->To the Most Noble and Distinguished Man,<-

->Gives and Dedicates:<-

# MARC ROSET

## OF THE RENOWNED REPUBLIC

->Of the Genevans; a most upright Senator, a most<-
->venerable former Consul, and his kinsman<-
->to be forever honored,<-

->Sends Greetings.<-

## ANTOINE CREGUT

FOR some time now, I have been considering by what means I might bring to light some <term>proof<note>original Greek: τεκμήριον (tekmērion), meaning a sign, mark, or piece of evidence.</note></term> of my deep affection and singular respect for you (Most Distinguished Man and kinsman to be honored from my very heart). This constant meditation has occupied my mind day and night, and certainly not without cause, for weighty reasons for carrying out this matter presented themselves to me from every side. First, there is the most worthy glory of our <term>kinship<note>The Latin 'affinitas' refers specifically to a relationship by marriage.</note></term> with you, and the illustrious nobility of your ancient lineage. For what could have happened more happily for me and my lot than to be joined with a man of such nobility of pedigree and integrity of character?

<summary>This page is a formal dedication by Antoine Cregut to Marc Roset, a prominent statesman in the Republic of Geneva, emphasizing their family ties and Roset's high social standing.</summary>
<keywords>Marc Roset, Antoine Cregut, Geneva, dedication, kinship, nobility, Senator, Consul</keywords>

# LETTER

...and to be joined by kinship with one outshining all others with the splendor of every virtue? What could be more just than to offer a <term>votive tablet<note>original Latin: "votiuam tabellam." Historically, a plaque or painting hung in a temple as a sign of gratitude; here, the author uses it metaphorically for the book he is dedicating.</note></term> to such great virtue? Nor, moreover, was I moved but little by that rare beauty of your face and of your whole person, as well as the admirable <term>grace<note>original Greek: χάρις (charis)</note></term> and <term>charm<note>original Greek: ἀφροδίτη (aphrodite), here referring to the quality of being attractive or persuasive in speech.</note></term> of your conversation, and the persuasive oratory of your tongue, which could bend even the most stubborn. For truly, in a <note>The author is making a pun on the name "Roset" and the Latin word "rosetum" (a rose-garden or bed of roses).</note> Roset there are rose-beds; in him, as in <note>Otho (32–69 AD) and Titus (39–81 AD) were Roman Emperors. Titus was famously described by the historian Suetonius as "the delight of the human race" due to his kindness.</note> Otho, are the wonders of the world, and as in Titus, the delights of the human race; nor did anyone ever depart from his presence feeling either somewhat sad or morose.

> Whoever comes as a spectator, departs as a lover;
> Either your virtue or your beauty captures him.

To these reasons are added your kind favors toward me, fixed in my deepest marrow, destined to remain there eternally and to be erased by no passage of the turning centuries; and finally, the noble subject of my <term>late-night labors<note>original Latin: "lucubrationum." This refers to scholarly work conducted by candlelight at night.</note></term> demanded this. To which of men, indeed, should I rather dedicate these new dissertations on the more hidden oracles of Scripture than to a man of more polished and sacred literature, who is able to search out the most hidden things intimately and penetrate most deeply the more difficult understanding of mysteries? Whose name would shine more worthily upon the frontispiece of my **Revealer of Secrets** than his to whom almost all secrets of nature and grace have been revealed from heaven by the supreme revealer of secrets—as if a veil had been drawn back?

All these things are rare, all these things are dear, all these things are
<meta>catchword: bright</meta>

<summary>Cregut continues his praise of Marc Roset, citing his physical grace, persuasive speech, and spiritual insight as reasons for dedicating this theological work to him. He characterizes Roset as a man uniquely capable of understanding the "secrets" of Scripture and nature.</summary>

### DEDICATION.
¶ iij

*I behold in you (Most Illustrious Man) qualities that are bright, for they are rare—indeed, I find such things in few people. They are dear, because I value them most highly; and they are bright, because they make you almost a peer to the heavenly beings themselves. But I find this to be your most excellent and altogether <term>worthy of victory<note>original Greek: ἀξιόνικον (axionikon). A term used to describe someone deserving of a prize in a contest; here, it refers to a crowning achievement of character.</note></term> trait: that you possess all these things not merely in theory, but also in practice. For you have not only a mind illuminated by the brilliant light of divine speech, but even your will itself and all the affections of your heart have been restored by the purity of the <term>Holy Spirit<note>original Latin: "Spiritus Sanctus."</note></term>. Thus, with light leading the way and the will following, you perform well those good things which you know. You know that <term>justifying faith<note>original Latin: "fidem iustificantem." A central Reformation concept where a believer is made righteous before God through faith rather than deeds.</note></term> occupies two seats—namely, the <term>intellect<note>original Latin: "intellectus."</note></term> and the <term>will<note>original Latin: "voluntas."</note></term>—and that what was celestial light in the mind is also the fire of the Spirit in the heart. This is what was called by <term>Blessed Augustine<note>original Latin: "B. August." refers to St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian of Western Christianity.</note></term> "that luminous charity," concerning which these are the main points:*
*Ignorance is diminished as the truth shines more and more; desire is diminished as charity burns more and more. You know also that our hearts are the beloved and chosen temples of Christ and the Holy Spirit, and that the soul is no more rooted in the heart—that part which is the first to live and the last to die—than Christ himself and the Spirit of sanctification are rooted in the heart, according to that word of Paul in <note>The author is citing the New Testament, Ephesians 3:17.</note> Ephesians 3:*

> *That Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith; that you, being rooted and grounded in charity, may be able...*

<summary>In this dedication, the author praises Marc Roset for bridging the gap between theological knowledge and spiritual practice, citing St. Augustine and St. Paul to emphasize the heart as the dwelling place of Christ.</summary>
<keywords>Marc Roset, virtue, justifying faith, intellect and will, St. Augustine, Holy Spirit, Ephesians 3, charity, spiritual illumination</keywords>

-># EPISTLE<-

...to comprehend with all the <term>Saints<note>original Latin: "Sanctis." In this context, it refers to the community of all true believers.</note></term> what is that breadth and length and depth and height, and to know that love of <term>Christ<note>original Latin: "Christi."</note></term> which surpasses all knowledge, etc. You know also that <term>sanctification<note>The process of being made holy through the Holy Spirit.</note></term> and <term>glorification<note>The final state of the believer in heaven, perfected in the presence of God.</note></term> differ not in kind, but only in degree. Therefore, just as *in glory no one could be called blessed in whose mind and heart the image of God was not perfectly restored, so too in the state of grace—and while we are still on the journey—no one can be considered reborn and sanctified whose mind and heart is not illuminated and sweetened by the brilliance of that divine <term>radiance<note>original Greek: ἀπαύγασμα (apaugasma). A term used in the New Testament (Hebrews 1:3) to describe Christ as the "effulgence" or "shining forth" of God's glory.</note></term> and heavenly sweetness, and finally intoxicated with a certain wonderful delight.*

*Those who do not know you (Most Distinguished Man) are those who have not known those exceptional gifts of soul that shine forth in you like stars, and by which you outshine all other stars, rising like a celestial Sun. I pass over the other ornaments with which nature and grace have enriched you; and lest I seem to do violence to your modesty, which rejects such praises, I vow them to <term>Sigalion<note>A name associated with Harpocrates, the Greco-Roman adaptation of the Egyptian god of silence. To "vow something to Sigalion" is a poetic way of saying one will remain silent.</note></term> as a faithful observer of <term>Pythagorean silence<note>original Greek: ἐχεμυθία (echemythia). A reference to the five-year vow of silence required of the followers of the philosopher Pythagoras.</note></term>. This one thing only I add, which makes your image more refined and perfect: namely, that your most beloved wife matches you in the same duties of piety and charity, and she is gifted with a mind no less open to understanding than a judgment wise in discerning. Her, as the <term>Chosen Lady<note>original Latin: "Electam Dominam." A reference to the opening of the Second Epistle of John, here applied to Roset's wife to praise her Christian character.</note></term> of whom...*

<meta>This page continues the dedication to the Genevan magistrate Marc Roset. Having previously praised Roset’s personal character and theological standing, the author now turns his attention to Roset’s wife and children, framing their domestic life as a model of Christian and civic virtue through a series of biblical and classical comparisons.</meta>

### DEDICATION:

John, <note>original: "Iohannes." Likely the author referring to himself in the first person.</note> I behold her; I see her born into virtue like a little bee in honey. **Susanna** <note>A biblical figure from the Book of Daniel (in the Apocrypha), celebrated as a model of wifely chastity and resilience against false accusation.</note> in her second bodily purity; **Esther** <note>The Jewish queen who saved her people, cited here as a model of courage and spirit.</note> revived in the excellence of her soul; **Elizabeth** <note>Likely referring to the mother of John the Baptist, known for her righteousness and piety.</note> in a renewed eminence of piety—so she is judged by all. Whatever talent is desired in serious matters; whatever refinement in civil life; whatever religion in **Church** affairs; whatever <term>household management<note>original: "Oeconomiae." In this period, the term referred to the governance and moral order of the home rather than just financial matters.</note></term> in domestic concerns, is found in her, and shines forth in a wonderful manner. From this it follows that this wife, equally abundant in children and in virtues within the walls of your home, joining her efforts with yours, raises with you the numerous offspring she received from you in the fear of God. And already both of you have sown such noble seeds of virtue in their souls that in a short time they shall be seen like new stars upon the soil of the **Genevans.** Those rosy buds, still closed, will at last grow into open roses, which will exhale a wonderful fragrance for the **Church** and the whole **State.** Their tender age, which that threefold aid—<term>nature<note>original Greek: φύσις (physis).</note></term>, <term>method<note>original Greek: μέθοδος (methodos).</note></term>, and <term>practice<note>original Greek: γυμνασία (gymnasia). In a classical education context, this refers to the disciplined exercise or training of the mind and body.</note></term>—cultivates, already tastes of a mature age, and foretells and promises great things to all **Geneva** just as once the <term>Younger Marcellus<note>The nephew and son-in-law of Augustus Caesar, who was famously praised by Virgil as a youth of immense promise whose early death was a tragedy for Rome.</note></term> did for ancient **Rome**; and thus in them that saying of <term>Horace<note>Quintus Horatius Flaccus (65–8 BC), a leading Roman lyric poet.</note></term> is most truly fulfilled:

> The brave are born from the brave and the good: there is in steers and in horses the virtue of their sires, nor do fierce eagles give birth to a timid dove. <note>original Latin: "Fortes creantur fortibus & bonis: est in iuuencis, est in equis patrum virtus, nec imbellem feroces progenerant Aquilae columbam." This is a famous quote from Horace’s *Odes* (4.4), suggesting that noble character is inherited and then refined by education.</note>

<summary>In this dedication, the author praises the wife of Marc Roset by comparing her to biblical heroines and describes their children as the future "stars" of Geneva. He emphasizes that their noble upbringing and education—combining nature, method, and practice—ensure they will serve both the Church and the State.</summary>

### DEDICATORY EPISTLE

Furthermore, <term>Most Distinguished Sir<note>original: "Vir Amplissimè." A formal honorific used for high-ranking magistrates or individuals of great social and intellectual standing.</note></term>, so that I may cease to diminish great matters with my humble words, I most submissively ask this one thing of God: that He may long preserve you and your entire family as distinguished lights and pillars of the **Church** and the **State** of **Geneva**, and that He may grant a prosperity equal to your virtues, so that He might fulfill the prayers of him who is forever:

->To Your Excellence<-

->Most dedicated and most devoted<-

->ANTOINE CREGUT.<- <note>original: "Antonius Cregutus." A 17th-century Reformed theologian and professor.</note>

<meta>This page follows the formal dedication to the Genevan magistrate Marc Roset. Having concluded his personal address to his patron, the author Antoine Cregut now turns to the "Honest Reader" to introduce the purpose and history of this specific volume. He bridges the gap between his previous academic work on theological "points" and this new, more interpretive work on biblical "secrets."</meta>

<page-type>preface</page-type>
<sig>¶¶</sig>

<image-desc>A woodcut headpiece featuring a central cherub's head with wings, flanked by symmetrical floral scrollwork and stylized marine or avian creatures at the outer edges.</image-desc>

### To the Sincere Reader.

<image-desc>Ornate decorative drop cap 'P' with a background of dense foliate and floral patterns.</image-desc>

**AFTER** our <term>Elucidations on the Points of Sacred Theology<note>original: "de apicibus SS. Theologiæ Elucidationes." This refers to Cregut's previous academic publication, which dealt with the "points" or minute, complex details of systematic theology.</note></term> were recently printed, behold, dear Reader, in a very short time we also present our **Gale Razaia**, that is, **The Revealer of Secrets**. <note>original: "Gale Razaia" is a Latinized form of the Aramaic phrase *Galeh Razaya*, meaning "Revealer of Secrets," a title famously associated with God in the Book of Daniel (2:28).</note> Just as in that prior treatise we unraveled the "points" of Sacred Theology—that is, the more hidden and difficult places of the entire system—so in this **Revealer of Secrets**, we clarify whichever more obscure oracles of the Holy Scriptures we find. We address those things which seem to us especially <term>hard to understand, which the ignorant twist to their own destruction<note>original Greek: "δυσνόητα, ἃ ἀγνοοῦντες, εἰς ἰδίαν ἀπώλειαν στρέβλουσι." A quotation from 2 Peter 3:16 referring to the difficult passages in the letters of the Apostle Paul.</note></term>, as **Peter** once said concerning certain difficult places in the **Pauline Epistles**.

But just as both treatises have something in common regarding their subject matter—since each claims for itself difficulty and "thorny points" even from the threshold of the title—so both have this in common regarding their publication: that they were published by chance and contrary to the author's intention. For while I intended to publish these dissertations of ours only in the <term>Theological Auditorium<note>The "Auditorium Theologicum" refers to the formal lecture hall of the Academy where Cregut taught; he originally intended these notes only for his students.</note></term>, and it was my intention to provide copies of them only to my listeners and to candidates of Theology, it quickly happened that once our **Revealer of Secrets** had stepped outside the barriers of the Academy, and by several people—not merely common folk, but foremost among friends—the prior parts...

<summary>In this preface, Antoine Cregut introduces his work "Gale Razaia" (The Revealer of Secrets), explaining that it aims to clarify the most difficult and "thorny" passages of the Bible. He notes that, like his previous academic work, this volume was originally intended only for his students but is being published more widely due to popular demand.</summary>
<keywords>Gale Razaia, Revealer of Secrets, biblical commentary, 17th-century theology, Academy of Geneva, hermeneutics, Antoine Cregut, Peter's Epistles</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's address to the reader. Following the mention of the Apostle Peter's warning about difficult scriptures, Cregut explains how he was encouraged by others to publish this work and defines his method of interpretation against more obscure philosophical and scholastic traditions.</meta>

<page-type>preface</page-type>
<sig>*</sig>
<meta>catchword: reader</meta>

...these oracles had been thoroughly read, and having been approved and praised by them beyond hope, they compelled me with further urgent prayers and warnings to ensure they were committed to the press and to pursue the work I had begun.

Furthermore, I believe the title should drive no one away, even though it suggests mysteries and difficulty—much like that **Heraclitus** of old, nicknamed the **Obscure** <note>original Greek: "σκοτεινὸς" (skoteinos), meaning dark or shadowy.</note>, who was understood by no one, not even by **Socrates**. Socrates, who was (according to the oracle) the only wise man among mortals, judged that all of Heraclitus's works required a **Delian**—that is, a deep-sea—diver <note>original: "Delio... natatore." Socrates famously remarked that Heraclitus's writings were so deep they required a swimmer from the island of Delos, famous for its expert divers, to reach the bottom without drowning.</note>. For in that philosopher, the mysteries of philosophical wisdom were veiled, and they were (as the **Stagirite** <note>A common name for the philosopher Aristotle, referring to his birthplace, Stagira.</note> said concerning his own <term>acroamatic works<note>Aristotle's "acroamatic" or "esoteric" lectures were advanced lessons intended only for his inner circle of students, as opposed to his "exoteric" works for the general public.</note></term>) **published and yet not published, for they are understandable only to those who have heard us** <note>original Greek: "δεδομένα καὶ μὴ δεδομένα, ξυνητὰ γὰρ ἐστὶ τοῖς ἡμῶν μόνον ἀκούουσι."</note>. But in the *Revealer of Secrets*, those things which were difficult and, as it were, covered by a certain veil, are clearly revealed once the veil is removed, and are made open even to children and newcomers.

Nor does a "difficult passage" mean the same thing to me as it does to the masters of the Hebrews: **it is written as a hard matter** <note>original Hebrew: "איכתיב קשה" (ichtiv kashah).</note>, that is, a *hard and difficult scripture*. Since among the <term>Talmudists<note>Jewish scholars who compiled and studied the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note></term>, a passage of Scripture is called "difficult" when it can be debated on both sides as a problem; this often makes the scriptural passage more tangled. This is also evident among the Scholastic doctors, commonly called <term>Quodlibetarians<note>From the Latin "quodlibet" (whatever you please). These were medieval academic debaters who would argue any side of a question for the sake of logic, often criticized for obscuring simple truths through endless hair-splitting.</note></term>, for through excessive arguing, the truth is lost. But we investigate the true and genuine sense of Scripture primarily from the context—the parts preceding and following the passage—and from other parallel texts, setting aside the many conflicting opinions of so many doctors and interpreters. It will therefore be pleasing to the
reader

<summary>Cregut explains that his book aims to clarify biblical "secrets" rather than obscure them, contrasting his direct contextual method with the confusing debates of ancient philosophers, Jewish Talmudists, and medieval Scholastics.</summary>
<keywords>biblical interpretation, Heraclitus, Socrates, Aristotle, Talmud, Scholasticism, Quodlibetarians, clarity of Scripture, hermeneutics</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's introductory address to the reader. Building on the previous page's comparison to the depth of Heraclitus and Aristotle, the author now explains that his work aims to uncover the hidden depths of scripture, following the tradition of great interpreters rather than claiming new, "fanatical" prophecies.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<sig>¶¶ ij</sig>

...reader eager to learn, to read these exercises of ours attentively, so that he may be able to examine difficult passages and ancient secrets; and thus look into things previously veiled with a thick curtain, now revealed. And whereas before it was only given to look at the surface itself and the bark, he may now rightly rejoice to see God <note>original Greek abbreviation: "Θῠ" (Theou)</note> himself.

Nor should anyone justly find fault that the author is titled the *Revealer*, as if we were claiming for ourselves some fanatic enthusiasm, or an Apocalypse or revelation of mysteries like John the Theologian, or as if we visionaries were claiming certain visions for ourselves; for everyone knows that these extraordinary gifts have now ceased. Nevertheless, who will deny that God daily reveals many things to His elect which were previously hidden? And although the gift of prophecy or interpretation was once extraordinary—just like the Spirit of prayer and other gifts—these gifts still thrive in the Church today, even if not with the same abundance and success.

Hence, just as among the Hebrews, *Shlomo Yitzhaki* <note>Commonly known as **Rashi** (1040–1105), the preeminent Jewish commentator on the Bible and Talmud.</note> is remembered as *Parshandata* <note>original Hebrew: פרשנדתא</note> or *Meforesh HaDat* <note>original Hebrew: מפרש הדת</note>, that is, the *Interpreter of the Law*, <term>par excellence<note>original Greek: "κατ' ἐξοχήν" (kat' exochen), meaning "pre-eminently" or "above all others."</note></term>, because many things were revealed to him that lay hidden to others. So among us, it is clear whom we mean when we say the *Most Learned Interpreter*. And no one doubts that certain difficult things were revealed to our **Beza** <note>**Theodore Beza** (1519–1605), a French Protestant reformer and scholar who succeeded John Calvin in Geneva.</note> which had been unknown to others. A single passage, **1 Peter 3:19**, *concerning the spirits in prison*, provides proof of this. Also, **Philips van Marnix, Lord of Saint-Aldegonde** <note>A Flemish-Dutch nobleman, diplomat, and theologian, famous for his role in the Dutch Revolt and his biblical scholarship.</note> was the first to correctly interpret the passage in **Acts 19:5**, *on hearing this, they were baptized* <note>original Greek: "ἀκούσαντες δὲ ἐβαπτίσθησαν" (akousantes de ebaptisthesan)</note>, from the original Greek text.

<summary>The author defends the title of his work, "The Revealer," clarifying that he is not claiming new divine visions but rather the scholarly "revelation" found in expert biblical interpretation. He cites historical examples of great interpreters like Rashi, Beza, and Marnix van St. Aldegonde who clarified previously obscure scriptures.</summary>

<keywords>biblical interpretation, revelation, prophecy, Rashi, Theodore Beza, Philips van Marnix, 1 Peter 3:19, Acts 19:5, scholarship vs. fanaticism</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's defense of his work's title, "The Revealer." As for us, even if we freely confess that we are not to be compared to those **vanguard of theologians** <note>original: "Theologorum Antesignanis," referring to the primary leaders or "standard-bearers" of theological thought.</note>; nevertheless, we have always deemed it servile and unworthy of an honorable man to be led by blind obedience like brute beasts, to swear by the words of a master, and—no differently than the disciples of Pythagoras—to keep repeating <term>he himself said it<note>original Greek: "αὐτὸς ἔφα" (autos epha), equivalent to the Latin "ipse dixit," used to indicate the unquestioning acceptance of a teacher's authority.</note></term>. For as was once said to those visitors at the dark cellar and humble hut:

> *Enter, for even in this place the immortal gods are not absent.* <note>A famous remark traditionally attributed to the philosopher Heraclitus, who invited guests into his modest kitchen to show that the divine exists in the mundane as much as the magnificent.</note>

In the same way, we also believe we possess the **Holy Spirit**, which, like the wind of Pentecost, blows where it wills and how it wills. However, a distinction must be made between us and the Apostles or apostolic men: while the Prophets of that time were called in an extraordinary manner and inspired by a charism infused by the Holy Spirit, now the "prophets" or interpreters of the New Testament are able to reveal certain secrets through immense labor, various late-night studies, untiring zeal, and constant meditation on the Scriptures and prayers—all with the Holy Spirit guiding and teaching, just as the supreme Prophet of the Church deigns to bestow from His Spirit.

I pass over the fact that **Petrus Galatinus** <note>Pietro Colonna Galatino (c. 1460–1540), an Italian scholar and friar known for his work "De Arcanis Catholicae Veritatis," which attempted to prove Christian doctrines using Jewish mystical texts.</note> very often mentions a certain book in his *Secrets of Catholic Truth* titled *Gale rasaia*, the *Revealer of Secrets*, or *Revealing Secrets* <note>original: "Gale rasaia," a Latinization of the Aramaic/Hebrew "Galei Razayya."</note>. For many Kabbalistic <term>Kabbalistic<note>Referring to Kabbalah, a school of thought in Jewish mysticism; the author suggests these specific interpretations are more human than divine in origin.</note></term> things are read there which savor of the human spirit rather than the revelation of the Spirit of God, and furthermore, many doubt his reliability.

But indeed, just as we observe these things concerning the edition and the title of the book, so regarding the subject matter, this is primarily observed

I wish to state that, from the difficult passages of <term>Scripture<note>original: "Scripturæ," referring to the books of the Bible.</note></term>, I have by no means selected those which savor even slightly of an "itch" for vain curiosity. In the investigation of such matters, one is prone to slip into error, and the knowledge or understanding of them brings minimal benefit; in these cases, it would be better to say **"I do not know."** Instead, we have selected those oracles which are momentous, which contain doctrine that is absolutely necessary to know, and which primarily concern the mysteries of grace.

In this first part (dearest Reader), I present to you my dissertations on the more difficult and more illustrious oracles of the <term>Pentateuch<note>The first five books of the Bible, also known as the "Five Books of Moses."</note></term>, or the five books of Moses. However, parallel passages from the New Testament are proposed and explained in the same chapter whenever the opportunity arises and such parallels are found, so that the Old and the New Testaments might mutually illuminate one another and bear witness to each other. In the following exercises, we will likewise run through the other books of Scripture and clarify the more illustrious and difficult passages, **God willing** <note>original: "favente Numine," literally "with the Divine Power favoring."</note>, in the same order—provided we find that this first part has been useful to the Church of God and acceptable to learned men, a favor we promise ourselves based on their fairness and the dignity of the subject matter.

It should also be noted (kind Reader) that in these exercises I avoid the <term>commonplace<note>original: "locus communis." In early modern theology, this referred to a standard method of organizing theology into general topics or "places" (like "Sin," "Grace," or "Justice"). The author is signaling that he is writing an analytical commentary, not a general textbook.</note></term>, nor have I wished to wander into that field as far as was possible. This is because the "commonplace" is already sufficiently treated in systematic works—whether theological works in theological matters, or political...

Furthermore, I have always held this to be certain: that a specific text of <term>Scripture<note>The Bible.</note></term> cannot be properly or accurately explained according to the author’s original purpose if it is turned into a <term>commonplace<note>original: "locum communem." In traditional rhetoric and theology, "commonplaces" were general themes or universal arguments used to categorize information, which the author feels can distract from the specific meaning of a unique verse.</note></term>.

Finally, this is because anyone who follows a commonplace writes nothing but ordinary things that are found everywhere in standard **theological systems**; on the contrary, he who examines and penetrates the very "entrails" of a specific context draws out new and unique insights—belonging to himself—from the inner sanctuaries of the divine oracle. He scrutinizes the purpose of the **Holy Spirit** more deeply, observes many things by his own effort, and brings forth as well as distributes new wisdom from the "good treasure of his heart." From this source, the depths and surpassing riches of divine wisdom are found like inexhaustible fountains, so that it can truly be said of the whole of Scripture what <term>Philo the Jew<note>A Hellenistic Jewish philosopher from Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE) known for তাঁর allegorical interpretations of the Hebrew Bible.</note></term> asserted regarding the Book of Genesis: **"All Scripture is an ocean of Theology, from which all rivers and every sea [flow]."** <note>original Greek: "πᾶσα γραφὴ ἐστὶν ὠκεανὸς τῆς Θεολογίας ἐξ οὗ πάντες ποταμοὶ & πᾶσα θάλασσα."</note>

Moreover, I have followed a method that has always seemed to me more correct and better suited for teaching clearly. For first, I have divided the entire **investigation** <note>original Greek: "συζήτησιν" (syzetesin)</note> into certain principal parts, which I then explain **in an orderly fashion** <note>original Greek: "τεταγμένως" (tetagmenos)</note> as clearly and transparently as possible, even employing subdivisions if the matter requires it. For as **Socrates** rightly said long ago: *“If I were to find someone who knew how to divide [a subject] correctly, I would follow his footsteps as if he were a great God.”*

Furthermore, before treating the subjects themselves, I always remove any **ambiguity of words** <note>original: "homonymiam," referring to words that sound the same but have different meanings.</note> and carefully search out the specific emphasis of the **terminology** <note>original: "nomenclationem"</note> in all languages, because...

Names are the signs of things, and are often given **by deliberate choice** <note>original Greek: "ἐκ τῆς προαιρέσεως" (ek tēs proaireseōs), meaning out of intentional purpose or preference.</note>; and as someone skillfully said: **"To teach correctly, one must first examine names."** <note>original Greek: "πρὸς τὸ ὀρθῶς διδάσκειν δεῖ πρῶτον ἐξετάζειν τὰ ὀνόματα."</note>

I prioritize the **instructional** <note>original Greek: "διδακτικὴν" (didaktikēn), referring to the didactic or teaching-oriented part of the work.</note> portion and the truth which the Italians call **positive** <note>original: "veritatem... positivam." In this context, "positive theology" refers to the study of truths established by authority or revelation, such as Scripture, rather than those reached through abstract philosophical speculation.</note>, so that the true sense of the divine oracle may be brought to light. For once the truth has been satisfied and fully asserted, it is easy from there to root out any errors through **refutation** <note>original Greek: "ἀνασκευαστικῶς" (anaskeuastikōs), meaning by way of dismantling or tearing down opposing arguments.</note>; because that which is straight is a rule for itself and for the crooked. 

However, sometimes when the occasion presents itself, I air those momentous controversies that are debated between **Catholics** and the **Pontificians** <note>In the context of the Reformation, the author uses "Catholics" to refer to his own side (claiming the "universal" or true faith) and "Pontificians" to refer to the Roman Catholic Church and its loyalty to the Pope/Pontiff.</note>. Omitting futile arguments, I select and refute only the stronger ones defended by the leaders of the Pontificians, such as **Bellarmino**, **Perron**, **Stapleton**, and others. Just as when I deal with Exodus 3 regarding the mission of **Moses**, I take the opportunity to refute all those claims, however plausible, which **Cardinal Richelieu** gathered in his posthumous book concerning the **calling of ministers** <note>referring to Richelieu's *Traité qui contient la méthode la plus facile et la plus assurée pour convertir ceux qui se sont séparés de l'Église*, where he argued against the legitimacy of Protestant clergy.</note>.

When I also draw out the meaning of any passage, I did not think it worth the effort to act like a <term>Rhapsodist<note>original: "Rapsodistam." Here used to describe someone who merely patches together the works of others without original thought or synthesis.</note></term>, and to recite the various opinions of theologians at great length—as others are accustomed to do—to the point of nausea. For through that rather lengthy enumeration, a book grows into a massive bulk, and it is easy to read those opinions in the books of authors published previously. Therefore, I decided not to weary the patience and attention of readers with these unnecessary things, nor to seek the glory of being a hardworking man of great reading or of a happy and tenacious memory. I preferred instead [to draw] from **Scripture** itself, its own interpreter, and from...

For the rest, I always reflect upon that saying of the Apostle to the Corinthians: 
> Paul plants, Apollo waters, but God gives the growth. <note>original: "Paulus plantat, Apollo rigat, at Deus dat incrementum." This is a reference to 1 Corinthians 3:6, emphasizing that while human effort is necessary, spiritual results come from God.</note>

Indeed, the labors and <term>late-night studies</term><note>The original Latin "lucubrationes" specifically refers to scholarly work performed by candlelight at night, implying great effort.</note> of men profit little, unless God, who sent us, causes a most abundant rain of blessings to descend. This we earnestly pray for with burning and most devoted vows from that giver of all good things. May that highest Parent of the Church grant that these exercises, such as they are, may be of service to His glory and the building up of the Church. May He daily increase in us the gifts and <term>graces</term><note>original: "charismata." In a theological context, these are spiritual gifts or talents granted by the Holy Spirit for the benefit of the community.</note> of the Spirit; may He kindle His light and heavenly rays more and more, so that we may be able to complete the work we have begun with alacrity, and—as He reveals His hidden mysteries to us through the Revealer of secrets—we may be able to make them clearly known to others. Amen.

## PREFACE.

Having recently presented the theological system of Friedrich Wendelin <note>Friedrich Wendelin (1584–1652) was a significant German Reformed theologian whose "Systema Maius" was a standard textbook of the era.</note> before a large audience, and with the year now drawing to a close, I have long hesitated whether I should finish the web I had begun weaving or rather start another. I sought a project that would be of greater benefit to more advanced students of theology, or at least one that considers both beginners and initiates alongside those who are more mature. Thus, I have decided to divide my nightly labors <note>The author uses the word *lucubrationes*, referring to study or writing done by candlelight late at night.</note> so that in one week I might explain Wendelin, and in the next—and so on alternately—I might examine the more illustrious oracles of Scripture and probe into its more hidden depths. I shall do this <margin>2 Peter 1:20</margin> not **by private interpretation** <note>original Greek: "κατ' ἰδίαν ἐπίλυσιν"</note> but by the guiding light of the Divine Word, which is a lamp to the feet and **a light shining in a dark place.** <note>original Greek: "λύχνος φαίνων ἐν αὐχμηρῷ τόπῳ"</note> <margin>2 Peter 1:19</margin>

Finally, the equal utility of both approaches won out. By dividing these modest labors into two parts, I have humbled myself to meet the needs of the beginners in their earlier stages, while not refusing to satisfy the desires of the more advanced. However, I have determined that we shall first select not only the more illustrious oracles, but specifically those of the Gospel—namely, those that concern Christ and His healing grace in both the Old and the New Testament. Thereafter (God willing), we shall discuss those things which pertain to nature and the law, so that the entire work may be divided into three parts.

The first, in order of dignity, is **On Grace**.
The second is **On Nature**.
The third is **On the Law**.

This division corresponds to that used by the Hebrews regarding the **Work of the Creation** <note>original Hebrew: מעשה בראשית (*mahasé bereschith*). This refers to the traditional Jewish study of the account of creation in Genesis and the mysteries of the natural world.</note>...

<summary>The author introduces his theological curriculum, explaining that he will alternate between teaching Friedrich Wendelin's system and performing deep exegesis of Biblical "oracles." He outlines a three-part structure for his work focusing on Grace, Nature, and the Law.</summary>
<keywords>Friedrich Wendelin, biblical exegesis, grace, nature, law, Hebrew theology, Ma'aseh Bereshit, pedagogy, 2 Peter 1:19-20</keywords>

## ANALYSIS.

*First, there is a general division of the topics to be handled, which consists of three parts. 1. The prohibition given to the first-formed humans <note>original Latin: *protoplastis*, referring to Adam and Eve as the first created beings.</note>. 2. The transgression of the divine command. 3. The deadly punishment that follows the guilt. Regarding the first part, it is observed that the prohibition given to the first-formed was hypothetical, since some of God's commands are absolute and others are hypothetical. These, in turn, are either affirmative or negative. How they are named by the Hebrews as affirmative and negative. Why are moral commands absolute, while ceremonial ones are hypothetical? Why the ceremonial law is called among the Hebrews <term>Chukkim</term> <note>original Hebrew: חקים (*chuqqim*), often translated as "statutes" or "decrees" whose reasons are not immediately obvious to human logic.</note>. Why negative precepts are more binding than affirmative ones. In what sense affirmative ones bind as equally as negative ones. Furthermore, there is a double precept: of Command and of Indulgence; what a precept of Command and of Indulgence is. When do precepts of Indulgence not apply, and why? The difference between a precept of Command and one of Indulgence. This distinction is indicated by the Hebrew word <term>Tzivah</term> <note>original Hebrew: צוה (*tzivah*), the root for "command."</note>. Permission is of two kinds: simple and moral. God's commands are not of equal authority regarding their subject matter.*

*II. The second part concerns the transgression of Adam. This is called by theologians "Originating Original Sin" <note>original Latin: *Peccatum Originale Originans*, referring to the actual act of sin committed by Adam, as opposed to the "originated" state of sin inherited by his descendants.</note>. This transgression of Adam is subdivided: 1. into Adam's sin. 2. into the causes of that sin. 3. into the process and timing of it. How Adam's sin is dissonantly <note>original Greek: *διαφωνικῶς* (diaphonikos), meaning "discordantly" or "at variance."</note> a sin, and why? Adam's sin was the greatest of all. It was greater than the sin against the Holy Spirit. Seven reasons are given to prove that Adam's sin was the greatest. Nevertheless, the sin of the Angels was greater than Adam's sin. No cause "by itself" <note>original Latin: *per se*</note> can be assigned for Adam's sin and his unbelief, but only an "accidental" cause <note>original Latin: *per accidens*</note>. What accidental cause is to be assigned. What the first root of evil is from Romans 5:12. Six momentous reasons concerning the entry of sin. Why there is a deep silence in Moses <note>The author refers to Moses as the traditional author of the Book of Genesis.</note> regarding providence when Adam's fall is described. Thus far, the consideration of Adam's sin as it was actual and personal; now it is considered as natural and habitual. How Adam was the root of the entire human race. Adam's sin becomes ours in two ways: by Imputation <note>term: *Imputation*—the legal assignment of Adam’s guilt to all humanity.</note> and by Propagation <note>term: *Propagation*—the biological or generational passing down of a fallen nature.</note>. Errors of the Papists <note>A common Reformation-era term for Roman Catholics; the author is likely preparing to argue against Catholic doctrines of original sin.</note>.*

<summary>This page provides a detailed outline for a theological treatise on the Fall of Man, categorizing divine laws into absolute and hypothetical types while arguing that Adam's first sin was uniquely significant in its impact on humanity.</summary>

<keywords>Protoplasts, Divine Law, Chukkim, Tzivah, Original Sin, Adam's Fall, Imputation, Propagation, Scholasticism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the systematic "Analysis" or table of contents for the treatise. ### THE REVEALER OF SECRETS.

*On the Imputation of Adam's sin. Imputation is twofold according to the Catholics <note>In this context, "Catholics" refers to the "universal" or mainstream theological consensus of the time, often including both Reformed and Roman Catholic views against radical sects.</note>: immediate and mediate, or antecedent and consequent. The question regarding the Imputation of Adam's sin can have a threefold meaning. The opinion of the Author, which is a middle ground between two extremes. The Author's opinion is explained more broadly. The Author's opinion is proven from Scripture and illustrated by the examples of Christ and Melchizedek.*

*It is concluded that Imputation is mediate. It is concluded to be mediate in a general sense, but not in a singular one. Mediate imputation does not conflict with God's justice and wisdom. Various distinctions of singular imputation: whether direct, collateral, or reflexive. Imputation properly so-called and improperly so-called. The imputation of Adam's sin is illustrated by the imputation of the Righteousness of the second Adam <note>The "Second Adam" is a traditional theological title for Jesus Christ.</note>. The true opinion is proven by the authority of Augustine. A mystery from the Kabbalah <note>The Kabbalah is a tradition of Jewish mysticism; here the author uses it to find deeper meanings in the Hebrew text.</note> concerning the name **Adam** <note>original Hebrew: אדם</note> and the secret of revolution <note>original Latin: *revolutionis*, likely referring to the "Gilgul" or the cycle of souls.</note>. An objection is answered regarding the soul, which seems to be created righteous by God.*

*How God concurs without sin while creating the soul. The opinion of the Academy of Bern regarding the Imputation of Adam's sin. Three types of habits <note>In philosophy, a "habit" refers to a stable disposition or quality of the soul.</note> and what kind of habit Original Sin is. The Author’s <term>Judgment</term> <note>original Greek: Ἐπίκρισις (*Epikrisis*), meaning a critical decision or final assessment.</note> on the opinion of the Catholics. The second part of Original Sin remains, namely Inherent Corruption. This is divided into three parts. # THE REVEALER OF SECRETS.

...let us uncover the origin of evil, so that we may reveal how it is imputed to future generations and the reason for this, while preserving the justice of God. Subsequently, we must undoubtedly confess—and tearfully lament without ceasing <note>original: "ἀδιαλείπτως" (adialeiptōs)</note>—the propagation of corruption and, finally, the lethal punishment for that fatal guilt.

But to condense this entire exercise into a few words, three things must be unfolded in an orderly fashion <note>original: "τεταγμένως" (tetagmenōs)</note>: 
1. The prohibition given to the first-formed humans <term>protoplastis; the first created people, Adam and Eve</term> in Genesis Chapter 2, verses 16 and 17.
2. The transgression of the divine command in Chapter 3, verse 6.
3. The lethal punishment that follows guilt.

I. God prohibits the first-formed from using the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. That prohibition (as is clear) is **hypothetical** <note>In this context, a 'hypothetical' command is one that is not inherently good or bad, but becomes so only because God specifically commanded it as a test.</note>. For God’s commands are of two kinds. Some are **absolute**, whether they are **affirmative**—which are called *hase* (עשה) by the Hebrews, meaning "**do**"—or **negative**, which are called *lo* (לא), meaning "**not**." Others, however, are **hypothetical** commands. 

**Absolute** commands are necessary because they relate to morals and, as such, are indispensable. For this reason, they are called *mitzvoth* (מצות) by the Hebrews by way of excellence <note>original: "κατ’ ἐξοχήν" (kat' exochēn), a Greek phrase meaning 'pre-eminently'</note>, and are called **commandments** <note>original: "ἐντολαὶ" (entolai)</note> by the Seventy Translators <note>The 'Seventy' refers to the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>, just as in Luke Chapter 1, verse 6 of the Gospel. Such are, first and foremost, the precepts of the first table <note>The first part of the Ten Commandments, which deals with duties toward God.</note>. God cannot allow an exception to these through "ethical permission," for to do so would be to approve of evil itself. Nor can He grant an exemption from them without denying Himself, stripping away the glory of His justice, and trampling upon His entire majesty. Is it even possible that He who said through the Prophets, *I will not give my glory to another*, would allow foreign gods to be worshipped or His venerable name to be blasphemed?

**Hypothetical** commands, however, are those which are not simply <note>original: "ἁπλῶς" (haplōs)</note> necessary to observe by their nature, but only because of the specific determination of the divine will. Such are all "middle things" <note>original: "ἐν μέσῳ κειμένα" (en mesō keimena)</note> or **indifferent matters** <note>original: "ἀδιάφορα" (adiaphora)</note>, which by their nature possess neither moral goodness nor malice; everything about the act itself is purely physical. Indeed, they do not even possess, in and of themselves, that goodness found in the secondary virtues, such as repentance, faith, grace, mercy, and so on—which are the streams of the primary virtues in both God and humans. In this sense, the entire ceremonial law <note>The ritual laws of the Old Testament, such as dietary restrictions or sacrificial rules.</note> contains commands of this kind. For in that law, things that are indifferent by their nature become necessary by the determination of the divine will, which...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the nature of divine law and the prohibition given to Adam in the Garden of Eden. It specifically explores why certain laws are considered "just" based on God's will rather than their own inherent nature.</meta>

### ANTHONY CREGUTUS
<meta>catchword: imposed-</meta>

Since it is the most upright rule and standard of justice, whatever God wills and commands obtains both the name and nature of justice. For He does not will something because it is just, but it is just because God wills it; and if He wills something because it is just—as is clear from the commands of the first table <note>Referring to the first part of the Ten Commandments, which concern duties toward God.</note>—it is because He wills Himself and His own image, and because that justice is nothing outside of His own nature. Therefore, once the will of God is established, those things which were <term>indifferent <note>original: ἀδιάφορα (adiaphora); things that are neither morally commanded nor forbidden in themselves.</note></term> become necessary because they are clothed in moral goodness. Hence, the performance of a command displays obedience, and conversely, the transgression of it displays disobedience, and indeed various sins. This is clear from Adam's sin, from whose unbelief and disobedience—as if through an open door—a troop of vices rushed forth in crowds, entered into men, and immediately occupied the citadel of the soul.

Not without merit, therefore, the <term>Ceremonial Law</term> is called by the Hebrews *Chukkim* <note>חקים; statutes or ordinances</note>, *statutes*, or *constitutions*. By the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> and by Luke 1:6, it is called a <term>requirement <note>original: δικαίωμα (dikaiōma); often translated as a decree or a righteous regulation.</note></term>. But why is this? For what purpose? The <term>Moral Law</term> contains justice in itself and yet is not called a "requirement," but a <term>commandment <note>original: ἐντολὴ (entolē)</note></term>; and conversely, the Ceremonial Law, which deals with indifferent things, is called a "requirement." The <term>Moral Law</term> is not called a "requirement" because it is obvious to anyone that this law is just and holy, and it is the law <term>by way of excellence <note>original: κατ’ ἐξοχὴν (kat' exochēn); meaning the law in its highest or most primary sense.</note></term>. Hence it is called a "commandment," because it mandates and prescribes with the authority of laws. But ceremonies are called <term>requirements <note>original: δικαιώματα (dikaiōmata)</note></term> so that even by the very naming of the law it might be impressed upon men that although the ceremonial law was in itself concerning indifferent things, nonetheless, by the hypothesis of the divine will—because God commanded them—they are among the necessary things. This is because God willed that so many ceremonies should be signs and types which would contain the justice of faith which is in Christ Jesus; and furthermore, their fulfillment would signify obedience toward God, which certainly denotes nothing other than moral justice. Therefore, even if things that are indifferent *abstractly as such* do not contain any moral justice, yet *concretely and with the hypothesis* of the Divine will, they undoubtedly display justice, since whatever God prescribes is not in vain or empty, but for His own glory and the salvation of the elect, all of which certainly embrace an exquisite justice. Therefore, this law was imposed on Adam as a sign of subjection—

is imposed. Otherwise, it made no difference to God whether he ate indiscriminately of any fruit. It was, therefore, a certain elementary test of obedience: so that man might know he has a ruler and master of his life, upon whose nod <note>The Latin *nutu* implies a simple gesture or command, suggesting man should be perfectly attuned to God’s will.</note> he ought to depend.

Observe moreover that this precept was highly obligatory, because it is prohibitive or negative. But negative precepts are more binding than affirmative ones. Whence the moral axiom: *negative precepts must be fulfilled and are practical in every "now" and "here"; that is, for always and everywhere.* And truly if ever affirmative precepts are practical in every "now" and "here," or are perpetual, this happens (as the <term>Scholastics <note>A group of medieval thinkers, such as Thomas Aquinas, who used logic and philosophy to explain Christian doctrine.</note></term> note) not from the force of the formula, but from the force of the matter. For example, when we are commanded to *love God with all our heart*, that command is perpetual, nor is it dispensable for even a moment; but this is from the force of the matter, because it is the sum of the law, and virtually encompasses all precepts of the law, both affirmative and negative.

It should also not be omitted that here there is a twofold precept of God: one which is called *of Command* <note>original: Imperij</note>, the other *of Indulgence* <note>original: Indulgentiae; here meaning a divine permission or grant rather than the Catholic practice of pardoning sin.</note>. The first is *of indulgence*, when God, in commanding, does not order but permits, as here in verse 16: *And God commanded the man, saying, "Of every tree of the garden you may freely eat."* So to Noah, every kind of food except blood in Genesis 9:3-4; and in Exodus 20, in the fourth commandment of the law, He commands us to *work for six days*. And in Deuteronomy 25, God commands the people *that they give money on loan to the Canaanite for interest.* All of these are precepts of indulgence, and therefore they were within the power of man’s choice; from their omission or commission, those sins which are called *of omission and commission* <note>In theology, a sin of "omission" is failing to do what is right, while "commission" is doing what is forbidden.</note> did not follow. The second kind is the precept of Command, which has its basis both in absolute and in hypothetical precepts (as mentioned above)—that is, in those things which are by their nature necessary, and in those which are of themselves <term>indifferent <note>original: adiaphora; things that are morally neutral unless a specific law is made about them.</note></term>.

This is evident in the curse of Amalek, which led to Saul being rejected in 1 Samuel 15. The nature of the distinction between the Precepts of Power and Indulgence, and how they are distinguished from one another, was fully explained by us in the *Treatise on Grace in General*, Thesis 21. There it is taught that in Precepts of Power, the duty that a creature owes to God is necessarily demanded; but in Precepts of Indulgence, God’s kindness toward the creature is prominent. Understand this as referring to benefits in a simple sense, for often the reasons for a benefit and a duty exist at the same time.

This distinction between the precept of *Power* and *Indulgence* is indicated by the word <term>vayetsav <note>original Hebrew: וַיְצַו</note></term>, meaning "and he commanded," which Moses uses in chapter 2, verse 16. <note>The OCR says "cap. 11," but the context of Adam and the "bill of divorce" later suggests a discussion of Genesis 2:16 or general Mosaic law.</note> For the Hebrews, the term <term>mitzvah <note>original Hebrew: מִצְוָה</note></term> signifies both power (or authority) and permission (or indulgence). However, this permission is understood in two ways depending on the subject matter. For it often signifies the approval of a thing when dealing with <term>adiaphora <note>From the Greek, referring to "indifferent matters"—actions that are neither morally commanded nor forbidden, such as what clothes to wear.</note></term>, and in this sense, that permission can be called *simple permission*. In this act, God influences matters <term>effectively <note>original Greek: ἐνεργητικῶς (energetikos)</note></term>, because in such an act there is no element of evil.

But there is another permission, which is rather a certain <term>concession <note>original Greek: συγχώρησις (synchoresis)</note></term> or tolerance of an evil that God cannot approve. Therefore, although that permission is called *moral permission* by some theologians of great name, it is not properly so called. For this reason, other learned theologians establish only a *physical permission* in God, but not an *ethical* one. While physical permission fits perfectly with God's providence—since He does not block a sin that He has the power to block—ethical permission would strike against God's justice and trouble both of God's rights: His *absolute right* as well as His *ordained right*. Therefore, if we call this "moral permission" (because Scripture seems to imply it through Hebrew idiom), we must immediately observe that it cannot be called moral in a simple sense, but only <term>in some respect <note>original Greek: πῇ τὶ (pē ti)</note></term> and <term>relatively <note>original Greek: σχετικῶς (schetikōs)</note></term> in comparison to greater sins. For God, not unlike a magistrate, permits lesser evils so that greater ones may be avoided, which is *simple tolerance*. It was in this way that He permitted the "bill of divorce," from which

<meta>This page continues the technical distinction between types of divine commands, specifically focusing on the difference between moral permission and civil permission (using the example of divorce) and the hierarchy of moral vs. indifferent actions (adiaphora).</meta>

->### THE REVEALER OF SECRETS.<-
B

what Matthew chapter 19, verse 7 has as <term>commanded <note>original Greek: ἐνετείλατο (eneteilato)</note></term>, it soon after in verse 8 places as <term>permitted <note>original Greek: ἐπέτρεψεν (epetrepsen)</note></term>. This word does not signify a simple moral permission—otherwise Moses would be acting contrary to God and would be approving of sin, which was truly adultery in the sight of God. Rather, it designates a "relative" permission, which belonged to Civil Law rather than Moral Law, occurring when sins are moderated so that they do not overflow like a torrent. In the same way, wise magistrates, since they cannot entirely prevent usury <note>The practice of lending money at interest, which was often restricted or debated in religious law.</note>, at least temper human excess and immoderate greed by prescribing a certain limit and boundary for interest through laws. There is, therefore, here a certain (as we have said) <term>concession <note>original Greek: συγχώρησις (synchoresis)</note></term> or rather <term>accommodation <note>original Greek: συγκατάβασις (synkatabasis); the idea that God or the law "steps down" to the level of human weakness.</note></term>. But here in the text of Moses, we are dealing with permission "simply stated," because it concerns <term>adiaphora <note>Matters that are morally indifferent; actions that are neither commanded nor forbidden by God.</note></term>. This is seen in the places praised above in Genesis 9, Deuteronomy 20, and 1 Kings 5:6, when Solomon asks Hiram to "command"—that is, to permit—the cutting of cedars in Lebanon.

From the foregoing, it can be gathered that God’s precepts are not of equal authority if they are considered with respect to their subject matter. Certainly, as far as God is concerned, all are of the same authority; hence, whoever violates one commandment of the law is made guilty of all, since he violates the majesty of the Lawgiver and the indivisible Law—namely, <term>charity <note>original Latin: charitatem; here meaning the divine love that binds all commandments together.</note></term>. But with respect to the subject matter, some things are good, others evil, and others indifferent. Evil things are prohibited absolutely because they defile the <term>image of God <note>original Latin: Dei imaginem; the theological concept that humans are created to reflect God's nature.</note></term>; good things are commanded because they participate in the image of God. But indifferent things have neither moral goodness nor moral malice, but only "physical" existence; therefore, they do not reflect the image of God in the sense of moral good, but only under the category of "being." Therefore, they become morally good only insofar as they are commanded by God and are intended for the ultimate end. Just as things that are morally good in themselves are more good the closer they approach the image of God—such as those commanded in the <term>first table of the Law <note>The first part of the Ten Commandments, which deals specifically with a person's relationship and duties toward God.</note></term>—or are less good the further they recede from God's image: so in indifferent matters, the degree of goodness is increased or diminished according to whether men recede from the ultimate goal or approach it. Therefore (as was said above), God wills and commands those moral goods because they are truly good, but indifferent things He does not will because they are [inherently] good, but rather...

# ANTOINE CRÉGUT

On the contrary, things are good because God wills them.

Therefore, when God forbade Adam from using the **tree of the knowledge of good and evil**, that which was only physically good became ethically evil by virtue of the prohibition. This is because God intended the ultimate end—that is, His own glory, which is the true form of every moral good. For if all actions are defined by their purpose and take on the nature of good or evil accordingly, this must be stated even more strongly regarding the ultimate end, since it is essentially good and the highest object of desire, and therefore the true standard of all good things.

So much for the **prohibition**. Now follows the **thing prohibited, namely the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil**. Many inquiries are made here concerning its name and the specific species of that fruit, but we gladly omit those as being overly curious and unnecessary, focusing only on what is essential. First, it should be noted that God forbade only two trees to the first-formed humans while providing an abundance of others, so that through such generosity, man might more willingly carry out the divine commands—though warnings were also added to strike him with fear.

->### Second part, which is the Transgression.<-

But let us descend to the transgression of the law, which is the second and most important part of this treatise. This is all the more worthy of attention because that sin is the first and the root of all others, and the source from which such a great change occurred in the entire universe. That transgression of Adam is correctly called by theologians **originating original sin** <note>original Latin: *peccatum Originale originans*</note>, or sin taken in the active sense. In that transgression of Adam, we will distinctly consider three things under divine guidance: I. The sin of Adam itself. II. The causes of that sin. III. Its process and timing.

I. The sin of Adam (as I said) is called **originating original sin**. It is a sin because it is so **uniquely singular** <note>original Greek: ἐξαιρετικῶς (*exairetikōs*)</note> or rather **uniquely destructive** <note>original Greek: ἐξασυρτικῶς (*exasyrtikōs*)</note>, for it is the greatest and most atrocious of all sins. 1. Because it was **most free**, for when Adam sinned, he excelled in the powers of **free will** <note>original Latin: *liberum arbitrium*</note> and was not tickled by any desire of the flesh <note>original: *concupiscentiali affectu*; referring to "concupiscence," or the disordered impulses that later theologians believed clouded human judgment after the Fall.</note> by which the height of the soul might be disturbed from its seat; rather, the will, of its own accord...

...and by his own inclination he rushed headlong into the abyss of such great evil. For this reason, that sin of Adam is greater than the **sin against the Holy Spirit**, because he who sins against the Holy Spirit is not endowed with free will. In such a person, there is a double <term>incapacity <note>original Greek: ἀδυναμία</note></term>, namely *natural and moral*. When someone is tickled by the lust of the flesh, which thereafter drags the will and the highest point of the mind into its service, no one can assert that they sin freely in every respect; indeed, the will is a slave to sin, acting like a bondservant because it is not its own master, but is moved by the whim and command of another.

If, therefore, the sin against the Holy Spirit is unforgivable, one should not rightly infer from this that it is the greatest of sins. This unforgivability occurs <term>incidentally <note>original Latin: *per accidens* — meaning it is not the nature of the sin itself that prevents forgiveness, but the circumstances surrounding it</note></term> and based on the hypothesis of the rejection of grace; because once the sacrifice of Christ is rejected, no other sacrifice is given to expiate <note>to make amends or atone for</note> that shameful sin. Therefore, the sin against the Holy Spirit is truly unforgivable, not in itself, but by the outcome. The same could truly be said of Adam's sin, had God not offered a <term>sacrifice of atonement <note>original Greek: ἱλασμὸν</note></term>. For no differently than the sin against the Holy Spirit, Adam's sin was a universal apostasy <note>a total desertion of faith</note>; indeed, he fell away entirely from the highest good and the ultimate end, turning toward a created thing and contemptuously abandoning the Creator. But because Adam lived in a state of nature and under the **legal covenant** <note>Also known as the Covenant of Works, the agreement between God and humanity before the Fall</note>, God struck another covenant with him—the **Gospel covenant**, for instance—and restored him anew to a state of grace. Yet, if that Gospel covenant is stubbornly despised, as is done by those apostates who trample the blood of Christ, a third covenant is not promised, nor is there any other propitiatory sacrifice for the expiation of that sin. For he who maliciously and obstinately scorns Christ's sacrifice would undoubtedly also reject countless other <term>atoning rites <note>original Greek: ἱλαστικά</note></term>.

I therefore make an exception only for the **sin of the Angels**, which is even greater than Adam's sin, because: I. The Angels possessed free will, no differently than Adam. II. Because their nature was more noble, in that Angels are "simple intelligences." Their minds are extremely sharp and they do not view objects through reasoning and <term>discursively <note>meaning step-by-step logic moving from one premise to the next</note></term>—moving from the unknown to the known and from the known to the unknown as humans do—but rather through simple apprehension. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the psychology behind Adam’s fall, specifically focusing on how the intellect (mind) and the will interact during the commission of a sin.</meta>

[from the delibera]tion and conception of sin, he passed to the birth itself, or the outward act; all of which cannot be anything but perfectly and **formally voluntary**. Therefore, a twofold voluntary nature is to be observed: one which acts upon the will, which we have called *radical* <note>original: *radicale*; referring to the "root" or source of the action</note>, and another which issues from the will, which we have called *formal* <note>original: *formale*; referring to the actualized form of the choice</note>. And indeed, if this act is truly voluntary because the will moves itself spontaneously and freely, why shall error in the mind not be considered voluntary, since the mind itself moves and directs the will? Therefore, the "voluntary" will be twofold: one which acts upon the will, and the other which issues from the will. This should certainly be judged of the mind with even greater right than of the body. For if Adam sinned with his very body—even though the body is not endowed with a will—simply because it is moved by the will, why should he not have sinned in his mind, since the mind itself moves the will? Indeed, the mind must necessarily move the will by reason of a **practical judgment**, which the will cannot resist, while nonetheless preserving its own liberty <note>The author is exploring the paradox of "free will": the mind presents a choice as "good" or "true," and the will follows that lead, yet the will remains free because it "wants" to follow.</note>. And this is confirmed by the fact that since the mind is "practical" when error and unbelief are brought forth, to that extent the mind and the will are either not distinguished at all from one another, or at least only **by reason** <note>original: *ratione duntaxat*; a technical term in Scholastic philosophy meaning a distinction made by our minds for the sake of analysis, rather than a physical separation of parts</note>. Thus, Adam’s mind infected the will by moving it toward evil *radically*, and in turn, the will confirmed the mind in evil by moving it *practically*. For just as a practical judgment necessarily moves the will by persuasion, so the will moves that intellect even more strongly and practically by determining it, because the will is formally free; hence the common phrase *freedom of the will* <note>original: *voluntatis libertas*</note>. And perhaps it is called *free judgment* <note>original: *liberum arbitrium*</note> rather than "judgment free," because although it begins from the mind and is in it radically, it is nonetheless formally seated in the will.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the psychology of the Fall, specifically asking why Adam’s will chose to sin. It builds on the previous page's distinction between the mind’s judgment and the will’s action.</meta>

<header>THE REVEALER OF SECRETS.</header>

Adam plucked and ate the forbidden fruit of the tree: Was it not because his appetite had first lusted after it? But why did the appetite lust? Was this not done by the nod and command of the will? But furthermore, why did the will command such a crime to the appetite? Truly, did it happen because a wandering or deceitful mind moved the will and drew it to itself? For just as Eve enticed her husband to sin, so the mind associated with the will, like a spouse, in that same outrage. Therefore, the **error of the mind** and **unbelief** is the first of all sins, nor can any cause be assigned to it "of itself" <note>original: *per se*; meaning an inherent or direct cause</note>. For just as in the order of "efficient causes" <note>An "efficient cause" is the primary source of a change or an ending; the agent that brings something about.</note> one must necessarily stop at the first cause to avoid an infinite progression; so in the order of "deficient causes" <note>A "deficient cause" is a Scholastic term for the cause of a moral failure or evil; it is a "falling away" rather than a positive creation.</note>, the first was the unbelief of Adam, for no prior cause can be assigned. 

It was not the instinct of the Devil; it was not the beauty of the fruit or the delicacy of its taste: for these things entice **from the outside** <note>original: *ἔξωθεν* (exothen)</note>, but they cannot compel the will. It was also not by God's permission, since that permission is not "efficient" but "efficacious." For God prohibits evil, and yet He permits it by **physical permission**, which is to say He does not impede it—which is not the same as bringing it about. Nor was it **ethical permission**, as if God were relaxing a law; for He who permitted Adam to sin certainly did not grant Adam *permission* to sin. Nor did it happen by the deprivation of some grace. For God does not desert man unless He is first deserted by man. Whence **Augustine** most wisely says: *Man was not forsaken so that he might forsake, but he forsook so that he might be forsaken.* (From *The City of God*, Book 13, Chapter 15). And in the same place, that holy Doctor adds: For his evil, his own will is prior; but for his good, the will of his Creator is prior. 

Therefore, there was no cause "of itself" for unbelief, because it is itself the highest or supreme cause of evil and the first of all. Whence a certain distinguished theologian—truly one not of the common herd—said acutely: *Adam sinned by a free choice more than by free-will* <note>original: *arbitrio libero magis quàm libero arbitrio*. This is a wordplay suggesting that the act was a result of a specific "free decision" made in that moment, rather than being an inherent defect in the faculty of "Free Will" itself.</note>. This is because, by the priority of nature, the act of the mind precedes that of the will, though in time, the act of the mind and the will were simultaneous.

But truly, although no cause "of itself" can be assigned for Adam's sin and his unbelief, nevertheless the **nature of mutability** <note>The capacity for a created being to change or fail, unlike God who is immutable.</note> is deservedly called the cause "by accident" <note>original: *per accidens*; an incidental or secondary cause</note>. For although the will was imbued with **original justice**...

...from the deliberation and conception of the sin, he passed to the actual delivery or outward deed; all of these aspects cannot be anything other than perfectly and **formally voluntary**. Therefore, we must observe a twofold voluntary nature: one which acts upon the will, which we have called <term>radical</term> <note>meaning the "root" or source of the action</note>, and the other which proceeds from the will, which we have called <term>formal</term> <note>referring to the completed shape or "form" the action takes</note>. Truly, if an act is considered voluntary because the will moves itself spontaneously and freely, why should an error in the mind not also be considered voluntary, since the mind itself moves and directs the will? 

Therefore, the voluntary nature is twofold: one that acts upon the will, and another that proceeds from the will. This should certainly be judged with greater right regarding the mind than the body. For if Adam sinned with his very body—even though the body itself is not endowed with a will—simply because it is moved by the will, why should he not be said to have sinned in his mind, since the mind itself moves the will? Indeed, the mind must necessarily move the will by reason of <term>practical judgment</term> <note>the rational decision to act in a specific way</note>, which the will cannot resist, while still preserving its own liberty. This is further confirmed by the fact that since the mind is "practical" when error and unbelief are brought forth, at that point the mind and the will are either not distinguished from each other at all, or at least only distinguished by logic. 

Thus, Adam's mind infected his will by moving it toward evil **radically**; in turn, the will confirmed the mind in that evil by moving it **practically**. For just as the practical judgment necessarily moves the will through persuasion, the will moves the intellect even more strongly and practically by determining its course, since the will is formally free. This is why it is commonly called the **freedom of the will**. And perhaps it is called **free choice** <note>original Latin: *liberum arbitrium*</note> rather than "unfettered judgment" <note>original Latin: *arbitrium liberum*</note> because, although the process begins in the mind and resides there radically, it is nonetheless formally situated in the will.

VII. Adam's sin is the greatest because it is the first in the order of causes. For just as God is the highest and greatest good—because in the scale of causes and accidental goods, one must ascend to that first good which is good by its very essence—so Adam's sin is the greatest evil. This is because, in the order of <term>failing causes</term> <note>original Latin: *causarum deficientium*; a philosophical term for a cause that produces an effect through a lack or failure of good rather than a positive action</note>, one cannot progress any further back. In Adam's unbelief is found the **root and sinkhole** <note>original Latin: *lærna*, a reference to the swamp of the Hydra; here meaning a deep source or breeding ground</note> of all evils, which further confirms the supreme nature of Adam's freedom. Therefore, they distinguish imputation into *mediate and immediate; or into consequent and antecedent;* which others call *common and singular.* *Immediate or antecedent imputation* is when Adam’s action—that is, the eating of the forbidden fruit—is imputed to his descendants directly and immediately simply because they are the children of Adam. *Mediate and consequent imputation,* however, is that which follows in view of the hereditary corruption derived to us from Adam, and happens by means of that corruption. Others prefer to distinguish (as I said) into *common and singular (or personal),* but that coincides with the others; for *common* corresponds to *immediate or antecedent,* while *singular* corresponds to *consequent and mediate.*
