# ANTHONY CRÉGUT

...born many centuries later, did they eat the forbidden fruit?
Truly, the Scripture cries out loudly in Ezekiel 18: *The soul that sins shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.* And indeed, when Adam is considered in this sense as <term>a particular individual</term> <note>original Greek: *τὸ δέ τι* (to de ti); an Aristotelian term referring to a specific, individual thing or person rather than a general category.</note>, a certain singular man and an individual person, then his actions can only be personal. They cannot be justly <term>imputed</term> <note>imputed: legally credited or assigned to someone's account, in this case, assigning Adam's guilt to his descendants.</note> to his posterity, no differently than the other sins Adam committed throughout his whole life's course, which are not imputed to his descendants. This was treated at length by us in the dissertation on the sin of <term>Achan</term> <note>Referring to the biblical story in Joshua 7, where Achan's individual theft led to the punishment of his entire family; the author explores how this collective responsibility is understood differently than original sin.</note> being imputed to his whole family, which is understood in a different sense. See, if you please, the exposition of this passage in Joshua 7.

II. That imputation of Adam’s sin can be weighed in another sense, insofar as it is *singularly mediate and occurs after generation*—when, specifically, the personal sin of Adam is imputed to us *consequently and mediately after the propagation* of <term>hereditary corruption</term> <note>The idea that humans are born with a "spoiled" or "corrupt" nature as a result of the Fall.</note>, which occurs through physical birth. But this second sense is likewise false. Since corruption is inherent in every one of Adam’s descendants, and they are therefore truly and formally called sinners because of that personal sin—which is not Adam’s, but our own—it is not worthwhile to say that first sin of Adam is imputed to us [afterward]. Rather, it is assumed to be imputed *antecedently*, that is, before the birth by which Adam’s corruption is propagated to his descendants. This is not in a <term>numerical</term> <note>Meaning it is not the exact same "count" or instance of sin.</note> sense but in a *specific* sense, taking *antecedently* not in an absolute or general way (as it precedes general corruption), but *antecedently with respect* to the singular and inherent corruption which exists in individuals and is propagated through birth. Indeed, it is so far from the case that Adam's actual and personal sin is imputed to his descendants after birth, that rather it is no longer imputed to the <term>regenerate</term> <note>Those who have been spiritually reborn or "saved" according to Christian doctrine.</note>, nor are their other sins. Psalm 32:1–2: *Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed iniquity.* And <term>Blessed Augustine</term> <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), the most influential Latin Church Father regarding the doctrines of grace and original sin.</note> says: *the guilt is removed, but the sin remains in act* <note>original: *tollitur reatus, sed peccatum manet in actu.*</note>—that is, the sin is not imputed. But corruption and the stain of evil still cling to the sinner.

III. There remains a third sense which is approved by us, and which being established, all the objections that can be made against the justice of God...

<meta>This page continues a complex theological argument regarding how Adam’s "Original Sin" is passed down to humanity. ...can be blown away with a single breath. We therefore establish a mediated and *consequent* <term>imputation</term> <note>imputation: The legal or theological act of attributing an action or quality to someone else’s account—in this case, attributing Adam’s sin to all humans.</note> which presupposes an inherent corruption. This does not occur in the specific individual who is born—for in that case, the imputation would happen because of an individual corruption spread through physical birth, a view we have already rejected and dismissed—but rather, we establish that mediated imputation which presupposes a common corruption of our shared nature. Thus, this third opinion will be the middle ground between the other two views.

But indeed, let us explain this opinion of ours a little more fully and clearly. That first sin of Adam can be viewed in two ways:

I. It is considered insofar as it was the personal act of that individual who, in reality and alone, moved his hand to the forbidden fruit and brought it to his mouth. In this sense, Adam's transgression is in no way imputed to his descendants. Anyone who would defend such an imputation would undoubtedly strike at God's justice in a way requiring atonement, and would impiously accuse God of being the author of sin. Since Satan alone had infected Adam with poison, God—by such an imputation (I shudder entirely while writing this)—would have declared the whole of humanity guilty by His own decree. Just as the other actual and personal sins Adam committed later were not imputed to his descendants (as everyone admits), so this first sin, insofar as it was purely actual and personal, ought not to have been imputed to us.

II. Adam's sin is considered not as a physical *act, but as something habitual and natural*. In this sense, that sin is imputed to his descendants, and it is done mediately and consequently because of the corruption of that same nature. Since, therefore, in this <gloss>disposition</gloss> <note>original Greek: *σχέσει* (schesis); referring to a relationship, state, or specific point of view.</note> Adam is considered the head and root of the entire human race, the whole of human nature was truly included in that one individual—much like how the entire nature and characteristics of the sun are contained within the sun itself. Just as nature was created by God’s hand when Adam was fashioned—for God fashioned all species within the span of six days—so too, when he and his nature were fashioned, all his natural gifts, namely <term>original righteousness</term> <note>original: *iustitia originalis*; the state of moral perfection and harmony with God that Adam possessed before the Fall.</note>, were created together with him, along with the rest of his bodily and mental faculties. And if Adam had persisted in that primeval integrity, without doubt that same integrity of nature and those natural gifts would have flowed down to his descendants...

Because it is a sin of the nature, it is considered to have been committed by them. From that point on, as nature is propagated through procreation to descendants, the original corruption inherent in that nature is also propagated and poured out.

Such an "inherence in nature" is so far from preventing a "proper imputation" to descendants that it actually confirms it. ...consequent, just, and worthy of God, unless that corruption of nature had remained.

But indeed, bravo! Let us illustrate and establish this most necessary doctrine by another even more necessary, and no less noble, which is concerning the **imputation of Christ’s righteousness**. Christ, as the "second Adam," is considered in a twofold **relation** <note>original: *σχέσει* (schesis)</note>: either as he was a single, individual person—and in this sense, as is evident, his actions are not ours (for he alone was born, performed miracles, died, etc.)—and in this respect, no imputation takes place. But in another **relation**, Christ is viewed as the mediator, the **God-man** <note>original: *θεάνθρωπος* (theanthropos)</note>, and the head of all the faithful. In this sense, everything he did and everything he earned, he did and earned not for himself, but for us. As Isaiah 9 says, *A child is born to us,* etc., and Romans 4, *he was handed over for our sins,* etc. And in this respect, the righteousness of Christ is imputed to us; and this is both **passive**, because he died for us, and **active**, because he fulfilled the law for us. This excellent doctrine is taught by the Apostle in Romans 5, especially throughout the entire chapter. And **Augustine** says it elegantly: *He made our sins his own sins, so that he might make his righteousness our righteousness.*

This being established, let us now see the kind of imputation: namely, *whether it is by imputation improperly so-called, or properly so-called; whether by mediated or immediate imputation; whether by a common or a singular righteousness of Christ that is imputed to us?* First, the imputation is not **improperly so-called**, because the righteousness of Christ is not in us **inherently** <term>inhæsiuè</term> <note>meaning it does not physically or essentially become part of our own nature</note>, but is truly **imputative** only. Therefore, the imputation is **properly so-called**. Second, that imputation is not **immediate**. For (as was said above) *God does not justify the ungodly in a composed sense* <note>original: *sensu composito*—a logical term meaning God does not declare someone "just" while they are simultaneously remaining "wicked" in their actual character</note>, that is, insofar as he is ungodly. For how could one be judged "just" who was, in reality, "unjust" in himself? Truly, this would seem to strike enormously against the justice of God; and in this sense, imputation would be chimerical, fictional, and imaginary (as even the **Papists** <note>original: *Pontificij*—referring to Roman Catholic theologians</note> assert, though they misunderstand it). For that imputation would be merely something relative with no absolute righteousness placed in the man, and therefore God would be justifying the ungodly in a "composed sense."

# ANTHONY CREGUT

<unclear>...sin]</unclear> is imputed mediately because of the corruption of nature which was corrupted in Adam, *in whom all have sinned* (Romans 5:12). In the same way, the righteousness of Christ is imputed to true Christians and members of Christ, because their nature is sanctified in Christ. Therefore, before God justifies us through the imputation of Christ's righteousness, he calls us effectively, and thus we "put off the old man and put on the new." This is so that the nature which we took from Adam might be cleansed and generated anew through the seed of the Spirit of regeneration (John 3), and that we might be a *new creation* (Ephesians 2). And thereafter, once we have been grafted into Christ through that new birth and coalesce in his communion—as members of a body grow together with the head—so God justifies us and considers us righteous, for the reason that through the communion of that same body, all the gifts and benefits of Christ become ours.

But just as that imputation of Adam's sin is common to all "Adamites" <note>A term for the descendants of Adam—all of humanity.</note> because of the sharing of that same nature, so the righteousness of Christ is imputed to all the faithful because of the sharing of the same human nature, which has been reborn and sanctified through the Holy Spirit and the *incorruptible seed of the Word*. And finally, just as individual corruption is passed down and communicated to descendants through physical birth, so in sanctification—in which progress in rebirth is made every day—the holiness and righteousness inherent in each believer grows *into a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ* <note>original Greek: *εἰς ἄνδρα τέλειον εἰς μέτρον ἡλικίας τοῦ πληρώματος τοῦ χριστοῦ*</note>.

This doctrine is supported by that bright light of the Church and <term>Pelagianomastix</term> <note>Literally "The Scourge of the Pelagians," a title for St. Augustine due to his fierce opposition to the Pelagian heresy, which denied original sin.</note> Augustine, who in *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, book 1, chapter 10, left this written: *"In Adam we were all included by virtue, and we were all that one man."* His footsteps were followed by the tireless <term>Antibellarminus</term> and <term>Antistapletonus</term> <note>Nicknames for the English theologian William Whitaker, highlighting his role as the primary Protestant challenger to Catholic theologians Robert Bellarmine and Thomas Stapleton.</note> William Whitaker, in *On Original Sin*, book 1, chapter 7: *"Therefore,"* he says, *"we are not only bound by habitual iniquity, but we sinned in Adam with an actual will. And this will must be considered primarily in original sin, without which we could neither be, nor be considered, sinners."* And Augustine, in *Retractions*, book 1, chapter 15: *"As if indeed sin—which we say they derive originally from Adam, that is, being involved in his guilt and for this reason held liable to punishment—could exist anywhere..."*

...human nature was truly corrupted in Adam. However, nature consists not only of the body but also of the soul. Although souls were not physically present in Adam—because (as I have said) they are not produced through natural descent <note>original: "ex traduce," referring to the theory that souls are passed down from parents like biological traits</note> but rather God infuses them into the body by creating them, and creates them by infusing them—nevertheless, since they never exist for even a moment outside the body, and because the soul of each individual is the "form" of the person and constitutes the more noble part of human nature, Adam's sin is therefore rightly imputed <note>legally assigned or credited</note> to them. For we say the same regarding souls as was said regarding the body and human nature. 

Human nature (as stated above) is considered either regarding its specific essence, or regarding its existence, or numerically <note>meaning as an individual unit</note>. It was present in Adam in the first way (as an essence), but not the latter (as individual descendants), and was thus corrupted. The same must be said of the soul, which is a part of that nature. For the nature of the soul is considered either specifically (as a type) or numerically and regarding its existence (as an individual). Souls, regarding their essence and with respect to their specific nature, were in Adam no differently than the body; and thus human nature was corrupted in Adam both regarding the body and regarding the soul. That total corruption of nature is imputed to his descendants, because the imputation is made to the whole person <term>supposito <note>a philosophical term for the individual subject or "subsistence" that possesses a nature</note></term>.

And therefore, since Adam was deprived of original righteousness <note>the state of perfection and grace before the Fall</note>—the seat of which was primarily in the soul—and since an unjust original corruption occurred, such a great stain is imputed to his descendants. But indeed, the soul considered regarding its individual existence is certainly not corrupted when it is created by God; that is, God does not create it corrupted, nor, if we pay close attention, will we say that God creates it deprived of original righteousness. Because God is not the author of sin; but because God creates the soul in the body, and it does not exist for even a moment outside the body, that sin is imputed to his descendants through a mediated imputation <note>an indirect legal attribution through the shared nature</note> on account of the corruption of the soul's nature in Adam. 

Hence, when God infuses that individual soul into the body by creating it, He imputes to it the corruption of the entire nature. God does not make the soul unjust through an *immediate* imputation (for such an imputation would be a direct act of making it sinful), but since the soul is by its nature corrupted in Adam, He judges and deems it unjust and corrupted at the moment of creation. Hence, that individual soul, by giving form to the body <note>the philosophical concept of "informing" or giving life and structure to matter</note> at the very moment of union, from the body and with the body...

Origen correctly explained this using the similarity of Levi being "tithed in the loins of Abraham" from Hebrews 7:10 <note>This refers to the biblical argument that because Levi was a descendant of Abraham, he was "present" within Abraham and thus participated in Abraham’s actions centuries before his own birth.</note>. Augustine also interpreted the passage from the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> in this way in Book 4 of his work *Against Two Epistles of the Pelagians* addressed to Boniface, and he cites Hilary there as being of the same opinion <note>original Greek: *homopsēphon*, meaning casting the same vote or being in full agreement</note>. Furthermore, no reason could be given why—as the Apostle speaks in 1 Corinthians 15:22—all (even infants, as Augustine elegantly teaches in his work *Against Julian*) die "in Adam" <note>original Greek: *en tō Adam*</note>, unless they had also sinned in him previously, because the wages of sin is death. And the Pauline dispute which he proposed in Romans chapter 5 returns to this point. This is the firm judgment of this Illustrious Church and Academy.

It must be observed, moreover, that the "actual" sin of Adam <note>The specific act of eating the forbidden fruit</note>, because it is not merely personal but also "natural" <note>Involving the whole of human nature</note>, thus contracted a "habit" of injustice in a single moment. For one must think one way about natural habits, another about supernatural ones, and another about acquired ones. **Acquired habits** are not obtained except through many repeated acts, as is clear from the habit of scientific knowledge. But **supernatural** or "infused" habits, such as the habit of faith or charity, are generated without any act of the will, as if by a "source cause" <note>original Latin: *à causa quâ*</note>. For "God works in us to will," etc. (Philippians 2:13). Finally, **natural habits** can be acquired from a single act of the will—or rather, they are not "acquired" in the strict sense, but are contained habitually within nature itself; this refers to evil habits, which remain habitually in a corrupted nature because free will has been lost.

But because Adam possessed a free will that was "self-inclining" <note>original Greek: *autirrhepes*, meaning having the power to tip the scales or incline oneself in either direction</note>, and because he was changeable, he corrupted the whole of nature by a single act of disobedience and contracted the habit of injustice. Thus, Adam’s sin was first personal and actual, then natural and, as it were, habitual, because nature is permanent like a habit. From there, that vice of nature is propagated to his descendants; so, what was at first an "actual" act and contracted by "accident" <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that is not essential to a thing's nature, like the color of a shirt.</note> thereafter becomes natural. It is not unlike how the Ethiopians first contracted their darkness from the heat of the sun; but what happened to the parents by accident and from the outside becomes natural in their descendants. For Ethiopians, though black by accident [originally], beget children who are naturally black. This can also be excellently illustrated by the example of the "Macrocephali" <note>Literally "Long-heads."</note> about whom Hippocrates wrote, who were made such by the artifice of their nurses, and then...

# ANTHONY CREGUT

...they naturally produced children with elongated heads <term>Macrocephalos</term>. This was originally done artificially by binding the soft heads of newborn infants, because those with long heads were commonly believed to be of nobler birth.

Up to this point, the thorny doctrine regarding the "imputation" of Adam’s sin <note>In theology, 'imputation' refers to the way God 'counts' or 'credits' the actions of one person to others—in this case, Adam's first sin being credited to all of humanity.</note> has been explained. Now it will be easy to reconcile the differing opinions of Catholic theologians among themselves. For as far as "immediate imputation" is concerned, I believe no right-believing theologian follows it exclusively, because all assert **with one mind** <note>original Greek: *homothymadon*</note> that we were in Adam as our head, and that in him we sinned and were corrupted. From this, they praise that clever saying of Bernard: *Adam and Eve were our destroyers before they were our parents.* And very often Augustine asserts that our entire nature was corrupted in Adam.

That particular opinion which posits imputation without corruption was defended by Albert Pighius and Alphonsus Salmeron. For Pighius wrote explicitly that original sin is not a corruption of human nature, but rather the very same "actual" sin committed by Adam; this is also the opinion of the Jesuit Salmeron. Regarding "mediate imputation" with respect to the individual corruption that is spread through physical birth, that view seems to appeal to some Catholic Doctors. However, we have already rejected this sentiment above, both because Scripture and the ancient fathers assert that human nature *in common* was corrupted in Adam, and because that use of "imputation" is (as we said) an improper use of the term. Furthermore, it does not sit well with the doctrine of the **imputation of Christ's righteousness** <term>iustitiæ Christi</term> <note>The belief that just as Adam’s guilt was credited to humanity, Christ’s perfection is credited to the believer.</note>.

Nevertheless, we consider this to be a pardonable error and of such little importance that we think it a waste of leisure time to publish books or compile massive volumes because of it, or to **make a tragedy** <note>original Greek: *tragōdein*</note> out of it, or to stir up a **tempest in a teapot** <term>simpulo</term> <note>original Latin: *fluctus in simpulo*, literally "waves in a small ladle."</note>. Since essence and existence differ only in their "mode" <note>A philosophical distinction: essence is *what* a thing is; existence is *that* it is; a mode is just the *way* it exists.</note>, the question is merely whether that mediate imputation concerns the corruption of nature in general, or the nature of the individual, or whether it occurs before or after physical birth. Is this not "quarreling over goat's wool"? <note>A Latin idiom for a completely useless argument over something of no value.</note> Let those who over-dramatize these minutiae and fight so fiercely see to it; they act as if the salvation of the entire Church and the very peak of Religion were at stake...

And today the usage has prevailed that it is properly called "original sin."

<meta>This page continues the theological analysis of the Fall, moving from the legal definition of "imputation" (how Adam's guilt is assigned to humanity) to the biological and spiritual "propagation" of original sin. It addresses the difficult question of why the children of baptized, "cleansed" parents are still born with sin.</meta>

# ANTHONY CREGUTUS

...originating original [sin] and taken in an active sense.

III. Original corruption is considered insofar as it is derived and poured into descendants through carnal generation. This is a topic constantly on the lips of Scripture and theologians alike, because the medicinal grace [of Christ] could not be properly recognized if the disease were unknown. This corruption is what is properly called "original sin" today, or **concupiscence** <note>original Greek: *epithymia*, referring to an inclination toward sin or disordered desire</note>, which is specifically forbidden by the commandment of the Law. Even though it is not within our power—being involuntary—it is simultaneously both a fault and a punishment. Regarding this, the Apostle says in Romans 7: **I would not have known desire was sin unless the Law had said, "You shall not covet."** This is involuntary both in its nature and its action, and it necessarily precedes the "voluntary desire" that is understood within every commandment of the Law, of which Christ speaks in the Gospel: **He who looks at his neighbor's wife to lust after her, etc.**

This corruption is propagated to each and every person, with the exception of Christ—even into the most Blessed Virgin <note>Cregutus, writing from a Reformed Protestant perspective, rejects the doctrine of the Immaculate Conception, arguing that all humans except Jesus inherit original sin</note>. Hence, each and every person dies because of that sin, as is evident even in infants from Genesis 2:17, Romans 5:12, and the end of Romans 6. This corruption is not removed in baptism or in the regenerate <term>regenerate</term> <note>those who have been "born again" through faith and the Holy Spirit</note>, even if it is not held against them; as Augustine said, **the guilt is removed but the condition remains.**

This is why those who are "born again" still beget children with the same original corruption they themselves possess—not indeed the exact same "numerical" instance of sin, but the same "specific" kind. Even if original sin is not imputed to the regenerate parents due to the grace of their new birth, they do not pass this gift of grace to their children through the act of begetting. This is because they father children not in their capacity as "faithful and reborn" people, but as humans descending from the first Adam, not the second [Christ]. Thus, sin passes through natural birth, while faith and holiness are implanted in us through spiritual rebirth. For this reason, Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from Carthage, c. 155–220 AD</note> once wisely said: **Christians are not born, but made.**

From this, the ancients—following the Sibylline verses <note>A collection of oracular utterances composed by early Christians to mimic ancient pagan prophecies</note> (if they are indeed genuine)—called them **fish** <note>original Greek: *ichthyas*. The Greek word for fish, *ICHTHYS*, was an early Christian acrostic for "Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior"</note>, because the "little Christian fish" are born from the baptismal waters. In the same way, circumcised men used to beget uncircumcised children, and a clean grain of wheat produces ears of corn along with the chaff and the husks.

This doctrine concerning the imputation of Adam's sin and the propagation of inherent corruption was once a great concern to the Blessed Augu... <note>The text cuts off mid-name, likely "Augustine," as indicated by the catchword "stinus" intended for the following page</note>

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of original sin, specifically addressing the mechanism of how sin is passed from Adam to all humans. ### THE REVEALER OF SECRETS.

Augustine found the task troublesome when he was being attacked by the Pelagians <note>Followers of Pelagius, who argued that humans have the free will to achieve perfection without divine grace and denied original sin</note>; hence it is that this holy Doctor was failing, as if weighed down under a great burden. From this, he would often repeat that vital phrase: One should not search so much for how sin entered the world, but rather how we are to be liberated from it through medicinal and liberating grace. He illustrates this with the comparison of a pit and a man who has fallen into it <note>Augustine’s famous analogy: if you see a man fallen into a pit, don't waste time asking how he fell in; focus on how to pull him out</note>.

The argument of the Pelagians regarding the soul—arguing that it is not transmitted from parents <term>tradux...the "traducian" theory that souls are generated from parents like bodies</term>, but through direct creation—tormented Augustine. Indeed, he freely confessed the difficulty, but said (in Letter 28): **whichever opinion is chosen (concerning the origin of the soul), let it not attack this faith of which we are certain: that for the soul of every person, even a tiny infant, liberation from the obligation of sin is necessary; and that there is no liberation except through Jesus Christ and Him crucified.** Therefore, even if it must be confessed that not everything is clear—whether regarding the origin of the soul or the propagation of sin—nevertheless we firmly believe that the soul is originally corrupted by sin, and that this corruption passes from Adam to his descendants, even if the method of propagation is difficult to know. And truly, if there are many secrets and hidden things in nature that escape us, where even the sharpest minds complain about the hidden causes of things and "idiosyncrasies" <note>original Greek: *idiosynkrasias*, meaning unique temperaments or hidden properties</note> as they flee to their "sacred anchor" <note>a classical Greek idiom referring to a last resort or final refuge</note>. Who will doubt that there are also many "unprovable things" <note>original Greek: *anapodeikta*</note> in Scripture, in which it is necessary to depend simply on the authority of the Speaker; so that one thing remains for us: "He Himself said it" <note>original Greek: *autos epha*, a phrase used to indicate that the master's word—in this case, God's—is the ultimate authority</note>.

Yet Pelagius and his followers did not go without an accurate response, just as the Pelagians of today do not. For they pose this dilemma: either the soul is created pure, or impure, or "not pure." It is not created "pure," because according to the universal Christian opinion, it is originally corrupted by the transferred sin of Adam. It is not "impure," because it is created by God, who can be the author of no corruption. Nor is it "not pure"—that is, in a middle state where it has neither purity nor impurity—for that middle state cannot be conceived, since in its intellect and will there is either something moral and something of the image of God, or there is not. To that, I say, we respond that in truth the soul is not created pure, nor is it created "not pure,"

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the transmission of original sin, moving from Saint Augustine’s struggle with the origin of the soul to Cregut’s specific arguments for why the soul is considered "impure" from the moment of its creation due to its union with the body.</meta>

### ANTOINE CREGUT

...but that it is created impure. 

**I.** It is not created pure because (as was stated above) human nature was corrupted in Adam; his sin was not merely personal, but natural <note>Meaning it affected the very "nature" of what it is to be human</note>, and thereafter that corruption is propagated to his descendants. 

**II.** It is not created in a "not-pure" state <note>original: "non pura"; referring here to a neutral state that is neither holy nor sinful</note> for the reasons already brought forward. Indeed, if it were created merely deprived of **original righteousness**, yet not "positively unjust" (as certain Catholic theologians wish to argue, as is clear from our treatise on original sin), it does not fully satisfy the problem. Nor can it be easily conceived how a soul could be deprived of original righteousness and yet not be positively unjust—as if it were like a stone without any moral character, even though it possesses faculties far above a stone. Furthermore, if the soul were merely deprived of original righteousness, Adam's sin would be "imputed" to it <note>In theology, "imputation" refers to the legal assignment of guilt or merit from one person to another</note>, which could not happen without a prior and mediated imputation; otherwise, God’s justice would be called into question, as has been proven above by many arguments. Therefore, the soul must have been positively corrupted in Adam. 

**III.** The soul is created impure, and yet (as was demonstrated above) God is not the cause of that impurity. This is because the soul is corrupted *accidentally* <term>per accidens...a philosophical term meaning something that happens as a side effect or through a secondary circumstance rather than by its primary essence</term> from the **contagion of the body**, specifically because of the intimate and most close union of the body and soul at the very moment of creation. 

Hence, although the soul is specifically the same in all humans regarding its nature, there are various inclinations—not only natural but also moral—toward virtues and vices. These arise from the diversity of physical temperament, and consequently from the "contagion" that emerges from the body. Indeed, the Scripture indicates this regarding Adam’s sin in **Genesis 3**: *She saw that the tree was good for food and beautiful to the eyes and delightful to behold.* <note>Genesis 3:6</note> For from this, the progress of sin is shown: through the contagion of the eyes and the appetite, that soul of Adam, which was then pure, was corrupted. 

If Adam’s pure soul was corrupted and consented to the allurements of the body, why should not those souls created in the womb—willingly consenting to a body that is already corrupted—be corrupted themselves? Therefore, I say that God creates the soul impure, not insofar as it is impure (for God is not the author of sin), but He creates it as a **punishment** for the first sin. This act of imputation is judicial, in which God, as a **just judge**, punishes sin because of the corruption of our nature.

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS.

For the same sin, when viewed from different perspectives, is both a fault and a punishment; indeed, God punishes sin with further sin, as when He hardened Pharaoh’s heart. To sum up <note>original Greek: συλλήβδην (*syllēbdēn*), meaning "collectively" or "in a word"</note>, God creates a soul that is impure, yet He Himself did not corrupt it. 

**I.** Because the soul, in respect to its nature, is impure; for it was corrupted in Adam. God created all species within the six days at the beginning, and consequently, He created the "species" of the human soul when He created the soul of Adam. But since the human species was corrupted in Adam (as has been frequently stated), when God creates individual souls every day, He creates souls that are impure in relation to that nature which was corrupted in Adam. 

**II.** God creates the soul impure not "of itself" <note>original: *per se*</note> from God’s own act, but "accidentally" <term>per accidens... meaning a result that follows indirectly from a primary action</term> because of the contagion of the body; for in this way, that individual soul is corrupted by the body with which it is united. 

**III.** God creates the impure soul through a **judicial act**, not simply as a **Creator**. In the initial creation, He exercised His role as Creator by forming the species, an act which ended in the production of His creatures as creatures. However, by creating new souls daily, He exercises the act of His **Providence**, which is concerned not only with governing good things but also with evil things. In this role, He concurs with events not merely "effectively" <term>efficaciter... ensuring a result comes to pass</term> but even "efficiently" <term>efficienter... acting as the producing cause</term> when He punishes sin with sin. 

And since He had seen from eternity the entire "lost mass" <note>original: *massa perdita*; a theological term referring to all of humanity as fallen and deserving of judgment</note> of mankind in His decree of predestination, and from that mass had predestined some and rejected <note>original: *reprobasset*; to "reprobate" or leave some in their fallen state</note> others, so too in time—while He unites all souls with matter and with a body corrupted by universal corruption—He unites them with a specific body suitable as a means to reach His determined ends, in order to execute His decree of election and rejection. For the soul receives either good or bad inclinations from the "temperament" <note>In the 17th century, "temperament" referred to the physical balance of humors in the body, which was believed to dictate one's personality and moral tendencies</note> of the body (as I have said); and thus, in the work of Providence, God performs the office of a **just judge**.

Thus ends the second part of our dissertation, namely Adam’s transgression or sin <note>original Greek: ἁμάρτημα (*hamartēma*)</note>; now follows its effect, the final punishment. The punishment is explicitly expressed in these most emphatic words <note>original Greek: ἐμφατικωτάτοις (*emphatikōtatois*)</note>: *On the day that you eat of it, you shall surely die* <note>original Hebrew: מות תמות (*mot tamut*), literally "dying you shall die," indicating absolute certainty</note>. Here, three things must be briefly <note>original Greek: βραχὺ (*brachy*)</note> examined: 

**I.** The punishment, namely death. 
**II.** The immediacy of the punishment. 
**III.** The certainty of the punishment.

<meta>This page continues Cregut’s theological exploration of the consequences of the Fall. # ANTOINE CREGUT
<meta>Catchword: Gospel</meta>

*The wages of sin is death.* It would strike against God’s justice if sin were committed without punishment; since sin is "lawlessness" <note>original Greek: ἀνομία (*anomia*), meaning a violation of divine law</note>, a transgression of the Law cannot occur without a violation of justice, and it necessarily deserves the penalty and curse of the law. Hence, there is a form of justice in God called "avenging and punitive," and God is a protector of His own glory; in *Exodus 20*, under the second commandment, He punishes the iniquity of the fathers, etc. God necessarily wills that satisfaction be made to Himself, which is clearly demonstrated by the satisfaction <term>satisfactio... the theological concept of Christ paying a debt to divine justice on behalf of humanity</term> of Christ, since *God did not spare his own son, but gave him up for us, etc. Romans 8:32.*

Next, that punishment is considered in two ways: either as *particular* or as *universal*. *Particular* punishment was in Adam immediately after his sin. For just as he himself sinned by an "actual" or "personal" sin, so he was primarily and by himself liable to punishment; but because his sin was also a "sin of nature," and we all sinned in Adam, it is a universal punishment that rightly afflicts all descendants of Adam. Hence, Christ did not only free Adam from punishment, but also each and every person who has been made a partaker in Christ's death.

Therefore, it is not without mystery that Christ, the "second Adam," redeemed the first Adam from that punishment—regardless of what the Tatian heretics <note>The Tatianists were a 2nd-century sect who, among other unorthodox views, believed Adam could not be saved</note> once falsely dreamed. This was done so it would be clear that Christ came into the world to exempt us from both particular and universal punishment—that is, from the sin belonging to individual persons and the sin belonging to human nature. Hence, if what Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Salamis known for his "Panarion," a massive catalog of heresies</note> reports in his 46th Heresy is true, it is deeply symbolic: namely, that Adam was buried in the very place where Christ, hanging on the cross, poured out His blood. Therefore, this place received the name "Calvary" <term>Calvaria... Latin for "skull," referring to the site of the crucifixion, Golgotha</term> from the skull of the first man found there. For why else would Divine Providence have seen to it that the corpse of the first man was covered by that specific earth which was to be sprinkled with the blood of the Redeemer, unless we were to understand that the first man himself was cleansed from his sin by the blood of Christ? And so, in those two men—the first and second Adam—the ruinous and fatal destruction of sin on the one hand, and the glorious restoration on the other, are displayed to the eyes of the whole world. And so—

...let that voice sound out from the trumpet of the Gospel: *Awake, you who sleep in the dust, and rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you.* <note>original: "Surge qui dormis in puluere..." — a paraphrase of Ephesians 5:14, often associated with the tradition that Christ’s blood dripped onto Adam’s skull at Calvary</note> Truly, this account belongs not only to Epiphanius, but also to Origen, Athanasius, Basil, Chrysostom, Anastasius Sinaita, Euthymius, and Theophylact; and among the Latin Fathers, the most ancient is Tertullian, who wrote in his second book *Against Marcion* in verse:

->*Golgotha is the place of the skull, once called Calvary;*<-

The same was later written by Cyprian, Ambrose, and Augustine—indeed, by Jerome himself in his letter to Marcella, in which he urges her to come to Palestine. However, Jerome elsewhere, in his commentaries on Matthew chapter 27 and Ephesians chapter 5, thinks this opinion should be rejected based on Joshua chapter 14, where it is said that *the great Adam was buried in Kiriath-arba*. That place, as it is told, was called Kiriath-arba—that is, the "City of the Four"—because it contains the bones of four of the greatest men: Adam, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Yet, on the contrary, Hebron (previously called Kiriath-arba) was not the tomb of Adam the "first-formed" <term>protoplastus... the first-created human</term>; rather, it was the tomb of the greatest man among the Anakites <note>The Anakites (Hanakæos) were a race of giants mentioned in the Old Testament</note>. For the word *Adam* <note>original Hebrew: אדם</note> is used specifically for the first-formed man, and generically for "men" in general. Conversely, *Arba* is not used here as a common noun meaning "four," but as a proper name; for Arba (or Arbahi) was the father of the Anakites, as is clear from Joshua chapter 15:13 and chapter 21:11. Since these were all giants, they were truly called "the greatest men" because of their physical stature. The Jews who had scouted the Promised Land indicated this sufficiently in Numbers 13. Furthermore, the annotation of Baronius in his *Annals* (Volume 1, year 34) supports this; he says *Calvary is so called because it was a place of execution and of those beheaded, so that the banner of martyrdom might be raised where the field of the condemned used to be, and where sin abounded, there grace might overflow.* Just as Baronius’s reasoning is correctly applied to our subject, so the naming he attributes to Calvary could also have held true in the time of Christ.

Therefore, punishment must necessarily be inflicted for Adam’s sin, and that by a twofold necessity: I. By absolute necessity. II. By hypothetical necessity. I. # ANTHONY CREGUTUS

...of the whole <note>Continuing the thought: "Adam" is used generically for the whole race</note>, would He not exercise His right? And Psalm 119:137 says: *You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgments are upright.* And the Apostle [Paul] in many places records God's *righteous decree* <note>original Greek: δικαίωμα — a judicial sentence or requirement</note> and His *indescribable* <note>original Greek: ἀνεκδιήγητον</note> nature. Necessarily, therefore, either God will deny Himself, or He will punish sin. Hence, punishing justice <term>iustitia vindex... justice that claims a penalty or avenges a wrong</term> is no less a part of God than rewarding justice. Nor does that "autocratic right" <note>original Greek: αὐτοκρατορικὸν — referring to absolute, sovereign, or unaccountable power</note> of God seem to hold weight here—the idea that He could be judged to remit the sins of a creature without any penalty. This is similar to what theologians commonly assert: that God, by His absolute power, could have annihilated His creatures even if they had never committed any sin.

For that "autocratic right" of God is spoken of in respect to the creature, over whom the Creator can exercise the highest authority. Because His authority is supreme, it can never violate justice; for in the supreme right of God, there is no sharing in iniquity. Otherwise, it would not be "supreme." This is not the case among men, of whom the well-worn proverb is told: *the height of law is the height of injustice* <note>original Latin: "summum ius summa iniuria" — a Roman legal maxim warning that the strict application of the letter of the law, without equity, can lead to the greatest wrong</note>. This is because human laws have sanctioned many things that are not born of right and equity. But "autocratic right" cannot be used against God Himself, because it would strike at His own justice. If it did, the saying "the height of law is the height of injustice" would apply to God just as it does to men, which is a thought unworthy of God’s nature. Therefore, the "ordained right" in God coincides with His "autocratic right"—that is, with His supreme right—for nothing is higher than the nature of God. Thus, just as the necessity of punishment is absolute, it was also absolutely impossible for God to have forgiven Adam’s sin without a reckoning.

This necessity of punishment flows directly from the nature of "vindicative justice." For that justice is not absolute, but relative. An absolute property is one that is entirely arbitrary and completely independent of any external condition. For example, God’s power or His mercy are absolute properties; they are exercised by God with total freedom, without any condition in the creature moving God to act. But justice is a relative virtue. It presupposes a condition—namely, sin. Once sin is present, God necessarily exerts His justice, such that He cannot *not* punish and cannot *not* hate sin. And although mercy presupposes the misery of sin, that misery does not necessarily move God’s mercy, which (as we have said) is arbitrary...

...trary, and that misery is like a "cause without which not" <term>sine qua non — a necessary condition</term>; but justice not only presupposes sin, but is also necessarily moved by it and as if by a "cause by which" <term>causa qua — the active or efficient cause</term>, which puts justice into actual exercise. Hence it is that the necessity of justice and the liberty of mercy—the former in punishing and the latter in forgiving—were blended in Christ’s ransom <note>original Greek: λύτρῳ — a price paid for the release of a prisoner or slave</note>, when, as the Psalmist says, *justice and mercy have kissed each other* <note>A reference to Psalm 85:10</note>.

For although that vindicatory justice <term>iustitia vindicatrix — justice that avenges or claims a penalty</term> and mercy are not "primary" virtues in God, but "secondary," because they would not be in actual exercise unless sin had entered into the world, nevertheless this does not prevent those virtues from being essential and immutable to God, and the very nature of God himself. For the very essence of goodness and justice has been in God from eternity and before sin was committed, and in (so to speak) an "indicated act" <term>actu signato — a scholastic term for a power or quality that exists in principle, even if it isn't currently being used</term>. But if justice becomes a punisher in "exercised act" <term>actu exercito — a quality in active operation</term> on the hypothesis of sin—just as grace and mercy find a place where there is guilt—this happens by circumstance. The change is not in God, but in the creature. In God there is a perennial and inexhaustible fountain of justice and goodness, from which the streams of vindicatory justice and grace bubble up; all of these, in respect to their source, are not really distinct, but only differ in respect to where they end. Therefore, punishment is a necessary consequence of divine justice given the hypothesis of sin. The Pagans themselves indicated this well enough by establishing various judges of crimes such as Minos and Rhadamanthus <note>In Greek mythology, these were the legendary judges of the dead in the underworld</note>, as well as Nemesis and Justice <note>original Greek: Δίκην (Dike) — the goddess of moral order and fair judgment</note>; indeed, punishment was even worshipped as a goddess by the Assyrians. And repentance, which the ancient Pagans named from "punishment" <note>original Latin: "poenitentia" (repentance) derived from "poena" (punishment)</note>, was worshipped as a goddess among the Romans, and her statue was preserved; hence the poet says in an Epigram:

> *I am the goddess who exacts penalties for what is done and undone:*
> *Indeed, so that one may repent, I am called Metanoia.* <note>original Greek: μετανοια — a change of mind, often translated as repentance</note>

Since, therefore, Adam’s sin violated the majesty of the Lawgiver, since its foulness defiled the image of God (which is holiness), and since such lawlessness <note>original Greek: ἀνομία — literally "without law" or "iniquity"</note> struck against God’s justice, necessarily likewise that most just Judge had to inflict punishment, either upon Adam himself, or upon a sponsor <note>Refers to Jesus Christ acting as a legal guarantor or substitute</note>, so that there would be true satisfaction by which the wounded majesty of God might be appeased.

### ANTHONY CREGUT

<margin>F iij</margin>

...on the hypothesis of the divine decree and will, since God—whose word is immutable—said to Adam in Genesis 2:17: *on the day that you eat of that fruit, etc.* Therefore, in the legal covenant <term>fœdus legale — a covenant based on works and obedience</term>, the substance was, *do this and you shall live*. This shows the agreements of the covenant and the mutual promises: man pledges obedience and the observance of the Law, while God pledges life and immortality.

Thus, since Adam was a breaker of the covenant, God is not bound to bestow life. Therefore, an inescapable punishment follows. Hence that passage in Deuteronomy 27:26: *Cursed is he who does not remain in all things, etc.* Romans 5:12: *Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin, death.* Romans 6:23: *The wages of sin is death.*

But (as was shown above in the first part) just as Paul testifies in the aforementioned passage that all have sinned in Adam, so the punishment has pervaded all mortals; and just as God had established the law for both Adam and for his descendants, so he also threatened punishment for Adam and his descendants.

For although that law given to Adam was ceremonial—or concerned a matter that is in itself "indifferent" <note>original Greek: ἀδιάφορά (adiaphora) — things that are neither morally good nor evil in themselves, but become a duty when commanded by God</note>, and therefore might seem to have been given specifically to Adam alone—nevertheless, it was in truth a moral law in that God demanded man’s obedience and wished to test it.

Yet Adam and all human beings are bound to observe the moral Law; and for transgressors of the law, inevitable destruction remains—whether for those who sin *formally* and *actually*, like Adam; or for those who sinned *causally* and *radically* in Adam. Paul points this out even with the example of infants in Romans 5:14, who had not sinned *in the likeness of Adam's transgression* <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ τῷ ὁμοιώματι τῆς παραβάσεως Ἀδάμ</note>.

Because Adam sinned knowingly and willingly, whereas infants sinned in Adam before they were born. Therefore, that threat—*on the day you eat, etc.*—was absolute, not conditional. For although God’s promises and threats in Scripture are frequently conditional—as can be seen in the Prophets and the famous example of the Ninevites <note>Referring to the Book of Jonah, where God decided not to destroy Nineveh after the people repented</note>—nevertheless, they cannot apply here. This is because, firstly, God established the law for Adam as the supreme Legislator, and it was to be observed inviolably; therefore, rewards and punishments had to be decreed for those who observed or failed to observe it. It is one thing, therefore, to speak of the first enactment of the law in which God

VII. God is no more able to relax the punishment due for sins than He is able to relax His own natural right. According to all theologians, God does not permit sin by an *ethical permission*; for He cannot relax the law, which is indispensable, any more than God can deny Himself. <meta>This page continues the logical exploration of divine justice, specifically arguing that punishment is not just an external response to sin, but an inherent part of sin's nature. It builds on the previous page's assertion that God cannot simply set aside the penalty for lawbreaking.</meta>

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS.

...necessity arises from the very *nature of sin*. For punishment is a necessary consequence of guilt; indeed, guilt does not differ in reality from punishment, but only in our way of thinking about them. Since guilt is lawlessness <note>original Greek: ἀνομία (anomia)</note> and a straying from the standard of justice—which is, in truth, the erasing of God’s image—that state itself is also a punishment. And since sin is *spiritual death*, it will likewise be both guilt and punishment at the same time. For what greater punishment, what greater torment can there be, than the separation of the creature from the Creator? This is the beginning of eternal death and the cause of bodily death. From this, it follows that those words of God addressing Adam, "*on the day you eat of it, etc.*" <note>Genesis 2:17</note> are not only a threat, but also a prediction of the destruction to come. It is as if God had said, "*on the day you eat, you shall die the death*." 

That is to say: you will transgress my law. Although eating from that fruit might seem to be a <term>neutral matter — an "adiaphoron," or something neither good nor bad in itself</term> <note>original: adiaphorum</note>, it will nonetheless be a horrific sin. *You shall die the death*; by feeding on that fruit, you will take in poison and death. This is why that tree was called the *tree of death*, just as the other was the *tree of life*. These names are understood to refer to both bodily and spiritual death and life. In truth, that original corruption, even if it is now involuntary for us, is nevertheless called sin because it is simultaneously guilt and punishment—though punishment itself is involuntary. Since that corruption is "original," being spread through carnal reproduction, it is the cause and the first root of death and suffering. Hence the common saying: *all things capable of being generated are subject to corruption*, because after Adam’s sin, since all of nature is corrupted, this corruption is spread through the act of generation, and therefore both types of death follow.

Note, however, that there is no contradiction when we say that punishment is necessary by both absolute necessity and *hypothetical* necessity; for the will of God and His freedom agree perfectly with His nature. For all types of necessity—whether the *immutability and absolute necessity which belongs to the divine nature*, or the *necessity of infallibility (God's foreknowledge)*, or the *necessity of the immutability of a decree*, or the *necessity of law*, or the *necessity of practical judgment*—all of these conspire perfectly with the freedom of the will. However, *physical necessity* (such as that of brute animals), *fatal necessity* (which was held by the <term>Stoics — ancient philosophers who believed all events were strictly fated</term>), and the *necessity of compulsion* do not; for these cannot coexist with the freedom of the will. # ANTOINE CRÉGUT

...inflicts punishment in various ways, yet not by some "physical necessity" <note>Physical necessity refers to an automatic, unthinking reaction, like a stone falling to the ground.</note>, because He chooses the type of punishment with the highest degree of freedom. He sets its limits according to His own judgment, and likewise most freely selects the persons He might punish or those to whom He might show favor. For this reason, He willed to punish sin not in mankind, but in His beloved Son; and He did not wish to torment His Son with eternal punishment, as He does the damned, but rather that His justice might finally be satisfied. Therefore, God’s attributes are natural and necessary, and yet they exert their actions in the manner of moral virtues. They do not act by force or by some physical necessity—like brute animals or inanimate objects—but by an <term>Ethical necessity</term>, which cannot be anything other than free and <note>original Greek: ἐκ τῆς προαιρέσεως (ek tēs proaireseōs)</note> "by deliberate choice."

...an intensity <note>original Greek: ἐπίτασις (epitasis); in this context, the highest point or peak of intensity required for fulfillment</note> was required, which it was necessary to reach; for God demanded the death of the Son with respect to both body and soul. Hence, when He suffered on the cross, He remained in agony and was subject to the scourges of divine justice, until He had reached that intensity of punishment by which God would be appeased—a peak which the damned can never reach because of the weakness or finiteness of their nature; and therefore they are forced to satisfy justice extensively and by extension <note>original Greek: κατ' ἔκτασιν (kat' ektasin); referring to a punishment stretched out over infinite time because the person cannot bear an infinite weight all at once</note>.

II. To the minor premise <note>A term from formal logic, referring to the second part of an opponent's argument that Crégut is dismantling</note> I respond that God can diminish some degree of punishment without prejudice to His justice; indeed, according to justice, He ought to inflict various degrees of punishment so that the penalty is proportionate to the crimes. For since the degrees of a thing are accidental <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are qualities that can change without changing the essential nature of the thing (like the heat of water)</note>, they do not vary the nature of the thing itself, according to the principle that "more or less does not change the species." Thus, according to various theologians, there will be various degrees of glory in heaven, and yet in all the blessed there will be the enjoyment of that highest degree of happiness which fulfills the intensity <note>original: ἐπίτασιν (epitasin)</note> of glory, such as is required for a perfect beatitude that is complete in all its parts—which is signified by the "full stature of Christ" and by the intuitive vision <note>The "Beatific Vision," or seeing God face-to-face as He is</note>. 

Therefore, on the contrary, there can be many degrees of punishment while that intensity of punishment required for the satisfaction of divine justice remains; this degree, although unknown to us, is very well known to the Judge. And although it is infinite in itself—because a fault committed against the Infinite deserves an infinite punishment—nevertheless, with respect to persons and with respect to time, God either changes or moderates the punishment. Thus, Christ's punishment was infinite in intensity <note>original: κατ' ἐπίτασιν (kat' epitasin)</note> because of the infinite Person who suffered: who was also able to endure the infinite weight of divine wrath. But in the damned, a change of the punishment occurs: since a finite creature cannot suffer a punishment infinite in intensity, it is necessary that they suffer at least a punishment infinite in extension <note>original: κατ' ἔκτασιν (kat' ektasin)</note>.

They not only deny that **satisfaction** <note>The legal payment or compensation required to resolve a debt or a crime</note> and punishment are necessary by absolute necessity; they even boldly deny that they are necessary based on the premise of God's will. For since degrees of a thing are "accidents" <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a quality that can change without changing the essential nature of the thing itself</note>, they do not vary the nature of the thing itself, according to the rule: *more or less does not change the species.* 

Just as various theologians hold that there will be different degrees of glory in heaven, yet in all the blessed there will be the enjoyment of that highest degree of bliss which fulfills the **intensity** <term>original Greek: ἐπίτασιν (epitasis)</term> of glory. This is what is required for perfect and complete happiness in every respect, which is signified by the "stature of Christ" and by the **intuitive vision** <note>The "Beatific Vision," or seeing God face-to-face as He is</note>. Therefore, on the contrary, there can be many degrees of punishment while that **peak intensity** <term>original Greek: ἐπιτάσει (epitasei)</term> of punishment required for the satisfaction of divine justice remains. That degree, though it is unknown to us, is perfectly known to the Judge. 

And although the punishment is infinite in itself—because a fault committed against the Infinite deserves an infinite penalty—nevertheless, in respect to persons and in respect to time, God either changes or moderates the punishment. Thus, the punishment of Christ was infinite **in intensity** <term>original Greek: κατ' ἐπίτασιν (kat' epitasin)</term> because of the infinite Person who was suffering, who was also able to endure the infinite weight of divine wrath. But in the case of the damned, a change in the punishment occurs: since a finite creature cannot endure a punishment that is infinite **in intensity**, it is necessary that they suffer at least a punishment that is infinite **by duration** <term>original Greek: κατ' ἔκτασιν (kat' ektasin)</term>.

But truly, the Socinians proceed further, and not only [deny] satis-

...they not only go on to deny that satisfaction and necessary punishment are required by absolute necessity; they even audaciously deny that it is necessary based on the hypothesis of the divine will. For they pretend that God remits all sins to a repentant man, and therefore requires no satisfaction from us nor from a **surety** <note>original: vade; a legal term for a guarantor or someone who stands bail for another</note>. Otherwise, they argue, God would be mockingly deceiving humanity by everywhere laying open the **depths of unheard-of mercy** <note>original: viscera; literally "bowels," a common Hebraism for deep, heartfelt compassion</note> in both testaments of the covenant, while on the contrary demanding that His justice remain <term>unrequited <note>original Greek: ἀνεκδίκητον (anekdikēton); meaning a debt of justice that is not "venged" or "punished"</note></term>, and inflicting its infinite weight upon the heads of mortals.

They strive to prove this with various arguments.

**I.** The first is taken from *faith and repentance*. For the Prophets and Apostles preach everywhere that the door of mercy is open to the penitent, and as often as they make mention of sins, they promise salvation to those who repent. This is evident primarily from the passage in *Ezekiel 18:23: "Do I take any pleasure at all in the death of the wicked? Is it not rather that he should turn from his ways and live?"* To this end also look the vehement sermons of John the Baptist concerning faith and repentance in *Matthew 3:2: "Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand."*

But these arguments are brought forward in vain by the heretic Socinus <note>Faustus Socinus (1539–1604), a theologian who denied the divinity of Christ and the traditional doctrine of the Atonement</note> and the Socinians. For is not the mercy of God toward men illustrious in that He gave His only-begotten Son over to death, so that He might be a <term>ransom-price <note>original Greek: ἀντίλυτρον (antilytron); a price paid to redeem a captive, specifically a "substitute-ransom"</note></term> for our sins? Thus, Scripture so often emphasizes both the mercy and the justice of God: the former because He has forgiven the sins of men; the latter because sin neither could nor should be remitted without satisfaction.

Furthermore, what they claim regarding faith and repentance does not oppose the truth, but rather confirms it. For (as we said above) repentance is Evangelical; it is not distinguished from faith, but necessarily includes it. Now, **justifying faith** is the instrumental cause of our justification, insofar as it embraces the righteousness of Christ which is imputed to us. But this is **passive righteousness** <note>In Reformation theology, "passive" righteousness refers to the righteousness of Christ that we receive as a gift, as opposed to "active" righteousness which we would earn by works</note>, which is nothing without the punishment and satisfaction of Christ.

Therefore, the <term>objection <note>original Greek: ἔνστασις (enstasis); a formal logical or legal challenge</note></term> of that abominable heretic is empty, which he brought forward concerning Abel from *Hebrews 11:4*, and *verse 5* concerning Enoch, and thereafter regarding that cloud of witnesses recorded by Paul: who...

->## ANTHONY CRÉGUT ##<-

all are declared to have been accepted by God through faith. And in verse 6, describing the nature of this faith, the Apostle speaks thus:

> *For he who approaches God must believe that God exists, and that he bestows rewards on those who seek him.*

By these words, the **Socinians** <note>followers of Fausto Sozzini, who denied the Trinity and the necessity of Christ's death as a legal satisfaction for sin</note> pretend to demonstrate that God is a rewarder to the faithful and the repentant; so far is He from inflicting any punishment upon them, whether directly upon themselves or considered in a **surety** <note>original: vade; a legal guarantor who takes on another's debt</note>. But in truth, no one can approach God who has not first been called and justified in Christ by **operating grace** <note>the theological concept of grace that begins the process of salvation in a person</note>; and these things necessarily include the **satisfaction of Christ** <note>the idea that Christ paid the legal penalty for human sin</note>. Furthermore, no one can approach God unless He is appeased in the Mediator. Acts 4:12: *There is no salvation in any other.* Moreover, Paul adds that faith is required *to believe that God exists*: but that faith is not merely **ethical and legal** <note>based on human behavior or the Old Testament Law</note>, but **Evangelical** <note>based on the Gospel of Christ</note>, which embraces the merit of Christ and which believes God to be truthful, who without doubt carries out His promises, which faith applies to itself.

Hence the words that follow, <term>He becomes a rewarder <note>original Greek: μισθαποδότης (misthapodotes)</note></term>, sufficiently indicate that Paul is not dealing there with the existence of God, but with the truth of His promises; for in reality, He would not be God unless He were most truthful and stood by His promises. For in the Gospel, there is a perpetual relationship between <term>reward <note>original Greek: μισθὸν (misthon)</note></term> and <term>promise <note>original Greek: ἐπαγγελίαν (epangelian)</note></term>, and therefore that reward which is granted to faith and repentance is **gratuitous** <note>given freely as a gift, not earned as a wage</note> according to the promises of God. This is clear from Romans 4:4–5 and from Matthew 5:46, where "reward" is explained in Luke 6 by the word <term>grace <note>original Greek: τὸ χάρις (to charis)</note></term>, to intimate that the reward is free. Therefore, God is a "rewarder" who bestows rewards according to the Evangelical covenant because of the satisfaction of Christ. Nor does it stand in the way that the Apostle adds, <term>to those who seek him <note>original Greek: τοῖς ἐκζητοῦσιν αὐτὸν (tois ekzētousin auton)</note></term>, because God cannot be found except in Christ; indeed, He cannot even be sought by those who are destitute of true faith.

Of no better quality is what **Socinus** <note>Fausto Sozzini (1539–1604), the namesake of the Socinian movement</note> impudently adds: that the very substance of the **New Covenant** <note>the relationship between God and humanity established by the Gospel</note> is entirely gratuitous, since God promises the free remission of sins with no consideration of satisfaction. Jeremiah 31:33: *For this is the covenant that I will strike with the house of Israel, etc.* And in verse 34, *God is said to forgive iniquities and remember sin no more.* And Psalm 103:3–4: *Who forgives all iniquities, etc.* Auda- <meta>catchword: Audaciter (Boldly)</meta>

<meta>This page continues Anthony Crégut’s refutation of the Socinians. Having previously argued that faith and grace do not exclude the legal "satisfaction" of Christ, he now appeals to the broader witness of Scripture—from Genesis to Revelation—to show that Christ’s death was a necessary payment for sin, distinguishing between the "free" gift received by man and the "full price" paid by the Mediator.</meta>

->### REVEALER OF SECRETS ###<-

The heretic asserts this far too excessively and <note>original Greek: αὐτεγράφως; in his own hand, meaning he asserts it on his own authority</note>, for the whole of Scripture cries out against it. Scripture establishes Christ as the base and the **firm foundation** <note>original Greek: στερεωματικὸν</note> of the Gospel covenant, insofar as he is the *Lamb slain from the foundations of the world* (Revelation 13:8). The Passover lamb and the other sacrifices of the Old Testament were illustrious types <note>symbolic foreshadowings</note> of this; hence that saying of the Theologians: *The blood of Christ stops all blood.* And the very first oracle of grace clearly points to this in Genesis 3:15: *The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent.* Indeed, the entire Epistle to the Hebrews repeats and emphasizes that Christ's sacrifice is a **propitiation** <note>original Greek: ἱλασμὸν; a sacrifice that turns away divine wrath</note>. Therefore, Socinus and his followers maliciously twist the aim and substance of the Gospel covenant when they eliminate every kind of legal satisfaction based on the fact that the covenant is called "free" or "gratuitous." For indeed, in respect to humans, it is purely a free gift, because God requires no compensatory punishment from them. If any punishments are inflicted on the faithful, they are either **disciplines** <note>original Greek: παιδείαι</note>, **testings** <note>original Greek: δοκιμασίαι</note>, or **martyrdoms** <note>original Greek: μαρτύρια</note> and other such things. These are temporal and transitory, and are in no way proportional to compensatory punishments—in fact, they are distant by **infinite leagues** <note>original: parasangis; a Persian unit of distance used here metaphorically to show a vast difference</note>. However, in respect to Christ the **surety** <note>original: sponsor; one who takes legal responsibility for another's debt</note>, the satisfaction is plenary and absolute in every detail. Paul demonstrates this in Hebrews 7 by comparing the legal sacrifices of the old Law, which had to be repeated often, with the sacrifice of Christ; and in chapter 10:14: *By a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.* Since, therefore, the covenant is a free gift toward men, it would be entirely unjust and **baseless** <note>original Greek: ἀνύστατον</note> if God required any satisfaction from men; but He does not require it from men, but from the guarantor and surety, Christ. Indeed—and this is even more convincing—He requires it from the surety whom God Himself granted to us out of paternal favor, and who is His own most beloved Son.

Nevertheless, the adversary still insists and more obstinately contends that sins and their punishment are in no way truly "forgiven" if the payment was made by a surety. *As if indeed* (he says) *a debt can be said to be forgiven to a debtor by a creditor when it has been paid, regardless of how it is paid, whether by the debtor or by a surety.* But the heretic is deceived, since one must judge differently **concerning things**, differently **concerning persons**, and differently **concerning monetary debts**:

<meta>This page continues Anthony Crégut’s defense of the doctrine of satisfaction against Socinian objections. # ANTHONY CRÉGUT #

...another [distinction] regarding crimes or personal guilt. In ancient times, the Jews used to judge one way <note>original Hebrew: בדיני ממונות; *be-dinei mammonot*</note>, that is, **in monetary disputes**, and another way <note>original Hebrew: בדיני נפשות; *be-dinei nefashot*</note>, **that is, in criminal disputes**. For in monetary matters, it is all the same regardless of who pays the debt, whether the payment is made by the debtor or by a guarantor. Indeed, a creditor would speak quite wrongly if he claimed a debt was "freely forgiven" when he had actually received the money from a sponsor; would he not be mocking his debtor by claiming to remit the debt as unpaid in this manner? 

But the judgment is far different regarding guilt and crime. For guilt is personal; according to the law, it makes the specific person a "guilty party" and therefore worthy of a deserved punishment. If, therefore, that punishment is not inflicted on the guilty person, but is transferred to another person by the permission and indulgence of the judge, can it not be rightly said that the punishment has been remitted <note>meaning "forgiven" or "sent away" from the original offender</note>? This is even more true because the Judge Himself provides the person who makes the satisfaction. Thus, it is not the guilty party, but the Judge Himself who presents the price of satisfaction and the **price of redemption** <note>original Greek: λύτρον ἀπολυτρώσεως; *lytron apolytroseos*</note>. All these things are to be seen in God the Father, who delivered up His own Son **as a ransom for all** <note>original Greek: εἰς ἀντίλυτρον ὑπὲρ πάντων; *eis antilytron hyper panton*</note> (1 Timothy 2:6). 

According to the Law, every legal action for damages is brought against the guilty person, according to that maxim of the Legal Scholars: **The offense follows the person** <note>original Latin: *Noxa caput sequitur*; a principle from Roman law meaning that the liability for a wrong attaches to the individual who committed it</note>. The "sons of the law" have commented extensively on this in the *Institutes*, Book 4, Title 8, which concerns "noxal actions" <note>legal actions regarding damage caused by a person or their property</note>. Nevertheless, God, by relaxing the Law, set aside the person who was the source and the offender, and transferred the punishment to His innocent and blameless Son.

From these points, any other quibbles and **hiding places** <note>original Greek: κρησφύγετα; *kresphygeta*, referring to intellectual loopholes or evasions</note> of the ill-omened Faustus Socinus <note>Faustus Socinus (1539–1604) was a controversial theologian who denied the deity of Christ and the doctrine of substitutionary atonement</note> easily fall away—those with which he stuffed his book *On the Savior* and his *Lectures*, where he barked against the glorious satisfaction of Christ and blasphemously vomited his poison. 

For the point he presses regarding the emphasis of **to forgive freely** <note>original Greek: τοῦ χαρίζεσθαι; *tou charizesthai*</note> in Colossians 2:13—**having forgiven you all your trespasses** <note>original Greek: χαρισάμενος ὑμῖν πάντα τὰ παραπτώματα</note>—does nothing to weaken the satisfaction of Christ. On the contrary, it confirms it and highlights God’s most generous grace. It is in this act above all that God unlocked the depths of His everlasting grace: that He bestowed upon us the fullness of grace through His beloved Son. Truly, the Apostle Paul alludes here to the passage in Psalm 103:3, where the word is <note>original Hebrew: סלח; *salach*</note> **pardon**, which signifies to condone or forgive, just as the Psalmist uses the words <note>original Hebrew: חסד; *chesed*</note> **mercy**, and 

<meta>catchword: ורחמים (and mercies)</meta>

they were called **life-for-life substitutes** <note>original Greek: ἀντίψυχοι, *antipsychoi*, those who give their lives to save others</note>, a concept which Paul seems to approve in Romans 5:7, when he asserts that *for a good man perhaps someone might even dare to die.*

No other humans can be called absolutely guiltless, nor can the innocent be punished for the guilty among them; for both in the **court of earth** <note>original Latin: *foro soli*, literally "the court of the soil"</note> and the **court of heaven** <note>original Latin: *foro poli*, literally "the court of the sky"</note>, God finds them all guilty and offensive, worthy not only of temporary but even eternal punishments.
