<meta>This page continues Anthony Crégut’s defense of the doctrine of satisfaction against the Socinians. Having established that God sometimes punishes descendants for the sins of their ancestors based on a shared corrupt nature, Crégut now transitions to the core of his argument: how God’s justice and mercy are perfectly balanced in the unique sacrifice of Christ.</meta>

-> ### THE REVEALER OF SECRETS. ### <-

<margin>H ij</margin>
<gloss>justice, mercy, sin, propitiation, Isaac, Moriah, Lamb of God, Golgotha, hypostatic, Word, satisfaction, divine plan</gloss>

...as we have said) it is the essential and eternal right of God, immutable and perfectly ordered, that sin should not go unpunished; without this, God’s justice would be enormously assaulted. Yet, a change of the person who is punished can in no way strike at God’s justice, because at that same moment, through wondrous wisdom, a marvelous **balancing** <note>original: *temperamentum*, a mixing or tempering of two qualities</note> is seen of both justice and Divine mercy. It is a balancing of justice, by punishing sin **without change** <note>original Greek: ἀνανταπαλλάκτως (*anantapallaktos*), meaning the penalty itself is not waived</note>, and of mercy, by transferring the penalty from the sinful man—who is worthy of the highest punishment—with the greatest **equity** <note>original Greek: ἐπιεικείᾳ (*epieikeia*), meaning fairness or leniency in the application of the law</note> onto the innocent Christ.

II. This harmonic balancing is all the more wonderful because God, the offended and injured party, prepared the victim who would be a sufficient **propitiation** <term>propitiatio: an offering that turns away divine wrath and restores favor</term> for our sins, as is held in 1 Timothy 2. This was vividly foreshadowed long ago in the sacrifice of Isaac prepared on Mount Moriah. For just as Isaac was to be sacrificed by God’s command, and yet in reality was not sacrificed, but a lamb was substituted in his place; so the human race was to be sacrificed by God's decree, but that **Lamb of God** who takes away the sin of the world (John 1) opportunely arrived, offering himself to the Father to be slaughtered on Golgotha—which was the same place as Moriah. <note>This refers to a traditional theological belief that Mount Moriah, where Abraham nearly sacrificed Isaac, was the same hill as Calvary/Golgotha where Christ was crucified.</note>

And thus, He provided the whole world with a shining example of both immense mercy and exquisite justice, and even unheard-of wisdom. For if He had wished to use the **strict letter of the law** <note>original: *summo iure*</note>, He could have punished the entire human race for its guilt and, according to the threat, *on the day you eat of it, you shall die*, subjected them to fatal punishment. Thus the whole human race would have perished, with no example of Divine mercy left behind. 

If, on the contrary, He had pleased to forgive the sin of the whole species by a **free dismissal** <note>original Greek: ἀφεσίᾳ (*aphesia*), meaning a simple pardon or sending away of the debt</note> without any expiatory **satisfaction** <term>satisfactio: the legal payment of a debt or penalty to fulfill the requirements of justice</term> intervening, then that most just Judge would have seemed too little concerned for His own justice. That justice would not only have been trampled by men because of **lawlessness** <note>original Greek: ἀνομίαν (*anomian*)</note>, but would also have been miserably neglected and violated by the Judge Himself because of the lack of punishment—which would indeed be unworthy of God's wisdom. 

Therefore, that most wise governor preferred to send His Son, who by a marvelous **divine plan** <term>œconomia: the systematic arrangement of God's dealings with humanity</term> would assume human nature—formed and sanctified in the Virgin’s womb—uniting it to Himself according to the **hypostatic union** <note>original Greek: κατὰ τὴν ἕνωσιν ὑποστατικὴν (*kata tēn henōsin hypostatikēn*), the theological doctrine of the union of Christ's divine and human natures in one person</note>. In assuming this nature, He united it, so that thereafter that human nature, by the Divine person of the **Word** <note>original Greek: τοῦ Λόγου (*tou Logou*)</note>...

wondrously sustained, He suffered death on the cross—not <gloss>by extension</gloss> <note>original Greek: κατ᾽ ἔκτασιν (*kat' ektasin*); referring to a satisfaction that is spread out over time and thus incomplete</note>, extensively and imperfectly satisfying divine justice, but <gloss>by intensity</gloss> <note>original Greek: κατ᾽ ἐπίτασιν (*kat' epitasin*); referring to a satisfaction that is complete and perfect in its concentrated power</note>, intensively and most perfectly. It is for this reason that we are said to be redeemed by both merit and efficacy: by *merit*, because of the suffering of His humanity; by *efficacy*, because of the infinite power of His divinity. 

And so (if it is permitted to compare great things with small) something almost identical happened, at least symbolically, to Zaleucus, the lawmaker of the Locrians <note>Zaleucus was a 7th-century BCE Greek legislator famous for his strict justice. When his son was sentenced to be blinded for adultery, Zaleucus gave up one of his own eyes and one of his son's eyes so the law was fulfilled without destroying the son entirely</note>. He also tempered justice with mercy; the father mercifully came to the rescue even while he exerted justice upon his law-breaking son. Regarding this, Valerius Maximus wisely noted these words in book 6, chapter 5: *with an admirable balance of equity, he divided himself between being a merciful father and a just lawmaker.* 

However, this same divine "management" <note>term: œconomia; the way God governs or arranges the salvation of the world</note> did not need to be observed for the Angels. For (omitting other weighty reasons), this alone is sufficient: not all the Angels fell, but countless numbers were confirmed in grace. For this reason, Christ *did not take on the nature of Angels* <margin>Hebrews 2</margin> because He wished to provide examples of justice and mercy within the angelic species. But among men, because all were descended from one man, and when Adam sinned *all sinned in him* <margin>Romans 5:12</margin>, everyone likewise would have perished and been the objects of divine justice, unless God's mercy had intervened to provide us with a guarantor <note>term: vadem; a legal term for someone who provides a guarantee or bail for another</note> from our own species.

III. God willed that satisfaction be made to His justice <gloss>without deficiency</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἀνελλειπῶς (*anelleipōs*); perfectly or fully</note>. But the entire human race would have been unable to satisfy it in this way, because full satisfaction must be <gloss>by intensity</gloss> <note>original Greek: κατ᾽ ἐπίτασιν (*kat' epitasin*)</note>. For this alone is satisfaction properly so-called, and only this is capable of appeasing an angry God. Hence the damned, who provide satisfaction in hell <gloss>by extension</gloss> <note>original Greek: κατ᾽ ἔκτασιν (*kat' ektasin*)</note>, will never fully atone for their sins, nor will they satisfy the judge so that He might finally be appeased; since their punishment will be eternal, that word shall be fulfilled in them forever: *you shall surely die.* <margin>Genesis 2:17</margin>

IV. Justice could not be satisfied, such that sins were atoned for and God appeased, unless a victim appeared who would present himself not by force, but voluntarily and with a ready mind. Yet among men, there never was nor ever will be a victim so holy that he would have undergone both deaths—of the body as well as the soul—of his own accord; but

A sacrifice without a heart was not pleasing to God. Christ, however, was that true sacrifice, so sanctified by the Holy Spirit that *he was obedient to God the Father even unto death, even death on a cross. Philippians 2:8. And Hebrews 10:9: Behold, I am here to do your will, O God.*

V. A most wise and just **economy** <term>oeconomia: the way God organizes and manages the salvation of the world</term> appears in this, because God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit wonderfully conspire and agree in a satisfaction of this kind. For the Father most freely gave up the Son, and benevolently accepted that sacrifice as a most sufficient **ransom** <note>original Greek: λυτρον, *lytron*, the price paid to release a slave or captive</note> to appease His justice. Then the Son also, of his own accord, willed to appear both to appease God’s justice and to redeem the human race, and toward this end to endure a horrific and cursed death. And finally, the Holy Spirit sanctified that **chosen vessel** <note>a reference to Christ's human nature</note> in the womb of the Virgin. What injustice is there then, since God—who has absolute right over all creatures—has so decreed it? This is especially true because that **absolute right** <term>ius absolutum: the sovereign power of God to act according to His will</term> matches perfectly with **ordered right** <term>ius ordinatum: justice that follows established laws and moral order</term>. Indeed, in this case, the two are the same. Therefore, it was far more permissible for God to substitute the human nature of Christ as a sacrifice for the whole human race than it was for Abraham, in former times, to substitute a ram as a sacrifice in place of his son Isaac. But above all, this is confirmed by the fact that the Son himself offered himself voluntarily; he is the master of his own right and his own life, which he was able to either give or retain at his pleasure. According to the scripture: *No one takes my soul, I can surrender it, etc.* This cannot be said of any mortal, for they do not possess **independent right** over their lives, which is why **suicide** <note>original Greek: αὐτοχειρία, *autocheiria*, the act of taking one's own life by one's own hand</note> is condemned.

VI. Furthermore, the justice of this "economy" is confirmed by the fact that Christ, as a most holy sacrifice, was able to free himself from the bonds of death by his own infinite power. For this reason, many illustrious perfections of God were highlighted by this same admirable satisfaction, which raised His glory to the highest degree: **Justice**, because it was satisfied; **mercy**, because the human race was redeemed; **power**, because *He raised His Son from the dead through the eternal Spirit. Romans 1:4*; and **glory**, because He defeated all enemies—Satan, sin, and death—and triumphed over them gloriously. **Right and power**, since forever...

->*On the cross death died: never from death shall it rise again:*<-
->*Your death was the sting of death: the cross its tomb.*<-
<note>original: *In cruce mors obiit : nunquam de morte resurget: / Mortis erat stimulus mors tua : crux tumulus.*</note>

**VII.** Because countless benefits emerged from that **satisfaction** <term>satisfactio: the theological idea that Christ's death paid a debt of justice owed to God</term> of Christ, while no harm resulted. **I.** With respect to God’s justice: it was fully satisfied, and at the same time, His mercy shone forth with absolute clarity. **II.** With respect to humanity: beyond the fact that they are **justified** <note>declared righteous in a legal sense before God</note> through Christ’s satisfaction and the **imputation** <term>imputatio: the legal "crediting" of Christ's perfect righteousness to the believer's account</term> of his righteousness, they are furthermore sanctified day by day. Once washed in the most sacred bath of Christ’s blood, they are perpetually cleansed and so purified by the spirit of **regeneration** <note>spiritual rebirth or renewal</note> that they grow into the full measure of Christ. *Ephesians 4:13*. Finally, with respect to Christ: no loss resulted, but rather the most brilliant splendor of glory shone forth, since he emerged as a most powerful victor from those straits of death and pain; and having laid his enemies low, he acquired friends and subjects for his Father.

**VIII.** In this, God’s justice shines: that the same nature which had first sinned is the one punished, not a foreign nature. For just as Adam’s sin is imputed to his descendants (as demonstrated above) through a mediated imputation—because the entirety of human nature was corrupted in Adam—so, because the guilt is identical, the entire nature in all and every individual human was meant to be punished and cut off by **piacular** <note>relating to an offering that atones for sin</note> punishment. But truly, since on the contrary human nature was to be restored in Christ, the "second Adam," it was necessary that all the faithful be grafted into Christ as their head. He acts as the radical and seminal source of spiritual life, so that while Christ suffered on the cross, the whole of human nature suffered. Thus, all and every individual who embraces the merit of Christ through faith might participate in his death and passion, applying this satisfaction of God’s justice to themselves just as if they themselves had truly paid the debt. For just as Adam’s guilt and punishment would not descend to his descendants unless they themselves had sinned in Adam and were already consenting in sin...

[...suffice], just so this **righteousness** of Christ and his **satisfying punishment** <term>satisfactoria pœna: a penalty paid to satisfy the demands of justice</term> cannot be **imputed** <term>imputari: legally credited to another's account</term> except to those who are grafted into Christ, who live with him and have fellowship with him. To this I reply, what of it! If we look at it in the first way, when he suffers, the entire nature suffers, which is one and the same in everyone, as was said before. If we look at it in the second way, God’s justice is accused in vain. For since the entire human race was subject to death, and therefore that individual as well (since he was contained within the human species), was it not better for that one individual to be sacrificed for the salvation of the people—as Caiaphas <note>The Jewish High Priest who, in the Gospel of John, argued it was better for one man to die than for the whole nation to perish</note> prophesied—than for the whole human race to perish? This is especially true since the satisfaction <note>The legal payment of a debt</note> of that victim was more than sufficient.

But they press further: they say that most holy person was not contained under the human species in the same way, nor was he guilty of a crime like other men descended from Adam. Yet I, in turn, say: fine, Christ was not corrupt in himself. But for what reason? Only because he was sanctified by grace for this very purpose: so that he might satisfy the debt for others. Therefore, he who was sanctified in the Virgin’s womb by the Holy Spirit was the same one who had to sanctify himself on the cross, so that he might likewise sanctify his members <note>The "members" of the Church or the body of believers</note>. Thus, he became a sacred victim who would atone for the sins of all. He himself hinted at this in John 17:19: *And for their sakes I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth.* And in Hebrews 10:14: *For by a single offering he has consecrated forever those who are being sanctified.*

Therefore, Christ was innocent not simply by his nature, but by grace, so that he might satisfy divine justice on our behalf. Do you see, then, the impious complaints of men? After they have corrupted nature through sin and violated the eternal Law and the most perfect order of right, they go even further. When God sets out to restore nature and his own justice through his Son—so that he might justify even the ungodly (Romans 4)—the "little man" <note>original: *homuncio*, a diminutive of "man," used here to highlight human insignificance or arrogance</note>, ungrateful for such great kindness, [opposes] the divine counsel...

But this was in vain, because an infinite price of blood and a satisfaction *according to the full extent of the debt* <note>Original Greek: *κατ' ἔκτασιν* (*kat’ ektasin*), a technical term for a payment that matches the full scope of the obligation.</note> was required.

But this was also in vain, because there is no true and sufficient satisfaction to be found through shadows and figures, but only a symbolic one. For that reason, Isaac was not actually sacrificed, but a ram was substituted in his place, *which was held back in a thicket of thorns by its horns* <margin>Genesis 22:13</margin>. This ram vividly prefigured Christ, the *Lamb slain from the foundations of the world* <margin>Revelation 13:8</margin>.

**Thirdly** and finally, Christ appeared at Golgotha. By repairing the insufficiency of the others, he offered to God a blood of infinite value as a price and was actually sacrificed on the cross. In him and with him, as in their head, both Adam and Isaac and all his other members <note>The "members" refer to the community of believers who make up the "body" of Christ.</note>—who by faith apply that shed blood to themselves—are present, and to them the satisfying justice of Christ is truly credited. For just as Christ, by taking on our crimes, was made a sinner, so in turn, we, clothed in his justice, appear before God as just and blameless. As Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential Latin Church Fathers.</note> skillfully said: *He made our crimes his own crimes, so that he might make his justice our justice.*

And let these things be said sufficiently concerning the punishment for sin, which the first man and his descendants had deserved. ### OF ANTHONY CRÉGUT ###

<meta>catchword: highest</meta>

The blasphemies of Lorinus <note>Jean Lorin (1559–1634), a French Jesuit theologian and commentator.</note> and the Jesuits; who (alas! I shudder all over) have dreamed these most foul dreams while sleeping, or, if they were awake, have raved these delusions: that God, by His **absolute power**, could bring it about that a righteous man might not be blessed or enjoy eternal glory; and that a sinner might not be punished with eternal torment, but rather be given eternal bliss. And—what surpasses all horror—that God, without injustice, could by His own will hand a man over to eternal tortures and reduce him to nothing, for this reason alone: because He possesses absolute dominion and is the author of life and death.

Indeed, I consider these impious ideas to be of such great horror that the glory of truth would be better and more honorably defended if we stopped our ears to such atrocious impieties, and if we refuted them by shaking the dust from our feet against them. This is especially true since it was demonstrated above that punishment is by necessity attached to sin, and it would be contrary to God's justice if sin were to remain unpunished. 

The reason for that necessity is not primarily because God ordained it so by some specific choice of His will, but rather from the very sanction of the **eternal law**. God can no more act against this law than He can act against Himself, since that law is nothing other than the eternal and immutable reason or will of God—indeed, it is the immutable God Himself. For the eternal law is that which Augustine defines in Book 1 of *On Free Choice of the Will*, Chapter 6: <note>original: "quod iustum est ut omnia sint ordinatissima"</note> *it is just that all things should be perfectly ordered.* 

This law is no less stable than God Himself. Furthermore, it is perfectly ordered that, just as bliss is owed to the righteous, so punishment or misery is owed to sinners. Therefore, I judge it so incompatible for sins not to be punished, that I do not say for eternity, but not even for a single moment. For he who sins is truly punished without interval, because the bliss of justice is so great that no one can depart from it except into misery. As Blessed Augustine skillfully puts it in Book 26 of *Against Faustus*, Chapter 3: <note>original: "Sicut qui non vigilat, dormit, sic quisquis non facit quod debet, sine interuallo patitur quod debet"</note> *Just as he who does not wake, sleeps, so whoever does not do what he ought, suffers without interval what he ought.* 

And so that you may better understand Augustine’s mind, know that by "justice" he does not mean a good quality or a right affection of a human being, but rather that **divine justice** which shines immutably above the mind; by sinning, one departs from it, and by loving, one approaches it. This is the **highest**...

<summary>Crégut refutes the Jesuit claim that God’s absolute power allows Him to punish the innocent or reward the wicked arbitrarily. He argues instead that punishment is an immediate and necessary consequence of sin according to the Eternal Law, which is identical to God's own nature.</summary>

is the highest justice and God Himself. But a rational creature is such a great good that it can find happiness in nothing other than God; and God is so great a good that no one departs from Him through sin without falling into punishment and misery.

Therefore, the great Augustine—that divinely granted scourge of heretics—proposed four reasons for the necessity of punishment:

I. Because if sin remained unpunished, it would be against justice and truth, both of which are immutable.
II. Because this is unjust, and anyone who thinks so is himself unjust—and in this, even more unjust because he makes God out to be unjust.
III. Because it is against the integrity, beauty, and order of the universe, which is disturbed and defiled by such deformity.
IV. Because it fundamentally destroys providence and God Himself. 

This is why Augustine long ago shuddered at the mere recollection of those monstrous ideas <note>original: *portentorum*</note> which are today being recalled from the underworld by the aforementioned Jesuits as if by a "right of return" <note>original: *postliminiò* — a legal term for the restoration of rights or status to someone returning from exile; here used sarcastically to describe the revival of old heresies</note>; he asserts that nothing more cruel could be devised against God.

Now, since there are two kinds of punishment, namely the **punishment of loss** <note>original: *pœna damni* — the spiritual pain of being deprived of the sight and presence of God</note> and the **punishment of sense** <note>original: *pœna sensus* — the active suffering or "felt" torment of hell</note>, sin has rightfully earned both.

I. The **punishment of loss** is required because, since there is a separation of the rational creature from the Creator, nothing but sin can cause such a great separation. For since the rational creature is the image, and God is the model <note>original: *exemplar*</note> and the Archetype of that creature, who could separate these two without injustice except for injustice itself—that is, sin—which does not emerge before it has erased the image of God? From this, the delusions of the Pelagians <note>A 5th-century group who argued that humans could achieve salvation through their own will without divine grace, and denied the doctrine of original sin</note> become apparent; they claimed that infants are born without sin and exist in a "state of pure nature," yet are nevertheless excluded from the kingdom of heaven.

II. The **punishment of sense** follows the guilt, which is customarily called "damnation" in the most specific sense <note>original: *Antonomasticè* — using a specific name or title as a stand-in for a general concept</note>. It is not called the "punishment of sense" because it is more bitter to the physical senses, but primarily because it secretly burns those senses and stings sharply in the innermost recesses of the conscience. Therefore, the horror of the pain and the torture of the conscience is so great that it has often been the cause of death and despair for sinners, since that pain is heavier and more intolerable than death itself. From this comes the perpetual restlessness of the soul tossing itself here and there; for when [one falls] from the highest...

<meta>This page continues Crégut's theological argument regarding the necessity of punishment for sin. He is building on the idea that even if God appears not to punish, the internal state of the sinner or the very nature of sin acts as a penalty under the Eternal Law.</meta>

# ANTHONY CRÉGUT

...the soul slips away from the Good; wherever it turns, it finds no place for its foot to rest, unless, like the dove, it returns to God as if to the ark <note>A reference to the dove in the story of Noah (Genesis 8:9), which found no resting place until it returned to the safety of the Ark; here, the "Ark" represents God's presence.</note>. Hence Augustine says in the *Confessions*, Book 1, Chapter 1:
> *You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.* <note>original Latin: "Fecisti nos ad te & inquietum est cor nostrum, donec requiescat in te."</note>

And indeed, either the sinner grieves, or he does not grieve because of his blindness—or, what is worse, he glories in that blindness. However it is viewed, sin does not remain unpunished. For **I. if the sinner grieves**, what is grieving but punishing the sin and reclaiming it for salvation? It is for this reason that **penitence** <term>penitence: Crégut is highlighting a Latin wordplay where *poenitentia* (repentance) is etymologically linked to *poena* (punishment)</term> begins with punishment and is named after it. And although God forgives the penitent, nevertheless, even when God forgives, the remission of sin does not happen without the punishment of the penitent, though it is handled most mildly because of the **satisfaction of Christ** <term>satisfaction of Christ: the theological doctrine that Jesus's suffering and death "satisfied" the debt of punishment owed by humanity to God's justice</term>; thus, "justice and peace kiss each other" <note>A reference to Psalm 85:10</note>, the sweetness of the one tempering the rigor of the other. On this matter, Augustine discusses beautifully in his book *On Continence* (Chapter 6) and his *Sermon on Various Subjects* (the final chapter); indeed, he suggests that the manner of punishment differs between God and man.
> *Sin must be punished,* he says, *either by you or by God. If it is punished by you, then it will be punished without you <note>meaning: you will not be destroyed along with the sin</note>; but if it is not punished by you, it is punished with you.*

Therefore, the very grief over a committed sin is the punishment for that sin. **II. If the sinner does not grieve because of blindness**, then the sin is punished and avenged unto his destruction. For what greater punishment can there be than blindness of the mind? What greater punishment than when punishment is absent in the impenitent? On this, Augustine says most skillfully (as he always does) in the *Confessions*, Book 1, Chapter 18:
> *God alone is great, scattering penal blindness over unlawful desires by an indefatigable law.*

**III.** Sin is punished when the sinner glories in his blindness. For the punishment is all the more severe the further it is removed from the recovery of salvation. In this way, God strikes sins that seem unpunished with many torments.

But why say more? This dogma—namely, that sin could remain unpunished—seemed so monstrous and unjust to Augustine that he concluded men could more easily embrace **atheism** (according to which the soul is extinguished with the body, and the just and unjust alike cease to exist) than they could accept that portentous dogma of the impunity of sins. To him, it was utterly disordered and contrary to the most orderly eternal law that the just should be miserable after death while, conversely, sinners should be most blessed.

<summary>Crégut uses Saint Augustine to argue that sin is never truly unpunished: it is either punished through the "medicinal" grief of repentance or through the "penal blindness" of a hardened heart. He concludes that a universe where sin goes unpunished would be so illogical that even atheism would be more believable.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Crégut's exploration of the nature of divine punishment. # THE REVEALER OF SECRETS.

So far we have discussed the wages or punishment of sin in general. Come now, let us discuss the type of punishment through a **more precise** <note>original Greek: akribesteran</note> investigation, which Moses clearly hinted at with those words: *dying, you shall die* <note>Genesis 2:17</note>. By these words, a double death is properly understood: namely, the **first death and the second death**; or temporal death and eternal death, which double death simultaneously includes the death of the body and of the soul.

**I. The first death**, or the **death of the body**, is nothing other than the separation of the soul from the body, which (as experience witnesses) entered into the world when sin entered. Romans 5:12 and Hebrews 9:27: *it is appointed for men to die once, and after this the judgment.* Hence, death is called in Scripture the *way of all nature*. And in 1 Corinthians 15:51, the changing of bodies on the day of resurrection will be a form of death; this can be said of Enoch and Elijah <note>Biblical figures who were taken to heaven without experiencing standard physical death</note>. Nor is the most blessed Virgin exempted from that common law, because she was conceived in sin <note>Crégut, writing from a Reformed/Protestant perspective, here argues against the doctrine of the Immaculate Conception, asserting that Mary was subject to mortality like all humans</note>.

Hence arises that fatal necessity of death which presses upon all men; and for this reason, they were named *mortales* (mortals) by the Latins, just as the Hebrew word **anaschim** <note>original Hebrew: אנשים</note> is derived from sickness and mortality. Psalm 8:4: *What is mortal man that you are mindful of him?* <note>original Latin: "Quis est mortalis quod memor sis eius?"</note> Even the **Cabalists** <term>Cabalists: Jewish mystics who interpreted the Bible through hidden meanings and the numerical/symbolic value of letters</term> expressed this from their mystical theology when, in the name **Adam** <note>original Hebrew: אדם</note>, they find through **notaricon** <term>notaricon: a Cabalistic method of forming a word by using the initial letters of several words (an acronym), or vice versa</term> these three things: **ash, blood, and gall** <note>original Hebrew: אפר (Epher), דם (dam), and מרה (marah)</note>. That is to say, man is nothing but ash, blood, and gall, or bitterness; these signify mortality and corruptibility. On this point, the Pagan author Valerius Maximus wrote in Book 5, Chapter 10: *a law is declared for all mortals by the nature of things, both for receiving the breath of life and for returning it in the same moment; and just as no one is accustomed to die who has not lived, so no one can live who is not destined to die.*

Therefore, the **Pelagians** <term>Pelagians: followers of Pelagius, a 5th-century monk who argued that human nature was not fundamentally corrupted by original sin and that death was a natural process rather than a punishment</term> were gravely hallucinating when they dreamed that death was natural and not a punishment for sin. From their view, it would follow that Christ died without sin; and that Adam would have died even if he had not sinned; and that infants die even if they are without sin; and that for the martyrs themselves, death is not an evil but a cause for rewards. This was also the opinion of certain Roman Catholics, and among others, **Augustinus Steuchus** <note>Agostino Steuco (1497–1548), an Italian humanist and theologian</note> "Pelagianizes" in Chapter 2 of his work on Genesis, where he explicitly says that death is natural and is not a punishment for sin, since infants die who are immune from sins...

Just as, conversely, "to die to sin"—when the word is used in the dative case and *actively*—means to live spiritually and to put sin to death by the grace of the Holy Spirit. This is the sense used in Romans 6:2: *We who died to sin, how shall we live in it any longer?* and in verse 11: *consider yourselves to be dead indeed to sin, but alive to God through Christ.* However, just as spiritual life does not differ specifically from eternal life, but only in degree—since both consist of the union of God, the supreme good, with our soul—so too spiritual death and eternal death do not differ except in degree, for both consist of the separation of the supreme good from the rejected man. Therefore, when Moses said *dying, you shall die* <note>original Latin: "morte morieris"; a reference to Genesis 2:17</note>, he could have understood not only eternal death but also spiritual death, because the latter is the start and the beginning of the former, just as the former is the completion of the latter; it is no different than how the life of grace (or spiritual life) is the beginning or the "first fruits" of the life of glory and eternity.

Nevertheless, even if spiritual death is included within eternal death, Moses does not therefore mean spiritual death specifically as it has the nature of sin, but rather as it is the punishment for sin. For sin is not a punishment insofar as it is sin; indeed, those two types of evil—namely, **guilt** <note>term: *culpa* (guilt/fault), referring to the act of wrongdoing itself</note> and **punishment** <note>term: *pœna* (penalty), referring to the judicial consequence of the act</note>—must not be confused. Certainly, sin (or spiritual death) insofar as it is guilt and a transgression of the law is not a punishment "properly and strictly so called," such as the law threatens with those words *dying, you shall die*, and such as justice necessarily demands to be satisfied. For how can justice demand that justice be violated by transgressing the law? How can justice be satisfied in the very way and at the very moment that justice is being harmed? And finally, how can the debt of punishment be paid in a way that actually makes the obligation more binding and increases the debt? If, therefore, Moses understands spiritual death in that dreadful threat *dying, you shall die*, it is only insofar as it has the nature of punishment properly speaking, not guilt; he sees it as the beginning of eternal death, like the "suburbs of hell" and the true **Limbo** <note>Crégut is likely using "Limbo" here metaphorically to mean a state of separation or a "borderland," while dismissing the Roman Catholic theological concept of Limbo as "mythical"</note>, if I may speak so, while others are mythical.

This, then, is the admirable thing in the order of God’s justice and in its exercised act: that sin and the punishment of sin coincide from different perspectives. Sin is like the lethal blow by which the soul...

the soul is killed; yet the loss of the Supreme Good is its death. For just as the soul is the life of the body, so God is the life of the soul: in His presence it lives, and in His absence it dies. From this it follows that the death of the soul is not so much sin itself as it is the punishment for sin. This is what the great Doctor of the Church, Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian for Western Christianity.</note>, intended to teach in Book 12 of *The City of God*, Chapter 1, when he demonstrates the inseparable and internal punishment of sin in a rational creature: *“By attaining the Supreme Good, the creature is blessed; by losing it, the creature is wretched.”* <note>original Latin: "Hoc adepto summo bono beata est, quo amisso misera est."</note> Because God is such a great good that even if no other punishment were imagined to follow, the rational creature would still be wretched and thus subject to penalties. For between enjoying the Supreme Good and not enjoying it—between being blessed and being wretched—there is no middle ground.

It is no wonder, then, considering that double aspect of **guilt** and **punishment**, that spiritual death is partly voluntary and partly involuntary. It is voluntary insofar as it is sin; it is involuntary insofar as it is the punishment for sin. For although no one sins except by choice, no one loses the Supreme Good except against their will; yet because the free will turns away from that Good (which cannot be held alongside evil desire), it follows that in a certain sense the soul is both willing and unwilling. Thus, sin and the punishment of sin must necessarily occur together. In this way, nothing prevents sin from being involuntary and its own punishment. Hence the holy Doctor Augustine says in Book 8 of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Chapter 13: *“Evil wills have their own internal punishment within themselves, which is their very own iniquity.”* <note>original Latin: "In seipsis malæ voluntates habent interiorem pœnam suam eandem ipsam iniquitatem suam."</note> And as the same Sainted Doctor holds in his commentary on Psalm 7, the beauty of the universe is preserved by these two things: rewards and punishments. Thus, the whole of creation is adorned with a beauty that is wondrous and known to few. This ensures that while each is given what they deserve, the beauty of the whole universe is not violated in any part.

Since that three-fold kind of death is rightly assigned as the penalty for original sin, why then were so many evasions and riddles <note>term: *gryphi* (riddles/enigmas), here referring to complex or obscure theological arguments.</note> stirred up by those “little fathers” <note>A likely dismissive reference to the theologians at the Council of Trent (1545–1563), which defined Catholic dogma in response to the Reformation.</note> at the Council of Trent while they were investigating the punishment for original sin? # ANTHONY CRÉGUT

The man of Rimini <note>Gregory of Rimini (c. 1300–1358), a prominent Scholastic theologian.</note>, who was the only one among the Scholastics to cause a rift by defecting from the Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard, the author of the standard Medieval theological textbook; Crégut uses the term "Gnomodidascalo" or "Rule-teacher."</note>, was nicknamed "the nursery of hell" <note>Gregory was famously known as the *tortor infantium* or "torturer of infants."</note> because he believed that infants were tortured by the fire of Gehenna on account of original sin. However, even the other Doctors of the Council were not of one mind <note>original Greek: ὁμοψηφῶντες</note>, because there was a wide discrepancy of opinions between the Dominicans and the Franciscans. Some placed infants in "limbo" and darkness, though without fire; others placed them above the earth and in the light. Some claimed they would spend their time philosophizing, while others dreamed in various and dispassionate <note>original Greek: ἀπαθῶς</note> ways that they were to be refreshed by the visits and consolations of Angels and Saints.

We, therefore, setting aside the ravings of that Little Council, believe that the disobedience of our first parents was not a "little sin," but a horrendous crime. Likewise, along with the Scripture, we judge its punishment not to be some light graze or a mere sting of the heart and attrition, nor the loss of some secondary good, but a most fatal and horrible penalty, the first taste of which often drives the damned into despair. May God grant that we perceive its weight through thought alone, so that we may pursue sin with a hatred more than Vatinian <note>A classical reference to Publius Vatinius, whose name became a proverb for a person who is intensely and deservedly hated.</note>, and let us record these funeral verses on this little page as a healthy memorial <note>original Greek: μνημόσυνον</note> of that great ruin and of Adam’s fall:

->*Adam’s fall subjected the soul to theologians,*<-
->*The body to doctors, and goods to lawyers.*<-

To these, join also those most true "funerals" of our first parents, by which we perform the funeral rites and due honors as if in the mourning of the whole world:

->*Adam lost a rib for the sake of the woman:*<-
->*For the sake of his wife, he lost his very soul.*<-

And those of the same sort:

->*Eve, mother of death, a false fruit deceived you with a lie;*<-
->*And while it was building your "Woe," it said to you "Hail."*<-
<note>This is a wordplay on the Latin "Eva" and the angelic greeting "Ave," and "malo" which can mean both "evil" and "apple."</note>

<meta>This page continues Crégut's argument against the "light" view of original sin held by some Scholastics. # THE REVEALER OF SECRETS.

Moses expressed this with those words: *in the day that you eat*. This immediacy of punishment is proved by two primary arguments. I. Because (as we said above) sin is simultaneously the evil of guilt and the evil of punishment, although from different perspectives. For sin pierces the soul with a lethal blow, which cannot happen without punishment and the greatest pain. Hence, sin is a continuous and unending executioner of the soul, wounding it incessantly <note>original Greek: ἀδιαλείπτως (*adialeiptōs*)</note>, so that, as Prudentius <note>A Roman Christian poet (c. 348–413 AD).</note> testifies, *a wound rises from a wound*. For the punishment inseparable from sin is the horror and torture of the conscience, which, since it is a fearful wickedness, gives testimony of its own condemnation. Indeed, a disturbed conscience always anticipates everything cruel and fierce; its distress, because it has often been the cause of death for sinners, was a pain more intolerable and heavy than death itself. Hence Augustine, in his commentary on Psalm 45, skillfully says:

> Among all the tribulations of the human soul, no tribulation is greater than the conscience of one's sins. Wherever a person flees, they drag themselves behind them; and wherever they drag themselves, they torture themselves. The tribulations are all the more bitter because they are internal.

But the conscience does not feel this when a callous has formed, or when a mind soothed by other delights even congratulates itself. Yet this is an even heavier punishment for a sinful conscience. For something is not right just because it is hard, nor is it healthy just because it is numb. For numbness <term>Stupor: a state of spiritual insensibility or "deadness" where a person no longer feels the weight of their sins.</term> in the soul is a more serious disease than the pains themselves, no less than in the body. Numbness does not hurt (says Augustine on Psalm 55):

> It has lost the sense of pain; it is all the more incurable the worse it becomes. Indeed, the horror and torment of a fearing conscience is left as the final stimulus for coming to one's senses; if even that is taken away, just as when feeling is removed from a sick body, all hope for health is lost.

It is, therefore, a great sign of abandonment and rejection when guilt and punishment coincide, and when God punishes sin with more sin; this cannot happen without a massive hardening of the heart, as is seen in the clear example of Pharaoh.

II. That immediacy of guilt and punishment is clearly expressed by the Hebrew idiom. For the same word חטאת <note>original Hebrew: *Chattah*</note> signifies both "guilt" and "punishment." Because of this, Christ is said to have been made חטאת <note>original Hebrew: *Chattah*</note>—*sin for us*—by a metonymy <note>A figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it.</note> for the punishment of sin, or a sacrifice for sin. Indeed, in two ways Christ was sin...

...for us. First, according to a Hebraism, "sin" means "sinner," because he carried our sins, just like Hazazel <note>The "scapegoat" described in Leviticus 16, which was sent into the wilderness bearing the sins of the community.</note>. John 1:29: *The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world* <note>original Greek: ὁ αἵρων τὴν ἁμαρτίαν τοῦ κόσμου (*ho airōn tēn hamartian tou kosmou*)</note>. For what else do those words *on the day* mean than the immediacy of the punishment? Namely, that on the very same day Adam sinned, he immediately felt the wages of sin, which is death itself. Romans 6:23: *For the wages of sin is death* <note>original Greek: τὰ γὰρ ὀψώνια τῆς ἁμαρτίας, θάνατος (*ta gar opsōnia tēs hamartias, thanatos*)</note>. For even if Adam did not appear to have died instantly at first glance, he nevertheless truly died a triple death.

1. **Physical death**, because he suddenly became mortal, whereas before sin he was immortal in the sense explained above. For death begins from our birth, according to the words of a certain poet: *We die as we are born, and our end hangs from our beginning* <note>A quote from the Roman poet Manilius in his work *Astronomica*.</note>. And truly, since our life is in a continuous flux and consists of perpetual generation and decay, we are also continuously dying. For just as in a <term>clepsydra: a water clock used in antiquity to measure time by the flow of liquid</term> or a mechanical clock, the final moment or segment of time does not mark the hour on its own, but rather all the segments that preceded it do; so too, death is not merely the separation of the soul from the body, but also the preceding changes and decays.

For this reason, illnesses are called "scourges" in the Scriptures, as in Mark 3:10: *they were held by scourges* <note>original Greek: εἶχον μάστιγας (*eichon mastigas*)</note>, meaning they were seized by diseases as if they were being corrected by God with lashes. This word has great emphasis, indicating not only the origin of diseases but also God's purpose in sending them to humanity. Paul also indicated this using the terms *weak*, *sick*, and *to sleep* (meaning to die) in 1 Corinthians 11:30. And in Hebrews 12:6, he uses the same word: *he scourges* <note>original Greek: μαστιγοῖ (*mastigoi*)</note>. Therefore, although this way of speaking is new, it rightly agrees with the reality itself and with the primary origin of disease and death.

III. On the same day that he sinned, he died an eternal death—not because he endured the punishment <term>extensively</term> <note>original Greek: κατ' ἔκτασιν (*kat' ektasin*). In theology, this refers to a punishment that lasts forever in time.</note> and in respect to an infinite duration, for duration is not part of the essence of the punishment; but rather, he sustained the punishment <term>intensively</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπίτασιν (*epitasin*). This refers to the depth or weight of the suffering rather than its length.</note>, insofar as he was separated from the highest good and turned away toward the creature, and a great **chasm** <note>original Greek: χάσμα (*chasma*)</note> was created between God and man. For (as we said above) spiritual death does not differ specifically or essentially from eternal death, but only in degree; for spiritual death is the beginning of eternal death. If, therefore, Adam did not suffer eternal death in terms of duration (that is, extensively), it is because he was liberated by Christ, who suffered it **equivalently** <note>original Greek: ἰσοδυναμῶντος (*isodynamōntos*). This implies Christ's suffering had the same spiritual value or power as an eternity of human punishment.</note>. For although Adam suffered it intensively within his spiritual death, this must be understood according to the limited measure of a creature, not in the highest intensity as Christ did, which allowed Him to satisfy divine justice. For even Christ himself, if he had been a **mere man** <note>original Greek: ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος (*psilos anthrōpos*). A term used in Christological debates to describe the view that Jesus was only human and not divine.</note>, would not have been able to sustain that infinite weight of divine wrath.

Nor does that passage in Hebrews 2:9 pose an obstacle, where Christ is said *to taste death* <note>original Greek: γεύσασθαι θανάτου (*geusasthai thanatou*)</note>. For the Apostle does not mean that he only tasted death lightly, as one who might sample food with the tip of his lips; rather, he speaks in the Hebrew manner, signifying that Christ experienced death and underwent it—the cause being substituted for the effect, because through taste, an experience of a thing is gained. To this corresponds the Hebrew word **ta'am** <note>Hebrew: טעם (*taham*)</note>, which the **Septuagint** <note>The influential third-century BCE Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> translates as "to know" <note>original Greek: γνώσεσθαι (*gnōsesthai*)</note>. Thus the word *ta'am* and *ta'ama* among the Rabbis signifies *the demonstration, sense, and proof of a thing*. Indeed, there is a metaphor here taken from the **offered cup**, according to the custom of Scripture, which Christ also maintained in his agony on the mountain [Gethsemane] while praying to the Father as he hurried toward death. A similar expression is found in John 8:51: *If anyone hears my word, he shall not see death for eternity* <note>original Greek: θάνατον οὐ μὴ θεωρήσῃ εἰς τὸν... (*thanaton ou mē theōrēsē eis ton...*). The sentence is cut off by the page break.</note>.

However, it can be added that this "taste" of death is not to be understood by the sensation of death in itself, but with respect to time. He returned alive to the heavens by swallowing up death, so that it might be truly said, as in 1 Corinthians 15: **Death is swallowed up in victory** <note>original Greek: κατεπόθη ὁ θάνατος εἰς νῖκος (*katepothē ho thanatos eis nikos*)</note>. 

This was certainly unique to Christ, which is why he is truly called the "firstborn of the resurrection" in two ways: first, because he rose in such a way that he would never die again, unlike others; and second, because he merely *tasted* death, for he was not swallowed by it, but rather he himself swallowed death <term>lanetsach</term> <note>Hebrew: לנצח, meaning "forever" or "unto victory"</note>, that is, *forever*, or as Paul says according to the Septuagint, *unto victory* <note>original Greek: εἰς νῖκος (*eis nikos*)</note>; for the Hebrew word signifies both. In this sense, in Hebrews 6:4, the Apostle says apostates *taste the good gift of God*, because they immediately vomit it out.

I. The opinion of those who think God was not speaking of corporal death, but of the death of the soul, because in reality Adam did not die on the day he ate of the fruit, but lived for 930 years; but this is easily refuted by what was said before. 

II. The opinion of those who feel that God’s words were not a definitive sentence, but merely a conditional threat, like the decree pronounced against the Ninevites <note>Referring to the Book of Jonah, where God threatened destruction but relented when the people repented.</note>. 

III. The opinion of Justin Martyr and Irenaeus—the former in his *Dialogue with Trypho*, the latter in Book 5 of *Against Heresies*—who feel that Adam truly died on the same day he ate; but they distinguish between a natural day and a **mystical day**. The natural day is defined by 24 hours, while the mystical day is defined by a thousand years, citing Psalm 90: *A thousand years in your eyes are like yesterday when it has passed.* 

IV. The opinion of others who believe that these words, *on the day you eat*, should be joined together so that *on the day* refers to the act of *eating*, but not to the following word *you shall die*; this would mean Adam would know that he would surely die—

[he would] die on the same day he ate from the fruit; but so that it might be established for him that the fruit of the tree of knowledge of good and evil was forbidden to him not just for any one day of the year or of his life, but throughout the entire course of his life, such that if he ate of it even once in his life, he would eventually die.

**vi.** He explains these words *dying you shall die* <note>original: *morte morieris*</note> not only regarding the necessity of dying, but also concerning the act of death—not indeed completed, but begun. For as soon as sin arose, heat and cold, hunger, diseases, and other precursors of death, as well as *congenital mortality* <note>original Greek: θνησιγενεῖαι (*thnēsigeneiai*), referring to things born already tending toward death</note>, rushed in in troops. 

**vii.** Jerome reports this. In his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, he praises Symmachus <note>A 2nd-century translator of the Old Testament into Greek</note>, the translator of the Bible, who did not render it *you shall die*, but *you shall be mortal*. This signifies not a natural capacity for dying stemming from man's particular temperament—which surely existed in Adam even in his state of integrity—but rather the inescapable necessity of dying to which man was condemned because of sin. This interpretation also pleased Theodoret (Question 38 on Genesis), Augustine (Book 11 of *The City of God*, Chapter 23), and countless others. And indeed, if it is well understood, it agrees perfectly with our opinion explained above. For our life is not unlike those little animals which, according to Aristotle in Book 2 of the *History of Animals*, are born at the ninth hour, begin to die at the noon hour, and die entirely at the third hour <note>Aristotle refers to "day-flies" or *ephemera*; the author is using these specific hours to show how life and the process of dying can overlap</note>. # ANTHONY CREGUT #

[per] ...wanted to weaken by this expression. Genesis 3:4: *By not dying, you shall die* <note>original: *Non moriendo moriemini*</note>, that is, you will most certainly not die. Just as God, who is most truthful, threatens a most certain and infallible punishment so that Adam might stand more firmly with the penalty hovering before his eyes, so on the contrary, Satan insults and breaks through with a certain force from the opposite side by accusing God of lying. He attempts to portray the most explicit and eloquent words—*on the day you eat, dying you shall die*—as if they were a delusion, opposing them with these: *by not dying, you shall die*. Oh, the Satanic impudence! He offers a simple negative, and not without mockery, which indeed points toward the fatal and deadly numbness of our first parents.

Thus far we have seen Adam's transgression and the punishment that followed it, all of which perpetually place before our eyes those four lethal wounds: **ignorance, malice, weakness,** and **lust**. Ignorance resides in the mind; malice in the will; weakness in the <term>irascible appetite</term> <note>The part of the soul traditionally associated with anger, courage, and the drive to overcome obstacles</note>; and lust in the <term>concupiscible appetite</term> <note>The part of the soul associated with basic desires for pleasure and comfort</note>. Now, from the opposite side, as God's healing grace comes to our aid, Christ the Savior approaches. He is that heavenly Adam who <note>original Hebrew: *beiad haram*</note> **with a raised hand** <note>An idiom meaning "with great power" or "triumphantly"</note> repaired the ruins of the first Adam and made our condition much more glorious. Since He has raised us from a state of nature into a state of grace, and from a changeable state into an unchangeable one, we may truly cry out with that Athenian: *We would have perished, had we not perished.* <note>original: *Periissemus nisi periissemus*. This famous paradox suggests that if humanity had not fallen and "perished" in sin, we would never have experienced the even greater glory of salvation through Christ.</note>

Therefore, as appeared above, there is a contrast between both Adams in respect to the sin or disobedience of the one, and the righteousness or obedience of the other. For just as Adam's sin is <term>imputed</term> <note>In theology, to "impute" is to legally credit the actions or status of one person to another</note> to us and thereafter an inherent corruption is propagated to his descendants through birth, so Christ's righteousness is first imputed to us in **justification**, and then, in **sanctification** through spiritual rebirth, an inherent righteousness and the gifts of Christ are communicated to us because of our union with Him as our head. The same must now be thought regarding the punishment as we asserted regarding the guilt. For the Apostle also observes this contrast in Romans 5:17: *For if by the fall of one man, death reigned through that one, much more will those who receive that abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness reign in life.*

-> ### REVELATOR OF SECRETS ### <-

...through the one Jesus Christ; and in verse 18, Paul opposes the **transgression** <note>original Greek: *paraptōma*</note> of Adam to the **righteous act** <note>original Greek: *dikaiōmati*</note> of Christ. And again, regarding the punishment, he opposes the **condemnation** <note>original Greek: *katakrima*</note> of Adam to the **justification of life** <note>original Greek: *dikaiōsei zōēs*</note> of Christ. And in verse 19, he opposes the **disobedience** <note>original Greek: *parakoēn*</note> of Adam to the **obedience** <note>original Greek: *hypakoē*</note> of Christ. In these passages, the Apostle's phrasing must be especially observed. For just as that "chosen vessel" <note>A traditional title for St. Paul, referring to Acts 9:15</note> wonderfully revisits and unfolds the mysteries of salvation, so too does he use specific concepts which represent the matter itself with the utmost exactness, and which one is not permitted to change. Therefore, I would not easily agree with those who treat **righteous act** <note>Greek: *dikaiōma*</note> and **justification** <note>Greek: *dikaiōsin*</note> as synonymous words.

For in truth, "righteous act" <note>Greek: *to dikaiōma*</note> is taken here for the *material* or substance of our justification, named thus from its effect—as if you were to say "the justifier" or "the justifying-matter," if those words were in common use among theologians in the same way the word **Justification** is. For the "righteous act" of Christ signifies that righteousness or obedience which is <term>imputed</term> <note>The theological concept where Christ's righteousness is credited to the believer's account</note> to us, which in verse 15 he called a **free gift** <note>Greek: *charisma*</note>, because God bestows it upon us freely. 

But, on the other hand, **justification** <note>Greek: *dikaiōsis*</note> is opposed to the **condemnation** <note>Greek: *katakrimati*</note> or the "sentence of damnation." Just as condemnation follows guilt, so the **justification of life** follows the acquittal and the forgiveness of guilt through Christ. Through this, we are declared righteous, and therefore we obtain eternal life. Furthermore, in verse 16, the Apostle makes a beautiful <term>antithesis</term> <note>A rhetorical contrast of ideas</note> between Adam’s **judgment** <note>Greek: *to krima*</note> (that is, his guilt) and Christ’s **free gift** <note>Greek: *to charisma*</note> (that is, <term>sanctifying grace</term> <note>original Latin: *gratia gratum faciens*; grace that makes a person pleasing to God</note>). He also contrasts Adam’s **condemnation** <note>Greek: *to katakrima*</note> and Christ’s **righteous act** <note>Greek: *to dikaiōma*</note> or justification. 

The Apostle also uses the word for **benefit** <note>Greek: *dōrēmatos*</note> to signify the spiritual gifts which God imparts to those who are justified, so that it is "grace freely given" or accepted. Thus, the distinction between these Pauline terms will be this: the **benefit** <note>Greek: *to dōrēma*</note> is the consequence of the **free gift** <note>Greek: *charismatos*</note> itself, just as the **judgment** is the consequence of the **transgression**. For the fall must precede the guilt, just as the justification which occurs through "sanctifying grace" precedes those benefits and gifts which are "grace freely given" <note>original Latin: *gratia gratis data*; refers to spiritual gifts given for the benefit of the church</note> and which are conferred during <term>sanctification</term> <note>The process of being made holy</note>. If anyone also wishes to examine closely the word for **donation** <note>Greek: *dōrean*</note> found in verse 15 and compare it with **benefit** <note>Greek: *dōrēma*</note>, he will say that the former is the act of giving, while the latter is the benefit received, that is, a **good deed** <note>Greek: *euergetēma*</note>. All these things are rightly and judiciously observed in these passages by our most learned Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major Protestant reformer and successor to John Calvin</note>; see more if—

<meta>This page continues the theological comparison between the first Adam and Christ, the "second Adam." # ANTHONY CREGUT #

...as you see in our treatise *On Grace in General.*

From that Pauline antithesis between Adam and Christ, it is easy to gather that the same evils transferred from Adam to his descendants were removed by Christ, the second Adam. Just as Adam propagated a triple kind of death and communicated it to his descendants, so Christ healed all these evils; and as the former spat out the lethal poison and venom of the serpent, so Christ prepared the **antidote** <note>original: *alexipharmacum*, a Greco-Latin medical term for a protective remedy against poison</note>. Furthermore, as Adam brought the punishment of loss and of sense <note>In traditional theology, the "punishment of loss" is the deprivation of the vision of God, while the "punishment of sense" refers to the actual suffering or torment of the soul and body</note>, Christ removed both. Finally, as the former inflicted the four aforementioned wounds, the latter successfully consolidated them all.

First, regarding **bodily death**, the matter is clear. For in 1 Corinthians 15:54: *Death is swallowed up in victory.* On this point, Cyprian <note>Saint Cyprian, a 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage</note> states brilliantly: *Death is the door to life, the victory of war, the harbor of the sea.* And in Ecclesiastes 7:2: *The day of death is better than the day of birth.* Indeed, among the Ancients, the day of a Saint’s death was called their **birthday** <note>original Greek: *genethlion*</note>. Hence Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine, a highly influential Jesuit theologian and Cardinal</note>, in *On the Beatitude of the Saints*, book 1, chapter 6, writes: *We now call the day of death the "birthday," because the Saints, dying on earth, are born in heaven.* And in 1 Thessalonians 4:13, the Scripture (as it often does elsewhere) uses the word **to fall asleep** <note>original Greek: *koimasthai*</note> to describe being placed in a tomb as if in a bed, from which we shall eventually be awakened. This same concept is designated in the Old Testament by the word <term>shakhab</term> <note>Hebrew: "to lie down" or "to sleep"</note>, but almost always with an addition, such as "with his fathers." Hence the frequent phrase: *He fell asleep with his fathers.* At other times it is used on its own, as in Isaiah 14:8 and Daniel 12:2, where <term>ieschenim</term> <note>Hebrew: "those who sleep"</note> is used to mean the dead. This phrasing was also common among the Latins, which is the origin of the story within the Papacy of the "Seven Sleepers" <note>A famous legend of early Christians who hid in a cave during persecutions and miraculously slept for nearly two hundred years</note>.

Nor can I help but mention here the brilliant epitaph of the Spaniard Ferdinand Nonius, recorded by the most illustrious Thuanus <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou, a famous 16th-century French historian and statesman</note>. For in his *History*, book 11, he writes: *Ferdinand Nonius, a great light of Spain, fell asleep in the Lord; on his tomb were inscribed four words—no more, for he had so commanded in his final instructions: "Death is life's greatest good."* How, I ask, has it come to pass that a horrific evil is now the greatest good of life? Surely it is from the death of Christ, which rendered the sting of death blunt, because he was made a <term>capporeth</term> <note>Hebrew for the "Mercy Seat," the gold lid of the Ark of the Covenant where God met with man; it implies a covering or atonement for sin</note>, as Paul has it in Romans 3:25: *whom God set forth as a* **propitiation** <note>original Greek: *hilasterion*, a word meaning a place or means of atonement, directly linking back to the Mercy Seat</note>...

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS #

<margin>The Mercy Seat</margin> <term>The Mercy Seat</term> <note>Hebrew: *kapporet*, the golden lid of the Ark of the Covenant, considered the place where God’s presence rested and where atonement was made</note>. Alluding perhaps to the Ark of the Covenant, whose cover was called by this name. And indeed, just as in Genesis 2, *God breathed into Adam’s nostrils the breath of life*, it was therefore God’s role to give breath, and man’s role to breathe and live. This is suggested by the word <term>to take breath</term> <note>Hebrew: *naphasch*, a verb meaning to breathe, be refreshed, or recover one's life</note>. In the same way, Christ "expiring" (breathing out) on the cross was the "respiration" (breathing again) of mankind. This was signified in John 11 <note>While the text cites John 11, the event of Christ breathing on the disciples is found in John 20:22</note> when He breathed on the Apostles, saying, *Receive the Holy Spirit.* Therefore, Christ truly introduced into the world a <term>good death</term> <note>original Greek: *euthanasia*</note>. This Greek name is more fitting for the faithful than for those whom the Emperor Augustus spoke of; according to Suetonius <note>A Roman historian</note> in his biography of Augustus, whenever the Emperor saw someone die without agony, he would exclaim: *O immortal Gods, grant a similar <term>good death</term> to me and mine.*

Secondly, concerning **spiritual death**, the matter is clear. For in Romans 6:11: *We are dead to sin and live to God through Christ Jesus.* And in verse 18: *And having been set free from sin, you became slaves to righteousness.* This occurs in justification and sanctification. In the former, the guilt of sin is removed; in the latter, the inherent corruption is removed—at least regarding its "reign" and "habit" <note>its power to dominate a person’s character</note>, even if the "act" or impulse of sin remains while we are **wayfarers** <note>original: *viatores*, a term for humans still on their earthly journey toward heaven</note>. Finally, the very act of sin will be completely removed in the resurrection, when He will free us through the power of redemption. Then, with sin and death utterly extinguished, we shall "put off the old man" and "put on the new."

Thirdly and finally, Christ has freed us from **eternal death**, since He Himself endured it for us <term>in its highest intensity</term> <note>original Greek: *kat’ epitasin*</note>, and as a victor and conqueror, He entered the heavenly sanctuary to prepare a place for us (John 14:3). For this reason, we have rightly rejected the impious ravings vomited out by Socinus <note>Fausto Sozzini, whose followers denied the divinity of Christ and the necessity of His sacrifice</note> and the Socinians against Christ’s "satisfaction" <note>the theological idea that Christ's death paid a debt to divine justice</note>. Likewise, we reject the foolish fantasies of the Muslims and the Quran <note>original: *Muhammedanorum & Alkorani*</note>, who fabricate a story that Christ was secretly snatched from the cross and another substituted in His place. They rave in that same Quran that original sin is forgiven without Christ’s satisfaction, and thus they <term>talk utter nonsense</term> <note>original Greek: *lêron lêrousi*</note>. For even if they believe Christ to be a great Prophet *in this world and the next life*, they nevertheless deny that He was a Priest who offered Himself for the sins of the world. Thus, they plead for God’s mercy outside of Christ. Hence that confession in the Quran: *When Adam was cast out of paradise...*

*That enmity is perpetual. There is an emphasis on the word <term>enmity</term> <note>Hebrew: *eybah*</note> which signifies that this hostility is not by nature, but by accident <note>In Aristotelian terms, an "accident" is a quality that is not essential to a thing's nature; here, it means the enmity arose because of the Fall, rather than being part of God's original creation</note>. This enmity exists mystically between the faithful and the reprobate, and between Christ and Satan. These are two opposing kingdoms of Light and darkness. *Finally, the fourth part concerns the victory of the woman’s seed. The victory is signified by the crushing of the serpent’s head. Various observations are made on the Hebrew words <term>to crush</term> <note>Hebrew: *shuph*</note> and <term>head</term> <note>Hebrew: *rosh*</note> which designate that victory. The victory is confirmed in respect to Christ and the faithful. The symbols of the victory of Christ and the faithful are the palm branch and the white stone <note>A reference to Revelation 2:17, where a white stone is given to "him who overcomes"</note>. The *Literal* <note>original: *Proprius*</note>, which is drawn directly from the words themselves, such as *God is one, just, good, etc.* The *Figurative* <note>original: *Tropicus*</note>, which is drawn from words used metaphorically, such as *Christ is the Shepherd, the Lamb, the Vine, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, etc.*
The *Composite* sense is found in oracles that have the character of a type, of which one part is in the *type*, and the other part in the *antitype* <note>In theology, a "type" is an Old Testament person or event that foreshadows a "antitype," usually Christ or a New Testament reality</note>. So teaches *Moses the Egyptian* <note>Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher</note> in the *Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: *Moreh Nevuchim*</note>.

Indeed, the sense cannot be complete without the antitype, which is therefore expressed through a likeness, whose <term>proposition</term> <note>Greek: *protasis*</note> contains the type, while the <term>conclusion</term> <note>Greek: *apodosis*</note> contains the antitype, as *can be seen in John 3:14 concerning the bronze serpent: as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must [the Son of Man] be lifted up, etc.*

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of biblical interpretation, shifting from a focus on the Hebrew text of the "Protevangelium" to a broader theological framework. It defines how "types" (historical precursors) and "antitypes" (divine fulfillments) function within Scripture, contrasting Christian interpretive methods with those of Jewish scholars like Maimonides.</meta>

# REVEALER OF SECRETS.

(as Wendelin <note>Marcus Friedrich Wendelin (1584–1652), a German Reformed theologian</note> observes) which occurs in plain oracles that do not function as types, and which is either proper or figurative. The **Proper** sense is that which is drawn immediately from the words themselves, such as *God is one, just, good, etc.* The **Tropic** <note>from the Greek 'tropos,' meaning a turn of phrase; a figurative or metaphorical use of a word</note> sense is that which is drawn from words used non-literally, such as *Christ is the Shepherd, the Lamb, the Vine, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, etc.* The **Composite** sense is found in oracles that function as types, where one part is in the **type** and the other part is in the **antitype** <note>In biblical study, a 'type' is a person or event in the Old Testament that foreshadows a 'antitype'—the reality or fulfillment in the New Testament</note>. As seen in *Exodus 12* regarding the **Paschal Lamb**, many things apply to it literally as a **type**; and many things also apply literally to **Christ** as the **antitype**. Similarly, in *Psalm 22*, various things are said of **David** literally as the **type**, and of **Christ** also literally as the **antitype**. For instance, in verse 1: *My God, my God, why [have you forsaken me]? etc.* And in verse 17: *They have pierced my hands and my feet.* These things the **Holy Spirit** seems to intend even more regarding the **antitype** than the **type**. Therefore, I would not agree here with the **Talmudists** and other teachers of the Hebrews, who, despising the literal sense, call it the "rind" and <term>דבר קטן</term> <term>davar katon</term>, <term>a small thing</term>. However, they call the mystical and spiritual sense <term>דבר גדול</term> <term>davar gadol</term>, <term>a great thing</term>. They call the literal sense <term>משל</term> <term>mashal</term>, an *example* or *parable*; and they compare it to a candle that is bought for a farthing. But the **Allegorical** sense they call the <term>certainty of the law</term> <term>בורית של תורה</term> <term>borit shel torah</term> <note>Literally "the purity of the law."</note>. They compare it to a pearl hiding in a dark house, which is eventually found by seekers by means of such a candle—that is, through the example. So teaches **Moses the Egyptian** <note>The famous Jewish philosopher Maimonides (1135–1204)</note> <term>in the Guide for the Perplexed</term> <note>original: "in more neuochim"</note>.

But indeed, this must be observed above all in the composite sense: that primary consideration must be given not to the **type** but to the **antitype**, since the former is merely a figure and image, while the latter is rightly judged to be the truth and reality. For this reason, the **Holy Spirit** does not intend the former <term>σχέσιν</term> <term>schesin</term> <note>relation or connection</note> for its own sake or properly, but only incidentally and because of the <term>σחέσιν</term> <term>connection</term> it has to the antitype—just as a shadow is nothing real in itself, but is only intentional and exists by means of the body from which it results. Indeed, the sense cannot be complete without the antitype, which is therefore brought forth through a likeness, whose <term>πρότασις</term> <term>protasis</term> <note>the opening premise or "if" clause of a comparison</note> contains the type, while the <term>ἀπόδοσις</term> <term>apodosis</term> <note>the concluding fulfillment or "then" clause</note> contains the antitype. This can be seen in *John 3:14* regarding the bronze serpent: *just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must [the Son of Man] be lifted up, etc.*

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous discussion on the "composite sense" of Scripture. Having criticized those who ignore the deeper literal meanings intended by the Holy Spirit, the author now provides a biblical illustration using the friendship of Jonathan and David to explain how one event can carry two simultaneous meanings—one immediate and one prophetic.</meta>

->### ANTHONY CREGUT<-

The example found in *1 Samuel 20* regarding Jonathan, the son of King Saul, making a covenant with David, fits this perfectly. For Jonathan, by shooting three arrows and instructing his armor-bearer to go and collect them, was signaling two things: what he was saying and what he was intending. The first was in respect to the armor-bearer, who looked to nothing but his master’s command, being completely ignorant of anything else; the second was in respect to David, who was secretly waiting for the agreed-upon plan and its outcome. Thus, it is not absurd to say that the Holy Spirit very often intended two things in a **composite sense**, doing so literally by looking both at the **type** and the **antitype**, because the former serves the latter <note>original: "παχυλῶς καὶ ὡς ἐν τύπῳ" (pachylos kai hos en typo) — meaning roughly, broadly, or as in a general sketch/figure</note>.

And just as Jonathan intended the retrieval of the arrows as a secondary matter, but primarily intended the news brought to the hidden David concerning Saul’s anger and the need for a swift flight—even if at first glance he seemed to be speaking more literally about the retrieval of arrows—so also the Holy Spirit frequently intends that which is mystical and the **antitype**, even when the opposite appears to the reader. Such a reader is unable to look within to see the **marrow** hidden in the **husk** <term>cortex and medulla</term> <note>These are common scholarly metaphors: the "cortex" is the outer shell or literal words, while the "medulla" is the deep, spiritual "marrow" or inner meaning</note>, or to see the "body" within the shadowy or overshadowing figure. This often happened to the fathers of the Old Testament while the synagogue and its ceremonies occupied their attention. 

Therefore, just as Jonathan’s armor-bearer, not being informed of the private consultation between the two friends, thought of nothing but the arrows and was not in the least bit concerned for David’s safety, David, on the contrary, looked to the reality foreshadowed by the arrows. Likewise, the Jews of today, wearing a veil and hardened by <note>original: "πωρώσει" (porosei) — a spiritual "callousness" or hardening of the heart/senses</note> blindness, cling to the **husk**. Thus, they live perpetually blinded in the valley of the shadow of death. On the other hand, the Apostles and the faithful, driven by the Spirit of God, spread before the eyes of all the mysteries of faith with the "husk" removed, and being placed in the open, they are satisfied to the very marrow. 

These things are clearly established from the passage in *Hosea 11:1*, which is cited by *Matthew 2:15* and applied to Christ: *Out of Egypt I called my son.* Although the Prophet, in respect to the **type**, understands this literally as the people of Israel being called out of Egypt. To this end, there are the passages from *Psalm 22*, *Psalm 18*, and *Isaiah 8:18* which are applied to Christ by the Apostle in the *Epistle to the Hebrews 2:12 and 13*: *I will announce your name to my brothers.* And: *I will put my trust in Him.* And: *Behold, I and the children whom [the Lord has given] me.*
