<meta>This page continues the author's discussion on the "composite sense" of Scripture. Following the illustration of Jonathan and David, the author now establishes a systematic framework for how truth exists in the Bible—sometimes explicitly stated, sometimes implied, and sometimes present as a "type" pointing toward a future "antitype" like Christ.</meta>

->## THE REVEALER OF SECRETS. ##<-

God gave. Thus, in *Psalm 22*, many things are said concerning David which properly apply to Christ. And John rightly observes that the saying about not breaking the bones of the Passover lamb was fulfilled in Christ, the true Lamb, and he points out the distinction between him and the thieves in that same place.

Therefore, it is not out of season or inappropriate to observe in this place that some things in Scripture are not said, some are said not to be, some both are and are said to be, and some neither are nor are said to be. Thus, the doctrine of the Trinity *exists*, but it is not *stated* word-for-word <note>original: "αὐτολεξεὶ" (autolexei)</note> in Scripture; so also the procession of the Holy Spirit, the "consubstantiality" <term>homoousia—the theological concept that the Son is of the same essence as the Father</term> of the Son, and the baptism of infants. All these things are in Scripture according to the substance <note>original: "κατ' πρᾶγμα" (kata pragma)</note>, not according to the literal wording <note>original: "κατ' τὸ ῥῆμα" (kata to rhema)</note>; not word-for-word, but according to their equivalent meaning <note>original: "κατ' ἰσοδυναμίαν" (kata isodynamian)</note>. 

Conversely, some things are said which are not literally true, such as when human limbs and emotions of the heart are attributed to God; for those things are spoken in a human-like way <note>original: "ἀνθρωποπαθῶς" (anthropopathōs)</note>, but must be understood in a way worthy of God <note>original: "θεοπρεπῶς" (theoprepōs)</note>, unless we wish to rave with the delusions of the Anthropomorphites <note>A group of early Christians who were accused of believing that God possessed a physical human body</note>. Other things both exist and are stated, such as the Word made flesh, Christ crucified, and so on. Still others neither exist nor are stated, such as the Popish purgatory, the transubstantiation of the Mass, and the like. 

When, however, we deal with the "composite sense" and with **types** and **antitypes** <note>A 'type' is a person or event in the Old Testament that foreshadows a 'antitype'—usually Christ or a New Testament reality</note>, many things are not explicitly said which nevertheless exist. Indeed, they are partly said and partly not said depending on the perspective: they are said either in the type, or in the antitype, or in both. Or, quite clearly, they are not said in respect to the antitype but rather the type, even though they are more truly present and intended in respect to the antitype. Thus, what the painter Timanthes used to say of his paintings may be more rightly found in Scripture: namely, that in it *few things are said, but many—indeed, innumerable things—are understood*. For things exist in Scripture in three ways: either by the literal word and "word-for-word" <note>original: "κατ' τὸ ῥητὸν & αὐτολεξεὶ"</note>, or by equivalent meaning <note>original: "κατ' ἰσοδυναμίαν"</note>, or by logical consequence <note>original: "κατ' συνακολόυθησιν"</note>. Indeed, they exist much more so by synonymy <note>original: "κατ' συνωνυμίαν"</note>, such that perhaps that famous Bishop Spyridon was a bit too fussy. According to the historian Nicephorus, Spyridon rose up offended in the middle of an assembly because a more eloquent Bishop had not cited Scripture word-for-word while preaching; for where *Mark 2:4* says "they let down the bed" <note>original: "χαλᾶσι τὸν κράββατον" (chalasi ton krabbaton)</note>, the preacher had instead used the synonyms "low-bed" or "pallet" <note>original: "σκιμπόδας & σκιμπόδια" (skimpodas & skimpodia)</note>.

Since, therefore, this particular oracle <note>Referring to the biblical prophecy currently under discussion in the book</note> must be explained by us in this manner, and since it includes a composite sense within itself, what we have said thus far in advance should rightly be applied to it. First, therefore, we must consider how these things applied literally to the brute serpent—

...come together, and likewise the woman and her seed are to be investigated indiscriminately; then, how it must be searched out mystically regarding the ancient serpent, that is the Devil, and regarding the seed of the woman by excellence <term>antonomasia—the use of a title or epithet (like "the Seed") as a proper name</term>, that is Christ. But all these things are for the sake of analysis <note>original: "ἀναλυτικῶς" (analytikōs)</note> and clarity. Therefore, there is a fourfold commentary:

I. What is the *seed of the serpent and the woman* <note>original Hebrew: "זרע הנחש והאשה" (zera‘ ha-nachash ve-ha-ishah)</note>.
II. Concerning the hatred or enmity between both, when God says *I will put enmity* <note>original Hebrew: "ואיבה אשית" (ve-eyvah ashit)</note>, etc.
III. Concerning the struggle between them.
IV. Concerning the *victory of the seed of the woman.* Because it is said *He shall bruise your head* <note>original Hebrew: "הוא ישופך ראש" (hu yeshuphcha rosh)</note>.

Regarding the first point, Moses literally deals with the animal serpent and the seed of the serpent, that is, other serpents born from it or to be born in the future. For there was indeed a real serpent which Satan used as a suitable instrument to seduce the first-created woman, Eve. This is clear, first, because Moses frequently calls it a serpent. And Eve said, *The serpent deceived me;* surely she could not even have guessed it was a demon. 

Secondly, because God does not interrogate the serpent as he did the man and the woman. For God said to the woman in verse 13, *Why have you done this?* but in verse 14, he said only to the serpent, *Because you have done this, you are cursed, etc.* Thus he does not question the serpent, but punishes it with a penalty. This is because in a beast there was no sense of sin, nor did any hope of pardon shine upon the Devil. 

Thirdly, because a penalty and curse are inflicted upon the brute serpent; for although it performed these things through the fraud of another, nevertheless, since the serpent was created for the sake of man, it is justly cursed as soon as it was miserably turned toward man's destruction. 

Fourthly, because the word of God is considered "mixed": for God addresses the serpent in such a way that it also pertains to the Devil. For although these things are properly said of the serpent—*Cursed shall you be above every animal, etc. upon your belly shall you go, and dust shall you eat all the days of your life*—nevertheless, the concluding clause also strikes the Devil in verse 15, and especially that part: *he shall wound you in the head, etc.* For in truth, Christ, the seed of the woman, crushed the head of Satan. 

Fifthly, from the outcome: for from the beginning until the end, there is enmity between the serpent and the woman and the seed of both. Indeed, by a certain secret antipathy and instinct of nature, man shrinks from serpents;

...and as often as the sight of serpents strikes horror into us, so often is the memory of our fall refreshed; but if for some people serpents are a delight, this is to be considered among the marvels <note>original: "prodigia"</note>.

The Ancient Doctors agree, and furthermore Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople</note> investigated in his 16th Homily on Genesis why the Devil chose the serpent on purpose. He responds that it was done because it was most fit for an ambush due to its natural and versatile cunning. But Saint Augustine <note>Augustine of Hippo (354–430), a foundational Christian theologian</note> teaches that Satan could not have used any other instrument than the mouth of the serpent. Since the Devil’s mind aimed to cunningly seduce the first-created parents <note>original: "protoplaſtos"</note>, he could more easily hope to obtain what he sought if he covered his snares rather than opening them. He would have covered them if he had assumed the form of a sheep or a dove, which are animals of a simple and innocent nature. But God willed that he should undertake the temptation through the serpent, so that just as He permitted the Devil to tempt, so He might warn man by the very form of the serpent—which man knew to be a cunning animal—to beware of the snares. 

Regarding Chrysostom, when he says the Devil sought an animal suitable for an ambush, this would only hold true if Eve could have been seduced by that same cunning which is naturally in a serpent. But since the cleverness not of a mute serpent, but of the Devil himself, was necessary to seduce man, the Devil could have carried out the business of seduction just as well through a dove as through a serpent—and indeed with a more hidden plan and greater fraud through a dove. Others add that the Tempter wished to attack Eve in secret, as the weaker part to be conquered; therefore, so that he might construct his snares secretly away from the true one and the Word <note>original Greek: "λόγῳ" (logō), referring here to divine reason or perhaps Adam as the representative of the Word</note>, he used the serpent, which, prone and crawling among the bushes of Paradise, would slither toward the woman and fraudulently deceive her without the man’s knowledge. But let all these things be considered as probable explanations.

Therefore, not without merit is that most ancient Ophite heresy hissed away <note>The author uses the Latin "exsibilatur," literally to hiss off the stage, playing on the snake theme</note>, named from the serpent <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄφεως" (apo tou opheōs)</note> according to Irenaeus <note>Irenaeus (c. 130–202), a Greek bishop and theologian known for his work "Against Heresies"</note> in Book 1, Chapter 34. This sect dreamed and blasphemed that this serpent was the "Wisdom of God," which opened the eyes of the first-created parents so they might distinguish between good and evil; and they did this out of hatred for the Creator...

Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–253 AD), a scholar known for his symbolic or "allegorical" interpretations of the Bible</note> also, indulging in allegories in his usual fashion whenever something seemed absurd to him, argued that the serpent should be understood as *pleasure* <note>original: "delectationem"</note>. He suggested that pleasure twists itself like a serpent from the lower parts of the body to the upper; it titillates and seduces the senses—represented by Eve—and then the senses bend the mind—represented by Adam—toward consent and sin. Ambrose, Bishop of Milan <note>Ambrose (c. 339–397 AD), a patron saint of Milan and teacher of Augustine</note>, published this same opinion in his book *On Paradise*, chapter 2, though he suppressed Origen's name. Nor were there lacking those (according to Procopius <note>Procopius of Gaza (c. 465–528 AD), a Christian commentator on the Octateuch</note>) who argued that the Devil took on a "phantasmal" or spectral body in the likeness of a serpent. Finally, Julian <note>Julian the Apostate (331–363 AD), the last pagan Roman Emperor, who attempted to revive Roman polytheism</note>, as Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria (c. 376–444 AD), who wrote a massive rebuttal to Julian’s anti-Christian works</note> reports in his third book *Against Julian*, contended that Moses’ account of the serpent was a mere fable—specifically on the grounds that a serpent is described as speaking with a human voice. Yet, Julian contradicts himself and forgets his own principles; for as Cyril argued, the Pagans themselves admitted that horses and rivers had occasionally spoken. Nevertheless, all these heretics are proven wrong by the actual context of Moses’ writing.

Furthermore, we cannot accept the interpretation of Blessed Augustine, who asserted that before the Fall, the serpent walked and stood with an upright posture. He inferred this from the curse God inflicted upon it. But (if I may say so with all due respect to him) this is an over-extension; for the curse was the burdensome crawling upon its belly—much like the pain of childbirth is to a woman, or the eating of dust—and being cursed above all the beasts of the field.

From what has been said, it is clear what the "seed of the serpent" refers to. Indeed, we are taught all too well by daily experience what great horror this serpent-born <note>original: "serpentigena"</note> offspring strikes into mankind.

But we must look further at what Moses indicates mystically through the serpent and its seed. The serpent is the Devil, so called for good reason because, as is clear from Genesis 3:4, he used that creature as his instrument to deceive Mother Eve. Hence, in 2 Corinthians 11:3, the Apostle says that the serpent seduced Eve by his cunning; likewise in Revelation 12:9, he is called the *Ancient Serpent* and the *Dragon*. And...

*...the great Dragon was cast out, that ancient serpent who is called the Devil and Satan, who deceives the whole world. And truly that nomenclature fits the Devil for various reasons. I. Because long ago, when he was about to tempt Eve, he assumed the body of a serpent and moved its limbs and organs. II. Because just like crawling reptiles, he creeps secretly by laying snares; but also like birds, or "presteres" <note>A type of venomous snake mentioned in classical literature whose bite caused burning and swelling</note> and fiery serpents, he flies, rushing down unexpectedly from above. > *The demon prowls and seeks whom he may devour, like a lion;*
> *He drives wandering souls by force, as if by a wind.*
> *Satan prepares hidden frauds, like a little fox;*
> *Those he could not destroy by force, he ruins by deceit.*

->DIABOLOS: Force, Deceit.<-

As for the explanation that the commentators of the Decrees <note>Legal scholars of Canon Law</note> devise—that the word comes from *Duo* [two] and *Bolus* [a morsel or swallow], meaning that the Devil wants to eat "two morsels" of a man, namely the body and the soul—it is laughed at as ridiculous. Hence, as it says in *Proverbs 30:19: The way of a serpent on a rock is hidden.* In the same way, the ways of the Devil are most hidden, and it is very difficult to detect his cunning or penetrate his "depths"; which is why Scripture emphasizes the "depths of Satan."

III. Just as the serpent is a *most venomous animal*, whose bite is most deadly because the poison is in its head and tongue and is suddenly shot out, as is clear from *Numbers 21:6* regarding the Israelites who died from the bites of serpents. Hence the poet Lucan <note>Marcus Annaeus Lucanus (39–65 AD), author of the epic poem *Pharsalia*</note> wrote of serpents:

> *They carry poison in their bite, and threaten fate in their teeth.*

In this way, Satan shoots out an immense amount of poison, intoxicating and lethally wounding men with the *most deadly venom of sin*.

This is illustrated by a most potent poison, which was reportedly found in a bronze chest in a Babylonian temple. Once opened, it infected the entire world and laid it waste as a plague spread far and wide. <note>This refers to a legend regarding the "Antonine Plague" (c. 165 AD), which soldiers supposedly unleashed by opening a golden or bronze casket in the temple of Apollo in Seleucia, near Babylon.</note>

IV. Serpents are said to be shrewd, as in Matthew 10:16: the faithful, and especially the ministers of the Church, are commanded to be "wise as serpents and simple as doves." <note>original: "prudentes sicut serpentes, & simplices tanquam columbæ"</note> This shrewdness of the serpent is either *useful* to itself or *harmful* to others. It is **useful** in managing and protecting its own health: for instance, every year during the spring, it sheds its old skin by squeezing through a narrow hole to put on a new one. It also restores its vision, which becomes dimmed from the long darkness of the place where it hides in winter, and makes it sharper by applying its eyes to fennel. <note>original: "marathrum seu fœniculum"</note> Furthermore, because it knows it is hated, it avoids humans; it flees the cry of peacocks and the breath of stags, who (according to Solinus <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a 3rd-century Roman chronicler of wonders</note> in chapter 22) draw serpents out from their hidden caves with the breath of their nostrils. When its head is targeted, the serpent offers its whole body to the blows to preserve its life by shielding its head; for if its head is crushed, it cannot be healed, whereas it easily heals other wounded parts of its body. It also stores all the body’s poison in its neck so that, in an emergency, it has a defense ready at hand. Finally, when entering water, it hides its poison in a safe place on land, so that it may reclaim it upon leaving the water.

Furthermore, the cunning of the serpent is **harmful** in its ambushing and injuring of others. When it intends to harm a passing human, it does not lie in wait near its own hole or in a deserted place, but *beside the road or path*. Genesis 49:17. <note>"Dan shall be a serpent by the way, an adder in the path..."</note> From these hiding places, it stealthily attacks the unwary and, with a hidden bite, brings down both the horse and its rider, precisely because no one would suspect it to be in such a well-traveled place. Its cunning also appears in the way it stops its ear against incantations, lest it be prevented from biting. Psalm 58:4-5:
> Their venom is like the poison of a deaf asp that stops its ear. <note>original: "Venenum sicut aspidis surdæ quæ obturat aurem suam."</note>

Whether this was said by the Prophet according to a common folk belief, or because such incantations truly occur—not through any real art, but through the mere illusions of the Devil, as was once done by the Marsi <note>An ancient Italian people famous in antiquity for their supposed power over snakes</note> in Italy. Countless other examples are mentioned by Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of "Natural History"</note> in his books on natural questions in six hundred places, which can be consulted if one wishes. # THE REVEALER OF SECRETS

## Augustine’s *On Christian Doctrine*, Book 2, Chapter 16, which recounts four shrewdnesses of the serpent. <note>Saint Augustine (354–430 AD) was a foundational Christian theologian; in this cited work, he discusses how the natural traits of animals mentioned in the Bible can be interpreted allegorically.</note>

But who will deny the practiced, ancient cunning of the serpent Satan, who in infinite ways deceives wretched mortals by twisting himself about like a snake? At one moment, he transforms himself into an **Angel of light**, though he is in fact an **Angel of darkness**; at another, like a hyena, he mimics the voices of shepherds so that he might tear them apart. <note>According to medieval bestiaries, the hyena was believed to imitate human speech to lure people out of their homes at night.</note> This base craftiness—to the misfortune of humanity—was displayed in Paradise. Indeed, his cleverness was exerted everywhere: in the way he insinuated himself into that place; in his choice of the forbidden tree, as he well knew; in his assault and attack upon the woman; in the sweetness of his voice so as not to terrify her; in the question he posed to stir up doubt and suspicion; in his reply so that mistrust might arise; in his most firm protestation, *“You shall surely not die”*; in his suggestion of envy on God’s part and of resentment and injury on man's part; and finally, in his promise of profit and happiness if she ate from that forbidden fruit. That shrewdness is even proven by an anagram of the Devil. <note>Early modern scholars often used "anagrams"—rearranging letters—to find hidden spiritual meanings in names.</note>

**V.** Serpents are *horrible and formidable*, as is clear from Exodus 4:3. When Moses' staff was turned into a serpent, he immediately trembled with horror and took to flight. By that transformation—both of the rod into a serpent and then the serpent back into a rod—two things were represented:

I. From the serpent and the horror it inspired, it was shown that Moses would be a source of terror and dread to all of Egypt and to Pharaoh, who would be struck down by repeated plagues and wonders. This was so even though Moses was otherwise destitute of outward glory and protection, while Pharaoh, by contrast, was surrounded by so many forces and defenses, and crowned with royal glory and a diadem.

II. The staff signified Moses’ safeguard: the protection and divine aid against all the schemes of Pharaoh and the Egyptians, just as shepherds use a staff to lead their flock and defend it against wild beasts. But truly, who is more dreadful and formidable than that ancient serpent? This is clear from experience itself, as witnessed by the many horrors and terrors he once struck into the pagan idolaters, and now strikes into witches, sorcerers, and his own slaves, and from the damage and venom of the serpent which he perpetually spits out. But he is put to flight by the staff of divine providence, etc.

VI. *The serpent is cursed above every beast. Genesis 3:14.* But is the Devil not cursed above all creatures? For if the instrument of sin and temptation was so cursed by the most just decree of God, what is to be decided regarding the tempter himself and the very source of sin? Shall he not himself be devoted and subject to every kind of curse? This can be illustrated from the Hebrew Kabbalah <term>Kabbalah: An ancient Jewish tradition of mystical interpretation of the Bible.</term> or *Notaricon* <term>Notaricon: A shorthand method of treating the letters of a word as an acronym for a phrase.</term> regarding the word **serpent** <note>original Hebrew: נחש (*nachash*)</note>, which is commonly written with Hebrew letters. This is not to be explained (as some have suggested) as merely *those things in the serpent*, but through *rashei tevot* <note>original: ראשי תיבות, literally "heads of words," the Hebrew term for acronyms.</note>. For this reason, Rabbi Levi Gersom <note>Levi ben Gershom (1288–1344), also known as Gersonides, was a major medieval Jewish philosopher and commentator.</note>, who is called the **Light of the Exile** <note>original Hebrew: מאור הגולה (*Maor HaGolah*), a title of great respect for a legal or spiritual authority.</note>, established the penalty of anathema <term>anathema: a formal curse or ban that excommunicates someone from a community.</term> for those who open letters addressed to others. Therefore, to them, "serpent" [נ-ח-ש] mystically and Kabbalistically signifies three types of anathema under which the aforementioned Rabbi Gersom forbade the opening of letters: *Niddui*, *Cherem*, and *Schammata* <note>The three Hebrew terms for excommunication: *Niddui* (temporary exclusion), *Cherem* (a more severe ban), and *Shammata* (the most extreme form of exclusion). The letters of the word "serpent" (N-Ch-Sh) serve as the initials for these three curses.</note>. 

Thus, that word which literally means *serpent* mystically designates for the Hebrews three horrible types of curse. These are surely hurled at the ancient serpent, as a vessel of the curse devoted to the punishments of God, the supreme judge. For this reason, he is continually terrified by that formidable word designating a curse, *Maranatha*; for he shudders when **the Lord comes** <note>original Aramaic: מרן אתא (*Maran atha*), which means "Our Lord has come" or "Come, Lord."</note>—specifically, to judge. This is why in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 8, the demon said to Christ: *“Have you come here to torment us before the time?”* <note>original Greek: ἦλθες ὧδε πρὸ καιροῦ βασανίσαι ἡμᾶς;</note> And therefore, those who mock that final day and the coming of the Lord can be said to be worse than the demons themselves. From this it follows that the Ancients used to conclude their exorcisms with these words: *“by him who is to come to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.”*

But observe in passing that just as the Devil was formerly designated by the serpent, so in the Book of Revelation <note>original: *Apocal.*</note> he is often named the **Dragon**, as in chapter 12:7, 13, 17; and chapter 13:2, 3; and 16:13; and 20:2. And he is soon called the **Red Dragon**, as in chapter 12:3, and then the **Great Dragon**, as in chapter 12:9. This is not without mystery; for just as a dragon is a very poisonous animal whose venom is especially lethal (Deut. 32:33), dragons are also most fierce and usually large, swallowing animals whole (Jeremiah 51:34).

<margin>Revelation 12:3</margin>In the same way, that infernal Dragon is the most poisonous, the most savage, and the worst of all. Since, therefore, *in the final times* <note>original Greek: ἐν τοῖς ἐσχάτοις χρόνοις (*en tois eschatois chronois*)</note> the rage and fury of the Devil has increased, with which he rages against humans; so, while of old in the very beginnings of the universe he was called a "serpent," at length in the most recent times—and especially in the Book of Revelation, where many things concerning the end of the world are recounted—he was nicknamed "Dragon." This was because, as his poison and malice increased, he grew from a serpent into a Dragon, and spat out whatever fury and extreme madness and virulence he possessed upon wretched mortals.

Since, therefore, the Devil is understood mystically through the serpent, so the "seed of the serpent" refers to the reprobate <term>reprobate: those rejected by God or considered beyond salvation due to their wickedness</term>, who are often called the "children of the Devil" in Scripture. <margin>I. Evil Angels</margin>they are rightly called the offspring of the Devil, insofar as they adhered to the Devil when he rebelled against God. Here, the Devil is called the *source of evil* <note>original Greek: ἀρχεκακός (*archekakos*)</note>, and elsewhere *Beelzebub* is named the prince of the angels.

The wicked perform the works of the Devil because they enjoy the characteristics of that mystical serpent. Foremost among these is a cunning and shifty prudence, as Scripture testifies: *The children of this world are more prudent in their generation.* And in Acts 13:10, because those enslaved to Satan are said to be full of *every kind of villainy* <note>original Greek: πάσης ῥᾳδιουργίας (*pasēs radiourgias*)</note>, as Paul testifies concerning Elymas the sorcerer when he opposed the conversion of the proconsul Sergius Paulus: *O man full of all deceit and all villainy, you son of the devil.* Yet this is understood primarily regarding those sorcerers <note>The Latin *maleficiis* here refers to practitioners of harmful magic or "black" witchcraft.</note> who are entirely in the power of the Devil; therefore, there is no crime so great that they do not immediately dare to commit it.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 97 regarding the identity of the Devil and his relationship to the "seed of the serpent." ### ANTHONY CREGUT ###

...is called, the Devil—who is that ancient serpent and a sinner in the absolute sense—will be named the unclean and impure spirit, and pre-eminently <note>original Greek: ἐξοχητικῶς (*exochetikos*)</note> **the evil one**, as in Matthew 6:13: *deliver us from the evil one* <note>original Greek: ῥῦσαι ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ (*rhysai hēmas apo tou ponērou*)</note>. This is because he is the primary root of sin, the author of the original stain, and the first who revolted from the Creator. For just as Scripture, when speaking of Adam's sin—which is "original sin" simply and as the source—calls it pre-eminently **sin** in the singular (John 1:29), but calls actual sins **sins** in the plural (Romans 5:12), because they are the rotten and bitter fruits budding from that root; so much more should the Devil’s defection and rebellion be designated by the name of **sin**. This is because it is sin in the absolute sense and in no way a "punishment for sin" (as inherited original sin is); rather, it was the most free sin of all, because it was committed spontaneously and without the enticement or persuasion of another. In contrast, the sin of Adam first drew its origin from the temptation and seduction of the Devil. Therefore, in the Devil's sin, one sees pure and simple malice; but the sin of man was not committed without a certain ignorance, which is why Eve, according to the testimony of the Apostle <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul in 2 Corinthians 11:3 or 1 Timothy 2:14</note>, is said to have been **deceived**.

For this reason, so that Scripture might indicate that Satan and man are the primary fountains of evil, when Moses penned the history of the first fall, he spoke only of the Devil, the serpent, and the <term>protoplasts: the "first-formed" individuals, referring to Adam and Eve</term>, but maintained a profound silence regarding God and God's providence. Why was this? Was it because providence was then idle and God was sleeping? Not at all; rather, Moses intended by this deep silence to signify that God is **not the author of sin**, even though none of these things were done except by God decreeing, permitting, ordering, directing, and determining them. Instead, he wished to indicate that the Devil is the primary origin of sin, the first author of evil, and the principle from which all evil flows. Therefore, the reprobate are the "seed" and progeny of that ancient serpent, and their entire lineage is serpentine and vipers’ work, according to the proverb: *from a bad crow comes a bad egg* <note>original Greek: κακοῦ κόρακος, κακὸν ὠὸν (*kakou korakos, kakon ōon*)</note>. Hence, in Matthew 3:7, John the Baptist said to the Pharisees: *Brood of vipers* <note>original Greek: Γεννήματα ἐχιδνῶν (*Gennēmata echidnōn*)</note>.

11. Because Eve had seen not the Devil but the serpent, and had seen it speaking, he <note>Moses, the author of Genesis</note> accommodates himself to Eve’s perception. Nor did Eve suspect that any trickery lay beneath when she heard the voice of the serpent, but she marveled at it as a truly extraordinary thing. And perhaps she burned with a greater desire to listen, and was not struck with horror, because at that time all animals were familiar to man; indeed, some have thought that Eve believed it had been granted to other living creatures as well to speak with a human voice. Accordingly, the wicked are rightly called "serpents" and the "seed of the serpent." From this arose the Greek proverb: *You cherish a serpent, and a serpent [bites] you* <note>original Greek: ὄφιν θάλπεις καὶ σὲ ὄφις (*ophin thalpeis kai se ophis*)</note>. Likewise, Tiberius Caesar, looking at the savage nature of his successor Gaius <note>Caligula</note>, predicted that *he was educating a nurse (of that kind of serpent) for the Roman people* (Suetonius). And Isaiah 14:29 says: *from the root of the serpent shall come forth a basilisk, even a flying fiery serpent.* Uzziah, in afflicting the Philistines, is compared to a serpent; but his successor Hezekiah is compared to a basilisk or a flying fiery serpent.

Thus far it has been demonstrated, unless I am mistaken, what the serpent and the seed of the serpent are; but it is now better to investigate further what is the **seed of the woman.** The "seed of the woman" is understood in two ways: either broadly and generally, or strictly, or most strictly and by way of excellence <note>original Latin: *antonomasticē*</note>. *Broadly*, all humans in general are understood by the "seed of the woman." For Eve was the mother of all humans living a physical life; for she was called **woman** <note>original Hebrew: אשה (*Ishah*)</note> from **man** <note>original Hebrew: איש (*Ish*)</note> because from the union of the man and the "woman-man"—that is, from that primeval coupling of both the first-formed <note>original Latin: *protoplasti*</note>—the generation of all <term>hysteroplasts</term> <note>original Latin: *hysteroplastorum*; a term for all human beings formed after the original creation of Adam and Eve</note> was brought about. *Strictly*, all the faithful are understood by the "seed of the woman" in a mystical sense; since they are the blessed and sanctified seed of the woman, they rightly declare eternal war against the ancient serpent—that is, the Devil—and trample and crush him under their feet. As it says in Romans 16:20, though by the power of Christ: *The Lord shall shortly crush Satan under your feet.* Hence the faithful are not called the *seed of the slave girl, or the handmaid*; but the *seed of the free woman*; they are not the sons of Hagar, but of Sarah: the seed of Abraham according to the spirit (Genesis 12:3; 22:18). -># ANTOINE CREGUT #<-

...of David, the *seed of Isaac*, *that seed to whom the promise was made* (Galatians 3:19).

Finally, in the strictest and most characteristic sense <term>antonomastically|The use of an epithet or title in place of a proper name, or a proper name to designate a type</term>, the "seed of the woman" is Christ, because in a singular and defining way, he truly is the woman’s seed. For just as he is called in Scripture, by way of excellence, the *Son of Man*, it is not because other men are not also sons of men—since all share the same human nature—but because Christ is the Son of Man in a unique way. This is either because he is the Son of Man in such a way that he is also the Son of God; or because that Son of Man does not exist in the common way as a mere person, but because he exists in a most singular way within the Word <note>The Logos or Second Person of the Trinity</note>. Or it is because that Son of Man was not born from the seed of a man, but of a woman. Or because he was not made "from sowing" <note>original Greek: ἐκ σπορᾶς (*ek sporas*)</note> but "according to the flesh" <note>original Greek: κατὰ σάρκα (*kata sarka*)</note>. Romans 1:3: *who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh* <note>original Greek: γενομένος ἐκ σπέρματος Δαβὶδ κατὰ σάρκα (*genomenos ek spermatos Dabid kata sarka*)</note>. Hence, in the first place of Scripture where the Messiah is designated by such a name—namely Daniel 7 <note>The text says Daniel 2, likely a citation error for Daniel 7:13</note>—he is not simply called the Son of Man, but *like a son of man* <note>original Aramaic: כברנש (*ke-bar enash*)</note>; because he was similar to a son of man and yet was the Son of Man in a singular way, being extraordinarily conceived and the "seed of the woman" in the highest sense. Thus, in Scripture, he is not called the Son of Man "by way of disparagement" <note>original Greek: κατ' ἐμφαύλισμον (*kat' emphaulismon*)</note> but "by way of preeminence" <note>original Greek: ἐξοχῆς (*exoches*)</note>, as is clear from the aforementioned passage in Daniel and frequently in the Gospels.

So, when Christ is called the "seed of the woman," it is understood in a most singular and eminent sense. **I.** Because he is the seed of the woman alone, and not of a man; hence, in his temporal birth, he has no father but only a mother, just as conversely in his eternal generation he has a father but no mother. Thus, in respect to the former, he is the seed of the woman; but in respect to the latter, he is the seed of the Eternal Father, "of the same substance" <note>original Greek: ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*)</note>. Yet in respect to both joined together, he is another Melchizedek, "without father, without mother" <note>original Greek: ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ (*apator, amētor*), referring to Hebrews 7:3</note>. **II.** Because he is the seed of *the virgin* <note>original Hebrew: העלמה (*ha-almah*) from Isaiah 7:14</note>. This is said emphatically with the definite article <note>the Hebrew prefix *ha-*</note>, meaning "this specific kind of woman," namely a virgin—indeed, a "hidden virgin" <note>original Greek: κατακλείστου (*katakleistou*)</note>, staying concealed at home outside the commerce of men according to the custom of the Hebrews. This is in contrast to a woman of ill repute, who is called by the Chaldeans <note>The Aramaic of the Targums</note> "one who goes outside" <note>original Aramaic: נפקת ברא (*nafqat barra*)</note>, which was a descriptive way of referring to harlots. Hence, in the Targum on Genesis 34:31, the Hebrew word for "harlot" <note>original Hebrew: זונה (*zonah*)</note> is rendered by the Paraphrast as "one who goes outside" <note>original Aramaic: נפקת ברא (*nafqat barra*)</note>. For this reason, Jerome, in his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, interprets *Almah* as a "Virgin kept with extreme diligence"...

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological examination of the term "seed of the woman," specifically focusing on the Hebrew word for "virgin" (almah) used in messianic prophecies. The author is moving from the identity of Christ to the linguistic proofs of his miraculous birth from a virgin.</meta>

-># THE REVEALER OF SECRETS #<-

...carefully guarded; and adds, *she who is a hidden Virgin*, has an extension <note>original Greek: ἔκτασιν (*ektasin*)</note> of virginity, so that she is both a virgin and hidden; and she who is hidden is consequently also a virgin. However, for one who is a virgin, it does not immediately follow that she is hidden. For *almah* <note>original Hebrew: עַלְמָה</note> comes from the Hebrew root *alam* <note>original Hebrew: עָלַם</note>, which is unused in the simple active voice <term>Kal|The most basic form of a Hebrew verb</term>, but appears in the passive voice <term>Niphal|The reflexive or passive form of a Hebrew verb</term> as *ne’elam* <note>original Hebrew: נֶעְלַם, meaning "hidden"</note>. Among the Chaldeans <note>Speakers of Aramaic, a language closely related to Hebrew</term>, however, the root is used even in the simple form, for whom *alam* not only signifies to be strengthened or *to be strong*, but also in the reflexive form <term>Ithpael|The reflexive voice in Aramaic</term> *to be hidden*. 

Here the Jesuit Alfonso Salmero must surely be an object of mockery for the reader when, in his *31st Treatise*, he says that word is partly Hebrew and partly Latin—a claim he swallowed without judgment from Porchetus <note>Salvagus Porchetus, a 14th-century monk who wrote against Jewish interpretations</note> in *Victory against the Hebrews, part 2, chapter 14*. For *almah* <note>original Hebrew: עַלְמָה</note> and the Latin word *alma* <note>meaning "nurturing" or "kind"</note> agree only in their sound. Therefore, the Hebrew *almah* corresponds to the "secluded" <note>original Greek: ταῖς κατακλείσοις (*tais katakleisois*)</note> among the Gentiles; or the "chambered" <note>original Greek: θαλαμευμέναις (*thalamemenais*)</note>, as if they were girls raised in private bedchambers. 

This observation, however, does not excuse the ritual and superstition of Nuns, because that name was common to all honorable girls who did not leave their parents' homes for reasons of modesty and virginal shame. Therefore, those girls had virgin-quarters <note>original Greek: παρθενῶνας (*parthenonas*)</note> in which they were raised apart from the sight of men, nor did they go out in public except for divine worship or to perform other necessary duties; for otherwise an *almah* was "hidden, recluded, or concealed" <note>original Hebrew: נַעְלָמָה (*ne’elamah*); original Greek: ἀπόκρυφος (*apokryphos*)</note>. These things are most skillfully observed by Casaubon <note>Isaac Casaubon, a famous 17th-century Protestant scholar</note> in *Exercise 1 on the Apparatus of the Annals, number 53*, and Baronius—that great annalist <note>Cesare Baronius, a Catholic Cardinal and historian</note>—is rightly lashed for twisting the "secluded girls" mentioned in 2 Maccabees 3:19 to justify his nuns. 

And here one must observe the excellent contrast <note>antithesis</note> between the *almah*, the hidden and unknown Virgin, and the woman "known" by a man, whose "nakedness" <note>original Hebrew: עֶרְוָה (*ervah*); original Greek: αἰσχημοσύνη (*aischēmosynē*)</note> has been uncovered. And not only was that custom and education of virgins in use among the Hebrews, but also among the Greeks. Hence it happened that for Hesychius <note>An ancient Greek lexicographer</note>, the "unveiling" <note>original Greek: ἀνακαλυπτήριον (*anakalypteriōn*)</note> was the day "when they first lead out the bride." Thus, "unveiling gifts" <note>original Greek: ἀνακαλυπτήρια (*anakalypteria*)</note> were the gifts offered to the bride when she first used to come out into the sight of men, just as "seeing gifts" <note>original Greek: ὀπτήρια (*optēria*)</note> were what the groom offered the bride when he first saw her. These were also called "conversation gifts" <note>original Greek: θεωρητήρια (*theōrētēria*)</note> from the first time they spoke to one another. 

And indeed, that word *almah* occurs seven times in Scripture: namely, Genesis 24:43; Exodus 2:8 (concerning the sister of Moses, just as in the first instance it was concerning Rebecca, or another virgin); and Psalm 68:26, *young women playing timbrels* <note>original Hebrew: עֲלָמוֹת תּוֹפֵפוֹת (*alamot topepot*); original Greek (LXX): ἐν μέσῳ νεανίδων τυμπανιστριῶν (*en mesō neanidōn tympanistriōn*)</note>.

For in this prophecy, we are dealing with that seed of the woman who shall crush the head of the ancient serpent. But to whom besides Christ can such great strength and such great victory belong? Indeed, who else possesses such greatness of soul that they would dare to enter the battle and not shrink from so horrific a fight! Truly, only Christ could "cast out the prince of this world"; he alone could destroy death and him who held the power of death.

But just as the bronze serpent was merely *Nehuschtan* <note>a Hebrew term meaning "a piece of brass"; used by King Hezekiah to describe the serpent when it became an object of idolatry in 2 Kings 18:4</note> to the idolaters, so Christ will be destruction for the impious and unbelieving, as the defiant Jews said of His blood: *let his blood be upon us and our children* <note>Matthew 27:25</note>.

This same point can be illustrated by an observation from Epiphanius, if indeed that story he tells is true. That Bishop of Salamis <note>Saint Epiphanius, a 4th-century Church Father</note>, in his work on *Heresies*, book 46, relates—as do Origen, Athanasius, Basil, Chrysostom, Anastasius of Sinai, and others—that Adam, the first-created, was buried not without mystery in the very same spot where Christ, the second Adam, hung on the cross. This was so that the droplets of blood, which dripped from the body of the suffering and dying Christ, might water the ground where the first Adam lay buried. Thus, that place was called *Golgotha*, and took the name *Calvary* <note>from the Latin *Calvaria*, meaning "Skull"</note> from the skull of the first man. This (as the ancient Doctors of the Church used to say) seems to have happened by no small mystery. For why would divine providence have arranged for the corpse of the first man to be covered by that specific earth, which was to be sprinkled with the blood of the Redeemer, if not so we might understand that even the first man himself was expiated from his sin by the blood of Christ? Hence the Apostle said: *Wake up, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you* <note>Ephesians 5:14</note>. Besides the authors mentioned above, Germanus, Euthymius, and Theophylact confirm the same; and among the Latins, the most ancient Tertullian, in a poem written in his second book *Against Marcion*:

> *Golgotha is the place of the head, once called Calvary*
> *In the earlier native tongue, for so he named it, etc.* <note>original: *Golgotha locus est capitis caluaria quondam / Lingua paterna prior, sic illum nomine dixit*</note>

The same was later written by Cyprian and Ambrose, as Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine, a prominent Jesuit cardinal and scholar of the Counter-Reformation</note> reports—

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS #

...it was by God’s design that He was crucified, namely to awaken Adam and his descendants from death and the grave, and so that His blood, washing the tomb of the first parent <note>The "first parent" refers to Adam; tradition held that Christ's blood dripped through the ground of Calvary onto Adam's skull to redeem him.</note>, might be a glorious monument to the washing of souls and the atonement for sins. Indeed, it should be noted in that story of Isaac that the Hebrew word <term>qarah (קרה)</term> <note>original: קרה; meaning "to happen" or "occur."</note> appears, which means "it happened," from which comes the word <term>miqreh (מקרה)</term> <note>original: מקרה; meaning "chance" or "accident."</note> for "event" or "chance." By this, Moses signifies that even things that appear entirely accidental or contingent are extended from divine providence. Therefore, God much more so governs and directs those things which concern the redemption of mankind.

Furthermore, someone has observed that in Genesis 22:13, these words are expressed: <note>original: והנה איל אחר נאחז בסבך בקרניו (*V'hinneh ayil achar ne'echaz bas'bak b'karnav*)</note> **"Behold, a ram was behind him, caught in a thicket by its horns."** This commentator claims that the word <term>sabak (סבך)</term> <note>original: סבך; meaning a thicket, entanglement, or perplexity.</note>, which in Hebrew signifies "entanglement," corresponds to the words of Christ fixed to the cross: *“Eli, Eli, lamma sabachthani,”* etc. <note>original: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46).</note> For just as the ram was entangled in the thorns, so the Lamb of God was greatly "perplexed" on the tree of the cross during His agony, crying out to His Father, *“Lamma sabachthani,”* as if looking back to Moses, who used the same word when speaking of the ram. But here it might be said, as was once said of <term>Tertullian</term> <note>Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus (c. 155 – c. 220 AD), a prolific early Christian author known for his complex and sometimes overly rigorous logic.</note>, **"because he was too sharp, he was therefore blunt."** 

For all these arguments regarding *sabak* and *sabachthani* are not very solid, even if they are clever. Indeed, the Syriac word in the New Testament does not truly correspond to the Hebrew word used by Moses. First, the word used by Moses is written with the letters *caph* and *samech*, while the Syriac word is written with *schin* and *qoph*. Furthermore, <term>sabak (סבך)</term> signifies "to be entangled," whereas the Syriac <term>shabaq (שׁבק)</term> in the <term>Peal</term> <note>The "Peal" is the basic verb form in Aramaic and Syriac, similar to the "Qal" in Hebrew.</note> form means "to permit" or "to leave behind." I am not unaware, however, that *sabak* is sometimes found spelled with a *schin*, because those letters are interchangeable, as seen in 2 Samuel 18:9, 1 Kings 7:17, and 7:41.

Up to this point, the first part of this Oracle <note>The "Oracle" refers to the prophecy of the "Seed of the Woman" in Genesis 3:15, which the author is analyzing.</note> has been examined, and thus we have sufficiently demonstrated that its meaning is composite. First, it is stated **literally** regarding the animal serpent, the woman, and her descendants. Second, it is understood **mystically**, yet still literally, regarding Christ, who is the "Seed of the Woman" by <term>antonomasia</term> <note>Antonomasia is a rhetorical device where a title or epithet (like "The Seed") is used as a proper name for a specific person (Christ).</note>; and conversely, the Devil is understood by the "Serpent." Third, by the "Seed of the Woman," all the faithful are also understood, who are grafted into Christ, the firstborn Seed.

Rather, they believe the Fall of the first man is enigmatically signified by this phenomenon: that the deceit of the serpent was the cause of death for humanity.

It is also extraordinary what David says in Psalm 58 <note>In the Latin Vulgate, this is Psalm 57.</note>: that the asp stops up its ears so as not to hear the voice of charmers, which is why the Psalmist calls it "deaf." For when an asp begins to endure the charmer, who calls it out of its cavern with songs, it presses one ear against the earth and stops up and covers the other with its tail so that it cannot hear the magical voices. Some hold that this happens through the operation of a Demon, since the snake does not understand by itself what is being uttered. However, it is probable that because the serpent once served as a servant to Satan, it can—as a punishment—be easily enchanted by the diabolical hissing and mutterings of magicians, so much so that it is then unable to cause harm. But what is worse is that there is not only enmity between the serpent and the woman, but that it is perpetual. Whence God, the supreme judge about to inflict punishment, says *I will put*. Truly, however, just as that perpetual enmity flourishes between serpents and the seed of the woman, so this is especially true in respect to that exacerbated enmity which exists between the Devil and the Church—which is the woman and the bride of Christ—and between the reprobate, who are the seed of the serpent, and the faithful, who are the blessed seed of the woman. ## XXII. 

Since, therefore, their crimes were so enormous, they were nevertheless only in the Babylonian captivity for 70 years. But the Jews of the second temple—who, as it is said in the book *Yoma* <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning the Day of Atonement</note> in the Talmud, were for seven days in the temple, and were studious in the Law, in the commandments of God, and in works of mercy—nevertheless have been punished with a captivity of 1,660 years, and there is still no end to it. Therefore, what cause shall we assign for such a long-lasting captivity, except for their enmity toward that blessed **seed of the woman**, which is Christ? This was predicted long ago by David in *Psalm 35:19*: *Let them not rejoice over me who are my enemies* **falsely** <note>original Hebrew: שקר (*sheker*)</note> *and without merit, nor let them wink with their eyes who are my* **haters without cause** <note>original Hebrew: שנאי חנם (*son’ai chinam*)</note>. And *Psalm 69:5*: *They who hate me without cause are multiplied more than the hairs of my head; my lying adversaries, who desire to destroy me, have grown powerful;* **my deceitful enemies** <note>original Hebrew: איבי שקר (*oy’vei sheker*)</note>. Here, "deceitfully" is frequently paired with "haters without cause," because enemies who have been harmed by no injury and provoked by no wrongdoing are eagerly driven to do harm. Therefore, it is out of pure, unadulterated hatred and a serpentine enmity—which is to be understood typically <note>as a symbolic "type" or foreshadowing</note> of David, but truly and antitypically <note>as the final fulfillment or reality</note> of Christ; just as Christ explains concerning himself in the Gospel: *that the word of the law might be fulfilled, because they hated me without cause.*

Nevertheless, in this enmity between the serpent and the woman, many things must be observed. 1. One must think differently about the **type** than about the **antitype**; or rather, differently about the literal sense than about the mystical. In the first [literal] sense, that enmity which exists between the serpent and the woman, just as between the seed of the serpent and the seed of the woman—that is, all human beings—can in some way be called an **antipathy**, because it breaks forth as if by an instinct of nature; when a person finds a serpent, they are immediately struck by a certain natural horror. For even if (as was said above) this was done by the judgment of God, as the word **"I will put"** <note>original Hebrew: אשית (*ashit*) from Genesis 3:15, "I will put enmity..."</note> indicates, it has nevertheless turned into nature and antipathy. This is shown in the thesis on original sin regarding original corruption, using the example of the Ethiopians: for **blackness** <note>original Latin: *atror*</note> has turned into nature <note>The author uses a 17th-century "scientific" theory that an environmental trait—black skin—eventually became a permanent biological nature, just as God's decree of fear toward snakes became an instinctual "antipathy."</note>. Whatever the ancients might say—such as *Epiphanius* (Heresy 37), *Tertullian* (in his book *On Prescription against Heretics*, ch. 47), *Augustine* (in his book *On Heresies*, addressed to Quodvultdeus), etc., concerning the **Ophites** <note>A Gnostic sect that supposedly worshipped serpents</note>, who both worshipped serpents and held them in high regard—these are extraordinary cases. They are like monstrous and irregular bodies that are **deviations from nature** <note>original Greek: παρεκβάσεις ἀπὸ τῆς φύσεως (*parekbaseis apo tēs physeōs*)</note>, which cannot violate the universal order of nature.

->REVEALER OF SECRETS.<-

But indeed, that enmity which exists between the Devil and Christ, between infidels and believers, is something beyond antipathy and greater, because the wicked, out of a certain obstinate malice of the will, hate the good; and that powerlessness <note>original Greek: *ἀδυναμία* (adynamia)</note> to love is twofold, namely **natural and moral**.

II. Note that a different judgment must be made regarding the Devil and his seed, and another regarding Christ and the seed of Eve. For the enmity of the Devil toward Christ, and of infidels toward believers, is depraved and blameworthy; but that of Christ and believers is good and praiseworthy. For the first group hates the person himself, while the second group does not loathe the person, but the vice of the person. The former pursue with hatred for an evil end; the latter for a good end. The former hate in fact but not by right; the latter hate both in fact and by right. Therefore, God does not command that enmity for the former, but merely predicts the outcome. But in respect to the latter, just as God predicted the outcome, so He also approves of that enmity, because it is by right and by reason of the vice, not the person.

III. Note therefore, when God says in Genesis 3, "I will put" <note>original Hebrew: אשית (*ashit*)</note>, He can in no way be called the author of sin, as if He himself truly placed the enmity, and consequently other sins which follow it according to that principle: "that which is the cause of the cause is the cause of the effect." I. God cannot be called the **physical cause** of sin and of that enmity, because it was already in the Devil before God pronounced this decree—by which, having been driven out, he seduced Eve—and it was in Adam himself immediately after the sin; for as the fire of charity fled and vanished, the heat of hatred and enmity boiled over. II. God was not the **moral cause** of the enmity, because He did not persuade man toward it nor demand it by right, as we said above. Therefore, even if "I will put" <note>Hebrew: *ashit*</note> is in the *Hiphil* conjugation <term>the causative stem in Hebrew grammar</term>, and is consequently a transitive verb, nevertheless it is sometimes, though rarely, intransitive, and belongs to those which are called in Hebrew Grammar **standing and not transitive** <note>original Hebrew: עמדים (*amadim*) or יוצאים בלתי (*yotzim bilti*)</note>. Indeed, "I will put" in Scripture is sometimes taken not **positively**, but **negatively**, so that God does not put some quality into a subject, but leaves it to its own nature. Thus, God is said to "put" enmity between believers and infidels when He abandons them...

### ANTHONY CREGUT

...unbelievers in their natural enmity and when He does not communicate the grace of charity to them, which occurs by *forsaking* them; for in respect to the faithful, the enmity exists by right. Therefore, God could positively establish that enmity because (as we have said) the faithful do not shutter at the person, but at the "poison" within the person; they hate it just as men shudder at and hate the venom of a serpent, while serpents hate men themselves. Therefore, the word "I will put" <note>original Hebrew: אשית (*ashit*)</note> is used in this place just as in 2 Samuel 8:2, where it says "he gave life" <note>original Hebrew: חייה (*chiyah*)</note>—not because he gave life **affirmatively** <note>original Greek: θετικῶς (*thetikos*)</note>, but because **privatively** or **negatively** <note>original Greek: στερητικῶς (*steretikos*) or ἀποφατικῶς (*apophatikos*)</note> he did not take it away, because he did not kill them. This is similar to Genesis 6:20, where Noah is said to have "kept the animals alive," and Exodus 1:17, regarding the midwives and the Hebrew children. It is the same in the previously praised passage from Samuel regarding David and the Moabites, and in Jeremiah 1:10: *See, I have set you this day over these nations and over kingdoms, to root out and to pull down.* In this way, the sun darkens the hemisphere negatively when it sets and hides its light.

IV. God can "put" enmity **incidentally** <term>per accidens: an effect that is not the primary intent, but follows as a side effect</term> when the Law is promulgated and when the Gospel is preached; this is also how the previously cited passage from Jeremiah 1:10 is understood. Hence, as the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul</note> testifies, the Law increases sin because *we always strive for what is forbidden and desire what is denied* <note>original Latin: "nitimur in vetitum semper cupimusque negata"—a famous quote from the Roman poet Ovid</note>. In the same way, the sun "kills" by stirring up diseased humors, even though by its own nature it gives life.

V. The word "I will put" can also be understood positively, not in respect to the **fault** <note>original Latin: *culpa*</note>, but to the **punishment** <note>original Latin: *poena*</note>. This is because God, by a just judgment, punishes sin with sin; in such a case, as a just judge, He is not the author of the fault, but He inflicts the punishment upon the sinner. This may be for the **testing** <note>original Greek: δοκιμασίαν (*dokimasian*)</note> of the believer, or for the **hardening** <note>original Greek: πωρωσίαν (*porosian*)</note>, **judgment** <note>original Greek: κρίμα (*krima*)</note>, and **destruction** <note>original Greek: ἀπωλείαν (*apoleian*)</note> of the unbeliever.

VI. When He says "I will put," this must be understood not in respect to the **production** of the act, but to its **efficacy**; that is, not that God concurs **effectively** in respect to the formal "disorder" <note>original Greek: ἀταξίας (*ataxias*)</note> which is in sin, but because He concurs **efficaciously**. For God does not behave merely **permissively**, as if His providence were idle; on the contrary, God’s power and efficacy are wonderful in directing, ordering, limiting, and determining both the sin and the sinner. In these matters, men are merely instruments, while God is the principal cause. Is it any wonder, then, if the effect is attributed to God? This is clear from the history of Job, and from the incest of Absalom, regarding which God said, *I have done this*. So it was also when Shimei <note>original: "Scimhi"</note> cursed David; and so...

VII. The word *I will put* <note>Hebrew: אשית (*ashit*)</note> denotes not only God's wisdom and providence, which shines forth in directing, ordering, and determining—whence in this sense it signifies "to establish" <note>Greek: καθισάναι (*kathistanai*)</note>, "to restore" <note>Greek: καταρτίζειν (*katartizein*)</note>, "to arrange" <note>Greek: τάττειν (*tattein*)</note>, or "to subject" <note>Greek: ὑποτάττειν (*hypotattein*)</note>, that is, to establish a certain order, rather than simply "to place" <note>Greek: τιθέναι (*tithenai*)</note>, "to give" <note>Greek: διδόναι (*didonai*)</note>, or "to bring upon" <note>Greek: ἐπάγειν (*epagein*)</note>—but it primarily demonstrates the severity of God as the supreme judge. For since that sin of the serpent and Eve was an absolute sin, and original sin was committed with no "tickling concupiscence" <note>The author suggests that because Adam and Eve had no prior fallen nature to tempt them, their choice to sin was a more direct act of the will, requiring a more severe judgment</note>; so it was necessary that the judge’s severity and the example of punishment be formidable to all ages, so that from the contemplation of such a perennial enmity, the horror of sin might move mortals all the more, and the memory of that first lapse might be perpetually refreshed.

VIII. When He says *I will put* <note>Hebrew: אשית (*ashit*)</note>, God seems to look toward those two spiritual kingdoms opposed to each other in an irreconcilable war <note>Greek: πολέμῳ ἀσπόνδῳ (*polemo aspondo*)</note>, namely the kingdom of darkness and the kingdom of light, and consequently the citizens of each kingdom, between whom no communion and no treaty can ever be struck. As the Apostle witnesses, *there is no communion of light with darkness, and of Christ with Belial* <note>2 Corinthians 6:14-15</note>; whence arise two cities: the City of God and Babel.

IX. That word *I will put* <note>Hebrew: אשית (*ashit*)</note> designates not only enmity, but even—by way of intensification <note>Greek: καθ’ αὔξησιν (*kath’ auxesin*)</note>—the sharpest enmity and a "more than Vatinian" hatred <term>Vatinian hatred: a proverbial expression for an intense, uncompromising hatred, named after the Roman figure Publius Vatinius who was famously loathed by Cicero</term>. It is as if God were saying: "I will put an enmity that is in every way horrific, both in its extent and its intensity," because it was never to cease, but was even to be most vehement. Nevertheless, just as there is not an equal venom among all serpents, but one is more lethal than another, so the enmity of men differs in degrees. For it is sharper, for example, between Jews and Christians; between Ishmaelites <note>A historical term for Muslims or Arabs</note> and Persians, etc. Whence it is said in the Talmudic tractate *Shabbat*: *Better to dwell under an Ishmaelite than under a Gentile, better under a Gentile than under a Samaritan, and better under a Samaritan than under a Chaver* <note>Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 11a</note>. <meta>This page continues the philological and mystical analysis of the Hebrew word "ashit" (I will put) from Genesis 3:15, moving into Cabalistic interpretations and a comparison between the judgment in Eden and the grace of the Gospel.</meta>

->### ANTHONY CREGUT<-

*Moreover*, **Gaber** <note>Hebrew: גבר (*Gaber*)</note> *is a word which is found in a Persian proverb: "Even if a Gaber tends a fire for a hundred years, yet if he falls into it even once, he is burned." In this context, Gaber denotes fire-worshippers, who remain in Persia to this day, most tenacious in their superstition, which is the deadly venom of the serpent and thus the fuel of enmity. However, others call them Gaor, and seek the reason for the name from the worship of the ox, which is called Gao by the Persians; or, as is more rightly believed, it comes from the Turkish Gaur, by which infidels are designated. But without a doubt, Gaor is a corruption of Gaber.*

X. **I will put** <note>Hebrew: אשית (*ashit*)</note> according to the Cabalists <note>Jewish mystics who seek hidden meanings in the scriptural text</note> signifies the fire of enmity; for in the word *ashit*, through *Temurah* <note>A Cabalistic method of rearranging or substituting letters to reveal hidden concepts; original: תמורה</note>, one finds **it ash** <note>Hebrew: אית אש</note>, which means "fire exists"—specifically, the fire of enmity. For **it** <note>Chaldean: אית</note> in Chaldean is the Hebrew **yesh** <note>Hebrew: יש; meaning "there is" or "exists"</note>. This is symbolic of that **bundle of myrrh** <note>Hebrew: צרור המור (*tseror ha-mor*)</note> in the Torah portion **Shemini** <note>Hebrew: שמיני; refers to the weekly reading from Leviticus 9:1–11:47</note> in Leviticus 11. There it is said that in the words **man** <note>Hebrew: איש (*Ish*)</note> and **woman** <note>Hebrew: אישה (*Ishah*)</note> is contained the name of God, **Yah** <note>Hebrew: יה; the first two letters of the Tetragrammaton</note>, which is the symbol of God's gracious presence. If the husband and wife live **in one accord** <note>Greek: ὁμοθυμάδον (*homothymadon*)</note>, God's name remains with them; but if, on the contrary, **Yah** and the God of peace withdraw from them, then only **ash** <note>Hebrew: אש; meaning "fire"</note> remains. This is because the fire of enmity and discord will consume them; and then, as Moses says, there is **enmity between you** <note>Hebrew: איבה בינך (*eivah benecha*)</note>. And then the spirit of strife and whirlwinds dwells between both; whereas, among the faithful, the **Shechina** <note>Hebrew: שכינה; the Divine Presence of God dwelling on Earth</note> dwells, which is the spirit of peace and concord, according to that saying of the ancient Hebrews: "When two sit together and between them are words of the Law, the **Shechina**—that is, the Spirit of God—is among them." The Spirit of God is called a "dwelling," because when God speaks of the Spirit in the Old Testament, He says in the New Testament, "I will dwell among them." From this it followed that the Holy Spirit is called the *Shechina*. If, therefore, God in His severe judgment and in His wrath once said, "I will put enmity," which is in truth the habitation of an evil spirit and a demon; so, on the other hand, in the Gospel covenant He said, "I will dwell among you," because that God of peace and the *Shechina* remains among the faithful, which extinguishes the poison of all enmity and strife. And hence there is the greatest difference between the **woe** <note>Latin: *vae*</note> of the serpent and the **hail** <note>Latin: *aue* (ave)</note> of the Angel: for the serpent’s "hail" to Eve was a "woe," but on the contrary, when Gabriel was about to congratulate the Virgin, he truly said "hail" and not "woe." Just as the first was an Angel of war and enmity, the other was truly an Angel of peace and concord. Therefore, no one among the poets has spoken more elegantly and acutely:

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of Christ’s triumph, specifically how his victory differs from earthly conquests and the symbolic use of palms and white stones in scripture. It also begins a philological critique of the Vulgate’s translation of Genesis 3:15.</meta>

### ANTHONY CREGUT ###

...prevailed and bore the palm of victory, Blessed Augustine gives the reason in the aforementioned passage: because he was certain of victory, and because he was to bring about this victory through his own death. Others triumph after the battle and the victory, either because they are not certain of winning, or because they do not conquer by dying. But both are truly said of Christ: he was certain of victory, and he conquered by dying. Therefore, he ought to have triumphed before death, and become the heir of that kingdom which he was to obtain through death. 

While the faithful could not triumph on earth, the Martyrs triumph in the heavens; hence Revelation 7:9: *They are clothed in white robes and carry palms in their hands,* <note>original: "Albis vestibus induti sunt & palmas in manibus gestant"</note> as a symbol of the victory won over enemies, for which they triumph gloriously among the heavenly citizens. And Ezekiel said that the walls of his temple were carved with palms; a vision which, according to the testimony of Gregory the Great, seemed to foreshadow the heavenly temple where the symbols of victory and triumph reside. 

And *Revelation 2:17: To him I will give a white stone, and on the stone a new name written, which no one knows except him who receives it.* By the "white stone" <note>Greek: ψῆφον λευκὸν (*psephon leukon*), literally a white pebble used for voting or as a token</note> victory is understood, for Arethas <note>An early medieval commentator on the Apocalypse</note> records that such a stone was customarily given to athletes competing in the theater. Hence, a stone signified two things among the ancients:
I. Victory, of which it was a symbol.
II. A symbol of acquittal or condemnation. Of acquittal, when it was white; of condemnation, when it was black. As Ovid testifies in Book 15 of the *Metamorphoses*:

-> *It was the custom of the ancients, with snow-white and black pebbles,* <-
-> *To condemn the accused with the latter, and to absolve from guilt with the former.* <-
<note>original: "Mos erat antiquis, niueis atriſque lapillis, / His damnare reos, illis abſoluere culpa."</note>

It is no wonder, then, if Christ bore the palm: Why should he not have the symbol of victory since he won the victory? Regarding him, that saying of Themistocles <note>A famous Athenian general and statesman</note> can rightly be said: *He conquered his friends with patience and his enemies with speed.* And that aphorism of Julius Caesar (or according to others, Alexander the Great): *losing nothing.* <note>Greek: μηδὲν ἀποβαλλόμενος (*meden apoballomenos*)</note> Rightly, therefore, Moses said *He shall crush* <note>Hebrew: הוא ישוף (*Hu yashuph*)</note>, that is, the *Seed* <note>Hebrew: זרע (*Zera*)</note>, because the seed of the woman crushed the serpent's head.

It is not without cause, therefore, that the common translator <note>The "common translator" refers to Jerome, the author of the Latin Vulgate</note> is criticized when he translates this passage as *she shall crush* <note>Latin: "ipsa conteret"</note>, as if the Hebrew were *she* <note>Hebrew: היא (*Hi*)</note> instead of *he* <note>Hebrew: הוא (*Hu*)</note> in the masculine. And the Papal Doctors <note>A polemical term for Catholic theologians</note> are much more deluded still, and deceive the poor common people, when from that corrupt...

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological critique of the Vulgate translation, specifically focusing on the translation of Genesis 3:15 and its implications for the status of the Virgin Mary in Catholic doctrine.</meta>

->### REVEALER OF SECRETS ###<-

By this translation, they wish to imply that the Most Blessed Virgin Mary, the Mother of God, crushed the head of the serpent. What is even worse is that, relying impiously on this corruption of the version, they blasphemously claim that the Virgin Mary is the redeemer of the human race. In doing so, they are unmindful of their own minor distinctions, for they typically establish two types of mediators: those of redemption and those of intercession. They usually make Christ the mediator of redemption, while the male and female saints are mediators of intercession. Yet, forgetting this, they now appoint the Virgin Mary as a mediator of redemption and associate her with the priestly office of Christ—who, in his death, crushed the head of the serpent and redeemed the human race through the merit and ultimately the efficacy of his sacrifice. And who would not shudder to read these impious claims in P. Galatinus, *On the Secrets of Catholic Truth*, book 7, chapter 10? <note>Pietro Galatino (1460–1540) was an Italian Franciscan friar and theologian whose work attempted to prove Catholic doctrines using Jewish mystical texts.</note>

> *Because the Virgin Mary was undefiled, she never fell ill, nor suffered the monthly course of women. She died not because of Adam's sin, but because, since she was to give birth to a son subject to suffering, she herself had to be subject to suffering; and she rose soon after and was assumed into heaven together with her Son. But you might ask: if the Virgin Mary had died before her son, where would her soul have gone? To the depths or to paradise? Not to paradise, since it was closed; nor to Limbo, since the Holy Fathers descended there because of original sin. Therefore, you might argue she also went there because of original sin. I respond: Regarding the place, she would have descended to neither, but would have ascended to another most holy place in the heavens. II. I say it was impossible for her to die before Christ. First, because God decreed that she should see the death of her son. Second, because she necessarily had to intervene in the remission of sins; for just as sin was committed by means of a woman, so it had to be forgiven by means of a woman, so that just as a sinful woman brought sin and death into the world, so a most holy woman might bring life.*

Thus far P. Galatinus, with whom the rest of the Catholics <note>original: "Pontificii," referring to supporters of the Pope</note> agree. From this comes the corruption of Genesis 3:15: *She shall crush,* <note>original Latin: "Ipsa conteret." Most Protestant scholars argued the Hebrew text says "He" (the Messiah) or "It" (the seed) shall crush the serpent, not "She" (Mary).</note> etc. As for what other Catholics say—that the Virgin is the "mediatrix of preservation" because she preserves us from sin—this is likewise an impious figment of the human brain, devised unscripturally and contrary to scripture. <note>Greek: ἀγράφως καὶ ἀντιγράφως (*agraphos kai antigraphos*)</note> Because of this error, the Virgin Mary is also called the "Queen of Heaven" by the Papists; a title which was once used with great flourish and elaborate display in a sermon before Henry IV, the greatest and best King of the French, by a certain monk...

# ANTHONY CREGUT #

...had been proven as far as possible: to this the King, after the sermon, indeed said, "I do not believe it, because the kingdom of heaven, like that of the Franks, is not ruled by the distaff and spindle according to Salic law." <note>The Salic Law was the ancient Frankish civil code that, most famously, excluded women from inheriting the throne or land. The "distaff and spindle" were traditional symbols of female domestic labor.</note> The King said this mockingly before his courtiers, execrating the horrible blasphemies of that preacher and scoffing at his trifles; and perhaps that common Rabbinical proverb pleased him: <note>original Hebrew: *אין חכמה לאישה אלא בפלך*</note> *There is no wisdom in a woman except in the spindle.* <note>original Latin: *Non est sapientia in fæmina nisi in colo.*</note>

All these monstrosities emerged from the corruption of the Vulgate edition, <note>The Vulgate is the late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible that became the Catholic Church's official version.</note> or rather, once this heresy was born in the minds of some, the translation was subsequently adapted to establish it. But oh, the impiety of these little men! Oh, the great monstrosity! The Papists <note>The author uses "Pontificij" (Papists) as a polemical term for Roman Catholics loyal to the Pope.</note> dared what no heretic had ever attempted. For, alas, it pains me to write of such impiety, and I shudder at the very thought: the Papists dared (I say) to lay sacrilegious hands not only on the translation, but even on the Hebrew original itself. For in the Hebrew it was *הוא* <note>hu</note> in the masculine gender, and therefore referred to *זֶרַע* <note>zera</note>, that is, the *seed*, because in truth the seed of the woman—that is, Christ—crushed the head of the serpent. Those plagiarizers, on the contrary, substituted *הִיא* <note>hi</note> in the feminine gender, so that it would be said of the woman, *she herself shall crush*, etc. Thus, it was mystically and symbolically attributed to the Virgin, of whom Eve (who was also a virgin at that time) was a type, or so they fabricate. 

And so that their impiety might grow, and lest anyone should scent out a fraud of this kind, a Masoretic note <note>The Masoretes were Jewish scholars between the 6th and 10th centuries who compiled a system of notes to preserve the exact text of the Hebrew Bible.</note> was added to the Interlinear Royal Bibles from the first edition in the form of a small circle, as if there were a substitution <note>original Greek: *αντιστοιχία*</note> of the letter *Vau* for *Yod* and it should be read as *היא* (she herself). But in truth, the Hebrew text was not corrupted by the Masoretes, but by the Jesuits; and that Masoretic note was added by them against the consensus of all manuscripts and the analogy of faith. This was reported by Raphelengius while he was still alive, <note>Frans van Ravelingen (1539–1597), a scholar and printer who worked on the Antwerp Polyglot Bible.</note> who oversaw the edition of the Royal Bibles; he says this was obtained through the fraud of certain Jesuits without any supporting example from a manuscript. This is observed by A. Walaeus in his *Common Places on the Translation of Scripture*, page 141. <note>Antonius Walaeus (1573–1639) was a Dutch Reformed theologian.</note> Furthermore, Salomon Glassius, the superintendent in the Duchy of Saxe-Gotha, adds in his *Philologia Sacra* that this corruption was made in the edition of the year 1572, but in the second edition of 1584, the true reading was restored
