...and the masculine *hu* <note>original Hebrew: הוא; the third-person masculine singular pronoun "He."</note> was expressly placed there. This change was made out of compelling necessity, either because of the scandal of such an enormous corruption even in the Hebrew sources—a crime so sacrilegious that even Satan himself was struck with horror—or perhaps because of the sting of sin from a pricking conscience, whose worm continually gnawed at the corrupters and falsifiers. It may even have been due to the divine *economy* <note>original Greek: οἰκονομίαν; referring to God's plan or management of the world.</note> and dispensation, which could no longer leave such an enormous stain on the sun of Scripture, nor such muddy and foul dregs in the Hebrew sources.

Wherefore the aforementioned Raphelengius <note>Frans van Ravelingen (1539–1597), a celebrated scholar and printer who worked on the Antwerp Polyglot Bible.</note>, just as he was about to breathe his last and give an account of this monstrous crime before God’s tribunal, spontaneously confessed that the persistence of the Jesuits had extorted this corruption from him. Who would deny that the testimony of such a man—and a dying one at that—is deservedly momentous and of great weight? Compelled by the truth, Santes Pagninus, a monk from Lucca, <note>An Italian Dominican and leading philologist of the Renaissance, known for his literal translation of the Bible from original languages.</note> also translated it as *it* <note>original Latin: *ipsum*; referring back to the "seed" (semen) rather than a person.</note>, referring it back to the "seed." So too did Andradius, a Portuguese Jesuit, and Melchior Canus, a Spanish Bishop, the latter conceding that the feminine *she* <note>original Latin: *ipsa*</note> had been substituted by the unskilled. Sacroboscus <note>Christopher Holywood (1562–1626), an Irish Jesuit.</note> acknowledges this, judging those copies to be more correct which read *it*. Likewise, Agostino Steuco, the Pope’s Librarian, called the interpretation regarding the Virgin "bad," as did Francesco Giorgio <note>A Venetian Franciscan friar known for his synthesis of Christian theology and Kabbalah.</note> before them.

The exceptions raised by Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Cardinal and one of the most important figures in the Counter-Reformation.</note> are invalid. For he objects as follows: **I.** He writes that the Vulgate edition varies, having *she* in some codices and *he* or *it* in others; therefore, it is not an absolute *error*. <note>original Greek: σφάλμα (*sphagma*)</note> But these things are said preposterously, since whichever copies are printed among the Papists retain the error; thus it appears to be a fault not of the scribes, but of the edition itself. And indeed, out of the infinite abundance of ancient codices, scarcely one was found by Franciscus Lucas and Hentenius <note>Johannes Hentenius (1499–1566), a Flemish biblical commentator.</note> that read otherwise. **II.** Bellarmine objects that it is not improbable that it should be read as *she*. This is because he himself saw a Hebrew codex in which there was *hu* [he] and not *hi* [she]; therefore, if the vowel points <note>In Hebrew, the same consonants (H-W-A) can sometimes be read as different genders depending on the vowel markings (niqqud) added later by the Masoretes.</note> are removed, the word could be translated in the feminine gender, as in Genesis 3:12 and Exodus 3:8. To Bellarmine's second exception, I respond that he stumbles over the same stone, and from a single little codex [attempts to judge] all Hebrew codices...

...to attack the faith. That volume of Bellarmine was cited by us above and lashed for its impious <term>error <note>original Greek: σφάλμα (sphālma); a slip, error, or false step.</note></term>. My good man, that volume is the Antwerp edition for the apparatus of the Royal Bibles <note>The Plantin Polyglot Bible (1568–1572), sponsored by King Philip II of Spain.</note>, where the text is accompanied by an interlinear version.

And indeed, *Franciscus Lucas* <note>Lucas Brugensis (1548–1619), a Flemish biblical scholar and critic.</note> does not want this to be considered an error, nor does he want it to have been corrected by the authority of ancient codices; rather, he claims it was changed deliberately by *Guido Fabricius Boderianus* <note>Guy Le Fèvre de la Boderie (1541–1598), a French Orientalist who worked on the Antwerp Polyglot.</note> upon the authority of *Pico della Mirandola*. As for Bellarmine’s retort that *He* <note>original Hebrew: הוא (*hu*); the third-person masculine singular pronoun.</note> sometimes occurs as a feminine gender, I admit this is true, but it occurs very rarely, and the grammatical construction here removes all ambiguity. This is clear from the previously praised passages where the nouns and verbs are feminine; but here, every element removes ambiguity. For the verb "he shall crush" <note>original Hebrew: ישופו (*yashuphu*); a masculine verb form.</note> is masculine, and in the second part of the verse, [it says] "you shall crush him" <note>original Hebrew: תשופנו (*teshuphunnu*); the suffix "-nu" is the masculine object "him."</note>. When Bellarmine further objects that it is not unprecedented for masculine pronouns or verbs to be joined to feminine nouns, one or two or even three examples can certainly be given; however, those are grammatical anomalies. Moreover, when this does occur, the sense of the passage justifies the construction. But here, on the contrary, it is manifest that *Mary* did not crush the head of the serpent, but rather *Christ the Lord*, who was born from her.

III. *Franciscus Lucas* also offers the exception that the Mother of Christ is understood to have crushed the serpent’s head because she gave birth to Him who did the crushing. But good God! How tasteless is that exception! Is this how they mock the poor common people? By this logic, you masters of Rome will even boldly infer that *Mary* was crucified and sits at the right hand of the Father, because she gave birth to Him who fulfilled all these things. By such reasoning, a Jesuit’s mother "sang the *Mass*" <note>original Latin: *Missam*; the central act of worship in the Catholic Church.</note> because she gave birth to a son who is a singer of the Mass.

The Carthusians, in their commentary on Genesis 3:15, included a note by Peter Blomevenna of Leiden <note>Peter Blomevenna (1466–1536) was a Dutch Carthusian monk and prior who defended traditional Catholic doctrines against the Reformation.</note> which claimed the authority of Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian whose works were often cited in biblical debates.</note>. It alleged that Josephus said in the third book of his *Jewish Antiquities* <term>Antiquities <note>original Greek: ἀρχαιολογίας (archaiologias); the title of Josephus’s history of the Jewish people.</note></term>: *He commanded that the woman should inflict blows upon its head.* Thereupon, Blomevenna exclaims with excessive joy: "Let those who are more curious than pious go now, relying on the modern copies of the Jews, and let them show that the ancient Jews read it differently than Josephus did!" But that "mole" does not see that he has been deceived by a Latin edition of Josephus. The Greek text sounds quite different: <term>having designated an enemy for them, he suggested that they should direct their blows against its head <note>original Greek: πολέμιον ὑποδείξας αὐτοῖς, καὶ ὑποτιθέμενος κατὰ τῆς κεφαλῆς φέρειν τὰς πληγὰς (polemion hypodeixas autois, kai hypotithemenos kata tēs kephalēs pherein tas plēgas).</note></term>. In this passage, Josephus says nothing about the "woman," but speaks generally of human beings, whom he knew to be the "seed of the woman." He was not considering a mystical sense here, and he certainly said nothing of the woman specifically striking the blow.

IV. The next exception is that of <term>Gordon Huntly <note>James Gordon of Huntly (1541–1620), a Scottish Jesuit and controversialist who wrote on biblical chronology and grammar.</note></term>, who wrote too boldly that the word *hu* <gloss>He <note>original Hebrew: הוא</note></gloss> is found among the Hebrews as a feminine gender, and indeed with great emphasis, so that it signifies not just "she," but "she herself," or "this very one and no other." Furthermore, he argues that because collective nouns in Hebrew (such as "woman," here signifying the entire Church) can be of either gender—masculine or feminine—as witnessed by the grammarian Pagninus <note>Sante Pagnini (1470–1541), an influential Hebraist of the Dominican Order.</note> in his *Grammar*, Book 2, Chapter 2.

Truly, did that Gordon not "untie the Gordian knot" <note>An idiom for solving a complex problem by a bold stroke; here used sarcastically.</note> most excellently? Shall he now appear to us as a great Hebrew grammarian? For he forges new grammatical rules and the rarest little observations. Alas, you learned master in Hebrew and <term>our teacher <note>original Hebrew: מורנו (morenu); a title of respect for a rabbi or teacher.</note></term>! Where on earth did you observe this "beautiful emphasis" of yours? It is rare indeed, because it is unheard of; it is singular, because it was invented and used by you as the sole author. Pagninus never said that collective nouns among the Hebrews are of both genders, nor is it true. He only said that names of genera and species—in which both masculine and feminine individuals are found under one category—comprehend both sexes regardless of their grammatical ending (even if ending in <term>h <note>original Hebrew: ה (He); a common feminine suffix.</note></term>). For example, the word <term>bird <note>original Hebrew: עוף (oph).</note></term> includes both males and females within the same masculine gender. But to what end is this argument? For Churches are not "masculine and feminine." And even if this were true, the word *hu* <gloss>He</gloss> would never actually be of the feminine gender.

Truly, here the saying will apply: *Clodius accuses adulterers* <note>A reference to Juvenal’s Satires, meaning a hypocrite who accuses others of the very crimes he commits himself. Clodius was a Roman politician notorious for his own scandals.</note>, or *Catiline accuses Cethegus*. The story mentioned involves the general Joab and a dispute over a single vowel in a biblical command, emphasizing the life-and-death importance of textual accuracy.</note></term> concerning Joab.

But truly, although the Virgin cannot be said to have crushed the serpent’s head *abstractly*—as if she alone had conquered the Devil—nevertheless, she crushed it *concretely* in respect to the "mystical body" <note>The "mystical body" refers to the Church, of which Christ is the head and the faithful are the members.</note>. For the "seed of the woman" is also understood to be the Church; and since Mary was a member of the Church, she—in this sense, just like other believers in and with Christ the head—crushes the serpent's head and overcomes the Devil. Indeed, because the Blessed Virgin was endowed with various prerogatives and excellent gifts, she also, in her own way, crushed the serpent's head more significantly, and vigorously conquered with her stronger faith, according to the saying: *faith has overcome the world*.

Therefore, truly the Church will crush the serpent's head and overcome the Devil. Scripture teaches this primarily in that famous passage, Romans 16:20: *The Lord will soon crush Satan under your feet*. By these words, the Apostle signifies that the power of crushing Satan is spread among all the faithful. Here, he seems to allude to the passage in Genesis 3; for the Greek word <term>will crush <note>original Greek: συντρίψει (*syntripsei*).</note></term> corresponds to the Hebrew <term>he shall bruise <note>original Hebrew: ישוף (*yashuph*).</note></term>. And therefore, it is better to read it—along with all the Greek manuscripts—as <term>may he crush <note>original Greek: συντρίψῃ (*syntripsē*); the author is arguing for a specific grammatical mood (the optative or aorist subjunctive) that implies a promise or blessing.</note></term>, so that it serves as a promise or an obligation by which the Romans are confirmed to persevere. This is better than the version of the "old translator" <note>The Latin Vulgate.</note> and the Syriac, who read it as a simple "he will crush," as if it were a prayer that the Lord might give a prosperous success to their own efforts. And the Savior hints at this in John 12:31: *Now the judgment of this world is here; now the prince of this world will be cast out*. But just as the faithful achieve victory over the Devil, so they triumph much more over unbelievers, whether in respect to the truth of doctrine or in respect to conduct. **In respect to truth**, because the truth of the Church cannot be conquered; for this reason, the Blessed Augustine used to call it the **eternal victory** <note>original Latin: *æternam victoriam*</note>. This is something the Romans falsely claim for their *eternal Rome*. However, although the Virgin cannot be said to have crushed the head of the serpent in the *abstract*—as if she alone had conquered the Devil—nevertheless, she crushed it in the *concrete* with respect to the "mystical body" <note>A theological term for the Church as the body of Christ.</note>. This is because the "seed of the woman" is also understood to be the Church; and since Mary was a member of the Church, she—in this sense, like other believers—crushes the head of the serpent in and with Christ the Head, and overcomes the Devil. Indeed, because the Blessed Virgin was endowed with various prerogatives and distinguished gifts, she also crushed the serpent's head more so in her own way, having strenuously conquered through her robust faith, according to the saying: *faith has conquered the world.*

Therefore, the Church truly shall crush the head of the serpent and overcome the Devil. Scripture teaches this primarily in that celebrated passage in **Romans 16:20**:

> *The Lord will shortly crush Satan under your feet.*

By these words, he signifies that the power to crush Satan is poured out upon all the faithful. Here, the Apostle seems to allude to the passage in Genesis 3; for the Greek word <gloss>will crush</gloss> <note>original Greek: *συντρίψει* (syntripsei)</note> corresponds to the Hebrew <gloss>he will bruise/crush you</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: *yeshuphcha*</note>. For this reason, it is better to read it as <gloss>will crush</gloss> in accordance with all the Greek manuscripts—rendering it a promise or a prophecy by which the Romans might be encouraged to persevere—rather than following the ancient translator <note>The Vulgate.</note> and the Syriac version which read it as <gloss>may he crush</gloss> <note>original Greek: *συντρίψῃ* (syntripsē)</note>, as if it were a prayer that the Lord might grant a prosperous outcome to their efforts. The Savior also hints at this in **John 12:31**:

> *Now is the judgment of this world; now the prince of this world shall be cast out.*

[the serpent] crushes the heel, which, if not a total victory, at least signifies harm. However, the word <note>original: שוף (*shuf*)</note> "to crush" does not seem to be used as properly regarding the heel as it is regarding the head; nor regarding the serpent as regarding the seed of the woman, because a serpent bites rather than crushes the heel. Yet, this is also said in a certain sense regarding the bite of a serpent, because it is also the property of teeth to crush; hence we have "molar" teeth, because they crush food no differently than millstones <note>The Latin *mola* means millstone.</note>. Next, one must observe the emphasis of the Hebrew word <note>original: עקב (*akev*)</note> for "heel." From this comes the verb <note>original: עקב (*akav*)</note> *to supplant* or *to trip up*. This fits wonderfully with the cunning of the serpent, who "supplants" the seed of man and secretly bites and crushes his heel. From this we get the name <note>original: יעקב (*Ya'akov*)</note> Jacob, meaning *supplantor*, who seized the sole of his brother Esau's foot while being born. For when he had first struggled with his brother in his mother’s womb, striving for victory and dominance, he then gripped the heel during birth, contending for the birthright; and finally, in his youth, what he had first attempted by instinct, he then fulfilled by mind and will: for in truth he supplanted his brother. Truly, in the same way, the serpent biting the heel of man supplants him, and what he cannot achieve by force and "open Mars" <note>An idiom for open, honorable warfare.</note>, he finally accomplishes through fraud and guile.

All these things, so stated literally regarding the serpent, also fit Christ and the faithful mystically. For: 1. Christ, as was proved above, reported a grand victory over the Devil; but the victory was bought dearly, because the serpent bit his heel, and the bite of that ancient serpent was so venomous that the death of Christ followed. Yet it happened in such a way that, being raised up on the cross—no differently than the bronze serpent <note>A reference to the story in Numbers 21, where looking at a bronze serpent on a pole healed those bitten by snakes; here it is a "type" or foreshadowing of the Crucifixion.</note>—he broke the teeth of the ancient serpent, destroyed its venom, and completely crushed its entire head. These same things are to be observed in the "other seed" of the woman, that is, the faithful. For the faithful conquer with Christ as their leader, but the victory is very bloody; because if, as is said in Romans 16, they crush Satan under their feet, so too does that serpent crush their heel. And even if sin does not reign (Romans 6), it at least dwells within, and no <term>alexipharmacum</term> <note>A historical medical term for an antidote or a preservative against poison.</note> is prepared for us by which the venom of the serpent can be entirely erased. Hence, *the flesh lusts against the spirit* (Galatians 5) and *the law of the members fights against the law of the mind* (Romans 7).

**A**we-struck, we now approach the exposition, under Divine auspices, of a most illustrious oracle—illustrious both because of the celebrated subject matter treated within it, and because of the various circumstances and deeds that so nobly distinguish and honor it. For therein is treated not only marriage, but even the **marriage of marriages**, whether because it was the most celebrated of all marriages, or because it was the first cause and root of all marriages. Therefore, the marriage of Adam is most illustrious, both as he was a singular person and as he was the head of the whole human race; that marriage was celebrated insofar as it is Adam’s—and thus a unique marriage—and insofar as it is taken as the norm for all others, or insofar as marriage is defined specifically.

I. The marriage is celebrated because it was the *norm and rule for all others*. 

II. *On the part of the one instituting it*, since God himself instituted it. 

III. *On the part of the bridal attendant*, <note>original: "paranymphi". In ancient Greek and Roman weddings, the paranymph was the friend of the bridegroom who escorted the bride.</note> because God himself was the attendant who led the bride to the groom, according to that passage in *Genesis 2:22: And the Lord God built the rib which he had taken from Adam into a woman: and he brought her to Adam.* 

IV. *On the part of the contracting parties*, for they were the noblest pair of spouses, being the <term>protoplasts|The "first-formed" humans, Adam and Eve</term> fashioned by God's own hand. 

V. *With respect to time*, because it was contracted in the <term>state of integrity|The theological state of perfect innocence and harmony before the fall of man</term>, before sin had entered into the world. 

VI. *With respect to place*, because it was (so to speak) solemnized in the earthly paradise—and without a doubt also in the heavenly one, since God was present there and played the greatest part. 

VII. *With respect to the extraordinary action*, because a great miracle was performed there in the formation of the bride from the rib of Adam, just as Christ performed his first miracle at the wedding in Cana, as recorded in *John 2*. 

VIII. *With respect to the purpose*, since it was not a purpose by accident—as happens among men today—hence the distinction of a marriage of *Choice and consideration*, and of a marriage *equal and unequal*. 

IX. *By reason of its symbolic significance*, since the marriage of Adam marvelously foreshadowed the spiritual marriage of the <term>Second Adam|A common theological title for Jesus Christ</term>, as will be seen below <note>original: "σὺν Θεῷ", Greek for "with God's help"</note>.

But indeed, so that this entire matter may be treated more distinctly, come now, let us divide it into these parts. I. *Concerning the institution*...

### ANTHONY CRÉGUT ###

...[resto]red, even with the more solemn blessing of marriage itself urged and repeated: *Be fruitful and multiply*.

Second, among the Romans, who seemed the most refined of all the Gentiles <note>The author uses "Gentiles" or "Ethnici" to refer to non-Christian/non-Jewish ancient peoples.</note>, marriage was observed. According to Festus <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus was a Roman grammarian whose work preserved many ancient customs.</note>, three boys "with living fathers and mothers" <term>patrimi et matrimi; children whose parents were both still alive, considered an auspicious sign</term> would lead the bride as she married. One would carry a torch made of white thorn—for they married at night, as Plutarch says in his *Roman Questions*—and two others would hold the bride. Indeed, the various names given to this act by the Romans point abundantly to its solemn practice:

*   **Matrimonium** comes from the name for "mother" (*mater*), because its specific purpose is the procreation of children.
*   **Connubium** or **nuptiæ** comes from "veiling" (*nubendo*), because just as the sun is covered by a cloud (*nubes*), so the bride was led to the groom covered with a veil as if by a cloud.
*   **Coniugium** comes from "joining together" (*coniungendo*), because husband and wife were joined to each other by a family bond.

Hence Virgil, in the first book of the *Aeneid*, notes both in the same verse: *I will join her in stable wedlock, etc.* <note>Original: *connubio iungam stabili* (Aeneid 1.73)</note>.

Finally, the institution of marriage prevailed among all nations, but it became mixed with so many corruptions and unbridled lusts, and was so miserably defiled by either divorces or remarriages and polygamy, that the entire essence of marriage was effectively destroyed. Nothing remained but an idol of such a great institution and a certain empty representation. This is clear from the practices of the Numidians, Moors, Egyptians, Indians, Garamantes, Parthians, Nasamones, Thracians, Scythians, and other barbarians, as well as the Greeks and more polished peoples, as can be seen in Polydore Vergil’s *On the Inventors of Things*, Book 1, Chapter 4. 

Therefore, the union of male and female for the propagation of the species is indeed a matter **of natural law**; but marriage as an institution is a matter **of the law of nations and civil law**, and is thus something political. However, for it to be contracted truly and according to the law as it was originally instituted, it is a matter **of divine law**. Therefore, it holds the status of a holy and religious observance. Yet, the Gentile nations have strayed an immense distance from this original institution. Although they seem to have received the ritual of marriage from the tradition of the Hebrews, they subsequently worshipped God according to their own whims (as in other matters of religion) and here poured themselves out into various and promiscuous lusts...

...tablishment was ruined. Indeed, the wise of this world have rejected marriage as something quite harmful to man, and for many centuries past it has had a bad reputation. Hence, the most prudent Cato is read to have said: *if the world could exist without women, our company would not be without gods.* <note>Original: "si absque fœmina posset esse mundus, conuersatio nostra non esset absque diis." This quote, often attributed to Cato the Censor, suggests that women are a distraction from divine or intellectual pursuits.</note> From this comes that common saying, *woman is a necessary evil.* <note>Latin: "fœmina est necessarium malum."</note> Likewise: *a wise man should not take a wife.* But these things are said wrongly; for if any truth is found in them, it is not due to marriage itself, but by accident, arising from the poison of the serpent and of sin—and furthermore, such cases are specific to certain individuals, not to the condition and status of marriage itself.

Therefore, there are many things that greatly adorn marriage:

I. **Divine institution**, which cannot be anything but most useful and necessary; we have said much about this from the beginning.

II. **His peculiar assistance or presence in the marriage of the faithful**, just as His absence is felt in the marriage of the reprobate—namely, when God either grants or does not grant marital blessings. Hence that common saying: *marriages are made in heaven.* <note>Latin: "matrimonia fiunt in cœlis."</note> Or as another said: *good things are made in heaven, but bad things in hell.* <note>Latin: "bona fiunt in cœlis, mala verò in orco."</note> This was the response that James, King of Great Britain, received from an English knight; for when that king sought a marriage for his son with a Spanish woman <note>A reference to the "Spanish Match," the failed attempt by King James I to marry Prince Charles to Infanta Maria Anna of Spain, which was highly controversial in Protestant England.</note> and boastfully claimed before the court that not even demons could prevent it, that knight wittily retorted that none of those impure spirits were then in hell, because they had all flown to Castile to be present at that wedding and to pronounce their "woe" upon it. Indeed, that undertaking, begun without God, had a similar end and catastrophe. For as it is held in Proverbs 18:22:

> *A prudent wife comes from the singular blessing of God; he who finds a wife finds a good thing, as favor comes from Jehovah.* <note>The author provides a slightly expanded paraphrase of the Vulgate/Hebrew text.</note>

And in chapter 19:14:

> *House and wealth are a possession from fathers, but a prudent wife is from Jehovah.*

And God willed that union to be so close and holy that it cannot be dissolved by any mortal, but only by Him who first joined the spouses—when He deigns to join one or the other to Himself in a closer marriage in that place where "they neither take wives nor are given in marriage, but are like the Angels of God" (Matthew 22:30). The word used by Matthew—"joined together" <note>original: συζεύξεν (syzeuxen)</note>—rightly applies to spouses and to marriage; indeed, metaphorically it refers to a "yoke," which, having been placed by God, no one ought to tear apart or cast off from their necks, but rather carry it gently as long as it pleases the divine "joiner" <note>original: συζεύκτῃ (syzeukte)</note> or "overseer" <note>original: ἐπιστάτῃ (epistate)</note>. VII. Because of that divine union and the institution of marriage, its nature is not the same as other political societies, which are easily contracted and dissolved by mutual consent. For although contracts are said to be voluntary before they are made, and necessary after they are made, yet once mutual consent is added, they immediately become valid or void; but marriage must be judged differently, since God first joined spouses infinitely in the marriage of Adam and in its institution; and then definitely in the marriage of each individual, both by the power of that first institution and by the unique blessing of this specific marriage which occurs according to the formula of the institution. Therefore, that union of spouses is closer than any other, such as that of parents and children. According to Genesis 2:24: *Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and shall cleave to his wife.* Note here that Moses uses the word "clinging" <note>original: דבק (*davak*)</note>, which signifies an attachment of love and the most ardent affection, as it is used in Genesis 34 regarding Shechem loving Dinah, the daughter of Jacob. # ANTHONII CREGVTI

...admits. Indeed, that word **"cleave"** <term>to adhere or stick <note>original: דבק (dabaq)</note></term> signifies a complete and total union, like that of the skin, flesh, and bones. Just as in **Job 19** and **29**, it is said *the tongue cleaves to the roof of the mouth.* And in **Jeremiah 13**, a belt is said to cling to the loins: *As a belt clings to the loins of a man, so I have made the whole house of Israel cling to me.* 

But this adherence [in marriage] is the narrowest of all, not only because it encompasses both soul and body, but also because the union of the body is so great that two become one flesh, though they were two before. Thus, in many ways, all people are from one man and are one man. 

I. *With respect to the species*; because the entire human species was in Adam, as if all men were one man, because they were all in him fundamentally <note>The author uses the term "radically," meaning "at the root."</note>. 

II. *With respect to sex*, since Eve was made from Adam’s rib, and therefore from Adam and Eve come all people, both male and female. 

III. *With respect to marriage*, because there would be no marriage without a bridegroom and a bride; yet the bride was drawn from Adam; and therefore marriage was in him from the beginning. Truly, then, the Apostle, alluding to this in **Ephesians 5:29**, says: *For no one ever hated his own flesh.* And in **verse 31**, he uses an emphatic term **"shall be joined"** <term>to be glued to <note>original: προσκολληθήσεται (proskollēthēsetai)</note></term>, that is, he shall be "glued," as if two were joined together by a kind of glue and thus became one. 

This fits wonderfully with that "gluing" of the food we eat to our own bodies. Therefore, physicians call the final stage of digestion **"assimilation"** <term>the process of food becoming part of the body's substance</term>, and that "dew"—the purest and most subtle part of nourishment which is converted into substance—is called **"gluten"** from the act of "gluing," and is called **"Cambium"** <note>A medieval medical term for the fluid that nourishes the tissues.</note> by Arabic physicians. 

And what is called **"Gluten"** <term>glue <note>Arabic script: אלעילן (al-aylān)</note></term> by the Arabs—for example, **"the glue of the bone"** <note>original: אלעילן אלעטם (al-aylān al-atam)</note>—is interpreted through this phrase **"cleaving"** <term>adherence <note>original: הלאון דבק (halaon dabaq)</note></term>, which is the very word **"cleave"** <term>dabaq</term> Moses uses in **Genesis 2:24**. 

It is for this reason, due to that most narrow union, that neither spouse has power over their own body. This is what Paul clearly taught in **1 Corinthians 7:4**: *The wife does not have power over her own body, but the husband; and likewise, the husband does not have power over his own body, but the wife.* Here, Paul seems to have pointedly used the word **"likewise"** <term>in the same way <note>original: ὁμοίως (homoiōs)</note></term> to show that the same judgment applies to the husband as to the wife, both because of the same reason for the union and the identity of the body (which belongs no more to one than to the other), for the bond is common and binds both equally, and also because...

VIII. That institution of marriage, although it was established <term>by covenant <note>original Greek: κατ' συνθήκην (kat' synthēkēn)</note></term> and by divine decree, nevertheless also seems in some way physical and engraved into the very inner chambers of nature. For this reason, the moral law—which was also engraved <term>by nature <note>original Greek: φύσει (physei)</note></term> upon the hearts of the Nations, as seen in **Romans 1**—prohibits fornication. *You shall not commit adultery,* says **Exodus 20**, and the law of nature itself demonstrated to them that wandering sexual unions and debauchery were contrary to nature. Therefore, from those <term>common notions <note>original Greek: κοιναῖς ἐννοίαις (koinais ennoiais)</note></term> and <term>preconceptions <note>original Greek: ἐγκαταλήψεσι (enkatalēpsesi); refers to innate ideas or mental grasps</note></term>, they recognized, albeit obscurely and as if through a mist, that marriage was not something purely human but was <term>divinely taught <note>original Greek: θεοδίδακτον (theodidaktos)</note></term> and, as it were, a celestial gift and institution. They observed this with some degree of worship and religion, however coldly. Indeed, they even imagined that their own gods celebrated weddings and entered into marriages; and for this reason, they assigned their own wedding songs and marriage hymns <note>The author uses the terms "Epithalamia" and "hymenaeos," both referring to traditional songs performed for a bride and groom.</note> to the gods of both the greater and lesser nations.

IX. And truly, that primeval institution of marriage had its origin in the first and most ancient foundation of all nature and the creation of the world, and since this was known to the Nations, marriage could not be ignored by them either. For God indeed created ranks of Angels, but He created only a single human being, who was alone in his species. Therefore, so that the human species might be propagated and thereby preserved, that conjugal society necessarily had to be instituted, in which God, through so many ages of the world, might display examples of His goodness, wisdom, and presence. For He willed to bless humanity in this way, according to the first formula: *Increase and multiply.* And in that first "economy" <note>From the Greek 'oikonomia,' meaning household management or arrangement.</note> of families, He willed to propagate the holy economy of His own family—that is, the Church—so that in this way another and more noble marriage might arise, namely that of Christ and the Church. And in truth, the first foundations of the Church are laid in piously established families, and its first seedlings sprout there, which thereafter send out branches far and wide and flourish happily. For as Paul testifies in **1 Timothy 3**: *If someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God’s church?*

Here, Cregut explores why God deemed it "not good" for man to be alone and defends the dignity of marriage against those who view it as a burden or a distraction.</meta>

X. That institution of marriage seems to possess a certain **moral quality**; for since the moral law is the image of divine justice, holiness, and purity, marriage displays for us to some extent the chastity and holiness of God—reminding us that He, who is most chaste, requires from us a chastity of heart and body. So that just as:
> *God is a chaste mind, and wishes to be called upon by a chaste mind,*
> *Thus He commanded chaste prayers to have weight.* <note>original Latin: *Casta Deus mens est, & casta vult mente vocari, / Sic castas iussit pondus habere preces.* A common poetic sentiment in early modern theology emphasizing that the internal state of the believer affects the efficacy of their prayer.</note>
So it must be added that He hates unholy hands, a self-indulgent body, and wandering lusts.

XI. God Himself added the definitive reason for the institution of marriage, as reported by Moses in **Genesis 2:18**: *It is not good for the man to be alone; I will make him a helper who is suited for him.* These words have a wonderful emphasis. *It is not good*, etc. This is true in many ways:
I. *With respect to the nature of man*, because he is <term>by nature a social animal <note>original Greek: φύσει εστὶ ζῶον πολιτικὸν (*physei esti zoon politikon*); a famous Aristotelian concept that humans are naturally inclined toward living in a community or "polis."</note></term>. Therefore, he naturally loves society and cannot live in solitude; hence that saying, "Woe to the one who is alone" <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 4:10.</note>. Indeed, nature itself acts as our teacher and instructs us: she who gave us two ears for the sake of society and communication.

III. *With respect to the comfort of life*; hence it is added, *I will make a helper*, whereby God kindly provided for the tranquility of men.
IV. *With respect to desire*, but this is secondary and came after sin, so that marriage might be a remedy against the lusts of the flesh. Therefore, let those profane men be gone who defined a "blessed life" as living far from a wife. Indeed, Jerome himself, in his first book *Against Jovinian*, did not blush to defame and disfigure holy marriage with insolent insults, because he himself lived a celibate life. <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) was famous for his asceticism and his polemical writing against Jovinian, where he argued that virginity was vastly superior to marriage.</note> Yet let no one seize this as an occasion to defame women, because God said *I will make him a helper* in the singular number, not *Let us make*, as he did earlier when dealing with the creation of man. First, before the flood, the "sons of God" contaminated themselves with the "daughters of men," whence from an ill-fated union an ill-fated offspring also sprouted, a **brood of vipers** <note>original Greek: *γεννήματα ἐχidνῶν* (*gennēmata echidnōn*)</note> (Genesis 6:2). Adah and Zillah. Genesis 4:19. From here came the first origin of polygamy—an evil egg from an evil crow <note>original Latin: *mali corvi malum ovum*, a classical proverb suggesting that a corrupt source produces corrupt results.</note>—for he [Lamech] was a fierce and savage man. Perhaps he did this to propagate his race so that he might become stronger and a terror to others through a numerous offspring, or perhaps it was out of burning lust. At the very least, his impiety is clear because he dared to violate the most holy law of God. Though that law was to be the perpetual order of nature, that scoundrel <note>original: *nebulo*</note> set out to corrupt the laws of nature with a beast-like contempt for God. Let polygamists be ashamed of such a father—truly an outstanding stock, that of Cain and Lamech!

But indeed, even among the Hebrews, a law was established against marriage by the Legislator Moses himself <gloss>because of the hardness of the hearts of the Jews</gloss> <note>original Greek: *διὰ τὴν Ἰουδαίων σκληρότητα καρδίας* (*dia tēn Ioudaiōn sklērōtēta kardias*)</note>, which concerned divorce. It was not that Moses established that law of his own accord as something good, but "by accident" <note>In a philosophical sense, meaning a provision made due to external circumstances rather than the ideal essence of the law.</note> as a lesser evil so that greater evils might be avoided, as magistrates are often forced to do by the insolence of wicked men. That law of divorces did not approve of, but rather disapproved of divorces, and merely tolerated them. Since he could not prevail upon them to keep their wives, he commanded that they should at least give a bill of divorce, so that the women might be provided for against the cruelty of their husbands; nevertheless, in the eyes of God, they were committing adultery.

Divorces, therefore, were not done among the Hebrews without rituals. First, a bill of divorce was delivered, according to the command of Moses. Deuteronomy 24:1. 

> *When a man has taken a wife and been her husband, and it happens that she finds no favor in his eyes (because he has found some uncleanness in her), that he, writing her a bill of divorce and delivering it into her hand, shall send her out of his house, etc.* 

He adds in the following verses that the husband cannot take her again after the divorce if she has married another man, whether that later husband has hated her or when that later husband has died, because it would be an abominable thing.

...to be detested before Jehovah, and by that deed, it would be polluted. This signifies that God hated polygamy and sexual immorality; therefore, He did not wish this law to be extended into the future, which was tolerated for the present **because of hardness of heart** <note>original Greek: πρὸς τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν (*pros tēn sklērokardian*); a reference to Jesus’s explanation in Matthew 19:8 that Moses allowed divorce only because the people were spiritually stubborn.</note>. For if the ancients looked for omens in the solemnity of marriages as signs—auspices, as it were—of a lucky or unlucky union, then how much more should the omens which portended abominable things be observed in divorces? Truly, the naming itself was, among other things, a bad omen: for *sepher cerithuth* means a **scroll of cutting off**, which is the same word the Hebrews used in an excommunication <note>original: *anathemate*</note>, just as they used the word **devoted to destruction** <note>original Hebrew: חרם (*cherem*); refers to something excluded or banned from the community.</note>, because such a person was cut off from the people. Likewise, the word **apostasy**, which signifies a departure, is attributed to apostates who have deserted the Christian religion, as if they were cut off and exiled from the family of Christ the bridegroom. Hence, that word is clearly biblical and unknown to secular writers, no differently than other words that signify Christian mysteries.

For although divorces were in use even among the Heathens or secular nations, they were not observed with the same ritual and the same **legal precautions** (as the Jurists say). For in the previously praised passage of Deuteronomy 24, Moses prescribes divorce so cautiously—or rather, permits it—that from the very words of the permission, it is easily gathered to be something permitted and tolerated with difficulty. Indeed, there seems to be a certain regret for the permission implied in the one who permits it. In the very act of permission, certain precautions are placed and required from the spouse that are so rigid that it seems divorce is being discouraged rather than permitted. For instance, when it is explicitly forbidden that a reunion of the spouses ever take place, whether the second husband is alive or dead, words of horror and detestable abomination are even employed, which denotes a bad omen. Certainly, among the Heathens, no such thing was observed, and by private law, a man could put away his wife...

# ANTHONII CREGVTI
<page-num>150</page-num>
<meta>The text begins mid-sentence, completing the word "hated" from the previous page's catchword "odio".</meta>

...hated [each other], and in turn, the wife her husband; then, once repudiated, they were often joined together again. Divorces happened with a very fickle spirit over the slightest triviality. For the husband merely sent a messenger to the wife and ordered her to "keep her own belongings" <note>This refers to the Roman legal formula *tuas res tibi habeto*, the standard phrase for announcing a divorce.</note>. Indeed, they made distinctions between *divorce* and *repudiation*, as is still done today by some, just as the Greeks distinguished between **separation** <note>original Greek: διαζύγιον (*diazygion*)</note> and **dismissal** <note>original Greek: δίεσιον (*diesion*)</note>. For a **separation** occurred when a marriage could not be restored, while a **dismissal** seemed to be less severe than a divorce. A **separation** unjoined the matrimonial yoke, whereas a **dismissal** denotes a simple sending away. They distinguished between "repudiation" and "divorce" in this way: "repudiation" was between a betrothed man and woman (so named because of a shameful matter), but "divorce" was between a husband and wife (from "turning away" from each other). This distinction did not exist among the Hebrews, nor can it be proven from Scripture.

Therefore, these things are to be observed in Hebrew divorces according to the Scripture:

I. God commands that a **bill of divorce** be written (Deuteronomy 24), **"and he shall write for her a scroll of cutting off,"** <note>original Hebrew: וכתב לה ספר כריתת (*ve-katab lah sepher keritut*)</note> and given to the wife. By this delay, the impulse of the mind could be restrained, and a space for deliberation was given; just as the philosopher Athenodorus advised the Emperor Augustus to recite the 24 letters of the Greek alphabet before he allowed his anger to boil over and commit some imprudent act.

II. Because Moses expressly ensures that once the divorce was made, the severing of the bond was final, and no return between the spouses was ever granted—which was done differently among the Pagans.

III. A bill of divorce was not given easily, but only for a great crime, when the wife committed something shameful and abominable, which the Scripture points out emphatically with the word **nakedness** <note>original Hebrew: ערוה (*ervah*); often translated in this context as "uncleanliness" or "indecency".</note>. It calls this **"to uncover the nakedness or shame,"** which means being **brazen-faced** <term>brazen-faced: literally "with a rubbed forehead" (*perfrictae frontis*), a Latin idiom for someone who has lost the ability to blush or feel shame</term> and impudently casting off modesty, contrary to the saying, "He blushed; the matter is saved" <note>A quote from the Roman playwright Terence, suggesting that a sense of shame is a sign of a redeemable character.</note>.

IV. It was permitted for the husband to hand over the bill of divorce, but not the wife, because there is no equality of rights, since the man is the head of the woman. In the same way, a father—rightly or wrongly, by law or by injury—often rages against his son; indeed, in other times, he even held the power of life and death. But it would be an unspeakable crime for a son to rage against his father, and it would never go unpunished. Furthermore, when a wife was hated by her husband, he dismissed and repudiated her, lest something worse...

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS
<page-num>151</page-num>

<meta>The text begins mid-sentence, completing the thought from page 150 regarding a husband's power.</meta>

...[hatred] <note>original: "odio"</note> against her, but it was not permitted to the wife, even if the husband were detestable, because the husband had nothing to fear from the wife's hatred due to her powerlessness, according to that saying: *anger without strength is vain.*

But indeed, after Moses, the abuse of divorces grew greatly among the Hebrews, and much more so after that people were cut off from God's covenant; for the evil spread daily, and finally, more than two hundred years ago, the cruel license of husbands increased so much that specific Teachers were appointed to restrain their insolence and unbridled license. For they created Masters above the ordinary **Rabbis** <note>original: "Rabbamin"</note> whom they called **our teacher** <term>Morenu: A title of high rabbinic authority, literally "our teacher," used particularly in Ashkenazi communities to denote those authorized to decide on complex legal matters.</term>, who were the heads of the rest and the leaders of the Synagogue, to correct the overly loose license of the common Rabbis in delivering bills of divorce. Hence it is that those *Morenu* took care specifically of divorces, and within their power was the right of granting those bills of repudiation: therefore, after their institution, if anyone had repudiated his wife without obtaining a bill of repudiation from this *Morenu*, his repudiation was illegitimate. This was also observed by the most learned **Buxtorf** <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629) was a celebrated Christian scholar of Hebrew and Jewish tradition.</note> in *Hebrew Abbreviations*, and he adds that the first *Morenu* were appointed as **Maharash** and **Maharil**, that is, **Our Teacher the Rabbi Shalom** and **Our Teacher the Rabbi Jacob Levita** <note>These refer to Shalom of Neustadt and Jacob Moelin, influential 14th-century rabbis who standardized many Jewish customs.</note>.

If anyone, however, desires to know the formula for the **bill of repudiation** <note>original: "libelli repudij"</note>, he will find it described at length in **Maimonides** <note>Moses Maimonides, a preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and legal scholar.</note>, part 2, and that in the **Talmudic dialect of Babylon** <note>Aramaic, the language of the Babylonian Talmud.</note>, where the day of the week is expressed on which the bill of repudiation or expulsion was delivered, or the Letter which they call of dismissal: **"A scroll of expulsion, and a bill of release, and a letter of dismissal"** <note>original Hebrew: ספר תירוכין וגט פיטורין ואגרת שבו קין (*sefer tironin ve-get piturin ve-iggeret shebukin*)</note>; also placed in that instrument of dismissal are the day of the month, the year, and the year since the creation of the world; which circumstances having been set down beforehand, the substance of the formula is added in this manner:

> *I wish, not by compulsion, but by the free will of my mind, both to repudiate you and dismiss and expel you, so that you may no longer be my wife, but may become free and mistress of yourself to go away and marry whatever man you wish, and let no one reject you on account of my name from this day even forever. Therefore, be permitted to every man, and let this be to you...*

...by me a bill of expulsion, and a bill of repudiation, and a letter of dismissal, according to the law of Moses and Israel. <note>These terms—*libellus expulsionum*, *libellus repudij*, and *epistola dimissionis*—refer to the *Gett*, the formal document required for a Jewish divorce.</note>

However, besides that common type of repudiation when a husband would repudiate his wife, there was—and is today—among the Jews another type of repudiation, when a kinsman repudiates a kinswoman according to the law of the **Levirate** <term>Levirate: From the Latin *levir* (brother-in-law). The biblical law (Deuteronomy 25:5–10) requiring the brother of a man who died childless to marry the widow to continue the deceased's lineage.</term>. For they use this formula in matters of kinship, where they treat the question of whether the wife of a deceased brother should be married or repudiated; and when a widow is repudiated by her kinsman, a shoe is pulled off for him, and at the same time his face is spat upon, and then those standing by in this rite would cry out.

Others wish, moreover, for a third type of repudiation to have had a place between a groom and a bride <note>i.e., between betrothed but not yet fully married persons</note>; and this was the opinion of the Jesuit **Salmerón** <note>Alfonso Salmerón (1515–1585), an original member of the Society of Jesus and a prominent biblical scholar.</note> and other Papists, but it is merely supposed, not proved. Indeed, nowhere in Scripture or in the books of the Hebrews is mention made of this kind of repudiation; rather, it only takes place between married spouses. Therefore, Salmerón wrongly wonders why Joseph did not hand a bill of divorce to the Blessed Virgin when he wished to leave her—or rather, if he wished to leave her according to our opinion. Salmerón is hallucinating (I say) when he thought both that a bill of repudiation was handed from a groom to a bride among the Jews, and further, that a bill of repudiation was not written according to the command of the law unless the causes of the repudiation were cited and witnesses produced, lest the document be believed to be a forgery. For the causes of repudiation were not added, nor can an example of any such formula be given in the Hebrew rituals. The Jesuit **Lorin** <note>Jean Lorin (1559–1634), a Jesuit commentator known for his massive volumes on the Bible.</note>, also of that same society, confesses this in his commentary on Leviticus chapter 21, for he says: *In which bill it was not necessary, and indeed was not accustomed, for the cause to be expressed, since another might sometimes marry the dismissed woman, which he would hardly do if the cause were expressed.*

...was practiced among the Jews, but also by wives against their husbands; for it was reciprocal. With the reins loosened to unbridled license, men killed their wives, as witnessed by Calpurnius Bestia <note>A figure mentioned by St. Jerome; he was said to have outlived and perhaps poisoned many wives</note>, who, on account of his frequently repeated marriages, was said to "poison them with his finger"; or, having performed a divorce, they married richer, younger, and more beautiful women, a practice which St. Jerome wrote was also prevalent among the Jews.

> *And bid him to keep his own things for himself.*

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 153. # ANTHONY CREGUT

This is not true, since divorce began among the Gentiles before it was ever introduced among the Jews; indeed, it was very much in practice among the Egyptians, by whose "contagion" the Hebrews were undoubtedly corrupted. Therefore, later on, as the population increased and Moses carried out his duties as a magistrate, he used forensic or judicial law—which, for that nation, was political in nature. He did not so much command repudiation as he intended to use the law to restrain a loose and unbridled license. Thus, it was not an <term>epitaghé<note>original Greek: "ἐπιταγὴ" — an authoritative command or order.</note></term> or an <term>entolé<note>original Greek: "ἐντολὴ" — a religious injunction or commandment.</note></term>, but merely a <term>synchōrēsis<note>original Greek: "συγχώρησis" — a concession, permission, or allowance.</note></term>. By this, Moses was not commanding divorce, but only intending that if husbands were to dismiss their wives, it should not be done without a "bill of divorce." This was done so that the fickleness and license of husbands might be restrained according to the various reasons laid down above. Furthermore, that law was not meant to be perpetual, but was only for a time, granted for the sake of a "stiff-necked" people and to ensure that women were not subjected to a perpetual <term>carnificina<note>original: "carnificinæ" — literally a butchery or place of execution; here used metaphorically to mean a state of constant torment or domestic misery.</note></term>. Therefore, that law was *permission, not a command; tolerance, not approval; immunity from civil penalty, but not immunity from guilt.*

Nevertheless, a difficulty arises here. In a certain sense, it could be said that repudiation is immune not only from civil penalty, but also from guilt—not only in the <term>court of the soil<note>original: "foro soli" — a legal term referring to earthly or secular courts.</note></term> but also in the <term>court of the sky<note>original: "foro poli" — a theological term referring to the court of heaven or God’s judgment.</note></term>. This same point can be asserted regarding the polygamy of the Patriarchs. For who would dare presume that the holy Patriarchs and so many of the faithful would have violated God’s law concerning marriage so many times and so stubbornly if polygamy and divorce were truly something blameworthy and actually a sin? I respond, therefore, that divorce and polygamy were sins in and of themselves insofar as they violated the law of God, which states: *The two shall be one flesh.* Thus, there should have been no immunity from either punishment or guilt. Such was the nature of the Jews' divorce, resulting from the Egyptian contagion, before the law of Moses was delivered in Deuteronomy 24. But truly, after that law of Moses was passed—which is also considered God’s law insofar as it tolerated both divorce and polygamy—divorce and polygamy seem to be immune even from guilt by the indulgence of God. For it pleased God to grant a <term>dispensation<note>A "dispensation" is a formal exemption from a law or rule given by a higher authority.</note></term> from that law in Genesis 2:24, which was established at the institution of marriage. For the mandates of the law are twofold: some are *necessary*, others are *arbitrary*. First, the *necessary* ones are those which regard the image of God, and the transgression of which...

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of divorce, specifically distinguishing between eternal moral laws and temporary legal concessions—referred to as "arbitrary laws"—granted by God due to human weakness.</meta>

### REVEALER OF SECRETS. 155

...so strikes God’s justice that He can in no way ignore nor tolerate it, any more than He could deny Himself. For this reason, those precepts are indispensable. However, the precepts we call **arbitrary** do not, by their own nature, violate the image of God, because they are not inherently just or unjust; rather, whatever justice they contain depends upon God’s arbitrary sanction and His most free will. Therefore, when God commands such a thing, it is a sin to transgress it. On the other hand, if God, out of fatherly indulgence toward human weakness, later wishes to remit the law and dispense with the execution of the mandate for a time, then it appears there is no guilt. Therefore, <term>by comparison<note>original Greek: "συμβολὼ" (likely a variant of συμβάλλω) — to compare or bring together; here used to mean "by comparison" or "consequently."</note></term> it is a sin when the first law of marriage from Genesis 2:24 is violated. It is *not* a sin when the other law from Deuteronomy 24 concerning divorce is not violated. Furthermore, if adulteries followed after these divorces, this happened "by accident" <note>An "accidental" consequence in logic is one that follows indirectly rather than being the essential purpose of the law itself.</note>; and indeed, Christ in Matthew 19:9 did not say that divorce was the cause of adultery in and of itself, nor that he who divorces his wife immediately commits adultery, but rather He says that he commits adultery who marries another wife. Therefore, that law of divorce, as it seems, was brought forth out of fatherly indulgence for the sake of the woman in particular, so that they might be freed from the **butchery** <note>original: "carnificina" — literally a slaughterhouse or place of execution; a vivid term used here to describe a state of domestic torment.</note> of their husbands. Likewise, with respect to the husbands who voluntarily handed over a "bill of divorce," the law seems to have been decreed by the just judgment of God: for it was just that those who spurned the most holy institution of marriage, and who rejected that remedy against the lusts of the flesh, should themselves be deprived of the help of marriage, and either burn with the fire of concupiscence or weave the very snares in which they would be entangled. Hence, Christ said in the place praised above: *Whoever dismisses his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, I say he commits adultery; and he who marries her who is dismissed commits adultery.*

Do not wonder, moreover, that the law concerning divorces in Deuteronomy 24:1, 2, etc., derogates <note>To "derogate" means to partially repeal or take away the force of a previous law.</note> from the law in Genesis 2:24. For often particular laws do not follow the general law, yet they do so without a transgression of the laws: for that general law always subsists and remains firm, even if a certain particular law makes exceptions in specific cases and circumstances, on account of reasons and causes of great weight. Hence the saying: **the exception does not weaken, but strengthens the rule.** <note>original: "exceptio non infirmat sed firmat regulam" — often translated as "the exception proves the rule."</note>

<meta>This page continues the theological argument regarding the nature of the Mosaic law on divorce. It distinguishes between eternal moral laws and "arbitrary" laws—those established by God for specific historical circumstances or out of mercy for human frailty. The author reconciles the apparent contradiction between the lifelong union described in Genesis and the allowance for divorce in Deuteronomy.</meta>

->THE REVEALER OF SECRETS.<-

...strikes at God’s justice in such a way that God can in no way ignore it or tolerate it, any more than He could deny Himself. Therefore, those precepts are indispensable. But the precepts which we call **arbitrary** <note>In this theological context, "arbitrary" does not mean "random," but rather "positive laws"—rules established by God’s specific choice for a certain time or people, rather than laws inherent to the very nature of morality.</note> do not, by their own nature, violate the image of God, because they are not just or unjust in and of themselves. Instead, whatever justice they possess depends on God’s sovereign sanction and His most free will. Therefore, when God commands such a thing, it is a sin if it is transgressed; but conversely, if God—out of fatherly indulgence due to human weakness—wishes to remit the law and grant a temporary dispensation from the execution of that mandate, then it appears there is no guilt. 

Therefore, <term>sympathetically<note>original Greek: "συμπαθῶς" (sympathōs) — here meaning "with allowance for human feeling" or "out of compassion."</note></term> a sin is committed when the first law of marriage from Genesis 2:24 is violated. However, it is not a sin when the second law from Deuteronomy 24 regarding divorce is not violated. If, however, adulteries followed after these divorces, this happened as an incidental consequence; indeed, Christ in Matthew 19:9 did not say that divorce was the cause of adultery in itself. Nor did He say that he who repudiates his wife immediately commits adultery, but rather He says that he who marries another wife commits adultery. 

Therefore, that law of divorces was—it seems—enacted out of fatherly indulgence primarily for the sake of the woman, so that they might be liberated from the **butchery** <note>original: "carnificina" — a repeat of the metaphor used on the previous page to describe the cruel or life-threatening conditions wives endured in abusive marriages.</note> of their husbands. Thus, in respect to the husbands who voluntarily provided a bill of divorce, the law seems sanctioned by God’s just judgment: for it was just that those who despised the most holy institution of marriage, and who rejected that remedy against the lusts of the flesh, should themselves be deprived of the help of marriage. They would either burn with the fire of concupiscence or weave the very snares in which they would be entangled. Whence Christ says in the aforementioned passage: ***I say to you, whoever dismisses his wife, except for fornication, and marries another, commits adultery; and he who marries her who is dismissed commits adultery.***

Do not wonder, however, that the law regarding divorces in Deuteronomy 24:1-2 (and following) detracts from the law in Genesis 2:24. For often particular laws do not strictly follow the general law, yet they do so without being a transgression. That general law always subsists and remains firm, even if a particular law makes certain exceptions in specific cases and circumstances for very momentous reasons and causes. Hence the saying: ***the exception does not weaken, but strengthens the rule.***

<meta>This page continues Cregut’s theological defense of the Mosaic law regarding divorce. Having established that God may grant temporary dispensations from general moral laws due to human weakness, he now provides scriptural and historical examples of such exceptions to prove that the "bill of divorce" was a tool of divine mercy and social order rather than a promotion of sin.</meta>

# ANTOINE CREGUT

Various examples are brought forward in the Scriptures to support this: for instance, when God commands the Israelites to take the vessels and furnishings of the Egyptians by stealth and not restore what was borrowed from them, does this not deviate from the general law against theft? Similarly, regarding the **law of the levirate** <note>The "Levirate" was a Jewish custom where a man was required to marry the widow of his deceased brother to continue his lineage.</note>, which was quite celebrated among the Jews; did it not introduce a mixing of blood and remove the usual reverence for such relations? If these were permitted, why should it be judged absurd if, despite the general law of marriage, another specific law regarding divorce <note>original: *repudio* — a formal rejection or casting off of a spouse.</note> was enacted for special causes?

Furthermore, I will not refuse to review here the special causes for the bill of divorce recorded by **Augustine** in Book 19 of *Against Faustus*, chapter 26, as his words are most skillful:

> *The Lord did not say, "let whoever wants to, send away his wife"; rather, He did not want a wife to be sent away by her husband, and so He interposed this delay: I. So that the mind, rushing headlong into discord, might be restrained by the requirement of writing a document, and might reflect on how much evil there is in divorcing a wife. II. Since among the Hebrews no one was permitted to write letters except the **Scribes** alone, who professed a more excellent wisdom and were endowed with equity and piety. The law intended the husband to go to those who ought to be prudent interpreters of the law and just dissuaders of discord; He commanded the husband to give a bill of divorce only if he still insisted on sending her away. For the document could not be written except by these men, who—as this occasion and necessity came into their hands—might govern with good counsel, and by acting peacefully between the man and his wife, might urge love and harmony. But if the hatred between them was so great that it could not be extinguished or corrected, then certainly the document would be written, because it would be in vain to refuse the release of a woman whom he hated so much that he could not be recalled to the proper love of a spouse by any persuasion of the wise.*

**Maimonides** adds a similar reason in *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: *More Neuochim* (Hebrew: *Moreh Nevukhim*)</note>, Book 3, chapter 49. He argues that this cause was established so that if a woman were removed from her husband’s house by mere words, any woman could simply leave and claim she had been repudiated; or, when caught in adultery, she and the adulterer might claim she had already been divorced. Therefore, the bill of divorce was necessary so that there would be legal proof of the repudiation.

Thus far, we have brought forward the causes—whether just or unjust—by which Jews and Gentiles were moved to hand over a bill of divorce. However, according to civil law, various others are cited. 1. The New Testament follows the first cause of divorce from Matthew 5...

->*If by chance the husband is taken to heaven, the wife to hell,*<-
->*Or vice versa, they are no longer one flesh.*<-

This is proven by the example of **Adam and Eve**, for there were no more than two of them. What is most important is that this is further illustrated by the explanation of **Christ**; for while Moses had said in Chapter 2, verse 24, *And they shall be in one flesh*, Christ explains from the context and the institution itself: *And the two shall be in one flesh*. Matthew 19:5 <note>original Greek: καὶ ἔσοvται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν</note>. # ANTHONY CREGUT
V iij

...the conjugal [bond] between them, a union is made, and the two coalesce into one body: as when the Latins say, *Be unto me a protector,* that is, *become a protector.* II. The emphatic article should be noted, **the two** <note>original Greek: οἱ δύο (*hoi dyo*)</note>, those two—that is, those who were truly two persons before marriage, after they are joined in wedlock, are made one body. Indeed, he repeats this in verse 6 and introduces it like a conclusion: *And so they are no longer two, but one flesh.* The **Syriac** <note>The *Peshitta*, an ancient Syriac translation of the Bible.</note> translates it as *and those two shall be one flesh* <note>original Syriac: ונהוון תריהון חד בסר (*wa-nehuun terehun chad besar*)</note>. For the word *tereyn* <note>original: תרין</note> means "two," even though the Latin translator of the Syriac edition translates it as "both of them." The **Arabic** translator expresses the same thing with these words: *both of them* and *they shall both be* <note>original Arabic: שניהם כלא המא & ויהון כלא המא (*wa-yakun kalla huma*)</note>, for the phrase *kalla huma* corresponds to the Greek article. III. **Into one flesh** <note>original Greek: εἰς σάρκα μίαν (*eis sarka mian*)</note> is a **Hebraism** <note>A grammatical structure or idiom reflecting the influence of the Hebrew language.</note> which is not usually expressed [literally] by the Latins; hence our [Theodore] **Beza** <note>A famous 16th-century Protestant reformer and colleague of John Calvin.</note> translates it as "one flesh," and the **Vulgate** <note>The standard 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible used by the Western Church.</note> translator as "in one flesh." IV. *One flesh*, that is, one body: as Paul explains in 1 Corinthians 7:4.

Therefore, **polygamy** <note>The practice of having more than one spouse at the same time.</note> was wrongly introduced against those express words. As for the **Patriarchs** <note>The biblical fathers, such as Abraham and Jacob, who often had multiple wives.</note> among whom it was tolerated, **Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian of Western Christianity.</note> brings forward various reasons for it in his book *On the Good of Marriage*. He says it was tolerated either by a certain **dispensation** <note>A special exemption from a general law granted for a specific reason.</note>, for the sake of the "blessed seed" <note>The lineage intended to lead to the birth of Jesus Christ.</note> that was to be born from that nation, or to symbolize the future joining of the Jews and Gentiles in the Church of Christ. But examples [of past behavior] should not override divine law, according to the rule of **Tertullian** <note>An early Christian author (c. 155–220 AD) known for his rigorous defense of Christian doctrine.</note>, who established three types of legal prescriptions:

> *Neither the passage of time, nor the patronage of persons, nor the privileges of regions can dictate to the truth.*

This, however, was the true polygamy of **Lamech** <note>The first man in the Bible described as having two wives (Genesis 4:19).</note> and the Patriarchs, because they had multiple wives at the same time. However, that **digamy** <note>Literally "second marriage." Here Cregut refers to the practice of remarrying after the death of a spouse.</note> or polygamy which was introduced by **Montanus** <note>A 2nd-century leader of a Christian movement that forbid second marriages even after the death of a spouse.</note> and other heretics after the time of Christ was falsely called digamy and polygamy; this occurs when someone has several wives successively [one after another]. The Apostle [Paul] does not condemn this in 1 Timothy 3:2 when he commands that a Bishop be **the husband of one wife** <note>original Greek: μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄןדρα (*mias gynaikos andra*)</note>. For once a wife has died, the previous bond is dissolved. 1 Corinthians 7:39: *A wife is bound by the law as long as her husband lives; but if her husband falls asleep [dies], she is free to be married to whom she wishes.* But the Apostle is arguing against the **bigamy** <note>The legal or religious state of having two spouses at once.</note> and polygamy of that time, which was of two types: when someone [kept] wives at the same time...

From there, a law was even established in Athens, as witnessed by Diogenes Laertius in his *Life of Socrates*. It is no wonder, then, if [Rudolph] Goclenius <note>A German philosopher and lexicographer (1547–1628) known for his "Critical Observations."</note> says on page 104 of his *Critique* that Lamech was the "first murderer," because he was the first to create a break in the continuity of marriage. What God joined together, he separated—not indeed the soul from the body, as Adam and Cain did, but two persons, man and wife, joined by an unbreakable bond that should not be severed by any human being. Well known is the law of Valentinian Augustus <note>Valentinian I, Roman Emperor (reigned 364–375 CE).</note> concerning the taking of two wives, as he himself had been captured by the love of the Virgin Justina when the opportunity was given by his wife Severa, who also loved Justina.

Nor do the heretics restrain their momentum there; for after the prohibition of second marriages, they even began to repeatedly say that even first marriages were disgraceful, at least for Churchmen. This is what Satan attempted at the First Council of Nicaea <note>The first ecumenical council of the Christian Church, held in 325 CE.</note>; but the famous Bishop Paphnutius vehemently refused, even though he himself was unmarried <note>original Greek: ἄγαμος (*agamos*)</note>, teaching with Paul in Hebrews 13:

> *Marriage is honorable, and the bed undefiled.* <note>original Greek: καὶ κοίτη ἀμίαντος (*kai koitē amiantos*)</note>

Yet, although Satan did not obtain his goal in this Council—that Bishops should be celibate—nevertheless, his effort was not entirely in vain. For it was decreed that those who were inaugurated [ordained] as celibates should always remain in this state and should not take a wife, with Paphnutius himself even supporting this.

But thereafter, not content with this blow, the evil spirit further urged celibacy so that it might completely exile marriage from Churchmen. From this, innumerable pollutions and foul deeds would later sprout, by which the priesthood would be defiled like the Augean stable <note>In Greek mythology, a stable that had not been cleaned for thirty years; here used to signify extreme corruption.</note>, and at last—oh, infamous uncleanness!—brothels would be established. Thus, the abuse proceeded by degrees: first, the celibate clergy looked down on those who were married; then, certain others...

# ANTHONY CREGUT

...those accepted into the priesthood <term>clericatum: the clerical state or priesthood</term> voluntarily vowed continence; later, it was even sanctioned by decree that those who were celibate before being ordained as Bishops should not contract a marriage after their inauguration. Finally, marriage was forbidden to all clergy by the decrees of the Popes. Although the clergy resisted this for many centuries, that monster of a man, Gregory VII—commonly called Hildebrand—finally achieved it with a heavy hand. The Germans called him *Hellebrand*, that is, *the firebrand of hell* <note>A German pun on his name: "Hölle" (hell) and "Brand" (fire/brand)</note>, being greatly supported in this by Henry V, a servant of the Pope and the "parricide" of his own father, Henry IV <note>Henry V overthrew his father, the Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV, after the Pope turned the son against the father during the Investiture Controversy.</note>. This effort, begun by Gregory I around the year 600 when he sent a certain Roman monk named Augustine to England, was finally completed by the other Gregory around the year 1100.

It is no wonder, then, if there has been a struggle on both sides for so many centuries, with some fighting fiercely for marriage and others for virginity and celibacy. The first occasion for this was given in the time of Jerome by Jovinian <note>A 4th-century Christian monk who argued that virgins, wives, and widows were of equal merit if their lives were otherwise holy.</note>, who, in his effort to raise marriage to the heavens, spoke far too dismissively of virginity. In response, Jerome and Ambrose found a wide field in which to range, preaching the praises of virginity, often, as frequently happens, by disparaging marriage. This was depicted with a beautiful metaphor by Basil the Great <note>One of the "Cappadocian Fathers" of the early church.</note>: just as gardeners, when they strive to correct the crooked state of a tender tree, often err by bending it too far in the opposite direction. Hence arose the many slanderous insults against marriage in the following centuries, through which that well-worn proverb was fulfilled: *Slander boldly, for something always sticks.* And likewise that saying of the Emperor Claudian: *He is acquitted, but the smudge remains.*

From this came that famous saying of Jerome: "Marriage fills the earth, but virginity fills paradise" <note>original: "matrimonium terram implet, virginitas autem paradisum"</note>. He furthermore said that God approved the work of each day of creation and repeated the phrase, *He saw that this was good.* But He did not say this on the second day because (Jerome says) the number two represents marriage, and the "unclean" animals entered Noah's Ark in pairs, not individually. He even calls married people "vessels for dishonor and shame" <note>A reference to 2 Timothy 2:20.</note>. Indeed, he applies that passage from Romans 8 concerning the unregenerate to marriage: *Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.* The supporters of the Pope also preach wonders concerning Saint Henry, the "Virgin Husband" Emperor (d. 1024), and Saint Kunigunde the Empress...

<meta>This page continues Anthony Cregut’s theological exploration of marriage.
