# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS.

As was stated above, from Genesis 2:24: *They shall be two in one flesh.* These two parts are emphatically expressed in all languages, especially the Oriental ones. For in Latin they are called *vir* and *uxor* <note>original: "vir & vxor," meaning man and wife.</note>, and in Greek *anēr* and *andris* <note>original: "ἀνὴρ ἀνδρὶς." While "andris" is a rare, poetic Greek term for woman, it is used here to mirror the word "man" (aner).</note>. But among the Hebrews, the name for "woman" is taken from the name for "man." It is for this reason that the Hebrews assert that Adam used their language, for in truth, *Ishah* <note>אשה</note> is derived from *Ish* <note>איש</note>, as if you were to say "man-ess" from "man" <note>original: "virissa à viro." The author is highlighting how the Hebrew word for woman is simply the word for man with a feminine ending.</note>. Furthermore, from the word *Anashim* <note>אנשים - "men" (plural)</note> is formed the word *Nashim* <note>נשים - "women" (plural)</note>. It is as if there were some mystery in these words, as if God wished to signify emphatically by the very character of the language:

I. That Eve was taken from the rib of the man and is flesh of his flesh, just as *Ishah* is taken from *Ish*.

II. That when *Ishah* is formed from *Ish*, the letter *Yod* <note>י</note>—the sign for the number ten—is removed, and the letter *He* <note>ה</note>—the sign for the number five—is added. This is to signify the perfection of the husband over the wife, just as the number ten is more perfect than five. Indeed, ten is considered absolutely perfect because we ascend from unity up to ten, and then immediately from ten back to unity, and so on into infinity; hence, among the followers of Pythagoras <note>A Greek philosopher who believed that numbers were the fundamental reality of the universe; the "Decad" (ten) was his most sacred number.</note>, there are ten principles of things.

III. From the name *Anashim* <note>men</note> comes *Nashim* <note>women</note> by removing the *Aleph* <note>א</note>, which is the letter that signifies primacy or dominion. This is done as if to designate the primacy of the man over the woman. These things are asserted by the Hebrews; they are more clever than they are solid, and they smack somewhat of Gematria <note>A Jewish mystical tradition that interprets the numerical values of Hebrew letters to find hidden meanings in texts.</note>; nevertheless, I would not deny that these allusions are consistent with the reality and the truth of the matter.

IV. *Ish* and *Ishah* signify the conjunction between two things so effectively that they were even attributed metaphorically to all other things besides a husband and wife. For according to the testimony of Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Jewish scholar and physician.</note> in *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: "More Neuochim," Maimonides' most famous philosophical work.</note>, part 1, chapter 6:

1. *Ish* and *Ishah* are attributed to the male and female among humans.
2. They are attributed to the male and female among all other species of living creatures. In Genesis 7:2: *From every clean animal you shall take to yourself sevens, a man and his woman* <note>original: "isch veischto." In English Bibles, this is usually translated as "a male and his mate."</note>.
3. *Ishah* is also adapted to any thing that is fit and suitable to be joined with another. For example, in Exodus 26:3: *Five curtains shall be joined, a woman to her sister* <note>original: "ischah & achotah." This is a Hebrew idiom meaning "one to another," but the author notes it uses the gendered language of "woman" and "sister."</note>, that is, one with the other. From this it becomes manifest that these two words, *Ach* <note>brother</note> and *Achoth* <note>sister</note>, are used equivocally just like *Ish* and *Ishah*.

Secondly, just as the parties entering into a marriage must be only two and no more, so they must not be too...

...nearby. For this reason, the degrees of blood relation <term>consanguinity; relation by birth</term> and relation by marriage <term>affinity; relation through a spouse</term> forbidden in Leviticus 18 must be avoided, whether in the ascending line <note>ancestors like parents or grandparents</note> or in the collateral line <note>siblings, cousins, aunts, and uncles</note>. In the ascending line, these prohibitions extend infinitely. Therefore, if Adam were still alive today, he could not legally marry anyone in his direct line of descent. In the collateral line, marriage is not permitted in the first and second degrees; indeed, according to civil law, it is forbidden up to the fourth degree in the equal transverse line. However, marriages between first cousins <note>original: "consobrinorum"</note> are not forbidden by Divine Law in Leviticus 18. <meta>This page continues Anthony Cregut’s critique of the Roman Catholic Church’s handling of marriage laws. The previous page ended with examples of royal marriages within forbidden degrees, and here Cregut argues that the Papacy's power, built on granting these legal exceptions, ultimately led to its own decline, specifically through the English Reformation.</meta>

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS

<note>This page continues from the previous discussion on kings who married close relatives with Papal permission.</note>

...sisters. The power of the Popes was increased more through the granting of dispensations for forbidden marriages than any kings and princes were increased by their own marriages; thus, by the just judgment of God, those monstrous acts often turned toward their own destruction. For England defected from the Pope and the Roman Church because he had refused a dispensation of this kind to Henry VIII—not out of a holy observance of divine law, but out of fear of Charles V, who was the nephew of Henry’s wife <note>Catherine of Aragon</note>. Thus, the same thing occurred which is well known among legal experts regarding contracts: *It is dissolved in the same way it was bound* <note>original: "Eodem modo soluitur quo ligatum est"</note>. In this same way, by the just judgment of God, the Roman Church perishes by the very means through which it was enriched: the dignity and wealth of the Papacy grew greatly through marriage dispensations, and so through those same means, it greatly decreased. The same can also be said of Indulgences and Purgatory, since those things gave Martin Luther the push and provided the occasion for the Reformation.

However, two passages of Scripture that seem to weaken the law in Leviticus 18:9, 16, and 18 cannot be brought forward in defense of this error. Specifically, in Deuteronomy 25:5, the wife of a brother who died without children is commanded to marry the surviving brother. And in Genesis 38:8, there is the example of the patriarch Judah, who gave to his <term>second-born son <note>original: δευτερογόνῳ</note></term> the wife of the deceased <term>first-born son <note>original: πρωτοτόκου</note></term>, and when he also died, he promised her to a third son. But in the aforementioned place in Leviticus 18, it is forbidden <term>in so many words <note>original: αὐτολεξεὶ</note></term> *that a brother should take his brother’s wife*. Those passages (I say) do not defend the error, because—as the sons of legal experts say—exceptions do not weaken the law, but rather strengthen it. The Law of Leviticus is general and common to all nations, but the law of the <term>levirate <note>The "levirate" (from the Latin 'levir', meaning 'brother-in-law') was a Jewish law requiring a man to marry his deceased brother's widow to continue the family line.</note></term> is special and had specific reasons. For this privilege was granted to the Jewish people in this specific case so that the family might be preserved in the name of the firstborn, and so that the "firstborn" of Christ, who would never die, might be mystically signified. Augustine also relates this in his 61st Question on Leviticus. Indeed, there were many prerogatives of the firstborn among the Jews, which also looked toward Christ, the *firstborn of all creation* (Colossians 1). For some people say these passages should not be understood as referring to a biological brother, but—according to the Hebrew custom—to a relative in another degree (as when Abraham and Lot are called "brothers," even though the former was the uncle and the latter the nephew). Although that is a true feature of the Hebrew language, it cannot fit the context here.

He also reconciles the biblical prohibition against marrying a brother's widow with the specific Jewish exception of the levirate marriage.</summary>

Deuteronomy 7:3–4. And although that law may seem to be judicial or political <note>Laws specific to the ancient state of Israel</note>, nevertheless the reason offered by Moses is moral, and therefore it still applies today. For after he said: *Neither shall you make marriages with them; your daughter you shall not give to his son, nor his daughter shall you take for your son,* he adds a moral reason in verse 4: *For he would turn away your son from following me, and they would worship foreign gods.* The same point is repeated in 1 Kings 11 and is confirmed by the example of Solomon; and truly that pestilential union is so deadly and ominous that, of old, from the beginning of the world, the entire human race was corrupted by it. For in Genesis 6:2, it is related that because of that impure marital union of the "sons of God" with the descendants of Cain, a flood-gate <note>literally "a Lernaean marsh," a classical reference to a source of many evils</note> of all evils broke into the world, which could not be washed away except by the lye of a universal Flood <note>original: "Cataclyfmi vniuersalis lixiuio"</note>; indeed, they could not be entirely purged until the first world was cut off and a second was established anew.

Hence, in the New Testament, marriages of this kind are explicitly prohibited, and Paul says in 1 Corinthians 7:39: *Let her marry whom she will, only in the Lord.* And in 2 Corinthians 6:14: *Do not draw the yoke with unbelievers.* For this reason, a famous man who served the Church well <note>Possibly a reference to a Reformer like Calvin or a Church Father</note> quite rightly wrote that those marriages were joined by the Devil’s own hand, not in heaven but in hell; he who, with a strange and fatal cunning—no differently than that ancient tyrant <note>A reference to King Mezentius, who famously tied living people to rotting corpses</note>—joins the living with the dead; not to revive the dead person, which is impossible for nature, but to kill the living one, which almost always happens because of human weakness and lukewarmness in those things which concern the glory of God. Indeed, what is worse, truly speaking, both can be said to be dead. For that marriage is actually a "work of the flesh"; and as the Apostle testifies in Romans 8: *They who are in the flesh cannot please God.* Pope Siricius wrongly applies this passage to marriage—if indeed those Decretal letters <note>Letters by popes that established church law</note> are truly attributed to Siricius.

Fourthly, according to Civil Law <note>The Roman "Ius Civile," which influenced church law</note>, there are five impediments which do not allow parties to contract marriage. I. By reason of kinship, whether natural or civil (that is, through adoption). II. By reason of affinity <note>Family relationships created by marriage</note>. III. By reason of public decency. IV. By reason of...

### THE REVEALER OF SECRETS. 169

...by reason of power and office; and as far as Canon Law <note>The body of laws and regulations made by ecclesiastical authority (the Church)</note> is concerned, in the descending line <note>Lineage from parents to children, grandchildren, etc.</note> it certainly agrees with Civil Law <note>Roman law or the secular legal code</note>. In the transverse line <note>Collateral relatives, such as siblings, cousins, or aunts/uncles</note>, however, it has its own peculiar prohibitions. Hence it is that Canon Law prohibits marriage up to the fourth degree, whereas in the Law of God, the degree is further removed from the first to the second degree, such as the union of an uncle and a niece. The Lateran Council, over which Pope Innocent III presided (chapter 50), offers a reason for this that is, above all, jocular and facetious—worthy indeed of the Pontifical majesty and the gravity of the Council: *Marriage is prohibited up to the fourth degree because there are four humors <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—which medieval medicine believed controlled health</note> and four elements <note>Earth, air, fire, and water</note>.* Oh, what sagacity! Oh, what invincible reasoning! Do not be surprised, for he holds the law in the shrine of his breast <note>A legal maxim suggesting the Pope is the living embodiment of the law</note>.

But in truth, in marriages it is not only required that the contracting parties be "legitimate" <note>Legally eligible to marry</note>, but also that those who are considered legitimate (insofar as the aforementioned defects are not found in them) should also contract the marriage in a legitimate manner. Therefore, there is required:
I. The consent of the contracting parties.
II. Free consent (Law 30 *on the Rules of Law*; Law 11 *on Betrothals*).
III. If the contracting parties are under the power of their parents, their consent must furthermore intervene—even for a son who is a soldier (Law 35 *on the Ritual of Marriage*), without distinction of age. In the case of a daughter, this holds until her twenty-fifth year (Principles of the Institutes, New Constitution 115, chapter *aliud*, section 11).

And that parental consent seems to be hinted at and clearly indicated in Matthew 22:30 by the emphatic phraseology used by the Holy Evangelist: *for in the resurrection they neither marry, nor are they given in marriage* <note>original Greek: ἐν γὰρ τῇ ἀναστάσει οὔτε γαμοῦσιν, οὔτε ἐκγαμίζονται</note>. For the word *gamein* <note>γαμεῖν - to marry</note> (they lead wives) is said of men, just as *gameisthai* <note>γαμεῖσθαι - to be married</note> is said of women; but *ekgamizontai* <note>ἐκγαμίζονται - they are given out in marriage</note> is said because of the parents, who *ekgamizousi*, that is, they hand them over to be married and into the power of others. Likewise in 1 Corinthians 7:38: *So then he who gives her in marriage* <note>original Greek: ὥστε καὶ ὁ ἐκγαμίζων</note> *does well; but he who does not give her in marriage does better.* From this it is clear that in the placing of daughters, the consent of the parents—or of those in whose power they reside—is required, and that they are said to be "married" <note>original: γαμεῖσθαι</note> in the passive sense, in respect to those by whom they are given in marriage. The Vulgate <note>The standard 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> has *nubentur* <note>literally "they will be clouded/veiled"</note>, which is barbarous <note>Cregut considers this poor Latin compared to the original Greek</note>. Yet, I would easily concede that the distinction between *to gamein* <note>active: to marry</note> and *gameisthai* <note>passive: to be married</note> is not permanent; for Paul wrote in 1 Timothy 5:14 that widow women...

### ANTHONY CREGUT

...to marry <note>original Greek: γαμεῖν</note>. And in 1 Corinthians 7:34, the woman is said "to have married" <note>original Greek: γαμήσασα</note> in the passive sense, instead of "having been married" <note>original Greek: γαμηθεῖσα</note>. Nevertheless, in Matthew 22:30 and most other places, that distinction seems to be observed. <note>In ancient Greek, different forms of the verb "to marry" were used depending on whether the subject was the man (who "took" a wife) or the woman (who "was given" to a husband). Cregut is examining how the New Testament handles these linguistic roles.</note>

Thus far we have spoken of the institution of marriage and the parts necessary to it—that is, the legitimate way of entering the contract. Now follows the third part of this discussion <note>original Greek: συζητήσεως</note>, which concerns the union between the contracting parties, or the "conjugal union." Truly, the conjugal union is the soul and the bond of the entire society and contract; without it, marriage is a hollow and intolerable yoke—not merely a heavy burden <note>original Greek: δυσβάστακτον</note>, but an unbearable one <note>original Greek: ἀβάστακτον</note>. Indeed, that union is twofold: namely, corporal and spiritual. It is corporal when the husband and wife become "one flesh," and spiritual when they become "one heart."

This union is foreshadowed in the formation of Eve. For since, as Moses testifies in Genesis 2:22, she was formed from Adam’s rib, is not that conjugal union symbolized right from the start? For just as God drew the entire human race from a single beginning, He did so so that from the unity of the root, the union of the branch and the shoots might also sprout (Acts 17:26). Thus, from the man was made the "man-ess"; from <term>Man (*Ish*)</term> arose <term>Woman (*Ishah*)</term>; from Adam's rib Eve was formed, so that woman might be "bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh" (Genesis 2:23). For here, God’s providence shines forth wonderfully. For, 

> *so that the joining of the human race might be more holy (says a most learned interpreter in his commentary on that passage), He willed that both males and females should arise from one and the same principle. Therefore, He established human nature in the person of Adam, and from there He formed Eve, so that the female might only be a portion of the whole race. This is the meaning of Moses's words in chapter 1:28: "God created man: male and female He created them." In this way, Adam was warned to recognize himself in his wife, as if in a mirror. Eve, in turn, was warned to submit herself willingly to the man, as one taken from him. For if the two sexes had flowed from different origins, it would have provided an occasion for either mutual contempt, envy, or strife.*

Indeed, Moses does not use the word <term>Built (*Banah*)</term> without purpose, meaning "he built," to signify that in the person of the woman, the human race was finally finished—which previously had been like an incomplete building. Or perhaps it is because in the male and female are the two principles of generation ordained—

...materials by which the household <note>original: *oeconomia*</note> and the families of the whole world are built up. Furthermore, from the word *build* <note>original Hebrew: בנה, *banah*</note> are derived the words for *son* and *sons* <note>original Hebrew: בן & בנים, *ben* & *banim*</note>, which signify the children through whom the foundations of families are laid. This is why those words of Moses are so emphatic: *this time* <note>original Hebrew: זאת הפעם, *Zoth happaham*</note>, as if denoting that he had lacked something until now; it is as if he had said, "Now at last I have found a fitting partner, who is part of my substance and just like myself, in whom I contemplate myself as if in another."

Therefore, people can be said to be "one" in four ways:

I. *Naturally or physically*: in this way all people are one through participation in the same human nature, by which all are equally human. II. *Ethically*: through familiar conversation, they become one in will and heart, as seen in *Acts 4*. III. *Bodily* <note>original Greek: Σωματικῶς</note>: in this way a husband and wife are joined even *corporally* in marriage <note>term: *coniugium* (marriage), from the Latin for "yoking together"</note>, just as they are joined *ethically* or *morally*. IV. *Mystically and supernaturally*: in this way all the faithful, as members of Christ, become one body among themselves and with Christ the head. The first and third types of union exist in all married couples, but the second and fourth are often lacking. However, in many, all four types of union are found. For the well-known story in the history of the Franks regarding noble and illustrious couples can apply to many: "Neither could a man be found with a better wife, nor a wife with a better husband," since the final year of the marriage equaled the earlier ones in love, sweetness, honor, and delight. In others, however, the "zeal of Mandrabulus" <note>A Greek proverbial reference to someone whose devotion decreases over time; Mandrabulus found a treasure and offered a gold sheep to Hera, then silver the next year, then copper, then nothing.</note> often occurs; he offered a golden sheep the first year, a silver one the second, a bronze one the third, and finally nothing at all, even though he had vowed to offer a golden one every year.

Therefore, the union between spouses is like the *connective and indivisible essence of marriage*, just as, according to the Theologians, charity <note>original: *charitas*, referring to the highest form of Christian love</note> is the connective and indivisible essence of the Law—not the whole of the Law, but the "all" of the Law. This rightly holds a place in the law of marriage; for union and charity are the "all" of the marriage law, without which the primary bond of society is broken. It is necessary, therefore, that a wife be our "essential friend," as those who love to write on household management <note>original: *oeconomia*</note> are fond of saying. And certainly, if union and charity are required in political society among citizens, how much more are they required in the society of the household, since...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the marital bond, moving from the general definitions of union provided on the previous page to the specific legal, philosophical, and biblical nature of the relationship between husband and wife. # ANTHONY CREGUTUS #

Indeed, that is the first of all societies, and it is established not so much by civil or international law as by natural law; this is evident from the existence of the two sexes and from the purpose of marriage, namely the procreation of children. Therefore, a husband ought to rule his wife with a civil rather than a servile authority <note>In political philosophy, "civil" rule implies the governance of free people, whereas "servile" rule refers to the mastery over slaves</note>. It belongs only to Barbarians to treat women as slaves, which (as Aristotle says) is not surprising, since all Barbarians are slaves by nature; among them, no one exercises true mastery, and in their natural reasoning, "slave" and "Barbarian" mean the same thing. Indeed, the Greeks ruled over them as if they were incapable of self-governance.

Aristotle added a reason why nature intended for a woman to be distinguished from a slave: because, he says, nature created woman for different purposes than a slave. Nature intended for these "instruments" to be distinct. If anyone should object that many instruments can serve various uses—such as the "Delphic sword" <note>original: *gladius Delphicus*; a multi-purpose tool mentioned by Aristotle in his *Politics*</note> which the ancients used for fighting, sacrifices, and household tasks—he responds aptly with this axiom as a concluding summary: *Nature makes nothing like the Delphic sword.* For nature’s instruments are perfect only if each serves a single use rather than many. It is therefore something monstrous and a deviation from nature <note>original Greek: παρέκβασις τῆς φύσεως (*parekbasis tēs physeōs*)</note> if a husband scorns his wife as a slave, and much more so if he treats her with injustice. Hence the household law of Pythagoras:
> *Let all violence be absent from her who is like a suppliant,*
> *and who has been led from her father’s hearth to our home.*
Marcus Aurelius recorded this household precept:
> *A wife is often to be warned; rarely to be rebuked;*
> *never to be handled with violent hands.*
To this, we add Aristotle’s judgment regarding the people who can disturb this union, when he declares:
> *Those marriages are dangerous where the father-in-law and mother-in-law are still living.*

That union between spouses is sufficiently foreshadowed by the rib and the side; for the word *rib* or *side* <note>original Hebrew: צלע (*thelah*)</note> signifies both. First, because that rib was taken from the man and is a part of him, "bone of my bones, flesh of my flesh" (Genesis 2). By this, the mutual union between spouses is most strongly confirmed. Second, because the rib was taken from his side, this signifies that the wife is at the man’s side; for she ought to be a partner, as if standing alongside him <term>collateralis: literally "side-by-side," implying an equal status in the household</term>, reclining at the husband’s side and also constantly present in the home; not taken from his feet...

So great, therefore, is that union between spouses that they may rightly be called one flesh and one heart, or one mind, and one substance; hence it is that marriage can most truly be called the legitimate and oldest consubstantiation <term>consubstantiatio: the philosophical concept of two distinct things becoming one substance</term> of the world, which those verses point out clearly and not unskillfully:

> You do not have the same soul, but the two of you have one mind,
> You are not one body, but one flesh.

<margin>VI.</margin> The rib from which Eve was formed signifies not only the union between husband and wife, but also the union of a mother with a daughter. For Eve arose from the rib of Adam, and so she existed as if his daughter; and then that daughter was joined in marriage with the parent, because they were *flesh of flesh* from *Genesis 2*. This is what the clever poet hints at enigmatically:
> *Tell me, who was the mother who married her daughter?*
> *Whose mother was male, and had no father.* <note>This riddle refers to Adam as the "male mother" of Eve, who was then joined to him in marriage.</note>

That marital union, understood ethically, existed truly between Joseph and the Blessed Virgin, since she was betrothed to him; however, it was not a physical union, on account of her perpetual virginity—namely before birth, during birth, and after birth. Therefore, those words in *Matthew 1:18*, "before they came together" <note>original Greek: *prin ē sunelthein autous*</note>, ought not to be understood in the way that the word "come together" <note>original Greek: *sunerkhesthe*</note> is used in *1 Corinthians 7:5*, "and come together again"; to which the Latin word *coire* <note>to go together, often used as a euphemism for sexual intercourse</note> corresponds, though it is less modest. It is for this reason that Erasmus translated it poorly as "before they had met" <note>original: *priusquam congressi essent*</note>, as if Mary were already Joseph's wife from whom he nonetheless abstained, and indeed because of a vow of virginity.

Not without merit, therefore, do we say that all of nature is preserved by unity and union; indeed, there are primarily three kinds of unions: namely, the *union of the world*, the *union of spouses*, and the *union of earth and water*. I. The union of the world preserves it from destruction; hence it is said that nature abhors a vacuum, just as all animals and living things abhor imminent death. II. The union of spouses preserves the human species, which without marital union...

...would altogether cease to exist; nor would that common saying hold true: *The destruction of one is the birth of another.* <note>original: *Corruptio unius est generatio alterius*; a classic Aristotelian principle suggesting that for a new thing to be born, something else must be transformed or "corrupted."</note> This is surely what the poet hints at in that verse:

III. The union between earth and water makes all things fertile; no differently than a woman is made pregnant by a man, the earth is fertilized and impregnated by water. Not without skill, therefore, did a clever poet compose a wedding song for the earth and water, singing in this verse:

->*No birth occurs except on land or in the waves:*<-
->*Therefore, wise God joined these elements together.*<-
->*So that the human race lacks nothing that can be born,*<-
->*Earth lies as a wife beneath the water poured over her.*<-
->*Earth is the wife of water; water and earth are one globe,*<-
->*The reality matches the words: moisture and soil.*<- <note>original: *humor humus*; a Latin wordplay where *humus* (earth) and *humor* (moisture/liquid) share a linguistic root, suggesting they are inherently part of one another.</note>

Therefore, marriage is not called "death" in this sense, since it is not only the life of the married couple, but also—through the procreation of offspring—the life and preservation of the entire world. Thus, that saying does not always hold true:

->*The youth is born, the married man dies,*<-
->*The widower rises again, a second Phoenix.*<- <note>A cynical proverb suggesting that a man loses his independent identity or "freedom" when he marries, only regaining it when he becomes a widower.</note>

Therefore, not without reason did that man exalt the marital union, who considered it more precious than a "union"—that is, a pearl <term>unio: a Latin term for a large, unique pearl, used here as a pun on "union" or "oneness"</term>—and thus sang its praise:

->*Who but a fool would reject gold when it is offered?*<-
->*A pearl is offered to us, yet it is rejected.*<-

In truth, the praises of union are so great that it is considered even more excellent than "unity" itself. For in unity there can be no union, as a union requires at least two—such as exists between a married couple, which was the first of all unions. Indeed, God himself, lest he be alone and so that he might be united with his creation in the swiftest marriage, deigned not only to create that world, but to re-create it; hence the Prophet says: *God has betrothed us in eternal mercies.* <note>A reference to Hosea 2:19. The author suggests God's relationship with humanity is modeled on a marriage.</note> Therefore, just as the Scripture rightly says of all solitude, *Woe to the one who is alone*, <note>original: *vae soli*; from Ecclesiastes 4:10.</note> so it is also said in respect to him who leads a celibate life, devoid of marriage.

From this, the Hebrew Doctors claim that the marital union is foreshadowed in the Hebrew names for man and woman, *ish* and *ishah* <note>original: איש (*ish*) and אשה (*ishah*)</note>. For when there is union between husband and wife, *Yah*—the Name of the Lord—dwells in the midst of the couple, just as His name *Yah* <note>original: יה (*Yah*), composed of the letters *Yod* and *He*</note> is found within those words. <note>The letter *Yod* (י) is found in *Ish* (man) and the letter *He* (ה) is found in *Ishah* (woman). Just as marital union is the work of God, so are marital strife and discord the work of Satan. On the contrary, nothing dissolves the marital union and separates those joined together more than polygamy and fornication or adultery. True union can only exist between two spouses; for if it is divided among many, the bond is loosened too much, and the knot—which ought to be a Gordian knot <note>An ancient metaphor for an unbreakable or extremely complex bond.</note>—is untied. I. For the union and the essential nature of marriage is broken no more by many wives than it is by two. Therefore, in this subject, polygamy and bigamy mean the same thing, just as in Hebrew the word for "two" <note>original Hebrew: שנים (*shnayim*)</note> can signify "many." For example, in Psalm 62:11: *God has spoken once; twice have I heard this* <note>The author cites Psalm 62:12 following the Latin Vulgate numbering; in modern Bibles, this is Psalm 62:11.</note>, meaning "I have heard it often." The reason is that whoever departs from "one" falls away into nothingness or into multiplicity.

This must be understood, however, as referring to illicit polygamy, not to that which is licit, conceded, or tolerated. As stated above, there are three types of polygamy:
I. Licit, when one enters a second marriage after the first has been legally dissolved, either by death or by some other legal right.
II. Doubtful or tolerated, when one had several wives at the same time. Among the Jews, God tolerated this through a certain <term>divine condescension</term> <note>original Greek: συγκαταβάσει (*synkatabasei*), a theological term for God's willingness to accommodate human weakness or historical context.</note>, though it was prohibited by Roman laws.
III. Permitted, when men married another after divorcing a wife. This was permitted by Roman laws for both men and women; however, among the Jews, as mentioned above, divorce <note>original Latin: *repudium*</note> was permitted for husbands but not for wives. For among those people, many things were allowed for men that were forbidden for women. Thus in Numbers 5, the privilege was given to husbands alone to investigate a suspected woman through the "waters of proof" <note>The "ordeal of the bitter water" described in Numbers 5:11–31, a ritual used to determine if a wife had been unfaithful.</note>. II. Fornication and adultery dissolve the conjugal bond, since the husband and wife are then no longer "two in one flesh," but the adulterer becomes one with the adulteress or the prostitute. He affirmed that the latter two are dissolved by adultery, but not the first, because even if a husband and wife do not live together and there is no carnal cohabitation at home, they are nonetheless bound by a perpetual conjugal bond. Finally, he adds that this conclusion is supported by Apostolic tradition, but the words of the Gospel are not so clear that the Lutherans can be easily convinced by them. Regarding polygamy, he asserted it is condemned by the law of nature and cannot be permitted; and that the Patriarchs <note>Biblical ancestors such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.</note> were either granted a dispensation by God, or they sinned.

Given that specific bond and conjugal union, it is no wonder that in the creation of the beasts there is no mention of "male and female" in the same way as "man and woman"; for the lusts of beasts are wandering by the impulse of nature. If, however, it happens otherwise in a certain kind of animal, this is done for the sake of example, as when the wise man sends us to the ants <note>A reference to Proverbs 6:6: "Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise."</note>.

But sexual immorality <note>original Latin: *scortatio*, referring to fornication or the use of prostitutes.</note> dissolves the bond and essence of marriage, because a man with a prostitute becomes "one flesh," and thus he sins against his own body, not outside the body as happens in other sins. However, that which is being abused is *outside* the body—for example, when someone gorges himself on wine, he uses his limbs as instruments but abuses the wine; likewise, a thief abuses his neighbor’s goods, or a murderer abuses a blade. But indeed, the fornicator uses himself as the organ and additionally abuses his own body, which he foully defiles and lustfully pollutes; whereas, by contrast, in other sins the stain is more internal than external. Add to this that in no other sin do bodies merge into one, as a man merges with a prostitute.

...and one flesh with a prostitute: but through marriage, she becomes his own person and his spouse, and, as it were, a lawful "matter" in the act of lying together, in which those waves of lust may be broken. This occurs without sin (says Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian whose views on sex and marriage—specifically that sex is only truly "sinless" when intended for procreation—dominated Western thought for centuries.</note>) if the union is done for the sake of procreating offspring. However, it is done with sin and the disgrace of fornication if any abuse of an otherwise lawful thing should intervene; for indeed, the procreation of children is the natural and primary end of marriage itself, while by accident—and because of sin—the secondary end is a bridle and restraint for boiling lust. 

Just as in another kind of desire—namely, for food—certain foods are forbidden, such as those sacrificed to idols <note>original: *idolothyta*. This refers to the early Christian debate over whether it was permissible to eat meat that had been offered to pagan gods.</note>; others are permitted. One is never and nowhere allowed to eat forbidden things like those sacrificed to idols, but one is indeed allowed to use permitted things, yet without excess, because one is not allowed to abuse them. In the same way, it is not lawful for those who are single to lie with any woman, nor is it lawful for the married to do so indiscriminately with everyone, but only with one's wife—and even with one's wife, not intemperately or for the sake of lust. 

Augustine teaches this same principle regarding all the senses, and regarding the lust of the flesh, the enticements of curiosity, and pride, whenever someone crosses the boundaries of natural decency, for which all things were instituted by God so that they might be perfectly ordered. This is why Augustine, in Book 2 of *Against Julian*, chapter 7, praises Ambrose <note>Ambrose (c. 339–397), the Bishop of Milan and a mentor to Augustine.</note>, the Bishop of Milan, who calls a man who is intemperate in marriage with his wife an "adulterer." Augustine also says in his 53rd Sermon *On Various Subjects*, chapter 13:

> *Whoever desires his wife's flesh more than that boundary prescribed for the sake of procreating children acts against the marriage tablets themselves. The solemn clause of these tablets is read out in the sight of all witnesses: "for the sake of procreating children." For who, with a healthy mind, gives his daughter over to another man’s lust? But so that parents do not have to blush, the tablets are read aloud, so that they may be fathers-in-law and not pimps <note>original: *lenones*. The author is highlighting the legal and social distinction between a father arranging a marriage and a person facilitating prostitution.</note>. The father's brow is wiped clean and cleared once the words of the tablets are heard.*

This refers to Philip's famous bigamous marriage to Margarethe von der Saale, which he justified as a "remedy" for his high libido after his first wife, Christine of Saxony, gave her consent.</note>. When his body was inspected by physicians, he was found to be a **triorches** <note>original: *triorches*. A Greek-derived term for someone born with three testicles; in this period, it was often cited as a biological explanation for extreme sexual drive.</note>.

Rightly, therefore, according to those ends of marriage, the sons of the Jurisconsults <note>Legal scholars or experts in Roman law.</note> define "nuptials" or "marriage" in this way: *Nuptials, or marriage, is the union of a man and a woman, containing an inseparable partnership of life.* Title 9, Section 1. To Modestinus <note>Herennius Modestinus, a celebrated Roman jurist of the 3rd century AD.</note>, it is thus: *Nuptials are the union of a male and a female, and a consortium of the whole of life, a communication of divine and human law.* Law 1, *Digest on the rite of marriage*. 1. It is called a **union**, not of bodies (since that can exist without marriage in wandering lusts), but of **minds**; for which reason **it is consent, not cohabitation, that makes a marriage.** Law on nuptials, *Digest on the rules of law*. And that union of minds, or consent, is not regarding the future (as are **betrothals** <note>original: *sponsalia*. These were formal promises to marry later, which carried legal weight but were distinct from the marriage itself.</note>, Law 1, *Digest on betrothals*), but nuptials are spoken of regarding the present; and a "betrothal regarding the present" is rightly judged as a true marriage, and therefore cannot be dissolved. Chapter penultimate, Chapter 13, *On the betrothal of two*.

II. Nuptials are said to **contain an inseparable habit of life.** This is because civil law prohibits the **separation of the bed** <note>original: *thori separationem*. Commonly known as "separation from bed and board," where a couple lives apart but remains legally married.</note> (Law 8, *Code on Repudiation*), which is admitted more easily under Canon Law. III. It is called **of all life**, because the spouses share the same fortune. IV. **Communication of divine and human law**: **Human**, because the wife enjoys the status of the husband, and therefore follows his domicile and his legal jurisdiction (Law 65, *On Judgments*; Law 19, *On Jurisdiction*). Likewise, she participates in his honors (Law 13, *Chapter on Dignities*). **Also of divine law**, because wives become participants in the **private rites** <note>original: *sacrorum privatorum*. In ancient Rome, each family had its own specific religious rituals and household gods; a bride would leave her father's rites to join her husband's.</note> of the husband, which was the custom among the Romans who once worshipped gods privately in addition to the public rites (Law 4, where Gothofredus <note>Denis Gothofredus (1549–1622), a famous jurist who edited the Corpus Juris Civilis.</note> comments on the *Code on criminal expenses*). The ancient Hebrews designated all these things with an emphatic phrase when they said a man **spread the wing of his cloak** over his wife, as is said in the Book of Ruth regarding Boaz and Ruth, Chapter 3:9: *And he said, "Who are you?" and she replied, "I am Ruth..."*

*...your handmaid said, that you should spread your wing over your handmaid, because you are a redeemer.* <note>A reference to Ruth 3:9, where Ruth asks Boaz to marry her. In the ancient Near East, spreading a cloak over someone was a symbolic act of marriage and protection.</note> In the Hebrew, it is *ci goel attah* <note>original: כי גאל אתה</note>, a word that signifies a kinsman or close relative who had the legal right to redeem property and to father children on behalf of a deceased brother. In Genesis 20:16, the Scripture uses another most expressive phrase when Abimelech said to Sarah, *Behold, I have given a thousand pieces of silver to your brother; behold, he is to you a covering of the eyes before all who are with you.* <note>Sarah was Abraham's wife, though Abraham initially told Abimelech she was his sister. This signifies the right that a husband has over his wife and his duty to protect her; conversely, it explains the duty of wives toward their husbands through a synecdoche <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole.</note>—namely, that they should revere their husbands and be subject to them. Ephesians 5:9. For as a sign of subjection, the wife is veiled. In Genesis 24:65, Rebecca, upon seeing Isaac, took a veil and covered herself. And in 1 Corinthians 11, verses 6 and 7, it says of the woman, *let her be covered* <note>original Greek: καλυπτέσθω</note>. But of the man in verse 7: *A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but woman is the glory of man.* For a veil would be a disgrace to a man, since he is subject to no one, but in this world reflects the majesty of God in respect to absolute dominion; thus he is His image and glory, just as princes and nobles in a court are the glory of the king, which is why they are splendidly adorned. But a woman wears a veil in the presence of her husband without disgrace, because she rejoices to be subject to her husband, and that subjection is voluntary; in this way, she is the glory of the man, just as the subjects of a king boast of their prince. It is for this reason that the Apostle in verse 10 calls the woman’s veil "power" or "authority" <note>original Greek: ἐξουσίαν</note>. *For this reason a woman ought to have power on her head, because of the angels.* "Power" <note>original: ἐξουσίαν</note> here is a metonymy <note>A figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it.</note> for the veil, because it serves as a testimony of her subjection. From this, among the Latins, women who passed into the power of a husband were said *to veil themselves* <note>original: *nubere*. The Latin word for a woman getting married, *nubere*, literally means "to veil oneself," related to the word for a cloud or "nuptial" veil.</note>. Just as a cap <note>original: *pileus*. A felt cap worn by freed slaves in Rome to signify their new status.</note> was a sign of the condition of freedom among the ancients, so the veil was a sign of subjection for women toward their husbands, and of reverence toward the "Angels"—that is, the Pastors and those prophesying in the Church.

The Apostle confirms and illustrates this doctrine from the formation of the woman in verses 8 and 9: *For man is not from woman, but woman from man. Neither was man created for the sake of the woman, but woman for the sake of the man.* And in Ecclesiasticus 17...

# ANTHONY CREGUT #

184

*He created from him (namely, the man) a helper like unto himself (namely, the woman).* And Thomas Aquinas <note>A hugely influential 13th-century philosopher and theologian.</note> in the first part of his *Summa Theologica, question 92, article 2*, brought forward very beautiful reasons for this. For he says:

I. That man might be the principle <note>The source or origin.</note> of the whole species, just as God is the principle of the whole universe, it was fitting for the woman to be formed from the man in that first institution, more so than in other animals. Acts 17: *God made from one every race of men.*

II. So that the man might love the woman more and adhere to her more inseparably, while knowing that she was produced from himself. Hence in *Genesis 2*, it is said she was *taken from the man*, and *a man shall leave*, etc. And this was especially necessary in the human species, in which the male and female remain together for the whole of life.

III. Because, as the Philosopher <note>This refers to Aristotle, specifically his work *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book 8.</note> says in the *8th book of Ethics*, the male and female in humans are joined together not only for the necessity of procreation, as in other animals, but also for domestic life, where the man is the head of the woman.

IV. The reason is sacramental. For it is symbolized through this that the Church takes its beginning from Christ. Ephesians 5. Thus far Aquinas. 

Aquinas adds in article 3 that the woman was formed from the rib of the man to signify a social union between the husband and wife; for the woman ought not to rule over the man, because she was not formed from his head; nor should she be despised by the man as a slave, because she was not formed from his feet. Furthermore, it foreshadowed the Church; because from the side of Christ sleeping on the cross, the sacraments—that is, the blood and the water—were to flow, by which the Church was established.

Since, therefore, this is the social union between husband and wife, and that helper like unto the man is so necessary, it is not without reason that so many praises are told in Scripture concerning a wise woman, and conversely, so many reproaches against a moody woman. *Proverbs 19:14*: *House and wealth are a possession from fathers, but from the Lord is a prudent wife.* *Proverbs 21:9*: *It is better to dwell in a corner of the roof than with a contentious woman in a shared house*—that is, a most inconvenient place under the open sky, where the sun, winds, rain, and storms of every kind harass the inhabitants.

It is therefore clearly established from what was said above that marriage was instituted for those purposes already explained, but not so that it would be a Sacrament of the Church, as the Romanists <note>original: *Pontificij*; followers of the Pope. Cregut is writing from a Protestant perspective.</note> claim. Indeed, there is no passage of Scripture from which this can be proven, neither in its exact words <note>original: *autolexei*</note> nor by logical consequence. If any passage is brought forward by the Romanists, it is not cited in its pure and genuine <note>original: *gnēsion*</note> form, but is corrupted by a faulty translation or a fake commentary, such as Ephesians 5:32: *This is a great mystery: but I speak of Christ and the Church.* In the Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible used by the Catholic Church.</note> the word **Sacrament** is used, for it always translates the Greek word for mystery <note>original: *to mysterion*</note> in this way. Thus, the Romanists err in two ways:

I. In their translation, by confusing "mystery" with "Sacrament." For "mystery" is a broader term; while every Sacrament is a mystery, the reverse is not true. In fact, by the power of the word itself, mystery does not mean **Sacrament**, but **secret** or **hidden thing** <note>original: *arcanum*</note>. Nevertheless, I would not deny that the nine Christian nations counted in the world today designate their liturgy with the notion of a mystery (as observed by that great and incomparable man among the learned, Joseph Scaliger <note>A famous 16th-century scholar and philologist known for his work on chronology and linguistics.</note>, in his notes on the New Testament). This naming was undoubtedly taken from the Greek *mysterion*, which is the mother tongue of both the name and the thing, telling wonders about all things <note>original: *panta peri pantōn teratologoumenē*</note>.

Hence, the Mass among all peoples and languages is called *myster, mystir, mystiri, mysterion*. Indeed, even for the Latins themselves: for the word "Mass" <note>original: *Missa*</note> was still foreign and unknown to them, as is clear from the Cotonian derivation <note>Referring to Pierre Coton, a Jesuit who attempted to find Hebrew origins for Catholic terms.</note> of the Hebrew phrase *missath nidbath* <note>original: מסת נדבח; "a voluntary offering"</note> in Deuteronomy 16. This is hissed out with a laugh by other Jesuits—specifically Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine, a leading Catholic theologian and cardinal.</note>—in his first book on the Mass, chapter 1. The word *raz* or *raza* <note>original: רז, רזא; meaning "secret" in Aramaic/Chaldean.</note> corresponds to this word "mystery," which, according to Bellarmine, is more in use among the Chaldeans than the Hebrews, which is why the Hebrews have not yet found its true root.

II. The Romanists are hallucinating regarding the sense of the text. For in that passage of Ephesians 5:32, the topic is not physical marriage—which they want to be a Sacrament—but mystical marriage, which he explains with these words: *but I speak of Christ and the Church.*

Therefore, it is not faith and the Holy Spirit speaking in Scripture that instituted marriage among the Sacraments, but the Roman faith and the spirit of the Pope speaking in tradition, lured by ambition and greed. For that most crafty spirit saw *with efficacy*...

It is therefore clearly established from what was said above that marriage was instituted for those ends explained beforehand, and not so that it would be a Sacrament of the Church, as the Papists <note>original: *Pontificij*; a common 17th-century Protestant term for Roman Catholics who follow the Pope.</note> claim. If any passage is brought forward by the Papists, it is not cited in its pure and genuine <note>original: *γνήσιος* (gnēsios)</note> form, but corrupted by a depraved version or a false gloss, such as Ephesians 5:32: *This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the Church.* In the Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible translation used by the Roman Catholic Church.</note> it is put as *Sacramentum*, for thus it always translates the Greek term for "the mystery" <note>original: *τὸ μυστήριον*</note>.

And so the Papists err in two ways:

**I.** In the translation, by confusing "mystery" with "Sacrament." For a "mystery" is a broader category; while every Sacrament is a mystery, the reverse is not true. Indeed, by the very force of the word, "mystery" does not mean "Sacrament," but "a secret, a hidden thing" <note>original: *secretum, arcanum*</note>. Nevertheless, I would not deny that the nine Christian nations numbered in the world today designate their liturgy by the notion of "mystery" (as that great and, among the learned, incomparable Joseph Scaliger <note>A famous 16th-century scholar of history and linguistics.</note> observed in his notes on the New Testament). This naming was undoubtedly taken from the Greek *mysterion*, which language is the mother of both the name and the thing, [the Greeks] speaking wonders about everything <note>original: *πάντα περὶ πάντων τερατολομεύη* (panta peri panton teratologoumenē)</note>.

Hence the Mass among all peoples and languages is called *myster, mystir, mystiri, mysterion*; indeed, even by the Latins themselves. For the word "Mass" <note>original: *Missa*</note> was still foreign and unknown to them, as is clear from the "Cotonian" origin <note>Referring to the Jesuit Pierre Coton, who argued the word "Mass" came from Hebrew.</note> from the Hebrew *missath nidbath* <note>See Deuteronomy 16:10: "a tribute of a freewill offering."</note>. This etymology is hissed off with laughter by other Jesuits—for instance Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine, a leading Catholic theologian and Cardinal.</note>—in his *On the Mass*, book 1, chapter 1. To this word "mystery" responds the word *raz, raza* <note>The Aramaic/Chaldean word for "secret."</note>, which, according to Bellarmine, is more in use among the Chaldeans than the Hebrews, which is why the Hebrews have not yet found its true root.

**II.** The Papists are deluded by reason of the sense. For in that passage of Ephesians 5:32, the subject is not physical marriage—which they want to be a Sacrament—but the mystical marriage, which the Apostle Paul explains in these words: *but I speak of Christ and the Church.*

Therefore, it was not faith and the Holy Spirit speaking in Scripture that instituted marriage among the Sacraments, but the Roman faith and the spirit of the Pope speaking in tradition, lured by ambition and greed. For that most crafty spirit saw, which *with efficacy*

<meta>This page continues Anthony Cregut's critique of Catholic arguments regarding clerical celibacy. On the previous page, he discussed the nature of marriage as a sacrament. Here, he shifts to a grammatical and historical refutation of Cardinal Duperron's interpretation of Church councils and Scripture, specifically focusing on how the word "forbid" is used in the context of marriage and dietary laws.</meta>

<page-num>188</page-num>
->### ANTHONY CREGUT<-

Cardinal Duperron <note>Jacques Davy Duperron (1556–1618), a French cardinal and diplomat known for his polemics against Protestants.</note> argues that marriage should be forbidden to bishops and other clergy; but the text rather prohibits them from *abstaining* from marriage. Otherwise, Hosius of Corduba <note>A 4th-century bishop who was a prominent figure at the Councils of Elvira and Nicaea.</note>—who presided over that Council <note>Likely referring to the Council of Elvira.</note>, and who also attended Nicaea and is believed by many to have presided there—would undoubtedly have opposed Paphnutius <note>An Egyptian bishop at the Council of Nicaea (325 AD) who famously argued against mandatory clerical celibacy, suggesting that "marriage is honorable."</note> in the Council of Nicaea when he spoke against enforced celibacy. *Therefore, to forbid one from abstaining from their spouse is not the same as ordering them to abstain.* Nor should Jacques Davy <note>Another reference to Cardinal Duperron.</note> find support in the passage from 1 Timothy 4:3, *forbidding to abstain from foods*, which they claim signifies *ordering to abstain from foods*. The Cardinal explains this incorrectly; for in the original text we do not read *forbidding to abstain from foods*, but *forbidding to marry* <term>κωλυόντων γαμεῖν</term>, and *[commanding] to abstain from foods* <term>ἀπέχεσθαι βρωμάτων</term> <note>original Greek: *kōlyontōn gamein, apechesthai brōmatōn*.</note>. In this instance, "to abstain" should not be linked with the word "forbidding," but rather the word *ordering* must be supplied from the sense of the passage, along with the conjunction "and," since the sentence has two parts. Indeed, Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his works against heresies.</note> supplied that missing word, *ordering* <term>κελευόντων</term> <note>original Greek: *keleuontōn*.</note>, in his writing against the Cataphrygians; the very diligent Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a key Protestant reformer and biblical scholar.</note> also observed this in his notes. It is like the phrasing in Homer: *eating food and [drinking] wine* <term>σῖτον καὶ οἶνον ἔδοντες</term> <note>original Greek: *siton kai oinon edontes*. Here, the verb "eating" applies to the food, but a verb like "drinking" is implied for the wine.</note>. Thus, the omission <term>ellipsis</term> <note>A linguistic term for when a word is left out because it is understood from the context.</note> must be filled: *forbidding to marry, and ordering to abstain from foods*. In this way, a verb of related or connected meaning is supplied to draw out the sense; this also occurs in 1 Corinthians 14:34, where there is an omission of the word *must*, when it says *it is not permitted for women to speak, but to be submissive*—supply: *but it is necessary that they be submissive*. Thus the scholars of Leuven <note>The Catholic University of Leuven, which produced influential Bible translations.</note> filled the omission in the Vulgate version by saying *commanding to abstain*, just as our French version does. Indeed, among the Hebrews there are countless examples of omissions, of nouns as well as verbs and other parts of speech, and in the New Testament the Apostles generally follow these "Hebraisms" of the Old Testament. This even occurs occasionally among Latin authors, such as in Virgil: *He himself sat with the Quirinal staff and the small robe, girt in the trabea* <note>Referring to the *Aeneid*, Book 7. The *trabea* was a ceremonial robe; the *lituus* (Quirinal staff) was an augur's wand.</note>. Here there is an omission of a verb that would be of a similar meaning to the word *staff* <term>lituo</term>, which signifies the curved wand first used by Romulus, and later by the augurs to mark out the sacred spaces <term>templa</term> with birds. One was not "girt" with a staff as they were with a robe. Therefore, there is a missing verb. For this reason, the Syriac translator also fills the omission in the previously praised passage of 1 Timothy 4:3...

<meta>catchword: ...omission [psin]</meta>

He refutes Cardinal Duperron's interpretation by citing historical figures like Paphnutius and linguistic examples from Homer and Virgil.</summary>

...supplying the verb that is missing in the Greek: <term>ומפריקן מן מאכלתא</term> <note>Syriac: *vemaphrekin men mecolotho*.</note> *and they make [them] abstain from foods.* The Arabic version, which almost always follows the Syriac, here contains the omission of the verb along with the Greek original. The most learned Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major Protestant reformer and scholar who succeeded Calvin in Geneva.</note> also explains this omission of the verb differently based on an observation of a Hebrew idiom: namely, that among the Hebrews, the same word <term>צוה</term> <note>Hebrew: *tzavah*.</note> can signify contrary things—both *to command* and *to forbid*. There are other words of this kind among the Hebrews; for instance, <term>ברך</term> <note>Hebrew: *barak*.</note> signifies both *to bless* and *to curse* in the *piel* <note>The *piel* is a Hebrew grammatical "stem" usually indicating intensive action; here it refers to the euphemistic use of "bless" to mean "curse."</note> form. Therefore, <term>צוה</term> (*tzavah*) or *tzivah* in the first part of the verse would signify *to forbid marriage*, and in the second part *to command abstaining from foods*, just as that specific sense of *tzivah* is found in Deuteronomy 1:37: "Finally, all things which *Jehovah our God had forbidden*." <term>וכל אשר צוה יהוה אלהינו</term> <note>Hebrew: *ve-kol asher tzivah Yehovah Eloheinu*.</note>. From all of this, it is clear that Cardinal Duperron's excuses are empty, and the passage from Paul does not agree with the position of the Council. Indeed, after that Council of Elvira was convened in Spain, the Spanish Bishops remained married, which sufficiently explains the meaning of the canon <note>Cregut argues that if the Council of Elvira (c. 306 AD) had actually banned clerical marriage, the bishops would have separated from their wives immediately, which historical records suggest they did not.</note>.

It remains at present, as a conclusion to this article, for us to discuss the **mystical marriage** and see how it was foreshadowed from the beginning. 

**I.** We explain <term>τὸ ὅτι</term> <note>Greek: *to hoti*, a philosophical term meaning "the fact of the matter."</note> and the reason for it: namely, that the marriage of Adam was a **type** <note>A "type" is a person, event, or institution in the Old Testament seen as a prophetic foreshadowing of something in the New Testament.</note> of the marriage of Christ. For there seems to be a reason for doubting this that should not be ignored: if Adam’s marriage was instituted for the purpose of being a type of Christ’s, and if Eve was formed from the man's rib so that the union of Christ with the Church might be signified, it would seem that God thought about Christ and the Church *before* the creation, and consequently, about grace *before* sin. This would completely overturn the order of the divine decrees <note>This refers to a complex Calvinist debate (Supralapsarianism vs. Infralapsarianism) regarding whether God decided to save humanity before or after He decreed that humanity would fall into sin.</note>. Hence it is that Paul in Ephesians 5:25 brings in the reason of sin when he says: *Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the Church and gave himself up for her.* 

I respond that "types" must be distinguished, for they are of two kinds: some are **according to nature** <note>original Greek: *kata physin*.</note> and others are **according to convention** <note>original Greek: *kata synthēkēn*.</note>. The former signify naturally because of a certain similarity found in nature...

And although a work of nature can never produce a state of grace (since the power of nature is not a privation from which the form of grace is drawn out, but rather a logical or negative one), nevertheless God sent nature first as a teacher, intending later to submit grace to her, so that we might more easily believe in grace and <term>the wisdom in a mystery</term> <note>original: *τῇ σοφίᾳ ἐν μυστηρίῳ* (*te sophia en mysterio*)</note> when it was revealed. Hence it is that the mysteries of faith are above reason, not against reason; rather, God revealed them in Scripture according to our way of conceiving them. Indeed, even those things which are called "internal works" <note>Theological term for the inner relationships of the Trinity.</note> have been revealed to us, not as they are identical in God, but according to our formal concepts.

...with **eternal mercies, when he chose us in Christ.** <note>original: *misericordiis aeternis, quum nos elegit in Christo.*</note> Ephesians 1. Finally, the consummation of that marriage will take place in heaven, when we shall enjoy the bridegroom and his blessings perfectly and for eternity.

V. In the marriage of Adam, three distinct things are considered: namely, **uniting, union, and unity.**
*   **Uniting** <note>original: *vnitio*</note> precedes the **union** <note>original: *vnio*</note> which results from that act of uniting.
*   The **union** is, by the priority of its nature, prior to the **unity** <note>original: *vnitas*</note>, because the male and female do not become "one" except after the union of the two, according to that passage in Genesis 2 and Matthew 19: *they shall be two in one flesh.*
*   Furthermore, **uniting** refers to a "transient act" passing from the one who unites to the one who is united.
*   **Union**, however, refers to a permanent state in those who are united, since the union lasts and perseveres.
*   But **unity**, since it exists inwardly from the union, lasts as long as the union lasts, and if the union is dissolved, the unity is also dissolved.

**Uniting** comes from God, who joins the spouses; **union** comes from the spouses, who join themselves to one another. **Unity** comes from the union that has been made between the contracting parties. **Uniting** depends on God as its starting point, but its goal is reached in the spouses. **Union** exists relatively in the husband and the wife, as the "related" and "correlated" parties. But **unity** is the fulfilled end of this union, and like a final form in which the spouses find rest.

Finally, that whole—or that "one"—which emerges from that uniting and union is not a <term>Physical whole</term> <note>original: *totum Physicum* - a single biological organism.</note> or a <term>continuous whole</term> <note>original: *totum continuum* - like the parts of a single limb.</note>, such as the union of limbs in a body. Rather, it is a <term>Political whole</term> <note>original: *totum Politicum* - a social or legal body made of distinct individuals.</note>, or an "economic" or "discrete" whole, such as the union of a king and his subjects, or a shepherd and his flock. Add to this the bond of this union, which is the spirit and charity. Add also—

the mode or reason for the union, because Adam and Eve are not united simply as human beings—since there is already an identity of nature in them, and therefore they are already "one thing." Indeed, <term>unity</term> <note>original: *vnitas*</note> implies something more than <term>union</term> <note>original: *vnio*</note>. Rather, they are considered "united" as male and female, in respect to their sex, and in this way they were merely similar. For things that are similar are "united," but things that are exactly the same are not; whether that similarity is a visible quality or a hidden property—just as things are united by a sympathy arising from their <term>unique temperament</term> <note>original Greek: *ἰδιοσυγκρασίᾳ* (idiosyncrasy), referring to the specific physical or mental makeup of an individual</note>, just as they are separated by antipathy.

But truly, all these things are found in a more eminent way in the mystical marriage of Christ with the Church. 

I. The **uniting** <note>original: *vnitio*</note> is performed by the entire Trinity, just like the incarnation of the Son, because it is an "external work" of God. For although Christ—in whom the uniting finds its end—is the Son of God, nevertheless that work is "external." This is because in that union, Christ is not considered as he is the Son of God and <term>of the same substance</term> <note>original Greek: *ὁμοούσιος* (homoousios), the theological term meaning Christ is of the exact same essence as God the Father</note> begotten of the Father from eternity, but as he is the Son of God through the grace of the **hypostatic union** <note>The theological doctrine that Christ is one person with two natures: fully divine and fully human.</note>. Furthermore, that union is not only with Christ, but also with the Church; therefore, the uniting is completed externally, both in respect to the bridegroom and the bride. 

II. Just as in Adam and other married persons the "act of uniting" precedes the "state of union," and "union" precedes "unity" by a priority of nature, so it is in the mystical marriage. And just as in the former, so in the latter, **unity** belongs to the same thing, while **union** belongs to two things. Thus, unity regards the species (the type of being); but union regards the individuals. So in human society, men are "one thing" specifically (as a species), but individuals are united among themselves. Among spouses there is also a "specific unity" when they become **one flesh**, but this is in the "species" of marriage; for a husband and wife are not only "one human" specifically, but also relatively—and if I may say so—*conjugally one flesh*, even though they remain two in terms of their persons and their sex. 

III. Just as in Adam and other married persons the "uniting" is transient (a passing act) and the "union" and "unity" are permanent; so it is in the mystical marriage of Christ and the Church. For once the uniting of the head and the members has been made, the union remains forever. For this mystical union does not end at the death of the faithful, as the physical union of spouses does, but it is indissoluble for eternity—not unlike the **hypostatic union** of the two natures in Christ, which was not dissolved even in the death of Christ.

No man or Angel has been found who would dare to claim both the nature and the title of the groom for himself, except for that "son of perdition" and the Antichrist. In this respect, the act of uniting is attributed to the Father as the source and origin, but to the Son as the one in whom the union is completed. The union itself relates to the head and the members, to the groom and the bride. It is no different than in the **spiritual anointing**: God the Father is the one who anoints, the Son is the one who is anointed—which is why He is called the **Messiah** or **Christ** (both meaning "The Anointed One")—and the Holy Spirit is called the anointing itself. <meta>This page continues the theological exploration of the "mystical marriage" or union between Christ and the Church. Having established in the previous page that the Holy Spirit is the bond of this union, the author now distinguishes this specific spiritual connection from other types of unions—such as the Trinity or physical marriage—and describes the mutual affection between Christ and his followers.</meta>

...and this union is proper and eternal to Christ because He was the conciliator of this mystical and eternal union. Indeed, with respect to the faithful, He is the Mediator of **redemption** <note>original: *ἀπολυτρώσεως* (apolytrōseōs)</note> and **recapitulation** <note>original: *ἀνακεφαλαιώσεως* (anakephalaiōseōs); a theological term for "bringing all things together under one head"</note>; however, with respect to the Angels, He is only the **mediator of recapitulation**.

Furthermore, that mystical union of Christ and the Church is entirely unique. Therefore, it differs specifically from every other kind of union, even those that are "hyper-physical" <note>beyond the laws of nature</note> or unique in their own category. For it differs:

i. **From the hypostatic union**, which is the joining of two complete natures <note>divine and human</note> in the one person of **the Word** <note>original: *τοῦ λόγου* (tou logou); refers to Christ as the eternal Son of God</note>.

ii. **From the substantial union**, which is the joining of three persons in one divine substance or essence within the Trinity.

iii. **From the natural union** found in man, where two incomplete natures—namely the body and the soul—are joined together to form one complete physical whole.

iv. **From the carnal union** of a husband and wife.

v. **From the corporal union** of two touching bodies, which contact one another **physically** <note>original: *σωματικῶς* (sōmatikōs)</note> because their outer edges are joined together.

vi. Therefore, this union is **spiritual** and is called **mystical** in a **spiritual sense** <note>original: *πνευματικῶς* (pneumatikōs)</note>, because it explains that "great mystery" mentioned by Paul in Ephesians 5:32—namely, the mystery concerning Christ and the Church. It is rightly called "spiritual" based on 1 Corinthians 6:17: *But he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit with him.*

Nevertheless, it must be especially noted that this mystical union is considered under a different **relationship** <note>original: *σχέσει* (schesei); a Greek term for the "disposition" or "aspect" of a relationship</note>: either as it refers from Christ to the Church (that is, from the head to the members, or from the groom to the bride), or as it refers to the faithful reciprocally and to one another, as they are members of the same body.

In the **first relationship**, Christ and the Church kiss and embrace one another. Christ embraces the Church by His Spirit, while the Church embraces Christ through faith. Christ kisses the Church, His bride, with a kiss of peace, blessing, and love; the Church, in turn, kisses Christ as her groom with a kiss of love, reverence, and adoration, according to Psalm 2:12: *Kiss the son.*

In the **second relationship**, the faithful embrace one another, even if they are separated by vast stretches of time or distances of place. The bond of those embraces is charity and peace, as stated in Ephesians 4:3: *Eager to maintain the unity of the spirit through the bond of peace.*

<meta>catchword: And so</meta>

<summary>Cregutus defines the "mystical union" of Christ and the Church by contrasting it with other theological and physical unions (like the Trinity or marriage). He describes a two-fold relationship: a vertical "embrace" between Christ and the Church via the Spirit and faith, and a horizontal bond of peace among all believers across time and space.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the mystical union between Christ and the Church. After distinguishing this union from physical or biological ones, the author now categorizes the various types of unities that arise from this relationship and explores the symbolic parallels between the Church and the Virgin Mary.</meta>

<header>REVEALER OF SECRETS</header>

And from this, it follows that from both of those types of union-relationships <note>original: *σχέσει* (schesei); a Greek term for a state of relationship or connection</note>, various kinds of unities emerge. I. Unity of the same body. II. Unity of spirit within the unity of the body. III. Unity of the same head. IV. Unity of faith. V. Unity of charity <note>or brotherly love</note>. VI. Unity of the same homeland. VII. Unity of inheritance. VIII. Unity of God and the Lord. IX. Unity of baptism—specifically the internal one. Ephesians 4:3-6. X. Unity of the shepherd and the flock. John 10:16. *And there shall be one flock and one shepherd* <note>original: *μία ποίμνη, εἷς ποιμὴν* (mia poimnē, heis poimēn)</note>. "Flock" <note>original: *Grex*</note>, not "fold" <note>original: *ouile*</note> as the Vulgate edition translates it. As Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major Protestant reformer and scholar</note> correctly observed, that word describes not the flock itself, but the stable for the sheep; such a thing was hardly ever a single place, and it is not only falsely but foolishly located at Rome. XI. Unity of the building. Ephesians 2:20-21. XII. Unity of the city, which is Jerusalem, the city of the living God. Hebrews 12. XIII. Unity of the whole discrete and the whole continuous—that is, unity by gathering together (collective) and the unity of a single subject—and thus the Church is called a dove, a bride.

Furthermore, from that twofold relationship <note>original: *σχέσει*</note> and the many relations between Christ and the Church, between the mystical groom and the mystical bride, it is easy to discern in what sense those things attributed to the Blessed Virgin in a different respect apply to the Church: namely, that she is the bride of her groom Christ, the parent of her parent, the daughter of her son, and that she was a virgin. Indeed, she is always a virgin and yet betrothed to a husband, and finally she was a mother and gave birth to a young son, and nonetheless without a man. How these things, I say, apply to the Church—either in part or in its entirety—is a delight to investigate, just as the poet truly and sharply said of the Blessed Virgin:

> ->*Bride of God, parent of her father, and daughter of her son:*<-
> ->*A virgin, yet not without a husband; but a mother without a man.*<-

From this, the ancients recorded in writing that Christ solemnly celebrated a threefold marriage. I. **Personal**, such as the marriage of the divine Word with human nature in the mystery of the Incarnation. John 1: *The Word was made flesh*. II. **Mystical marriage**, such as that of Christ with the Church. III. **Spiritual marriage**, which is celebrated in the hearts of the faithful. All are said to be foreshadowed in the wedding at Cana in Galilee (John 2), and indeed the opinion of the learned...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the mystical union between Christ and the Church.
