The most venerable Augustine taught that those [mysteries] were signified through physical marriages, based on Ephesians 5. Furthermore, concerning those three marriages of Christ, it is said more truly than of a physical marriage, that *what he once assumed, he never laid aside*. Regarding the first marriage of Christ, Augustine wrote on the passage in Psalm 19:6. For *he is as a bridegroom coming out of his chamber*, etc. "The Word," he says, "is the bridegroom; the flesh is the bride; the womb of the Virgin is the bridal chamber." The place where the wedding was celebrated was *Cana*, which means *Zeal* or *Love* <note>The author uses a common Hebrew etymological interpretation: "Cana" (קָנָה) is linked to "zeal" or "possession."</note>. For the fervent love and affection of God was the antecedent cause <note>original: *προηγουμένη* (proēgoumenē); the primary or leading cause</note> of those marriages of the incarnation. John 3:16. *For God so loved the world*, etc. The most ardent love of that bridegroom was prefigured in Shechem, son of Hamor in Genesis 34, who was desperately in love with Dinah, daughter of Jacob, and who wished to be circumcised for her sake—indeed, he truly died. So Christ wished to be circumcised and to die for the Church, which was also to be baptized in both ways: namely, by the river <note>water baptism</note> and by blood.

Next, in that wedding at Cana, water was changed into wine; so in the marriage of Christ, water was changed into wine. This means that what was diluted in the flesh passed over into the wine of grace and divine nature—not indeed by mixing <note>original: *κατὰ κρᾶσιν* (kata krasin)</note> or confusion <note>original: *σύγχυσιν* (synchysin)</note>, or by blending <note>original: *κατὰ φύραμα* (kata phyrama)</note>, or by alteration <note>original: *κατ' ἀλλοίωσιν* (kat' alloiosin)</note>, but rather by <term>transelementation</term> <note>original: *κατὰ μεταστοιχείωσιν* (kata metastoicheiōsin); a change of the fundamental elements or "re-elementing"</note>, "not changing the nature, but adding grace to the nature," as Theodoret says in his *Dialogues*, or by regeneration <note>original: *κατὰ παλιγγενεσίαν* (kata palingenesian)</note>, as when the Apostle said that *we become partakers of the divine nature*. Or, with respect to the incarnation, by <term>hypostatic union</term> <note>original: *κατ' ἕνωσιν ἐνυπόστατον* (kat' henōsin enhypostaton); the union of Christ's divine and human natures in one person</note>, which happened without change, without division, without confusion, without separation, and without distance <note>original: *ἀτρέπτως, ἀδιαιρέτως, ἀσυγχύτως, ἀχωρίστως, ἀδιαστάτως*</note>. According to that verse:

> *I am what I was, and I was not what I am now; I am called both:*
> *You do not know me unless you grasp me by both lineages.*

St. Augustine wrote in his treatise *On the Trinity* that the changing of water into wine at Cana foreshadowed the change made in Christ's incarnation: from the rigor of the Law to the sweetness of grace, and from the justice of God to mercy, as the Psalmist says: *Your mercy is in heaven, and the earth is full of justice.* For in the <term>economy of the Law</term> <note>The "economy" refers to God's plan or management of human history in different eras</note>, mercy was in the heavens, but justice was on the earth; yet in the economy of grace in the incarnation, justice flew up to heaven, and mercy descended to the earth.

<meta>This page continues the discourse on the "marriages" of Christ. The previous page discussed the first marriage—the Incarnation—where the Word took on human flesh. This page moves to the second (mystical) and third (spiritual) marriages, explaining how Christ’s sacrifice and the individual believer's faith complete this divine union.</meta>

<page-num>197</page-num>
<header>REVEALER OF SECRETS.</header>

The **second mystical marriage of Christ**, namely that which exists between Christ and the Church, consists of those redemptions sanctioned with blood. The contract for this union was finalized on the cross, and its twin bridal gifts **are not gold or silver, or any precious thing, but the blood of Christ.** <note>The author contrasts worldly dowries with the "price" paid for the Church.</note> The Church, as the bride of Christ, could say to him what Keturah <note>original: *Cethura*; the author likely means Zipporah, Moses's wife, who speaks these words in Exodus 4:25. Keturah was Abraham’s second wife.</note> said to Moses in Exodus 4: *You are a bridegroom of blood to me*, since he redeemed the Church with his own blood and life itself, as in Ephesians 5:25.

The **third marriage of Christ**, namely the **spiritual** one, is in truth not distinct from the mystical marriage, but is included within it like a part within a whole. This is because every individual believer is a part of the whole and universal Church; and Christ cannot be the head of the Church without also being the head of every single member. However, from those two marriages—the personal or natural <note>The Incarnation</note> and the mystical <note>The Church</note>—there emerges a third bond which some call **forensic and legal**. <note>The term *forensic* refers to a legal standing, as in a court of law, where Christ takes on the legal debt of humanity.</note> This bond is rooted both in the agreement of wills and in the decree of the Supreme Judge, since Christ, as our guarantor <note>original: *sponsor*</note>, voluntarily took our personhood upon himself by the Father's decree so that he might pay our debts. Matthew 20:28: *Even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.*

Therefore, just as physical marriages are celebrated with solemnity according to ancient custom (as is clear from John 2 at the wedding in Cana), because men rejoice and exult cheerfully for a "rib" <note>An allusion to Eve being formed from Adam's rib.</note> recovered in a wife, even with an added bonus <note>original: *mantissa*; a Latin term for a "makeweight" or an unexpected addition/increase.</note>, when it had previously been lost; so much more solemnly should the marriage of Christ with the Church be celebrated. For in this union, it is not a rib that is recovered, but the **image of God** which was lost through the Fall of Adam. This image is restored in Christ, and thus the Church is born from his blood. This was foreshadowed by the fact that from the side of Christ—as if from a rib—there flowed blood and water, which are the two sacraments of the Church <note>Baptism and the Eucharist.</note>, signifying its birth and its nourishment.

Furthermore, it should be observed that this union we have discussed so far belongs to the **invisible Church**, and therefore in the dowries...

and consists of internal gifts, but it is worth the effort that this union also be viewed in respect to the visible Church; whether that visible Church is considered in itself regarding its own members and those joined in covenant, or regarding those who are outside the covenant, and who are called "the Church" in name only <note>original: *æquiuocè*; meaning they use the name but do not possess the reality</note>.

That union consists primarily in two things, namely **in the union of charity and in the union of truth**. The **union of truth** <note>original: *unio veritatis*</note> is sufficiently demonstrated from the marks of the visible Church, namely the pure preaching of the divine word and the healthy administration of the Sacraments. Since the truth of the articles of faith and the institution of the Sacraments are perfectly contained in the word of God, the union of truth will truly remain there where those two marks remain undefiled. **The union of charity** <note>original: *unio charitatis*</note> is also necessarily required in the visible Church, just as in the primitive Church in Acts 4, which was **one heart and one soul**. From this, others add a third mark of the visible Church, namely **the exercise and practice of ecclesiastical discipline**. The union of truth is founded upon the first two marks; the union of charity is founded upon this latter one. From the former union, heresies are uprooted; from the latter, the roots of schisms and divisions are eradicated. And surely the vitals of that common mother <note>The Church</note> are wounded when Jacob and Esau struggle within her womb and batter it with hands and feet <note>A reference to Genesis 25:22, symbolizing internal conflict between brothers/believers</note>. Nor is it fitting for the holy Jerusalem to be built with a confusion of tongues, no differently than proud Babel. Nor should the tunic of Christ, which is seamless <note>original: *inconfutilis*; see John 19:23</note>, be rent or torn in any way. Whoever, therefore, deviates from those two centers—namely of truth and of charity—doubtless also devises a defection from the Church, and busies himself with writing a bill of divorce to the groom. They are no different than lines receding from a center point, which grow distant from one another; and the more they are removed and distant from the center, the more they also grow distant from each other. Indeed, their separation is more conspicuous the further they are extended from the point of union.

Wherefore, since the Reformed Churches <note>original: *Ecclesiæ reformatæ*</note> lean most firmly upon those two marble columns, it is no wonder if a most constant union flourishes among them, such that it cannot be broken by any opposing effort; for they would sooner suffer every last drop of blood to be drained from the body before that healthy...

...lest that vital kinship of truth or doctrine be snatched away from her. Rather, that union of the Church ought to be valued at such a high price that even if its Teachers are not always of one mind <note>original Greek: <term>ὁμοψηφῶντες</term> (*homopsēphountes*), meaning "voting together" or "unanimous"</note>, nevertheless, because of "stubble or hay built upon the foundation," schisms ought by no means to arise in the Church, as the Apostle teaches in 1 Corinthians 3 <note>The author refers to 1 Cor 3:12, suggesting that minor errors in teaching—the "stubble"—should not destroy the foundation of the Church's unity.</note>. Specifically, they celebrated Easter on the fourteenth day of the Moon, not on the following Lord’s Day, for which reason they called them contemptuously **Tessarecadecatites** or **Quartodecimans** <note>From the Greek and Latin words for "fourteen"; these Christians followed the Jewish dating for Passover/Easter rather than the Roman Sunday tradition.</note>. This scandal proceeded so far that Christians, because of those dissensions, were mocked in theaters and ridiculed on stage by the infidel pagans; just as today, Christians are a laughingstock to the Turks and Muslims on account of civil wars and discords. 

And in our times, the dissensions that have arisen among Protestants have given an immense opportunity for the Papists <note>The "Pontificii" or followers of the Pope.</note> themselves to quibble, mock, and slander—as if there were some fundamental disagreement in the chief articles of faith between us and the "Lutheran brothers," as they are called. Yet, in truth, we both agree in all articles of religion, even if we do not admit the exposition of the brothers regarding the Sacrament of the **Eucharist** <note>The Lord's Supper</note> as being in agreement with the sense of Scripture, nor do we accept the consequences that follow from it.

However, the Papists do us an injury by numbering us and the Lutheran brothers with **Anabaptists**, **Libertines**, and such fanatics; since heaven is no further from the earth than our doctrine differs from their dreams and "enthusiasms" <note>A 17th-century term for people claiming direct, private revelations from God apart from Scripture.</note>. For this reason, we deservedly cast our complaints against **Bellarmine** <note>Cardinal Robert Bellarmine, a leading Catholic theologian of the Counter-Reformation.</note>, who in Book 4 of *On the Marks of the Church*, Chapter 10, peddles the most foul deceptions of **Friedrich Staphylus**, a Roman sycophant.

Well known is the *Henoticon* <note>An edict issued by Byzantine Emperor Zeno in 482 AD in an unsuccessful attempt to reconcile the differences between the supporters and opponents of the Council of Chalcedon.</note> of Zeno, well known the *Ecthesis* <note>A letter or "statement of faith" issued by Emperor Heraclius in 638 AD which defined Monothelitism as the official imperial religious form.</note> of Heraclius, well known the "Type" <note>An imperial edict issued by Constans II in 648 AD that forbade any further discussion on the nature of Christ's will, attempting to quiet religious controversy by silence.</note> of the Emperor Constans. Therefore, they establish politically that they cannot exist without the Pope or apart from him, like members without a head: hence it is that some of them prefer the name "Papists" over "Catholics." For example, Caesar Baronius <note>A prominent Catholic historian and cardinal (1538–1607).</note> states in his *Martyrology* for October 16 that no title of dignity is more sublime than that of "Papist," and the Jesuit Becanus <note>Martinus Becanus (1563–1624), a Jesuit theologian and polemicist.</note>, speaking of the universal Church, calls it not "Christian" from its head Christ, but "Papal" from the Pope.

But let the Papists boast as much as they wish about the Pope; we Christians will certainly boast forever in Christ, the true and only head of the Church. And just as the Hebrews sing to the Triune God, because of the unity and simplicity of His essence, the *Song of Unity* which they call *Shir Ha-yichud* <note>original Hebrew: שיר היחוד, a hymn of praise regarding the oneness of God.</note>, so we will give the greatest thanks forever both to the Triune and "three-personed" <note>original Greek: *trisyprostato*</note> God and to Christ the "God-man" <note>original Greek: *theanthrōpō*</note>, because He has caused us to grow together into the unity of His mystical body, and has adorned us with the benefits of that union and unity. And this is because it has been given to us *to keep the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace, and because there is one body and one spirit.*

This is why the temple of God is specifically called by Christ the **house of prayer**; not because the temple served only for prayer, since other exercises of piety were performed and carried out in the temple, but because a name is commonly taken from its most important part.

Now, as for the text itself, nothing prevents the word "invocation" from being taken in both ways: for in truth the Church, which was gathered from the family of Seth, then began to devoutly pour out prayers to God. For the true faithful saw that no sacrifice is more excellent and more acceptable to God than that <term>bloodless one</term> <note>original: "ἀναίμακτον" (anaimaktos) — a term often used for the Eucharist or spiritual worship as opposed to animal sacrifice</note>, which is the sacrifice of praise: according to that passage in *Psalm 50:14: Sacrifice to God praise and render your vows to the Most High.* And all remaining sacrifices would be tasteless unless they were seasoned with the salt of our prayers. Indeed, without them, the very salt of the sacrifices would become foolish <note>or "lose its savor"</note>; but if the salt has lost its savor, with what shall it be seasoned? as Christ says in *Matthew 5:13.* 

Therefore, it will be more truly said of that spiritual sacrifice than of sacrifice properly so-called (when a victim was slaughtered) that there is no religion without sacrifice. This is because there was a time when the Church and religion existed without sacrifice properly so-called and <term>atonement</term> <note>original: "ἱλασμῷ" (hilasmo) — a propitiatory sacrifice meant to appease God</note>, namely before the first sin. But truly, there was never a Church or religion without spiritual sacrifice, because even before sin, God was adored by men and Angels. Now, invocation is the peak and summit of adoration, and therefore it is the more sublime and highest worship of God. The very word for "adoration" indicates this, for the concept itself signifies that God cannot be adored without prayer. This is denoted by both the Hebrew and Greek terms, since no one can bow themselves before God except by supplicating and praying. But yet there is this distinction: a gesture represents the act of adoration more physically, but the voice expresses the invocation itself and the petition of the matter and of the sinful man, according to the common saying.

### ANTHONY CREGUT

->*I entreat God with my voice, but with my gesture I adore His Divinity.*<-

To this we should refer that remark of Erasmus of Rotterdam in his *Adages* <note>original: *Adagiis* — a famous collection of Greek and Latin proverbs compiled by the Renaissance scholar Erasmus</note>, when he says that adoration must be performed by a turning of the body. This was surely done in imitation of the heavens, which are driven in a perpetual rotation <note>original: *vertigine*</note>, a movement that antiquity believed was God. By this turning of the body, it is signified that nothing in human affairs is stable or permanent; rather, in whatever way it has seemed good to God to turn or roll our lives, it is right that we should be content. 

And that which we said above concerning adoration and prayer seems to have been sufficiently hinted at by the common translator <note>The "common translator" refers to the author of the Vulgate, the standard Latin Bible</note> in Matthew 18:26. There, the translator renders the Greek word for "to prostrate oneself" or "to adore" <note>original: *τὸ προσκυνεῖν* (to proskynein)</note>—a word which in the New Testament is always to be understood as a religious act or the adoration of God—using the word for "to pray" <note>original: *τὸ orare*</note>: *that servant, falling down, prayed to him.* <note>original: *προσεκύνει αὐτῷ* (prosekynei autō) — "he did him homage" or "he fell on his knees before him"</note> In other instances, the Latin translator would not have hesitated to translate it as "to adore" <note>original: *τὸ adorare*</note>, since he uses that word indiscriminately for both religious and non-religious honor. This is contrary to the practice of all foreign authors <note>Greek authors</note> who, without exception, always use the term for religious honor.

But indeed, although "Invocation" in this divine oracle <note>Referring to the passage in Genesis regarding the family of Seth</note> can be taken for that most noble species of religion, the words of Moses must be expanded even further: namely, to the entire practice of religion. This is done by synecdoche <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole</note>, the part for the whole, and the word is used in this same way in Romans 10:13: *Whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.* For this sounds the same as: "whosoever shall have confessed the name of the Lord shall be saved." For "confession" in the Scripture signifies piety and the whole worship of God; hence that word is accepted in this sense a little earlier in verse 9: *Namely, that if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thy heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved.* And verse 10: *For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.* 

From this, the Martyrs who had endured death or various punishments for the Christian religion were commonly called **Confessors**. So it was for that pious Bishop Paphnutius <note>A 4th-century Egyptian bishop who was mutilated during the Diocletianic Persecution</note>, whose eye was gouged out and whose leg was broken for the sake of Christ; he was enrolled in the white-list of Confessors. On account of that confession of Christ, the Emperor Constantine the Great used to kiss the hollowed-out eye of that holy man. And to this confession of the Christian faith, shame <note>original: *αἰσχύνη* (aischýnē)</note> was opposed. For just as that special confession, which among...

### THE REVEALER OF SECRETS
<meta>catchword: q</meta>

Among the Catholics <note>original: *Pontificios* — literally "the followers of the Pontiff"</note>, it is commonly called "auricular confession" <note>the practice of confessing sins privately into the ear of a priest</note>, and while that which is specifically a confession of sins is truly called confession because it is done before God, it is here used in contrast to shame <note>original: *αἰσχύνω* (aischynō)</note> or the bashfulness of those who do not dare to confess their sins before the whole eldership or Church, nor to perform penance. Thus, in a general sense, the "confession of the name of God" is spoken of in contrast to the shame <note>original: *αἰσχύνω* (aischynō)</note> of those who blush to confess and profess the name of Christ—whether because of the reproach of Christ and his "form of a servant," for the cross is a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Greeks, or because the Gospel is everywhere spoken against and suffers the hatred of the world. Hence Christ said, *whoever confesses me before men*, etc. And then, *whoever is ashamed of me and the Gospel*. Paul implies the same in Romans 10:11: *Whoever believes in him will not be put to shame* <note>original: *non pudefiet* and *καταισχυνθήσεται* (kataischunthēsetai)</note>. For although Paul is looking back to the passage in Isaiah 28:16, where the Hebrew truth has *he shall not make haste* <note>original: *לא יחיש* (lo iachiš)</note>, the meaning coincides: for he who hastens is often put to shame by the outcome because he hurried too much, whence the proverb: *Make haste slowly* <note>original: *Σπεῦδε βραδέως* (Speude bradeos)</note>, and that other saying: *A hasty dog gives birth to blind puppies*. Or even because he who hastens already seems, by that very fact, to be ashamed; for why does he hasten unless to avoid an imminent shame? But on the contrary, he who believes rests upon the promises of God, relying on which he finds peace, as is held in Psalm 18:3: *I will trust in Him* <note>original: *πεποιθὼς ἐπ’ αὐτῷ* (pepoithōs ep’ autō); Hebrew: *חסה* (chasah), meaning "I took refuge"</note>. And here the rule applies: *Quick enough if well enough*. Nevertheless, it can also be said that the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> read in the Hebrew not *he shall not make haste* <note>original: *לא יחיש* (lo iachiš)</note>, but rather *he shall not be put to shame* <note>original: *לא יביש* (lo iabiš)</note>, with only a single letter changed.

Hence it is that this "confession of the divine name" suggests not so much a private as a public celebration, as in Psalm 118: *Confess to the Lord, for He is good*. This is what the Apostles did when they were converted from timid doves into noble eagles after the day of Pentecost. And Christ demonstrated this by his own example before Pilate; he remained silent in his own defense and kept his mouth closed, but for the confession of the truth, he opened his mouth and said to Pilate: *You would have no [power...]*

...authority over me, etc. However, among the Hebrews, the term *opening of the mouth* <note>original: פִתְחוֹן פֶּה (*pithchon pe*)</note> is used to signify an excuse or a self-defense, as in: *and they shall have no excuse* <note>original: ולא יהיה להם פה (*velo vhieh lahem pitchon pe*) — literally "and there shall not be to them an opening of the mouth"</note>. In this sense, Christ did not "open his mouth" to defend himself; yet, on other occasions whenever it concerned the glory of his Father, did he not speak with an "opening of the mouth"?

The confession of God's name occurs in two ways: either in the *heart* or with the *mouth*. That which occurs in the heart is called faith; hence the Apostle says in Romans 10: *With the heart one believes, and with the mouth confession is made.* For just as the "internal word" <note>original: *verbum mentis* or *λόγον ἐνδιάθετον* (logon endiatheton)</note> of the mind is expressed through the "spoken word" <note>original: *λόγον προφορικόν* (logon prophorikon)</note>, so too the heart's confession is expressed through the mouth's confession, which Paul explains in Romans 10:13 as an "invocation" <note>the act of calling upon God in prayer or worship</note>. Therefore, where there is no confession, there is no faith—just as where there is neither heat nor light, there can be no fire. This should be understood as referring to the confession of the heart rather than just the mouth. On this point, Leo the Great <note>a 5th-century Pope known for his influential writings on the nature of Christ</note> offered these noteworthy remarks regarding Peter’s denial of Christ:

> Faith did not fail in his heart when confession failed on his lips; his love was not so much overturned as his constancy was disturbed. He loved within him the one he denied outwardly, even though his affection was numbed, gripped by fear. Faith remained in its essential state, but the fear of danger cut off its outward expression.

Nevertheless, the confession of the mouth—which is the same as calling upon God—is called "confession" in an absolute sense because it is a public and solemn act of obedience to faith and a celebration of the Divine name. This is why, in the ancient Church, those known as "Martyrs" or "Confessors" <term>Confessor: In the early Church, this title was given to those who suffered for their Christian faith—often through torture or imprisonment—but were not killed</term> bore physical "badges" of their confession on their bodies. This is clear from the *Ecclesiastical History* of Rufinus of Aquileia, Book 10, Chapter 17, regarding Paphnutius the Confessor and Maximus, the Bishop of Jerusalem, who was also a confessor. Both men had an eye gouged out and a hamstring cut, which served as conspicuous signs of their confession. When Maximus was sitting in an assembly of "malignant" <note>ill-willed or corrupt; here referring to the bishops opposing the orthodox leader Athanasius</note> bishops who were acting against Athanasius in favor of the imposter Arsenius <note>Arsenius was a bishop whose "severed hand" was used in a famous false accusation against Athanasius of Alexandria</note>, Paphnutius spoke to him with great gravity:

> "Maximus," he said, "I share with you the very same mark of confession; with you, I had my mortal eye gouged out, only to gain a clearer vision of the divine light. I will not allow you to sit in a council of the wicked, nor to enter among those who act with injustice."

...they called <note>The text likely concludes a sentence from the previous page regarding how certain people or practices were named</note>. But **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century historian and bishop known as the "Father of Church History"</note> feels the opposite; for he explains it as referring to the faithful, among whom, since the worship of God was flourishing, they began to be called by the name of God, so that they were termed "sons of God." Furthermore, Moses speaks concerning the object of **Invocation**, which he designates by the name of God when he says: <term>אז הוחל לקרא בשם יהוה (*az huchal likro beschem Iehovah*)</term> <note>original: "Then it was begun to call on the name of Jehovah" (Genesis 4:26)</note>; "then it was begun to call upon the name of Jehovah." In this instance, Moses first attributes a name to God, which is done according to our human way of conceiving things. For in reality, it is hardly fitting for a name to be assigned to God. Indeed, by what reasoning would you impose a name upon God? Would it be <term>by chance</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τυχῆς (*apo tyches*)</note>, or indeed <term>by deliberate choice</term> <note>original Greek: ἐκ τῆς προαιρέσεως (*ek tes proaireseos*)</note>?

Not the first, for who would assert that a name is imposed upon God by accident or through "Lady Luck"? Especially since nothing can be affirmed concerning God without a sacred mystery. Nor is it by deliberate choice; for what would be the reason and cause for a name in God? It is not for the first reason, <term>distinction</term> <note>original Greek: διακρίσεως (*diakriseos*)</note>—namely, so that he might distinguish one from another, just as among men one is surnamed **Peter** so that he may be distinguished from **Paul**. This is because Peter is "one" in a relative and arithmetic sense (so to speak), numerically distinct from Paul and other men. But God is "one" in an absolute and metaphysical sense, because He is unique. Therefore, since there are no other Gods, He does not need to be discerned from others <term>by a distinguishing mark</term> <note>original Greek: διακριτικῶς (*diakritikos*)</note> or a proper name.

But if God is named so as to signify His essence, persons, and perfections—just as Christ is <term>nameless</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνώνυμος (*anonymos*)</note> as **Immanuel** with respect to His person (*Isaiah 7*) and **Jesus** with respect to His office (*Matthew 1*)—by what adequate name could He be denominated?

Regarding **Essence**: this is itself infinite and incomprehensible, and since it embraces all species—not only those created, but even those possible—it seems He cannot be nicknamed by a proper and adequate name, but only by that common name of "essence" <note>the state of "being"</note> which applies to every being.

Regarding **Person**: God would be <term>three-named</term> <note>original Greek: τριώνυμος (*trionymos*)</note> since there are three persons, but here we are dealing with the name of God in the passage of Moses.

Regarding **Perfections**: since those are infinite, anyone would labor in vain to comprehend them in a single name. Therefore, speaking properly and accurately, God has no name by which He may be fully encompassed, since He is incomprehensible; but as God [has revealed] Himself...

He understands everything and as a whole <note>original Greek: ὅλον καὶ ὅλως (*holon kai holōs*)</note>, so he has no need for a name, since he himself is the very thing that would need to be named; just as a man does not need his own name to call himself, so neither does God.

However, why does Scripture attribute a name to God, and why does Moses now say that the name of God is invoked? I respond that this is done according to our way of conceiving things <note>Theologians often argue that God "accommodates" himself to human language so we can understand him</note>, because otherwise we would hardly be able to conceive of God's attributes; hence, there are various names for God according to the variety of his perfections and operations. Just as the angels do not strictly have names, but names are assigned to them according to our perspective <note>original Greek: καθ᾽ ἡμᾶς (*kath’ hēmas*)</note> in the Scriptures, according to the various offices they are allotted, and as they are called ministering spirits <note>original Greek: πνεύματα λειτουργικὰ (*pneumata leitourgika*); see Hebrews 1:14</note>. Thus they are called in a general sense by the Hebrews **messengers** <note>original Hebrew: מלאכים (*mal'akhim*)</note> from their duties, just as the Greeks call them **angels** <note>original Greek: ἄγγελοι (*angeloi*), meaning messengers</note>; so specifically, from their different duties toward men, one is called Raphael, another Gabriel, another Uriel, etc. In the same way, Scripture imposes various names upon God by reason of his perfections and operations, so that in this way at least God may be acknowledged by us in some manner, and we may distinctly conceive of his various perfections.

Truly, however, among the various names attributed to God in Scripture, none is more emphatic <note>original Greek: ἐμφατικώτερον (*emphatikōteron*)</note> than that which Moses employs here, namely **Jehovah** <note>original Hebrew: יהוה (*Yahweh*)</note>, which is the same as that which God imposes upon himself in Exodus 3:14. For when Moses inquired after his name, *God said to Moses: I am that I am.* For in the name Jehovah, both the very essence of God and his eternity are contained. **Essence**, because it is the same as that "Being" <note>original Greek: ὁ ὢν (*ho ōn*), the One who is</note> in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> to which Christ alludes in John 8 when he says: *Before Abraham was, I am.* **Eternity**, because it includes all the differences of time, whence in the Apocalypse he is called *the one who is, and who was, and who is to come. The Alpha and the Omega.* Hence, if any is considered the proper name of God, it will be Jehovah; for although it may seem common, since it signifies "essence" (which is a metaphysical notion and therefore common to every Being), yet it properly designates God, because "Being" is said analogously with respect to God and creatures; and since God is Being by essence, creatures are beings by accident <note>In traditional philosophy, God's nature is to exist, whereas creatures only exist because they were created</note>. Therefore, Jehovah is not undeservedly called by the Hebrews the **unique name** <note>original Hebrew: שם המיוחד (*shem hamiuchad*), literally "the appropriated" or "distinctive" name</note>, because it fits no one but God, whence the Aramaic paraphrase <note>The Chaldaic or Aramaic Targums, which were interpretive translations of the Hebrew Bible</note> expresses it as the **great and glorious name** <note>original Aramaic: שמא רבא ויקירא (*shema rabba veiakkira*)</note>. <meta>This page continues the philological study of the divine names, moving from the philosophical necessity of God's names to a detailed linguistic analysis of the Tetragrammaton and its perceived influence on the languages of the world.</meta>

# ANTHONY CREGUT #

The **Explicit Name** <note>Hebrew: *Shem HaMephorash*; often translated as the "distinct" or "uniquely explained" name</note>.

The **Name of Four Letters** <note>Hebrew: *Shem shel Arbah Otioth*</note>, which is called the **Tetragrammaton** <note>Greek: *tetragrammaton*, meaning "four letters"</note> by the Greeks and, due to the superstitious reverence of the Jews, the **Unutterable** <note>Greek: *anekphōnēton*</note>.

The fame of that glorious name seems to have spread through all nations. From this, it appears that the Pagans named the greatest of the Gods, **Jove**, from **Jehovah**; and because it is a four-letter name, by a superstitious imitation, the name of God has been adopted as a four-letter word among almost all peoples. For just as in Hebrew it was preeminently a four-letter name <note>Hebrew: יהוה (YHWH)</note>, so it is for the Chaldeans <note>אלהא (*Elaha*)</note>, the Syrians <note>אלהא (*Elaha*)</note>, and the Arabs <note>אללה (*Allah*)</note>. In Greek, it is **God** <note>Greek: θεός (*Theos*)</note>; in Latin, *Deus*; in Spanish, *Dios*; in Italian, *Idio*; in German, *Gott*; and in English, *God*. In Egyptian, it is *Thauth*, perhaps derived from the Greek *Theos*. In Persian, it is *Syre*, perhaps from the Greek for **Lord** <note>Greek: Κύριος (*Kyrios*)</note>, just as the French call a king *Sire*. According to others, the Persian word is *Khoda* <note>כודא</note>, for that is what they call God, which approaches the German *Gott*. This seems to be taken from the Chaldean *Gad* or *Gada* <note>גדא גד</note>, meaning a **favorable star** or **fortune**. Thus, in Genesis 30:11, "In Gad" is read as "Good fortune comes." Others interpret *Gad* as God, or as Jupiter, because the planet Jupiter is considered benevolent. Hence that passage in Isaiah 65:11, "those who prepare a table for Gad," which Arias Montanus <note>A famous 16th-century Spanish Orientalist and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible</note> rendered as **preparing a table for Jupiter**. In French, it is *Dieu*. I even hear that in the recently discovered New World, the name is four letters, *Zimi* <note>A reference to "Cemi," the ancestral spirits or deities of the Taíno people in the Caribbean</note>, by which they designate God. Thus, that mother tongue [Hebrew] has been fabulously told concerning all things <note>original Greek: πάντα περὶ πάντων τερατολογημένη (*panta peri pantōn teratologēmenē*)</note>.

From this, it has come about that He who, in respect to Himself, properly has no name, is nevertheless called by the Hebrews, in respect to us, preeminently **The Name** <note>Hebrew: השם (*HaShem*)</note>. This is used emphatically—that is, *the* name—because He has a name above every name, as the Apostle says in Philippians 2:9 concerning Christ: *He has bestowed on him the name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, etc.* For the word **The Name** <note>Hebrew: *HaShem*</note> sounds the same as "God" among the Rabbis, even if by the force of the word it simply signifies "name"; just as in Syriac, it means **to impose a name** <note>Syriac: *shamma* or *shammi*</note>. Indeed, it does not only signify God in a general sense, but specifically **Jehovah**; for by "The Name," Jehovah is designated exclusively. Hence these phrases are found everywhere in the books of the Rabbis: **If The Name helps** <note>Hebrew: *Im ya'azor HaShem*; equivalent to "God willing"</note>, or **If The Name decrees** or **permits**, or **If The Name wills**. For "The Name" is that divine and ineffable name **Jehovah** <note>יהוה</note>.

It also explains the Rabbinic use of "HaShem" as a substitute for the ineffable divine name.</summary>

They claim no one from that time had dared to pronounce it until Peter Galatinus <note>Pietro Galatino (1460–1540), a scholar who popularized the spelling "Jehovah" in the West</note>, but instead of it, *Adonai* <note>Lord</note> or *Elohim* <note>God</note> was pronounced. Truly, these are the fictions of dreaming and raving Rabbis; for Moses did not intend to signify this, as if that Jewish superstition concerning the **Unutterable Voice** <note>Greek: *peri tēs phōnēs anekphōnētēs*</note> had already taken deep roots back then. Rather, Moses intended to suggest something more solid and holy: that by using the term "The Name" <note>Hebrew: השם (*HaShem*)</note>, he showed that the blasphemy is more horrible when the name of God is explicitly expressed and immediately "pierced" by a blaspheming tooth and tongue, than if it had been suppressed.

It will not seem unnecessary here to mention what the teachers of the Hebrews observe concerning the name **Jehovah**, namely, that the first place in Scripture in which mention of it was made is Genesis 2:4: *In the day that Jehovah God made the heaven and the earth.* This **Four-Letter Name** <note>Greek: *tetragrammaton*</note> (they say) is first read there because the creation of things was now finished, and the majesty of God shines more clearly in the completed workmanship of the world. Furthermore, the name **Elohim** is added, which pertains to office and attribute; as if Moses were saying, "He who is properly called **Jehovah** is the Lord, Judge, director, and governor of all things." And indeed, some reason for this matter seems to be required: for since Moses, in narrating the history of creation, repeated *Elohim* thirty-two times, he uses the name **Jehovah** only in Genesis 2:4 and joins it with *Elohim*, the [reason] of which matter...

...the reason (if I am not mistaken) can still be added. **Jehovah** is the essential name of God, representing God's essence and eternity; however, since that essence and eternity of God are unsearchable depths, and before the creation of the world these two were hidden from eternity in God's bosom, finally, in the creation of the world, God exhibited himself to be seen as if in his own image—the essence of God in the species of created beings, and his eternity in time and the perpetual motion of celestial and sub-celestial things. Yet he adds the name **Elohim**, because it fits marvelously with creation and signifies right and dominion. For he who is **Jehovah**, Being by essence, from whom all created beings come, is also **Elohim**, and he possesses the supreme and <term>absolute power <note>original Greek: *autokratōrikon*</note></term> over the creatures established by him, whom he can break like potter's vessels. But then in the same Chapter II, verse 7, when Moses says that man was formed from the dust of the earth, he repeats both names of God: *and so **Jehovah God** formed man*, etc. This was done so that, just as in that <term>microcosm <note>the "little world" of the human being</note></term> the workmanship of the entire <term>macrocosm <note>the "great world" of the universe</note></term> is to be contemplated as if in a mirror—because there the sensible and intelligible worlds are enclosed—so in a more illustrious way, God is visible as both **Jehovah** and **Elohim**, because man was made more expressly in the image of God.

From this, one should observe that among the ten names of God which are attributed to him in Scripture, these two—as they are the oldest, one being essential and eternal, the other truly relative and from the beginning of the world—are thus the principal and <term>most unique characteristics <note>original Greek: *idiōtata*</note></term>. Therefore, if God were to be designated by any name from eternity, he would without doubt have been designated by that absolute and essential name, **Jehovah**; but indeed, in the very cradle of the world, he wished to be marked by a relative name. For **Elohim** began to exist in time, when after creation God held dominion over creatures and began to exert his force and power. By reason of this meaning, this name is often bestowed upon magistrates and angels on account of their dominion. The name **Jehovah**, however, is not common to creatures, except perhaps symbolically and figuratively, as when the Ark of the Covenant is called **Jehovah**, just like the "glory of God," because it is his symbol.

<meta>This page continues the philological investigation into the divine names. Having previously discussed why Moses combined "Jehovah" (the essential name) with "Elohim" (the name of power and judgment) in the creation account, the author now addresses why the specific name "Jehovah" is so frequently replaced by the title "Lord" in translations like the Septuagint and by modern scholars.</meta>

->### THE REVEALER OF SECRETS<-
->217<-

...constantly interpreted **Jehovah** <note>original Hebrew: יהוה</note> as *the Lord*, as in the formulas of blessings: *Blessed be the Lord God of Israel* <note>original Hebrew: ברוך יהוה אלהי ישראל, *baruc Iehoua Elohim Iisrael*</note>. Certainly, regarding the <term>moderns <note>original Latin: *neotericos*, referring here to 16th and 17th-century Christian scholars</note></term>, the solution is easy: following the Jewish superstition that arose long ago after the coming of Christ, they read *Adonai* <note>meaning "My Lord"</note> instead of **Jehovah**, which is a word that signifies *Lord*. But truly, what should be thought of the <term>Septuagint <note>original: LXX; the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible from the 3rd century BCE</note></term> translators, who constantly rendered it as **the Lord** <note>original Greek: τὸ κύριος</note>? Were they also blinded by the blind superstition of the Jews? I do not think so. Rather, it is better to say that since they were unable to properly write or pronounce **Jehovah** in Greek—due to the guttural letter *he* <note>the Hebrew letter ה</note> and because of the letter *vav*, whose value the Greeks cannot express—just as they did not render the aspiration of the *he* in the middle of the word, they used **the Lord**, as it sounds like the other name, *Adonai*. Indeed, all Christians until the time of <term>Pietro Galatino <note>An Italian scholar (1460–1540) credited with popularizing the pronunciation "Jehovah" in the Christian world</note></term> followed the Hebrew custom and rendered it as *the Lord*.

But indeed, a difficulty still arises: why did the Septuagint use the word **the Lord** <note>original Greek: τὸ κύριος</note>—a word which means the same as *Adonai*—rather than **God** <note>original Greek: θεὸς</note>, or some other word that expresses a divine name other than *Adonai*, if the Septuagint were not following the Jewish superstition? I answer that the Septuagint were moved by the same reasoning as the superstitious Jews were, and are still moved today. For why did the superstitious Jews not use another name of God—such as **Yah** <note>original: *Iah*</note> or **El**—to express the name of **Jehovah**, but instead all expressed it through *Adonai*, just as the Septuagint did through **the Lord**? Truly, the reason for this choice among so many names of God must have been common to both; but that common reason (as we have said) is not superstition, which the Septuagint did not follow. Therefore, there must be another reason drawn from the nature of the thing—specifically from the notion of this name. For in truth, **Jehovah** also signifies "dominion"; for since its primary meaning implies **Being by essence**, and thus the principle of every being—whence **Jehovah** is called **He Who Is** <note>original Greek: ὁ ὤν</note> and in the Book of Revelation is called the **Beginning and the End** <note>original Greek: ἀρχὴ καὶ τέλος</note>—so too it signifies dominion over those things which have a beginning, namely, the creatures. Therefore, since **Jehovah** could be expressed by neither group—not by the Jews because of superstition, and not by the Septuagint because of the <term>poverty <note>original: *inopia*, meaning the linguistic limitations or lack of specific phonemes</note></term> of the Greek language—the meaning of the name **Jehovah** was expressed by both through equivalent words.

The author argues that while Jews avoid the name out of superstition, the Greek Septuagint translators used "Lord" because the Greek language lacks the sounds necessary to pronounce Jehovah correctly, and because "Lord" captures God's essential dominion over creation.</summary>

Our conjecture is proven by the opinion of the Hebrews, who assert that there are two names of God: one essential and eternal, namely the name of God or **Elohim**; the other, however, is relative, namely **Jehovah** or **the Lord**, which He manifested to us in time. They say that Scripture always places this name first to signify the love of God, which, according to the Hebrews, is also designated by that name. Hence: *Blessed be the Lord God of Israel* and *You shall love the Lord God with all your heart*. In Genesis 2:7: *the Lord God formed man*. Furthermore, it will still be a pleasure to observe that remarkable point which the Hebrews write regarding the concept of **Jehovah**: that **Jehovah** and **Elohim** signify two further things. For they maintain that **Elohim** implies judgment, or is the name of God as Judge, according to Deuteronomy 1:17, Psalm 75:8, and Psalm 50:6. **Jehovah**, however, is the name of grace. Hence, in the book titled *The Gate of Light* <note>original Latin: *Porta Lucis*; this refers to the *Sha'are Orah*, a famous 13th-century Kabbalistic text by Joseph Gikatilla</note>, these words are found: "when the decree goes forth toward mercy, then He is called **Jehovah**—that is, the name of **Jehovah** is attributed to Him—but when the decree goes forth toward judgment, then He is called **Elohim**." They prove from Exodus 34:6 that **Jehovah** is the name of grace: *Jehovah is a gracious God*. But why is He called **Elohim** in the creation when there was no sin, and therefore no cause for judgment? They say that God created the world as **Elohim** out of His primary intention; for He knew the instability of man, who would have need of a judge. Yet, moved by His surpassing grace and mercy, He soon joined the name of grace with that of Judgment in Genesis 2:4: *In the day that the Lord God made the heaven and the earth*. Sometimes, however (say the <term>Kabbalists <note>original Latin: *Cabalistæ*; scholars of Jewish mystical tradition</note></term>), judgment is attributed to God as **Jehovah** <note>original Hebrew: יהוה</note> just as to **Elohim**, but that judgment is to be understood as a "judgment of grace," namely when the rigor of justice is turned into the sweetness of grace. And these teachings of the Hebrew philosophers, who are called **Kabbalists**, surely contain excellent doctrine; for they do not always dream, but for the most part they bring to light sharp and fruitful insights.

By these names of God, they first implore mercy for themselves as innocents; then they were obliged to call upon *Elohim* regarding judgment and the undergoing of punishments for their crime, had they truly established a new cult. Finally, they employed the name of God, *Jehovah*, because this naming tempers God’s justice with the equity of clemency and kindness—as if they were saying: may *Jehovah*, who is the mediator, moderate the judgment according to the intent of our hearts; and let that most just Judge decide whether we have earned punishment or reward. Therefore, they wisely joined those three names, as they contain the mysteries of the greatness, power, and glory of God.

Those excellent teachings of the Hebrews are certainly not foreign to the promises of God in Exodus 6:3, when God addresses Moses thus: **I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob by the name of God Almighty; but by my name Jehovah I was not known to them.** This was not because God had not revealed His name *Jehovah* to the Patriarchs, or because He had not sealed His promises with that name—for indeed in Genesis 15:7 and 28:13 He is called *Jehovah*, and in Genesis 26:25 Isaac calls upon Him by this name. > ->*Ah, my God, your name*<-

> ->*May you, at last, vindicate it.*<-

Therefore, when Moses says that the name of God began to be invoked, let us be far from understanding that superstitiously or technically <note>original Greek: τεχνικῶς, *technikos*</note> as referring to mere syllables. Rather, we conceive of the very reality signified by that name, which is what ought to be invoked.

and creatures should be understood <note>original Greek: ἀναλόγως, *analogōs*</note> analogously, as the greatest theological principle holds; and since they were revealed according to our way of perceiving, just as among men we understand the person himself, his attributes, and his reputation through a proper name, so through the name of God we analogously conceive of God's very essence, the persons [of the Trinity], His attributes, His authority, and other things of this sort. And surely, since *there is only one God* (1 Timothy 2:5), so He alone is to be invoked. For as Paul testifies in Romans 10, the object of faith and invocation is the same: *How shall they call on him in whom they have not believed?* As we believe in God, so we invoke Him. behold their salvation. Nor does there exist anywhere in Scripture any example of any believer who invoked anyone other than God, as <term>Bellarmine</term> <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Cardinal and influential Catholic theologian during the Counter-Reformation</note> admits—at least regarding the believers of the Old Testament. However, he offers a ridiculous reason, which is nothing more than a <term>begging of the question</term> <note>original: *petitio principii*; a logical fallacy where one assumes the truth of the very thing they are trying to prove</note> and an <term>old wives' tale</term> <note>original: *anilis fabula*</note>. He claims that the fathers of the Old Testament were in <term>limbo</term> <note>In traditional Catholic theology, the "Limbus Patrum" was a temporary place for the souls of the righteous who died before Christ's resurrection</note> and therefore did not yet enjoy the clear vision and the "wonderful mirror" of the divine face or essence.

Since, therefore, the name of God is the object of invocation, it is no wonder if, conversely, the profanation of that name was inevitably punished, a fact confirmed by various examples from Scripture. Indeed, even among the heathens, the name of God was held sacred; the <term>Pythagoreans</term> <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, known for their strict ethical and mystical rules</note> themselves were afraid to wear it on their rings and insignia lest it be profaned. Hence the Pythagorean law:

> *Do not wear the image of God in a ring.* <note>original Greek: ἐν δακτυλίῳ θεοῦ εἰκόνα μὴ περιφέρειν</note>

Even though we may frequently invoke God and yet not be heard, we should not conclude from this that God does not wish to be invoked, or that He is not the proper object of prayer. For that best of fathers often hears us by *not* hearing us when we ask for things that are harmful—just like the sons of Zebedee—following the sentiment of an ancient philosopher among the heathens:

> *O immortal Gods, grant me good things even if I should not ask for them; but turn away from me evil things, even if I should ask for them.*

Indeed, when Christ himself (Matthew 26, Mark 14, and Luke 22) prayed in the garden and was not "heard" <note>In the sense of having the request granted</note>, he taught us not to take it poorly when we do not obtain from God what we ask. For in this prayer, Christ was partly heard and partly not heard. He was heard in that which he asked for absolutely—according to John 11: *I know that you always hear me.* However, he was not heard in what he asked for out of natural human feeling, according to Psalm 22 <note>original: *Psalm xxi* (Vulgate numbering). This refers to the opening of the Psalm: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"</note>: *I will cry out by day and you will not hear.* Unless, however, we say that Christ was heard in that which he prayed for conditionally:

> *Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.*

He asked, therefore, to be freed from death only under the condition of its possibility.

Nor is that vain argument of a "greatest philosopher" of any better quality, by which he seeks to prove that God is not to be invoked at all. He argues as follows: *God is not to be prayed to because He bestows good things of His own accord. For He does not hear the wicked even if they pray, and the good [He hears] even [without] invocation...*

...the remains of the body are venerated on earth; as someone among the ancients once truly said. In this way, men who live on earth place other men in the heavens—and the worst people place the worst men there—so that they might then be adored by humanity. 

Indeed, often those are canonized and adored who never even existed, such as Saint Ursula <note>The text reads "Viſula," likely a variant or error for Ursula</note> from whom the Ursuline nuns take their name; Saint Christopher; and George. In truth, since Canonization occurs through an inquiry and scrutiny into the life of the candidate, the decision depends on a matter of human fact; in such matters, according to their own decrees, the Pope is not <term>infallible</term>, as he is claimed to be in questions of Law. This is the formula: *In the name of God Almighty, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and of the Blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, and in our own name and authority, by the counsel of the brothers, we decree and define that [Name], of blessed memory, is a saint, and is to be enrolled in the catalog of Saints.*

But before that decree of canonization is pronounced by the Pope, the matter is litigated in the Papal court by patrons. Once the dispute has been aired, the Pontifical decree goes out, and then the entire Roman Church is commanded to invoke that saint—except that, on the other hand, Cardinal Perron and the Jesuit Peter Cotton have taught that it is a matter of indifference whether one invokes the Saints or not.

Sometimes, however, during the canonization process, the votes of the Cardinals are sought after by princes, either to procure or to block a canonization. This was done in the case of Ignatius Loyola <note>The founder of the Jesuit Order, canonized in 1622</note>, who was made "Blessed" (which is a step toward Sainthood) for a long time before he was finally decreed a saint. it was sanctioned by laws that no one should be enrolled in the list of the gods who had not first been declared a God by the Senate through a decree of <term>apotheosis</term> <note>The process of elevating a human being to divine status</note>. Just so, among the Romans today, it is not permitted to worship Saints unless they have first been canonized by the Pontifical Senate. Hence Cicero writes in book 2 of *On the Laws*: *No one shall have gods separately, nor new gods; nor shall they worship even foreign gods in private unless they have been publicly adopted.* <note>original Latin: "Separatim nemo habessit Deos, neue nouos, sed ne aduenas nisi publicè adscitos, priuatim colunto."</note> Thus the canonized Roman Emperors were called the *indigenous gods*, as Suetonius testifies in his biography of Vespasian. Vespasian himself used to mock this impious arrogance; for while he lay dying in his bed, he would say, *“Soon I shall become a god.”* <note>original Latin: "mox Deus euadam"</note> This ceremony used to take place at the Emperor’s funeral: an eagle would suddenly fly out from the funeral pyre and the ashes of the deceased toward the heavens. Then, that superstitious crowd of common people standing by believed that the soul of the Emperor had flown into the heavens, and thus they recorded him in the catalog of the gods. From the pyre of an Empress, however, a peacock would emerge—with the exception of Augusta Sabina <note>Vibia Sabina, wife of Emperor Hadrian</note>, who, on account of her strength of mind, had the privilege of having the Romans perform her funeral rites in the same manner and with the same birds as they did for the Emperors.

It is no wonder, therefore, if there was no canonization of Saints as long as the power and glory of the Roman Empire flourished. For as long as that greater force of subsequent times occupied the seat of proud tyranny, it could not be revealed, according to 2 Thessalonians 2:7: *only he who now restrains [will do so] until he be taken out of the way.* <note>original Greek: "μόνον ὁ κατέχων ἄρτι ἕως ἐκ μέσου γένηται"</note> *The one who restrains*—that is, *he who stands in the way*, or *he who holds power*—was at that time the Roman Emperor. Then, it pertained to the Emperors themselves and to the Senate to perform an <term>apotheosis</term>; but finally, when the glory of the empire was extinguished and its strengths prostrated, the second beast <note>A reference to the Beast of the Earth in the Book of Revelation, often interpreted by Protestant reformers as the Papacy</note> ascended from its ruins. From that point, the canonization of Saints immediately began. This is why the Jesuit Rainaudus <note>Théophile Raynaud (1583–1663), a prolific Jesuit scholar</note>, in his *Chronology*, traces the ritual of canonization only back to the year 710. For he says that Saint Suibertus <note>Saint Suidbert of Kaiserswerth (d. 713), a Northumbrian missionary</note> was the first to be decorated with a solemn canonization in the year 710. Nor should anyone think to argue against the novelty of canonization by pointing to the added word *solemn*, because no mention of canonization is found among the ancient writers. Indeed, those listings of the names of Saint Peter, Paul, Ignatius, Augustine, and others are more recent and do not imply a formal canonization, since the ancients followed a different custom...

# ANTONIUS CREGUT #

Scripture calls those "saints" who live on earth, not those dwelling in the heavens after death. <note>Cregut argues that in the New Testament, "saints" usually refers to the living community of believers, whereas the Catholic Church uses the term for the deceased who have been officially recognized.</note> Therefore, Tertullian <note>An early Christian author (c. 155–220 AD) from Carthage.</note> and other Doctors of the Church most truly said under the empire of the first beast, *“he who makes divines and gods is by this very act greater than God.”* <note>original Latin: "qui diuos deoſque facit hoc ipſo maiorem eſſe Deo"</note> But what would they have said about the man who recorded an assassin and parricide in the catalog of the divine? For Pope Sixtus V had previously praised him in a delivered speech on account of the murder of Henry III, <note>In 1589, King Henry III of France was assassinated by the Dominican monk Jacques Clément. Pope Sixtus V famously delivered a speech praising the act as a "remarkable, noble, and memorable work."</note> and he compared that crime (*oh, the impiety!*) with the mystery of redemption. *Oh, the wickedness!* These Vatican deities are put on display; these monsters—not of men, but of demons—are not located in the heavens, but are thrust down into <term>Tartarus</term> <note>The deepest abyss of the underworld in classical mythology, here used to mean Hell.</note>.

That canonization of Saints is truly, according to the opinion of the Papists, an <term>apotheosis</term> <note>The process of elevating a human being to divine status.</note> or **deification**, seeing as they judge seven honors to be owed to a canonized saint:

I. To be held and judged publicly as a Saint.
II. To be invoked in public prayers within the ecclesiastical assembly.
III. To have temples and altars consecrated to them.
IV. To have the divine office and sacrifice performed in their veneration.
V. To have feast days dedicated and hallowed for them.
VI. To have an image with lights <note>Referring to candles or lamps placed before icons or statues.</note> as a sign of glory.
VII. To have relics and chests—holy boxes and repositories—preserved and carried publicly on an anniversary feast.

Now, I ask you, what is this other than exhibiting the entire worship of religion to a creature? What else do the followers of the Pope do when they worship God? What special thing do they grant to God that they do not also grant to the Saints? *Oh, impious idolatry!*

From this, I gather that there are generally three illegitimate objects of invocation. I. That which is nowhere, and never was, is unlawfully worshipped and invoked. II. That which does exist can also be unlawfully worshipped and invoked if it is a creature; whether animate, like Angels and men, or inanimate, like the heavens. III. That which is God himself can be invoked unlawfully if he is worshipped superstitiously and with <term>will-worship</term> <note>original Greek: ἐθελοθρησκείᾳ (ethelothreiskeia); a term from Colossians 2:23 referring to self-imposed or man-made religious practices.</note>, such as through images and visible rituals. Thus, among the followers of the Pope, invocation is illegitimate in these three ways; hence it is that their most eagle-eyed Doctors frankly confess that *scarcely any distinction can be noted between Ethnic <note>i.e., Pagan or non-Christian.</note> and Roman idolatry.* Let one suffice for us: Ludovicus Vives <note>Juan Luis Vives (1493–1540), a Spanish humanist and student of Erasmus.</note> in his commentary on Augustine’s *City of God*, Book 8, Chapter 27, who reports thus: *“Nor do I see in...”*

From this canonization and invocation of Saints has flowed **patronage**, which also reeks immensely of <term>Gentilism</term> <note>A term used by early modern Protestants to refer to paganism or the practices of the "Gentiles" (non-Christians/heathens).</note>. Hence it is that **St. Crispin** is, among them, the patron of cobblers because they make sandals <note>original: "crepidas"</note>, according to that warning of the most excellent painter: *“let the cobbler not judge beyond his last.”* <note>original: "ne sutor ultra crepidam." Whatever cause he might set forth, I would have perished by now. Therefore, the name of God alone, and not that of a creature, is to be invoked.

Although there had been pious and religious men before this who without doubt worshiped God and invoked His name—such as Adam, Seth, Enoch, and the others—nevertheless the Church and the assembly of the faithful, who might invoke God with collective prayers, had not yet been gathered. That era, therefore, is notable in the history of the universal Church: For if the creation of the world is distinguished by the existence of creatures—from which the first counting of years began—so too the first gathering of the Church of God ought to be memorable, since the name of God was invoked by the faithful alone. But the holiness of the Church did not last long, seeing as before the Flood, another "flood" of impiety preceded it, which caused *God to repent that He had made the world* (Genesis 6:6). And thus the smallness of the Church was so great that its number was reduced to the family of the righteous Noah alone, while the other inhabitants of the world perished in the flood of waters. Then, after the Flood, the name of the Lord began to be invoked in the family of Shem and Eber (from whom the Hebrews are named), but more illustriously in the Patriarchs such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and the twelve Patriarchs and their descendants; and more magnificently in the time of David and Solomon, when the Temple was built. But it was in a more illustrious way still at the coming of Christ, when Christ first gathered the Apostles, who thereafter, through the calling of the Gentiles, would assemble the Church from all nations by the trumpet of the Gospel, according to the prophecy of Genesis 49:10 concerning the coming of the Messiah, in which there is the *gathering of the peoples* <note>Hebrew: *yiqhat ammim*</note>. Although this physical act was still in the future with respect to us, it was nevertheless always present to God in His eternity, in which there are no divisions of time. For when Christ intercedes for us, it should not be thought of crudely—as if He were kneeling down and prostrating Himself before the Father. But rather:

1. That by the power and efficacy of His sacrifice, like a most sweet fragrance, He makes the Father favorable toward us.
2. Because Christ is like the **mouth** through which we address the Father, the **eye** through which we look upon God, the **hand** by which we offer our prayers to God, and the **altar** upon which all our spiritual offerings are placed. In Him they are consecrated and become like incense pleasing to God. 

All of these things can truly be attributed to the faithful of the Old Testament, provided they embraced the Mediator with saving faith; for to faith, things absent are made present. Whence Augustine says: *This is what your Savior says: you have nowhere to go except to me; you have no way to go except through me.*

**R**he remarkable **taking up** <note>original: *raptus*, a term used here to describe a bodily ascent or "translation" into heaven without dying</note> of three remarkable persons, which occurred in the three ages of the world, and which prefigured the final and universal taking up of the whole **Church Militant** <note>the Christian church currently on earth, seen as being "at war" against sin and the devil</note> after the resurrection, has had almost all—both predecessors and successors—as its admirers; indeed, to many, because of the uniqueness and wonder of the matter, it has seemed incredible. We now approach the discussion of this matter under divine auspices, and we shall submit these three things alone to examination. I. We will deal with the taking up. II. Concerning the circumstances of the taking up. III. Concerning its end <note>meaning its goal or purpose</note>.

Scriptural history explicitly describes that unique taking up. Genesis 5, verse 24, Moses says concerning Enoch: *And Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him.* 2 Kings 2:11, concerning Elijah: *it happened as they went along walking and talking, that behold, a fiery chariot and fiery horses made a separation between them both: thus Elijah ascended in a whirlwind into heaven.* Concerning Christ, Acts 1:9: *And when he had said these things, while they looked on, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him and took him away from their eyes.* These testimonies of Scripture are so clear that there seems to be no reason for doubting, and one taking up illustrates the other; indeed, the more that times approach the **newest things** <note>the end of the world or "last things"</note>, that is, to the manifestation of the **sun of righteousness** <note>a biblical title for Christ, often used to signify the fullness of revelation</note>, the more the mysteries are revealed. Therefore, the taking up of Enoch is more obscure, because it occurred before the Law; the taking up of Elijah is more evident, because he lived under the Law; indeed, before he was actually taken up, there was a rumor among men and among the sons of the Prophets that Elijah was going to be taken up—whence Elisha was able to ask for gifts before the taking up, and Elisha was a witness of that taking up, which cannot be said of Enoch—that he had anyone as a witness of his taking up. Finally, in a more illustrious manner, Christ is taken up into the heavens in the sight of the disciples and the Angels. Concerning Enoch it is said more obscurely <term>enennu</term> <note>Hebrew: איננו</note>, "**he was not**," and <term>lakach otho</term> <note>Hebrew: לקח אתו</note>, "**he took him**." Yet from the whole context of the history, it becomes plain that something unique and extraordinary is being recounted there by the sacred historian. For what is cited in Ezekiel 24:16 concerning the Prophet's wife is entirely different and nothing unique occurs; indeed, in verse 18 the death of the wife is explicitly narrated: *my wife died in the evening.* For although the Prophet uses the word **took** <note>original: לקח (*lakach*)</note>...

The word **take** <note>original: לקה *lakach*</note>, as used by Moses, is not sufficient on its own; for we do not emphasize the word alone, but the entire narrative of the history. Yet, if we say that this phrase is quite unique within a singular mystery—as often happens in Scripture, which signifies unique doctrines to us through emphatic words and singular phraseology—it is clear from Luke 1:35 concerning the unique conception of Christ. There, the Angel said to Mary, **the power of the Most High will overshadow you** <note>original Greek: *δύναμις ὑψίστου ἐπισκιάσει σοι*; Latin: *virtus Altissimi inumbrabit te*</note>. Similarly, that phrase **he took him** <note>original: לקה אתו *lakach otho*</note> is scarcely found twice or thrice in Scripture when discussing someone’s departure from the living—specifically in the aforementioned passages of Genesis 5:24 and Ezekiel 24:16. You might also add the prayer of the Prophet Jonah in Jonah 4:3: *Now therefore, O Lord, take my life from me, I beseech you; for it is better for me to die than to live,* where he also uses the word **take** <note>original: *lakach*</note>.

Nevertheless, even if the "rapture" <note>the bodily ascent to heaven</note> of Enoch is not fully inferred from the word **take** <note>original: *lakach*, "he assumed" or "took up"</note> alone, but from the whole historical narrative, the word לקה <term>lakach; to take or receive</term> itself seems to me to designate something rare and specific in these passages when death is discussed. For although death is the "most terrible of terrors" and the **king of fears** <note>a reference to Job 18:14, describing the dread of dying</note>; yet because Genesis 5 speaks of Enoch as a holy man walking in the sight of God, God removed the horrors of death from him and peacefully **took him up** <note>original: *assumpsit*</note>. Moses speaks in such a way so that the faithful might be comforted against the terrors of death by that example of Enoch's benevolent "taking up," and against that terrifying decree: *in the day you eat of it, you shall surely die.* For this same reason, because the death of Ezekiel’s wife was sweet, and she departed from life as if in a moment—to be gathered into the "bundle of life"—the Scripture uses the word **take** <note>original: לקה *lakach*, "he assumed"</note>. This is what the Catholics <note>original: *Pontificii*, referring to the Roman Catholic Church</note> look back to (though they wander from historical truth) when they fashioned the "Assumption of the Blessed Virgin." We say the same of Jonah’s prayer, by which he undoubtedly desired not a painful death, but a tranquil and peaceful **taking up**.

Now, however, as far as Elijah is concerned, the words are crystal clear: **he ascended into heaven in a whirlwind.** There, the text is not discussing Elijah’s death, but his ascension into heaven in both body and soul. And Elisha, filled with wonder, cries out as if witnessing a singular and...

Here, he addresses the intermediate state of these translated figures and refutes Jewish and Catholic interpretations that suggest Enoch merely died an early death.</meta>

in a state that is better than that of the first humans <note>referring to Adam and Eve before the Fall</note>, but not as good as they will finally possess after the resurrection has occurred. This is the state in which He wills humans to have been held, had they not fallen, for as long as it took until they were to be transferred—together with everyone else afterward—into supreme happiness with a glorified body.

Since, therefore, that "taking up" of Enoch is confirmed by so many monuments of antiquity, it is a wonder that the Jews themselves have kicked against those testimonies. For Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note> thinks Enoch is said to have been "taken by God" because he perished sooner and at an immature age, so that his wickedness would not be changed <note>i.e., to prevent him from falling into sin</note>. To confirm this opinion, they bring forward the previously praised testimonies of Ezekiel 24 and Jonah 4, where <term>lakach <note>Hebrew: לָקַח</note></term>—that is, *he took* or *assumed*—is said of those who truly died and were not "translated" <note>moved to heaven without dying</note>. Aben Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a celebrated Spanish Jewish scholar</note> adds that this death of Enoch was sweet and without pain. Moreover, it is said <term>einennu <note>Hebrew: אֵינֶנּוּ</note></term>, *he was not*. Because if his years are compared with the age of the fathers, since they were quite short, it might seem as if Enoch himself "was not." Indeed, certain ones from the number of the Rabbis explain *einennu* to mean he was transformed into an Angel, so that he was no longer a man. Since these things are uttered from the vain reasoning of little men without the authority of the Scriptures, they are to be eliminated far from us with the same ease [with which they were proposed], according to that saying: <note>original Greek: ἄτερ γραφῆς</note> *without Scripture*.

Nor is the truth of this "taking up" hindered by what Paul wrote in Hebrews 9:27: *it is appointed for all to die once*. For besides the fact that the Apostle speaks of the ordinary way of all the earth, not of the extraordinary—for exceptions do not weaken but confirm the rule (as the Jurists say)—it must furthermore be added that death is not always the dissolution of the human body into a corpse, or the separation of the soul, but a transformation from a mortal and corruptible state to an immortal and incorruptible state. This is clear from the example of the people remaining alive at the final coming of Christ, who will not die in the ordinary way by a separation of the soul from the body, but <note>original Greek: ἐν ῥιπῇ τῷ ὀφθαλμῷ</note> *in the twinkling of an eye* they will be transformed. 1 Corinthians 15:51 and 52; 1 Thessalonians 4:17: *Then we who are alive and remain <note>original Greek: ἁρπαγηסόμεθα</note> shall be caught up <note>or "raptured"</note>.*

The Papists <note>original Latin: Pontificii; referring to Roman Catholics</note> also, no less than the Hebrews, deny the "taking up" of Enoch and Elijah, or at least entangle the history in fables. For in the *Hebrew* it reads simply: *Behold, I send you Elijah.* The *Septuagint* translates it: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the Tishbite" <note>original Greek: ἰδοὺ ἐγὼ ἀποστελῶ ὑμῖν Ἡλίαν τὸν Θεσβίτην</note>, as if the Prophet understood this specifically regarding *Elijah the Tishbite* by name, whereas he speaks instead allegorically and signifies *John the Baptist*, as *Christ* explains in the *Gospel*, who was like a second *Elijah*, for he came in the spirit and power of *Elijah*. 

This *Septuagint* corruption deceived *Chrysostom* <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Church Father</note>, who writes in a homily on *Matthew* that *Elijah* would return to the world. To this the *Papists* apply the prophecy of *Revelation* <note>original: Apocalypseos</note> concerning the two witnesses who are going to fight against the *Antichrist*, and whom the *Antichrist* will kill; but by such fictions <term>they invite much ridicule <note>original Greek: πολὺν γέλωτα ὀφλισκάνουsi (polyn gelōta ophliskanousi)</note></term>.

Therefore, we utterly hiss off the stage <note>original: exisibilamus</note> the fables the *Papists* tell about their dwelling in some sort of earthly paradise, and about their coming before the judgment, as <term>unwritten <note>original Greek: ἄγραφα (agrapha)</note></term> and <term>contrary to Scripture <note>original Greek: ἀντίγραφα (antigrapha)</note></term> ideas.
