...extraordinary <note>Continuing from the previous page: "extraordinary event."</note> Scripture attributes this to the <term>First Cause <note>A philosophical term for God, who initiates all things without being initiated by anything else.</note></term>, since its entire determination, direction, and ordering depend on that highest cause. Nevertheless, because it is a work of providence, it is not unreasonable to affirm that God, in that taking up of **Enoch** and **Elijah**, used the ministry of some creature—specifically an Angel. This is much like how our souls, when separated from the body, are carried into heaven by the ministry of Angels, no differently than the soul of **Lazarus** was carried into the "bosom of Abraham," and just as we will be caught up into the air after the resurrection. For although God could accomplish a rapture of this kind immediately and by a single act of will, He always prefers to act through intermediaries in the work of providence. And Scripture, dealing with the taking up of **Elijah**, expressly says he was taken up by a whirlwind, and **Christ** by a cloud, because God wanted some symbol of such a great event and unique effect to appear for the consolation of the faithful, so that the truth might be more fully witnessed.

Next, as to the state of the men taken up, without doubt their bodies were changed in an instant, as will happen after the resurrection to those humans still living, as **Paul** testifies in *1 Corinthians 15* and *1 Thessalonians 4*. This change will be equivalent to death. For just as in other men, that mortal body was destroyed to put on immortality, and the corruptible to put on incorruption—since the mortal and corruptible do not dwell in the heavens—the purpose of those raptures was to display specimens of the future resurrection to the eyes of men. This would not happen if those bodies always remained in their prior <note>Original: "priori," meaning their earthly, mortal state.</note> state. God, therefore, wished to prefigure the existence of the universal resurrection as if by a certain preliminary resurrection. For at that time, God wished to effect in those two faithful ones, many centuries before, what He would eventually perform in everyone. And just as **Christ**, long before His coming, gave "preludes" (*as **Tertullian** <note>An early Christian author (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) from Carthage.</note> likes to say*) of the future incarnation, so **Enoch** and **Elijah** gave preludes of the future resurrection. For on the day of resurrection, **Enoch** and **Elijah** will come just like the others; and they will be caught up into the air in the sight of the Lord.

Thus, having confirmed the truth of the rapture and its manner, we must now deal with the circumstances of the rapture, which also [make] the rapture more...

and they further illustrate and confirm the point. Regarding **Enoch**, Moses says that he walked with God, *and he was not, for God took him.* In this way, Moses intended to indicate the <term>procatarctic cause <note>The initial or triggering cause that sets a sequence of events in motion.</note></term> of that taking up: because he walked with God, he was pleasing and accepted by Him. Therefore, so that he would not associate with impure men and be corrupted by them, God took him. The Hebrew word is emphatic: <term>התהלך</term> <note>original: *hithhallec*</note> in the <term>Hitpael <note>A Hebrew verb form often used to express intensive, frequent, or reflexive action; here implying a habitual lifestyle.</note></term> stem; that is, properly, he "walked about," or walked frequently and assiduously. This was to signify not some faint or fleeting act of piety in **Enoch**, but a firm habit that was <term>more lasting and unchangeable</term> <note>original Greek: χρονιώτερος καὶ ἀμετάβλητος</note>.

Many circumstances are noted regarding the taking up of **Elijah**, for Scripture speaks of various instruments of his departure, such as the *chariot* <term>רכב</term> <note>original: *receb*</note>, *fiery horses*, and a *whirlwind*. All these surely demonstrate a magnificent departure and a kind of triumph for that great servant of God. Having suffered many anguishes and tortures from the impious **Ahab** and **Jezebel**, at last, after they were wretchedly destroyed, the prophet entered the heavens in triumph before all Israel—indeed, before the whole world. Thus, what the Hebrew masters say of mystical theology or philosophy can truly be applied to this mystery: <term>the Work of the Chariot</term> <note>original Hebrew: מעשה מרכבה (*ma'aseh merkavah*). In Jewish mysticism, this refers to the study of Ezekiel's vision and the divine realm.</note>. This is what they call the works of grace, as distinguished from <term>the Work of Creation</term> <note>original Hebrew: מעשה בראשית (*ma'aseh bereshit*)</note>, which refers to the works of nature. This alludes to the chariots found in the vision of **Ezekiel**, chapter 1. In this way, **Elijah’s** departure had to be magnificent amidst the terrors, lightning, and thunder of the Law.

Yet these earlier departures cannot be compared with that of **Christ**, which possessed this unique quality: that after death was conquered, along with sin and Satan, having risen from the dead, He entered the heavenly sanctuary in triumph with a glorious body by His own power. It also has this unique feature: that besides the disciples, the Angels themselves stood by as heavenly witnesses of His ascension, just as they were the heralds of His future coming at the Last Judgment, as is clear from Acts 1. And perhaps just as **Enoch** and **Elijah** preceded Christ's ascension from afar as "preludes," so they will closely precede His descent from heaven with the Angels when Christ comes to judge the living and the dead, so that of all...

But come now, let us specifically discuss all the circumstances of that triple taking up. These are three: namely, of *persons, places, and times*. 1. *As to persons*, there are three distinguished Prophets: Enoch prophesied before the Law, as seen in Jude verse 14: *“Now Enoch, the seventh from Adam, also prophesied about these men, saying, ‘Behold, the Lord comes with ten thousands of His saints.’”* Elijah prophesied under the Law, and Christ under the Gospel; but these Prophets differ from Christ just as servants differ from a Lord, as Paul conveys the distinction between Moses and Christ in Hebrews 3:5: *“Moses indeed was faithful in all His house as a servant, but Christ as a Son presides over His own house.”* Therefore, in comparing Enoch with Elijah, the latter stands ahead of the former by many <term>parasangs <note>An ancient Persian unit of distance, used here metaphorically to mean a great distance or degree.</note></term>; yet in comparing Elijah with Christ, the latter is higher by infinite parasangs and is incomparable due to his <term>excellence <note>original Greek: ὑπεροχὴν (hyperochēn)</note></term>. Nevertheless, if it please you, let them be set in parallel.

### *Three persons taken up in a triple taking up*

->*Setting them in parallel* <note>original Greek: παραλληλίζοντες (parallēlizontes)</note><-

I. Enoch and Elijah were not taken up by their own merit—for on the contrary, by their own demerit they were liable to be snatched away and thrust down into the abyss—but they were taken up by the merit of Christ alone, which exerted itself from the foundations of the world. For Revelation 13 says: *“The Lamb of God was slain from the foundation of the world.”* Therefore, before Christ’s entrance into the sanctuary, the heavens were open to the faithful of the Old Testament, whatever the <term>Papists <note>A common term in 17th-century Protestant writing for members of the Roman Catholic Church.</note></term> may babble regarding the <term>limbo of the fathers <note>original: limbo patrum; a theological concept of a place where the souls of the righteous were held until Christ's resurrection.</note></term>.

II. Enoch and Elijah were taken up into the heavens before they had tasted death; but Christ ascended into heaven after he had been crucified, had died, was buried, and had descended to the lower regions, so that, having conquered his enemies, he might triumph over principalities, powers, etc.

III. Enoch and Elijah did not ascend into the heavens by their own power, but were snatched up by the hand of God; hence, the term "taking up" <note>original: raptus</note> is properly used for Enoch and Elijah because they were translated by another’s force, but Christ ascended by his own divine power and will; hence it is that

Christ is said to have ascended, rather than to have been snatched away, because he ascended by his own power and is not carried off by a force external to himself.

VI. The ascension of Enoch and Elijah benefited themselves but not others, except only as an example; for they were by no means able to open heaven for others; but Christ's ascension profits all the faithful, because he himself, as the Holy Priest, opened heaven, and penetrating the veil, proceeded to the sanctuary, where he intercedes for us <term>without ceasing <note>original Greek: ἀδιαλείπτως (adialeiptōs)</note></term>. Hence in Hebrews 6:20: *“Christ the forerunner has entered heaven for us.”*

VII. Enoch and Elijah were snatched into heaven out of God’s favor and benevolence toward them, which is called <term>sanctifying grace <note>original Latin: "gratia gratum faciens," a theological term for the grace that makes a soul pleasing to God and grants salvation.</note></term>, because God loved them in his beloved one. But Christ ascended into heaven so that he might become a partaker of his own glory; because the throne of glory is there, and he ought to be the head of Angels and men, therefore he was exalted so that all things might be subject under his feet, according to Ephesians 1:22.

VIII. Enoch and Elijah did not give gifts to men after their ascension. Christ, however, when he had ascended on high, gave gifts to men, because on the solemn feast day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit was sent in the sign of tongues of fire. Acts 2 and Ephesians 4.

IX. Elijah could not give Elisha the double portion of the Spirit which Elisha requested from him, for he confesses the thing to be difficult, as it is something given only by God, not by men; but Christ, as he received the spirit without measure, so he distributes various portions of his Spirit, until we come <term>to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ <note>original Greek: εἰς μέτρον ἡλικίας τοῦ πληρώματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ (eis metron hēlikias tou plērōmatos tou Christou)</note></term>.

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS

And let these things suffice concerning the distinction of the persons. Regarding the circumstance of place, it is viewed either in respect to the *starting point* <note>original: "termini à quo"</note> or in respect to the *destination* <note>original: "termini ad quem"</note>. In respect to the *starting point*, sacred history does not relate the specific place from which Enoch was snatched away, and indeed it was not necessary; for although the circumstance of place is required for the certainty of historical truth—according to that well-known saying, *history without chronology and topography is like a house without light and a bell without a clapper*—nevertheless, in every particular history, that circumstance is not always exactly observed without some special reason. Concerning Elijah, the place is noted, namely near the Jordan; and after Elijah had performed a miracle by striking the waters with his cloak and both had walked through on dry ground, the river Jordan was thus distinguished by so many miracles. For also in the time of Joshua, the Israelites crossed on dry ground, and at their entry, the divided river yielded to those about to cross (*Joshua 3*). So Naaman the Syrian was healed of his leprosy by being dipped seven times in the Jordan; so spiritual leprosy was cleansed by John the Baptist baptizing in the Jordan. Now also because of Elijah’s rapture, that river was ennobled. But especially that circumstance is noted by the Evangelists in the ascension of Christ, which is said to have taken place from the Mount of Olives, and that not without a mystery: since on that mountain he endured various anguishes and tortures, as is clear from *Matthew 26:37–38*. For it was fitting for Christ to give a proof of divine glory and his own Majesty in the same place in which he had previously exhibited the signs of his weakness; thus the same mountain could witness the <term>emptying <note>original: "exinanitionem," referring to the "kenosis" or Christ's voluntary humbleness during his earthly life</note></term> of Christ and his exaltation. In the same place where he fought strenuously against the Father’s justice and spiritual powers, so there he brought back the fruits and triumphs of victory.

In respect to the *destination*, Moses does not speak explicitly of the rapture of Enoch; however, we gather from the words of Scripture that it is said implicitly that he was translated into the heavens, because God took him and he was no longer among men. Since God dwells in the heavens, and the faithful become heavenly beings after this life, there is no doubt but that Enoch was snatched into heaven. Concerning Elijah, however, and Christ, the matter is clear, since it is expressly said that they were translated into heaven; and truly if Lazarus and the good thief are in the heavens,

<meta>This page continues the theological discussion regarding the destination of Enoch and Elijah after their "translation" or departure from Earth, specifically refuting the idea that they are held in a terrestrial paradise rather than the highest heavens.</meta>

### ANTHONY CREGUT

...why should Enoch and Elijah be exiled from the heavens?

Nor should anyone object by citing the passage in John 3:13: *No one has ascended into heaven, except he who descended from heaven,* etc. For this is wrongly understood as a physical, local ascent, whereas in that context it refers to a **metaphorical ascent**, that is, to the spiritual understanding of the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven. This is a wisdom that only the Son, who is the Wisdom of the Father, could grasp—He who was in the heavens and is the only-begotten from the bosom of the Father <note>John 1</note>. In this same metaphorical sense, the passage in Romans 10:6 can also be explained: *Do not say in your heart, "Who will ascend into heaven?"*—although this can also be explained in terms of a local, physical ascension.

The objection brought from the passage in Ecclesiasticus 44:16 <note>also known as the Book of Sirach</note> is also invalid. In the Greek, the text reads: *Enoch pleased the Lord God, and was translated, an example of repentance to these generations.* But in the Vulgate edition <note>the standard Latin Bible used by the Catholic Church</note>, it is wrongly recorded against the **Greek original** <note>original: "ἀυτόγραφον"</note> as: *he was translated into paradise, that he might give repentance to the nations.* Here, Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine, a prominent Jesuit theologian and Cardinal</note> hallucinates in various ways, or rather, he deliberately misuses the passage. 

I. Having dismissed the Greek original, he follows the Latin translator and fails to correct the error. 
II. From the fact that the Vulgate translator uses the word "paradise," Bellarmine wrongly infers that this paradise is **terrestrial** (on Earth), when it is better explained as the **celestial** (heavenly) paradise. This is illustrated by the "rapture" of Elijah, who was translated into the heavenly paradise, for he **ascended into the heavens** <note>original Hebrew: *alah ha-shamayim*</note>. 
III. He errs in imagining a terrestrial paradise, since none exists on earth today; for the paradise that existed in the time of Adam perished in the waters of the Flood. It was located in Mesopotamia, as is clear from the mention of the river Euphrates. 
IV. The Jesuit disagrees even with his own associates, who place those who were "snatched away" in the regions of the air—unless they wish to claim that the terrestrial paradise reaches the highest region of the air and stands 16 cubits higher than the mountains, as some dream. They imagine it was raised one cubit above the waters of the Flood, which, according to the testimony of Moses in Genesis 7:20, rose to a height of 15 cubits.

Of the same sort are the fables told about their coming to fight against the Antichrist, which they claim could not happen if they were already in the heavens. But they devise these things in vain against the Scriptures, which predicted nothing regarding their return. For as to what they bring forward from Malachi, chapter 4, verse 5: *Behold, I will send to you...*

<meta>This page continues the theological argument by Anthony Cregut regarding the fulfillment of biblical prophecy. Having previously discussed the translation of Enoch and Elijah, Cregut now addresses the specific prophecy of Elijah's return found in the book of Malachi, arguing that it refers to John the Baptist rather than a literal return of the ancient prophet.</meta>

# REVEALER OF SECRETS.

"...to you Elijah the prophet, before the great and venerable day of the Lord comes," <note>original Latin: "vobis Eliam prophetam, antequam veniat dies Iehovae maximus & reuerendus"</note> they interpret this passage poorly. For the prophet is not speaking literally about Elijah the Tishbite <note>the Old Testament prophet who was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind</note>, as the **Septuagint** <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, often abbreviated as LXX</note> mistakenly understood (as mentioned above). Rather, through "Elijah," he signifies **John the Baptist**, for whom the prophet Elijah served as a <term>type</term> <note>a "type" is a historical figure or event in the Old Testament seen as a symbolic precursor to someone in the New Testament</note>.

There are many similarities between Elijah and John the Baptist: in their persons, in their way of life, in their burning zeal, in their strict and severe ministry, and finally in the time in which they lived—comparing the biblical King Ahab and Queen Jezebel to King Herod and Herodias, both pairs being bitter persecutors. I bring forward an interpreter beyond all reproach, namely **Christ**, who in Matthew 11:10 and 14 explains this as referring to John the Baptist, asserting that "Elijah" has already come as the forerunner who prepared the ways of the Lord, in accordance with Malachi’s prophecy.

Furthermore, those words, *before the great and venerable day of the Lord comes*, do not signify the Day of Judgment or the final coming of Christ, but rather his first coming. For in the Hebrew it is *Yom Ha-Nora* <note>original: יום הנורא</note>, words which do not always mean a "terrible day," but a "**venerable day**," which properly matches Christ's first coming—truly great and venerable—for which John the Baptist was the herald. 

And besides, even if one chooses to translate the Hebrew word as "terrible day," it still fits Christ's first coming; in this sense, "terrible" would mean "to be feared," and fear arises either from terror or from **reverence**. This is seen in Genesis 28, when God appeared to Jacob in a dream; upon waking, Jacob said, *How awesome is this place!* <note>original Hebrew: מה נורא המקום הזה — "ma nora hammakom hizze"</note>. The Latin translator renders this as "**how terrible is this place**" <note>original: "quàm terribilis locus iste"</note>, yet who cannot see that the place is venerable because of the signs of the divine presence?

Indeed, it can be understood as a sense of dread, just as when God is called the *Fear of Isaac* <note>original Hebrew: פחד יצחק — "pachad iitshchak"</note>, meaning the one whom Isaac fears. Among the Hebrews, the faithful are called *those who fear the Lord* <note>original Hebrew: יראי יהוה — "yirei Yehovah"</note>, and among the Syrians, *those who fear God* <note>original Syriac: דחלי אלהא — "dechli Alaha"</note>, a term which also implies something "terrible." Among the Chaldeans and Syrians, the word *Dachala* <note>original: דחלא</note> signifies an idol or a false god, which idolaters fear as if it were the true God. And certainly, the Septuagint translates this as *the great and glorious day of the Lord* <note>original Greek: ἡμέραν κυρίου μεγάλην καὶ ἐπιφανῆ</note>.

It was also terrible for other nations to whom, because of their unbelief, it was—as **Simeon** witnesses in **Luke 2:34**—*Behold, this child is destined for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be spoken against.* <note>original Latin: "Ecce poſitus eſt iſte in caſum & reſurrectionem multorum in Iſrael, & in ſignum cui contradicatur."</note> This also extends to the Gentiles and all unbelievers, to whom the cross of Christ is either a stumbling block or foolishness. But indeed, although the circumstances of the location have been proven by us from the testimonies of the Scriptures—both regarding the <term>translation</term> <note>the miraculous taking up into heaven without dying</note> of Enoch and Elijah as well as that of Christ—let it be far from us to borrow the fables and vain inventions of little men <note>a dismissive term for superstitious or unreliable authors</note> to demonstrate the truth of this notable history. This is especially true when discussing the **Ascension of Christ**, as **Cardinal Caesar Baronius** <note>a powerful Catholic historian (1538–1607) known for his "Annales Ecclesiastici"</note> did in the first volume of his *Annals* for the year 34, number 232, when he says: *An outstanding monument to the ascension into heaven are the footprints of the sacred feet impressed upon the earth. Concerning these, the prophet Zechariah once said in chapter 14: "His feet shall stand in that day upon the Mount of Olives, which is opposite Jerusalem to the East"; therefore, Christians turned toward the East when they prayed.* <note>original Latin: "Egregium aſcenſionis monumentum ad cælum eſt ſacrorum pedum terræ impreſſa veſtigia..."</note> Similar things are certainly found among the ancient writers, but these things are said without proof and without the support of Scripture.

**Jerome**, writing *On Hebrew Places* as cited by Baronius, has this to say: *The last footprints of Christ on the Mount of Olives are shown today impressed into the earth; and although the earth is continually carried away by the faithful, it remains. And when the Church was built there, the highest peak could never be covered or vaulted over because of the passage of the Lord’s body, but the place remains open.* <note>The legend suggests that because Christ ascended from that spot, human-made roofs would miraculously fail to cover it.</note> **Optatus of Milevis** <note>a 4th-century bishop in North Africa</note> feels the same way, as does **St. Paulinus, Bishop of Nola**, in his 11th letter to Severus. As for the circumstance of time, it is worthy of observation; for not without reason did **Enoch**, **Elijah**, and **Christ** ascend into heaven during different periods of time. Since there are three ages of the world—before the Law, under the Law, and under the Messiah—God willed that symbols of the future resurrection should exist in those three ages. For **Enoch** was the example and prelude of the resurrection for those who lived before the Law; **Elijah** for those under the Law; and **Christ** for those under grace and under the Gospel.

And from this, the purpose of this triple <term>rapture</term> <note>original Latin: "raptus," referring here to being "caught up" or translated into heaven</note> becomes clear. For the common purpose is that they should all be symbols and illustrious monuments of the future resurrection for the consolation of the faithful amidst the various hardships of this earthly pilgrimage. The specific purpose regarding **Christ** is that he might prepare a place for us in heaven; and where the head is, there also the members should gather. Furthermore, it was so that he might intercede for us in heaven as if in a sanctuary, insofar as he is our **Priest**; for (as the Apostle witnesses in the **Epistle to the Hebrews**) <note>Referring to Hebrews 8:4</note> he would not have been a Priest if he had remained on earth forever.

**Just as pride** is the greatest of all sins, so it draws after it punishments more fatal and lethal than all others. Because of the fall of the Angels through pride, they immediately plunged into the most deadly punishment: <note>original Greek: Θεὸς σειραῖς ζόφου ταρταρώσας; from 2 Peter 2:4</note> *God, casting them into Tartarus, delivered them into chains of darkness.* Adam likewise, having fallen through pride, devoted himself and his posterity to eternal and unending torments. The same thing also happened to the architects of the Tower of Babel; for as they, puffed up by pride, busied themselves to raise a tower even to heaven, so by the most just judgment of God the greatest punishment for sin was inflicted upon them: namely, the confusion of tongues, which is truly a <term>cacoethes</term> <note>A medical or rhetorical term for a "malignant habit" or "bad custom"</note> of horrible evils. 

Regarding this, in the elucidation of this oracle <note>referring to the biblical text or prophecy being analyzed</note>, a discussion is incumbent upon us—provided that the Pentecostal Spirit, who once sent out tongues distributed like fire, breathes peacefully upon us—and this under a threefold examination:
I. *Concerning the confusion of languages.*
II. *Concerning the causes of that confusion, both the principal cause and the less principal or <term>procatarctic</term> <note>original Latin: procatarctica; a technical term in logic and medicine meaning the immediate or inducing cause</note> cause.*
III. *Concerning the effects of that confusion of tongues—that is, first regarding the dispersion, and by contrast, we shall contemplate the blessings in every member of the gift of tongues within the economy of grace.*

I. As for the confusion of tongues, it should be noted what Moses recounts in Genesis 11:1: *The whole earth was of one lip and of the same words.* This was truly a great blessing from God; for since humans are by nature <term>social animals</term> <note>original Greek: ζῶα πολιτικὰ (zōa politika); a reference to Aristotle's definition of humanity</note>, and the concepts of the mind cannot be explained except by the tongue, it was fitting that all should be of "one lip," so that they could communicate among themselves. Without this, the sacred bond of society would be immediately dissolved. 

Therefore, a variety of languages is a <term>deviation from nature</term> <note>original Greek: παρέκβασις τῆς φύσεως (parekbasis tēs physeōs)</note> and seems to represent something of a monster or a portent. For although that first language was not natural, but existed <note>original Greek: κατὰ τὴν συνθήκην τοῦ Θεοῦ (kata tēn synthēkēn tou Theou)</note> *according to the covenant of God*, nevertheless, the commonality of it was truly <note>original Greek: κατὰ φύσιν (kata physin)</note> *according to nature*, so that the concepts of the mind might be more easily communicated. That variety of languages, then, is accidental, and was inflicted upon men as a punishment for sin. By these [varied languages], humans are, as it were, <term>tortured</term> <note>original Latin: excarnificantur; literally "flayed" or "racked," referring to the intense difficulty of learning many languages</note> from their youth.

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of the "original language" of humanity. While the previous page discussed the confusion of tongues at Babel as a punishment and the possibility of a return to a single language in the afterlife, this page focuses specifically on identifying that original language as Hebrew and explaining why it only received its specific name later in history.</meta>

# ANTHONII CREGVTI

…and this language is called holy and chosen before sin and Babel, because the earth was of "one lip"; and this shall be the language under the kingdom of the Messiah. Thus says Petrus Galatinus <note>a 16th-century Italian theologian and scholar of Hebrew</note>.

However, leaving aside those speculations about the future state in the resurrection—at least regarding the language men will speak, since Scripture maintains a deep silence on these things, withholding what is merely curious—one thing remains clear: before the confusion of languages, there was not only one single language, but that language was Hebrew. This is evident from the proper names given to things from the beginning, such as Adam, Cain, Seth, etc. All of these names have meanings and etymologies <note>the study of the origins of words</note> confirmed in Scripture, and they cannot be derived from anything but a Hebrew origin. Indeed, since those names were not given by chance <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ τύχης" (apo tyches)</note> but by deliberate choice <note>original Greek: "ἐκ προαιρέσεως" (ek proaireseōs)</note>, the reason for their origin is sought from Scripture. Therefore, since that language existed in the state of innocence, the opinion of the Hebrews is very probable: that it will also remain in the resurrection—unless we think it even more probable that in the world to come, the Hebrew language will be changed and made even more perfect, as befits a state of glory. Just as all other things will be changed for the better.

When, therefore, Augustine in Book 16 of *The City of God*, final chapter, says that the Hebrew language was invented after the time of Noah, he does not mean to deny that Hebrew existed before then. Rather, he simply means that it began to be *called* "Hebrew" in the time of Noah's descendants. For (as Eucherius <note>a 5th-century bishop and exegete</note> rightly explains) before the division of tongues, the Hebrew language was common to all, and therefore did not have a specific name. But in the time of Heber <note>or Eber, a biblical figure from whom the term "Hebrew" is traditionally derived</note>, when many languages had begun to exist, that common language was called "Hebrew" to distinguish it from the others, because it remained in the house of Heber. From him, the Hebrews were named, as if "Hebereans" descended from Heber; this was the name by which Abraham was first called by the Canaanites (Genesis 14:13). Or it may be derived from *avar* <note>original Hebrew: "עבר"</note>, meaning "across," as if to say "from across the river" or "from across the Euphrates."

Thus, the Hebrew language has this advantage over all others: it was passed down as a blessing, not as a curse, unlike the other languages that arose from the confusion at Babel. For this reason, Hebrew is the most noble and most significant of all; for while the rest are of human institution, Hebrew alone…

<header>THE REVEALER OF SECRETS</header>

...[He]brew is by divine institution. For to say that languages signify **by nature** <note>original Greek: "φύσει" (physei)</note> as Plato maintained, would be plainly ridiculous; rather, we should agree with Aristotle that they signify **by convention** <note>original Greek: "θέσει" (thesei); the idea that words get their meaning from human agreement rather than an inherent natural link</note>. Therefore, three things must be observed in languages: I. *The material aspect*. II. *The formal aspect*. III. The **institution** <note>original Greek: "συνθήκη" (synthēkē); a formal agreement or establishment</note> or imposition. The *material* is the sound of the letter and syllable, whether pronounced or written; the *formal* is the meaning or the relationship to concepts. The **institution** or establishment is the foundation and the efficient cause of that meaning. Since this institution is divine in the Hebrew language, it is undoubtedly elegant and emphatic, having borrowed nothing from elsewhere.

Hence it is that Hebrew alone, among all languages, possesses words that signify not only with reason, but a single word often has various meanings. These agree wonderfully and emphatically with the thing signified. What is even more remarkable is that if a word is changed in various ways—whether from the beginning to the end, from the end to the beginning, or if you begin a **transposition of letters** <term>metathesis: the rearranging of letters within a word</term> from the middle—the word will always signify something, and that meaning will fit the thing itself beautifully. This is truly extraordinary and cannot be observed in any other language; in others, if even the slightest transposition occurs, the word becomes unarticulated or rather signifies nothing at all.

It is from this principle that the masters of the Hebrews, in their **Kabbalah** <note>the ancient Jewish tradition of mystical interpretation of the Bible</note> or mystical philosophy, have discovered various mysteries through sharp philosophical reasoning, as well as by calculating or rearranging letters from the richness of the language. Any person skilled in the language can experience this for themselves. However, human **institution** <note>original Greek: "Συνθήκη" (synthēkē)</note> is found in other languages, which were born from the punishment of pride <note>referring to the Tower of Babel</note> and were mixed in various ways, partly from Hebrew and partly from each other. In them, you can see the clear traces of Babylon. Indeed, these are counted as seventy-two languages, not including the various dialects of a single tongue. See Conrad Gesner in his little book on the differences of languages, which he titled *Mithridates* <note>Published in 1555, this was one of the first works of comparative linguistics</note>.

Therefore, those three things must be distinguished: **onomatopoeic sounds** <note>original Greek: "τὰ πεποιημένα" (ta pepoiemena); literally "things made," referring to words that imitate natural sounds</note>, the use of speech (or discourse), and the articulation of languages. The first two are **by nature** <note>original Greek: "φύσει" (physei)</note>; "made" sounds like bleating, lowing, roaring, etc., are seen naturally in beasts. Discourse is also natural to every human and to humans alone, because since man is a **social animal** <note>original Greek: "πολιτικὸν" (politikon); an Aristotelian term meaning an animal meant to live in a community</note>, nature gave him the use of speech, which is the **instrument of community** <note>original Greek: "κοινωνίας ὄργανον" (koinōnias organon)</note>. But the third, that is, the articulation of languages, is not natural; as...

This is clear from the history in Genesis 11 regarding the confusion of tongues; because languages undergo various changes, so much so that within a hundred or two hundred years they are not understood by descendants, just as if they were foreign languages—yet natural things do not change. Since the Hebrew language (as was said above) is of such great dignity, it must be confessed that the confusion of tongues is a horrible punishment, which deprived us of the use of the Hebrew language and, conversely, introduced barbarism through the variety of the remaining languages. 

But indeed, so that we may feel the punishment of the sin of Babel and its gravity all the more: Come now, let us briefly consider the dignity of the Hebrew language. 1. Its dignity is derived from its *simplicity*. For if you except certain proper names, you would hardly find compound words; almost all are simple, just as the power of the letters is simple. Next, every primary root consists of three letters, with very few exceptions—which, for that reason, might seem spurious or foreign. Add to this that in a single radical letter <note>The "root" or foundational letters of a word</note>, the entire meaning of a word is sometimes found no less than in three letters. This is clear in the word <term>שדי</term> <gloss>Shaddai</gloss>, a name for God, where the letter <term>ש</term> <term>shin</term> signifies <term>asher</term> <note>original: "אשר"; meaning "who" or "which"</note>, as if you were to say <term>ש די</term> <gloss>asher dai</gloss>, which means <gloss>He who is sufficient</gloss>. It is also seen in the names <term>מיכאל</term> <gloss>Michael</gloss> and <term>מכבי</term> <gloss>Maccabeus</gloss>: <term>מי כה אל</term> <gloss>Who is like You, strong God?</gloss> and <term>יהוה מי כמוכה באלים</term> <gloss>Who is like You among the gods, O God?</gloss> <note>original: "Mi camocha ba-elim Adonai" from Exodus 15:11</note> 

Furthermore, many words are derived from any common root. Moreover, a single tense includes many timeframes; for since the "past tense" is the only one used among the Hebrews, it contains the other types of the past—the imperfect, the pluperfect, and the <term>aorists</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀορίסטους"; a Greek tense referring to a past action without specifying its duration or completion</note> of the Greeks—in an eminent and somewhat superior way. Indeed, the past is often taken for the present and for the future when it is preceded by the <term>vau hippuk</term> <gloss>vav-conversive</gloss>, that is, the <term>vav conversivum</term> <note>A grammatical rule where the letter 'vav' (and/or 'waw') attached to the front of a verb reverses its tense, turning a past-tense form into a future-tense meaning</note>. Its simplicity also appears in its moods, for the indicative mood encompasses the others. Yet, such great simplicity does not (wonderfully enough) produce obscurity, because the meaning is easily drawn from the whole context, as those who are skilled in the holy language know. I omit here the various mysteries which some wish to extract from this property of the Hebrew language to demonstrate the simplicity of the Divine essence, the Trinity of persons, the infinity of God, His sufficien—

...[wis]dom, etc., which, because they possess more cleverness than substance, I voluntarily omit.

II. A property of the language, which also elevates its <gloss>excellence</gloss> <note>original: "ἐξοχὴν"</note>, is **brevity**. For while other languages luxuriate in almost innumerable roots—such as Greek, Latin, Arabic, etc.—Hebrew alone has few roots. Therefore, just as a single gemstone is preferred over many common stones, so one Hebrew word contains several Greek and Latin words in its meaning; and conversely, a single thing is expressed by various Arabic words, especially important things, so that it is a sign of a thing's greater nobility whenever it is expressed by various notions among the Arabs. And yet, sometimes the opposite occurs, as is clear from the story of the cat by the Arabic historian Timur: just as the four-letter name of God, <term>Jehovah</term> <note>The Tetragrammaton, the sacred four-letter name of God in Hebrew</note>, is more perfect the more it signifies God's greater or more numerous perfections, so too is the Hebrew word, because it designates more things within its meaning.

III. Its <gloss>excellence</gloss> <note>original: "ἐξοχὴ"</note> is its **perfection**; for a single word and root is inflected through eight conjugations <note>The different patterns or "stems" a Hebrew verb can take to change its meaning</note>, which wonderfully increase, strengthen, change, or reciprocate the meaning, and sometimes signify the same sense, and sometimes the contrary, as is clear from <term>בָּרַךְ</term> <gloss>barak</gloss>, which signifies both "to bless" and "to curse" when the conjugation is changed. Hence the Hebrews call conjugations <term>בִּנְיָנִים</term> <gloss>binyanim</gloss>, that is, **buildings** or **structures**, because from them are drawn the ingenious and emphatic devices of Hebrew expression, countless examples of which exist in the New Testament.

IV. Its <gloss>excellence</gloss> <note>original: "ἐξοχὴ"</note> is **modesty** and **decorum**. For while other languages often use obscene vocabulary, Hebrew alone substitutes honorable words, so that it truly appears to be the **Divine language** <gloss>the language</gloss> <note>original: "τὴν γλῶσσαν"</note>. Thus in Genesis 4:1, and often elsewhere, the word <term>יָדַע</term> <gloss>iadah</gloss>, that is, **he knew**—"Adam knew his wife"—is used for conjugal love. There are also many honorable words which the <term>Masoretes</term> <note>Jewish scholar-scribes who preserved and standardized the Hebrew Bible text</note>, the critics of the Hebrews, placed in stead of obscene ones. For example, in 2 Kings 18:27, where the text mentions <term>שֵׁינֵיהֶם</term> <gloss>their urines</gloss>, the Masoretes (for the sake of modesty), as well as the Chaldean translator, read it as <term>מֵימֵי רַגְלֵיהֶם</term> <gloss>the waters of their feet</gloss>. Likewise, in 2 Kings 6:25, <term>חֲרֵי־יוֹנִים</term> <gloss>excrement of doves</gloss>, the Masoretes substitute <term>דִּבְיוֹנִים</term> in the margin. In this way, the ancient Hebrews look out for the modesty of the holy language, so that words used in a profane way...

**V.** Its properties include **unity and antiquity**; for since it existed from the beginning at the creation of the world and before the confusion of languages, it is rightly considered both one and the most ancient. **VI.** Its property is **holiness**. For the Hebrew language is commonly called the **"Holy Tongue"**; and this is for many reasons.

II. Because it was the language of a holy people and of God’s Church.
III. Because in that language God was called upon and the name of God was sanctified.
IV. Because in that language the Old Testament and the Law of God were written, which are holy and just.
V. Because, as we said above, it eliminates obscene words and substitutes holy and decent ones. ...and so forth. In the same way, our French tongue is unable to express the force of the Greek words *phronēma* <note>original: φρόνημα; referring to a mindset, purpose, or the "mind of the flesh"</note> and *phronein* <note>original: φρονεῖν; to be minded or to think in a certain way</note>, and indeed, neither can Latin. For this reason, the common translator <note>the Latin Vulgate</note> wrongly expresses it as **wisdom** <note>Latin: *sapientiam*</note> in Romans 8. This is because *phronēma* and *phronein* are sometimes taken in a good sense and sometimes in a bad sense, which cannot be said of "wisdom." It is for this reason that Beza <note>Theodore Beza, a 16th-century Protestant reformer and linguist</note> correctly renders it thus: **What the flesh savors is death**. Similarly, there is a distinction between "reprobate" and "rejected" <note>Latin: *reprobum* and *reprobatum*</note> found in 1 Corinthians 9:27: **lest I myself should be a castaway** <note>original Greek: αὐτὸς ἀδόκιμος γένωμαι</note>. For "reprobate" is the opposite of **proven** <note>Latin: *probo*</note> and **sincere**, but not necessarily the opposite of "elect." Likewise, that distinction which Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine, a prominent Jesuit theologian</note> places between **refusing** and **not-willing** <note>Latin: *nolle* and *non velle*</note>, or **willing** and **not-refusing** <note>Latin: *velle* and *non nolle*</note>, no language besides Latin is able to express, because others use the negative particle disjunctively, as those who are skilled in other languages know. Nevertheless, even if other languages have their own unique idioms, they are all impoverished compared to the riches of the Hebrew language and the emphasis of its Hebraisms.

VIII. There is also **Singularity**. This differs from "Hebraisms," which represent unique features only in parts of a language—features which other tongues strive to imitate for the sake of their singular emphasis. But "singularity" regards the language as a whole, which surpasses all others by many parasangs <note>a Persian unit of distance, used here to mean "by a great length"</note>, as is evident from the properties mentioned above, such as, primarily, its **simplicity** and **brevity**; and indeed its **perfection**, which arises from the variety and emphasis of its conjugations. To be sure, the illustrious historian Jacques Auguste de Thou <note>Latin: Thuanus</note>, in the second book of his *History of His Life*, page 25, has some memorable observations regarding the singularity of languages, especially concerning the Basque or Cantabrian tongue. *For when he visited the district of Béarn and arrived at La Bastide-Clairence in Lower Navarre, he saw and spoke with Joannes Leizarraga <note>Latin: Licarraguem</note>, the pastor of that place, who, by order of Queen Jeanne <note>Jeanne d'Albret, the Protestant Queen of Navarre</note>, translated the catechism and the New Testament into the Basque or Cantabrian language. For the Cantabrian language, just like our British <note>referring to the Breton language of Brittany</note> and Irish, is singular and has nothing in common with others; for this reason, it was once thought that it could not even be written down.* These are the words of De Thou in his autobiography: but observe, even if those languages were unique, that singularity is...

### REVEALER OF SECRETS

...the punishment of the confusion of tongues, and was therefore harmful because it increased the difficulty of language; but the singularity of the Holy Tongue comes from divine institution, which does not make the language worse, but raises its extraordinary <term>superiority</term> <note>original Greek: ὑπεροχὴν (hyperochēn); meaning pre-eminence or excellence</note> above others, so that other languages cannot imitate its unique character.

**IX.** There is also its (so to speak) *motherhood*. For the Hebrew language is the mother and root of all languages, since it borrows nothing from others, while the rest take many words from Hebrew. For since Hebrew was the only common language before the confusion at Babel, those bold men retained many of its words. This is especially observable in the Oriental languages, for the change was not as great immediately as it became later with the passage of time, as is evident in the Western languages. However, if anyone wishes to notice the roots of words, they will find that most originate from the "radical" language and from the matrix of the Holy Tongue. A single Latin word, *amaritudo* <note>bitterness</note>, will suffice for us; for if you trace it back to the absolute original word, you will find it is the Hebrew word for *bitterness* from *bitter*, and *bitter* from *sea*; and *sea* is from the Hebrew <term>מרה</term> <note>transliterated: Marah; meaning bitterness</note>, which signifies bitterness. It must be observed, therefore, regarding that confusion of languages, that the same thing happened with respect to the punishment as usually happens with respect to a fault. For as it is commonly said of a fault: *No one becomes extremely wicked all at once*; so that punishment of the architects of Babel was not immediately fatal or extreme, since in those early times there was a great affinity between languages. 

Thus, Abraham speaks in Egypt, Chaldea, and Canaan without an interpreter and understands others. In Genesis 31, Laban calls the *heap of testimony* one thing in his native tongue, and Jacob calls it another, yet each understands the other; for when the stones were taken and the heap made, Laban called it *Iegar Sahadutha*, but Jacob called it *Galhedem* <note>Genesis 31:47; both names mean "Heap of Witness," the former in Aramaic/Syriac and the latter in Hebrew</note>. Furthermore, Laban's daughters gave their sons Hebrew names while they were in Syria. Likewise, in Genesis 41, Joseph in Egypt speaks through an interpreter to his brothers, and yet the surname given to Joseph by Pharaoh sufficiently shows the affinity of the languages, for he was called *Tsaphenat Paaneah* <term>צפנת פענח</term> <note>traditionally interpreted as "Revealer of Secrets," the title of this book</note>. ### ANTHONY CREGUT

...and so forth. Thus, our French language cannot express the force of the Greek words for *mindset* and *to think* <note>original Greek: φρόνημα (phronēma) & φρονεῖν (phronein)</note>, nor can Latin; hence the common translator <note>The "Vulgate" or standard Latin Bible of the time</note> wrongly expresses it using the word *wisdom* <note>original Latin: sapientiam</note> in Romans 8. This is because the Greek terms for "mindset" can be used in either a good or a bad sense, which cannot be said of "wisdom." This is why Beza <note>Theodore Beza, a 16th-century Protestant reformer and linguist</note> correctly renders it: *What the flesh relishes is death.* <note>original Latin: Quod sapit caro, mors est</note>

Similarly, there is a distinction between being *reprobate* and being *rejected* <note>original Latin: reprobum & reprobatum</note> which comes from 1 Corinthians 9:27: *lest I myself should become disqualified.* <note>original Greek: αὐτὸς ἀδόκιμος γενώμαι (autos adokimos genōmai)</note> In our French, this cannot be expressed without a long explanation. Therefore, to remove any ambiguity, Beza renders it: *lest I myself become a castaway.* <note>original Latin: ipse reiectaneus fiam</note> For "reprobate" is the opposite of being *proven and sincere* <note>original Latin: probo & syncero</note>, but it is not necessarily the opposite of being "elect." 

Likewise, that distinction which Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine, a prominent Jesuit cardinal</note> makes between *to be unwilling* and *to not will*, or *to will* and *to not be unwilling* <note>original Latin: nolle & non velle, & velle & non nolle</note>, no language besides Latin is capable of expressing. This is because other languages use a negative particle in a way that separates the ideas, as those who are skilled in other languages know. Nevertheless, even if other languages have their own unique idioms, they are all impoverished compared to the riches of the Hebrew language and the power of its "Hebraisms" <note>specific Hebrew linguistic patterns</note>.

**VIII. There is also singularity.**
This differs from "Hebraisms," which only represent the unique qualities of a language that others try to imitate because of their special emphasis. "Singularity," however, regards the entire language, which surpasses all others by many miles <note>literally "parasangs," an ancient Persian measure of distance</note>. This is clear from the properties mentioned above, such as its primary *simplicity and brevity*, and indeed its *perfection* owing to the variety and emphasis of its conjugations. 

Truly, the illustrious historian Jacques Auguste de Thou <note>original Latin: Iac. Aug. Thuanus</note> has some memorable things to say about the singularity of languages in the second book of his autobiography, page 25, especially regarding the Basque or Cantabrian tongue:

*When he visited the district of Béarn <note>original Latin: Benearni pagum</note> and had come to La Bastide-Clairence <note>original Latin: Bastidam Clarentia</note> in Lower Navarre, he saw and spoke with Joanes Leizarraga <note>original Latin: Iohannem Licarraguem</note>, the local pastor. By the command of Queen Jeanne <note>Jeanne d'Albret, Queen of Navarre</note>, he translated the catechism and the New Testament into the Basque or Cantabrian language, and arranged for it to be printed in very elegant type by Pierre Haultin at La Rochelle <note>original Latin: Rupellæ</note>. He himself oversaw the work (for who else could have done it?). The Cantabrian language, just like our Breton <note>original Latin: Britannica</note> and Irish <note>original Latin: Hibernica</note>, is unique and has nothing in common with the others; for that reason, it was once thought that it could not even be written down.*

These are the words of De Thou in his life story. But observe: even if those languages were unique, that singularity is...

# THE REVELATOR OF SECRETS.

[Gre]ek, Latin, and Oscan (as Aulus Gellius reports) were said to have "three hearts" <note>original: "tria corda"; the author refers to the poet Ennius, who claimed to have three hearts because he spoke three languages</note>, and Porcius Cato himself in extreme old age wished to learn the Greek language.

Nevertheless, it should be observed that even if illustrious men learned the **Cardinal languages** <note>primary or principal languages of the era</note>, yet for the sake of the majesty of the Empire, that nation which held power and in whose hands the majesty of the Empire resided, propagated its language along with its Empire. This is why the Roman Senate was gravely angry with Cicero because he answered the Syracusan Senate in Greek, as Cicero himself confesses in the *Verrines* <note>Cicero’s speeches against Verres, a corrupt governor of Sicily</note>. And truly, just as the Greek language was spread far and wide while the Greek monarchy flourished, so when the Romans were the masters of affairs, Latin reached the very borders of the Empire. Finally, with the Roman Pontiff taking hold <note>the Pope</note>, he desires the same language to be propagated as the successor to the Emperors; this is even seen in sacred rites, in which everything is conducted in Latin. The Scripture, or its authentic edition, is Latin <note>the Vulgate</note>, and others are prohibited; prayers are made in Latin; the Mass is chanted in Latin by priests before the laity and the **unlearned** <note>original: "idiotis," referring to the common people who did not know Latin</note>; the sacraments are administered in Latin; and thus civil contracts were previously made in Latin. Even the exorcists, when they address demons, perform their exorcisms in Latin.

Therefore, just as it is a sign of Empire and dominion on the part of the ruler and victor to propagate a language, so it is no small punishment for a conquered people to have a foreign language forced upon them and their own abolished. Hence, God in His word threatens that He will speak to His people through nations of an exotic tongue. For once the natural language—which flows spontaneously from the mother’s womb—is abandoned, foreign ones are learned only with great labor. This is why Jerome calls the study of the Hebrew language a **grindhouse** <note>original: "pistrinum," a place of hard labor or a mill; Jerome used this term to describe the difficulty of learning Hebrew</note>. What shall we say of those who learned ten or fourteen languages? The skill of Frederick II, the Roman Emperor, is well-known; he spoke elegantly in Latin, French, Spanish, Italian, German, Turkish, and Greek. What shall I say of Mithridates <note>King of Pontus, famous for his linguistic abilities</note>, who was proficient in the dialects of all the peoples he ruled, who were very many? Or shall we omit that wonder of the world, Joseph Scaliger, who eloquently used thirteen languages? Surely such a great abundance of words could not have been learned without swallowing a great deal of hardship.

But they devise these things in vain against the Scripture.*

*Just as the Apostles spoke in various languages extraordinarily and by a miraculous gift, so in these most recent times, in the reformation of the Church and the preaching of the Gospel, there flourished like a portent and a great miracle those **highly gifted** <note>original: εὐφυεῖς (euphueis)</note>, and indeed **polyglots** <note>original: πολυ-γλωττοί (polyglottoi)</note>, who elegantly mastered various languages; so that they could truly be nicknamed* Mithridates, *as* Conrad Gesner *entitled his book on the differences of languages; because that King of* Pontus *mastered* 22 *languages of the nations over which he ruled, according to the testimony of* Pliny *in book 7, chapter 24. Let one suffice: **Joseph Scaliger** <note>A towering figure of 16th-century scholarship, famous for his incredible linguistic range and his work on historical chronology.</note>, the great son of a great father, who in his immortal book* On the Emendation of Time *made it openly known to the learned that he was perfectly skilled in all the languages of the entire world.*

*Since, therefore, the word of man is twofold, namely the **internal word** <note>original: λόγος ἐνδιάθετος (logos endiathetos); the internal thought or concept before it is spoken.</note> and the **spoken word** <note>original: λόγος προφορικός (logos prophorikos); the thought as it is uttered in speech.</note>: the first word is known by God alone, who is the **searcher of hearts** <note>original: καρδιογνώστης (kardiognostes)</note>, but the other is brought forth in vain to reveal the word of the mind unless it is pronounced in a known language; for it would be no better known than the word of the mind itself. Indeed, there would be a confusion of tongues even for the Angels themselves, unless whenever they speak among themselves through some word (as I might call it) that is **spoken**...*

to signify their concepts. For as Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and philosopher.</note> skillfully taught in the 1st part, question 107, article 1, the will moves the intellect to its operation. *Now, the intelligible is in the intellect in three ways. I. habitually, or according to memory, as Augustine says in book 10 of On the Trinity, chapter 5. II. as considered or conceived in act; III. as related to another.* <note>original: "Intelligibile autem est in intellectu tripliciter. I. habitualiter, vel secundum memoriam... When, however, the mind turns itself to considering in act what it holds in habit, a person speaks to himself: For the very concept of the mind is called the internal word. Truly, from the fact that the concept of the angelic mind is ordered toward manifesting it to another, through the will of the Angel himself, the concept of the mind of one Angel becomes known to another. And thus one Angel speaks to another. For to speak to another is nothing else than to manifest the concept of the mind to another. Thus far Thomas. From these things it is clear that those who speak in an unknown tongue do not truly address others, because they do not manifest the word of the mind, just as tongues would be unknown to the Angels themselves if their concepts were concealed.

...he would use them as ministers, but this is erroneous, because no mention of Angels is made by Moses. Then he says *let us go down*, by which word God signifies that he places those whom he addresses on an equal level and calls them into judgment with himself. Furthermore, that descent would have been local <note>Meaning a literal movement from one place to another in physical space.</note> in respect to the Angels, but God does not speak of a local descent; rather, he speaks *anthropopathically* <note>original: "κατ’ ἀνθρωποπάθειαν" — a theological term for attributing human emotions or physical actions to God to make Him understandable to humans.</note>. From this it is clear that God did not wish to call for outside help; but rather, to further despise the pride of those architects, he willed to take from within his own wisdom what was sufficient for destroying them. One might also add that there is emphasis in the phrase *let us go down*, by which it is signified that God did not wish to come into judgment suddenly, incited by anger, and condemn those scoundrels as if they had not been heard; but he willed first to descend, so that he might know their crime and audacity at close hand, and having known the facts, declare the law, according to the maxim of the Jurists, *law arises from the fact* <note>original: "ex facto ius oritur" — a legal principle suggesting that the specific circumstances of a case determine how the law is applied.</note>. These things are said of God *in a human manner* <note>original: "ἀνθρωποπαθῶς"</note>, but for judges they are truly precepts and laws concerning the declaration of the law.

Therefore, if the Jews would open their eyes here, they would truly see in this word *let us go down* <note>original Hebrew: נרדה (*nerdah*)</note> the mystery of the Trinity, or at least a plurality of persons. For why would God have called upon the earth as a helper for that reason? What did the earth accomplish in this solemn judgment? But the Ancient Hebrews say that here is the *House of Judgment* <note>original Hebrew: בית דין (*Beth Din*)</note>: that is, of the persons of the Trinity, because among the Hebrews, a *House of Judgment* <note>term: <term>Beth Din</term> — a rabbinical court. <meta>This page continues Anthony Cregut's theological defense of the Trinity. Having argued on the previous page that God's use of the plural "let us" in Genesis (regarding the Tower of Babel) indicates a plurality of persons rather than a consultation with angels, he now focuses on the linguistic distinctions of the Trinity and the internal "processions" within the Godhead. He concludes by comparing human and divine Trinities and evaluating the strength of different scriptural proofs.</meta>

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS

*judgment, that is, lawful*: and they judged <note>original Hebrew: דיני ממונות *dine mammonoth*</note> *monetary laws or civil lawsuits*. There was, moreover, among them a <note>original Hebrew: סנהדרי גדולה & סנהדרי קטנה</note> *Lesser Sanhedrin and a Greater Sanhedrin*. <note>The Sanhedrin was the supreme council and court of justice in ancient Israel. The "Great" Sanhedrin had 71 members, while "Lesser" ones in various cities had 23.</note>

From this it is evident that the persons of the Trinity are distinct from one another, yet this distinction is grounded more in the reality of the thing itself than in mere words. For the word "emanation" <note>The concept of something flowing out from a source.</note> is common to all three persons, who are internal emanations; nevertheless, the word "procession" is specifically attributed to the Holy Spirit. Nonetheless, it also seems to be said of the Son; for Scripture frequently attributes <note>original Greek: τὸ ἐξελθεῖν — *to exelthein*</note> "to go out" to Him, which, as far as the words are concerned, is the same as <note>original Greek: τὸ ἐκπορεύεσθαι — *to ekporeuesthai*</note> "to proceed." Therefore, the term "procession" should not be stubbornly restricted only to the Holy Spirit, but the force of the distinction ought to be established in the underlying realities rather than in the vocabulary. However, we judge it safer, in this ineffable mystery, not only to think in accordance with the Scriptures but also to speak with them, since their words are from the inspiration of God no less than the things themselves.

But truly, when God says *let us go down*, the Father addresses the Son and the Holy Spirit, and thus the word is taken <term>hypostatically | referring to the distinct individual persons of the Trinity rather than the single divine essence</term>. For the word "Father" is taken in two ways in Scripture. First, <note>original Greek: οὐσιωδῶς — *ousiodōs*</note> "essentially," specifically when divine things are contrasted with human things, eternal with fleeting, or heavenly with earthly; in this way, that word is used in the Lord’s Prayer: *Our Father*, etc. Second, it is taken "hypostatically" when the persons are contrasted with one another, as happens in this passage. And here it is pleasing to bring forward the excellent testimony of Gregory Nazianzen <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and one of the "Cappadocian Fathers," famous for his definitions of Trinitarian theology.</note>, the prince of the Greek Fathers: *There is one God: the Father from whom are all things, and the Son through whom are all things, and the Holy Spirit in whom are all things. For these prepositions—"from whom," "through whom," and "in whom"—do not divide the nature, but rather characterize the unique properties of the one and unconfused nature.*

We perceive an image of this Trinity within ourselves, about which Augustine writes in *Book 15 of On the Trinity*. There is a very great difference between this trinity which is in us and the Divine Trinity. Therefore, we see the trinity that is in us rather than believe it; but we believe God to be a Trinity rather than see it.

The mystery of the Trinity is therefore better proven from this passage in Genesis than from the word *Elohim* <note>The Hebrew name for God, which is plural in form but usually takes a singular verb. Many theologians used this grammatical oddity as proof of the Trinity.</note>, by which Peter Lombard <note>A 12th-century bishop and author of the *Sentences*, the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages.</note> and others attempted to prove the Trinity.

<meta>This page continues Anthony Cregut's theological discussion regarding the Trinity and the names of God. # ANTHONY CREGUT

...they attempt to demonstrate; for that reasoning seems to me not only weak but even quite dangerous, as other theologians of great name have also observed. If, therefore, *Elohim* <note>The Hebrew word for God, which is plural in form (*-im* being the masculine plural ending).</note> in the plural is joined with a singular verb, as in "God created" <note>original Hebrew: ברא אלהים — *bara Elohim*</note> in Genesis 1, this happens because of a linguistic idiom, just as in the Greek language and style it is said, "living things runs" <note>original Greek: ζῶα τρέχει — *zoa trechei*. In Greek, plural neuter subjects take singular verbs; Cregut is arguing that the grammar of *Elohim* is a similar quirk of language rather than a mathematical proof of the Trinity.</note>. And indeed, all the Hebrews teach, as do most Christians—even those who use this argument to prove the Trinity—that it results from a property of the language that *Elohim* is joined with a singular verb. In 2 Samuel 7:23, it says, "God went to redeem the people" <note>original Latin: *Iuerunt Elohim ad redimendum populum*. Note: In this specific Hebrew verse, unlike Genesis 1:1, the verb for "went" is actually plural, matching the plural noun *Elohim*.</note>. 

But they do this with this limitation: that it is understood as a Hebrew idiom regarding the second and third person, but not regarding the first person. That is, that *Elohim*, by a property of the Hebrew language, is constructed with a singular verb in the second and third person, as in Genesis 1 and 2 Samuel 7:23—just like the word *Adonim* <note>original Hebrew: אדנים — *Adonim*, meaning "lords" or "masters," often used in the plural for a single great lord.</note>. But when it is constructed with a singular verb in the first person, they say it is not from a property of language but to signify a mystery, as in Exodus 20: "I am the Lord thy God" <note>original Latin/Hebrew: *Ego sum Iehoua Eloheca*</note>. Truly, these things are asserted without evidence and are not proven. And indeed, it is difficult to provide a reason why it would be a Hebrew idiom in the second and third person, but not in the first. 

Nevertheless, we should not omit that the Hebrews, according to the Cabala <note>A tradition of Jewish mysticism that interprets the hidden meanings of Hebrew letters and words.</note>, draw a mystery from the word *Elohim*. For to them, *Elohim* <note>original Hebrew: אלהים</note> is said as if it were *El Hem* <note>original Hebrew: אל המ</note>, meaning "God they are," or "God themselves." And from this, the letter *Yod* <note>The Hebrew letter י.</note> is expressed as a mystery in these words: "remember thy Creators" <note>original Hebrew: זכור בוראיך — *zechor boreicha*. In Ecclesiastes 12:1, the word "Creator" appears in a plural form, which Cregut notes as a point of mystical interest.</note>, that is, "your Creator," and in *Elohim*, because "God they are." 

The things written by Rabbi Ibn Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a famous Jewish scholar and grammarian.</note>, the prince of Hebrew grammarians, and other Hebrews—namely, that the use of the plural number with the singular is "for the sake of honor" <note>The "plural of majesty," where a ruler refers to themselves as "we."</note>—is rightly debunked by the most illustrious Antonius Walaeus <note>A prominent Dutch Reformed theologian (1573–1639) at the University of Leiden.</note>, Professor of Sacred Theology in the Academy of Leiden, in his *Theological Commonplaces* on the divine names. This Rabbinical "refuge" <note>original Greek: προσφύγετον — *prosphugeton*, meaning a place to flee or an excuse used in an argument.</note> is refuted by experience itself; for the Emperor would not have said, "We, Charles, the Emperors, I will," or "I command," and so on.

Furthermore, God not only prepares Himself for judgment when He said, "Come, let us go down"; but He also immediately inflicts and decrees punishment, saying: "Let us confound their tongue." This certainly accords perfectly with the unbridled audacity and insolent pride of those men; for that most wise...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of divine power and linguistic history. # THE REVELATOR OF SECRETS
<meta>catchword: punishment,</meta>

The Ruler and Judge approached those scoundrels with great display, just as the Poets have told myths about their Jove, who was nearly cast down from his throne by the God-fighting <note>original Greek: Θεομάχοις — *theomachois*</note> Giants, and who was forced to hurl lightning bolts from heaven to protect his Empire; and this was done in great haste while the Giants piled mountains upon mountains—Ossa upon Pelion <note>A reference to the Greek myth where giants attempted to scale Mount Olympus by stacking two mountains.</note>—so they might ascend into heaven against the will of the gods. 

But the history of Moses thinks and speaks more gravely and sublimely regarding the true God. For it shows that God despised the bold efforts and attempts of those little men, who were like Pygmies. Therefore, He did not use many machines, but with a single breath <note>original: *sufflamine*</note> He checked them, scattering them into the breezes. *Come now, let us confound their speech* <note>original: *Agedum confundamus labium*. From Genesis 11:7.</note>; I will only blow a breath, and they will fly apart as laughingstocks with confused tongues. Do you see how such great efforts vanish with a single puff of a fan? 

The same thing happened in this most recent century to the army of King Philip II of Spain, prepared for the destruction of England. This was commonly called the **Invincible Armada** <note>original: *Exercitus inuincibilis*</note> by the Spanish, the most arrogant of all nations. It carried chains with which to damn all of England—conquered and bound—to prisons, and which not even God Himself (O, the impiety! for they blasphemed thus) would be able to defend and protect. Do you hear the unheard-of audacity of the Spanish giants? But with a single breath of the winds, God confounded that blasphemous tongue, which could not even be heard over the storms of the sea and the winds, much less was it heard by God. After Philip had learned of this slaughter, he replied coldly and with a stupidity and insensibility more than Stoic: *I did not send them to fight against the winds* <note>original Latin: *non miseram pugnatum aduersus ventos*. A famous remark attributed to Philip II after the 1588 defeat.</note>. Is it really so, O King? But God, the King of Kings, stirred the winds to repress your audacity and your unbridled, untamable lust for dominion. O, Giant-like audacity, divinely avenged and restrained!

The punishment of Babel was the confusion of languages, by which the work already begun necessarily ceased and could not be finished. For how could so many people have completed such a great building without mutual communication? For when the architects asked for mortar, others brought stones, and vice versa. From this arose the story **about the sack**. For it has been observed in all languages that a sack is named by the same word: sack <note>original: *sac*</note>, sack <note>original Latin: *saccus*</note>, sack <note>original Italian/Spanish: *sacco*</note>, sack <note>original Greek: *σάκκος*</note>, sack <note>original Hebrew: *שק*</note>, sack <note>original Aramaic: *סקא*</note>, sack <note>original Syriac: *סק*</note>.

they attempt to demonstrate; for that reasoning seems to me not only weak but also quite dangerous, as other theologians of great renown have also observed. In 2 Samuel 7:23: *Elohim went to redeem the people* <note>original Latin: *Iuerunt Elohim ad redimendum populum*</note>. 

However, they add this limitation: it should be understood as a "Hebraism" regarding the second and third persons, but not regarding the first person. That is, they argue that *Elohim*, by the property of the Hebrew language, is constructed with a singular verb in the second and third person (as in Genesis 1 and 2 Samuel 7:23), just as the word *Adonim* <note>A plural form of "Lord" used for God or high-ranking masters.</note> is; but when it is constructed with a singular verb in the first person, they claim it is not from a linguistic property, but to signify a mystery, as in Exodus 20: *I am Jehovah your God* <note>original Latin: *Ego sum Iehoua Eloheca*</note>. Truly, these things are asserted without cost and are not proven. And indeed, it is difficult to provide a reason why it would be a "Hebraism" in the second and third person, but not in the first. 

Nevertheless, we should not omit that the Hebrews extract a mystery from the word *Elohim* according to the Kabbalah <note>A school of thought in Jewish mysticism.</note>. For to them, *Elohim* <note>original Hebrew: אלהים</note> is spoken as if it were *El Hem* <note>original Hebrew: אל המ</note>, meaning "God they are," or "God they themselves." From this, the letter *Yod* <note>original Hebrew: י</note> is expressed as a mystery in the words: *Remember your Creators* <note>original Hebrew: זכור בוראיך (*zekhor bore'eykha*). From Ecclesiastes 12:1. The Hebrew word for "Creator" is here in a plural form.</note>, meaning "your Creator," *Elohim*, because "God they are" <note>original Hebrew: אל המ</note>.

The writings of Rabbi Aben Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a distinguished Spanish Jewish grammarian and philosopher.</note>, the prince of Hebrew grammarians, and other Hebrews—who claim that the use of the plural number with the singular was "for the sake of honor" <note>original Latin: *honoris causa*; often referred to today as the "plural of majesty."</note>—are rightly exploded by the most famous Antonius Walaeus <note>Antonius Walaeus (1573–1639), a prominent Dutch Reformed theologian and professor at the University of Leiden.</note>, Professor of Sacred Theology at the Academy of Leiden, in his *Theological Commonplaces on the Divine Names*. He argues that this rabbinic "refuge" <note>original Greek: κρησφύγετον (*kresphugeton*)</note> is refuted by experience itself. For an Emperor would not have said, "We Charles, Emperors, I will, or I command, etc." <note>original Latin: *Nos Carolus Imperatores volo, aut iubeo*. Walaeus points out that even a ruler using the "royal we" would not pluralize the title "Emperor" if only one person was speaking.</note>

Furthermore, God does not only prepare Himself for judgment when He said, *Come now, let us descend*; but He also immediately inflicts and decrees punishment, saying: *Let us confound their tongue*. This certainly fits perfectly with the unbridled audacity and insolent pride of those men; for that most wise Ruler of the world...

<meta>This page continues Cregut’s discussion on divine power and the history of languages. Having previously discussed the name of God (Elohim) and its grammatical properties, he now shifts to historical and mythological examples of human pride being humbled by divine intervention, specifically focusing on the Tower of Babel and the Spanish Armada, concluding with a philological note on universal words.</meta>

->REVEALER OF SECRETS<-

The Ruler and Judge approaches those scoundrels with great preparation—much like the poets told fables about their own Jove <note>The Roman god Jupiter (Jove).</note>, who was nearly toppled from his throne by the **"God-fighting" Giants** <note>original Greek: θεομάχοις (*theomachois*).</note>. According to these myths, Jove was forced to hurl lightning bolts from heaven to defend his empire, and he had to do so in great haste because the Giants were stacking mountains upon mountains—piling **Mount Ossa** upon **Mount Pelion** <note>In Greek mythology, the Giants attempted to scale Olympus by stacking these two mountains in Thessaly.</note>—to climb into heaven against the will of the gods. But the history recorded by Moses <note>The book of Genesis.</note> speaks and thinks of the true God in a far more serious and sublime manner. For Moses shows that God looked down with contempt upon the daring efforts and strivings of those little men, who were like **pygmies**. Therefore, God did not use complex war machines, but scattered them into the winds with a single breath: *Come now, let us confuse their lips; I shall merely blow, and with their languages confused, they will fly apart in ridicule.* Do you see how such great labors vanish with a single puff of a fan?

The same thing happened in this most recent century to the army <note>The Spanish Armada of 1588.</note> of **Philip II**, the King of the Spaniards, which was prepared for the destruction of England. This fleet was commonly called the "Invincible Army" by the Spaniards (the proudest of all nations). They carried chains with them, intending to condemn all of England—once conquered and bound—to their prisons. They even claimed that not even God (oh, what impiety! for they blasphemed thus) would be able to defend or protect the island. Do you hear the unheard-of audacity of these Spanish "Giants"? Yet, with a single blast of the winds, God confused those blasphemous lips; their voices could not even be heard over the storms of the sea and the winds, much less were they heard by God. After King Philip learned of this disaster, he responded coldly, with a stupidity and insensibility greater than any **Stoic**: *I did not send my fleet to fight against the winds.* <note>original Latin: *non miseram pugnatum aduersus ventos*.</note> Is that so, O King? But God, the King of Kings, stirred those winds to restrain your audacity and your unbridled, untamable lust for dominion. Oh, Giant-like audacity, avenged and restrained by the divine!

The punishment of **Babel** was the confusion of languages, by which the work they had already begun necessarily ceased and could not be finished. For how could so many people have completed such a massive building without mutual communication? When the architects asked for cement, others brought stones, and vice versa. From this arose the "fable of the sack." For it has been observed that in all languages, a **sack** is called by the same name: *sac*, *saccus*, *sacco*, **sack** <note>original Greek: σάκκος (*sakkos*)</note>, **sack** <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: שַׂק (*saq*), סַקָּא (*saqqa*), סַק (*saq*)</note>.
