# ANTHONY CREGUT #

<page-num>272</page-num>

In Hebrew, Chaldean, Syriac, and Arabic, although the word for "sack" can be expressed by six different names, it is also called—just as it is in almost all other languages—<term>saq <note>original Hebrew: שק (*saq*). Cregut is noting that the word for "sack" or "bag" is remarkably similar across many unrelated language families.</note></term>. This appears to be an extremely ancient concept that originated at Babel. From this, a popular story arose: that when everyone was about to depart and was already prepared for their journey, each person asked for or took up their "sack," and thus all the nations agreed upon this same name.

This punishment at Babel seems all the greater because it was so universal. In truth, it was inflicted upon all descendants—not that the sin of those builders is held against their descendants in the same way Adam’s original sin is (for that was a personal sin of the builders, not a sin of human nature itself, and we did not "sin in them" as we did in Adam); yet, although the guilt was not shared, the punishment remains common to us all. This is because, had those builders not sinned, the **Holy Language** <note>The "Lingua sancta," traditionally identified by theologians as Hebrew, believed to be the original language of humanity before the fall of Babel.</note> would have been passed down to us, and the whole human race would still be of "one lip" as it was once. Instead, we now face a vast variety and confusion of languages. 

Therefore, just as Adam killed his descendants with a natural death when he introduced sin into the world, those Babylonians killed their descendants with a **"civil death"** when the confusion of languages entered the world as their punishment. However, just as the chosen—by shedding the "old man"—are freed from Adam’s sin and punishment through Christ, so too are those who do not partake in the pride and sin of Babel. Those who depart from the **mystical Babylon** <note>A term often used by Protestant reformers to refer to the Roman Catholic Church, which they viewed as the spiritual successor to the corrupt biblical Babylon.</note> in both mind and body are not struck by its plagues. For just as Christ brought life into the world so that we might be freed from natural death, he also sent the gifts of languages through his Spirit <note>A reference to the Pentecost, where the Apostles were granted the ability to speak in many tongues.</note>. By these gifts, we are redeemed from "civil death"—which consists of <term>aphonia <note>original Greek: ἀφωνίᾳ (*aphonia*), meaning speechlessness or the inability to communicate.</note></term>—and the prophecy of Isaiah (chapter 19:18) is fulfilled, which predicted that *under the kingdom of Christ, the language of Canaan would be common to all.* Although people may differ in the sound of their speech, they all speak one and the same thing when they cry out, "Abba, Father." Thus, those who were previously miserably scattered have been united into the unity of faith.

On the other hand, for those who prefer to be members of the mystical Babylon rather than the Church of Christ, is it any wonder if they love the confusion of ancient Babel, or at least undergo its punishment? For in the **Papacy**, everything is obscure, unknown, entangled, and barbaric.

...scriptures, etc. Forbidden Scripture, images as "silent scripture," the Latin office of the Mass, the Latin liturgy, and the "implicit faith" <note>The theological concept that a layperson's faith is sufficient if they simply believe whatever the Church teaches, even if they do not understand it.</note> of the Priest. What is this but the confusion of Babel? Certainly, in the ancient Roman Church, they used the Latin language in their liturgies, but at that time it was not an unknown language; it only became so later, even in Italy, due to the invasions of the Goths, Lombards, and Gauls.

To this point belongs a memorable story, which is found in Sulpitius Severus's *Life of St. Martin*. He recounts that a certain man named Defensor <note>A local bishop who opposed Martin’s election.</note> opposed the promotion of St. Martin to the Bishopric under the pretext of his "squalor" and "lack of decorum" <gloss>original Greek: ἀκοσμιότητος (*akosmiotētos*)</gloss>, because, as Paul testifies in 1 Timothy 3:2, a Bishop must be "orderly" <gloss>original Greek: κόσμιον (*kosmion*)</gloss>. However, when on the solemn day of prayers and assembly <note>original: *synaxeos*, referring to a liturgical gathering.</note>, someone from the gathered people—in the absence of the Deacon—took up the Psalter to read some of the Psalms, he happened upon the 8th Psalm, where these words are found:
> *From the mouths of infants and nurslings you have ordained praise, because of your enemies, to silence the foe and the defender.* <note>The Latin *defensorem* matches the name of Martin's opponent, Defensor.</note>

Immediately upon hearing the name of the "defender," a huge rumor spread from the Church among all the people against that troublesome man named Defensor, as if that reading of the psalm had happened by divine providence, and God had condemned the man’s unlucky opposition against St. Martin by an omen. By this example, it is clear that worship was conducted in a known language and understood by everyone.

The Papists, therefore, do not imitate the rites of the ancient Church, but rather the barbarism of the Heathens, who considered the mysteries of religion more profound if their listeners understood nothing, as Arnobius teaches in *Against the Heathen*. Thus, the Magi <note>Sages or sorcerers.</note> had barbarous words and formulas in their invocation of Demons, Furies, Erinyes, Hecate, and Proserpina; likewise today, those pseudo-Christians—who falsely claim the name of the religious—control things using barbarous voices in magical matters. They use words such as *Barnasa*, *Leucias*, *Bucella*, *Agla*, *Tetragrammaton*, *Adonai*, and other such terms, which they carry on amulets, just as superstitious Jews do with their *hanging charms* <gloss>original: *Appensa kamea*</gloss>.

The initial <term>procatarctica <note>A Greek-derived medical and philosophical term meaning the "preceding" or "triggering" cause of a condition.</note></term> cause of the confusion of tongues was the pride of the architects, which God willed to punish with such a great penalty. For Moses says in verse 4: *And they said, "Come, let us build for ourselves..."*

...a city and a tower, whose top may reach even unto heaven: and let us make a name for ourselves, lest perhaps we be scattered across the face of the whole earth. <note>original: Genesis 11:4</note> These words of those little men surely breathe an unheard-of **pride**; for they presume that they will attain a great name throughout the whole world by that proud building. And even if they were perhaps scattered through different regions of the world, yet that lofty monument to their name would remain forever, which they hyperbolically extol by raising the building even unto heaven. This is the perpetual madness of worldly men: that, having abandoned heaven, a name and immortality are sought on earth. But as the Psalmist testifies in *Psalm 49:7* <note>The author likely refers to the Vulgate numbering; the theme of God laughing at human vanity is more famously found in Psalm 2:4.</note>, God laughs from heaven and renders their vain attempts useless. Justly, therefore, did God punish their pride, because these great efforts were made in contempt of God—not because they feared a second flood, as some suggest, and wished to protect themselves with that most high tower. For such ideas are ridiculous: first, because the covenant established with Noah makes us cautious and secure from that fear—the symbol of which is the **Iris** or the *heavenly bow* <note>The rainbow, promised to Noah as a sign that God would never again destroy the earth by flood.</note>—and also because it would have been impossible to include so many people in that fortress. Therefore, the sole cause was human **pride** and **ambition**, which is a garment a man never takes off.

Although, therefore, the confusion of languages and such great variety has its origin in pride (insofar as it is the punishment for it), yet today most men boast of that variety. Thus, although that punishment should have corrected pride, pride still lifts its head in many.

i. When someone today boasts of a variety of languages and the knowledge of them—whom Paul also rebukes in *1 Corinthians 14*, as those who proudly abused those gifts. The same thing happens to them as to those devoted to luxury, who boast of the luxury and pomp of their clothes, even though clothes are signs of sin and were originally given to cover nakedness. 

ii. The "barbarism" of languages in the **Papacy** <note>The Roman Catholic Church</note> today arises from pride and ambition. For the Doctors <note>High-ranking theologians and teachers</note> foster the ignorance of the people so that they themselves may be held in greater admiration, as those who—like the Pharisees of old—hold the **key of knowledge** within themselves and "bind and loose" <note>A reference to Matthew 16:19, regarding the authority to declare what is permitted or forbidden.</note>. Thus, having proudly contempted the true divinity, they polluted themselves with various, wandering, and promiscuous lusts; for they adored fictional gods and vain idols, which is an **idolatry** that is nothing other than spiritual fornication.

But indeed, just as God allowed those abandoned Gentiles to walk in their own ways, even for a long time disregarding the "time of ignorance" (as the Scripture speaks in *Acts 17*), so He gathered His own people and Church from elsewhere. This was done by establishing a covenant with the Patriarchs and their descendants, among whom the **Hebrew language** was preserved in its purity. From this, the Scripture of the Old Testament was written in Hebrew, and the entire worship of God was performed in that language. Thus, at that time, the punishment of the nations was not inflicted upon the people of God, because they were neither dispersed, nor did the confusion of tongues erase that first language; rather, because it was preserved among the Hebrew people, it was called the Hebrew language.

<page-num>276</page-num>

...affixed Him to the cross, they were also at last rejected by God. Hence, by the just judgment of God following the **destruction of Jerusalem**, a confusion of tongues was sent upon them, and the entire nation was either destroyed or scattered into various parts of the world. This dispersion, as well as the confusion of languages, continues even to this day, as the remnants of such a great scattering are found throughout the earth.

And first, there were two famous **dispersions** <note>original: *διασποραὶ* (*diasporai*)</note> of the Jews. The first **dispersion** was the Asian one, whose head and metropolis was the city of Babylon. These Jews used the **Chaldaic paraphrase** <term>Aramaic translations or expansions of the Hebrew Bible, known as Targums, used because many Jews no longer spoke Hebrew fluently.</term> or **Targum Onkelos** in their synagogues; it was to them that Peter once wrote from the metropolis of Babylon, where he was at that time. The second **dispersion** was the European one, whose metropolis was Alexandria in Egypt. Those Jews used the **version of the Seventy Interpreters** <note>The Septuagint (LXX), the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible into Greek.</note>, and they possessed a temple just as those in Jerusalem did.

This is why those Hebrews in *Acts 6:1* and *11:20* are called **Hellenists** <note>original: *ἑλληνισταὶ* (*hellēnistai*)</note>, not because they lived in Greece, but because they used the Greek language. This dispersion had taken place even before the Ascension of Christ, as is clear from *John 7:35*: *The Jews therefore said among themselves, "Where is this man intended to go, that we shall not find him? Is he going to those who are dispersed among the Greeks, and to teach the Greeks?"* For in that passage, it is not the pagan nations scattered here and there that are meant, but the Jews dispersed throughout the world—since (as **Beza** <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major Protestant reformer and successor to John Calvin, known for his work on the Greek New Testament.</note> rightly observes) the very name of "dispersion" can hardly apply to native inhabitants.

But thirdly, there were other Jews whose metropolis was Jerusalem, and these are called **Hebrews** in *Acts 6:1*, distinct from the others who are named there as **Hellenists**. This was not because they were Greeks, but because they were Jews using the Greek language. Thus, there is a distinction between **Greeks** <note>original: *ἑλλήνας* (*hellēnas*)</note> and **Hellenists** <note>original: *ἑλληνιστὰς* (*hellēnistas*)</note>: the former are Greeks by nation, while the latter are "Greecianizing" Jews who belonged to the European **dispersion**; whereas the **Hebrews** <note>original: *ἑβραῖοι* (*hebraioi*)</note> were the Hebrews who lived in Jerusalem.

For there were three metropolises of the **commonwealth** <note>original: *πολιτείας* (*politeias*), referring here to the organized Jewish community or civil structure.</note>: namely, Jerusalem, Babylon, and Alexandria. In the first, the Jews used the **Jerusalem Paraphrase** <note>The Targum Yerushalmi.</note> which survives today. In the second, they used the **Targum Onkelos**, and in the third, the **Version of the Seventy**. Others hold a different view and think those **Greeks** were Greeks by nation but proselytes by religion, of whom it is said in *John 12:20*: *Now there were certain **Greeks** <note>original: *ἑλληνες*</note> among those who came up to worship at the feast.*

*Various curious writings about Melchizedek. The aim of the Jerome-influenced writings regarding Melchizedek. The division of the topics to be treated into three parts.*

*The first part concerns the person of Melchizedek. The person of Melchizedek is graphically depicted in Hebrews 7. Melchizedek can be understood in two ways as being "without father" <note>original: *ἀπάτωρ* (*apatōr*), a Greek term meaning fatherless or without a recorded genealogy</note>, etc.; namely, in nature and in the divine economy <note>The "economy" refers to God’s plan or arrangement for human salvation.</note>. In what sense Melchizedek is the name of a person. The true opinion regarding the person of Melchizedek. Various opinions about Melchizedek are refuted.*

*What the Ancients thought about the person of Melchizedek. The naming of Melchizedek foreshadowed Christ. A refutation of a more recent opinion regarding the person of Melchizedek. Objections from an author of great reputation are brought against our opinion on the person of Melchizedek. His objections are refuted. His exception regarding the passage in Hebrews 7:3 is refuted.*

*The second part concerns the offices of Melchizedek. Only Melchizedek rightly held both offices, namely the Royal and the Priestly. Whether by right among the Gentile nations the same person held both offices? Christ, as the true Melchizedek, is a true king. The Kingdom of Christ is spiritual. The dreams of the Jews regarding a temporal kingdom. The threefold excellence <note>original: *ὑπεροχὴ* (*hyperochē*), a Greek word for superiority or preeminence</note> of Christ over the kingdom of Melchizedek. The first is the eternity of that kingdom. II. The dignity of the subjects. III. His victory. IV. An excellence is added because Christ is at once king and father.*

JUST AS the person of Melchizedek was extraordinary, so much more have restless minds and a compulsive itch for writing <term>original: *cacoëthes*; a Greek-derived medical term used by the satirist Juvenal to describe an incurable or malignant habit, here applied to the urge to write</term> about new and extravagant fantasies seized people here and there. Indeed, in the time of Blessed Jerome, a certain volume was circulating that was anonymous and unauthored <note>original: ἀνώνυμον καὶ ἀδέσποτον (anōnymon kai adespotoon)</note>, in which vain and futile ideas about Melchizedek were peddled. Since Jerome suspected these things were dangerous and contentious <note>original: φιλεγκαιμονα (philenkaimona); literally "fond of making accusations" or "argumentative"</note>, he did not easily allow himself to be involved in them, until, urged by the pressing entreaties of his friends, he finally gave his consent; he could not bear to reject his petitioner, Evagrius. Therefore, in his letter to Evagrius, Jerome both revealed the truth and outlawed the commentaries of others regarding Melchizedek, according to the sense of the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul’s discussion of Melchizedek in the Book of Hebrews</note>. We also, after so many centuries have passed since his time—and thus with so many bright lights shining before us, especially the lighthouse and radiant beam of the Scriptures—do not blush to offer our small effort here. We do not disdain to carry a little light in an earthen vessel, like the soldiers of Gideon <note>A biblical reference to Judges 7, where Gideon's soldiers hid torches inside clay jars to surprise their enemies</note>. And we do this by applying a paraphrase to the passage in Genesis 14:18, 19, and 20, where, when Melchizedek came out to meet Abraham, he brought out bread and wine; and because he was the priest of the Most High, he blessed him and received tithes. Therefore, all these things must be discussed in order:

I. Who that person Melchizedek was.
II. What were his offices, both royal and priestly.
III. What were his deeds: whether from his royal office in receiving Abraham sumptuously and magnificently, or from his priestly office in blessing and receiving tithes.

<header>THE REVEALER OF SECRETS.</header>

I. The person of Melchizedek is vividly portrayed in Hebrews 7:3 where, as Paul says, he is "without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God." <note>original Greek: Ἀπάτωר, ἀμήτωρ, ἀγενεαλόγητος, μήτε ἀρχὴν ἡμεרῶν, μήτε ζωῆς τέλος ἔχων ἀφωμοιωμένος τῷ υἱῷ τοῦ θεοῦ (Apator, amētōr, agenealogētos...)</note>

These things are stated by the Apostle in such a way that we should look not so much at the person of Melchizedek himself as at Christ, his antitype <term>antitype: the person or reality in the New Testament that fulfills a "type" or symbolic foreshadowing in the Old Testament</term>. For in this prophecy, as in most of Scripture, the meaning is multi-layered; it fits partly the type and partly the antitype—indeed, it fits more truly and accurately the antitype than the type. And in truth, when Melchizedek is called "without father, without mother," etc., by Paul, this should not be understood as if he were actually born without a father or a mother. Rather, it is because Moses, in Genesis 14:18, speaks so sparingly and almost in passing about Melchizedek that there is a profound silence regarding his genealogy—not only in that specific passage, but in the entirety of Scripture. It is as if that man had dropped from the clouds or from heaven to bless the father of the faithful [Abraham] and, immediately after the blessing, was carried back up into heaven.

From this, some in the past took the opportunity to believe that he was an Angel sent from heaven in a bodily form, just as others appeared to Abraham at other times; or that he was the Holy Spirit taking on a body as a garment, just as the Son of God frequently did (according to Tertullian) as a prelude <note>original: praelusurus; a rehearsal or "pre-play"</note> to his future incarnation. Therefore, Melchizedek can be understood in two ways as "without father, without mother," etc.: I. In nature. II. In the economy <term>economy: (from Greek *oikonomia*) the divine plan or arrangement for human salvation through history</term>.

In the first way (nature), it is not at all believed that Melchizedek was "without father or mother," because no man can exist in that way, nor has anyone ever existed who, as a human being, is a natural thing; therefore, he cannot be called "without beginning" <note>original Greek: ἄναρχος (anarchos)</note>. In the second way, then, he is called "without father," etc., because according to the divine economy and arrangement, his genealogy is not recorded in Scripture; hence, he is presented to us by Moses as a man "without genealogy" <note>original Greek: ἀγενεαλόγητος (agenealogētos)</note>. Thus, Melchizedek is not "without genealogy" in himself or in an absolute sense, but "in a certain respect" and "relatively" <note>original Greek: κατὰ τί & σχετικῶς (kata ti kai schetikōs)</note>—namely, with respect to the Scripture, which remains entirely silent about his family tree.

The Syriac translator explained this clearly when he wrote on Hebrews 7:3: "Whose father and mother are not written in the genealogies, nor the beginning of his days." <note>original Syriac: דלא אבוהי ולא אמה אתכתבו בשרבתא ולא רישיתא דיומוהי (D’lā abūhy w-lā emmeh etkatebū b-sharbatā...)</note> Therefore, since Melchizedek was the most illustrious type <term>type: a historical person or event that serves as a prophetic symbol of a future reality</term> of Christ the Mediator, those qualities are sometimes attributed to the "figure" (the symbol) which truly and in reality belong only to the "antitype" and the one symbolized.

For just as a shadow which accompanies a body is not truly something real like the body itself, but is only an intentional being and a "body" <term>in name only</term> <note>original Greek: ὁμωνύμως (homōnymōs). This refers to two things that share a name but have different definitions, like a "man" and a "painting of a man."</note>, just as a painted man is a man <term>in name only</term>. So, since the figures of the Old Testament are certain shadows which foreshadow for us the body and the truth in the New Testament, is it any wonder if the truth and reality of the things proclaimed belong properly and really to the thing prefigured and the <term>antitype</term> <note>antitype: the New Testament reality (Christ) that fulfills the Old Testament symbol (the type).</note>, but to the figure and shadow less properly? Indeed, they do not truly belong to the shadow, but only <term>in a certain respect</term> <note>original Greek: κατά τι (kata ti)</note> for that purpose and regard, so that it may be able to represent the thing prefigured.

Therefore, since Melchizedek was a shadow and figure representing Christ—who was the body of that shadow and the truth of that figure—when he is called <term>without genealogy</term> <note>original Greek: ἀγενεαλόγητος (agenealogētos). This refers to the fact that his lineage is not recorded in Genesis.</note> in Scripture, this does not belong to him really or with respect to his nature (which was like that of other men), but only figuratively and with respect to the "economy" <note>economy: here used in the theological sense of the "divine arrangement" or plan of salvation.</note>. Or, if I may put it this way, that naming is attributed to him not **positively**—as it is to Christ, who is eternal and the beginning without a beginning—but **negatively**, because his fatherhood, motherhood, and <term>genealogy</term> <note>original Greek: γενεαλογία (genealogia)</note> are denied in Scripture, or at least are not affirmed. 

Since, therefore, figures are things of the weakest existence, it is no wonder if attributes belong to them in the weakest way, but to the thing prefigured in the most real way. Thus it is said of David in Psalm 22: *They have pierced my hands and my feet.* Those things are attributed to him as a figure and by a certain external naming, but not really, because David was not crucified, nor were his hands and feet pierced. But Christ truly and really was fastened to the cross, and could say, *They pierced my feet*, etc. It is sufficient that these things are attributed to the figure <term>analogously</term> <note>original Greek: ἀναλόγως (analōgōs)</note> and <term>according to the order</term> <note>original Greek: κατὰ τάξιν (kata taxin)</note> of their resemblance.

Therefore (as was observed in the preceding <term>pronouncement</term> <note>original Latin: oraculo. Likely referring to a previous section of the text or a specific scriptural authority.</note>), since the meaning is composite—as it is in types and antitypes—the antitype must be considered first of all, because it is the center to which all the lines of the circumference are combined as if into a single point. And as long as the body lay hidden under the shadow, like the marrow under the bark, for so long was the shadow to be considered; but as the shadow disappears and vanishes, only the body ought to arrest the rays of the eyes. Thus in the Old Testament, while the shadows and figures were flourishing, the faithful turned their eyes there; but as they set...

...[manifesting] clearly in the New Testament, we behold the body itself. Therefore, Christ is our true Melchizedek, who is *without father, without mother* <note>original Greek: ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ (apatōr, amētōr)</note>, etc. Hence, just as in *Isaiah* 7 he is called *Immanuel* <note>original Hebrew: עִמָּנוּאֵל, meaning "God with us"</note>, which is a name of a person designating both natures [divine and human], so too Melchizedek will be the name of a person, because it represents both the divine and human nature; the eternal and the temporal generation. For he is called *without father* <note>original Greek: ἀπάτωρ (apatōr)</note> insofar as he is man and with respect to his temporal birth, and *without mother* <note>original Greek: ἀμήτωρ (amētōr)</note> insofar as he is God and with respect to his eternal generation. He is *without beginning of days*, as he is God, and *without end of life*, insofar as he is both God and man. These titles can also fit him not only with respect to his person, but also with respect to his <term>Priestly office</term> <note>original Latin: officij Sacerdotalis</note>, in which he had neither predecessor, nor any to follow or succeed him. Therefore, just as *Jesus* is a name of office, so Melchizedek is a name of office, because it represents a double office—namely, the kingly and the priestly.

Having set forth this true exposition of Melchizedek, let all those vain and futile interpretations of certain ancients, as well as several moderns, be rejected <note>original Latin: explosa sunto; literally "be hissed off the stage"</note>. These writers, beyond and against Scripture, devised the idea that Melchizedek was, according to some, an Angel; according to others, the Son of God himself; and according to others, the Holy Spirit. But it is not believable that any man existed who was not a son of Adam. Others, such as the Hebrews <note>referring to Jewish tradition, such as the Targums</note>, have maintained that Shem and Melchizedek were the same person; an opinion also followed by Sander and Coccius among the <term>Papists</term> <note>a historical term used by Protestant authors to refer to Roman Catholics</note>. But even if a few Jews assert and imagine this—with their usual audacity, leaving nothing untouched even without a foundation—nevertheless they are seriously mistaken. For Paul says Melchizedek was *without genealogy, without father, without mother* <note>original Greek: ἀγενεαλόγητον, ἀπάτορα, ἀμήτορα (agenealogēton, apatōra, amētora)</note>, descriptions which cannot apply to Shem, whose genealogy among both his ancestors and his descendants Moses accurately described; indeed, Moses even recorded the beginning and end of his life. Shem had all these things, and while no one doubts that Melchizedek also had them [physically], Shem’s were explicitly recorded in Scripture. This is exactly what Paul denies regarding Melchizedek. ...miss the mark, those who curiously inquire into the lineage of Melchizedek, for God willed these things to be hidden from us so that the figure might foreshadow its fulfillment in Christ. And those are hallucinating much more who have too boldly and as if it were certain claimed that Shem <note>The son of Noah; a common identification in Jewish and some Christian traditions</note>, the son of Noah, was Melchizedek. Even more mistaken are the Melchizedekians <note>A group of early Christians who were thought to hold heretical views regarding Melchizedek as a divine power</note> who used to say repeatedly that he was the Son of God appearing to Abraham; and thus, in place of the true history related by the sacred historian Moses, they substitute a ghost for us. Erasmus also errs not a little in his version of this passage in *Hebrews* 7:3, who translates *without father, without mother* <note>original Greek: ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ (apatōr, amētōr)</note> as "of unknown father, of unknown mother," and *without genealogy* <note>original Greek: ἀγενεαλόγητος (agenealogētos)</note> as "of unknown lineage," not only failing to be explicit but even distorting the sense. For Melchizedek is represented to us by Paul in such a way that he signifies the eternity of the <term>antitype</term> <note>The reality or person foreshadowed by a "type"; here, Christ is the antitype of Melchizedek</note>, Christ; but if you substitute "of unknown father" for "without father," the symbol of eternity is immediately removed. 

Jerome, moreover, in his letter to Evagrius, cites various authors who had searched too curiously for Melchizedek’s parents, such as Origen, who says in his first homily on *Genesis* that he was an Angel; and according to Jerome, his follower Didymus says the same. Likewise Hippolytus, Irenaeus, Eusebius of Caesarea, Emesenus, Apollinaris, and Eustathius, the first Bishop of the Church of Antioch—all of whom, by various winding paths, arrived at one common crossroads, saying that Melchizedek was a Canaanite man, the king of Jerusalem, which was first called Salem, then Jebus, and finally Jerusalem.

All these things sufficiently indicate the nature of the curiosity of little men throughout all time, and the insatiable <term>itch</term> <note>original Latin: cacoethes, a term often used for a persistent, malignant habit or a "mania" for doing something incorrectly</note> of small minds, which on the slightest occasion pry into hidden mysteries and strive to snatch away the veil spread by God. Although God wisely and for a good purpose wished to hide these things, nevertheless those busybodies intend to frustrate God’s purpose and pretend to look into the <term>Ark</term> <note>The Ark of the Covenant, which was kept in the Holy of Holies</note> without the <term>mercy seat</term> <note>original Latin: propitiatorio; the lid of the Ark, which covered the Law and where God's presence rested</note>. Thus the Holy Spirit veiled the genealogy of Melchizedek in Scripture and willed it buried in silence, yet the human spirit struggles against it and rummages through genealogies immoderately; hence it is no wonder if the Apostle in his own time complained that many curious questions about genealogies were being raised. <page-num>287</page-num>

### THE REVEALER OF SECRETS. ###

Augustine, in Question 109, attempts to show that Melchizedek was not a human being; it is clear that Hierax <note>A 4th-century Egyptian teacher known for his rigorous asceticism and allegorical interpretations</note> and the Melchizedekians held the same view. For according to Epiphanius in *Heresies* 55 and 67, Hierax asserted that Melchizedek was the Holy Spirit, and the Melchizedekians used to say he was greater than Christ and the one who introduces us to God. Tertullian also attributes this view to the heretic Theodotus in his book *On Prescription Against Heretics*. 

Others, as we saw above, said he was an Angel. For Augustine says in Book 1 of *Questions on Genesis*, question 72: *"For so great was the excellence of Melchizedek that it is doubted by some whether he was a man or an Angel."* The Samaritans, however, judged Melchizedek to have been a man—specifically Shem, the son of Noah—but these people have been refuted by us above with various arguments. Epiphanius wanted to refute them with an argument drawn from chronology—namely, that Shem could not have lived long enough to reach the age of Melchizedek—but in this he is mistaken by an anachronism. Shem could indeed have been a <term>contemporary</term> <note>original Greek: σύγχρονος (synchronos)</note> of Melchizedek, which is evident if the years are accurately calculated from Scripture. See the calculation in Jerome’s *Epistle to Evagrius* regarding Melchizedek according to the opinion of the Hebrews, by which it is proved that Shem outlived Abraham, his descendant of the tenth generation, by forty years. 

Furthermore, Epiphanius claims that Melchizedek was from the race of the Sidonians or Canaanites, which he seems to have taken from Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian</note>, who calls Melchizedek a "ruler of the Canaanites"; however, he could have reigned among the Canaanites even if he was not born of their nation. Nor is that tradition of any better quality which is mentioned by Epiphanius when he says *he discovered that the father of Melchizedek was called Heraclas, and his mother was said to be Astaroth or Asteria.* That is surely deservedly judged as a fable. 

Also impious is the assertion of the Jews who, according to Epiphanius, said that Melchizedek was the son of a prostitute, and that this is why no mention was made of his genealogy. For the true cause of that silence, and the reason why Scripture is silent about Melchizedek's genealogy, is because he was a "type" or figure of Christ whom he was meant to foreshadow, and who was in truth <term>without father</term>, <term>without mother</term>, and <term>without genealogy</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἀγενεαλόγητος (apatōr, amētōr, agenealogētos). In theology, this refers to Christ having no earthly father and no divine mother.</note>. But indeed, just as Melchizedek foreshadowed Christ because he was "without father," etc., so too his naming graphically represents the person of Christ...

[The text] depicts [him], for he is called **Melchizedek** not without mystery—that is, *King of Justice*, *King of Righteousness*, or *My King is Just* (Hebrews 7:2)—just as he could also be called **Melchisalem**, that is, *Peaceful King*, *King of Peace*, or *My King is Peace*, and **Solomon** (Hebrews 7:1). It is fitting that all these things correspond excellently to Christ, the <term>antitype</term> <note>In biblical studies, an "antitype" is the person or event that fulfills a symbolic "type" established earlier in the Bible.</note>. For He is the true Melchizedek, *King of Justice* <note>original Hebrew: מלך צדק (Melekh-Tzedek)</note>, who is called in the abstract by the Prophet "Our Justice" (Jeremiah 23:6), who is the "Sun of Justice" (Malachi 4:2), and "who was made justice for us by the Father" (1 Corinthians 1:30). Christ is also truly "Melchisalem," the King of Peace, and the *mystical Solomon*, because He is that peaceful one; and His bride, the Church, is called the "Shulammite," the *peaceful one*, because she obtained every kind of peace from the King of Peace. Hence in Isaiah 9, that child who was born—who in chapter 7 is called *Immanuel* <note>original Hebrew: עִמָּנוּאֵל, meaning "God with us"</note>—is called in chapter 9 the "Prince of Peace" <note>original Hebrew: שר-שלום (Sar-Shalom)</note>, which is the same as Melchisalem, "King of Peace." Just as He is also king of **Salem**—taking "Salem" not generically for "peace," but specifically for the city of **Salem**, which was later called **Jerusalem**; indeed, also mystically, because the Messiah was the King of the Jews. Thus He once entered the royal city of Salem (or Jerusalem) and surveyed His temple as if it were a royal citadel. And finally, triumphing over His enemies on the cross, although His rebellious subjects were raging with madness, He was named *Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews*. These points regarding the person of Melchizedek could suffice.

But since some of the ancients, as well as several <term>modern scholars</term> <note>original Latin: Neotericorum; referring here to contemporary 17th-century theologians</note>, believe there was no such real king named Melchizedek, but that he was Christ Himself, the Son of God, who (as He often did elsewhere) gave a preview of His future incarnation when He appeared to the fathers of the Old Testament. We did not consider it out of place to refute this opinion and further confirm our own view, which was already proven above. First, we consider it very dangerous and injurious to the eternal truth of the Scriptures to wish to call into doubt the history described by Moses with its various circumstances, and to bring to trial something that is a matter of fact, not just of law, against the truth after so many thousands of years—weighing it as if in a scale; indeed, to mock Moses’s historical narrative with mere groundless conjectures. Moses commends Abraham's victory with various details.

...and [Moses] records, among other things, that two kings came out to meet him [Abraham], namely the king of **Sodom**—that is, of Sodom—and **Melchizedek**, the king of **Salem**. Therefore, if the historical truth is corrupted and it is asserted that Melchizedek did not actually appear to Abraham, but rather the Son of God did, why would the meeting with the king of Sodom not be invalidated by the same reasoning? Who would not then dispute his appearance as being illusory? Indeed, one might more easily be persuaded regarding the king of Sodom, since Moses does not record as many details about him as he does about Melchizedek. 

For Moses only says that the king of Sodom came out to meet Abraham, but that king is not even named <note>The King of Sodom is named Bera in Genesis 14:2, but Cregut is highlighting that in the specific scene of the meeting (v. 17), he is referred to only by title, unlike Melchizedek.</note>—which cannot be said of Melchizedek, whose name is preserved in the sacred text. And if the former is called "king of Sodom," the latter is presented in exactly the same way as "king of Salem." 

Furthermore, if it is permitted to think and speak so boldly concerning the histories of Scripture, what will remain certain in others? Whenever some history, like that of Melchizedek, is treated as most mystical <note>original Latinized Greek: "mysticotata"</note>, will not the ancient secrets be too curiously corrupted? It is holier, therefore, to venerate with silence and faith those things we do not understand, than to rashly hesitate over them. 

Add to this that not only is the truth of Moses attacked, but the Apostle's [Paul's] brilliant commentary is neglected, who in *Hebrews 7:4* explicitly said: *Consider how great this man was, to whom even the Patriarch Abraham gave a tenth of the spoils.* As if that great Apostle were saying: if Melchizedek surpassed Abraham, how much more excellent is Christ, of whom Melchizedek himself was a <term>type</term>? <note>In biblical interpretation, a "type" is a historical person or event that foreshadows a future reality (the antitype), like Christ.</note>

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS.

Even if his father were unknown, he could not be said to be "without a father" simply for that reason, because in that case Nimrod, Elijah, and Jeremiah would also have been "without a father." Likewise, Melchizedek would be *sinless* <note>original Greek: ἀναμάρτητος (anamartētos)</note>—that is, *without sin*—simply because the Scripture does not accuse him of sin. But indeed, all these arguments are in vain and are easily resolved by applying the distinction set down previously. For Melchizedek is considered in two ways: either in nature, or in the <term>economy</term> <note>In theology, the "economy" refers to God’s plan or arrangement for human salvation throughout history.</note>. He is seen either as a natural man and a son of Adam, or as a mystical man and a <term>type</term> and figure of the **second Adam** <note>A common title for Jesus Christ, contrasting him with the first man, Adam.</note>. In the first way, he was not *without a father* <note>original Greek: ἀπάτωρ (apatōr)</note>, etc., because no son of Adam arises except through the ordinary generation from a male and female. But in the second way, Melchizedek is *without a father* and *without genealogy* <note>original Greek: ἀγενεαλόγητος (agenealogētos)</note>, because in this "economy" of the Scripture (or of God speaking in the Scripture), he is considered a mystical man.

Therefore, so that the figure might represent the one it prefigures, it was necessary that he be presented to us in Scripture as *without father*, *without mother* <note>original Greek: ἀμήτωρ (amētōr)</note>, and *without genealogy*; just as he is presented as both king and priest forever. All these things belong to Melchizedek in an indirect sense as a figure, but to Christ truly as the one prefigured. To the former, they apply as one hiding in the shadows and under the economy of shadows; to the latter, they apply as one shining forth in the body and in the economy of grace. It does not follow, then, that Nimrod, Elijah, and others were of unknown fatherhood, because they are considered only in nature, not in the economy. As natural sons of Adam, they cannot be called "without father"; they are not mystical men or types of Christ regarding a *lack of genealogy*, a perpetual Priesthood, and eternity of life. In the same way, one could also infer that Melchizedek was *sinless*, because as a mystical man in the economy, he was without father and mother, and therefore without sin.

III. It seems absurd to [our opponents] that a petty king of Canaan was greater than the Patriarch **Abraham**, unless he had been Christ himself, since Abraham was the father of the faithful and the origin of God’s people, both the natural-born and the spiritual Abrahamites. <margin>Hebrews 7</margin> But on the contrary, the Apostle <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul, the traditional author of the Book of Hebrews.</note> testifies at length in that entire chapter that he was greater: because Melchizedek was the High Priest, because he blessed Abraham, because he received tithes from him, and finally because Melchizedek was an illustrious type of Christ in respect to both his person and his offices, such as his royal dignity and his priestly duty. Nor is it truly asserted that Melchizedek was not a type of Christ, when Paul says so explicitly in the place cited above.

He maintains that while Melchizedek was a human king of Canaan, he was spiritually superior to Abraham in his role as a priest.</summary>

Hebrews 7:11 states that Christ is a Priest *according to the order* <note>original Greek: κατὰ τὴν τάξιν (kata tēn taxin)</note> of Melchizedek, and verse 15 says *according to the likeness* <note>original Greek: κατὰ τὴν ὁμοιότητα (kata tēn homoiotēta)</note>. The objection that Abel also had no successor, and that the state of being *without genealogy* <note>original Greek: τὸ ἀγενεαλόγητον (to agenealogēton)</note> is also found in Job and Elijah, is invalid. This is because there is a <term>fallacy of division</term> <note>A logical error where one assumes that what is true for parts of a group must be true for the whole, or that characteristics found separately in different people are the same as finding them all combined in one person.</note>; for even if those traits are found separately in others, they are found—or presented—all together in no one except Melchizedek. Secondly, it is false that Abel had no successor; Seth succeeded him, whom God substituted in his place in Genesis 4:25—hence the name **Seth** <note>original Hebrew: שֵׁת (Shet)</note> because he was "appointed" or "added."

IV. Many objections are raised from the history written by Moses, but they are nothing more than mere conjectures. 1. Why would Abraham not have sought help from Melchizedek, a neighboring king, rather than from Mamre and Eschol—who were pagans—to rescue his nephew Lot? But the response is ready at hand from Moses himself in Genesis 14:13. There, Moses teaches three things: first, that Abraham lived among the oaks of Mamre, and therefore, in that sudden raid, those pagans were more immediately available so that Lot could be rescued as quickly as possible from the victorious and fast-retreating army. Indeed, the slightest delay would have prevented Lot's liberation. Secondly, it is expressly stated in that 13th verse that Mamre, Eschol, and Aner were allies joined in a covenant with Abraham. Therefore, what is more common than to seek help from allies, since these are the very terms of a treaty? Thirdly, Moses does not say that Abraham sought help from those pagans, but only that he armed his own servants. Verse 14: *And when Abraham heard that his brother was taken captive, he armed his trained servants, born in his own house, three hundred and eighteen, and pursued them unto Dan.* Even **Bellarmine** <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a highly influential Jesuit Cardinal and Counter-Reformation theologian.</note> admits this when he wittily observes that at the First Council of Nicaea, three hundred and eighteen bishops were assembled, just as Abraham recovered Lot with that many servants.

II. They object that Abraham sent to Mesopotamia to find a wife for his son Isaac, which he would not have attempted if he had a pious king living right next to him. Truly, this is easily refuted from the text of Moses itself in Genesis 24:4, when Abraham says to his senior servant, *But thou shalt go unto my country, and to my kindred, and take a wife unto my son Isaac.* And surely a wife would come more willingly from there, to marry a fellow countryman; on the other hand, he forbade taking a wife from

### [The Separation from the Canaanites]

Abraham did not take a wife for his son from the Canaanites because God, by a sacred covenant, had separated him from them. For this reason, he did not want his lineage to be mixed with the Canaanites, whom he knew were already divinely destined for destruction. Indeed, his descendants were to be introduced into that land as the true owners once the current inhabitants were wiped out; therefore, there was a sworn discord as if with perpetual enemies. For even if Melchizedek was faithful, he was nonetheless an extraordinary man, inspired by God as if by a peculiar divine breath; and it is not established whether he had daughters, and if he had them, whether there was a nubile virgin or not—*already ripe for a husband, already in her full years for marriage.* <note>original Latin: "Iam matura viro, iam plenis nubilis annis." This is a poetic reference, likely from Virgil's Aeneid, describing a young woman of marriageable age.</note> Nor is it true that Abraham's relatives lived in Mesopotamia at a distance of three hundred leagues. For in the Hebrew text it is *Aram Naharaim*, <note>original Hebrew: אֲרַם נַהֲרַיִם (Aram Naharayim), literally "Aram of the Two Rivers."</note> that is, "Syria of the Rivers," which began not far from Judea, even if it extended far and wide.

### III. [Abraham’s Journey to Gerar]

Some wonder why Abraham, in Genesis 20, set out toward the South country and lived between Kadesh and Shur, and stayed as a foreigner in Gerar, where Abimelech, a pagan man, was king. If Melchizedek was the king of Jerusalem, why (they ask) did Abraham not live with him? But these people inquire with too much curiosity; the question is no longer *about the "why,"* but *about the "fact."* <note>original Greek: "περὶ τοῦ διότι" (peri tou dioti) vs "περὶ τοῦ ὅτι" (peri tou hoti). Cregut is using Aristotelian logic to distinguish between the reason for a thing and the factual occurrence of it.</note> It is not a matter of what should have been by right, but what was done in fact. If any reason can nonetheless be given, we say that God directed the life of the Patriarch by a peculiar instinct, leading him now here, now there, as it seemed best to Providence. This was done so that his miraculous preservation amidst so many difficulties might reveal to us and to the whole world the riches of divine favor and protection, as happened in the territory of Abimelech. Furthermore, it pleased God to exercise the father of the faithful in various travels before he could quietly set foot in the land of Canaan, of which—after so many journeys and wanderings—he was to be the future inhabitant and true possessor through his descendants.

### IV. [The Status of Jerusalem and the Jebusites]

They add that whenever Scripture speaks of Jerusalem, it always calls it a pagan city from the time of Abraham until David, by whom the Jebusites were finally expelled. Yet, on the contrary, in the time of Abraham its king is called Melchizedek, who is the Priest of the Most High. But if later, in the time of Adoni-zedek (mentioned in Joshua 10) and in the time of David, its inhabitants were Jebusites—men who were not only pagans but also wicked sinners—as the Chaldean paraphrast <note>This refers to the Targum, an Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note> translated those words in 2 Samuel 5:6:
> You shall not enter here unless you remove the blind...

### [The Meaning of Likeness in Scripture]

Finally, they raise one objection against the words of the Apostle in Hebrews 7:3, where Melchizedek is said to be *made like* <note>original Greek: ἀφωμοιωμένος (aphōmoiōmenos), meaning "made to resemble" or "assimilated to."</note> the Son of God. They claim that because in Scripture that which is said to be "similar" is often also "the same"—as in Philippians 2:7, where *Christ is said to have been made in the likeness of man*, and yet he was truly a man—the same must apply here. 

But on the contrary, Paul not only says Melchizedek was made like the Son of God; he also says conversely that the Son of God was a *priest* <note>original Greek: ἱερέα (hierea).</note> according to the order of Melchizedek in chapter 6:20 and chapter 7:15, *In the likeness of Melchizedek*. Furthermore, these phrases in Scripture do not simply denote identity. For in Philippians 2:7, Jesus Christ was made in the likeness of man; but he was not a mere man, or a *simple human* <note>original Greek: ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος (psilos anthrōpos). This refers to the heresy that Jesus was only human and not divine.</note> (as Nestorius <note>Nestorius was a 5th-century Archbishop of Constantinople whose views led to the belief that Christ had two distinct natures, sometimes interpreted by his critics as denying the full union of God and man.</note> dreamed), but truly the *God-man*. <note>original Greek: θεάνθρωπος (theanthrōpos).</note> 

Finally, observe that Scripture intends one thing when dealing with "types" (symbols), and another when it speaks properly and considers the Truth itself separately. When dealing with types or speaking figuratively, words and notions do not signify "identity" (being the same thing), but "likeness," because a figure is like the thing it represents, and vice versa—it is not the thing itself. If "identity" is attributed to them, this is done in an improper sense, specifically because of the very close union between the sign and the thing signified, and the most perfect *likeness* <note>original Greek: ὁμοίωσιν (homoiōsin), meaning "assimilation" or "resemblance."</note> between the figure and the reality. But it happens differently outside of signs and figures; where then the marks of likeness, such as "as"... <meta>catchword: word [ἔπος]</meta>

<meta>This page continues Anthony Cregut's theological argument regarding the identity of Melchizedek. Having previously argued that Melchizedek was a real historical human rather than a divine apparition, Cregut here uses linguistic analysis of Greek and Hebrew to distinguish between "similarity" and "identity" in the biblical text.</meta>

<header>->THE REVEALER OF SECRETS<-</header>

**"Thus"** <note>original Greek: οὕτως (*houtōs*)</note>, that is "in this way," as used here, does not signify a mere similarity but an identity <note>meaning the things are one and the same</note>, as in John 1:14: *glory as of the only begotten from the Father* <note>original Greek: δόξαν ὡς μονογενοῦς παρὰ πατρός</note>. In this instance, the word "as" <note>original Greek: ὡς (*hōs*)</note>, which corresponds to the Hebrew **"Caph of similitude"** <term>Caph similitudinis: a Hebrew prefix (כּ) usually meaning "like" or "as," which can sometimes emphasize the reality of a thing rather than just a comparison</term>, does not signify a similarity, but the very truth of the matter. It should be observed, however, that whenever these particles are doubled—**"thus as"** <note>original Greek: οὕτως ὡς</note>—they always denote a metaphor or a similarity; as in 1 Corinthians 3:15: *but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire* <note>original Greek: αὐτὸς δὲ σωθήσεται οὕτως δὲ ὡς διὰ πυρὸς</note>. *But he himself shall be saved, yet so as if through fire.* In this case, it is not a matter of literal fire, but fire spoken of metaphorically.

Finally, the argument they bring forward concerning other appearances of Christ cannot support this fabrication <note>the theory that Melchizedek was a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ</note>. They point to the angels who appeared to Abraham, among whom was Christ, and who are called "men." However, those appearances can be turned back against them: for in those cases, Scripture testifies that those who appeared were in truth angels. In contrast, regarding Melchizedek, Moses nowhere denies that he was a son of God <note>Cregut argues that while angels are identified as such, Melchizedek is consistently described as a human king</note>; and if for a time he was believed to be a man by Abraham and others, their opinion is soon corrected when those messengers of God manifest themselves.

Thus far let these things be said concerning the person of Melchizedek; now follow his offices, which are two: namely, the **royal** and the **priestly**. Both are evident from this oracle in Genesis 14:18: *And Melchizedek king of Salem* <note>original Hebrew: ומלכי צדק מלך שלם</note>. And then it is added: *and he was a priest of the Most High* <note>original Hebrew: והוא כהן לעליון</note>. And Paul says in Hebrews 7:1: *For this Melchizedek was king of Salem, priest of the Most High God.* This dual office is utterly extraordinary and unique to Melchizedek. For no one has ever been found, besides Melchizedek, who by right obtained both dignities, both the Royal and the Priestly. Moses held the magistracy <note>the leadership of the people</note> both by a clearly divine calling and by a power and authority most eminent of all—emanating either **sovereignly** <note>original Greek: αὐτοκρατορικῇ</note> or immediately from God, the King of kings—yet he never stepped into the priestly dignity, but instead let his brother Aaron perform that duty. And David was called king and the firstborn of kings in Psalm 89:27—that is, *the greatest of kings* in the Hebrew idiom—yet he never performed the parts of a High Priest. And when King Uzziah <note>referred to here as Osias</note> moved his hand toward the censer <note>to offer incense, a task reserved for priests</note>, he was immediately defiled by leprosy through God’s vengeance; and therefore, by **usurping** an office not his own...

...was deprived of his own [office], and was unfit for its function. If, however, certain individuals are found among the pagan nations who performed both duties <note>the offices of King and Priest</note>, this was done tyrannically, and was a matter of actual practice rather than of law; just as everything in the religion of those idolaters was corrupted. And so, tyrants, distinguished by a new dignity, wished to expand their power and make it venerable by means of the sacred office. Thus, under the pretext of religion, they might tame even the most ferocious people—an approach that succeeded for Numa Pompilius <note>the legendary second king of Rome (c. 715–673 BCE), credited with establishing many of Rome's religious and political institutions</note>, the second king of the Romans. This also included his fictional conversations with the nymph Egeria <note>Numa claimed a divine nymph taught him his laws in secret to give them divine authority</note>. This same strategy eventually succeeded for the Roman Pontiff <note>the Pope</note>, to the greatest destruction of Christianity; he joined the highest dignity, both secular and spiritual, in his own person. From this comes his head crowned with a triple diadem, and those famous lines from the poem of Mantuan <note>Baptista Mantuanus (1447–1516), a Carmelite poet famous for his Latin verse</note> regarding that threefold or unbridled audacity:

->*Powerful with a double sword, whose footsteps*<-

->*By the oracle of your voice, you guide the reins of the world,*<-
->*And you are rightly believed to be God on earth.*<-
<note>original: "Oraclo vocis mundi moderaris habenas, / Et meritò in terris crederis esse Deus."</note>

Therefore, although we freely admit that formerly among the Nations <note>the Pagans</note> one and the same person sought and held both offices, as is found in Plato and frequently occurs in the Poets; nevertheless, among the people of God under the Law <note>the Mosaic Law of the Old Testament</note>, these two offices were so distinct that it was a sin for Kings to seize the priesthood. Therefore, it was unique to Melchizedek to possess both dignities. Thus, according to the axiom of theologians: that most singular and extraordinary thing in the Old Testament foreshadowed some distinguished mystery in the New Testament. But what mystery? Truly, none other than that of Christ the antitype <term>antitype: the New Testament reality that fulfills or corresponds to a "type" (a person or event) from the Old Testament</term>, who is the true Melchizedek, being both King and High Priest at the same time. Therefore He is called Messiah and Christ—that is, "Anointed"—because He was anointed with the oil of gladness above His companions so that He might be our King, Priest, and Prophet.

14. He is called **King of kings**. So it is said in Zechariah 9:9, *The King of the daughter of Zion.* In Matthew 2:2 and 27:11, *The King of Israel or of the Jews.* In Psalm 2:6, *God’s King*, <note>original: "Rex Dei"</note> because he was appointed king of the Church by God. In Hebrews 7:1 and 2, he is described as the *King of righteousness and peace*, prefigured by Melchizedek <note>Melchizedek is a mysterious king-priest in Genesis whose name means "King of Righteousness."</note>. Therefore, it was not without a great mystery that the title on the cross was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin letters: **King of the Jews**. This was so the whole world might acknowledge that Christ, through his suffering, had triumphed over the Devil and won a kingdom for himself. 

But this kingdom of Christ is one of spirit and grace, which was followed by the kingdom of glory that he acquired for himself in his resurrection and ascension, although it had been destined for him from the moment of his conception. For just as David—who was also a figure representing Christ—was anointed king in his youth by Samuel, yet did not obtain possession of the kingdom except after many labors and sorrows; so Christ began to be the Lord of glory from the beginning of his conception, but it was necessary for Christ to suffer and so enter into his glory, as noted in Luke 24. 

Of this kingdom of glory, Luke 19 speaks under the parable of a certain nobleman who went into a distant country to receive a kingdom for himself and then return. Here he speaks of his passion, through which he was to go away to receive the kingdom of glory, and finally return on the Day of Judgment. However, Scripture does not recognize a temporal <note>meaning "earthly" or "limited by time"</note> kingdom of Christ. 

But you will say: was he not prefigured through Moses, Melchizedek, David, and others whose kingdoms were temporal? I respond: Christ did not have to be a temporal king simply because he was prefigured by them; rather, the reality <note>the "antitype"</note> is more excellent than its symbolic figure. It is not without reason, then, that the kingdom of Christ is called the **kingdom of heaven** or the **kingdom of God**. This naming signifies the state of the Christian Church as it is opposed to the Jewish state; for the Jews constantly dreamed of a temporal and earthly kingdom for the Messiah, because Moses promised earthly happiness to the Jews in a symbolic <note>typological</note> way. 

Thus the Talmudists <note>scholars of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note> think of nothing but an earthly kingdom; and so too the Muslims in the Quran have imitated the Talmudists. Sounder mystical theologians—namely the *Mecubbalim* <note>the Hebrew term for "those who receive," or Cabalists</note> or Cabalists—reject these carnal dreams and instead preach spiritual freedom and the release from original sin through the Messiah.

Therefore, observe the triple superiority <note>original: ὑπεροχὴν</note> of Christ's kingdom over the kingdom of Melchizedek and David, as is clear from Daniel 2:44.

1. That it shall not be destroyed, but he shall remain king without successors. Other kingdoms have successors. Hence among the Greeks those sons are called **born in the purple** <note>original: πορφυρογέννητοι; a title given to children born to a reigning Emperor in the purple chamber of the palace</note>, and they are deemed blessed because they are sprung from royal blood, just as at Rome the **Patricians** <note>the hereditary aristocratic class of ancient Rome</note> are regarded. But regarding the Messiah's kingdom, it is not those **born in the purple** but the **regenerated** <note>original: παλιγγενηταὶ; those "born again"</note>—the faithful born anew—who are partakers of Christ’s royal dignity, because we are a *royal priesthood*. The kingdom or Empire of the Romans was believed to be eternal; hence that phrase found everywhere among authors: ***Eternal Rome***. Nor was it permitted for Christians to think otherwise. Hence Paul speaks obscurely in 2 Thessalonians 2: *He who now restrains, let him restrain* <note>Early Christian interpreters often believed the "restraining force" was the Roman Empire, which delayed the coming of the Antichrist</note>. And the Church Fathers also wrote obscurely when, fearing the arrival of the Antichrist, they prayed *for the delay of the end* <note>original: pro mora finis</note>, that is, for the preservation of the Roman Empire. But the outcome proved that Rome was not eternal; which is a claim that must be asserted of Christ's kingdom alone.

Therefore, when the Psalmist says in Psalm 110: *Sit at my right hand **until** I make your enemies*, etc., it does not follow that Christ's kingdom is to be abolished, for it must be eternal. This remains true even after he has subdued all enemies, among whom death is considered the last, according to 1 Corinthians 15:26: *The last enemy to be destroyed is death.* For as Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian of the Western Church</note> testifies, that little word ***until*** <note>original: donec</note> does not signify some determined time, but an indefinite one—indeed, often an infinite one—as he illustrates with various examples: 

Matthew 5 and Luke 12, concerning the last penny: *Until you pay the last penny*; which Blessed Augustine understands as the eternal punishments of Hell. So too Matthew 1:25: *Joseph knew not Mary **until** <note>original: ἕως οὗ</note> she had brought forth that firstborn son of hers* <note>The author uses this to argue that "until" does not imply Joseph had relations with Mary afterward, reinforcing the doctrine of her perpetual virginity</note>. 1 Corinthians 15: *He must receive heaven **until** all things are put under his feet.* Many other passages can be added, such as Genesis 28:15: *I will not leave you **until*** <note>original Hebrew: עד אשר — ad asher</note> *I have done what I have spoken to you.* Deuteronomy 34:6: *No one has known the tomb of Moses **until** this day.* 1 Samuel 15:35: *Samuel did not see Saul **until** the day of his death.* 2 Samuel 6:23: *Michal is said to have had no child **until** the day of her death.* Psalm 71:18: *While I am old and gray-headed, O God, do not forsake me, **until** I have declared your arm to this generation.* Matthew 28:20: *Behold, I am with*

...I am with you **until the end of the age** <note>original: ἕως τῆς συντελείας τοῦ αἰῶνος; Matthew 28:20</note>. 1 Corinthians 15:25: **It is necessary for him to reign until** <note>original: ἄχρις οὗ</note> **he has put his enemies under his feet.** 1 Timothy 4:13: **Until I come** <note>original: ἕως ἔρχομαι</note>, **attend to reading.** In the same way, when we are about to depart, we often wish our friends good health **until we return**, yet we do not wish the opposite for them afterward. Likewise, he will reign without enemies or obstacles; without any limitation of power or justice; and without any distinction of times, varied economy, or the distribution of works and other circumstances which are administered in the Kingdom of Grace on this earth and are most suitable to it.

The sages of the Hebrews confess that eternity of the Messiah's kingdom. Beyond the passage in Daniel 2 and other oracles of Scripture, they also observe a certain mystery in Isaiah 9, where, after various titles of the Messiah are listed—such as **Wonderful, Counselor, Prince of Peace**, etc.—it is finally added: **to the increase of the government** <note>original: לםרבה המשרה</note>. Therefore, they say, there is a hidden mystery there. For in the book **Shabbat** <note>The Talmudic tractate on the Sabbath</note>, in the chapter titled **The Builder** <note>original: הבונה; "Ha-Boneh"</note>, the **closed Mem** signifies a closed word or a hidden matter...

...becomes either Caesar or nothing. This has been observed, not without mystery, in the Emperors of the East and the West. For in Rome, the first Emperor created was Augustus, in whose hands (as Tacitus says at the beginning of the *Annals*) the majesty of the Empire began; but Augustulus <note>The diminutive name "Little Augustus" given to Romulus Augustulus, the last Western Roman Emperor</note> was the last Emperor. So too in the East, Constantine the Great first fixed his seat at Constantinople and founded the city, but Constantine <note>Constantine XI Palaiologos</note> was the last Emperor; for he was conquered by Mehmed III <note>The text reads "Mahomete III," though historically it was Mehmed II who captured Constantinople in 1453</note>, Emperor of the Ottomans and the Turks, and the city of Constantinople was captured. By this allusion of names, it seems signified that kings do not reign by their own force and power, but by Him who says, *through me kings reign* <note>Proverbs 8:15</note>; who makes an Augustulus out of an Augustus; and from Constantine the conqueror of the world, another Constantine who was a slave of the Turks; and finally, who makes him who was shortly before Caesar suddenly become nothing—or, as the saying goes, *from Consul to Rhetorician, from Rhetorician to Consul.* <note>A reference to the unpredictable "Wheel of Fortune" where high-ranking officials could be reduced to lowly teachers, or vice versa</note> Truly, therefore, all kingdoms except that of Christ have a beginning and an end; hence that funeral verse of the noble poet:

> *Every just power has a beginning and an end;*
> *God alone lacks an end and a beginning.*
> *The power of Caesar is undefined, not infinite;*
> *No one on earth can do all things.*

IV. To this may be added the **preeminence** <gloss>original: ὑπεροχήν (*hyperochēn*)</gloss>, that Christ is at once King and Father. For although good princes are commonly called *parents of the fatherland and the people* <note>original: *parentes patriae & populi*</note>—which was the surname of Louis XII, King of the Franks—they are nonetheless not properly fathers as Christ is. For a father has begotten us, and so has Christ; but on the contrary, regarding earthly kings, the king does not create the people, but rather the people create the king. And if kings beget natural sons to be successors of the kingdom, they cannot, however, beget the whole people; but Christ, the spiritual king, begets all subjects in the kingdom of grace spiritually through the incorruptible seed of His Spirit and Word. From this the horrendous crime of the Jews is evident, who committed at once the two most wicked of all crimes: namely, the crimes of **high treason** <term>high treason: *perduellio*, a crime against the state or its ruler</term> and **parricide** <term>parricide: *parricidium*, the murder of a parent</term>; one against their king, the other against their father. And so they cut off, as it were, a double head; and therefore it is no wonder if they brought upon themselves death and eternal destruction.

V. To this let **Shaddai** <note>Hebrew: שדי, a name for God usually translated as "Almighty," though the author focuses on the root meaning "sufficient."</note> be added. Christ the King is truly and by his very title the Lord, because he is *Shaddai*—sufficient for himself and for all others—since he alone requires nothing from anyone; yet, on the contrary, all things have need of him. Hence Augustus (during whose reign Christ was born) forbade by edict that anyone should call him "Lord," as if divinely instructed that the true Lord of the whole world had arisen, to whom others ought to offer gifts as a symbol of subjection, as in Psalm 72:10: *The kings of Tarshish and of the isles shall bring presents: the kings of Sheba and Seba shall offer gifts.* For gifts are brought to such a Lord of lords, not because he lacks them, but so it may be clear that all things are subjected under the feet of that Head—even the powers of the world. Therefore (as the Political theorists like to say), all men, even kings, are "Feudatories" and vassals to that King of kings. And since the word <term>Feudum</term> <note>A "fief" or "feud," the land held by a vassal in the feudal system.</note> is a Lombard word said to be derived from *fide* [faith], or as if it were *Fedum*, according to Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a prominent French jurist and political philosopher.</note> in Book 1 of *The Republic*, chapter 9; the initial letters of this word signify: *Fidelis Ero Domino Vero Meo* [I will be faithful to my true lord]. To whom can these words be more rightly applied than to Christ? We, as his feudatories receiving benefits from him, are bound to pledge: *I will be faithful to my true lord.* For we are truly his Feudatories or <term>Timariots</term> <note>The author compares Christian subjection to the "Timariot" system of the Ottoman Empire, where cavalrymen (Timariots) were granted land (Timars) by the Sultan in exchange for military service.</note> paying our allegiance. Just as a *Feud* or a *Timar* (a Turkish word, but derived from the Greek *Timan*, "to honor") is a benefit conferred by a prince upon a subject, so Christ the highest Lord confers all things upon us and receives nothing, needing nothing himself. The Apostle indicates this excellently in Ephesians 4:8; for when he cites the words of Psalm 68:18, *you received gifts* <note>original: "לקחת מתנות"</note>, he did not render it word-for-word <note>original: "αὐτολεξεί"</note>, but looking to the deeper sense, he said *he gave gifts* <note>original: "ἔδωκε δώματα"</note>, or *he gave presents* <note>original: "נתן מתנות"</note>. Here he does not follow the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament (LXX).</note> translators, who render it *you took gifts* [ἔλαβες δώματα], because the kingdom of Christ differs from earthly kingdoms. While the fruits of other kingdoms go to the benefit of the kings, in the kingdom of Christ, everything is done for the sake of the subjects. Therefore, the word "received" [לקחת], which refers to earthly kings...

### ANTHONY CREGUTUS

...you have received, truly signifies the taking of a gift. This is because earthly kings take spoils from their enemies and gifts from their subjects, as is clear from the example of the Persian kings, before whom no one dared to appear without a gift. Yet, regarding Christ, the King of the Church, Paul rightly said <note>original: ἔδωκε (*edōke*)</note> **he gave**, reflecting the underlying meaning. For if He <note>original: לקח (*lakach*)</note> **received** (as the Psalmist has it), He surely received so that He might give and distribute to the faithful; for since He received the Spirit without measure, this was done so that from His fullness the members of His body <note>The Church</note> might draw. Therefore, the words of the Prophet are to be explained thus: <note>original: לקחת מתנות באדם (*lakachta matanot ba-adam*)</note> **you received gifts for men, that is, which you were to give to men.** For although giving and receiving differ greatly, the Apostle nevertheless looked to the genuine sense. Indeed, a thanksgiving immediately follows: **"Blessed be God,"** who daily adorns us with his gifts. Therefore, the Hebrew letter <term>Beth</term> <note>ב</note> is taken to mean <note>original: בעבור (*ba'avur*)</note> **for the sake of**, or "to," so that a verb of subsequent action is understood. Thus, in *Genesis 32:13*, regarding the gifts to be handed over by Jacob to his brother Esau, which Jacob first "received" <note>or "took in hand"</note>. In *Acts 7:9*, **"They sold him into Egypt,"** meaning for the purpose of being transferred there. In *Numbers 23:27*, **"I will take you to another place,"** namely, to be led there. The <term>Chaldean Paraphrast</term> <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note> holds the same view as Paul regarding this way of speaking, except that he interprets these things ineptly as referring to Moses, as does even the impious <term>Rabbi Solomon</term>. <note>Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator. The author's use of "impious" reflects the standard religious polemics of the 17th century.</note>

But this observation is even more clear in the word <note>original: לקח (*lakach*)</note> **received**, which includes a relationship between the giver and the receiver: when someone receives only for the purpose of handing it over, the Hebrews then use the word **received** rather than **gave**. And yet, because when we deal with a gift, we receive it for the purpose of giving it, it follows that by looking at the sense rather than the literal property of the word, "received" is expressed by Paul as "gave" in the previously praised passage, when he said **"He gave gifts."** In truth, one who intends to give a gift is accustomed first to take it into his hands, to arrange it and adorn it, and only then to offer it once it is arranged and adorned. Just as in the cited passage of *Genesis 32:13*, Jacob prepared the gift that he would send to his brother; and in *Deuteronomy 12:26*, when God requires an offering from His people, He says, **"take"**—meaning the gift to be given to me. Paul, therefore, placed <note>original: διδόναι (*didonai*)</note> **to give** in the place of <note>original: λαμβάνειν (*lambanein*)</note> **to take**. And in this way, he likewise reveals the royal magnificence of Christ, who does not receive these gifts from men...

VI. The **excellence** <note>original Greek: ἐξοχὴ (*exochē*), meaning preeminence or distinction</note> of this kingdom of Christ is that it is heavenly and spiritual. Hence, Rabbi Aben-Esra <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra, a prominent 12th-century Jewish scholar and biblical commentator</note>, explaining the passage in *Daniel 2*, says that the **Kingdom of Heaven** <note>original Hebrew: מלכות השמים (*malkhut ha-shamayim*)</note> signifies the **Kingdom of the Messiah** <note>original Hebrew: מלכות המשיח (*malkhut ha-mashiach*)</note>. It is called by this name, firstly, because the King is from heaven. For although earthly kings are said to be ordained by God in *Romans 13* and sent by God—not having emerged by mere chance; for which reason (as Isidore of Pelusium <note>A 5th-century monk and prolific letter writer known for his scriptural interpretations</note> writes) in the most ancient paintings, a hand was seen extended from heaven, placing a crown upon their heads—nevertheless, this is attributed to Christ in a special, indeed unique way, so that no other king can be compared to him, with the exception of Melchizedek. 

This is not because Melchizedek had actually fallen from heaven, or had descended from there as Christ did, but because he is presented in Scripture as a "figure" or foreshadowing of Christ. Therefore, his genealogy is not recorded, as if he were not sprung from the earth and from men like an ordinary earthly king, but so that we might suspect him to be a heavenly king—if not properly and in reality, then at least **analogously** <note>original Greek: ἀναλόγως (*analogōs*)</note>, insofar as he was an illustrious figure and type of Christ, the heavenly King. Now, the figure must represent the thing it prefigures (the "antitype"), and what is said of one must be said of the other, at least by analogy. Whence, as was said above, the meaning is composite; it is not complete unless the things said of the "type" <note>the historical foreshadowing</note> are applied to the "antitype" <note>the spiritual fulfillment</note>. Thus, the **premise** <note>original Greek: πρότασις (*protasis*)</note> and the **conclusion** <note>original Greek: ἀπόδοσις (*apodosis*)</note> emerge: the premise fits the type, while the conclusion truly fits the antitype. Therefore, Christ alone is truly and in reality called the Heavenly King, and the Kingdom of the Messiah is called the Kingdom of Heaven.

1. Because Christ is from heaven, both regarding his divine nature and his human nature, and regarding his eternal generation as well as his temporal generation. In the first way, because he was begotten by the Father from eternity (*Psalm 2*). In the second way, because he was conceived by the Holy Spirit. 

2. Because the King dwells in the heavens, as in *John 3*: 
> *No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.* 

3.
