# ANTHONY CREGUTUS

The Apostle says our citizenship <note>original Latin: *conuersatio*; often translated as "conversation" or "way of life," but here referring to citizenship or the place where one truly belongs</note> is in heaven (*Philippians 3*), and in the *Epistle to the Hebrews 6*, faith is called the **anchor of hope**. Yet, as Saint Augustine witnesses, just as when a sailor casts the ship’s anchor—which is a symbol of hope—by casting it toward the land, he is said to have already reached the land even though he still tosses about on the sea; so too the faithful, although they navigate this ocean of life, their citizenship is said to be in heaven because they cast the anchor of their hope there. Therefore, just as sailors cast the anchor into a dark and deep place hidden from us, and as long as it remains fixed there, the ship is safe in the midst of storms; so our hope is placed in God, who is entirely invisible to us and who dwells in the heavens. There is, however, this distinction: a sea anchor is cast downward toward the earth because it finds the bottom there, but our hope is an anchor of a different kind, which is cast **upward into the heavens**. This is because here on earth it can find no firm base where it might cling and rest. And just as the rope tied to the anchor joins the land with the ship—even though a great and obscure distance lies between them—so by the anchor of hope and the bond of the Word <note>original Latin: *verbi vinculo*; referring to the promises of Scripture</note> we are united with God, even though He seems very far from us, invisible, and like a most profound abyss.

IV. Because the seat of the subjects is certain in heaven; for on earth they are pilgrims and are regarded as foreigners by the world.

# ANTHONY CREGUT

...Salem is more a corruption than a name taken from those mountains.

Therefore, the Etymology of the word Jerusalem is not from the Greek <note>original: ἱερὸν (*hieron*), meaning "holy" or "temple"</note>, but as we have said, from <note>original Hebrew: יראה (*yireh*)</note> "He will provide" and <note>original Hebrew: שלום (*shalom*)</note> "peace." This is because of the words of Abraham when he was about to perform the sacrifice, when he said: *The Lord will provide*. But on this point, what did the Rabbi in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>An ancient Jewish commentary on the Psalms</note> say regarding that verse in Psalm 76: *And I will place my tabernacle in Salem* etc.? The Holy One, blessed be He, said: "How then shall I call this place? For if I call it Salem, I will erase the words of my friend Abraham, who called it <note>original Hebrew: יראה (*yireh*)</note>. But if I call it <note>original Hebrew: שמה (*shammah*)</note> <note>Likely referring to the name "Salem" or the "Name" associated with Shem/Melchizedek</note>, the name of the righteous man will cease. What then did the Holy One, blessed be He, do? He mixed the names by which both had called that place, and called it **Jerusalem**." 

Where one should note that more recent Hebrew scholars corrupt the passage in Ezekiel 48:35: <note>original Hebrew: ושם העיר מיום יהוה שמה (*ve-shem ha-ir mi-yom YHWH shammah*)</note> "and the name of the city from that day [will be] The Lord is there." Here it is written as <note>original Hebrew: שמה (*shammah*)</note> "there," not <note>original Hebrew: שמו (*shemo*)</note> "His name." As Jonathan the Chaldean <note>Referring to the *Targum Jonathan*, an Aramaic translation and commentary</note> has it: <note>original Aramaic: ושמא דקרתא דמתפרש מיומאדי ישרי שכינתיה יהוה תמן</note>—that is, *they shall explain the name of the city from the day on which God placed His Divine Presence there.* 

Finally, by Aelius Hadrian, who rebuilt the city, it was called **Aelia Capitolina**; from this comes the canon of the Council of Nicaea <note>The first ecumenical council in 325 AD</note> regarding Aelia and the honors of the Patriarch of Jerusalem. Others wish for "Jerusalem" to be formed from *Jebus* and *Salem*, with the 'B' changed to an 'R'; by others it is believed, though incorrectly, to come from *Luza* and *Bethel*. Hence this two-line verse regarding its many names:

->*Solyma, Luza, Bethel, Jerusalem, Jebus, and Aelia,*<-
->*The holy city is called Jerusalem, and also Salem.*<-

These matters have been discussed by us at length so that it may appear that such grand names were imposed on this place by divine will and clearly <term>according to correctness</term> <note>original Greek: κατ' ὀρθότητα (*kat' orthotēta*)</note>—as Plato speaks in his work *Cratylus*—because of the most holy mystery of the <term>economy of Christ</term> <note>The divine plan for human salvation through Jesus</note>, which was once to be fulfilled there. Therefore, those things which are foreshadowed in <term>type</term> <note>A historical person or event serving as a prophetic symbol</note> concerning Melchizedek, and *Zedek* [Justice], and *Salem* [Peace], and Jerusalem, have all been found to be fulfilled mystically and as the reality the symbol pointed to; as will be obvious to anyone examining the spiritual connections. For this reason, Jerusalem is not undeservedly called the mother of all Christian Churches, since the Gospel broke forth from there into the whole world and the gifts of the Holy Spirit were poured out there, just as Caesarea was the mother of all Gentile Churches. Thus say the Hebrews.

XII. Paul defines **Jerusalem as the Church and the assembly of the firstborn, whose names are written in heaven** <note>Reference to Hebrews 12:23</note>. And in Galatians 4, he calls it the **Jerusalem above** and the mother of us all. This will be especially prominent in the three periods of the Christian Church. **I.** In its infancy, when the Gentiles were called by the preaching of the word. **II.** Its glory will shine at the end of the ages, in the calling of the Jews and the fullness of the Gentiles after the destruction of Babylon and the Antichrist, at which time all nations and their glory shall be led to Christ the King. **III.** The brightness of Jerusalem will be most radiant after the glorious resurrection. Since all these things magnificently proclaim the glory of Jerusalem, and that city was mystically the throne of our Melchizedek, is it any wonder if we teach that all these things fit perfectly in Christ, who is truly Melchizedek, the King of *Tsedek* <note>original Hebrew: צדק (tzedek), meaning "justice" or "righteousness"</note>, the King of *Salem* <note>original Hebrew: שלום (shalom), meaning "peace"</note>, and the King of Jerusalem?

But indeed, just as Christ is the true Melchizedek, so the Pope is a Pseudo-Melchizedek; for he is by no means the King of Jerusalem—that is, the Church—but a tyrant and usurper, who, according to 2 Thessalonians 2, comes <term>καθίσαι εἰς ναὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ (*kathisai eis naon tou Theou*)</term> <note>to sit in the temple of God</note>, to sit in the temple, or as Saint Augustine preferred to interpret it, against the temple of God. Therefore, just as there is no communion of Christ with Belial, so there is none between the true and the false Melchizedek. The former is the King of *Tsedek*, that is, of justice; the latter of injustice. The former is the King of *Salem*, that is, of peace; the latter the king of war and fury. Whence in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>, the beast wages war against the saints and kills the two witnesses. The former is the King of Jerusalem, because in Him is the true vision of peace; the latter is the king of mystical Babylon, where there is *Jerubabel*, the vision of confusion, and *Jerusalal*, that is, the vision of prey <note>The author is using wordplay here: Jerusalem (Vision of Peace) vs. Jerubabel (Vision of Confusion/Babel) and Jerusalal (Vision of Plunder/Prey)</note>; because he is a great plunderer of souls, and another Nimrod, a mighty hunter of men before the Lord. They only agree in this: that just as the King of Jerusalem was the King of **Jebus**, so this one is the king of the **Jebusites**—or rather those who are called "Ab-Jesuits," who are commonly said to be the very marrow of the Pope.

Furthermore, the kingdom of Christ is spiritual and heavenly, whence (as we saw above) it is called the kingdom of heaven, according to that well-known hymn:

> ->*Wicked enemy Herod, why do you fear Christ’s coming?*<-
> ->*He who gives heavenly kingdoms does not snatch away mortal ones.*<-

But this man's kingdom is earthly, even if he falsely claims for himself the "two swords"—that is, the temporal and the spiritual power. Not without reason, then, did King Louis oppose coins with coins and sword with sword, ordering his own to be struck with this other inscription: *I will destroy the name of Babylon*. ...stumbled over the basic elements. He did not know that in the Hebrew it is read *tero'em*, meaning **you shall break them**. <note>original: תְּרֹעֵם (Psalm 2:9)</note>. This comes from the roots *ra‘a‘* and *hara‘*, and the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> verb *ra‘a‘*, which means **to crush** or **to shatter**. This is why the Chaldean paraphrase <note>The Targum</note> renders it as "you shall shatter them." <note>original: תתברנון (tetabberinnun)</note>. Therefore, that Jesuit was deceived by the similarity of the words, as if the root were *ra‘ah*, which means **to feed** or **to pasture**. However, the text cannot support that meaning, since it is immediately followed by: *and you shall scatter them like a potter’s vessel*. From what has been said, it is clear that the Hebrew saying once applied to the kingdom of Antiochus can rightly be said of the Pope’s reign. Later, regarding the Roman Empire, they used the acronym <note>original: רָאשֵׁי תיבֹוֹת (rashei tevot)</note> **Kingdom of Impiety** <note>original: מלכות הרשעה (Malkhut ha-Resha'ah)</note>, for this is what Paul calls the **mystery of impiety** <note>2 Thessalonians 2:7; usually translated as "mystery of iniquity"</note>. *Elias* <note>Likely Elias Levita, a 16th-century Hebrew scholar</note> prefers the term **impious kingdom**.

So much for the first office of Melchizedek, which is the kingly office; now follows the second office, which is the Priestly one. For Moses does not only say that Melchizedek was King of Salem, but also that **He was Priest of the Most High** <note>original: והוא כהן לעליון (Genesis 14:18)</note>. Now, in truth, there were two kinds of **priests** <note>original: כהנים (Cohanim)</note>. 
I. **Political priests**, who were the chief ministers of the king and served his majesty. 
II. **Ecclesiastical priests**, who served God and His supreme majesty. 
Just as the same distinction is in use today regarding the **Ministers and Pastors of the Gospel**. For some are **political ministers**, who are the leading men before kings and who hold the rudder of the kingdom; others are **ecclesiastical ministers**, who devote themselves to sacred things. From this, all pastors are called **Ministers**, and the Apostles too are **ministers of Christ**, and Christ himself is called in *Romans 15* the **Minister of the Circumcision**, and in *Hebrews 8*, the **Minister of the Sanctuary**. The first group were properly **Ecclesiastical Priests**, and because this office was the highest, the name was later extended to the primary ministers and officials in political affairs. This is why this word is rendered in the Targum <note>The Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible</note> as **prince** <note>original: רבא (Rabba)</note> and in the plural as **princes, nobles, or governors** <note>original: רברבין (Ravarvin)</note>. Thus, those who are called **Priests** <note>original: כהנים (Cohanim)</note> in *2 Samuel chapter 8*, are called in *1 Chronicles 18* **the king's sons, the chief assistants at the hand of the king**. For David’s sons were priests of this kind. This was a position of the highest dignity; and if we believe the Jews, Absalom conspired against his father David to drive him from the throne of the kingdom because he was not admitted into the fellowship of this dignity. However, the heretic *Socinus* <note>Faustus Socinus, a 16th-century Italian theologian known for denying the divinity of Christ and traditional views on the atonement</note> should not have seized upon this as an opportunity for mockery when he ignorantly inferred—because David's sons were "priests"—that David must have been a King-Priest in the same sense as Christ, and so on.

...Priest, no differently than Melchizedek. Hence, in 1 Peter 2, the Church is called a *royal priesthood*, and in Exodus 19, a *kingdom of priests*. Onkelos <note>The author of a famous Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Torah</note> renders this as *kings and priests*. Besides those political "priests" <note>referring to civil leaders or magistrates who were sometimes called by this title in a broad sense</note>, there were primarily ecclesiastical priests who performed sacred rites. These ecclesiastical priests were again of two kinds: some ministered to the true God and were properly called *Cohanim* <note>original Hebrew: כהנים, meaning priests</note>; others, however, served the gods or idols of the Gentiles and were named *Komray* or *Komrin* in the Targum <note>original Aramaic: כומרא כומרין</note>. These were, as it were, "black-clad little sacrificers," so called because they walked about in dark garments according to a superstitious ritual. In the same way, modern Jews today call Monks by this name, and a nun is called a *Komrit* <note>original: כומרית</note>.

Furthermore, the *Cohanim*—the priests who ministered to God—were of two kinds: either before the Law or after the Law. The priests before the Law <note>The "Law" here refers to the Mosaic Law given at Mount Sinai</note> were *all the firstborn in the families of the godly*, as is evident from Exodus 19:22, 24. For this reason, the Patriarchs sacrificed as priests. And Esau is called "profane" by Paul in the Epistle to the Hebrews, not without cause, because he had sold his birthright <note>which included the right to the priesthood</note>. Priests after the Law are understood either in a *broad* sense or a *strict* sense. In the *broad* sense, all *the faithful are called priests, because in Romans 12:1 they present their bodies as living sacrifices. And in Revelation 1:6, Christ is said to have made us kings and priests to God and his Father.* Also, in 1 Peter 2:9, he calls Christians a *royal priesthood*. Hence, the people of God are called "peculiar" <note>original Greek: λαὸς περιούσιος, *laos periousios*; Hebrew: סגולה, *segulah*</note>, meaning a *special possession*. For among the Greeks, *periousia* means abundance. Now, ornaments and things that are precious are "abundant" <note>in value</note>; therefore, they are stored away and held in higher esteem than common things. Thus, although God is the ruler of the whole world, he nevertheless possesses the Church in a special way, like a crown upon his head and a seal upon his hand, and like a *segulah* <note>original: סגולה</note>, that is, a "possession," but a precious one, which God has acquired for himself. Just as in olden times a "peculium" <note>term: peculium - a small hoard of property or money held by someone who could not legally own it, like a son or a slave; here used for God's private treasure</note> was said to be acquired through labor with livestock <note>original: pecude</note>, which can be said in respect to Jacob. Indeed, Rachel was his own special treasure above all; nor is Rachel named so without a beautiful allusion, because *Rachel* signifies a "sheep" <note>original: Rachel; Hebrew: רחל, meaning ewe</note>. This "possession" of God, therefore, is rightly called *God’s priesthood*. In the *strict* sense, priests are those who are consecrated to God by a public office. And these are further of two kinds: either typical or antitypical. Typical priests are figures <note>symbols or "types"</note> that foreshadow the truth in the New Testament. There are furthermore three types of priests. 1. There are the *Ordinary* and common priests or ministers who performed ecclesiastical duties in the Old Testament, but did not have the right to offer sacrifices or burn incense. *Psalm 132:9: Let your priests be clothed with righteousness, and let those you kindly receive sing.* <note>original Latin: *Sacerdotes tui induantur iustitia, & quos benignè accipis cantent*</note>. Of this sort were the Levites, who were the lowest among all the priests. Thus, in Joshua 18:7, the name "Priesthood of God" also encompasses the ecclesiastical ministry which they performed. Perhaps to this group we can refer that "crowd of priests" mentioned in Acts 6:7: *And a great crowd of the priests obeyed the faith.* <note>original Greek: πολύς τε ὄχλος τῶν ἱερέων ὑπήκουον τῇ πίστει</note>. This indeed (to mention this in passing) greatly commends the efficacy of the Word of God, since in those early days of the Gospel, it won over even a crowd of priests to Christ, the High Priest.

However, I am not unaware that the Syriac edition reads *from the Jews* <note>original Syriac: מן יהודיא, *men Iihudaie*</note>, that is, *out of the Jews* <note>original Greek: ἐκ τῶν Ἰουδαίων</note>, though this is not generally approved. For why would that be noted, since the Gospel was then being announced only to the Jews? The Arabic version reads simply "a great crowd." Beza <note>Theodore Beza, a major Protestant theologian and scholar of the Greek New Testament</note> does not reject the sharp conjecture of Isaac Casaubon <note>A famous classical scholar known for textual criticism</note>, who suspects the text was written as: *and a great crowd, and [some] of the priests obeyed the faith* <note>original Greek: καὶ πολὺς ὄχλος, καὶ τῶν ἱερέων (sub. τινες) ὑπήκουον τῇ πίστει</note>. This would mean there was a great crowd [of common people] and also some of the priests who listened to the faith. This type of ellipsis <note>a grammatical omission where words are understood rather than stated</note> is also found in Matthew 23:34 and John 16:17. Ignorance of this omitted particle "and" <note>original Greek: καὶ</note> gave occasion for the corruption of this passage. For it is scarcely probable that even some priests—much less a "crowd" of priests—embraced the doctrine of salvation. As it says in John 12:42: *many from the rulers believed in him; but because of the Pharisees they did not profess it, lest they be moved out of the synagogue.* To these priests we can refer those whom the Rabbis call *Common Priests* <note>original Hebrew: כהנים הדיוטות, *Kohanim Hedyotot*</note>, meaning vulgar, plebeian priests, or "commoners" in the Targum, from the Greek word *Idiotes* <note>original Greek: Ἰδιώτης; used here to mean a private person or layman rather than someone with special status</note>.

II. There were other priests who in Scripture are called *Chief Priests* <note>original Greek: Ἀρχιερεῖς; Latin: *Principes Sacerdotum*</note>, who were divided into two families: namely, those of Eleazar and Ithamar <note>the sons of Aaron</note>. From these there were twenty-four families: specifically, sixteen from Eleazar and eight from Ithamar. These families ministered in rotation, as is evident from Luke 1 regarding Zechariah. From among these chief priests was formed the Sanhedrin <note>the supreme judicial and ecclesiastical council of the Jews</note>. Hence, in Matthew 2, Herod is said to have assembled—

Chief priests <note>original Greek: ἀρχιερεῖς</note>. From this group, a deputy for the High Priest was chosen, who performed his duties when the High Priest was kept in seclusion for seven days before the Day of Atonement <note>Yom Kippur</note> to prevent ritual impurity. From this group also came the "Head of the Assembly" <note>original Hebrew: ראש כנושתא, *Rosh Knesseth*</note>, that is, the ruler or head of the synagogue <note>original Greek: ἀρχισυναγωγῆς</note>, such as Jairus who is mentioned in the Gospel; regarding these, see Maimonides <note>A preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note>. III. There were the High Priests, who were exalted above all others; for this reason, there could not be multiple High Priests at the same time, but there was only one High Priest. He was therefore called simply and in the singular "the chief priest" <note>original Greek: ἀρχιερεὺς</note>, or "the priest who is great" <note>original Hebrew: כהן הגדול, *Kohen HaGadol*</note>, namely the greatest and highest of all priests. Therefore, in respect to the Priesthood itself, Aaron was not inferior to Moses; but insofar as Moses was the leader of the entire people, and thus also of the priests, he was superior to Aaron in his capacity as a Magistrate.

The Bishop of Rochester <note>original Latin: *Roffensis*; refers to John Fisher (1469–1535), the Catholic Bishop of Rochester who wrote against the Reformers</note> therefore wrote foolishly that in all matters pertaining to God, Moses was superior to Aaron, and that Moses was the High Priest in an absolute sense, while Aaron was only a High Priest comparatively, in respect to other priests. He says that in the New Law, Christ is the High Priest in an absolute sense, while Peter and the Pope are High Priests in a comparative sense to others. These things (I say) are asserted foolishly by the Bishop of Rochester, since Moses was not a priest after Aaron was established—certainly not a high priest—but rather a magistrate.

This is sufficiently demonstrated in Exodus 4, according to the Hebrew truth <note>a scholarly term for the original Hebrew text</note>, and not according to the Latin translator <note>the Vulgate</note>, who wretchedly corrupted this passage by introducing God speaking to Moses in this way: *He shall speak for you to the people, and he shall be your mouth: but you shall be to him in those things which pertain to God.* These final words are ambiguous. But in the Hebrew it is read: *And he shall speak for you to the people, and he himself shall be as a mouth for you to the people: and you shall be to him as God.* These words the Chaldean Paraphrast <note>the Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> expressed thus: *He shall speak for you with the people: and he shall be to you as an interpreter <note>original Aramaic: למתרגמן, *le-metargeman*</note>: and you shall be to him as a prince <note>original Aramaic: לרב, *le-rav*</note>.* To this interpretation Solomon Jarchi <note>Rashi, the famous medieval French rabbi</note> lends his support when he says that "mouth" <note>Hebrew: פה, *peh*</note> stands for "interpreter" <note>Hebrew: מליץ, *melitz*</note>, and "as God" <note>Hebrew: לאלהים, *l'Elohim*</note> is placed for "master" or "prince" <note>Hebrew: לרב vel לשר</note>. So also say Lyranus <note>Nicholas of Lyra</note> and Vatablus. This interpretation is confirmed in Exodus 7:1: *Aaron shall be your Prophet*, that is, your interpreter, according to the Chaldean Paraphrast. It seems the translation of the Latin translator—

[...tion] <note>Continuing from the previous page's discussion on the description of Moses's role</note> taken from the Septuagint <note>The early Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>: *“And you shall be to him in the things pertaining to God.”* <note>original Greek: σὺ δ’ αὐτῷ ἔσῃ τὰ πρὸς τὸν θεὸν</note> And here, observe in passing the weak remedy <note>original Latin: *Malagma*, literally a softening plaster or poultice; used here metaphorically to mean a weak scholarly excuse</note> applied by Agostino Steuco <note>A 16th-century Italian humanist and Old Testament scholar</note>, who, since he could not excuse the common Latin translator <note>The Vulgate</note>, attempted to downplay it in this way: he claimed the Latin translator spoke thus for the sake of modesty—as if indeed Moses had been immodest when the Hebrew truth reads, *“You shall be to him* <note>original Hebrew: לאלהים, *lo-elohim*</note> *as God”*; or as if he had attributed more to himself than was necessary. Therefore, it was not Moses, but Aaron alone and his descendants who were the High Priests. Although these High Priests were of the Levite tribe, they are specifically called the "sons of Aaron," because from the lineage of Levi, no others except the descendants of Aaron were granted access to that office.

It must therefore be noted that when Moses entered the Sanctuary, he did so not by the right of a High Priest, but by the privilege of a Mediator. For this reason, he entered the Holy of Holies freely at his own discretion, above all other Prophets and Priests, and appeared there before God. The High Priest, however, entered only once a year, with a singular display of various ceremonies. Moses alone received the voice of God without terror, except during the publication of the Law. Hence, among the excellencies <note>original Greek: ὑπεροχὰς</note> of Moses, this was the chief: to speak with God *face to face, as a man with his friend.* Indeed, he was a Mediator both because he interceded between God and the people, and furthermore between the people and God. But Moses was a *typical* <note>In the sense of being a "type" or a prophetic foreshadowing</note> mediator, whereas Christ is the *real* mediator. Just as the typical Redeemer freed them from Egyptian slavery without a price, Christ is the real Redeemer who freed us from spiritual slavery; the former was without a price because they were held in unjust slavery, but the latter was with a price, because it was necessary for the justice of God to be satisfied.

Just as among the Pagans <note>original Latin: *Ethnicos*</note>, those from a single family were sometimes placed in charge—just as at Rome, the priests of Hercules were the ***Potitii and Pinarii***, as is clear from Livy, Decade 1, Book 1. This occurred, however, not without <term>disorder <note>original Greek: ἀταξίᾳ (ataxia)</note></term> and in a most corrupt time; nay, by the ancient institution, the High Priest performed this duty for his whole life, nor should he have been removed from office without grave cause—which happened to Abiathar (1 Kings 2:26). But in the time of Annas and Caiaphas, both held the office alternately; and in one year Annas was the secondary, in the next the primary, and vice versa, as is clear from John 11:49, 51, compared with Acts 4:6. Therefore, when Christ was born, he found everything among the Jews to be most corrupt; and truly speaking, no legitimate King, Prophet, or Priest then existed. No King, because Herod was a tyrant and, moreover, a slave of the Romans; no Prophet, because Malachi was the last of the Prophets; no Priest, because Annas and Caiaphas were usurpers. This happened not without a mystery, to signify that Christ is the High Priest, King, and Prophet, because the true Messiah was anointed for those three roles.

...now we shall set [other matters] aside. Furthermore, Melchizedek and Christ agree in that each performed both a royal and a priestly duty, a combination which, besides Christ, happened to no one in ancient times. For if Moses is called a priest, and it is established from Exodus 29 and 40 that he performed priestly functions, this was done outside the normal order and only for a certain time until the Levitical priesthood could be instituted; once that was instituted, one nowhere reads of Moses performing the duties of a priest. When, however, the Maccabees <note>A Jewish family that led a rebellion against the Seleucid Empire and later ruled Judea, combining the roles of King and High Priest.</note> later joined both the royal and priestly dignity, this was a matter of fact <note>original Latin: *de facto*</note> rather than a matter of legal right <note>original Latin: *de jure*</note>; and although it might have seemed legitimate, the practice was extraordinary and based on the requirements of the times, from which no general rule can be inferred. The same must be thought regarding Eli, who was simultaneously the High Priest and a political Judge (1 Samuel 4:18); that is, <term>to spin together things that do not match <note>original Greek: τὰ ἀσύκλαστα κλώθειν (*ta asyklasta klōthein*). II. Melchizedek was the High Priest of the Most High. In the same way, Christ is the High Pontiff <note>High Priest</note> of God.

III. The former was a priest forever and without successors. The latter is also a priest in perpetuity.

IV. Melchizedek never had any successors; likewise, no High Priest can succeed Christ.

V. Melchizedek was High Priest even though he was not from the tribe of Levi, a status which could not apply to any priest according to the order of Aaron. In the same way, Christ was not from the tribe of Levi, but from Judah; nevertheless, he is declared High Pontiff, as is clear from Hebrews 7:14.

VI. Melchizedek was not made a priest according to the Law and through a fleshly commandment, but by the power of an indestructible life. Likewise Christ, to whom it is said in Psalm 110:4: *You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek*. For in both cases, nothing fleshly is employed when dealing with the institution of the priesthood, but rather the living image of eternity shines forth. For although it is said of the Levitical priesthood that it would endure <term>forever <note>original Hebrew: לְעוֹלָם (*le’olam*)</note></term>, this word is nevertheless understood differently there than when it concerns the priesthood of Christ and Melchizedek, in which an infinite eternity is understood. <note>The author is distinguishing between "forever" meaning "for the duration of an age" (Levitical) and "forever" meaning "without end" (Christ).</note>

VII. Melchizedek blessed Abraham and received tithes. Thus Christ is the source of blessings and the blessed God to whom the tithes of all good things ought to be paid—indeed, as to the High Pontiff, the tithes of tithes.

...according to the order of Melchizedek, because "according to the order" <note>original Greek: κατὰ τάξιν (*kata taxin*)</note> means the same as "according to the likeness," as is clear from Psalm 110:4, from which the words of Paul are taken. For in the Hebrew, it is *al-divrati* <note>original Hebrew: על־דברתי</note>, which signifies "after the manner" or "according to the reason and likeness." Whence the Syriac translates it as *be-dmutheh d-malki* <note>original Syriac: כדמותה דמלכי</note>, "to the likeness of Melchizedek." And Abraham ibn Ezra <note>A distinguished 12th-century Jewish scholar and biblical commentator.</note> explains *al-divrati* as "according to the course, order, or reason"; he notes that the *Yod* is paragogic <note>A "paragogic" letter is an extra letter added to the end of a word in ancient languages that does not change the meaning but often affects the rhythm or style of the text.</note> and explains it as *al-minhag* <note>original Hebrew: על מנהג</note>, "according to custom and habit." The Apostle [Paul] uses "according to the order" <note>original Greek: κατὰ τὴν τάξιν (*kata tēn taxin*)</note> as in Hebrews 5:6, and then "according to the likeness" <note>original Greek: κατὰ τὴν ὁμοιότητα (*kata tēn homoiotēta*)</note> as in Hebrews 7:15. The Chaldean [Targum] has *al-divrat* <note>original Aramaic: על־דברת</note>, "for the cause of," or simply "because of," as in the Hebrew *al-devar* <note>original Hebrew: על דבר</note>.

Now, Christ and Melchizedek differ as the shadow and the body; the figure and the truth; the type and the antitype <note>In biblical interpretation, a "type" is a historical person or event that foreshadows a future "antitype"—in this case, Melchizedek foreshadows the reality of Christ.</note>. Therefore, whatever is said of Melchizedek belongs by a greater right and *hypostatically* <note>original Greek: ὑποστατικῶς (*hypostatikōs*); meaning in a way that relates to Christ’s actual person and divine substance.</note> to Christ; indeed, they truly apply only to the antitype. For it is not properly Melchizedek, but Christ, who is without father, without mother, without genealogy <note>original Greek: ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἀγενεαλόγητος (*apatōr, amētōr, agenealogētos*)</note>, etc. <note>These terms are used in Hebrews 7:3 to describe Melchizedek's sudden appearance in Genesis without family records, symbolizing the eternal nature of Christ.</note> Nevertheless, these things are deservedly attributed to Melchizedek in Scripture because, since the mysteries of the Gospel were foreshadowed through figures, and these were eventually fulfilled under the Messiah so that the harmony of the Old and New Testaments might become clear, it was necessary that these traits be found in some respect in Melchizedek. And in truth, these things can fit no creature except Melchizedek. For the objection that Abel had no successor, and that the "lack of genealogy" <note>original Greek: τὸ ἀγενεαλόγητον (*to agenealogēton*)</note> is also found in Job and Elijah, is a fallacy of division <note>A logical error where one assumes that because a trait exists in parts of several things, those things are the same as a single thing that possesses all those traits at once.</note>; for even if those things are found separately in others, they are presented together in no one except Melchizedek. 

Secondly, it is false that Abel had no successor; since Seth succeeded him, whence his name was called from *Sheth* <note>original Hebrew: שת (*Seth*), meaning "appointed" or "placed."</note>, because he was added to Abel after he was killed by his brother; for God substituted him as noted in Genesis 4:25. Thus others followed until Noah and the subsequent Patriarchs. Furthermore, Melchizedek and Christ differ primarily in this: although both are called Priests, one nowhere reads that Melchizedek sacrificed, and there is deep silence in Scripture regarding his victim; conversely, Christ sacrificed on the cross and is himself the offered victim. Nor is Melchizedek undeservedly called a priest; however, Scripture adds nothing about a victim because he foreshadowed Christ, who was at once the priest and the victim.

But Melchizedek did not receive tithes from his brothers, but from the great Patriarch and the father of all the faithful; and he blessed the one who held the promises. Yet, as the Apostle rightly teaches us in the same chapter, verse 7: *that which is lesser is blessed by that which is greater.*

VI. Aaron and the Levitical priests are mortal. But Melchizedek is described as immortal and eternal, "without beginning of days or end of life" (same chapter, verses 3 and 8). *But there, it is witnessed of him that he lives* <note>original Greek: ὅτι ζῇ (*hoti zē*)</note>. For the silence regarding his death is taken as a testimony of his life.

VII. The Levitical priesthood was "ordinary," and one priest succeeded another; but Melchizedek was an "extraordinary" priest and without a successor.

IX. The Levitical priesthood was abolished. That of Melchizedek, however, remains forever. 

X. The Levitical priesthood was not perfect. But that of Melchizedek is perfect and was meant to perfect the Levitical one, as Paul testifies in the same chapter, Hebrews 7:11: *“Furthermore, if perfection were by the Levitical priesthood (for under it the people received the Law), what further need was there that another priest should rise after the order of Melchizedek, and not be called after the order of Aaron?”* And indeed, since Melchizedek was a priest of a different kind than the Levitical, it follows that the others were not perfect and had to be perfected by another. Just as there was also a change of the law. For as the Apostle says in verse 12: *“For the priesthood being changed, there is made of necessity a change also of the law.”* 

In these words, the Apostle proposes two things: first, that the Levitical priesthood was imperfect, which he proves by the fact that another priesthood was added; for otherwise, why would such an introduction be necessary? Second, that the priesthood of Melchizedek was introduced not only to perfect the other, but what is more, to abolish it, because it is not of the same but of a different order. Hence it is expressly said "according to the order of Melchizedek" <note>original Greek: κατὰ τάξιν μελχισεδὲκ (*kata taxin Melchisedek*)</note>, and the Syriac version uses the word *shuhalapha* <note>original Syriac: ܫܚܠܦܐ (*shuhalapha*), which refers to a change, transformation, or substitution</note>, which signifies a change and abolition rather than a mere transfer. Hence Paul says in verse 12: "For the priesthood being changed" <note>original Greek: μετατιθεμένης γὰρ τῆς ἱερωσύνης (*metatithemenēs gar tēs hierōsynēs*)</note>. 

XI. The Levitical priesthood had to be taken from the tribe of Levi according to the institution of the Law, but not from the tribe of Judah—concerning which tribe Moses spoke nothing regarding the priesthood, as noted in the same chapter, verse 14. But Melchizedek was not from the tribe of Levi. 

XII. The Levitical priesthood was not instituted with an oath. But concerning Melchizedek, David said in Psalm 110:4: *“The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.”* This certainly exalts the priesthood of Melchizedek wonderfully above the Levitical one, for God is not accustomed to interpose His own name by swearing regarding trivial matters. Therefore, this priesthood which is sanctioned by God's oath is of great weight—something never said of the Levitical priesthood. For that reason, that oath signifies several things. First, that we are not dealing here with a trivial matter, but one of great...

Because he is called a priest *forever* <note>original Hebrew: לעולם (*le‘olam*)</note>, which—since it is highly extraordinary and singular—had to be confirmed by an oath and by that solemn formula. 4. Hence in the formula of the Oath it is added, *the Lord will not repent*, because He rested entirely in it, and as if concerning a priesthood and a priest *who is unchangeable* <note>original Greek: ἀμεταμελήτῳ (*ametamelētō*)</note>, He cries out, *in whom I am well pleased* <note>original Greek: ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησα (*en hō eudokēsa*)</note>. 

XIII. The Prophet David attributes to that priest the *beauty of holiness*, and a people offering *freewill offerings* <note>original Hebrew: נדבות (*nedavot*)</note>. This is found to be not entirely fulfilled in the Levitical priesthood. 

XIV. The Levitical priests were many, *because death prevented them from continuing* (Hebrews 7:23). But this priest is unique, and his priesthood is called perpetual—not in respect to a succession, where priests succeed one another forever, but in respect to the priest himself, who is also *permanent* <note>original Greek: ἀπαράβατος (*aparabatos*), meaning a priesthood that cannot be transferred or pass away</note>. 

XV. The Levitical priests ministered in the tabernacle, but this one is the *minister of another sanctuary, and of that true tabernacle which the Lord pitched, and not man*, as Paul states in Hebrews 8:2. 

XVI. The Levitical priests performed sacrifices on earth, because there was the earthly sanctuary. But the other priest according to the order of Melchizedek, since his sanctuary is heavenly, could not complete his sacrifice on earth. For according to the testimony of the Apostle in chapter 8:4, *If he were on earth, he would not even be a priest, while those priests remain who offer gifts according to the law*. 

XVII. The Levitical priests were the intercessors of the old covenant; but this one is the intercessor of a new covenant, sanctioned by more excellent promises (Hebrews 8:6), according to that passage in Jeremiah 31:31–33 and Romans 11:27: *Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will strike a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah.* And at the end of chapter 8, Paul says in the same Epistle to the Hebrews: *In saying "new," he has made the first one old; now that which is becoming old and growing gray is near to vanishing away.* 

XVIII. The Levitical priesthood had established rites of religion and a worldly sanctuary, namely the tabernacle in which was the lampstand, and the table...

But in the priesthood of Melchizedek, the priest does not enter the sanctuary every year, but only once.

xx. In the Levitical priesthood, that continual entering and exiting of the priest signified that the way to the sanctuary had not yet been made open while the first tabernacle was still standing. But in the priesthood of Melchizedek, the High Priest enters the sanctuary once, because the first tabernacle has been abolished.

xxi. In the Levitical priesthood, while the first tabernacle lasted, brute victims were sacrificed, such as goats, calves, and bulls; but in that of Melchizedek, no such victims are offered, but rather a rational sacrifice <note>original Latin: *rationalis victima*; a theological term for a sacrifice involving the mind and soul, referring to Christ’s self-offering as the Logos or "Reason" of God</note>.

xxii. In the Levitical priesthood, the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer sprinkling the defiled person sanctified them only **for the purity of the flesh** <note>original Greek: *πρὸς τὴν τῆς σαρκὸς καθαρότητα* (*pros tēn tēs sarkos katharotēta*)</note>, as the Apostle writes in Hebrews 9:13. This means it was a legal and external purification, so that they would not be barred from sacred rites; yet it was not able to sanctify by an internal and spiritual purification. But in the priesthood of Melchizedek, the blood of the rational sacrifice, sprinkling the defiled, cleanses their conscience from dead works to serve the living God.

xxiii. In the Levitical priesthood, nothing was cleansed except by blood; so the Apostle testifies in Hebrews 9:18, 19, etc. *The Old Testament was not dedicated without blood. For when Moses had recited every commandment according to the law to all the people*

to the people, and having taken the blood of calves and goats, with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, he sprinkled both the book itself and all the people. Furthermore, he sprinkled both the tabernacle and all the sacred vessels of the ministry with blood. And nearly everything is purified with blood according to the law, and without the shedding of blood there is no remission <note>referring to Hebrews 9:22; the idea that divine forgiveness requires a life-sacrifice</note>. But that purification by the blood of victims was merely legal and external; in the Melchizedekian priesthood, however, the blood of an infinite price and of a rational victim <note>original Latin: *rationabilis victimae*; a sacrifice involving a conscious, reasoning being rather than an animal</note> purifies the mind, and is the fulfillment of all those shadows.

XXIV. In the Levitical priesthood, victims were sacrificed and died daily, and once one was slaughtered, others followed in succession; hence there was both an evening and a morning sacrifice. In the Melchizedekian priesthood, the victim was slaughtered only once, namely, in the evening of days <note>a poetic or prophetic reference to the end of the ages or the finality of Christ's era</note>.

XXV. In the Levitical priesthood, victims were slaughtered very often because the sacrifice was imperfect, nor could sins be wiped away through it; for that reason, it was continually repeated. In the Melchizedekian priesthood, a single offering sufficed, nor should the sacrifice be repeated, since it was most perfect.

XXVI. In the Levitical priesthood, God said of its sacrifices: *sacrifice and offering I do not want; burnt offerings and a sacrifice for sin I do not approve* <note>original Latin: *sacrificium & oblationem nolo: holocautomata & hostiam pro peccato non approbo*; see Psalm 40:7</note>. In the Melchizedekian priesthood, it was said of its sacrifice: *You have prepared a body for me. Behold, I am here (in the scroll of the book it is written of me) to do your will, O God.* <note>Hebrews 10:5-7, quoting the Septuagint version of the Psalms</note>.

XXVII. In the Levitical priesthood, the priests continually minister and sacrifice in the presence of God. But in the Melchizedekian priesthood, the priest no longer sacrifices or ministers in the presence of God once the sacrifice has been performed once; but because he is a heavenly king, he has sat down at the right hand of God <note>Hebrews 10:12</note>.

XXVIII. In the Levitical priesthood, once a single sin was committed, a victim was immediately offered, and then another; hence it was called a "sacrifice for sin." In Hebrew, therefore, a single word expresses both "sin" and "the victim" or "sacrifice for sin": חטאה <note>Hebrew: *chatta* or *chatt'ah*; Cregut is noting that the language itself links the act of sin with the requirement for its ritual cleansing</note>. And so there was a solemn festival of the "Day," because it was יום הכפור <note>Hebrew: *Iom hakkippur*; the Day of Atonement</note>, the day of propitiation. In the Priesthood of Melchizedek, if we sin willfully after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins.

...blood [of Moses' law] despised, *he died without mercy on the testimony of two or three.* <note>original Latin: *absque misericordia ex duorum aut trium testimonio moriebatur*; quoting Hebrews 10:28</note>. Heb. 10:28. In the priesthood of Melchizedek, whoever tramples upon the priest, the covenant, the victim, and His blood, will inevitably die an eternal death.

XXX. In the Levitical priesthood, no matter what victims were offered, and however exquisitely the various rites and many-layered ceremonies were observed, the fathers nevertheless *did not receive the promise* <note>original Latin: *non obtinuerunt promissum*</note> Heb. 11:39; that is, that promise in which all others are "Yes and Amen." <note>original Latin: *Etiam & Amen*; quoting 2 Corinthians 1:17</note> 2 Cor. 1:17. For they saw the coming Christ only from a distance, He who was shown to us through a singular favor. But in the priesthood of Melchizedek, the promise itself is obtained, and in that unique sacrifice, salvation itself is won. For He has appeared who was to reconcile all things, both those in heaven and those on earth. Eph. 1:10. Whence in the Epistle to the Hebrews 11:40, the Apostle says: *Because God had provided something better for us, that they should not be made perfect without us.* Here he uses the word *teleiōsai* <note>Greek: τελειῶσαι; to bring to completion or perfect</note>, which signifies primarily the perfection that comes through consecration. Thus, in chapter 2:10, it is attributed to Christ himself *dia pathēmatōn teleiōthēnai*, *to be consecrated through suffering.* <note>Greek: διὰ παθημάτων τελειωθῆναι; originally meaning to be made perfect/complete through what he endured</note> For the hardships of Christ were, as it were, the sacred solemnities by which He was initiated and consecrated into His High Priesthood.

XXXI. In the Levitical priesthood, the sacrifices were not *hilastika* <note>Greek: ἱλαστικὰ; propitiatory or sin-cleansing</note>, that is, propitiatory in truth and reality, but only figuratively. But in the priesthood of Melchizedek, the sacrifice is truly *hilastikon* <note>propitiatory</note>, *diallaktikon* <note>reconciling</note>, and *apolytrōtikon* <note>redemptive</note>. And this offering and sacrifice put an end to the Levitical sacrifices.

XXXII. In the Levitical priesthood, sacrifices were of various kinds. Some were *shelamim* <note>Hebrew: שלמים; peace offerings</note>, which are of a lower order. Others were *chatat* <note>Hebrew: חטאת; sin offering</note> and *asham* <note>Hebrew: אשם; guilt offering</note>, called by the Rabbis *kodashim kalim* <note>Hebrew: קדשים קלים; light holy things</note>, which, as Rambam <note>Rabbi Moses Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher</note> records in the *Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original Latin: *more Neuoch.*; referring to the work Moreh Nevochim</note>, page 3, could be eaten in Jerusalem only, and indeed only on the day they were offered and the following day, but not after that, because they contract defilement. But in the Melchizedekian priesthood, there was a single propitiatory sacrifice, the perfection and completion of all others.

Thus far have been the excellences <note>original Greek: ἐξοχαὶ (*exochai*); the superior qualities or heights</note> of the Melchizedekian priesthood over the Levitical priesthood. -># THE REVEALER OF SECRETS.<-

...nothing else can be said than that he is the very person of Christ, our High Priest and the true Melchizedek. II. That the sacrifice of the Mass is opposed to it and Antichristian, so far is it from having been foreshadowed by it. Regarding the first point, if you enumerate in order the aforementioned excellences <note>Greek: *hyperochas*; meaning superiorities or pre-eminences</note> of the Melchizedekian priesthood over the Levitical, you will find that they properly belong to Christ as the fulfillment <term>antitype|The reality or person that a "type" or symbol points toward.</term> of Melchizedek.

**I.** Melchizedek was "without father, without mother," etc. <note>original Greek: *apatōr, amētōr*; referring to the lack of recorded genealogy in Genesis</note>; so was Christ, hence the name of the person *Immanuel* in Isaiah 7, in which two natures <note>The divine and human natures of Christ</note> are signified.

**II.** Melchizedek was king and priest; likewise, Christ was truly king and priest, a combination which was permitted to no one else among the people of God. For this reason, Uzziah, the King of Judah, was struck with leprosy because he had set his hand to the censer <note>See 2 Chronicles 26:16-21; Uzziah attempted to perform the priestly duty of burning incense and was punished by God.</note>. Therefore, the Jews falsely interpret Psalm 110 as referring to King David, for in that passage the word *Kohanim* <note>Hebrew: כהנים; plural for priests</note> is not used to mean "princes" (as they would have it), as it is elsewhere, but "priests." Because the Messiah is figured there by Melchizedek, it is as if to say: although He shall be a King, He shall nevertheless exercise the priestly dignity, because the figure of that role preceded Him in Melchizedek. Indeed, because He was also prefigured by the Prophet Moses, the Messiah was King, Priest, and Prophet, so that the entire dignity of many illustrious "types" might be included in a single "antitype."

**III.** Melchizedek is called King of Justice and King of Salem, which means peace. All these things, as said above, are excellently fulfilled in Christ.

**IV.** Melchizedek blessed Abraham and received tithes. But did not Christ bless Abraham? Indeed, *in that seed shall all the nations be blessed?* <note>Quoting the promise made to Abraham in Genesis 22:18, fulfilled in Christ.</note> And should not both Abraham and all peoples pay tithes to such a great priest, and even kings themselves offer incense? As the Psalmist testifies, and this will be seen further below.

**V.** Melchizedek blessed the Patriarch and took tithes from the father of the faithful, but Christ is God, blessed above all, to whom Abraham was bound to offer and consecrate both his son Isaac and himself and all things.

**VI.** Melchizedek is described as an eternal priest; but Christ is truly such a high priest, because He is God with the Father and of the same substance <note>original Greek: *homoousios*; the theological term defining the Father and Son as one in essence</note> with Him.

**VII.** Melchizedek was an extraordinary priest and without a successor; so is Christ, who remains forever, which is why no other priests were instituted in the New Testament. <note>This is a standard Protestant argument: because Christ is the eternal priest after the order of Melchizedek, there is no need for a human "priesthood" to offer sacrifices like the Mass.</note>

**VIII.** Melchizedek is not said to have died, unlike the Levitical priests; thus Christ is immortal.

**IX.** The priesthood of Melchizedek was never to be abolished: so neither is Christ’s,

### THE REVEALER OF SECRETS

### Page 327

heavenly. Therefore, if Christ had remained on earth, all those things would not have been fulfilled, and the Levitical priest would have continued to sacrifice and enter into the sanctuary. But two different kinds of priests cannot be maintained by law at the same time. For although the sacrifice of Christ on the cross was perfect, that priestly action did not reach its completion until he entered into the sanctuary <note>referring to Christ's ascension into heaven</note>. Therefore, that perfection of the sacrifice is judged as the perfection of a part, not the perfection of the whole, because intercession and the prayer that obtains grace are required for the completion of the entire action.

Now, therefore (as Camero <note>John Cameron (c. 1579–1625), a Scottish theologian and scholar</note> rightly noted), this is the logic of the **type and the thing typed** <note>original Greek: *tō typō & typōthenti*; original Latin: *figuræ & rei figuratæ*</note>: that the figure does not give way to the truth piece by piece, but in its entirety. That is, the whole figure stands until the whole truth comes into its place. Therefore, since there was one action of the High Priest consisting of two parts—to immolate the sacrifice outside the Holy of Holies, and to enter into the Holy of Holies—the entire action of the [Levitical] Priest gave way to the entire action of Christ. 

And even though Christ had offered the sacrifice on the cross, the Levitical priest still had to enter the Sanctuary—unless the sacrifice had first been offered outside the Sanctuary—because the Levitical priesthood was not abolished by Christ's death alone. Rather, it was necessary for the abolition of the Levitical priesthood that Christ enter into heaven. Therefore, when the Apostle said, *if Christ had remained on earth he would not have been a priest*, this is true for two reasons: 

**I.** Because he would have occupied the place of the Levitical priesthood. But two priesthoods could not stand together, and the figure <note>the symbolic type</note> gives way to the thing figured <note>the reality</note>. 

**II.** Because he is not a true priest who cannot finish the priestly action, which Christ could not perform while on earth. For as long as the tabernacle stood, the **service and worship** <note>original Hebrew: *avodah*; original Greek: *latreia*</note> had to remain. 

**XVII.** Christ, no differently than Melchizedek, is the intercessor of a new covenant, because in Christ all things are made new. A new law, a new covenant, a New Testament, a new day (that is, the Lord’s Day, which succeeded the Sabbath), a new earth, a new heaven (that is, a **new creation** <note>original Latin: *noua creatio*</note>), a new generation, a new lump <note>referring to a "new batch" of dough, a metaphor for a purified community</note>, a new man, a new Passover, which Christ himself mentions; a new commandment (concerning charity even toward enemies), and a new song, of which we read in the Apocalypse and the song of the Angels in Luke 2.

<meta>This page continues the point-by-point comparison between the priesthood of Melchizedek and Jesus Christ, establishing that the transition from the old Levitical law to the new covenant was a shift from physical, temporary rituals to a spiritual, eternal reality centered in heaven.</meta>

# ANTOINE CRÉGUT <note>Antoine Crégut (1602–1674) was a French Reformed theologian and professor.</note>

For Melchizedek, no physical tabernacle is described, nor so many fleshly rites and ceremonies as can be seen in the Levitical priesthood. In the same way, Christ rejects all fleshly forms of worship and wishes to be worshipped in spirit and truth. John 4: *God is Spirit, therefore he must be worshipped in spirit and truth.* Romans 14: *The Kingdom of God does not consist in food and drink, but in joy and peace through the Holy Spirit.*

xix. Christ is the true Melchizedek because he did not enter into the sanctuary once every year like the high priest, but entered once after his death, where he intercedes for the Church militant <note>The "Church Militant" refers to Christians currently living on earth, struggling against sin and trial.</note> on earth (Romans 8), until after the judgment he shall again enter the Church triumphant <note>The "Church Triumphant" refers to the saints in heaven who have overcome the world.</note> to rule with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

xx. Christ entered the sanctuary once because he abolished the ceremonies, and that frequent entering and leaving of the sanctuary by the high priest has been done away with. For this reason, the Sanctuary was destroyed immediately after the ascension of Christ.

xxi. In the priesthood of Melchizedek, animal victims <note>original Latin: *brutæ victimæ*, literally 'brute' or 'irrational' animals</note> are not offered as they are in the Levitical priesthood; thus Christ is that true victim offered for the life of the world. By the testimony of Scripture, he was made a **propitiation** <note>original Greek: ἱλαστήριον (*hilastērion*), the place of atonement</note>, a **ransom** <note>original Greek: λύτρον (*lytron*)</note>, a **substitute ransom** <note>original Greek: ἀντίλυτρον (*antilytron*)</note>, and a **redemption** <note>original Greek: ἀπολύτρωσις (*apolytrōsis*)</note> (Romans 3:24, 1 Timothy 2:6). For this reason, he was foreshadowed in the past by the **Mercy Seat** <note>original Latin: *propitiatorium*, the gold lid of the Ark of the Covenant</note>, which covered two things at once: namely, the Ark and the Law. This was to represent symbolically two mysteries: that Christ covers the Church with his power, and the Law with his obedience. And just as the book of the law was sprinkled with the blood of victims, so the law could not be satisfied except by the blood of the Son of God. Therefore, as is clear from Hebrews 9:19, the sprinkling was performed over both the book of the law and the people; by the former, the atonement for sins was signified; by the latter, we understand that the application of this blood is entirely necessary for us. There were, moreover, two Cherubim around that Mercy Seat, which embraced the Ark and looked toward the Mercy Seat in such a way that they gazed upon one another. Thus the Hebrew name is derived from "ascending," while the Greek name is derived from "burning completely." Indeed, by this means mortals were thought to consecrate themselves entirely to God and—as if having cast down the body—to lift up the soul into heaven with the smoke of their victim. This rightly foreshadowed the burnt offering of Christ on the altar of the cross, entirely consumed by the fire of divine justice, just as the Paschal lamb was eaten roasted; and the smoke of this burnt offering ascended into the nostrils of God the Father, who smelled the odor of a pleasing fragrance. ## ANTHONY CREGUT

Hypocrites and the ungodly daily trample the blood of Christ underfoot, empty the cross of its power, and profane this most sacred burnt offering of the cross; hence, the same fate befalls them as befell those who crucified Him: **"His blood be upon us and upon our children"** <note>original Latin: *Sanguis eius sit super nos & filios*; a reference to Matthew 27:25</note>. However, the **Peace Offerings** <note>original Hebrew: *Shelemim* (שלמים)</note>, which we call **peaceable offerings**, and the Greeks call *eirenaia* <note>original Greek: *eirēnaia* (εἰρηναῖα); things pertaining to peace</note>, and sometimes *soteria* <note>original Greek: *sōtēria* (σωτήρια); things pertaining to salvation or deliverance</note>, that is, **salutary offerings**, were a type of victim of which they burned only the fat, but consumed the meat in a feast. Indeed, this was done on the same day it was slaughtered, so that no remains could be kept until the morrow, except in one specific variety, concerning which laws are prescribed in many places in Leviticus (Leviticus 7:19, 22). Hence Moses says in Deuteronomy 27:7, "You shall sacrifice **peace offerings** and eat, and you shall rejoice before your God." These sacrifices are called *Shelemim* <note>original Hebrew: *Shelemim* (שלמים)</note> because they were made for the happy success of affairs, which the godly either earnestly requested from God or attributed to Him after receiving them; hence in Leviticus 7 they are called **Eucharistic** <note>In the sense of "thanksgiving" or "gratitude."</note> and **congratulatory** offerings. All these were shadows and illustrious types foreshadowing that most sacred victim of the cross, which was not only consumed on the altar of the cross by the fire of divine wrath burning from above and blazing in the furnace of justice, but is also entirely consumed in the sacrament of the Eucharist, just as the Paschal lamb was of old. Through that victim, most pleasing to God, prosperous outcomes arise, and because of it, all the promises of God are **"Yea and Amen"** <note>original Latin: *Etiam & Amen*; reference to 2 Corinthians 1:20, meaning "certain and fulfilled."</note>. Therefore, those who sacrificed according to this rite were publicly testifying and professing that the one God is the author and giver—and, if I may put it this way, the **steward and provider** <term>original Latin: *promus condum*; a Roman household term for the person in charge of the storeroom who distributes provisions</term>—of all happiness arising for mortals. This matches excellently with the sacrifice of our Melchizedek <note>A reference to Christ as the ultimate High Priest in the line of the biblical figure Melchizedek.</note>, without whom all things are hopeless.

Therefore, all Mosaic sacrifices look toward the sacrifice of Christ in an **anagogical** <note>Anagogical: an interpretation that sees earthly rituals as symbols of spiritual or heavenly realities.</note> sense. Though the Hebrews designate them by various names, such as *Olot*, *Shelemim*, *Chatat*, and *Asham* <note>original Hebrew: *Olot* (עולות - burnt offerings), *Shelemim* (שלמים - peace offerings), *Chatat* (חטאת - sin offerings), and *Asham* (אשם - guilt offerings)</note>—for the *Chatat* and *Asham* were also sacrifices involving blood and were made for the expiation of sins, and are called by the Greeks sometimes a *thysian* <note>original Greek: *thysian* (θυσίαν); a sacrifice</note>, sometimes a *prosphoran* <note>original Greek: *prosphoran* (προσφοράν); an offering</note>, and sometimes a *teleten* <note>original Greek: *teletēn* (τελετήν); a religious rite or initiation</note>—nevertheless, all can be referred back to the two primary kinds: namely, the *Olot* and the *Shelemim*. These we, along with other theologians, distinguish in such a way that the former are called *latreutika* <note>original Greek: *latreutika* (λατρευτικὰ); pertaining to divine service or worship</note>, or (if you prefer) *sebastika* <note>original Greek: *sebastika* (σεβαστικά); pertaining to reverence</note> or *eucharistika* <note>original Greek: *eucharistika* (εὐχαριστικά); pertaining to gratitude</note>, because they were offered to God with veneration and worship...

The latter can be called **propitiatory** <note>original Greek: *hilastika* (ἱλαστικὰ); offerings intended to appease or reconcile</note>, by which it was believed that sins were wiped away and divine justice was satisfied. The former were a symbol of Divine worship and a testimony of religion—sometimes used as a prayer to ask for God’s favor, sometimes as an act of thanksgiving to testify to a grateful soul for benefits received, and sometimes as a simple exercise of piety to renew the confirmation of the covenant. To this former category belong **burnt offerings** <note>original Hebrew: *Olot* (עולות)</note>, **libations** <note>original Hebrew: *Nesachim* (נסכים)</note>, and **grain offerings** <note>original Hebrew: *Minchot* (מנחות); often translated as oblations</note>; as well as **firstfruits** <note>original Hebrew: *Bikkurim* (בכורים)</note> and **peace offerings** <note>original Hebrew: *Shelemim* (שלמים)</note>. But the latter sacrifices were called in Hebrew either a **guilt offering** <note>original Hebrew: *Asham* (אשם)</note> or a **sin offering** <note>original Hebrew: *Chattat* (חטאת)</note>. In these, the purpose was to appease the wrath of God, to satisfy His justice, and thereby to wash away and wipe clean one's sins. This was not because those Mosaic victims were equal to such a great task, but because they foreshadowed the victim of the cross, which was the perfection and fulfillment of all ancient sacrifices. As the Great High Priest himself testified with his own voice in John 19:30: **"It is finished"** <note>original Latin: *consummatum est*</note>.

Therefore, although all Mosaic sacrifices may seem widely varied in nature and divided into various species—whether by reason of their material, which consisted of different animals (and these were called **sacrificial victims** <note>original Hebrew: *Zevach* (זבח)</note>); or from dry earthly material, such as bread, fine flour, frankincense, salt, etc. (and these are **grain offerings**); or from liquid material, such as wine, oil, etc. (and these are properly **libations** <note>original Hebrew: *Nesachim* (נסכים)</note>, just as the preceding are *Minchot* <note>original Hebrew: מנחות</note>)—or whether they are categorized by the manner and cause of the offering; nevertheless, sacrifices of any kind are easily reduced to those two species mentioned above: namely, to the **worshipful** <note>original Greek: *latreutika* (λατρευτικὰ)</note>, **reverential** <note>original Greek: *sebastika* (σεβαστικὰ)</note>, and **eucharistic** <note>original Greek: *eucharistika* (εὐχαριστικὰ); meaning "of thanksgiving"</note> on one hand, and to the **propitiatory** <note>original Greek: *hilastika* (ἱλαστικὰ)</note> on the other. The former species includes within itself burnt offerings, grain offerings, libations, and peace offerings. The latter species includes the guilt offering and the sin offering. However, "sacrifice" <note>original Hebrew: *Zevach* (זבח)</note> is a general name denoting all sacrifices, just as "offering" <note>original Hebrew: *Korban* (קרבן)</note> is a word signifying all offerings in general. Yet all these sacrifices, of whatever kind they may be, foreshadowed Jesus Christ, who is our High Priest, who has entered the sanctuary in heaven and opens the way for us; who is the victim, who brings to an end the blood of all other victims and renders God merciful; and who is the altar upon which we place our gifts, so that in Him we may dare whatever we dare. Furthermore, the fact that these kinds of sacrifices were fulfilled in Christ, and thus finally abolished, is sufficiently proven by the destruction of the Temple. For we condemn whatever is now performed by the Jews as superstitious and empty. These things are contained in the **Order of the Standing Men** <note>original Hebrew: *be-Seder Ha-Ma’amadot* (בסדר המעמדות); a liturgical collection of prayers and biblical readings used by the Jewish community to replace the physical Temple service</note>. When the Temple was still standing, the author says, if anyone sinned at night, he brought a sacrifice in the morning; if he sinned during the day, he sacrificed in the evening, and then the priest would remit his sins. Later, since the Temple was destroyed and the priest and all sacrifices ceased, they instituted "sacrifices of the lips" in place of physical sacrifices, with a mere commemoration of the ancient sacrifices. For, being persuaded that a remembrance here is worth as much as the offering itself, they ordained triple readings for every day of the week, to be spoken from the Bible, the **Mishnah** <term>Mishnah: The first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions</term>, and the **Gemara** <term>Gemara: The component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis and commentary on the Mishnah</term>. Those who wish to be more holy recite these daily. To this service they added this excellent praise: **"And everyone who says these things is assured that he is a son of the World to Come."** <note>original Hebrew: *ve-kol ha-omerim muvtach lo she-hu ben ha-Olam Ha-Ba* (וכל האומרים מבוטח לו שהוא בן העהב)</note>. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of Old Testament sacrifices, moving from the replacement of physical sacrifices with prayers ("sacrifices of the lips") to a specific theological debate about whether those sacrifices covered only accidental sins or willful ones as well.</meta>

-># THE REVEALER OF SECRETS.<-

...for the errors of the people. In Greek: *on behalf of himself and for the people’s sins of ignorance* <note>original: ὑπὲρ ἑαυτοῦ καὶ τῶν τοῦ λαοῦ ἀγνοημάτων (*hyper heautou kai tōn tou laou agnoēmatōn*)</note>. By this word "sins of ignorance," it is indicated that he offered sacrifices only for sins committed through ignorance, and not for those committed willfully and out of malice. II. To this point, it is argued that in private sacrifices, almost no account was taken of grave crimes. But to the first point, we respond that by the word "sins of ignorance," sins of any kind are understood, even willful ones. For here, "sins of ignorance" are not set in opposition to willful sins—whether committed out of weakness or out of malice—but "sins of ignorance" (and in Hebrew *sh’gi’ot* <note>שגיאות</note>, as we said above) designate all sins. For even if you sin willfully, there is still some error in your conscience which Satan has fascinated <note>In the sense of being "bewitched" or "blinded" by a deceptive charm or delusion</note>. Hence, the Vulgate edition and Desiderius Erasmus translate this too narrowly and obscurely as *ignorances*; it should rather be translated as *errors*. This is because that "ignorance" regarding sins is a matter of law, or is an "affected" ignorance <note>A legal/theological term for "deliberate ignorance," where one chooses not to know the law to avoid guilt</note> and a result of a depraved disposition. It is at once both a sin and the punishment for sin; therefore, even if it is "invincible" <note>A term for ignorance that cannot be overcome by reasonable effort</note>, it is still blameworthy. Psalm 19:13 <note>Verse 12 in modern English Bibles</note>: *Who understands his errors?* <note>original Hebrew: שגיאות מי יבין (*sh’gi’ot mi yavin*)</note>. 

To the second point, we respond that it is false to say that, absolutely speaking, no account was taken of grave crimes. For even if an explicit confession of grave crimes was not made, those grave crimes were nevertheless understood to be implicitly included. But observe the reason for this: those who offered sacrifices separately for their offenses were required to confess the offense; yet God had commanded in the Law that every grave offense be punished by death. Therefore, since He is clement and merciful, He did not wish to impose upon wretched men, conscious of their own secret crimes, the necessity of offering sacrifices separately, lest they face the danger of execution—or rather, lest they be subjected to the ultimate punishment. Nevertheless, **on the Day of Atonement** <note>original Hebrew: ביום הכפורת (*be-Yom Ha-Kippurim*)</note>, which was preeminently called **The Day** <note>original Aramaic/Hebrew: יומא (*Yoma*)</note>, this annual sacrifice was instituted so that no sin would pass away without being <term>typically</term> <note>In theology, a "type" is an Old Testament person, event, or object that foreshadows a New Testament reality</note> expiated. In this sacrifice, it was not the sins of individuals (as in private sacrifices) but the sins of everyone, whatever they may have been, that were expiated. This typical expiation of sins clearly foreshadowed the real <term>propitiation</term> <note>The act of appeasing God's justice or regaining His favor</note> made by Christ on the cross.

### ANTHONY CREGUTUS

Therefore, one will observe here quite opportunely that in the law of old, God did not prescribe any kind of works so that the expiation <note>The act of making amends or reparation for guilt or sin</note> of sins might occur, but rather instituted sacrifices alone for satisfaction. Why does the Supreme Judge seek no satisfaction in works, but requires all compensation in sacrifices? Truly, this was done to show that there is only one sacrifice of the cross, which was foreshadowed through the sacrifices of the law. For the sacrifices that were immolated <note>Offered as a sacrifice, typically by killing</note> by the Jews were not considered the "good works" of men; rather, they obtained value and efficacy only in respect to the truth and the antitype <note>The historical reality or person—in this case, Jesus—that a symbol in the Old Testament points toward</note>. "What is propitiation <note>The act of appeasing a deity; original: propitiatio</note> with the Lord," says Augustine, "except sacrifice? And what is sacrifice except that which was offered for us in the death of Christ?" All these things are clearly confirmed in *Hosea 14:3, Isaiah 53:5, Romans 3:24, 1 Corinthians 1:30, Ephesians 1:7, Colossians 1:14, 1 Timothy 2:6, 1 Peter 2:24.*

This doctrine concerning the priesthood of Melchizedek, just as it shows that all the Levitical sacrifices and the entire priesthood of the ancient law have been abolished, so it also clearly strikes against <note>original: *arietat*, literally "to ram" or "strike like a battering ram"</note> the priesthood of the Mass <note>original: *sacerdotium Missaticum*</note>. For this reason, the Church rightly rejects and abominates it as something impious and devised by Satan in mockery of the sacrifice of the cross. We intend to demonstrate the vanity and horrendous impiety of this priesthood of the Mass with a single argument, which will stand in place of many. For if a priesthood of this kind and a sacrifice of the Mass were granted in the New Testament, one could assign to it some priest, some victim, an altar, fire to consume the victim, and the sacrifice itself or the action of sacrificing. But none of these things can be assigned. Therefore, there is no such priesthood or sacrifice of the Mass in the New Testament. This must be proven point by point. 1. No priest can be assigned. For what kind of priest would he be? And of what <term>order</term> <note>original Greek: τάξεως (*taxeōs*)</note>? Not that of Aaron, because this priesthood has been abolished, as Paul testifies in *Hebrews 7:8, 9, etc.* Nor is it according to the order of Melchizedek; for that priesthood was unique, extraordinary, and without a successor. ...ordinary, they are not **without genealogy** <note>original Greek: ἀγενεαλόγητοι; a reference to Hebrews 7:3 describing Melchizedek as having no recorded lineage</note> like Melchizedek; and as they have a father from whom they were born, so even if they are **unmarried** <note>original Greek: ἄγαμοι; referring to clerical celibacy</note>, they produce many sons. Wherefore the Apostle [Paul], in Ephesians 4, when he enumerated all ecclesiastical offices—such as Apostleship, Prophecy, Teaching, etc.—kept a profound silence concerning the presbyterate <note>the office of elders or priests</note> or the priesthood of the Mass, because those **little sacrificers** <note>original: sacrificuli; a derogatory term for those who perform the sacrifice of the Mass</note> are the "Melchizedeks of the new law," without father, without mother, etc. And so that Scripture might even better expose those new and egregious Melchizedeks, it did not deign to honor them with the name of "priests," but instead called the whole Church, or the entire multitude of the faithful, "Melchizedeks"—that is, priests and kings. In Revelation 1 and 1 Peter 2, it is called a "royal priesthood," because as members of the mystical body, we are adorned with the gifts of Christ the head.

But if the name of "priest" is to be granted to those little sacrificers, it will be by the same title that the masters of the Hebrews <note>the Rabbis</note> grant to their own priests regarding **slaughtering and inspection** <note>original Hebrew: שחיטות ובדיקות (Shechitot u-Bedikot); the ritual laws for slaughtering and checking animals for kosher consumption</note>.
