# ANTHONY CREGUTUS

->*That wonder so far exceeds my understanding:*<-
->*In what way a Wolf keeps the sheepfold safe.*<-

II. Just as no priest could be designated in that fictional priesthood of the Mass <note>original: *Missatico*; referring to the office of the Catholic priest performing the Eucharist</note>, so too no victim can be conceived for it. For—I ask you—what and of what sort would that victim be? Would it be bread and wine? Or the "species," that is, the "accidents" <term>accidents: in Aristotelian philosophy, these are qualities like color, shape, or smell that exist in a substance but are not the substance itself</term> of bread and wine? Would it be the body of Christ? Would it be some animal, either irrational or rational? Or something else entirely? Truly, nothing can be conceived that could hold the status of a victim in that fictional sacrifice.

It cannot be bread and wine, since the substance of bread and wine does not remain after the consecration; rather, according to the whims of those "Transubstantiators" <note>original: *Metusiastarum*; a polemical term derived from the Greek word for transubstantiation, *metousiosis*</note>, it is changed into the body and blood of Christ. Yet, what kind of conversion this is—whether Physical, Metaphysical, or beyond the physical <note>original: *hyperphysica*</note>; whether it is properly a conversion, a creation, or an annihilation—is a dispute still before the judge. The scholars of the *Summas* and the debaters of "any-topic-you-please" <note>original: *quodlibetarij*; referring to medieval university debates called 'quodlibets'</note> from the schools are perpetually inquiring into this and fighting like blindfolded gladiators <note>original: *andabatarum*; ancient gladiators who fought in helmets without eye-holes, here used to mock theologians arguing blindly</note>.

This victim also cannot be the "accidents" or the "species" of the bread and wine. First, because even by Divine power, the existence of accidents without the substance of bread and wine is impossible—and not only impossible, but "in-com-possible" <note>logically contradictory</note>. This is because the very nature of an accident implies that its being consists in being *within* or adhering to a subject. Hence, the Papists speak somewhat timidly, as they do not dare to say that accidents exist without a subject, but instead use the word "species" <note>appearances</note> so that they might, in some way, cover their impudence and shame.

Second, a victim must be slaughtered, but accidents—such as lengths, breadths, dimensions, lines, surfaces, colors, shapes, and so on—cannot be slaughtered; they cannot be called victims even equivocally <note>original Greek: ὁμωνύμως; having the same name but different meanings</note>.

Furthermore, the body of Christ can hardly be called a victim of that sort, for it would have to be either a "passible" body <note>capable of suffering</note> or an "impassible" body <note>incapable of suffering</note>. It is certainly not passible, since it was already sacrificed on the cross and cannot be sacrificed again; both because no such passible body now exists, and because **by one sacrifice Christ has preserved forever those who are being sanctified** (Hebrews 10). Nor can it be an impassible body: 1. because it is a contradiction for a body to be sacrificed and slaughtered in a propitiatory <note>an offering intended to appease God</note> and properly-defined sacrifice, and yet remain incapable of suffering. For...

to be sacrificed is to suffer, and thus that which cannot suffer would become capable of suffering, and vice versa. For what the Papists chatter about regarding an "unbloody sacrifice" <note>original: *sacrificio incruento*; the Catholic doctrine that the Mass is a real but non-bloody re-presentation of Christ's sacrifice</note> is a mockery they offer us; they provoke laughter by this stupid contradiction. For it is an "opposite in the appositive," and a contradiction in terms <term>contradiction in adjecto: a logical fallacy where the modifier contradicts the noun, like "a cold sun"</term>, just as in their "Roman Catholic Church"—which claims to be both "universal" and "particular"—or a "world within a city," or "heaven in a house" <note>original Greek: *οὐρανόν ἐν οἴκῳ*</note>. Furthermore, if the body of Christ were sacrificed by these little priests <note>original: *sacrificulis*; a derogatory diminutive for Catholic priests</note>, the victim would be more worthy than the priest, and yet the little priest wants to appear more worthy, since he believes and presumes that he "creates the creator" (as Pierre de Besse <note>original: *Bessæus*; a prominent 17th-century French preacher</note> says in his *Theological Conceptions*) and that he himself makes the victim and blesses it in the "species" <term>species: the outward appearances (bread and wine) that remain after the substance has supposedly changed</term>, as is clear from the Canon of the Mass itself. Finally, that victim to be sacrificed could not be any animal, whether rational or irrational.

It could not be an irrational animal, because that kind of victim has ceased to exist by now; though it flourished in the Levitical priesthood <note>the Jewish priesthood of the Old Testament</note>, it is now considered abolished along with that entire ministry. As is clear from the Epistle to the Hebrews, that kind of victim was merely "typical" <note>a "type" or shadow prefiguring a future reality</note> and was not able to purify souls and consciences.

Nor could it be a rational animal <note>meaning a human being</note>, because it would have to be either one man, or many, or all. It could not be just one man: first, because that would reek of the idolatry of Molech or Milcom <note>pagan deities associated with child sacrifice in the Old Testament</note>, which was long ago expressly condemned and severely punished, due to "excessive self-chosen worship" <note>original Greek: *ἐθελοπερισσοθρησκεία*</note> and the monstrous "perverse imitation" <note>original Greek: *κακοζηλία*</note> of the sacrifice of Isaac. Second, because the blood and death of one "little man" would not suffice to expiate the sins of all sinners. Third, because it would be unjust for one individual to pay and perish for everyone.

Nor could it be several or all men. For that victim would have to satisfy Divine justice either *extensively* (as the Schools love to speak) or *intensively*. It cannot be the latter [intensively], because neither all men, nor Angels, nor creatures in the entire universe would be equal to such a sacrifice. Because no creature, since it is finite, is able to bear and sustain the infinite weight of Divine justice—since that abandonment of creation is so great and so excessive, and that desertion so infinite, that it would be necessary for the wretched and finite creature to be "finished" an infinite number of times and reduced to nothing. Nor can it be the former [extensively]; for if that victim were to satisfy *extensively*, since that...

<meta>This page continues Cregut’s argument regarding the theological impossibility of the Catholic Mass. After arguing that no human or animal can serve as a sufficient "victim" for the sacrifice, he now turns to the concept of "satisfaction"—the payment or penance required for sin. He distinguishes between the ancient Church's use of public discipline and what he views as the corrupt later system of indulgences.</meta>

# ANTOINE CREGUT

[...that] satisfaction were to last forever, it could not be called true satisfaction. First, because true and properly defined satisfaction must be *intensive* <note>meaning concentrated or sufficient in its power to fulfill a debt</note>, so that the Judge may be appeased and therefore sins may be wiped away. Second, those who would satisfy in this way [eternally] could never truly say "I have satisfied," because it would be eternal and extended—or extendable—into infinity. Third, because this is the sort of satisfaction belonging to devils and all the damned, who make satisfaction in the fire of Gehenna <note>the biblical term for hell</note>, yet satisfaction will never be reached; they are scorched but not consumed, they die but are never dead or extinguished. Finally, that victim <note>referring to Christ in the Mass</note> cannot be considered any other kind of expiatory thing, as the Papists dream regarding the satisfactions they call *Canonical* or *Ecclesiastical*. 

For the goal of the ancient Church when it instituted Canonical or disciplinary satisfactions was not that those satisfactions should be considered propitiatory <note>original: *propitiatoriæ*; meaning to regain God's favor or atone for the guilt of sin</note>, as the Papists claim, but so that by ecclesiastical penalties they might test whoever had denied the faith during persecutions or had fallen into heinous crimes. Hence those public penalties were not "satisfactions" or like expiatory sacrifices of the penitents standing either in *weeping* <note>original Greek: *prosklausi*; the first stage of public penance where the penitent stood outside the church door weeping and begging for prayers</note>, or in *hearing* <note>original Greek: *akroasei*; the second stage where they were permitted to enter the back of the church to hear the scriptures read</note>, or in other places; rather, they were *penalties or punishments* <note>original Greek: *epitimia e timoriai*</note>. 

Therefore, the purpose was not (as the Monks now wish) to satisfy for sins as if the penitents were being offered like victims in a sacrifice for sin. But rather: 

I. To test whether they were hypocrites. 
II. To remove scandal from the Church. 
III. So that others might fear the Church's severity. 
IV. So that the horror of sin and God's wrath would appear to the fallen, and thus contrition and faith would be born. 
v. To witness that the Church abhors the license of sinning and hates all sinful actions, so that the mouths of pagan mockers might be blocked. 

Hence the canons of Ancyra and Nicaea <note>early Church councils from the 4th century that established rules for readmitting those who had lapsed in their faith</note>. See also 2 Corinthians 5 concerning the incestuous man of Corinth. 

But afterwards, the Bishops relaxed that rigor, from which arose *indulgences and the concessions of the fathers, and even the invented device of redeeming imposed satisfactions through commutation* <term>commutation: the practice of substituting a difficult penance, such as a long fast, with a more manageable one like alms-giving</term>. Namely, so that a fast could be "redeemed" by alms-giving or prayer. Then they were even redeemed by money, and at last Canonical satisfactions became obsolete, and the monetary redemptions of indulgences [turned] into another kind of trade...

III. In that Mass-priest-hood <note>original: *sacerdotio Missatico*</note>, no altar can be assigned. For either that altar would be an altar properly so-called, or improperly so-called. It is not properly so-called, because 1. there is only one altar of this kind in the New Testament, namely the altar of the cross. 2. Because according to them [the Catholics], the sacrifice of the Mass is unbloody and therefore is not properly a <term>propitiatory <note>original: *ἱλαστικὸν* (hilastikon); meaning a sacrifice that actually removes the guilt of sin</note></term> sacrifice, and for that reason an altar properly so-called is not required. It is not improperly so-called, because according to them the sacrifice of the Mass is propitiatory; but in a propitiatory sacrifice, the altar must be not improperly, but properly so-called. Therefore, since neither an altar properly so-called nor one improperly so-called can be assigned, certainly none can be granted at all, because none can be found except of these two kinds. Therefore there will be no sacrifice of the Mass, because these are relative terms—sacrifice and altar—and when one is established, the other is also established. Hence, among the Hebrews and Greeks, they are denoted by the same related concepts; as <term>sacrifice <note>original Hebrew: *זבח* (zebah)</note></term> and <term>altar <note>original Hebrew: *מזבח* (mizbeah)</note></term>. So in Greek: <term>sacrifice <note>original: *θυσία* (thusia)</note></term> and <term>altar <note>original: *θυσιαστήριον* (thusiasterion)</note></term> from the word <term>to sacrifice <note>original: *θύειν* (thuein)</note></term>, just as other names come from the same root <term>to sacrifice <note>original: *זבח* (zebah)</note></term>. For the Latins preferred to derive the words from form and ritual. *Altare* [Altar], as if from *altum* [high]; and *Aram* [Altar], as if from *ansam* [handle], according to the most learned Roman, Varro; because the Priest was accustomed to hold the Altar with his hands while he offered the sacrifice. Hence the poet <note>Virgil, in the Aeneid</note>:

IV. Just as there is no victim and no altar, so too no fire descends, nor is it kindled to consume the victim—a failure which we read also happened to the priests of Baal in the time of Elijah (1 Kings 18:38). From this, Jerome observes in his *Hebrew Questions or Traditions on Genesis* that Cain could not have known that God had accepted the gifts of his brother Abel, or rejected his own, except for the fact that fire descended from heaven upon Abel's gifts. For this reason, Theodotio <note>Theodotio was a 2nd-century translator of the Hebrew Bible into Greek</note> interpreted the passage thus: *And the Lord set fire above Abel and above his sacrifice, but above Cain and above his sacrifice He did not set fire.* <note>original Latin: "Et inflammauit Dominus super Abel..."</note> Jerome adds that fire used to come from heaven to devour a sacrifice: we read of this both in the dedication of the temple under Solomon, and when Elijah built the altar on Mount Carmel. It is for this reason that some have thought the generation of Cain worshiped fire—as was done in Ur of the Chaldeans <note>a biblical city associated with Abraham; the name 'Ur' also means 'fire' or 'light' in Hebrew</note>—because their ancestor Cain saw fire descend from heaven. And therefore he believed God was fire, which to the Hebrews is <term>Or אור</term>. ...just as we see them [the Jews] even now, having remained without sacrifices—unless perhaps the fact that they slaughter a sheep for the Passover is considered among the sacrifices. Furthermore, suppose that the Passover is a sacrifice; for some affirm it, while others deny it. Yet it is certain that it was not an **atoning sacrifice** <term>ἱλαστικὸν</term> <note>original Greek: *hilastikon*; a sacrifice meant to appease God’s wrath or remove sin</note>. The reason is that the Passover was not offered for sin, nor was it slaughtered either in its entirety or in part as a sacrificial offering. However, the Hebrew terms for **offering** <term>קרבן</term> <note>original: *korban*</note> and **gift** <term>מנחה</term> <note>original: *mincha*</note> do not always signify a propitiatory sacrifice.

And in Mark 14:12, when it is said: *On the first day of Unleavened Bread, they **slaughtered** the Passover* <term>ἔθυον</term> <note>original Greek: *ethuon*; often translated as "sacrificed," but here Crégut argues it refers to the domestic killing of the animal</note>. It was not being "sacrificed" in the ritual sense; for it was a domestic feast distinct from the sacrifices performed in the temple by the priests, which were **whole burnt offerings** <term>ὁλοκαύτωματα</term> <note>original Greek: *holokautomata*</note>, a magnificent example of which exists in 2 Chronicles 35.

But even if we concede that the Passover was a sacrifice (for I see that this has pleased a most learned interpreter), it would still not support the sacrilege of the Papal Mass; rather, it would foreshadow the sacrifice of the cross and the sacrament of the Eucharist. For there were two parts to the Passover, according to that most learned interpreter: first, the sacrifice itself; second, the sacred feast. It was a sacrifice because the people were reconciled to God by the sprinkling of blood, which could not happen without a sacrifice. Indeed, a lamb was slaughtered every year, followed by a feast whose celebration lasted seven continuous days.

But *Christ is our Passover*, says Paul in 1 Corinthians 5:7; He was slaughtered once, and indeed under this law: that the power of the slaughtering is eternal, even though He was slaughtered but once. As for the eating, we do not feed upon the lamb, Christ, in the sacrament once a year, but perpetually. No one, I think, will assert that this happens in the Mass, in which they dream that Christ is slaughtered not once, but daily.

Furthermore, the sacrifice of the Passover lamb was **bloody**, but in the Mass, it is established as **unbloody**; yet the fulfillment should correspond to the figure. Finally, nothing was preserved from the lamb, which had to be eaten entirely according to the law. But on the contrary, in the Mass, there is a **preservation of the host** <note>Referring to the Catholic practice of "reserving" the consecrated bread in a tabernacle</note>.

11. They are greatly deluded when they imagine that the sacraments of the Old Testament foreshadow the sacraments of the New Testament as their own fulfillments. For although Baptism succeeded Circumcision, and the [Lord's] Supper succeeded the Passover, they did not do so as fulfillments of their own figures, or as a sacrifice...

**Page 343**

[...the sacrifice of the cross], but as a sacrament to a sacrament, or as a new rite to an old rite. Hence, both sacraments—those of the Old as well as the New Testament—contained the reality itself. For this reason, they were not bare figures, but were joined with the truth they contained within themselves. This is why they should be called **antitypes** rather than types; they certainly contained the same thing, but not in the same manner or with the same degree of clarity and fullness. 

*Blessed Chrysostom* <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Church Father known for his preaching.</note> *illustrates this with a simile in his homily "Do not be ignorant."* A painter (he says), wishing to paint a king, is accustomed first to sketch his appearance **coarsely** <term>παχυλῶς</term> <note>original Greek: *pachylos*; meaning roughly or in broad strokes</note> with dark or dim and yellowish colors; nevertheless, the king is recognized in the face. But when the same king is portrayed in bright and vivid colors and finished in every detail, there is certainly a great difference, yet it is the very same king. 

And it is in this sense that 1 Peter 3:21 must be explained when it calls baptism the **antitype** <note>In theology, a "type" is a foreshadowing (like the Great Flood), and an "antitype" is the fulfillment (like Baptism).</note> of the flood. For a **type** <term>τύπος</term> <note>original Greek: *typos*</note> is often said to be that in which something is represented to us—as if in a model—by a certain impressed form **analogously** <term>ἀναλόγως</term> <note>original Greek: *analogos*</note>.

<margin>1 Corinthians 10:6</margin>

As it says, *Now these things were our types*, speaking of the Israelites *baptized in the cloud and the sea and drinking from the spiritual rock*. Which the Vulgate and Erasmus translate as "figures." From this was born the error of those who believed the sacraments of the Old Law were merely figurative and did not bestow grace; as if Israel were not the true Church, but only a shadow and figure of the true Church, from which countless other errors have sprouted. 

However, Paul says they were **types** not so much in respect to the Israelites as in respect to us. Therefore, they are not so much types as **antitypes** <term>ἀντίτυποι</term> <note>original Greek: *antitypoi*; things that correspond to a previous pattern</note>: that is, types corresponding directly to our types. Thus the manna was a sacrament of the heavenly bread for the Israelites (about which John 6 speaks), but for us it is a type of the bread we break in the Eucharist (1 Corinthians 10). Likewise, Circumcision was for those same Israelites a seal of the righteousness of faith, but in respect to us, it is a type of baptism; the same can be said of the Passover. 

But some types were extraordinary and incidental, such as the crossing of the sea which happened once. Others are ordinary, such as the sacraments. Wherefore the Apostle uses not only the word **type** <term>τύπῳ</term>, but also **pattern** <term>ὑποδείγματος</term> <note>original Greek: *hypodeigmatos*; a sign, copy, or suggestive representation</note> in Hebrews 8:5 and 9:23, where the legal requirements are called **patterns of heavenly things** <term>ὑποδείγματα τῶν ἐπουρανίων</term>. Thus he uses the word **symbol** <term>παραβολῆς</term> <note>original Greek: *parabolēs*; often translated as "parable," here meaning a symbolic representation</note> in Hebrews 9:9: *Which was a symbol for the present [time]...*

<summary>Crégut argues that Old Testament rituals were not empty symbols but contained the same spiritual reality as New Testament sacraments, using a painting analogy from John Chrysostom to explain the progression from "type" to "fulfillment." He challenges the idea that the ancient Israelites were merely a "shadow" of the Church, asserting they were the true Church in an earlier form.</summary>

-> ### ANTOINE CRÉGUT ### <-

...at that present time. In short, there are two kinds of types. 1. When types are compared with the truth itself, as in sacrifices, or when persons—such as Samson, Solomon, etc.—foreshadowed Christ; and thus in Hebrews 9:24, the sanctuary of the tabernacle is called an **antitype** <term>ἀντίτυπον</term> <note>original Greek: *antitypon*; a fulfillment or corresponding reality to a previous symbol</note> of the heavens. 2. When types are not compared as figures with the truth itself (of which they are models), but when they are compared with other secondary types which are models of the same thing. Thus, in the previously cited passage of 1 Peter 3:21, the Great Flood foreshadowed baptism as a **type** to an **antitype** <note>The author is explaining that the Flood was a first "type" of salvation, and Baptism is a second "type" (antitype) of that same salvation.</note>. And both signified the sanctification of the Church or the emerging from the abyss of sin and death.

Neither is that argument valid for proving the sacrifice of the Mass which the Council of Trent <note>A major 16th-century council of the Catholic Church that defined its doctrines against the Protestant Reformation.</note> brings forward in Session 22, Canon 2, from John 13:27: "**Do this**" <note>original Latin: *Hoc facite*. The author is critiquing the Catholic view that these words at the Last Supper turned the Apostles into priests with the power to sacrifice.</note>. It pronounces an anathema <note>A formal curse or excommunication.</note> against those who say Christ did not institute the Apostles as priests with these words, "**Do this**." As if the discussion there were truly about sacrifice and little priests <note>original Latin: *sacrificulis*; a diminutive term used here to dismiss the Catholic priesthood.</note>. In that way, even Judas could have been instituted as a priest, since Christ speaks to him thus: "**What you do, do quickly**" <note>original Latin: *quod facis, fac citò* (John 13:27)</note>. Thus the traitor would be a priest and the betrayal a sacrifice. 

Nor is the argument of any better quality which they press from the Hebrew word **asah** <note>Hebrew: עשׂה; meaning "to do" or "to make"</note> when used with the accusative case in a complete construction (as they say). For *asah* joined with only a pronoun never means "to sacrifice." Therefore, if *asah* for the Hebrews, **rezein** <term>ῥέζειν</term> <note>original Greek: *rhezein*; to do or perform a ritual</note> for the Greeks, and **facere** for the Latins denote "to sacrifice," this does not happen by the inherent force of those words. Instead, it occurs when some noun is added that determines the general meaning of those words toward a specific thing. Thus *asah* will sometimes mean **to create** <note>original: *creare*</note> when something is made from nothing; sometimes **to beget** <note>original: *generare*</note> when nature acts; and sometimes **to form** <note>original: *formare*</note> when art acts. 

All of these are denoted by their own proper names, namely: **bara** <note>Hebrew: ברא; to create</note>, **yatzar** <note>Hebrew: יצר; to form</note>, and **yalad** <note>Hebrew: ילד; to beget</note>. This is why *asah* joined with the word for a **heifer** <note>original Latin: *vitula*</note> means **to prepare**, or with **calf** <note>original Latin: *vitulum*</note>, as in Genesis 18:7, when Abraham **prepared a calf** <note>Hebrew: עשׂה</note> for the three angels by sending a servant. But we have treated these matters more extensively in our *Apology for the Synod of Charenton* <note>The 1623 Synod of Charenton was an assembly of the Reformed Church in France; Crégut wrote a defense of its decisions.</note> regarding communion with the Lutherans; there, it was demonstrated that **to do** <note>original Latin: *facere*</note> among the Latins never meant "to sacrifice" unless a victim is added, such as "**to do [sacrifice] a kid**," "**a lamb**," and in the poet [Virgil], "**to do [sacrifice] calves**" <note>original Latin: *facere vitulas*</note>; or "**to perform a divine rite**," and this...

-> ### REVELATOR ARCANORVM <note>The Revealer of Secrets</note> ### <-

...more in use among Poets than among Orators; and even then, only rarely. Regarding the word *to do* <term>ποιεῖν</term> <note>original Greek: *poiein*; Crégut is arguing that this common verb does not carry a specialized sacrificial meaning in the New Testament</note>, which Christ uses—*do this* <note>original Greek: *touto poieite*</note>—it is never read as being used to mean "to sacrifice" among authors.

Then, even if *to do* <note>original Latin: *facere*</note> were the same as *to sacrifice*, nevertheless this meaning would in no way fit here; for *do this* denotes the action which Christ was performing, which was to eat and to distribute bread to be eaten; but who ever heard of an "action" being sacrificed? What priest ever offered a victim of this kind? Finally, that interpretation is refuted by the following words: *In remembrance of me*. For how could Christ be sacrificed in remembrance of himself, since memory is of absent things? Nor is the argument valid which Cardinal Perron <note>Jacques Davy du Perron (1556–1618), a prominent French Cardinal and diplomat known for his skill in theological debate</note> used to exclaim elsewhere with a great seduction of words and gestures while preaching in the Church of Auxerre <note>original Latin: *Altisiodorensi*</note>:

> "Are there not," said that prelate, "many saints buried in this temple? Are there not the bones of martyrs in this place? They are present, and yet there are monuments and memories, or a memorial, of them."

But he repeated these things in vain before the common folk and the ignorant masses, who did not see that Davy <note>Referring to the Cardinal by his surname, Jacques Davy</note> was acting the sophist; because the saints and martyrs are not memories of themselves, but of their own illustrious deeds, which were in the past, not the present, and which were set before the faithful to be imitated. Add to this that in 1 Corinthians 11, Paul said to all the faithful—at least to the Corinthians to whom he wrote—*do this* <note>original Greek: *touto poieite*</note>; but if that were so, there would be as many sacrificing priests as there are faithful—unless the Papists, who introduced the Mass without communicants, are now busy thrusting upon us a sacrifice without priests as well. Away with such peddlers of nonsense <note>original Latin: *nugiuendulos*</note>.

Indeed, why say more? Perron yields the field to us <note>original Latin: *herbam porrigit*; a Latin idiom meaning to admit defeat or give up the struggle</note> in his response to the King of England, page 926, when he distinguishes between the sacrifice of *redemption* and that of *religion*. The sacrifice of *redemption*, he says, which is *both in itself and original*, is the sacrifice of the cross, which, according to Hebrews 9, was performed once; but the sacrifice of *religion* applies that of the cross to us, and is perpetual in the Eucharist. And while other priests, as Paul says in Hebrews 10, *stand ministering*, Christ, after he had offered himself once, sits at the right hand of the Father. When Perron had said these things in the speech which he delivered in...

Among the assembly of Dominicans <note>The Order of Preachers, a major Catholic religious order</note>, many murmured and repeatedly said that this was the "old ferment of heretics" and belonged to their father <note>original: *vetus hæreticorum fermentum*; a reference to the biblical metaphor of leaven/yeast representing corrupting influence</note>. But Gabriel Biel <note>A late-medieval German theologian (c. 1420–1495) whose works on the Mass were highly influential</note> contradicts himself; for at one moment he says the sacrifice of the Mass is an "application" of the sacrifice of the cross, and at another that it is the same thing, differing only in the "mode" of offering. *The sacrifice of the Mass (he says) differs from the sacrifice of the cross only in its unbloody mode of offering. In substance and in the operation of similar effects, it is the same; the end is also the same. And whatever Christ obtained on the cross in general for the faithful, that is applied in the Mass in particular. But it is applied most generally to the Catholic Church; most specially to the petty priest; and specially to the founder and the one in whose name the Mass is performed.* By these last words, he values the price of Masses in a marvelous way; therefore, do not be amazed if they are sold dearly, or if so many precautions are employed in the celebration of the Mass, as is evident from the "Drama of the Mass" described in an elegant <term>vivid sketch</term> <note>original Greek: *hypotyposis*; a rhetorical term for a lifelike description</note> by Sleidan <note>Johannes Sleidanus (1506–1556), the primary historian of the Protestant Reformation</note>.

Thus far our commentary on the second part—that is, on the offices of Melchizedek, namely his royal and priestly office. There now follows the third part, which concerns the <term>Fulfillments</term> <note>original Greek: *apotelesma*; referring to the practical results or completion of an office</note>, both the royal fulfillment and the priestly fulfillment. And first, the royal fulfillment is his magnificence, seen when he sumptuously received Abraham as he returned from battle. Moses hints at this briefly with these words: *he brought out bread and wine*. For he received Abraham and his companions with hospitality, and refreshed the weary and hungry army with royal liberality. For although Moses only makes mention of bread and wine, he speaks first in the Hebrew manner, among whom all types of food are signified by "bread"; hence also the word <term>Lechem</term> <note>original Hebrew: לחם</note>, which to the Hebrews means *bread*, signifies *meat* to the Arabs. <meta>This page continues Crégut's argument against the Roman Catholic interpretation of the Mass as a literal sacrifice. Having previously cited the "Master of Sentences" (Peter Lombard) and Gabriel Biel to show that even Catholic theologians have described the Mass as a "memorial," Crégut now transitions to a detailed linguistic analysis of the story of Melchizedek in Genesis 14 to dismantle the claim that Melchizedek’s offering of bread and wine was a priestly sacrifice foreshadowing the Eucharist.</meta>

-> ### REVEALER OF SECRETS ### <-

In the Lord's Prayer we ask for daily bread; which in the Syriac version is <note>original: לחמא דסונקנאן, *lachma de-sunkanan*</note> *the bread of our necessity*. Yet we do not lack bread alone, but also other things necessary for food and clothing. Second, Moses speaks in favor of the frugality of that time, when kings themselves lived soberly, and the stimulants of the throat and various seasonings and foods <note>original Greek: ἐδέσματα καὶ ἡδύσματα, *edesmata kai hedysmata*</note> had not yet become common, as happened later with the spreading of delicacies and allurements.

But truly, although that action of Melchizedek was purely civil and royal, it was ignorantly turned into something ecclesiastical and priestly by the ancient writers of the Church. This error was born from the <term>Vulgate edition</term> <note>The standard Latin translation of the Bible used by the Roman Catholic Church</note>, in which these are the words: *But Melchizedek, king of Salem, bringing forth bread and wine, for he was a priest of the Most High.* These words certainly do not express the Hebrew truth, for in the original manuscript it is written thus: <note>original Hebrew: ומלכי־צדק מלך שלם הוציא לחם ויין והוא כהן לאל עליון; *u-Malki-tzedek melech Shalem hotzi lechem ve-yayin ve-hu kohen le-El Elyon*</note>. In this passage, two expressions must be considered: namely, *hotzi* and *ve-hu*. The first does not signify "to offer," as if the bread and wine were Melchizedek's offerings made to God in his capacity as a priest; rather, it signifies "to bring forth" or "to produce," because Melchizedek brought out the bread and wine not for God, but for Abraham, so that he might refresh him and his soldiers after their victory, and to welcome such a victor—a servant of the most high God and the father of the faithful—with royal liberality. 

The second expression to be considered is *ve-hu*, meaning "and he." For that particle *vau*, which is called the <term>copulative vau</term> <note>original: *vau copulatiuum*; a Hebrew grammatical term for the letter "and" (waw) used to join sentences</note> by Hebrew Grammarians, is poorly translated by the Latin interpreter as "for he was," as if it were a causal particle. By this, the translator would imply that Melchizedek offered the bread and wine to God and not to Abraham, and did so from a priestly rather than a royal office, because he was a priest of the Most High. This would certainly utterly overturn the Mosaic context and place the entire mystery in a very small matter, leaving aside that which is momentous and which was divinely observed by the Apostle in the <term>Epistle to the Hebrews</term> <note>Referring to Hebrews 7, where the author compares Christ to Melchizedek based on his eternal priesthood, rather than any offering of bread and wine</note>. Would that this had been prudently weighed by the ancients! For they would not have so weakly transferred the likeness of Christ and Melchizedek to bread and wine—a likeness which consists in far different things. For they want to claim that Christ offered his body, which is the life-giving bread, and his blood, which is the spiritual drink.

# ANTHONY CRÉGUT #

And yet (which is worthy of great attention) while the Apostle <note>Paul</note> in the Epistle to the Hebrews most exactly gathers and follows in detail whatever Melchizedek had in common with Christ, he does not make even a tiny word of mention regarding the bread and wine. But if the clever arguments of <term>Tertullian</term> <note>An influential early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD)</note> or other doctors <note>original Greek: ὁμοψηφάντων, *homopsēphantōn*</note> *sharing the same opinion* were true, it would have been no small negligence to examine individual parts of trivial importance while not deigning to spare even a single syllable for the chief point. Truly, since the Apostle disputes so at length and accurately concerning the priesthood, it would be a mark of the crudest forgetfulness to in no way touch upon the distinguished sacrifice in which the whole power of the priesthood was included. But such a <note>original Greek: ἁμάρτημα μνημονikὸν, *hamartēma mnēmonikon*</note> *failure of memory* would be unworthy of the divine Apostle.

Truly then, do the <term>Roman Catholics</term> <note>original: *Pontificij*. Crégut uses this term to refer to those loyal to the Pope (the Pontiff)</note> presume to cleverly demonstrate their sacrifice of the Mass? Surely, if wherever the word <note>original Hebrew: הוציא, *hotzi*, meaning "he brought out"</note> *brought out* is found they could prove offerings to us, there would be innumerable offerings and innumerable sacrifices! But it is well that they fittingly demonstrate their Mass from the word <note>original Hebrew: מוצאות, *motzaot*, meaning "outgoings" or "exits"</note> *outgoings*. For from "brought out" and "went out" and "going forth" and "outgoings" <note>original Hebrew: הוציא & יצא & צאת & מוצאות; *hotzi*, *yatza*, *tzat*, *motzaot*</note>—by grammatical analogy—these names rightly suit the Mass; no less than that of the pious Poet:

->*May God himself send back the Mass which Satan sent,*<-
->*Soon may the Mass perish, which was sent so ill.*<-
<note>This Latin couplet relies on a pun: "Missa" (the Mass) is derived from the same root as "missa" (sent). The poet mocks the rite as something "sent" by the devil that God should "send back."</note>

But nevertheless, let us freely grant to the Roman Catholics that Moses spoke of an offering, and that Melchizedek brought it forth not as a king, but offered the bread and wine as a priest; yet what does this do for the sacrifice of the Mass? Why would it foreshadow a sacrifice rather than a <term>sacrament</term>? Indeed, why not rather a sacrament, and specifically that of the Eucharist? Since bread and wine are not sacrificed, but are offered in the sacrament of the Eucharist; indeed, they are not offered, but consecrated, and God himself in those symbols not only offers but also confers his signified grace to us—that is, Christ. Therefore it should be noted that offerings are of two kinds: some are from men, namely when they offer to God himself; others are from God, when God offers to us. The first were in sacrifices, whether <term>propitiatory</term> <note>intended to appease God's anger over sin</note> or <term>Eucharistic</term> <note>offerings of thanksgiving</note>. In the propitiatory ones, when the victims were offered for sin—

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS. 349 #

...the expiation of sins, and these (as we said above) were called <note>original Hebrew: חטאה, *Chattah*</note> **Sin Offerings** and <note>original Hebrew: אשם, *Asham*</note> **Guilt Offerings**. In <term>Eucharistic</term> <note>From the Greek *eucharistia*, meaning "thanksgiving." Crégut is using the term in its literal sense of "gratitude" rather than specifically the Christian sacrament</note> offerings, they were not offered for the expiation of sins, but as an expression of gratitude for a benefit received. Indeed, there were many offerings or sacrifices so-called in an improper sense, which we termed above <note>original Greek: χαριστικὰ, *charistika*</note> *thank-offerings*, <note>original Greek: σεבαστικὰ, *sebastika*</note> *reverential offerings*, and <note>original Greek: εὐκτικά, *euktika*</note> *votive offerings*. And the Hebrews designate these by various names: <note>original Hebrew: עולות, *Oloth*</note> **Burnt Offerings**, or <note>original Hebrew: שלמים, *Shelamim*</note> **Peace Offerings**, or <note>original Hebrew: מנחות, *Minchot*</note> **Grain Offerings**, or <note>original Hebrew: זבח, *Zevach*</note> **Sacrifice**, or <note>original Hebrew: קרבן, *Korban*</note> **Offering**, or <note>original Hebrew: תרומה, *Terumah*</note> **Contribution**, or <note>original Hebrew: נדבה, *Nedavah*</note> **Free-will Gift**. For all those words signify "offerings" in a general sense, but in different ways.

For instance, <note>original Hebrew: עולות, *Oloth*</note> *Burnt Offerings* were <term>holocausts</term> <note>From the Greek *holokaustos*, meaning "burnt whole"</note>, where the victims were entirely consumed by fire, as was said before. <note>original Hebrew: שלמים, *Shelamim*</note> *Peace Offerings* were offerings or sacrifices for peace and successful outcomes. <note>original Hebrew: מנחות, *Minchot*</note> *Grain Offerings* were both "profane" gifts (which one person gives to another) and "sacred" gifts (which we offer to God); among the Hebrews, these were offered morning and evening. From this evening offering, the time of day itself was called *Mincha*. Hence the <note>original Hebrew: מנחה גדולה, *Mincha Gedolah*</note> *Great Mincha* and the <note>original Hebrew: מנחה קטנה, *Mincha Ketanah* <margin>Small Mincha</margin></note> *Small Mincha*. In place of these, the evening and morning prayers were substituted. The first, that is the evening ones, were called <note>original Hebrew: תפלת מנחה, *Tephilat Mincha*</note> *the Mincha prayer* and <note>original Hebrew: תפלת השחר, *Tephilat Ha-shachar*</note> *the morning prayer*.

According to <term>Maimonides</term> <note>Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon (1138–1204), a preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher and Torah scholar</note>, this morning prayer began at sunrise. It is regarding this that we read in Acts chapter 2, when the Apostles prayed until our ninth hour before noon, which is when they received the Holy Spirit. Likewise, at the time of the "Great Mincha," Peter prayed while going up to the roof in Acts 10:9. At the "Small Mincha," or the ninth hour of prayer, Peter and John went into the temple in Acts 3:1.

Furthermore, <note>original Hebrew: זבח, *Zevach*</note> *Sacrifice* is used in two ways: either for a sacrifice properly so-called, or for one improperly so-called, as in Psalm 50 and Psalm 51, where a "contrite spirit" is called a <note>original Hebrew: זבח, *Zevach*</note> *Sacrifice*. Next, <note>original Hebrew: קרבן, *Korban*</note> *Corban* is a general offering by which all legal offerings are signified in Leviticus 1:3 and chapter 2, verses 1, 4, 5, etc. From this, the Evangelist Mark calls *Corban* a "gift." <note>original Hebrew: תרומה, *Terumah*</note> *Terumah*, however, was an offering given spontaneously, for which there was neither a fixed measure nor a set value. The wealthier gave one part out of forty; those of middle means, one out of fifty; and the poorer, one out of sixty. If someone had gathered a barn full of sheaves of grain, he would set aside a portion for the priest based on "equity and the good" <note>A legal principle of fairness</note>, and then the entire barn was <note>original Hebrew: פטור, *Patur*</note> *exempt* or free for its owner. <meta>This page continues Crégut's systematic breakdown of biblical offerings. Having established the various types of Hebrew sacrifices in the previous page, he now details the specific ritual procedures for voluntary offerings and traces how these ancient practices influenced—and, in his view, were misinterpreted by—the Christian church.</meta>

-> # ANTHONY CRÉGUT # <-

...a voluntary offering made with generosity. According to the teachers of the Hebrews, seven conditions were observed in these offerings (if I may mention this in passing):

I. The heads of families brought those offerings of firstfruits as far as the courtyard; while carrying them on their shoulders, they recited these words from Deuteronomy 26 to the priest: <note>original: "vobis annuntio coram Deo me venisse in illam terrā quam Deus patribus nostris promiserat, &c."</note> *“I declare to you today before God that I have come into the land which God promised to our fathers,” etc.*

II. The priest would take the basket from each person's hand and place it before the altar.

III. That passage from Deuteronomy was read from beginning to end, in which the misery of the people and the mercy of God are proclaimed.

IV. A sacrifice of <term>Eucharist</term> <note>Crégut uses the Greek-derived term for "thanksgiving" to link Jewish gratitude rituals with the later Christian sacrament.</note> or thanksgiving was added to the offering of firstfruits.

V. The singing of Psalms took place, without which no sacrifice was performed.

VI. The offering was lifted up by the priest himself, according to God's command, as is evident throughout the Law.

VII. Those making the offering were required to remain in the city for the entire night, to show that they had not traveled to the city <note>original Greek: παρέργως (*parergōs*)</note> *incidentally* or in haste, but to truly give thanks to Jehovah.

Eventually, the offerings of the Christians arose from those Jewish ones, as is clear from Philippians 4 and Hebrews 13. Later, in the time of <term>Cyprian</term> and <term>Augustine</term> <note>Two influential early Church Fathers from North Africa (3rd and 4th–5th centuries AD).</note>, a **table** stood in the middle of the temple upon which the offerings were placed; Augustine, in his 122nd letter to Victorinus, calls this **“God’s altar.”** These were offered before the celebration of the <term>mysteries</term> <note>Refers to the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper or Communion.</note>, as Nicephorus relates concerning the Emperor Theodosius. Among the Greeks, these offerings were called <note>original Greek: τὰ δῶρα, τὰ θύματα, τὰ καρπώματα (*ta dōra, ta thymata, ta karpōmata*)</note> ***the gifts, the sacrifices, the fruits***. Hence that phrase in the Liturgies: <note>original Greek: τὰ σὰ ἐκ τῶν σῶν (*ta sa ek tōn sōn*)</note> ***“Your own from Your own.”*** From this comes the <note>original Greek: κακοζηλία (*kakozēlia*)</note> ***misguided imitation*** found in the Papist Mass. For that “ape” of the ancient Church prescribes offerings and has named them the **Offertory**.

But in truth, there are other offerings which are offered *by God to men*, and these are found in every sacrament. In a sacrament, the minister of God offers us the symbols, but God offers the reality of the sacrament itself, which is <term>metonymically</term> <note>A figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it; here, the bread/wine represent the spiritual grace.</note> contained within those symbols. Therefore, if Melchizedek, as a priest, had offered bread and wine, he would have foreshadowed the **Sacrament of the Eucharist** rather than the **Sacrifice of the Mass**. This is because he would have been offering the symbols to Abraham, and God would have been offering the signified grace. But in a **sacrifice**, *we* offer to God; we do not receive from God. Indeed, a sacrament and a sacrifice differ as much as ***giving and receiving***.

<summary>Crégut outlines seven ritual requirements for Hebrew firstfruit offerings and argues that Christian offerings evolved from these. He concludes by distinguishing a "sacrament" (God giving to man) from a "sacrifice" (man giving to God), using this to critique the Catholic Mass.</summary>
<keywords>firstfruits, Deuteronomy 26, Hebrew traditions, Church Fathers, Augustine, Offertory, Melchizedek, Sacrament vs Sacrifice, Eucharist, Liturgy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of biblical offerings, moving from the specific ritual laws of the Hebrews to the interpretation of the meeting between Melchizedek and Abraham. Crégut is arguing against the Catholic (Pontificial) interpretation that Melchizedek's "bringing forth" of bread and wine was a sacrificial "offering" that prefigures the Mass.</meta>

### THE REVEALER OF SECRETS ###

In the first, God gives; in the second, He receives. But in truth, Melchizedek did not offer bread and wine to God, but brought them out to Abraham. This is clearly gathered from the history written by Moses, although the divine historian touched upon this meeting quite briefly. Note here in passing from this history how religiously we must handle the word of God, and how it must not be touched with "unwashed hands" <note>original Latin: "haud illotis manibus"—a proverbial expression meaning to approach a sacred subject without proper preparation or reverence</note>. For if anyone should criticize Moses for treating such a great man with so few words—indeed, having omitted those things which the laws of history especially seemed to require—nevertheless, let that critic <note>original: "Momus criticus," referring to Momus, the Greek god of mockery and censure</note> immediately be silent and see what a grand mystery Moses shadowed forth with these very few words. Indeed, let him carefully notice how he himself is *without excuse* <note>original Greek: ἀναπολόγητος (*anapologētos*)</note> who scrutinizes secrets; like those who curiously investigate Melchizedek's father and genealogy, and—what is worse—sanction a hidden matter as most certain in a dictatorial manner, as we saw above from Jerome's letter to Evangelus. I shall now bury in silence the monstrous ideas of Postel <note>Guillaume Postel was a 16th-century mystic and linguist often accused of heresy for his eccentric universalist views</note>, that "cobbler of heresies," and others from his fellowship.

Therefore, the Roman Catholics <note>original: "Pontificij"</note> abuse the word *hotzi* <note>Hebrew: הוציא (*hotzi*), meaning "he brought out"</note> which signifies *to produce* or *bring forth*; thus they contradict both the Vulgate translator and the Septuagint <note>The "LXX," the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> and the Church Fathers, who interpret it no differently than we do: "bringing forth." The Septuagint says: *He brought out loaves of bread and wine* <note>original Greek: ἐξήνεγκεν ἄρτους καὶ οἶνον (*exēnegken artous kai oinon*)</note>. Here "loaves" is said in the plural because they denote provisions or supplies, according to the Hebrew idiom, as was previously stated. Nor can the Catholics prove the contrary from the passage in Judges 6:18–19, when Gideon *brought out his gift and meat and broth to the Angel* <note>referring to the Hebrew verb הוציא (*hotzi*)</note>. For there it also signifies "he brought forth," because it is not a matter of sacrifice or ritual offering, but of food brought for eating, since Gideon believed the Angel (or Jehovah) to be a man. Therefore, the Vulgate translated it as *brought* or *carried*, not as *offered*.

And thus let this royal <term>Apotelesma</term> <note>A theological term for the completion or practical fulfillment of a prophetic "type" or symbol.</note> concerning this "type"—that is, Melchizedek—be explained. Now indeed, it is more certain than certainty itself that this was truly prefigured regarding the "antitype"—that is, Christ—in whom this is magnificently fulfilled. For He, the Monarch of the Church, sent His gifts to men from on high. First, as King of kings, He received gifts from other kings...

<meta>catchword: Petrum</meta>

...receives, as is clear from Psalm 68, from the word *lakach* <note>original Hebrew: לקח; this verb can mean both "to take/receive" and "to bring/fetch"</note> which can be explained in two ways, as was said above. And in Psalm 72:10: *The kings of the ocean’s shores and the islands shall pay tribute; the kings of Sheba and Seba shall offer gifts.* And in Matthew 2, the gifts offered by the Magi: gold, frankincense, and myrrh. This was according to the custom of the Eastern peoples, who did not appear before their kings—or before those to whom they owed honor—without a gift. Among the Persians, whenever the king traveled through the provinces, everyone offered him gifts: some brought oxen, others sheep, grain, or wine; those of humbler means offered milk, cheese, dates, fruit, and so on.

There is a well-known story of a Persian named Synætæ (mentioned by Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a 3rd-century Roman author who wrote "Varia Historia," a collection of anecdotes</note>) who was surprised by King Artaxerxes Mnemon; having nothing else, he ran to the river Cyrus and brought the king water in both his cupped hands. The same custom (according to Seneca) passed to the Parthians. Thus in Genesis 43, the sons of Jacob carry gifts to Joseph; and in 1 Kings 10, the Queen of Sheba won over Solomon with her gifts. Just as God commanded in Exodus 23:15: *You shall not appear in my sight empty-handed.* The reason is added in Deuteronomy 16:17: *Everyone shall bring according to what his hand can give, according to the blessing of the Lord your God which He has given you.* 

Secondly, Christ, as King of the Church, sent "gifts to men" (Ephesians 4). Indeed, He sent the Holy Spirit, who is the gift above all gifts, and the cause and beginning of every gift. For this reason, they are pre-eminently called *eminent gifts* and *spiritual graces* <note>original Greek: ἐξοχῶς δωρήματα (*exochōs dōrēmata*), χαρίσματα (*charismata*)</note>, which that great King poured out in a solemn and magnificent way on the day of Pentecost, according to the prophecy of Joel, chapter 2. Indeed, He gave himself as a *ransom for redemption* <note>original Greek: λυτρὸν εἰς ἀπολύτρωσιν (*lytron eis apolytrōsin*)</note>.

The Pope arrogantly imitates this royal magnificence of Christ, as he also falsely claims Christ's dignity for himself. He does this either by taking gifts and offerings from men—as was evident in England with "Peter's Pence" <note>term: Peter's Pence (denarius B. Petri); an annual tax of one penny from every householder in England paid to the Papal See</note>, with coveted palfreys <note>original Latin: "parafredis concupiscibilibus"—expensive riding horses often demanded as tribute</note>, and from other extraordinary tributes as well as annual revenues. 

Or, he does this by sending out trivial gifts such as "blessed roses," wax *Agnus Dei* pendants <note>term: Agnus Dei; small wax discs blessed by the Pope, often depicting a lamb, used as devotional objects</note>, and empty titles like "Defender of the Church." He also makes imaginary and conditional divisions of empires—provided the recipients can conquer them—just as Alexander III <note>note: The author likely intends Alexander VI, who famously divided the New World between Spain and Portugal in 1493, though Alexander III also exerted significant temporal authority over kingdoms like Ireland in the 12th century</note> divided the whole world on a globe between the Kings of Spain and Portugal. In this, he used the same legal right used in "dividing estates" <note>term: herciscundis hæreditatibus; a Roman legal term for the judicial division of an inheritance among co-heirs</note>, acting contrary to the practice of Christ. And finally, on his anniversary, he ridiculously scatters small coins like *baiocchi* and *bagutini* <note>term: baiocchi and bagutini; small-value Italian coins of the period, used here to highlight the Pope's perceived pettiness compared to Christ's spiritual gifts</note> among the common people, out of a perverse affectation <note>original Greek: κακοζηλίᾳ (*kakozēlia*)</note>.

...imitating Peter by saying, *I have neither gold nor silver,* <note>original Latin: "Neq; aurum neque argentum habeo"; a reference to Acts 3:6</note> etc. but rather after the fashion of the Roman Emperors, who used to throw "scattered gifts" <note>original: "missilia," objects thrown by emperors to a crowd during games or festivals</note> to the people, such as sweets, ointments, linens, perfumes, and so on. So much for the kingly fulfillment <note>original: "apotelesma," a term referring to the completed work or outcome of an office</note> of Melchizedek; let us now proceed further to track his two priestly fulfillments: namely, his blessing and his receipt of tithes. First, he blessed Abraham—that is, a priest blessed a priest. However, an extraordinary priest blessed an ordinary priest. Indeed, he blessed not only that particular priest of a single family (just as the Patriarchs and heads of households were once priests), but also the public priests of the whole people, such as Aaron and all the Levites. These were blessed and tithed through Abraham, since they were "in the loins of Abraham" <note>A biblical concept from Hebrews 7, suggesting that descendants are spiritually present in their ancestors</note>. These preeminences <term>superiorities</term> <note>original Greek: ὑπεροχὰς (hyperochas), referring to higher ranks or dignities</note> are extolled by the Apostle in the Epistle to the Hebrews. Therefore, if the blessings of particular priests, like the Patriarchs, were valid—as is clear from Isaac blessing Jacob and not Esau, and from the blessing of Jacob as he blessed his sons—and if the blessings of ordinary priests like the Levites and even pastors are valid; then how much more shall the blessing of Melchizedek, an extraordinary priest, be valid and most acceptable to God. And if the blessings of the pastors of the Church are like a pledge of the good things which they pray for on behalf of those they bless, as is clear from Numbers 6:27:
> And putting their hands upon the children of Israel, they shall invoke my name: and I will bless them.
How much more the blessing of Melchizedek, who was indeed a unique and extraordinary priest, whose gifts and duties were also required to be unique and extraordinary?

And truly, there was a double blessing. One is common to all the faithful when they bless one another and one prays for another. The other is a solemn blessing or prayer, by which he who excels in public dignity commends others subject to him to God; and this cannot be done except with great authority. With such a blessing did the High Priest of old bless the people with hands lifted up toward heaven; which was also observed by Christ, as Luke testifies—

# ANTHONY CREGUT

...prophets, who blessed the Apostles with that same rite, so that he might signify that he is that High Priest foreshadowed by the men of old.

Truly, however, that which was done symbolically by Melchizedek was fulfilled perfectly and with great <term>preeminence</term> <note>original Greek: ὑπεροχῇ (hyperochē), meaning excellence or superiority</note> in Christ, just as the reality <note>original: "antitypus," the person or thing represented by an earlier symbol</note> surpasses the symbol <note>original: "typus"</note>. For in truth, Christ not only blessed Abraham and the rest of the faithful, but he is also the inexhaustible fountain of all blessings. Indeed, for him, to "bless" is to "do good," just as for him to "speak" is to "decree" and "to act." This is as when the Word created all things in Genesis 1: God spoke, and all things were made. So when Christ blessed the loaves and the fishes, he multiplied them (John 6); and conversely, when he cursed the fig tree, it immediately withered away. 

For men, to bless can sometimes mean to curse, which is proven by a Hebrew <term>idiom</term> <note>a phrasing or grammatical structure unique to a specific language</note>, where the same word *barak* <note>original Hebrew: ברך</note> in different conjugations signifies both to bless and to curse. This is known from the story of Job’s wife, and in 1 Kings 21:10, where false witnesses testify against Naboth, saying: *you have cursed God and the king*. The Hebrew actually says: *you have blessed*. 

Yet God turns the cursing of men into blessing, as is clear from the story of Balaam <note>A prophet in the Book of Numbers who was hired to curse Israel but was compelled by God to bless them instead</note>; and when God blessed the living creatures in Genesis 1, he granted them fertility by that blessing. Hence Origen <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 185 – 253 AD)</note> notes a distinction between the blessing of God and that of men. God’s blessing always brings with it some gift. Men are said to "bless" God in the sense of praising him or giving thanks. And in Romans 12, "blessing" one's enemies is to pray for good things in exchange for evil. In the phrasing of Scripture, not only does Christ’s "blessing" imply a gift and a benefit, but even his "saying" is an affirmation or an asseveration <note>a solemn declaration</note> of some great thing. 

Therefore, one must not read the Gospel phrases <term>I say to you</term> <note>original Greek: λέγω σοι (legō soi) or λέγω ὑμῖν (legō hymin)</note> with indifference. For sometimes it signifies <term>I strongly affirm to you</term> <note>original Greek: διϊσχυρίζομαί ὑμῖν (diischyrizomai hymin)</note>, and in Hebrew, *making them trust* <note>original Hebrew: מבטח אותם (mivtach otam)</note>. Thus, the Seventy Interpreters <note>The translators of the Septuagint, the Greek version of the Old Testament</note> translated that blasphemous saying of Rabshakeh <note>A messenger of the Assyrian King Sennacherib who threatened Jerusalem</note>, "Do not let Hezekiah make you trust," as "Let not Hezekiah say to you."

That blessing of Melchizedek upon the blessing Abraham is all the more illustrious because Abraham is raised above all other men. Whence it is said of Abraham in Genesis 12:2: *And I will make you the father of a great nation and I will bless you; and I will magnify your name: and so now be a blessing.* and in verse 3: *they will be blessed*

Just as in the Law all fruits were sanctified by the offering made from the **firstfruits** <note>the first portion of a harvest, given to God as an act of sanctification for the whole crop</note> in Leviticus 19:24 and Deuteronomy 26:2, and just as in the order of nature the branches follow the nature of the root; so since Abraham was a father to the faithful—functioning as the root to the branches and the firstfruits to the harvest—all the faithful are said to be blessed in him. Yet the firstfruits and the root themselves are blessed only in the "Firstfruits and Root" of all blessings: that is, Christ. Indeed, they were blessed by that Christ and Melchizedek, which is why the Apostle writes in Ephesians 1:3: *Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavens in Christ.*

Hence it is that among the Hebrews all blessings were performed through the name **Jehovah**. According to Numbers 6, the people were blessed by pronouncing the **tetragrammaton** <note>the "four-letter" name of God, YHWH, considered too sacred to pronounce in common speech</note>; this blessing—as Pietro Galatino <note>an Italian friar and scholar of Jewish mysticism (1460–1540)</note> reports in *On the Secrets of Catholic Truth*, book 2, chapter 9—was performed with three fingers of both palms held erect and two pressed down, to signify the Trinity of the Divine Persons. This practice ceased with **Simeon the Just** <note>a High Priest who, according to tradition, was the same Simeon who held the infant Jesus in the Temple</note>, who took Christ up in his arms...

For this reason, Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides, the influential medieval Jewish philosopher</note> states: from the time Simeon the Just <note>a high priest from the Second Temple period</note> died, his fellow priests ceased to bless the people using the "name of four letters" <note>the Tetragrammaton, the sacred name YHWH</note>, but instead they blessed them with a "name of twelve letters." This should be understood (says the same Galatinus <note>Pietro Galatino, a 16th-century scholar of Jewish tradition</note>) not as meaning that this name could be pronounced like other words, but rather to signify the ineffable essence of God which is expressed by this name. Therefore, the ancient Jews desired that the name *Jehovah* not be pronounced, but rather *Adonai* <note>meaning "Lord"</note>, because they said Moses had commanded this. On account of this ineffability, Rabbi Hakkadosh <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince, known as "the Holy One"</note> used to say that God has no known name, following the saying of Hermes Trismegistus: "He who exists is nameless; that is his name, for it cannot be spoken by a human mouth" <note>original Greek: *ὅτι ὁ ὢν ἀνώνυμος ἔστι τὸ ὄνομα, οὐ δύναται ἀνθρωπίνῳ στόματι λαληθῆναι*</note>. Even the "evil demon" <note>a term the author uses for pagan spirits behind oracles</note> did not remain silent on this. For the Delphic Apollo, when someone asked what God was, replied: "whatever the name, it is not even contained by a word" <note>original Greek: *ὅ τι τὸ ὄνομα, μηδὲ λόγῳ χωρέμενον*</note>. His name cannot be captured by speech. Yet the Jews say that this name will be made manifest in the time of the Messiah. This is most true, since in the name of the Messiah all shall be blessed, and he himself will reveal his own name and the name of the Father. The Talmudic scholars record these traditions in the tractates *Yoma* (folio 39, verse 2) and *Eruvin* (folio 18, verse 2). From this, the blessings of the Gospel are set in opposition to the curses of the Law; this was once foreshadowed on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal <note>the locations where Israel declared blessings and curses upon entering the Promised Land</note>. And Nachmanides <note>Moses ben Nahman, a prominent medieval rabbi and scholar</note>, who is by no means an ordinary teacher among the Hebrews, suggests by a probable conjecture that Gerizim was positioned toward the South because that has always been considered the "right side" of the world (since we face toward the East). The right side is considered more auspicious, whereas Ebal was toward the North, a region which Jeremiah often cries out is ill-omened (Jeremiah 1:14, 4:6, 6:1, and other places), as it was destined to eventually release great destruction upon the human race.

Just as the figure of Joshua <note>The Latin text uses *Iosue*, which is the same name as Jesus in both Hebrew and Greek, highlighting the typological link</note> led the Israelites by the hand into the land of Canaan, rather than Abraham or Moses, so too has Christ, the true Joshua, opened the way for us into the heavenly Canaan—a path not provided by the law of nature or moral law. For this reason, in Psalm 37, the possession of Canaan is presented by the Psalmist as a distinguished blessing or gift, since nothing was more pleasing to the Israelites than the possession of that land. In Scripture, this land is called such pre-eminently <note>original Greek: *κατ' εξοχην*</note> and by its very title, because it serves as a type for the "land of the living." And so, in Daniel and elsewhere, it is called the "beautiful land" <note>original Hebrew: *צבי ארץ* (*Tzvi Eretz*), referring to the land of Israel as a place of glory</note>. See Ezekiel 20:6 and Daniel 11:16. From this comes that promise in the fifth commandment of the Law: that children who obey their parents shall be "long-lived" <note>original Greek: *μακροχρονίους*</note> in the land which God was to give them.

Furthermore, we shall now proceed to demonstrate with a clear example that Christ, the true Melchizedek, was the foundation and origin of all blessings; namely, through the blessing of Jacob and the rejection of Esau. For the blessing seemed rightfully to belong to Esau, and almost every legal right demanded it. Thus, the father’s blessing should have deservedly rested upon the head of Esau, not Jacob, for the following reasons:

I. **By natural law**, because Jacob was the younger, while Esau was the firstborn. 
II. **By the law of nations and custom**, for the custom had become established that the firstborn should be the masters of their brothers and the heirs to the father's goods and blessing. 
III. **By the intention of the father, Isaac**, who wished to bless Esau and not Jacob. 
IV. **Because Jacob was not blessed except under the name**, person, clothing, voice, and appearance of Esau himself; indeed, he received it under the firm assertion that he *was* Esau. Therefore, he acted as a proxy for the other, and was promising and stipulating on behalf of his brother. 
V. **Because fraud and deceitful cunning were involved**, even at the very moment when Esau was engaged in an act of obedience. 

No defense will hold weight if someone objects that the brothers had made a pact, and that Esau had sold his birthright for a bit of food. For, in the first place, Esau was "supplanted" by Jacob—hence his name was truly Jacob <note>original Hebrew: *יעקוב* (*Ya'akov*), meaning "supplanter" or "one who trips up by the heel"</note>. Secondly, there was an "enormous loss" <note>term: <term>læsio enormis</term>; a legal concept where a contract is voided because the price paid is so vastly lower than the value of the item</note> (as the legal scholars say); for what proportion is there between a bit of stew and the right of the firstborn? Moreover, the brothers could determine nothing that went against the father’s right and free power. At the very least, Jacob should not have deceived and mocked his father, who was old and blind.

And so that we may examine these things more deeply, consider the rule established by St. Augustine and (so to speak) canonized in the Church: it holds that whenever something "irregular" occurs in the lives and deeds of the saints—something that strikes against laws, good morals, or the light of nature—one must most firmly believe that some mystery lies hidden and concealed there. In such cases, a cause is given for those effects which is sublime and above the order of nature, which must necessarily move all other natural and ordinary causes, just as secondary things supply whatever they are to the primary cause. 

This mystery is all the more evident because it has been clearly revealed by God, such as this matter concerning Jacob and Esau, which is revealed to Rebecca in Genesis 25: namely, that there are two nations in the womb, and that, contrary to the law of nature, the firstborn would be a servant to his brother. Here, several brilliant mysteries shine forth:

I. **The cutting off of the Jewish people and the grafting in of the Gentiles.** For in them the oracle was fulfilled: *the elder shall serve the younger*. For Esau, the firstborn, was deprived of the blessing; thus, mystically, the Jewish nation, which was God's firstborn, was cut off, and the wild olive tree <note>A reference to the metaphor in Romans 11 of the Gentiles being grafted into the lineage of faith</note> was grafted in its place.

II. **The dominance of the spirit over the flesh** in that struggle of the holy twins during the "generation of grace." Since our regeneration <note>The spiritual process of being "born again" or renewed in faith</note> is imperfect and the flesh lusts against the Spirit, the "elder" in that fight nevertheless serves the "younger," because the flesh is subjected to the dominion of the Spirit, and is finally subdued and tamed.

With these things established, the previously mentioned arguments fall apart. **I.** Regarding **natural law**, because the privileges of the flesh cannot hinder God’s free arrangement; He is a debtor to no one, and as the **High Priest according to the order of Melchizedek** <note>original Greek: <term>κατὰ τάξιν Μελχισεδὲκ</term></note> He bestows blessings on whom He wills. And Melchizedek, the divine giver of blessings, reveals hidden wisdom when He uses wicked instruments so wisely; just as He displays goodness when He bestows a blessing at the very moment when the sins of mortals would invite and even provoke Him to strike with the lightning of terrible **anathemas** <note>A formal curse or total rejection by God.</note>. That Apostolic blessing (the same Thuanus says in that place) is believed to have had its origin in an old sleepless man’s dream <note>original: *agrypnij somnio*. Cregut is mockingly suggesting that a foundational political legitimacy was based on a hallucination.</note>; that is, from a letter of Pope Stephen II recorded by Regino, Abbot of Prüm, in his *Chronicles* under the year of salvation 753. 

In that letter, it is said that when the Pope had come into Gaul to seek help from Pippin against Aistulf, the King of the Lombards, he suffered a dangerous illness; whether he was delirious while awake or dreaming while he rested, he says that Saints Peter and Paul appeared to him in the shrine of Saint-Denis. He claims they healed him with their very touch in the presence of Dionysius <note>Saint Denis, the patron saint of France.</note> himself. At their prompting, while he was consecrating the altar, during the offering of the sacrifice, he anointed Pippin and his two sons, Charles and Carloman, as kings. He also marked Pippin’s wife, Bertrada <note>original: *Bertrandam*</note>, with the grace of the Holy Spirit. Then, the Frankish nobles, having been consecrated by the Apostolic blessing through the authority of Saint Peter granted to him by Christ, bound their faith so that they would never thereafter appoint a king for themselves from any other lineage, nor from those descending from their progeny, except from the blood of those whom Divine Providence had chosen to protect the Apostolic faith, and whom it had deigned to consecrate to royal sublimity by the heavenly anointing through the Vicar of Saint Peter. 

The same story is brought forth by Sigibert <note>Sigebert of Gembloux (c. 1030–1112), a medieval chronicler.</note>, who also writes that every foreigner is forbidden from invading the Franco-Gallic kingdom by an Apostolic anathema <note>A formal curse or excommunication.</note>. From this, the Guises wanted it to seem that the Apostolic blessing was granted only to the Carolingians <note>The dynasty of Charlemagne and Pippin.</note>, which Hugh <note>Hugh Capet, founder of the Capetian dynasty, whom the Guises viewed as a usurper of the Carolingian line.</note> violated by usurping the kingdom. Thus far, Thuanus has been mocking "The United" and especially the Guise faction, who, by abusing the beautiful name of "blessings," were striving to invade the kingdom. They falsely claimed that the successors of Hugh were rebellious toward the Church, and that for the kingdom's destruction, they had introduced that abominable error which the French call the "Liberty of the Gallican Church" <note>The Gallican Liberties were a set of traditions that limited the Pope’s power in France in favor of the French monarch.</note>, which they claimed was the sole refuge for the Albigensians and now for the Lutherans.

But truly, before you observe this one thing concerning Papal blessings from the languages—which will be judged a paradox by most—namely, that even if no royal family ever existed...

Although the family of the French kings from the lineage of Charlemagne <note>original: *Caroli magni*</note> was so closely joined with the Papacy, and obtained so many blessings from the Roman Pontiff, yet none is found to have been exposed to such sudden ruin and such a mournful catastrophe. For in the span of twenty-eight years elapsed between the year 862 and the year 889, the lineage of Louis the Pious <note>original: *Ludovici Probi*</note> lost twelve kings and eight other princes, all of whom died in the flower of their youth; and from that numerous progeny, once the twenty-eight year cycle had passed—indeed, scarcely had it passed—no one remained except for four natural or adulterous sons: Arnulf <note>original: *Arnoldus*</note>, born of Carloman, King of Bavaria; and Zuentibold, Ratold, and Bernard, the sons of Charles the Fat <note>original: *Caroli Crassi*</note>; and a single legitimate son, a minor and so contemptible that he was reserved to be the plaything of storms and tempests. This was, of course, Charles the Simple <note>original: *Carolus Simplex*</note>, who after a captive life of miseries left his inheritance to Louis "From-Beyond-the-Sea" <note>original: *Ludouico vltramarino*; Louis IV of France, so named because he was raised in exile in England</note>, which was then passed on to his descendants as well.

Therefore, if the Papal blessing has always been so deadly—and as deadly as the blessing of the symbolic Melchizedek is restorative—then surely that ominous blessing ought not to be called a blessing so much as a curse; unless you would call it a "blessing" in the same way that among the Hebrews "to bless" <note>original: בּרך (*barak*)</note> in the *Piel* <note>A Hebrew grammatical form that can sometimes express the opposite of a word's root meaning as a euphemism.</note> signifies "to curse." And it is as the Apostle uses the word "blessing" <note>original: εὐλογίαν (*eulogian*)</note> in Romans 16:18; though this word otherwise signifies a benediction, in this place it denotes flattery. *For they that are such* (says the Apostle) *serve not our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly; and by good words and fair speeches <note>original: εὐλογίας</note> deceive the hearts of the simple.* Of this sort are the "blessings" of the Roman sycophants, with which they are accustomed to flatter the kings whom they strive to fascinate with their sycophancy. For since "to bless" <note>Greek: εὐλογεῖν</note> is, in Greek, "to praise" <note>Greek: ἐπαινεῖν</note>, and a "blessing" <note>Greek: εὐλογία</note> becomes a laudatory speech, this will primarily pertain to flatterers, as Plutarch beautifully describes in his published book on how to tell a flatterer from a friend. And although "blessing" <note>Greek: εὐλογία</note> is also taken for a favorable prayer, it nevertheless rightly fits the Pope and his emissaries—those bread-cutting <note>Greek: ψωμοκόποις (*psomokopois*); a term for parasites or those who live off others’ tables</note> dealers in trifles who devour the simple-minded under the pretext of blessings. From this come those monstrosities of the Canonists in Canon Law: *Although touch and kisses are preludes to incontinence...*
