## Zz iii

...in the case of laypeople, but it is otherwise in the case of Clerics; for a Cleric is presumed to do *these things out of charity and good zeal. And in the gloss of the Decree <note>A reference to the *Decretum Gratiani*, the fundamental collection of canon law for the Roman Catholic Church in the 12th century.</note>: If, therefore, a Cleric embraces a woman, it shall be interpreted that he does this for the sake of blessing her.* And lest the reader should pass over this "beautiful" interpretation without fruit, he is thus cautioned in the margin: <margin>A Cleric embracing a woman is presumed to be doing good.</margin> An excellent blessing, truly! Was it in this way that the Apostles burned with charity? This is that saying: *love thinks no evil* <note>original Greek: *ἀγάπη οὐ λογίζεται τὸ κακὸν*</note>, *Charity thinketh no evil.* 1 Cor. xiii. 5.

Thus far we have explained the first priestly action, namely blessing; the second follows, which is to receive tithes. From this, the superiority <note>original Greek: *ὑπεροχή*</note> of Melchizedek over Abraham is further evident. For who is greater: the one who gives, or the one who receives tithes? Surely, whoever receives them—indeed, it is a great thing to receive tithes from anyone—but what about receiving them from a priest, from a Patriarch, from the Father of the faithful? For tithes in the Old Testament were threefold:
I. **Common tithes**, which were given to the Levites <note>The tribe of Israel designated for religious duties.</note> in compensation for the twelfth part of the land, which otherwise might have been owed to the Levites. Concerning these, see *Levit. xxvii. 30.*
II. **The tithe of tithes**, which the Levites paid from their own tithes to the priests for their ministry. *Num. xviii. 26.*
III. **The tithes of the poor**, which in every third year from the Sabbath of the land were yielded not only to the Levites, but were held in common with the poor, widows, orphans, and travelers. *Deut. xiv. 28.*
The wealthy gave to the poor, and even superiors gave to inferiors, not in recognition of power, but either as compensation for services or as alms. And although in this third manner it does not seem true that the one receiving tithes is more excellent than the one giving them; nevertheless, this is rightly established regarding tithes of the first and second kind. Tithes were for the Levites in place of an inheritance, for they possessed nothing except a few cities to inhabit. Therefore, at that time tithes were necessary by the prescription of the law; but before the law they were free and at one's discretion (*Gen. xiv. 20.*), by the example of Melchizedek and Abraham. The same should be thought concerning vows. *Gen. xxviii. Jacob vowed, etc.*

Therefore, from what has been said, it is clear that Melchizedek was a High Priest...

# ANTHONY CREGUT

...priest raised up with great eminence <gloss>original Greek: ὑπεροχῇ, meaning superiority or excellence</gloss> above others; for if the High Priest according to the order of Aaron <gloss>original Greek: κατὰ τάξιν Ἀαρὼν</gloss> excelled other Priests and Levites—insofar as the other Priests paid the "tithes of tithes" <note>Under Mosaic Law, the Levites received a tenth (tithe) from the people, and then gave a tenth of that portion to the High Priest.</note> to the High Priest—how much more shall Melchizedek himself be more excellent than the High Priest, since the High Priest was himself tithed by Melchizedek? For by tithing Abraham, he also tithed Levi and all the Levites who were "in the loins of Abraham" <note>A biblical idiom meaning they were his future descendants, yet to be born.</note>, as the Apostle himself gathers in the Epistle to the Hebrews. 

Nor can the same immediately be inferred concerning Christ, as if he himself had also been tithed by Melchizedek; even though he was also in the loins of Abraham, from which in Scripture he is called the "son of Abraham." For besides the fact that Melchizedek was a "figure" <note>In theology, a "figure" or "type" is a historical person who foreshadows a future person; here, Melchizedek foreshadows Christ.</note> of Christ—and therefore the figure cannot be more worthy than the one it represents, nor consequently can it tithe him—it must be added that Christ was indeed in the loins of Abraham, and therefore called the son of Abraham, but in an extraordinary manner. For he was conceived by the Holy Spirit, and the blood of the Virgin from which Christ was to be formed was sanctified by the Holy Spirit working through a creative act <gloss>original Greek: δημιουργικῶς</gloss>; which is expressed in Luke 1:35 by a very rare phraseology: *The power of the Highest shall overshadow you* <gloss>original Greek: δύναμις ὑψίστου ἐπισκιάσει σοι</gloss>. 

And in Romans 1, Christ is not said to be born from the flesh, but *having become* <gloss>original Greek: γενόμενος</gloss> of the seed of David according to the flesh <gloss>original Greek: κατὰ σάρκα</gloss>, so that the extraordinary mode of his generation might be understood. Wherefore, Christ is specifically called the son of Abraham and of David; why, to be sure, is he called the son of those alone, and not of other ancestors? Because, clearly, the promises were made to Abraham and David: and because the seal of those promises was given to Abraham—which is circumcision, the seal of the righteousness of faith—and David was peculiarly chosen by God to be the leader of his people. These things are surely so observed in Scripture that it appears the generation of Christ was supernatural, not carnal, and thus Christ was the "blessed seed" of Abraham with respect to the promise. 

Therefore, although he was thus the son of Abraham and of David, such that he was truly their Lord as well, he was not tithed by Melchizedek, because he was not in the loins of Abraham in the same manner as Levi, but was born in an extraordinary way. ### REVEALER OF SECRETS

...the true Melchizedek and the High Priest of the faithful receives tithes. These tithes, however, in the New Testament are no longer physical, but spiritual, just as all offerings and sacrifices have become. Regarding the tithes for pastors, no specific law is established in the Gospel. To be sure, God commanded that pastors be supported by the faithful, as in 1 Corinthians 9:14: *Those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel.* Also Matthew 10:10: *The laborer is worthy of his reward.* Likewise in Galatians 6 and 1 Timothy 5:17. But concerning the method—whether pastors ought to be supported by tithes, as the Levites were under the Law, or by some other means—the Scripture of the New Testament prescribes nothing. Nor is the same reasoning now supplied as it was for the Levites of old; for since the Levites (unlike their brothers and the other tribes) were not permitted to possess a portion of the land of Canaan, God willed that this lack be compensated by tithes. In this way, the Levites could live among their brothers and more easily manage the affairs of the Church.

Absurdly, therefore, the Roman Pontiff <note>The Pope.</note>—acting as if he were a second Melchizedek—receives tithes not only from those he calls the "laity," but even from the clergy; indeed, other priests pay him "tithes of tithes." <note>A reference to the *decimae decimarum*, a tax where the lower clergy paid a tenth of their income to the higher hierarchy.</note> The first king in France who permitted the extraction of those tithes was Charles, nicknamed "the Fair" <note>Charles IV, reigned 1322–1328.</note>, the son of Philip, who intended to divide them with the Pope in the year 1326. The Pope then abused these funds to wage war against the Emperor. Now, since all legalistic requirements of the Law have been abolished in the New Testament, are the Papists not "Judaizing" <note>original: *Iudaizant*; a theological term for Christians who improperly adopt Jewish Mosaic laws.</note> when they demand tithes? Indeed, are they not "Gentilizing" <note>original: *Gentilizant*; acting like pagans or heathens.</note>, since the Devil (that "ape of God") <note>A common medieval and early modern phrase suggesting that Satan imitates divine rituals to lead people into idolatry.</note> long ago taught his own priests to imitate the customs of the Levites? Thus the Romans paid tithes to Hercules; and Lucullus, according to Plutarch, consecrated a tenth of the spoils to the gods which he had brought back from the Mithridatic War. Liber (also known as Bacchus) <note>The god of wine and ecstasy.</note>, after he had conquered the Scythians, destined a tenth part of the spoils for Jove <note>Jupiter.</note>, according to Ovid in Book 3 of the *Fasti*. The same was performed by King Cyrus after the Lydians were subdued.

But just as none of these things are rightfully owed to false priests, so on the contrary, we owe ourselves and all our possessions to the true Melchizedek—that is, to Christ. Therefore, we should offer those things cheerfully...

JUST AS that war undertaken by Abraham was not for the purpose of plundering, but was begun for the glory of God and love for one's neighbor, so too the final part of it—the division of the spoils—is directed toward the same end. This is shown by the Patriarch in two ways: first, by the oath, which is a celebration of the Divine name; and second, by his disdain for the spoils, even down to the smallest part. Here, three things are to be considered, with God's help <note>original: σὺν Θεῷ (syn Theo)</note>: I. *The Oath itself.* II. *The object of the oath.* III. *The formula of the oath.*

I. Regarding the *Oath*; Not every oath is lawful. Therefore, in this matter, the blessed have held the middle ground and avoided extremes. For we must not, like the Anabaptists <note>A radical Protestant group that, among other things, strictly interpreted the Bible to forbid all swearing of oaths, which they believed were prohibited by Jesus.</note>, rigidly condemn all oaths because of what is said in Matthew 5:34: *Do not swear at all: neither by heaven, for it is God's throne: nor by the earth, etc.* For those fanatics judge those words to apply to certain "perfect" individuals. In the original Greek <note>original: autographo</note> it is: *neither by heaven; nor by the earth* <note>original: μήτε ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ; μήτε ἐν τῇ γῇ</note>. This follows the Hebrew idiom, where the letter *beth* <gloss>the second letter of the Hebrew alphabet (ב)</gloss> is often placed as a marker for swearing, as in Genesis 22:16 and Joshua 2:12. It is similar among the Arabs: *by God* <note>original: billahi</note>; and *by the earth* <note>original: bilardi</note>. The formula for swearing an oath was also common among the Pagans, as in Virgil: *I swear by the stars* <note>original: per sidera iuro</note>.

Nevertheless, if the Anabaptists themselves would look more closely at the nature of an oath, they certainly would not condemn them entirely. For properly speaking, an oath is a true confession and invocation of the true God, by which we call upon God as a witness to our conscience, and also as a Judge and avenger if we lie, or if we behave with fraud or deceit in our assertion. From this it is clearly established that an oath is made for the glory of God. Far from being something to be blamed, we should instead judge it to be a splendid means of glorifying God. For whenever human affairs are tangled and uncertain, such that no way out can be found—just as nothing is safer than to flee to God's providence, as Abraham did, saying, *The Lord will provide*; so too in uncertain and doubtful matters, when no human counsel or help is available, we flee to God when we swear, seeking His truth, omniscience, justice, and authority—

strictness and supreme law we call *sovereign* <note>original: αὐτοκρατορικὸν (autokratorikon), referring to absolute or imperial authority</note>. The words of Basilides found in Eusebius’s *Church History*, book 6, chapter 5, do not favor the error of the Anabaptists <note>A radical Reformation group that refused to take any oaths, citing a literal interpretation of Jesus's command in the Sermon on the Mount.</note>. Basilides said before his martyrdom that it was not lawful for him to swear that he was a Christian. However, he understood this to refer to the vain and reckless oaths into which he was being provoked by his companions.

First, therefore, an oath is a confession and invocation of the name of God; it is indeed an act that makes one weigh a matter of the greatest value. For we value the confession and invocation of God’s name so highly because, through *synecdoche* <term>Synecdoche is a figure of speech where a part of something is used to represent the whole; here, "swearing" represents the entirety of religious worship.</term>, these acts signify the whole of religious worship and piety. This is according to Romans 10: *Whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.* What should we then think of the oath, which likewise, according to the style of Scripture, signifies the whole of religious worship? The words of Isaiah in chapter 19:18 are explicit: *In that time there shall be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the language of Canaan and swearing to the Lord of hosts* <note>original Hebrew: נשבעות ליהוה צבאות (nishba'ot l'Yehovah tzeva'ot)</note>. This is a prophecy concerning the calling of the Gentiles, in which Egypt is used as a synecdoche for all nations, just as in verse 24 Egypt and Assyria are mentioned. To this we should also refer what is found in Romans 14:11: *and every tongue shall confess to God* <note>original Greek: καὶ πᾶσα γλῶσσα ἐξομολογήσεται τῷ Θεῷ</note>. *Shall confess*, that is, shall worship me and acknowledge me as God. For in Isaiah 45:23, these are the words: *By myself I have sworn* <note>original Hebrew: בי נשבעתי (bi nishbati)</note>; *the word has gone out of my mouth in righteousness and shall not be recalled, that unto me every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall swear.* Where Isaiah says, *Every tongue shall swear*, Paul explains it with these words: *Every tongue shall confess.* This is because a sworn oath is a true and open confession of that God whom we call upon as a witness and an avenger of perjury. To use God’s name reverently and religiously in weighty and just causes is truly to worship God, and to believe that all things are known and seen by Him, and that He rewards those who swear truly and affects those who swear falsely with punishments. Hence, besides the previously praised passage of Isaiah 45, in chapter 48:1, Jehovah speaks thus: *Unto me every knee shall bow: every tongue shall swear.* He is speaking of the nations that would one day worship God. It is for this reason that the same Scripture testifies that swearing by anything other than God is a species of false worship, since no creature can be worshipped in place of God. And to this pertains that passage of Deuteronomy 6:13 and 10:20: *You shall swear by His name, not [by others]—*

...you will follow other Gods and swear by his name: *He is your praise, and your God.* <note>Deuteronomy 10:21</note> For this reason, Tertullian <note>An early Christian author (c. 155–220 AD) known for his defense of Christianity against Roman paganism.</note> asserts against the heathens that when Socrates mocked the Gods of his fellow citizens, he was accustomed to swear by an oak, a goat, or a dog. is an oath, *But the word of the oath, which came after the law, appointed the Son, who has been consecrated forever.* <note>original: *At sermo iurisiurandi post legem concepti, filium constituit, qui in æternum est sanctificatus*, quoting Hebrews 7:28.</note> This is because the Levitical priesthood was established without an oath; but, by contrast, the priesthood <term>according to the order</term> <note>original Greek: κατὰ τάξιν (*kata taxin*).</note> of Melchizedek was established with an oath. Likewise, the Angel of the Covenant in Revelation 10:5-6 &c. *swears by Him who lives forever and ever that there should be time no longer.*

Therefore, since an oath is proved to be legitimate both by God’s command and by His own example, yet men so frequently abuse the oath that they do not glorify God's name with it, but impiously profane it. This is expressly forbidden by the third commandment of the Law, where the Law says, *You shall not take the name of God in vain.* <note>Exodus 20:7.</note> These words <note>original Hebrew: לא תשא לשוא (*lo tisa lishav*).</note>—*you shall not take*, or *you shall not swear in vain*—signify universally any abuse of the name of God. For:

i. It is taken in vain when men swear <note>original Hebrew: שקר (*sheqer*), meaning "falsely" or "lyingly".</note> falsely; for in doing so, they call upon the God of truth to bear witness to a lie as if He were a false witness, which is a heinous sin.

ii. The name of God is taken in vain when an oath is made rashly, or for a trivial matter of no value. For to continually call upon God for the most insignificant reasons is seen as an affront to the majesty of such a great divinity; nor is the habit free from the danger of perjury. But (as was said above) the name of God must be used reverently and religiously in serious and just causes.

iii. When those who are furious, frantic, children, or those who are not in control of their own legal standing swear; for just as they could not make vows to God under the Law, so it is not lawful for them to swear.

iv. When someone swears for illicit things, because then the oath is a bond of iniquity and cannot be fulfilled except through crime.

v. Whenever any of these three conditions are missing from the oath: namely, *truth*, *justice*, and *judgment*. <note>A reference to Jeremiah 4:2, often cited as the three "companions" of a lawful oath.</note>

vi. When someone uses lots and illicit methods of this kind, such as <term>Geomancy</term> <note>Divination by interpreting markings on the ground or patterns formed by tossed handfuls of soil.</note>, <term>Hydromancy</term> <note>Divination by water.</note>, <term>Necromancy</term> <note>Communicating with the dead.</note>, <term>Lecanomancy</term> <note>Divination using a basin of water.</note>, <term>Onomancy</term> <note>Divination by names.</note>, <term>Arithmancy</term> <note>Divination by numbers.</note>, <term>Botanomancy</term> <note>Divination by plants or herbs.</note>, <term>Stichomancy</term> <note>Divination by pulling random lines from books.</note>, &c. Add to this games of dice and gambling, and furthermore the abuse of incantations, "little prayers," and magical symbols for sorcerous deceptions, spells, charms, for love knots and bonds, for amulets, for taming animals, and for either inflicting or driving away diseases; for these symbols...

It is for this reason, out of a horror for blasphemy, that the Jews used to tear their clothes. And St. Augustine observed from Matthew's account that the veil of the temple was torn at the same time that Christ breathed his last; where Theophylact <note>A Byzantine archbishop and biblical exegete.</note> noted quite skillfully that, just as the Jews—upon hearing blasphemies—immediately tore and shredded their garments in horror, so too when those same Jews were impiously blaspheming against God and the <unclear>Messiah</unclear>

The veil of the temple was torn, just as all nature roared and, as it were, paid its last respects at the death of Christ. This is why in Jeremiah 26, it is charged as a crime against the king and his servants that when the prophetic book was surrendered to the fire, they did not tear their garments—just as King Hezekiah did when he heard the blasphemies of <term>Rabshakeh</term> <note>A high-ranking Assyrian official whose taunts against God are recorded in Isaiah 36-37.</note> in Isaiah 37. For the same reason, in Acts 12, Herod Agrippa perished because he did not tear his royal robe <note>original Latin: *vestem regiam non scidit*. In context, Herod allowed himself to be worshipped as a god; his failure to show the ritual horror of a mortal usurping divine glory led to his divine punishment.</note>. However, in Leviticus 21, the law forbade only the Priests from doing this, because their ornaments were holy. Therefore, <term>Caiaphas</term>, driven by fury to incite those present toward the destruction of Christ, was the first of all the High Priests to tear his garment—and he did so wrongly. For if Jonathan the High Priest is said to have torn his garments in 1 Maccabees 11, most scholars argue that those were not priestly garments but military ones; this is evident because he is said to have returned to the battle. For when verse 71 says, *“So Jonathan, tearing his clothes, put dust on his head and prayed,”* verse 72 adds, *“And turning back against them in battle, he put them to flight.”* Therefore, Jonathan was not in a formal assembly, but in the heat of conflict, and he tore his clothes not because of blasphemy, but because of the shameful flight of his soldiers—imitating, as a leader, the commander Joshua, as seen in Joshua 7. Thus, in Numbers 14, when Israel grumbled in the wilderness, the leaders of the people tore their clothes, but Moses and Aaron did not.

Furthermore, so great is the horror of blasphemies that the <term>Holy Tongue</term> <note>A traditional term for the Hebrew language.</note> did not dare to express them by their own or explicit name, but by an opposite word. It does so not <note>original Greek: *δυσφημικῶς* (dysphemistically, or using harsh words)</note>, but by <term>euphemism</term> <note>original Greek: *κατ’ εὐφημίαν* (speaking well to avoid offense)</note>. For it uses the word <note>Hebrew: *barak* (ברך)</note>, which in the <term>Piel</term> <note>An intensive form of the Hebrew verb.</note> form means "to curse," even though the primary root in the <term>Kal</term> <note>The simple or basic form of the Hebrew verb.</note> form means "to bless." Thus, just as the Holy Tongue covers indecent words with decent ones, it wished to veil the horror of blasphemy under the cover of a word of praise. We see this in Job 1:5: *“perhaps my sons have cursed God”*—though the Hebrew says *“blessed.”* So too in verse 11: *“unless he curses you to your face,”* which means openly and with all reverence for the divine cast aside. Likewise, in 1 Kings 21:13: *“Naboth cursed God and the king.”*

An ancient metaphor for condemnation, derived from using black stones for a "guilty" vote in court.</note> the impious blasphemies of Pseudo-Christians, which strike horror even into the Jews and Turks. Is this the humility of the "servant of the servants [of God]"? <note>The author is mocking the Pope's official title, *Servus servorum Dei*, contrasting it with his perceived arrogance.</note>

Without a doubt, all these things draw their origin from the First Deceiver <note>original: *protopseusto*, a Greek term for the Devil as the "first liar."</note>, as is evident from his various oracles recorded by ancient authors. *I say to you, son of Aeacus, that the Romans you can conquer,* <note>The famous ambiguous oracle given to Pyrrhus: *Aio te Aeacida Romanos vincere posse*. In Latin grammar, it could mean "you can conquer the Romans" or "the Romans can conquer you."</note> and *Croesus, by crossing the Halys, [will destroy a great empire],* <note>Croesus destroyed his own empire, not his enemy's.</note> or *Lord, be secure, the enemies shall enter,* and so forth. Also, in the 28th chapter of the first book of Samuel, he [the spirit] gave an ambiguous answer to Saul: *You and your sons shall be with me tomorrow*; which is not to be understood as being in the same state or condition as Samuel.

And let these things suffice regarding the vices that occur in the taking of oaths. Now, however, before we proceed further, might it not seem to someone that Abraham’s oath <note>Referring to Genesis 14:22–23, where Abraham swears to the King of Sodom that he will take nothing from the spoils of war.</note> was perhaps rash and taken for a trivial cause? For why did he not refuse those spoils of the King of Sodom with a single word? Ought he to have leaped so easily into swearing an oath? Especially since it is right to use the name of God sparingly and only in cases of urgent necessity. Calvin <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), the French theologian and reformer.</note> rightly responds that Abraham had two reasons for swearing. For because crooked men are accustomed to measuring others by their own yardstick, they rarely have faith in simple words. Therefore, that King would have thought Abraham was not seriously waiving his right to the spoils unless the name of God had been invoked. Secondly, it was of great importance that it be obvious to everyone that he had not waged a mercenary war. He had to be carefully on guard against this, not so much for his own sake, but out of zeal for the glory of God, upon which some stain of ill-repute might have been cast. Furthermore, Abraham wanted to arm himself with the name of God as a shield against all the enticements of greed; for the King of Sodom would not have ceased to test his mind in various ways, unless the opportunity had been cut off early by these flatly-rejected flatteries. Thus writes Calvin, judiciously as he always does.

# THE WORKS OF ANTOINE CRÉGUT <note>Antoine Crégut (1612–1701) was a French Reformed theologian and professor at Die and Valence.</note>

...and the invocation of the name of God signifies the whole of piety <term>synecdoche <note>original: *συνεκδοχικῶς*; a figure of speech where a part is used to represent the whole. Here, the author argues that "calling on God's name" stands in for all religious devotion.</note></term>. Nevertheless, this must also be treated explicitly at the present time. First, Scripture expressly commands that we swear by the name of God, not by created things; because the former is an act of piety, while the latter is impiety and a most wicked crime. For this reason, in Deuteronomy 6:13, three things are specifically claimed for God: fear, worship, and the oath. *Fear the Lord your God, and serve him, and swear by his name.* These instructions are repeated again in Deuteronomy 10:20.

Secondly, the oath—as even the Scholastic <note>The medieval "Schoolmen" or academic theologians, such as Thomas Aquinas.</note> thinkers themselves confess—is an act of <term>latria <note>original: *latriæ*; a Greek-derived term used in theology to describe the supreme worship reserved for God alone, as distinguished from *dulia*, the honor given to saints.</note></term>, which is reserved for God alone. Hence Thomas Aquinas, the father of the Schools, in *Summa Theologiae* II-II, question 89, article 6, in his response to the third point, writes: *The worship of latria is given to Him whose testimony is invoked by swearing.* And therefore it is commanded in Exodus 23: *You shall not swear by the name of foreign gods.* However, *the worship of latria is not given to creatures who are included in an oath according to the aforementioned ways—that is, as he said in his conclusion, insofar as divine truth shines through them, not according to the creatures themselves.* He demonstrates this in his response using the example of the Gospel: *Just as we swear by the Gospel—that is, by God, whose truth is revealed in the Gospel—and by the Saints, who believed and observed this truth.* And this type of oath he calls **by contestation** <note>original: *per contestationem*; calling upon God to stand as a witness to the truth of one's words.</note>; but he adds another kind, **by execration** <note>original: *per execrationem*; an oath where the speaker calls down a curse or divine punishment upon themselves or something they love if they are lying.</note>. And thus he begins: *In this oath, some creature is brought in so that divine judgment may be exercised upon it. And thus a man is accustomed to swear by his own head, or by his son, or by another thing which he loves.* In 2 Corinthians 1, Paul says: *I call God as a witness upon my soul.*

Furthermore, in the same question, article 4, Thomas has words most worthy of note: *An oath is an act of latria and of religion, by which one professes that God is of unfailing truth, and exalted and wise above all. Therefore, in that a man swears by God, he professes God to be the superior; as His truth is unfailing and His knowledge is universal.* And he brings forward the passage from Hebrews 6: *men swear by one greater than themselves.* and from the first book of the *Metaphysics* <note>By Aristotle.</note>: *an oath is the most honorable thing.* Hence it is that Scripture condemns oaths by creatures or by artificial and fictitious gods, except insofar as creatures are employed only as symbols and pledges of divine glory, not that the religious obligation of the oath is directed toward them. Hence Jeremiah 7...

<note>REVELATOR ARCANORVM: The title of Crégut's work.</note>

->*They swear by those who are not gods, which sufficiently indicates that one must swear by God alone.*<-

Furthermore, the conditions of the object by which one swears sufficiently prove that one must swear by God alone. For the object of the person swearing must be *omnipresent, omniscient, and omnipotent*—<term>the Knower of Hearts <note>original Greek: *καρδιογνώστης* (kardiognōstēs); a theological term for God's unique ability to see into the human soul and judge the truth of one's intentions.</note></term>. Finally, men would swear in vain by creatures, who lack the aforementioned conditions, nor could they even be the avengers of perjuries. 

But if examples are brought forward from Scripture concerning holy men who swore by creatures—such as Joseph in Genesis 42:16 swearing by the life of Pharaoh; Moses in Deuteronomy 4:26 by heaven and earth; or Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:31 by the glorying of the Corinthians—one of several explanations applies. Either those examples are proposed in Scripture merely as a matter of fact, not as a matter of law <note>original: *de facto, non de iure*; meaning the Bible records that they happened, but does not necessarily endorse them as legal or moral precedents.</note>; or they are only examples and not rules; or they are to be understood by us not *literally*, but *figuratively* and *symbolically*, as said above, insofar as creatures are symbols of God's glory. Or even, in those examples, they are not so much noted as oaths but as <term>obtestations <note>A solemn appeal or protestation calling something to witness.</note></term> and assertions.

Therefore, the Papists swear wrongly, and not without idolatry, when they swear religiously by creatures, such as by the Saints and by relics. Well known is the story in Serranus <note>Jean de Serres (1540–1598), a French historian and advisor to Henry IV.</note> and other historians concerning the Cross of Saint Lau <note>Saint Laud (Laudus), a 6th-century Bishop of Coutances. The "Cross of Saint Laud" in Angers was a famous relic used for swearing particularly solemn oaths.</note>, which was kept from ancient times among the people of Angers with old confidence and certainty: that if anyone should swear upon this cross and turn out to be a perjurer, he would die a tragic and mournful death before the year’s end. Hence it is that Louis XI, King of the Franks, when urged by his master of the horse, never wished to swear upon that cross; and because the King refused, the other man, accused of high treason, did not dare to commit himself to the King’s faith.

Therefore, that superstition of the Papists tastes of Heathenism. For the Heathens swore by Jupiter, Hercules, by the fortune of the Caesars, and by the stars. And just as the *Pater Patratus* <note>The "Father Spokesman," the chief official of the Roman college of priests (the Fetiales) who oversaw treaties and international oaths.</note> was the superintendent of oaths in Rome, Horace writes in Book 2, Epistle 1:

> *To you, while present, we bestow timely honors,*
> *And we set up altars for swearing by your name.*

Thus today the Papists, with <term>misguided zeal <note>original: *cacozelia*; a term used in rhetoric and theology to describe a perverse or poorly executed imitation of something good.</note></term>, swear upon the arms of Saint Anthony...

# ANTOINE CRÉGUT

This stands against what is held in Zephaniah 1:5, where those are condemned who *swear by their Milcom* <note>original: *Molechum*. This refers to the pagan deity of the Ammonites; the biblical passage condemns those who try to split their loyalty between God and idols.</note>. As for the Stoics, they considered an oath to be a trivial or playful matter. Zeno openly condemned them, and if ever he did swear, he did so mockingly "by the goatherd," just as Socrates swore "by the dog" or "by the plane tree." Unless, as we said above, we argue that Socrates condemned the superstitious oaths of the pagans—just as he condemned their idolatry—since they worshipped and swore by innumerable fictitious gods when there is, in fact, only one God.

However, in this regard, the Roman Pontiff <note>The Pope.</note> attempts something that exceeds all impiety, inasmuch as he <term>dispenses <note>To "dispense" in a legal or ecclesiastical sense means to grant a formal exemption from a law or a previously taken vow.</note></term> the subjects of a prince from their **oath of loyalty**. Indeed, he often releases others from oaths as well, which is surely to exalt himself above God. For he who releases a servant from the obedience he owes to his master claims for himself a status greater than that master. In this way, the Pope makes men perjurers, which is the extreme of impiety and a horrendous profanation of the divine name. Perjury breaks the bond of society among men; this is why the Turks refuse to enter into treaties with Christians, because the Pope grants dispensations from oaths. <note>Crégut refers to a common 17th-century Protestant argument that Catholic diplomatic reliability was undermined by the Pope's power to annul treaties made with "heretics" or "infidels."</note> This was something Murad <note>original: *Amurathes*; likely referring to the Ottoman Sultan Murad II.</note> experienced in the Hungarian war, but (as we said above) to the ruin of the Christians, the plundering of the kingdom of Hungary, and the death of the king. <note>This refers to the Battle of Varna (1444), where King Wladyslaw III broke a peace treaty with the Ottomans at the urging of a Papal legate, resulting in a disastrous Christian defeat.</note> Many examples of this kind of dispensation are found in the <term>Decrees <note>referring to the *Decretum Gratiani*, the foundational collection of Canon Law.</note></term>, Case 15, Question 6. Such is the case in the history of Pope Formosus, and likewise Paul IV, who violated oaths and drove others to do the same, not without great disgrace to the Christian name—even in the judgment of the Papists themselves. The history of the Gibeonites in Scripture is well known, regarding the descendants of Saul who were crucified because Saul had violated an oath of trust. For as related in 2 Samuel 21, when a famine pressed upon the Israelites for three years, David was warned by an oracle that it was because of the Gibeonites slain by Saul; he handed over seven of Saul’s descendants to be hanged, and after this was done, God was reconciled.

The first of all dispensations of an oath was made in the year of the Christian era 752, when Pope Zachary cast Childeric, King of the Franks, into a monastery, and Pepin was elected and substituted in his place. <note>This marks the end of the Merovingian dynasty and the rise of the Carolingians. Pope Zachary authorized the deposition of Childeric III, releasing the Frankish nobles from their oaths of allegiance so they could crown Pepin the Short.</note> He openly declared that he who exercised the functions of a king ought to bear the name and the royal insignia of a king.

# REVEALER OF SECRETS. 383

Before that dispensation <note>The practice of the Pope releasing subjects from their oaths of allegiance, discussed on the previous page.</note> no example exists in all of antiquity; on the contrary, history shows conduct entirely opposed to it. This business began under a bad omen, and was subsequently imitated by successors in the worst possible way.

Furthermore, in this section regarding the **object of the oath**, the words of Moses must be observed. For he records that Abraham spoke thus: *I have lifted my hand to the Lord God Most High, the possessor of heaven and earth.* <note>original Latin: *Levavi manum meam ad Dominum Deum excelsum, possessorem caeli & terrae.* See Genesis 14:22.</note> All of these words signify that He is the true object of an oath—He who is our Lord, and who holds over us the supreme and sovereign right <note>original Greek: $\alpha\upsilon\tau\omicron\kappa\rho\alpha\tau\omicron\rho\iota\kappa\grave{\omicron}\nu$ (*autokratorikon*). This refers to an absolute, independent power that answers to no one else.</note> by which He has the power to punish perjurers. Only *God* is the object of an oath; for this reason, He whom Abraham calls "Lord," he also calls "God." Moses also adds the title *Most High*, because He is so far exalted above men; and since He sits in the highest heavens, we must lift our hands toward Him when invoking and swearing by His name. Finally, he adds *possessor of heaven and earth*, because the matter at hand <note>In the biblical narrative, Abraham had just rescued people and property from four kings but refused to take any of the spoils for himself.</note> concerned spoils and the property of those who had been redeemed. Therefore, Abraham intended to show that it belongs to God, as the possessor of heaven and earth, to grant him possessions and temporal goods by blessing his labors. For this reason, he swears sacredly by God's name that he does not wish to possess the property of others unjustly, nor does he wish to own even a thread or a sandal-strap which the possessor of heaven and earth had not first bestowed upon him.

There remains the final chapter: namely, the **formula of the oath**. For men have hardly ever been more prolific or excessive than in their formulas for swearing. But to explain those formulas more distinctly, it is necessary to distinguish between the formulas used by the saints and those of profane men. Furthermore, these kinds of holy formulas can be examined in two ways: either as they were practiced in the <term>dispensation <note>The author uses the word "economy" (*oeconomia*), a theological term for the way God manages human history in different eras.</note></term> of the Old Testament, or as they were used in the dispensation of the New Testament. Likewise, the oaths of profane men are considered either as they were used by the Rabbis and other Jews, or by the Heathens, or even by Christians.

The formulas of the Saints in the dispensation of the Old Testament were:
1. By placing a hand under the thigh (Genesis 24:2). *And he said*

-> # ANTOINE CRÉGUT <-

Abraham spoke to the senior servant of his house, who was in charge of all that he had: ***put your hand now under my thigh.*** <note>original Latin: *pone nunc manum tuam sub femore tuo.* This refers to Genesis 24:2, where Abraham asks his servant to swear an oath regarding a wife for Isaac.</note> This rite has puzzled interpreters in various ways as they have searched for the reasons behind this ceremony, with some preferring one explanation and others another. Some believe that Abraham required this ceremony from the servant so that he might testify to his submission by the act of lowering and placing his hand. Augustine prefers to think this was done to signify his faith in the promised Messiah, in whom all the promises of God and his oaths were "Yes and Amen." <note>original Latin: *Ita & Amen.* A reference to 2 Corinthians 1:20, implying that all divine promises are fulfilled in Christ.</note> Or, perhaps by this sign he bound the servant by an oath in the name of the Messiah, who was destined to come forth from his "thigh" at the appointed time; for as Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Archbishop of Constantinople known for his preaching.</note> notes, <note>original Greek: ἐντεῦθεν ἡ ἀρχὴ τῆς γενήσεως τοῦ Ἰσαὰκ γέγονεν (*enteuthen hē archē tēs genēseōs tou Isaak gegonen*) — "from here the beginning of the generation of Isaac took place."</note> However, to the very learned Spanheim <note>Friedrich Spanheim (1600–1649), a Calvinist theologian and professor.</note> in his *Evangelical Doubts*, these views seemed more subtle than solid, as did the conjecture regarding the designation of circumcision.

Therefore, he considers a better reason to be that among the Eastern peoples, the **thigh** <note>Hebrew: ירך (*yarekh*)</note> was conceived as the principle of generation; hence the descendants of anyone are said to be **those coming out of his thigh.** <note>original Latin: *exeuntes è femore eius.* See Genesis 46:26.</note> This was done so they might testify how truly they desired their posterity to remain faithful to them (which was held among the chief blessings of God), and how truly they would fulfill this or that promise. Hence, this custom was ordinary in oath-taking, for in Genesis 47:29, Jacob requires the same from his son Joseph when he swore not to bury his father in Egypt. And in Josephus, <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note> Book 1 of *Antiquities*, chapter 16: <note>original Greek: γίνονται δὲ αἱ πίστεις αὗται τοῦτον τὸν τρόπον, ὑπὸ τοῖς μηροῖς ἀλλήλοις τὰς χεῖρας ἐπαγαγόντες, ἐπικαλοῦνται τὸν θεὸν μάρτυρα τῶν ἐσομένων (*ginontai de hai pisteis autai touton ton tropon, hypo tois mērois allēlois tas cheiras epagagontes, epikalountai ton theon martyra tōn esomenōn*).</note> *These pledges are made in this manner: by placing their hands under each other's thighs, they call upon God as a witness of things to come.* Therefore, just as Abraham lifted his hand according to the solemn rite (as we do today), so according to another rite, the hand was placed under the thigh. Nevertheless, the most learned interpreter judged the Christian interpretation to be very plausible—that the ancients swore in this way by Christ—yet he judges more simply that while servants swore to be faithful to their masters, they were accustomed to testify to their subjection by this ceremony, especially because (as it is said) this custom is still preserved in certain parts of the East.

<sig>Ccc</sig>

this ceremony was as if the servant had sworn by the holiness of the Divine covenant: because Circumcision was performed upon that part of the body. But whether Abraham was the original author of that rite is very uncertain, since he could have inherited it from his forefathers, as the custom appears to have been a formal one even then. There are others among the Jews who assert it was a symbol of subjection whenever a servant swore upon his master's thigh. 

As for us, to bring forward what we also think of this rite, we say that it should first be noted who had the right to demand an oath. Surely, those have the right who exercise some lordship or authority over others; for instance, a father can demand an oath from a son, especially in that time when fathers held supreme legal rights over their children, as is clear from the example of Jacob and Joseph in the previously cited passage of Genesis 47:29. Likewise, a master can demand it from a servant, as Abraham demands from his servant in this passage of Genesis 24:2. Finally, a magistrate may demand it from subjects, as is still observed today. 

Therefore, when those inferiors swore, they looked toward two superiors: namely, the father, master, or magistrate; and on the other hand, toward God, the supreme Lord of all. In the first position <note>original Greek: θέσει (*thesei*). In this context, it refers to the physical or social aspect of the ritual.</note> they used that symbol of subjection by placing the hand under the thigh. This was the simple meaning of this rite, as well as its original practice, just as even today inferiors place a hand above the knee as a sign of subjection when greeting their superiors. But in the second position <note>original Greek: θέσει (*thesei*). Here referring to the theological or spiritual aspect of the ritual.</note> because an oath is also added, we lift the eyes of the mind toward God, the supreme and unique object of all swearing. By looking toward God in this way, the Jews could contemplate His covenant, and therefore Circumcision; and those who knew the Messiah could also look to Him here as the "blessed seed" <note>A reference to the promise that all nations would be blessed through Abraham's offspring (the Messiah).</note>.

II. There is also an elliptical <note>In grammar, "elliptical" refers to a sentence where some words are omitted but understood by the reader.</note> mode of swearing in the Old Testament. For the conditional word *if* <note>original Hebrew: אִם (*im*)</note> in oaths or more serious assertions creates an elliptical way of speaking. This is clear in the following divine declaration, when Abraham said: *if from a thread even to a shoestring*, indeed, *if I shall take anything of all that is yours.* <note>Genesis 14:23. Abraham is swearing to the King of Sodom that he will not keep any of the spoils of war for himself.</note> In such cases, through *aposiopesis* <note>A rhetorical device where a speaker breaks off a sentence and leaves it unfinished, usually for dramatic effect or out of reverence. In oaths, the unspoken part is usually a curse: "If I do this, [then may God strike me dead]."</note> the part of the speech containing the calling down of a curse—should the swearer fail—is usually kept silent.

<meta>This page continues Crégut's analysis of oaths, moving from the physical ritual of "hand under the thigh" to the linguistic structure of Hebrew oaths. He explains how the Hebrew language uses omission (ellipsis) to avoid speaking aloud of curses or evil outcomes.</meta>

<page-num>386</page-num>

<header>ANTOINE CRÉGUT</header>

For just as nature shrinks from calling down evil upon itself, and charity shrinks from doing so to another, so the Hebrew language—here as often elsewhere, being most devoted to decency and holiness in speech—loves silence and does not express curses directly but uses an ellipsis <note>An ellipsis is the deliberate omission of words that are understood from the context.</note>. From this it follows that when the conditional particle *im* <note>original Hebrew: אם (*im*), meaning "if"</note> is used alone, it indicates a negative; but if the negative particle *lo* <note>original Hebrew: לא (*lo*), meaning "not"</note> is added to it, then it affirms. 1 Samuel 3:14: *I have sworn to the house of Eli: if the iniquity of the house of Eli shall be atoned for* <note>The implied meaning is: "it shall NOT be atoned for."</note>. Psalm 89:36: *Once have I sworn by my holiness: if I should lie to David* <note>The implied meaning is: "I will NOT lie."</note>.

But if a curse is sometimes expressed by men in an oath, even then, pious men do not give free rein to imprecations; instead, they restrain the evil through a decent periphrasis <note>A roundabout way of speaking to avoid blunt or offensive language.</note>, in this manner, 1 Kings 2:23: *May God do so to me and more also, if Adonijah has not spoken this word against his own life.* The same phrasing is found in 1 Kings 19:2 <note>Original text cites 19:3; modern Bibles place this in 19:2.</note>, Ruth 1:17, and Jeremiah 22:5.

There was also another elliptical form of swearing, in this manner: 1 Samuel 14:45: *As the Lord lives, if a hair of his head shall fall to the ground*—the sense is, *as he lives, as truly as God lives, etc.* The same reasoning applies when God himself swears, or when men swear by their own lives. As in Ezekiel 5:11: *As I live, says the Lord God, if I do not, etc.*—which is to say, *as I live, so shall I do to you, etc.* 2 Kings 2:2: *As the Lord lives and as your soul lives, if I leave you.* <note>original Hebrew: חי יהוה וחי נפשך אם אעזבך (*Chai Yehovah ve-chai napshecha im e’ezvecha*)</note>. Here it should be noted in passing that in these kinds of oath formulas, the Scripture speaks of God in one way, and of false gods or men in another. For concerning the true God, the word is said absolutely as *chai* <note>original Hebrew: חי (*chai*), meaning "living"</note>, but concerning gods and men it is said in the construct form as *chē* <note>original Hebrew: חי (*chē*), a grammatical variation used when the word is linked to the following noun</note>, as is clear from Amos 8:14 and 1 Samuel 20:3. Scripture thus suggests a distinction between God and men regarding the object of the oath; for we swear by the name of God primarily and by itself, because He is the true and sole object of an oath, but by creatures only secondarily, and only insofar as they are symbols of Divine glory.

III. Sometimes, in more serious protestations to defend their innocence and the glory of God, the pious seem to express curses of evil, as in Psalm 7:4: *David said, O Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is this iniquity in my hands, etc., let the enemy pursue...*

...the enemy [pursue] my soul, etc. <note>original: *inimicus animam meam*. This refers to Psalm 7:5, where David uses a conditional oath: "If I have done this... [then let] the enemy pursue my soul."</note> Likewise in Psalm 139 and Job 31; but strictly speaking, neither David, nor the Levites and all of Israel, nor Job are calling down curses upon themselves. Instead, they are testifying to their own innocence and piety, and thus they sufficiently confirm that they are not liable to those evils, insofar as they have not committed the things with which they are charged by their enemies.

Since, therefore, the Scriptures use *aposiopesis* <note>A rhetorical figure where a sentence is deliberately broken off, leaving the ending to be understood by the listener.</note>, do you see how rightly those people should be rebuked who, in their translations, express the curse explicitly? This is correctly argued by Johannes Buxtorf in his *Treasury of the Holy Language* <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629) was a famous scholar of Hebrew; his *Thesaurus Linguae Sanctae* was a standard reference work for biblical scholars.</note>, who noted all these things most excellently and piously. Therefore, it is wrongly read in those versions as, *May I perish and be destroyed, may God punish me*. And in the oaths of God, they translate in this way: *may I not live, I shall not be God, I shall lie*; these are things which can truly be said of a mortal and changeable creature, but concerning the immortal and immutable God, they can only be conceived of as impious. It is not, therefore, without reason that Scripture uses *aposiopesis*; since it is a figure of rhetoric, why should we eliminate it from Scripture, especially when there is a great reason for using it?

IV. The formula for an oath in the New Testament, which is used above all, is **Amen**. This is a Hebrew particle signifying truth, certainty, and trust. From this trust in prayers arises that solemn *epiphonema* <note>A striking concluding sentence or exclamation.</note> **Amen**; which they sing together like a song of victory <note>original Greek: ἐπινίκιον (*epinikion*)</note> over the already conquered enemies of calamities and miseries, with a certain holy dance of the heart. Christ often uses this assertion in the Gospel when he says, *Amen I say to you*. For example, in Luke 23:43, he said to the thief: *Amen I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise*. This solemn appeal was rightly suited to Him who truly is the *Amen, the faithful witness*, in whom all the promises of God are *Yes and Amen*.

Furthermore, it should be observed that Christ often uses that expression *Amen*; but he frequently emphasizes it by repeating it twice, doubling it in this manner: *Amen, amen*, for the sake of greater trust and certainty. Indeed, it has been noted by more than one person that John the Evangelist reports Christ doubling *Amen, amen* much more often than the other Evangelists, because John dealt with higher mysteries, and this [is suited to] the eagle [flying] higher... <note>In traditional Christian art and theology, St. John is symbolized by an eagle because his Gospel is considered the most spiritually elevated.</note>

# ANTOINE CREGUT

...is compared to a flying <note>The author is referring to the eagle, the traditional symbol of John the Evangelist, often depicted as an eagle because his Gospel "soars" to the heights of divine theology.</note> eagle, and is commonly surnamed John the Theologian. Because mysteries of this kind were quite abstract from the senses and difficult to believe, John introduces Christ repeating a solemn declaration in this way: *Amen, Amen* <note>original Latin: "Amén, Amén." In English Bibles, this is often translated as "Verily, verily" or "Truly, truly."</note>.

But indeed, although the previous formula—which is elliptical <term>elliptical: a grammatical structure where words are omitted because they are understood from context</term>, such as *if [I take] from a thread even to a shoe-latchet, etc.* <note>A reference to Genesis 14:23, where Abraham uses a partial sentence to swear an oath.</note>—is said to be common in the Old Testament, and the other, *Amen and Amen*, is also very common in the New Testament; nevertheless, a single passage occurs in the Gospel in which both are expressed. This is in Mark 8:12: *Truly I say to you, if a sign shall be given to this generation.* <note>original Greek: Ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, εἰ δοθήσεται τῇ γενεᾷ ταύτῃ σημεῖον.</note> For here the New Testament expression *Amen* is read, and a rhetorical silence <term>aposiopesis: a sudden breaking off in speech, leaving a sentence unfinished</term> is noted in the conditional particle *if* <note>original Greek: εἰ; original Latin: si</note>, which corresponds to the Hebrew *if* <note>original Hebrew: אם (im)</note>, about which enough was said above.

However, before we pass by this declaration of certainty, namely *Amen*, we thought we should not omit two things which confirm the certainty of an oath, which surely ought to be very great. 1. The particle *Amen* designates this not only in the first sense designated above, but also because He who swore is the *Amen* <note>A reference to Revelation 3:14, where Jesus is called "the Amen, the faithful and true witness."</note>. Therefore, when He repeated *Amen*, saying *Amen, amen, I say to you*, this can be the meaning: *I, who am the Amen—the Truth—speak the Amen—that is, the truth—to you.* The second thing to be noted regarding the certainty of an oath is the root of the word *shebuah* <note>original Hebrew: שבועה</note>; this word signifies an "oath," and it comes from the root *sheba* <note>original Hebrew: שבע</note> which signifies "seven." From this come the arguments of the Cabbalists <note>Cabbalists: followers of Jewish mysticism who often find deeper meanings in the numerical values or roots of Hebrew words.</note> that the word for swearing is derived from the number seven, because an oath ought to be as valid and certain as if it had been made in the presence of seven witnesses. This is reported by A. Masius <note>Andreas Masius (1514–1573) was a famous linguist and scholar of the Ancient Near East.</note> in his commentary on Joshua, chapter 2, verse 17, citing Rabbi Bahaias <note>Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish rabbi and biblical commentator.</note> in his commentary on Genesis 21:24, when he discusses the oath of Abraham, by which he—the first of all in the sacred history—bound himself to Abimelech.

V. A common form of oath in Scripture is when God swears by His own life: *As I live* <note>original Hebrew: חי אני (Chay ani); original Greek: ζω ἐγώ (Zō egō)</note>. This is found in Romans 14:11, which the Apostle cites from Isaiah 45:23: *By myself I have sworn* <note>original Hebrew: בי נשבעתי (Bi nishbati)</note>. For although Isaiah does not have the phrase *As I live*, as Paul alleged in the previously mentioned place, nevertheless the Apo- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, leading into "apostle" on the next page.</note>

-># THE REVEALER OF SECRETS<-

The Apostle <note>Referring to Paul in the Epistle to the Hebrews</note> looks to the underlying sense, since God could not swear by His life without swearing by Himself, because the life of God does not differ from His essence. Nor could He swear by Himself without swearing by His life, because the essence of God is active through His life; He does not understand, will, or act wisely except because He lives. He truly exists by His own unique force and power. This identity of life and essence seems to be foreshadowed for us in the Hebrew language, where *Chayah* <note>original Hebrew: חיה</note> was "to be," and *Chai* <note>original Hebrew: חי</note> meant "he lived"—or *Being and living*. These are signified by nearly the same naming and differ only by a point <note>A reference to Hebrew vowel points or "niqqud," which change the meaning of similar-looking consonant clusters</note>, by which the Holy Tongue, handed down by God’s institution, mystically indicates that in God, to exist and to live are truly identical; yet they are distinguished virtually and according to our formal concepts.

VI. In addition to those formulas of swearing by both God and the Saints contained in Scripture, there are also others used by both Jews and Gentiles and Christians outside of Scripture.

1. *The Rabbis*, who commonly swear thus: *Chai* <note>original Hebrew: ח"י</note> *by your life*, or *Chai*. From this, Rabbi Kimchi <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), a famous medieval Jewish grammarian and biblical commentator</note> supposes in 2 Kings 11:2 and elsewhere, where it is said: *Chai Yehovah ve-chai napshecha* <note>original Hebrew: חי יהוה וחי נפשך</note>, *As the Lord lives and as your soul lives*. The word *Che* is placed for *be-chai*, *by the life*, as the Rabbis say in oaths: *by your life, as you live*. Or conjunctively: *by your life and the life of your soul*. Furthermore, the Rabbis also swear *by the faith of the law*, as is evident from Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and jurist</note>. The Rabbis and all Jews indiscriminately also swear by their own name. For they say when swearing negatively: "If I am not a Jew, I shall not do this." Or affirmatively: "May I be a Jew, if I have done this." And to this, Petrus Galatinus <note>Pietro Colonna Galatino (1460–1540), an Italian friar and scholar of the Kabbalah</note> applies that passage from Isaiah 65:15: *And you shall leave your name for an oath to my chosen*. Or according to the version of Junius <note>Francis Iunius (1545–1602), a Reformed theologian</note>: *And you shall leave your name that it may be a curse to my chosen*.

II. The oaths of the *Gentiles* <note>Non-Jewish peoples, particularly the ancient Greeks and Romans</note> were varied. 1. Among the Romans, that form of swearing, *Mehercule* <note>By Hercules</note>, was religious and holy, and women could not use it, just as males could not use the oath of *Castor and Pollux*. However, both males and females were able to swear by *Edepol* <note>By Pollux</note>. Moreover, when some great necessity pressed, they used a no-common oath, namely *by Jupiter's stone* <note>original Latin: Iouis lapidem. A Roman ceremony where the swearer threw a stone, asking Jupiter to cast them out of the city like the stone if they lied</note>. To this, some Christians wish to relate the mystery of Christ, the stone rejected by the Jews but nevertheless placed at the head of the corner.

This much is certain: the oath was considered most sacred among the Pagans <note>original Latin: "Ethnicos." In this context, it refers to the non-Christian, classical world of Greece and Rome</note>. Hence Aulus Gellius, in Book 1, chapter 21 of his *Attic Nights*: *But indeed, when I had read Hyginus’s commentary with Favorinus, and the arrogance and unpleasantness of his bitterness immediately displeased him. "By Jupiter of Stone," he said—which was considered the most sacred oath—"I am ready to swear that Virgil never wrote this."* <note>The oath "Iovem lapideum" (Jupiter of Stone) was one of the oldest and most solemn Roman oaths, involving the casting away of a stone to symbolize the gods casting away a perjurer</note>.

Furthermore, among the Pagans, the most sacred oath was *to swear by Orcus* <note>A name for the underworld or its god, similar to Pluto</note>, who was not only believed by the ancients to be the God of the underworld—whom they also called Pluto and Father Dis—but others also claimed he was a river of Thessaly flowing out of the Stygian marsh. Hence, among the Gods, it was considered the most sacred oath; and therefore Orcus was named <term>from the Greek word for "oath" (*horkos*)</term>, because there was no oath firmer or more sacred among the gods above. From this came the belief among the Pagans in the <term>Gods of Oaths (*Theoi horkioi*)</term>, who presided over swearing and were armed with lightning bolts for the punishment of perjurers. In Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedic lexicon</note>, the <term>God of Oaths (*horkios theos*)</term> is the presiding officer and judge of swearing. Thus the Styx, the river destined for perjurers, was called the <term>Sacred water of Zeus (*hydor tou Dios horkion*)</term>, whence the <term>Oath-bound (*horkioi*)</term> and the <term>Devout (*hosioi*)</term> were called the same thing by the Pagans. And here Spanhemius <note>Friedrich Spanheim (1600–1649), a noted Calvinist theologian and scholar</note> truly asserts in his *Evangelical Doubts* that the Pagans were more sacred and religious in this matter than the Jews, who played with oaths like boys play with knucklebones <note>An ancient game similar to dice or jacks</note>, or who considered oaths made by the temple as nothing compared to oaths *by the gold of the temple* <note>A reference to Matthew 23:16, where Jesus criticizes the legalistic maneuvering used to invalidate certain oaths</note>.

The ceremony observed among the Pagans was to swear by the limbs of idols or fictional gods, just as among the Papists <note>A term used by the author to refer to Roman Catholics</note> today people swear by the limbs and bodies of the Saints; and therefore by that sacrament, trust was bound as if God were present. Polybius records that the Pagans used this form of oath, saying <term>touching the sacred objects (*apsamenous ton hieron*)</term>, and Livy—who often copies Polybius—rendered this as *having touched the sacred things*.

But indeed, among all the Pagans, the form of swearing used by the Pythagoreans was famous, who most holily swore *by the tetrad* <note>The number four, represented as a triangle of ten dots, which the Pythagoreans considered the source of all nature</note> or the threefold number <note>The original Latin here says "ternarium" (threefold), though the "tetrad" is four. This may be a scribal error or a specific numerical theory</note>. Moreover, since Pythagoras saw that the nature of number was completed in the ten, he made it the beginning of all things, since all nations count up to ten, and when they have reached it, they return to that unity...

When they perceived that the power of this number [ten] was entirely contained within the <term>quaternary (the number four)</term>, for within it are included 1, 2, 3, and 4, which added together make ten, for this reason they believed the quaternary was the most holy number. When they wished to solemnly confirm something, they used it as an oath, saying: *I swear by the Almighty who instilled the tetrad into our soul, which contains the eternal fountains of nature.* <note>original Latin: "Iuro per Omnipotentem animæ qui tetrada nostræ perpetuos fontes naturæ infudit habentem." This refers to the Pythagorean Tetraktys, a triangular figure of ten points arranged in four rows, which they considered the source of all wisdom.</note> For they imagined the soul consisted of a quaternary, such that the <term>monad (*monas*)</term> is *mind*, the <term>dyad (*dyas*)</term> is *knowledge*, the <term>triad (*trias*)</term> is *opinion*, and the <term>tetrad (*tetras*)</term> is *sense*. Furthermore, they assigned the numbers four and nine to justice, because four is the first square number and is "even times even." Nine, however, is the first solid number <note>While mathematically a "solid" number usually refers to a cube, the author here refers to the first square of an odd number (3x3), symbolizing stability and retribution</note> resulting from three multiplied by itself, and in this way they demonstrate the parity and equality of justice. Indeed, the disciples of Pythagoras would assert nothing except by the quaternary, unless they occasionally called upon their teacher as a witness; hence that famous phrase <term>*autos epha*</term> <note>Greek: "He himself said it," known in Latin as "Ipse dixit." It implies that the master's authority is the final word.</note>.

### III. Oaths of the Christians
The oaths of the *Christians* remain. The ancients swore by the life and safety of the Emperors—not for a religious reason, as the Pagans would have intended, but these were <term>votive oaths (*dotika*)</term> due to the prayers made for the Emperor. Hence Tertullian says in his *Apology against the Gentiles*: > *We swear not by the guardian spirits (genii) of the Caesars, but by their safety, which is more venerable than all genii.* <note>Early Christians refused to swear by the "Genius" of the Emperor because it implied worship of his divine spirit, but they would swear by his physical well-being or "safety" as a citizen.</note> These words can be understood in the same sense as some explain that passage regarding Joseph <margin>Genesis 42:16</margin> when he swore *by the life of Pharaoh*. 

Likewise today among the Spanish, an oath *by the life of the king or queen* is inviolable and cannot be revoked. A clear story from Spanish history concerns Ruy Gomez <note>Ruy Gómez de Silva (1516–1573), a primary advisor to King Philip II of Spain</note>, who was playing a game of dice with the Emperor Charles V. When the Emperor had sworn he won *by the life of the Empress*—and this was in vain, since victory surely belonged to that nobleman—the nobleman, knowing this well, surrendered the prize and declined to continue the game so that the Emperor’s oath would not be violated <note>i.e., to prevent the Emperor from committing perjury by swearing falsely on his wife's life</note>. When the Emperor learned of this from the conversation of those standing around, he immediately replied: "Truly, you are worthy to be the governor of a Prince." Thus he placed his son [the future Philip II] under Gomez’s care and wisdom. However, that Spanish oath *by the life of kings*...

Therefore, this form of swearing is most ancient; indeed, it particularly took place in four areas: namely, **in sacrifices, in prayers, in voting, and in oaths.**

### ANTHONY CREGUT

Names imposed by men are often by chance <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τύχης (*apo tyches*)</note>, but none are imposed by God that are not by design <note>original Greek: ἐκ τῆς προαιρέσεως (*ek tēs proaireseōs*), meaning by deliberate choice or purpose</note>. For it would be unworthy of the wisdom of God to bestow names upon things that were without a fixed purpose or as if by accident; indeed, and this is of greatest importance, God not only imposed names with design, but also instilled in things and persons the virtues that are signified through those names and symbols. Hence it is that names are imposed in two ways:

I. By chance.
II. By design.

First, names are imposed **by chance** when no reason can be assigned as to why that name was given rather than another, and thus they seem to be given by accident and fortuitously; for example, why one person is called *Peter* and another *Paul*, and so on. Second, they are imposed **by design** when there is an underlying reason for such an imposition. Thus, the Jews of old wondered why *Zacharias*, as is held in *Luke 1*, would impose the name *John* on the infant, since no one from his kindred was called by that name; nevertheless, he himself had recognized reasons for this naming—indeed, this name was given as if divinely, because *John the Baptist* was to be the first herald of Gospel grace.

However, that imposition of a name which is by design is either from the counsel of God or of man. In the first way, God not only imposed names by a fixed counsel and with great reason, but he also implanted all the gifts which were signified by that naming. Thus, when he imposed the name *Cephas* <note>The Aramaic word for "Rock," translated into Greek as *Petros*</note> upon *Simon Peter*, he likewise brought it to pass that he would truly be *Cephas* and a rock of firmness with respect to doctrine; and when he called the sons of *Zebedee* *Boanerges* <note>A Hebrew/Aramaic expression meaning "Sons of Thunder"</note>, he truly made them sons of thunder and resounding trumpeters of the Gospel.

In the second way <note>referring to names given by human design</note>, it happens differently. For men usually impose names with a fixed purpose, but they do not have—nor can they have or confer upon others—the virtues which are signified by those distinguished names. Thus, many are called *Alexanders* and *Caesars* who nonetheless are quite unable to imitate the fortitude and heroic spirits of those men; indeed, many have obtained qualities contrary to those which are indicated by their proper names. This can be seen in the promotion to the Papacy; for in the election, the name is changed, and often he is called *Clement* <note>meaning "Merciful"</note> who is instead *Inclement* <note>meaning "Unmerciful" or "Harsh"</note>,

Therefore, a name is never imposed by God without that act of naming being mystical and significant; but on the contrary, when men impose names, it is mostly done superstitiously and without reason <note>original Greek: ἀλόγως (*alogōs*)</note>. In this way, all the names attributed to God and the Angels in Scripture are highly significant and full of meaning. For the perfections of God are expressed primarily through ten names. So too are the names of the Mediator <note>A title for Jesus Christ as the bridge between God and humanity.</note>, whether it be the name of his person or the name of his office. Likewise, the names which God imposed upon men cannot be anything other than most significant <note>original Greek: ἐμφατικώτατα (*emphatikōtata*)</note>, as is clear from the cases of Abraham, Jacob, and others.

Regarding Christ, he rightfully and deservedly changed the names of only three Apostles. Since the names of things are signs and symbols, who would deny that those images and symbols handed down by Christ were not in vain or meaningless <note>original Greek: ἀσημάντικα (*asēmantika*)</note>? And indeed, for those three disciples upon whom Christ imposed a name, there was a great preeminence and dignity <note>original Greek: ὑπεροχὴ (*hyperochē*)</note> in the Church above the others, as is clear from Galatians chapter 2 and from 2 Corinthians 12:11, where those three Apostles are called "pillars" according to the opinion of the Church. Christ himself, whenever he performed momentous and more extraordinary deeds, called those three disciples aside as future witnesses of his great glory; this is evident when Jesus recalled the daughter of Jairus from death back to life, when Christ was transfigured on Mount Tabor, and when he struggled against the wrath of God in the garden.

But on the contrary, names are mostly imposed by men superstitiously and carelessly <note>original Greek: παρέργως (*parergōs*), meaning as a side-matter or without serious intent</note>. Thus, the Popes, when they are created, repudiate their baptismal name and choose another by their own will. Yet, what is notable is that they never take the name of Peter for themselves, silently indicating that they wish to have nothing in common with Peter, not even the name itself. This happened to Benedict XIII, who was previously called Peter of Luna; and Gregory XII used to call him "Peter" contemptuously <note>original Greek: ἐξουθενικῶς (*exouthenikōs*)</note>, either because he condemned his election or because he disdained the name imposed during that election. ### ANTHONY CREGUT

Peter of Pavia wished to be called John XIV. However, Marcellus II refused to change his name, a thing that had never happened before from the time when the Pontiffs <note>A title for the Pope.</note> began to change their names. For when Germans were elected to the Papacy, they were called by foreign and "barbarian" names that were unknown and unpleasant to Roman ears; it was then that they began to be called by more common names and to change their original ones. This practice was afterwards maintained by others, even if they were not German but descended from other nations. 

Nevertheless, this was not observed by Marcello Cervini, Cardinal of the Holy Cross <note>original: "Sanctæ Crucis"</note>, because since he was serious and severe in his character and of an unshakable mind, he wished to signify by neglecting this ceremony that he was always the same man, whether before his Papacy or during it. Others, however, claim that the first who changed his name upon entering the Papacy was Sergius II, because of the "horror" of his name, since he was previously called by an obscene and shameful name <note>Sergius II's birth name was reportedly *Os Porci*, meaning "Pig's Snout."</note>. Yet the Jesuit Theophilus Raynaud <note>original: "Th. Raynaudus"</note> denies this in his *Chronology*, asserting that the first of all to change his name was John XII, who was previously called Octavian.

It is to be observed, moreover, that besides names imposed superstitiously, there are others adopted out of excessive affectation. Just as among the Egyptians there were the *Pharaohs* and later the *Ptolemies*, so among the Romans there were the *Caesars*; among the English, the *Henries*; among the French, the *Charleses*; in Flanders, the *Baldwins*; and formerly in Aquitaine, the *Williams*. Indeed, for the most part, those names were fatal and ominous. On the other hand, the Papists commonly despise the names of the Old Testament, such as Zachariah, Jeremiah, Isaac, etc., choosing instead the names of Pagans such as Diana, or Catherine—that is, *Hecatarina* from Hecate—which are the names of false deities and vain names of the heathens.

There were, however, learned and illustrious men who changed their own names, not out of superstition or rashness, but moved by a specific reason, as may be seen in the history of Thuanus <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a famous French historian and book collector.</note>, book 26. Thus Reuchlin <note>Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a pioneering German humanist and scholar of Greek and Hebrew.</note> preferred to be called *Capnio*, from the Greek word for smoke <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ κάπνος (*apo tou kapnos*)</note>, since "Reuchlin" means the same thing in German. So too Philipp Melanchthon loved to be called by that name, meaning "black earth" <note>original: "à terra nigra"</note>, since he was previously named *Schwartzerdt*, a word which signifies the same thing...

IV. The fourth polity of the Church was in Abraham, with whom God established a special covenant, the sign of which was the sacrament of Circumcision. For this reason his name was changed, and he was called *Abraham*, as if you were to say *father of a multitude*. For although he was about a hundred years old and his wife was ninety, she conceived beyond hope and against hope. Thus, he fulfilled the meaning of his name, which is to be understood in a narrow sense regarding his physical offspring, but in a more grand sense regarding his spiritual offspring and the promise, according to Genesis 22: *In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed.*

V. The fifth <term>polity <note>Greek: *politeia*.</note></term> had its beginning with Moses. Under his leadership, God determined to rule the Church with various laws and statutes and to deliver it from various hardships—most notably from Egyptian servitude. This was an illustrious "type" <note>In biblical interpretation, a "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament that foreshadows something in the New Testament.</note> of spiritual redemption from the yoke of hell and the spiritual Pharaoh. Hence the mystical imposition of his name: Moses is from <term>to draw out <note>Hebrew: *mashah*.</note></term>, not only because he himself was rescued from the waters, but also because he delivered the people of God (the Church) from many waters and abysses—for the Scripture is fond of calling great troubles and afflictions by such names. Yet Moses did not lead the Church into the land of promise, or Canaan; therefore, this fifth polity was not sufficient, but a sixth still remained.

VI. Therefore, the <term>polity <note>Greek: *politeia*.</note></term> of the Church began its [new] period with Joshua. For it was after the son was called Isaac at the laughter of Abraham that we read that Sarah also laughed.*

But indeed, just as we rightly venerate the naming and imposition of names found in the Scriptures above all others because they contain singular mysteries, so we also marvel at the emphasis and propriety of the Hebrew language in general. Through both proper names and common nouns, it signifies things so excellently that all words seem to have been imposed on things **from their very utterance** <note>original: "ek tēs prophoras"</note>, and here that saying holds true: **names often suit the things they represent** <note>original: "conueniunt rebus nomina saepe suis"</note>. For from the beginning, Adam imposed names on all living creatures according to their nature, when by God's command they passed before him according to their species; and therefore, from their name, anyone might be able to philosophize and [understand] their natural history...

As for fish, the Hebrews imposed more general names because these living creatures are, as it were, in another world, remote from human society. Hence, they are assigned three names according to their size: the common ones are called in general <term>fish <note>Hebrew: "dagim."</note></term>; the larger ones <term>sea monsters <note>Hebrew: "thannim," often translated as whales or great serpents.</note></term>; and the greatest of all is the **Leviathan**.
