And Origen, who was most skilled in this language, cleverly wrote that Hebrew words, when translated into the words of other languages, lose much of their value and emphasis; indeed, the other languages reveal, in contrast to Hebrew, the manifold confusion of Babel.

I would wish this to be understood regarding common nouns; for proper names are often transferred <term>word-for-word <note>original Greek: "autolexei"</note></term> into other languages, with only the ending slightly changed according to the idiom of each language. Thus, the Arabs are sometimes called by Greek names. For the proper name **Theodore** was shared with them, just as **Cypris** was the name of Herod’s mother, who was an Arab by nation; so too the name **Beryllus** belonged to a Bishop of Bostra in Arabia. Indeed, the name **Theodore** is expressed <term>with equivalent meaning <note>original Greek: "isodynamountos"</note></term> in all languages: among the French it is *Dieu donné* <note>God-given</note>; in the African language, when it was Latin, it was *Adeodatus*; to the Hebrews it is *Elnathan*, or *Nathanael*; to the Syrians and Arabs *Il nathan* or *Nathannail*.

Observe, however (my dearest listeners), that as often as those names are so meaningful, beautiful allusions are frequently formed from them when the occasion arises, which have an excellent emphasis either for **confirmation** or for **correction**. Thus, in the former manner, it was said of the Emperor **Probus** that he was "Probus truly upright" <note>A pun on the Latin name *Probus* and the word *probus*, meaning honest or virtuous.</note>. Nevertheless, for a name to be asserted as truly imposed upon someone, two conditions are necessary.
I. That the name be attributed to someone always or <note>original Greek: "hōs epi to poly"</note> *for the most part*; for a name that is attributed to someone only once cannot truly be called a "name." For example, **Peter** was once called **Satan** by Christ, yet who would dream of this being Peter’s name? Similarly, in the Apocalypse, **Rome** is called **Babylon** mystically—and according to the Jesuit **Ribera** and others, also in the Epistle of Peter—and yet Babylon is not the proper name of Rome. **Bellarmin** also observed this, and because this condition was lacking, he wished to weaken the significance of the name **Boanerges** <note>Meaning "Sons of Thunder."</note> which was given to two disciples.
II. That the name be truly proper, and not common; since common names, as they apply to many things, are called names <term>catachrestically <note>A term for using a word in a forced or technically incorrect way.</note></term>. These are the sorts of names which are attributed to someone <term>antonomastically <note>From "antonomastic," a rhetorical device where a title or epithet is used instead of a proper name, such as calling a judge "Your Honor" or a King "His Majesty."</note></term>, as when **Paul** is called *the Apostle*, **John** is called *the Theologian*, the King of the French is called the *Most Christian King*, or the King of Spain is called the *Catholic King*. For the former is not more Christian than others, nor the latter more Catholic, but they are called so in this way on account of a certain <note>original Greek: "hyperochēn"</note> *eminence*.
III. It can be added that when names are even more common, they are not even attributed to someone antonomastically or for a specific reason, but are shared indiscriminately with others. For instance, the name of **Bishop** is given to others indiscriminately, and formerly the name of **Pope** was common to many Bishops—at least to those in whom there was a certain visible dignity above the rest, whether because of their see, or as the ancients say, *because of the primacy of the city* <note>original: "propter principalitatem vrbis."</note>. <page-num>404</page-num>

-># ANTHONY CREGUTUS<-

...more distinguished Bishops; whether due to their virtues and personal gifts, or by reason of age (as was noted by **Daniel Chamier** <note>A 16th-century French Reformed theologian known for his massive work against Catholic doctrines.</note>, who can never be praised enough, whether for his exceptional learning or his singular piety), **Cletus of Rome** calls **Cyprian** "Pope" in Epistle 3 among the letters of Cyprian. Likewise, **Alexander of Alexandria**, in the Synod of Seleucia, is addressed as: <note>original Greek: "Μακαρίῳ πάπᾳ ἐπισκόπῳ ἡμῶν Ἀλεξάνδρῳ"</note> **"To the blessed Pope, our Bishop Alexander."** Furthermore, **Lindanus** <note>Wilhelmus Lindanus, a 16th-century Catholic Bishop and polemicist.</note> in his *Panoplia*, book 4, chapter 80, states: "Although the name 'Pope' is today attributed among Latins to the Roman Pontiff alone, there are no small conjectures that among the ancients it was common to the entire order of elders."

And therefore, it should be observed that the name **Pope** was by no means immediately appropriated to the Roman Pontiff as if it were a <term>Unique Name <note>original Hebrew: "shem ha-miyukhad." In Jewish tradition, this refers specifically to the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God that is not to be pronounced.</note></term>, as the Rabbis call the **Tetragrammaton** <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</note>; rather, that naming convention crept in by degrees and step-by-step. 

I. That name "Pope" was common to **Bishops** in general; for they used that title interchangeably. 

II. Specifically, **Patriarchs** <note>The highest-ranking bishops in the early church, such as those of Alexandria, Antioch, and Constantinople.</note> were honored by that title as an eminent one, because the Bishops living under their patriarchate looked to them as the bishops of the primary sees, as **Theodore Balsamon** <note>A 12th-century Byzantine canonist and Patriarch of Antioch.</note> reports regarding the privileges of Patriarchs. 

III. Finally, this title was reserved for the **Roman Patriarch** when he proudly raised himself above the rest of the Bishops, Archbishops (or Metropolitans), and Patriarchs; and it was then that this voice of pride was heard: **"There is only one name in the world, namely Pope."** This is found in the short decrees of **Gregory VII** <note>Likely referring to the *Dictatus Papae*, a list of 27 statements of papal power issued in 1075.</note>, as cited by **Baronius** <note>Cesare Baronius, a 16th-century Cardinal and church historian.</note> in Volume 2 for the year 1076. 

IV. It should be observed that the name "Pope" was not handed down nor used by any of the first **Councils**, such as Nicaea, Ephesus, Constantinople, Sardica, and so on. 

V. The name "Pope" is not a badge of any particular **Ecclesiastical rank**, such as the name of Bishop, Archbishop, Patriarch, etc. Hence, no one used to call themselves by that name; for since it was an honor bestowed by others, no one said or wrote that they were the "Pope," just as no one calls themselves "Lord." However, no one hesitated to call themselves a Bishop or a Patriarch. 

VI. Most often, that naming convention is found among the Ancients as **"Pope of the Universal Church,"** which, if understood correctly, signifies nothing harsh, no differently than the phrase **"Bishop of the Universal Church."** It does not...

<summary>Cregutus argues that the title "Pope" was historically a common honorific for all bishops and patriarchs, only becoming an exclusive and supreme title for the Bishop of Rome in the 11th century under Gregory VII.</summary>

...that he is the **Pope** or **Bishop of the universal Church**, in such a way that he would rule it as a head and as an **Ecumenical Bishop** <note>A title implying authority over the entire inhabited world.</note>—which belongs to **Christ** alone—but because all Orthodox Bishops are truly Bishops of the universal Church, even if they are assigned now to this flock, now to that; and they cultivate and water the one Church like a plot of earth.

Furthermore, just as among the Papal prelates and <term>cardinals <note>original: *purpurati*, literally "those dressed in purple," referring to the high-ranking officials of the Catholic Church.</note></term> arrogant names are usurped, so do private **Doctors** <note>In this context, "Doctor" refers to a high-level teacher of theology or law.</note> delight in the vainest titles and praises. Just as among the Hebrews and the Jewish nation—the most arrogant of all under heaven—we constantly hear them casting out pomposities and "foot-and-a-half-long" words to the point of nausea; hence the titles **Rab**, **Rabbi**, **Ribbi**, **Rabbanam**, **Morenu**, **Chachamim**, etc. <note>These are various Hebrew titles of honor: "Master," "My Master," "Our Teacher," and "Sages."</note>

But indeed, even more intolerable in the Papacy are the most vain names of the [religious] orders; when some are called **Franciscans**, others **Dominicans**, others **Benedictines**, others **Augustinians**, others **Jesuits**, etc. What is this other than claiming—contrary to **Paul’s** exhortations—one for Paul, another for **Apollos**, another for **Cephas** <note>The Apostle Peter.</note>, and no one for Christ? This is condemned in **Jerome’s** book against the *Luciferians*: <note>The Luciferians were a 4th-century schismatic group; Jerome argued against their sectarian identity.</note> "If you should ever hear those who are called Christians being named not after the Lord **Jesus Christ**, but after someone else, such as **Marcionites** or **Valentinians**, know that they are not the Church of Christ, but the synagogue of Antichrist."

And let these things be said regarding the abuse that occurs in the giving of names. As for proper names which are ordinarily given at **baptism** among Christians, the legal right of giving a name or denomination belonged to the father among the Hebrews, as is clear from the history recorded in **Luke 1** concerning the name of **John the Baptist**, which was given by **Zechariah** his parent at the boy’s circumcision; and since he could not speak, **having asked for a writing tablet, he wrote.** <note>original Greek: "αἰτήσας πινακίδιον ἔγραψε" (Luke 1:63).</note> Hence it is that **Calvin** wisely observed on **Isaiah 7:14** that no mention is made of a man in the giving of the name **Immanuel**. ***Behold, a Virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and she shall call his name Immanuel.*** Wherefore...

...that? Is it not because the birth of **Immanuel** <note>Meaning "God with us."</note> was extraordinary? Therefore, something unique occurred there; since the **Virgin** conceived without a man, no one except the Virgin had the privilege of bestowing the name. For otherwise, whenever that duty was performed by mothers, it was done with the consent and authority of the fathers. Indeed, the man himself gives the name to his wife. For just as the wife of Adam was called **Eve** by Adam—for as she was taken from man, and thus called *Isha* <note>original Hebrew: אשה</note> from *Ish* <note>original Hebrew: אש</note>, a "man-ess" <note>original: *virissa*, a Latinized term created to mirror the Hebrew derivation of "woman" from "man."</note> from "man"—so Adam bestowed the name upon her. Likewise today, all wives leave behind the name of their father's family and are surnamed by their husband when they become spouses.

The same custom is also observed among the **Turks** <note>Referring to the Ottoman Empire.</note> at the time of circumcision. They do not superstitiously reject Old Testament names as the <term>Papists <note>A common Protestant term for Roman Catholics.</note></term> do; rather, their names, like the Hebrew ones, are emphatic and signify **by choice** <note>original Greek: *ἐκ τῆς προαιρέσεως*, meaning names are chosen for their specific meaning or purpose.</note>. Hence **Amurathes**, that is, *the Desirous*. **Hali**, that is, *Eli*. **Eses**, *Jesus*. **Ebraim**, *Abraham*. **Soliman**, *Solomon*. **Iagub**, *Jacob* <note>Cregut correlates this with Joseph in the text, though it traditionally refers to Jacob.</note>. **Scander**, *Alexander*. **Chetir**, *George*. And those four names very well known to them—and perhaps more well known to Christians than is proper—**Baiazet** or *Paiazet*, **Orthogules**, **Orchanes**, **Tzimifces**, which are taken from the language of the Tatars. Diminutive names are very much in use among them; thus for **Mustapha**, which in Arabic signifies *pure*, *refined*, or *elect*, they use the abundant diminutive **Musslacaifites**, and for **Chetir**, they use **Charaitin**.

Since names are given in this way **by choice**, it is easy to find the root and provide the reasoning for the etymology or derivation. In our **French language**, the more established words have their origin in Latin, although I would not deny that some are Greek and a few are Hebrew due to the mixing of peoples. But those names which are commonly derived from the French language itself I consider to be trivial, such as *mors* (death) because it *mordet* (bites), and others of that kind, which certainly show some cleverness but have little solidity. It is just like among the Latins when they want to say **war** <note>original: *bellum*</note> is named after **beasts** <note>original: *belluis*</note> because war first began against beasts, or by **Antiphrasis** <note>A rhetorical device where a word is used in a sense opposite to its proper meaning.</note>, because war is the least "beautiful" <note>original: *bellum*, which in Latin can mean "war" (noun) or "beautiful" (adjective). The joke is that war is called "beautiful" because it is not beautiful at all.</note> thing there is.

Let this conclude the treatment of the first part of the dissertation, namely **the thesis on the bestowing of a name**. Now the hypothesis follows immediately...

...the thesis, namely the bestowing of the name of **Abraham**. For while he was previously called ***Abram***, he was later named ***Abraham***. The first name signified *exalted father*, while the latter signified *father of a multitude*; for it is a common practice among the Hebrews to form compound names, as is evident from ***Absalom*** <note>Meaning "Father of Peace," from *Ab* (father) and *Shalom* (peace).</note>, ***Adonizedek*** <note>Meaning "Lord of Righteousness."</note>, ***Melchizedek*** <note>Meaning "King of Righteousness."</note>, and so on. This practice is also in use among the Greeks.

Now, from what has been discussed above regarding the thesis, it is clear enough that the name **Abraham** is **by choice** <note>original Greek: *ἐκ τῆς προαιρέσεως*, referring to a name intentionally selected to convey a specific purpose or character.</note> and is highly emphatic, because it was bestowed by divine command, which can never be in vain. The reason for this name can be assigned a twofold meaning: one with respect to his physical descendants, and the other with respect to his spiritual descendants and the promise. In the first sense, Abraham was truly the *father of a multitude*, since the nations that naturally flowed from that patriarch were innumerable, as the stars of the firmament and the sand of the sea. This was evident from the very beginning in that most numerous offspring that came out of Egypt, who were so formidable to the Egyptians themselves that Pharaoh issued a cruel command to the midwives regarding the slaughter of the Jewish male children by their hand.

The second reason relates primarily to his spiritual offspring and the promise, for this is what God chiefly considers, since physical things are merely **types** <note>In biblical scholarship, a "type" is a person, event, or institution in the Old Testament that foreshadows a greater reality in the New Testament.</note> of spiritual realities. This is demonstrated and explained in the passage of **Genesis 22:18**: *In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed.* Therefore, it is not only the Jewish nation. For Abraham is called the *father of all believers*; and the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul.</note> in **Romans 4:13** says of Abraham in this sense: **that he should be the heir of the world** <note>original Greek: *κληρονόμον αὐτὸν εἶναι τοῦ κόσμου*.</note>. For to be the heir of the world declares that he has the whole world as his children, and thus, as it were, he possesses the entire world. This is proclaimed with even greater right regarding **Christ** in **Hebrews 1:2**, when it is said that he was appointed heir of the whole world, in whom even the father Abraham, along with the whole world adopted as sons, is blessed. Hence, believers are truly called both **Christians** and **Abrahamites**.

And it is from this that whenever the Jews speak of the Patriarch Abraham, they emphasize his fatherhood. Hence that phrase so often repeated in the Gospel: *we have Abraham as our father.* Even today, they never name him except with that **honorable title** <note>original: *Euphemia*, a Greek term for an auspicious or respectful phrasing used for the deceased.</note> **Abraham our father, peace be upon him** <note>original Hebrew: אברהם אבינו עליו השלום (*Avraham Avinu alav ha-shalom*)</note>, that is, one who rests in peace. For when after a name...

<meta>This page continues Anthony Cregut's analysis of the significance of names in the Bible. <page-num>408</page-num>

### ANTHONY CREGUT

When the Jews mention **Abraham** <note>original Hebrew: *Abraham*</note>, they add "our father" <note>original Hebrew: *Avinu*</note>, always understanding it to mean the Patriarch, and not anyone else of the same name. Furthermore, the following blessing <note>original: *euphemia*, a term for a respectful or auspicious expression</note> "peace be upon him" <note>original Hebrew: *Alav Ha-Shalom*</note> is never attributed to anyone except Moses, the Patriarchs, and the Prophets; for this is the constant custom of the Hebrews.

That naming of Abraham is also confirmed by the change of his wife’s name. For just as **Abraham** is named from "father of a multitude" because of the multitude of nations of which he was the father, so his wife—who was previously called ***Sarai***, meaning *my Lady*—was called absolutely and without the possessive suffix ***Sarah***, meaning *Lady*, because she was the mother of many nations. Genesis 17:15: *God said to Abraham: as for Sarai your wife, you shall not call her name Sarai, for Sarah shall be her name. And verse 16: I will bless her so that she may be the mother of many nations; kings of peoples shall come from her.* Therefore, that most noble pair of spouses, though differing in words through the change of their names—for **Abraham** and **Sarah** sound very different from each other—nevertheless, in respect to their sense and mystical significance, those two names signify the same thing <note>Both names reflect a shift from a limited, personal role to a universal, royal status over many nations.</note>.

In a similar way, the first bestowing of a name recorded as being done by a human corresponds to this: **Eve** in Genesis 3:20. *And Adam called the name of his wife Eve.* For **Eve** <note>original Hebrew: *Chavah*</note> was also so named from the word "lived" <note>original: *vixit*; Hebrew root *chayah*</note>, because she was the mother of all living. The Hebrews say she was not called *Chayah* <note>meaning "living thing"</note>, even though she could have been, because that word signifies the same as *Chavah*, and thus from either word she could have been called Eve, the mother of the living. However, Adam chose the word *Chavah* instead, due to the ambiguity <note>original: *homonymiam*</note> found in the word *Chayah*, which also signifies *animal* or *wild beast*; he chose the alternative so that he would not seem to have taken a beast as his wife. 

But indeed, it is more likely what Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to the famous 11th-century commentator Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki)</note> adds: that the name of **Eve** was bestowed here to show that the task of giving names was not completed immediately when it began; and truly, names were given according to various events as they occurred. The sense of ***Eve*** (that is, her naming) can also be mystical, for she signifies the Church, which is the mother of all who live a spiritual life. In this way, faith has secured a new name for four especially distinguished persons: namely, **Eve**, **Abraham**, **Sarah**, and **Cephas** <note>The Aramaic name for the Apostle Peter, meaning "Rock," illustrating a New Testament example of a divinely changed name.</note>.

# REVEALER OF SECRETS.

But if the faith of Abraham brought about that remarkable change of name, then surely the infidelity of Socinus <note>Faustus Socinus (1539–1604) was an Italian theologian whose followers, the Socinians, denied the pre-existence and divinity of Christ, arguing he was a man who became divine only after his resurrection.</note> maliciously corrupts that naming of Abraham. He does this so that the origin or significance of the name—which was established by God to signify a mystery full of the greatest comfort, namely the calling of the Gentiles—is unfortunately inverted and perverted by that detestable and ill-omened Faustus Socinus <note>Cregut is making a pun here: *Faustus* means "favored" or "lucky," while he calls him *infaustus*, meaning "unlucky" or "ill-omened."</note> to undermine the divinity and eternity of Christ the Son, who is **of the same substance** <note>original Greek: *homoousios*, the key term from the Council of Nicaea asserting that Christ is of the same essence as God the Father.</note> as the Father.

For those words of Christ in John 8:58, *“before Abraham was made, I am,”* he corrupts in this way: *“before Abraham was made”*—that is, before **Abram** <note>original Hebrew: *Abram*</note> became **Abraham** <note>original Hebrew: *Abraham*, meaning "father of a multitude." Genesis 17:5</note>, the father of many nations through the preaching of the Gospel when the time for the calling of the Gentiles arrived—I was the Messiah. This is because (Socinus says) in the Greek it is *before Abraham came to be, I am* <note>original Greek: *prin Abraam genesthai, ego eimi*</note>. These words are not to be translated as Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536), the famous Renaissance humanist and editor of the Greek New Testament.</note> did, *“Before Abraham was born,”* but *“before Abraham became,”* because, as Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), the primary successor to John Calvin in Geneva and a renowned biblical translator.</note> believes, the phrase **to become** <note>original Greek: *to genesthai*</note> is contrasted with **I am** <note>original Greek: *tō eimi*</note>, which is properly attributed only to Him who alone truly exists.

But while we do not disapprove of that version by our Beza—since the passage deals with the existence of Him who was yesterday and is today, and therefore the contrast had to be preserved—who would not, on the other hand, detest the wicked corruption of the heretic regarding the sense of the passage? Is it not immediately refuted by the evidence of the context alone? For Christ proved that Abraham had seen Him and that He existed in Abraham's time—which the Jews were denying—otherwise Christ would have answered equivocally. Oh, the unbridled audacity of the heretic! Oh, the monstrous audacity of Satan! Who, with his "dwellers in darkness," completely subverts the venerable mysteries of religion so that they may pervert everything higher and more sacred: **being wickedly ignorant of the mysteries, they distort them to their own destruction.** <note>original Greek: *ta mysteria kakistōs agnoūntes eis idian apōleian streblousi*</note>

Observe furthermore (dearest listeners) that two things seem unique to us in that naming of Abraham. First, the change of name made by God; second, a certain divine instinct in the first naming, which was done by his parents. For how could such a great similarity of names between Abram and Abraham have occurred, unless God had intended all these things in His work...

# ANTHONY CREGUT

...had [Providence] not directed [him] according to the eternal decree? And so God ordained that the parents would bestow the name Abram, so that God, by adding a single little letter, might signify a great mystery. O Divine Providence, whose Lyncean eyes <note>original: *Lyncei oculi*. In Greek mythology, Lynceus was an Argonaut with sight so keen he could see through trees, stones, and the earth itself.</note> were able to foresee not only things, but even the names of the things themselves! This would be even more conspicuous if there is any weight to be found in the observation of the Hebrews, who noted that the letter added to the name was *he* <note>The Hebrew letter ה (H), which is the fifth letter of the alphabet.</note>, one of the four letters of the **Tetragrammaton** <note>original: *τετραγραμμάτου*, the four-letter sacred name of God, YHWH.</note>; for he was called Abraham, *because in his seed all nations will be blessed.* (Genesis 22). But that blessed seed, and the cause of all blessing, is signified by Jehovah and is Jehovah himself, by which name eternity and the truth of the divine promises are signified.

Of the same sort are the observations that can be made regarding other names, such as *Sarai* and *Sarah*, or *Peter* and *Cephas*. For why was she called *Sarai* by her parents—a name which has such close kinship with the name *Sarah*—unless it was because she who was previously the mistress of her own family was made the mistress of the whole world, just as Abraham was made the heir of the whole world? But how could there be such affinity between those names, unless the parents who first bestowed the names were led by a certain divine instinct? We say the same concerning the name Peter changed into Cephas; for Peter is named from *petra* <note>The Greek word for "rock."</note>, and Cephas in Syriac <note>Meaning Aramaic, the language spoken by Jesus and the Apostles.</note> signifies a rock, and in the Attic dialect of Greek, *petta* <note>original: *πέττα*</note> is the same as *petra*, from which the proper name of the Apostle, *Pettos* <note>original: *πέττος*</note>, is derived.

Furthermore, one might still not unreasonably inquire here why God bestowed or changed the names of two Patriarchs, Abraham and Jacob, but did not change the name of Isaac at all? It can be answered that God did not change Isaac's name alone because God had already assigned him that name before his birth, based on "laughter" (Genesis 18:13), when Sarah was rebuked because she had laughed. This was subsequently considered by Abraham in Genesis 21:3 when he called his son Isaac. And in verse 6, Sarah says, *“God has brought me laughter; whoever hears will laugh with me.”* It can also be added that there was no reason for changing the name of Isaac, because nothing new or extraordinary happened to him as it did to the other patriarchs.

Cregut interprets the "stones" allegorically as the hardened hearts of the Gentiles who were eventually converted.</note> And God looked primarily toward this spiritual progeny, as is evident from the words of the covenant recited in this chapter. These words certainly do not merely suggest a gathering of Arabs, Edomites, and others who might merge into Abraham’s family, but He includes here even foreign and far-distant nations, which are united throughout the whole world by the bond of faith and charity and recognize the "father of the faithful." And therefore, in this sense, most were actually excluded from the physical seed and were hardly able to merge with Father Abraham, since Abraham and the Church had vomited them out like cancers <note>original: *carcinomata*. In 17th-century polemics, "cancer" or "canker" was a common metaphor for heresy or those cut off from the religious body.</note>. It is not, therefore, because of the scattering of a physical lineage into many nations that Abraham is called the "father of many nations," but because of the joining together of the nations of the whole world through an extraordinary path. This is why God so often emphasizes the reason for that naming in Scripture, which surely would not happen unless something singular was being designated.

And the things mentioned by the Hebrew teachers <note>Refers to Rabbinic scholars or Jewish commentators.</note> fit this commentary quite well: namely, that Abraham lived near the middle age of the world and was brought onto this world's stage so that he might, by his own virtue, support both the ages that had come before and those that were to come after, as if acting as a pillar. For because Abraham was the "father of a multitude of nations," he deservedly earned the title of their "pillar." But truly, a pillar is not placed in some corner of the house, but is set right in the very center to hold up the building. And in truth, the name of Abraham, the reasoning behind that name, and the covenant established with the patriarch, display the sweetest and most peaceful voice of God. For once the Divine Will had been offended by sin, the voice of God had never rang out more sweetly among men than in the time of Abraham; nor had a greater hope shone upon posterity than from that divine oracle: *Your name shall be called Abraham, for [I have made you] a father of a multitude, etc.* <note>Genesis 17:5.</note>

According to this sense, the Apostle in Romans 4:13 calls Abraham the "heir of the whole world." *For the promise to Abraham or his seed that he should be heir of the world did not come through the law, but through the righteousness*

...the righteousness of faith. For since Abraham is called the "father of the faithful" because of the righteousness of faith, he is therefore the heir of the whole world, because the faithful are scattered throughout the whole world, whether those faithful be from the Jews or from the Gentiles. Indeed, in this passage the name "heir" is not used in its literal sense, but according to a Hebrew idiom <term>idiotismo: a linguistic feature unique to a specific language, in this case, Hebrew</term>, because, as is clear from Psalm 127:3, children are called a *nachalah* <note>Hebrew: נחלת</note> or "possession." *Behold, children are a possession of the Lord: the fruit of the womb is a reward.* Paul asserts the same thing about Christ in Hebrews 1:2: *Whom He has appointed heir of all things, through whom also He made the world.* Likewise, in Romans 8:17, all the faithful are called "heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ." This is because we are all the children of God, adopted in Christ. To the Latins and Greeks, those who succeed to someone’s goods after death are called "heirs"; but to the Hebrews, an "inheritance" is a possession in general, used when someone enjoys the goods granted to them even while the donor or parent is still living. Thus, we are heirs of God, even though that heavenly Father lives forever.

It is so far from the truth, therefore, that through "Abraham"—that is, the "multitude of nations"—only a physical lineage should be understood (meaning the Jews primarily), that the Jews themselves and the Scripture itself rather understand "the Nations" <note>original: *Gentes*, often translated as Gentiles</note> to mean all other nations and peoples besides the Jews. For throughout the Scripture, all people are divided into Jews and Gentiles, just as they are divided into Jews and Greeks in 1 Corinthians 1:22 and 24. Likewise, they are divided into Jews and Syrians according to the Syriac version in the previously mentioned passage of 1 Corinthians 1:22. And the Rabbis call all other peoples *lo’ez* <note>Hebrew: לועז</note>, that is, "barbarians" <note>This term originally referred to those speaking a foreign or "stammering" tongue</note>. But now, the Jews of today call Christians alone *Goyim* <note>Hebrew: גוים, meaning "Nations" or "Gentiles"</note> maliciously and insultingly <note>original Greek: *ὑβριστικῶς* (hybristikos), meaning with insolence or abuse</note>, thus restricting a general name to Christians alone—whether calling them in the plural *Goyim* or in the singular *Goy*. From this comes that hateful superstition of the Jews, that no one should cut food with the knife of a Christian man—*she-chatach be-sakkin shel Goy* <note>Hebrew: שחתך בסכין של גוי</note>—which means "because he cut it with the knife of a Christian man." Moreover, the Jews do not cut just anything with any knife; for they always keep two knives with them: one is a *sakkin shel basar* <note>Hebrew: סכין של בשר</note>, a "meat knife," because they use it for cutting meat; the other is a *sakkin shel chalav* <note>Hebrew: סכין של חלב</note>, a "milk knife," or rather for dairy products and fruits. Now, however, they inquire scrupulously whether it is permissible to eat from those things which have been cut or slaughtered by a Christian’s knife.

Nevertheless, it must be observed that although Scripture often distinguishes between Jews and Gentiles *distinctively* <note>original: διακριτικῶς (diakritikōs); used here to mean "making a clear, neutral classification"</note>, it does not always do so *scornfully* <note>original: συγχυτικῶς (synchytikōs); a rhetorical term for blending or blurring terms, often to imply contempt or a "smear"</note>. This is evident primarily from this passage where Abraham is called the "father of many nations," and where the calling of the Gentiles is discussed. However, the Jews constantly use the term *scornfully*, especially when they apply that name to Christians alone—a figure of speech the Jews themselves call "a shameful manner" <note>original: גנאי דרך (G'nai Derekh); a Rabbinic idiom for a disparaging way of speaking</note>. Rhetoricians and grammarians call this a "blended or derogatory expression" <note>original: λόγον συγχυτικὸν (logon synchytikon)</note>. Indeed, this figure of speech is frequently found in Scripture. For instance, in Ephesians 2, Paul speaks *scornfully* <note>original: συγχυτικῶς</note> when he commands the Ephesians to remember what they once were—namely, "Gentiles"—as a way of showing contempt for their former condition. He does not do this a little later in chapter 3:1, saying: *I, Paul, the prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles*; in that instance, he is not speaking figuratively or with contempt. 

For this reason, Scripture refers to those as "nations" *scornfully* whom the Chaldean paraphrase <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible</note> calls "Syrians" <note>original: ארמיא (Aramaya)</note>, as in Leviticus 25:47. The Syriac version also commonly translates "Greeks" as "Syrians," perhaps *scornfully*, as seen in the aforementioned passage of 1 Corinthians 1:22 and Acts 16:2. But in one particular place, Paul pushes the figure of speech so far that he does not even deem the "Nations" worthy of the name "nation." In Romans 10:19, he says: *I will provoke you to jealousy by a nation that is not a nation* <note>original: ἐγὼ παραζηλώσω ὑμᾶς ἐπ’ οὐκ ἔθνει</note>. In this place, the Apostle calls all profane peoples a "non-nation," as if they were unworthy of even the name "nation"—just as to live in sin is not truly "living," and a gift from an enemy is "no gift." Thus, those who were called "nations" in an absolute sense were not truly a "nation."

But what will the Jews say—they who so hate this naming convention—if we demonstrate from Scripture that they themselves are designated by that very name, *Goi* <note>original: גוי (Goy); usually translated as "Gentile" or "Nation," often used by Jews to refer to non-Jews</note>, meaning "nation"? These most stubborn of two-legged creatures refuse and kick against it, but "willingly or unwillingly" <note>original: ἑκόντι ἀέκοντίγε (hekonti aekontige)</note> they are forced to confess it, as is clearly evident from Scripture, even if they never stop weaving their sophistries. The passages are Joshua 5:6 and chapter 10:13. In the former, it is written: *For the children of Israel walked forty years through the wilderness, until all the nation of men of war was consumed* <note>original: כל הגוי אנשי המלחמה (Kol Ha-Goy Anshei Ha-Milchamah)</note>. Here it should be noted that those wicked men, guilty of rebellion, are not called "the people" <note>Cregut is contrasting the Hebrew word 'Am' (God's people) with 'Goy' (a profane nation)</note>, but *Goi*—that is, a "nation"—a word used here as a term of hatred, signifying profane men (as we said above) who are estranged from the sacred covenant of Abraham.

For it was of no benefit to those Jews to be circumcised when they neither trusted in God nor were obedient. For as Paul testifies in Galatians 5:6: *Neither circumcision is of any value, nor uncircumcision; but faith which works through love and a new creation.* <note>The author combines elements of Galatians 5:6 and 6:15 here.</note> Additionally, in verse 8, the entire nation is called a <term>גוי</term> <note>Hebrew: *Goy*; meaning "nation" or "Gentile."</note>—doubtless because they were still uncircumcised in the manner of the barbarians before they were actually circumcised. 

But another passage in Joshua 10:13 is also clear: *And the Sun stayed and the Moon stood still, until the nation took vengeance upon its enemies.* <term>עַד יִקֹם גּוֹי אֹיְבָיו</term> <note>Hebrew: *Ad yikom goy oyvav*; "Until the nation avenged its enemies."</note>. The Chaldean Paraphrase <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary.</note> translated this as *the people of Israel*, using the word <term>עַמָּא</term> <note>Aramaic: *Amma*; a term for "people" often used with more dignity than "Goy."</note> which signifies a "people." 

But the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translates it: *until God avenged their enemies* <note>original Greek: ἕως ἠμυνάτο ὁ Θεὸς τοὺς ἐχθροὺς αὐτῶν</note>. Thus, they substituted the word *God* (Theos) for the word that would express <term>גּוֹי</term> <note>Goy</note>, as if they were unwilling to apply the vocabulary of a "nation" or "Gentile" to Israel, because in sacred history that term is almost always applied to profane or pagan nations. 

Undoubtedly, those translators thought that <term>גּוֹי</term> (*Goy* / "nation") was not placed in the nominative case—meaning the nation itself took vengeance on its enemies (that is, the nation of Israel against other nations)—but rather they wanted it construed in the accusative case. This was also the view of the translator Symmachus, who rendered it: *until [God] avenged the people of their enemies* <note>original Greek: ἕως ἠμυνάτο τὸν λαὸν τῶν ἐχθρῶν αὐτοῦ</note>. It is no objection that this speech is bound by certain poetic meters, and therefore the word <term>גּוֹי</term> (*Goy*) was used for the Israelites; for the same thing is done more than once in ordinary prose, as the most learned man Andreas Masius also testifies in his commentary on Joshua.

Since, therefore, even the Jews are "Goiim"—that is, "Nations," taking the word in its broad sense—it is clearly evident from this that both Jews and Gentiles are included in those words: *Your name shall be called Abraham, for I have made you a father of a multitude of nations.* For in truth, he is the father of all the faithful, whether born of the Jews or of the Gentiles, since all peoples are "nations." 

Indeed, Christ, who is the true seed of Abraham in whom all the nations of the earth are blessed, came first for the Jews and then for the other nations. This is why the Apostle [Paul], whenever he mentions the calling of the Gentiles, attributes such a great benefit to the mercy of God; but whenever he says the Messiah was presented for the Jews, he commemorates the "truth" of Christ and emphasizes the promises repeated to the fathers. ...mercy did not also abound toward the Jews, just as God’s truth did toward the Gentiles—not because the calling of the Gentiles was not frequently predicted in the Old Testament and foreshadowed in <term>types</term> <note>A "type" is a person, event, or institution in the Old Testament seen as a "shadow" or prefiguration of something in the New Testament.</note>, but because that truth was most conspicuous in the Gentiles and the former mercy was most evident in the Jews.

Yet finally, once the Gentiles were called, Paul was chosen beyond the number of twelve, so that he might be the Teacher of the Gentiles.

The prophets long ago provided a specimen of this truth whenever they prophesied the coming of the Messiah: for they immediately annexed the promise regarding the calling of the Gentiles, as a great benefit that would immediately follow the manifestation of Christ in the flesh. Hence, in Genesis 49:10, after Jacob had said: *The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh comes* <note>original: "Schilo." This is a messianic title meaning "the one to whom it belongs."</note>, he immediately adds: *and to him shall be the obedience*—or the gathering—*of the peoples*, words which clearly signify the calling of the Gentiles. 

And in Micah 5:2–3, after the prophet had said: *And thou, Bethlehem Ephrata, though thou be little among the leaders of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel,* etc. After that prophecy regarding the Messiah’s coming, there is added in verse 3 [the promise] regarding the calling of the Gentiles: *when the remnant of his brethren shall return with the Israelites.* There are certainly significant reasons why mention is usually made in the same prophecy of both Christ’s arrival and the calling of the Gentiles. 

I. The first is taken from the name of Abraham; because since he was the "father of a multitude of nations," the promises made to all of Abraham's descendants—both Jews and Gentiles—are included in the prophecies regarding the <term>blessed seed</term> <note>A reference to the promise that through Abraham's offspring all nations would be blessed.</note>. 

II. The second is because God willed, even from the beginning, to provoke the Jews to jealousy by a nation that was no nation <note>original Greek: παραζηλῶσαι ἔθνος ἐπ᾽ οὐκ ἔθνει (*parazēlōsai ethnos ep' ouk ethnei*)</note>. Thus, when mention was made of the calling of the Gentiles, they would know they should not be proud of their lineage, nor haughtily repeat those words, *we are the children of Abraham*, because the Gentiles...

The prophecy of the calling of the nations is annexed to the prophecy of Christ's coming so that, in the fullness of time when these things occurred, the people would not be too greatly terrified, as if God had suddenly changed His plan. They could only be confirmed by the aforementioned prophecies, which they did not understand before the pouring out of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Hence Paul, in Colossians 1:26, proclaims a **mystery** hidden from the ages and says it is wonderful even to the Angels.

...signified, yet God did not immediately wish the thing signified to be fulfilled, nor was it without mystery. First, that fatherhood took place in the family of the Patriarchs; then, as the descendants of Abraham grew, it spread into the Jewish people; and thereafter at various times some shoots from that root were propagated among foreign nations. This resulted in the grafting of **proselytes**, who were previously called *gerim* <note>original: גרים (*gerim*)—a Hebrew term for resident aliens or strangers.</note> or foreigners, and soon after being grafted they were called proselytes or "newcomers," because they were coming to the family of Abraham. Finally, in the fullness of time, the shoots flourished far and wide, and that spiritual fatherhood was extended in the calling of the nations *from sea to sea, and from the rivers even to the ends of the world.* <note>Psalm 72:8</note>. Therefore, just as before the first advent of Christ the Lord wished to give a prelude to His future incarnation; so before the second advent, through the preaching of the word in the calling of the Nations, He also wished to show a prelude of that future calling, when He chose some from among the foreigners who were called proselytes.

But as to why that most wise Moderator <note>A common theological term for God as the ruler and director of history.</note> wished to delay the calling of the nations for so long, there were serious reasons. 
I. Because from that massive transformation, the advent of Christ was far more magnificent, whose glory shone throughout the whole world. II. So that there might stand out a most illustrious <term>type</term> <note>In biblical studies, a "type" is a historical person or event that serves as a prophetic symbol or foreshadowing of something to come later.</note> of predestination—namely, of **election** in the choosing of the Gentiles, and of **reprobation** in the rejection of the Jews.

Furthermore, if it pleases us to examine these matters even more minutely <note>original Greek: εξονυχιζειν (*exonychizein*)—literally "to the quick of the nail," meaning to investigate with extreme precision.</note>, we shall extend the fatherhood of Abraham even further. For we shall divide the Christian Church into three different periods: the first will be in the beginnings of the Christian Church, when the calling of the Nations arrived in the time of the Apostles. The second is at the end of the ages when the Jews shall be converted, and the "fullness of the Gentiles" shall enter after the destruction of Babylon and the Antichrist, at which time all nations and their glory shall be brought to Christ. And the third regards the state after the glorious resurrection. The Prophets speak often of the first period, as in Isaiah 2:2-3 etc.: *It shall come to pass in the last days, that the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be established on the top of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills; and all nations shall flow unto it.*

From other things that follow in that chapter, it is demonstrated that the Devil still wishes to gather **Gog and Magog** <note>Biblical figures representing the enemies of God's people who gather for a final battle.</note> for battle against the Church, but in vain. And then in chapter 21: *John saw a new heaven and a new earth;* because after the judgment, a renewal of the whole world took place.

<meta>This page continues Anthony Cregut's theological exploration of the "First Resurrection." Having established that the Church is promised a period of glory after the fall of the Antichrist, Cregut now categorizes the different types of divine callings and resurrections to clarify how the "First Resurrection" of Revelation 20 should be understood—not merely as a physical event at the end of time, but as a spiritual and historical restoration of the Church.</meta>

<page-num>420</page-num>
<header>ANTHONY CREGUT</header>

Threefold is the calling according to Scripture and the Theologians: *universal*, which is for each and every human being, who are called through the heraldry of nature and the whole universe <note>original: *ex naturæ & totius uniuerfitatis præconio* — Referring to the idea that the natural world "preaches" God's existence</note> according to Psalm 19; *general* or *common*, which occurs through the preaching of the Divine word according to Matthew 28 and Romans 10; and *special*, which occurs inwardly through the Holy Spirit according to Romans 8. In the same way, there is a threefold resurrection. First, the universal resurrection of each and every human being, which will occur at the end of the world, and which is often called in Scripture the *second resurrection*. Second, the *general* or *common* resurrection is the resurrection of the visible Church, which lay as if dead and lifeless in the tomb under the tyranny of the **Antichrist**, but which, having been liberated by the wonderful power of God, is seen to have risen again. And this is called in Revelation 20 the *first resurrection*; specifically in relation to the universal resurrection, which, as we said, is called the second resurrection. After that resurrection of the Church, there will be continuous peace and tranquility for a thousand years—a certain number being placed for an uncertain one, and a definite for an indefinite <note>Cregut suggests the "1,000 years" is a symbolic long period rather than a literal millennium</note>. Finally, the *special* resurrection corresponds to the special calling, and it belongs to the Church of the elect, or the invisible Church; hence it is also called the resurrection of the soul, because although the soul was dead in a moral death <note>original: *morte Ethica*</note> through sin, it thus rises again through efficacious grace. This is also called the "first resurrection" in opposition to the second resurrection (which will be universal); it is also called *regeneration* <note>original: παλιγγενεσία — *palingenesia*, meaning "rebirth" or "new birth"</note> or a "second generation," distinct from the first generation which was from Adam, as Paul says in Philippians 3:11.

Furthermore, just as in the universal calling "in the knowledge of God" <note>original: *ἐν γνώσει τοῦ Θεοῦ*</note> both the power of God and His divinity are manifested (Romans 1) within the subjective nature—that is, in man, though that knowledge was obscured through sin—so in the universal resurrection, the power of God and the glory of His divinity will shine forth wondrously. Matthew 22: *You err, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God.* And Romans 1:4, by raising up the nature of man which had been cast down by sin and death. Next, in the general calling, the Church is called to go out from **Babylon** <note>In Reformation-era theology, Babylon was frequently used as a code for the corrupt Roman Church or the realm of the Antichrist</note> and from the kingdom of the Antichrist through the preaching of the word; likewise, in the general resurrection, the Church of God will rise magnificently and be liberated from the Babylonian captivity and the kingdom of the Antichrist—not by weapons of physical warfare, but by the living and efficacious word of God, *piercing more than any two-edged sword* (Hebrews 4). Of which resurrection...

### ANALYSIS.

*Why Circumcision was instituted after the name of Abraham was bestowed, which signifies the calling of the Nations. Division into two parts: I. The Institution of Circumcision. II. The Purpose for which it was instituted.*

*Observations on the name of Circumcision in various languages. The metaphorical application to the pruning of trees. Whether Circumcision is absurd to human reasoning. That Circumcision was rightly instituted in those regions* <note>The author likely refers to the Middle East, where the climate or local customs made the practice more medically or culturally appropriate.</note>.

*Circumcision was an object of ridicule to the Gentiles, who were ignorant of such great mysteries of God's promises. Two topics will therefore be suitably discussed here: I. *On the institution of Circumcision*. II. *On the purpose for which Circumcision was instituted*. For other matters pertaining to this common topic are sufficiently taught by others in the general systems of Theology.

Circumcision is called <term>peritomē</term> <note>original: "περιτομὴ"; a Greek term meaning "a cutting around."</note> by the Greeks, and among the Hebrews it is <term>milah</term> <note>original: "מילה"; the standard Hebrew word for circumcision.</note>, as it is also for the Rabbis. From this we get <term>brit milah</term> <note>original: "ברית מילה"; "covenant of circumcision."</note>, meaning the *covenant of Circumcision*, and <term>ba'al brit</term> <note>original: "בעל ברית"; literally "master of the covenant," referring to the person who holds the infant during the ceremony, often called a "sandek" or godfather.</note>, the *Master of the covenant*, who is the supporter of the infant to be circumcised. But among the Arabs, it is known by the single word <term>khatan</term> <note>original: "חתאן"</note> derived from <term>kh-t-n</term> <note>original: "חתן"</note>, which means *son-in-law, kinsman, or relative by marriage*; perhaps because it was not permitted by the mandate of divine law to contract a marriage alliance with an uncircumcised man. Hence, in Genesis 34:14–15, the sons of Jacob refused a marriage alliance with Shechem, the son of Hamor, and his marriage with their sister Dinah, unless he were first circumcised, because (they said) *a foreskin is a reproach to us*. Although these things were done through deceit, their reasoning was nevertheless true, since the foreskin was considered unclean. Thus the law was inviolable that males should be "de-foreskinned," as is clear from verse 14 of this chapter: *And the uncircumcised male, whose flesh of his foreskin is not circumcised, that soul shall be cut off from his people, because he has broken my covenant.* This was not only strictly required of men, but was even derived by metaphor to trees and fruits; as in Leviticus 19:23: *Also, when you come into that land and plant any tree for food, you shall count its foreskin as forbidden, the foreskin of its fruit: for three years each shall be as uncircumcised to you; none of them shall be eaten.* This is because, according to Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, 1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French commentator on the Torah.</note>, the tree was considered impure, and its fruits polluted and abominable, just like the foreskin in a man, or the skin blocking the male member. The Chaldean <note>Referring to the Targum, the Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> expresses this emphatically according to the idiom of the language: <term>removing, you shall remove its fruit</term> <note>original: "תרחקון רחקא ית אביבה"; an Aramaic phrasing emphasizing the total rejection of the early fruit.</note>. All these things are signified by the Hebrew word <term>arel</term> <note>original: "ערל"; meaning uncircumcised, clogged, or blocked.</note>, which signifies being uncircumcised or blocked; just as the Arabic <term>alafa</term> <note>original: "עלף"</note> signifies, besides the foreskin, a covering or small cloth in general, as well as a sheath or casing. This is the same meaning as the Greek word <term>akrobystia</term> <note>original: "ἀκροβυστία"; the term for foreskin or uncircumcision used frequently by the Apostle Paul.</note>, so often repeated by Paul, as if "covered at the extremity," from <term>buō</term> <note>original: "βύω"</note>, meaning to obstruct or plug up.

Cregutus notes that the concept of being "uncircumcised" extended even to young fruit trees, which were considered "impure" for the first three years after planting.</summary>

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS. #

Since this is the case, this institution of circumcision seems plainly absurd to human reasoning. For who would not wonder that the most holy God—who, in His glorious majesty, is supremely adorable to both men and Angels—wished to establish the sacrament of so many mysteries in the private parts? And that by removing the foreskin, or baring the anatomy, He similarly uncovered man’s shame, which nature and modesty have desired to keep covered ever since the fall of Adam? This is why Ham was cursed: because he so irreverently and impudently uncovered the nakedness of his father Noah while he was overcome with wine. 

But let "flesh and blood" <note>A biblical idiom for human nature or limited human perspective.</note> cease to quibble here. Is any part of the body truly more shameful than another in the sight of God? What made those members shameful in our eyes, if not sin—which cannot be attributed to God? Therefore, God chose to select those members which are shameful not to Himself, but to man, so that He might make the wisdom of the world look foolish. He did this the more to cast down the pride of the flesh; even the first circumcised man <note>referring to Abraham</note>, though he was over ninety years old, had to "become a fool" in the world's eyes so that he might show himself obedient to God. And so in that mystery, just as in the mystery of the cross, it pleased God to reveal to the world the truth of the Apostle’s words: *that the foolishness of God is wiser than men* <note>original Greek: "μωρίαν τοῦ Θεοῦ"; see 1 Corinthians 1:25</note>, so that we might think piously and speak soberly regarding the mysteries of faith.

Nevertheless, even if these things seem foolish to men at first glance, would anyone dare to claim that they were instituted discordantly, or *by chance and not by divine purpose* <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ τύχης non ἐκ τῆς προαιρέσεως"</note>? Truly, even those things which seem foolish in the judgment of men are ordered by God with great reason. For since God especially wished to emphasize man's natural corruption through original sin—lest the human race grow proud and so that it might seek a redeemer—He likewise wished to represent and graphically depict that corruption through various Sacraments. Therefore, God instituted Circumcision in those parts which are the instruments of procreation. He did this so that, by the cutting away of the foreskin, it might be signified that whatever is born of man is impure and unclean, according to the saying: *that which is born of the flesh is flesh* <note>John 3:6</note>. For this reason, the "old man" must be stripped off and circumcised through this ritual, lest the soul itself be cir-

...should be cut away, just as it was later shown in another sacrament in the New Testament, where baptism signifies the washing away of the filth of the flesh. Furthermore, that sacrament of Circumcision signified the "blessed seed" <note>A reference to the promised Messiah.</note> which was to come forth from the loins of Abraham; since His generation was not **from the flesh** <note>original Greek: "ἐκ σαρκὸς"</note> but **from the seed of David according to the flesh** <note>original Greek: "ἐκ σπέρματος Δαβὶδ κατὰ σάρκα"; see Romans 1:3</note>, a **rebirth** <note>original Greek: "παλιγγενεσία" (palingenesia), meaning regeneration or spiritual renewal.</note> has transformed us. By the first, the guilt of Adam is removed, and by the second, the very act of inherent corruption is stripped away. Therefore, whoever is ashamed of circumcision—the token of salvation—should also be ashamed of the salvation that flowed from the loins of Abraham.

It is no wonder, then, if the Gentiles—who were ignorant of such great mysteries—mocked Circumcision and everywhere traduced the circumcised with hateful and envious labels. Because of this, the Jews were called *recutiti* <note>A Latin slur meaning "skinned back" or "re-skinned."</note>, because the skin had been cut away from the glans. Thus Sidonius says: *He brings the origins of the "skinned-back" Jews.* And Martial, in Book 7: *You do not flee the loins of the "skinned-back" Jews.* And Horace, in Satires Book 1, Satire 5, calls them *Apellas*: *Let the Jew Apella believe it.* This was a fictional name derived from the prefix *a* (meaning "without") and *pellis* ("skin"), signifying one who is "skinless." It is no wonder (I say) since the Pagans saw only the external matter but were ignorant of the internal meaning; they saw the outer bark, but were unable to look within to see the marrow hidden inside. But on the other hand, the Jews—who knew a mystery lay hidden in Circumcision, even if they did not all discern it clearly—hated the uncircumcised because they knew God had instituted the rite. Therefore, they **contemptuously** <note>original Greek: "ἐξουθενικῶς" (exouthenikos).</note> called the uncircumcised "foreskinned." Indeed, they did not dare to enter the holy places or even eat with the uncircumcised; this is why Pilate went out from the judgment hall to speak to the Jews who were accusing Christ <note>To avoid them becoming "defiled" by entering a Gentile space.</note>. Hence, in 1 Samuel 18:25, Saul requested from David a hundred foreskins of the Philistines as a dowry for Michal, the daughter of King Saul. This was done by Saul so that David would be held in great hatred by the Philistines (who shuddered at circumcision), and thus they might conspire to kill David.

Nevertheless, even if circumcision tastes like foolishness to human reason, and the Gentiles moreover were ignorant of the thing it signified,

But for what reason do the Turks observe circumcision, which they call *Sunnah* <note>original: "Tsuneth"; referring to the *Sunnah*, the traditional customs and practices of the Islamic community.</note>, since no command for it is found in the **Quran**, nor was the false prophet Muhammad himself circumcised? They do not circumcise on the eighth day, but from the seventh year to the fifteenth and beyond, so that the ones being circumcised may be able to pronounce the ritual words. Nor does the circumcision take place in their temples, nor is it performed by the priests—whom they call *Talismans* <note>A term used here to refer to the *Ulema* or religious scholars, though "Talisman" is a curious Latinization in this context.</note>—but by an experienced surgeon. Regarding the giving of names: although they are bestowed at birth, they are nevertheless renewed at the circumcision. And those names are almost always meaningful; such as *Solyman* (**Solomon**), that is, "peaceful"; *Sultan Selim*, "Prince of peace"; *Muhammed*, "Praiseworthy"; *Mahmut*, "Desirable"; *Ali*, "High"; *Mustapha*, "Sanctified"; and *Sophi*, "Holy."

Since he was first a Samaritan and later became a Jew, he was therefore circumcised a second time. For Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403), a bishop known for his "Panarion," a massive work refuting heresies.</note> testifies that it was the custom for those who converted from the Samaritans to the Jews to render their prior circumcision void. This refers to *epispasm*, a surgical procedure used in antiquity to reverse circumcision.</note> and then cut it off again. For this reason, Symmachus's edition of the Old Testament is frequently corrupted, because he translated incorrectly in order to refute the Samaritans. For Epiphanius mentions several Emperors together, namely **Hadrian**, **Antoninus Verus**, both **Commoduses**, **Pertinax**, and **Severus**; nevertheless, since he places **Theodotion** <note>Another 2nd-century translator of the Hebrew Bible into Greek.</note> after Symmachus, and indicates twice that he lived under that Commodus who followed Marcus Antoninus, it is sufficiently clear that Symmachus lived under Antoninus Verus, while Theodotion lived around the beginning of the reign of **Quintus Commodus**. These facts are evident from his book *On Weights and Measures*.

But indeed, what shall we say of those Jews who believe that circumcision was at one time repeated within the very people of God, and who attempt to prove this from the Scripture in **Joshua 5:2** <note>The OCR says "v. 1," but the text refers to verse 2.</note>: *At that time, Jehovah said to Joshua, prepare for yourself sharp knives, and, repeating a second time, circumcise the children of Israel.* <note>original Hebrew: "ושוב מל את בני ישראל שנית," *V’shuv mol et b’nei Yisrael shenit*.</note> According to the Chaldean <note>The Aramaic translation or Targum.</note>: *And repeating, circumcise the children of Israel a second time.* The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> says: *And sitting down, he circumcised the children of Israel a second time.* <note>original Greek: "Καὶ καθίσας περιέτεμε τοὺς υἱוὺς Ἰσραὴλ ἐκ δευτέρου."</note> For the word "return/repeat" <note>original Hebrew: *shuv*.</note>, they seem to have read "sit" <note>original Hebrew: *yashav*.</note>, since they rendered it as *sitting down* or *having sat* instead of *repeating*, although the words for "return" and "sit" are often confused in Hebrew. It is from this that the **Talmudists** devise in the *Chapters of Rabbi Eliezer* <note>original: "capitulis Eleazaris," referring to the *Pirke De-Rabbi Eliezer*, a midrashic work of Jewish tradition.</note> the idea that the complete rite of circumcising the foreskin was not handed down to **Abraham** by God; and therefore, that the phrase "a second time" refers to the perfection of the ceremony. For this reason, they argue that those who had been circumcised once according to the rite of Abraham were required to be cut again in a more perfect manner. These things certainly seem foolish and impious at first glance, unless we understand that something mystical lies hidden beneath the surface—as often happens with the Talmudists. That is to say, this refers not to the historical **Joshua** who foreshadowed things to come, but to the **Jesus** <note>In Latin and Greek, the names "Joshua" and "Jesus" are identical (Iesus/Iesous). The author is making a "typological" argument: the historical Joshua's actions pointed forward to the spiritual actions of Christ.</note> who was prefigured and foreshadowed, by whom that old circumcision was made perfect, and through whom the faithful are circumcised with a circumcision...

# BY ANTHONIUS CREGUTUS

...not made with hands <note>original: "ἀχειροποιήτῳ"</note>, by which it is not the flesh and the foreskin of the flesh that is amputated, but the body of sins that is cast off—a spiritual circumcision in which only the children of Abraham according to the promise participate.

However, the Talmudists <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic law and tradition.</note> offer vain and obscene reasons for a "second circumcision," which we shall omit in order to propose one for consideration that seems to us to carry some weight. For they say that most Jews in the time of Moses were correctly circumcised by their parents in their tender youth, yet they had to be circumcised again if they wished to be joined in the communion of sacred rites with the rest of the Jews. The reason is that those wretched people, pressed by the cruelty of the Egyptian slavery, used a certain medical art to draw down and stretch the skin to form a new foreskin, covering the glans with skin. For this reason, they were called *Meshukim* <note>original: "משוכים," a Hebrew term for those who have undergone epispasm to hide their circumcision</note>, as if you were to say "one who draws over the skin" <note>original: "ἐπισπαςικὸς"</note>, from the skin having been drawn forward.

This was likewise done by their descendants when the Romans held power after the Temple and the City were utterly destroyed. For many Hebrews, failing under the yoke of their enemies, used the same art to hide their Jewish religion, striving to be recognized as uncircumcised rather than circumcised. But later, by the order of **Bar Kokhba** <note>The leader of the second Jewish revolt against Rome (132–136 AD). His name is recorded here as "Bar Cosba."</note>, they were circumcised again. For he was a False Messiah <note>original: "Pseudomessias"</note> truly worthy of his name, which signifies "son of a lie" <note>A pun on his name: while "Bar Kokhba" means "Son of a Star," his critics called him "Bar Koziba," meaning "Son of a Lie."</note>. Liberty was promised to the Jews, and the city of **Betar** <note>original: "Bitter," the final fortress of the Bar Kokhba revolt.</note> was even occupied, but he did not hold his kingdom for long; for immediately under **Aelius Hadrian** <note>The Roman Emperor Hadrian, who suppressed the revolt.</note>, Betar was captured, and four million <note>original: "quadragies centena millia"—a traditional historical figure that may be exaggerated</note> Hebrews fell. 

It seems **Paul** alluded to this in 1 Corinthians 7:18: *Was anyone called who was circumcised? Let him not draw over his foreskin; was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised* <note>original: "περιτετμημένος τις ἐκλήθη; μὴ ἐπισπάσθω, ἐν ἀκροβυστίᾳ τις ἐκλήθη, μὴ περιτεμνέσθω"</note>. Since the word "to draw over" <note>original: "ἐπισπᾶσθαι"</note> is opposed to "to be circumcised" <note>original: "περιτέμνεσθαι"</note>, it is clear enough that Paul is speaking of the drawing forward of the foreskin, which was done by a surgeon's hand so that the glans would be covered. Many ancient authors mention this, such as **Celsus** <note>A 1st-century Roman medical writer.</note> in Book 7, Chapter 25; **Epiphanius**, whom I mentioned above in his book *On Weights and Measures*; and **Josephus** <note>A 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> in *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 12, Chapter 6.

Nevertheless, that Jewish rite of repeated circumcision can in no way be proven from the passage in Joshua. Let us, therefore, search out the true double meaning of this commandment; we boldly assert that the Jewish people were not circum—

...[circumci]sed, and concerning the repeated circumcision, whatever those words <note>original Hebrew: שוב (*shuv*), "return/again," and שנית (*shenit*), "a second time"</note> might seem to designate; it is because those who were circumcised in the time of Joshua had not been circumcised in the time of Abraham or Moses; for that generation had passed away, and a new one succeeded it. Since, therefore, the rite of circumcision had been interrupted for about forty years during the wandering in the desert, God willed that it should be renewed once again. For since God gathered the Church in Abraham and his descendants, upon whom He impressed the promises of the land of Canaan, He also willed to seal those promises with the sign of the covenant. However, because that symbol had been omitted for a long time in the desert, and almost all those who had been circumcised had died, it was necessary that, after the crossing of the Jordan and the gathering of a new assembly, the people should be circumcised again. In this way, the covenant made with Abraham and his seed might be sealed anew by the solemnly repeated Sacrament. Therefore, the same individuals were not circumcised twice, as we heard above that the Talmudists <note>Scholars of Jewish law and tradition; the author suggests their interpretations are groundless "dreams."</note> dream. This is sufficiently explained in verse 3 with these words: *Now this is the reason why Joshua circumcised them: all the people who had come out of Egypt as males, all the men fit for war, had died in the desert, on the journey itself, after they had come out of Egypt.* And it adds later that their children had been substituted in their place. Joshua circumcised these, as they were uncircumcised <note>original: "præputiati," literally "possessing a foreskin."</note>.

Nevertheless, we do not deny that many of those who had been circumcised in Egypt were still living. For it does not seem likely that the rebellion of the Jews committed at Kadesh-barnea <note>A site in the desert where the Israelites rebelled against God, leading to their forty-year wandering.</note>, which brought such great slaughter upon the nation, applied to those who had not yet reached their twentieth year. Add to this that the Jews exempt the entire tribe of Levi from that crime. Therefore, the sense of Scripture is to be understood according to the majority of the people. Indeed, Scripture expressly forbids that Caleb, Joshua, and Eleazar should be included in that destruction. Thus, Augustine, in his *Questions on Joshua*, once solved the problem by explaining the repetition through a rhetorical figure called <term>Synecdoche</term> <note>A figure of speech where a part is used to represent the whole (e.g., saying "the people were circumcised" even if only the majority were).</note>. The people (he says) had been circumcised before, because some part of them lacked a foreskin: such as Caleb, Joshua, Eleazar, and perhaps all the Levites, and those who at Kadesh-barnea had not—

...while they were twenty years old. However, the people are circumcised now for a second time, because the greatest part of them is being circumcised—specifically in the manner explained above.

Andreas Masius <note>A 16th-century Flemish scholar and Hebraist renowned for his commentary on the Book of Joshua.</note> relates yet another exposition in his work on Joshua, taken from Rabbi Levi son of Gerson <note>A 14th-century Jewish philosopher and commentator often known as Ralbag.</note> and many others. He reasoned as follows: that when Moses was returning to Egypt to be the leader of his kin, he had learned through his own personal danger how poorly God takes the neglect of that sign of adoption. <note>This refers to the "Bridegroom of Blood" incident in Exodus 4, where God nearly kills Moses for failing to circumcise his son.</note> Therefore, Moses immediately circumcised the entire multitude, which had long neglected to do so because of the harshness of their slavery. For they could not have celebrated the Passover without laying aside the foreskin, nor could they set out to possess the land of Canaan, which had been promised only to the circumcised. Furthermore, since those whom Moses had circumcised in Egypt had almost all died out during the long wandering on the journey, and those born in the meantime were not circumcised, there was now a need to circumcise the multitude collectively. This view of Rabbi Levi and many other Jews coincides almost exactly with our explanation provided above, except for what he adds about the neglect of circumcision in Egypt (which is asserted without Scriptural evidence), as well as its restoration by Moses—a point which the Christian author Tertullian <note>An early and influential Christian theologian from Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD).</note> once approved and followed.

I will not pass over another explanation <term>glossema <note>A marginal note or explanation of a difficult word.</note></term> by Rabbi David Kimchi <note>A medieval Jewish grammarian and biblical commentator known as Radak.</note>, cited by the same Andreas Masius. He wrote that those words <term>return/again <note>original Hebrew: שוב (*shuv*)</note></term> and <term>a second time <note>original Hebrew: שנית (*shenit*)</note></term> found in the aforementioned passage of Joshua do not refer to the act of circumcision itself—as if the people were being circumcised twice—but rather to the *oversight* of the procedure. Therefore, Joshua was commanded that, moving back and forth through the camp again and again, visiting each and every person, he should ensure that no one remained uncircumcised. For the word <term>secondly <note>original Hebrew: שנית (*shenit*)</note></term>, which is derived from the word <term>to repeat <note>original Hebrew: שנה (*shanah*)</note></term>, does not strictly mean "a second time," but "frequently." Thus, something is not to be done twice, but repeated often, because the command regarding circumcision must be constantly impressed upon the people. However, to indulge in such clever subtleties is not truly to search for the genuine sense of Scripture, but rather to violently twist the most sacred oracles to fit one's own mind.

...applying that Jewish <term>circumcision</term> <note>The ritual removal of the foreskin, which the author is here interpreting as a spiritual metaphor.</note> skillfully to the mysteries of the Christian religion. In Joshua chapter 5, it is recorded that the people were circumcised again, and indeed with small stone swords; certainly, that event was a foreshadowing of that circumcision by which Christ himself circumcises for us stony statues and idols. For those foreskins—that is, the delusions of this world—are cut away by stony swords (the words of Jesus our Lord) and are piled up into heaps everywhere. God then warned that they should be circumcised through Jesus—even those who already possessed that circumcision which took its beginning from Abraham. 

Justin <note>Justin Martyr (c. 100–165 AD), an early Christian apologist whose "Dialogue with Trypho" is a famous debate between a Christian and a Jew.</note> then adds: "For in your first [circumcision] iron is used and continues to be used, because you remain in the stubbornness of your heart and soul. For the first day of the week, while it remains the first of all days, is again called the eighth in the numbering of all the days which revolve in a cycle, and yet it remains the first. 

Thus says Justin; and those things which he said concerning Christ the Rock and the little stony swords align correctly with the Hebrew text, <note>original: חרבות צורים (charvot tzurim)</note> "stony or flinty swords."
