Truly, the word *tsur* <note>original: צוּר</note> always signifies a stone or a rock; it never signifies "an edge" in the Sacred Scriptures. For those words in Psalm 89:44, "You have turned back the *edge* of his sword," <note>original: תָּשִׁיב צוּר חַרְבּוֹ (*tashiv tsur harbo*). Modern translations often render this as "the edge of his sword," but the author argues the literal meaning is "the rock/hardness of his sword."</note> are a metaphor derived from the hardness of flint, rather than from the proper meaning of the word itself. The <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, often abbreviated as LXX.</note> translates the passage as: *Make for yourself sharp knives from stone.* <note>original Greek: ποιήσον σεαυτῷ μαχαίρας ἐκ πέτρας ἀκροτόμους</note> Here it should be noted in passing, according to the opinion of the ancient Jews in the book *Vayikra Rabba* <note>A homiletic commentary (Midrash) on the Book of Leviticus.</note> or the "Great Leviticus," that there was such a vast quantity of discarded foreskins in one place that they formed a hill in a place that was otherwise flat and level; for this reason, that place was called *Givat Ha-Aralot*, <note>original: גִּבְעַת הָעֲרָלוֹת</note> which is to say, "The Hill of the Foreskins." However, the <term>Chaldean</term> <note>Referring to the Targum, the Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> thought that the small hill took its name from the foreskins. Therefore he translates it thus: *And he circumcised the sons of Israel on the hill, which they named the Hill of Foreskins.* This is more likely.

Truly, however, even though the Jews were strictly circumcised according to that severe command of God in Genesis 17:14—*The male who is not circumcised shall be cut off*—and the example of Moses, whom the Angel sought to kill because he had not circumcised his son, nevertheless that rite was omitted for forty years in the desert by God’s permission. This was due to the hardships of the journey, since the physical suffering of those who were circumcised was extreme. This is evident from Genesis 34:25, where just two of Jacob’s sons, on account of the violation of their sister, brought a deadly slaughter upon an entire city. <note>Referring to the story of Simeon and Levi attacking the Shechemites while the men were incapacitated and healing from circumcision.</note> Therefore, one wonders why, after the crossing of the Jordan when Joshua circumcised the whole people by God’s command, those Canaanite petty kings did not destroy the entire nation while they were in such great pain. But without a doubt, their minds were struck with such great terror that they were utterly stunned, nor did they think of what ought to be done.

Nevertheless, although the Jews were circumcised by God’s prescription and were "the Circumcision" in contrast to the "uncircumcised" Gentiles—hence the distinction made by Paul between the <term>Circumcision</term> and the <term>Uncircumcision</term> <note>In the Pauline epistles, these terms often serve as shorthand for Jews and Gentiles.</note>, and the resulting great hatred that grew between the Jews and the Nations—nonetheless, many people professed the Jewish religion who were not themselves circumcised. Thus, four types of people can be observed with respect to religion: 1. The Jews, who were necessarily circumcised, and without circumcision there could be no fellowship among them; indeed, as was said above, if anyone [sought] another circumcision...

...which he held as a Jew, he was circumcised again when he defected from his own people to the Jews, as was shown by the example of the Samaritans. II. The Gentiles, who were most alienated from the Jewish religion and circumcision, whom they mockingly <note>original Greek: σκωπτικῶς (*skōptikōs*)</note> used to call *Apellas* <note>A Roman nickname for Jews, likely meaning "without skin," referencing circumcision.</note> and "the skinless" <note>original Latin: *recutitos*</note>. III. Those proselytes who exactly observed all the rites of the Jews and did not refuse to be circumcised. IV. There were other proselytes who indeed followed the Jewish religion in many things, who honored the Jerusalem sanctuary with peculiar veneration, and who sacrificed victims in the temple courtyard, but nonetheless were not circumcised.

The first group were called "proselytes" in the absolute sense, from the Greek word *proselytoi* <note>original: προσήλυτοι</note>, as if "those who have approached" <note>original Greek: προσελθόντες (*proselthontes*)</note> since they were coming toward the Jewish religion. Among the Hebrews, they were also called *gerim* <note>original: גֵּרִים</note>, meaning "residents" or "newcomers," because they lived in the Promised Land which God had bestowed upon His people as a special favor. The Chaldean <note>The Aramaic translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> calls such a person *totav* <note>original: תּוֹתָב</note>, meaning "newcomer" or "proselyte," while the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> uses the term *paroikos* <note>original: πάροικος, meaning a sojourner or neighbor</note>.

These were also called "proselytes of righteousness" because they followed the righteousness of the law exactly, were circumcised, and embraced all the Mosaic observances. These proselytes transitioned into Judaism in three ways: *by circumcision, baptism, and offering* <note>original Hebrew: בְּמִילָה בִּטְבִילָה וְקָרְבָּן (*be-milah, be-tevilah, ve-korban*)</note>. 

Women transitioned through baptism and offering; men through the three requirements mentioned above. For the circumcision of women (which was mentioned earlier) was not practiced among the Jews, but rather among the Muslims of Egypt and Syria, and among the Abyssinian Christians—thus does superstition drive men mad.

The second type of proselytes were called "proselytes of the gate." These observed only certain precepts of the Patriarchs, such as the prohibition against consuming blood or animals that had been strangled <note>These are part of the "Noahide Laws" believed to apply to all humanity.</note>, a rule dating back to the time of Noah and eventually upheld after the Council of Jerusalem in Acts 15. In the Scriptures, these people are often called *Hellenes* <note>original Greek: ἕλληνες</note>, that is, "Greeks." This creates a distinction between "Hellenists" and "Greeks." 

The "Hellenists" <note>original Greek: Ἑλληνισταὶ (*Hellenistai*)</note> were Hebrews who were said to "Hellenize" <note>To adopt Greek language or customs.</note>—not because they were residents of Greece or lived there, but because they used the Greek version of the <term>Septuagint</term> translators. The "Greeks," however, were Gentiles who were accustomed to "Judaize" <note>To follow Jewish customs without fully converting.</note>, because they honored the Temple of Jerusalem with a particular religious devotion due to the magnificence of the temple itself. Many examples of these are found in the writings of <term>Josephus</term> <note>Flavius Josephus, a first-century Jewish historian.</note> and in Acts 8:27 <note>The account of the Ethiopian eunuch traveling to worship at the Temple.</note>.

It also clarifies the linguistic distinction between Greek-speaking Jews (Hellenists) and God-fearing Gentiles (Greeks).</summary>

# ANTHONY CREGUT

"The Eunuch, a high official of Candace" <note>original Greek: Εὐνοῦχος τῆς Κανδάκης δυνάστης (*Eunouchos tēs Kandakēs dynastēs*); see Acts 8:27</note>. Such a man was also Cornelius the Centurion, and that other Centurion whose faith Christ praised, and others of whom it is spoken in John 12:20. Luke, in the book of Acts, is accustomed to calling these people **worshippers** <note>original Greek: σεβομένους (*sebomenous*), often translated as 'God-fearers'—Gentiles who worshipped the God of Israel without full conversion to Judaism.</note>. Oecumenius <note>A 10th-century Bishop and commentator on the New Testament.</note> once wrote that the Gospel was spread from the Jews to the Samaritans, and from them to the pure Gentiles, among whom were the Ethiopians. Therefore (to say this in passing), Peter was not the first to preach to the Gentiles, as the supporters of the Pope <note>original Latin: *Pontificij*</note> claim; for Philip preached earlier to the Samaritans and to the Eunuch who was an Ethiopian.

Observe, however, that the converts from the Gentiles at that time were not called *proselytes*. This is because in that **dispensation** <note>original Latin: *œconomia*, referring to the theological era or 'divine plan' of the early Church.</note>, the calling of the Gentiles was not an extraordinary thing—as it was when they became proselytes under the Old Law—but was the ordinary way; a single Church was being made out of Jews and Gentiles. Having set aside the notion of "proselytes," the ancient Church adopted the term **Neophytes**, following that passage of Scripture in 1 Timothy 3:6, where it forbids a Bishop to be a **neophyte** <note>original Greek: νεόφυτον (*neophyton*)</note>, meaning a *novice*. Properly speaking, it signifies a **new plant** <note>original Latin: *nouam plantam*</note>; for, as Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, the 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople known for his eloquent preaching.</note> observed, the Apostle did not say **young** <note>original Greek: νέον (*neon*)</note>, but **neophyte**, that is, someone recently grafted into the Church. Paul wrote this to Timothy while he was in Asia, where it was necessary to summon many from among the Gentiles to lead the Church. However, the term "Neophytes" was also used generally by the ancients in regard to age. Hence, in the Fourth Council of Carthage—where two hundred and fourteen Bishops were gathered—in Canon 86 (for there are 104 Canons in that Council), we find these words: *“Let the Neophytes for a time abstain from more sumptuous banquets, public shows, or from their wives.”* Thus, the name "Neophyte" was a new designation in the New Testament Church and is very rare in Scripture; from its origin, the naming of "proselytes" faded away in the Church.

After the proselytes had come to the Jews, the way the Hebrews themselves should conduct themselves toward their **residents** <note>original Latin: *inquilinos*, referring to foreigners living among the Jews.</note> is taught in the book *Mechilta*, which is a commentary on Exodus. For since Moses said in Exodus chapter 22, verse 21: *“Do not mistreat a stranger, nor oppress him: for you were strangers in the land of Egypt,”* the Rabbis wrote on that passage that proselytes are to be loved for three reasons: I. Because they are loved by God. II. Because in Scripture they are always named and treated just like Israel. III. Because the holy

Because God does not exclude any creature, but receives all. For his gates are open at every hour, and whoever wishes to enter and be joined, enters and is joined. And the **proselytes** <note>original Hebrew: הגרים (*ha-gerim*)</note> shall eat of the **bread of the presence** <note>original Hebrew: הפנים (*ha-panim*), literally "of the faces." The author suggests that converts are welcome even to the sacred Showbread of the Temple.</note>, that is, the bread of proposition. In Deuteronomy 10, God will give them food and clothing, which is what Jacob asked for in Genesis 28: *If God will give me bread to eat and raiment to put on, etc.* Therefore, they shall be sojourners like Jacob, the firstborn of God. Petrus Galatinus <note>A 16th-century Franciscan friar and scholar of Jewish mysticism and the Talmud.</note> reports these things in book 9, chapter 13 of *The Secrets of Catholic Truth*.

It is therefore clearly evident from the above that King Herod was by no means a Jew by nation, but an <term>Idumaean</term> <note>A person from Idumaea (Edom), a region south of Judea; traditionally the descendants of Esau.</note>. Yet, he was not a "proselyte" either, even though he lived in the communion of the Jews and was among the number of those who are said to **Judaize** in Esther 8:17 <note>original Hebrew: מתיהדים (*mityahadim*); original Greek: ἰουδαΐζουσι (*ioudaïzousi*), meaning to adopt Jewish customs or pass oneself off as a Jew.</note> according to the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>. For between these two categories, a middle ground is given: 1. He was not a Jew, because he was an Idumaean, as I have said. 2. He was not a proselyte, because he himself was not a convert or a stranger, having been born of circumcised parents. Thus, he is incorrectly called a proselyte by Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his writings against heresies.</note> (as Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger, a leading 16th-century scholar of chronology and history.</note> testifies), since not even his grandfather was a proselyte, but was born from one who was already circumcised.

The historical truth, therefore, according to Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> in *Antiquities*, book 14, chapter 17, is this: Hyrcanus, King of the Jews, defeated the Idumaeans. After they were conquered, he handed down the law to them and established a treaty on the condition that they would remain with the Jews provided they were circumcised and observed Jewish rites. Therefore, from that time until the destruction of the Temple, they lived with the Jews, professed the same religion, and were regarded as true Jews. Thus, Herod’s parents migrated to the Jews **from foreign nations** <note>original Greek: ἀλλοφυλισμοῦ (*allophylismou*)</note> and were circumcised; therefore, those earlier ones were the proselytes, not Herod and the other Idumaeans of his time, whom the ancients rightly called **men of the same race** <note>original Greek: ἄνδρας ὁμοφύλους (*andras homophylous*)</note>. Thus it is clear in what sense the Rabbis called the reign of Herod the **kingdom of the proselytes** <note>original Hebrew: מלכות הגרים (*malkhut ha-gerim*)</note>. *Truly I would rather be Herod's pig than his son* <note>original: "Certè mallem esse Herodis suem quàm filium." This is a famous quip attributed to Augustus Caesar, playing on the Greek words for pig (*hys*) and son (*hyios*).</note>, because as a Jew he did not eat pork. Nevertheless, it can truly be said that this Herod was an **Amphibian** <note>The author uses "Amphibian" metaphorically to describe someone who lives in two different "elements"—in this case, Jewish and Roman cultures.</note>, because he practiced Judaism with the Jews and lived like a Gentile with the Romans.

However, a difficulty could arise here, and one might ask: was it lawful to make <term>proselytes</term> <note>From the Greek *proselutos*, meaning a convert or "one who has come over."</note> even while the law of circumcision was still in effect? The reason for doubting this comes from Matthew 23, where Christ rebukes the Pharisees in this manner: *Woe to you, Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, for you traverse sea and land to make a single proselyte*, etc. For even if this word "proselyte" corresponds to the word **Ger** <note>Hebrew: גֵר (*ger*)</note>, which among the Hebrews signifies any kind of stranger or newcomer, usage specifically established that it also signified only those proselytes who professed the true religion with the Jews. Therefore, why does Christ rebuke the Scribes and Pharisees for making proselytes?

I respond: Christ does not condemn them for making proselytes as such—for in doing so, He would be condemning the very religion He Himself professed—but because they specifically made *such* proselytes; that is, men converted more to **Pharisaism** than to Judaism. These converts were steeped in Pharisaic doctrine and behavior; indeed, because recent converts are often more tenacious and rigid observers (as is frequently the case), they became **twice as much the sons of Gehenna** <note>original Greek: διπλότεροι υἱοὶ γεέννης (*diploteroi hyioi geennes*); referring to the fires of judgment or hell.</note>.

Another explanation can also be brought forward, such as that of the most learned **Cameron** <note>John Cameron (c. 1579–1625), a renowned Scottish theologian and scholar of the New Testament.</note> regarding that passage. He wrote that the parts of this verse should not be explained separately, as if Christ were rebuking two different things: 1. that they made proselytes, and 2. that they made them sons of Gehenna. Instead, they should be rendered thus: *Woe to you Pharisees, because after you have moved every stone to make one proselyte, you afterwards make him worse.* A similar expression exists in Romans 6:17: *Thanks be to God that, though you were slaves to sin, you obeyed from the heart,* etc. <note>In both cases, the first part of the sentence sets the stage for the second, more important point.</note>

Thus ends the first part of the **investigation** <note>original Greek: συζητήσεως (*syzeteseos*), meaning a systematic inquiry or discussion.</note>. The second part follows, namely: the purpose for which circumcision was instituted, which Moses sufficiently hinted at when he said, *It shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you.* That "sign" (as is evident) does not signify in the way that smoke from a furnace is a sign of fire; rather, it signifies **by convention** <note>original Greek: κατ' συνθήκην (*kata syntheken*)</note>, that is, by divine appointment. Therefore (as observed above), lest anyone should quibble—

Moreover, it is a sign of the covenant between God and the offspring of Abraham. But just as in olden times, covenants were not only recorded in public registers but were also usually engraved in bronze or carved into stone so that their memory might be more witnessed and celebrated; so now, God carves His covenant into the flesh of Abraham. For Circumcision was, as it were, a solemn monument of that adoption by which the race of Abraham had been chosen as God's own special people.

It must be noted, however, that this covenant of God with Abraham was established as a **special covenant**. For a **general covenant** had preceded it, which God had struck with all creatures, even those without reason (Genesis 9:8), by which He promised that He would no longer send a universal flood to submerge the world again; the sign of this was the rainbow in the sky. This covenant with Abraham, however, is special because it regards only the descendants of Abraham—that is, the children of the promise, or the elect, from among both the Jews and the Gentiles. For Abraham was named such because he was the father of a multitude of nations. Romans 9: *It is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God; rather, the children of the promise are counted as the offspring.* Galatians 3: *If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to the promise.*

Furthermore, it should be observed that although that covenant regarded all the elect from every nation, for a long time it was restricted to the offspring of Abraham according to the flesh—that is, to the Jews alone. Thus, it was foreshadowed by the sign of circumcision, which was a <term>sacrament</term> <note>In this context, a "sacrament" refers to a holy rite that serves as a visible sign of an inward grace or a divine promise.</note> belonging only to the Jews, if you exclude the very few <term>proselytes</term> who were converted from the Gentiles to Judaism. Indeed, long before Abraham, that same special covenant was in force in Adam and Noah, the substance of which was proclaimed from the beginning in Genesis 3, while God says to the first parents <note>original: "protoplastis," referring to Adam and Eve.</note>: *The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent.* Yet, in those first beginnings of the Church, it was announced obscurely; indeed, before Abraham's time it was signified by no sacraments; but in Abraham's time, since God had decreed to gather a Church for Himself out of one nation, He thus renewed and enriched the covenant, and foreshadowed it with an ordinary sacrament—namely, circumcision—from which flowed the distinction between the circumcised and the uncircumcised.

That covenant is signified by the Hebrew word *Berit* <note>original: ברית</note> which in that language sounds the same as *covenant* <note>original: "foedus" in Latin.</note>. Therefore, I cannot restrain myself from censuring here either the excessive boldness or the ignorance of Cardinal Jacques Davy du Perron <note>A prominent 17th-century Catholic diplomat and theologian known for his debates with Protestants.</note>, who stubbornly defends that the word *Berit* properly and in its primary meaning signifies a *cutting* or *fission* because (he says) it is derived from a word which is the same as *to cut* or *to cut off*; and then in a secondary sense denotes a covenant, because (he says) the Chaldeans and Hebrews of old, when making a covenant, would cut a sacrificial victim into two parts, and both parties to the contract would pass through the middle of them; and by this rite they sealed the covenant and asked that God should cut apart the violator or breaker of the covenant in this way (Jeremiah 34:18, Genesis 15:10). That ceremony was observed by God when He sanctioned the covenant with Abraham; hence the Hebrews, not unlike the Latins, say *to strike* or *to hit a covenant* <note>In Latin, the phrase "icere foedus" (to strike a covenant) literally refers to the striking of the sacrificial animal.</note>. And from this, the Cardinal tries to infer that these words *Circumcision is the covenant* are to be properly translated as *Circumcision is the cutting*, and therefore he argues the phrase is not figurative <note>Perron's goal was to argue that sacramental language is literal, not symbolic, a key point of contention between Catholics and Protestants regarding the Eucharist.</note>.

...observe: Do not words gain value through use, just like coins? Thus, he who first represented Moses with horns in the temples of the Papists <note>The author uses "Pontificiorum" (Papists), a common 17th-century Protestant term for Roman Catholics.</note> became an object of mockery for posterity, because in the writings of that Prophet, the word <term>קרן</term> <note>Hebrew: *karan*, meaning to shine or radiate.</note> is used. This word comes from the noun <term>קרן</term> <note>Hebrew: *keren*, which can mean "horn" or "ray of light."</note>, that is, *horn*; from this, it was believed that Moses wore horns on his forehead. However, in the usage of Scripture and among all Hebrews, that verb signifies *to gleam* or *to shine*, which denotes that Moses' face shone because of his recent conversation with God on Sinai. 

Secondly, according to the analogy of grammar, <term>ברית</term> <note>Hebrew: *Berit*, meaning "covenant."</note> more likely arises from the verb <term>ברה</term> <note>Hebrew: *Barah*.</note> which means *to choose*, because the persons between whom a covenant is entered are chosen, as are the matters and conditions for which it is established. But even if <term>ברית</term> is taken from the root <term>ברא</term> <note>Hebrew: *Bara*.</note> which in the *pihel* form <note>A specific grammatical intensive form in Hebrew.</note> signifies *he fell* or *he cut* in addition to *he chose*, the etymology will still fit by reason of its meaning; for victims were usually slaughtered in the striking of covenants. But it does not follow from this that *Berit* properly signifies a "splitting" or "cutting," because even if it signifies a covenant, the reason for the etymology will always remain consistent. 

Thirdly, Perron’s interpretation would be ridiculous. For what is this: "Circumcision is a cutting"? Does not a great mystery lie hidden there? Who does not know that Circumcision was a cutting, or an amputation of the flesh of the foreskin? 

Fourthly, Perron stands alone in his opinion. He is contradicted by the Seventy <note>The Septuagint (LXX), the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> who always translate the name <term>ברית</term> as <term>διαθήκη</term> <note>Greek: *diathēkē*, meaning "covenant" or "testament."</note>, a word which signifies *covenant*; likewise the New Testament in Acts 7 and Hebrews 9. He is also contradicted by the Vulgate edition <note>The standard Latin Bible of the Catholic Church.</note>, which everywhere translates it as *foedus* (covenant). 

Fifthly, Moses explains himself in this <term>v. 11</term> <note>Referring to Genesis 17:11.</note>. For when he had said at the beginning of the verse, *And you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin*; he immediately adds, *it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you.* <term>לאות ברית</term> <note>Hebrew: *le-ot berit*.</note> But if *Berit* were the same as "cutting," in what sense would Moses have said "as a sign of a cutting," when it was properly a cutting itself, according to Davy <note>Cardinal Jacques Davy du Perron.</note>? 

Sixthly, I omit that some, as Mestrezat <note>Jean Mestrezat (1592–1657), a notable French Reformed theologian.</note> testifies, derive it from the word <term>ברק</term> <note>Hebrew: *Barak*.</note> which signifies *to flash* or *to shine*, because those striking a covenant explain their minds to each other without ambiguity; but because these points are twisted against the analogy of grammar, I do not dwell on them. It is established that one should not focus on that foreskin of the flesh, which in itself would be foolishness, but rather the thing signified must be weighed. This is the very marrow within the husk <note>Crégut uses "medulla" (marrow) and "corticis" (husk/bark) as a metaphor for the hidden spiritual meaning inside a physical ritual.</note>, and the spiritual mystery: namely, the circumcision of the mouth, the heart, and the lips. From this, it is clear that there are four kinds of foreskins, and just as many kinds of circumcision. In the *Bereshit Ketanna* <note>original: "Bereſchit Ketanna" — likely referring to a Midrashic commentary on Genesis.</note>, Rabbi Akiba used to say there were four types of foreskins.

I. *The foreskin of the ear. Jeremiah 6:10: Behold, their ear is uncircumcised, so that they cannot give heed.*

II. *The foreskin of the mouth. Exodus 6:11: How should Pharaoh heed me, who am of uncircumcised lips?* <note>The standard citation for "uncircumcised lips" is Exodus 6:12 or 6:30.</note> This passage, cited by that Rabbi, speaks of a stutter; for in those who stutter, such as Moses was, many superfluous syllables fall out, which are like a foreskin that must be cut away so that the speech might be made pure.

III. *The foreskin of the heart. Deuteronomy 10:16: Circumcise the foreskin of your heart.* So also in Jeremiah 4:4.

IV. *The foreskin in the flesh. Genesis 17:11: He who has not circumcised the flesh of his foreskin, that soul shall be cut off.*

From this, it follows that there are four kinds of circumcisions. Three are spiritual—namely of the heart, the ear, and the lips—which are always necessary for everyone. But the fourth, that of the flesh, ceased upon the rising of the Messiah, the spiritual teacher. Galatians 5:6: *For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything; but faith acting through love.* And Romans 2:25: *For circumcision indeed is of value if you obey the law; but if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision.* Because Circumcision was like a solemn obligation for the Jews, by which they were bound to the complete performance of the moral law, with the penalty of being "cut off" set before them in the rite of circumcision if they should sin against the law in even the slightest way. 

In this respect, Paul in Colossians 2:14 calls the ceremonial law a handwritten document of condemnation; it is so far from the case that circumcision <term>χειροποίητος</term> <note>Greek: *cheiropoiētos*, meaning "made by human hands."</note> could procure righteousness. But in verse 26 of the same second chapter of Romans, "uncircumcision" is understood in two ways: for the person and for the thing. Therefore: *If the uncircumcised man keeps the requirements of the law, will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision?* At the beginning of the verse, "uncircumcision" is used for the "uncircumcised man"—that is, for the person himself, by way of metonymy <note>A figure of speech where a thing or concept is referred to by the name of something closely associated with it (e.g., using "the crown" to mean "the king").</note>. In the second part of the verse, "uncircumcision" is not used for the uncircumcised man (the person), but for the state and condition of the person himself,

When, therefore, in Scripture, Circumcision is called a **covenant of salt** <note>original: *berit melach*</note>, it means it is irrevocable, not unlike the decrees of the Medes and Persians; and an **eternal covenant** <note>original: *berit le'olam*</note>. This is especially to be understood in respect to spiritual circumcision, which ought to be perpetual and unchangeable, since the covenant of God cannot be made void, according to that saying of Paul: **the gifts of God are irrevocable** <note>original Greek: *charismata tou Theou eisin ametameleta* — See Romans 11:29.</note>. That also holds a place in the sense of Scripture regarding circumcision made by hand, but less properly; for that was intended to last **forever** <note>original: *le'olam*</note>, not in an absolute sense, but **until the time** <note>original: *ad zon* (likely a corruption of *ad zeman*)</note> fixed and ordained: which was **until the world to come** <note>original: *ad olam ha-ba*</note>. Thus do the teachers of the Hebrews call the **days of the Messiah** <note>original: *yemei ha-mashiach*</note>.

However, Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), also known as the Rambam, a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note>, who was the first among the Rabbis to begin to be sober <note>By "sober," Crégut means rational or philosophical, as opposed to the more mystical or legendary interpretations of other rabbis.</note>, does not seem sufficiently sober in this place. For when, in the book *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: *More Neuoch.* (Moreh Nevuchim), Part 3, Chapter 49.</note>, he takes up the discussion on the purpose of Circumcision, he seems to look more at that which belongs to the flesh than that which belongs to the spirit; though, forced by the truth, he considers the covenant itself as the thing signified. For he begins thus: *Circumcision was instituted, in my judgment, so that the lust of men might be diminished, and this member might be weakened for that act as much as possible. Secondly, because it is a sign of the covenant; and those who have some common sign, which has the form of a covenant, love each other intensely; and those circumcised enter into the covenant of Abraham, and this reason is the stronger.* But Maimonides fails even in respect to the covenant, because he seems to hold the reasoning of some external covenant with the seed of Abraham according to the flesh, rather than the spiritual covenant, according to the seed of the faithful. This is to look at carnal Circumcision rather than spiritual; but when that spiritual part is lacking, you have heard Paul asserting above in Romans 2:25 <note>The text incorrectly cites Romans 11:25, but the quote "Circumcisio tua facta est praeputium" is from Romans 2:25.</note>: **Your circumcision has become uncircumcision.**

Maimonides adds in that same place certain "rabbinical delusions" which it is a burden to write out. *Some* (he says) *have thought that Circumcision was a perfection of a defect of birth, but this...*

<summary>Crégut argues that biblical "eternal" covenants regarding circumcision refer primarily to the spiritual state rather than the physical rite, which was only intended to last until the Messianic age. He critiques Maimonides for focusing too heavily on the physical and social aspects of the ritual rather than its internal spiritual necessity.</summary>

# ANTOINE CRÉGUT
<page-num>456</page-num>

...it is not performed to supply a defect of creation <note>original: *defectum creationis*</note>, but to correct a defect of morals <note>original: *defectum morum*. Crégut is arguing that the body is not "broken" by God at birth, but the ritual serves a psychological or ethical purpose.</note>. Moreover, it is certain that circumcision weakens the intensive power of the member, as well as the pleasure. For since that member sheds blood and loses its covering immediately after birth, it is undoubtedly weakened from that point on. Hence the **Rabbis** say that a woman joined in marriage to an uncircumcised man can only with difficulty be pulled away from him.

In the same chapter, **Maimonides** <note>Moses Maimonides, the 12th-century Jewish philosopher, discusses this in *The Guide for the Perplexed*, Book 3, Chapter 49.</note> adds a threefold reason why circumcision is performed in infancy:
I. If one waited until the infant grew up, perhaps he would no longer perform it.
II. Not as much pain is felt then, both because of the tenderness of the skin and because of the weakness of the imagination <note>Meaning the infant lacks the cognitive capacity to anticipate the pain with fear.</note>.
III. Because parents have a lesser degree of affection for children in their infancy <note>Maimonides' argument is that the father's bond with a newborn is not yet so overwhelming that it would prevent him from performing the painful command.</note>. 

But it is commanded (he says) to be done on the **eighth day**, because before that day animals are weak due to moisture, as if they were still in their mother's womb. But after the seventh day, they begin to be counted among those seeing the air of this world. **Exodus 22:30**: *Seven days it shall be with its mother, but on the eighth day you shall give it to me.* It is as if before seven days it were a premature birth. Yet all these things are brought forward by Maimonides more as a **physician** than as a **theologian**; and all those reasons which are recounted by him are more physical than metaphysical <note>original: *hyperphysica*, literally "above-physical."</note>, and they regard that which is external to circumcision rather than the most wise institution of God and its mystical end.

Furthermore, regarding the purpose of Circumcision, **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Catholic Scholastic philosopher.</note> says in Part 1 of the 2nd part, Question 102, Article 5: That all the sacraments of the Old Testament had rational and **literal** causes, insofar as they were ordained for the worship of God for that time, and **figurative** causes, insofar as they were ordained to prefigure Christ. But the literal reason (he says) of Circumcision was principally for the **protestation of faith in one God**. And because **Abraham** was the first who separated himself from the unfaithful, going out from his house and from his kindred, he therefore was the first to receive circumcision; and the Apostle assigns this cause in **Romans 4**: *He received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of faith, which he had while in uncircumcision, that he might be the father of all who believe while uncircumcised, that it might be imputed also to them.*

He aligns himself more with Thomas Aquinas, who views the ritual as a literal profession of faith and a figurative prestructure of Christ.</summary>

...righteousness. Because he believed in hope against hope <note>original: *contra spem in spem*; a reference to Romans 4:18 regarding Abraham’s faith</note>—that is, against the hope of nature, in the hope of grace—so that he might become the father of many nations: since he himself was old, and his wife aged and sterile. And so that this profession and imitation of Abraham’s faith might be strengthened in the hearts of the Jews, they received a sign in their flesh which they could not forget; hence it is said in *Genesis 17: My covenant shall be in your flesh for an everlasting covenant.* Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the influential 13th-century theologian</note> adds two other reasons, which coincide with those brought forward by **Maimonides**. But the figurative reason, according to Thomas, is the removal of corruption to be achieved through Christ, which will be perfectly completed in the eighth age, which is the age of those rising again <note>The "eight day" of circumcision was often linked by theologians to the "eighth age" of eternity following the seven ages of human history</note>. And because all corruption of guilt and punishment comes upon us through carnal origin from the sin of our first parent, therefore such circumcision was performed on the member of generation. Hence the Apostle says in *Colossians 2: You were circumcised in Christ with a circumcision not made by hand, in the stripping away of the body of the flesh: but in the circumcision of our Lord Jesus Christ.*

Since, therefore, that expression "Circumcision is the covenant" <note>original: *Circumcisio est fœdus*</note> is truly figurative and sacramental, why should this other one concerning the Sacrament of the Eucharist not also be sacramental: "The bread is the body of Christ"? Why then do the **Metusiasts** <term>Metusiasts: A term derived from the Greek *metousiosis* (transubstantiation), referring to those who believe the bread literally becomes the body of Christ.</term> perpetually beat us over the head with this common point <note>original: *κοινὸν caput*</note>? "Christ, who is truthful and almighty, truly said, 'this is my body,' and he can do it. Therefore, the bread is properly the body of Christ, namely through transubstantiation." Since he spoke so clearly, why do they want Christ to have spoken figuratively and ambiguously, so as not to be understood? It will be very appropriate in this place to prove with the strongest reasons that this figurative phraseology <term>Tropic: From 'trope,' meaning a metaphorical or non-literal use of a word.</term>—"Circumcision is the covenant," or "the bread is the body of Christ"—is of all things the easiest and most evident. If, however, they were understood literally, the pronouncement would be most difficult, most obscure, and beyond the conception of any man or Angel, because of inevitable contradictions <note>original: *antilogias*</note>. Our reasons are as follows:

1. No expression could have been more suitable than that which properly fits the subject matter: For since words are signs of things, in order to signify them adequately, they must correspond to them—

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page regarding the linguistic nature of sacramental language. The author, Antoine Crégut, is explaining why "is" (est) should be interpreted as "signifies" in the context of both Circumcision and the Eucharist, countering literalist interpretations (like Transubstantiation) by appealing to Hebrew linguistics.</meta>

# ANTOINE CRÉGUT
<page-num>458</page-num>

...to agree, according to the well-known saying: *names often fit their subjects.* <note>original: "conueniunt rebus nomina sæpe suis." A common Latin legal and literary maxim suggesting a natural link between a thing's name and its essence.</note> But truly, when we are dealing with the Sacraments, is it any wonder if the phrasing is "sacramental," according to the very nature of the matter? 

**II.** That way of speaking is not foreign, but is very familiar to the Holy Spirit speaking in Scripture—as in the case of Pharaoh’s dream, when seven cows are said to be seven years because they *signify* them; or when baptism is called the "washing of regeneration" because it is a *sign* of it; and so it is a thousand times in Scripture. 

**III.** Because it stems from the idiom <note>original: *idiotismo*, referring here to a specific linguistic quirk or grammatical structure peculiar to a language</note> of the Oriental languages, especially their mother tongue, namely Hebrew, which idioms occur everywhere in the Old and New Testaments. For in the Hebrew language, there is a constant use of the verb **hayah** <note>Hebrew: היה; the verb "to be"</note>, that is, **Is**, in place of **signifies**. 

Note that we do not say—as do some theologians of no low rank—that there is no word among the Hebrews to express the same thing as *signifies*, and that therefore Christ did not say "the bread *signifies* my body" but "the bread *is* my body" (just as "Circumcision *is* the covenant") out of a necessity or "poverty" of the language, as if it were unable to express the concept of **it signifies** <note>original Greek: τὸ significat</note> with any single word. This argument (I say) is not of great weight, because there are other words among the Hebrews that have the same value as "to sign" or "to seal"—and sacraments are not only signs, but also *seals* of grace. 

Furthermore, even if the Hebrew word for "signifies" was not used, could not Christ have used the word for "sign," which is found among the Hebrews, just as Moses does in this passage when he says Circumcision is the **sign of the covenant** <note>original Hebrew: *ot berit* / אות ברית</note>? But what else is "Circumcision is the sign of the covenant" than "Circumcision *signifies* the covenant"? 

Therefore, it must be said that Christ and the Scripture often use the word **hayah** (is) because the Hebrews, by their idiom, express **signifies** this way; this is thus very easy to understand from the "genius" <note>the inherent character or spirit of a language</note> of the language. 

**IV.** Christ wished to speak this way because that expression is more emphatic; for it expresses more to say "circumcision *is* the covenant" or "the bread *is* the body of Christ" than if he had said "it *signifies*" or "is a sign." For by the word **is**, that most close union is denoted which exists between the sign and the thing signified, since the thing signified is contained within the sign. From this it follows that the name of the sign is attributed to the thing signified, and the name of the thing signified is attributed to the sign **metonymically** <note>Metonymy is a figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something closely associated with it (e.g., "the crown" for "the king"). Here, Crégut argues "body" is used for "bread" because they are sacramentally linked.</note>; hence Theodoret in his *Dialogues* says—

<summary>Crégut argues that when the Bible says a sign "is" the thing it represents (like bread being the body of Christ), it is following a standard Hebrew linguistic idiom where "to be" means "to signify." He rejects the idea that this was due to a lack of vocabulary, arguing instead that it is a deliberate, emphatic way to show the close union between a sacrament and its spiritual meaning.</summary>

...[he attributed] to the body the name of the symbol, and to the symbol the name of the body, not changing the nature, but adding grace to the nature. <note>original: "τῷ σώματι τῷ συμβόλῳ, καὶ τῷ συμβόλῳ τῷ σώματι τέθεικεν ὄνομα, οὐ τὴν φύσιν μεταβάλων, ἀλλὰ τὴν χάριν τῇ φύσει προστεθεικώς." This is a famous quote from the 5th-century theologian Theodoret of Cyrus, often used by Protestants to show that the early Church viewed the bread and wine as symbols rather than a literal change of substance.</note> Just as, therefore, the statement "the son is the father himself" is more emphatic than "the son is the image of the father"—because the former expresses a greater similarity between father and son, which is like an identity of nature—so when Christ said, "the bread is my body," he said more than if he had said, "the bread signifies my body." 

**v.** Christ spoke in Syriac, because that was the dialect used in Jerusalem; but the Aramaic speakers do not express the verb "to be," but imply it, as is clear from the Syriac version, where we read *Hano pagri* <note>Syriac: הנו פגרי</note> "**this my body**." This is found in Matthew 26 and Luke 22. However, in Mark 14, the substantive verb is expressed—*Hano itohi pagri* <note>Syriac: הנא איתוהי פגרי</note>—with the same emphasis mentioned above and following the same Hebrew idiom. 

**vi.** Our explanation is easy to accept because it follows the phrasing commonly used among Christ's disciples, who spoke in the same manner as their teacher, Christ. For example, when they say in Matthew 26:17: *Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?* Now, if "Passover" <term>Pascha: literally "the passing over," referring to the Exodus</term> were understood in its proper sense, it would mean the act of transition. Therefore, it is used improperly <note>meaning "figuratively" or "metonymically" in 17th-century logic</note> to denote the Paschal lamb. 

**vii.** Christ speaks according to the custom of all the Jews who, when celebrating the Passover in Christ's time, did as follows: the head of the family would bless the bread before distributing it with these words: **This is the bread of misery which our ancestors ate in the land of Egypt.** <note>original Greek: "οὗτος ὁ ἄρτος ταλαιπωρίας ὃν ἔφαγον οἱ πρόγονοι ἡμῶν ἐν τῇ γῇ Αἰγύπτου."</note> Yet, it was not strictly the same bread that the fathers had eaten, but a commemoration of that bread of misery, or a "mnemonic sign." <term>signum μνημονικόν: a sign intended to assist the memory</term> These things are found in the rituals of the Hebrews, as reported by Scaliger in *On the Emendation of Time*, book 6. <note>Joseph Scaliger (1540–1609) was a renowned scholar of chronology and history.</note>

**viii.** Christ speaks according to the usage of all languages and nations, among whom the figurative sense is more common than the literal sense; just as we commonly say, "This is the King of the French," when we mean an image of him. In the same way, the bread is the body of Christ, that is, a figure of Christ’s body, as Tertullian explicitly explains in book 4 of *Against Marcion*. 

**ix.** Our explanation agrees with that which the Papists <note>original: "Pontificij." This refers to Roman Catholic theologians.</note> themselves hand down when dealing with other Sacraments, both of the old and the new law. ## CHAPTER XI.

### On Chapter 22 of Genesis, from verse 1 to 15. Wherein the sacrifice of Isaac is treated, which Abraham was approaching to slaughter his son, but with an Angel forbidding it, a ram was substituted.

---

### ANALYSIS.

*The fame of this history of the sacrifice of Isaac and why it is so. Its division into four parts, and what they are.*
*The first part: what kind of trial it was. The reasoning for the trial is very much in doubt according to Maimonides. <note>original: "Maiemonide." Moses Maimonides, the 12th-century Jewish philosopher.</note> Mention is made of six trials in the Law according to Maimonides. Why the trial of Abraham was the greatest of all. In a trial, there are two: the one who tests and the one who is tested. How God is said to test. God tests humans in a threefold way. God is not inactive even if He tests in a negative way. How God participates in a trial. The sacrifice of Abraham was not <term>satisfactory</term>. <note>In a theological context, a "satisfactory" sacrifice is one that pays the debt for sin; the author argues Abraham's act was one of obedience, not atonement.</note> The difference between the temptations of Satan, of men, and of one's own <term>concupiscence</term>.* <note>original: "concupiscentia." Disordered desire or the human inclination toward sin.</note>
*The emphases of the words for "trial" or "temptation" in various languages are weighed. Who are the <term>Sycophants</term> <note>original: "Sycophantæ." In the classical sense, these were professional informers or false accusers.</note> and spies. Who were the <term>quadruplatores</term> among the Romans. <note>original: "quadruplatores." Public informers who were rewarded with one-fourth of a convicted person's property.</note> Why mention is made of Satan whenever the Scriptures deal with temptation. Why God permits appearances of demons and not of Angels. The difference between the Spirit of God and the unclean spirit regarding their association with men. The success of Satan's temptation, or the contrary. How the world tempts. That the worst of temptations comes from lust. Who they are who are tested.*
*God is tested in two ways by men. Men are tested by men in two ways. Men are tested by themselves in two ways.*

The passage in 2 Timothy 4:6 is explained. <note>2 Timothy 4:6: "For I am already being poured out like a drink offering..."</note> In what sense the zeal of Jephthah was preposterous. The various impulses of Jephthah, both from the Spirit of God and from the human spirit. God's wisdom shines forth wonderfully from the sins of men. Indeed, if testing, according to that Rabbi <note>likely a reference to Maimonides, mentioned on the previous page</note>, is not the least among the doubtful reasons for Divine law, then surely that eminent Master of the Hebrews would likewise freely confess that among the six testings mentioned in the law of Moses, this one of Abraham was not the least, but indeed the most dangerous of all. Whence, deservedly because of his victory in so difficult a contest, Abraham earned the name "Father of the Faithful." For although the Holy Patriarch, by the strength of his faith, was destined to be superior to his natural affections for his son, he nevertheless had to fight not only against nature, but even against the word of God, upon which alone his faith ought to have rested as its firmest foundation; yet another word of God, contrary to the preceding one, strongly shook the Patriarch's faith, since it rendered void the promises founded in Isaac—hence that most skillful phrase of the Apostle: *He believed in hope against hope*, namely, because he hoped with a strengthened faith, even though otherwise there seemed no reason for hoping. Therefore, this pious man could have suspected this latest word of God about sacrificing Isaac to be the snares of Satan the tempter, since it conflicted with the word of promise: and surely the fall of our first-formed ancestors <note>original Greek: *προπλάστων* (*proplastōn*), referring to Adam and Eve</note> could have greatly increased these suspicions; nevertheless, the Patriarch recognized the voice of God, by which he was able to distinguish the word of the spirit of lies from the word of the most truthful God; whence he immediately replied, *Here I am*.

Therefore, in that testing, two beings are manifest: namely God, who truly tests, and Abraham, who is tested. God tests, nor does James contradict this in *chapter 1:13: Let no one say when he is tempted, I am tempted by God; for God cannot be tempted by evils, nor does he tempt anyone.* For just as God is not tempted—*he is untouched by evils* <note>original Greek: *ἀπείρασός ἐστι κακῶν* (*apeirasos esti kakōn*)</note>, that is, he is not affected by sins or wicked impulses—so too he does not lead men into evil, but they are carried toward sins by their own movement; we say the same regarding that petition of the Lord’s Prayer, *Lead us not into temptation*, and regarding that complaint of the Church in *Isaiah 63:17: Why have you made us wander from your ways?* For, according to the style of Scripture, those words must be understood *negatively, not positively*; for although those words designate an action in a twofold way, because they are not only transitive in the thing, as in the <term>kal</term> <note>The basic, simple active voice in Hebrew verb conjugation</note> conjugation, but also in

<meta>This page continues the theological analysis of how God "tests" humanity. The previous page discussed Abraham's trial and the linguistic nuances of God's commands. This page moves into a systematic explanation of how God can be said to "cause" or "permit" actions without being the author of sin, using grammatical analogies from Hebrew and Greek philosophical terms.</meta>

<page-num>465</page-num>
# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS #

the person [of the actor] from the analogy of the **Hiphil** <note>original: *hiphil*; this is a Hebrew verb conjugation that usually indicates a causative action—i.e., making someone else do something</note> conjugation, nevertheless in phrases of this kind they do not signify an actual causing of the event in a strict sense. On the contrary, God does not act and indeed suspends His action; yet He is nonetheless said to "do" it because He does not prevent the perverse actions of man which He could have prevented. This is said **anthropopathically** <note>original: *$\alpha\nu\theta\rho\omega\pi\omicron\pi\alpha\theta\tilde{\omega}\varsigma$* (*anthropopathōs*); this refers to speaking of God in human terms or attributing human passions to Him</note>, because men are punished by God whenever they do not prevent an evil they were able to prevent; in such a case, they are judged to have "done" the deed as accomplices to the evil. This, however, is conceived of in God without any sin, because God is not bound to prevent sin in the way that men are; indeed, it is better for the sake of a greater good not to prevent it. Thus He "made the Church wander from its ways" when He allowed it to wander, and (as is said of the Gentiles in *Acts 17:30*) *when He overlooked the time of ignorance.* Just as in *2 Samuel 8*, *He gave life to the Moabites because He allowed them to live, and did not kill them when He could have killed them.*

Therefore, it must be established that there are three ways God tests men without sin:

I. **By Acting**, and this in three ways: **through punishment or discipline** <note>original Greek: *$\delta\iota\grave{\alpha} \ \tau\tilde{\eta}\varsigma \ \tau\iota\mu\omega\rho\acute{\iota}\alpha\varsigma \ \ddot{\eta} \ \pi\alpha\iota\delta\epsilon\acute{\iota}\alpha\varsigma$*</note>, as a fatherly correction; or **through testing or probation** <note>original Greek: *$\delta\iota\grave{\alpha} \ \tau\tilde{\eta}\varsigma \ \delta\omicron\kappa\iota\mu\alpha\sigma\acute{\iota}\alpha\varsigma$*</note>, to examine their faith, patience, obedience, etc.; or **through testimony** <note>original Greek: *$\delta\iota\grave{\alpha} \ \tau\omicron\tilde{\upsilon} \ \mu\alpha\rho\tau\upsilon\rho\acute{\iota}\omicron\upsilon$*</note>, for the sake of witnessing to true and saving doctrine, as seen in the confessors <note>those who maintain their faith under persecution</note>.

II. **By Permitting**, when He allows evil to happen; *For* (says Augustine):
> *that which is done against His will is not done apart from His will; for if He did not want it to be done, it certainly would not happen.*

Therefore, because God is able to prevent evil and yet does not prevent it, He is judged to "will" it; indeed, as stated above, the Scripture says **anthropopathically** that God "does" it. Since the will is the principle of human actions, yet speaking truly and properly, God wills sin **permissively** <note>original: *permissivè*; meaning He allows it rather than actively creating it</note>. He neither wills nor is able to effect sin, for that would imply weakness and injustice in God; rather, He merely permits it to be effected by others. It is in this sense that He is said to test without sin.

III. God tests **by not acting**, that is, by abandoning man to his native corruption, not imparting to him the grace by which he might restrain the force of temptation and shake off its power. For He is a debtor to no one, and He is independent; concerning which...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of God’s "testing" of humanity. While the previous page categorized three ways God tests without sinning, this page focuses on the third method: "negative" testing through the suspension of divine grace or action. It uses the examples of the Lord's Prayer and the hardening of Pharaoh's heart to explain that God's "non-action" is still a deliberate act of His will.</meta>

<page-num>466</page-num>
->ANTHONY CREGUT<-

a creature cannot be spoken of which is not only dependent upon God, but also depends upon others of its kind, not only in fact, but also by right; for the highest Maker of these things willed that all should be connected among themselves, or joined by a stable marriage. Thus can that phrase be explained: *Lead us not into temptation*: <note>From the Lord's Prayer (Matthew 6:13).</note> that is, let your helping grace not desert us, such that we fall into the snares of the tempter and he triumphs over us; which always happens whenever we fight with our own strengths without the assistance of grace. The same must be thought regarding that phrase of Scripture, when God is said *to have hardened Pharaoh's heart*. <note>A reference to Exodus 9:12, a classic theological problem regarding free will and divine sovereignty.</note> Since the human heart is stony by nature, it is therefore not necessary for it to be hardened by some new action—as if it became hard from being soft, or harder from being hard—but rather by the suspension of action, by not softening it.

Nevertheless, even if God tests in this negative way—by not acting and by deserting—be careful not to say that God is idle, as if the will of God did not concur, even if there were some suspension of the divine action. For the act of the divine will is not negative in respect to itself, since God necessarily has a "willingness" or "unwillingness" <note>original: *volitionem vel nolitionem*</note>; for just as in the work of providence, that divine <term>providence</term> <note>original: *πρόνοια* (*pronoia*); the Greek concept of divine forethought and care for the universe</note> and <term>divine impulse</term> <note>original: *νεῦσις* (*neusis*); literally a "nod" or "inclination," referring here to the subtle divine movement that maintains the order of the world</note> cannot close the gaze of the eyes even for a moment, or blink even a little, without a huge confusion of the world occurring immediately, and the whole mass of the machine [of the universe] being resolved into the first chaos and <term>formless void</term> <note>original: *tohu vabohu*; the Hebrew phrase from Genesis 1:2 describing the primordial state of the earth before creation</note>; so not even for a moment would the will of God be suspended, or His willing or unwilling cease, without everything being immediately reduced to nothing. For as the world was created from God’s will, so now it is ruled and preserved by His command. Therefore, the act of the will shall not be negative in respect to itself, but in respect to the immediate result: since a suspension of action follows it. Thus, there is a difference between *willing not to act* and *not willing to act*; because in this latter case, the act of will itself is denied, but in the former, the act of will is not denied, but a negative result is established.

It is now clear from what has been said how God tested Abraham by commanding that he sacrifice his son. For He did not test him in the second and third way *by permitting sin* and *by not acting*—that is, by deserting and abandoning him in his native corrupt[ion]... <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword *ptione* indicates the next word is *corruptione* (corruption).</note>

Yet that ordeal was not "satisfactory" <note>In traditional theology, an act that pays a debt or makes amends for sin.</note>, for Abraham and Isaac could not satisfy it in any way, nor was it properly a "chastising" punishment, which we previously called <term>paideia</term> <note>original: *παιδεία*; Greek for disciplinary instruction or training</note> or <term>timoria</term> <note>original: *τιμωρία*; Greek for retribution or vengeance</note>. This was not because God was ignorant of what would happen—since from eternity He decreed it and, just as He directed the end, so He ordained all the means—but rather to reveal such great faith and obedience to all mortals, which would earn the Patriarch the title and surname "Father of the Faithful."

One must feel quite differently about the temptations of Satan, of men, and of one's own lust. For those are mixed with sin; indeed, they intend sin as their goal and the highest thing to be desired. This is why Scripture so often emphasizes the temptations of Satan, the world, and the flesh. Satan tempts, which is why he is called <term>diakritikos</term> <note>original: *διακριτικῶς*; Greek for "distinctively" or "by way of distinction"</note> in Matthew 4:3 and 1 Thessalonians 3:5 as "the tempter" <note>original: *ὁ πειράζων*</note>, or as the Syriac puts it with the emphatic *he*: "the tempter" <note>original: *המנסה* (*hammenaseh*)</note>. This signifies the same thing as "the one tempting," since the Greek participle serves as a noun. And thus the Latin translator correctly rendered Matthew 4, but incorrectly in the passage of 1 Thessalonians 3:5: *Lest perhaps he who tempts should have tempted you*; for it should have been translated not as "he who tempts," but as "the tempter." Otherwise, there would be a redundancy and a vain repetition of the word: "lest he should have tempted you who tempts." It is for this reason that the Syriac uses the noun *menasiona* <note>original: *מנסינא*</note>, meaning "tempter," not a participle. Therefore, the title "the tempter" <note>original: *ὁ πειράζων* or *πειραστής* (*peirastēs*)</note> is attributed to the unclean spirit not only distinctively, but also <term>diasyrtikos</term> <note>original: *διασυρτικῶς*; Greek for "scornfully" or "reproachfully"</note>. For the word *dokimazein* <note>original: *δοκιμάζειν*</note>, which means "to explore," is more general than *peirazein* <note>original: *πειράζειν*</note>, "to tempt," because the latter is taken in both a good and a bad sense; for just as the Devil tempts, so God tempted Abraham. Likewise in Exodus 17:7, the Israelites rashly tempted God; hence the place was called *Massah and Meribah* <note>original: *Massa & Meriba*; Hebrew for "Testing" and "Quarrel"</note>, namely from "temptation" and "contention." But just as Satan is called "the tempter" <note>original: *πειράζων*</note> from the act of tempting—following the Hebrew custom where a participle is used as a noun, "the one tempting" for "the tempter"—so among the Syrians he is called scornfully...

...is also called <term>akhel kartza</term> <note>original Aramaic: אכל קרצא; literally "eating a piece," a common idiom for slander or backbiting</note>, that is, a *detractor* or *slanderer*. This usage is found throughout the New Testament, as well as the Greek terms <term>diabolos</term> <note>original: διάβολος; the root of "devil," meaning slanderer</note> and <term>kategoros</term> <note>original: κατήγορος; accuser</note>. He is so named because he both tests people with his slanders and drags them before God to be accused, as is clearly seen from the story of Job. This Greek word *kategoros* corresponds to the Aramaic <term>kategor</term> <note>original: קטיגורא or קטיגור</note>, meaning *accuser*.

Indeed, according to Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides, the influential 12th-century Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note>, this term does not designate just any accuser, but a fierce slanderer, a <term>sycophant</term> <note>original Greek: συκοφάντην; here used in its classical sense of a malicious informer</note>, and a denouncer before the king. This is similar to the spies in ancient Persia who observed everything done and said across the land and immediately reported it to the kings, though usually in a slanderous manner. Consequently, they were commonly known as the *eyes and ears of the king*. 

Among the Romans during the reign of Nero, there were similar figures called <term>quadruplatores</term> <note>Latin: informers who received a fourth (quadrans) of the accused's property as a reward</note>. They were so named because Nero granted them a fourth part of the assets belonging to those they had denounced. The Emperor Tiberius believed these informers were so necessary to the Republic that he called them the *guardians of the laws*, and he asserted that the foundations of justice would be subverted if these "quadruplatores" were removed from the protection of the Empire.

In fact, some political writers apply the words of Ecclesiastes 10 to these sorts of spies: *Even in your thoughts do not curse the king, for a bird of the heavens will carry that voice, and the winged creatures will reveal the word.* They also cite 2 Samuel 18: *Nothing can be hidden from the king.* This is achieved, of course, through the work of spies. Satan is just such a sycophant and accuser <note>original: κατήγορος</note>; for the purpose of scouting out everything so that he may denounce mankind, he circles the entire earth. As it says in Job 1:7: <term>mishut ba'aretz</term> <note>original Hebrew: משוט בארץ</note>, *from wandering through the earth*. This is why in Revelation 12:10 he is called the *accuser of the brothers*.

However, just as an accuser and slanderer is called a *kategor* among the Syrians (as noted above from Rabbi Maimonides), the same author notes that the one who interceded for someone before the king was called a <term>paraclete</term> <note>original Aramaic/Greek: פרקליטא / παράκλητος; an advocate or defense attorney called to one's side</note>. This title is very frequently attributed to Christ, the Son of God, and to the Holy Spirit: to Christ in 1 John 2:1, and to the Holy Spirit in John 14 and Romans 8.

And from this emerges a consideration worthy of notice, which the most learned John Cameron <note>A prominent Scottish theologian (c. 1579–1625) who taught in France and was known for his insights into the Greek New Testament</note> also mentions in his lectures on Matthew 17: that as often as the Scriptures deal with temptation, mention is made of Satan and his traps. For the tempter constantly watches and lies in wait night and day for the 
<margin>•</margin> destruction of our souls, so that he may rush down upon us most swiftly, like a bird-catcher upon birds, and he is always...

For the Spirit of God has a commerce of love; indeed, that divine guest rejoices to dwell with us, whence, as Scripture testifies, He is saddened if anyone casts Him out by sinning. of redemption. But Satan takes no delight in human company; if he seeks people like a **roaring lion**, he seeks them so that he may devour them; if he dwells in the body of a possessed person, this is done so that he may be their constant executioner and torturer. It is for this reason that Scripture banishes them to desert places and solitude whenever they lose hope of causing harm to humans.

However, even if Satan tempts, the temptation does not always succeed; therefore, by inciting someone toward evil, he sometimes does not overcome those whom he tempts. Thus he tempted Christ, but did not overcome Him (Matthew 4:3; Luke 4:2). Sometimes he overcomes those he tempts, but he overcomes either for a time—as with Adam and Eve (Genesis 3:2; 2 Corinthians 11:3), or David (1 Chronicles 21), or Peter (Luke 22:31)—or he overcomes them completely, as with Judas the betrayer (John 13:2) or Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5:3). These temptations of the Devil are designated by various names in Ephesians 6:11, such as *his wiles* <note>original: "insidias eius"</note>, and in verse 16, as the *fiery darts of that evil one* <note>original: "iacula mali illius ignita"</note>.

But indeed, it is not Satan alone who tempts and lures us toward evil, but also the *world*; and it does so through various enticements, whether through wicked conversations and examples, or through promises, or threats, or flatteries and other things of that sort. Very often Satan attacks the faith of the elect with those <term>ballistae</term> <note>original: "balistis"; large ancient engines used for throwing heavy missiles</note> and most powerful war-machines, and busies himself with shaking the stability of that faith. In this way, that most vain and impudent spirit did not even spare Christ in the desert, and he endeavored to cloud Him with ambition and the empty glory of the world, just as he used the worst possible instruments at other times when he drove the Pharisees to tempt Him. For Satan himself, by himself and directly, never dared to do so after that first temptation, as we are taught in the Gospel, nor did God permit it to him. It was sufficient for Christ to have been tempted by the Devil once so that He might succor His tempted members <note>The "members" refers to the individual believers who make up the "body" of the Church</note>, and that He might carry back the victory over the tempter. Thus His members would know that they too shall overcome Satan through faith, and finally, so that the great difference between the first and the second Adam <note>In Christian theology, the "first Adam" is the biblical first man who fell into sin, while the "second Adam" is Jesus Christ, who remained sinless</note> might be shown in the struggle of temptation.

Nevertheless, in respect to humans, all those temptations of both Satan and the world would be empty and ineffective unless others followed within us that are more harmful—those, namely, which arise from our own...

It concludes by noting that external temptations only succeed when met by internal human weakness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the sources of temptation from page 470. The text transitions from external temptations (the devil and the world) to internal ones (the flesh), specifically focusing on how human weakness differs from malicious intent and how God reacts to being "tested" by figures like Gideon and Ahab.</meta>

<page-num>471</page-num>
<header>THE REVEALER OF SECRETS</header>

...weakness and from the desires of the flesh; but within us lies hidden the poison of the serpent, the lustful affection—the source and fuel of all evils. James records the stages of this desire in chapter 1, verse 14:

> *Each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire.*

This temptation is therefore called *human temptation* by Paul in 1 Corinthians 10:13, not only because God is indulgent toward men by permitting—and indeed even sending—temptation for the sake of chastisement and testing (which does not exceed human strength), but also because it arises from within a person, from the weakness of the flesh rather than from stubborn malice.

Thus far we have spoken of those who tempt, whether for good or for evil. For good, as when God tempted Abraham to test his faith and obedience. For evil, as when the devil, the world, and one's own desire tempt. Now we must also observe those who are tempted; and these are either God or humans. God is tempted by humans, but in two ways: either for good or for evil. He was tempted for good by Gideon in Judges chapter 6:39:

> *Furthermore, Gideon said to God: "Let not your anger burn against me, and I will speak only once: let me test just once with the fleece. Let there be dryness only upon the fleece, I pray, and let there be dew upon all the ground."*

For his faith is praised in the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 11; for even though it is a sin to waver in faith, it is nevertheless permitted to seek a sign to strengthen it in due time, according to that saying:

> *I believe, Lord, but help my unbelief.* <note>original: "Credo Domine, sed tu adiuua meam incredulitatem"; a reference to Mark 9:24.</note>

Hence Gideon asks for opposite signs; for the first sign might not have seemed so very wonderful—namely, that the surrounding ground was dry while the fleece was soaked—since it is the nature of wool to easily attract moisture, and even to contract it by its innate oiliness. Therefore, it was much more likely for the dew to be absorbed even if the ground were not wet. But for the wool to remain dry while the ground around the fleece was wet—this is foreign to the nature of a fleece. On the contrary, God was angry with Ahab because he refused to ask for a sign even when invited by God <note>This refers to Isaiah 7:10-14, where King Ahab refuses a sign from the prophet Isaiah.</note>, doing so with a presumption of "stronger faith" that allegedly had no need of such aids. But the <term>Searcher of Hearts</term> <note>original: "καρδιογνώστης" (*kardiognōstēs*); a Greek theological term for God's ability to know the innermost thoughts of a person.</note> punished this hypocrisy by giving the sign of the virgin birth, which did not pertain to the hypocrite.

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of temptation, moving from God testing humans for good to the ways in which humans improperly test God, each other, and themselves. It specifically addresses the concept of "testing the Spirit" and the dangers of self-love.</meta>

<page-num>472</page-num>
<header>ANTOINE CRÉGUT</header>

God is often tempted toward **evil** by men, as the Israelites tempted Him in the desert. *Exodus 17:3; Numbers 14:22 <note>Original OCR reads iv. 22, likely a typo for xiv. 22, where Israel tests God ten times.</note>; Hebrews 3:8, 9.* This is evident from the places named Massah and Meribah <note>Massah means "testing" and Meribah means "quarreling."</note>. Likewise Ananias and Sapphira. *Acts 5, verse 9: But Peter said to her, "How is it that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord?"* <note>original Greek: πειράσαι τὸ πνεῦμα κυρίου</note>. It must be noted (as Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major Protestant Reformer and successor to Calvin.</note> most skillfully says on this passage) that this manner of speaking is indeed unknown to secular writers, but it is worthy of the constant reflection of the children of God. For as often as something is done with a bad conscience, so often do men bring judgment upon themselves, and as much as lies within them, they provoke God to anger, as if intentionally wishing to make a trial of whether He is just and almighty. But on the other hand, there are others who tempt the mercy of God; for although they provoke God with their horrendous sins and do not cease to kindle His anger, they nevertheless securely presume that they will obtain mercy from God. Indeed, there are the impious who sarcastically mock God’s mercy, such as those in *Romans 6:1* who say, *we should sin so that grace may abound.*

Furthermore, men are tempted by men; sometimes for **good**, as when a master wishes to explore the loyalty of a servant; or for **evil**, namely so that they may seize an opportunity to maliciously carp at the words and deeds of a neighbor, in the manner that the Scribes and Pharisees in the Gospel are recorded to have tempted Christ. *Matthew 16:1, 19:3, and 22:18; John 8:6;* and throughout the New Testament.

Finally, men are also tempted by themselves. But this temptation occurs in two ways. **i.** Through the temptation of the flesh, concerning which we spoke above in the previously cited passage of *James 1:14*, namely when we are drawn away and enticed by our own desires. **ii.** Through trial and <term>examination <note>original Greek: δοκιμασίᾳ (*dokimasia*), a formal testing or scrutinizing.</note></term>. *2 Corinthians 13:5: Examine yourselves, whether you be in the faith; prove your own selves. Do you not know your own selves, that Jesus Christ is in you? Unless indeed you are disqualified.* This kind of temptation is very necessary, because men are either so wonderfully blind that they cannot judge what they are like at first glance—which is why one of the wise men of Greece repeatedly emphasized **know thyself** <note>original Greek: γνῶθι σεαυτὸν (*gnothi seauton*)</note>—or they so flatter themselves and are fascinated by <term>self-love <note>original Greek: philautia</note></term>, that they are the first of all mortals to be deceived by themselves as if by a false dye. Hence Saint Augustine says: **self-love** even to the contempt of God built Babylon <note>A reference to Augustine's *City of God*, where "love of self" builds the earthly city (Babylon) and "love of God" builds the heavenly city (Jerusalem).</note>.

<meta>catchword: But</meta>
