<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of self-examination and temptation. While the previous page focused on how humans wrongly test God or others, this page shifts to the necessity of testing one's own faith, using the Apostle Peter’s "sifting" by Satan as a primary case study.</meta>

# REVEALER OF SECRETS.

But you might ask: how can anyone truly examine themselves when they are so blind to their own faults and so prone to self-flattery? I answer that certain marks are given in the Scriptures by which this testing can be most effectively carried out, and everyone is capable of experiencing the meaning of those marks within themselves. For do not the outward <note>original Greek: ἔξωθεν</note> fruits of the Holy Spirit, and the inward <note>original Greek: ἔσωθεν</note> sealing of divine promises through the Spirit’s seal and the pledge of our inheritance, serve as the proofs <note>original Greek: τεκμήρια, meaning clear signs or evidence</note> of our faith? Blindness cannot prevail forever; for although the state of faith may lie hidden for a time, it is soon recognized by subsequent actions. A small fire hidden under the ashes quickly gives off not just little sparks, but actual flames. As Pope Leo the Great <note>Leo I (c. 400–461), a Bishop of Rome known for his influential theological writings.</note> once skillfully wrote concerning the Apostle Peter:

> *Faith did not fail in his heart when confession failed on his lips; nor was his love so much overturned as his constancy was disturbed. He loved within him whom he denied without, even if his affection, constricted by fear, was sluggish. Faith remained in its first act; the fear of danger intercepted the second.*

These golden words, written in the large, bold hand of an ancient Doctor of the Church, clearly show that Peter’s wavering faith could only be made firm through his own trial and testing.

Yet, it must also be admitted that sometimes the temptation of Satan and the flesh is so great, and the believer is so violently shaken and sifted by them, that in their wavering they refuse another kind of testing, or at least forget it; this continues until their strength is restored and the Holy Spirit is renewed within the heart of the believer, at which point they test and prove themselves to see if they are in the faith. Peter’s temptation was of this very dangerous and almost fatal kind. This is why the Gospel writers describe it in the most emphatic terms <note>original Greek: ἐμφατικωτάτοις</note>. First, they use the word "demanded" <note>original Greek: ἐξαιτεῖσθαι, which implies asking for someone to be handed over for punishment or interrogation</note>, much like the Syriac word *sha’al* <note>original: שאל</note>. Then they use the word "to sift" <note>original Greek: σινιάσαι</note>, derived from the word for a sieve. This is a very rare word that corresponds to the Syriac *arab* <note>original: ערב</note>, meaning to winnow or sift, and the Chaldean <note>A language closely related to Hebrew and Syriac</note> *arbla* <note>original: ערבלא</note>, meaning a sieve. This verb, in its intensive form, also means to throw into confusion or to disturb—which is certainly part of temptation. This matches the interpretation of the ancient scholar Theophylact <note>An 11th-century archbishop and biblical commentator</note>, who explained it as "to disturb and to harm" <note>original Greek: ταράξαι καὶ βλάψαι</note>. In the Arabic version, the word used is *garbala* <note>original: גרבלא</note>, which also means to sift.

<meta>This page follows a discussion on the Apostle Peter’s trial of faith. It transitions from the specific "sifting" of Peter to a broader theological categorization of who can and cannot undergo temptation, specifically contrasting humans and Christ with the angelic host.</meta>

# ANTHONY CREGUT
<meta>catchword: words</meta>

Let these things be said concerning those who are tempted, whether we speak of God or of men. Now, by way of exception <note>original Greek: κατ' ἄρσιν, a logical term meaning to define something by what it is not</note>, it must be observed that Angels—whether they be good or evil—are never tempted. Nowhere in the Holy Scriptures can a mention of "angelic temptation" be found. This, however, rightly causes a doubt to arise, since they are endowed with minds, and God Himself (the Supreme Intelligence) is said to be tempted, as was shown above. 

Nevertheless, it is truly observed that we never read of Angels being tempted. The reason is this: it would be useless for the good Angels to be tempted, for they adhere firmly to what is good. Because they are confirmed in grace and granted beatitude <term>beatitude: the state of perfect, eternal happiness and the "vision" of God enjoyed by the saved</term>, they are no longer subject to the shifting circles of temptation. On the other hand, the evil Angels have become stubbornly hardened and fixed in evil by their own will. Therefore, there is no need for them to be tempted, especially since they have already been judged and the wrath of God remains upon them.

The example of Christ does not contradict this, even though He was tempted by Satan. Although the tempter’s efforts were in vain, because Christ was made sinless <note>original Greek: ἀναμάρτωλος, meaning impeccable or incapable of sinning</note>, the example does not apply here. I say it does not apply because the tempter tried to tempt Him out of ignorance. Without a doubt, from the beginning, Satan was ignorant of Christ’s person, His status, and His offices. After all, not even the good Angels (as Peter testifies) fully knew the mysteries of our redemption, which is why they "bent down to look into them" <note>A reference to 1 Peter 1:12, describing the curiosity of angels regarding the Gospel</note> as they grew in understanding. Indeed, there are specific reasons why Christ willed to be tempted, which we have cited previously. As for God, when He is said to be "tempted" by men, it happens because of their own ignorance and weakness; for in this way, they dare to "test" or explore His knowledge, power, and will.

Since, therefore, we do not read of Angels being tempted, but only humans—of whatever kind they may be, including Christ—it is necessary for a full understanding of this matter to see what is similar and what is different between the temptations of men and the temptations of Christ. Paul presents both aspects in Hebrews 4:15:

> *For we do not have a High Priest who cannot be affected by the feeling of our infirmities, but one who was tempted in all things in a similar way, yet without sin.*

First, in these words, the Apostle demonstrates the similarity of these temptations in two ways: namely, by the "matter" (the substance) of the temptations, and by their "form" (the manner). He demonstrates the former in these...

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of Christ’s temptation, specifically addressing how He could be "tempted in every way" while remaining fundamentally different from other humans due to His sinless nature.</meta>

### THE REVEALER OF SECRETS

...stating in his words that Christ was able to **sympathize with us** <note>original Greek: συμπαθῆσαι ἡμῖν</note> and be tempted **in all things** <note>original Greek: κατὰ πάντα</note>. This signifies not only that Christ, while He lived on earth, endured every kind of affliction and was subject to them just as we are, but also that even now, sitting at the right hand of the Father in heaven, He **suffers with** <note>original Greek: συμπαθεῖν</note> His members. From there He cries out, *Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?* <note>A reference to Acts 9:4, implying that when the Church—the body of Christ—suffers, Christ Himself feels it.</note> Paul later explains this through the phrase **according to likeness** <note>original Greek: κατ' ὁμοιότητα</note>, used in place of **similarly** <note>original Greek: ὁμοίως</note>. This is because He was locked in conflict in various ways just as we are, to the point that He underwent the same punishments and felt the various agonies and anxieties of pain.

However, in the second place, Paul shows the distinction when he adds **without sin** <note>original Greek: χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας</note>. The Syriac version expresses the Greek word for word: **separated from sin** <note>original Syriac: מן חטיא פריש</note>. This is a better phrasing than in John 15:5, "**apart from me** you can do nothing" <note>original Greek: χωρὶς ἐμοῦ</note>, where the Syriac has **without me** <note>original Syriac: דלא אנא</note>. That translation of "apart from" <note>original Greek: ἀπ' ἐμοῦ</note> is surely diluted; for Christ does not influence us merely as a co-cause <term>co-cause: a secondary factor that works alongside another to produce an effect</term>, but He is the sole cause of life for the faithful, outside of whom there is no life or spirit. Just as branches not clinging to the vine draw no sap and consequently wither away. 

In this way, Paul says Christ was tempted just like other men, yet with the exception of sin. While others who are tempted frequently fall into sin, Christ never did. He was both **lacking sin** <note>original Greek: ἄτερ ἁμαρτίας</note> and **separate from sin** <note>original Greek: χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας</note>. Unlike the rest of us, He was not conceived in sin, but was "separated from sin and sinners"—which is a Hebrew way of saying He was "sanctified." Therefore, He was not tempted like other men by the cravings of the flesh <term>concupiscence: the internal inclination or desire toward sin</term>. He was "separate from sin," which Paul refers to in the singular as **Sin** <note>original Greek: ἁμαρτία</note>, from which **sins** <note>original Greek: ἁμαρτίαι</note> emerge as its fruits. Hence Augustine says: *Christ took the punishment upon himself, but not the fault, so that he might take away both the punishment and the fault.* 

This can be illustrated by a very fitting comparison. It is just as if one were to repeatedly stir up clear water; it will not become murky or muddy. But if you move pure water that has mud or sand settled at the bottom, it immediately becomes cloudy. In the same way, though Christ was tempted and struggled with pains, He always kept His soul most pure and clear without the filth of sin—something that cannot be said of other men, even the holiest among them.

<meta>This page continues the theological discussion of Christ’s temptation. Having established that Christ was tempted but remained "without sin," Cregut now moves to a specific historical example—Abraham—to show how even the greatest human faith involves a level of internal struggle and doubt that differs from the perfect sinlessness of Christ.</meta>

-># ANTHONY CREGUT<-

Finally, to come down to a specific case <term>specific case: Cregut uses the word 'hypothesis' in the classical sense of applying a general rule to a particular person or event</term> and narrowing our focus on this subject: Abraham was tempted by God Himself. Although he eventually emerged as the victor (as is clear from the outcome), it cannot be said of him, as it is of Christ, that he was **without sin** <note>original Greek: χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας</note>. This is because, in that struggle, Abraham doubted. Even though his soul was clear and pure, it appeared a little clouded in the midst of such a great storm of temptation. 

For, O good God! What turmoil, what various and conflicting thoughts raced through his mind as he considered that God was commanding things that were contradictory and at odds with one another. He saw that God’s word seemed to oppose His own word. All those brilliant and magnificent promises regarding Isaac were now perishing because of this latest, bloody command. Abraham was able to doubt whether the one now speaking to him was the same God who had recently promised him such great blessings and a most fruitful lineage through Isaac, or whether Satan was attempting to tempt him, just as once happened to our **first parents** <term>first parents: the 'protoplasts,' Adam and Eve</term>. 

The Patriarch could have reasoned thus: "Either the one speaking to me is the true God, or he is Satan, the father of lies. If it is the latter, I will not obey, for he commands a bloody act, contrary to nature and contrary to God’s word. But if it is God speaking to me, why does He, who is most true, command contradictory things? And why does He, who is unchangeable, change His decree?" Certainly, amidst so many opposing thoughts, Abraham hesitated and wavered in his faith. But at last, the constancy of his faith and obedience conquered; he trusted in the power of God, who was able to raise his slaughtered son from the dead.

I will not omit the fables that the Jewish teachers tell here in the book *Yelamdenu* <note>original Hebrew: ילמדנו, a collection of midrashic homilies</note> regarding that passage in Genesis 22: *And Abraham took the wood for the burnt offering and placed it on Isaac, etc. And the two of them walked on together, etc.* Rabbi Johanam says that while the two were walking together, Satan came and stood at Isaac's right hand and said to him: "O you who are suffering a wrong, son of a woman who has suffered! How many afflictions did your mother endure before you came to her? This old man has gone mad, and therefore he goes to sacrifice you and tear you apart." Then Isaac turned and said to his father, "Father, look at what this one is saying to me." His father said, "Do not look at him, for he has come for no other reason than to subvert us, and such has been his work from the beginning of the world." can be seen from the Mosaic text; indeed, the opposite is asserted by the fact that Isaac was ignorant of what his father was about to do, or whether he was going to sacrifice himself or a ram. For this reason, Isaac said, *“Here is the wood, but where is the victim for the burnt offering?”* These things, therefore, are said by the Rabbis <note>The author refers here to Jewish scholars who provided expansive commentary on the Torah</note> following the tradition of the fathers; or rather, they wished to conjecture in this way what the thoughts and temptations of Abraham and Isaac might have been, and also what the snares of Satan were. The second part of this dissertation now follows, namely the substance of the temptation, or its specific type, which is **testing** <note>original Greek: *δοκιμασία* (dokimasia)</note>. For God, by this most rigid and difficult-to-reconcile command, wished to test the faith and obedience of Abraham. This was not because there was any ignorance in God—for the all-knowing God is the **Searcher of Hearts** <note>original Greek: *καρδιογνώσης* (kardiognōstēs)</note> and knew what the faith of the holy Patriarch was and what he was weighing in his heart; indeed, He knew what He Himself was going to do in Abraham, for faith and obedience are the gifts of God. Rather, these things were provided for a specific purpose for the sake of the Church of God according to the divine economy <term>divine economy: the plan by which God manages human salvation throughout history</term>, so that in this famous story, distinguished mysteries might be foreshadowed. This was not only with respect to Abraham—who from that time was called **Father of a Multitude** <note>original Hebrew: *אב המון* (Ab Hamon), the etymological root of 'Abraham'</note>, the father of the faithful, and **heir of the entire world** <note>original Greek: *κληρονόμος τοῦ κόσμου* (klēronomos tou kosmou)</note> according to Romans 4:13—but also with respect to Isaac, whose sacrifice foreshadowed that singular sacrifice of Christ. That sacrifice was truly and actually performed on that same Mountain of Moriah, so that it might be a **propitiation** <note>original Greek: *ἱλαστήριον* (hilastērion), a means of reconciling humanity to God</note> for our sins.

The first point is easily proved; for since God had determined, according to His eternal decree, that Abraham should be not only a father **according to the flesh** <note>original Greek: *κατὰ σάρκα* (kata sarka)</note> of both Isaac and all the Jews, but also that he should be the father **according to the spirit** <note>original Greek: *κατὰ πνεῦμα* (kata pneuma)</note> and **according to the promise** <note>original Greek: *κατ' ἐπαγγελίαν* (kat’ epangelian)</note> of all the faithful, it was certainly necessary that this spiritual fatherhood be demonstrated by some extraordinary deed. For if a miracle shone forth in his fatherhood of the flesh...

<meta>This page continues Antoine Cregut’s theological dissertation on the trial of Abraham. On the previous page, Cregut explored the internal psychological and demonic temptations Abraham faced. Here, he shifts to the dual nature of the trial: how the command to sacrifice Isaac threatened both natural law and religious faith, and how Abraham’s spiritual love triumphed over earthly ties.</meta>

### ANTOINE CREGUT ###

...[natural]ly, when sterile Sarah conceived by her aged husband, all the more in spiritual fatherhood something most singular and extraordinary ought to occur. But what is more singular than a father in his hundredth year sacrificing and cutting the throat of his only-begotten and most beloved son, who was miraculously born of a sterile wife, and in whom all the promises of God were founded? In truth, that command seemed to destroy two very significant things: namely, *nature* and *faith*. 

First, *nature*: For to what end does God command such a crime of Abraham? Did God wish to slaughter and flay that wretched old man and that tender youth with one and the same blow? Did it please Him to playfully disembowel them both with the same command? Indeed, did He delight in striking three victims with a single blow and piercing them with a sword—namely the father, the mother, and the only son—three rational and human victims? 

Second, God even seems to nullify *faith* by this precept: For faith is founded on the word of promise, of which Isaac was the foundation and that most precious <term>pledge</term> <note>original: *arrhabo*</note>; but with Isaac sacrificed, upon what could Abraham’s faith lean concerning the blessed seed? If Isaac perishes, does not the faith of Abraham perish? If the word of God is made void, does not the faith born from it vanish? This is surely a vast mountain of temptations, which might rightly terrify all men.

Nevertheless, with God's help, Abraham emerged victorious on both counts. First, he overcame nature and subjected his fatherly affections to God, the author of nature; for the holy Patriarch knew that faith must be raised above nature, and that supernatural love transcends every kind of love by infinite leagues <note>original: *parasangis* (parasangs), a Persian measure of distance used here metaphorically</note>. Nor does that super-celestial fire have anything in common with this elementary fire, but neglecting all else, it must fly up to its own sphere. Hence Christ says in the Gospel: *“He who loves father or mother, or husband or wife, etc.”* <note>A reference to Matthew 10:37, where Jesus speaks of the necessity of loving God above family</note>. Indeed, reason itself dictated by right and equity what the Patriarch’s duty was. For he was bound to hand over to God what was His; and since God is the Father of bodies and spirits, as Scripture witnesses, and holds the <term>absolute central authority</term> <note>original Greek: *αὐτοκεντρικὸν* (autokentrikon), referring to God's inherent right as the center and source of all things</note> over all creatures, it was only right that...

<summary>Cregut argues that God’s command to sacrifice Isaac was a supreme test that challenged both the laws of nature and the stability of religious faith. Abraham’s victory is portrayed as the triumph of supernatural love and divine right over human emotion and logic.</summary>

### THE REVEALER OF SECRETS ###

...who was able to reclaim what was His own.

Secondly, he stood as a victor through faith, even beyond faith itself. For the work of faith is to believe in those things which are invisible and impossible to nature; indeed, the work of faith is to humbly carry out God’s commands, even if the reason for them is unsearchable to us. For this reason, the Apostle says in *Romans 4:18* that Abraham *against hope, believed in hope, that he might become the father of many nations.* Nor, as it says in verse 19, *did he consider his own body, already dead (since he was about a hundred years old), nor the deadness of Sarah’s womb.* Thus, the Holy Patriarch did not look at exhausted nature, but at the power of God, who could raise up children to Abraham from the very stones. Likewise, when God commanded Abraham to sacrifice his only son, he also looked to the infinite power of God, which was able to raise Isaac from the dead; thus, God's promises would not be made void, but would be fulfilled according to God’s word. Abraham therefore clung tenaciously <note>original: *mordicus*, literally "with his teeth"</note> to the divine promise, and subjected to that power whatever obstacles Satan raised to disturb his mind. Consequently, he perceived a blessing even from his son's ashes, and thus emerged splendidly from the labyrinth of temptation.

The reason for that command is twofold: one is *moral*, the other *mystical*. The moral reason was so that Abraham’s faith and obedience might be made manifest, as was said above. The mystical reason was so that the sacrifice of Christ on the cross might be foreshadowed <note>original: *adumbraretur*, meaning "sketched out in shadow"</note>. These reasons were certainly unknown to Abraham at the beginning and before the revelation; nevertheless, he believed through faith in what he did not see, according to the saying: *Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.* It is from this that this history corresponds <note>original: *αναλογως* (analogously)</note> most beautifully and truly to Christ. Isaac was born miraculously and beyond the powers of nature from a sterile mother, in whom there was no physical power to give birth or conceive seed. Christ was born of a Virgin without the seed of man. Sarah laughed in amazement and said, *"After I have grown old, shall I have pleasure? My lord being old also?"* But the Virgin Mary replied to the Angel, *"How can this be, since I do not know a man?"* Then, in this 22nd chapter, verse 2, God said to Abraham: *"Take now your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering <term>holocaustum</term> <note>A religious animal sacrifice that is completely consumed by fire</note> upon one of the mountains of which I shall tell you."* All these things truly foreshad—

...in which they were fulfilled. For God the Father gave us his son, his only one, whom he loved—Christ—and sent him to the land of Moriah, which was in truth Calvary, and offered him as a **burnt offering** <note>original: *holocaustum*, a sacrifice entirely consumed by fire</note> upon that mountain which God had foretold.

And in **Verse 6**: *Abraham took the wood for the burnt offering and placed it upon Isaac his son, and took in his hand fire and a sword.* These things were fulfilled in Christ, the true Isaac; for God placed the wood of the burnt offering upon his son, since Christ carried the wood of the cross on which he was sacrificed. God the Father also took the fire of his justice and the heat of his wrath, by which Christ, the burnt offering, was consumed from heaven; likewise the sword of the destroyer, by which that firstborn of God was pierced because of our sins.

**Verse 9**: *And they came to the place of which God had told him: and there Abraham built an altar, and arranged the wood, and bound Isaac his son, and placed him upon the altar on top of the wood.* These things depict the passion of Christ vividly <note>original: *graphice*, meaning with graphic detail or like a drawing</note>. For Christ had to be sacrificed outside the gates of the city; therefore, departing from Jerusalem, he came to the place which God had spoken of long ago, **and built the altar of the cross**. Just as Abraham constructed a new altar on which no one had sacrificed before, so Christ was slaughtered on a new altar.

For the fabrication <note>original: *commentum*</note> of the Jews is false, who say that Noah, Adam, Cain, and Abel had once sacrificed on that same altar. Nor was it polished from cut and smoothed stones, as God later commanded in the Law, but it was rough and hastily constructed; all these things properly align with the altar of the cross. *And he arranged the wood.* Thus the wood of the cross was correctly set out and arranged in the shape of a cross. *And he bound Isaac his son;* thus Christ, the Son of God and the true Isaac, was bound; *and placed him upon the altar and the wood*, because he was made a curse, according to that saying: *cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.*

Finally, in **Verses 10, 11, and 12**, when Isaac was to be sacrificed, God forbade him from being slaughtered, a ram having been handed over in his place. These things were also fulfilled in Christ, since just as Isaac was offered as a sacrifice, so Christ was truly offered as a <term>propitiatory sacrifice <note>original Greek: *ἱλαστήριον* (hilastērion), a sacrifice meant to appease or turn away divine wrath</note></term>. Just as Isaac is offered as a rational and living victim at a time when brute and irrational victims were displeasing, so what was figuratively true of Isaac was truly and really true of

### THE REVEALER OF SECRETS ###

The Apostle said of Christ in Hebrews 10:5: *Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you have prepared for me.* This is also found in Psalm 40:7. Then, just as Isaac is not actually sacrificed, but a ram is offered in his place—even though Isaac had been destined for death—so too the human race was destined for eternal death and to be sacrificed to divine justice. However, humanity is not actually sacrificed; instead, a ram is offered in its place. This ram is Christ, the *Lamb slain from the foundations of the world* (Revelation 13:8). Finally, when Abraham was so perplexed as he was about to slaughter his son, the merciful Jehovah is present, accepting the offering of his son without requiring his death. Abraham looks back and sees a ram caught in a thicket by its horns, which he offered instead of his son.

In the Hebrew text, the word for "thicket" is *sabak* <term>Hebrew: סבך, meaning a dense thicket or entanglement</term>, which can also imply "in perplexity." The translators of the Septuagint <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> left the word *Sabech* as if it were the specific name of a tree from which the ram hung. What you might find even more surprising is that Rabbi Solomon <note>the medieval commentator Rashi</note> says it was an *elah* <note>Hebrew: אלה</note>, that is, an oak or an oak grove. These details certainly fit wonderfully with the cross of Christ: for He was truly that "perplexed" ram who hung from the tree of the cross—indeed, if some learned doctors are to be believed, he hung *on an oak*. 

Furthermore, and more surprising still, because of that "perplexity" or entanglement, Christ cried out *Eli lamma sabacthani* <note>“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46)</note>. According to some Doctors, these words seem to allude to the Hebrew word *sabak*. What increases the wonder is that the Septuagint does not translate *sabak* into a Greek word, but retains the word *sabech* itself, just as the Evangelists Matthew and Mark retain the Syriac word *Seba* (and with the suffix, *sabactani*), so that this beautiful linguistic connection might shine more clearly. Whether these things happened by chance <note>Greek: ἀπὸ τύχης</note> or by design <note>Greek: ἐκ τῆς προαιρέσεως</note> and divine ordination, they are all truly worthy of great admiration.

Nor should we omit that this place was named *Moriah* by Abraham, meaning "The Lord will see" <note>often interpreted as "The Lord will provide"</note>. From this came a proverb used even in the time of Moses: *In the mountain of Jehovah it shall be seen.* This phrase was used by those who were perplexed and did not know what to do. In such moments, nothing is safer than to flee to God's providence. This is why God is called *Theos* <note>Greek: Θεὸς</note>, a word derived from "running," not only because of the heavens—whose course is most swift and which the ancient Pagans believed was God—but also because of the sudden and unhoped-for help that comes "from the machine" <note>Greek: ἀπὸ τῆς μηχανῆς; a reference to the *deus ex machina* in ancient theater where a god was lowered onto the stage to resolve a hopeless plot</note>. But mystically, all these things are to be referred to the cross of Christ and to Calvary or Golgotha; for...

<meta>This page continues Antoine Cregut’s theological interpretation of the Binding of Isaac. On the previous page, Cregut discussed how the "perplexed" ram caught in the thicket represents Christ's entrapment in the human condition and His crucifixion on the cross.</meta>

### ANTOINE CREGUT ###

...while the Church is in perplexity, that saying holds true: *In the mountain of the Lord it shall be seen* <note>original Latin: "in monte Iehoua videbitur." This refers to Genesis 22:14, suggesting God provides in times of crisis</note>. For prayers are heard because of Christ's sacrifice, and He intercedes for us in heaven (Romans 8). Hence that saying of Christ: *Whatever you ask of the Father in my name, it will be given to you.*

Nor is it without mystery that the Jews held this sacrifice of Abraham in such high regard that, at the beginning of the year when they observe the Feast of Atonement <note>Yom Kippur</note>, they celebrate the memory of this event. According to Jerome <note>a 4th-century Church Father</note> and the ancient Hebrew interpreters, they sound a horn trumpet <note>the shofar</note> to recall the horns of that ram. For they say: "Since we were entangled in the sins of the entire past year, so that we were liable to great punishments because of them, through the benefit of this sacrifice, we return to grace." Truly, if the Jews were not blind and did not perpetually have the *veil* <term>Greek: κάλυμμα (kalymma), referring to the spiritual blindness or "veil" over the heart mentioned in 2 Corinthians 3:15</term> of Moses before their eyes, they would instead look upon the cross of Christ and His majestic sacrifice, which was foreshadowed by that of Isaac; for those things are found more effectively in the reality than in the figure <note>the symbolic type</note>.

For the ram is rescued from its entanglement and then sacrificed; this is done first to signify the redemption of the human race which—while it was entangled because of its sins like the ram, and destined for death like Isaac—is nevertheless graciously liberated by Christ being substituted in its place. Second, it is because from this, both natures of Christ are signified: namely, the human nature, which is handed over to death; and the other, which is immortal and incapable of suffering. Thus, from Leviticus, two goats prefigured Christ: one, namely the *Azazel* <note>the "scapegoat" sent into the wilderness</note>, is released alive, while the other is sacrificed. Furthermore, many other *similarities* <term>Greek: ὅμοια (homoia)</term> and *dissimilarities* <term>Greek: ἀνόμοια (anomoia)</term> could be gathered here between Isaac and Christ, and between the sacrifices of both, but the aforementioned things should suffice for the purpose of our goal.

But indeed, although that command of God was extraordinary and unique to Abraham—and in fact, it was not fulfilled, because God intended only that which was moral, namely the faith and obedience of Abraham—nevertheless, human restlessness, which usually runs riot against and beyond the law of God with an intolerable *misguided zeal* <term>Cacozelia: a perverse or distorted imitation of a virtue, in this case, a twisted imitation of Abraham's willingness to sacrifice</term>, wanted to imitate Abraham's sacrifice. For because God had said to Abraham, *Take now your only son Isaac and offer him as a burnt offering* <note>original: "holocaustum"</note>, from this, religion...

...these deeds were done, and confirmed by monstrous examples in Jeremiah 7:31, Jeremiah 19:2, and 2 Chronicles 28:3, against the express command of God in Leviticus 18:21 and 20:2. For the idolaters, with detestable idolatry, sacrificed their sons to the idol Molech, or Milcom, "passing them through the fire" or burning them. The *place* in which this monstrous idolatry occurred was outside the city of Jerusalem in גיהנם <note>original Hebrew: *Ge-Hinnom*, the Valley of Hinnom</note>, in the *Valley of Hinnom*, where there was a high place called תפת <note>original Hebrew: *Tophet*</note>. The *statue or image* that stood on that high place was made of bronze, having the face of a calf, with hands stretched out like those of a man opening his hands to receive something from another; it was hollowed out within. It is added, moreover, in the book *Yalkut* <note>The *Yalkut Shimoni*, a prominent medieval collection of Jewish midrash or scriptural commentary</note> on Jeremiah 7, that seven shrines were built there, before which this image was placed. He who entered the first shrine brought a young pigeon; he who entered the second offered a lamb; in the third, a ram; in the fourth, a calf; in the fifth, a steer; in the sixth, an ox; and finally, in the seventh shrine, a man offered his own son, first kissing the calf or Molech. As it says in Hosea 13:2: *The sacrificers of men kiss the calf.* The *rite* by which the sacrifice was made was of this sort: Molech was heated by fire placed beneath him until he became glowing like light. Then the priests took the infant and placed him in the glowing hands of Molech; and lest the parent hear the wailing of the child, they beat drums <note>The text suggests an etymological link between *Tophet* and the Hebrew word *toph*, meaning "drum"</note>. From this, the place was called Tophet. This abominable place was defiled by the pious King Josiah (2 Kings 23:11) by throwing in dung, filth, corpses, and other unclean things. As Rabbi David Kimchi <note>A famous 12th-13th century Jewish commentator and grammarian</note> observes, for this reason a perpetual fire—אש תמיד <note>original Hebrew: *esh tamid*</note>—was kept there to burn the filth and the corpses. Hence it happened that because of those horrendous tortures of the little boys—whose wailing was called נהם <note>original Hebrew: *naham*, meaning "roaring"</note>, which by a transposition of letters <term>metathesis: the rearranging of sounds or letters in a word</term> became *Hinnom* הנם—and because of that continuous fire, the place and the torture of the damned is called in the Gospel of Matthew 5:22 "Gehenna" <note>original Greek: γέεννα (geenna)</note>. See more on this in Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf, a renowned 17th-century Christian scholar of Hebrew and Jewish tradition</note> under the word *ge* <note>valley</note>.

Nevertheless, if God so severely condemned the idolatry of Molech and the barbarity of the nations whenever they offered human victims, alas! what will be the prompt answer regarding the deed...

<meta>This page continues Crégut’s discussion of human sacrifice in the biblical context. After discussing the pagan horrors of the Valley of Hinnom on the previous page, he now examines the controversial biblical case of Jephthah’s daughter to determine if it was a true sacrifice or a symbolic devotion.</meta>

# ANTOINE CRÉGUT #

-> Page 484 <-

The case of Jephthah, which is described in Judges chapter 11, concerns a man who sacrificed his only daughter after she was devoted to God. His sacrifice seems to be approved by Scripture, which testifies that "the Spirit of the Lord came upon him" <note>original Latin: *Spiritum Domini factum esse super eum*</note>. Furthermore, Paul, in Hebrews chapter 11, numbers Jephthah among the saints. Setting aside the various opinions of interpreters—both Hebrew and Christian, ancient and modern, which are cited by Peter Martyr <note>Peter Martyr Vermigli (1499–1562), a leading Reformed theologian</note> and others on this passage of Judges—we will briefly respond that this question concerns first the *matter of fact* <note>original: *de facto*</note>, and then the *matter of law* <note>original: *de iure*</note>. 

Regarding the **matter of fact**: most commentators deny that Jephthah actually sacrificed his daughter, claiming instead that he merely dedicated her to God, and thus she died only a "civil death" <note>A legal status where a person is alive but loses all civil rights, often used here to mean she lived a secluded, celibate life</note>. They argue this type of vow was not *cherem* <note>original Hebrew: חרם; a "ban" or "devotion" where something is utterly destroyed as an offering</note>, or that specific curse which was devoted to God rather than simply promised; for that which is *cherem* must be destroyed, as is clear regarding the Amalekites. Rather, they argue it was another kind of vow, an *anathema* <note>original Greek: ανάθημα; here meaning a gift or person dedicated to a temple</note> which remained forever sacred to God and never returned to profane use. For example, if someone had vowed a Nazirite vow <note>term: Nazirite; a person who took a vow of separation and service to God, involving hair growth and abstinence from wine</note>, as long as they lived, they could not be anything but a Nazirite. They gather this from the fact that she "bewailed her virginity." And Rabbi Levi ben Gerson <note>also known as Ralbag, a 14th-century philosopher and commentator</note> observes that it does not say, "Jephthah sacrificed her," but "he did according to his vow." 

However, the contrary opinion is the true one, which is followed by the Targum <note>original: *Thargum*; an ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note>; for it says explicitly that the girl was sacrificed. It even rebukes Jephthah for not consulting the High Priest. The older Rabbis feel much the same way; they further criticize the High Priest for not warning Jephthah of his sin and restraining him, even if he had not been consulted. But what is more significant is that this second opinion conforms to the literal and internal sense of the Scripture itself.

Since the *matter of fact* is established <note>i.e., that she was actually killed</note>, the more difficult question is the **matter of law**: whether this sacrifice should be praised or condemned. There is great reason for doubt, and interpreters are not of one mind. Some praise the deed, others rebuke it, bringing forth arguments on both sides. Having carefully considered the history, we will defend a middle opinion: we intend to prove that in Jephthah’s action there is something to be praised, but something else worthy of blame. First, his most fervent zeal is to be praised; he burned with such love toward God that he was ready to [consecrate] <note>The Latin ends mid-word with "con-"; the catchword suggests it completes as "consecrated" or "sacrificed"</note> all his possessions to God spontaneously and eagerly...

...he consecrated, and in gratitude for the victory brought back (or to be brought back) from the enemies, he willingly vowed to the God of Hosts whatever should come out from the doors of his house. For since God had preserved him and the entire army of Israel from the rage and cruel slaughter of the enemies, he deemed it just to also consecrate himself and his own to God and to face death for His glory. Therefore, as evidence <note>original Greek: τεκμήριον (*tekmērion*), meaning a proof or sure sign</note> of his zeal and great fervor, he vowed certain "firstfruits" to his Savior—namely, whatever came out of the doors of his house. Hence, it was the fervor of his zeal and his desire for liberation that produced these words and this vow (verse 30): *And Jephthah vowed a vow to Jehovah and said: "If you will indeed deliver the children of Ammon into my hand, then whatever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the children of Ammon shall be Jehovah’s, or I will offer it as a burnt offering."* <note>original: *holocaustum*</note>.

For although God is not delighted by human blood, nor has He specifically commanded the sacrifice of children to us—which would undoubtedly smack of some barbarity—nevertheless, while this is true, one must also confess that God wishes to be loved above all others, and that the soul must be generously surrendered for His glory. Therefore, when martyrs and confessors—driven by a strenuous and undaunted impulse of faith and zeal because of the urgent necessity of the Church—have voluntarily surrendered themselves to be tortured and tormented by executioners, that zeal pleased God. By the strength of His Spirit, He favored those heroic movements and brought the constancy of such strong heroes to a most joyful conclusion, having finally obtained the victory and the crown of martyrdom.

In this act of Jephthah, there is a similar fervent zeal; and since the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart, it easily erupted into the words mentioned above. This is proven by what is said in verse 29: *The Spirit of God was upon him.* And: *The Spirit of Jehovah was upon Jephthah.* A little later it adds: *And Jephthah vowed a vow to Jehovah, and said: "If you will indeed deliver,"* etc. This is further confirmed by the Apostle in Hebrews 11, who numbers Jephthah among the saints and the truly faithful. Furthermore, it is evident from the outcome: God did not prevent this kind of sacrifice as He did with Abraham when he was about to sacrifice his son <note>Referring to the "Binding of Isaac" in Genesis 22, where an angel stops the sacrifice</note>, but in His secret counsel, He wished to permit it for the instruction of the faithful. For in the victims, it was signified that death was...

<meta>This page continues Crégut's theological exploration of sacrifice, moving from the general theory of substitutionary atonement to the specific and controversial case of Jephthah’s daughter. He compares the concept of human sacrifice to Christian martyrdom and concludes by critiquing the rashness of Jephthah’s vow.</meta>

# ANTHONY CRÉGUT #

-> Page 486 <-

...the wages of sin <note>original: *stipendium peccati*</note>; this was testified by the one who offered a sacrificial victim to God—namely, that he himself deserved to be killed, but by the goodness of God, his own death was transferred onto the victim. This is even more evident in a human victim, who suffers a well-deserved death because of sin; yet, by the fatherly mercy of our God, we believe that eternal death is remitted and turned into a temporal death. Indeed, it becomes a temporal death which is not properly a punishment for sin or a means of making satisfaction, but which is merely for the sake of correction and is either **discipline** <note>original Greek: *παιδεία* (*paideia*)</note>, or a **testing** <note>original Greek: *δοκιμασία* (*dokimasia*)</note>, or a **witness/martyrdom** <note>original Greek: *μαρτύριον* (*martyrion*)</note>. Ultimately, that human victim pointed more directly toward the sacrifice of Christ; for it was a kind of visible sermon on the cross of Christ and on the necessity of transferring our death to him. Since, therefore, God is inclined toward mercy, he did not delight in human blood, nor did he demand those rational victims from men for that reason. On the contrary, even though the firstborn of men were bound to him, he did not wish them to be sacrificed, but rather to be redeemed at a price. And in **Deuteronomy 12**, it says: *The nations which I shall expel before you sacrifice their sons and daughters: but see that you do not do likewise.* <note>The author summarizes the prohibition in Deut. 12:31</note> Nevertheless, when an extraordinary and singular human victim is offered to him once by an extraordinary vow, God seems to have accepted this sacrifice, just like the martyrdom of the confessors, which is accepted by God in the manner of a sacrifice. Hence Paul says in **2 Timothy 4:6**: *For I am already being poured out.* <note>original Greek: *ἐγὼ γὰρ ἤδη σπένδομαι* (*egō gar ēdē spendomai*)</note> *Indeed, I am now a drink offering, and the time of my departure is at hand.* He uses the word **being poured out** <note>original: *spendomai*</note> rather than "being slaughtered" <note>original Greek: *σφάζομαι* (*sphazomai*)</note> or "being sacrificed" <note>original Greek: *θύομαι* (*thyomai*)</note>, alluding to the sprinkling of blood or even wine that was customary in sacrifices. And in **Philippians 2:17**: *Yes, and if I am being offered as a libation upon the sacrifice and service of your faith, I joyfully congratulate you all.* Here Paul predicted his own death, not as a means by which the Philippians would be reconciled to God, but as a means by which they would be confirmed in their faith.

But truly, while Jephthah’s sacrifice can be praised in this sense—or at least not condemned—we nevertheless judge that his zeal was in some way preposterous and "without knowledge." This is because he made his vow without exercising any discernment, but inconsiderately, regarding the first thing that should come to meet him as he stepped out from the doors of his house. He certainly did not consider that what actually happened could occur: that his only daughter would be the one to come out of those doors. Thus, he soon paid the price for the rashness of his vow...

<meta>This page continues Crégut's analysis of the sacrifice of Jephthah’s daughter. Following the previous page’s discussion on the nature of human sacrifice and redemption, Crégut now examines the specific psychological and spiritual motivations behind Jephthah’s actions, contrasting them with the sacrifice of Christ and the near-sacrifice of Isaac.</meta>

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS. 487 #

...dismayed by the meeting with his daughter. For as it is stated in verse 35:

> He tore his clothes and said, "Alas, alas my daughter! You have truly bowed me down, and you are among those who trouble me. For I have opened my mouth to Jehovah <note>The Hebrew name for God, often used in older translations where modern ones might use "the LORD."</note>, and I cannot take it back."

Therefore, several "movements" or motivations of Jephthah must be considered here. The first movement was of the Spirit of God, when, burning with zeal, he dedicated himself and all he owned to God. However, in that movement there was something mixed in from the human spirit, since he made the vow without making a distinction—promising whatever should first come out of the doors of his house. Next, there was a movement of human emotion when he was shaken by the sight of the girl, for then the very depths of his heart were moved. Furthermore, there was a movement of the human spirit and a certain superstition rather than true worship when he insisted on fulfilling the vow rigidly and **unreasonably** <term>ἀλόγως (*alogos*)</term>, <gloss>thoughtlessly</gloss> <note>original Greek: *ἀπερισκέπτως* (*aperiskeptos*)</note>, as it seemed to him. For according to the Law, he could have redeemed the girl, just as the firstborn sons were redeemed <note>The Mosaic Law allowed for a monetary payment to "buy back" a person dedicated to God's service, rather than performing a sacrifice.</note>. 

Nevertheless, here, as in the other sins of the ancient fathers and saints, Blessed Augustine observes that the illustrious wisdom of God flourished and was present. From these events, various reasons are drawn forth for the instruction of the Church and for preaching and illustrating the mysteries of the Christian faith. And so, God wished to use Jephthah's sacrifice **for instruction** <term>εἰς παιδαγωγίαν (*eis paidagogian*)</term>, signifying the sacrifice of Christ, which was made holy by the decree of God the Father when He handed over His only-begotten Son to death. 

For since mortals were far too stunned—and did not lift the eyes of their minds toward Christ as was fitting—God wished to rouse these "snoring" men by means of Jephthah's singular and extraordinary sacrifice. He intended that, by seeing a throbbing and dying human victim, they might look toward Christ, the true victim and the only offering acceptable to God—the one who would give His life and be the victim for the human race. 

Let these things be said concerning this most unique history. In this matter, we have preferred to follow a middle path rather than either praising Jephthah’s action entirely (with Augustine) or, turning to the other extreme, criminalizing it according to the opinions of the Rabbis and certain other Fathers. Among others, Jerome wrote the following: *Jephthah was foolish in making the vow because he lacked discernment, and he was impious in fulfilling it.*

Observe, therefore, on one hand, the mercy of God, who prohibited Abraham from sacrificing his son; and on the other hand...

<meta>This page continues Crégut’s examination of human sacrifice, moving from the specific case of Jephthah’s daughter to a broader critique of pagan "savagery." He contrasts the bloodthirsty demands of "demonic" pagan gods and the customs of the Gauls and Greeks with the mercy of the Christian God, who accepted animal substitutes until the ultimate sacrifice of Christ.</meta>

# ANTOINE CRÉGUT #

...of the gods of the Nations, that is, the monstrous savagery of the Demons who demanded rational victims <note>In this context, "rational victims" refers to human beings—creatures possessing reason—as opposed to "irrational" animal sacrifices.</note> from wretched mortals, as noted among others by Jerome in his letter regarding the epitaph of Nepotian which he wrote to Heliodorus, and Erasmus in his *Scholia* <note>Erasmus of Rotterdam was a famous Renaissance scholar whose "Scholia" were explanatory notes on the writings of the Church Fathers like Jerome.</note> on Jerome. Erasmus mentions that Saint Jerome emphasized their monstrous savagery, for they not only sacrificed to the spirits and shades of the deceased as if they were gods, but even slaughtered human beings. For each person’s ancestors, after they had departed from life, were held in the place of deities. 

Hence Jerome says: *“The ferocity of the Bessi <note>A Thracian tribe known in antiquity for their fierce and predatory nature.</note>, and the throng of skin-clad peoples, who once sacrificed men to the rites of the dead, have broken their harsh cry into the sweet melody of the cross, and the voice of the whole world is Christ.”* Indeed, according to Jerome (as witnessed by Erasmus), "rites for the dead" <note>original Latin: *inferiæ*</note> are funeral ceremonies or the "just dues" which are paid to the deceased. The word is derived from "bringing in" <note>original Latin: *inferendo*</note>, so that it corresponds to the Greek <term>sacrifices to the dead (*enagismata*)</term>, rather than being derived from "the underworld" <note>original: *inferis*</note>. 

The Nations and the Barbarians, therefore, used to slaughter men for the shades of the deceased, either to appease them or to please them. Thus, in the Tragedies, the ghost of Achilles is appeased by the blood of Polyxena. And in Virgil: *“Ufens seizes living sacrifices to immolate to the shades.”* And in Homer, in the penultimate book of the *Iliad*, at the funeral rites of Patroclus, Achilles sacrifices twelve Trojan youths, as well as dogs and horses, for the sake of his deceased friend. 

Caesar, in the sixth book of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*, testifies that this was a public custom of the Gauls: in times of serious illness or the dangers of war, they would sacrifice human beings as victims, because they believed that the divine power could not be appeased for the life of a man except by the life of a man. Furthermore, slaves and clients, who were known to have been loved by their masters and patrons, were burned together with them once the proper funeral rites were completed. 

How much, then, must the mercy of our most clement God be praised above the savagery of men and false gods! For He did not demand rational victims but rather animal sacrifices <note>original Latin: *brutas hostias*, literally "brute" or non-rational victims.</note>. For even if, by His just judgment due to the transgression of the law, the whole human race was devoted to eternal curses and handed over to death, nevertheless, through the interceding mercy of God, He not only becomes appeasable by His own Son being delivered to death for us, but also, when it was necessary for the sacrifice of His Son to be foreshadowed by various victims, He never permitted that...

<summary>Crégut contrasts the "demonic" practice of human sacrifice in pagan cultures (Greek, Roman, and Gallic) with the mercy of God, who substituted animal sacrifices for human ones as a precursor to the sacrifice of Christ.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Crégut’s discussion on the nature of sacrifice. After contrasting the "barbarism" of pagan human sacrifice with the animal sacrifices of the Hebrews, he now explores the specific case of Abraham and Isaac as a prophetic "figure" of Christ's sacrifice on the same geographical site.</meta>

-> # THE REVEALER OF SECRETS # <-

...barbarism, as if it were to be represented through the immolation of men; instead, it was represented through brute victims <note>That is, animal sacrifices rather than human ones.</note>. And if, through one rational victim—namely Isaac—He wished to foreshadow the sacrifice of Christ, this was performed only as a figure and not in reality. This is just as Melchizedek—not in truth but in figure, and not according to his actual nature <note>original Greek: *kata to eidos*</note> but according to how he is described <note>original Greek: *kata to legesthai*</note>—was "without father, without mother," <note>A reference to Hebrews 7:3, describing Melchizedek as a type of Christ because his genealogy is not recorded.</note> etc. Indeed, God would not even have condemned Christ Himself, our guarantor, to death if it could have happened otherwise while preserving His justice; since the mercy of God is the greatest of His works, He did not wish His wrath to burn forever. To prevent His justice from causing constant terror, He created a refined tempering of justice and mercy, which can truly be called a mystical **temperament** <note>original Greek: *idiosynkrasia* (idiosyncrasy), here meaning a perfect blending of distinct qualities</note>, specifically when those two distinguished virtues of God kissed each other.

The place in which Abraham was commanded to sacrifice his son was Mount Moriah, for it is said in *verse 2: Go to the land of Moriah.* And in *verse 14: And Abraham called the name of that place, The Lord will see.* That place was surely mystical and therefore most famous because in it the "mystery of mysteries" was first foreshadowed and finally fulfilled in the fullness of time. For that Mount Moriah is the same mountain as Golgotha, upon which Christ, the redeemer of the human race, was sacrificed for the expiation of sins. For why else would God have said to Abraham: 

> *Go to the land of Moriah, and offer your only son as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I shall tell you.* 

Why did God want Abraham to walk for three or four days before he reached that mountain? Was not the land in which the Holy Patriarch then resided sufficient and suitable for a sacrifice? In truth, a mystery lies hidden here; these details, so religiously observed, were hardly in vain. **God and nature do nothing in vain.** <note>original Greek: *Theos kai physis ouden matēn poiousi*</note> God wished to give a prelude to the future passion of Christ in that blessed seed. For just as when the Son of God appeared in human form to the fathers of the Old Testament, He gave a prelude to the future Incarnation; so Christ appeared in human form and in the figure of Isaac on Mount Moriah to create a prelude to His future passion. And so that the figure might more closely correspond to the truth, God wisely ordained that this entire, great business be celebrated on the same mountain, so that even from the topography itself, the truth and meaning of such a famous history might be confirmed...

-> ### ANTOINE CRÉGUT ### <-

...be established. This is why that distinguished mountain was made noble by so many names.

First, it was called *Moriah* by Abraham, not only so it would be a **memorial** <note>original Greek: *mnemonikon*</note> name for the deed performed and past with respect to the ram and Isaac, but also so it would be a **significant** <note>original Greek: *semantikon*</note> name for a future event with respect to Christ, the redeemer of all. For *Moriah*, from the etymology of the name, is capable of signifying several things emphatically. Jerome explained it as the "land of vision," deriving it from the root **to see** <note>original Hebrew: *ra’ah*</note>, perhaps because *Jerusalem* was located there, which was so named from the **vision of peace**. Others interpret it as **the myrrh of God**. Others derive it from the word **to teach** <note>original Hebrew: *yarah*</note>; others from **to fear** <note>original Hebrew: *yara*</note>; and these two better fit the matter itself and the grammatical analogy. For the "land of Moriah" would be the same as the "land of divine worship," either because God had chosen it for performing the sacrifice, or because the location of the Temple was destined to be there. Therefore, that sacred place then began to be the site where God, by a secret plan, had determined to eventually establish regular worship. Sacrifices rightly receive their name from "fear," as they testify to a reverence for God. However, Abraham seems to allude to *Moriah* and explain it differently when he said, *The Lord will see.* And perhaps our translators had this in mind when they call it the **land of vision**, or perhaps they looked to the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> who translate it as **high land** <note>original Greek: *gen hypselen*</note>, for those things which are high are easily held to be conspicuous. Those who wish that mountain *Moriah* to be named from "myrrh" look to the passage in the Song of Songs: *I will hasten to the mountain of myrrh; because that soil was very fertile in myrrh and cinnamon.*

Next, that place was called *Golgotha*. Matthew 27:33: *And when they had come to a place called Golgotha, which is the place of a skull.* For so it is read (according to Beza) in all the manuscripts, but incorrectly since the *L* <note>The Greek letter lambda (λ).</note> is removed; for it should be said *Golgaltha*, or *Gulgoltha* from the Hebrew **skull** <note>original Hebrew: *Gulgoleth*</note>, from the word **wheel** or **orb** <note>original Hebrew: *galal*</note>, and these from the root **to roll** <note>original Hebrew: *galgal*</note>. The Syriac version has *Gugultha*, with the first *L* <note>original Hebrew: *lomad*</note> removed. The reasoning for that etymology is not the same among everyone: for some wish the place to be so named from the abundance of skulls, since those condemned to death would suffer the ultimate punishment there, and after they...

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of Mount Moriah, moving from the etymology of the site to the specific mystical significance of Christ’s crucifixion at Golgotha and the nature of Abraham’s obedience.</meta>

-> ### THE REVEALER OF SECRETS ### <-

...where there were corpses, the skulls remained for a long time. But truly, although those things which were carried out in the person of Christ were done according to the custom and habit of the nation, they were nevertheless **most mystical** <note>original Greek: *mystikōtata*</note> in Christ. For he was cast out from the city as if unworthy of human company, so that he might receive us into the heavenly kingdom with the Angels. Therefore, the Apostle in Hebrews 13:12 testifies that this was done according to the ancient figure of the Law; for God commanded that the bodies of the animals, whose blood was brought into the Sanctuary for atonement, be burned outside the camp. Thus, he says that Christ went out from the gate of the city so that, having taken up the curse, he might become like a rejected thing, and thus atone for sins. Others, however—indeed most of the ancient writers—claim this place was called *Golgotha* because Adam was buried there, and his skull was found there. This is the opinion of Epiphanius, Origen, Athanasius, Basil, Chrysostom, Anastasius Sinaita, etc.; but we have written more extensively on these matters elsewhere in our dissertation on the passage in Genesis 3:6 and chapter 11:17, which you may consult if you wish.

Finally, the last part of this **discussion** <note>original Greek: *syzētēseōs*</note> remains: namely, the *outcome*. This can be considered either in respect to Abraham himself, or in respect to God. In respect to Abraham, it is the manifestation of faith and obedience. In respect to God, it is the prohibition made to Abraham that he should not strike or slaughter his son. First, the faith and obedience of the holy Patriarch are eminent and conspicuous; for which reason he was named the "father of the faithful" not without cause. Truly, Abraham’s obedience can be subject to no quibbling. Nor will anyone say what the impious apostate Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who famously critiqued Christianity</note> blasphemously said regarding the faith and obedience of the Apostles—that they showed signs of great fickleness when they immediately followed Christ's call with a blind impulse, without any preceding examination of his person or office. Nor can any stain of a certain "blind obedience" be branded upon it, such as the Jesuits have vowed to the Pope, and which they themselves call "blind," or as Cusanus <note>Nicholas of Cusa, a 15th-century cardinal and philosopher</note> called "irrational." For the Jesuits, he said, blind obedience stands in place of reason, much as a soul serves a pig instead of salt <note>A common historical idiom suggesting the soul only exists to keep the body from rotting, implying a base, unthinking existence</note>. But truly, the obedience of our Patriarch is truly the "obedience of faith," which is certainly not rational <note>in a worldly sense</note>, yet is not irrational, but rather above...

# ANTHONY CREGUTUS #

...might be confirmed. Hence it is that this distinguished mountain was ennobled by so many names.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Abraham’s sacrifice from the previous page, specifically regarding the manifestation of his obedience as a "reason" or "rationale" for his faith.</meta>

-> ANTHONII CREGVTI <-

...reason, because this obedience acts as a handmaid to faith, and it believes even those things which it cannot comprehend, since it humbles all the powers of the soul until a brighter light and revelation illuminates the mind.

And in truth, the necessity of obedience is so absolute that we are not only bound to obey God even when He commands something contrary to nature—as was done with Abraham when He commanded him to sacrifice his own son—but even disobedience is condemned although the action might otherwise be done for the glory of God. Thus those two blind men who received sight sinned, for they spread the miracle everywhere against Christ’s command. Regarding them, see Matthew 9:31. For we must comply with God’s commands, no matter how much it seems to us that something better could be done. For who is wiser than the wisdom of God? And who shall say that God is playing, or that He desires something other than what He said? It is well known what happened to Saul because he preserved the devoted things of Amalek <note>original: *anathema*; referring to the spoils of war that God had commanded to be totally destroyed</note>, even though he was preparing a magnificent sacrifice. 1 Samuel 15:22. Also well known is the story of the man who refused to strike the prophet, and for that reason was killed by a lion. 1 Kings 20:35. To him, the killing of a prophet of God seemed a crime; yet it was not an evil since it was commanded by God. In the same way, Peter wrongly dissuades Christ from His passion in Matthew 16:22. And in John 13:8, with misguided humility, he takes care that Christ should not wash his feet.

From this it follows that obedience is beautifully signified in Scripture by three signs. For just as in the military of this world Caesar formerly defined the best soldier as one who behaved correctly <note>original: *morem gereret*; to comply with custom or orders</note>. And Vegetius <note>Publius Flavius Vegetius Renatus, a writer of the later Roman Empire known for his treatise on military matters</note>, in *Concerning Military Matters*, said that nothing is more beneficial for victory than to obey the leader. Commanders, moreover, give orders through three signs: I. By a vocal sign, such as the commands of superiors. II. By a semi-vocal sign <note>original: *semiuocale*; sounds produced by instruments rather than the human voice</note>, such as a trumpet or horn. III. By a silent sign, such as banners and the signals of weapons. Thus in the spiritual warfare there are three signs. I. The vocal, concerning which Hebrews 13 says: *Obey your leaders and submit to them.* and Matthew 23: *Whatever they tell you, do.* For as it is held in the Digest <note>The *Digest*, or *Pandects*, a massive collection of Roman legal jurists' writings compiled under Emperor Justinian</note>, in the section *On Military Matters*, law "militum": "He who does not observe the commands of princes is to be punished by death, even if he has performed the matter well." Thus also he who is disobedient is to be punished with eternal punishment. II. The semi-vocal, namely the riddles <note>original: *ænigmata*; obscure or symbolic messages</note> of the prophets and of the figures.

For Adam, as soon as he was created, was bound by the command of obedience. (Genesis 3). Noah was saved from the flood by building and entering the ark. (Genesis 7). Abraham was called the father of many nations by the offering of his son. (Genesis 22). III. The *silent sign* <note>original: *Signum mutum*</note> consists of the examples found in the created world. Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose, a 4th-century church father and doctor of the Church</note> says that bees who do not comply with the laws of the queen bee <note>the original uses "king bee" following the biological understanding of the time</note> are killed. The sea naturally obeys the influences of the heavens. Thus, in every kind of thing, God established certain superiors and more excellent beings whom He wished to be obeyed. But that obedience consists of a threefold subjective consent according to the Scholastics <note>medieval university theologians who used logic to explain Christian doctrine</note>: namely 1. Of the inferior to the superior. 2. Of sensuality <note>the physical senses and desires</note> to reason. 3. Of reason to the Creator or to the Mind <note>Greek: *νοῦν* (noun)</note>. And that first intelligence, that threefold kind of obedience shines forth in Abraham, who indeed willingly and most humbly submitted his sensuality, his reason, and everything that belonged to his nature to the Supreme Ruler.

Therefore we truly assert that in that remarkable obedience of Abraham, his singular piety and fear of God shone forth; for the primary effect that sprouts from that cause and root is obedience. For what is obedience but the submission of a pious mind, by which the revealed divine voice is followed eagerly, diligently, and constantly? Not as in sacrifices by slaughtering the flesh of another, but by slaughtering and offering one’s own will. This is the sacrifice of a contrite heart, pleasing to God, which the Psalmist <note>referring to King David, the traditional author of the Psalms</note> discusses. Or that which Paul mentions in Romans 12:1:

> *Present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your rational worship.* <note>original Latin: *Sistite corpora uestra hostiam viuam, sanctam, acceptam Deo, rationalem illum cultum uestrum*</note>

And in truth, just as God is the first mover of all things that are moved in both the physical and ethical realms, so it is necessary that all agents, both natural and voluntary, obey Him; the former indeed from the necessity of nature, which is carried by a blind impulse without choice <note>Greek: *ἄνευ τῆς προαιρέσεως* (aneu tēs proaireseōs)</note>; the latter indeed from the necessity of justice, which occurs with moral motion and out of choice <note>Greek: *ἐκ τῆς προαιρέσεως* (ek tēs proaireseōs)</note>.

Rightly and most skillfully, therefore, Gregory I <note>Pope Gregory the Great, known for his writings on the spiritual life</note> said: Obedience is the only virtue that plants the other virtues in the mind and guards them once they are planted. Hence Christ repaired the crime of Adam’s disobedience by His own obedience even unto death <note>Greek: *μέχρι θανάτου* (mechri thanatou)</note>. The action of Martha was holy,

->**THE VISION AT BETHEL**<-

IF indeed that well-known maxim of the theologians is true—that nothing wonderful or performed with great ceremony and preparation was ever seen in the Old Economy <note>The "Old Economy" refers to the era of the Old Testament and the Mosaic Law</note> that did not foreshadow a notable mystery in the New Economy—then surely, if ever, that maxim holds its place in this remarkable vision. For what can appear more magnificent to men than a ladder set up from the earth to heaven, at whose base the great Patriarch <note>Jacob</note> sat, at whose summit Jehovah stood, and through whose steps the Angels moved by ascending and descending? And while this stood, an oracle was heard promising all most favorable things to Jacob and his seed. Did not all of paradise then descend from heaven to earth? Or did Jacob not see there all the delights of paradise? Therefore <note>The Latin catchword at the bottom of the page is *Idcirco* (Therefore)</note>, ecstatic and full of wonder, he exclaimed:

> How venerable is this place! This is nothing else but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.

Therefore, let us contemplate with the eyes of faith, and not merely as if in a dream, that mystical ladder of Jacob, and let us investigate the mysteries which it foreshadowed. But so that we may confine the history and its discussion within certain bounds, we shall propose only four points to be examined: I. *The appearance made to Jacob in a dream.* II. *The outward form of the vision.* III. *The oracle thundering from heaven.* IV. *Jacob’s wonder, his vow, and the words he spoke and deeds he performed.*

First, Moses noted that God appeared to Jacob in a dream. Appearances of God were frequent in the <term>Dispensation of the Old Law<note>The "Economy of the Old Law" refers to the way God managed His relationship with humanity and revealed His plan before the coming of Christ.</note></term>; for God appeared to Adam twice, before the fall and after the fall. He appeared to Noah twice, before the flood and after the flood; ten times to Abraham; he appeared to Isaac twice; to Jacob seven times; to Moses very often, and to others without number, as is clear from sacred history. But however much Scripture relates these appearances of God, it does not explain which person of the Trinity appeared to the fathers of the Old Testament—whether the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, although there is deep silence in both <term>instruments of the covenant<note>Referring to the Old and New Testaments.</note></term>, the ancient Doctors of the Church felt that the Son of God appeared. For they say that He was that "face of God" which <gloss>the letter "ę" representing "ae"</gloss> walked before His people Israel, sometimes under the form of a pillar of fire, and sometimes under the form of a pillar of cloud, of which Moses brings forth God speaking in Exodus 33:14: *My face shall go before you, that I may give you rest.* <note>original Latin: "Facies mea præcederet, vt quietem darem tibi." Most modern Bibles translate "Facies" here as "Presence."</note> And the ancient Doctors say that He also appeared to Moses in the burning bush (Exodus 3) and to Israel <note>meaning Jacob, who was renamed Israel</note> when he wrestled with Him—from which victory the name of "Israel" is derived. The most ancient of the fathers, such as **Tertullian** <note>An influential early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD).</note> among others, add that the Son, appearing to the ancients in human form, *gave a prelude to the future incarnation.*

From this it follows that the **Arian heretics** <note>Followers of Arius who argued that Jesus Christ was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father.</note> used to harass the Catholics with this argument: since the fathers who lived in the three centuries after Christ had unanimously taught that those very frequent appearances of God related in the Old Testament were not to be understood as the Father (who is invisible) but as the Son, the **Council of Sirmium** <note>A series of 4th-century councils that attempted to find a middle ground between Arianism and the Nicene Creed.</note>—gathered from the Bishops of the East against the errors of **Photinus** <note>A 4th-century bishop who taught that Jesus was a mere man and did not exist before his birth.</note>—decreed an anathema against those who said it was not the Son who was seen by Abraham, or who wrestled with Jacob—

...him, but the invisible God or the Father. From the authority of those [early] fathers, the **Arians** <note>Followers of Arius, who taught that Jesus Christ was a created being and therefore not equal to God the Father.</note> inferred that the Son was less than the Father, because he had been made visible and had performed the duty of a messenger to men on behalf of the Father for so many centuries. And so **Ambrose** <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 339–397 AD), a prominent Bishop of Milan and defender of Nicene Christianity.</note> says: *“This is the cause of error; this is the origin of the Arian heresy.”* <note>original: "haec est caufa erroris, haec origo haerefis Arij."</note> And **Blessed Augustine**, even though in his age the Arian heresy was only twitching in a half-dead state, intended to cut out the root of this pestilential heresy and drain the bilge-water of that Arian objection which breathed out the poison of the whole heresy. He believed this could be done in no better way than if he denied that those appearances made to the fathers were truly the Son of God, but were instead an **Angel**. Therefore, he was the first of all, with sails spread—with great daring and effort, and with a great weaving of the sharpest reasons—to depart from the opinion of the ancient fathers. In his books *On the Trinity*, he demonstrated that those appearances of the Old Testament should be attributed not to God, but to an Angel. This was perhaps the reason why he suppressed those books for so many years.

Nevertheless (let this be said with the leave of that highest Doctor), that Arian objection was not of such strength that it should have forced the illustrious Doctor to depart from the consensus and kinship of doctrine of the fathers of previous centuries, and—what is most important—from the authority of Scripture. In many places, Scripture cannot admit the interpretation that these appearances were of some *created* Angel, but rather of the *uncreated* Angel, who alone is **Michael the Archangel**, or the **Angel of the Covenant**. By granting that those appearances were not of a created Angel but of the Son of God, we must nevertheless deny the Arian conclusion: that he was lesser than the Father because he was made visible and served as the Father’s messenger. For those appearances of the Son of God were not of the Son insofar as he is simply the Son of the Father, having a single nature and being the same as the Father (in which way he is neither visible nor the Father's messenger); rather, they were insofar as he is the Mediator and <term>God-man<note>Original Greek: θεάνθρωπος (theanthropos). A theological term describing the union of divine and human natures in the person of Christ.</note></term>. For in this way he has two natures in a single person, and thus was made visible with respect to his human nature, and was the Father’s messenger according to his perso[n]—
