...for these are the works of the Mediator, which do not make the Son less than the Father in regard to his divinity, but only in regard to his humanity. For the **hypostatic union** <note>The theological doctrine that in the person of Jesus Christ, a divine nature and a human nature are united in one single person (hypostasis).</note> of these natures was achieved **without confusion** <note>original: "ἀσυγχύτως" (asynchytōs). This term was central to the Council of Chalcedon (451 AD) to explain that Christ's two natures remained distinct even when united.</note>, without any mixing of the two.

Nor does it help to say that the Son had not yet been incarnated at the time of the Fathers of the Old Testament when he appeared to them. For although he had not yet been revealed in the flesh and born of the Virgin, nevertheless, from the very beginning of the world, Christ was performing his **mediatorial office** <note>The role of acting as a bridge or go-between for God and humanity.</note>, and by the most wise **dispensation** <note>original: "oeconomia," referring to God's plan or management of the world.</note> of his Father, he was the legate and messenger. For as it is said in **Hebrews 13:8**: *Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.* And in **Revelation 13:8**: *He is the Lamb slain from the foundations of the world.* It is for this reason that, long ago (as previously reported from **Tertullian** <note>An early Christian author (c. 155–220 AD) from Carthage.</note>), he was giving "preludes" to his future incarnation. Therefore, as he is God, the Son is not less than the Father, but is **of the same substance** <note>original: "ὁμοούσιος" (homoousios). The keyword of the Nicene Creed asserting the Son's equality with the Father.</note> with the Father; and as he is the Son **hypostatically** <note>original: "ὑποστατικῶς" (hypostatikōs); that is, in his distinct personhood.</note>, he is also not less than the Father, because the divine **processions** <note>The theological concept of how the Son and Spirit originate eternally from the Father.</note> and the order of existence do not imply any "greater" or "lesser" status. Rather, the Son, as he is the Mediator between God and men, was the messenger of the Father by divine arrangement; for it pleased the Son to humble himself, and *though he was **in the form of God** <note>original: "ἐν μορφῇ τοῦ Θεοῦ" (en morphē tou Theou).</note>, he did not think equality with God something to be grasped; but he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.* (**Philippians 2:6–7**). Therefore, there will be no inconsistency in what is said if we claim that the Son also appeared to Jacob in this vision, and was the one who spoke to him.

Those appearances were frequent in the time of the Patriarchs in those early days of the Church, because God had not yet instituted the **Levitical priesthood** <note>The formal religious system and hereditary priesthood of ancient Israel described in the book of Leviticus.</note>, nor any ordinary or extraordinary ministry. Therefore, he wished to instruct the people himself—or at least his principal servants, such as the Patriarchs. He deigned to establish a **covenant** <note>original: "foedus," a formal, binding agreement between God and his people.</note> with them and their descendants, which it was necessary to present in person. Thus he first appeared to **Adam** as the head of the entire human race, to establish a covenant with him and his posterity: before the Fall, the **natural covenant**; after the Fall, the **Gospel covenant**, though more obscurely, in **Genesis 3**: *The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent.* Afterward, he appeared to **Noah**:

...after the flood, so that He might strike another covenant, though this one was general and made with all living creatures, promising never again to send a universal flood. Next, He appeared to Abraham and the Patriarchs to establish a more splendid, special covenant with them and their descendants, and to renew it often, repeating its beautiful and magnificent promises. But above all, He appeared to Moses to enter into a **legal covenant** <note>The covenant of the Law given at Mount Sinai.</note> with him and the entire Israelite people, so that the Law might be proclaimed and so that Moses might receive from the hand of God the tablets of the law, carved by God’s own finger. 

Because Moses was the **Mediator** <term>A go-between or representative; in this context, someone who bridges the gap between God and the people.</term> of the Law and a symbolic Redeemer, the appearances of God became rarer from that time onward, except occasionally to the Prophets, whom He sent to kings and noblemen whenever the needs of the Church required it. Yet the greatest and most illustrious of all appearances was that of the Son of God, when the fullness of time arrived. This is the appearance Paul boasts of in **Hebrews 1:1**. There was also the appearance of the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost, in the sign of tongues of fire, as recorded in **Acts 2:1-2**.

However, just as these appearances were frequent, they were also very diverse, as Paul indicated in clear words. In **Hebrews 1:1**, he says: *God spoke of old to the fathers at many times and in many ways* <note>original Greek: "πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως" (polymeros kai polytropos), meaning "in many portions and in many manners."</note>. These words signify not only multiple appearances but also those of different kinds and varied natures. 

For sometimes God appeared in the symbol of the **pillar of cloud and fire**; sometimes **in the bush**; sometimes **in smoke**; and sometimes **in flame and earthquake and the wind of Elijah** accompanied by a voice. At other times, the Prophets saw **thrones cast down, books opened, the form of judgment, myriads of Angels, and the empires of the world**, as seen in **Daniel 7, 10, and 11**. Likewise, Zechariah saw **variegated horses, horns, a measuring line, a golden lampstand, a flying scroll twenty cubits long and ten cubits wide, four chariots, and mountains of bronze** <note>original: "montes chalybei," literally "mountains of steel or hard iron," referring to the "mountains of brass" in Zechariah 6:1.</note>, and so on. 

All these manifestations are reduced to a single category: visions. This is why the Prophets are called "seers," or those who understand visions, or "those with open eyes," or "dreamers of dreams." These visions were of two types regarding the people experiencing them: they occurred either to those who were awake or to those who were sleeping and dreaming. Regarding waking visions, they happened in two ways: either through external signs presented to the senses of men from the outside, to signify something...

<page-num>303</page-num>

...what God intended in the vision, just as the burning bush seen by Moses in Exodus 3 was an external sign signifying the affliction of the Jewish Church in Egypt, when it was burned but not consumed. Or revelation occurs through *internal signs* impressed from within; and this happens in two ways: either through *sensible forms* <note>original: "species sensibiles"; mental images that correspond to the five senses</note> newly produced in the imagination, or arranged in a certain way and directed and ordered toward a certain end; or also through *intelligible forms*, by immediately affecting and moving the intellect above the sphere of its own natural activity. In this way, men understand in an extraordinary manner those things which they could never achieve by themselves through their own power of thought. Thus, the intellectual power is raised to such a high level of understanding, not by its own reasoning, but through revelation and celestial influence. For how could the Prophets, such as Isaiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and others, and John the Theologian have known so many mysteries and prophecies, which are related in the Prophetic books and in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>, unless God had revealed these things to them?

It must be observed, however, that those revelations varied according to the different **Dispensations** <term>Oeconomias; the historical stages or "households" of God's plan, such as the era of the Old Testament Law versus the New Testament Gospel.</term> of the Old and New Testaments; not only regarding the physical movements of those to whom the revelations were made, but also regarding their degrees. First, regarding physical movements: sometimes there were no external movements or changes in the body, especially in the Dispensation of the New Testament. For the inspirations of the Apostles were more sedate and tranquil than those of the Prophets. In that Dispensation, characterized by the Spirit of adoption, all things were composed toward peace and a calm state. On the other hand, in the other Dispensation—in which the spirit of servitude reigned—all things were arranged for fear and terror, which were fitting for the ministry of the Law.

Sometimes, however, in both the first and second Dispensations, physical changes or agitations occurred in the body. But sometimes these were slight, as when Elisha orders a musician <note>original: "Psaltem"; a harpist</note> to be summoned to calm him. Thus, very often the bodies of the Prophets were affected and shaken by a kind of trembling, and they broke out into less composed gestures, so that they were sometimes seen as if driven by madness; this is why the Greek word for diviners <note>original Greek: μάντεις (*manteis*)</note> comes from the word for "to be mad" <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ μαίνεσθαι (*apo tou mainesthai*)</note>. And as is clear from Numbers 24, they were prostrated on the ground; hence it is that there Balaam calls himself *the man falling down with his eyes open*.

# ANTOINE CREGUT

<page-num>504</page-num>

...those movements were also highly agitated; and for that reason they were called by the specific name of "ecstatic." This is because through those movements, the mind was so elevated that the soul was snatched outside of itself. In this way, a certain stupor remained in the body—a "deep sleep" <term>tardemah; the Hebrew word תרדמה used in the Bible for a divinely induced trance or deep sleep</term>—in which the person seemed to suffer a lapse of consciousness. This led to a temporary suspension of the soul's powers, specifically the sensory and motor functions.

Thus, ecstasy stood in relation to the contemplative and intellectual faculty just as the heroic virtues of the ancient heroes stood in relation to the practical part of the will; these virtues elevate the soul so far above the senses that, disregarding all danger, they nobly undertake and most powerfully overcome any difficult task. To this, certainly, we can refer the "snatching away" <term>raptus; a mystical transport or rapture</term> of Paul into the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12). This experience so elevated his soul from his body, and its abstraction from the senses was so great, that he did not know whether he had been snatched away "in the body or out of the body."

However, I do not agree with the Scholastic philosophers <note>The medieval university theologians, such as Thomas Aquinas, who often debated the physical limits of mystical states</note> that this abstraction and rapture of the ecstatic soul was so total that the body remained motionless without breathing. For that rapture occurred within the *superior part* of the soul, at the very "peak of the mind" <note>original: "mentis apicem"; a technical term for the highest, most spiritual part of the human intellect</note>, which is by its nature abstracted from matter and the senses. It did not, however, affect the *inferior part* of the soul, and much less the vegetative and sensory faculties. Therefore, only the rational life—that is, the specific and physical process of understanding—was suspended, but not the vegetative or animal life <note>The basic biological functions like breathing and heartbeat</note>.

This is how we should understand the wisest of Rabbis, Maimonides, in his *Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: "More Neuoch." or *Moreh Nevukhim*, a foundational work of Jewish philosophy</note>, Part 2, Chapter 46:

> Many things happen to the Prophets during a prophetic vision. Thus, what is said in Hosea 1—"Go, take for yourself a wife of harlotry and children of harlotry"—is not to be understood as a physical act perceived by the senses, but as something occurring within the prophetic vision. The same applies to what Jeremiah 13:4 says regarding the loincloth: "Take the loincloth that you bought, which is on your waist; and arise, go to the Euphrates, and hide it there in a hole in the rock," and so on.

Thus far, Maimonides.

But just as revelations varied in their physical movements, they also varied in their degrees; for God first manifested himself more obscurely to the Patriarchs, then more clearly, and finally, under the New Dispensation <term>Oeconomia; the historical era of the Gospel</term>, the veil was entirely removed. Paul indicates this especially in:

<margin>Hebrews 1</margin> ...through the phrase "in many ways" <note>original Greek: *polytropos*; referring to Hebrews 1:1, "God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets"</note>, from which even the ancient teachers of the Hebrews counted up to sixty types or categories, all of which were grouped under the title of Prophecy. Regarding this, the same Rabbi Moses the Egyptian—commonly known as Maimonides, or simply by the name **Rambam** <note>An acronym for his name, Rabbi Moses ben Maimon (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher</note>—wrote in *The Guide for the Perplexed, Part 2, Chapter 36*: *Prophecy and dreaming do not differ in kind, but in degree—that is, in abundance or scarcity; hence (he says) there is a common saying of our wise men: dreaming is one of sixty parts (or types) of Prophecy.* And in *Genesis Rabbah* <note>An ancient collection of Jewish homiletic interpretations of the Book of Genesis</note>, when it is said that *the unripe fruit of Prophecy is dreaming*, it is a most fitting comparison. For just as an unripe fruit—or a fruit that has fallen—is still a fruit in its own right and individual nature, except that it fell before its perfection and maturity; so too the imaginative faculty is the same during sleep as it is in a time of Prophecy, except that it is still imperfect and has not yet achieved its full completion. In the same place, this Rabbi, along with his fellow Rabbis, adds regarding dreaming:

> *The Rabbis say that Prophecy does not exist in times of persecution, but in the time of the Messiah (may he be revealed soon!) Prophecy is destined to return to us again, as God promised.*

He put these things forward according to the mind and faith of the Jewish people.

And these revelations occurred to those who were awake in these various ways and degrees; as for those who were sleeping, God also manifested Himself to them in many ways <note>original Greek: *polytropos*</note> through various appearances, both internal and external. These were so powerfully impressed upon them that the sleepers perceived things that those who were awake might have perceived if they had gazed upon objects with focused eyes. To this we can refer the vision of Jacob, who saw that marvelous ladder while dreaming. As for why God spoke most often at night and to those sleeping—since that communication was more obscure and seemingly less fitting for God, or less useful to the one receiving the revelation—there are various weighty reasons. This is aside from that highest reason taken from the will of God, which is the "cause of all causes." But because these matters are fully and learnedly treated by Spanheim <note>Friedrich Spanheim (1600–1649), a significant Calvinist theologian and professor</note> in his *Evangelical Doubts, Volume 2, Doubt 56*, we shall purposefully omit them here.

Now, Hebrew interpreters observe here that there are three types of dreams. 1. *Natural dreams*, which arise from natural causes and are either meaningless <note>original Greek: *asemanta*</note> or, if they are significant <note>original Greek: *semantika*</note>, represent nothing more than natural things

significant. <term>Indicative signs</term> <note>original Greek: *Sēmanta*</note> often arise from accidental causes—for instance, from things seen during the day which then occupy the imagination at night. Regarding these, the poet says:

> Rash dreams play in the deceptive night,
> And bid trembling minds to fear false things.

Hence the saying of the Son of Sirach: *Dreams give wings to fools* <note>A reference to the deuterocanonical Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 34:1, which warns against trusting in vain dreams</note>. <term>Signifying dreams</term> <note>original Greek: *Sēmantika*</note>, however, truly signify something if they depend on the humors predominating in a person, or upon their temperament. For this reason, physicians sometimes order that dreams be observed; there are notable examples of this in the works of Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire (c. 129–216 AD) whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> and other doctors. II. Dreams are *divine* and *superphysical* when a deep sleep is sent by God, and through these dreams, God reveals hidden things. This happened to Adam, who, upon waking, prophesied, saying: *This is flesh of my flesh*, and for this reason, she shall be called <term>Woman</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Ishah*</note>. III. **Mixed** dreams occur when the sleep is purely natural and arises from natural causes, but God uses it to reveal hidden things, such as the dreams experienced by the Prophets; Jacob’s dream of the ladder was of this kind. The poets Homer and Virgil tell many fables here; for they imagined two gates of dreams, one of **Horn** and the other of **Ivory**. The gate of *Horn* relates to true things, while the *Ivory* gate relates to the false. They say that the greater part of dreams pass through the ivory rather than through the horn. There are also turbulent dreams, which is why the followers of Pythagoras in ancient times did not dare to eat beans, because they stirred up all sorts of turbulence in the mind.

But while these three types of dreams can be truly established, the "itch" of human curiosity has often run wild in this area. This is why all dreams were once superstitiously observed, and various predictions were made based on the wordplay of names. For example, when Alexander the Great was besieging Tyre and despairing of its capture, he dreamed that he saw a satyr dancing on his shield. When he asked what this might mean, a courtier replied flatteringly, <term>Tyre is yours</term> <note>original Greek: *Sa Tyros*, a pun on the word for satyr, *Satyros*</note>. Upon hearing this, Alexander attacked the city with all his might and captured it. Likewise, when the Emperor Constantius was about to fight against his enemies, he dreamed that he would enter the city of Thessalonica; but someone ominously interpreted this based on the outcome as <term>Give the victory to another</term> <note>original Greek: *Thes allō nikēn*, a pun on the name *Thessalonikēn*</note>. The ambiguity of a demon and Serapis <note>Serapis was a Greco-Egyptian deity often associated with healing and oracular dreams</note> concerning a creditor and children occurred when the Greek word *tōkō* <note>original Greek: τóκῳ</note> was used, which signifies both "usury" (or interest on a loan) and "birth" or "offspring." There are countless other examples of this kind which have nothing in common with Jacob’s dream, and so we omit them here of our own accord.

Whether dreams are good or bad, or even <term>neutral</term> <note>original Greek: ἐν μέσῳ κείμενα (*en mesō keimena*), literally "lying in the middle"</note>, is a matter on which not everyone holds the same opinion. Truly, among the Hebrews, Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Jewish historian whose works were widely read by later Christian scholars</note> believed that no dreams are bad, since he even maintained that the wicked thoughts themselves to which men give consent are not sins, unless an outward action follows. Therefore, he mocks Polybius <note>A Greek historian of the 2nd century BC</note> for writing that Antiochus was chastised and punished by God merely because he had resolved in his mind to plunder the Temple of Jerusalem and reduce it to ruins or ashes. But James judged far more correctly in his epistle, chapter 1, when he judges not only <term>conceiving</term> <note>original Greek: τὸ συλλαμβάνειν (*to syllambanein*)</note> and <term>bringing forth</term> <note>original Greek: τὸ τίκτειν (*to tiktein*)</note> to be sin, but also <term>being lured</term> <note>original Greek: τὸ δελεάζειν (*to deleazein*)</note> and <term>being drawn away</term> <note>original Greek: τὸ ἐξέλκεσθαι (*to exelkesthai*)</note>. Therefore, since there are many dreams which arise from lustful desires and which produce wicked thoughts, we shall not deny that they are also wicked, because they are inclinations of the flesh which cannot be restrained even by the understanding and will of those who are awake. Hence, Epiphanius <note>Saint Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403 AD), a prominent bishop known for his defense of orthodoxy</note> says in Book 2 *Against Heresies*, chapter 4: *It is not in my power to keep from thinking absurd things.* And Gregory the Great <note>Pope Gregory I (c. 540–604 AD), an influential theologian of the early Middle Ages</note> in Book 4 of his *Moralia*, chapter 28, said: *A dream is the thought of those sleeping, and a thought is the dream of those waking.* These things should be understood as referring to physical or natural dreams; for as for divine dreams, they are always good and for a good end. To these also can be referred the dream of the Blessed Anthony <note>Saint Anthony the Great (c. 251–356 AD), an early Christian monk and Desert Father</note>, who lived in the year 368 <note>Historical sources usually date his death to 356 AD; Cregut may be following a different chronological tradition</note> and shortly before his death, when he had already lived one hundred and five years, dreamed that he saw pigs which were destroying the sacred altars with their feet. Upon waking from sleep, he interpreted this as referring to churchmen who would one day devastate the Church with fornications, adulteries, and other pollutions. Philip Melanchthon <note>A German Reformer and close associate of Martin Luther (1497–1560)</note> mentions this prophecy and indicated that it denounced the fornications and lustful lives of priests and monks.

Let these things be said, just as they were regarding various appearances and revelations; there follows next the specific type of vision produced in that dream, which was a ladder set up from the earth to heaven. Revelations from God are primarily signified by *visions and dreams*, because these two modes were the most common and customary. Numbers 12:6: *If there is a Prophet among you, I, Jehovah, make myself known to him through a vision, or I speak to him through a dream.* <note>original Latin: "Si est Propheta ex vobis per visionem meipsum Iehouam notum facio ei, aut per somnium alloquor eum."</note> The same is taught in Job 33:15, Jeremiah 23:15, and elsewhere. Hence, in Joel 2:28 and Acts 2:17, a clearer revelation of mysteries is signified through *visions and dreams*, which was to be communicated to believers under the <term>Economy of the New Testament</term> <note>A theological term referring to God's management or "arrangement" of the world and the church during the Christian era</note>, especially to the Apostles themselves. *And it shall be in the last days (says God), I will pour out from my Spirit upon all flesh: and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy: and your young men shall see visions, and your elders shall dream dreams.* <note>original Latin: "Et erit vltimis temporibus (dicit Deus) effundam ex Spiritu meo in quamuis carnem: & prophetabunt filij vestri & filiæ vestræ, & iuuenes vestri visiones videbunt, & seniores somnia somniabunt."</note> This is why Jerusalem and Judea are called the *valley of vision* in Isaiah 22:1, because God delivered oracles there and manifested himself, and because Jerusalem was the assembly of Prophets, who were called "seers of God" and those "understanding the vision of God." There are, moreover, innumerable examples of visions in both the Old and New Testaments. Thus, the Book of Revelation <note>original Latin: "Apocalypseos"</note> is named after the revelations and visions of John, just as in 2 Chronicles 9:29, the book concerning the deeds of King Solomon written by the Prophet Iddo is called the *vision of Iddo*.

But indeed, if the visions of the Prophets were notable—because God never manifested himself in an extraordinary way without also intending an extraordinary purpose—then surely among the rest of the visions, that of Jacob will also be wonderful, and without a doubt, it will signify something notable. For who would believe that God wished to appear here with his Angels, and to show a ladder of such height, or to deliver a magnificent oracle, if all these things did not signify something most worthy of commemoration? Theologians therefore ask, and not without cause, what extraordinary and memorable thing was foreshadowed by this wondrous ladder? The ancient Hebrews wish to see here a sign of God's special providence for the protection and blessing of Jacob; and in truth, that sense contains nothing foreign to the vision—rather, it seems appropriate to Jacob’s circumstances and his journey—

...coming. For when that good Patriarch <note>Jacob</note> left his father's house and the embraces of his parents to flee the fury of his brother—who breathed nothing but threats and death—and set out for distant regions and unknown men, no hope remained except that placed in God and His providence. Therefore, so that this pious man might be most firmly supported by this prop, that ladder was seen, like a most stable column upon which he might lean. Lest he think God was far away, since he himself was a wanderer on earth while God dwelt in the heavens where there is **the unapproachable light** <note>original Greek: $\tau\text{ò } \phi\alpha\tilde{\omega}\varsigma\ \dot{\alpha}\pi\rho\text{ó}\sigma\iota\text{ov}$ (to phōs aprositon); a reference to 1 Timothy 6:16</note>, there was set before his eyes the interaction of God with men through the ministry of Angels, who continually ascend and descend; indeed, they encamp around those who fear Jehovah.

Although that work of providence is general and regards the whole of nature—which, once created by God, is preserved and governed—nevertheless, it is easy to observe a Special Providence, by which God deigns to preserve His elect above all, like the apple of His eye and **a chosen people** <note>original Greek: $\tau\text{ò}\nu\ \lambda\alpha\text{ó}\nu\ \pi\varepsilon\rho\iota\text{o}\acute{\upsilon}\sigma\iota\text{o}\nu$ (ton laon periousion); a phrase used in the Septuagint and New Testament to describe God's special treasure or "peculiar people"</note>, as was demonstrated by us at length and in full in the treatise on providence. It is for this reason that many remarkable things are recorded by Moses in this vision. Mention is made of God, Angels, man, the heavens, and the ladder; of God standing above the ladder; of man lying beneath the ladder; of Angels ascending and descending the ladder; of the heavens, so that the height and summit of the ladder might be measured; mention is also made of the earth, so that the length and depth of the ladder might be known. Furthermore, God leans upon the ladder because He governs and moderates the changes of the world by a stable and constant order of things, and by a perpetual or everlasting duration. Jacob measures the base of the ladder at its <term>podismo</term> <note>From the Greek *podismos*, referring to the measurement of the base or the "footing" of a structure; here it implies Jacob is positioned at the very foundation of the divine structure</note> and lies there, to signify that the faithful are covered under the shadow of the wings of God's providence, and depend trustfully upon it against all accidents and whatever distresses, wants, and anxieties of affairs. The Angels move along the ladder because in the work of providence God does not act without means as He does in miracles, but uses various means and secondary causes; yet He flows in with them as the primary cause. Indeed, not to use the means ordained by God is to tempt God and, as much as lies within us, to disturb the order of providence. But among so many means...

Mention is made of the Angels here above all for several reasons: first, because they are the most noble of intermediaries; second, because they are most powerful against all the attacks of the world; third, because they are most swift, so that they may promptly bring help to those in labor—which is why they are depicted with wings. Furthermore, if earthly means should fail, God provides from the heavens, showing that in the work of providence, no less than in miracles, He may display something extraordinary—namely, the assistance of Angels to those who are not familiar with them. This fact has been proven quite often, as in the examples of Daniel in the lions' den, the three Hebrews in the furnace, Peter in prison, and others. And in Psalm 91:11:
> *For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways.* <note>original Latin: "Nam Angelis suis præcipiet de te ut conseruent te in omnibus viis tuis."</note>
And in Hebrews 1, they are called <term>ministering spirits</term> <note>original Greek: πνεύματα λειτουργικὰ (pneumata leitourgika); spirits who serve or perform a public office</note>. Furthermore, this mention is made because no human was capable of this kind of commerce—to be able to travel from earth to heaven, nor to ascend or descend by a ladder. For this was so ordained by God in nature: that men, like Jacob, lie beneath the ladder, while the Angels ascend and descend because they must execute God's commands.

Additionally, God wished to show the very close connection of all things in nature, both celestial and sub-celestial <note>The "sub-celestial" or "sublunary" world refers to the Earth and its atmosphere, which ancient science believed was subject to change and decay, unlike the eternal heavens.</note>, because God created all things in number, weight, and measure. Therefore, all species of nature are joined not by chance, but harmoniously like a mathematical sequence, which was foreshadowed by the rungs of the ladder. Homer does not differ much from these ideas when he depicts his Jupiter holding a chain in his hand, with which he grasped all created things, connected and bound together <note>A reference to the "Golden Chain of Being," a concept from the Iliad often used by later theologians to describe the hierarchy and interconnectedness of the universe.</note>. Finally, mention is made of Angels because in the work of providence, those three—God, the Angels, and the heavens—are like universal causes that flow into the production and preservation of things. God is the absolutely primary cause, which flows into all effects and acts immediately by both forms of immediacy: namely, of virtue and of person <note>original Latin: "virtutis & suppositi." A scholastic distinction meaning God is present both through His power (virtue) and His actual being (supposit) in every action in the universe.</note>. The heaven is also universal in its causing, because by its influences it moves and variously alters all sublunary things; but the Angels stir both the elements and mixtures, both the celestial and the sub-celestial, at their own nod—yet always by God's permission and command. For this reason, no mention is made in this vision of other creatures, which are governed by providence rather than governing it; rather, they are merely foreshadowed in the image of the ladder—

For the measurement of that wonderful ladder measures the whole of nature, which reaches from the earth to the heavens, but it does not pass into <term>imaginary spaces</term> <note>Scholastic philosophers used this term to describe the infinite void they believed existed beyond the boundaries of the physical universe.</note>, because (as Moses says) God leans upon the ladder. Indeed, there is nothing above nature except God who fills all things—not those imaginary spaces, which are nothing real. Therefore, not even the highest tip of the ladder could reach there, but only to God. For just as all nature comes from God, the **Being of Beings** <note>original Latin: *Ente Entium*</note>, so it ends in God; because He is the **Alpha and Omega** <note>The first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, symbolizing the total span of existence.</note>, the beginning and the end.

Furthermore, everything we have said about this vision can be very fittingly illustrated by that vision of Ezekiel, found in Ezekiel chapter 1. For there, mention is made of wheels, living creatures, and the most vivid color of God from the midst of the fire. For the Hebrew word which has troubled many interpreters, namely **chaschmal** <note>original Hebrew: חשמל (*ḥašmal*); often translated in Bibles as "amber" or "glowing metal."</note>, signifies a **glowing coal** that is highly ignited, and thus most burning; it is as if it were **chash mal** <note>original Hebrew: חש מל</note>, that is, *quickly or hastily cutting off and consuming.* But what are those wheels other than the celestial orbs or spheres, which are turned around in perpetual motion? What are those four living creatures, depicted by their faces, wings, and movement, other than the **Angels**, who move at God's command? What is the *Chaschmal* but a symbol of the presence of the divinity? From this, the sense of that chapter and the goal of the vision is to reveal to the Prophet the singular works of providence through the obedience of the Angels, their administration of the whole world through the Spirit of God, and the glory and authority of Christ over the Angels and all created things, for the fulfillment of His will.

Those who believe Jacob was comforted here by this vision of God's providence add further that the Moderator of the world appeared like a most magnificent king. Such a king desires to know everything that happens in his kingdom, and therefore employs various ministers who run back and forth so that, being aware of all things, they may report to the king, and then immediately execute his commands, perpetually ascending and descending. And here the saying of Jacob in verse 17 fits perfectly:

> There is nothing here but the house of God and the gate of heaven; for by this the family of God goes out and enters.

[The vision of] ascent and descent revealed to the Patriarch that God governs the growth and decline of empires, or the states and cycles of the **four Monarchies** <note>A traditional interpretation of the Book of Daniel, referring to the four successive world empires: Babylon, Persia, Greece, and Rome.</note>. Indeed, whatever joyful and pleasant things we encounter in providence and in prayer, they are all founded in the **Mediator** <note>A theological title for Jesus Christ, acting as the bridge between God and humanity.</note>, without whom it would happen that we could obtain nothing for our salvation.

What, then, does the vision of the ladder represent to us concerning the Messiah? In truth, his manifestation in the flesh was clearly foreshadowed by that shadowy vision. For here the entire mystery of Christ is pre-signified: here his person is seen in the vision; here his natures, status, and office are shown as if **in a figure** <note>original Greek: *ἐν τύπῳ* (en typō)</note>. First, Christ and his person are signified by the ladder; Christ himself explains this in John 1, the last verse: *After this you shall see the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.* Second, his dual nature is seen in this ladder. For the top of the ladder, which touches heaven, signifies his divine nature; however, the foot of the ladder denotes his human nature. Hence it is said of the person of Christ in the concrete that he was in heaven even though he was on earth; for in respect to his human nature he was on earth with Nicodemus, but in respect to his divine nature he was in heaven. John 3:13: *No one has ascended into heaven, except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.*

God leans upon this ladder, because Christ is truly *Immanuel*, that is, *God with us* <note>original Latin: *Deus nobiscum*</note>; for the Divine nature is united with the human nature. And as it is said in John 1, *Christ is in the bosom of the Father*. The *Office* of Christ is also shadowed forth in this mystical ladder. For just as a ladder joins two extremes that are very far apart from one another—namely, heaven and earth—so Christ our Mediator unites God with men, the Creator with the creature. These were previously two extremes so separated by sin that they were removed by infinite parasangs <note>A *parasang* is an ancient Persian unit of distance, roughly equivalent to 3.5 miles; here used metaphorically to describe an immeasurable gap.</note>; nor could they ever be joined except through that Mediator, Christ. Christ, therefore, opened heaven to us, and through him access and entry to the heavenly sanctuary is made. Hence, in John 10, he is called the *door of the sheep*. And in John 14, he is called the *Way by which one goes to the Father*. And he himself first ascended so that he might prepare a place for us, and at his birth, Angels were seen descending and proclaiming that peace had been made between God and men.

Furthermore, a twofold state of Christ is shadowed forth in this ladder: namely, the state of exaltation and the state of humiliation. For in that ladder there were higher rungs which reached closest to heaven, and lower rungs which were less distant from the earth. These lower rungs figured the stages of Christ’s <term>emptying</term> <note>original Latin: *exinanitionis*, referring to the concept of *kenosis* or Christ "emptying himself" of his divine glory to become human.</note>—namely, his conception, birth, passion, death, and burial. Those higher rungs, however, were stages of his exaltation, specifically his resurrection, ascension, and his sitting at the right hand of the Father. Truly, all those things were obscure in the Old Testament, seen only in vision and sleep; but in the New Testament they have been clearly displayed. Thus today, we do not merely believe in future things, but we learn of the deeds and past events of Christ as they now appear splendidly in both Covenants, like the Sun at midday. For as Paul testifies in Hebrews 13:8, *Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever*. And in chapter 9:8 of the same epistle: *The Holy Spirit indicating this, that the way into the sanctuary was not yet made manifest while the earlier tabernacle was still standing.*

Moses notes, moreover, that Angels appeared on that ladder ascending and descending. The naming of "Angels" is attributed to many in the Scripture, either properly or improperly. Properly to those...

<page-num>515</page-num>

is attributed to those spiritual substances that stand perpetually before the throne of God; it is said <term>improperly</term> <note>In 17th-century logic, "improperly" means figuratively or metaphorically, rather than literally.</note> of the pastors of the Church and, in general, of the faithful. First, the vision can be rightly understood as referring to **Angels** properly so-called, since they ascended and descended through the stages of Christ’s humiliation and exaltation; for they were the heralds of his conception and birth, and thereafter they ministered to him during his temptation. In his agony or passion, they descend to comfort Christ; in his resurrection and ascension, they also perform their duty toward the faithful.

However, if the vision is considered accurately, it seems better understood as referring to Angels improperly so-called [metaphorical angels]. For first, it is said in the text of Moses that those angels were to *ascend* before they *descended*, which hardly seems to fit Angels properly so-called <note>The author argues that literal angels, already being in heaven, would usually be described as descending first.</note>; second, Angels are not properly "citizens" of the Church, and *Christ did not take on the nature of angels, but the seed of Abraham*, as stated in Hebrews 2:16. Therefore, they are participants neither in the person of the Mediator, nor in his offices, nor his benefits. 

Yet, if we establish that Angels properly so-called are signified here, let it be weighed in this sense: that the Son of God is also the Mediator for Angels—not indeed a Mediator of <term>redemption</term> <note>original Greek: *apolytrōseōs*</note>, but of <term>recapitulation</term> <note>original Greek: *anakephalaiōseōs*; the act of bringing all things together under one "head" or focal point.</note>. For Christ is that foundational <term>firmamental medium</term> <note>original Greek: *stereōmatikon*; describing a structural or solid intermediary that holds things in place.</note> by which all creatures are inseparably united with the Creator—not only because the creature is infinitely distant from the Creator, but also because the creature is prone to failing unless it is confirmed in grace. Therefore, in a twofold sense, Christ is also the Mediator of the Angels:

1. **In nature**, because he joined two infinitely distant extremes: the Creator and the creature. 
2. **In grace**, because since the good Angels could have fallen just as the evil ones did, they were confirmed in grace so that they would not fall. In this sense, Scripture says the Angels were "chosen," and in Ephesians 1 they are said to be "gathered together" in Christ the head. 

In this sense, therefore, the mystical ladder pertains to the Angels. However, "Angels" improperly so-called can also be understood as ascending and descending via this ladder of Jacob, namely the **Pastors** or **Teachers** of the Church. For in Malachi 3 and frequently in Revelation 1, they are called "Angels" <note>In the Book of Revelation, the "angels of the seven churches" are traditionally interpreted as the bishops or leaders of those congregations.</note>. And just as the title applies to them, so the vision can rightly fit them. For the true Teachers of the Church, not only as believers but also in their capacity as Pastors and Teachers, must perpetually [ascend and descend] through that ladder.

We are easily able to achieve this with that Master teaching us, of whom it is said in John 3: *No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.* <note>John 3:13.</note> In that passage, the phrase *to ascend into heaven* is to be understood metaphorically: that is, to grasp the heavenly doctrine which Christ, having come forth from the bosom of the Father, revealed to us. Likewise, in **John 12:28**, when Christ said, *Father, glorify your Son,* a voice was heard responding from heaven, *I have both glorified it and will glorify it again.*

These supports were represented to Jacob by the voice of God and the symbols—namely, the **Word of God and the sacraments.** Therefore, no one can ascend or descend through that mystical ladder unless they lean firmly on these two side supports: the Word of God on the right, and the sacraments on the left. This refers to Joshua 7, where lots were cast to identify Achan as the one who had stolen forbidden items from Jericho.</note>, which we will discuss in its proper place; or in the **distribution of inheritances**, examples of which are found throughout the Book of Joshua; or in **Election**, as in Acts 1:26, when Matthias was chosen by lot to replace Judas.

<meta>This page continues Antoine Crégut’s commentary on the vision of Jacob’s Ladder (Genesis 28). Having previously categorized visions as "mute" (symbol only), he now moves to the third category: "mixed" visions, where both sight and sound cooperate to reveal divine truth.</meta>

## ANTOINE CRÉGUT

Finally, there are others that are *mixed*, which consist of both: namely, a symbol shown to the eyes and a voice striking the ears. Such were the angelic appearances, and such is the vision Jacob now receives; for in addition to the ladder, a heavenly voice of God is heard. Indeed, it usually happens this way; for these kinds of mute visions would be cold and, as it were, dead, unless the Word of God, like a soul, gave them life. Therefore, just as the **Sacraments** <note>In Reformed theology, Sacraments (like Baptism and Communion) are "visible words" that require the preaching of the Gospel to be understood.</note> are signs and attachments to the Word of God, and the Word is like the soul that gives them life and explains their meaning—as if the voice itself were thundering from heaven—so something similar occurs in this vision and in other mixed visions. To this point, that well-known saying of the ancient fathers can be applied: *Add the word to the element and it becomes a sacrament.* <note>Original Latin: "Adde elemento verbum & fiet sacramentum." This is a famous quote from St. Augustine, emphasizing that a physical ritual only becomes a holy sacrament when joined with the divine Word.</note> For this reason, the sacraments of the Papal party <note>Original Latin: "Pontificiorum," referring to the Roman Catholic Church.</note> are lifeless, for they put forward bare symbols without the Word of God.

And these things are clearly evident if we apply the present oracle to the symbol seen. For since we have said that the ladder signified God's **providence**, which specifically keeps watch for His servants, this heard oracle now explains that sign. For what does this mean: *I will be the God of Abraham, of Isaac, etc.*? Do not the many promises made to Jacob wonderfully illuminate the whole vision? What does this mean in verse 15: *And behold, I am with you and will keep you wherever you go, etc.*? Does not the miraculous providence of God shine forth? And truly, so many and such great promises manifest what we are saying in abundance, both by the event itself and by their fulfillment.

Furthermore, if by that **mystical ladder** we understand what we brought up above regarding the opinion of the Hebrews—that it signified the prayers of the faithful and the temple of prayer, or **Bethel** <note>Hebrew: "House of God."</note>—that will also harmonize with the oracle. For what is this: *In you all the families of the earth shall be blessed, and in your seed?* (verse 14). And that: *This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven* (verse 17). Does not the oracle promise the hearing of the prayers of Jacob and the faithful, and the subsequent flow of divine blessings? And did not the holy Patriarch firmly believe it? Both because he said, *this is none other than the house of God, etc.* and because he made this vow, saying: *If God will be with me and keep me, etc.* (verse 20).

But indeed, the final exposition encompasses all the others...

And what is most significant, it adds a mystical depth—namely, that this mystical ladder foreshadows **Christ the Mediator**, both in his person and his natures, as well as in his statuses, offices, and benefits. For in truth, God neither preserves nor governs his people through special providence, nor does he hear their prayers, except through Christ the Mediator, who reveals himself kindly and graciously in the ladder. The divine oracle in verses 13, 14, and 15 also explains this explicitly. 

For first, God calls himself **Yahweh** <note>The Hebrew Tetragrammaton יהוה. Crégut follows the common Reformation-era view that this name signifies God as the fulfiller of promises.</note>, by which name he signifies the truth of the promises to be fulfilled in Christ. Then he calls himself the God of Abraham and the other Patriarchs, because a special covenant was sanctioned with them; yet Christ is the foundation and fulfillment of the entire covenant. Thirdly, he adds: *in your seed all the families of the earth shall be blessed*; which is to be understood mystically of Christ, the blessed seed, who is so often called the "Son of Abraham" and "of David" in Scripture. As seen in Romans 1: *descended from the seed of David according to the flesh* <note>Original Greek: ἐκ σπέρματος Δαβὶδ κατὰ σάρκα.</note>. Indeed, his person is represented in the mystical ladder. 

Fourthly, when God promises that the seed of Jacob will be like the dust of the earth to the East, West, North, and South, the oracle sufficiently hints at the children of Abraham according to the promise—that is, all the faithful who are united to Christ the head. Finally, when he says in verse 13: *The land on which you lie, I will give to you and to your seed*. He speaks of the land of Canaan, which was a **type** <note>In biblical studies, a "type" is a historical person, place, or event that foreshadows a future reality, usually Christ or the Church.</note> of the heavenly Canaan, to which entry is granted only through Christ (foreshadowed in the ladder), just as Joshua alone led the Israelites into the earthly Canaan. In summary <note>Original Greek: Συλλήβδην (*Syllēbdēn*).</note>, this clear oracle proclaims that no special blessing was ever granted except in the name of Jesus Christ, the blessed seed.

Since, therefore, symbols shown to the eyes ought to clearly reveal the oracles, we do not approve of the interpretations of the **Kabbalists** <note>Jewish mystical scholars. Crégut here refers to a traditional Jewish commentary regarding King Saul's failure to fully exterminate the Amalekites as commanded in 1 Samuel 15.</note>, who say that Saul was deceived by the ambiguity of the oracle found in Exodus 17:14: *Afterwards the Lord said to Moses: Write this as a memorial in a book, and recount it in the ears of Joshua: that I will utterly blot out the memory of the Amalekites from under heaven.* <note>Original Hebrew: אמחה את זכר עמלק (*Amcheh et zekher Amalek*).</note> Because the word *zekher* <note>Hebrew: זכר.</note> signifies both "male" and "memory," depending on the different punctuation <note>The Hebrew consonants Z-Kh-R can be read as *zekher* (remembrance) or *zakhar* (male). The story suggests Saul’s teacher taught him to kill only the males, leading to his disobedience.</note>; yet Saul believed he was satisfying God's command...

For once, those who practiced the rituals of the **Saturnalia** were deceived by this ambiguity and sacrificed a man to **Saturn** every year, when the sacrifice could just as well have been performed with **lit lamps** according to the oracles. Thus, that foolish nation, cruel in its worship to its own destruction, finally came to its senses under the teaching of **Hercules**. Away with the frauds of that impure Spirit in divine oracles; now **Jehovah** speaks clearly to **Jacob** in this oracle, from which there arises not ambiguity or perplexity of mind, but the fullest **assurance of faith** <note>Original Greek: πληροφορία (plērophoria), meaning "full conviction" or "certainty."</note>.

These terms in the New Testament often refer to receiving a divine warning or instruction.</note>. <meta>This page continues Crégut's theological commentary. While the previous page focused on the clarity of God’s commands to King Saul, this page moves into a linguistic and historical analysis of how God speaks to humanity, specifically focusing on Jacob’s vision of the ladder and distinguishing true divine communication from pagan oracles.</meta>

# REVEALER OF SECRETS.

->**Divine revelation** and **divine instruction.**<- <note>original: κεχρηματισμὸν & χρηματισμὸς</note> Thus, in this oracle, God is said to **instruct** Jacob <note>original: χρηματίζειν</note> as He speaks to him; and Jacob is said to be **instructed** <note>original: χρηματίζεσθαι</note> or "divinely warned," just as it is said of the Magi in Matthew 2:12. And the speech delivered to Jacob, which is contained in verses 13, 14, and 15, is the **divine revelation** or **instruction**. That specific word <note>original: κεχρηματισμὸν</note> is found in Matthew 2:12, Romans 11:4, and Hebrews 12:25, even if it is used with a rare meaning when someone is divinely warned without having first called upon God. 

However, the pagans distinguished between **prophecies** and **the sayings**; <note>original: χρησμοὺς & τὰ λόγια</note> because the former word signified oracles expressed in verse, while the latter signified oracles delivered in prose. Paul uses this latter word in Romans 3:2: *chiefly because to them were committed the **sayings of God**.* <note>original: τὰ λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ</note> And in Acts 7:38, Moses is said to have *received **living sayings**,* <note>original: λόγια ζῶντα</note> or living utterances. By this term they signify the Legal Covenant. The most learned **Beza** <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major Protestant reformer and scholar.</note> translates this as "Utterances" rather than "oracles," so that the vocabulary would not smack of heathenism; for the pagans were constantly boasting of the "oracles" of demons. Nevertheless, our French version retains the term "oracles," as a more expressive one was not available.

Observe furthermore that the **Devil**, acting as **God's ape**, <note>A common medieval and early modern concept (*Simia Dei*) suggesting that Satan can only mimic or parody God's true miracles and institutions to deceive people.</note> long ago imitated those oracles of God in **manifold ways**, <note>original: πολυτρόπως</note> so that under the pretext of religion and worship he might fascinate wretched men. For according to the calculation of scholars, there were two most ancient and famous oracles: namely, that of **Ammon** and that of **Dodona**. 

The first was established in the same place where the school of **Ham** <note>original: Chami</note> and his descendants first existed—hence **Jupiter Ammon**, as if it were "Chammon" from Ham. The other, which belonged to the **Dodonian Apollo**, was in the same place where the settlement of **Dodanim** <note>Mentioned in Genesis 10:4 as a grandson of Noah.</note> was, who was the grandson of Noah through Javan. For Satan wished to occupy those places and corrupt them with his poison.

The fourth and final part of the **discussion** <note>original: συζητήσεως</note> still encompasses four things: namely, Jacob’s wonder, his deeds, his words, and his actions. His wonder is contained in verses 16 and 17; for having awakened from his sleep, he cries out in amazement: *Surely the Lord is in this place,* etc. Truly, many things inspired this wonder: that miraculous ladder, God leaning upon the ladder, the angels ascending and descending, the voice thundering from heaven into his ears, and other things of that kind. Two things especially create wonder: 1. Ignorance of the causes. 2. The effect...

# ANTHONY CRÉGUT

<margin>
The rarity of the effect. <note>original: "Effectus raritas"</note>
</margin>
This first thing gives rise to wonder; whence the poet says:
> To wonder at nothing is almost the one thing, Numicius, 
> and the only thing that can make and keep one happy. <note>original: "Nil admirari propè res vna Numici, Solaque quæ poßit facere & seruare beatos." A famous line from Horace, *Epistles* 1.6.1, arguing for stoic equanimity.</note>
This is why Pythagoras once said that the goal of philosophy is to wonder at nothing. The other thing gives rise to no less wonder; for those things which are extraordinary, and which happen rarely, strike our eyes and minds most forcefully, according to that saying of the poet:
> The sun has no spectator except when it fails; 
> no one observes the moon unless it is struggling. <note>original: "Sol spectatorem non nisi cùm deficit habet; Nemo obseruat Lunam nisi laborantem." From Seneca’s *Natural Questions*, referring to solar and lunar eclipses as moments where humans finally pay attention to the heavens.</note>
These two elements are found especially in this vision; for Jacob is immediately struck with awe because he is ignorant of its cause, nor is he able to fully investigate its reason. That the vision was extraordinary is so clear that we judge any further proof to be unnecessary.

It is no wonder, therefore, if such great admiration brought forth these words from Jacob: *Truly the Lord is in this place, etc.* and in *verse 17*: *How terrible is this place, etc.* <note>Genesis 28:16-17. Here, "terrible" carries the archaic sense of "awe-inspiring" or "dreadful" in the presence of the divine.</note> Jacob thought he was alone in that place, but unexpectedly he felt the presence of God, who is truly the guardian of Israel, perpetually watching over the faithful, and who, even if not summoned, is nevertheless present through the presence of His grace. And although He is present in grace, Jacob nonetheless affirms the place to be "terrible," because such great majesty cannot appear to the eyes of "little men" <note>original: "homuncionum," a diminutive for humans, emphasizing our smallness compared to God.</note> without them being immediately struck by such great brightness and the flashing glory of the divine power. It is indeed necessary that this happens so that men may be bent toward humility.

Jacob’s actions are described in *verse 18* with these words: *And Jacob arose in the morning, and took the stone which he had placed under his head, and set it up as a pillar, and poured oil upon the top of it.* <note>Genesis 28:18.</note> Such an admirable vision ought not to lie hidden hereafter, nor was it fitting that it should benefit Jacob alone. Truly, it was worthwhile for posterity to have knowledge of so great a mystery. Therefore, the pious Patriarch prepares a monument—at first glance and in its outward appearance small and lowly, yet by God’s providence ordering all these things, it is "more lasting than bronze." <note>original: "ære perennius," a reference to Horace, *Odes* 3.30, meaning an immortal legacy.</note> For he erected a pillar <note>term: "statua" / "statuam" — in this biblical context, it refers to a *matzevah*, a standing stone or pillar used as a memorial marker.</note> so stable that as long as the world shall stand, that pillar also shall stand in the memory of men. This firmness seems to arise from the very...

...designated by the word **monument** <note>original Hebrew: מצבה (*matzebah*), which signifies a pillar or standing statue</note>. And although that word **monument** <note>original: מצבה (*matzebah*)</note> sounds like "statue" in a general sense, and is even used specifically for those statues that became idols—as is clear from Leviticus 26:1, where God forbids statues to be erected for Him because they stood for veneration as if they were images of God—nevertheless, it is not erected by Jacob here for that purpose, but rather to be a **memorial** <note>original Greek: *μνημόσυνον* (*mnemosynon*), a physical reminder or token of remembrance</note> of the vision.

It is also not without mystery that Jacob poured oil upon the stone; for this is not a sign to be assigned to a superstitious rite, but rather he intends to piously signify something mystical. For even though no law had yet been brought forth concerning anointings and pourings of this kind (as was later done by solemn ritual), the Patriarchs nevertheless had many **foreshadowings** <note>original: *vmbratilia*, literally "shadowy things"</note> and, as it were, preludes of future institutions. This is clearly seen in the case of sacrifices, which were in use among the Patriarchs immediately from the time of sin and the fall of man, even if no law existed for their formal sanction. Therefore, the holy Patriarch was not ignorant that this pouring of oil was a sign of consecration. Since the erection of that pillar and **memorial** <note>original Greek: *μνημόσυνον*</note> was an act of religion and of Jacob’s gratitude, he wished by this external rite to signify the consecration of the Spirit, without which all efforts would be vain and useless. Without that **oil of gladness** <note>A common biblical metaphor for the Holy Spirit, citing Psalm 45:7</note>, nothing happy or pleasant can be provided; nor without the oil of the Spirit would he have stood forth as the **strongest athlete** <note>A traditional term for Jacob, referencing his later wrestling with the angel and his spiritual endurance</note>, in which, however, having been anointed by that oil of the Spirit, he emerged as victor. However, I do not think we should dwell on those things which others report: that the stone signified Christ, and the oil the Spirit (the oil of gladness by which Christ was anointed above his companions). For although it is most true that Christ is often designated in Scripture by a stone—because he is that **corner stone** <note>original: *Petra angularis*</note>—and that he was **historically** <note>original Greek: *ἱστορικῶς* (*historikōs*), meaning in the literal or factual sense of the narrative</note> anointed by the Holy Spirit; nevertheless, in that **early stage of instruction** <note>original: *pædagogia*, referring to the "childhood" of the faithful before the full Law of Moses or the Gospel</note> and those **rudimentary elements** <note>original: *rudibus elementis*</note> of the Fathers, it is not probable that those mysteries were revealed so explicitly to the Patriarch. ...because they are superstitious, nor do they possess the conditions required for true and legitimate vows. I. Regarding the *object*, they err, because vows should not be named for the Saints, but for God alone, because a vow is a type of invocation and oath, which are owed to God alone; nor does there exist in Scripture any example or precept of a vow named for any Saint. II. By reason of the *subject*, because among them, those who make vows are for the most part not under their own legal control <note>original: "sui iuris" — a legal term for someone who has the full power to act for themselves.</note>, such as children without the consent of parents, or a wife without the consent of her husband. *Numbers 30:4, 5, 6, etc.* III. By reason of the *matter*, because they vow illicit things or things bad in themselves; as in Judges 17:3, *the mother of Micah*, who vowed silver for the making of idols and ritual garments. And in *Acts 23:12*, mention is made of the vow of those who had sworn with a curse to bring about the death of Paul. Likewise, when they vow things that are not in their own power; as when Monks and Nuns vow chastity: furthermore, when they vow *indifferent things* <note>original: "res indifferentes" — things that are neither commanded nor forbidden by God, but are neutral in themselves.</note>, and so these neutral things are made necessary by them and weave a snare for consciences, such as the monastic vows of *continence, obedience, and poverty*. IV. By reason of the *manner*, because vows are made by them rashly and without consultation, like the vow of Jephthah in Judges 11:30 <note>Jephthah rashly vowed to sacrifice the first thing that came out of his house, which turned out to be his daughter.</note>, and when they are made *under compulsion*, as when parents force Nuns to take monastic vows so that the inheritance for their other children might be larger. V. By the *end*, because they presume to merit eternal life from these actions.

Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a highly influential Jesuit Cardinal and Counter-Reformation scholar.</note> observes in Book 2, *On Monks*, chapter 14: The word for "vow" among the Latins is ambiguous, for it signifies a promise, a prayer, and a desire. For (he says) we say *I have undertaken a vow of continence*, that is, I have promised continence to God; and *I have poured out vows for continence to God*, that is, I have prayed to God for continence. However, the same Bellarmine adds that among the Greeks there is not the same word for vow and prayer, but two others closely related, namely *euchē* <note>original Greek: εὐχὴ</note> and *proseuchē* <note>original Greek: προσευχὴ</note>; the former signifies a *vow*, while the latter signifies a *prayer*. For a vow is called *neder* <note>original Hebrew: נדר</note> and a prayer is called *tephillah* <note>original Hebrew: תפלה</note>. He gives this reason for the matter: that among the Greeks and Latins, when these names were invented, there was no true piety, and therefore men vowed nothing to God or the gods except to obtain that which they desired, and for that reason always—

<meta>This page continues Anthony Crégut’s theological examination of religious vows. Having previously listed the conditions for a valid vow, he now turns to a linguistic and historical analysis, comparing how Pagans (Greeks and Romans) and Hebrews understood the relationship between a vow and a prayer.</meta>

# ANTHONY CRÉGUT
<meta>catchword: More</meta>

they used to join prayers to their vows; following that line of Virgil, *Are you slow to offer vows and prayers?* <note>original: "Cessas in vota precesque" from Virgil's Aeneid, Book 6. Crégut is showing that in Roman culture, a "vow" was almost always a bargain-style request to a god.</note> Whence, as Gregory of Nyssa <note>a 4th-century church father from Cappadocia</note> observed in his second oration on the Lord’s Prayer, the Greeks called a prayer *proseuche* <note>original: προσευχή</note>, because it happened after the vow, which they called *euche* <note>original: εὐχή</note>. But the Hebrews, because they worshipped God piously and made vows without the hope of a reward like hirelings, did not pray to God so that He might repay them for the vow, but made their vows absolutely; hence it is that among them, a vow had nothing in common with prayers. Therefore they used names which are not related to signify "vow" and "prayer," namely *neder* <note>original: נדר — a vow or a thing promised to God</note> and *tephillah* <note>original: תפלה — a prayer or intercession</note>, as was said before.

Robert Bellarmine <note>a highly influential Jesuit Cardinal and defender of Catholic doctrine, whom Protestant writers like Crégut frequently attempted to refute</note> observed these things quite sharply and learnedly, but nevertheless it is difficult to investigate the reasoning behind many words, because they are for the most part imposed by chance <note>original: ἀπὸ τύχης — "at random" or "by luck"</note>; and so perhaps those two Hebrew concepts were named by chance. But indeed, if anything plausible can be said, we shall instead bring forward another reason for this naming convention, which seems more probable. 

Since the Latins and Greeks were from the Gentiles and were not God’s people, God had not commanded vows to them; nor had He taught them any form of worship. Whenever, therefore, those nations pronounced vows to God, they did this in "will-worship" <note>original: ἐν τῇ ἐθελοθρησκείᾳ (*en tē ethelothrēskeia*) — a term from the New Testament (Colossians 2:23) referring to man-made or self-imposed religious rituals</note> and by their own arrangement. And because human nature is not very inclined toward piety, men never made vows to God without looking toward some useful benefit or so that they might be freed from some evil. For that reason, they commonly added prayers to their vows, from which were born the related terms *euche* and *proseuche*. 

But among the Hebrews, whose religion was based on God’s establishment, vows were commanded by God’s law; and so, in order that they might not transgress the Law of God, they pronounced and fulfilled vows only for their own sake and intended them as an end in themselves. Therefore, they did not add prayers as if they were requesting something from God. Add to this that in that nation, basic principles were established which, since they were coarse, unrefined, and external, were not dedicated to internal and spiritual worship (such as prayers), but the greatest part of their religion was situated in rites and ceremonies by which the Jews intended to appease God. This is why in the Old Testament (as Peter Martyr <note>Peter Martyr Vermigli, a prominent Italian Reformer and theologian</note> observes), mention of vows is frequent, while in the New Testament a vow is not even named, except when the conversation is about Jewish vows, as in Acts 21.

...both by which he may assist his own piety, and at the same time profess it among men; thirdly, as an offering by which he may practice benignly helping his brothers. For as the **Most Learned Interpreter** <note>This likely refers to a prominent Protestant commentator, possibly John Calvin, whom Crégut frequently cites.</note> rightly perceives, tithes were ceded for that use. In another sense, "vows of charity" are still understood, not of piety; this is when they are not declared for some specific worship of God, but for the sake of bearing with the ignorance of the weak, just as Paul says he "became a Jew to the Jews." For this reason, he did it only once and for a short time, so as to accommodate himself to the Jews for that interval. 

But today among Christians, they are used as an empty *Cacozelia* <term>misguided zeal or a poor imitation of a foreign style</term>, whenever those Judaizing Nazarites and Clerics are ordered not to grow their hair, but to shave it in the likeness of a sphere. But indeed, just as there is now a massive abuse of vows among Judaizing Christians, so formerly among the Jews before the time of Christ—and even today—the abuse has prevailed. Maimonides <note>A preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note> in *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: "More Neuoch" (Moreh Nevuchim)</note>, part 3, chapter 49, begins thus: *The Rabbis say: Vows are a fence for separation* <note>original Hebrew: נדרים סיג לפרישות (Nedarim seig l'perishut). This implies that vows act as a protective boundary to keep a person focused on a holy life.</note>, *that is, for a separate and holy life or abstinence, as is evident from the Nazirites.* But in the time of Christ, this was the solemn formula of swearing or rather vowing among the Hebrew Doctors: *Let it be an offering, whatever it is by which I might benefit you; or whatever utility you might take from me.* <note>original Hebrew: קורבן כל מה דתהנה מני (Korban kol mah d'tehaneh mini). This refers to the "Corban" practice rebuked by Jesus in the Gospels, where a man avoids helping his parents by claiming his resources are a gift dedicated to God.</note> This Jewish *Halacha* <term>traditional Jewish law or custom</term> is read in the treatise on oaths and on vows. When someone used this vow toward another, no matter how closely bound by necessity—even toward his own parent—the Rabbis established that it was a sin for that person to help the other with any kind of benefit or duty, lest what he had devoted to God should serve human comforts. This is why devoted things were formerly called *Cherem* <note>original Hebrew: חרם</note> among them, and *Anathemata* or *Ananeimena* among the Greeks, referring both to those things dedicated in sacred places and those things burned and destroyed. But in later times, the Hebrews called it *Corban* <note>original Hebrew: קרבן</note>, with the letter *K* <note>the Hebrew letter Kaph (כ)</note> being elided as a harsher sound...

# ->ANTHONY CRÉGUT<-

<margin>קָרְבָּן *Corban*</margin> Christ once alluded to this tradition in Matthew 15:5 and Mark 7:11 and criticized it: *But you say, whoever says to father or mother, whatever help you might have received from me is a gift, he shall be innocent.* <note>original Greek: Δῶρον ὃ ἐὰν ἐξ ἐמוῦ ὠφεληθῇς</note>. But Mark says, *Corban, which is a gift* <note>original Greek: Κορβᾶν ὅ ἐστι δῶρον</note>. Since those hypocrites used the appearance of religion as a pretext, they denied the duties of charity to their neighbor, as if they were saying: "I have already consecrated everything from my goods that could have relieved you in this your poverty." Since these passages are quite obscure due to ellipses <term>the omission of words for brevity</term> in the Greek original, it is no wonder that interpreters have labored over this place. The Syriac interpreter is less obscure, at least in Matthew, even if the ellipsis still makes the passage difficult enough. For thus the Syriac of Matthew 15:5 is to be rendered word-for-word: *My offering, or my Corban, is that from which you might take benefit from me.* However, the Syriac in Mark is a little more obscure, for it has: *By my offering of Corban, which is from me, you shall be helped.*

From these things it is clearly established that the Jews, as soon as they had pronounced some vow, observed it quite rigidly, even if it were unjust or rash; which the example of Jephthah <note>A biblical judge who made a rash vow to sacrifice the first thing that came out of his house—which turned out to be his daughter (Judges 11).</note> also sufficiently confirms. The same was practiced among the Gentiles and today among "Judaizing Christians," <note>A polemical term Crégut uses for Roman Catholics, suggesting their rituals and vows are overly legalistic and similar to Old Testament law.</note> whose religion for the most part degenerates into superstition. Hence it is that among secular authors, when men sought something most passionately, they were said to *have it in their vows*. Thus it was said of old regarding Eudoxus, the celebrated astronomer <note>Eudoxus of Cnidus (c. 390–337 BCE), a Greek astronomer who allegedly died from observing the sun too closely.</note>, that he so desperately loved the Sun—the primary object of his science—that he had it in his vows to gaze upon it so near and at such close quarters that he would not refuse to be blinded by its light and most brilliant glare, or even to be scorched by its vivid flames. Following this phraseology, Jacques Auguste de Thou <note>A famous French historian and statesman (1553–1617) known for his "History of His Own Time."</note> in his *History*, book 37, volume 2, page 310, reported these things concerning Suleiman, the most proud Emperor of the Turks. They record that three things were lacking for his total happiness and his highest vow: First, to bring under his power Vienna, the bulwark of the German Empire and as it were the key—which he boasted was owed to him as the heir of the Empire after Constantinople was captured by his great-grandfather Muhammad [II]; second, [to finish] a stupendous temple in Byzantium [Istanbul] built by himself...

# ->THE REVEALER OF SECRETS<-

...could not finish the work begun and the aqueducts started in imitation of the Romans; if fortune had made him master of these vows <note>In this context, "vows" refers to the ruler's solemn desires or grand designs.</note> before death, he would have considered himself the most fortunate of all kings.

Therefore, leaving aside the superstitious vows of superstitious men, let us imitate Jacob’s vow and his manner of vowing. For as it was the first vow of all recorded, so it ought to be the exquisite norm and rule <term>amussis: a mason’s leveling tool, used here to mean a perfect standard</term> for others, both in respect to the object, as well as the matter and the goal. Nor should anyone here quibble that Jacob was a mercenary <note>A "mercenary" piety refers to the critique that Jacob only promised to serve God in exchange for physical rewards.</note>, and that his piety was not true and praiseworthy, since he promises worship and honor to God only if God should grant him goods and the necessities of life. As if the holy Patriarch’s piety truly depended on those earthly and corruptible goods! Without doubt, his piety was more deeply rooted than to be uprooted by a lack of earthly things; for it was given freely and without hope of reward. As he had received freely, so he also gave back freely. Therefore, the Patriarch looked toward God’s promises and embraced them with faith; for that reason, he confirmed his faith even more with those words and added a vow, so that he might be bound even more strongly, as if by a sturdy chain. Therefore, that vow is founded upon the covenant; and because God had promised the Patriarch protection, preservation, and all things necessary for his life, so he, relying on God’s promises, in turn promises that he will be a religious observer of the divine will if God should graciously provide life and daily bread according to the promises.

## ANALYSIS.

The oracle regarding Shiloh is noble in many ways. The whole oracle is divided into the four endowments of Judah. 1. The <term>preeminence<note>original Greek: ὑπεροχὴ</note></term> of Judah is derived from the Scepter. This is proven from the etymology of the name "Judah." An answer is provided to the objection taken from the <term>preeminence<note>original Greek: ὑπεροχῇ</note></term> of Joseph, who received a double portion of the inheritance. Joseph’s preeminence was only temporary, and for what reason? The right of the firstborn was taken away from Reuben, and why? The election of Saul as king did not hinder the truth of this prophecy. The ambiguity of the word <term>shebet<note>original Hebrew: שבט; this word can mean a staff, a scepter, or a tribe</note></term>, from which the obscurity of this passage arises. The threefold meaning of the word <term>shebet</term>. Why <term>shebet</term> is not understood here as a physical rod or staff. Why <term>shebet</term> is not understood here as a "tribe." Why this latter opinion nevertheless possesses a great deal of probability for several reasons. The confusion of the genealogies of the ten tribes. The preservation of the genealogies of the tribe of Judah. The Messiah as the <term>precious treasure<note>original Greek: Κειμήλιον; refers to a stored-up heirloom or highly valued object</note></term> found within the genealogies. Several reasons why the Scribes preserved genealogies. These reasons were either Sacred or Civil. Four civil reasons for which genealogies were preserved among the Jews. The sacred reason derived from the Messiah is the most powerful. The dreams <note>In this context, "dreams" refers to the speculations or interpretations of the Jewish scholars.</note> of the Jews regarding the future Messiah in relation to genealogies. Why the ancients had so many questions concerning genealogies. There would be no <term>preeminence</term> for Judah if <term>shebet</term> were interpreted merely as "tribe." Matthew wove together the genealogy of Christ from the public archives of the Jews. Why did the Jews not find fault with the genealogy of Christ as composed by Matthew? The true opinion is established: that Moses understood <term>shebet</term> to mean a "scepter." This opinion regarding the Scepter is twofold and **is divided** <note>This completes the thought from the catchword "pescitur" (divided/split) at the bottom of the page.</note>
