**In many ways** noble and illustrious is that prophecy of Genesis 49:10, whether because it offers us an exceptional prediction concerning Christ, or because it reveals the excellent gifts and symbols of the tribe of Judah, or because it has been illuminated by the commentaries and labors of so many learned men, or finally because it is a point of controversy between Jews and Christians, and has thus been made famous by the various reflections of both Rabbis and Christian Doctors. We also, under divine auspices and relying on the luminous help of the Spirit, shall look into these inner sanctuaries so that we might be able to uncover the core <note>original: "nucleum enucleare," literally "to de-shell the nut."</note> of the matter. Indeed, so that we leave nothing of importance untouched, we shall seek out four distinguished gifts and prerogatives of Judah, in which the whole prophecy will be found to be examined. 

I. The *Prerogative* shall be the *Scepter* <note>original: "Sceptrum"; a symbol of royal authority and tribal leadership.</note> placed in that tribe. 
II. There shall be the *duration of the Scepter*, which is signified by these words: *until* <note>original Hebrew: עַד כִּי (ad ki); original Latin: "donec."</note>. 
III. The *Eminence of the Scepter*, because *Shiloh* <note>A traditional title for the Messiah, often interpreted as "He to whom it belongs."</note> shall reign: *until Shiloh comes* <note>original Hebrew: עַד כִּי יָבֹא שִׁילֹה (ad ki yabo Shiloh).</note>. 
IV. The *Breadth of the Scepter*, which extends even to the Nations; *and to him shall be the gathering, or the obedience, of the peoples* <note>original Hebrew: וְלוֹ יִקְּהַת עַמִּים (ve-lo yikhat ammim).</note>.

The first prerogative of Judah is rightly drawn from the Scepter. The Patriarch Jacob sufficiently suggests this when blessing his sons in verse 8, where he speaks thus: *Judah, you are he whom your brothers shall praise*. Here he alludes to the name Judah, which is taken from a root that means *to praise, to celebrate, or to confess*. This was partly because he had been so named by his mother <note>Leah, who said "Now I will praise the LORD" at his birth.</note> because he was the cause for praising God. But it is primarily because the great Patriarch, through a prophetic spirit, foresees a new reason for this etymology. For he knew by divine inspiration that the scepter was to be placed in that tribe, and therefore the name of Judah would be famous and splendid among his brothers, so that he would be honored by all like a firstborn. 

Nor does it stand in the way that Jacob assigned a double portion to his son Joseph as if to a firstborn, for this was the right of primogeniture <note>The legal right of the eldest son to inherit a larger share of the estate.</note>. For the firstborn *obtained a double portion of the father's goods*, as is clear from Deuteronomy 21:17. Since, therefore, Reuben the firstborn had deservedly fallen from his right because he polluted his father's bed by incestuous union with his stepmother, Jacob wished that right to be transferred to Joseph,

->### TO THE REVEALER OF SECRETS<-

as is explained in 1 Chronicles 5:1–2 and following. When Reuben had defiled his father’s bed <note>original: "prophanasset strata patris sui"; referring to Reuben's sin with Bilhah in Genesis 35:22.</note>, his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph, the son of Israel. However, this was not so that Joseph could claim the entire right of the firstborn for himself, for Judah prevailed over his brothers. Thus, in the distribution of the land of Canaan, two portions fell to the descendants of Joseph, as can be seen in Joshua 14:4 and chapters 16 and 17, as well as Ezekiel 47:13. Elisha seems to allude to this law of the firstborn in 2 Kings 2:9 when he asks for a *double portion* of Elijah’s spirit; that is, he sought to obtain that prerogative among the "sons of the Prophets." As if he were Elijah's firstborn son—or his most beloved disciple—he wished to succeed him in the prophetic office and the spiritual gifts in which Elijah had excelled.

From this, therefore, it is gathered that the right of Reuben actually transferred to his brother Joseph. For this reason, and not without cause, Jacob concludes the blessing of Joseph in Genesis 49:26 in this manner:
*Let these blessings be on the head of Joseph, and on the crown of the one separated from among his brothers.*
First, Jacob indicates that his prayers would not be scattered into thin air, because they would rest "upon the head," which denotes their substantial fulfillment. Second, he calls Joseph <term>Nazir<gloss>consecrated or separated</gloss></term> among his brothers, either because he is their "crown" due to the shared glory that flows from him to all the others, or because he is "separated" from all of them by the dignity in which he excels. Nevertheless, that prerogative of Joseph was not able to take away the <term>eminence<gloss>original Greek: ἐξοχὴν (exochen); meaning superiority or prominence</gloss></term> of Judah. This is because the excellence of Joseph was merely temporary and, indeed, not long-lasting; he eventually had to be brought back into line with the others to submit himself to the scepter of Judah. But Judah's dominion was meant to be permanent and enduring, according to the divine oracle: *The scepter shall not depart from Judah, etc.* By this oracle, God instituted a monarchy among His people as the most perfect state of government.

Furthermore, the history of King Saul does not obscure the light of this truth. In that case, the beginning of the kingdom and the appearance of that regime seem to have sprung from the "wanton lust" of the people, who tumultuously demanded a King be given to them before the proper time and under unlucky omens. Indeed, it even seemed to go against the oracles, since the scepter was placed not in the tribe of Judah, but in another; for Saul was a man from the tribe of Benjamin. But—

nor shall <unclear>his own</unclear> Scribe <note>original: "Scriba propria"; referring to the "lawgiver" or "ruler's staff" in Genesis 49:10.</note> depart from between his feet until Shiloh comes—that is, the Messiah. They argue, therefore, that Jacob foretold that the remaining tribes were to be confused, or rather scattered, but the tribe of Judah alone was to be preserved until the coming of the Messiah, along with the Scribe in the midst of his feet.

This opinion holds no small amount of probability. **I.** Because it attributes a great <term>preeminence<gloss>exochēn</gloss></term> <note>original Greek: εξοχην</note> to Judah, which was the very purpose of his father Jacob in blessing him. For what could be greater than his preservation while the others were scattered and mingled with idolaters and profane nations? What greater preeminence is there than the <unclear>continued</unclear> presence of the Scribe "between his feet"? For it was their duty to preserve the genealogies of the families with the greatest care in the public archives, so that the genealogy of the Messiah would not be obscure, and thus he might be recognized by the most certain <term>distinctive marks<gloss>characterismo</gloss></term>.

**II.** Because this sentiment seems to be proven by the facts themselves, and does not disagree with the accounts of historians. It is clear from both Scripture and ancient writers that the remaining tribes were mixed with the Gentiles and were long ago carried away to Assyria, never to return. From this arose the "Vatinian hatred" <note>A proverbial expression for an intense, irreconcilable hatred, named after the Roman politician Publius Vatinius.</note> between the Jews and the Samaritans (who were mixed with the Gentiles). Because of this, those who were circumcised by the Jews were circumcised again by the Samaritans; the poet Horace mockingly called them *Apellas*—that is, *without skin* <note>original: "sine pelle"; a pun on the Greek 'a-pella' used by Horace to refer to a circumcised Jew.</note>—using a made-up word, and Martial called them *docked* or *re-skinned* <note>original: "curtos sive recutitos"; Latin terms used by Roman satirists to mock the physical signs of circumcision.</note>. This is why Christ, in the first mission of the disciples, explicitly forbade them from entering the cities of the Samaritans. And in John 4, the Apostles are amazed that Christ would hold a conversation with a Samaritan woman.

In contrast, the tribe of Judah remained unmixed and untainted until the time of the Messiah. However, we cannot agree with this opinion in every respect. For even if we must admit that the tribe of Judah was preserved above all others—and its genealogies maintained because the Messiah was certainly to be born from it (which was his indubitable <term>criterion<gloss>kritērion</gloss></term> <note>original Greek: κριτηριον; a standard or test for identification.</note> so that he might be recognized by the Jews according to the prophecies)—nevertheless, other tribes also remained. Most notably the *tribe of Levi*, which was the Priestly tribe; this was to ensure that no one might seize the priesthood who was not from that tribe, for God had wished to destine this honor to them by a peculiar right. The same judgment should be held regarding the others.

...from which Paul notes his lineage, and while addressing Agrippa he mentions the "twelve tribes" <note>original Greek: δωδεκαφύλου; referring to the collective body of the twelve tribes of Israel</note>, Acts 26:7. *To which promise our twelve tribes, serving God continually night and day, hope to attain.* And in Luke chapter 2, verse 36, he mentions Anna the Prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. But until this very day, the genealogies of the Hebrews have been preserved with wonderful care and concern, whether by private authority within individual families, or publicly in the archives of the temple and authentic monuments; whether by the fathers of the family or by the Scribes, whose duty among other things was to preserve the genealogies correctly and distinctly, just as they acted as Notaries and public Registrars, because they provided authority <note>original Greek: ἀυθεντίαν; legal authenticity</note> and trust in controversies more than private descriptions could. From these records, perhaps, the Evangelists Matthew and Luke described the genealogy of Christ; these records agreed perfectly with those Hebrew archives, since no dispute was ever raised against the genealogy of Christ, neither against Matthew, nor Luke, nor the other Apostles and Christians—which sufficiently demonstrated that the Jews were convinced by the very evidence of the truth. They could not accuse the Evangelists, and much less condemn them, without striking their own genealogists with the same blow and rendering them condemned, or at least erasing the genealogies with which our own were in harmony. And certainly, if it had not been so, and clearer than the sun itself, the Scribes and Pharisees would have immediately seized the opportunity for mockery.

Many causes exist for this exact preservation of genealogies by the Scribes and heads of families, some of which may be called *sacred*, and others *political*.

*Political or Civil reasons:* 
**I.** So that the distinction of tribes might be maintained, as well as the families within the tribes, so that neither would the Gentiles be mixed with the people of God—who were then a *treasured people* <note>original Greek: λαὸς περιούσιος; a people of special possession</note> and as if God's own property—nor would the Israelites themselves be mixed among one another, whether by their own will and accord, through marriage, or by chance from a lack of observing the genealogical succession.

But in contrast, the tribe of Judah remained unmixed and untainted until the time of the Messiah.

Yet up to that day, the genealogies of the Hebrews were preserved with wonderful care and diligence, whether by private authority within individual families, or publicly in the temple archives and authentic monuments; whether by the fathers of the family or by the Scribes. Among other duties, it was the office of the Scribes to preserve the genealogies correctly and distinctly, acting as public Notaries and Recorders, so that they might provide **authority** <note>original Greek: αὐθεντίαν (authentian)</note> and proof in disputes, more so than private descriptions. From these sources, perhaps, the Evangelists Matthew and Luke described the genealogy of Christ; these accounts agreed wonderfully with those Hebrew archives, since no quarrel was ever raised against Matthew, Luke, or the other Apostles and Christians regarding the genealogy of Christ. This sufficiently demonstrated that the Jews were convinced by the evidence of the truth itself; they could not accuse the Evangelists—much less condemn them—without simultaneously striking a blow against their own genealogists and making them out to be at fault, or at least striking out the genealogies with which our writers were in total agreement. And indeed, unless this had been the case and clearer than the sun itself, the Scribes and Pharisees would have immediately seized the opportunity for mockery.

Several reasons exist for this exact preservation of genealogies by the Scribes and heads of families, some of which can be called **sacred**, others **political**.

**Political** or **Civil Reasons**:
I. So that the distinction of the tribes and of the families within those tribes might be preserved, lest either the Gentiles be mixed with the people of God (who were then a **chosen people** <note>original Greek: λαός περιούσιος (laos periousios); literally "a people for his own possession"</note> and, as it were, God's own possession), or even lest the Israelites themselves be mixed among one another, whether voluntarily, through marriage, or by chance through a failure to observe the genealogical sequence.

[God] willed the tribes to be distinct. For although the sale of lands and possessions was permitted, everything first had to be offered to fellow tribesmen; or, if it happened to pass into another tribe, the property was reclaimed by the original owners during the following Jubilee <note>A Year of Jubilee occurred every 50th year in ancient Israel, where debts were forgiven and ancestral lands returned to their original family owners (Leviticus 25)</note>. From this, one can derive the just excuse of Naboth, who refused his field and paternal inheritance to King Ahab because he had received it as a succession transmitted from his ancestors <note>Referring to the story in 1 Kings 21, where Naboth refused to sell his vineyard to the King because it was a sacred family inheritance</note>. 

III. The description of genealogies <term>genealogy</term> <note>original Greek: γενεαλογ. (genealogia)</note> served for the distinction of firstborn sons and those descended from them, so that they might subsequently obtain, by right of primogeniture, both a double portion of the inheritance and authority over their brothers—rights which were passed down from the firstborn of the firstborn, and so on. 

IV. The preservation of genealogies was also useful for rooting out the seeds of litigation among the Jews which could arise from property ownership, or for settling and resolving those disputes that had already arisen. Thus, in **Ezra chapter 2, verse 59**, it is related that some could not show their father’s house or their descent, whether they were of Israel, and therefore they were believed to be <term>strangers</term> <note>original Hebrew: נכרי (nokhri)</note> or <term>converts</term> <note>original Greek: προσήλυτοι (prosēlytoi)</note>, or <term>resident aliens</term> <note>original Greek: πάροικοι (paroikoi)</note>. Whence in **Nehemiah chapter 7, verse 5**, Nehemiah performed the census of the people by the benefit of these genealogies. But indeed, beyond those civil reasons, there remains that most powerful reason, which concerns sacred and most mystical matters, and which was intended above all in the recording of genealogies: namely, the recognition of the Messiah. He was to be born from the tribe of Judah, from the trunk and root of Jesse (**Isaiah 11**), from David, and from the royal family. Therefore, those exquisite genealogies had to be preserved so that, when the Messiah was born, his genuine identifying characteristics might shine forth so clearly that he could not be ignored. 

Hence, by the singular providence of God, it happened that after the Messiah was revealed and the ministry of the ancient tabernacle was abolished, there arose a confusion of tribes beyond what can be described. This was due to the dispersion <note>The Diaspora, or the scattering of the Jewish people across the world</note> of the entire Jewish nation, which the Jews themselves are forced to admit, being well aware of such great confusion; for each person has proof within himself of which tribe...

...it would follow [from the opposing argument] that the phrase *nor a Scribe* <note>original Hebrew: מחוקק (*mechokek*), often translated as lawgiver or staff</note> *from between his feet* <note>A reference to Genesis 49:10</note> would be invalid, since Scribes were not only found among the tribe of Judah, but also among Asher, Levi, and the other tribes; and Scribes recorded and preserved the genealogies not only of the tribe of Judah, but of the other tribes as well. For although those genealogical tables were copied by private individuals and kept quite carefully at home, because those private copies were not official or trustworthy <note>original Greek: $\dot{\alpha}\xi\iota\acute{o}\pi\iota\sigma\tau o\iota$ (*axiopistoi*)</note>, there existed in addition public tables compiled by the Scribes. It is likely that Matthew composed the genealogy of Christ from these public tables, since he reports several details that are not expressly found in the genealogies of the Old Testament, such as the fact that Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab. 

As *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a pioneering Christian historian</note> *observes in book 1 of his History, chapter 7*, Herod zealously sought out these tables to destroy them. He did this partly to hide the royal lineage of the Messiah, the King of the Jews, whose temporal kingdom Herod feared because he himself had usurped it; hence he busied himself with removing the royal offspring not only from the genealogical tables but also from the living. He also did this because, since he himself was of low-born origin, he did not want to be surpassed in nobility by any of the Jews who traced their lineage from kings and patriarchs as if from a high and ancient source. However, if Matthew had disagreed with the public documents or genealogical tables, he surely would have been denounced as a forger from the very start. Yet, because he was not stained by such a blemish, no one before the age of those wicked men—Celsus, Porphyry, and Julian <note>Famous early critics and philosophers who argued against Christian doctrines</note>—dared to tear apart or revile the holy Evangelist.

Therefore, having rejected that opinion concerning the tribe, it now remains that the word *scepter* <note>original Hebrew: שבט (*shevet*)</note> be explained through metonymy <term>metonymy: a figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it, such as "the crown" referring to a King</term>, and thus be understood as *dominion*, or by a double figure of speech as "royal dignity." This is similar to how the word for *Lawgiver* <note>original Hebrew: מחוקק (*mechokek*)</note> signifies the person holding authority. Thus the meaning would be that royal dignity would remain in the tribe of Judah; or, if the royal dignity were abolished, the judicial or legislative <note>original Greek: $\nu o\mu o\theta\epsilon\tau\iota\kappa\acute{\eta}\nu$ (*nomothetikēn*)</note> power denoted by the *Lawgiver* would remain in that tribe until the coming of the Messiah. Nevertheless, this opinion regarding the scepter is still divided into two interpretations. For that scepter is understood either as physical or as spiritual.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Scepter of Judah" from Genesis 49:10, shifting the focus from the royal line of kings to the "Lawgiver"—the judicial authority and the structure of the Jewish court system (Sanhedrin) that maintained Judah's prominence even during periods without a king.</meta>

# ANTHONY CREGUT
### Page 148

...by Moses, not only was the scepter established—whether that signifies royal dignity or dominion—but also the <term>mechoqeq: Lawgiver <note>original Hebrew: מחוקק</note></term>, or judicial power. By this term, the Great Sanhedrin is commonly designated, which did not exist in the other tribes, but only in Judah and in the city of Jerusalem, the metropolis of the entire kingdom, and "in the midst of the feet of Judah." For by the admission of the Rabbis themselves, even in the midst of the Babylonian captivity, the Jews were presided over by a certain descendant of David, whom they called the <term>Head of the Exiles <note>original Latin: "caput deportatorum"; Hebrew: "Resh Galuta"</note></term>. 

After they were liberated from captivity, the descendants of David also held dominion under the title of "leadership," for Zerubbabel was the Leader and Prince of the Jews. In his time, the House of God was rebuilt by those living in Jerusalem, as is evident from the Book of Ezra, chapter 5. Indeed, even later, when the Hasmoneans or Maccabees were in power, the supreme power of judging remained with the <term>Sanhedrin <note>The supreme council and tribunal of the ancient Jewish people</note></term>.

Among the Jews of old, there was a threefold judicial power:

I. The first consisted of **three judges**, and was established only in those places where there were fewer than one hundred and twenty <term>heads of households <note>original Hebrew: בעלי בתים, "ba'alei battim"</note></term>. From this comes that saying of the Rabbis: <term>The Father of the House of Judgment <note>original Hebrew: אב בית דין, "Av Beit Din"</note></term> *does not consist of fewer than three*; so that there may be a majority and a minority—that is, if one of them dissents, two are always in agreement. Likewise, if only two judge, their judgment is not legitimate. Furthermore, it is said: <term>Do not judge alone <note>original Hebrew: אל תהי דן יחידי</note></term>. This assembly judged only <term>monetary disputes <note>original Hebrew: דיני ממונות, "dinei mamonot"</note></term>.

II. The second was constituted of **twenty-three judges** in places where one hundred and twenty or more heads of households lived. That court judged <term>criminal cases <note>original Hebrew: דיני נפשות, "dinei nefashot"</note></term>—those which concerned life—and it was called the <term>Minor Sanhedrin <note>original Hebrew: סנהדרי קטנה</note></term>. It exercised judgment in the gates of the cities, according to the verse: *Establish justice in the gate*, Amos 5:15.

III. The third consisted of **seventy-one judges** and judged only at Jerusalem; it was called the <term>Great Sanhedrin <note>original Hebrew: סנהדרי גדולה</note></term>. This was sanctioned in the Law in Numbers 11:16: *Gather for me seventy men of the elders, etc.* These were to join themselves to Moses, which results in the number seventy-one. <meta>This page continues the analysis of Jewish governance and the Great Sanhedrin, specifically interpreting the famous prophecy of Jacob in Genesis 49:10 regarding the "Scepter" and the "Lawgiver." The author is moving from a description of the council's structure to a linguistic and theological debate over the duration of Jewish authority.</meta>

### ANTHONY CREGUTUS

The **synedrion** <note>original Greek: $\sigma\upsilon\nu\epsilon\delta\rho\iota o\nu$</note>, or Council of 71. Broadly speaking, "scepter" and "Lawgiver" signify in a general sense any kind of dominion and command, whether of one person or many; whether it be Monarchical, Aristocratic, or of another kind; whether simple and purely Political, or a mixture of the Political and the Ecclesiastical or Priestly. Thus the sense is:

> The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor a Lawgiver from between his feet.

Command, or dominion and power, shall not depart from the tribe of Judah until **Shiloh** <note>A title for the Messiah, often interpreted as "he to whom it belongs" or "the bringer of peace"</note> comes; and thus it is not understood specifically as a kingdom or the **Sanhedrin** <note>The supreme judicial and religious council of ancient Israel</note>, but as dominion of whatever kind it might be. Most interpreters embrace the former opinion, for they want "scepter" to be understood strictly as a kingdom, and "Lawgiver" as the judgment of the Seventy. They argue that the royal line lasted until the times of the Messiah, because **Antigonus**, **Hyrcanus**, **Aristobulus**, and the brother of **Mariamne**—the last of the **Hasmoneans** <note>The ruling dynasty of Judea prior to Herod the Great</note>—were suppressed by **Herod**; just as they maintain the Sanhedrin was a council composed of various descendants of David.

But we choose the latter interpretation, though with this limitation: we establish that Jacob, by "scepter" and "Lawgiver," understood any dominion broadly. However, through a Prophetic spirit, he definitely and **significantly** <note>original Greek: σημειωνῶς, meaning by way of a distinct sign</note> designated the *kingdom* as the primary form of government, mentioning it as a more sublime and magnificent dominion. Just as we understand by the term <term>Mechoqeq: Lawgiver <note>original Hebrew: מְחֹקֵק</note></term>—which term the interpreters translate as *Lawgiver*—any kind of power in general that was customary among the Jews. Thus, in this sense, leaders, Priests, and even leaders and Priests joined together can be designated; all of these forms of government prevailed among the Jews at various times.

Several reasons persuade us of this opinion. 1. Because no violence is done to the meaning of the words; the word <term>Shevet: Scepter <note>original Hebrew: שֵׁבֶט</note></term> signifies both a "kingdom" definitely and "dominion" indefinitely, and we assert that both notions fit correctly here. Also, the word *Lawgiver* (<term>Mechoqeq <note>Hebrew: מְחֹקֵק</note></term>) designates something general from its native meaning; for it is the same as one who *establishes, decides, or prescribes*: which can certainly apply perfectly to any government, whether divine or human, civil or ecclesiastical.

<summary>This page explores the interpretation of Genesis 49:10, arguing that the terms "scepter" and "lawgiver" refer to Jewish authority in a broad sense—including priests and leaders—rather than strictly to a king or the Sanhedrin alone. Cregutus argues this flexible definition explains how Jewish rule persisted through various political shifts until the coming of the Messiah.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the linguistic and legal analysis of the "Lawgiver" mentioned in Jacob's prophecy. # THE REVEALER OF SECRETS.

...whether Monarchical or Aristocratic. Hence, in Deuteronomy 4:5, the **statutes of God** are called *statutes* <note>original Hebrew: חקים (*chuqqim*)</note>. Likewise, in Psalm 2:7, the time of the Messiah is called a **decree** <note>original Latin: *statutum*</note>. From this comes that famous division of the threefold Law of God: namely, the **Moral, Ceremonial, and Judicial**, which are denoted by these three words: *commandments, statutes, and judgments* <note>original Hebrew: מצות חקים משפטים (*mitzvot, chuqqim, mishpatim*)</note>. These are often joined together in Holy Scripture when discussing the Law of God, as in Deuteronomy 6:1, and which the Greek translators render as **commandments, ordinances, and judgments** <note>original Greek: ἐντολὰς, δικαιώματα, κρίματα (*entolas, dikaiomata, krimata*)</note>. 

However, the term "Lawgiver" is truly used in respect to that threefold law, although by the usage of Scripture, **statutes** <note>original Hebrew: חקים (*chuqqim*)</note> specifically designates **ordinances** <note>original Greek: δικαιώματα (*dikaiomata*)</note> or sacred rites and the entire ceremonial law. If, in Luke 1:6, only two of those words are joined and **judgments** <note>original Greek: κρίματα (*krimata*)</note> are omitted, the reason is readily apparent: in respect to **ordinances**, Zechariah was one of the leading priests; therefore, it is no wonder if he walked in all the **ordinances**, rites, and constitutions, as Luke records. As for the **commandments** <note>original Greek: ἐντολὰς (*entolas*)</note>—that is, the mandates of the moral law—no faithful person rejects them, least of all Zechariah, who is praised by the same Luke. 

But as for why the Evangelist omitted **judgments**; this happened because the judicial power was for the most part in the hands of the Romans. Yet truly, just as **judgments** <note>original Hebrew: משפטים (*mishpatim*)</note> and **statutes** <note>original Hebrew: חקים (*chuqqim*)</note> are spoken of regarding the ceremonial law, so they are also spoken of regarding the judicial law, which is then explained by the Greeks as **legislation** <note>original Greek: νομοθεσίαν (*nomothesian*)</note>. Indeed, the Apostle seems to have understood it this way in Romans 9:4 when he says: *Who are Israelites; to whom pertain the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises.* In the Greek it reads: *the covenants, the legislation, and the worship* <note>original Greek: καὶ αἱ διαθῆκαι καὶ ἡ νομοθεσία, καὶ ἡ λατρεία</note>. By these, he denotes the **Moral, Judicial, and Ceremonial** Law, so that God’s benevolence might better appear; and he uses the plural "covenants" because there were two **tables of the covenant** <note>original Hebrew: לוחות הברית (*luchot habrit*)</note>. 

Therefore, **judgments** <note>original Hebrew: משפטים (*mishpatim*)</note> and **legislation** <note>original Greek: νομοθεσία (*nomothesia*)</note> are spoken of regarding the supreme power, of whatever kind it might have been—whether royal, or belonging to some High Prince and leader; whether Monarchical or Aristocratic; whether Political, or Ecclesiastical and Priestly; whether separately or combined, such as existed in the **Hasmonean family**, in which the supreme authority, both civil and priestly, was joined. And for that reason, a threefold kind of judges is rightly proved from this:

1. Those who brought the law, the **decreers of the law** <note>original Hebrew: חקקי חק (*choqeqe choq*)</note>, such as were found among the Greeks: Draco, Lycurgus, Solon, and other Lawgivers.

II. From *Chuqqim* <note>original Hebrew: חקים (*chuqqim*)</note>, which sound like **statutes**.
III. From *Mishpatim* <note>original Hebrew: משפטים (*mishpatim*)</note>, which we interpret as **judgments**, laws, or a judicial norm.

The second kind of law depends solely on the will of God; otherwise, no logical reason could be given for regulations of this sort—such as the law that a field must not be sown with different kinds of seeds <note>A reference to the Mosaic prohibition in Leviticus 19:19 against mixing seeds</note>, or that certain sacrifices must be performed with one ritual and others with another. IV. Because our interpretation of those words seems not only to align with the spirit of the sacred authors, but is also consistent with secular writers, both Greek and Latin, ancient and modern. For among those authors, the "sceptre," although it broadly denotes rule and governance, is attributed not only to kings but also to leaders, princes, and lords. Thus, in Homer, not only are kings (and specifically Agamemnon) called *sceptre-bearers* <note>original Greek: σκηπτοῦχοι</note> or *those holding the sceptre* <note>original Greek: σκῆπτρον ἔχοντες</note>, but also the princes who served in the Greek army. This is why Achilles in Homer swore by his sceptre as a symbol of justice, and in the work of the same poet, a sceptre is attributed to the leader Ulysses, with which he struck the back and shoulders of Thersites <note>A character in the Iliad known for being a commoner who criticized the leadership; Ulysses used the sceptre to physically discipline him, demonstrating it was a tool of authority, not just ornament</note>. And truly, since the sceptre is a symbol of *uprightness and severity*, we rightly say it belongs to any supreme rulers and *governing authorities* <note>original Greek: ἐξουσίαις ὑπερεχούσαις</note>, as those in whom uprightness and severity must necessarily hold the primary place.

V. Because no less from this are the *preeminences* <note>original Greek: ὑπεροχαὶ</note> or prerogatives of Judah affirmed; indeed, manifold forms of power and dignity are claimed for the tribe, which from the beginning to the end stood out like a head thrust forward or raised their crests high. The earlier instances were like a prelude: just as there was priority in the order of setting up camp, so too in the offering of gifts; that tribe was also the first in perceiving the inheritance of the land of Canaan, and first in military expeditions, and that by divine oracle. All of these things were certainly, if not the sceptre itself, at least the preludes to the sceptre; but at last, it attained the possession of the sceptre and the governance of the Lawgiver. And although it was later led into the Babylonian captivity, nevertheless (according to Eusebius of Caesarea <note>A 4th-century Christian historian</note>) the *preeminence* <note>original Greek: ὑπεροχὴ</note> of Judah was extraordinary. This was not without the singular providence of God, because that tribe emerged from the Babylonian captivity while the remaining tribes—led away across the Euphrates by Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians—never returned in their entirety to their ancestral soil. And because of those prerogatives of Judah, the "Jews" were named after Judah. By this name all Israelites were called—even those very few who returned from the Assyrian captivity and (according to Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note>) passed into the name and lineage of Judah. For since that people had been disfigured by so many slaughters, and worn down by adverse affairs—

Although I do not deny that others—among whom is Josephus in *Antiquities*, Book 11—claim that this name arose from Judas Maccabeus, under whose leadership the liberty and dignity of the nation breathed again and revived after it had lain collapsed and nearly buried or extinguished for some time. And so, by this naming, the dignity and **ruling authority** <note>original Greek: ἀξίωμα ἀρχικὸν</note> of Judah flourished again, which lasted both in the time of Christ (who is called the *King of the Jews*) and in the time of Paul, who wrote in Romans 11:17, *Behold, you are called a Jew*. And today also it flourishes, as that people is commonly called the Jewish people. Everywhere in Scripture, these prerogatives are proclaimed, as in Romans 3:1: **"What then is the advantage of the Jew?"** <note>original Greek: τί οὖν τὸ περισσὸν τοῦ Ἰουδαίου</note>. The word **advantage** <note>original Greek: περισσὸν; literally "the extra" or "abundance"</note> here signifies excellence and eminence, even if elsewhere, such as in Matthew 5:37, it is taken in a negative sense, where it concerns an oath beyond "yes, yes," and what is added as **extra** <note>original Greek: περισσὸν</note> is from evil. In that passage, the word does not signify a simple addition to the oath, but a superfluous redundancy. Therefore, since the terms "sceptre" and "Lawgiver" are taken so broadly, they are not always spoken of reciprocally as "king" and "law," because for the most part "law" and "Lawgiver" have a broader application than "king" and "kingdom," since they pertain to other rulers and to various states and republics in which both laws and Lawgivers flourished. Thus, the saying of the noble poet is not always valid:

->*Law without a King would have been like light without the Sun.*<-
->*A King without Law would be like the Sun without light.*<-
->*The flock first chose the King; the King with the flock established*<-
->*The Law: hence the King governs both the Law and the flock.*<-

And since law is light—and according to the Hebrews, **the Law is light** <note>original Hebrew: תורה אור (Torah Or)</note> and in Chaldean **the Law** <note>original Chaldean/Aramaic: אורייתא (Oryaita)</note> is called "light," and **an observer of the law** <note>original Aramaic: אוריין (Oryan)</note> is one who follows that light—deservedly that light is extended not only to kings, but also to other lords and **authorities** <note>original Greek: ἐξουσίας</note>.

Thus far the first part has been explained by us, and the first [concerning] Judah...

...prerogative, namely the sceptre and the Lawgiver. Here we have seen, unless I am mistaken, quite fully what the breadth of those notions is and how they are understood in this prophecy. Now follows the second prerogative of Judah, namely the duration of the **sceptre** and the **Lawgiver**. Indeed, that prerogative and the period of its duration will be very clear according to our interpretation and opinion; however, according to the views of others, it will differ not a little from the actual historical outcome, and the truth of this prophecy will not be preserved entirely **intact** <note>original: *sarta tecta*; a Latin legal idiom literally meaning "patched and roofed," signifying something kept in good repair or preserved completely</note>. 

For if by "sceptre" we strictly understand royal dignity, and by "Lawgiver" the Sanhedrin <note>The *Sanhedrin* was the supreme judicial and religious council of the Jewish people, traditionally composed of 71 or 72 members</note>, how will the truth of this oracle stand? Will it really fit correctly with the historical events? It would be as if royal dignity and the authority of the seventy-two judges remained unimpaired until the Messiah. 

But on the contrary, with experience itself as a witness and both sacred and secular authority agreeing, the royal dignity and the supreme council failed before the advent of Christ. First, in the Babylonian captivity, the royal spirit expired when the King of the Chaldeans led Jehoiachin and Zedekiah captive, and those who remained from the sword he carried away into Babylon. Later, under Cyrus king of Persia, those returning from captivity returned not under kings, but under other leaders, such as Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and Nehemiah, as is held in Ezra 2:2 and Nehemiah 1 and 2. 

As long as the Babylonian captivity lasted, there existed that leader who was called the <gloss>Head or Prince of the Captivity</gloss> <note>Hebrew: *Resh Galuta*; Greek: *Aichmalotarches*. This was the title given to the leader of the Jewish community in Babylon</note>. Nor did those leaders and princes (who bore some likeness of royal dignity and monarchical or single-rule governance) hold power much longer; for immediately there succeeded the High Priests, in whose hands was the Majesty and supreme authority. 

This is sufficiently demonstrated by the history of Alexander the Great and Ptolemy Philadelphus. Regarding the former, that king received the High Priest Simon the Just most amicably, even dismounting from his horse and entering into a peace treaty with him. For when he had gone out to the city of Jerusalem to lay it waste, Simon the Just went out to meet him with other priests in priestly attire, after he [Alexander] had previously been warned in a dream. Struck by the sacred majesty of Simon, he showed a reverence that Alexander certainly would not have shown toward a High Priest <meta>catchword: toward</meta>

Since all these things happened before the manifestation of Shiloh <note>A cryptic title from Genesis 49:10 widely interpreted by both Jews and Christians as referring to the Messiah.</note> or the Messiah (I beg you), how will this oracle be plain if interpreted rigidly and according to that literal opinion: *The sceptre shall not depart from Judah until Shiloh comes*? We also want this understood regarding the "Lawgiver," if we interpret that as the Sanhedrin, since by the time of Christ it had already departed. During the reign of Herod and while Roman power occupied supreme command, the majesty of that council was utterly extinguished, and all of Judea was exposed to the mockeries of a powerless tyrant—even if that "fox" <note>A likely reference to the cunning of the Herodian dynasty; in the Gospels (Luke 13:32), Jesus refers to Herod Antipas as "that fox."</note> sometimes flatteringly ensnared the Jews, even professing the Jewish religion, albeit <term>in part</term> <note>original Greek: *ἐκ μέρους* (ek merous)</note>, because he was not fully a Jew but a "half-Jew."

And for this reason, it has been rightly observed by others that three things failed upon Christ’s arrival, which he himself had to fulfill and supply:

I. Royal dignity had long ago failed in that nation; indeed, the line of David was utterly pierced through or extinguished by the tyrant Herod.

II. In Malachi, the last of the Prophets, prophecy also failed, as the Jews themselves admit. They say this was succeeded by the <term>daughter of a voice</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Bat Kol* (בת קול). Hence, regarding Haggai 1:8, Hebrew commentators write that among those five things which were not found in the Second Temple, the spirit of prophecy is numbered.

III. There were no true High Priests before the arrival of Christ, since everything was done at the whim of the Romans...

# ANTHONY CREQUITIUS

<page-num>560</page-num>

Furthermore, it must be admitted that Roman rule was not yet so absolute that a small measure of liberty—however obscure—did not still appear among the Jews. Some spirit and vigor of Jewish laws and rituals still breathed; the soul was still acting and giving life to that political body, even if it resided in some corner in a somewhat languid state, or like a heart palpitating and frequently suffering from deadly fainting spells. This is the source of those bold and unpunished boasts of the Jewish people in *John 8:33*: *We are the seed of Abraham and have never served anyone; how can you say, "You shall be set free"?* Although these words were false and insolent—as is evident from the Egyptian servitude, the Babylonian captivity, and the present Roman yoke—they nonetheless exhaled a certain breath of liberty.

To this we can also relate the "horned dilemma" <note>A logical trap or "catch-22" where both options are designed to incriminate the speaker</note> of the Pharisees posed to Christ in *Matthew 22:17*: *Tell us then, what is your opinion? Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar or not?* For Christ responds in verse 21: *Render therefore unto Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and unto God the things that are God’s.* By this response, the Savior implies that Judea was under the Roman Empire—which was evident from the coinage—and yet not entirely oppressed by the Roman yoke or utterly destitute of power and a Lawgiver. For Christ adds: *Render the things that are God's to God*, by which words he seems to indicate the Sanctuary Shekel <note>original Latin: *siclum Sanctuarij*; a specific tax paid by Jews for the upkeep of the Temple</note>. For just as the "coin of the census" <note>original Greek: *τὸ νόμισμα τοῦ κήνσου*</note> was paid to Caesar as the prince, so the Sanctuary Shekel was weighed out for God, who held dominion over his people by a special right. 

Wherefore, in *1 Samuel 8:7*, Jehovah is angry that the people had demanded a king; thus he said to Samuel: *They have not only rejected you, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.* Yet He could not make the covenant struck with Abraham entirely void. For God reigned over the Jews as long as they remained the people of God, until the coming of the Messiah. For this reason, the Messiah himself was believed by them to be the "King of the Jews," and they expected his kingdom to be a temporal one. This was what Herod feared when he committed that cruel infanticide <note>Refers to the Massacre of the Innocents</note> in the lands of Bethlehem, so that he might strike down the Messiah while he was still a youth. Hence the saying:

->*Wicked enemy Herod, why do you fear the coming of Christ?*<-
->*He who grants heavenly kingdoms does not snatch away mortal ones.*<-

Therefore, when in *Matthew 17:24* Christ pays the *didrachma* <note>original: δίδραχμα; a silver coin worth two drachmas, used here to refer to the half-shekel Temple tax</note>, it is not understood as a poll tax paid to the Romans, nor as the half-shekel of the Sanctuary diverted by the Romans. Rather, it refers to that half-shekel still weighed out for the Sanctuary, which had not yet been diverted by the Romans but was still being paid annually, as can be seen in the writings of Josephus and Maimonides in the *Yad* <note>original: יד; the "Strong Hand" or Mishneh Torah</note>, book 3, which concerns the "Treatise on Times," section 7, regarding shekels. This payment made to the sanctuary displayed a certain image of the "Sceptre" and the "Lawgiver," and proved that it had not departed from Judah until Shiloh <note>A messianic title from Genesis 49:10, often interpreted as "He to whom it belongs"</note> should come.

But afterward, it happened—not without a great mystery—that once the Messiah had been revealed and the Temple, the city, and the entire nation had been cut off and overturned (and thus the Lawgiver and the legal worship utterly abolished), that which was owed to the Temple was diverted by the Romans and consecrated to Jupiter Capitolinus. This was a palpable proof of the rejection of the Jews and the seal on their "bill of divorce." For (as a man of great reputation has rightly observed), that which was for the Jews a pledge of the service they owed to God for their redemption from Egypt was instead consecrated to an idol. Thus, that people would no longer appear to be the people of God, nor would God reign over them, since the Sceptre and that Lawgiver—who had delivered the moral, ceremonial, and judicial Law to the Jewish people—had departed from Judah. These laws were the *commandments, statutes, and judgments* <note>original: מצוות חקים ומשפטים / ἐντολὰς, δικαιώματα & κρίματα</note>.

Hence there is a great distinction between those things that happened during the first Temple and those of the second. Certainly, when the first Temple was destroyed, the shekel was not intercepted; indeed, Belshazzar is punished because he had polluted the vessels of the Temple. But by contrast, during the second Temple, God tolerates the crime of Vespasian when he orders the Sanctuary shekel to be carried to the Roman Capitol. Why was this? It was because, at the destruction of the first Temple, the *Days of the Messiah* <note>original: ימי משיח</note> had not yet arrived, during which the Sceptre and the Lawgiver were to depart from between the feet of Judah.

But truly, with *Shiloh* rising during the time of the second Temple, the Sceptre and the Lawgiver departed from Judah. Hence, although the Scripture proclaimed the glory of the second Temple to be greater than that of the first, nevertheless, no mention is made of a restoration of the second Temple like that of the first. For the Prophets defined the destruction of the [first] Temple, the captivity, and the duration of that captivity. Furthermore, in the first captivity, not all the Jews were transported, but a seed remained...

<meta>This page continues the analysis of how the "Sceptre of Judah" prophecy (Genesis 49:10) aligns with historical transitions of power. The previous page established that Jewish authority was in a state of decay during the Roman era, leading up to the birth of Christ.</meta>

# ANTHONIUS CREGUTIUS
<page-num>564</page-num>

...begins its descent until it finally falls and undergoes a precipitous drop. In the beginnings of its ruin, or its glory destined to fall, liberty is not immediately extinguished even by the victors. The sceptre and the Lawgiver—that is, dominion and power—are not taken away instantly. Instead, by gradual soothing and by prolonging the fruits of victory for a time, the wild beast is finally tamed, and the people are stripped of their rights of their own accord. 

This is evident from the Roman Empire itself, the strongest of all, which did not go to ruin in a single moment. Rather, its liberty was first agitated or tested by Sulla and Pompey, then more strongly and boldly attacked by Caesar, and finally conquered by the Triumvirate and, most of all, by Augustus. Nevertheless, some authority of the Senate still remained; for many centuries after Augustus, good Emperors attempted nothing without the authority of the Senate. Even today in Rome, in its most corrupt state, the authority of the Senators has not entirely failed. Indeed, in the year 1267, **perpetual Senators** were created—just as **perpetual Dictators** once were—such as Charles, the brother of King Saint Louis of France. These perpetual Senators even presided over the election of the Pope, as Charles did when Nicholas III was elected, as is clear from the history of Platina <note>Bartolomeo Platina (1421–1481), a papal historian</note> regarding Nicholas III, from Stella, and others. 

A similar change occurred in the Jewish kingdom; for after various shifts, authority and power failed gradually. First, the royal majesty was extinguished under the dominion of the Chaldeans <note>The Neo-Babylonian Empire under Nebuchadnezzar</note>. Then followed the governorship in the time of Zerubbabel. Later, the entire authority of the nation devolved to the Priests. Finally, their authority passed to the Hasmoneans <note>The Maccabean dynasty that ruled Judea</note>, who joined both the political and priestly regimes. When these, along with their entire lineage, were exterminated under Herod the Great, that tyrant—with the Romans nodding their heads and even granting it—usurped civil power, leaving the priesthood to the Priests. It was under that state of affairs that Shiloh <note>original: "Schilo"; a traditional title for the Messiah</note> was revealed according to the oracle. Therefore, in that prophecy of Jacob, when it is said:

> *the sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a Lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh comes.*

These words cannot be understood, first, as referring to the royal sceptre, since it is clear that the Kings failed under Nebuchadnezzar during the Babylonian captivity. Jacob is also not speaking of governors, since before the times of Alexander the Great...

...they had failed, and yet Shiloh had not yet arrived. Moreover, this is not understood as referring to the Priests who preceded the **Hasmoneans** <note>The ruling dynasty of Judea between 140 and 37 BCE, also known as the Maccabees</note>, nor to the Hasmoneans who held both the royal and priestly powers joined together, because their authority also failed under **Herod**, and still Shiloh had not come. What, then, shall we choose in these perplexed and intricate thickets of argument? For on both sides there are difficulties and riddles in this wrapping of the oracle; for if we say the time of the Hasmoneans is precisely noted—since it was then that the sceptre and the Lawgiver departed from Judah—someone might object, and not undeservedly, that Shiloh had not yet come; and according to the prophecy, the sceptre shall not depart *until* Shiloh comes. 

If, however, to solve this knot, you extend the time until the destruction of the city and the temple, you will fall into **Scylla while trying to avoid Charybdis** <note>A classical metaphor for trying to avoid one danger only to fall into another</note>; for the sceptre and the Lawgiver seem to have already departed under Herod once the Hasmoneans were subdued and destroyed. 

But so that we may at last extricate ourselves from these intricacies, we assert that both are true, and nonetheless the sound truth of the oracle remains protected. For even if the dominion and legislative authority were expiring under the Romans and Herod, it did not breathe its last breath until Shiloh, or the **Messiah**, himself expired. Since the true King of the Jews was rejected and crucified by ungrateful and treacherous subjects, their liberty and power also had to die and be utterly extinguished. The **shekel** <note>original: "siclo" — refers to the Temple tax formerly paid to God/the Jewish King, which after the Roman conquest was diverted to the Temple of Jupiter in the Roman Capitol</note> formerly paid to the legitimate King was by then transferred to the Capitol, so that those who had crucified the King of the Jews and demanded Caesar as their King should thereafter serve a tyrant in perpetual servitude **in the kingdom of impiety** <note>original Hebrew: במלכות הרשעה (*be-malkhut ha-resha'ah*)</note>; for so the Rabbis themselves today call the Roman Empire. 

Therefore, all these things were done not without mystery and the highest wisdom of God, nor could they have been managed by a wiser **economy** <note>In this context, "economy" refers to God’s plan or administration of human history</note>. Since Christ came while the dominion of the Jews was expiring under Herod, he did so timely to bring help to his people struggling in the greatest straits, so that as the true King, Prophet, and Priest, he might restore the kingdom, prophecy, and priesthood that were fallen and wavering. The Gospel parable in Matthew 21:33 describes how the owner sought the fruits of the vineyard from the farmers and suffered a rejection before he would destroy them, and before he would take away the kingdom of God and give it to a nation that would produce its fruit, as is held in the same chapter, verse 43. For *he was sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel* <note>original Latin: "missus erat ad oues perditas domus Israel"</note> Matthew 15:24. This was also because if the glory and liberty of the Israelite people, or the authority of the Priests, had utterly collapsed, the Messiah could not have been judged and condemned by them according to the Prophecies and decrees. This follows what is written in Psalm 118:22, Matthew 21:42, Acts 4:11, Romans 9:33, and 2 Peter 2:7: *The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner; this was done by the Lord, and it is wonderful in our eyes.*

For this reason, even after the death of Christ, the authority of the "first men" or rulers <note>Greek: ἀρχόντων, *archonton*</note> and the elders is recounted in various places in Scripture; as is clear in Acts 4:5–6: *And it happened on the first day that their rulers, and elders, and Scribes were gathered together in Jerusalem, as well as Annas the High Priest, and Caiaphas, and John, and Alexander, and as many as were of the high-priestly lineage.*

These rulers <note>Greek: ἀρχόντες, *archontes*</note>—that is, the "first men"—were still a certain shadow and specimen of that Sanhedrin <note>The supreme council and tribunal of the Jews</note>, or council <note>Greek: συνεδρίῳ, *synedrio*</note>, which was from the tribe of Judah, before Herod raged most cruelly against the lineage of David. These rulers or "first men" seem to correspond to the "princes" or "first men" <note>Hebrew: השרים, *ha-Sarim*</note> mentioned in Jeremiah 26:10. This will be apparent to anyone considering the similar gathering and the similar form of judgment used against both the Prophet Jeremiah and the Apostle Peter. For on both sides, there are the "princes" or "first men," the Elders, the Priests, and the Scribes—whom Jeremiah calls "the prophets" <note>Hebrew: הנביאים, *ha-Nebiim*; Greek: Προφήτας, *Prophetas*</note>. However, the name of the Scribes is missing in the Arabic version, which supports the fact that Peter, in his later defense, does not address them specifically by name; hence one might rightly say they were included under the name of the elders.

Therefore, the rulers <note>Greek: οἱ ἀρχόντες</note>—that is, the "first men" or "princes" as the Vulgate translator renders it—according to that passage in Jeremiah 26:10 <note>Hebrew: השרים, *ha-Sarim*</note>, were certain remnants of the Sanhedrin, or some obscure shadow of the Lawgiver and his weak power. The *Elders* were truly those from among the people who were influential in authority and dignity, and who sat together with them in solemn judgments. Joined to these were the Scribes and the Priests <note>Hebrew: הכהנים, *ha-Kohanim*</note>, that is, the High Priests <note>Greek: Ἀρχιερεῖς, *Archiereis*</note>, whose authority was the greatest, as those who...

...who would gather the council; as is clear from Acts 5:21. And truly the words of Christ in Matthew 5:22 concerning the judgment <note>Greek: περὶ τῆς κρίσεως, *peri tēs kriseōs*</note>, the council <note>Greek: συνεδρίῳ, *synedriō*</note>, and the hell of fire <note>Greek: γεέννης τοῦ πυρὸς, *geennēs tou pyros*</note> indicate sufficiently that after the coming of Shiloh <note>A reference to the Messiah, based on the prophecy in Genesis 49:10</note>, some shadow of judgments and the Council or Sanhedrin remained among the Jews. For there, by "the council" <note>Greek: τὸ συνέδριον, *to synedrion*</note>, Christ understands the *small council* <note>Hebrew: *Sanhedrin ketanna*</note> consisting of 23 judges; and by "the hell of fire," he understands the *great council* <note>Hebrew: *Sanhedrin gedola*</note> of 71 judges, whose penalty was fire. For the small Sanhedrin judged *financial disputes* <note>Hebrew: *dinei mamonot*</note>; but the great Sanhedrin judged *capital cases* <note>Hebrew: *dinei nefashot*</note>; therefore, Christ adapted the passage in Matthew 5:22 to the civil law of the Israelites, among whom (as is established from the Babylonian book of the *Sanhedrin* <note>A tractate of the Talmud dealing with law and punishments</note>) that supreme council used a fourfold type of punishments; before Herod—and after Herod the Romans—had disturbed this whole order: namely, strangling, the sword, stoning, and burning. 

Therefore, in the time of Christ, there stood a Lawgiver and a certain form of jurisdiction among the Jews—indeed, the great Sanhedrin itself—but it was greatly fractured and disempowered because the time of Christ's death was imminent. Thus, the power of capital judgment had been taken away from them by the Romans, which is why Christ necessarily had to be condemned by the Romans, the masters of the Jews, according to that passage in John 18:31: *It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death* <note>Greek: ἡμῖν οὐκ ἔξεστιν ἀποκτεῖναι οὐδένα, *hēmin ouk exestin apokteinai oudena*</note>. This was because Judea was administered by the Emperor's procurator <note>Latin: *rationalem*</note>, in whose hands was the <term>ius gladii: the "right of the sword," or the legal power to execute a person</term>. 

Therefore, when Pilate says, *Judge him according to your law* <note>Greek: κατὰ τὸν νόμον κρίνατε αὐτὸν, *kata ton nomon krinate auton*</note>, he speaks insultingly, it seems, and ironically <note>Greek: εἰρωνικῶς, *eironikōs*</note>. Nor did this fall sluggishly upon their ears, but touched by his biting word, they respond: *It is not permitted for us to kill anyone*. You know that the right of the sword has been taken from us; it is your place, therefore, not ours, to punish him. But if Pilate did not speak ironically, then our opinion is all the more confirmed: that civil authority and judgments had not yet completely departed from the Jews. It is no wonder, then, if Christ was fixed to a cross, because crucifixion <note>Greek: σταύρωσις, *staurōsis*</note> was in use only by the Romans, who used that kind of punishment on obscure, despicable men and lowly slaves. And the Rabbis themselves deny that it was the custom of their ancestors to fix criminals to a cross. This is what Christ himself had predicted...

This legal context explains why Christ was tried by the Jews but executed by the Romans via crucifixion, a non-Jewish penalty.</summary>

Matthew 20:19. *And they shall deliver him to the Gentiles to be mocked, and scourged, and crucified.* This is read as fulfilled in John 18:32: *signifying by what death he was about to die* <note>original Greek: σημάνων ποίῳ θανάτῳ ἔμελλεν ἀποθνήσκειν</note>. Therefore, from the things said above, one should observe that a wonderful Divine Providence shone forth in the fulfillment of this oracle and in this entire divine plan <note>original: *oeconomia*—referring to God's management of human history</note>. Then, under Pompey <note>The Roman general who conquered Jerusalem in 63 BCE</note>, although Judea was struck and crushed by a great disaster, with taxes exacted and the threshold [of the Temple] profaned; nevertheless, the Lawgiver <note>Hebrew: מחוקק</note> and self-governance <note>original Greek: αὐτονομία (*autonomia*)</note> had not yet departed, because Pompey restored the High Priesthood <note>original Greek: τὴν ἀρχιερωσύνην (*tēn archierōsynēn*)</note> to the Jew Hyrcanus, as Josephus testifies in *Antiquities*, Book 14, Chapter 8; and thus some form of government remained among the Hasmoneans <note>The ruling dynasty of Judea before the Herodian period</note>. Finally, under Herod and the powerful Romans, under whom the Jewish Empire seemed utterly defeated and destroyed without hope, some small spark of glory still flashed, which indicated that freedom was not entirely dead, but nearly so, gasping its last breath; for the Council of the first men, elders, scribes, and High Priests <note>original Greek: ἀρχιερέων (*archiereōn*)</note> was still assembled, as is clear from the previously praised passage in Acts chapter 5. Some Sanhedrin <note>The supreme judicial and religious council of the Jews</note> still remained, although mutilated in one arm, because it did not judge criminal cases, the "right of the sword" <note>the power to execute capital punishment</note> having been forbidden to them by the Romans; hence Christ, in Matthew 5:22, did not wish to think lightly of its authority, since he made honorable [mention of it]...

But furthermore, observe the most wise moderation of God in this entire Divine Plan <note>original: *Oeconomia*—referring to God's management of human history</note>; for that highest Moderator of all things did not want the matter established in extremes. He did not want it to occur in the highest glory and authority of the Jews, such as existed in the magnificence of David or Solomon; nor did God want Shiloh <note>A title for the Messiah derived from the prophecy in Genesis 49:10</note> to be revealed in the extreme oppression of the Jewish nation when their empire was entirely destroyed. Instead, He held a middle path between these extremes: namely, so that the authority of the Jews would be greatly weakened and almost lifeless, yet not entirely dead or extinguished. First, that Jewish glory ought not to have shone out while glowing at its zenith, because this would have been contrary to the goal of the Prophecy. The prophecy points out a characteristic sign <note>original Greek: τεκμήριον (*tekmērion*)</note> for us to recognize the Messiah based on that removal of the scepter and the Lawgiver; without this, he would not have been so graphically depicted. Second, it ought not to have occupied the other extreme, because if the entire nation had been cut off and deleted by total destruction <note>original Greek: πανολεθρίᾳ (*panolethria*)</note>, as happened in the later destruction of the temple, how could the Messiah, the King of the Jews, have visited his people? How could he have promised them liberation, provided they did not refuse their freedom? How could that greatest Prophet have instructed his disciples? How could that High Priest have purified his temple and soon sacrificed himself? How could that stone have been rejected by the builders? Therefore, it was divinely brought about that there should be this balance between the extremes; namely, so that the power of the Jews would be greatly undermined and their empire as if expiring, so that the Messiah might thus be recognized. By this sign, it would be made clear that the time was at hand for the oracles to be fulfilled—especially that one in Genesis 49. Because of this, everyone at that time was waiting for the Messiah with intent eyes and perked ears, as if he were standing on the threshold. God wished to reveal him in that moment of agony and desperate affairs, so that the most afflicted nation might breathlessly embrace its liberator. But Shiloh was manifested before the total destruction, so that by embracing him and adoring him as the legitimate King, the Empire might be restored; or, on the contrary, for those guilty of rebellion, and on account of **hatred without cause** <note>original Hebrew: שנאת חנם (*sinat chinam*)—a Rabbinic concept explaining why the Second Temple was destroyed</note>...

Nor is the objection of some people valid—that the scepter was not removed immediately after the death of Christ according to our view and the words of the prophecy: *the scepter shall not be removed until Shiloh <note>A traditional title for the Messiah from Genesis 49:10</note> comes.* For this removal was only fulfilled many years later when the city was cut off and the temple burned. It is not valid, I say: First, regarding the prophecy, because it does not intend that the Jewish empire and nation be destroyed immediately upon the Messiah being presented. For the prophecy does not say this; but merely that the scepter is not to be taken away until Shiloh comes. Therefore <note>Hebrew: *ad ki yavo*</note> "Until he comes" defines the past time that preceded the arrival of Shiloh, so that by that sign <note>original: *charactere*</note> he might be recognized when he had arrived. It does not, however, accurately determine the future time as if it were necessary that immediately after the Messiah was presented, the Jewish nation should perish by total destruction <note>original Greek: πανωλεθρίᾳ (*panolethria*)</note>. For if the words of the prophecy were so strictly applied, that nation would have been cut off not only after the death of Christ, but even shortly after his birth.

Second, I add that according to our opinion, that nation ought not to have been exterminated immediately after the death of Christ, because the Apostles had to be sent to the Jews; the Gospel was to emerge from Zion <note>original: *Tsijon*</note> according to the Prophets; and on the day of Pentecost, while the Disciples were gathered in Jerusalem, the Holy Spirit had to be poured out abundantly according to the prophecy of Joel, chapter 2, so that there might be a passage from the Synagogue into the Church, and from the Jews to the Christians. Hence Acts 13:46: *It was necessary for the word of God to be spoken to you first; but since you reject it, and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles.* Therefore Jacob adds: <note>Hebrew: *v'lo yiqhat ammim*</note> "and to him shall be the gathering of the peoples."

Nevertheless, I do not favor the opinion of those who claim the scepter was not taken away in the time of Herod on the grounds that he was himself a Jew and thus the ruling dignity <note>original Greek: ἀρχικὸν ἀξίωμα (*archikon axioma*)</note> did not depart from Judah; they cite the words of the Midrash <note>A genre of ancient Jewish rabbinic biblical commentary</note> on Deuteronomy 17:15. For when that Royal Law was read to the King: *In appointing a king, you shall appoint over you a king whom the Lord your God chooses, from among your brothers, etc. You may not appoint a foreigner, etc.* Herod Agrippa <note>King of Judea, grandson of Herod the Great</note>, as it is recorded in the Midrash, when he came to that passage and remembered that although he was a Jew by religion, he was an Idumean <note>A descendant of Esau/Edom, rather than a native Israelite</note> by birth, began to wail aloud...

began. Indeed, he ordered the people to be of good cheer, for they knew him to be their brother, even though he was born of a servant. This was also observed by <term>the late</term> <note>original Greek: ὁ μακαρίτης (*ho makarites*)</note> Philippe de Mornay <note>A prominent French Protestant writer and statesman (1549–1623)</note>, a man distinguished by nobility, learning, and heroic and Christian gifts, in his book *On the Truth of the Christian Religion*, chapter 29. Herod was succeeded by Archelaus, who, although banished by the Romans after ten years, nevertheless saw the royal dignity pass into Herod's bloodline—specifically to Herod Agrippa, his grandson through his son Aristobulus, and then to Agrippa the Younger, the son of the former...

-> # ANTHONY CREGUT <-
<note>Anthony Cregut (1623–1697) was a Reformed theologian and professor; this work likely reflects a 17th-century academic defense of Christian prophecy.</note>

In the <insert>eighth</insert> year of the Emperor Claudius, he was granted the kingdom of Chalcis; in the twelfth year of Claudius, he was granted the territories of his uncle Philip and of Lysanias. Later, Nero granted him part of Galilee, Tiberias, and other places. He survived until the third year of Trajan <note>Agrippa II, the last of the Herodian dynasty, who died around 100 AD</note>, and for thirty years after the destruction of Jerusalem, he still enjoyed <term>the dignity of authority</term> <note>original Greek: ἀρχῆς ἀξιώματι (*archēs axiōmati*)</note>. Therefore, if Herod and the Herodians had been true Jews, <term>the logic would falter</term> <note>original Latin: *aqua hærebit*, literally "the water will get stuck," a Roman idiom for being in a difficult position</note> in the explanation of the Prophecy, because the scepter would not have been removed from Judah before "Shiloh" <note>A cryptic title for the Messiah from Genesis 49:10</note> arrived; thus, this <term>sign</term> <note>original Greek: σημείον (*sēmeion*)</note> of the Messiah, by which he was to be recognized, would have been marked in vain. Since Herod was not of the Hebrew race, the scepter began to depart from Judah as if wounded by a lethal blow; yet (as we have seen) the Empire was not utterly destroyed until the destruction of the city and the temple. At that time, once the Jews were completely cut off, that King of the Jews—the Messiah—conquered the Nations with the scepter of the word of God and acquired them for himself.

Since Christians today interpret that oracle in such various ways and do not at all <term>agree in opinion</term> <note>original Greek: ὁμοψηφῶνται (*homopsēphōntai*)</note> regarding the time of his arrival, it is no wonder if the ancient Jews themselves were anxious about the Messiah, his name, and the time of his coming. For the writers of the <term>Talmud</term> <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism</note> in the volumes *Pesachim*, *Nedarim*, and *Sanhedrin* list various names for him. Those from the school of Rabbi Shela say the Messiah’s name is **Shiloh**, based on the verse: *until Shiloh comes*. Those of the school of Rabbi Janna insist it is **Jinnon**, based on: *Jinnon is his name* <note>Referring to Psalm 72:17</note>. Others say **Chanina**, based on: *I will show you no favor* <note>A play on the Hebrew word for "favor" or "grace," Chanina</note>. Others say **Menachem**, based on: *Menachem, that is the comforter, has gone far from me*. Others say **the Leprous one**, based on: *surely he has borne our infirmities* <note>Isaiah 53:4; in the Talmud, this led to a tradition of the Messiah sitting among the lepers at the gates of Rome</note>. However, when later Jews—worse than their predecessors—noticed that all the deadlines established by the ancients had passed and the Messiah they sought (that is, a temporal King) had not come, they forbade anyone from calculating the time of his arrival under a curse; hence the saying: **May the spirit of those who calculate the ends be broken.** <note>original Hebrew: תיפח רוחן של מחשבי קצין (*Tippach ruchan shel mechashei kitzin*)</note>

And let this conclude the discussion on the second <term>excellence</term> <note>original Greek: ἐξοχῇ (*exochē*)</note> or prerogative of Judea. Now, let us begin the third, which is the eminence of the scepter and the Lawgiver, which is expressed in these words:

-> ### REVEALER OF SECRETS ### <-
<note>The header "REVELATOR ARCANORVM" suggests this is part of a series of theological revelations or a specific treatise on hidden meanings in Scripture.</note>

It is taken from the phrase <note>original Hebrew: עד כי יבא שילה (*ad ki yavo Shiloh*)</note> **until Shiloh comes**. For when the temporal scepter and the earthly Lawgiver had failed in that notable period discussed previously, Shiloh finally approaches—He whose scepter is eternal and who is the heavenly Lawgiver, who has the power to save and to destroy. For as long as Judea was the Church of God, the scepter remained in the tribe of Judah and the Lawgiver stayed "between his feet"; but once that nation killed the Lord of Glory, the Messiah, the scepter was taken away from Judah. Yet, immediately, a more eminent and more splendid rule emerged: namely, that of the King of the Jews, whose Empire was extended from sea to sea. Therefore, let the third prerogative of Judah be the eminence of this second scepter, which appeared when Shiloh emerged from that tribe. For if it is said in **Matthew 2:6**: *“And you, Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for out of you shall come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel,”* then much more shall the tribe of Judah be called "not the least"—by <term>meiosis</term> <note>a rhetorical figure of speech where an understatement is used to emphasize the greatness of something</note>, that is, "most excellent"—because from her emerged that leader and king, Shiloh. He is the **shoot from the root of Jesse**, who expanded his branches and leafy vines far and wide to the ends of the earth.

That the name **Shiloh** signifies the Messiah, we proceed to prove by various reasons:

I. It is evident from the **Jerusalem Targum** <note>an Aramaic translation and expansion of the Hebrew Bible</note> and the **Chaldean Paraphrase**, which translate this word as <note>original Aramaic: משיחא (*Meshicha*)</note> **the Messiah**. Most Rabbis also agree with this.

II. It is evident from the origin of the word itself, as it is derived from the word *shil*, which denotes **the afterbirth or placenta**, and by <term>metonymy</term> <note>a figure of speech where a related term stands in for the thing itself</note> refers to the **offspring**. The afterbirth is that membrane in which the infant is wrapped in the mother's womb; this is intended to signify that the Messiah had to be born as an infant and procreated not by a man, but by a woman. In this word, the letter *He* (ה) is used as a suffix in place of *Vav* (ו), as often happens. Therefore, **Shiloh** will be the same as <note>original Hebrew: בנו (*beno*)</note> **his son**—that is, the son of Judah, born of his lineage. Hence, **Abraham Ibn Ezra** <note>a celebrated 12th-century Spanish rabbi and scholar</note> says Shiloh is the same as **his son**, and the *He* is in place of the *Vav*, as seen in the word for <note>original Hebrew: אהלה (*aholo*)</note> **his tent**. **Rabbi Bechai** <note>Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century commentator</note> in his commentary on Genesis 49:10 also states that *Shiloh* is a word derived from the meaning of the word <note>original Hebrew: בשליתה (*be-shilyatah*)</note> **in her afterbirth** (Deuteronomy 28:57). Jacob used the word "Shiloh" rather than "his son" to hint that he was speaking specifically about the Messiah, etc. 

As for the fact that the **Septuagint** <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translates this as <note>original Greek: ᾧ ἀπόκειται (*hō apokeitai*)</note> **to whom it is reserved** or **the things laid up for him**—that is, the one for whom the scepter is reserved, or he to whom the empire belongs—just as...
