The same <term>Chaldean Paraphrast</term> <note>This refers to the *Targum*, an ancient Aramaic translation and interpretation of the Hebrew Bible</note> also holds that the word **Shiloh** is placed for **to whom it belongs** <note>original Hebrew: *lo asher*</note>. This interpretation can be confirmed from **Ezekiel 21:27**: *“A ruin, a ruin, a ruin I will make it; this also shall not be, until he comes to whom judgment belongs; and I have delivered it.”* In this passage, the Prophet alludes to the text of **Genesis 49:10**. However, from these things it is clear that the Chaldean and the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament, often abbreviated as LXX</note> read **Shiloh** <note>Hebrew: שילה</note> in the original manuscript, rather than **Sheluh** <note>Hebrew: שלה</note>, as the <term>Vulgate</term> <note>The standard Latin translation of the Bible</note> translator did when he rendered it as *“he who is to be sent,”* deriving it from the root *shalah* (to send). Unless, perhaps, it is better to say that the translator followed the intended sense of the oracle rather than the literal meaning of the word—since in truth Christ was to be "sent" to redeem the human race. Or, we might say he indeed read **Shiloh** in the Hebrew just as the Chaldeans and the Septuagint did, but because he was ignorant of that word's <term>etymology</term> <note>the origin and history of a word</note>, he thought it should be read as *Sheluh*, both because the two words sounded similar and were thus easily interchangeable, and because the sense fit: for the Messiah was to be sent by the Father. Therefore, the Jews are falsely and unjustly accused of the crime of <term>plagiarism</term> <note>here meaning "textual corruption" or "forgery"</note>, as if out of hatred for Christ and Christians they corrupted this passage and wrote *Shiloh* instead of *Sheluh*.

**iii.** By deriving **Shiloh** from *shalah*, which means "to be tranquil." Thus, in the word *Shiloh*, the "h" at the end is not a grammatical suffix but part of the root, because the Messiah is *Shilo* <gloss>quiet/tranquil</gloss>, the author of eternal tranquility. 

**iv.** If **Shiloh** is read as a compound word made of *shai* (meaning "gift") and *lo* (meaning "to him"), it signifies that gifts are to be offered to the Messiah as King as a symbol of subjection.

**v.** Finally, the entire assembly of Hebrew Teachers can be brought forth in support. For not only does the triple <term>Targum</term> support us—namely the Chaldean paraphrases of Onkelos, Jonathan, and the Jerusalem Targum, in which **The Messiah** <note>original Aramaic: *Mashiacha*</note> is read in place of *Shiloh*—but also the <term>Talmudists</term> and the ancient book **Bereshit Rabbah** <note>An early Jewish commentary (Midrash) on Genesis</note>, as well as later Jewish scholars like Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note>, Kimchi, Bechai, and others.

**vi.** I add the mystical theologians themselves, or <term>Cabalists</term>, who through <term>Gematria</term> <note>a system where letters represent numbers, and words with the same numerical total are thought to be related</note> find in the letters of the phrase **Shiloh shall come** <note>original Hebrew: *Yavo Shiloh*</note> the number **358**, which is the exact same number found in the word **Messiah**. Thus, it is understood mystically that Shiloh is truly the Messiah. But immediately they spit their venom against the Messiah when they deny that this Shiloh, or Messiah, was **Jesus of Nazareth**; whom for that reason they do not—

O nation blinded by the thickest <term>scotoma</term> <note>A medical term for a blind spot in the vision; here used metaphorically for spiritual blindness</note>! O raging and unbridled malice! VII. There is a wondrous allusion between the words **Shiloh** and **Siloam**, not only regarding their sound and endings, but also regarding their meaning. For just as **Shiloh** is the Messiah, so **Siloam** (in Hebrew, *Shiloach*) means **Sent**; which is truly said of the Messiah. For this reason, in **John 9:7**, the blind man was sent by Christ into that pool to wash his eyes, which had been blind from birth, in order to recover his sight. By this, Christ seems to hint that our natural blindness can be healed nowhere else but in his own blood—that is, in himself, who had been sent by the Father as our Redeemer. 

Because of this, that spring is believed by some to have been the pool of **Bethesda** (**John 9:7, 11**) <note>The author appears to link the pool of Siloam in John 9 with the pool of Bethesda in John 5</note>, which means **house of outpouring**, or according to the Syriac translator, *Beth Chesda* <note>original Hebrew: בית חסדא</note>, the **house of kindness**. This title truly fits Christ, who is the perennial fountain of all graces and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. As Josephus testifies in *The Jewish War*, Book 6, Chapter 6: it was **a sweet and abundant fountain** <note>original Greek: πηγὴ γλυκει̃α τε καὶ πολλὴ</note>. 

And yet, the same author in **chapter 11** reports that Siloam and all the springs outside the city failed before the arrival of Titus <note>The Roman General, later Emperor, who destroyed Jerusalem in 70 AD</note> when he was about to besiege it; but once the city was besieged, the waters flowed generously for the Romans. Josephus says the same thing happened when the Babylonians besieged and conquered Jerusalem during the reign of Zedekiah. Mystically, this signified that the Messiah—the springing fountain and the true Siloam—had "failed" among the Jews, and the streams of grace had dried up for them so they might overflow abundantly upon the Gentiles.

I will pass over the fact that in **Nehemiah 2:13**, that spring is called the **Serpent’s Well** or (in Hebrew) the **Dragon’s Well**, because of its slow and creeping flow; but mystically it signified Him who extinguishes the lethal poison of the serpent or dragon. For that fountain was like a regular miracle in Judea, healing all diseases and ailments, but it lost its supernatural property after **Shiloh** <note>The Messiah</note> deserted the Jews; for then both Shiloh and Siloam failed.

Since, therefore, the Messiah is understood by the name **Shiloh**, and the Prophet says **until Shiloh comes** <note>original Hebrew: עד כי-יבא שילה (*Ad ki-yavo Shiloh*)</note>, this passage concerns the coming of the Messiah, in which the prerogative of Judah is further exalted; and this...

# ANTHONY CREGUTUS

In this way, Judah is preferred over the other tribes; for either the scepter was never among them, or if it was briefly in Israel, the scepter immediately departed from **Ephraim** <note>The leading tribe of the northern Kingdom of Israel, often used as a name for the whole northern kingdom</note>, since the ten tribes were carried away into the **Assyrian** captivity, from which they never returned. But truly, in **Judah**, the scepter remained until the final times, which occurred under the Messiah. For Jacob said, *the scepter shall not depart from Judah until...* At which time a more splendid and powerful scepter would arise from Judah—namely, that of the Messiah, just as it had been mystically promised to **David** when his kingdom was said to be eternal. Therefore, that arrival of the Messiah is rightly considered by us to be the third **blessing** <term>εὐλογίᾳ (*eulogia*): a Greek term for a formal blessing or praise</term> of Judah. 

For if that tribe was then rejected along with the others and the temporal kingdom taken away from it, this happened incidentally because of the unbelief of the Jews, who first drove out and crucified the Messiah himself. Indeed, that prediction by Jacob concerning the removal of the scepter was not only a identifying sign for recognizing the Messiah, but also a threat against the Jews regarding the taking away of the scepter due to their rebellion. Although all these things were decreed from eternity in the secret counsel of God, nevertheless their fulfillment and outcome have specific causes depending on human freedom, which can in no way be forced or hindered by the necessity, infallibility, or immutability of God’s decrees.

It is clear, however, that this oracle refers to the second coming of Christ. For although Scripture describes various "comings" to us—such as the first in "prelude," when (**Tertullian** says) he gave a prelude of his future incarnation by appearing to the Patriarchs and taking on a body like a garment, not as a form giving life to the soul, and much less in a **hypostatic union** <term>The theological doctrine that Christ is one person with two distinct natures, divine and human</term>, but as an assisting form. Whence (the Church Fathers say) *he had not come to be born, and therefore not to die.* 

And such was the other coming in the preaching of the cross through the proclamation of the Gospel, of which **John** himself speaks in chapter 21:22 when he responded to Peter: *If I wish him to remain until I come, what is that to you?* For that passage does not concern the final coming on the Day of Judgment—a point not sufficiently considered by those **charlatans** <note>original: *agyrtæ*, referring to wandering quacks or religious impostors</note> who, abusing this passage, devised various fables. Indeed, in this past century, the impostor of **Toulouse** <note>original: *Thelozæ*. This likely refers to a 16th-century religious pretender or heretic executed in the French city of Toulouse</note> was burned.

...there was one who openly claimed to be John, and whom another scoundrel, Postellus <note>Guillaume Postel (1510–1581), a French linguist and mystic known for his eccentric religious theories</note>, called his brother at Paris, and who boasted that he possessed the soul of Adam, the first-formed. Nevertheless, Scripture has declared to us two advents of Christ in particular. The first advent was in the appearance of the flesh of sin, so that it might be *concerning sin* <note>original: περὶ ἁμαρτίας (*peri hamartias*)</note> (Romans 8:3), that is, that He might offer Himself as a sacrifice for sin. But the other Messiah will be the son of David, who will destroy **Armilos**, that is, the anti-messiah. Do these things not seem to foreshadow, as if through a cloud, the double advent of Christ? # ANTHONY CREGUT

...for whenever they <note>Referring to the Jewish prophets or contemporary Jewish interpreters mentioned on the previous page</note> prophesy concerning the coming of the Messiah, they always seem to have confused his double advent into one. The same thing happens to them as happens to those who look from a distance at two towers; though they are far apart, because they are positioned in the same line of sight, the viewer assumes they actually merge into one. Yet, once one has traveled closer to them, the gap and the distinction between them is easily perceived. In this way, if the Jews of today were not blind, and if their minds had not been clouded <note>original: *mens non læua*, a classical idiom suggesting a foolish or ill-fated mindset</note>, they would recognize that double coming of Christ. Indeed, far from the first coming having not occurred, the second is already pressing near and Christ is already "greeting the threshold," as Christ himself hints in the Gospel. For as often as he speaks of his coming, he speaks of it as a thing most near at hand; a manner of speaking which the Apostles did not disdain to imitate.

Since, therefore, it is clear that there is a double coming of Christ, Christians do not doubt which advent the Prophet speaks of in this oracle <note>Likely referring to the prophecy of the "Scepter of Judah" in Genesis 49:10</note>, since it is clearer than the sun that the Prophet designates the first coming of Christ there. For the events would not correspond to a second coming. Nor does it stand in the way that this first coming was humble and in the "form of a servant," and therefore might not seem to fit with the eminence of a scepter, nor relate to us a third aspect of Judah in an <term>inglorious</term> <note>original: ἀδόξῳ (*adoxō*), meaning without fame, honor, or glory</note> state. For of old, the light shone in the midst of darkness, and the form of a servant did not hide the form of God; for even as an infant in the manger he was adored by the Magi, the Angels sang their chorus, and the Father and the Holy Spirit bore witness to the Son when he was dipped in the waters of baptism. From this, note the remarkable skill of Paul in the 2nd chapter of 2 Timothy, verse 10, where speaking of this prior advent he uses the word <term>appearing</term> <note>original: ἐπιφανείας (*epiphaneias*), the root of the word "Epiphany"</note> when he says: **grace given in Christ... revealed now through the appearing of our Savior Jesus Christ** <note>original: χάριν ἐν Χριστῷ δοθεῖσαν φανερωθεῖσαν νῦν διὰ τῆς ἐπιφανείας τοῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ</note>. What sort of phraseology is this from the Apostle? Was that prior coming, however humble it may have been, to be called "illustrious" and an "epiphany," just as that later coming is magnificent—and so very magnificent? Yes, indeed; it pleased the Apostle to speak by divine inspiration so that he might lift our souls from the contemplation of external things to the contemplation of the power and veneration of that coming. And in truth, even in that lowly form of a servant, the demons themselves were forced, trembling, to adore and confess the divine majesty of Christ.

...in the preceding oracle concerning Melchizedek <note>Melchizedek was a mysterious priest-king from Genesis often seen by Christian scholars as a "type" or precursor to Christ.</note> we touched upon these matters, especially because in these scholarly labors of ours, we do not intend to treat mere <term>locos communes</term> <note>original: "locos communes"; these are "commonplaces" or standard, simplified theological topics found in textbooks.</note>; for we have already sufficiently accomplished that in our *Theses*. Instead, we seek only those things which naturally flow from the very heart of the oracles. Having set those aside, then, I shall ensure that we complete the fourth and final prerogative of Judah along with the entire oracle. That fourth <term>epoch</term> <note>original: "ἐποχὴ"; a distinctive period of time or a turning point in history.</note> of Judah is that from her a King emerged, whose scepter or dominion shall be spread through the whole world, and whose breadth is from sea to sea. This is what the Prophet hints at when he adds <term>and to him shall be the gathering of the peoples</term> <note>original Hebrew: "ולו יקהת עמים" (v’lo yikhat amim). From this, it is clearly established that the Patriarch Jacob predicted, through a prophetic spirit, the more remarkable things that were to happen to Judah. In this way, he predicted the <term>epoch</term> of his son and the entire tribe, yet he immediately seized upon their ingratitude and disobedience when he fixed the limits of the scepter. He notes the rejection of the Jews, but points toward the obedience and collection of the Gentiles under the Messiah. Therefore, this is worthy of note: whenever Scripture speaks of the coming of the Messiah, it immediately commemorates the calling of the Gentiles and connects these things together. 

As in Micah 5 <gloss>verse</gloss> 2, after the Prophet had said, *And you, Bethlehem Ephrata, though you are small among the judges of Judah, out of you shall come forth to me the future ruler in Israel*, etc., he soon adds in <gloss>verse</gloss> 3, <term>the remnant of his brothers</term> <note>original Hebrew: "יתר אחיו" (yeter achiv).</note> *shall return with the children of Israel*. By these words, he predicts the calling of the Gentiles, because the remnants of the nations, chosen by God in Christ, will join themselves to the Church. Paul shows this fulfilled in Romans 11:25 when he says, *that blindness in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in*. 

Therefore, it is not entirely true what certain theologians have asserted—namely, that whenever Paul commemorates a benefit bestowed upon the Jews at the coming of Christ, he makes mention of "Divine Truth," because the promises were made to the Jews and the covenants belonged to them; thus, when all these things were fulfilled in Christ, God’s Truth is rightly preached by the Apostle. However, they claim that when the same Apostle announces the benefits bestowed upon the Gentiles through Christ, he speaks instead of "Divine Mercy"...

Scripture, or even at times people in general, divide the world into Jews and Greeks, as seen in 1 Corinthians 1:22: *For the Jews demand a sign, and the Greeks seek wisdom* <note>original Latin: "Quandoquidem & Iudæi signum petunt, & Græci sapientiam quærunt"</note>. However, the Syrians distinguish differently, namely into Jews and Syrians; hence, in the Syriac version of this passage, the word used is *aramai* <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: ארמיא (Arameans)</note>. I will set aside the Rabbis, who speak differently today, for they call others *lo'ez* <note>original Hebrew: לועז (foreign speakers)</note>, meaning **barbarians**, with the exception of Christians, whom they specifically call *goyim* <note>original Hebrew: גוים (nations/Gentiles)</note> contemptuously <note>original Greek: "ἐξουρτικῶς" (exourtikōs); likely a Greek-inflected term for "scornfully"</note>, and *bedik bannay* <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: בדיק בנאי</note>, which means **in a shameful manner**. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;However, I would like to observe here in passing a remarkable skill of the Apostle and something quite unique. In Hebrew, this is *lo am* <note>original Hebrew: בלא עם (not a people)</note>. Here, he calls all profane peoples a "nation that is not a nation"; just as those who are condemned to eternal punishments are not said to "live" but to "die." Thus, those who were called **nations** in an absolute sense were not truly a **nation**, because (as the Apostle adds) they were a nation devoid of understanding: *I will provoke you to anger by a foolish nation* <note>original Greek: "ἐπὶ ἔθνει ἀσυνέτῳ παροργιῶ ὑμᾶς" (epi ethnei asynetō parorgiō hymas)</note>. Conversely, I observe that in Scripture, this specific naming is once attributed to Israel in the singular; in Joshua 5:6, they are called a *goy* <note>original Hebrew: גוי (nation/Gentile)</note> in the singular: *For the children of Israel walked forty years through the wilderness, until all the nation of men of war was consumed* <note>original Hebrew: עד תם כל הגוי אנשי המלחמה (ad tam kol ha-goy anshei ha-milchamah)</note>. It must be noted, however, that those wicked men, guilty of rebellion, are called in this place not a "people" but a *goy*—that is, a **nation**—using a word that is usually hateful and which generally signifies profane men who are strangers to the sacred covenant of Abraham. And not without merit, since they had alienated themselves from that covenant through a detestable crime. One can also add the passage in Joshua 10:13: *And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed, until the nation avenged itself upon its enemies* <note>original Hebrew: עד יקם הגוי איביו (ad yakom ha-goy oiyvav)</note>. This is found in the translation of Saint Jerome <note>The Vulgate</note>, and the Chaldean Paraphrase interprets this as referring to the people of Israel. ...in this way the Hebrew words [were rendered in Greek as]: "until God took vengeance on the enemies" <note>original Greek: ἕως ἠμυνάτο ὁ Θεὸς τοὺς ἐχθρούς</note>. Truly, they intended that the word *goy* <note>original Hebrew: גוי; meaning "nation" or "Gentile"</note> be placed in the accusative case; this was also the view of Symmachus <note>an author of a 2nd-century Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, who translates it as: "until he took vengeance on the people of their enmity" <note>original Greek: ἕως ἠμυνάτο τὸν λαὸν τῆς ἐχθρᾶς αὐτῶν</note>. The Chaldean <note>referring to the Aramaic Targum, a translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible</note>, however (as I mentioned), as if bound by a similar religious scruple—or rather superstition—does not translate *goy* as "nation," but as "the people of Israel."

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Furthermore, before we conclude these definitions regarding the word *goyim* <note>original Hebrew: גוים; the plural form of "nation," usually referring to non-Jewish nations</note>, I ask that it still be observed that—although (as we said above) "Gentiles" is understood by the term "Greeks" when they are contrasted with the Jews, as in the previously cited passage of **1 Corinthians 1:22**—nevertheless, sometimes these two are not contrasted, but signify indiscriminately either the faithful or the wicked. For example, in **1 Corinthians 10:32**, Paul forbids giving *offense to Jews and to Greeks and to the church of God*. Here, by "Jews and Greeks" joined together, all people in general are understood. Likewise, in **Romans 1:16** <note>The source text cites Romans 1:26, but the quotation follows 1:16</note>: *For I am not ashamed of the Gospel of Christ, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.* 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;There, by "Greeks," he understands the Gentiles; for whenever they are contrasted with Jews (as stated above), the "Nations" are signified. This habit of speaking arose, of course, because the greatest part of the East spoke Greek. Yet those Greeks are considered as the faithful. In the same **Epistle to the Romans**, chapter 2:9 <note>The source text cites Romans 11:9, but the quotation follows 2:9</note>, speaking of the wicked among both Jews and Greeks, he wrote in this manner: *There will be tribulation and distress for every human soul who does evil, the Jew first and also the Greek.* There he understands all the wicked, whether they are members of the visible Church or outside the communion of the Church. But in the previously cited passage of **1 Corinthians 10:32**, by "Jews and Greeks," he includes each and every person estranged from the covenant; this is evident from the fact that he contrasts both Jews and Greeks with the "Church of God."

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;As for our Prophet; he certainly uses the word *amim* <note>original Hebrew: עמים; "peoples"</note> rather than *goyim* <note>original Hebrew: גוים; "nations"</note>; that is, "of peoples" and not "of nations." But who does not see that by "peoples" in the plural, the Gentiles are signified? These are they who, at the coming of Shiloh <note>a messianic title from Genesis 49:10, often interpreted as "he to whom it belongs" or "the bringer of peace"</note>, were to be ruled by his powerful scepter and were required to submit their necks under his yoke. Therefore, here we see an expansion of the Messiah's kingdom and the greatest breadth of his scepter, which was the final *epoch* <note>original Greek: ἐποχὴ; a significant point in time or a historical period</note>. Thus, we have there an evident prophecy concerning the Calling of the Gen[tiles]...

[na]tions. Much could be collected here regarding the **calling of the Nations** <note>original Latin: *vocatione Gentium*</note>, if the goal were to treat this as a common theological topic. Indeed, I took up that task in my *Theological Theses*, where these points are sufficiently and accurately examined. For now, it is enough to note that through the phrase **the obedience—or gathering—of the peoples** <note>original Hebrew: *kehat amim* (קהת עמים)</note>, a clear proof <note>original Greek: *tekmerion* (τεκμήριον)</note> of the Messiah’s manifestation is shown to us. 

For was this not fulfilled immediately after Christ was revealed? Did the peoples not run to the foot of the cross and the Crucified One at the proclamation of the Gospel? This was prefigured, as it were, in the genealogy of Christ, since two Gentile women are explicitly mentioned by the Evangelists, from whom that **Shiloh** <note>A messianic title from Genesis 49:10, often interpreted as "the one to whom it belongs" or "Prince of Peace."</note> was descended. This hints that the wild olive branch was to be grafted into the holy root, and would become a sharer in the richness of the olive tree <note>A reference to the Apostle Paul’s imagery in Romans 11:17 regarding the inclusion of non-Jews in God's promises.</note>. 

Just as in that same genealogy mention was made of two native women who were guilty of great crimes—namely **Tamar** and **Bathsheba**, for incest and adultery—because Christ took upon Himself the persona of the sinners He would redeem; so too mention was made of two foreigners in the same genealogy—namely **Rahab**, of prostituted modesty and from Jericho, and **Ruth**, an idolater and a Moabite. This was so that the Holy Spirit might early on prefigure that Christ came to save the Gentiles as well. 

For this reason, the ancient Doctors of the Church call **Rahab** a "type" <note>A "type" is a historical person or event seen as a symbolic foreshadowing of a later reality.</note> of the Gentile Church. Although she was an idolater and a harlot before her calling, she was finally chosen into one body with Israel. Casting aside her Heathenism and her shameful life, she held out the scarlet cord tied to her house as a saving sacrament of her redemption <note>In Joshua 2, Rahab saved her family by hanging a red cord from her window; early Christian writers saw this as a symbol of the blood of Christ.</note>. 

I omit other allegorical subtleties of the ancient Doctors, which are more pleasing to the palates of those who live on weeds <note>The author is criticizing scholars who prefer overly decorative or "fluff" interpretations over solid theology.</note>. For instance, they claim that **Rahab** signifies "breadth," because she represented the breadth of the Gentile Church, previously living in the world represented by **Jericho**, a "moon-like" city and a symbol of inconstancy <note>The name Jericho was often etymologically linked to the Hebrew word for "moon."</note>. Truly, these are the most trifling of trifles, tasty only to those who know how to **babble nonsense** <note>original Greek: *leron lerein* (λῆρον ληρεῖν)</note>.

it did not resound to the Nations through the ministry of men as it did to the Jews; nevertheless, it pleased the supreme Governor of the universe to thunder His voice to the Pagans themselves through the heraldry of creation, as the Prophet David teaches in Psalm 19 and Paul in Romans 10. For even then, when God willed His grace to be enclosed within the covenanted Jews alone, little sparks of knowledge still flew out toward the Nations. Therefore, the Jews (as Calvin <note>Jean Calvin (1509–1564), a principal figure of the Protestant Reformation.</note> rightly observed) were like household listeners; but when God spoke to the Nations through the sky, the moon, and other creatures, it was a sign that He would one day call them into a true knowledge of Himself.

However, it must be admitted that the voice of creation is quite obscure compared to the oracles and prophecies of the Old Testament which predict that calling of the Nations—especially those prophecies announcing the eminence and splendor of Jerusalem or the Church. We believe this should be understood not only regarding the **Triumphant Church** <note>The Church in heaven</note> and the heavenly Jerusalem, but also regarding the **Militant Church** <note>The Church on earth, currently engaged in spiritual warfare</note> and its external appearance. This can be seen, and not without merit, in various periods of the Church:

I. In its beginnings, namely in the time of the Apostles and their successors, when the Gospel was preached to the **entire inhabited world** <note>original Greek: *pasē oikoumenē* (πᾶσῃ οἰκεμένῃ)</note>, and the Nations, flowing together from every side, were gathered into the fold of the Great Shepherd; according to that oracle of ours: **And to him belongs the obedience—or gathering—of the peoples.** <note>original Hebrew: *ve-lo yikkehat ammim* (וְלוֹ יִקְּהַת עַמִּים). This refers to the Messianic prophecy in Genesis 49:10.</note> Notable examples of this are found in the first sermons of Peter in Acts 3 and 4, when several thousand men were converted. For the efficacy of the Gospel had to exert its power first upon the Jews, and thereafter far and wide among the Nations, who were no longer strangers to the covenant, but grafted into the natural olive tree.

II. That splendor of the Church will shine forth in the last times in the conversion of the Jews and the fullness of the Nations, after the destruction of Babylon and the Antichrist. At that time, all nations and their glory shall be brought to Christ, about which the Apostle divinely prophesies in the Epistle to the Romans 11:25 and 26: *For I would not have you ignorant, brothers, of this mystery (lest you should be wise in your own conceits), that a partial hardening has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the nations has come in, and so all Israel shall be saved: as it is written...*

**Isaiah 59:20 and 27:9.** *The Deliverer will come from Zion, and He will turn away ungodliness from Jacob.* Here the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul in Romans 11:26.</note>, just as in verse 12, sets out certain contrasting terms—namely, the **diminution** <note>original Greek: *hēttēma* (ἥττημα), referring to a loss, defeat, or a decrease in number</note> of the Jews and the **fullness** <note>original Greek: *plērōma* (πλήρωμα)</note> of the Nations, and the **hardening** <note>original Greek: *pōrōsis* (πώρωσις)</note> that has happened in part to Israel, until the **enlightenment of all Israel** <note>original Greek: *phōtismō pantō Israēl* (φωτισμῷ πάντῳ Ἰσραὴλ)</note>; according to that which is said in verse 26, **all Israel will be saved** <note>original Greek: *pās Israēl sōthēsetai* (πᾶς Ἰσραὴλ σωθήσεται)</note>. For the word *hēttēma*, that is, *diminution*, signifies the small number of the Jews; for a people who do not worship God in Christ is regarded as "not a people." Thus, it is rightly said that the Jews, by their own stubbornness, have been reduced to a small number; and conversely, their conversion is called in that same passage a **fullness**. For it is destined to happen that the whole nation shall one day come to Christ. Indeed, although they are dispersed throughout the whole world and most miserably tossed about, they are nonetheless numerous beyond what can be said, so that even today that blessing made to Abraham in Genesis 22:17 <note>"I will multiply your seeds as the stars of heaven."</note> still exerts itself.

The same must be established regarding the "fullness of the nations," of which Paul speaks in verse 25: *until the fullness of the Nations has entered*, using the verb "to enter" according to the custom of the Scriptures, which speaks of the assembly of the Church as if it were a specific designated place. However, it must be diligently observed here that Paul is discussing the Jews and the Nations in a general sense, and is not speaking of every individual person. He evaluates these nations in respect to their **diminution or fullness** <note>original Greek: *hēttēmatos ē plērōmatos* (ἡττήματος ἢ πληρώματος)</note>; for as long as that diminution lasts, various branches are broken off, and a remnant survives, concerning which he says at the beginning of the chapter in verse 5: **In the present time there is a remnant according to the election of grace** <note>original Greek: *en tō nyn kairō leimma kat’ eklogēn charitos gegonen* (ἐν τῷ νῦν καιρῷ λεῖμμα κατ᾿ ἐκλογὴν χάριτος γέγονεν)</note>. Among these was Paul himself, as he says in verse 1. But truly, under the state of "fullness," many are said to be grafted in; yet if you look at individual men, he who once comes to Christ and has learned from Him shall never be cast out.

III. Finally, the splendor of the Church will be greatest after the final resurrection. For then, from all nations, tribes, peoples, and tongues, the elect shall stand before Christ the Judge. Those who, at the first coming of the Messiah, were the **obedience and gathering of the peoples** <note>original Hebrew: *Yiqhat Ammim* (יקהת עמים). A reference to Genesis 49:10, often interpreted as the gathering of nations to the Messiah.</note> shall, at His second coming, be the **glory of the peoples** <note>original Hebrew: *Kevod Ammim* (כבוד עמים)</note>. For then there will be a greater breadth to those words, "the gathering of the peoples," since the fullness of both Jews and Nations will have occurred—referring to the nations as a whole rather than every single individual (as we said above). For those who are converted from Judaism today are either very rare, or, if they are converted in great numbers as in Spain, they are in truth not converted from the heart. <note>A reference to the *Conversos* or "New Christians" in Spain, many of whom were forced to convert during the Inquisition but secretly practiced Judaism.</note>

...but they are driven to the abjuration of Judaism by threats, terrors, and tortures. These Christian proselytes are commonly called **Marranos**, **New Christians**, or **Neophytes**; they are of Jewish, Moorish, and Arab descent, and have been washed in the waters of baptism. In Spain, they are said to exceed the number of one hundred thousand families, and for this reason, they are a source of dread to the Spanish themselves. These Marranos, struck by the terrors of the Spanish Inquisition—including the rack and the most cruel tortures—have preferred to profess Christianity outwardly rather than bid a final farewell to their fatherland; nevertheless, they follow Jewish superstition inwardly and are circumcised in secret.

Finally, in these words of the Prophet <term>and to him shall be the gathering of the peoples</term> <note>original Hebrew: *ve-lo yikkehat ammim* from Genesis 49:10, a famous Messianic prophecy</note>, three notable allusions can be observed.

i. In the word <term>gathering</term> <note>original Hebrew: *kehat*</note>, which seems to allude to the synagogue; for just as the synagogue stood and was assembled among the Jews under the Old Testament, so in the New Testament there is a <term>gathering</term>, namely of the Christian people. This was to signify that at the coming of **Shiloh** <note>A title for the Messiah</note>, the scepter would be taken from Judah and the Lawgiver removed from between his feet, and the synagogue likewise would be buried in the ruins of the city or temple. Meanwhile, another scepter, Lawgiver, and synagogue—that is, a <term>gathering</term>—would arise among the nations.

ii. That word <term>gathering</term> signifies not only "assembly" but also **obedience**, so that a contrast might be shown between the first and second synagogue. In the first, there was no obedience, but rather disobedience; therefore the scepter, Lawgiver, and synagogue were taken away. But in the second, there was the **obedience of the peoples**, because they are the spiritual subjects of a spiritual king. Therefore, that scepter and Lawgiver shall never be taken away but shall endure forever. This obedient gathering of that heavenly king has disdained the naming of the former synagogue and has obtained the venerable name of the **Church**, a concept which signifies four things:

i. <term>gathering</term>: a meeting or assembly in a simple sense.

ii. An assembly gathered by the calling of the divine word, because it is named from the Greek word <term>to call forth</term> <note>original Greek: *akalein* (ἀκαλεῖν). The word "Ecclesia" is derived from *ek-kalein*, meaning to call out of or summon.</note>.

iii. It signifies, by way of excellence, an assembly gathered by an **effectual calling** <note>A theological term for a divine call that successfully brings a person to faith</note>; for it is also said of the Church **invis-**...

Upon hearing this, those unruly children are immediately provoked to zeal—that is, seized by grief and anger—and in this way return to a better state. But while mothers do this in play, God threatens that He will do so in earnest. To this, one can also refer the words of Christ pronounced over Jerusalem in Matthew 23:37:
> *How often I wanted to gather your children together, just as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing!*

But the Messiah called his people together by the most sweet word of the Gospel, because he himself endured the penalties of the law, and now the Spirit of adoption predominates.

If we weigh the matter by its original meaning, those three words *Eheie* <note>original Hebrew: אהיה (*Ehyeh*), meaning "I will be" or "I am"</note>, *Jehovah*, and *Jah* denote the very essence of God; for their origin is the same, differing only slightly in their endings. *Jah* is simply a shortened form of the name *Jehovah*, just as it is commonly shortened by the Chaldeans when they write it with two "yods" like this: יי <note>a common scribal abbreviation for the Name of God</note>, adding, as the Rabbis usually do, <term>acronyms</term> <note>original Hebrew: ראשי תיבות (*rashei tevot*), literally "heads of words"</note> with marks painted above. Furthermore, *Jehovah* is essentially the same as *Eheie*, not only in its root but also in its tense; this is evident from their first letters, which are formative markers of the future tense. This remains true unless we say that the first letter of the name *Jehovah* is an indicator and formative of a proper name, as seen in the names *Israel*, *Jacob*, and similar examples.

This point can certainly be confirmed from that passage in Revelation 1:4: *Grace to you and peace from him who is, and who was, and who is to come* <note>original Greek: χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη ἀπὸ τοῦ ὁ ὢν, καὶ ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος (*charis hymin kai eirēnē apo tou ho ōn, kai ho ēn, kai ho erchomenos*)</note>. For the Apostle is alluding to the words of Moses, *I am that I am* <note>original Hebrew: אהיה אשר אהיה (*Ehyeh asher Ehyeh*)</note>, and the four-lettered name <term>tetragrammaton</term> <note>The sacred four-letter name of God, YHWH</note>, *Jehovah*. 

Otherwise, there would be no grammatical construction in the Apostle’s words, since he ought to have said *from the one being and the one coming* <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄντος, καὶ τοῦ ἐρχομένου (*apo tou ontos, kai tou erchomenou*)—the author is noting that John uses the nominative case where the genitive is grammatically required</note>. John intended, therefore, to explain the name of God, יהוה (*YHWH*), just as Moses explained it by saying אהיה אשר אהיה (*Ehyeh asher Ehyeh*), or rather as God did when speaking to Moses. If John had declined "the one who is" and "the one coming" as participles, and "he was" as a verb, he would have expressed the meaning of the words, but there would have been no sign or characteristic mark of a proper name. Therefore, so that everyone would recognize that specific proper name of God, he refused to decline the words according to grammatical rules. 

Furthermore, he added the emphatic article as another characteristic of a proper name; indeed, to make us believe even more firmly that it is a proper name, he did not hesitate to add the article to the verb *was* <note>original Greek: ἦν (*ēn*)</note>, so that the sentence might be translated into Latin as: *Grace to you and peace from "Is" and "Was" and "Will-come."* Therefore, in this passage, the Greek article is not used technically <note>that is, as a standard part of speech</note>, as often happens, but significatively, as an index and mark of a proper name.

But perhaps someone might object: are not even proper names declined? What, then, prevented John from saying "from the one who is" <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄντος (*apo tou ontos*)</note>, etc.? He certainly could have; but in that case, someone might have suspected these names were merely descriptive titles <note>original Latin: appellativa</note>, and not the unique proper name of God. But come now! I shall demonstrate through several observations how clearly that Greek name corresponds to the Hebrew *Jehovah* or *Eheie* <note>I shall be</note>.

I. The Hebrew names include all distinctions of time; for in the word *Jehovah* is found *He was, He is,* and *He will be* <note>original Hebrew: היה (*hayah*), הוה (*hoveh*), and יהוה (*yihyeh*)</note>, that is: *He is, He was, He will be*. And in the word *Eheie* <note>I shall be</note> is found *I shall be, I was, I am* <note>original Hebrew: אהיה (*ehyeh*), היה (*hayah*), הוה (*hoveh*)</note>. These three distinctions of time are designated in the Greek name as *the one who is, and who was, and who is to come* <note>original Greek: ὁ ὤν, καὶ ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος (*ho ōn, kai ho ēn, kai ho erchomenos*)</note>.

II. Note that John said *He was* <note>Greek: ὁ ἦν (*ho ēn*), using the imperfect "was/used to be"</note> rather than simply "he has been," so that the perpetuity of the divine essence might be signified; for God was so from eternity that He did not cease to be, because His being has not passed away, but remains unchangeably.

III. It is worthy of observation that John did not say *He shall be* <note>Greek: ὁ ἔσται (*ho estai*)</note>, as he said *He who is* and *He who was*; instead, he said *the one who is coming* <note>Greek: ὁ ἐρχόμενος (*ho erchomenos*)</note>. This was done partly so he would not seem to indicate some new beginning or a new kind of existence that did not exist before, and partly because he frequently presents God to us as a Judge. Thus, He is "the one who is to come," and who, by His illustrious advent and solemn judgment, will make it plain before the whole world that He shall exist for eternity.

IV. That name is not without merit called <gloss>the unique</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: המיוחד (*Ha-Meyuchad*), meaning the "distinguished" or "proper" name</note> *proper, or appropriated name*, since it expressly signifies the divine essence itself. Since this essence in God is most simple, it is truly called God Himself; according to that common saying of the Hebrews, and also of Rabbi Ha-Kadosh <note>Judah the Prince, a 2nd-century CE rabbi and chief redactor of the Mishnah</note> in the first petition of the book: *Nothing is found in God which is not God* <note>original Hebrew: לא נמצא שום דבר באל לא אשר יהיה אל (*Lo nimtza shum davar ba-El lo asher yihyeh El*)</note>. For the very essence <note>original Greek: οὐσία (*ousia*)</note> of God is perpetually signified in the Old Testament by the name *Jehovah*, but in the New Testament by the name *God* <note>original Greek: Θεὸς (*Theos*)</note>, which is read 600 times therein.

Those words "I will be who I will be" <note>original Hebrew: אהיה אשר אהיה (*Ehyeh asher Ehyeh*)</note>, or "I am who I am," denote the simplicity of God or His most simple essence, inasmuch as in Him "being" and "essence" are not distinguished. Hence, in Maimonides’ *Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original Latin: *More Neuoch.*, part 1, chapter 63</note>, the name of the Lord <note>original Hebrew: יהוה (*YHWH*)</note> and "The Existing One" <note>original Hebrew: נמצא (*Nimsa*)</note> are synonyms to the Talmudists <note>Jewish legal and theological scholars</note>. However, a mystery lies hidden in the repetition of the same word, which signifies existence by way of attribution or predication. For the relative "who/which" <note>original Hebrew: אשר (*asher*)</note> contains within itself mention of an attribute inherent to itself (for it is always imperfect by itself and notes that something else is still to be joined to it, just like the word *alladhi* <note>original Latin/Arabic: *Aldi*</note> among the Arabs); and the first name is placed, which takes the place of the subject, "I will be" <note>original Hebrew: אהיה (*ehyeh*)</note>, and the second name, which is its attribute, is likewise called "I will be" <note>original Hebrew: אהיה (*ehyeh*)</note>, as if it wished to signify that the named subject and its attribute are one and the same in substance. That is to say, God exists, but not through a separate "existence" added to His nature. Therefore, it is the same as saying "The existing one who is the existing one" <note>original Hebrew transliteration: *Hannimsa ascher hu hannimsa*</note>. That is, He who necessarily exists and is found, because He always was and will be. The Rabbi Moses <note>Moses Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher</note> noted this skillfully and wisely. 

vii. That name "I shall be" <note>original Hebrew: *Eheie*</note> is proper to the Son of God; for since He appeared frequently to the Patriarchs and Prophets to give preludes of the future Incarnation, He wished to express His person and natures by this most emphatic <note>original Greek: ἐμφατικωτάτῳ</note> name, and thus it would correspond to "Immanuel" <note>meaning "God with us"</note> in Isaiah 7:14. 

First, "I will be" <note>original Hebrew: אהיה (*ehyeh*)</note> denotes the divine nature of that Immanuel: for who besides God can truly say "I shall be"? Is not God alone absolutely immutable, while every creature is defectible and mutable, whether externally or internally? <margin>VIII.</margin> "I Will Be" <note>original Hebrew: אֶהְיֶה (*Ehyeh*)</note> denotes that God is and shall be not only in Himself and absolutely, but also relationally <note>original Greek: σχετικῶς (*schetikōs*)</note> and in relation to the Church. Was not the name *Jehovah* known from the beginning of the world, just as *Shaddai* was? Was not this name of God revealed immediately from the creation? (Genesis 2:4). To be sure, Moses intended to demonstrate that *Jehovah* was the most perfect author of a perfect work once the work of creation was finished. Therefore, this must be understood not as a simple knowledge of the name—for that, as is clear, had been known long before—but regarding its effect and the thing signified. For God was known to the Patriarchs by the name *Jehovah* only when He stood by His promises and liberated His people from the yoke of their enemies. At other times, He had manifested Himself by the name *Shaddai*, because He had supplied them with everything that was then necessary and which sufficed in that Economy <note>The "Divine Economy" refers to the way God manages the world and relates to humanity across different historical eras.</note>; this is clear from the word *Shaddai*, which is composed by the Hebrews from *She* <note>original Hebrew: שֶׁ</note> (a contraction for *Asher* <note>original Hebrew: אֲשֶׁר</note>, meaning "who" or "which") and *Dai* <note>original Hebrew: דַי</note>, which is "enough" or "sufficient." Thus it means *He who is enough* or *the Sufficient One*. For as the Rabbis commonly say regarding that name of God: *For so it was spoken to him from the mouth of the Almighty* <note>original Hebrew: שכך נאמר לו מפי גבורה; "Gevurah" (Power) is a traditional Rabbinic term used to refer to God Himself</note>. From this comes the Kabbalistic <note>Referring to Jewish mystical tradition</note> word and abbreviated name **AGLA** <note>אגלא</note>, which is explained thus: *You are mighty forever, O Lord* <note>original Hebrew: אתה גבור לעולם יהוה; "Atah Gibor Le-olam Adonai"</note>.

But further, for a greater illustration of this passage, let us bring forth another explanation which pleases us not a little. When God first established a covenant with Abraham, as found in Genesis 17:1, he wished to manifest himself by the name **Shaddai**, saying: *I am God Almighty* <note>original Hebrew: אני אל שדי; "Ani El Shaddai"</note>. For in striking a covenant, it was essential for God to promise an all-sufficiency and necessary abundance, so that Abraham might have the requirement of the covenant—namely faith and **confidence** <note>original Greek: πεποίθησιν</note>. He had to believe firmly that God is that *Shaddai* who possesses sufficiency in and from Himself, so that He lacks no one's help, but is able to assist all, protect them, destroy enemies, and finally keep all promises and fill the needs of His people. Therefore, so that God might make all these things known to the patriarchs, He rightly said, *I am God Almighty*. Indeed, this name of God wonderfully strengthened Abraham’s faith.

Yet at length, when God had decided to fulfill those remarkable promises at the appointed time, He then had to reveal Himself by another name, namely **Jehovah**, by which God indicated His truth and constancy. He showed that He was no longer exhibiting the fulfillment of all things through words and authentic promises alone, but in very deed and by the outcome of events. Therefore, immediately in chapters 3 and 6 <insert>of Exodus</insert>, regarding the mission of Moses to Pharaoh and the liberation from Egyptian slavery, that wonderful name **Ehyeh** <note>meaning "I Will Be"</note> and **Jehovah** is proclaimed, so that the faithful might look to Jehovah the Redeemer, who was before Abraham and had struck the covenant with him. From this comes that saying in John 8: *Before Abraham was, I am* <note>original Latin: "priusquam Abraham esset, ego sum"</note>; and also, *Abraham saw my day and was glad*. Indeed, He joined His name **Shaddai** with **Jehovah** with so many miracles, and liberated the people *with a high hand* <note>original Hebrew: ביד רמה; a biblical idiom for acting with great power and publicity</note>. These names the Scripture wished to combine thereafter in the new <term>economy|The theological arrangement or "plan" of God's dealings with humanity</term> with that customary name of God. For the origin of the Latin word <note>referring to *Deus* (God)</note> seems to have come from the Aeolic dialect *theis* <note>original Greek: θείς</note>, which proceeds from the Hebrew *dai* <note>דיי</note>; that is, "sufficient." From this comes *Shaddai*, the name of God.

### THE REVEALER OF SECRETS:

IX. The name **אהיה** **Eheie** <note>original Hebrew: "Ehyeh," typically translated as "I am" or "I will be" from Exodus 3:14</note>, meaning **I will be**, implies a perfection of every kind; for the very essence of God contains within itself, in a virtual sense, every other thing. Indeed, since no human language is suitably <note>original Greek: κατ’ οἰκὴν</note> sufficient to denote the perfection of God, only God’s own instruction was able to express that most eminent perfection of His. For to the Latins, the word *perfectus* <note>meaning "perfect" or "finished"</note> implies a state of imperfection, since it is defined as something "made" <note>original Latin: "factus"</note>, which can hardly be said of God. Likewise, for the Greeks, the word **τέλειος** <note>teleios</note> implies something that has reached its end or limit. Therefore, only the Hebrew language is capable of expressing the perfection of God without implying imperfection; for He is called perfect, **כליל** <note>Klil</note>, from the root **כלל** <note>Klal</note>, which means *to possess all things*. This is expressed preeminently by God’s name **Eheie**. For since His "being" is infinite, He will certainly contain all perfections—not merely in a formal sense, but in an eminent sense <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "formally" means possessing a trait directly, while "eminently" means possessing it in a higher, more foundational way</note>; just as a King contains all political offices eminently, since he bestows them upon his subjects, yet he does not contain them formally, as he does not exercise those specific roles himself.

X. Note well that although **Eheie** implies "being" itself—which might therefore seem to be a most common and thus most indeterminate concept, as is evident from the study of Metaphysics—one must nevertheless think quite differently regarding **Eheie**. This is because the essence of God is the most singular and determined of all things, which is why it is the proper name of God. Indeed, it is so proper that it can apply to no other; thus He ought not only to be called "one," but "the only," which cannot be said of any other thing, even if it is singular. For a man like Peter is called "one" in a relative and numerical sense, but God is called "one" in an absolute and metaphysical sense, because He is unique, and there is no other God or **Eheie**. It is for this reason that by the Syrians, Assyrians, Phoenicians, and other Eastern peoples, the Sun (whom they worshiped as a God) was called *Adad*, because he is "alone," or "unique." The Persians expressed this same thing clearly in their own idiom, for among the names of God they held the word **הו** <note>Hu</note>, as did other Easterners. But what is this **הו** to them other than *He* or *Himself*? And what is *He*, if not *Jehovah* or *Eheie*, *He who is*? For by this demonstrative pronoun, the most singular essence is demonstrated in an eminent manner and nomenclature. Hence the Persians are accustomed to place that unique word separately at the head of their letters; and by a common formula they say **יה הו** <note>ie hu</note>, *O God* <note>The author is likely connecting the Hebrew "Yah" with the Persian/Arabic "Hu" (He)</note>. The Kabbalists <note>Jewish mystics</note> do not disagree, for they reckon the syllable **יה** <note>Yah</note> among the attributes of God. Whether this can be proven from Scripture...

<summary>This page analyzes the Hebrew name "Eheie" (I am/I will be), arguing that it represents a unique, metaphysical perfection that Latin and Greek terms fail to capture. The author also draws parallels between the Hebrew name of God and the divine titles used by the Persians and other ancient Near Eastern cultures to signify absolute oneness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the divine name "Eheie" (I will be). The previous page concluded by suggesting that while the name implies "being" itself, whether this "being" can be shared with others is a matter of debate.</meta>

...can be, is a matter of controversy among the learned.

XI. Observe that the eminence of the name **Eheie** is so great that it cannot be attributed to creatures even by analogy; for this reason, it is called **incommunicable** <note>original Greek: ἀκοινώνητον (akoinōnēton), meaning something that cannot be shared</note> by the Hebrews. Therefore, the common axiom of theologians does not apply here: *Names common to God and creatures are understood analogically, or rather equivocally.* <note>In traditional theology, "analogy" suggests a partial likeness between God and humans, while "equivocation" suggests the words mean entirely different things. Cregutus argues this specific name is so unique that no such comparison is possible.</note> For in this case, there is nothing in common, no less than in those properties of God which are called **Incommunicable Attributes**.

XII. When God says to Moses **Eheie Asher Eheie**, **I will be who I will be**, it is a Hebrew idiom, just as in that Hebraism found in Exodus 33:19: **I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy** <note>original Hebrew: ורחמתי את אשר ארחם (ve-rachamti et asher arechem)</note>. Likewise, the Septuagint <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> and the Apostle in Romans 9:15 render it: **I will have mercy on whom I have mercy** <note>original Greek: ἐλεήσω ὃν ἂν ἐλεῶ (eleēsō hon an eleō)</note>. This Hebrew practice of repeating a word signifies several things:

1. That mercy comes from God’s **good pleasure** <note>original Greek: εὐδοκίᾳ (eudokia)</note>, not from any **triggering cause** <note>original Latin: causa procatarctica; a technical term for an external cause that prompts an action</note>, and is therefore sovereign.
2. That it is free and unmerited.
3. That it is constant and unchangeable.
4. That it is immense and ineffable.

In these words, **Eheie Asher Eheie**, all these meanings are included. First, the **necessity of God’s Being**. Since God’s being is not sovereignly chosen like that of a creature, but necessary. For God exists by His very **essence**, whereas creatures exist by **accident** and dependency <note>In philosophy, "essence" is what a thing is by nature; an "accident" is a property that could be missing without the thing ceasing to be itself. God's very nature is to exist; a human's nature is to be human, but they might not have existed at all</note>. Therefore, a creature can either exist or not exist without any contradiction, because existence is not inherent to its essence. However, God cannot *not* exist, because non-existence is **incompossible** <note>a logical term meaning two things cannot happen at the same time</note> with His essence. For those things which exist by their essence are necessary, and that which is necessary cannot be otherwise.

For example, the essence of a human is to be **rational**; therefore, a human is necessarily rational and cannot be otherwise, for it is impossible to be a human and not be rational. It is a different judgment, however, regarding **whiteness**; because since a man is white by accident, he can still be a man even if he is not white. Since, therefore, God’s "to be" is His very essence, He necessarily exists. This is what is signified by that Hebrew phrase **Eheie Asher Eheie**. From this, it follows that God is the **source of all Being**; for that which exists by its essence is the source of all others. However, there is a distinction here between creatures and the Son of God: God is the source and **cause** of all creatures, but in respect to the Son, He is the **source but not the cause**; for the Father is the source of the Son by reason of the order of existence, but He is not His cause...

<summary>Cregutus explains that the divine name "Ehyeh" (I will be) signifies God's necessary existence and absolute uniqueness, which cannot be compared to created beings. He uses the Hebrew idiom of repetition to show that God's being and mercy are sovereign, constant, and the fundamental source of all existence.</summary>

...of Him as He is God, because the Son is **God in His own right** <term>autotheos; a Greek term for a being who is God of Himself, rather than being God by derivation</term>. For this reason, He truly said to Moses **I will be who I will be** <note>original Hebrew: *Eheie ascher Eheie*</note>, because He is of Himself. And therefore, He is generated by the Father necessarily, by the necessity of nature, and not contingently like the sons of men.

II. From that Hebrew idiom is signified the constancy, eternity, and immutability of God’s being. Whence He says: **I am God, I do not change** <note>Malachi 3:6</note>. And in James 1:17: **In God there is no change nor shadow of turning.** And His eternity is defined by **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century Christian philosopher</note> as: *the whole, simultaneous, and perfect possession of a boundless life.* Indeed, constancy and immutability are denoted even more by this Hebrew phrase than by that other: **I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy**, because the latter immutability is **hypothetical** <note>meaning it depends on the "hypothesis" or decision of the divine will</note>, stemming from the decision of the Divine will and decree; whereas the former is absolute and entirely from the necessity of nature. Nevertheless, one should trust that **the Lord** <term>YHWH; the four-letter name of God, often translated as 'the Lord' or 'Jehovah'</term> signifies that power by which God is so eternal and immutable that He is constant in His promises; and that promise **par excellence** <note>original Greek: κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν (kat’ exochen)</note> is the promise of salvation. Hence it is that **Solomon Iarhi** <note>better known as Rashi, a preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note>, a Jewish man, in his commentary on Exodus chapter 6, verse 2, interprets the word **YHWH** as **faithful and certain** <note>original Hebrew: נאמן ודאי (ne’eman vadai)</note>.

III. It signifies His immensity and ineffability. For since the attribute is the same as the subject—**I am what I am**—is it not sufficiently indicated that this name is immense and entirely **ineffable** <note>beyond expression or too sacred to be spoken</note>? This is not because it is ineffable regarding its material pronunciation or as a sign **technically** <note>original Greek: τεχνικῶς (technikos)</note>, but regarding its very meaning and formal pronunciation, because its essence cannot be sufficiently expressed or explained by a creature. Truly, when I consider these things more accurately, it becomes clear to me that this was the meaning of the **Sages** <note>original Hebrew: חכמים (Chachamim)</note>, the ancient wise men among the Hebrews, when they called that name first the **Tetragrammaton** <term>meaning "the four-lettered name"</term>, which signifies His immensity. Since it is God’s proper name, not one little letter can be added or taken away, nor even changed, as we saw above from the passage in Revelation 1: **from Him who is, and who was, etc.** <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ ὁ ὢν, καὶ ὁ ἦν (apo tou ho on, kai ho en)</note>. This sufficiently demonstrates that the essence of God is infinite and immense, and therefore nothing can be added or taken away. All languages and nations have imitated this, among whom the name of God is a **four-lettered word** <note>original Greek: τετραγράμματον (tetragrammaton)</note>, as we have proven with various examples in our **inquiry** <note>original Greek: συזητήσει (syzetesei)</note> on Genesis chapter 4:25, "then men began to call upon the name of the Lord." For why did all the nations want the name of God to be four-lettered? Surely it does not seem...

...that this happened **by chance** <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τύχης (*apo tyches*)</note>; for since chance is accidental, it could not have produced such great uniformity across all languages. Nor was this done out of some imitation of Jewish superstition, where they merely weigh the numerical value of the name's letters; for other nations loathed the Jewish people, so they were far from following their superstitions. Furthermore, since God Himself in Exodus 3 called Himself **I will be** <note>original Hebrew: אהיה (*Eheie*)</note>, which is the same as in Exodus 6:2, **Jehovah** <note>original Hebrew: יהוה (*Iehoua*)</note>, they certainly intended the name to be, as they call it, a **Tetragrammaton** <term>a Greek term meaning "a word of four letters," specifically referring to the sacred four-letter name of God</term>, just as the Apostles in the New Testament used the word **God** <note>original Greek: Θεὸς (*Theos*), which also has four letters</note>. And the **Synod of Dordrecht** <note>A national assembly held in 1618–1619 to settle a theological device in the Dutch Reformed Church</note> decreed that the Tetragrammaton **Jehovah** <note>Hebrew: יהוה</note> should be expressed in the Dutch version by the word *Heere* <note>Lord</note>, which is also a four-letter word—unless you spell it with a double "e" as *Heere* <note>Cregutus notes that the spelling varies between four and five letters</note>—and they willed that **Elohim** <note>original Hebrew: אלהים, another name for God</note> be rendered as *Gott* <note>German/Dutch for "God," also four letters</note>. We must judge, therefore, that this was done rather because of the mystical sense of the ancient Hebrews, who drew out the immensity of God from His own proper name **I will be** <note>Hebrew: אהיה (*Eheie*)</note>. This religious reverence permeated all nations, even if it was eventually turned into superstition by the Jews and perhaps by others. The same thing happens to the **Papists** <note>A 17th-century term for Roman Catholics</note> regarding the name of **Jesus**; for because the thing signified is immense, and according to Paul’s testimony in Philippians 2:9-10, it *is the name above every name*, the followers of the Pope superstitiously venerate the physical material and the syllables themselves.

Secondly, the ancient sages of the Hebrews also called that name the **Schemhamphorasch** <term>a Hebrew term meaning "the Explicit Name" or the "Separated Name," referring to a hidden or expanded version of the divine name</term>, that is, the **explained name**. Why was this? Was it not because they saw the immensity of God contained within it, and therefore realized that no common wisdom was required to understand its mysteries? What does it mean when the Hebrew sages said that the Messiah, in the **world to come** <note>original Hebrew: בעולם הבא (*be-olam ha-ba*)</note>, would pronounce and explain that name **Schemhamphorasch**, and through it perform various miracles? Were not all those things fulfilled in the Messiah? Did He not Himself, in John 8, explain this name *Eheie*, just as He did in Revelation 1, as we have seen? Did He not pronounce it quite often? Since the Messiah is **I will be** <note>Eheie</note> and **Jehovah**, did He not perform various miracles through it? For miracles cannot be performed by a creature, but only by Him who is called **I will be**. Hence those rulings of the theologians coincide: that Christ alone saw the Divinity **as a whole but not entirely** <note>original Greek: ὅλῳ ἐκ ὅλως (*holoi ek holos*); a scholastic distinction meaning He perceived the entire divine nature, but as a human, He could not exhaustively comprehend the infinite</note>, insofar as He is man.

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS #

...but insofar as He is **Eheie** <note>Hebrew: אהיה (*Eheie*), meaning "I Will Be" or "I Am"</note> or **Jehovah**, He sees that idea **wholly and totally** <note>original Greek: ὅλῳ καὶ ὅλως (*holō kai holōs*)</note>, in its entirety and completeness.

**Thirdly**, from this we can understand those words so often repeated by the Hebrew Sages: that the proper name of God is **unutterable**, **ineffable**, **unpronounceable**, and **inconceivable** <note>original Greek: ἄῤῥητον (*arrhēton*), ἄφραστον (*aphraston*), ἀνεκφώνητον (*anekphōnēton*), ἀνόητον (*anoēton*)</note>. For those first Hebrew **Sages** <note>Hebrew: חכמים (*Chakhamim*)</note> who lived before the birth of Christ did not believe out of some superstition that the **Tetragrammaton** <term>The four-letter name of God, YHWH</term> could not or should not be pronounced. They held this for three reasons: **I.** Because God Himself pronounced it to Moses many times. **II.** Because Moses himself wrote it in the Law; and whatever can be written can certainly also be pronounced, since the **written word**, the **spoken word**, and the **internal thought** <note>original Greek: λόγος γεγραμμένος (*logos gegrammenos*), προφορικὸς (*prophorikos*), and ἐνδιάθετος (*endiithetos*)</note> do not differ in their reality. **III.** Because the High Priest pronounced it when blessing the people; and according to Hebrew witnesses, blessings were made through the name **Jehovah**, following the verse in Numbers 6:24-26. The people were blessed by the pronunciation of the four-letter name **Jehovah**; according to them, this blessing was performed with three fingers of both palms raised and two folded down. 

This practice ceased with **Simeon the Just** <note>A Jewish High Priest during the Second Temple period, famously said to have greeted Alexander the Great or, in Christian tradition, the elderly man who held the infant Jesus</note>, who took Christ into his arms. For as **Maimonides** <note>A profoundly influential medieval Jewish philosopher and Torah scholar</note> reports, from the time Simeon the Just died, his fellow priests ceased to bless the people with the four-letter name, but instead blessed them with a name of twelve letters: **Father, Son, and Holy Spirit** <note>original Hebrew: אב בן ורוח הקדש (*Ab Ben ve-Ruach ha-Kodesh*)</note>. Hence, in the **Codice Sotah** <note>A tractate of the Talmud</note>, chapter 7, folio 37: *In the Sanctuary, the Priest pronounces the Tetragrammaton as it is written; in the provinces (that is, outside Jerusalem), he uses a **by-name** <note>original Hebrew: כנוי (*kinuy*), an epithet or substitute title</note>, which is His surname.*

Therefore, when that name was no longer pronounced after Simeon the Just and was called **unutterable**, it was done to signify the inexpressible essence of God, which is honored more by silence than by speech—according to the words of the Prophet in the Psalms, *O God, silence is Your praise.* For this reason, **Rabbi Hakkadosh** <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah</note> used to say that God has no known name. And **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a syncretism of the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth</note> said, **"For He who is, is nameless"** <note>Greek: ἐστὶ γὰρ ὁ ὢν ἀνώνυμος</note> and **"The name cannot be spoken by a human mouth"** <note>Greek: τὸ ὄνομα οὐ δύναται ἀνθρωπίνῳ στόματι λαληθῆναι</note>. This pious reverence of the Hebrew Sages for the Divine Name was later wrongly turned into superstition by more recent Jews, who focused on the syllables rather than the reality signified. **Petrus Galatinus** <note>An Italian Renaissance friar and scholar of the Kabbalah</note>, seeking to cast off this superstition, was the first of all who dared to pronounce the **Tetragrammaton**.

Furthermore, beyond that reason drawn from the nature of the essence...

# ANTHONY CREGUTUS #

...concerning the ineffability of the divine, another reason is supplied from the nature of the Greek language. For the Greek language cannot pronounce a **rough breathing** <note>the aspirated "h" sound</note> in the middle of a word. This is why the **Seventy Interpreters** <note>The translators of the Septuagint, the ancient Greek version of the Old Testament</note> never used the word **Jehovah**, but always rendered it as **Lord** <note>original Greek: Κύριος (*Kyrios*)</note>; and from this, superstitious Jews in the following centuries, suspecting some mystery lay beneath it, did not dare to pronounce the **four-letter name** <term>The Tetragrammaton, YHWH</term>, but instead substituted the vowels of the name **Adonai** <note>Hebrew: "Lord"</note> so that they might express the word **Lord** as the Seventy did. Therefore, when the Seventy render the name **Joshua** <note>Hebrew: יהושוע (*Yehoshua*)</note>, they translate it as **Jesus** <note>original Greek: Ιησοῦς (*Iēsous*)</note> without the aspirated and guttural letters. Others add that it was **unutterable** <note>original Greek: ἀνεκφώνητον (*anekphōnēton*)</note> because of the letter **vav**, which is the **digamma** <note>an archaic Greek letter representing a "w" or "v" sound</note> known only to the Aeolians among the Greeks.

But if you consult the Jews, they say this was done because of the commandment of the Law: *You shall not take the name of Jehovah your God in vain.* For by interpreting this commandment incorrectly, they claim it should not be pronounced except by the High Priest on the tenth day of the month of **Tishri** <note>the day of Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement</note>, and even then only **in the Holy Place** <note>original Greek: ἐν ἁγίοις (*en hagiois*)</note>, in the Sanctuary; as Philo Judaeus reports in the third book of his *Life of Moses*. They do this, obviously, so it is not profaned by being pronounced outside the Sanctuary in Jerusalem. 

Note, however, that in certain places in Scripture it seems to have always been pronounced—specifically in **Psalm 8:2**: **Jehovah our Lord, how excellent...** <note>Hebrew: יהוה אדנינו מה אדיר (*Yehovah Adonenu mah addir*)</note> and in verse 10, where the same words are repeated. And in the **Song of Habakkuk**, according to some, in chapter 3, verse 19 of his prophecy; yet according to the vowel points, it is read as **Elohim** <note>God</note> in this manner: **Jehovah my Lord** <note>Hebrew: יהוה אדני (*Yehovah Adonai*)</note>. 

It is observed that by the time of **Theodoret** <note>A 5th-century Christian theologian</note> it was already **unutterable**, and the conjecture of those who say the Jews refused to pronounce it after the Temple of Jerusalem was leveled to the ground is not improbable, since it was only lawful to pronounce it **in the Holy Place**. For it can be inferred that it was pronounced more frequently by the Jews before then from the fact that the **Gentiles** <note>non-Jewish people</note> had knowledge of it. This is clear from the greatest of the gods, who took his name from it; for by **Ennius** and **Suidas**, he is called **Jove** <note>Jovis/Jupiter</note> in the nominative case. And **Orpheus** called God **Iao** <note>original Greek: Ἰάω</note>; whence **Diodorus Siculus** said that God is called **Iao** by the Jews. **Justin Martyr** says God was called **Iaoth** by the Hebrews, as does **Epiphanius**, but **Tertullian** says **Iao**. These examples sufficiently show that the name **Jehovah** was not **unutterable** in ancient times, since the nations heard it from the Jews, even if they themselves pronounced it somewhat corruptly, as often happens with words...

...ought not to mislead. For nowhere will you find that those [the Patriarchs] possessed a prophetic sense in such a way that they were commanded to cry out to the sons of men and to direct them in the way. Neither Abraham, Isaac, nor the others said: "God told me that you should do this," or "He sent me to you." Rather, God told them only what they themselves were to do, or what was to happen to their descendants. They themselves, however, instructed men by way of contemplation <note>A reference to the idea that the Patriarchs taught through philosophical or spiritual example rather than through a formal legislative mandate.</note>. (Genesis 12:5). Since, therefore, God appeared to Moses and sent him, it is no wonder if Moses said in Exodus 3: "They will not believe me, and they will say, 'What is his name?'" Therefore, God taught him the name אהיה אשר אהיה <note>original Hebrew: *Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh*</note> *I will be who I will be*. Thus far Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides, a preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher who discussed the unique nature of Moses's prophecy in his work *The Guide for the Perplexed*.</note>.

I assert, moreover, that the mission of Moses was unique, because he was sent in a unique and pre-eminent manner so as to foreshadow Christ. It is for this reason that Moses, when he was about to die, said to the people in the book of Deuteronomy: *The Lord your God will raise up for you a Prophet like me*, undoubtedly indicating Christ, who was the true and only Teacher and Prophet, and the highest interpreter of the Law. For this reason, Scripture, when speaking of Moses, says: *They have Moses and the Prophets* (Luke 16:29), distinguishing Moses from the Prophets *par excellence* <note>original Greek: κατ' ἐξοχὴν (*kat' exochen*)</note>. This is not because Moses was not a Prophet, but because, having been elevated above the others, he appeared to be more than a Prophet; for he was not only an interpreter of the Law, but also its promulgator. This is just as Christ was the interpreter and promulgator of the New Law in the New Economy—indeed, the supreme Legislator (John 1:17): *For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ*. Here, Christ is certainly preferred to Moses as the reality is to the shadow <note>literally "as the truth is to the figure"</note>, and as the son who is over the house is preferred to the servant who is in the house, as Paul speaks in Hebrews 4:5 and 6 <note>The text cites Hebrews 4, though the comparison of the servant and the son in the house is found in Hebrews 3:5–6.</note>. Nevertheless, in reality, the two are compared and paralleled <note>original Greek: παραλληλίζονται (*parallelizontai*)</note> with each other because of the analogies that can be observed between them. Therefore, just as Scripture says of the most blessed Virgin Mary, *Mary above all other women* <note>original Greek: Μαρίᾳ πὰρ' ἀλλas γυναῖκας (*Maria par' allas gynaikas*)</note>, because as the mother of Christ she excelled others; and as Homer frequently repeats this phrase, *Zeus and the other gods* <note>original Greek: Ζεύς τε καὶ ἄλλοι Θεοὶ (*Zeus te kai alloi Theoi*)</note>, because Jupiter was the greatest of the gods; so in the same way Moses is preferred to others by this phrasing on account of his unique office.

The High Priest used to enter the sanctuary only once every year, but Moses appeared before God more often in the tabernacle, and God spoke with him face to face. Furthermore, Moses was a typical redeemer <note>In historical theology, a "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament that foreshadows a "reality" in the New Testament.</note>, who liberated the people of God *with a raised hand* <note>original Hebrew: ביד רם (*be-yad ram*)</note> from the servitude of Egypt; which redemption certainly prefigured the redemption from spiritual servitude accomplished through Christ, who was not a typical but a real and true redeemer. Hence Moses, in the Book of Exodus where that redemption is discussed, at one moment uses the word *padah* <note>original Hebrew: פדה</note>, which signifies a redemption made without a price; and at another moment the word *ga'al* <note>original Hebrew: גאל</note>, which signifies a redemption with a price; so that in this way both redemptions might be signified: namely, the typical and physical one, which was done without a price, and the real or spiritual one, which was done with the price of the blood of the immaculate Lamb, as Peter speaks. And this is truly and properly called redemption, while the other is so called improperly. But since the mystery of redeeming grace is obscurely suggested in the economy <note>A theological term for the "plan" or "system" by which God governs a particular era of human history.</note> of the Old Testament, and the fathers of the Old Testament then noticed that temporal redemption more—clinging, as it were, to the husk <note>A metaphor for focusing on the literal or physical surface of a text rather than its spiritual core.</note>—Moses therefore uses the word *ga'al* only twice, but the word *padah* more frequently, so that after they had thirsted and panted for physical liberation, they might also expect the spiritual liberation with heads held high <note>original Latin: *exerto capite*, a phrase suggesting eager or straining anticipation.</note>; just as in the first economy, the Law was hammered home many centuries before, so that eventually, in the new economy of grace, it might stand out more prominently.

Since, therefore, a mission <note>Referring to a formal commissioning or being "sent" by God.</note> is twofold, namely *ordinary* and *extraordinary*. *Ordinary*, which is done mediately by God through men—such as was the mission of Timothy and the bishops who succeeded him, and of which Paul spoke in 1 Timothy 5 when he said to Timothy, *Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands*. It is also mentioned in the 4th Canon of the Council of Nicaea. *Extraordinary*, which is done immediately by God without the ministry of men—such as was the mission of the Prophets and Apostles. Indeed, the Son of God himself glories that he did not come or speak of himself, but from the Father. From this it is clear that the mission of Moses was extraordinary; indeed, it was something higher and more excellent than a standard extraordinary mission, because his mission was unique. ### BY ANTOINE CREGUT ###
