...even those sent extraordinarily, nevertheless their mission was not singular <note>Meaning unique or one-of-a-kind.</note>, as was that of Moses.

We therefore put forward three points regarding the mission of such a great Prophet. I. That it was the *very first*. II. That it was *extraordinary*. III. That it was *singular*. From the fact that it was the first, it cannot be inferred that it was extraordinary; for on the contrary, in every order there must be something first and last. Hence it is that Aaron the High Priest is the first of all by the institution of his office, and yet his mission, like his Priesthood, was ordinary and mediated <note>In theology, an "ordinary" office is one established to continue through successors, while "mediated" means he was appointed through another human (Moses) rather than directly by God.</note>, as is clear from the book of Exodus, chapter 4. Moses’s mission, therefore, was extraordinary. I. Because it was the first in such a way that it had no successor among men; for of no one except Christ is it said, *God will raise up for you another Prophet like me*. But Christ was not properly Moses’s successor, but rather the reality of that which was foreshadowed through that type. II. His mission was extraordinary because he was sent immediately by God <note>Directly, without human intervention.</note>, as is clear from this passage in Exodus 3: *I AM has sent me to you* <note>original Hebrew: אהיה שלחני אליכם (*Ehie shalakhani aleikhem*)</note>. III. It was extraordinary because it was singular and above the natural order of things. For since Moses handed down the law, since he was a symbolic Redeemer, and since he was a Mediator between God and the people, he surely could not have performed his office except in an extraordinary capacity. It is not without merit, therefore, that Scripture says on account of Moses's great excellencies <note>original Greek: <unclear>ὑπεροχὰς</unclear> (*hyperochas*)</note>, *There has not arisen since then a Prophet like Moses, whom God spoke to face to face.*

Nevertheless, however exceptional Moses's eminence <note>original Greek: <unclear>ὑπεροχὴ</unclear> (*hyperochē*)</note> may have been above other Prophets, if he is then compared with the Apostles, even in regard to his mission, he will be judged not only as not superior to them, but as much inferior. For, I. Moses was sent by God who sustained the role of judge and demanded the retribution <note>original Greek: <unclear>ἀνταποδόμασιν</unclear> (*antapodomasin*), referring to the legal penalties or "repayments" required by the Old Covenant.</note> of the law; but the Apostles were sent by Christ, the redeemer of the human race and Immanuel <note>A name for Christ meaning "God with us."</note>, a partaker of flesh and blood. From the most holy dictate of this Spirit, they brought forth the oracles of God and made them known to the whole world, carrying them hidden in their breasts like a most sacred trust.

For this reason, it was skillfully and weightily observed in the Fifth Council of Constantinople <note>The Second Council of Constantinople (553 AD), often cited in these debates regarding apostolic tradition</note> that the Apostles met in Jerusalem (as seen in Acts 15) not out of any necessity—since those servants of God were *secure* <note>original Greek: ἀσφαλεῖς (asphaleis)</note> and driven by the breath of the Spirit—but they were compelled by a certain divine arrangement to confer on doctrine. Indeed, in that first and most ancient Council, they wished to sketch a model for all Universal Councils, or rather to provide a Rule <term>Canon</term> in its decrees for the following centuries, by which Universal Councils might be directed and by which controversies or disputes concerning faith and morals might be settled. **XII.** The mission of the Apostles carried a certain *Legislative authority*; for just as they were able to authoritatively <note>original Greek: αὐθεντικῶς (authentikos)</note> rebuke guilt both privately and publicly by right of their mission, so too were they able to inflict punishment. This was not only a "satisfactory" penalty—which the ancients called *Canonical* or *Ecclesiastical*—but even, like a Legislator or magistrate, the penalty of death. This is sufficiently proven by the example of Ananias and Sapphira in Acts 5, who were punished by Peter with the capital penalty and ultimate execution, so that terror might be struck into the whole Church and the supreme authority of the Apostles might become known to everyone. <meta>This page continues Anthony Cregut’s discussion on the different types of divine missions. Having previously established the excellence of the Apostles' mission, he now shifts to a specific comparison with Moses, highlighting Moses’ unique role as a "type" or foreshadowing of Christ.</meta>

...sent, he who is the center and origin of every mission.

But in truth, although the mission of the Apostles absolutely surpasses the mission of Moses, nevertheless <term>in a certain respect<note>original Greek: κατ' τι (kat' ti)</note></term> Moses is deservedly considered to be preferred even over the Apostles themselves; specifically, insofar as he was a <term>typical mediator and redeemer<note>In historical theology, a "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament that serves as a prophetic symbol or "shadow" of Jesus Christ, who is the "antitype" or reality.</note></term> prefiguring the real and true Mediator, Christ—which can be said of no mortal besides Moses. Hence those singular things said concerning Moses: in *Exodus 14:31*, the people are said to have *believed in God and in Moses*; and in *Exodus 19:9*, God, commending the authority of Moses, wills that all the Jews believe in him forever. <note>original Hebrew: ויאמינו בך לעלם (veyaminu bekha le'olam)</note> "And they will believe in you forever," which is not only to be understood as historical faith, but also as that faith which embraces the special promises of God. This is indeed attributed to Moses as a typical Mediator and insofar as he reflects Christ, the Truth; however, faith is truly and realistically attributed to Christ the Mediator.

To this point agrees that passage in *1 Corinthians 10*, when the Israelites are said to be *baptized into Moses, in the cloud and in the sea*. This phrase does not only signify the ministry of Moses—that is, that they were baptized by the ministry of Moses, which the <term>Syriac<note>Referring to the Peshitta, the ancient Syriac translation of the Bible.</note></term> indicates with the common words <note>original: ביד משה (beyad Mosheh)</note> *by the hand of Moses*—but Paul’s words also designate something else extraordinary. For otherwise, Paul’s speech would have been cold, nor would he have raised Moses above others; for the faithful are baptized through the ministry of all pastors, and yet it is not said in Scripture that anyone was baptized *into Paul or into Peter, etc.* The reason is that the mission of Moses was singular insofar as he was a Mediator and Redeemer. Indeed, what must be observed is that Moses was a Mediator with respect to both ends: for he acted as an intermediary between God and the people, and between the people and God. Therefore, he spoke to the people in the place of God, since the people could not bear the terrifying voice of God. And furthermore, the people could not approach God; hence it is that through the intervention of Moses, God spoke to the people and conversely the people spoke to God. For a Mediator ought to both lead the people to God and reconcile God to the people. But all these things were magnificently fulfilled in Christ. Thus far we have observed three kinds of missions: namely, the ordinary, the extraordinary, and the singular; and we have said that the mission of Moses was

<meta>This page continues Anthony Cregut’s analysis of divine "missions" or vocations. ### THE REVEALER OF SECRETS ###
<meta>Catchword: grace</meta>

...to have been at once extraordinary and unique; moreover, a type of mission can be added which can rightly be called *mixed*. This is because a mission can be observed as being partly *ordinary* and partly *extraordinary*, such as the mission of John the Baptist. Since he was the son of Zechariah the Priest, his vocation was **ordinary** <note>Meaning it followed the established, inherited laws of the Aaronic priesthood.</note>; but because he was sent to proclaim grace and to be the forerunner of Christ, his vocation was **extraordinary**.

Cardinal Richelieu, in his *Method for the Conversion of those who have departed from the Roman Church* (Book 2, Chapter 3), further subdivides the extraordinary mission into *primitive (or original)* and *collateral (or subaltern)*. He calls "original or primitive" that which was given by God for the purpose of instituting a new law or a new priesthood and for promulgating new doctrine; such was the mission of Moses, and, in the new economy, the mission of Christ and the Apostles. However, the "collateral" mission was given for correcting the abuses spreading within an already established Church; this was the mission of the Prophets of the Old Testament, intended either to convert the unfaithful to the knowledge of the truth or to lead back those who had recently departed. Such was Elijah’s mission: to confound the false prophets of Baal and to lead the people back to the faith of the God of Israel.

And let these things thus explained suffice concerning the various kinds of mission, for the nature of Moses' mission is now clear enough. Now, indeed, it will be easy to respond to the persistent demands of the <term>Papists<note>A common Reformation-era term for followers of the Roman Catholic Church.</note></term> concerning our own mission and vocation; for I hear them perpetually repeating those <term>much-celebrated points<note>original Greek: πολυθρύλλητα (polythryllēta)</note></term>, shouting: *“What is your mission? From whom do you hold your mission or vocation? What was the mission of Luther or Calvin?”* And since recently Cardinal Richelieu, in the posthumous book mentioned above, treats this question <term>without proper examination<note>original Greek: ἀνεξετάστως (anexetastōs)</note></term>—and his commentaries on this matter have been greedily seized upon by his followers, and the Monks themselves have peddled them to the people from the pulpit—come then, let us also undertake a more accurate <term>investigation<note>original Greek: συζήτησιν (syzētēsin)</note></term> of this question.

First, to respond directly: the mission of Luther, Calvin, and others was *mixed*—that is, it was both *ordinary and extraordinary* in different respects. It was **ordinary** because Luther, for example, received his vocation within the Roman Church, for he was...

He argues that Luther and Calvin held "mixed" vocations, combining established church authority with a divine call to reform.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Anthony Cregut’s defense of the Protestant Reformation. Having established the different types of divine "missions" on the previous page, Cregut now applies these principles specifically to Martin Luther, arguing that Luther’s authority to preach and ordain was divine in origin, even though it was conferred through the existing structures of the Roman Church.</meta>

# ANTHONY CREGUT #
<meta>catchword: would suffice (Latin: faciat/fatiatè)</meta>

...was inaugurated to preach the word of God and to administer the Sacraments. Luther’s mission, at the time he was inaugurated, was not properly a human mission, but a divine one. For even though it was **ordinary** and **mediated** <term>In 17th-century theology, an "ordinary" mission follows established Church laws, and "mediated" (Latin: *mediata*) means God acts through human instruments, such as bishops, rather than speaking directly to the person as He did with Moses.</term>, it was nonetheless no less divine than an **extraordinary** vocation. For God Himself sends pastors, but He does so mediately through the ministry of men. 

Therefore, although Luther was consecrated by a Roman Bishop, he was properly sent by God to preach His word and administer His sacraments; for this reason, through the laying on of hands, God equipped him with various gifts and the graces of the Holy Spirit. If, therefore, through reading, meditation, prayer, and prophesying, he uncovered the various errors of the followers of the Pope, it was at a time when the "Papists"—both Bishops and Laity—were shouting: *The Church has need of reformation, both in faith and in morals; in both head and members.* <note>original Latin: "Ecclesia opus habet reformatione & in fide & in moribus: & in capite & in membris." This was a common legal and theological slogan used during the Great Schism and the Conciliar movement.</note> Indeed, everyone was shouting this in the Council of Pisa and the Council of Basel. Is it any wonder, then, if according to his conscience he condemned the Roman Church and accused it of various crimes before the whole world? 

Luther, therefore, did not lose his vocation and his ordination, since he had not received it properly from man, but from God, who uses the ministry of men in that **ordinary** vocation. For this reason, it is called *mediated*, because of the means <note>the human agents or "media"</note> which God uses. Indeed, if Luther had continued to teach "Popery" after knowing the truth, he would have abused his office, and it is *then* that he would have rather lost his vocation, since he would have violated the missions, covenants, and conditions of his office. For a true herald of God’s word is not bound to the Pope, but to God and His word. 

Just as the Emperor Trajan, when handing the sword of justice to a magistrate, used to say: *Draw this sword against me, if I do not practice justice.* <note>original Latin: "contra me hunc gladium stringe, ni iustitiam exerceam." This famous anecdote was often cited by early modern writers to justify resisting unjust authority.</note> So Luther said to the Pope, while handing over a "bill of divorce": *Keep your things to yourself.* <note>original Latin: "res tuas tibi habeto." This is a reference to the Roman legal formula for a divorce (*repudium*), signaling Luther's formal break from the Roman Church.</note> 

Since, therefore, Luther did not lose his mission by defecting from the Pope (as has been proven), he was certainly able to confer that mission upon others. For he was a priest and a herald of the Gospel, which office—according to Scripture—does not differ from that of a Bishop (that is, a herald of God’s word). For the Bishops of the Papacy, if they do not preach the Gospel, are but masks of Bishops—mere names and titles without the reality itself.

This reasoning should now be sufficient for any man who is not stubborn...

<summary>Cregut argues that Martin Luther’s authority was valid and divine because his ordination as a priest was a "mediated" mission from God, which he did not forfeit by breaking with the Pope. He concludes that as a valid minister of the Gospel, Luther had the right to reform the Church and ordain others.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Anthony Cregut’s polemical defense of Martin Luther’s authority. On the previous page, he argued that Luther’s mission was "ordinary" because he was a validly ordained priest. Here, he pivots to argue that Luther also possessed an "extraordinary" mission—a direct internal calling from God—to counter Catholic "Papist" arguments that Luther lacked the right to change established Church doctrine.</meta>

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS #

...it would sufficiently satisfy, since the followers of the Pope <note>Latin: *Pontificij*. A common 17th-century Protestant term for Roman Catholics.</note> have nothing they can solidly offer in response; but having thus lethally wounded their right side, I will make it so that I also strike the left side incurably. I say, therefore, that Luther’s mission was furthermore **immediate** and **extraordinary** in another respect, since, because it was a "mixed" mission, it was necessary for it to consist of two parts. But we must see how that mission of Luther was extraordinary. Indeed, a mission can be called extraordinary in two primary ways: either *on the part of the sender and the mode of sending*, or *on the part of the substance of the mission or its instruction*. 

*On the part of the sender*, a mission would not simply be extraordinary; for whether a mission is ordinary or extraordinary, it must always come from God. Therefore, something more is required regarding the *mode of the mission*—namely, that it be **immediate**, which is to say it proceeds immediately from God. Now, a thing can be immediate in two ways: 

Either **externally** <note>original Greek: *ἔξωθεν* (exōthen)</note>, when God calls and sends someone "through the spoken word" <note>original Greek: *λόγῳ προφορικῷ* (logō prophorikō)</note> by addressing them with a living voice. In this way, He called Abraham out of Ur of the Chaldeans; thus He called Moses from the bush; thus He sent Christ (Matthew 17:5), when the heavenly voice was heard saying: *This is my beloved Son, listen to him*, and also in Matthew 3. 

Or **internally** <note>original Greek: *ἔσωθεν* (esōthen)</note>, when God calls within by some more vehement and effective motion of the Holy Spirit. Luther’s mission was not of the first kind, since that belonged to the **Economy of the Old Testament** <term>In theology, an "Economy" (Latin: *Oeconomia*) refers to God's specific way of managing or interacting with humanity during a particular historical era.</term>, when God frequently appeared to His Prophets and Patriarchs. But once Christ was finally revealed as the Mediator, these types of appearances ceased. The voice of God ceased when the Word of the Father had spoken; He no longer speaks "in many parts and in various ways" (Hebrews 1), now that the "living and effective word of God" has been delivered to us (Hebrews 4), and we have the "Holy Spirit by whom those who are children of God are led" (Romans 8).

Therefore, Luther's mission was of the latter kind, which befits the economy of the New Testament. For God did not appear to him, but this entire business was carried out through the internal calling of the Spirit. For, first of all, the knowledge of the truth in that **Egyptian darkness** <note>A biblical metaphor for spiritual ignorance or the "errors" of the Roman Church, referencing the plague of darkness in Exodus.</note> could only have arisen from the illumination of the Spirit. Secondly, once the truth was known, the defense and publication of it—and Luther’s undaunted courage when that truth was oppressed by all the power, threats, and persecutions of the Papacy—was without doubt from the fervor of the Spirit...

<summary>Cregut argues that Martin Luther’s authority was "extraordinary" and "immediate," not through physical appearances like those in the Old Testament, but through a direct, internal calling of the Holy Spirit suited for the New Testament era.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Anthony Cregut’s argument regarding the "immediate" mission of the Reformers. On the previous page, he began distinguishing between an external immediate mission (like Abraham or Moses at the burning bush) and an internal one. This page focuses on the internal, "heroic" mission evidenced by biblical figures and the Reformers.</meta>

<page-num>618</page-num>
<header>ANTHONY CREGUT</header>

...from the matter itself and <term>of necessity</term> <note>original Greek: ἐξ' ἀνάγκη (ex anankē). Cregut is arguing that certain missions arise naturally from the urgent needs of the Church.</note> it flowed forth. We have examples of this kind of mission in various instances of heroes, such as in Samson against the Philistines regarding the various acts of his life, and in the very act of his death—a type of death which wonderfully represented Christ’s victory over death. 

So too Moses, when he struck down the Egyptian and liberated his Jewish brother, was already being sent <term>inwardly</term> <note>original Greek: ἔσωθεν (esōthen)</note> before his formal mission; by the movement of the Spirit, he was giving a prelude to the future liberation from Egyptian servitude. Likewise, Elijah was a brilliant example of this kind of mission when he reformed the Church, slaughtered all the priests of Baal, and with undaunted zeal opposed the cruelty of Ahab and the persecutions of the shameless Jezebel. 

Add to this John the Baptist, who in John 1:6 is said to be "sent by God." *There was a man sent from God, whose name was John.* In that passage, the Evangelist undoubtedly points to an extraordinary mission; and yet that mission was not performed by a spoken voice, for we nowhere read that God appeared to him and sent him in such an external manner. Hence, John is said to have *come in the spirit and power of Elijah.*

It must be admitted, however, that this kind of calling is not found in those who are sent by an **ordinary mission**. For even if they also feel an internal calling of the Spirit, they nevertheless do not reach that supreme level and summit of the <term>heroic Spirit</term> <note>Latin: Spiritus heroicus. A theological term for a special gift of courage beyond natural human capacity.</note> and undaunted fortitude which Luther attained, along with Calvin and other heroes of Christ. These are those <term>two witnesses</term> <note>A reference to the "Two Witnesses" in Revelation 11, whom many Protestant commentators identified as the succession of reformers like Hus and Jerome who stood against the Papacy.</note> who were killed, such as were the martyrs John Hus and Jerome of Prague. 

For just as in the moral virtues, an internal movement of virtue is felt by all who are endowed with it, yet that "heroic Spirit" which impels noble men to exceptional deeds—bursting forth from a certain unique temperament—is found in very few. Therefore, this has been observed much more throughout various ages in the constancy of the martyrs and in the fortitude of those teachers who, with an undaunted and most powerful soul, conquered death itself. Even the <term>Papists</term> <note>Latin: Pontificij. A term for supporters of the Pope.</note> themselves are compelled to admit this when they assign "aureoles" and "green crowns" to doctors <note>A "doctor" here refers to a highly learned teacher of the Church.</note> on account of heresies fought with a brave soul.

I grant, indeed, that Luther and other heroes of the Reformation suffered from human frailty, and that Luther at the beginning trembled...

### REVEALER OF SECRETS
<note>original Latin: REVELATOR ARCANORVM.</note>

...that he <note>Referring to Martin Luther.</note> doubled back and hesitated, and perhaps suffered something of human frailty out of anger and envy toward the Franciscans and Dominicans regarding the publication of indulgences <note>Indulgences were payments made to the Church to reduce punishment for sins. Cregut is addressing the common Catholic argument that Luther only started the Reformation because he was jealous that the Dominicans, rather than his own Augustinian order, were chosen to sell them.</note>; but everyone knows that God permitted these same blemishes to be found in all others, so that His power might be made more illustrious in human weakness. For at the very beginning of a calling, so many storms occur, so many dangers fly before one’s eyes—like a stormy sea—that the faithful man is held in great perplexity and his soul nearly fails. Consider how many excuses Moses made in this same situation, even though God was speaking to him from the burning bush? What shall I say of Jonah fleeing, and so forth? But at last, the Spirit of God triumphs and rouses the sluggishness of men. This is what happened with Luther, who, having been excommunicated by the Pope, in turn excommunicated the Pope himself.

Up to this point, it has been shown that the mission of Luther and others was <term>extraordinary</term> *on the part of the sender and the mode of the mission* <note>original Latin: "à parte mittentis & modi miſſionis." This means the way they were called by God was unusual compared to the standard bureaucratic process of the Church.</note>; but it is also extraordinary *with respect to its substance*. For Luther was sent so that he might reform the Church and purge its filth, which certainly has something extraordinary about it, as is clear from the example of Elijah and the Prophets. Even Cardinal Richelieu <note>Armand Jean du Plessis, Duke of Richelieu (1585–1642), a famous French clergyman and statesman who wrote works of pro-Catholic controversy.</note> confesses this, and he calls this mission "extraordinary"—not indeed a "primary and original" one, but a "collateral and subordinate" one, which is exactly what we also assert. Therefore, Luther was not sent to form some new doctrine—for if he were, the mission would be a <term>primary extraordinary mission</term>, like that of Moses and the Apostles, and miracles would be required for the confirmation of that new doctrine. Instead, Luther was sent so that he might reform the ancient doctrine which had been corrupted in the Papacy and depraved by a heap of traditions. For this reason, he had no need of miracles, but rather the Canon of the Scriptures, where both the doctrine and the miracles are already clear.

And truly, the <term>Papists</term> <note>A historical term for Roman Catholics used by Protestant writers.</note> themselves cannot deny that Luther held a true and legitimate mission within the Papacy; for among them, he announced the word of God for a long time (even if it was then adulterated by human traditions) and administered the sacraments. At that time, his calling was legitimate—not because he was preaching Roman doctrine, but because he announced the word of God, by which he was properly sent, even if it had been corrupted within the Papacy.

his mission and calling was much more legitimate afterwards, once he announced the pure and uncorrupted word of God; for, as is evident, the proclamation of truth could not interrupt his calling, but rather confirm it. Nor should the Catholic <note>original Latin: "Pontificius," referring to the Roman Catholic Church.</note> side object that Luther falsely claimed to be reforming the Church. Hence John Francis Pico della Mirandola sincerely wrote in his book *On the Order of Believing, Theory 16*: *One should believe a peasant or a small boy citing Scripture rather than the Pope or a thousand Bishops speaking without Scripture.*

...that they might lead out their <note>The OCR "fiam" is likely a fragment of "Ecclesiam" (Church), referring to the faithful being led out of Rome.</note> from the mystical Babylon <note>A common Reformation-era term for the Roman Catholic Church, referencing the corrupt city in the Book of Revelation.</note>. We have already discussed this testimony of the Spirit and heroic movement sufficiently above, when we examined the extraordinary mission of **Luther** and the reformers.

This includes **Elijah** and other Prophets, as is clear from the books of Kings; indeed, that duty of purging the Church and the temple of God belongs to the kings who are the foster-children of the Church, as was performed by **King Josiah**. And in the time of the Church Fathers, there was **John Wycliffe**, the **Albigensians** and those called **Waldensians**, as well as **Berengar, Archdeacon of Angers** <note>An 11th-century theologian who challenged the doctrine of transubstantiation.</note>, **Bertram the Priest** <note>Also known as Ratramnus of Corbie, a 9th-century monk whose writings on the Eucharist were influential to later Protestants.</note>, **John Huss** and **Jerome of Prague**, **Girolamo Savonarola the Dominican**, and finally **Luther** arose, and others without number both before and after **Luther**.

Observe, however, that the place of Scripture from **Jeremiah 1:5** is wrongly cited by the Cardinal to prove the extraordinary mission of **Jeremiah**. For the Prophecy of **Jeremiah** itself could not be proven by a testimony taken from that same Prophecy of **Jeremiah**, but from another testimony of Canonical Scripture. In respect to the people, this would be the same as if **Luther** tried to prove his mission using his own writings. But there was no need for **Luther** to give testimony about himself, since the Scriptures of the Old and New Testament have sufficiently provided testimony concerning his mission and that of others...

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS

...of the reformers. This is mystically taught in the Book of **Revelation** <note>original: "Apocalypseos"</note>, when it speaks of the two witnesses fighting against the **Antichrist**, being killed by him, and then rising again (Revelation 11). For those witnesses are the faithful Pastors of God, who at various times have provided testimony for the truth against heresies. They are called **"two"** because of the small number of witnesses to the truth—a certain number used for an uncertain one—and then **"two"** because **"by the mouth of two witnesses every word remains firm,"** as it says in the Gospel. Finally, they are called **"two"** because they utilize two witnesses that are beyond all reproach: namely, the **Old and New Testaments**. Hence, in verse 4, they are called **"the two olive trees and the two lampstands placed in the sight of the God of the earth,"** because through them, God kindles the light of the Gospel and nourishes the anointing of His Spirit in the hearts of the chosen against errors.

**Richelieu** <note>Armand Jean du Plessis, Cardinal-Duke of Richelieu (1585–1642), a powerful French statesman and Catholic prelate who wrote polemics against Protestantism.</note> furthermore insists that the mission of **Luther** and the others was not "extraordinary" because it was not confirmed by miracles. But in response, I answer first: that miracles were not absolutely necessary or essential for an extraordinary mission. This is evident from the fact that many Prophets did not perform miracles even under the Economy of the Old Testament; and in the New, **John the Baptist** was not distinguished by any sign, or as **Josephus** <note>Titus Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note> says of Christ, he was <term>a worker of no deeds</term> <note>original Greek: "οὐδὲν ἔργων ἐργάτης" (ouden ergōn ergatēs); likely referring to a specific lack of public miracles in certain historical accounts or a lack of magical artifice.</note>. On the contrary, many have performed signs who were not truly sent, as is clear from **Deuteronomy 13:1–3**: *"When a false prophet rises in your midst performing signs,"* etc.

II. Miracles were much less necessary in the mission of **Luther**, since they are required only when the doctrine of faith must be confirmed; and this happens whenever the doctrine being preached is *new*. However, when nothing new is brought forward, but the same doctrine is insisted upon that was previously handed down, there is no need for miracles. Since it was already confirmed by miracles when it was first preached, that was sufficient. **Pope Gregory I** <note>Also known as Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD).</note> and other ancient fathers illustrated this in earlier centuries with the example of a young plant and a budding shoot, which is watered until it grows into a tree; for then it is irrigated only by the rain from heaven. They also illustrate this with the similar example of a carriage in which infants walk and step forward little by little during their infancy, but for young men, such supports are useless. They also add the likeness of an arch, for whose stability at the beginning...

subsidiary supports are required, but as soon as the cement has hardened they are removed as useless, and nothing remains but the columns <note>original: "stylobates"</note>, capitals, and crossbeams. Therefore, since the doctrine of Luther and the Reformers is the same as that of the Apostles, the miracles of Christ and the Apostles, which sealed that doctrine, are sufficient.

III. I respond **conversely** <note>original Greek: "kat' antistrophēn"</note> that the Roman Bishops should have rather confirmed their doctrine with miracles; since their doctrine was new and recent, such as *the invocation of saints, free will, transubstantiation, the withholding of the cup* <note>original: "calicis mutilatio," referring to the practice of denying the sacramental wine to the laity</note>, *etc.* But either they performed no miracles, or they were false and **lying wonders** <note>original Greek: "terata pseudous"</note>.

IV. For the performance of miracles, a "faith of miracles" is required, by which one not only believes in God's infinite power to work miracles, but also in a covenant with God and a promise of God regarding the effecting of miracles whenever a believer implores it in prayer. But neither the Catholic Doctors <note>original: "Doctores Pontificiorum"</note>, nor Luther and others of this kind, had such a covenant with God, nor were they endowed with the faith of miracles.

V. Even if Luther had performed signs, this would not have been a true **proof** <note>original Greek: "tekmērion"</note> of his mission; because the Antichrist and his emissaries will perform signs, just as the Egyptian Magi often performed the same signs as Moses. Therefore, that mark is not essential.

VI. The very mission of Luther and the preaching of the Gospel was the greatest miracle; therefore, just as in the resurrection of Lazarus there was no need for another miracle to confirm that the resurrection of Lazarus was a miracle and a divine work; so, to prove that Luther’s mission was extraordinary, there is no need for any miracle other than the singular success of such a great Reformation, at which **Bellarmine** <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a powerful Jesuit Cardinal and key defender of the Catholic Church during the Counter-Reformation.</note> exclaims in amazement and wonder: **"O, what a portent!"** <note>original: "proh portentum!"</note> because in a mere moment of time, Luther's doctrine permeated so many nations and kingdoms, and had so many steadfast followers. For the example to the contrary—the Arian heresy <note>A 4th-century belief that denied the full divinity of Christ</note>, of which **Hilary of Poitiers** <note>A 4th-century Bishop and "Hammer of the Arians."</note> wrote: *"The whole earth groaned in amazement to find itself Arian"*—is wrongly cited. For the reasoning is surely different, since in Luther's time the true Doctrine was afflicted by tortures and torments, and yet that seed germinated immensely; so much so that the ashes of martyrs were the nursery of the Church. But on the contrary, regarding the Arian heresy and the **Quran** <note>original: "Alcorano"</note> of the **Muhammadans**, because [they grew] by the various armies and power of princes...

...increased, and this doctrine was spread by fire and sword. Truly, the same happened to Luther as to the Apostles, whose doctrine flourished in the midst of flames.

Of the same sort are the arguments the Cardinal <note>referring to Cardinal Richelieu (1585–1642), a chief adversary of French Protestant thought</note> brings forward concerning John the Baptist: that his whole life was miraculous; because he was born of a sterile mother, because he leaped in the womb, because Zechariah was mute, because he flourished in holiness of life. For all these things prove nothing about an "extraordinary mission," nor could they confirm such a mission to the Jews, because they had occurred long before and most were unknown to the Jews, or were even common to other men.

In vain also is that legal rule cited, namely that *the judgment is the same for those who do not exist and those who do not appear* <note>a Latin legal maxim: "idem sit iudicium et eorum qui non sunt et eorum qui non apparent"</note>; and consequently (says the Cardinal) Luther’s mission is false, since it is not proved by any testimony of Scripture or by miracle. But from the things said above, the mission of Luther and the others has been sufficiently proven, so that there is no reason for doubt.

Nor does Richelieu weaken the truth asserted above when he presses "step by step" <note>original Greek: κατ’ πόδας (*kat' podas*)</note> all the words of the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> concerning *the two witnesses, the time of prophecy for 1,260 days, their repentance, that they were clothed in sackcloth, that they performed great miracles, that they were killed, rose again, and finally ascended into heaven:* things which can be said of neither Luther nor any of the Reformers. 

But who does not see that all those things are narrated not indeed historically but prophetically, and therefore are not to be understood literally, but mystically, as is usually done in other Prophecies. Therefore, the number is a "definite for an indefinite" <note>a rhetorical device where a specific number represents a general large quantity</note>, as said above, and the "days" are mystical, as is often understood in this Prophecy and others; and because the Apocalypse imitates the style of the Prophets, repentance is signified by sackcloth, for nothing is more frequent among them than *to be clothed in sackcloth and ashes*. They performed miracles in the sense explained above, *and those two witnesses are killed and rise again and ascend into heaven*. For those witnesses or martyrs of the truth die, but soon they rise again in their successors, like phoenixes from their ashes; and finally they ascend into heaven, because those holy martyrs of God are crowned with the crown of martyrdom. Which indeed...

# ANTHONY CREGUT

Everything fits together perfectly without any distortion of the truth; but what the Catholics <note>original Latin: *Pontificij*</note> imagine regarding Enoch and Elijah <note>referring to the traditional Catholic view that Enoch and Elijah would return as the "Two Witnesses" to fight the Antichrist</note>, we consider to be empty and rotten fictions lacking the Word of God—indeed, they are unwritten <note>original Greek: *agraphōs*</note>. The Cardinal adds many other things wordily concerning miracles, which were fully refuted by us above, and therefore we would be repeating ourselves in vain here.

There remains a captious dilemma which the Cardinal uses:
> *When Luther withdrew from the Roman Church, either the Roman Church was the true Church or it was not. If it was not the true Church, I ask of him: was there then a true Church in the world, or on the contrary, was there no true Church? If there was any Church, let him tell us which one it was, and why he did not join with it—which would have been better than instituting a new one. If there was no Church, what would become of the promises of God, who promised that he would remain with the Church until the end of the ages, and that he would send the Holy Spirit to rule her?*

But indeed, this supposed sharpness of the Cardinal and his great effort is dispelled by even the slightest breath. It is not that we do not respect the talent and judgment of the most Eminent Cardinal—which has shown itself to be astounding and wonderful in many distinguished deeds—but because, due to the defect of his cause, any human efforts whatever cannot be anything but ruinous; for it is in vain and dangerous to attempt war against God and the Church. I respond, therefore, that when Luther came forth, the true Church was in the world, and yet it was not the Roman Church; rather, it lived *within* the Roman Church, and indeed *outside* the Roman Church in the Greek and other churches, since we believe, according to the Apostles’ Creed <note>original: *symbolum Apostolorum*</note>, in the Holy Catholic Church, which is spread throughout the whole world. Indeed, even as I write these things after Luther’s secession, the true Church is a "hidden mixture" <note>original Greek: *chimera*; here used to describe something that exists within another body but is distinct or obscured</note> within the Roman Church. 

For all these things to be understood, it must be known that the Catholics sweat greatly over this question and labor in vain in their various published writings, because they aim away from the target by playing in ambiguity, not distinguishing the notion of the Church according to its various aspects <note>original Greek: *schesis*</note>. For the true Church of God, which is treated in the Creed and throughout Scripture, and whose many praises and wonderful qualities are proclaimed, is not the visible and external Church, which also consists of hypocrites;

...but rather the Church which is gathered from the faithful alone through the preaching of the Word. For although the Elect <note>The "Elect" refers to those whom God has chosen for salvation, a central concept in Reformed theology.</note> are not separated from others, nor do they live apart, they must nevertheless be distinguished from the rest. Therefore, at the time when Luther was sent, the true Church existed within the Papacy <note>original Latin: *in Papatu*</note>, but it was the Church of the Elect, which groaned perpetually under the Roman yoke, just as the Jewish Church once groaned under the yoke of Pharaoh. Because of this, throughout various centuries, the Roman Church was accused of rebellion by faithful pastors, and that Roman tyranny was condemned by the Word of God; but those faithful witnesses and martyrs of Christ were killed, as it is written in Revelation 11. Yet soon they rose again from the ashes; for God raised up other heralds of the truth, and finally Luther and other reformers arose, who inflicted an incurable wound upon the Roman Church and the Pope. And then, as the trumpet of the Gospel sounded within the Papacy through Luther and others, countless people shook off the Pope's yoke—a burden they had previously borne with impatience, but which they finally broke with a strong and undaunted spirit at the time appointed in the counsel of God. This happened when Luther excommunicated the Pope and burned the papal bulls <note>In 1520, Luther publicly burned the "Exsurge Domine," the papal decree threatening him with excommunication, signaling his final break with Rome.</note>. There was also the Church of the Elect in the East, since many of those churches were purer than the Roman one itself, as is evident from the *Confession of Faith* by Cyril, Patriarch of Constantinople, recently published <note>Cyril Lucaris (1572–1638), the "Protestant Patriarch," who attempted to reform the Greek Orthodox Church along Calvinist lines.</note>. <margin>The Confession of Faith by Cyril, Patriarch of Constantinople</margin> I add further that even now within the Roman Church there is a Church of the Elect, such as those who come to join us every day from the Papacy. For whoever lives within the Papacy and comes to know the truth and the errors of the Popes, if they are a lover of their own salvation, they must immediately withdraw from that Church. This is because, due to idolatry, God cannot be rightly worshipped within the Roman communion, nor can salvation be obtained there. Therefore, Luther and the other faithful who were then in the Papacy could not flee *to* the true Church, since they themselves *were* that true Church; for in that case, the Church would have been fleeing to itself. Furthermore, that true Church could no longer remain within the Papacy, both because the yoke of Babylonian tyranny <note>A common Protestant metaphor comparing the Roman Church to the biblical Babylon that held the Israelites captive.</note> had to be shaken off at some point after such long servitude, and because God finally chose to hear the groans of His people at the preordained time (just as happened during the Egyptian servitude), and also because the Church, as a virgin and undefiled bride, could no longer persevere amidst such corruption of faith and morals as existed in the Papacy.

And these things have been said thus far concerning <term>extraordinary mission</term> <note>In this context, a "mission" is the authority or calling to preach. An "extraordinary mission" refers to a direct call from God, like that of the Prophets or Apostles, without human appointment.</note>. This is because the <term>succession of Bishops</term> <note>The continuous line of bishops tracing back to the Apostles, which the Catholic Church claimed as the sole source of authority.</note> remained among them. This is especially true when the essential parts of mission and ordination remain unchanged, just as baptism administered in the Roman Church is valid even if the doctrine is corrupted, because the essential parts of this sacrament remained. Even our baptism is considered valid according to the <term>Pontificians</term> <note>A term for Roman Catholics, referring to their allegiance to the Pope (the Pontiff).</note>, although they repeatedly assert the corruption of our doctrine. Even in the time of Christ and the Apostles, the doctrine of the Priests was corrupted, and yet the succession of Priests remained. Regarding the Pharisees, Christ said: *they sit in the chair of Moses, etc.* <note>Matthew 23:2. Christ instructs his followers to obey the teachings of the Pharisees because of their office, even if they do not follow their personal examples.</note>

Therefore, Luther truly had an ordinary mission and could be lawfully sent by the Roman Bishops. Thus the order of succession could not be interrupted in Luther and his successors. Since Luther was sent by the Roman Church, either the Roman Church can have no succession, or Luther had it; and Luther’s succession could not be interrupted just because he spoke out against the doctrine of the Roman Church. This is because, firstly, Luther was properly sent by God, of whom the Roman Bishops were only the instruments and means of the mission, insofar as it was a "mediated" and ordinary one. Therefore, Luther was bound to seek the glory of God, not the glory of the Pope. Secondly, Luther and others swore upon the most holy [Word] of God...

He treats everything according to political and topical standards, following human reasoning and the maxims of the world, rather than theologically and from the true principles of faith, which are the highest proofs of all. 

Hence it is that he deliberately disdains to examine faith controversies to the quick <note>Cregut uses the Greek "ἐξονυχίζειν" (exonychizein), meaning to examine minutely or "to the fingernail."</note>, treating them only broadly <note>Greek "παχυλῶς" (pachylos), meaning cursorily or roughly.</note> and in outline <note>Greek "ὡς ἐν τύπῳ" (hos en typo), meaning as a sketch or figure.</note>. He does this, of course, so that he might not discover something through too much searching and scrutiny that would disturb his aim and mind, or impose a delay on his secret plans. This same thing happens to those who busily try to reconcile the world and the glory of the age with religion. And truly, that "method" is a clear enough example of those things the Cardinal was meditating upon regarding <term>syncretism</term> <note>The attempted reconciliation or union of different or opposing principles, practices, or parties, often in a religious context.</note> and religious harmony.

## CHAPTER XV.

### A Dissertation on Exodus Chapter VIII, verses 16, 17, 18, 19: On the Miracle of the Lice.

### ANALYSIS.

The infestation of lice <term>phthiriasis: a condition where lice multiply rapidly on the body</term> in Egypt was unknown to the physicians. *This dissertation is divided into four parts.*

The first part concerns the miracle of the lice. It argues that the production of these lice was truly a miracle. There are eight conditions required for a true miracle:
1. That miracles are rare.
2. That they are external rather than internal works.
3. That they are above nature, not against nature.
4. That they transcend universal nature.
5. That they are examples of the power of creation.
6. That they do not happen gradually, but in an instant.
7. That they proceed from the immediate power of God.
8. That they proceed from the active power of God, and not from any active or passive power within nature itself.

The opinion of the Rabbis <note>The author is likely referring to Jewish commentators who attempted to provide naturalistic explanations for the plagues</note>, claiming that miracles come from nature, is refuted. The opinion of Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher</note> regarding miracles. Strictly speaking, there is no "instrumental cause" <note>an intermediate tool or agent</note> for miracles. There are two kinds of instruments: physical and moral. How faith in miracles serves as a moral instrument for performing miracles. What kind of covenant <note>original: "pactum"</note> is required in miracles. Whether the Prophets and Apostles performed signs. What are the signs of the Antichrist? What are the signs of the "Saints" within the Papacy? <note>The author, a Protestant, uses "Papatu" (the Papacy) to question Catholic claims of miracles</note>. Regarding the miracle of Muhammad in the Quran <note>original: "Alcorano"</note>. Stories of fabulous <note>legendary or mythological</note> miracles found in the works of Eusebius, Rufinus, and de Thou <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a French historian</note>. Signs of the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicorum"</note> from Valerius Maximus. Allusions to the names of Saints arising from miracles according to the Papists. A very strong argument proving that Saints could not have performed miracles <note>The author argues that human beings cannot perform miracles by their own power, only God can</note>. That the miracles claimed by the Papists are performed in secret.

->ANTOINE CRÉGUT<-
630

...they swore that they would teach the Gospels as pure doctrine and truth, an oath they could not have upheld unless they spoke out against the errors of the **Papists** <note>original: "Pontificiorum." A common 17th-century Protestant term for Roman Catholics, emphasizing their allegiance to the Pope (the Pontiff).</note>.

What we have said so far should be enough to prove the mission of **Luther** and his associates, so there is no need to resort to the arguments the **Cardinal** <note>Cardinal Richelieu (1585–1642), the French statesman and theologian who wrote works attempting to convert Protestants back to Catholicism.</note> brings up concerning the **Princes**, or the **Hussites** <note>Followers of Jan Hus, a 14th-century Czech reformer.</note> and **Albigensians** <note>A medieval religious group in Southern France. Early Protestants often claimed these groups as "spiritual ancestors" to show that their faith existed before the Reformation.</note>, from whom some derive **Luther’s** calling. For this should not be understood as if **Luther** and the other reformers received their mission directly from the **Hussites**; rather, this is said only regarding the lineage of **Doctrine**. When the **Papists** ask where the Church was before **Luther**, the answer is that it existed within the **Papacy**, as is clear from the **Hussites** and **Albigensians**, who were sent in the same way as **Luther**.

And so let this be the response to that specific chapter in Book 2 of Cardinal Richelieu's *The Method of Conversion*, in which the **Monks** and other **Catholic Doctors** presume to triumph in their sermons and pulpits before the people. They take their opportunity from the mission of **Moses**, which we explained in that passage of **Exodus 3:14** <note>"God said to Moses, 'I AM WHO I AM.'" Catholic critics argued that because Luther could not perform miracles like Moses, his "call" from God was fake.</note>. Since the **Cardinal’s** book was at hand, we could not leave his reasons untouched. From this sample, it is clear to anyone how easily one can dismantle the artful arguments found in that book. Indeed, these meditations (as is clear at first glance) savor more of a **Politician** overwhelmed by various business than of a profound and consummate **Theologian**. 

This is because he treats everything through a political lens and topical logic according to human reasoning and the maxims of the world, rather than theologically and from the true principles of faith (which are the ultimate proof of all proofs). Hence, he deliberately disdains to **examine to the quick** <note>original: ἐξονυχίζειν (exonychizein), a Greek term meaning to examine with extreme, "fine-toothed comb" precision.</note> the controversies of faith, instead treating them **roughly and only in a general sketch** <note>original: παχυλῶς καὶ ὡς ἐν τύπῳ (pachylos kai hos en typo).</note>. He does this, no doubt, lest he should find something by searching too deeply that would disturb his goals or his mind, and place a delay on his secret plans. This is what happens to those who try to reconcile the world and the glory of the age with religion. Truly, that method is a clear enough example of what the **Cardinal** was meditating on regarding <term>syncretism: the attempt to merge different or opposing religious beliefs into one</term> and regarding a forced peace in religion.

### A Dissertation on Exodus Chapter 8, verses 16, 17, 18, and 19. Concerning the Miracle of the Lice.

### A N A L Y S I S.

*The infestation of lice in Egypt <note>original: "Phtiriasis Ægypti." From the Greek 'phtheir', meaning louse.</note> was unknown to the physicians. The dissertation is divided into four parts.*
*The first part concerns the miracle of the lice. That the production of the lice was truly a miracle. Eight conditions required for a true miracle. That miracles are rare. That they are external works, not internal ones. That they are above nature, not against it. That they transcend universal nature. That they are specimens of creation. That they do not occur gradually but in an instant. That they proceed from the immediate power of God. That they proceed from the active power of God, and not from either the active or passive power of nature. The opinion of the **Rabbis**, that miracles come from nature, is refuted. The opinion of **Maimonides** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Jewish philosopher and scholar who sought to reconcile Aristotelian philosophy with Hebrew scripture.</note> regarding miracles. There is not, strictly speaking, an instrumental cause of miracles. Two kinds of instruments: Physical and moral. How the faith of miracles is a moral instrument for performing miracles. What kind of covenant is required in miracles. Whether the **Prophets** and **Apostoles** produced signs. What the signs of the **Antichrist** are. What are the signs of the Saints in the **Papacy**? Concerning the miracle of **Muhammad** in the **Quran**. Stories of fabulous miracles in **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339), an early Christian historian.</note>, **Rufinus** <note>Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 345–410), a monk and historian known for translating Greek church works into Latin.</note>, and **De Thou** <note>original: "Thuanum." Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a French historian and statesman.</note>. Signs of the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicorum." Here referring to non-Christian Greeks and Romans.</note> from **Valerius Maximus** <note>A 1st-century Roman author who compiled a famous collection of historical anecdotes.</note>. Allusions to the names of Saints arising from miracles according to the **Papists**. A most powerful argument by which it is proved that the Saints could not have performed miracles. That the miracles of the **Papists** are done in secret.*

SINCE the miracle of the lice was so astounding that the Magicians of Pharaoh, having given glory to God, were forced to exclaim, *This is the finger of God*. Thus, struck by that portentous lice-infestation <term>phtiriasis</term> <note>From the Greek 'phtheir' (louse); a condition where lice swarm the body, often used in antiquity to describe a horrific or divine punishment.</note>—unknown to physicians and incurable—we shall proceed to contemplate it a little more closely. This will be brought under examination in four chapters of discussion. I. Concerning that miracle of the lice performed by Moses and his brother Aaron. II. Concerning its purpose. III. Concerning the vain attempt of the Magicians to imitate it. IV. Concerning their confession, recognizing the finger of God.

In the first part, two things are yet to be distinguished: namely, the miracle itself and the true cause of that miracle.

->REVEALER OF SECRETS<-

I. That the creation of those lice was truly a miracle, we have clearly demonstrated from the true and essential conditions and requirements of a miracle. 1. A miracle must be rare and extraordinary; for those things which happen in the ordinary course of things by no means deserve the name of a miracle. Since they ought to produce wonder, which is why they are called *niphlaot* <note>original Hebrew: נפלאות</note> or "wonders" among the Hebrews, and *mophtim* <note>original Hebrew: מופתים</note>, that is, "prodigies," they must certainly be rare and unusual; otherwise, they would become commonplace. This follows the saying of **Augustine**: *Miracles grow cheap by the frequency of seeing them.* And that of the **Poet**: *The sun has no spectator except when it fails <note>The author refers to a solar eclipse.</note>.* No one observes the moon except when it is in labor <note>Meaning a lunar eclipse.</note>. Yet the light of the Sun and Moon is far more noble than their eclipse. Thus, in **John 2:1**, everyone wonders that Christ miraculously converted water into wine, and yet no one wonders that rainwater becomes wine in the vines, even though this is also the work of God, and no less a miracle, but it is "ordinary" because it happens every year.

II. Miracles must be external works, not internal; for those which are internal are called mysteries rather than miracles, and they affect the mind rather than striking the senses. Thus, the Trinity and the Incarnation and other works of God, although they are above nature, are nonetheless not "miracles" in this sense. Therefore, the <term>transubstantiation<note>The Catholic doctrine that the bread and wine of the Eucharist become the actual body and blood of Christ.</note></term> is wrongly placed among miracles by the <term>Papists<note>A historical, often polemical term for Roman Catholics.</note></term>, since no extraordinary sign of divine omnipotence appears, but instead something entirely contrary appears to the senses. That conspicuous mark of miracles was present in the miracles of Christ and the Apostles, which were exposed to the senses. The same is apparent from this miracle revealed by Moses.

III. Miracles are indeed above nature, but they are not against nature; and they indeed determine nature, but they do not exterminate it. Hence it is that God is able to perform *things impossible for nature* <note>original Latin: "impossibilia naturae"</note>, but not *things impossible by their nature* <note>original Latin: "impossibilia naturâ"</note> or what are called by the **Scholastics** <note>Medieval theologians and philosophers.</note> <term>incompossibles<note>Things that involve a logical contradiction, such as a "square circle."</note></term>, that is, things which involve a contradiction with the nature of the thing itself. Hence, as **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas, the highly influential 13th-century theologian.</note> rightly observed, those things are said to be "unable to be done" rather than saying that God "is unable to do them"; so that the impossibility is understood to reside not on the part of God, but on the part of the creature itself, because its nature is repugnant to it:

->ANTHONY CREGUT<-

A miracle, moreover, is an effect of power, not of powerlessness and weakness; this can be seen in the miracle of Moses, but not in the prodigy of <term>transubstantiation</term> <note>The Catholic doctrine that bread and wine become the actual body and blood of Christ; the author, likely a Protestant, is criticizing this as "overturning" nature rather than a true miracle.</note>, where there is not a conversion, but a subversion of natures.

**IV.** Miracles must transcend not only particular nature, but also universal nature. For those things which merely exceed the forces of a particular nature are not truly miracles, but only "wonders" (*mira*). Thus, angels and demons have frequently performed wonders which stirred the admiration of men, and for that reason were held to be miracles by men. In this way, the magicians of Pharaoh seemed to perform miracles in this place when they imitated the works of Moses; but they were either merely "wonders," or they were false and illusory. In contrast, the miracles of Moses were true and real, without deceit or incantations.

**V.** Every miracle has within it some specimen of creation. For since a miracle arises from the immediate power of God, and not from a mediated power (namely that of nature, which miracles transcend, as we said above), it is therefore always a work produced out of nothing. For the production that comes from art requires some whole natural composite of matter and form. But generation, which is the work of nature, necessarily requires matter so that a form may be introduced into it. Finally, creation, which is a work above nature and art, requires neither matter nor form, but produces Being out of nothing, "calling those things which are not as if they were" <note>A reference to Romans 4:17.</note>. This assertion of ours would be easy to confirm by examining any miracle. Thus, in the first miracle of Christ, when water is converted into wine, it is a specimen of creation; because in the water there was no <term>privative power</term> <note>A latent or inherent potentiality to become something else.</note> out of which wine could be drawn, but only a <term>negative power</term> <note>The simple absence of the thing, with no natural way to produce it.</note>. Therefore, that transmutation was made through a creation of wine from the "non-being" of wine. The same must be thought concerning the resurrection of Lazarus and other miracles.

**VI.** Miracles do not happen successively <note>Over a period of time.</note>, but in an instant. The reason is that all succession and motion belongs to nature, according to the definition of **the Philosopher** <note>Aristotle.</note> in his *Acroamatics* <note>original: "Acroamaticis," referring to Aristotle's "Physics."</note>: *Nature is the principle of motion and rest in that in which it exists primarily and of itself, and not by accident.* But miracles happen above nature. Therefore, they happen in an in—

...instantly and also indivisibly, as is clear here in the procreation of lice <note>Referring to the third plague of Egypt in Exodus 8:16–19. The author argues that whereas nature takes time to generate life, God did so here in an instant.</note>.

**VII.** Miracles proceed from the infinite power of God, which, since it acts immediately in miracles, means nothing can be achieved by a creature—whether as a primary cause, a lesser cause, or even an instrumental cause. Not as a *primary cause*, because then God would not be the one performing the miracle. Not *instrumentally*, both because in Psalm 72:18 <note>Psalm 71:18 in some numbering systems</note> God is said to do <note>original Hebrew: נפלאות לבד (*nifla'ot levad*)</note> *wonders alone*, and in Psalm 136:4 *great wonders alone*—or "separately from others," as the Hebrew word implies—and because an instrument must cooperate with the principal cause. This cooperation is denied in miracles with respect to any creature, as has been demonstrated above from other conditions.

**VIII.** Miracles proceed solely from the <term>active power</term> <note>The capacity to initiate an action or change in another thing.</note> of God, the author of nature; they do not proceed in any way from the active or <term>passive power</term> <note>The capacity of a thing to be changed by an external force.</note> of nature. Not from an *active power*, because then it would transcend the entire sphere of nature, and nature would be acting above itself. Not from a *passive power*, because since that is physical, a work which is above nature would be emerging from the very "bowels" of nature, which is <note>original Greek: ἀτοπώτατον (*atopotaton*)</note> *utterly absurd*. Therefore, the Rabbis—according to the testimony of Maimonides in *The Guide for the Perplexed, Part 2, Chapter 29*—erroneously assert that miracles in some way flow from nature. They claim the Prophets did not actually perform miracles, but merely gave a sign of when this or that thing would have a miraculous effect, which God had implanted in it from the beginning of its nature. 

However, Maimonides adds another point from his own mind which can be understood in a sound sense: namely, that *no miraculous change is constant and permanent; for the thing returns to its own nature, as the serpent back into a staff, the blood back into water, and so with the leprous hand.* According to the Rabbis, *the world follows its own custom.* <note>A common Jewish philosophical maxim: "Olam k’minhago noheg," meaning the natural order generally persists even if interrupted by a miracle.</note> *This is our opinion on miracles.* So far Maimonides.

We conclude, therefore, that no <term>instrumental cause</term> <note>A tool or agent used by a higher power to achieve an end, like a brush in the hand of a painter.</note> of miracles is given, and accordingly, neither Moses, nor the Prophets, nor the Apostles performed them by any power of their own. However, so that these things may be understood more distinctly, it must be known that there are two kinds of instruments: some are called *physical instruments*, and others are called *moral instruments*. *Physical instruments* are those which, upon a certain subject...

# ANTHONY CRÉGUT

...they pour in their power to produce an effect; just as heat is the instrument of fire by which water grows hot through the influence of its own power upon the subject being acted upon. In this way, there is no **physical instrument** for performing signs <note>miracles</note>; no more than in the act of creation, of which miracles are specific examples, for a creature is not even capable of creating a gnat. As for **moral instruments**, both Moses and others can be called instruments in this way: because they had the "faith of miracles," they obtained those signs from God through their prayers. For just as **justifying faith** in the faithful is a <term>moral instrument</term> <note>An instrument that does not produce the result by its own physical force, but by meeting a condition or an agreement—like a signature on a contract.</note> by which, because of the Gospel covenant, the believer embraces the special mercy of God and thus follows the remission of sins; so the **faith of miracles** is a moral instrument. Because of a special covenant established with those who possess this faith, when they embrace the power of God with the firmest trust, God performs miracles at their command. Thus, they themselves are judged to have performed the miracles, according to the saying, *All things are possible for one who believes* <note>original: "Credenti omnia sunt possibilia" (Mark 9:23)</note>, both actively and passively. Nevertheless, it is truly God who provides such things. Peter sufficiently hinted at this regarding the lame man <margin>Acts 3:12</margin> saying, *Men of Israel, why do you wonder at this? Or why do you look so intently at us, as if by our own power or piety we had made this man walk?* And Moses, striking the rock with his staff, could not draw out water because he wavered in faith, and therefore he struck it twice. So Christ said in the Gospel that he could not perform many signs because of the Jews' unbelief; because that "faith of miracles" was required as a moral instrument by which the power of God (so to speak) might be drawn out and miracles obtained from Him. Thus, Moses is said to have performed those miracles before Pharaoh, and the Apostles performed many so that their mission and the Gospel doctrine might be confirmed.

Therefore, the **Roman Catholics** <note>original: "Pontificij" (the Papists)</note> are seriously deluded when they attribute various miracles to the Saints and to the relics of Saints. For this reason, the <term>apotheosis</term> <note>The elevation of a human to divine status.</note> or **canonization** of Saints is usually decreed among them based on a report of miracles. This is why they stuff the *Lives of the Saints* with a hodgepodge of miracles, even employing obscene and almost scurrilous stories, the telling of which requires one to apologize to the listener's nose <note>A Latin idiom meaning the stories are "stinking" or highly offensive to good taste.</note>...

...they ought to be, such as those things which Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius (1538–1607) was a prominent Catholic cardinal and historian known for his "Annales Ecclesiastici."</note> relates regarding Saint Gingolphus <note>Saint Gangulphus of Burgundy. The author refers to a legendary punishment of the saint's unfaithful wife, involving involuntary flatulence—hence the "obscene rattling" mentioned.</note> at the year 756, concerning the obscene rattling of the saint and his wife. But indeed, even those miracles of the Papal saints are fictitious; just as Cardinal Bessarion <note>Basilios Bessarion (1403–1472), a Greek scholar and Catholic Cardinal who was famously skeptical of certain medieval traditions.</note> indicated, who, upon seeing a wicked man enrolled by the Pope in the catalog of the gods <note>i.e., the canonization of a saint</note>, exclaimed: *Truly, this man compels me to doubt all the others.* Or rather, they are "marvels" rather than miracles, performed by a <term>Cacodaemon</term> <note>A malevolent spirit or demon.</note>. For although that phrase is not added in Matthew 24:24 when Christ predicted the rising of false christs and false prophets who "will show great signs and wonders" <note>original Greek: δώσουσι σημεῖα μεγάλα κὶ τέρατα</note>, it must nevertheless be understood as such, as is clear from the following "so as to deceive" <note>original Greek: ὥστε πλανῆσαι</note>; this is done through impostures and feigned miracles. For in truth, miracles can be performed by the power of God alone, who, as He alone was able to establish nature, so He alone is capable of transforming it. Falsely, therefore, the Papists repeat this: *By the virtue of the cross and signs, the <term>transubstantiation</term> <note>The miraculous change of the substance of bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ.</note> of natures takes place.*

For this reason, we here hiss away the fake miracles of Francis Xavier, the Jesuit and "Apostle of the Japanese," as well as those of Loyola, the founder of the order. As for Mahomet <note>Muhammad, the prophet of Islam.</note>, he himself confesses that he was not sent to perform miracles—for miracles were attributed to Christ—but that he was girded with the sword, so that he might strike terror and destruction everywhere against those refusing the Alcoran <note>The Quran.</note>. However, they claim a single miracle was performed by him regarding the moon; the nature of this is not expressed in the Quran, but interpreters explain that the moon, having once been split in two, fell from heaven, but was joined back together by Mahomet and placed once more in its sphere. These are sheer trifles <note>original: "Gerræ Germanæ," a Latin idiom for nonsense or "stuff and nonsense."</note> and most foul lies.

It must be observed, therefore, that faith should not be rashly given to miracles of this kind. For men here usually indulge themselves too much and believe those <term>quacks</term> <note>original: "agyrtis," referring to wandering charlatans or street-performers.</note>, those triflers and peddlers, who hawk "old wives' tales" and superstitions to simple women. This happens today not only among the common people...

The partisans interpreted this in such a way as to say that God and the heavens were looking upon the slaughter with exultation. Jacques Charpentier <note>Iacobus Carpenterius (1524–1574), a philosopher and fierce opponent of the Protestant Reformers.</note>, alluding to that light in relation to the month, praised it as "August" <note>A pun on the month of August (when the massacre occurred) and the title *Augustus*, meaning venerable or imperial.</note> in a published writing, and said that once the Protestants were deleted, the Catholic religion would take on its ancient splendor. On the contrary, the Protestants argued that if this were to be considered a miracle, it was a sign signifying that even if the Church seemed extinguished, it would miraculously flourish back to life. They confirmed this by the example of the bush shown to Moses <note>The Burning Bush in Exodus 3.</note>, and argued that the innocence of the faithful was commended by it rather than the slaughter, since it occurred in a cemetery named for the "Innocents."

It is no wonder, therefore, if the ancients, such as Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father.</note> (on Matthew 24, homily 49), Cyril, Augustine, and others have said: *He is a great marvel who requires marvels in order to believe.* Because signs and omens contribute nothing to holiness, and the Antichrist will perform works wonderfully but deceitfully. The Pharisees sought signs from Christ. Among the Pagans, innumerable signs were peddled, as is clear from Valerius Maximus <note>A Roman author of the 1st century AD known for his collection of historical anecdotes.</note>, Book 1, Title 8. Their priests and prophets, like Calchas <note>A seer in Homer’s *Iliad*.</note> in Homer, the Vestals, and the Augurs produced various portents, but they smacked of the deceptions of demons.

...[they claim] that their miracles belong to the Saints, who lived piously and now enjoy glorious bliss, and that it would be quite blasphemous to attribute impostures to them; but everyone knows that Satan transforms himself into an angel of light. This is why the Egyptians long ago misused Jeremiah himself; when the Prophet was buried in that region, they transformed him into a god and worshipped him, sacrificed to him, and honored him no differently than their own gods, as Jerome also reports in his preface to Jeremiah. And when these idolaters were healed from the bite of serpents, they credited it to their own zeal and religion toward the Prophet.

Even today, the <term>Papists</term> <note>original: *Pontificij*; a term used by Protestant authors to refer to members of the Roman Catholic Church.</note>—who command us to be serious and sober when dealing with the miracles of the Saints—nevertheless make the matter a laughingstock and exult jokingly by playing on syllables. Thus, they want Saint Gothard to perform miracles by curing arthritis, which our French people call *la Goute* <note>original: *la Goute*; Crégut is mocking the linguistic similarity between the name Gothard and the word for "gout."</note>. Likewise, Saint Lucia heals the eyes because she is named *Lucia* from "Light" <note>original: *Lucia à Luce*.</note>. Saint Otilia cures the ears, because the Greek word signifies ears <note>original: *Otilia* derived from the Greek *ous/otos* (ear).</note>. And the <term>roasters</term> <note>original: *tostores* or *assatores*.</note> celebrate the feast of the <term>Assumption</term> because of the allusion to the name "roasted meat" <note>original: *assus*; Crégut is pointing out a pun between the Assumption of Mary and the Latin word for roasted or parched food.</note>. And many other things could be added, if it did not weary us to linger on these trifles and <term>frivolous nonsense</term> <note>original: *φλυαρίαις* (phlyariais).</note>.

Therefore, the Papists rashly claim miracles for themselves with this insoluble argument. For if they were able to produce miracles, they would do so either as a **principal cause** or as an **instrumental cause**. But they can do so in neither way. Therefore, they do not produce miracles. The <term>major premise</term> is evident, because there is no middle ground between a principal and an instrumental cause. The <term>minor premise</term> is proven: because if they acted as an instrumental cause, that instrumental cause would act either as a **physical instrument** or as a **moral instrument**. But they act in neither way. Therefore, etc. 

They do not act as a physical instrument, because humans—regardless of who they are—can contribute no power toward producing a supernatural effect, such as a miracle, which is raised above all nature and flows immediately from God, as was demonstrated above. Nor do they act as a moral instrument, because instruments of this kind presuppose a faith in miracles and some **covenant** between God and men, by which God promises an act of infinite power and a miraculous influence whenever the person who...
