# ANTHONY CRÉGUT

[Whoever] possesses the **faith of miracles** <note>The "faith of miracles" refers to a specific spiritual gift mentioned in the New Testament, distinct from saving faith.</note> will ask it from God for the confirmation and sealing of true doctrine. But in truth, no one is found among the **Papists** <note>original: *Pontificios*; a term used by Protestant authors to refer to members of the Roman Catholic Church.</note>, nor has anyone been found since the proclamation of the **Gospel**, who possessed this faith of miracles and, with it, the covenant and promise regarding the performing of miracles and obtaining them from God at will—whenever it might please the **Monks** to "discover" some image of the **Virgin** or of some **Saint** in some location, in order to clean out the purses of the superstitious common folk and enrich the **Cloister-dwellers** <note>original: *Coenobitas*; monks living in a community.</note> with offerings. 

And although the Monks may preach these wonders, performed at the feet of **idols** <note>original: *simulacrorum*; Crégut uses this word to imply that the statues are false gods or graven images.</note>, to those near and far, nevertheless, not without cause, clever and discerning men <note>original: *nasutuli & emunctae naris homines*; literally "people with big noses and wiped nostrils," a Latin idiom for those with a keen sense of smell or sharp wit who can "sniff out" a lie.</note> smell out these deceitful frauds. By this reasoning, they prove that miracles ceased after the manifestation of the Gospel throughout the whole world; for since the Gospel was sufficiently sealed by the miracles of the Apostles, as if with stamps, it is not now to be confirmed again by new miracles. Furthermore, miracles ought to be external and visible so that they may serve as seals for confirmation; but the miracles claimed in the **Papacy** have crept in secretly in hiding places and the little hovels of Monks, and have not been seen or made open to others in public—which is the opposite of what Christ and the Apostles did. Nor have we ever heard of any miracle performed in the presence of any **Catholic** <note>original: *viri Catholici*; Crégut likely uses this term here to refer to a "true" (Reformed) believer, arguing that no Protestant has witnessed a miracle convincing enough to make him "fly over" to the Roman Catholic side.</note> man, which nevertheless ought to have happened so that he might go over to the side of the Papists.

But indeed, however true these things may be in this current state of the **Church**, nevertheless in the time of Moses and the Apostles, those holy men of God were moral instruments who, with respect to the action, behaved merely **passively** <note>original: *παθητικῶς* (pathetikōs)</note>, because they receive [the power] rather than effect it themselves. They are not, however, like wooden stumps in this matter, since they are endowed with the faith of miracles, which cannot exist without knowledge and assent—indeed, without trust and **full assurance** <note>original: *πληροφορίᾳ* (plērophoria)</note> concerning the power of God, which by covenant must soon exert itself by embracing that faith. Therefore, because on account of that certainty of the outcome they *seem* to perform them, the Apostles are said to "produce" miracles. When, therefore, in Mark 16:20, God is said to **work with** <note>original: *συνεργεῖν* (synergein)</note> them, this is not to be understood as if God were a **co-cause** <note>original: *συναίτιον* (synaition)</note>, and as if a joint-cause working from one part—

...should work, on the other hand men themselves. For in truth, men do nothing with respect to the **Result** <term>original: *Apotelesma*; the final outcome or completed effect of a divine action</term>. And although, as far as ministry and the preaching of the word are concerned, God "waters" through men, yet regarding miracles, God is said to act *in* men rather than *through* men. Indeed, even the very humanity of God, although united to the **Word** <term>original: *λόγῳ* (logō); the divine Logos or Second Person of the Trinity</term>, could not by itself perform miracles, because all the results of that Divine Person proceed from the efficacy of the divinity, yet from the merit of the humanity; for Christ merited more through suffering than through acting, unless the efficacy is drawn from his divinity. 

Therefore, just as **justifying faith** <note>A central Protestant doctrine where faith is the instrument by which a person receives God's grace, rather than a "work" the person performs.</note> justifies us not by acting or ethically (insofar as it is a habit taken absolutely), but rather by receiving the **merit of Christ** (insofar as it is taken relatively as an instrument); so the **faith of miracles** does not produce miracles by acting as a habit, but as an instrument for receiving and obtaining the virtue and power of God. And for this reason, as faith is said to justify because it embraces God's mercy, so the faith of miracles is said to perform miracles because it firmly embraces God's power. And just as he who doubts and does not believe is not truly justified, so **Moses**, doubting while striking the rock with his staff <note>A reference to Numbers 20:11-12, where Moses's doubt resulted in him being barred from the Promised Land.</note>, did not obtain the act of God's power in bringing forth water.

But indeed, just as a creature cannot absolutely perform a miracle, so this can be confirmed with respect to the types and the three kinds of miracles. The **first kind of miracles** is when no matter lies beneath from whose potentiality a form might be drawn out; and thus, to produce something without underlying matter is not only to perform a miracle, but even to **create and to make something from nothing**, as when Christ fed a vast multitude from a few loaves and fishes. For that multiplication could not have happened without creation. The **second kind of miracles** is when matter is present, but it is a "raw and disordered mass" and by itself incapable of the production of a form, since there is no **passive power** within it from which a form can be drawn out, but only that power which is called in the Schools **obedientiary** <term>original: *potentia obedientialis*; a Scholastic term referring to the natural capacity of a creature to be acted upon by God to receive a supernatural effect beyond its own powers</term>, which is purely negative and is nothing with respect to the effect—for nothing could ever be produced through that power on its own—but nevertheless, that power is required with respect to God performing a miracle.

<header>ANTHONY CRÉGUT</header>
<page-type>text</page-type>

...obediential <note>From the Latin *obedientialis*; referring to a creature's capacity to obey a command of the Creator to perform a task beyond its natural ability.</note>, which excludes all contradiction; if such a contradiction were present, there would be no miracle, because miracles are above nature, not against nature. An example of this kind of miracle is seen in the man born blind, who is cured by mud; here, there is only an "obediential power" in the mud, just as there was in the dust from which Adam was formed. 

The third kind of miracle occurs when there is indeed a **passive power** <term>original: *potentia passiva*; the inherent capacity of a substance to be changed or to receive a new form</term> in the matter, from which an effect can be drawn out naturally and in an ordinary way. However, because no **active power** <term>original: *potentia activa*; the force or agent that causes a change to happen</term> of a creature is present to activate that passive potential of the matter—according to the axiom of the Philosophers: *Whatever is in potential cannot be brought into actuality except by that which is already in act*—the effect is not produced naturally. Instead, the immediate power of God supplies the lack of ordinary active power, and the effect emerges supernaturally, which is truly a miracle. 

In this way, Christ cured various diseases that certainly could have been cured by medicines; but because he did not employ those natural causes, and there was no such active power present, but rather he healed the diseases by himself immediately—such as a fever or other ailments—he is truly said to have performed a miracle. In these three ways, Moses and the other Prophets and Apostles performed signs, though they used the first mode more rarely. They chose to use some form of matter for the purpose of making it apparent to everyone that a miracle had been performed by them—or rather *in* them, since they were merely moral instruments <note>A "moral instrument" refers to a person who acts as a representative or tool for God's will, rather than being the source of the power themselves.</note>.

Since, therefore, God is the true and sole cause of miracles, he does not require means out of any necessity. He wished to signify this in the Creation by a famous example. For first he created light, not only to adorn the world with such excellent beauty and to begin the process of distinction, but also to show that he can accomplish whatever he wills without **secondary causes** <note>In scholastic philosophy, God is the "Primary Cause" of everything, while natural objects (like the sun) are "secondary causes" that God normally uses to achieve effects.</note>. For it was not by chance or accident that light preceded the Sun and the Moon. Since nothing is more easy for us than to bind God's power to the organs whose ministry he uses; and since light arises from the Sun and Moon, we conclude in our own opinion that this power is so confined to those two heavenly bodies that if they were removed from the world, it would seem no light could remain. But God willed to create light separately, to show that he holds the light in his own hand...

<meta>This page continues Crégut's analysis of how God uses "means" (instruments) to perform miracles. <header>THE REVEALER OF SECRETS</header>

...than he could bestow upon us without the Sun and the Moon. Indeed, he created the light in such a way that there would still be alternating turns for darkness.

Therefore, God sufficiently testifies that he does not need means to perform his works, since he uses either means in which there is only a **negative power** <term>original: *potentia negativa*; a capacity that does not naturally produce the effect being sought</term>, from which an effect cannot be naturally drawn; or he uses contrary means, which by their own nature would hinder the effect rather than help it. Examples include when Christ used mud to give sight to the blind man <note>John 9:6</note>, or when the Prophet used bitter wood to make the waters sweet <note>Likely a reference to Elisha at Jericho (2 Kings 2:19-22) or Moses at Marah (Exodus 15:23-25)</note>, or when the Prophet was fed by a raven, a bird of prey <note>Elijah in 1 Kings 17:4-6</note>. So in this history, Moses and Aaron use a rod to strike the water or the dust; in that rod there was no physical power to produce the effect, but only a logical and negative power. Therefore, God alone performed the miracle.

Thus far we have spoken of miracles and their **efficient cause** <term>original: *causa efficiens*; the primary agent or force that brings something into being</term>; there follows the second part, which is their **end** <term>original: *finis*; the ultimate purpose or goal</term>. The end of miracles is the confirmation or sealing of doctrine; for this reason, miracles must presuppose doctrine. For just as the Sacraments are ordinary signs by which the charters of grace are sealed—and thus are appendices to the Word—so miracles are extraordinary signs by which heavenly doctrine is confirmed. From this it follows that doctrine remains valid even without miracles, but miracles are nothing without doctrine; because doctrine is necessary for the very existence of the Church, like an incorruptible seed, while miracles are necessary only for its well-being. Hence, in Deuteronomy 13:1, that prophet is rejected who performs various signs but teaches against the Law of God.

Nevertheless, it must be established that the miracles of those false prophets are "signs and wonders of a lie" <note>original: *σημεῖα καὶ τέρατα ψευδοῦς* (*sēmeia kai terata pseudous*); a reference to 2 Thessalonians 2:9 regarding deceptive supernatural acts</note>. For since true miracles are not performed except by God, they will certainly confirm only true doctrine. "The works," Christ says, "testify of me; and believe the works that I do, if you will not believe me." From this, those who first believed in Christ were moved by the evidence of those miracles. Hence the Apostles say, "No one does such works as you do" <note>Though attributed here to the Apostles, this phrasing is most famously used by Nicodemus in John 3:2</note>. For who would believe that God would bear witness to a lie? This is why the Evangelists observe that Christ was "powerful in both word and in works."

# ANTOINE CRÉGUT

...sometimes false prophets produced true miracles, as can also be proved from the previously cited passage of Deuteronomy 13. This was permitted by God so that he might test his own people to see if they would persevere; as it is said in verse 3: *Do not listen to the words of that prophet, or to that dreamer of dreams; for Jehovah your God is testing you, to know whether you are lovers of your God with all your heart, and with all your soul.* <note>Deuteronomy 13:3</note>

However, the time in which miracles ought to confirm doctrine must be observed. For while the Gospel is to be preached until the end of the ages, this doctrine will not be perpetually confirmed by the brightness of miracles. If it were, they would not be "miracles," as they would be ordinary works that would become cheap <note>original: *vilescerent*; to lose value or become common</note> through the constant frequency of seeing them. Therefore, when the law was first given by Moses, it was then confirmed by various signs; likewise when the Gospel was promulgated by Christ and the Apostles. But now, with the Gospel revealed throughout the whole world, one would demand miracles in vain and at an inappropriate time; and surely this would be to "tempt God" <note>To "tempt God" in this context means to demand a supernatural sign when he has already provided sufficient ordinary means (like scripture and reason) for faith.</note> by not wishing to use ordinary means, and wishing to rely perpetually on the extraordinary power of God. Indeed, since today there is no "faith of miracles" <term>original: *fides miraculorum*; a specific gift or era where miracles are expected to operate</term>, nor are there any stipulated agreements between God and men for such things, for what good would God be compelled to use the law of his omnipotence?

Therefore, regarding the circumstance of time, these points are to be noted:

I. Miracles occurred when the state of the Church was changed, namely when the Law or the Gospel was first promulgated.

II. When there were extraordinary persons and offices—such as when Prophets approached with ecstatic movement and divine inspirations <term>original: *enthusiasmis*; in this context, it refers to a state of being filled with a divine spirit to deliver a message</term>—for then there was need for miracles, so that the true Spirit might be distinguished from the false.

III. When the Prophets uttered oracles and predicted the future; for it was necessary then to produce miracles so that faith might be applied to the prophecy before its future fulfillment or outcome.

IV. When the Prophets or Teachers attempted something singular, which displayed the authority of a magistrate <note>The authority of a civil leader or judge who has the power to punish.</note> beyond the duty of a Teacher. This was observed in the Prophet Elijah, who delivered the priests of Baal to slaughter <note>1 Kings 18:40</note>, and Peter who afflicted Ananias and Sapphira with the ultimate punishment <note>Acts 5:1-11</note>, and Paul who blinded the sorcerer Bar-Jesus <note>Acts 13:6-12</note>. All those things were done as singular acts and went beyond the usual duty of a Teacher, and thus had to be confirmed by some miracle.

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS

...[occurred]; although those very scourges <note>Likely referring to the plagues of Egypt or similar divine judgments mentioned on the preceding lost page.</note> were miraculous and extraordinary in their manner.

However, although it is very true that miracles were performed at those various times, they were also occasionally—though rarely—provided at other times. Indeed, in the time of Christ, there were what might be called "ordinary miracles," such as that of the pool of **Bethesda** (John 5). For an Angel would descend into the pool at a certain and defined time and stir the water, so that the first sick person—whether blind or paralyzed—who entered after the water was stirred would be healed of whatever disease or weakness they suffered. Of the same kind was the **Sabbatical River**, of which **Josephus** writes in *The Jewish War*, book 7, chapter 35 <note>The historian Josephus describes a river in Syria that flowed for six days and rested on the seventh, or vice versa, depending on the source.</note>. This river, which flowed between Arcas and Rapheneas, was seen by **Titus**; it would flow rapidly throughout the whole week, dragging stones along, but would rest on the **Sabbath**. And **Pliny** says in book 31 of his *Natural History*, chapter 2: *In Judea, a river is dried up every Sabbath.* <note>original: "In Iudæa fluuius Sabbatis omnibus ſiccatur."</note> This miracle surely and excellently confirmed the law of Moses and the Mosaic ceremonies; but once the Mosaic law was abolished, that miracle also ceased, for today no one is found who says they have seen it. One should judge the same regarding the scarlet portion between the horns of the scapegoat <note>Crégut refers to a Jewish tradition found in the Talmud: a scarlet thread tied to the goat would turn white if God accepted the people's repentance. It was said to have stopped changing color forty years before the Temple's destruction.</note>, a sign which also failed after the coming of Christ. The same was true in the first temple for the responses of God through the **Urim and Thummim** <term>Urim and Thummim: Ancient Hebrew oracular devices used by the High Priest to seek divine guidance.</term>.

Furthermore, since miracles were performed to confirm doctrine, one might wonder why Christ forbade the two blind men in Matthew 9:30 to spread news of the miracle, telling them to let no one know they had recovered their sight. Yet, although Christ did not wish it to confirm his doctrine at the very moment the miracle was performed—for very weighty reasons unknown to us which Christ kept hidden in his heart—it was nevertheless destined to happen eventually, so that the miracle would become known to all and confirm Christ’s person, his offices, his status, and his entire doctrine.

But indeed, just as there were "ordinary miracles" in the **Church** to confirm the truth of heavenly doctrine, so there are what we might call "ordinary miracles" in nature to manifest the power and goodness of God. For, unless our own vice and wickedness blinded us so that we looked at any other thing rather than God’s works...

# ANTHONY CREGUT

...[if we were to spend time] weighing and judging these things, we would daily observe miracles which would lead us to look up to our heavenly parent. Do you not see the waters suspended in the air, distilling drop by drop, clearly so that they might fertilize the earth rather than overwhelm it? Daily, the sea strikes the low-lying shore with a vast mass and a roaring force; and that shore is not firm or solidly packed, but composed only of thin and light shifting sand; and yet, as if restrained by the power of the present God, the sea is turned back upon itself there, and however much it rages and tosses, it is brought to a halt. But such is our madness that we more easily ascribe these things to nature itself than to the parent of nature and the craftsman, God. These things were said skillfully and piously by **Andreas Masius** <note>Andreas Masius (1514–1573) was a Belgian Catholic humanist and scholar of Oriental languages.</note> in his commentary on **Joshua**, chapter 3.

The third part of the inquiry <note>original: "συζητήσεως"</note> was the empty effort of the **Magicians**, who tried in vain to imitate the miracle of **Moses** regarding the lice. But indeed, what Moses wrote about that frustrated and vain attempt seems not to be without difficulty. For either the other portents of Moses were miracles, or they were not miracles. If they were not truly miracles, then they were either fakes, or if they were real, they were works of nature and brought forth from some private power. And yet, neither can be said. Not that they were fakes, for this would be unworthy of God, whose works are truly existing realities <note>original: "ὑφισάμενα," meaning they have a real, substantial existence rather than being mere illusions.</note>; nor were they works of nature, because neither the waters, nor the earth, nor the rod of Moses possessed any private power from which these forms could be brought forth. Therefore, it must be concluded that those portents of Moses were truly miracles. But if they were truly miracles, they were also truly the **finger of God** <note>A biblical metaphor (Exodus 8:19) signifying direct divine action.</note>; but if they were the finger of God, why did Moses say the Magicians of **Pharaoh** could not imitate them, and why did the Magicians themselves, being well aware of this matter, confess: *Here is the finger of God?*

I respond that in truth, the **finger of God** was no less present in the first miracles than in this one of the lice; because everywhere the immediate power of God was exerting itself. Nor was Moses a physical instrument, but a moral one <note>A "physical instrument" acts by its own properties (like a saw cutting wood), whereas a "moral instrument" acts because God has chosen to link His own power to that person's command or action.</note>. Nevertheless, the Magicians did not recognize the finger of God in the others, because in those instances their effort was not useless; they performed the same miracles as Moses—not that the devil or the Magicians could produce true miracles, but...

...because God, who willed to harden Pharaoh's heart, permitted that insane king and the Egyptians to be more and more driven mad or fascinated by deceptions and <gloss>through lying wonders <note>original: "διὰ τῆς τεράτων ψευδῶν"</note></gloss>, just as in 1 Samuel 28 He permitted Samuel to be summoned by the incantations of the Witch of Endor <note>The Latin text uses "Pythonissa," a term for a medium or necromancer, specifically referring to the woman consulted by King Saul.</note>, so that the power of error might be granted, and Saul might fall <gloss>into a reprobate mind <note>original: "εἰς νοῦν ἀδόκιμον," referring to a mind rejected by God or unable to judge rightly</note></gloss>. They did not actually create frogs or other insects, but used natural causes by God’s permission. Here, however, their efforts were in vain, because the Author of Nature did not permit nature to supply its forces to the Magicians, lest they be thought equal to Moses and the Devil be falsely believed equal to God. Furthermore, through this failed attempt, Pharaoh was meant to know that Moses was truly sent by God; therefore, by rejecting God's servant, he was more stubbornly hardened and rendered all the more inexcusable.

From this, it is clear that with respect to God and His infinite power, one miracle is not greater than another. For whatever God does, He completes by a single act of His will. Therefore, He does not act successively or by degrees; it was just as easy for God to create the whole world as it was to create a gnat <note>original: "culicem"</note>. When, therefore, one miracle seems greater than another, this is to be understood only in relation to us; hence Christ said in the Gospel, *this kind of demon is not cast out except by fasting and prayer*. And although the Disciples had performed various miracles at that time, they could not cast out these demons—either so that the power of Christ might be more illustrious and it might be shown that the disciples performed those various signs in the name of Christ, or even so that the degrees of faith might be recognized. For the more intense faith is, the greater the signs it can perform or obtain from God, as Christ said: *If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you would say to this mountain, etc.*

->## ANTHONY CREGUT ##<-

The doctrine mentioned above is supported by Thomas Aquinas in the First Part, Question 105, Article 8 <note>Referring to the *Summa Theologiae*, a foundational work of Catholic theology</note>. For when Christ spoke in John 14 concerning miraculous works, saying: *The works that I do, he shall do also; and greater works than these shall he do* <note>original: "Opera qua ego facio & ipse faciet, & maiora horum faciet"</note>; Aquinas skillfully adds in his conclusion that it happens that one miracle is greater than another, not according to a comparison to divine power, but in relation to the faculty of nature, insofar as it exceeds it more. Indeed, according to Aquinas, nothing can be called a miracle by comparison to divine power, because anything compared to divine power is very small. According to that passage in Isaiah 40: *Behold, the nations are as a drop in a bucket, etc.* <note>original: "Ecce gentes quasi stilla situlæ, &c."</note> Instead, something is called a miracle through comparison to the faculty of nature which it exceeds. And therefore, according to how much more it exceeds the faculty of nature, it is called a greater miracle. 

Now, something exceeds the faculty of nature in three ways. In the first way, regarding the **substance of the deed**, such as when the Sun moves backward, or that a human body is glorified, which nature can in no way perform. These hold the highest rank among miracles. Secondly, something exceeds the faculty of nature not regarding what is done, but regarding that **in which it is done**, such as the raising of the dead and the giving of sight to the blind. For nature can cause life, but not in a dead person. And it can provide sight, but not to one born blind. These hold the second place among miracles. In the third way, something exceeds the faculty of nature regarding the **manner and order of the doing**. For instance, when someone is suddenly cured of a fever by divine power without medicine and the usual process of nature in such cases; and when the air is immediately thickened into rain by divine power without natural causes, as happened at the prayers of Samuel and Elijah. Such things hold the lowest place among miracles. Yet each of these has different degrees, according to the different ways they exceed the faculty of nature. 

Thus says Thomas. Now, however, the miracle of Moses does not seem to have been of the first or second kind, since the generation of lice was not above the faculty of nature—for they are generated naturally in <term>phthiriasis <note>A medical condition of lice infestation, derived from the Greek word 'phtheir' (louse).</note></term>, even in beasts and men, as happened in Egypt. Therefore, that miracle was of the third kind, because natural things—namely, the lice— <meta>catchword: culi</meta>

But because the Magicians were able to imitate those earlier wonders with deceptive portents by God's permission, they continued to fascinate the impious king and refused to confess the finger of God. They persisted until, forced by their own impotence, they confessed the finger of God to shield themselves before Pharaoh. He could not demand divine power from them, nor the "finger of God" from mere mortals <note>original: "homuncionibus" (literally 'little men')</note>, unless he dared to transform men into God. Therefore, it is as if they had cried out in astonishment and wonder: "Do not marvel, O King, that we could not perform wonders of this sort, since they surpass all nature..."

Scholars are well aware of the nature of the book *Raziel* <note>A medieval grimoire of "Practical Kabbalah" claiming to contain secrets revealed to Adam by the angel Raziel</note>, which is Kabbalistic and magical, no less than Agrippa’s *On Occult Philosophy*. In it is described a use of the Psalms that is more than superstitious—prescribing that they be recited frequently, or written on clean parchment and worn around the neck as an amulet, adding the name of a specific Angel constructed Kabbalistically from the Psalm, and offering a small prayer addressed to that Angel. Whoever wishes to know more, as well as the Kabbalistic mysteries of the Angel’s name *Elohad* <note>original Hebrew: אלהד (Elohad)</note>, should consult the most learned Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf, a prominent 17th-century Christian Hebraist</note> in his *Rabbinic Library*.

<margin>Preeminently. <note>original: "κατ' εξ." (kat' ex.) — an abbreviation for "kat’ exochen," meaning preeminently or by excellence.</note> Galatians 3:19.</margin>Here, therefore, we propose two things to be discussed. I. *Moses' intercession for the people*. II. *The vow, when he desires to be erased from the book of life*. And in both, we will observe that Moses was an illustrious **type** <note>In biblical studies, a "type" is a historical person or event that serves as a prophetic symbol or foreshadowing of a future person or event, specifically Christ.</note> of Christ, the true Mediator and Intercessor.

Moses intercedes for the people in a more eminent way than his brother Aaron and other High Priests. For even though the High Priest was also an illustrious type of Christ—since he first offered a victim and then entered the sanctuary interceding for himself and the people—this was to represent Christ the High Priest **according to the order of Melchizedek** <note>original: "κατὰ τάξιν Μελχισεδέκ" — a reference to Hebrews 5:6 and Psalm 110:4, signifying a priesthood that is eternal and superior to the traditional Levite priesthood.</note>, who offered himself as a victim on the cross and then entered the heavenly sanctuary to intercede for us there. Nevertheless, Moses held a great **preeminence** <note>original: "ὑπεροχὴν" (hyperochen) — superiority or excellence.</note> over the High Priest. This is because he interceded for the people not merely as a Priest, but as a **Mediator**. For this reason, he did not enter the Sanctuary only once a year as the High Priest did; rather, he entered and exited frequently, ascending and then descending Mount Sinai to mediate between God and the people, and between the people and God. In this eminent way, he was a type of Christ, the true and actual Mediator who intercedes between God and men. Moses was the Mediator of the Law, but Christ was the Mediator of the Gospel. John 1:17: *The Law was given through Moses; grace and truth were provided through Jesus Christ.* For this does not only signify that the Law was given **by the hand of Moses**—that is, through the ministry of Moses—but also in a singular way because he was the Mediator. Hence, in the phrasing of Scripture in Exodus 14:31, it is said that they **believed in Moses**, and in 1 Corinthians 10, that they were **baptized into Moses**. Elsewhere, Paul said in 1 Corinthians 1:15: *Lest anyone should say I have baptized in my own name.* However, since Moses was the figure and Christ was the truth itself, there was a maximum distinction between the two. Paul clearly expresses this in Hebrews 3:5 when he says that **Moses was a faithful servant of God in the whole house of God, but Christ was the Son over the house.** For although in Isaiah 53 Christ is also called the servant of God—*My faithful servant shall justify many*—that servitude of Christ is **managerial** <note>original: "œconomica" — referring to the "economy of salvation," the specific role Christ took on in the divine plan, rather than his essential nature.</note>, not a servitude of nature like our own; for he then took the form of a servant when he was already in the form of God. Phil.

Nevertheless, because he was the Mediator of the Legal Covenant <note>The "Legal Covenant" refers to the Old Testament Law given at Sinai, which established a relationship based on obedience to rules.</note>, the conditions of which were impossible to meet, he brandished the lightning bolts of divine curses so that he might serve as a **guide** <note>original: *pædagogus* — in the ancient world, a tutor or guardian who escorted a child to school; Paul uses this term in Galatians 3 to describe the Law leading people to Christ.</note> toward Christ (Galatians 3). This is why it is nowhere stated that God took pity on His people because of Moses, as He did because of Abraham, Isaac, etc., and their descendants.

To this we may also refer that **redemption** <note>original: λυτρωσις (*lytrosis*)</note> performed by Moses, when he is called a Redeemer. For he was a symbolic redeemer who freed the people from Egyptian slavery; however, that redemption was performed without a price. This is signified by the word **redeem** <note>original: פָּדָה (*padah*) — often used for rescue or ransoming from power without necessarily implying a financial transaction.</note>, because that slavery was unjust. Therefore, the people had to be freed from the yoke of Pharaoh **with a high hand** <note>original: בְּיָד רָמָה (*bejad ramah*)</note>—that is, with great power—and without a price. Indeed, they even took the goods of the Egyptians in secret, since the wages for so much labor were rightfully owed to them. Yet, the Scripture twice uses—specifically in the first and last instances—the word **redeem** <note>original: גָּּאַל (*Gaal*) — a term for redemption that implies a price paid or the duty of a kinsman-redeemer.</note>, which signifies a redemption involving a price. This was done to foreshadow the spiritual redemption accomplished through a price: namely, by the blood of Christ.

Therefore, Moses truly interceded not as a Priest, but as a Mediator. Because he was a Mediator, he fulfilled all the requirements of a mediator, which the Jesuit Bellarmine lists as four in number in his work *On Christ*, Book 5, Chapter 1:
I. A Mediator must be an arbiter between God and men, discerning and judging the case.
II. A Mediator must act as an intermediary, reporting the pacts and conditions.
III. He must pray and supplicate to one party on behalf of the other.
IV. He must satisfy the demands of one on behalf of the other.

Moses did all these things, but only in a figurative sense. It was not that God could truly be appeased by Moses' mediation, nor that a mere man and a sinner could reconcile humanity to God; rather, it was because in that **administration** <note>original: *œconomia* — the historical arrangement or "dispensation" of God's dealings with humanity.</note> of the Old Testament, God willed to represent that most real and true mediation of Christ the Mediator through shadows and figures. Certainly, all these conditions are verified throughout the Scriptures concerning Christ:
I. Ephesians 3:12: *In whom we have boldness and access with confidence through faith in him.*
II. John 1:18: *No one has ever seen God; the only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known.* And John 3:13: *No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.* Indeed, the Son knows the innermost mind of the Father through His union with divinity. 
III. Romans 8:34.

> *Christ died, rose again, and sits at the right hand of the Father and intercedes for us.* <note>Though the margin cites Acts 20:28, this first sentence is a paraphrase of Romans 8:34.</note> *God acquired His Church with His very own blood.* (Acts 20:28).

But indeed, just as those conditions of a Mediator did not properly and realistically apply to Moses, but rather to Christ whom he was foreshadowing, so too the very naming and nature of "mediation" or of a "Mediator" could not truly and realistically apply to Moses. For a Mediator is so called <term>literally</term> <note>original Greek: αὐτολεξεὶ (*autolexei*)</note> because he stands in the middle between disagreeing parties. But Christ is truly the "middle" by participating in the extremes of the disagreeing parties, and He reconciles them because He possesses a divine nature in common with God and a human nature in common with men. He differs from God through His "emptying" <note>original: *exinanitionem* — referring to the concept of *kenosis* where Christ set aside his glory to become human.</note> and His voluntary stewardship <note>original: *oeconomiam* — the divine plan or arrangement of salvation.</note> (Philippians 2:6-7). He differs from other men through the union of grace with the **Word** <term>Logos</term> <note>original Greek: λόγῳ</note> (John 1: *The Word was made flesh*), and by His immunity from sin (1 Peter 2:22), which is why He is called <term>sinless</term> <note>original Greek: ἀναμάρτωλος (*anamartolos*)</note> (Hebrews 7). 

Moses, however, was a <term>mere man</term> <note>original Greek: ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος (*psilos anthropos*)</note> whose human nature was not united with the divine nature; therefore, he was not properly and truly a Mediator, but only figuratively so by divine arrangement. This was because God deigned to choose him and make him "a man after His own heart" (as the Scripture loves to say) so that he might intercede with God on behalf of the people.

Therefore, that intercession of Moses was not that of a private individual—which God often does not hear because there is no special covenant entered into with every single individual, nor has God promised that a private person will be heard every time they pray for someone. But Moses, insofar as he was a mediator, was *always* heard. When the people frequently murmured against God, and God, swelling with wrath, wished to destroy them utterly, Moses immediately interceded, and thus God was appeased and spared the people, as occurs everywhere in the books of Moses.

Consequently, when the Catholics <note>original: *Pontificii* — literally "the followers of the Pontiff," a common Reformation-era term for Roman Catholics.</note> assert that the Saints are intercessors, they are establishing just as many Mediators, and by consequence just as many redeemers—just as Moses is not only called a Mediator but also a Redeemer. And indeed, the "Papists" <note>original: *Papicolæ* — literally "Pope-worshippers," a polemical term used by the author.</note> suggest this enough, as witnessed by Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a highly influential Jesuit cardinal and defender of Catholic doctrine during the Counter-Reformation.</note>, who says that *the Saints are in some way redeemers.* They commonly distinguish between a "Mediator of redemption" and a "Mediator of intercession," calling Christ the Mediator of redemp—

of remission, but they consider the Saints to be mediators of intercession. This, however, is a contradiction, for no one can be a mediator of intercession without also being a mediator of redemption, as the second priestly act is built upon the first. Indeed, Christ himself could not be a mediator of intercession unless he had first been the mediator of redemption; this is why Paul in Romans 8:34 lists in order the death, resurrection, and ascension of Christ, and only then adds His intercession.

The purpose of intercession is that God might forgive the sins of the people. When Moses intercedes for the forgiveness of sin, he provides us with a vivid "type" or foreshadowing of the intercession of Christ. Christ prays to the Father in the heavenly sanctuary that He might be willing to forgive our sins. Because He had first offered a sacrifice on the cross, He later applies that sacrifice to us in heaven through intercession, by which we finally obtain the forgiveness of our sins. Hence, in the Gospel, Christ is said to forgive sins as the <note>original: *causa meritoria* — the "meritorious cause," meaning the reason or grounds by which a benefit is earned.</note> meritorious cause. Mark 2:7: *Who can forgive sins but God alone?* <note>original Latin: *Quis potest remittere peccata nisi solus Deus.*</note>

This is a power which the Pope impiously claims for himself. For this reason, it is recorded that Pope Martin IV <note>Pope Martin IV (r. 1281–1285) was often criticized by Protestant authors for his political involvements.</note> approved when the Sicilian assassins flatteringly shouted to him that verse from John 1: *Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, have mercy on us.* <note>original Latin: *Agne Dei qui tollis peccata mundi miserere nostri.*</note> And as Nangis <note>Guillaume de Nangis, a 13th-century French chronicler.</note> relates, because he did not give glory to God, he died a hidden death not unlike that of Herod. The Pope, therefore, exalts himself above Moses and occupies the very seat or throne of God. For even if Moses was a "typical" Mediator <note>A "typical" mediator here means a symbolic representative or "type" pointing toward the ultimate reality of Christ.</note>, he never dared to forgive sins in an absolute sense, but only prayed to God that He might forgive the people’s sins. Yet the Pope pretends to forgive sins absolutely, by supreme right, and <term>sovereignly</term> <note>original Greek: αὐτοκρατορικῶς (*autokratikorōs*)</note>. Thus he issues his decrees—which he calls by the ominous name of *Bulls* <note>The author is making a pun on the Latin *Bulla*, which means a lead seal but also a "bubble," implying something empty or fleeting.</note>—sealed with lead like legal arrests, dispatched by his own impulse and supreme authority. 

In truth, if the Bishop of Rome were to forgive sins conditionally, and speaking in accordance with the Gospel were to say, "If you believe the Gospel, your sins are forgiven," he would be thinking rightly. As a true Pastor of the Gospel, he would be using the "power of the keys" <note>The authority to "bind and loose" or forgive sins, traditionally associated with St. Peter and the papacy.</note> correctly. But as if this were his actual intent, on the contrary, he—though himself a sinful man—presumes to forgive sins absolutely and <term>destructively</term> <note>original Greek: ὀлеθρητικῶς (*olethrētikōs*)</note>. As in 2 Thessalonians 2, he acts as <term>the son of sin</term> <note>original Greek: ὁ υἱὸς τῆς ἀμαρτίας (*ho huios tēs hamartias*) — usually translated as "the son of perdition."</note>, even though he is not even certain if his own sins...

will obtain remission from God. But if the Pope remits sins conditionally, those conditions which are demanded by him all the more exalt and confirm his supreme right and authority. For he does not demand Gospel conditions like the faithful shepherds of God, but conditions devised from superstition. He does not say, *If you believe, if you repent*, etc., but *if you adore those relics, if you visit this or that Church, if you devoutly recite this or that prayer so many times, if you hear so many Masses*. All of these are not God's commands, but the Pope’s own laws and statutes, which he has sanctioned <note>original: αὐτοκρατορικῶς (*autokratōrikōs*) — autocratically, or by his own absolute power</note> and decreed as a Legislator.

Therefore, by that impious usurpation of the Pope, the momentous doctrine of the whole Christian religion—which is, as it were, the marrow and soul of Theology and the Gospel, namely the remission of sins—is exposed to mockery. Thus, it is no wonder if Pope Leo X <note>Leo X (r. 1513–1521) was the Pope at the start of the Reformation; Protestant writers often attributed this cynical quote to him to illustrate papal corruption.</note> used to call the Gospel the "fable of *Jesus Christ*" with the most horrific impiety. For if the Pope remits sins by his own impulse under the condition of observing his own law, what will become of the <term>meritorious cause</term> <note>the fundamental reason or "price" that makes a benefit valid</note> of justification? Why was Christ’s blood shed? Did the Pope die for us? Did he rise again for mankind? But on the contrary, Moses, the <term>typical Mediator</term> <note>a "type" is a historical person or event in the Bible that foreshadows a later reality, in this case, Christ</note>, fled to Christ; for when he asks God to pardon the sins of the people, who could doubt that he was looking toward the death and resurrection of Christ, the true Mediator? For from these two acts we fully obtain the remission of sins.

Since, from the idiom of the Syriac language <note>The author refers to Aramaic/Syriac, the language spoken by Jesus, where the word for sin and debt is the same.</note>, sins are called *debts* <note>original: חובין (*chobin*)</note>; as in Matthew 6: *forgive us our debts*. From this it follows that He who has freed us from the obligation of sins is said to have made <term>satisfaction</term> <note>the legal payment of a debt or penalty</note> for our sins. This Christ perfected in two ways, namely through *death and resurrection*. 1. *By death*. For when He was fixed to the cross and shed His blood, He was in truth paying the debt; but when He rose again and ascended into heaven, He *obtained the receipt* <note>original: *apocha* — a legal term for a written discharge or receipt of payment</note>. This is why the remission of sins is attributed to the cross, as the payment of the debt, and to the resurrection and ascension, as the receipt of the debt having been paid. Therefore, the remission of sins can be ascribed to two things: either to the *money* counted out by the guarantor himself—which is the blood of Christ—

...blood shed; or a <term>receipt</term> <note>original: *apocha* — a formal written discharge of debt</note>, which a guarantor, having paid the money, has obtained for the sake of the debtor. It is attributed to the money paid as the *cause*, and to the *receipt* as the *sign and symbol of the money paid*. Paul taught these things in the most <gloss>emphatic</gloss> <note>original: ἐμφατικωτάτοις (*emphatikōtatois*)</note> words in Colossians 2:14, handing down that *the Lord fastened to the cross, took from our midst, and blotted out the handwritten bond that was against us*. And the Pope, having despised the death and resurrection of Christ, while no payment of the debt has been made and the receipt is still outstanding, grants the remission of sins under some futile condition of a hair-shirt, a cowl, mortification, pilgrimage, fasting, etc.

Since, therefore, the Pope pretends that by these ridiculous satisfactions the sins of men are remitted and divine justice is entirely satisfied, he does not know the nature of true and real satisfaction; since no satisfaction exists if it is not of infinite price and weight. And therefore, that is true and properly called satisfaction which is according to <gloss>intensity</gloss> <note>original: κατ' ἐπίτασιν (*kat' epitasin*) — referring to the quality or internal "stretch" of the value</note>, but not that which is according to <gloss>extension</gloss> <note>original: κατ' ἔκτασιν (*kat' ektasin*) — referring to the outward duration or quantity</note>. This <gloss>intensity</gloss> or intensive virtue is truly derived not so much from the thing itself as from the infinite person. For just as sin or guilt is said to be infinite—not by reason of itself, but because of the infinite essence of God against whom it was committed—so punishment and satisfaction are called infinite because of the person of the Redeemer, which is infinite, as it is forged from the Divine nature.

Yet, because of the infinity of the person, that very common saying of some does not hold: namely, *that a single shed drop of the Mediator's blood could have satisfied God if He had so willed*. For this is to confuse the <gloss>intensity</gloss> of satisfaction with its <gloss>extension</gloss>; certainly, as far as <gloss>extension</gloss> is concerned, God could have taken something away from the time and duration of the satisfaction, because that was not essential to it; but truly, nothing ought to be taken away from the <gloss>intensity</gloss>, because it belongs to the nature of satisfaction. But what could a single shed drop of blood have in common with such <gloss>intensity</gloss>? For although the infinity of the person makes the satisfaction infinite—which otherwise could not be infinite of itself, since a passion of infinite weight would reduce the suffering nature to nothing—nevertheless the satisfaction and punishment ought not to have been so meager as to be ridiculous and unworthy of God's justice, which is not satisfied by a trivial punishment, such as a drop of blood would have been (which could even have existed without punishment). Instead, God had to increase that punishment of the guarantor, Christ, even unto the measure <note>original: *modulum* — the catchword for the next page is "dulum"</note>

<summary>Cregutus argues that Christ's suffering provides a legal discharge of debt that renders Papal penances (like fasting or pilgrimages) useless. He distinguishes between the "intensity" (infinite value) and "extension" (duration) of Christ's sacrifice, arguing that while Christ's divine personhood makes his merit infinite, the actual physical suffering had to be significant rather than a mere "single drop of blood."</summary>

...measure <note>original: *...dulum*, likely *modulum* (measure or standard)</note> by which the supreme wisdom of God ordained that divine justice could be satisfied.

From the aforementioned, it can be understood what those Jewish teachers meant—who are commonly called *Mekubbalim* or <term>Cabalists</term> <note>original: *Cabalistæ* — practitioners of Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition</note>—when they assert that Moses was not able to reach as far as the <term>Sefirot Chokhmah</term> <note>original: *Sefirot Chokhmah* (ספירות חכמה) — the 'emanations of wisdom'; in Kabbalistic thought, these are divine attributes through which the Infinite reveals itself</note>, that is, the *enumerations of wisdom*, at least inclusively; for he reached up to it exclusively <note>meaning he reached the boundary of this divine wisdom but could not enter or fully possess it through the Law</note>. For the ancient Jews mystically signify the weakness of the Law regarding justification; since the Law can indeed stir up a desire for forgiveness in the souls of men by revealing and increasing sin, as Paul taught in Romans 5, but it cannot effect the forgiveness of sins itself; it merely leads us by the hand to the true Mediator. For this reason, Moses reached as far as the shore and the border of the land of Canaan, but he did not progress further. However, Joshua—a <term>type</term> <note>original: *typus* — a person or event in the Old Testament seen as a prophetic symbol of Christ</note> of Christ, the true Joshua—led the people into that land of promise.

When, therefore, Moses interceded for the people and asked God to pardon the people’s sins, he was undoubtedly looking toward the Messiah, the Mediator, who was the moral and meritorious cause of the forgiveness of sins. Therefore, even then, His work was taking effect; for it is sufficient for a "moral cause" <note>a legal or intentional cause, like a signed contract</note> to exist in a **known act** <note>original: *in actu cognito* — existing in the mind and purpose of God</note>, even if it is not yet in a **physical or real act** <note>original: *in actu Physico seu reali* — the historical event of the crucifixion</note>. Hence, it is attributed to Christ in 1 John 5:6 *that He came in water and blood*. And in John 19:34, when the side of Christ had been pierced by a soldier’s spear, immediately there came out blood and water; these two symbols signify the forgiveness of sins and the absolution from the filth of sin, or the removal of corruption and stains. This is justification and sanctification; for blood signifies the forgiveness of sins in justification, while water designates sanctification. The words of Peter in John 13 pertain to this: *If I do not wash you, you will have no part with me.* Oh, if only the Jews today would take notice of this excellent and comfort-filled doctrine whenever they most earnestly ask God for the forgiveness of sins on feast days! Hence the book titled <term>Selichot</term> <note>original: *Selichot* (סליחות) — "forgivenesses"; a collection of penitential prayers and poems</note>, that is, *of Remissions*, which book of prayers they use on the more solemn feasts, because for mercy and forgiveness...

I shall therefore ensure that I expose its weakness to everyone by making it plain through six most solid responses.

That theologian’s argument is drawn from the mystical union that exists between the Saints and Christ in the mystical body. For (he says), if the human nature of Christ is adored by virtue of the <term>hypostatic union</term> <note>The "hypostatic union" is the theological doctrine that Christ's divine and human natures are perfectly united in one person</note>, because it is united in the <gloss>Word</gloss> <note>original: *λόγῳ* (Logoi) — referring to the second person of the Trinity</note>, why should the Saints not also be invoked by virtue of their mystical union with Christ the Head? The argument, therefore, proceeds as follows:

->Just as the union of the human nature in the Word stands, so stands the union of the Saints in the mystical body with Christ the Head; but because of that union of the human nature in the Word, the human nature is to be adored. Therefore, because of the union of the Saints with the Head in the mystical body, the Saints are to be invoked.<-

I respond to that argument in six ways. 1. I say the comparison limps badly: for if this were true, all the faithful who live on earth—and likewise that theologian himself, if he wishes to be called faithful—would have to be invoked; for each and every one of the faithful are members united with the Head in the mystical body. Nor does it help here to make an exception for Saints canonized by the Pope, since, in the first place, I firmly assert this: that the name "Saints" is never attributed in Scripture to the deceased saints, but only to the faithful of the <term>Church Militant</term> <note>The "Church Militant" refers to Christians currently living on earth who are "warring" against sin and the devil</note>. This is seen when Paul wrote his Epistles to the "saints" or the "sanctified," and in the Creed, *We believe in the Holy Catholic Church*, or at least it is very rarely attributed to the deceased. And often many are believed to be Saints whose souls are being tortured in the fire of <term>Gehenna</term> <note>Hell or eternal punishment</note>, as Cardinal Bessarion <note>Basilios Bessarion (1403–1472), a Greek scholar and Catholic Cardinal who sought to reconcile the Eastern and Western churches</note> confessed elsewhere. Furthermore—

the same reasoning for the union in the mystical body applies just as much to the faithful or saints living on earth as it does to those who have died.

II. If this argument were valid, it would apply equally to the Saints under the Old Testament dispensation; for the mystical body of Christ has existed from the beginning of the world, because *Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.* <note>Hebrews 13:8</note> Yet, as Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a highly influential Jesuit cardinal and defender of Catholic doctrine during the Counter-Reformation</note> admits, the Saints were not invoked in the Old Testament because they were in the <term>limbos</term> <note>original: *in limbis*; referring to the "Limbo of the Patriarchs," where the souls of the righteous were thought to wait until Christ's resurrection</note>; therefore, they did not say, "Saint Noah, Saint Abraham, etc., pray for us." And yet, those men were united with the Head in the mystical body. For here, a philosophical axiom holds true: *whatever applies to a subject because of its nature, applies to all who share that nature.* Therefore, if Saints are to be invoked because of their union in the mystical body, then all Saints who share in this union ought to be invoked <note>The author argues that if simply being part of Christ's "body" makes one a mediator to be prayed to, we should logically pray to holy people who are still alive on earth, which his opponents do not do</note>.

III. If that argument were valid, the Saints would not only be Mediators of intercession, but also of redemption—a claim which the Papists <note>original: *Pontificij*</note> nonetheless deny. For no reason can be assigned why that union should result in a mediation of intercession rather than one of redemption, since both belong equally to Christ the Mediator, and one cannot be shared any more than the other. Indeed, since the mediation of intercession is founded upon the mediation of redemption itself, Christ himself could not truly be called a Mediator of intercession unless he were also the Mediator of redemption. The Papists themselves are forced by the truth to assert this, such as Bellarmine himself, who wishes the Saints to be, in some way, "Redeemers," and they even call the Virgin the "Redemptress of the human race." They have even attempted to prove this through a horrible sacrilege by corrupting the original Hebrew of Genesis 3:15, in the particle **"he"** <note>original: *הוא* (hu)</note> for **"she"** <note>original: *היא* (hi)</note> <note>A famous theological dispute: Protestant scholars noted the Hebrew says the "seed" (he) will crush the serpent, while the Catholic Vulgate translated it as "she" (Mary) would crush it</note>.

IV. That theologian fails to notice that intercession is an act of Christ’s priestly office, which can belong to no one except our Mediator. This was prefigured long ago in the High Priest, who blessed the people with these words: *May Jehovah bless you...* <note>Numbers 6:24</note>, and who entered the sanctuary after the sacrifice to intercede for the people. Thus, Christ alone—who is the High Priest according to the order of Melchizedek—offered himself as an **atoning sacrifice** <note>original: *ἱλασθήριον* (hilastherion); a Greek term for a propitiatory offering or the "mercy seat" where God meets man</note> on the cross and [entered] into the sanctuary...

# ANTHONY CREGUTUS

having entered the heavenly sanctuary, He now intercedes for us, so that we need no other Priest.

That theologian is ignorant of the purpose of the mystical union, which is so that Christ our head may pour His gifts into us, that we might be partakers of all the benefits of grace—namely, calling, justification, sanctification, etc.—but not so that He might impart to us <term>pre-eminence</term> <note>original: *ὑπεροχὴν*; referring to a state of being superior or holding a higher rank</note> and the unique qualities of the Mediator. Nor does Christ hand over His glory to another, nor does He make them sit at the right hand of the Father, as Paul clearly noted in Romans 8:29: *For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers.*

VI. He is ignorant of what the mystical body of Christ actually is; for the nature of Christ’s physical body, born of the Virgin Mary, is one thing, and the nature of the mystical body—which is the invisible Church or the "Elect," consisting of both members and a head—is another. The body of Christ that is called upon and adored is the Physical body, because of that personal union <note>This refers to the "hypostatic union," the theological doctrine that Christ is one person with two natures, human and divine</note>; for since one person is formed from two natures, that subsisting person is adored, because the object of adoration can only be <term>that which exists as a singular thing</term> <note>original: *τὸ ᾗ τὶ*; an Aristotelian philosophical term for a specific, individual substance rather than a general category</note>. But in truth, the "mystical body" does not signify any single subsisting person that could be adored, but rather a certain universal nature of a supernatural body, just as "natural body" refers to a universal nature existing in lower things. Therefore, just as "image" in a general sense cannot be adored—but rather this or that specific image, such as that of Peter or the Virgin—so the mystical body of Christ cannot be invoked. This is so true that even the divine essence and nature itself would not be adored, insofar as it is an "essence," unless it also existed as a singular person, and unless its essence were its very existence.

But you will say: "We also admit that; in reality, the mystical body of Christ is not adored as if it were some common nature. But what prevents each individual believer—for example, Peter or Paul, who as saints enjoy that mystical union—from being adored or invoked separately?" I, in turn, retort and respond: Do those Saints, considered separately and abstractly, make one person...

->REVELATOR ARCANORVM. 603<-
->[REVEALER OF SECRETS. 603]<-

For either the believer, as a singular subsisting thing, makes a whole with the entire mystical body, or he does not. If the believer, considered in the abstract, does not form a singular whole with the mystical body, then he certainly ought not to be invoked in prayer. This is just as the human nature of Christ would not be invoked or adored if it were separated from the Word <note>The "Word" here refers to the *Logos*, the divine nature of Christ. The author argues that Christ's humanity is only worshiped because it is joined to his divinity</note>; for it would be idolatry to adore a creature and a <term>mere man</term> <note>original Greek: *psilòn ánthrōpon*; a term used in early Church controversies to describe the view that Jesus was only a human being and not God</note>. Therefore, if the human nature of Christ is adored, it is because it constitutes a single person with the Word. 

But if, on the other hand, believers are concretely fused into a mystical body and form one single entity, then that entire singular entity would exist as a composite of infinite individuals—composed of those who have been from the beginning of the world, those who are now, and those who are to be until the end of the world. I would very much like to be informed where on earth this person, or "singular whole," might exist, and whether he is descended from the lineage of Pygmies or of Giants!

Finally, there remains another part of the argument: namely, the *vow* of Moses: *blot me now out of your book which you have written* <note>original: *dele me nunc de libro tuo quem scripsisti*; quoting Exodus 32:32, where Moses offers his own soul to save the Israelites after the sin of the Golden Calf</note>. In this final section, two things must again be weighed:
I. What is meant *by the book which God wrote*?
II. Regarding the vow: that he desires to be blotted out from that book. 

As to the first point, four books of God can be identified:
1. The book of providence.
2. The book of Sacred Scripture.
3. The book of divine judgment.
4. The book of life. 

The first book is discussed in *Psalm 139:16*; and this is the book of God's counsels and decrees. The second book is discussed in *Isaiah 34:16*. The third is spoken of in *Daniel 7:10*; this same book is called the *book of remembrance* in *Revelation 20:12*. The fourth is the book of foreknowledge and the eternal predestination of those to be saved, mentioned in *Daniel 12:2, Philippians 4:3,* and *Revelation 3:5*. Those whom God chose, He inscribed, and by inscribing them, He chose them. 

Now, however, Moses is speaking of this fourth book. For it is clear he does not wish to be blotted out from the book of Providence, or of Judgment, or of Scripture, but from the book of life. For when God first predestined someone to eternal life from eternity, that person is said to be inscribed in the book of life. However, when He has rejected someone, theologians say that God has <term>passed them over</term> <note>original: *praeteriisse*; a technical term in the doctrine of predestination meaning God chose not to elect certain individuals</note> or <term>negatively not chosen them</term> <note>original: *non elegisse negatiue*</note>; that is, He did not inscribe them in the book of life. Thus, God willed to have only four books, whereas among men there is an infinite abundance of books. Hence Seneca noted quite skillfully in an epistle: *If my life span were doubled, or if it were given only to these...* <note>The quote likely refers to Seneca’s view that life is too short to waste on useless reading</note>

Nevertheless, it is from human depravity, no less than from ignorance, that such a multitude of books arises. Therefore, those books which we condemn—which deserve fire rather than light—are impious and harmful in various ways. 

Just as the book of Scripture is called <term>The Bible</term> <note>original Latin: *Biblia*</note> or "The Scripture" by way of a title, so those four books of God <note>Theologians of this era often spoke of four "books" through which God is known: Nature, Conscience, Scripture, and the Book of Life (Divine Decree)</note> ought to be called "Books" <term>pre-eminently</term> <note>original Greek: *exochōs*</note>. This is for an even stronger reason than that by which those two very ancient Rabbinic books are commonly called, <term>par excellence</term> <note>original Greek: *kat’ exochēn*</note>, <term>Siphra and Siphri</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Siphra, Siphri*, meaning "The Book" and "The Books"; these are ancient legal commentaries on Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy</note>.

Since, therefore, it is clear that through this written book Moses understood the *Book of Life*, how then will that vow of the Prophet stand: <term>Blot me now out of your book which you have written</term> <note>original Hebrew: *machēni na misiphrēcha asher katavta*; quoted from Exodus 32:32</note>? This passage seems parallel with that of Paul in Romans 9:3, <term>wishing to be accursed for his brothers and separated from Christ</term> <note>original: *Optantis esse anathema pro fratribus suis, & à Christo separari*</note>. Yet both were impossible; indeed, the Prophet and the Apostle knew the impossibility of each well enough. Why, then, did they long for what was impossible? Or rather, why did they long for what seemed to be against the glory of God? For no one can be <term>anathema</term> unless he is a sinner, nor can one be blotted out from the book of life unless he perishes in eternal death. But that cannot happen without spiritual death, which is sin. How then does he wish to glorify God by not being glorified?

The great difficulty of this matter has led some to say that by the "book of life" we should not understand the book of the *future life* or the decree of election, but the book of the *present life*, in which God has written the limits and boundaries of every person's life. However, this interpretation is rejected: first, because the words of the Prophet would be too weak, and second, because they would not properly align with Paul’s words, since becoming an "anathema" and being "separated from Christ" regard the future life, not the present one. For the Greek word <term>anathema</term> <note>original: *anáthema*</note> corresponds to the Hebrew word <term>cherem</term> <note>original: *herem*</note>, by which a thing or person consecrated and devoted to God is signified—and that with a specific consecration of the person's life. It comes from the word *cherem* or, in the causative form, <term>to destroy or cut off</term> <note>original Hebrew: *hecherim*</note>. Hence comes the vow of *cherem*, when someone completely renounces a thing from themselves so that it can never be redeemed; nor was it permitted...

Therefore, these words of both Moses and Paul are signs of distinguished love toward God and charity toward one’s neighbor. For what can be said that is greater or more burning than to desire eternal death and damnation for the glory of God and the salvation of brothers? Therefore, Moses, being so dismayed, could rashly burst into these words of excessive overabundance: *blot me out of the book of life*. But in respect to Paul, these considerations would not have a place, because he wrote his Epistles by the dictate of the Holy Spirit, and his writings were not produced <term>extemporaneously</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπροσχεδιασμένως (*aproschediasmenos*); meaning "off the cuff" or without preparation</note>, but deliberately and with meditation.

Nevertheless, it will be better if we say that both uttered these words for a certain end and purpose: namely, out of a vehement zeal for the glory of God and an ardent charity toward their neighbor. Therefore, when Moses said, *Blot me out of the book of life*, that distinguished Prophet was not ignorant that the decree of Election is immutable, and that therefore he could not be blotted out of the book of life; but his scope was to show, through that impossible vow, that he was ready...

# ANTOINE CRÉGUT

...to endure any things, however harsh or even fatal, rather than to wish to fall away even the slightest bit from the glory of God, or for the salvation of the brothers to perish; or even that he would have preferred himself to be blotted out from the book of life rather than the whole Jewish nation, especially since the cutting off of the people seemed to make God's glory void. Therefore, in this vow of Moses, the mode of limitation is kept silent, which is expressed in those words of Christ when he said: *Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me* <note>original Latin/Greek: *Pater si possibile est transeat à me* / παρελθέτω ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ τὸ ποτήριון τοῦτο</note>. *Let it depart from me, let it pass me by and leave me untouched*, which word "let it pass" <note>original Greek: παρελθέτω (*parelthetō*)</note> corresponds to the Hebrew word <term>abar</term> <note>original Hebrew: עבר; to pass over or through</note>, which often signifies the same thing. 

It is not that Christ was ignorant of the necessity of his passion, which he had so often foretold to his disciples; but he spoke thus out of a vehement sense of divine wrath and from a horror of God's terrible judgment, which the senses of human nature recoiled from, and which, if it had been possible, he would have gladly avoided—provided it could have been done without injury to God's glory. All these things in other men, being sinners, could hardly be conceived without some stain of vice; but in Christ, the <term>sinless one</term> <note>original Greek: ἀναμαρτήτῳ (*anamartētō*)</note>, it was not difficult. Therefore, whereas Christ expressed a modification by saying *if it is possible*, and not *let this cup absolutely depart from me*, Moses expressed it absolutely and without a limiting mode: *blot me out of the book of life*. 

Therefore, vows of this kind are expressed <term>by way of hyperbole</term> <note>original Greek: κατ’ ὑπερβολὴν (*kat’ hyperbolēn*); an intentional exaggeration for emphasis</note>. For although they are impossible in respect to the thing itself and according to the hypothesis of the divine decree (which is a necessity of immutability), nevertheless, because it was not absolutely impossible if one only considers the theoretical foreknowledge in God—or if one considers the decree of <term>reprobation</term> <note>The theological concept of being rejected by God or excluded from salvation</note> regarding Moses as it applies to others—that Prophet uttered this vow: *blot me out of the book of life*... 

Or, Moses speaks <term>humanly</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνθρωποπαθῶς (*anthrōpopathōs*); attributing human emotions or passions to a situation involving God</note>. For even though Moses knew that the decree of God is immutable and cannot be blotted out, nevertheless, in that vehement passion and burning affection, he speaks in a human manner. As the Hebrew <term>Maimonides</term> <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar</note> loves to speak concerning <term>anthropopathisms</term> <note>The attribution of human feelings to God</note>, he spoke "according to the language of the sons of men," as if the decree of God were conditional. God himself frequently reveals himself this way in Scripture, as when Moses says in the book of Genesis, chapter 6, that *it repented God that he had made man.* A similar vow occurs somewhere in the writings of Saint Augustine, who had desired for a time to endure all the torments of the fire of Gehenna, so that even for a moment...

This vow of Blessed Augustine <note>Referring to a famous tradition where St. Augustine wished to see Christ in the flesh, Paul in the pulpit, and Rome in its glory.</note> was undoubtedly impossible; nevertheless, that vow is not condemned, because a condition is understood that remains unspoken—namely, *if it be possible, or if it be not impossible*.

Regarding the passage from Paul, the answer will be easy based on what was said above; for he was moved by the same affection as Moses when he wished to be anathema <note>A term for something "accursed" or separated from God.</note> and separated from Christ. He expresses this vehemence of feeling with very clear and most emphatic words when he says: *I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie, my conscience also bearing me witness through the Holy Spirit* <note>original Latin: *Dico veritatem in Christo, non mentior, attestante mihi simul conscientia mea per Spiritum Sanctum*</note>. And then in verse 3: *For I myself was wishing to be accursed* <note>original Greek: Ἠυχόμην γὰρ αὐτὸς ἐγὼ εἶναι ἀνάθεμα (*Ēuchomēn gar autos egō einai anathema*)</note>. In these words, his vow and its fervor are wonderfully described. The vow is indicated by the word *ēuchomēn*, which means *I would have wished*; it comes from *euchē*, meaning *a vow*. The fervor of the feeling comes from the other words. For truly, to signify the most fervent affection, nothing further can be said; and thus from a burning and seething heart, the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart, and therefore brings forth these grand words: *For I myself would have wished to be accursed*, etc. 

I. Note that the Apostle says *I would have wished* <note>original Latin/Greek: *optarim* / Ἠυχόμην</note>, by which he notes the impossibility of the vow. In that word "I would have wished," he includes the equivalent phrase used by Christ: *if it were possible*. Therefore, when he makes an impossible vow, it must be explained in the same sense we used to explain that of Moses. 

II. It should be noted that the Apostle speaks of *will*, not of *power*; for although the will to be accursed was in him, the power was not. That lack of power arose from two things: 1. From God's decree, which is unchangeable and therefore does not allow him to be accursed. 2. From the Apostle's own lack of power, since his strength was not so great that he could become accursed for his brothers. Therefore, when he says *I would have wished to be accursed*, it is the same as if he said, *I would have wished to be able to be accursed*. That is: I would wish to be ignited with such fervent zeal for God's glory and moved by such great love for my brothers that I could become accursed for them—which, however, he could not perform because of the <term>incapacity</term> <note>original Greek: ἀδυναμίαν (*adynamian*); a lack of strength or power</note> of free will. For if he had possessed that perfect love and love for God, he would have perfectly fulfilled the law according to <term>absolute righteousness</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνεκδοδίκαιον (*anekdodikaion*); a theological term for a standard of justice that is beyond human reach</note>. ...was made a curse <note>original Greek: *katara*; original Latin: *execratio*</note> for us. This relates to what Paul says in Romans 7:19: *For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing.* For there Paul speaks as one reborn, but imperfectly; therefore he wants to do good by reason of the reborn part of his soul, but he cannot, because the unregenerate part and the "outer man" resist him. Paul could therefore say *ēuchomēn* <note>original Greek: *ηὐχόμην*</note>, "I would wish" to do good, but he was not able; just as he said in this place, *I could wish to be anathema.*

III. It should be observed that Paul alludes to Jewish rites, among whom there were three types of anathemas, namely <term>Niddui</term> <note>A minor form of social distancing or temporary exclusion from the community.</note>, <term>Cherem</term> <note>A more severe ban involving total exclusion and devotion to destruction.</note>, and <term>Schammata</term> <note>The most absolute form of excommunication.</note>. Thus, those who were struck by these various types of anathemas were considered separated from God and excommunicated. Indeed, they even sealed letters with the word <term>nachasch</term> <note>original Hebrew: *נחש*</note>, which is an acronym for *Niddui, Cherem, and Schammata*, so that whoever opened them would be struck with every kind of anathema. In a similar way, in the Christian Church, sinners were commonly struck with these anathemas. Now, therefore, the Apostle, alluding to all these external rites and Church discipline, looks primarily at that which is internal—namely, separation from Christ. Just as in an ecclesiastical judgment it was a horrendous punishment to be penalized with anathema and handed over to Satan, so it would have been the greatest charity if someone became anathema for his neighbor; how much more if someone were separated from Christ and became anathema for his neighbor's sake.

IV. Observe also this: when Christ said in the Gospel, *greater love has no one than to lay down his life for his friends*, he speaks of what is sometimes done in actual practice; he does not speak of what never occurs. For otherwise, it would be a greater charity to be anathema for one’s brothers, because laying down one's life concerns the present life, while being anathema concerns the future life. In this way, Christ was exalted above all men and Angels, since he was made anathema; for there was no charity, neither in Angels nor in men, which could even slightly approach that of Christ. The Apostle himself emphasizes <note>original Latin: *exaggerat*, in the sense of magnifying or heightening the importance of a concept.</note> this throughout his epistles, and especially in Romans chapter 5 and Ephesians chapter 3, with monumental <note>original Latin: *vncialibus*, literally "uncial" or large capital letters.</note> and most significant words.
