WITH that divine and uncreated Archangel who went before the Israelites leading us in this exercise, we shall explain these three things with favorable success: *I. What the naming and nature of Angels is in Scripture. II. What kind of Angel is designated here. III. His duty: to go before all the people.*

Regarding the first point, naming is considered in two ways: either as common or as proper. The common name is designated by that general word *malakh* <note>original: מלאך</note>, which properly signifies the same as the Greek *angelos* <note>original: ἄγγελος</note>—a messenger or envoy—from the verb *angellein* <note>original: ἀπὸ τῷ ἀγγέλλειν</note>, which denotes an office. The Hebrew word is derived from, or at least is related to, the word *melakah* <note>original: מלאכה</note>, which signifies "work." And indeed, just as the word for work (*melakah*) is included in the word *malakh* which signifies "Angel," so Angels are not idle, but are perpetually at work. Paul hints at this in Hebrews 1, calling them "ministering spirits" <note>original: πνεύματα λειτουργικὰ (*pneumata leitourgika*)</note>; for in this way he indicates they are not merely messengers, but also administrators. From this also comes the word *tzava* <note>original: צבא</note> which is attributed to them; it is an emphatic term that does not only signify an "army," but also encompasses everything that possesses a principle of order. For just as the Church of God is called *edah* <note>original: עדה</note> from the general word *ya'ad* <note>original: יעד</note>...

*In truth, there is no personal naming of Angels among themselves, nor is it necessary, since they are not distinguished from one another by these kinds of concepts, nor are they given surnames. If, however, proper names are attributed to them, this is done in respect to us, and because of the various duties they perform. Hence, names are imposed upon them according to those duties, as is clear from the proper names attributed to them in Scripture: such as Gabriel, from "strength"; Raphael, from "healing." And in other apocryphal books, Uriel (4 Esdras, chapter 4) is derived from "light," because he came to enlighten or instruct Esdras. There are various other names among the Rabbis, such as Nuriel, Metatron, Juhac, etc., which names are surely descriptive rather than proper names, because they are imposed for a time due to some duty. Other names are common names which apply to many Angels, such as Seraphim, Cherubim, etc.; and among the Rabbis and others, Mazaloth <note>Likely referring to the zodiac or constellations</note>, El, Ligion, Rihatton, Chirton, and Gistera, etc. Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi, the famous medieval Jewish commentator</note>, among others, says that the names of Angels are secrets; so much so that not even they themselves know their own names. Indeed, he claims that Angels do not have names, but only surnames are given to them from the very things they are sent to care for; and he brings forward the examples of Seraphim, Cherubim, and Raphael. Thus* יהך *Juhac is the name of the Angel set over the care of men, taken from the final letters of these words in Psalm 91:11:* כי מלאכיו יצוה לך, *for he shall give his angels charge over thee.* <note>The name Juhac (יהך) is formed by taking the last letters of the Hebrew words 'malachav' (his angels), 'yetzaveh' (shall command), and 'lach' (concerning you).</note>

*It must be observed, however, regarding the name Cherubim, that it is a general term and does not always signify Angels, but a form or figure in the general sense of any living creature. Hence, in the books of Kings and Exodus, statues are said to be made as "Cherubim," but never as "Angels." I admit, indeed, that Angels are sometimes called in...*

# ANTHONY CREGUT

Scripture mentions Cherubim, yet no one will deny that Cherubim are not always Angels. Indeed, the Rabbis, who were well-acquainted with their mother tongue, teach that *Cherub* <note>Hebrew: כרוב</note> is a general name for any type of image or form <note>original Hebrew: כולל לכל צורה (*kolel le-khol tzurah*)</note>, though in the Law <note>The Torah, or first five books of the Bible</note> it specifically refers to a human figure. David Kimchi, in his work on *Hebrew Roots* (citing Rabbi Ibn Ezra), and David de Pomis in his *Dictionary*, explain them as images having the form of a human, except for the fact that they are winged. The term is also used in Exodus for various figures—especially those of a man, a lion, an ox, and an eagle—on the curtains. The same is found in Ezekiel. Therefore, besides Genesis chapter 3, there is hardly any place in the Old Testament where they must necessarily be understood as Angels. In fact, one might reasonably doubt whether they must be understood as Angels even in that passage of Genesis. 

But let us hear Francesco Giorgio of Venice <note>A 16th-century Franciscan friar and Christian Kabbalist</note>, who explains those Cherubim on the Mercy Seat <note>The gold lid of the Ark of the Covenant; original Latin: *propitiatorio*</note> sometimes as sacrificing Priests, and sometimes as the dual nature of Him who was made an atonement for our sins. It is easy, then, to conclude that the Cherubim were not images of Angels, for they represented nothing by their outward form. Nor does Scripture say anywhere what the Cherubim actually expressed; to claim that they represented Angels is nothing more than an old woman's dream <note>An idiom meaning a silly or superstitious fancy; original Latin: *anile somnium*</note>. Nevertheless, Moses in Genesis 3 called the Angels "Cherubim" so that the people might better understand the nature of Angels, since Angels themselves are invisible. Others are found who say that the word is composed of a prefix signifying likeness <note>The Hebrew letter *Kaph* (כ)</note> and the word *rabi* or *rabia* <note>Aramaic/Chaldaic: רבי / רביא</note>, meaning "child" or "little boy," because Angels were often depicted in the form of children. That Chaldaic word *rabia* comes from a root meaning "to grow" or "to sprout."

But although that common naming of "Angels" usually pertains only to the good Angels and not the bad, nevertheless, in Scripture, evil demons <note>original: *Cacodæmones*</note> are sometimes simply <note>original Greek: ἁπλῶς (*haplōs*)</note> called "Angels." Usually, however, they are mentioned with some additional description, such as "angels of the Devil" or "angels of Satan." Nor are they usually called "spirits" simply, but rather "evil spirit" or "unclean spirit," etc. Yet they are rarely called "Angels" simply, as in 1 Corinthians 6, where the Saints are said to be those who will judge the Angels <note>Referring to the judgment of fallen angels</note>. But it should be observed that whenever they are called "Angels" simply...

For instance, in the previously cited passage of 1 Corinthians 6, Paul says that the **Saints shall judge the Angels** <note>original Latin: *Sanctos iudicaturos Angelos*</note>; this was said for the purpose of exalting the glory and prerogatives of the Saints. Among philosophers, there is still a certain common naming of Angels; they are called **intelligences**, because they understand by a simple grasping of ideas and without the need for a chain of reasoning; just as God is called <term>Mind</term> <note>original Greek: νοῦς (*nous*); the faculty of the human mind which is necessary for reaching analytical patience and an understanding of the divine</note> in an absolute sense, because He is the primary intelligence. In the Peripatetic <note>The school of philosophy founded by Aristotle</note> doctrine, these intelligences were believed to be the movers of the heavens, and Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar</note> describes them mystically and with a new phrasing and notion in his *Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original Latin: *More Neuoch.*</note> part 2, chapter 10, when he speaks of the *breadth of the Angels*:

This is stated in the *Genesis Rabbah* <note>A Jewish midrashic text containing homiletic interpretations of the Book of Genesis</note>, and is explained by us in our great Talmudic work, where we have taught that all creatures are divided into three parts: into the separated intelligences which are the Angels, into the bodies of the celestial spheres, and into prime matter—that is, into those bodies which are perpetually changing and are beneath the heavens. In this way, the enigmas of Prophecy are to be understood; one must wake from the sleep of oblivion and emerge from the sea of ignorance.

The same Rabbi Maimonides further hands down in the aforementioned book, *Guide for the Perplexed*, part 3, chapter 22, a distinction between the good and the evil Angel, or the good and evil inclination.

> *You know (he says) that our opinion in the Law is well-worn regarding the* <term>good inclination and the evil inclination</term> <note>original Hebrew: יצר טוב ויצר רע (*yetzer tov ve-yetzer ra*)</note>.

Regarding the evil inclination, the sages say that it arises in a human at the time of their birth; as in Genesis 8: *from his youth.* Regarding the good inclination, they say it begins to exist in a man only after the perfection of his intellect. Therefore, we say the evil inclination is called a *great king*:

Have the sons of men become so maddened that they have stubbornly attacked such great authority? If stubbornly, yet it is more certain than certainty itself that they did not dare this with impunity.

Certainly, Scripture says nothing explicitly about the creation of the **Angels**, as it does regarding other species which were established within the six days of the **Creation of the World** <note>original Latin: *Cosmopœiæ*</note>. Nevertheless, there is no doubt that they were created during that **six-day period** <term>Hexameron: the six days of creation as described in Genesis</term>. Indeed, Moses did not lack reasons for veiling the creation of the Angels in silence, which we may also track down through inquiry. 

Was it perhaps because Angels are invisible? And so, since their nature was hidden, the divine historian did not wish to detain a people who were still unrefined and **undiscerning** <note>original Latin: *obæsæ naris*, literally "of a fat nose," a classical idiom for lacking subtle judgment</note> with such abstract matters? Or was it because that people was prone to idolatry and had recently been led out of Egypt, where idols and "idol-madness" <note>original Latin: *idolomania*</note> burned everywhere? Since the nature, gifts, and habitation of the Angels shone forth with something sublime, there was a danger that the Israelites might ascribe some divinity to them—especially since Moses says during the creation of man in Genesis 1: *Let us make man in our image.* For to a people ignorant of the mystery of the **Trinity**, it was easy to suspect something about the Angels, as if God had called them into a council.

Such, indeed, was the mind of the Rabbis, as is evident from Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher</note> in the book *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original Latin: *More Neuoch* (Moreh Nevochim)</note>, part 2, chapter 6. Angels are **separate intelligences** <term>Separate Intelligences: in medieval philosophy, these are non-material beings that move the celestial spheres</term> through which God governs the world. From this, the **Sages** <note>original Hebrew: *חכמים* (*Chakhamim*)</note>, regarding what we read in our Law, *Let us make man in our image*, write in this sense—**if one may say so** <note>original Hebrew: *כביכול* (*kibbi-yakhol*), a term used to avoid anthropomorphism when speaking of God</note>—that God does nothing until He has gazed upon it; that is, until He has deliberated in the **heavenly household** <note>original Latin: *familia superiori*</note>.

In this saying, I wonder (says that Rabbi Moses [Maimonides]) why they use the word **gaze upon** <note>original Hebrew: *משתכל* (*mistakel*)</note>. For Plato says similarly that God looks into the world of intelligences and produces Beings from it. Elsewhere they express it thus: God does nothing unless He has first consulted about it with the **heavenly retinue** <note>original Hebrew: *פמליא* (*pamalia*)</note>. The word *pamalia* in the Greek language signifies a "battle line" <note>This is a common medieval etymological association, though the term is more directly related to the Latin *familia*</note>. Maimonides, however, explains these things in a favorable sense when he says: their meaning is not as if God actually spoke and consulted with a creature; rather, it signifies that even the smallest parts of the world are brought into being through the mediation of Angels. 

Or do we also say that Moses remained silent on the creation of Angels because he wished to compose a history of the **Church**, and because Angels do not properly belong to that history? For that reason, he said very little about them...

...is said in Scripture, and the things narrated there are not treated absolutely and for their own sake, but in relation to the **Church**. Just as in a history of the **Franks** mention is occasionally made of the **English** and the **Spanish**, it is only done relatively and by accident because of wars or because they are neighboring peoples. In this same way, it was useful for the Church to know that good **Angels** exist for the consolation of the faithful, because they "set up camp" <note>original Latin: *castrametantur*; a reference to Psalm 34:7, suggesting angels act as a protective military guard</note> around us. Finally, shall we say that the creation of the Angels was addressed when Moses said at the very beginning of Chapter 1, verse 1, that ***God created the heaven and the earth***? There, he could have included everything contained within the heavens—all the inhabitants of heaven, and consequently the Angels. This is why in *Matthew 24:36* and *Galatians 1:8*, they are called the ***Angels of the heavens***.

Since, therefore, the teachers of the **Hebrews** felt that the Angels belonged to the "higher household," they did not wish to count them among the works of creation, but rather among those things which are **Metaphysical** and **mystical**. Hence, they record two genres of works: namely, the **Work of the Beginning** <note>Hebrew: מעשה בראשית, *Ma'aseh Bereshit*</note>, which is the "craft of creation" named after the first word of the **Bible**; and the **Work of the Chariot** <note>Hebrew: מעשה מרכבה, *Ma'aseh Merkabah*</note>, the "craft of the chariot" based on the vision of **Ezekiel** in Chapter 1 <note>The "Work of the Chariot" refers to Jewish mystical traditions regarding the divine throne-chariot and the celestial realms</note>.

And let these things be said briefly regarding that first part concerning the naming and existence of Angels. For we voluntarily omit countless other things that could be said about their properties, operations, location, duration, and so on, because these belong to general theology <note>original Latin: *locum communem*, or "commonplace," referring to standard topics in a theological textbook</note>, and not to our specific purpose. Therefore, what falls to us to investigate in the second place is what kind of Angel it is specifically of whom Moses speaks when he says, ***Behold, my Angel shall go before you***. Truly, all these words indicate that this Angel was a singular, specific Angel, spoken of **Antonomastically** <term>Antonomastic: using a title or epithet as a proper name, such as calling a specific angel "The Angel" to denote their unique status</term>. For first, Moses said ***Behold*** <note>original Latin: *Ecce*</note>, a particle used in Scripture to demonstrate something extraordinary and singular, as in *John 1:29*: ***Behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world***. Secondly, this was because he was not just any common lamb, but that specific Lamb prefigured by the ancient types. Similarly, in *Isaiah 7:14*: ***Behold, a Virgin shall conceive***. ...was signified, but a unique Virgin and one uniquely pre-defined, which is why the Prophet does not use the common term *betulah* <note>original: בתולה</note>, that is, *Virgin*, but *almah* <note>original: העלמה</note>, that is, a *hidden Virgin* <note>original Greek: κατάκλεις (katakleis), meaning "enclosed" or "shut up"</note>, and with the emphatic article *ha* <note>original Hebrew letter: ה</note>. Elsewhere, *Scripture* uses the common name of *Angels* in the plural and teaches that God uses their ministry. Furthermore, his specific office designates something peculiar: he was to *go before the people*. Since, therefore, that *Angel* is unique, it is not difficult to recognize who that *Angel* is. For he can be none other than the **Son of God**, who, just as he is called by way of antonomasia <note>a rhetorical device where a title or epithet is used instead of a proper name</note> and uniquely the *son of man* in *Daniel 7:13*—*as the son of man* <note>original Chaldean/Aramaic: כבר אנש (kebar enash)</note>, so that the uniqueness might be designated by that Chaldean expression; and just as he is called the *seed of the woman* or *Shiloh* using a very rare word to indicate excellence and uniqueness; so now he is called by antonomasia *Malak* <note>original: מלאך, meaning Messenger or Angel</note>. This is because, according to the *Temurah* <note>a mystical Jewish method of rearranging the letters of a word to find hidden meanings</note> of the **Hebrews** (which we call an **Anagram**), *Malak* is in truth *Michael* <note>original: מיכאל</note>; and *Michael* is the *Archangel*, or the *Angel of God* and *God*. For *Michael*, with its letters transposed through *Temurah*, becomes *Malachi* <note>original: מלאכי, meaning "My Messenger"</note>. Concerning this, it is said in this place: *My messenger before you* <note>original: מלאכי לפניך (Malachi lefaneka)</note>. And in *Exodus 23:23*: *my Angel shall go before you*. Moreover, *Mi-ka-el* <note>מי כאל</note>, through the method of *notaricon* <note>a method of interpreting words as acronyms</note>, is the same as *Who is like the strong God?* <note>original Hebrew: מי כה אל (Mi kah El)</note>. 

These words can apply to none other than the **Uncreated Angel**, who in the *Epistle of Jude* is called *Michael the Archangel fighting for the body of Moses*. And in *Zechariah*, he is called the *Angel of Jehovah*. Likewise, in *Revelation 8:3*, he is *that Angel who held the golden censer and offered the prayers of the Saints to God while standing at the altar*. He is also believed to have been *that Angel of the covenant*, who intercedes for us in heaven as the *High Priest*, offering the most sweet sacrifice of his own oblation...

# ANTOINE CRÉGUT

680

...offers incense to God the Father.

Who, then, would not shudder at the Pope's perpetual insults against the glory of our Michael? For there is no unique title <note>original Greek: ἐπωνυμία (eponymia)</note> or singular naming of Christ that the Pope does not immediately seize for himself. Not only does Pope Clement V <note>Pope from 1305–1314</note> act as a substitute for the Archangel—having commanded the Angels themselves to carry the souls of those pilgrims into heaven who had died on their journey to Palestine—but there is also an image printed in Rome where the oracles of the Prophets concerning God and the Messiah, Jesus Christ, are attributed to the Pope. Furthermore, among other things, these verses appear there:

> *Michael himself first dissolved the angelic name;*
> *For he who was before Michael is as God.*

It is clearly evident, then, that the Archangel is in truth Christ—that divine Galen <note>Galen was the most famous physician of antiquity; here the author uses his name as a title for Christ the Great Healer</note> who, by his infinite power, healed all manner of diseases and weaknesses and raised the dead. He was the true Raphael <note>The name Raphael means "God heals" in Hebrew</note> of the bodies and souls of men. Concerning that supreme physician Galen, there is a most true anagram, for the name *Galenus* fits most beautifully with the reality: *Angelus* <note>The letters in the Latin name Galenus can be rearranged to spell Angelus, meaning Angel</note>.

> *Are you an Angel: a good or a bad one, Galen?*
> *Guardian of human health; therefore, a good Angel.*

These things were spoken of a mortal man, but they are most truly to be pronounced and firmly believed regarding our Archangel and Michael.

Since, therefore, Christ is the Archangel and the head of all Angels, that fictitious doctrine of the three Hierarchies or Eparchies <note>Provincial administrations or ranks</note> is rightly abolished. For just as in the mystical body of Christ—namely, the Church—Christ alone is both the head and the firstborn (Ephesians 1, Romans 8), and all others are members and brothers without spiritual dominion or jurisdiction; so among the Angels, Christ alone is the Archangel and Michael, the unique head of both Angels and men. Indeed, all Angels and even men are fellow servants, as the Angel said to John in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>. That fiction of the Hierarchies, therefore, is without foundation; rather, it was devised with reckless effort by that Dionysius the Pseudo-Areopagite <note>A 5th-6th century theologian whose "Celestial Hierarchy" established the traditional nine choirs of angels, though his identity was later proven not to be the Dionysius mentioned in the Book of Acts</note>, who...

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS

...who, while living on earth, dared to investigate the orders and hierarchies of celestial intelligences, even placing one hierarchy before another, subjecting the second to the first and supreme, and the third to the second. In this system, the Angels of the supreme hierarchy would send those of the second, and the Angels of the second hierarchy would send those of the lowest to humanity; furthermore, they fixed the seat and order in each hierarchy, so that in one were Angels and Archangels, in another Seraphim, Cherubim, and so on. <note>The author is critiquing the "Celestial Hierarchy" attributed to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, which established the traditional nine-fold ranking of angels common in medieval theology.</note> There are, moreover, other inventions which we spontaneously despise as old wives' tales. Therefore, to us, the provinces, middle-ranks, and sub-ranks <note>original Greek-derived terms: *eparchiæ, mesarchiæ* and *hyparchię*</note> of the angels in that fictitious hierarchy are nothing more than pure beings of reason <note>A philosophical term, *Entia rationis*, referring to things that exist only in the mind rather than in reality</note> and empty things fluttering in the air.

However, even if there is no head among the [good] Angels (since Christ alone was meant to be the Archangel and the sole head of the Angels), we must judge differently regarding the evil angels. For among them, there is a head and a leader of the rest. Thus, the Devil is called the **chief leader** <note>original Greek: *ἀρχηγὸς* (archēgos)</note> in the singular; *Matthew 25: Depart, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the Devil and his angels.* And *Revelation 12* mentions the Dragon and his angels. Regarding Christ the head, *Daniel 10:13* says that Michael is a great prince, **one of the chief [princes]** <note>original Hebrew: אחד הרא שונים (*achad ha-rishonim*)</note>. Note, however, that Christ is called an "Angel" not because He is an Angel by His nature and essence—for He did not take on the nature of Angels (*Hebrews 2*) nor is He endowed with an angelic nature—but He is called an Angel in the same sense that in the *Epistle to the Hebrews* He is called an Apostle: in His capacity as Mediator, because He performs an embassy on behalf of the Father. In this same respect, Pastors and Bishops (*Revelation 1*) are called "Angels," and figuratively John the Baptist, Christ’s forerunner, is called an "Angel" in *Malachi 3:1*: *Behold, I am sending my Angel, who shall prepare the way before me.*

Although this naming is common to many, nevertheless Christ the **chief leader** <note>original Greek: *ἀρχηγὸς* (archēgos)</note> is distinguished from other Angels. For in the Scriptures, He is now called the *Angel of Jehovah*, now the *Angel of God*, and likewise the *Angel of God’s face*; the *Angel of great counsel*; the *Angel of the covenant or testament*. And in *1 Thessalonians 4:16*, He is called the Archangel. All these names are highly emphatic and signify the various **relationships** <note>original Greek: *σϰέσεις* (scheseis)</note> of Christ. Other Angels, however, are allotted various distinguished names.

### ANTHONY CREGUT

...belongs to the Israelites. The familiar angel of **Abraham** was **Zadkiel**; of **Isaac**, **Raphael**; and of **Jacob**, it was **Peliel**. For **Moses**, it was **Metatron** <note>A high-ranking angel in Jewish mystical tradition (Kabbalah), often described as the celestial scribe or a mediator between God and humanity.</note>. Regarding other angels, **Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational Christian theologian.</note> was the first of all to say that they possess an allegorical "day," the boundaries of which are "morning" and "evening." From this arose the concept of **morning** and **evening** knowledge of God. **Morning** knowledge is that by which angels know God immediately and behold all things in God. **Evening** knowledge is that by which angels behold created things—and therefore themselves—and from there ascend all the way to God. These things concerning created angels are highly uncertain, and one might even be inclined to ask what the "allegorical noon" of that day would be; yet truly, regarding this **uncreated Angel** <note>Refers to Christ as the divine Word before his human birth.</note>, it is rightly asserted that the noon of His knowledge is continuous. For He is the very "face of God" and the **radiance of God** <note>original Greek: *apaugasma tou Theou*; a reference to Hebrews 1:3.</note>. Indeed, He is the wisdom of the Father, and He sees God **the whole and wholly** <note>original Greek: *holon kai holōs*; meaning He perceives the entirety of the divine essence in an exhaustive, infinite way.</note>, and He makes God visible and, as it were, tangible in Himself. Indeed, after that Angel of God was incarnated, He surpassed the angels even according to His human nature; because, on account of the **hypostatic union** <term>The theological doctrine that Christ is one person with two distinct natures: fully divine and fully human.</term>, He was raised above all creatures; hence in Psalm 110, He is said **to sit at the right hand of God**. And in Hebrews 1:13: **To which of the angels did He ever say, sit at my right hand**, etc. And by reason of knowledge, the soul of Christ sees God **the whole but not wholly** <note>original Greek: *holon ouch holōs*</note>; but with respect to His divinity, He sees God **the whole and wholly**. To the angels, however, neither of these applies.

The primary difference between the Moral Law and the Ceremonial Law is this: the moral law is, in itself, the image of God’s justice and the copy <note>original Latin: *Ectypus*; a philosophical term for a derivative copy of an original pattern or "Archetype."</note> of that original Pattern, containing even those virtues of God which theologians call "primary"; for this reason, it is perpetual and was inscribed on human hearts from the beginning. But indeed, the Ceremonial law is in itself indifferent—neither good nor bad, neither just nor unjust. Therefore, it has no power except by convention <note>original Greek: κατ' συνθήκην (*kata synthēkēn*); meaning by agreement or social contract rather than by nature</note>, namely, from divine institution. 

Nevertheless, it happened by accident and because of the stain of sin that the Ceremonial law became necessary. Hence it is that not only was it observed after God’s institution—through which (as we have discussed at length elsewhere) it was made a decree <note>original Greek: δικαίωμα (*dikaiōma*)</note>—but it was also observed in most cases even before God's formal institution and command. For, as can be seen in the book of Genesis, the Patriarchs frequently offered sacrifices, such as Noah, Abraham, and others; indeed, immediately after the first sin, Abel and Cain did so, as is clear from Genesis 4. 

But among all ceremonies, the observance of the Sabbath is rightly given greater weight; because before it was sanctioned by God’s law, and before it was observed by the Patriarchs under that law, God deigned to consecrate that ceremony by His own example even before sin existed, when (as held in Genesis 1) *He rested from all His work*. Not without merit, therefore, did that supreme Legislator later sanction that ceremony by law; indeed, what is more, He wished to include it in His moral law, or the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note>, so that it might be of perpetual observance—if not by reason of this specific seventh day, then at least by reason of some day. And for that reason, that fourth commandment of the Decalogue...

The Sabbath was confirmed by an almost regular *miracle* (if the historians are to be believed); hence the singular marvel concerning the Sabbatical river <note>The Sambation, a legendary river in Jewish literature that was said to flow wildly six days a week but stop and rest on the Sabbath</note>.

So many and such great qualities of preeminence <gloss>original Greek: ἐξοχὴν (*exochēn*)</gloss> caused the Sabbath not only to be observed religiously among the Jews, but even to the point of superstition: hence that very common phrase among the Hebrews, *techum ha-shabbat* <gloss>original Hebrew: תחום השבת</gloss>, that is, the *boundary of the Sabbath*, which comprised two thousand paces <note>approximately 1.2 kilometers or 0.75 miles</note>, beyond which it was not permitted to cross. For the guards were Roman soldiers, whose garrison was established in the **Antonia Tower**, according to **Josephus** <note>Flavius Josephus, a first-century Romano-Jewish historian</note>, and they were commanded by the **captain of the temple** <note>original Greek: *στρατηγὸς τοῦ ναοῦ* (*stratēgos tou naou*)</note>. Therefore, during festivals, he would station guards and watches around the temple, so that no riot would arise from that most seditious nation. Nonetheless, whenever there was a danger to life, no work was prohibited.

<margin>-</margin> Hence that most common saying of the Rabbis: *Danger to life pushes aside the Sabbath* <note>original Hebrew: *Saccanath hannefesch doche eth haschabbath*</note>. This is because it was permitted to do work on the Sabbath by which a neighbor’s life might be preserved. In this, it is evident that the hatred of the Jews toward Christ was **Vatinian** <note>an idiomatic expression meaning extreme, unrelenting hatred</note>; they were so often and so bitterly provoked against Him because He healed infirmities, saying that He had violated the Sabbath and transgressed the Law of Moses.

That the Jews magnified the institution of the Sabbath above other ceremonies could be proven by various Hebrew documents. The **Cabalists** themselves <note>Jewish mystics who sought hidden meanings in scripture</note>, who searched out the mysteries of religion more than others, proclaimed the Sabbath to be a mystery of the living God, saying: *The Sabbath is the secret of the living God* <note>original Hebrew: *schabath hu sod el chai*</note>. For it is a symbol of the higher world—that is, the **Jubilee of eternity**—where all labor will cease. They judge that both Sabbaths—namely, the Sabbath of the lower world and the Sabbath of the higher world—were signified by two words used in the Law of Moses. For Moses uses the words *Zakhor* and *Shamor* <note>original Hebrew: זכור & שמור</note>—that is, **Remember** and **Observe**—in the promulgation of the law in **Deuteronomy 5** and **Exodus 20**. The first is from **Exodus 20:8**: *Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.* The second is from **Deuteronomy 5:12**: *Observe the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.* They claim that this choice of words was made by Moses in...

# ANTHONY CREGUT

nothing was created in it. For "ceasing from speaking" is expressed by the word *shavat* <note>original Hebrew: שבת; the root of "Sabbath," meaning to cease or rest</note>. Job 32:1: *and they rested* <note>original Hebrew: וישבתו — *vavishbetu*</note>, or "those three men ceased to answer." Therefore, the words of Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> are to be understood in a sound sense, where he says in his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*: "And God completed on the sixth day his works which he made." In place of the "sixth day," the Hebrew text has the "seventh day." We shall therefore constrain the Jews—who boast of the Sabbath rest—by pointing out that even then, in the beginning, the Sabbath was "dissolved" while God was still working on the Sabbath, completing his works within it and blessing the day itself: because in it he had completed all things.

II. It should be observed that God rested on the Sabbath day, but in a unique way. For unlike "little men" [mortals], there was no exhaustion or weakness resulting from labor; rather, he merely ceased from speaking or from acts of will. For whether men labor with the body or the mind, they cannot help but eventually become weary from excessive toil, because they act through movement and change. But God acts without movement or change, through his word or through a simple act of will. Therefore, his Sabbath and rest is nothing other than the cessation of volition. Thus, there is no distinction other than between *amar* <note>original Hebrew: אמר — "he said"</note> and *lo amar* <note>original Hebrew: לא אמר — "he did not say"</note>; for *shavat* (that is, "he ceased") is the same as "he did not speak." For the Sabbath, or rest, signifies two things: either the end and limit of an action, or recreation and refreshment after movement and labor. The former is attributed to God, but not the latter, because (as stated above) he did not create the world with physical labor. The masters of the Hebrews express this enigmatically: God created the world in the letter *He* <note>original Hebrew: ה</note>, which is to say, by his breath. For this letter is produced only by a breath, which that supreme *demiurge* <term>demiurge: from the Greek *demiourgos*, meaning a craftsman or world-creator</term> of the world represented in the most noble of all creatures when he created the spirit of Adam by breathing; "the spirit of life," or "of lives" <note>original Hebrew: נשמת חיים — *nishmat chayim*</note>, by breathing into his nostrils—a metaphor taken from glassmakers who produce glass by blowing. This agrees with the words of the Psalmist in Psalm 33: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their host by the spirit of his mouth."

III. Observe that God rested on the seventh day and created all things in six days. Therefore, Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Jewish philosopher</note> wrote *contradictorily* <note>original Greek: ἀντιγράφως</note> in the *Guide for the Perplexed* (*Moreh Nevuchim*), part 2, chapter 30, when he says that God created all things simultaneously,

<summary>Cregut defines divine rest not as recovery from fatigue, but as the cessation of the creative "speech" or "will" that formed the world. He uses Hebrew linguistics and metaphors of breath to argue that God's work was completed through a simple, effortless expression of power.</summary>

### THE REVEALER OF SECRETS

...[had] created [all things], but then separated them from one another successively. He likens this to a farmer who sows various seeds in the earth at a single moment; some of these sprout after one day, others after two days, and others after three, even though the entire sowing was performed in one hour. But according to the testimony of Moses, God established all things in six days. He did not do this successively in the sense that he labored for six continuous days from morning to evening like a farmer, but rather in six distinct moments. These are signified broadly <note>original Greek: παχυλῶς (*pachylōs*); meaning roughly or in a simplified manner adapted for a general audience</note> by Moses as "six days" for the common people to understand.

Augustine was also mistaken in thinking that the world was established in a single moment in his work *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book 4, Chapter 33. Two reasons drove that holy man toward this error. 1. A passage from Ecclesiasticus: *God created all things together* <note>original Hebrew: יחדיו — *jachad*; often translated as "simultaneously" or "together." Cregut is citing Sirach 18:1</note>. He failed to notice the Hebrew idiom latent in the word *jachad*, which does not always mean "at the same time," but equally means "likewise," as if you were saying "these as much as those." For example, in Psalm 49:11: *they die alike, as do the foolish and the stupid* <note>original Hebrew: יחדיו ימותו — *yamutu jachad*</note>; and verse 3: *the rich and the poor alike* <note>original Hebrew: יחד עשיר ואביון — *jachad ashir ve-evyon*</note>. Here, therefore, more truly than in other matters, we might say with Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), an influential Jesuit Cardinal and scholar</note> that *Augustine was deceived by an ignorance of the Hebrew language.* 2. The cause of Augustine’s slip was that he wisely judged that God, by his infinite power, would have wished to establish all things in a single instant, since he wills and understands all things as light and matter <note>original Greek: φῶς καὶ ὕλη (*phōs kai hylē*)</note>. Nevertheless, that great Saint was not unaware that God, in Scripture, usually effects things according to his <term>ordained power</term> <note>God's power as expressed through the established laws and order of the universe</note> rather than through his <term>absolute power</term> <note>God's total, infinite potential to act beyond or outside established natural laws</note>. This is because it pleased him to temper and determine his infinite power by his own will and wisdom. This is no different than in the "new creation" <note>A theological term for the process of spiritual salvation or the renewal of the world</note>, where various acts, moments, and stages of progress are distinguished, after which finally the heavenly Sabbath-rest <note>original: *Sabbathismus*; referring to the eternal rest of the soul in God</note> follows, as was skillfully observed previously by the most learned John Cameron <note>John Cameron (c. 1579–1625), a famous Scottish theologian who taught in France</note>.

IV. Observe that God rested on the seventh day so that he might contemplate his handiwork and, as Moses witnesses, see *that all which he had made was very good.* And likewise, by his own example, he might teach us that the Sabbath must be celebrated, and that we must rest from all our work so that we might contemplate God’s works in this magnificent theater of the sun, the sea, and the sky.

# ANTOINE CRÉGUT

V. Since God rested from every work of creation, those impious delusions of the Rabbis must be outlawed and cursed; they imagined that God, caught off guard by the final evening of the sixth day, left certain creatures imperfect—such as Fauns and Satyrs—as if He were just one of the common craftsmen who needed more time. For since the Jews "look for a knot in a bulrush" <note>original Latin: *nodum in scirpo quaerant*; a common idiom for searching for a difficulty where none exists</note>, they argue from the words of Moses in Genesis 2:3, where it is said, *that God rested from all His work which He had created to make*. But those final words do not mean that God was to create and make other things after the sixth day; rather, they signify that all His subsequent works were finished. It is as if he had said that God so created His works that nothing was lacking for their perfection, or that creation progressed until the work was absolute in every way.

I add other Rabbinic fables regarding a "hole in the heavens." For the Talmudists wrote that God created the heavens imperfect with a hole in the North, so that if anyone could complete it, they might show themselves to be God. Galatinus <note>Pietro Galatino (c. 1460–1540), a scholar who sought Christian allegories in Jewish texts</note> explains this mystically as referring to Christ, who recreated the world, conquered the devil, and abolished idolatry. Truly, these Rabbinic fables are so ridiculous that one must confess the authors were struck by the thickest blindness <note>original Latin: *scotomate*; a medical term for a blind spot, used here for spiritual or intellectual darkness</note>, unless they were veiling some mystical meaning beneath those wraps of words.

For instance, when the ancient Hebrews write elsewhere that when they were asked what God was doing before He created the world, they replied that God had built and overturned worlds. They explained it this way: while He enjoyed His own immense wisdom, He saw that the world could be established and firmed up in infinite other ways, but He approved this one single method. Moses signified this with these words in Genesis 1:4: *God saw the light, that it was good*. This "looking" of God is nothing other than His approval. They say the same thing when they claim that seven things were created before the creation of the world: namely, *the Mosaic Law, repentance, paradise and Gehenna <note>the place of punishment or Hell</note>, the throne of glory and the house of the sanctuary <note>the Temple in Jerusalem</note>, and the name of the Messiah*. No one, unless I am mistaken, will deny that these are to be understood mystically.

II. Just as the holiness of the institution of the Sabbath was demonstrated by the example of God, who rested on that day from all work, so thereafter

This is confirmed by the miracle of the manna in Exodus 16. For that heavenly food was not found in the field on the seventh day; hence Moses says in Exodus 16:26: "Eat it today," said Moses, "for today is the Sabbath of the Lord <note>original: *Iehoua*; Jehovah or Yahweh</note>: today you will not find that food in the field." And for that reason, on the sixth day they gathered a double portion of food, two measures—an omer <note>original: *Homer*; an ancient Hebrew unit of dry measure, roughly 2 liters</note> for every person; and so it was done for forty years. Therefore, of old, even before the Law was officially proclaimed, the Sabbath was observed as a sort of prelude.

III. The sanctity of the institution of the Sabbath is further confirmed by the double proclamation of the Law in Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5, where the Sabbath is sanctified not only by the authority of the Lawgiver, but is expressed in emphatic and very distinct words. This is seen both in the terms <term>זכור</term> *Zacar* <note>original Hebrew: "Remember"</note> and <term>שמור</term> *schamar* <note>original Hebrew: "Keep" or "Observe"</note>, which were discussed above; from the command of sanctification itself; from the example of God considered therein; and from the specific list of persons who are bound to keep it holy. These are distinctly enumerated in that Fourth Commandment, not even omitting servants, strangers, or cattle; and finally, by the rigid prohibition of any work, even the smallest.

IV. The sanctity of the Sabbath is also abundantly demonstrated by the perpetual praises and commendations of the Prophets. For they continually emphasize that God primarily wills and exactly demands obedience in this matter, and that He cannot forgive the pollution of His Sabbath, since He would thereby be permitting the profanation of His own Name. This is why the sanctification of the Sabbath is placed in the "first table" of the law <note>The "first table" refers to the first four of the Ten Commandments, which traditionally concern humanity's direct relationship and duties toward God, as opposed to the "second table" concerning duties toward fellow humans</note>, which is entirely indispensable because it directly and immediately touches the nature and majesty of the Lawgiver. This is why the Prophets, when indicating the impiety of the people and the subversion of all religion, immediately complain of polluted, violated, unkept, and unsanctified Sabbaths—as if, once this obedience were omitted, nothing else remained by which God might be honored. Such complaints and rebukes from God are found everywhere among the Prophets, such as in Ezekiel 20:12, chapter 22:8, and 23:38; in Jeremiah 17:21; in Isaiah 56:2; and in Nehemiah 9:14. Likewise, one finds many *Praises of the Sabbath* <note>original: *Sabbathi Encomia*</note>.

V. It can be added regarding the institution of the Sabbath that the law appears to have been given not only in the time of Moses, but even immediately from creation, so that the Sabbath might be its <term>memorial</term> <note>original Greek: *μνημόσυνον*; a reminder or monument</note> and a remembrance of God’s rest. Thus, just as the first day was the beginning of successive duration (since before that there was nothing but eternity <term>from the past</term> <note>original: *à parte ante*; eternity looking backward</note>), so the seventh day was the boundary of duration, such that nothing more remained except eternity <term>to come</term> <note>original: *à parte post*; eternity looking forward</note>. By these witnesses, it appears that such a river once existed in Judea, but now no trace of it remains, nor is anyone found who says they have seen it. This sufficiently suggests that the Jewish Sabbath has long since failed after the resurrection of Christ, and the Christian Sabbath—that is, the **Lord’s Day**—has succeeded it. For just as the Sabbath looks toward the benefit of **creation**, so the Lord’s Day looks toward the benefit of **redemption**; and as He fulfilled the work of creation on the Sabbath day, so on the Lord’s Day He fulfilled the work of redemption through the resurrection. And as the work of redemption excels the work of creation, so the Lord’s Day excels the Sabbath day, because it shall never be abolished. Hence the Talmudists say: "the work of creation is less than the work of redemption." For in creation, God spoke and the world was made; but in redemption, it was necessary for God not only to speak, but also to do many things and to suffer. This certainly agrees with the words of the Messiah in Luke 24: *It was necessary for Christ to suffer and so to enter into His glory.*

Truly, God intended various ends when He instituted the Sabbath. 1. *That it might be a **memorial** <note>original Greek: μνημόσυνον (*mnēmosynon*)</note> of God’s rest.*

...after the work of creation; so that men might learn that God did not perpetually establish new species—even though he could have, according to his **absolute power**, which regards *all possible things* <note>original: πάντα τὰ δυνατὰ (*panta ta dynata*)</note>. Instead, he wisely arranged them into a fixed number, which he produced from his **ordained power**. <note>Theologians distinguished between God's "absolute power" (what He is capable of doing) and "ordained power" (the specific laws and order He chose to establish).</note> For although the power of God is infinite in itself, it pleased him to restrict and determine it by his own will and wisdom. Therefore, God created only *the things that were to be* <note>original: τὰ μέλλοντα (*ta mellonta*)</note>, which were destined to exist according to his decree, and he did so according to his wisdom *in number, weight, and measure*. <note>A reference to the Wisdom of Solomon 11:20, a popular verse used to describe God as a rational architect.</note> If, therefore, that most pure act [of God] is still working even now, as it says in **John 5**: *My Father is working until now, and I am working*, this is to be understood as the work of general and special **providence**, and not that he is producing entirely new species of creatures.

**II.** So that men might learn that the world was not created out of a necessity of nature—as certain philosophers have dreamed—but out of supreme freedom. It exists because that most free agent willed it; and because he willed it so, and because he willed it *then*, and not otherwise or at another time. For that reason, he also rested when he willed and how he willed, namely by ceasing from the work of creation. By contrast, when he begets the Son <note>Referring to the eternal generation of Jesus Christ in the Trinity.</note>, he never rests, because he begets him out of a necessity of nature (or naturally); therefore, he begot him from eternity, begets him today, and will beget him for eternity.

**III.** So that it would become manifest to men that God approved of the craftsmanship of the world. Therefore, he did not only rest so that he might contemplate his glory in that image of himself—the **Archetype** in the **Ectype** <note>In the philosophy of the time, the *Archetype* is the original idea in God's mind, while the *Ectype* is the physical copy or reflection found in the created world.</note>—but he also fully took pleasure in it, since (as **Moses** says) *he saw everything that he had made, and it was very good*. Therefore, if God will eventually consume the world in a great fire, just as he once submerged it in a flood, this happens as a result of the "accident" of sin, because of which *it repented God that he had made man*, as is said in **Genesis 6:6**, and *the earth was cursed* (**Genesis 3**).

**IV.** So that men might know that they too ought to rest following God's example, and cease from all servile work, so that they might attentively contemplate God's works. Thus, by leafing through that "**book of nature**," they might recognize God's goodness, power, and wisdom depicted there in great characters, and by recognizing them, they might glorify him.

**V.** That the Sabbath should be specifically for the Israelites a memorial of the wondrous liberation from Egyptian slavery, which is immediately emphasized in the very preface of the law in **Deuteronomy 5** and **Exodus 20**: 
> *I am Jehovah your God who led you out from the land of Egypt, from the house of slaves.*
For the Jews, snatched from the yoke of Pharaoh and redeemed from the harshest servitude, rested from all the labors of Egypt, under whose immense weight they were breaking down to a monstrous degree, groaning day and night while panting for rest.

**VI.** That the Sabbath should be that sacred and blessed day devoted to divine worship, on which sacred assemblies are held, the law of God is read and explained, heavenly hymns are sung, prayers are poured out to God, and sacrifices are offered (**Numbers 28:9**), sacraments administered, sacred collections made, and other such holy exercises performed. Hence it is that in **Nehemiah 9:14**, the Sabbath is called *Holy*. And it is used <term>Synecdochically</term> <note>A figure of speech where a part is used to represent the whole. Here, the word "Sabbath" stands in for the entire system of external religious practice.</note> for the whole of external worship.

**VII.** That it might be a sign of every blessing, even bodily, and of the cessation from all sickness and trouble. Hence that Hebrew proverb cited above: <note>original: סכנה הנפש דוחה את השבת (*Sakanat ha-nefesh doche et ha-shabbat*)</note> *danger to life sets aside the Sabbath*. Namely, that it is permitted to do some work on the Sabbath by which another’s life may be preserved.

**VIII.** That this bodily and external Sabbath might be a sign of the moral and internal Sabbath—namely, the ceasing from the works of the flesh, or (as the Apostle says) from the unfruitful works of darkness. For even if the Sabbath was instituted before sin, this does not prevent it from later signifying, by circumstance <note>original: *per accidens*</note> and by convention <note>original: κατ' συνθήκην (*kat' synthēkēn*)</note>, many things which it could not signify by its nature <note>original: φύσει (*physei*)</note>. For this is the logic of signs: they signify either naturally or by appointment. Thus, when marriage was instituted, it was not a remedy against the lust of the flesh, since sin had not yet arisen; rather, its purpose was based on the design of nature. But after man fell, it became a medicine by circumstance.

**IX.** The Sabbath was instituted to be a sign and monument of the covenant established between God and his people. For

**X.** So that, with respect to the works and labor of the entire week, the Sabbath might be a rest and recreation for men; just as night was given to us to be a rest after daily labors, so that with the senses lulled by sleep, the body might rest peacefully and tired limbs might be relieved. **XI.** That the Sabbath might be a <term>Type</term> <note>In theology, a "type" is a person, event, or institution in the Old Testament that foreshadows a greater reality in the New Testament.</note> of the heavenly and eternal Sabbath or rest, which the blessed shall enjoy in the heavenly Sanctuary. The Apostle teaches this in **Hebrews 4:4**, in which chapter it is shown that the rest of the Jewish people in the land of Canaan was a type of the rest of the faithful in the heavenly Canaan after their full redemption from spiritual Egyptian slavery. This is why Paul says in verse 8: *For if Jesus had given them rest, he would not have spoken thereafter of another day.* In this context, by "Jesus," he does not mean Christ (as some suppose), but Joshua, who is called "Jesus" by the Greeks. <note>In the Greek language of the New Testament, the names Joshua and Jesus are identical (Iēsous). Joshua led the Israelites into the physical Promised Land, while Jesus leads believers into the spiritual one.</note> For just as that land of Canaan was a type of the heavenly Canaan, so Joshua was a type of Christ leading us into the heavenly Canaan, just as Joshua led the Jews into the earthly Canaan. Therefore, Paul adds in verse 9: *There remains, then, a certain Sabbatism for the people of God,* using a Hebrew-derived word where he had previously used <note>original: "κατάπαυσιν" (katapausin)</note> "rest" to mean the same thing.

1. This is done to distinguish the names themselves (as <term>Beza</term> <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major French Protestant theologian and successor to John Calvin.</note> says in his notes). For in **Psalm 95**, rest is called <note>original: "מנוחה" (menuchah)</note> *menuchah*, but where the seventh day is discussed, it is called <note>original: "שבת" (shabbath)</note> *shabbath*.

2. It is also to distinguish heavenly rest from earthly rest; the former is that eternal "Sabbatism" symbolized by the external Sabbath, in which there will be everlasting rest from every work of the body and of darkness, and from all miseries. This is because there will be a total redemption of both body and soul, which theologians call <term>efficacious redemption</term> <note>The final, completed state of salvation where the believer is fully freed from the presence and effects of sin.</note>. Scripture, when speaking of those works from which we shall cease and rest, does not only call them *dead works*, *evil works*, *works of darkness*, and *fruits of the flesh*, but also understands other things which are burdensome <note>original: "pœnalia," meaning tasks involving hardship or punishment</note>, in which the pious are exercised in this life. XII. So that the Sabbath might be a symbol of great mysteries, both of things past and things future.

<margin>1.</margin> Of things past. For (as was said above) it was celebrated in memory of the first and most universal benefit, namely the creation of the world. For as Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy</note> writes in his book *On the Creation of the World*, just as kings command that the birthdays of their sons be honored, so God willed the "birthday" of His work to be honored. And among the distinguished <term>Epochs</term> <note>A significant point in time used as the starting point of an era</note>, that one is most excellent which begins from the creation of the world, because it refutes the errors of the Philosophers, who were inclined to believe in the eternal motion and eternity of the world.

<margin>II.</margin> It was a figure of *future things*. And this is in a threefold sense: in an <term>Allegorical</term> sense, in a <term>Tropological</term> sense, and in an <term>Anagogical</term> sense <note>These represent three of the four traditional levels of scriptural interpretation: Allegorical (relating to Christ/Church), Tropological (relating to moral conduct), and Anagogical (relating to the afterlife/eternity)</note>. 

First, in the allegorical sense, the Sabbath was a figure of Christ’s rest in the tomb; for just as God rested on the Sabbath from the work of creation, so Christ rested on the Sabbath from the work of redemption, which is the observation made by the Apostle in **Hebrews 4**. 

Secondly, it was a figure in the tropological sense of the rest of the human mind from the "servile works" of sin or darkness. For while the Jews rested on the Sabbath, they signified that a time of grace would come, in which men, liberated through Christ from the slavery of sin, would peacefully enjoy spiritual rest and leisure. This is noted by Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, the influential 4th-century theologian</note> in his 30th Tractate on John and elsewhere, as also reported by Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine, a prominent Jesuit Cardinal and Counter-Reformation theologian</note>. 

Thirdly, it was a figure in the anagogical sense of the eternal rest of the blessed in heaven—that "Sabbath-rest" <note>original: "sabbatismo"</note> of which the Apostle speaks in **Hebrews 4:9**, as mentioned above. For as for the anagogical sense about which Bellarmine babbles in *On the Worship of the Saints*, book 3, chapter 12—namely, that the Sabbath was a figure of the rest of holy souls which they expected after death in the "Bosom of Abraham"—he is greatly hallucinating, since he does not see that the souls...

The saints could not have been waiting for that most blessed rest in the "bosom of Abraham," since they were already enjoying that rest in the bosom of Abraham. Indeed, the "bosom of Abraham" mentioned in Luke 16 is the bosom of the Heavenly Father—that is, paradise—where the blessed enjoy the <term>beatific vision</term> <note>The direct perception and enjoyment of God in heaven</note>, and not those mythical <term>Limbos</term> <note>Limbus/Limbo refers to a theological concept of a temporary place for those who died before the time of Christ</note> about which the proponents of Limbo prattle on to the point of nausea. Nor should the authority of Augustine (in his 115th Epistle) move us in this matter, because many of the ancients were deceived by a corruption in the <term>Vulgate</term> <note>The common Latin translation of the Bible used by the Western Church</note> edition of the First Epistle of Peter, chapter 3, verse 19. In that version, it says: *and to those spirits who **were** in prison, coming he preached.* In the original Greek text, the substantive verb "were" is not expressed, but it is simply written: *to the spirits in prison* <note>original: "τοῖς ἐν φυλακῇ πνεύμασι"</note>. This corruption even misled our own [John] Calvin. But [Theodore] Beza <note>A prominent Protestant Reformer and colleague of Calvin</note> removed all occasion for doubt by judiciously emending the Vulgate and substituting "are" for "were," following the Apostle's meaning without making any change to the Greek original, where the verb is understood. Thus it is clearly evident, even to the blind, that those spirits were not in "Limbos," but are in the prison of hell—and were so even when Peter wrote his epistle—but they were those who lived when the Spirit of Christ preached repentance to them through Noah. But let these things be said in passing; for at another time, God willing <note>original: "favente Numine"</note>, that divine prophecy will be handled accurately.

Thus far we have discussed the true purposes for the institution of the Sabbath; however, the Pagans, who were ignorant of the Jewish mysteries or even maliciously slandered them, fabricated other purposes. For their authors wrote that the Sabbath was instituted in honor of Bacchus and Saturn, and therefore for the purpose that those false gods might be worshipped by them on that holy day. For Plutarch <note>A Greek historian and philosopher</note> reported that the Jews worshipped a donkey and Bacchus, and he thought that "Sabbath" was derived from the foreign name *Sabbos*, which was a name once used for Bacchus. And Apion <note>An Egyptian-Greek grammarian known for his anti-Jewish rhetoric</note> used to say, as reported by Josephus, that the Jews, having been expelled from Egypt, were afflicted with ulcers of the groin after a six-day journey, and for this reason they rested on the seventh day. They prattle on that this day was called the Sabbath because, in the Egyptian language, a disease of the groin was called *Sabbatosis*. Others, as can be seen in the writings of Cornelius Tacitus <note>A Roman historian who expressed many prejudices against the Jews</note>, [considered] Saturn [to be the God] of the Jews...

They used to say [the Jews worshipped Saturn as] God because they celebrated the Sabbath. For the pagans also consecrated the seventh day to Saturn, with individual days of the week assigned to a particular planet, and because they were believed to be gods, the days were sanctified in their honor. Hence it is that Faustus the Manichaean <note>A 4th-century follower of Manichaeism who famously debated St. Augustine</note>, as recorded in Augustine, book 18 *Against Faustus*, chapters 2 and 5, *called the leisure of the Sabbaths "Saturnian chains"* <note>original: "Sabbatorum ocium vocabat catenas Saturnicas." This implies that the Sabbath rest was a form of bondage to the planet/god Saturn.</note>.

Now follows the third part, namely the **punishment inflicted on violators**. That is expressed in the Law <term>verbatim</term> <note>original: "αὐτολεξεὶ" (autolexei) — word for word</note> in these words: *whoever does work on that day shall be put to death.* Hence it was a sin to gather **manna** on the Sabbath day (Exodus 16:27, 28, etc.), because it did not even rain on that day. It was also a sin to gather wood (Numbers 15:32); when one of the Jews had done this, by the command of Moses he was led out of the camp by the whole assembly and overwhelmed with stones. [Also forbidden:] *To kindle a fire in the houses* (Exodus 35:3). *To plow or reap* (Ibid. 34:21). *To tread the winepresses* (Nehemiah 13:15). *To carry burdens and bring them into the city* (Nehemiah 13:15). *To sell or buy anything* (Nehemiah 10:31). *To make a journey* (Isaiah 58, Matthew 24:20). And therefore *to go out from one's place* (Exodus 16:29). All these things were prohibited under penalty of death.

However, this was not to be taken so rigidly as if all those things were entirely forbidden. For in Acts 1:12, it mentions a "Sabbath journey," which was a certain fixed distance, as we explained above. Nor was it forbidden to do good on the Sabbath, to exercise works of charity and piety, or to attend to <term>worldly necessities</term> <note>original: "τὰ βιωτικὰ" (ta biotika) — things pertaining to daily life or survival</note>. For Christ and the Apostles often performed those things, as is clear from Matthew 12:1, 12; Mark 3:4; Matthew 12:5; John 7:22, 23; and Matthew 12:1-2. And the Jews lawfully slaughtered animals, performed sacrifices, circumcised, and so on. Likewise, everyone would untie an ox or a donkey from the manger and lead it to water (Luke 13:15), and when one had fallen into a pit, they would pull it out (Luke 14:5).

Therefore, the Pharisees were too rigid and superstitious, who, under the appearance of piety and observance of the Law, condemned works of charity performed on the Sabbath; hence it is that they accused Christ as a transgressor of the Sabbath because he had healed the sick. The *Sabbath*, whenever they slaughtered victims in the temple and offered them in sacrifice, must be understood according to the mindset <note>original: δοξασικῶς (doxasikos) — based on opinion or appearance</note> of the Pharisees and from their hypothesis. But on the contrary, the profane were worthy of the gravest punishment, and in general all the Heathens <note>original: "Ethnici" — non-Jews or pagans</note>, who, leaning toward the other extreme, condemned and mocked the celebration of the Sabbath and held it in derision, as is gathered from Lamentations 1:7. This is similar to when the lampstand is removed from the unbelievers because of their contempt for the Gospel, according to the warnings in Revelation 1. For since the Sabbath was a sign of great joy among the people of God, they could not be deprived of the Sabbath celebration without great mourning, as is clear from Lamentations 2:6 and Hosea 2:11.

This abrogation of the Sabbath clearly confirms the abrogation of the remaining ceremonies. For if the Sabbath ceased, which was the oldest ceremony of all, established long ago by God’s command and example; what will be the judgment for the other ceremonies of the law? Truly it must be said that they were all torn in the veil of the temple, died in the death of Christ, buried in Christ’s tomb, became lethal after Christ’s resurrection and ascension, were cut off in the destruction of the temple and city, dispersed in the dispersion of the people, and finally abolished in the abolition of the Synagogue and the Sabbath, so that henceforth a new name and a new day might succeed them, namely the Church and the Lord's Day <note>original: "dies Dominica" — Sunday, the day of the Resurrection</note>, so that once all old things were abolished, all things might become new in this new economy of the New Testament.

In truth, the abrogation is general with respect to all ceremonies of the Old Testament; for since they were signs of future things and figures foreshadowing the truth, they certainly had to be abolished after they were fulfilled and the truth arrived. Hence it is that while ceremonies were previously called *ordinances* <note>original: δικαιώσεις (dikaioseis)</note> or *decrees* <note>original: δικαιώματα (dikaiomata)</note> because God, by instituting them, *ordained* <note>original: ἐδικαίωσε (edikaiose)</note> them—even though in themselves they were indifferent <note>original: "adiaphoræ" — a theological term for actions that are neither inherently good nor evil</note>, neither good nor evil—after the time appointed for their duration passed, they are no longer *ordinances*, but *unrighteous acts* <note>original: ἀδικίαι (adikiai)</note>, because they are no longer prescribed by God, nor can they be called *statutes* <note>original: חקים (chukkim)</note> as before, because they have been abolished. Therefore, after their abolition, they are called rather in Scripture *will-worship* <note>original: ἐθελοθρήσκεια (ethelothreskeia) — self-imposed or superstitious worship</note> (Colossians 2) and the *traditions* <note>original: παραδόσεις (paradoseis)</note> of men.

# ANTHONY CREGUTI

...but that [the Sabbath] is truly ceremonial. Since, in a general sense, some day forever ought to be sacred to God, the fact that it was this specific day rather than another is entirely a matter of indifference; consequently, it depends on God’s decree, who establishes now this one, now that one according to various reasons. First, He willed to establish the seventh day so that it might be a memorial <note>original: "μνημόσυνον" — a remembrance or commemorative token</note> of God's rest; but in the new law, with the Sabbath having been abolished, it pleased God that a new day should succeed it, namely the Lord’s Day <note>original: "dies Dominica" — Sunday</note>, which would be a memorial <note>original: "μνημόσυνον"</note> of Christ's rest in the sepulcher and His resurrection on the first day. This was demonstrated long ago by a miracle, if we believe the ancient writers, who testify that once the Sabbath was abolished, the miracle of the Sabbatical River <note>A legendary river mentioned by Pliny and Josephus that supposedly flowed all week but stopped on the Sabbath; the author suggests the miracle stopped when the Sabbath was no longer required.</note> ceased.

Nevertheless, I would hardly agree with those who say that the abolition of the Sabbath was prefigured by the fact that the Sabbath was dissolved long ago at the beginning of the world. For where the Vulgate edition has Genesis 2: *And God finished on the sixth day his works which he made,* the Hebrew truth has **on the seventh day** <note>original: "בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי" — Bejon haschebihi</note>. And Blessed Jerome likewise reads according to the Hebrew in *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, page 152, last volume, as was observed by us above by citing the very words of Jerome. "Therefore," says P. Galatinus <note>Pietro Galatino, a 16th-century scholar of Jewish and Christian theology.</note> in *On the Secrets of Catholic Truth*, book 11, chapter 10: "This passage constrains the Jews, who boast of the leisure of the Sabbath, since God worked on the Sabbath." In the *Bereschith Ketanna* <note>The Midrash *Bereshit Rabbah*, an ancient Jewish commentary on Genesis.</note> it is held thus: *“This is one of the words which the wise men changed for King Ptolemy. For King Ptolemy asked the seventy elders <note>The traditional 70 translators of the Septuagint.</note>, saying: In how many days did the Holy God, blessed be He, create the world? They said to him: in six, as it is in Genesis 2.”* This was said by the Rabbis because the Septuagint version does not follow the Hebrew truth in this place, no differently than the Latin version. And in the book *Siphre* <note>Sifre, a legalistic commentary on the books of Numbers and Deuteronomy.</note> Rabbi Eleazar said: the people did not keep the Sabbath in the desert for forty years except for the first Sabbath. Rabbi Joses says: It was the Sabbath when there was the battle in Jericho, and it was captured on the Sabbath. on the seventh day all the works of God were completed; for when in six days (which were nothing other than six moments in respect to God speaking, even if in respect to our perspective they are measured as successive days) God had perfected all works by His word, at last in the final moment when He had fallen silent, and had said nothing further, nor consequently created anything, therefore it is said by Moses that He perfected on the seventh day His works which He had made, because He then kept silence, and thus showed that God had completed all works. That tradition regarding the dissolution of the Sabbath which is held among the Hebrew masters <note>The "masters" refers to Rabbinic authorities and commentators.</note> could also be brought forward. However, when the word <term>olam</term> is placed alone, or even (as Burgensis maintains) when <term>ad</term> is placed before it, it then signifies a perpetuity according to the condition of the thing to which it is joined. For instance, when it is said that *the word of God remains forever*, there it signifies an eternity without end. But when that word is predicated of a thing whose duration is periodic, then it signifies an eternity that is not absolute, but periodic—what the Latins call a *saeculum*, or the age of a specific thing. Thus, in Deuteronomy 15, concerning a servant who *does not wish to go out free in the seventh year, it is said: He shall serve you forever*, that is, through the whole period of his life, or up until the Year of Jubilee. Likewise, in 1 Samuel 1: *Samuel shall remain in the tabernacle of the Lord for an age*; that is, until his fiftieth year, which was the "age" of the Levites' ministry according to Numbers 8; or as Hannah says, *all the days of his life*. The same must be understood concerning the "age" of ceremonies. For the Mosaic age, or the age of ceremonies, lasts until the time of Christ. Hence the Rabbis call the last days or the final times <term>yeme mashiach <note>Hebrew: ימי משיח</note></term>, the "Days of the Messiah." Therefore, among the Hebrews, there were three <term>olamim <note>Hebrew: עולמים; plural of olam, meaning "ages" or "worlds"</note></term> *holamim*, that is, ages: I. The one beginning from the start of the world and ending with the coming of the Messiah. II. One that lasts for the whole time of the Messiah until the day of resurrection. III. The one extending from the resurrection into perpetuity.

From what has been said, it is clear that the word *le-olam* <note>Hebrew: לעולם; "forever" or "to eternity"</note> has a threefold meaning in Scripture:

II. It signifies a fixed time characterized by a solemn period, such as the Jubilee, or the era of the Old Testament and other similar spans of time.

III. It signifies eternity properly defined. The duration of the Sabbath and other ceremonies of the Law are understood according to the second meaning <note>that is, they lasted for a specific historical age</note>. But concerning the sacrifice of Christ, there is a true perpetuity.

Since, therefore, there have been three types of Sabbath: the Legal Sabbath of the Old Testament; the Spiritual Sabbath of the New Testament; and the Celestial Sabbath after both of these economies. The third will be perfect and everlasting, and will place an end to all our labors and distresses.

Therefore, to finally conclude this dissertation, this change from the Sabbath day <note>Saturday</note> to the Lord’s Day <note>Sunday</note> shows that all things were to be renewed in the new economy <note>the "economy of salvation," referring to the new order established by Christ</note>, and the old things were to become new. According to 2 Corinthians 5: *Old things have passed away, and all things have been made new.* Hence, Scripture speaks of a *new creature, a new people, a new man, new knowledge, the New Testament, a new commandment, a new name, a new way, a new song, new clothes, new wine, new vessels, the New Jerusalem, a new heaven, a new earth*, and finally, a *new Sabbath*. Because it is "new," it represents to us something excellent (following the Hebrew idiom), since that day represents the birth of the world and that very day on which created things began. 

On that day, light shone out of the darkness; the law was handed down from Mount Sinai; on that day, Christ rose again; the saints came forth from the grave; on that day, the Holy Spirit descended upon the Apostles; and finally, according to ancient tradition, on that day Christ will descend to judge the living and the dead. When the trumpet sounds, the Jericho of this world shall fall, and Christ, our true Joshua <note>the name Joshua and Jesus are the same in Hebrew, both meaning "The Lord Saves"</note>, will lead us into the possession of the heavenly Canaan. These things are certainly spoken more truly and more appropriately than the things the Muhammadans <note>a historical term for Muslims</note> say in their commentaries on the Quran: *God exalted Mecca among cities; Ramadan among months; and Friday among days. Why Friday? Because (they say) the sun rose on that day, Adam was created on that day, he was placed in paradise on that day, he was cast out onto the earth on that day, and the day of judgment will appear on that day.* Truly, let Muhammad perish with his Sabbath, and let Christ our Lord remain with His Sabbath, so that the Lord’s Day may endure until the consummation of the world. This was also done by an entire nation to expiate great crimes or to avert massive disasters, such as during a great pestilence. It was called a **hecatomb** <note>original Greek: ἑκατόμβη (*hekatombē*)</note> either from the number of victims or from the number of those sacrificing, because a hundred cities of the Peloponnese performed it. Hence among the Pagans, Proserpina was called **Hecate**, because she was placated with a hundred victims.

...pronounced by the priest, **"it will be a help to you"** <note>original Hebrew: יהיה לך עזר (*Yihyeh lecha ezer*)</note>, *it will be useful to you, it will be sweet to you, it will be a seasoning for you.*

This can easily be demonstrated in the case of the Romans from their own histories. For if the spoils of enemies were hung in the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus <note>The most important temple in Ancient Rome, located on the Capitoline Hill.</note>, all those things were done rather for their own honor than for the glory of God, since this was the final act of a triumphal procession.

They recognized a Majesty wounded by the sins of men and seized with fury, which could be soothed by sacrifices of this kind. Hence it is that immediately after the first sin, the rites of sacrifice became prevalent throughout the whole world among all nations. Therefore, those ancient men judged sacrifices to be so necessary to religion that without them, piety would not only have been weak, but even utterly extinguished. Hence it is that among them...

<meta>Continuing from page 723, which discussed the spiritual blindness of Pagans compared to the typology of Jewish sacrifice. Page 724 shifts to the linguistic and etymological origins of terms for "sacrifice" and "altar" across Hebrew, Greek, Latin, and Christian traditions.</meta>
