...almost all ceremonies and the entire pomp of religion are reduced to priests (or minor clerics), to sacrifices, to victims, and to altars. Indeed, under the premise of sin, sacrifices were absolutely necessary. This is emphatically shown by Hebrew naming conventions; for since **sin** <note>original Hebrew: חטאת (*chattah*)</note> signifies both **sin** and **a victim for sin**, and furthermore, by a change of name <term>metonymy</term>, it signifies the **punishment for sin**. We see it used for "sin" in Leviticus 5:18 and elsewhere; for a "sacrifice for sin" in Ezekiel 45:23 and Ezra 6:17; and often elsewhere for the "punishment of sin," as in Genesis 4:7.

It is not without reason that among the Hebrews and Greeks, the terms for "sacrifice" and "altar" share the same roots. For the Hebrews, a sacrifice is **Zevach** <note>original Hebrew: זבח</note> and an altar is **mizbeach** <note>original Hebrew: מזבח</note>, coming from the root **Zavach** <note>original Hebrew: זבח</note>, meaning to sacrifice or slaughter. Similarly, for the Greeks, the terms **sacrifice** <note>original Greek: ϑυσία (*thusia*)</note> and **altar** <note>original Greek: ϑυσιαστήριον (*thusiasterion*)</note> come from the verb **to sacrifice** <note>original Greek: ϑύειν (*thyein*)</note>.

However, the Latins had other reasons for their naming conventions. First, they used the word **sacrifices** <note>original Latin: *sacrificiorum*</note> because, as we have said, the most powerful part of religion consisted of sacrifices. They used this word because those sacrificing **performed sacred acts** <note>original Latin: *sacra faciebant*</note>; that is, they truly worshipped God and, through that exercise of piety, appeased his offended Majesty. Secondly, since the Pagans sought earthly goods from God in their sacrifices rather than heavenly ones, and because they primarily prayed to avert evil, they used the word **victim** <note>original Latin: *hostia*</note>, taking its origin from **enemies** <note>original Latin: *hostibus*</note>. This follows the well-known saying: ***The victim takes its name from conquered enemies*** <note>original Latin: *hostibus à victis hostia nomen habet*; a common etymological maxim in classical Latin literature.</note>. Finally, names were derived from the shape of the altar and from the rites of the sacrifices. For **altar** <note>original Latin: *altare*</note> comes from **high** <note>original Latin: *alto*</note> because its shape was elevated. And **altar-hearth** <note>original Latin: *ara*</note>, according to Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, an ancient Roman scholar and grammarian.</note>, is like a **handle** <note>original Latin: *ansa*</note>, because the priest was accustomed to hold the altar while he was sacrificing. Hence that line from the poet:

> *Praying with such words and holding the altars.* <note>A quote from Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book VI, line 124, describing a priest or suppliant performing a ritual.</note>

But later among Christians, countless names were adopted. For when they saw that all the Levitical sacrifices were abolished—and even though the sacrifice of the cross was perpetual—they nevertheless emphasized above all its application and commemoration. Therefore, they called them metaphorical sacrifices, or **Eucharistic** sacrifices, which the Greek Fathers used to call **unbloody sacrifices** <note>original Greek: ϑυσίας ἀναιμάκτους (*thysias anaimaktous*)</note>. From this come those names used by the Greek Fathers: **sacrifice**, **offering**, **rite**, **thanksgiving**, **worship**, **reverence** <note>original Greek: ϑυσία (*thusia*), προσφορά (*prosphora*), τελετή (*teletē*), εὐχαριστία (*eucharistia*), λατρευτικόν (*latreutikon*), σεβά[σμον] (*sebasmon*). The catchword σμον completes the final Greek term.</note>

<margin>**Sacrifices** <note>original Greek: θυσίαι (*thysiai*)</note></margin> For although **sacrifice** <note>original Greek: θυσία (*thysia*)</note> seems to correspond to the Hebrew **Zevach** <note>original Hebrew: זבח</note>, and **rite of initiation** <note>original Greek: τελετή (*teletē*)</note>—which comes from the word **to complete or consume** <note>original Greek: τελέω (*teleō*)</note>—corresponds to the **burnt offering** <note>a sacrifice where the whole animal was burned</note> because the victim was consumed; nevertheless, these terms are used metaphorically and not strictly regarding **propitiatory sacrifices** <note>sacrifices intended to appease God's anger for sin</note>.

It is therefore clearly established that the origin of sacrifices is most ancient. For since sin began long ago in the very beginnings of the world, it is certainly proven that sacrifices had their start then as well. However, I would not subscribe to the opinion of **Bellarmine** <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a powerful Cardinal and Jesuit theologian during the Counter-Reformation</note>, who made sacrifices co-existent with religion itself. In truth, religion existed before sin, and sin existed before sacrifices—which necessarily presuppose it. Religion existed in **Paradise** <note>the Garden of Eden</note>, but sacrifices existed only outside of Paradise. Indeed, **Johannes de Turrecremata** <note>Juan de Torquemada (1388–1468), a Spanish Dominican theologian</note> doubts whether **Adam** was the first Priest, and whether he truly ever offered a sacrifice. For **Moses** in Genesis 4, verses 3 and 4, makes the first mention of the sacrifices of **Abel** and **Cain**; indeed, he says expressly, *And it came to pass after many days that Cain offered, etc.* But who would say that the rite of sacrificing was thought up at random? Truly, it is more reasonable to believe either that sacrifices were instituted by God long ago—especially since the Apostle in Hebrews 11:4 reports that by faith Abel’s sacrifice was accepted by God—or it must be said that whatever was pleasing and grateful to God was handed down by divine instruction. This can be sufficiently confirmed by the fact that, under the **Law** <note>the Mosaic Law/Torah</note>, God later sanctioned and promulgated such sacrifices to be performed under the penalty of death. Therefore, when the **first-formed humans** <note>Adam and Eve</note> and their descendants were expelled from Paradise, they were deprived of the sacrament of divine benevolence—namely, the **Tree of Life**. So that some hope of salvation might shine upon them anew, the **token** of sacrifices succeeded it. By these sacrifices, something spiritual was surely prefigured, which those ancient fathers primarily looked toward; for who would believe those ancient and pious **Patriarchs** <note>the early biblical fathers</note> looked only at the **husk** <note>the outward ceremony</note> and not the **marrow** <note>the inner spiritual meaning</note>, or that they merely played with empty ceremonies?

But just as sacrifices in ancient times signified the worship of God, so **burnt offerings**—or **Oloth** <note>original Hebrew: העלה (*olah*)</note>—occupied the primary place among them. In these, the victims were reduced entirely to ashes and were, as it were, sent away from the earth to God, carried up into heaven with the smoke. For this reason, among the institutions of Moses, no other...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of ancient sacrifices from page 725, moving from the origins of sacrifice after the Fall to the specific distinctions between different types of Hebrew offerings and the unique status of the Passover lamb.</meta>

# -> ANTHONY CREGUT <-

...it was believed to be a sign of greater piety, since by it mortals consecrated themselves entirely to God, and, as if the body were cast down, they were thought to raise their soul to heaven with the smoke of their sacrificial victim. For this reason, God was wonderfully appeased by those sacrifices and promised that the victims of the faithful would be most acceptable to him; but on the contrary, whenever they were defiled by hypocrisy and feigned zeal, God was moved by burning anger, and therefore they were rebuked and harassed by the holy prophets as being little accepted by God.

It must be noted, however, that there was a primary distinction between **burnt offerings** <gloss>original Hebrew: עולה (*olah*)</gloss> and **peace offerings** <gloss>original Hebrew: שלמים (*shelamim*)</gloss>—that is, between whole burnt offerings and those for peace or prosperity—in that the former pertained to the atonement of sins, while the latter pertained to the happy success of affairs. Hence, such preliminary sacrifices were usually slaughtered before solemn covenants. This is clear from **Exodus 24:5** and from **Exodus 17:15**; for so **Moses** sacrificed when he was about to recite the law on **Mount Sinai**, and when he had defeated the **Amalekites** <note>an ancient nomadic tribe described as enemies of the Israelites</note> with his hands raised toward heaven.

Now, as to whether the **Paschal lamb** <note>the lamb sacrificed during the Jewish festival of Passover</note> should be numbered among the burnt offerings, there is no reason to doubt. Since those victims were burned entirely by fire except for the skin, this cannot be said of the Paschal lamb, which was eaten within the families. Nor was it even counted among those sacrifices where certain parts were burned while the Priests ate others; for according to the law, the whole lamb had to be eaten within the families. It is better, therefore, to assign the Paschal lamb to another class of sacrifices. Indeed, the ancient writers doubted whether the Paschal lamb belonged to any class of sacrifices at all. For although (they say) it was a **type** <note>a symbolic foreshadowing in Christian theology</note> of Christ, nevertheless it was not sacrificed. We read everywhere that it was to be slaughtered, but not at all sacrificed in the sense of a sacrifice properly so called. Hence it is sometimes called **Corban** <note>original Hebrew: קרבן</note>, which is a general name signifying all legal offerings in **Leviticus 1:3** and **chapter 2, verse 1**. From this, it is broadly explained in the Gospel of **Mark** as a **gift** <note>referring to Mark 7:11, where "Corban" is defined as a gift devoted to God</note>. And although it is called **Zevach** <note>original Hebrew: זבח</note>, this word often broadly signifies even spiritual worship and sacrifices. And if it is used properly when dealing with the Paschal lamb, this is done because of the slaughter of the lamb, which is properly designated by that word.

<summary>This page distinguishes between Hebrew burnt offerings (for atonement) and peace offerings (for gratitude), while arguing that the Paschal lamb occupies a unique category because it was eaten by families rather than being fully consumed by fire or shared with priests.</summary>

...designated. Nor for that reason was that ancient ceremony of the Paschal lamb numbered among the legal and external sacrifices.

It is confirmed that the Paschal lamb was not a sacrifice from the fact that nothing was found in it of those things which pertained to sacrifices. First, it was not slaughtered by Priests alone as other victims were; second, it was not slaughtered at the altar. Hence, when the **Papists** <note>a historical term for Roman Catholics, often used in Protestant polemics</note> argue that the Paschal lamb was sacrificed so that they might more easily defend the **Sacrifice of the Mass** <note>the Catholic doctrine that the Eucharist is a literal sacrifice of Christ's body and blood</note>, they "cut their own throats with their own sword" <note>an idiom meaning they defeat themselves with their own argument</note> by which they would have wanted the lamb slaughtered. For when they define sacrifice, they add this: *“When it is offered by a chosen minister, who indeed alone is considered a Priest.”* 

Add to this the passage in **Exodus 8**. For when **Pharaoh** permitted the Israelites to make a sacrifice to God, provided they sacrificed within Egypt, **Moses** denied that this was right, and openly denied that the Israelites were going to sacrifice in Egypt. Yet the sacred history in **Exodus 12** testifies that the Israelites celebrated the Passover in Egypt. Hence **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, an influential 4th-century church father</note> in his book *Retractions*, chapter 10, says: *“Among the Gentiles they could not sacrifice, just as we see them now having remained without sacrifices, unless perhaps because they slaughter a sheep for the Passover, this might be reckoned among sacrifices.”*

Nevertheless, on the other hand, there are men of great renown who place the slaughtering of the Paschal lamb among the sacrifices; among these, one shall be worth them all to us: the great **Calvin** <note>John Calvin, the primary French reformer and theologian</note>. In his commentary on **1 Corinthians 5:7**, he wrote that there were two parts of the Passover: a sacrifice and a sacred feast. For "even if" (he says) "some do not hold the Paschal lamb as a sacrifice, reason nonetheless proves it was properly a sacrifice: for there the people were reconciled to God by the sprinkling of blood. Moreover, there is no reconciliation without sacrifice. Then the Apostle <note>Paul</note> now openly confirms this: for he uses the word **to sacrifice** <gloss>original Greek: θύειν (*thyein*)</gloss>, which is appropriate for sacrifices; otherwise, his context would not stand. Therefore, the lamb was slaughtered annually, and then a feast followed, the celebration of which lasted seven continuous days." Thus far Calvin.

Nor yet, however, does that severe punisher of the Papists <note>referring to Calvin</note> favor their doctrine concerning the sacrifice of the Mass—namely, the idea that the sacrifice of the Paschal lamb was a **figure** <note>a symbolic foreshadowing or "type"</note> of the Eucharist, which therefore...

### ANTHONY CRÉGUT

...just as the Passover must be at the same time both a sacrifice and a sacrament. **Calvin** is not, I say, a supporter of their view on that account. For the Paschal lamb was not a figure <note>a symbolic representation or "type"</note> of the sacrament of the Eucharist, but rather of Christ, the true Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world (John 1:29; 1 Corinthians 5:7). Therefore, that hypothesis of the **Papists** <note>a historical term for Roman Catholics</note> is false: that the sacraments of the Old Testament foreshadowed those of the New Testament as "figures of figures." For both were truly sacraments, containing the very thing they signified, even though the later ones succeeded the earlier ones.

Hence, when baptism is called the **antitype** <note>original Greek: *antitypon*; a thing that corresponds to or fulfills a "type"</note> of the flood by Peter in 1 Peter 3:21, this word is not to be taken (as is commonly done) to mean the fulfillment that responds to some figure—as when **Melchizedek** <note>a mysterious priest-king from Genesis</note> foreshadowed Christ (Hebrews 7), or when the Paschal lamb foreshadowed that Lamb of God slain from the foundation of the world. Rather, the word **antitype** is used here as that which responds to a **type** <note>original Greek: *typo*</note> as if to an exemplar or model. Thus, just as baptism corresponds to the flood, and even to the cloud and the crossing of the Red Sea **analogously** <note>original Greek: *analōgōs*</note>, so also the Paschal lamb was a type of the Eucharist, to which this sacrament responded **analogously** as an **antitype**.

However, insofar as the Paschal lamb was slaughtered, to that extent it did not represent the Eucharist, but rather Christ sacrificed on the cross, as is clear from 1 Corinthians 5:7. Paul uses the word **types** <note>original Greek: *typoi*</note> in the same sense as Peter in 1 Corinthians 10:6, when speaking of the fathers of the Old Testament, he says that they ate the same spiritual food as us and drank the same spiritual drink, and then adds: *Now these things were our types.*

It is not that the sacraments of the Old Testament were merely figures of the sacraments of the New Testament. Those who hold that view have fallen into the gross error of thinking that the sacraments of the Old Testament were only figurative and did not actually **exhibit** <note>meaning to effectively provide or bestow</note> the thing they figured—as if the Israelites were not the Church of God and participants in His grace! Rather, they are called **types** because they were those models that related to us **analogously**. Hence our **Beza** <note>Theodore Beza, a prominent French Protestant Reformer</note> in his notes on 1 Peter 3:21 correctly translates it as "corresponding exemplar." Thus it means the same as the word for **model** <note>original Greek: *hypodeigmati*</note> in Hebrews 8:5, where the Levitical priesthood is called the **model and shadow** <note>original Greek: *hypodeigmati kai skia*</note> of heavenly things. These heavenly things were the **archetypes** <note>the original patterns or "first forms"</note>, just as was foreshadowed in Moses, who built the tabernacle according to the form of the archetype he saw on the

...mountain, which the Archetype <note>the original model or pattern</note> seen by Moses reflected as the heavenly Archetype. In the same sense as *type* <note>Greek: τύπος, typos</note> and *pattern* <note>Greek: υπόδειγμα, hypodeigma</note>, the word *parable* <note>Greek: παραβολή, parabolē</note> is used in Hebrews 9:9, where the tabernacle <note>Greek: σκηνή, skēnē</note> is called a "parable"—that is, a model for that present time, corresponding to the Hebrew *mashal* <note>original Hebrew: משל</note>, which broadly signifies all those things. For the word "parable" <note>Latin: parabola</note> found in the Vulgate <note>the standard 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> edition is too obscure and does not correctly express the meaning.

Furthermore, just as we denied the major premise of the Papist <note>a historical term for Roman Catholics</note> argument—namely, that the <term>Passover</term> <note>Latin: Pascha</note> was a figure of the Eucharist—next we can even deny the minor premise: that the Passover was a sacrifice. Many hold this view, including <term>Augustine</term> among the ancient fathers, and the previously cited passage from Exodus 8 seems to prevail. Or, if we admit that the Passover was a sacrifice (as <term>Calvin</term> felt) insofar as it was slaughtered, we can then turn the argument back against the followers of the Pope in this way: the Passover was a bloody sacrifice; but the Eucharist is not a bloody sacrifice. Therefore [they are not the same]. Next, the Paschal lamb was eaten entirely, and not even a tiny bit was saved; but the Papist host is saved for the next day. Therefore [they are not the same]. Thus, even if the Passover were a sacrifice, it does not follow that the <term>Eucharist</term> is a sacrifice, as is clear. When, therefore, the early Church fathers call the Eucharist a sacrifice, they are speaking figuratively <note>Greek: καταχρηστικώς, katachrēstikōs; a rhetorical term for using a word improperly or by extension</note>. For it cannot properly be called that.

But once one of the fathers had called it a sacrifice in this loose sense, another followed him and adopted this naming, and then another, and thus the thing itself grew and changed for the worse by expanding to a monstrous degree. It is much like birds in flight: sometimes seeds accidentally stick to their wings or claws, which they then drop by chance into the most fertile places; from these tiny beginnings, the plants gradually and slowly grow strong in a wonderful way. Or, as happens with a herd of goats: when their leader eats from the well-known <term>Sea Holly</term> <note>Latin: Eryngio; referring to a classical belief that a goat eating this plant causes the entire herd to stop still</note> plant, all the others immediately follow and eat from the same plant of their own accord. So it is very true what is commonly said: *We are most easily persuaded by examples.*

# ANTHONY CRÉGUT

...[authority] of Augustine, and also by the reasons cited above, if we maintain with Calvin that the Passover was a sacrifice? Truly, it will not be very difficult to untie those knots <note>to solve these logical difficulties</note>. For as to the passage in Exodus, although Moses did not wish to sacrifice to God in Egypt <note>fearing the reaction of the Egyptians to the slaughter of animals they held sacred</note>, and yet the Paschal lamb was sacrificed in Egypt, this was later ordained by a unique command of God, so that the passing over of the destroying Angel might be a memorial <note>original Greek: μνημόσυνον, mnēmosynon</note>. This is just as by a special command the Israelites were ordered to borrow vessels and utensils from the Egyptians and then carry them away with them in flight, even though the general law stated *thou shalt not steal* (Exodus 20). 

Indeed, it does not seem credible that the people of God lived for so long in Egypt without the rite of sacrifices, since at that time the primary worship of God consisted in that ceremony; for in that school of instruction <note>Latin: pædagogia, referring to the era of the Law as a "tutor" for mankind</note>, a certain external worship was required, without which internal and spiritual worship would have vanished. For although in Exodus 8:26 Moses said that the sacrifices of the Jews were an abomination to the Egyptians, it should not therefore be thought that the worship of God was entirely interrupted for that reason. 

As for the opinion of Augustine, he speaks quite perplexedly, since he finally concludes in this way: *unless perhaps the fact that they sacrifice a sheep for the Passover is counted among the sacrifices.* The reasons that are brought forward by others are also doubtful—namely, that the lamb was sacrificed neither by priests alone nor upon an altar; for this is asserted without authority. Nor is the argument of others valid when they say the Passover was not offered for sin; for since it was an illustrious type of Christ, our Passover who was sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7), and of the Lamb of God slain before the foundations of the world were laid (Revelation 13:8), it likewise will be an offering for sin; for the same reasoning applies by analogy <note>original Greek: ἀναλόγως, analogōs</note> to the figure <note>the Old Testament symbol</note> and the thing figured <note>the New Testament reality</note>.

And let these things be said in passing concerning the Paschal lamb. Furthermore, regarding <term>burnt offerings</term> <note>Latin: holocausta, where the entire animal was consumed by fire</note>, their types are to be observed, of which three are assigned according to Moses in Leviticus 1: 

I. From the *herds*, namely oxen. 
II. From the *flocks*, namely sheep or goats. 
III. From the *birds*, namely doves or turtledoves. 

This was done so that the circumstances of both the rich and the poor might be considered: a practice observed concerning the Virgin Mary in Luke 2:24, whose sacrifice <note>original Greek: θυσία, thysia</note> was *a pair of turtledoves and two young pigeons.*

<meta>This page continues Anthony Crégut’s theological examination of Old Testament sacrifices, moving from the specific case of the Passover (discussed on the previous page) to the general requirements for burnt offerings as established in Leviticus. He transitions from historical arguments about Egyptian customs to a typological interpretation, where Old Testament rituals are seen as "shadows" or "types" that point toward the reality of Christ.</meta>

->## THE REVEALER OF SECRETS<-

Furthermore, just as humans were not permitted to offer just any animal they pleased, but only those God decreed to test their obedience—and because God should not be worshipped with self-imposed rituals <note>original Greek: εθελοθρησκείαις (ethelothrēskeiais), meaning "will-worship" or religious practices chosen by humans rather than commanded by God</note>—so the rites of burnt offerings <term>holocausts; from the Greek meaning "burned whole"</term> had to be performed only according to God's instructions. This is why in the same first chapter of Leviticus, God commanded they be made from pure and clean animals, specifically domestic ones; then from males, and those being whole and without blemish. All these requirements were undoubtedly not without a "mystery" <note>a hidden spiritual meaning or "typology"</note>; for who would believe God wished to tire His people with empty ceremonies in vain? Truly: I. They typically foreshadowed Christ, who had to be slaughtered like the burnt offerings. He had to be from among his brothers, not from foreigners, and thus *domestic* <note>meaning He was human, of the same "household" as those He saves</note>; *male*, that is, endowed with masculine strength and divine virtue—the source of the cross’s efficacy, or *effective* redemption; *unblemished*, because as Hebrews 7:26 says, *For such a High Priest was fitting for us, holy* etc. And 1 Peter 1:19: *Know that you were redeemed with precious blood, as of a lamb without spot or blemish, even Christ.* II. Ceremonial cleanliness instructed the people about moral cleanliness, which God truly intended to be seen in the sacrifices. For as God said elsewhere, *I want obedience, not sacrifice*; thus He wants spiritual cleanliness and the sacrifice of a contrite heart, which was foreshadowed by that ceremonial rite.

Therefore, when the blood of the victim was sprinkled upon the altar, as found in Leviticus 1:5 and 11, this signified that the blood did not simply fall to the ground, but was consecrated to God as a pleasing aroma. This was not because it was the blood of an irrational animal, but because it foreshadowed Christ, the true victim, who was most acceptable to God the Father, and whose blood was meant to cleanse us from all sin (John 1). This is why Paul, in Hebrews 10, denies that sins could be removed by the legal sacrifices. And in 1 Peter 2:24, it is said that Christ "carried" <note>original Latin: *baiulasse*</note> our sins on the cross as the true victim. Here the Apostle uses the word *anapherein* <note>original Greek: ἀναφέρειν</note>, which means *with the body inclined, and the back and shoulders placed under, to take up a burden; then truly to raise oneself up as much as possible so that it is no longer carried*...

# ANTHONY CRÉGUT #

...but let the burden be taken away. And so he responds with the Hebrew term *sabal* <note>סבל; meaning a burden or load</note>, and the Rabbis call it *sabbit* <note>שביט; meaning a rod or staff</note>, which John Cameron <note>a 17th-century Scottish theologian famous for his insights into the covenants of the Bible</note> correctly noted.

It was therefore clearly foreshadowed—through the burnt offerings <term>holocausts</term> sacrificed upon the altar—that Christ would be lifted up on the cross. This was also represented by the bronze serpent raised up on a pole, as Christ himself testifies in *John 3:14*. From this comes the fact that the cross was a cursed kind of death, according to *Deuteronomy 21:23*: *He who is hanged on a tree is cursed by God.* For this reason, it was not permitted for the corpse of one hanged on a tree to remain overnight, but it had to be buried on the same day; for (says Moses) *He who is hanged is a curse to God: so that you do not defile your land which the LORD your God gives you as a possession.* Why someone hanged on a tree should be a curse to God is a question often asked by Jews, both ancient and modern; and because the mystery of the Messiah's crucifixion was unknown to them—since they were always dreaming of some kind of worldly kingdom—they frequently stumbled as if walking in the dark. 

The Chaldean Paraphrast <note>the *Targum*, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary of the Hebrew Bible</note> indeed believes a hanged man is called a "curse of God" because that punishment was destined only for those who had insulted the divine majesty with various blasphemies; since the sight of a hanged man renewed the guilt of a most foul crime and exposed it to the eyes of others. 

However, Rabbi Isaac Arama <note>a 15th-century Spanish Jewish philosopher and commentator</note> in his excellent book called *Akedath Itzchak* <note>עקידת יצחק; meaning "The Binding of Isaac"</note>—which is a commentary on the Law and the five scrolls—wrote that the hanged man is called a curse not of God, but of the judges, who are called *Elohim* <note>a Hebrew word for God that is also used in the Bible to refer to judges or powerful leaders</note> in the Scripture. Yet this interpretation is not proven by this passage in Deuteronomy 21:23. 

Moses of Gerona <note>also known as Nahmanides (Ramban), a leading medieval Jewish scholar</note> has a better sense of it; he wrote on this passage that no kind of death is more shameful or cursed than hanging, and therefore the corpse should be quickly removed from the sight of men—even though it must be admitted that the criminal’s guilt deserves a longer hanging than the space of a single day. Thus the masters of the Hebrews reason, showing the truth "only on the surface" <note>original Greek: ἐξ ἐπιπολῆς φαινόντες (ex epipolēs phainontes), meaning appearing superficially or without depth</note>, yet they do not look into the mystical sense. This is because they were never able to clearly see the Messiah's state of "emptying" <note>the theological concept of *kenosis*, where Christ humbled himself to take human form and suffer</note>, contemplating only his glory. But "most emphatically" <note>original Greek: ἐμφαντικωτάτως (emphantikōtatōs)</note> Paul, writing to the...

<meta>This page continues Anthony Crégut’s theological discussion on the nature of the cross. The previous page ended with a discussion of why the "hanged man" was considered a curse under Mosaic law. Here, Crégut explores Jewish terminology for the cross and interprets a famous Talmudic parable about a king’s twin brother as a hidden acknowledgment of the divine nature of the crucified Christ.</meta>

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS #

Paul, in *Philippians 2:8*, highlights the shame of the cross with that remarkable phrase—or rather, repetition: "even death on a cross" <note>original Greek: θάνατον δὲ σταυροῦ (*thanaton de staurou*)</note>. Likewise, in *Galatians 3:13*, he says that Christ became a "curse" <note>original Greek: κατάραν (*kataran*)</note> for us, specifically so that he might redeem us from the curse of the law. And truly, although the ancient Chaldean Paraphrast <note>the *Targum*, an ancient Aramaic translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> often openly translated it as "cross" or "gallows," the Jews from that time until today have spoken of it obscurely. They have sketched the cross through circumlocution <term>the use of many words where fewer would do</term> rather than designating it by a specific name. For example, they commonly use that silly nomenclature *ha-sh’ti ve-ha-erev* <note>השתי והערב</note>, which means "the warp and the woof" <note>terms referring to the vertical and horizontal threads in weaving, used here to describe the cross-shape without naming it</note>.

By this, they undoubtedly intended to obscure rather than clarify the cross, or perhaps to secretly hide some perceived "horrible crime" among themselves. This is similar to what they have done with the name *Yeshu* <note>ישו; a Hebrew name for Jesus</note>, which for them mystically signifies "may his name and memory be blotted out" <note>original Hebrew: *yimmach shemo* (ימח שמו)</note>, and also with the word *Goyim* <note>גוים</note>, meaning "Gentiles." For as Paul testifies in *1 Corinthians 1:23*, the cross of Christ was a "stumbling block" to the Jews. As for the seventy-two translators <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, they expressed the cross or gallows more clearly in the past; they used the words "double wood" <note>original Greek: ξύλον δίδυμον (*xylon didymon*)</note> whenever the Hebrew text has *ha-ets* <note>עץ; "the tree" or "the wood"</note>, such as in *Joshua 8:29* concerning the hanging of the King of Ai. This is also how the cross of Christ was formed—not from three pieces of wood or parts, as is the custom today in the Papacy <note>a Protestant critique of Roman Catholic crucifixes that include a footrest or *suppedaneum*</note>, where a small tablet is fixed beneath the feet of the one hanging.

Furthermore, the ancient Talmudists sensed that mystery of the cross in Chapter 6 of the *Sanhedrin* <note>a section of the Talmud dealing with legal procedures and capital punishment</note>. They proposed the example of two brothers who were exactly alike in their physical form and features. One of them was made a king, while the other happened to be captured by enemies and was crucified. Those who saw the brother hanging on the cross thought the king himself had been hanged. This is explained by Bahaiaus <note>Rabbi Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish commentator and Kabbalist</note> as follows:

> *That King (he says) is the Majesty of God, that which is called the 'image of God.' Therefore, when the image of His image is hanged, the Majesty of God is treated with contempt—unless it is removed from the scene in its proper time, that is, on that same day. For the night is dedicated to divine judgment.*

This Bahaiaus—an author and Kabbalist <term>a follower of Jewish mystical tradition</term> who gladly searches out more hidden meanings—does not write this unskillfully. These things were truly and in reality fulfilled in Christ, who was the "radiance" <note>original Greek: ἀπαύγασμα (*apaugasma*)</note> of God and the "exact representation" of His glory, as noted in *Hebrews 1:3*.

# ANTHONY CRÉGUT #

...nevertheless he was fixed to the cross and buried on the same day, so that he might rise again on the third day.

   What has been said above would suffice for this section, were we not to encounter an example of crucifixion that should perhaps not be observed only in passing <note>original Greek: $\pi \alpha \rho \acute{\epsilon} \rho \gamma \omega \varsigma$ (*parergōs*)</note>—namely, in *2 Samuel 21* <note>the Latin text cites 2 Regum, which in the Vulgate refers to the books of Samuel</note>, concerning the seven sons of Saul who were hanged at David’s command. This was done at the request of the Gabaonites, who did not allow them to be taken down from the gallows or buried until they had been soaked by rain. This act by David seems to have been done against the law in *Deuteronomy 21:22*, which forbade the body of a hanged man from remaining overnight for the reasons mentioned above. Nor is the response of Rabbi Nehmann valid, who argued that the Gabaonites were not from the people of God, nor the seed of Abraham, and therefore were exempt from the law when they hanged them. It is not valid (I say) because the Gabaonites were joined with the Jews and were subject to the same laws in the same land; furthermore, all these things were carried out at David's command and with his approval. We must respond, therefore, that this example was unique—an exception to the rule—because God, moved by great anger, had sent a famine upon the people due to Saul’s unpunished crime. Therefore, just as the punishment was inflicted by God's counsel, so too those bodies had to remain overnight until the offended Majesty of God was appeased, which was signaled by the rain dripping from above. For it had already been three years since God, angered at the family of Saul because of the slaughtered Gabaonites, had been afflicting the Israelites with a continuous famine arising from excessive drought.

   Thus far concerning the first kind of <term>sacrifices</term> <note>ritual offerings made to God</note>, namely, burnt offerings. The second was the <term>mincha</term> <note>Hebrew: מנחה</note>, a gift or offering. This was a sacrifice consisting of inanimate things, and it was fourfold: from raw flour, from cakes baked in an oven, from things fried in a pan, and from things cooked on a grate. It is called *mincha* from the root *nachah* <note>Hebrew: נחה</note>, meaning to lead or to bring, because it was brought by the people and offered for consolation and appeasement.

   Concerning its ritual, these points from *Leviticus chapter 2* should be observed: I. There was a general prohibition against using leaven or honey, but salt was to be sprinkled. II. That the *Mincha* be made in the four ways mentioned above; indeed, according to *Leviticus 23:7*, it was also made from the ears or grains of the first-fruits...

...offerings. III. That they should be offered to God by the Priests. IV. The Priests were required to eat them. 

I. He forbade leaven in sacrifices because it signified human traditions and **will-worship** <note>original Greek: εθελοθρησκείαν (*ethelothrēskeian*); refers to self-imposed religious practice not commanded by God</note>, as well as hypocrisy in one’s conduct. Christ explained this when warning his disciples to beware of the **leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod**. Paul also exhorted the faithful in 1 Corinthians 5 to abstain from the **leaven of malice and wickedness**. **Honey** was also forbidden because it signifies those human traditions that taste like honey to the palate and are usually sweet to the curious and to innovators; indeed, cooked honey has the power to cause fermentation. 

However, leaven was admitted in a different sense and for a different purpose in Eucharistic <note>In this context, "Eucharistic" refers to the *Todah* or "thank-offering," rather than the modern Christian sacrament</note> sacrifices (Leviticus 7:13). Two leavened loaves were also offered in the firstfruits (Leviticus 23:17). For just as a little leaven causes the whole mass to swell, so the firstfruits of the crops sanctified the entire harvest, and the Eucharistic sacrifices, like leaven, caused the abundant blessings of God to overflow and swell. 

II. Sacrifices were sprinkled with **salt**, which signified God’s institution and His word, without which the traditions of men and manufactured forms of worship are tasteless <note>original Latin: *insulsi*; can mean both "unsalted" and "foolish" or "absurd"</note> and unpleasing to God; hence Christ says in Mark 9:49: ***You are the salt of the earth. Every man shall be salted with fire: and every victim shall be salted with salt.*** This is fitting, as salt prevents decay. 

III. It pleased God that cakes should be offered to Him in four ways, to signify that we obtain every kind of food through God’s blessing, and that it is consecrated by His word. 

IV. He willed that they be offered through the **Priests** because they typically prefigured Christ, who makes us and our offerings acceptable to God, for nothing can be offered by us that is pleasing to God except in Christ. Hence those words of Christ himself: ***Whatever you shall ask the Father in my name, you shall receive.*** 

V. The Priests were required to eat those offerings so that the people would know the nature of God's care for the ministry, according to that saying of Paul: ***he who serves the altar, ought to live from the altar.***

The third type of sacrifice was the <term>זבח שלמים</term> (*zeuach schelamim*) <note>original Hebrew: "Sacrifice of Peace-Offerings"</note>. These sacrifices were therefore called **peace offerings** or **Eucharistic**. **Peace offerings**, because they signified blessings from...

...granted by God to men; for to the Hebrews, peace and "peace-making" signified every kind of blessing. Hence the common salutations: **Peace be with you** <note>original Hebrew: *shalom aleichem*</note>. These were called **Eucharistic** <note>From the Greek *eucharistos* meaning "thankful"; in this context, it refers to the *Todah* or thank-offerings</note> because they were acts of thanksgiving on the part of men for God’s blessings.

The rites of those sacrifices were as follows: I. Some parts, especially the fat, were burned in the fire; others were kept by the offerers; and finally, the priests claimed other parts for themselves, as is clear from Leviticus, chapter 3. II. They were offered through a priest. III. Food was consumed by fire as a pleasing aroma. The first rite signified that the sacrifices were in honor of God, from which their dignity was derived. This is why the fat—the more choice part—was yielded to God, as is also clear from Psalm 63:5: *My soul shall be satisfied as with marrow and fatness.* They were also performed for the sake of the faithful and the Priests, which is why other parts were reserved for them. Hence that saying about the **Corban** <note>A Hebrew term meaning a gift or offering dedicated to God</note> in the Gospel: *That gift will be useful to you.* The second rite signified Christ the Mediator, who in the heavenly sanctuary holds a golden censer in his hand, offering incense pleasing to God. The third was the pleasing aroma of the food, by which their acceptance was signified. Hence it was called the **food of Jehovah**. Moreover, those sacrifices were made from three kinds of four-footed animals: namely, from cattle, sheep, and goats.

The fourth kind of sacrifice was the <term>חטאת (*Chattah*): a Hebrew term for a sin offering</term>, for sin or for a sin committed through error. There were four types of this: namely, when it was offered for the High Priest, for the Church <note>original Latin: *Ecclesia*; referring here to the congregation or assembly of Israel</note>, for the Prince, and for any private individual, as is clear from Leviticus, chapters 4 and 6. And for this reason, the victims were offered according to the status and wealth of those persons. For the Priests offered a reddish heifer, or as it is in the Hebrew, a <term>son of an ox (*ben-baqar*): a literal Hebrew idiom for a young bull or calf</term> (Leviticus 4:13). In the same way, the whole Church <note>the assembly of Israel</note> offered a young bull (verse 22). The Prince offered a male goat (verse 27). Private individuals from the common people offered a female goat or a female sheep (chapter 4, at the end). Paul seems to refer to this kind of sacrifice in Hebrews 9:7, writing that the **High Priest offered, not without blood, for himself and for the errors of the people.** Here the Greek <term>ἀγνοημάτων (*agnoematon*): refers specifically to sins of ignorance or unintentional mistakes</term> corresponds to the Hebrew <term>שגגות (*sheghioth*): unintentional sins or "wanderings" from the path</term>, and therefore signifies sins committed through ignorance, the sacrifice [of which...]

<meta>This page continues the technical classification of Mosaic sacrifices. The previous page concluded by discussing "Peace Offerings" and began to touch upon the nature of sacrifices for sin.</meta>

->### THE REVEALER OF SECRETS. ###<-

...specifically called the **sin offering** <note>original Hebrew: *chattah*</note>. Indeed, because almost all sins—even voluntary ones—seem to be committed in some way through error (since there is always some error of conscience bewitched by Satan), it has come to pass that the term **sins of ignorance** <note>original Greek: *agnoemata*</note> is used broadly to designate every kind of sin. Strictly speaking, however, it refers to that specific type which is expiated by the **sin offering**, namely when the sin is not voluntary but committed entirely through ignorance. 

It should be observed, moreover, what Maimonides <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher and scholar</note> wrote in *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: *Moreh Nevochim*</note>, part 3, chapter 46: **peace offerings** <note>original Hebrew: *shelamim*</note> are of a lower order; the **sin offering** and the **guilt offering** <note>original Hebrew: *asham*</note> are called by the Rabbis **holy things of minor degree** <note>original Hebrew: *kodashim kalim*</note>, which could be eaten in Jerusalem only, and specifically on the day they were offered and the following morning, but not thereafter, because they would contract defilement.

The fifth kind of sacrifice is for **guilt** or **offense** <note>original Hebrew: *asham*</note>, so called because the victim was offered to expiate that kind of sin which was one of omission. Thus it was called an "offense" <note>Latin: *delictum*</note>, as if it were a "leaving behind" <note>Latin: *derelictum*</note>, from the act of abandoning; or it was called "guilt" <note>Latin: *reatus*</note> because the penalty of the sin was removed by it. Therefore, in Genesis 26:10, Leviticus 5:6, and Leviticus 7:2, the offering for guilt is explained. 

In this way, the **sin offering** <note>original Hebrew: *chattah*</note> would be a sacrifice for the **fault**, and the **guilt offering** <note>original Hebrew: *asham*</note> would be for the **punishment**. This corresponds perfectly to the twofold benefit of Christ: namely, **justification** and **sanctification**. In justification, redemption from the *guilt* (the legal liability) occurs, and through the death of Christ, we are liberated from eternal death. In sanctification, redemption from the *fault* (the moral stain) occurs, because we are morally sanctified through the imputation of Christ’s active righteousness, and physically through inherent righteousness, albeit imperfectly. To this twofold benefit is opposed the twofold evil of Adam: namely, the guilt that is imputed to us and the fault that inheres in our natural corruption. 

This interpretation of the **sin offering** and **guilt offering** is the more probable one. Otherwise, authors are quite doubtful about the true meaning of those terms. To some, the **sin offering** is taken for sin perpetrated through ignorance, according to Leviticus 4 and 5, while the **guilt offering** is for sins committed voluntarily and insolently. Nicholas of Lyra <note>A highly influential Franciscan biblical exegete of the Middle Ages</note> interprets it such that the former is a sin of **commission**, while the latter is a sin of **omission**; hence it is an "offense," as if a leaving behind, as stated above.

# ANTHONY CRÉGUT #

The sixth kind of sacrifice is the **consecration** <note>original Hebrew: *milluim*, meaning "fillings"</note>; this is properly defined as the sacrifice of completion. Concerning this, see Leviticus 6:20 and Exodus 29:22: **the ram of consecration** <note>original Hebrew: *el milluim*; literally, "the ram of fillings"</note>. According to Rabbi Solomon <note>original: R. Salomonem; referring to the medieval commentator Rashi</note>, it was so named because by it the priestly act was fulfilled and perfected. This can be confirmed from the passage in Numbers 3:3: **he filled their hand** <note>original Hebrew: *mille iadam*</note>, that is, he consecrated their ministry. From this, a common expression arose, as Buxtorf <note>Johann Buxtorf, a renowned 17th-century Hebraist</note> correctly noted, that by delivering certain portions of the sacrifices into the hands of the Priests, they were solemnly admitted into the possession of the office of sacrificing, and were most fully confirmed in it. Thereafter, the term was used broadly for any kind of consecration.

Thus far we have dealt with the first part of the dissertation, namely the burnt offerings and the remaining kinds of sacrifices; there follows the second part, specifically the *laying on of hands upon the head of the burnt offering*. This is expressly stated in the Law, Leviticus 1:4, in these words: *and he shall lean his hand upon the head of the burnt offering*. This rite was once accurately observed. For he who delivered the victim to be offered to God to the Priest, after he had approached the door of the tabernacle, would lay his hands upon the head of the burnt offering. This is also commanded for Aaron and his sons in Exodus 29:10. It is not, however, very difficult to know what that ancient ceremony prefigured in a mystical sense. Truly, just as the victim foreshadowed Christ, the true victim; so the laying on of hands upon the head of the victim signified that all our sins were laid upon the head of the Mediator, so that our guilt might be taken away. Hence that passage in Isaiah 53: *He has cast upon him our iniquities.* And 1 Peter 2:24: *He bore our sins in his body upon the tree, etc.* From this come the two goats: one sacrificed, the other for *Azazel* <note>original: *hazazel*; the "scapegoat"</note> sent into the desert bearing sins, which is therefore called the *scapegoat* <note>original Latin: *hircus emissarius*</note>.

It must be observed, therefore, that the laying on of hands was customary in the economy of the Old Testament and in the economy of the New Testament. In the former economy, the laying on of hands which was done upon the head of the burnt offering represented (as we have said) the laying of all sins upon Christ the Mediator, as if upon the symbolic victim, who, on the cross, [bore] all our sins...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "laying on of hands," moving from its role in Old Testament animal sacrifices to its spiritual fulfillment in Christ and its continued use in the Christian sacraments of baptism and ordination.</meta>

# REVEALER OF SECRETS #

...he carried, so that in this way, through the blood of that Mediator, we might be reconciled with God and justified from all sins. This is because, through the laying on of hands, all sins were imputed to Christ the Mediator, so that thereafter his righteousness might be imputed to us; according to that saying of Augustine, *he made our sins his own sins, so that he might make his righteousness our righteousness.* <note>original Latin: *delicta nostra sua delicta fecit, ut iustitiam suam nostram iustitiam faceret*</note> But indeed, in the new economy <note>or "dispensation"—a theological term for God's system of dealing with humanity</note>, the laying on of hands is performed not upon brute victims <note>animals</note>, but upon the heads of rational victims <note>human beings</note>, signifying that we are truly justified and sanctified through the blood of Christ. Hence it is that the laying on of hands in baptism represents those two benefits of Christ to us; for there are two parts of baptism, namely *remission of sins and regeneration*. This was solemnly demonstrated in the primitive Church whenever the Apostles, through the laying on of hands, extraordinarily conferred the gifts <note>original: *charismata*</note> of the Holy Spirit, and this took place after baptism, as is clear from *Acts 19:6 and from Acts 8:17.* For although those extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit were common to both the elect and the reprobate <note>those chosen for salvation and those who are not</note>, nevertheless they were not in vain; rather, those spiritual gifts were sent by God for the salvation and conversion of the faithful. Moreover, that rite is observed today in the election and inauguration of Pastors, by which is signified not the conferring of the gifts of the Holy Spirit *for benefit* <note>Latin: *ad beneficium*, referring to personal sanctification</note>, but rather *for office* <note>Latin: *ad officium*</note>; that is, for the proper execution of the pastoral duty, in which great office the kind and effective influences of the Holy Spirit are specifically required. This is clear from 1 Timothy 5:22: *Do not lay hands quickly on anyone,* and *Acts 6:6* regarding the election of the seven Deacons of the Church.

It is established, therefore, that this ceremony passed from the old economy into the new and had its origin from the Hebrews, who used that rite in various religious acts—for instance, in the public and solemn consecrations of sacrificial victims, as is proved from this passage of Leviticus. It was also used in private prayers and blessings, as is clear from *Genesis 48:14* and elsewhere whenever the Patriarchs blessed their sons. The story of the Patriarch Jacob is well known: when he blessed Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Joseph, he did so with crossed hands, so that his right hand would be placed upon the younger son because of the more abundant [grace] of God...

# ANTOINE CREGUT #

...blessings, for which reason he ought to have been preferred to his brother. This ceremony was thereafter practiced in the Christian Church primarily in a threefold act. First, in ordaining ministers, as seen in 1 Timothy 5:22 and frequently elsewhere. Second, in bestowing the spiritual gifts <term>charismata (spiritual gifts or graces)</term> of the Holy Spirit, as in Acts 8:16. Third, in offering favorable prayers, as in Matthew 19:13: *Then children were brought to him so that he might lay his hands on them and pray.*

In truth, no specific command for this ceremony is found in the New Testament; nevertheless, its frequent use in the Church of God is not without merit. First, because the precept is found in the Old Testament, as is already clear in Leviticus 1:4: *And he shall rest his hand upon the head of the burnt offering...* <note>original Latin: *Et nititur manu sua*</note> etc. For even though the ceremonial law has now been abolished, and no sacrifice of animal victims occurs, that which is moral is always preserved. Since something of the "thing signified" remains even today, the sign is not poorly applied to signify that thing. For just as with the Sabbath—the Sabbath was indeed abolished, and yet the Lord's Day is celebrated in the new economy <note>the theological system of the New Testament</note> because that which is moral remains, namely the sanctification of something to God. Likewise, burnt offerings are not offered today, and therefore hands are not laid upon the heads of sacrificial victims; yet because we are "rational victims" <note>human beings as "living sacrifices" (Romans 12:1)</note> to be consecrated to God, the laying on of hands is not out of place, so that those mysteries may be signified, as occurs in the ordination of Pastors. 

Second, although no command is found in the New Testament, the practice of the Apostles and the early Church suffices, as well as that of Christ: which, since it was so precise and perpetual, ought to stand as a command for us. And in truth, that ceremony is very useful; for just as victims of old were set apart and preserved for God from common use through the laying on of hands, so the faithful (by reason of the benefit they receive) and Pastors (by reason of their office) are specifically consecrated to God. Therefore, they are no longer their own masters <note>original: *sui iuris*</note>, but are devoted to God and the Church. Hence Paul excellently exhorted Timothy with these words in 2 Timothy 1:6: *I remind you to stir up the grace that is in you through the laying on of hands.*

Furthermore, because that rite was celebrated and signified illustrious mysteries, it ought not to be used in vain or rashly. Hence Paul wrote to Timothy in 1 Timothy 5:22: *Lay hands suddenly on no one...* <note>The Latin text cuts off here: *Manus citò nemini impo-*</note>

# ANTHONY CREGUTUS #

[primarily] for the sake of heavenly and spiritual blessings; yet the laying on of hands was also a symbol of earthly and physical things, namely the healing of diseases. Thus, in Luke 4:40, Christ healed the sick by laying His hands upon them. And in Acts 28 and Mark 16, the Apostles laid on hands for the healing of diseases. This indeed rightly corresponded with the power and virtue of God, of which the hand was a symbol, just as it was a symbol of authority—not unlike how the Egyptians used it as a hieroglyph and emblem for those same concepts. It is for this reason that the Egyptians were the first of all to carve the shape of a hand upon a scepter. Similarly, on the throne of Solomon, there were two carved hands that supported the throne; hence Scripture asserts that *all things are in the hand of God*.

The third part was the *purpose of the burnt offering* <term>holocausti (a sacrifice entirely consumed by fire)</term>, namely that sins might be expiated. This expiation was twofold: one was *legal or figurative*, the other *real and prefigured*. The former expiation was performed through brute victims <note>original: "victimas brutas" — animal sacrifices</note>; but the latter through Christ the Mediator, the true victim sacrificed on the cross, who was the reality of those figures and the substance <gloss>literally: the body</gloss> of those shadows. Paul speaks of both types of victims and both types of expiation in Hebrews 9:13–14:

> For if the blood of bulls and goats and the ashes of a heifer, sprinkling those who are defiled, sanctify for the purity of the flesh, how much more shall the blood of Christ—who through the eternal Spirit offered himself blameless to God—cleanse your conscience from dead works to serve the living God? 

For this reason, the same Apostle in Hebrews 10:8–9 prefers the latter sacrifice far above the former ones, when he says:

> Sacrifice and offering and burnt offerings and sin offerings you did not desire, etc.

By this variety of words, he alludes to the various sacrifices of the Law, but soon adds:

> Then he said, “Behold, I am here to do your will.” He takes away the first, so that he may establish the second.

Therefore, the general purpose of all sacrifices was the expiation of sins, which even the Pagans <term>Ethnici (Gentiles or non-Christians)</term> themselves intended. But this was the difference between the Pagans and the Jews: the former limited expiation to the blood and death of the animal victim, whereas the Jews looked further to the blood and death of the true Victim or Mediator, which was foreshadowed in the animal victim. They behold the body itself and the very truth. For when Caiaphas, prophesying, said, *It is expedient for one man to die for the people;* <note>John 18:14</note> he did not even understand what he meant himself; yet now, Christians clearly preach with Paul (in 1 Timothy 2 and Romans) that *Christ has been made a propitiation for our sins and for those of the whole world*. Paul says that He Himself is the *atoning sacrifice* <note>original: "ἱλαστήριון" (hilastērion), a term for the "mercy seat" or a means of appeasement</note> for us, and has given a *ransom* or *substitute ransom* <note>original: "λύτρον" (lytron) or "ἀντίλυτρον" (antilytron)</note>. From this comes that theological axiom: *The blood of Christ brings all [other] blood to a halt.* <note>original: "Christi sanguis sistit omnem sanguinem." This implies that Christ's death fulfilled and terminated the requirement for animal sacrifices.</note> Because in Him, all sacrifices were fulfilled.

To this point belongs what the Rabbis say regarding the *goat for Azazel* <note>original: "hirco hazazel," the scapegoat described in Leviticus 16</note>; for when, according to the law in Leviticus 16, it was sent out into the desert carrying the sins of the people, a piece of scarlet wool, shaped like a tongue, was bound between its two horns. Sometimes that scarlet tongue would turn white, and sometimes it remained red, depending on whether the sins were expiated or remained unatoned. If it turned white, there was great exultation and rejoicing throughout all Judea, because God was appeased, and this served as a symbol of the expiation of sins. But if the scarlet portion remained red, mournful laments and wailing were heard throughout Judea, because God was not appeased, nor was there true repentance among the people. This occurred to signify that the goat was not the true victim, even if it were sacrificed, but rather Christ the Mediator. 

And this was (as the Rabbis used to say) a miracle of the first Temple. All these things are recounted at length in the Talmudic Law, as was also observed by Johannes Buxtorf <note>A famous 17th-century Christian Hebraist and scholar of Jewish traditions</note> in his review of the Talmudic work. *For forty years before the destruction of the Temple, the lot no longer came up in the right hand, nor did the scarlet strip turn white anymore, nor did the evening lamp burn, and the doors of the Temple opened of their own accord:* Yoma, folio 39, page 2. This last point is expressed by the Syriac translator as *vmechada aphai tarha dehaikela etstari*; <note>original Syriac: ומהדא אפי תרעא דהיכלא אצטרי</note> and immediately the face of the temple gate was torn. Those things said regarding the *lot* allude to the passage in Leviticus 16:8. For whichever lot fell to the right hand was placed upon the goat situated to the right, which was sacred to the Lord and slaughtered for the expiation of sins; the other lot, falling to the left hand, was placed upon the goat for Azazel, which [was sent] into the desert...

For although they were atoned for only figuratively and typically through the [ancient] sacrifices, they were truly and in reality atoned for through the sacrifice of the cross; and therefore sins were not imputed to the faithful. From this it is said *not standing* <note>original Greek: "μὴ στήσας" (mē stēsas), a legal concept meaning a charge is not "made to stand" or upheld</note>; as is clear from Acts 7:60, when Stephen said, *Lord, do not hold this sin against them.* <note>original Greek: "κύριε μὴ στήσῃς αὐτοῖς τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ταύτην" (Kyrie mē stēsēis autois tēn hamartian tautēn)</note> For by the word "to stand" or "to set up," a firm and permanent imputation of sins before God is signified, just as, conversely, those which are not imputed are said to be "blotted out." For this reason also, among the ancient Jews, a solemn feast of atonement was celebrated, which was called "The Day" *par excellence* <note>original Greek: "κατ' ἐξοχήν" (kat’ exochēn), meaning preeminently</note>, or *Yoma* <note>original Aramaic/Hebrew: "יוֹמָא" (Yoma), the title of the Talmudic tractate on the Day of Atonement</note>, because it was the day of *Kippur* <note>original: "hakkipur"</note>, of atonement.

## CONCERNING THE SACRED FIRE.

### ANALYSIS.

What is the Hebrew <term>אש תמיד</term> <note>original Hebrew: "esh tamid"</note> *Continual Fire*? What is the *continual bread* <note>The Showbread or "Bread of the Presence"</note>? The division of the topics to be discussed.

*The first part concerns the commandment to maintain the fire.* The necessity of this commandment, and why was it given? Which is older in the Church: sacrifices or the sacred fire? By what sign did Cain recognize that Abel's sacrifice was more acceptable to God? <note>Referring to the tradition that fire from heaven consumed Abel's offering but not Cain's.</note> Fire was religiously preserved among all nations. Who was the God of the Chaldeans and the Persians? Concerning the fire-worshipers of the Persians. What does the term *Gaber* <note>A reference to the "Guebres," a historical term for Zoroastrians or fire-worshipers in Persia.</note> mean to them? What of *Mithras* <note>The Persian god of light and sun.</note>? What is the meaning of the fable of Epimetheus and Prometheus regarding fire? Concerning the fire of the Vestals <note>Virgin priestesses of Vesta in Rome who tended a perpetual sacred fire.</note> among the Romans. Concerning the double fire of the heathens according to Augustine. Concerning the ordinary and extraordinary fire among the Jews. The extraordinary fire in the more solemn sacrifices, and why? The opinion of the Rabbis concerning the sacred fire ascending upward into heaven. The story from Ruffinus <note>A 4th-century monk and historian.</note> regarding the fire-god of the Chaldeans. The fraud of the Egyptians involving a water jar. <note>original Greek: "πυρεῖον" (pyreion), meaning a fire-temple or fire-altar.</note> The fire-temple of the Persians destroyed by Bishop Abda. Concerning "strange fire" <note>Fire not taken from the authorized altar, as in the sin of Nadab and Abihu.</note>. Concerning "impious fire." What are the <term>כונים</term> <note>original Hebrew: "kavvanim," usually translated as sacrificial cakes offered to the "Queen of Heaven" in the book of Jeremiah.</note> *Cauuanim* to the Hebrews?

*The second part is the object of the commandment, namely the Priests.* A twofold reason why God commanded the Priests to maintain the fire: one historical, the other allegorical. This is illustrated by all the more solemn sacrifices. The two duties of the Priests regarding the fire: one ordinary, the other extraordinary. When did the Priests maintain the fire themselves, and when did they seek to obtain it from God?

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'C' containing a cherubic face surrounded by decorative foliage.</image-desc>As I conclude the preceding commentary on burnt offerings and the remaining sacrifices, that wonderful command of God concerning the perpetual fire occurs to me, which is commonly called among the Rabbis <term>אש תמיד</term> <note>original Hebrew: esh tamid</note> *continual fire*. Just as the *bread of faces*, or *showbread*, is called in Numbers 4:7 *continual bread*, because it was required to stand perpetually before the face of God upon the table. Therefore, we shall briefly observe four things here. I. *The commandment regarding the perpetuity of the fire.* II. *To whom a commandment of this kind is entrusted.* III. *The place where the fire is kept.* IV. *The purpose of the commandment.*

I. The commandment of God is expressly stated in this place: "The fire shall be kept burning continually." Therefore, there is a great necessity, which is commonly called the "necessity of the precept"; for since God rightly claims absolute right over all creatures, His will ought to be the highest and inviolable law for all mortals. But furthermore, besides other moral reasons which will be brought forward later in the final part, this one is momentous: that this fire was not common or hearth-fire, nor even merely elemental, but sacred and heavenly. Therefore, since it had once descended from heaven, it had to remain unextinguished so that the consumption of the burnt offerings might be accomplished. Indeed, it can scarcely be judged which was older in the Church: the sacrifices, or that heavenly fire, since—as sa- <note>The text ends mid-word with the catchword "sa-", likely continuing as "sacrificia" (sacrifices) on the following page.</note>

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS.

Just as sacrifices were in use among the ancient Patriarchs before they were formally instituted by God, so too, according to the ancients, that sacred fire descended from heaven. By consuming the burnt offerings, it served as a miraculous symbol by which God approved those sacrifices before the formal institution of the Law. For this reason, the ancient Hebrews record that Cain knew his brother Abel’s sacrifice was more acceptable to God because fire descended from heaven upon Abel's sacrifice, but not upon his own; by this sign, God approved the former and not the latter. St. Jerome <note>Eusebius Sophronius Hieronymus (c. 347–420 AD), a prominent Church Father and translator of the Vulgate Bible.</note> confirmed this from the edition of Theodotion <note>A 2nd-century scholar known for his Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> in his "Questions or Traditions on Genesis." Writing on the passage from Genesis: *And God looked upon Abel and upon his gifts: but upon Cain and upon his sacrifices he did not look, and Cain was very sorrowful.* <note>original Latin: "Et respexit Deus super Abel & super munera eius: super Cain autem & super sacrificia eius non respexit, & contristatus est Cain valde."</note> How could Cain have known that God had accepted his brother’s gifts and rejected his own, unless that interpretation which Theodotion set down were true: *And the Lord set fire upon Abel and upon his sacrifice: but upon Cain and upon his sacrifice he did not set fire.* <note>original Latin: "inflammauit Dominus super Abel & super sacrificium eius: super Cain verò & super eius sacrificium non inflammauit."</note> We also read that fire used to come from heaven to devour sacrifices at the dedication of the Temple under Solomon, and when Elijah built an altar on Mount Carmel. This most learned Father [Jerome] clearly suggests by these words that even in the ancient times of Abel and Cain, sacred fire fell from heaven. This was, as it were, a prelude to that law: *Let the fire be nourished continually; let it not be extinguished.* <note>original Latin: "Ignis iugiter alitor ne extinguitor." A reference to the commandment in Leviticus 6:13 regarding the altar fire.</note> Justin Martyr <note>An early Christian philosopher and apologist (c. 100–165 AD).</note>, in his explanation of questions posed by the Gentiles to Christians, asks why Cain’s sacrifice was rejected while Abel’s religious gifts were pleasing. He answers that because Cain worshiped God with the poorer fruits of the earth, he judged himself more worthy of the better things than God. Abel valued God more than his own needs; Cain valued his own necessary use more than God.

Yet truly, this wonder of the sacred fire became so prevalent among all nations that they did not refuse to venerate it with some religious cult. First, it was religiously preserved among the Hebrews, no differently than other wonders of God, such as the *Manna and Aaron’s flowering rod*, so that they might be "memorials" <note>original Greek: μνημόσυνα (mnemosyna), meaning tokens of remembrance or monuments.</note> of divine blessings. Then the Oriental peoples, namely the Chaldeans...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Sacred Fire" by tracing its history through the superstitions of the ancient Persians, Greeks, and Romans, contrasting their pagan practices with the biblical precedents discussed previously.</meta>

# ANTHONY CREGUT

And the Persians, being closer neighbors to the Jews, worshipped fire, as is evident from the name *Ur of the Chaldeans* <note>original: "Vr Chaldæorum"</note>; among them, as among the Hebrews, the word אור (*Ur*) signifies fire. For the Persians, it was the highest form of religion to worship fire—or even the Sun, which is heavenly fire—under the name *Mithra* or *Mithras*, from which we get the *Mithraic rites*. The same was true for the Assyrians and Phoenicians, by whom the sun was called *Adad*, derived from the Hebrew אחד (*Echadh*) and, by the dropping of the first letter, חדה (*chadh*), meaning *one* or *unique*; just as the Latin *Sol* [Sun] is thought to be named as if *solus* [alone]. From this Persian superstition arose the proverb: *Though a Guebre <note>term: <term>Guebre</term> (Gaber), a historical term for Zoroastrians, who are often called "fire-worshippers" in older Western texts.</note> kindles the fire for a hundred years, yet if he falls into it even once, he is burned.* For גבר (*Gaber*) denotes the fire-worshippers who remain in Persia to this day, most tenacious in their superstition. This same word occurs in the Talmud, in the tractate *Shabbat*: *Live under an Ishmaelite <note>A reference to Muslim rulers.</note> and not under a Christian; and live under a Christian and not under a Chauer.* <note>original Latin/Hebrew: "תחת ישמעל ולא תחת גוי ולא תחת חבר... Sub Ismaelita (sub. habites) & non sub Christiano... & non sub Chauer."</note> Where the Gloss <note>Interpretive commentary.</note> notes that a *chauer* is *a people from the sons of the Persians.* This Persian superstition is mocked more than others, as they appeared especially superstitious to the Hebrews.

Later, this superstition passed from the Easterners to the Westerners. For the Greeks, who mixed everything with their various fables and mythologies, devised a certain *Epimetheus* and his opposite, *Prometheus*. They considered the former foolish, as he clumsily and imprudently assembled all things from the beginning of the world, and among other living things, he made man alone unarmed and destitute of any protection. But they judged the latter [Prometheus] to be wise, who (as Plato once wrote) wishing to repair the defects of his companion Epimetheus, stole two most necessary things from the gods: fire from Vulcan, and wisdom from Minerva. Without these two aids, the entire *Cosmopoia* <note>term: <term>Cosmopoia</term>, the creation or making of the world.</note> would have gone to ruin and been reduced to ashes. From this comes the inevitable ruin of those who were "interdicted from water and fire" <note>A Roman legal formula for exile, where a person was cut off from the basic necessities of life.</note>.

Finally, this misguided zeal <note>original: "Cacozelia," a term for a distorted or bad imitation.</note> passed from the Greeks to the Romans. For it was a great sin for the Vestal Virgins to allow the sacred fire to be extinguished; if it ever happened, it was considered a terrible omen requiring atonement. In order for the offense to be repaired in some way, it was necessary that it be immediately relit by the rays of the sun, so that it might remain a sacred and heavenly fire, rather than one that was earthly and merely from a hearth.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of fire-worship, transitioning from the Persian Guebres to the classical Roman and Greek traditions, before contrasting these "superstitions" with the biblically ordained use of sacred fire in the Tabernacle and Temple.</meta>

# REVEALER OF SECRETS

Hence that indirect expression used by the Poet: *Who keep the hearths chaste with perpetual Virginity.* By this rite, the Hebrew אש תמיד <note>original: "esh tamid"</note> or *continual fire* was signified through the "evil-imitation" <note>term: <term>cacozelia</term>, a perverse or misguided imitation.</note> of Satan. He is "God's ape," who fascinated wretched mortals by abusing sacred things. This is why Saint Augustine, in his book *The City of God*, mentions the two types of fire used by the Heathens—namely, that of Vulcan and that of the Vestals. In Book 7, Chapter 16, he says the fire of the Vestals is "lighter," while the fire of Vulcan is "more violent." Here, the scholar Vives—drawing from Phurnutus <note>A reference to the Stoic philosopher Lucius Annaeus Cornutus (Phurnutus), who wrote on Greek mythology.</note>—adds that Vulcan represents this coarse fire that we use everywhere, for the more subtle fire is Jupiter himself.

However, just as that worship of fire and the superstition of the fire-worshippers was displeasing to God, He nonetheless willed that a sacred fire be preserved among His own people and in His temple for the sake of burnt offerings. For this reason, fire was either kept continually in the temple and upon the altar, or it descended from heaven in an extraordinary manner during more solemn sacrifices. In the very first sacrifice of all, that of Abel, fire descended from heaven, as was proven above from Jerome and the Greek edition of Theodotion. From this, idolatry emerged among the generation of Cain; for when their father Cain saw the fire sent down and descending from heaven, his descendants believed that God *was* the fire that consumed the burnt offering. From this came the idolatry in Ur of the Chaldeans <note>The author links the name "Ur" to the Hebrew word for "fire," suggesting the city was named for its fire-worship.</note>. Later, in that most solemn sacrifice of Aaron the High Priest during his inauguration, fire descended from heaven. By this symbol, God testified to the dignity of that most holy office, showing that He would hold the sacrifices of Aaron and his sons as valid, confirm the blessings made to the people, and hear their prayers. This event occurred, as recorded in Leviticus 9:24, during the first period of Aaron’s inauguration:

> *Then the glory of Jehovah appeared to all the people; for fire went out from the presence of Jehovah and consumed the burnt offering and the fat on that altar: which when all the people saw, they shouted and fell on their faces.*

Furthermore, we read that a similar miracle occurred in Judges 13:20, during the sacrifice of Manoah:

> *For it happened that when the flame went up toward heaven from the altar, the Angel of Jehovah ascended in that flame of the altar.*

In this instance, a great blessing from God was revealed; for not only did a sterile woman give birth, but she gave birth to Samson.

Psalm 20:3: *May Jehovah remember all your offerings and turn your burnt sacrifice into ashes most completely.*

Furthermore, it is not without merit to observe here the teaching of certain Rabbis, who report that after that fire sent down from heaven had consumed the burnt offering, it immediately ascended straight back to heaven toward its origin. They claim it could not be disturbed or deflected in any way, either to the right or to the left, by whirlwinds, fire-storms, or tempests. Since it was not "elementary" fire <note>term: <term>elementary fire</term>, the natural fire found on Earth, as opposed to celestial or divine fire.</note> but heavenly, the winds and storms—which are composed of the elements—were unable to act above the sphere of their own activity or influence the heavenly influx. Just as no natural force could hinder its descent, neither could it hinder its ascent. Pietro Galatino, in his work *On the Secrets of Catholic Truth*, <note>original: "Petrus Galatinus de arc. Cathol. uerit." Galatino was a 16th-century scholar who attempted to prove Christian doctrines using the Jewish Kabbalah and Rabbinic texts.</note> lists this among the miracles that were once seen in the Tabernacle.
