...of my hands as an *evening sacrifice* <note>original: "sacrificium vespertinum"; a reference to Psalm 141:2, comparing prayer to the ritual offerings in the Temple.</note>: and regarding the ascent into the temple, to which no mortal could arrive except by climbing; thus it is frequently said in the Gospel that the Jews "ascended" into the temple, as in Luke 18: *Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a Tax Collector.* If, therefore, what the Rabbis <note>Jewish scholars and teachers of the law.</note> relate concerning the sacred fire is true, David seems to have alluded to it there; indeed, if we give credit to those same Hebrews, it was a symbol of a bad omen among them if the fire did not ascend straight up, or if it were driven to the right or left by the force of the winds.

Since the miracle of the sacred fire was so illustrious, it is certainly no wonder if the Chaldeans and Persians (*as we have seen above*) so superstitiously worshipped fire as a God. From this, a memorable story is told in Rufinus <note>Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 345–410 AD), a monk and historian known for translating Greek church histories into Latin.</note>, Book 11, Chapter 26, concerning the Chaldeans carrying their god, Fire, around, who are said to have had a conflict with the gods of all the provinces; so that whichever god won would be held as the only God. But since the other gods were fashioned from gold, silver, bronze, stone, etc.—materials which are easily dissolved or damaged by fire—it happened that fire was truly believed to be a God above all others. However, later, the Priest of Canopus <note>Canopus was an Egyptian deity often represented as a jar with a human head; also a city in Egypt.</note> defeated the Chaldeans with a new trick: when the holes of a water jar were plugged with wax, and fire was placed beneath it, the fire was extinguished by the water flowing out. Thus, the water jar—painted in various colors, with very small feet, a drawn-in neck, and a swollen belly as if bruised, formed in the manner of a water jar with an equally smooth back—was worshipped by the Egyptians as the image of Canopus, and they boasted that they had defeated the Chaldeans.

It is further related in the *Tripartite History* <note>original: "hist. Tripartita"; a standard medieval textbook of church history compiled from three Greek historians: Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret.</note>, Book 10, Chapter 30, that Bishop Abda, adorned with many virtues, used divine zeal in Persia and destroyed that nation's <term>pyreion</term> <note>original: "πυρεῖον"; a fire temple, from the Greek word "pyr" meaning fire.</note>, that is, their hearth or Vesta <note>Vesta was the Roman goddess of the hearth; the author uses her name here to explain the concept of a sacred perpetual fire to a Latin-reading audience.</note>. For they call those temples <term>pyreia</term> in which they keep the fire, for they consider fire to be God. And in Book 11, Chapter 8: *when the Persians had embraced Christianity, the king nevertheless used to worship a burning fire perpetually and suppliantly in a certain house. However, the Magi* <note>The priestly class of ancient Persia, from whose name we get the word "magic."</note> *hid a certain man underground at the time the king was accustomed to worship, and they made him cry out these words: "Cast out the king, for he has acted impiously because he deems the Christian priest worthy of honor."*

But a little later it is added that the fraud of the Magi <note>original: "Magorum"; here referring to Persian priests or sorcerers often associated with fire rituals.</note> was detected; for it was not the fire that was speaking, but a man hiding within.

Therefore, a distinction must be made between the sacred fire and other fires. For just as the sacred fire is commanded in this place, and Jehovah prescribes by this law that it be a perpetual fire, which is to be nourished continually and kept from being extinguished; so other fires are severely prohibited in the sacred books. Thus, God forbade "common" or "foreign" and *extraneous* fire in sacrifices. For whatever burnt offerings were consumed by this extraneous fire were not only unpleasing to God, but He also reacted sharply against the transgressors of the law, as is clear from the example of the sons of Aaron, Nadab and Abihu. When they applied extraneous fire to the sacrifice, they themselves were consumed by the fire of Jehovah. *Numbers 26:61. But Nadab and Abihu died when they offered foreign fire before the Lord. And Leviticus 10, verses 1 and 2: But Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, each took his censer, put fire in them, and placed incense upon them, to offer foreign fire before the Lord, which He had not commanded them. Therefore, fire coming out from the presence of the Lord consumed them; so they died before the Lord.*

Furthermore, the sacred fire is contrasted with the impious fire, such as that fire of the fire-worshippers, who are called *Gaber* <note>original: "Gaber"; a term for Zoroastrians or "Ghebers," derived from the Persian word for an infidel or fire-worshipper.</note> among the Persians, as was said above; for that was kindled for the use of idolatry. Hence, the idolaters of Molech <note>An ancient Near Eastern deity associated with child sacrifice.</note> are frequently condemned in Scripture, who passed their sons through the fire. *Isaiah 50:11. Behold, all you who kindle a fire, who encircle yourselves with firebrands: walk in the light of your fire and among the firebrands you have set ablaze. This is what you shall receive from my hand: you shall lie down in pain. And Jeremiah 7:18. The children gather wood, and their fathers kindle the fire; and the women knead dough to make cakes for the heavenly things <note>often translated as "The Queen of Heaven."</note> etc.* Where, without a doubt, the Prophet censures various idolaters: both those who passed their sons through fire for Molech, and others who worshipped the host of heaven and made <term>cauuanim<note>Hebrew: כונים (kawwanim), sacrificial cakes used in pagan worship.</note></term>, a word peculiar to this Prophet, which signifies certain <term>ektypa<note>Greek: ἔκτυπα; relief-molded or embossed forms.</note></term> cakes—that is, forms pressed out according to the design of the idols to which they were to be offered. The second part was the *object of the precept*, that is, *to whom that law was prescribed*. Those, however, were the Priests; for just as it belonged only to the Priests to sacrifice, so it pertained to them to tend the sacred fire—not indeed to light it; for that was the duty of the High Priest, who was according to the order of Melchizedek <note>A reference to the eternal priesthood mentioned in Genesis and the Epistle to the Hebrews.</note>; but once lit, to cherish it, nourish it, and take care that it was not extinguished. And Lyranus <note>Nicholas of Lyra, an influential Franciscan teacher whose literal commentaries on the Bible were highly regarded.</note> says that two small pieces of wood were added daily, not out of the necessity of the matter, but because of God's command. The *Historical* reason was that since the fire had been lit from heaven, God willed that the burnt offerings be consumed by it as a sign of His approval of the victims. The *Allegorical* reason was that when God rejected "foreign" fire, He signified that no doctrine ought to flourish in the Church unless it is heavenly or revealed to us from heaven, rather than devised by men. That sacred fire had to be perpetually nourished by the Priest because it was a symbol of the Holy Spirit, who ought to be the perpetual Teacher of the Pastors and the Church through the word divinely handed down. Hence the Apostles are called *taught by God* <note>original Greek: Θεοδίδακτοι ("Theodidaktoi")</note>, and concerning the faithful, John says, *The Anointing will teach you all things*.

Before the Levitical priesthood <note>The lineage of priests descended from Levi, established in the book of Leviticus.</note> was instituted, there were truly legitimate Priests, for the priesthood was attached to the right of the firstborn, or to those who were more worthy of that right even if they were younger, such as Abel and Jacob. This is why Esau is called *profane* by Paul in the Epistle to the Hebrews, because he had traded such a sacred thing—that is, the right of the firstborn and the priestly office—for a morsel of food. Furthermore, when the Priesthood of Aaron was established, during the first and more solemn sacrifice, God even sent down fire from heaven to approve his office; and he did this for the rest of the Priests, both for his successors in the highest dignity, the <term>High Priests</term> <note>original Greek: ἀρχιερέων (archieréōn)</note>, and for the lesser Levites. This was also observed during the dedication of the temple performed by Solomon. For while he was sacrificing, fire descended from heaven so that God might prove the Holiness of the temple, all the rites, and especially the sacrifices that were to be offered there by the Priests. And finally, in the time of Elijah, fire also descended so that it might be known by all who were the true Priests of God—whether it was Elijah or the followers of Baal—and thus God won authority for his servants and Ministers. This is not unlike how he secured the highest authority for his son, the supreme Prophet and Priest of the Church forever, when fire descended from heaven at his baptism, namely the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove.

The Priests, therefore, did two things: First, in an ordinary capacity, they nourished and cherished the sacred fire on the altar so that it would not be extinguished. Second, in an extraordinary capacity, during solemn sacrifices, they obtained celestial fire from God; as is clear from the example of Elijah, whereas the <term>High Priests</term> <note>original Greek: ἀρχιερεῖς (archiereis)</note> such as those of Baal were unable to obtain it. This was because God did not approve of their sacrifices, nor did he allow Satan at that time to deceive men with his tricks, as he had done through the Magicians of Pharaoh when God had hardened his heart. This is also what John predicted the Antichrist would do in Revelation 13:13, when he says: *And he performs great signs, so that he even makes fire come down from heaven to earth in the sight of men.* By this miracle, he pretends to prove that he is sent by God, mimicking the deed of Elijah, who, to prove he was a true Prophet of God, made fire come down from heaven in 2 Kings 1:10, 12. In Zechariah 3:2 and 1 Corinthians 3:15, *to be saved or snatched from the fire* means to be delivered from the most serious calamities. From this comes the proverb *fleeing the smoke, he fell into the fire*, which is used when someone falls from a heavy evil into an even heavier one. 3. Specifically, fire is used to represent the *punishments of the damned*; hence Matthew 3:12 and Luke 3:17 call it unquenchable fire <note>original Greek: πῦρ ἄσβεστον (*pyr asbeston*)</note>. and Matthew 18:8 calls it *eternal fire*. All these things were truly fulfilled in Christ, who was the sacrificed Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5), and he was inwardly and entirely [consumed] by that fire. Finally, after the <term>holocaust</term> <note>A religious animal sacrifice that is completely consumed by fire; from the Greek *holokaustos* meaning "wholly burnt."</note> was finished, and truly *entirely burnt* <note>original Greek: ὅλως καυσὸν (*holos kauson*)</note>, he then cried out with a loud voice, "it is finished," and surrendered his soul to God the Father, so that even that most sacred fire might ascend to God the Father like the incense of a most sweet aroma.

The fourth part is the *purpose of the sacred fire*, or why that fire was maintained on the altar.

I. So that God might witness by this miracle that this form of worship was established by Him.

II. To prove the calling of His ministers, showing that He truly called Aaron and his successors to the duty of sacrificing and had instituted all the priests.

III. So that the Church might be certain that such worship was pleasing to God.

IV. To teach that our victims ought to be burned by heavenly fire—that is, that we ourselves must be plainly purified by the fire of the Holy Spirit so that we and our offerings might please God.

V. To be a symbol of God's benevolence and the forgiveness of all sins. This is why in Genesis 4 it is said that God looked upon Abel and his sacrifice—first upon his person, then upon his offering. Therefore, that sacred fire was a symbol of God's gracious presence. As seen in Leviticus 9:24 and Psalm 20:3: *May He remember all your gifts, and reduce your burnt offering to ashes, most fully.* <note>The author cites Psalm 40:4, likely following a different numbering system or referencing the Vulgate tradition; the text mirrors the sentiment of modern Psalm 20:3.</note>

VI. Conversely, in another respect, it was to be a symbol of divine wrath against sins and sinners. For just as the victims were consumed by that fire, so sinners would have been consumed by the fire of divine judgment or in the fire of <term>Gehenna</term> <note>A historical valley near Jerusalem used as a metaphor for a place of fiery spiritual punishment or Hell.</note>, were it not for the blood of the true victim being shed. This is evident in those who were not washed in the blood of that sacred victim, for they were devoured by heavenly fire—such as the two captains of fifty and their men in the time of Elijah (2 Kings 1:10, 12, etc.).

Thus, every faithful person, affected by this heavenly fire, should utterly consume their lustful desires, according to the words of the Blessed Augustine: *ignorance is diminished as the truth shines more and more; lust is diminished as charity burns more and more.* <note>original Latin: "ignorantia minuitur veritate magis magisque lucente; concupiscentia minuitur charitate magis magisque feruente."</note> 

ix. It was meant to signify the fire of the Holy Spirit, which descended visibly on the day of Pentecost in the form of tongues of fire (Acts 2). This Spirit causes our bodies to stand as living sacrifices, holy, rational, and acceptable to God, as described in Romans 12:1. By burning away the "old man" and our fleshly nature, the Spirit mortifies them, so that the "new man" may rise with the fire of charity. Hence, John 3 [says]: *He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.* Through a <term>hendiadys</term> <note>original Latin: "Endyadin"; a figure of speech where two words are used to express one complex idea. Here, "Spirit and fire" means a Spirit that acts like fire.</note>, this means the Spirit who is like fire or fiery, purifying us in the manner of fire. 

x. To signify the heavenly fire of truth, which does not originate from <term>will-worship</term> <note>original Greek: ἐθελοπερισσοθρησκείαις (*etheloperissothrēskeiais*); religious rites chosen by humans rather than commanded by God.</note>, but from heavenly revelation; thus, traditions are banished from the house of God like "strange fire." 

xi. It could also signify that fire of divine power by which the redemption of the body will occur, just as the redemption of the soul occurred previously. By this, the bodies of the living will be transformed <term>in the twinkling of an eye</term> <note>original Greek: ἐν ῥιπῇ ὀφθαλμοῦ (*en rhipē ophthalmou*)</note>, and this mortal nature shall put on immortality in the resurrection of the flesh. 

xii. It had to be that sacred and heavenly fire so that it might act more powerfully and effectively upon the victims to be consumed, and thus signify the infinite efficacy of the Holy Spirit. For often elemental fire was unable to consume the entire victim; for there are often small parts of an animal which, like <term>fire-moths</term> <note>original Latin: "pyraustarum"; refers to a mythical insect or moth believed by the ancients to live in fire.</note>, [escape] the power of the fire...

Since there were various kinds of festivals among the Jews, they were either based on days, such as the Sabbath returning every week; or on months, such as the New Moon or New Moons, held on the first day of every month; or on years. These year-based festivals were of two kinds: for they either returned after many years, such as the Sabbath of the land [the Sabbatical Year] and the Jubilee year; or they returned every year, and for that reason are called "annual." These latter festivals lasted for several days, but the first and last days [were kept] with equal solemnity...

...were to be celebrated. We have already treated several of these various festivals, either in our study on the Sabbath or elsewhere. For the present, we are undertaking a discussion only of the annual festivals under divine guidance. But so that these may be discussed in an orderly fashion <note>original Greek: τεταγμένως (*tetagmenos*); meaning in a systematic or arranged manner</note>: I. *We shall briefly present something concerning festivals in general.* II. *Specifically concerning the types of annual festivals.* III. *Concerning the purpose of those festivals.*

I. Festivals were most ancient among the Jews; long ago they were prescribed by God with great reason, so that on those days God might be most devoutly celebrated, assemblies might be held, victims sacrificed, and prayers poured out to God. Hence they are commonly called *the festivals of the Jews* (John 11:55), sometimes *appointed times* (Galatians 4:10), sometimes *fixed holidays*, or *solemnities of God*. Sometimes "festival" is taken to mean the sacrifice of the festival, as in Exodus 23:18; and on those days the people rejoiced, according to that passage in Deuteronomy 16:14: *And you shall rejoice in your festival day*. From this comes the fact that they used to dance on festival days. Wherefore the Hebrew <term>chag</term> <note>original: חג (*chag*)</note>, meaning "festival," is derived from a root which means not only *to celebrate a festival*, but also *to dance*. From this, the custom later prevailed among the Pagans <note>original: *Ethnicos*; non-Jewish nations</note> so that on festival days, games were held in honor of the gods. The Isthmian and Olympic games, etc., are known to everyone, to which all of Greece once flocked; from there was born the famous era called the Olympiads, just as the <term>lustra</term> <note>a purification ritual performed every five years following a census</note> were among the Romans, and as centuries were numbered *by the secular games*. There were, therefore, among the ancients <term>lawful days</term> <note>original: *fasti dies*; days when legal and public business could be conducted</note> and <term>common days</term> <note>original: *profesti*; days for ordinary work</note>; the former were those on which it was not permitted to do anything [secular], while on the latter, by contrast, it was lawful to handle private and public affairs.

But indeed, if the Pagans celebrated festivals superstitiously and in honor of false gods—indeed, even behaving themselves on those days quite immoderately and petulantly, being vastly wanton—the Hebrews expressed this with the word <term>chagag</term> <note>original: חגג (*chagag*)</note>, which not only means *to celebrate a festival* and *to dance* as said above, but also—at least by a <term>misuse of terms</term> <note>original: *catachrestice*; the use of a word in a way that departs from its strict meaning, here suggesting a linguistic irony</note>—*to stagger*, because those rascals were accustomed to stagger in the manner of drunks. In this way, the Jews observed festivals religiously, with various ceremonies and great solemnity, and this was according to God’s command and in honor of the true God; among them, just as the first day of each month was celebrated and sacred, from which...

<page-num>763</page-num>
<header>THE REVEALOR OF SECRETS.</header>

It has been observed by others that the Jews now use various names for the months which were brought over from the Persians, Medes, and Babylonians during the time of the exile. This is why those names of the months are not found in the earlier books of Scripture, but only in those of the Prophets or others who lived after the Babylonian captivity, such as Zechariah, Daniel, Ezra, and Esther. It was therefore worthwhile to know in which month the Jewish festivals are celebrated, and why in one month rather than another; for these matters were not arranged by chance.

It should be noted, however, that the days of the festivals were not equally solemn among the Hebrews; for the intermediate days between the first and the eighth were less solemn, while the first and eighth days were the most solemn. For this reason, on the first and eighth days, because they were entirely solemn, it was not permitted to do any work; on the other hand, during the intermediate days, because they were not entirely festive, it was lawful to do certain works that were not forbidden once the sacred rites were completed. And therefore all these were distinguished as *festivals, non-festivals, and intermediate-festivals.* *Festivals* were the feast days on which it was a sin to do work outside of sacred duties. *Non-festivals*, by contrast, were common days on which it was permitted to do any work whatsoever. *Intermediate-festivals* were the middle days, on which there was less solemnity, and in which not all works were forbidden—as is evident in the festivals of Passover and Tabernacles. This is similar to how today among the Catholics <note>original: "Pontificios", referring to the Roman Catholic Church</note> the first and last weeks of Lent are more strictly observed, and thus the latter is called <term>by way of excellence</term> <note>original Greek: kat’ exochēn</note> Holy Week. This is why among the Jews mention is made of the <term>great festival</term> <note>Hebrew: mohed gadol</note>, and the <term>small festival</term> <note>Hebrew: mohed katon</note>. For by "small festival," they understood the intermediate-festivals. In the second part of the Talmud, which they call the *Seder* <note>The "Order," specifically Seder Moed dealing with festivals</note>, it treats festivals in twelve books. The eleventh of these is called the *small festival* <note>Moed Katon</note>, because it deals with the intermediate-festivals; and the twelfth is <term>festivity</term> <note>Hebrew: chagiga</note>, so named because of the festive appearance of males three times a year in Jerusalem—namely, at the festivals of Passover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles—according to the command of God in Exodus 23:17. From this requirement, however, the deaf, the blind, the lame, the simple-minded, and those with obstructed knees <note>referring to those physically unable to make the journey or perform the rituals</note> are excused.

<sig>CCCCC ij</sig>

As has been observed by others, the Jews now use various names for the months which were brought over from the Persians, Medes, and Babylonians during the time of the exile. This is why those specific names of the months are not found in the earlier books of Scripture, but only in those of the Prophets or other writers who lived after the Babylonian Captivity, such as Zechariah, Daniel, Ezra, and Esther. It was therefore worth the effort to know in which month the Jewish festivals were celebrated, and why in one month rather than another; for these matters were certainly not arranged at random.

It must be observed, however, that among the Hebrews, the solemn days of the festivals were not all of equal status; for the intermediate days between the first and the eighth were less solemn, while the first and eighth days were the most solemn. For this reason, on the first and eighth days, because they were entirely solemn, it was not permitted to perform any work. Conversely, on the intermediate days, because they were not entirely festive, it was lawful to perform certain works that were not forbidden after the sacred rites were completed. Therefore, all these were distinguished as **festivals, work-days, and intermediate-days.** <note>original: *festa, profesta & interfesta*</note>. **Festivals** were the holy days on which it was a sin to do any work outside of sacred duties. **Work-days**, on the other hand, were common days on which it was permitted to do any work whatsoever. **Intermediate-days** were those days in between, on which there was less solemnity, and in which not all works were forbidden, as is evident in the Feast of Passover and the Feast of Tabernacles. This is similar to how, among the Catholics <note>original: *Pontificios*</note> today, the first and last weeks of Lent are more strictly observed, and thus the latter is called <term>Holy Week</term> <note>original: κατ' ἐξοχήν (kat' exochen), meaning "preeminently" or "par excellence"</note>. Because of this, mention is made among the Jews of the <term>Great Festival</term> <note>Hebrew: *Moed Gadol* (מועד גדול)</note> and the <term>Small Festival</term> <note>Hebrew: *Moed Katon* (מועד קטן)</note>. For by the "Small Festival," they understood the Intermediate-days. In the second part of the Talmud, which they call the **Seder** <note>Meaning "Order"</note>, the text treats festivals in twelve books. The eleventh of these is called *Moed Katon*, because it deals with the intermediate days; and the twelfth is called **Chagiga** <note>Hebrew: *Chagigah* (חגיגה), meaning "Festival-offering"</note>, which refers to the festive appearance of all males three times a year in Jerusalem—namely, at the festivals of Passover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles—according to the commandment of God in Exodus 23:17. From this obligation, however, the following are exempt: the deaf, the blind, the lame, the simple-minded, and those with defects in the geni- <note>The text likely concludes with *genitalibus* (genitals) on the following page; see catchword "piuntur" likely from *excipiuntur* (are exempted).</note>

<meta>catchword: piuntur</meta>

And yet, although ceremonies flourished under the economy of the Old Testament, and consequently there were many feasts—whereby even among the Arabs the same word that signifies a "feast" also denotes "ceremonies," namely *hadid had* <note>original: *hadid had*</note>—nevertheless, the Jews did not indulge in excessive luxury when celebrating their festivals. The number of their feasts was strictly defined (indeed, that Arabic word also means "to define"). But the followers of the Pope <note>the author uses the term *Pontificij*</note>, introducing not only Judaism but also Paganism <note>original: *Ethnicismus*</note> into the Christian Church, multiplied feast days into infinity. Just as the Pagans (according to the inventory of Varro, the most learned of the Romans) worshipped thirty thousand gods and three hundred Jupiters, so the Papists call upon countless Saints, to whom they have dedicated festive days and peculiar solemnities. And just as the *Pantheon* <note>A Roman temple dedicated to all gods</note> was established among the Pagans so that no god from such a great multitude would be forgotten, so among the Papists, lest they pass over anyone from that massive crowd of Saints, they celebrate the Feast of All Saints on a single solemn day every year. 

But just as many gods were worshipped among the Pagans who never actually existed, so too in the Roman Church, countless Saints are worshipped and their festivals celebrated who never lived among mortals—such as the eleven thousand virgins, the seven sleepers, George, Christopher, Photinus, Guerlicouus, Emenehouus, Longinus <note>traditionally the name of the soldier who pierced Jesus' side</note>, Gingolfus, and so on. And just as among the Pagans there were gods of the greater and lesser nations, as well as "middle" gods; so it is among the Papists. There are the *Blessed*, then the *Saints*, and the "little saints" <note>original: *sanctuli*</note>. Because of this, **Worship** <note>original: *Latria* — technically reserved for God alone</note> is owed to some, **Veneration** <note>original: *Dulia* — for saints</note> to others, and **High Veneration** <note>original: *Hyperdulia* — specifically for the Virgin Mary</note> to others. Great festivals are dedicated to some, while for others there are minor feasts and "between-festivals" <note>original: *interfesta*</note>.

It must certainly be confessed that this heap of festivals began long ago in the time of the Emperor Constantine, when peace was restored to the Church after so many great persecutions and "halcyon days" had arrived. -># ANTHONII CREGVTI<-
### 766

...[the daily] sacrifice signified the perpetuity of the sacrifice of Christ, who *once and for all* <note>original: *ἐφάπαξ* (ephapax)</note> and through a single offering consecrated those to be sanctified forever. (Hebrews 10). Or, according to Thomas Aquinas <note>A 13th-century Italian theologian whose *Summa Theologica* became a foundation for Western Christian thought.</note> (Part 1-2, question 102, article 4), it signified the perpetuity of Divine blessedness.

II. Temporal feasts, such as the Sabbath and the New Moons <term>New Moons: *Neomeniæ*, monthly festivals marking the beginning of the lunar month</term>, signified the memory of the creation and governance of the world; these were repeated more frequently because they were common benefits to the whole human race. And according to Thomas, the feast of the New Moon was celebrated at the new moon, and not at the full moon, to avoid the cult of idolaters who sacrificed to the Moon at that time. And that solemnity occurred with every moon, because these lower earthly things vary principally according to the course of the moon.

III. Anniversary feasts were celebrated because of peculiar benefits granted to the Jewish people: **Passover** <note>original: *Pascha*</note> in memory of the liberation from Egypt; **Pentecost** in memory of the giving of the Law; the **Feast of Trumpets** in memory of the deliverance of Isaac, when Abraham found the ram caught by its horns—which were represented by the horns they used as trumpets. The **Feast of Atonement** in memory of the atonement for sins, especially the idolatry of the [golden] calf.

**The Feast of Tabernacles** <term>Scenopegia: from the Greek for "tent-pitching," referring to the festival of Sukkot</term> was held in memory of Divine protection in the desert when they lived in tents; for this reason, in this feast, they were required to have the fruit of a most beautiful tree, that is, the citron <note>original: *citrum*, the etrog used in Jewish ritual</note>, and the wood of thick-leaved branches, that is, the myrtle, which are fragrant, and palm fronds and willows of the brook, which retain their greenness for a long time. And these are found in the promised land to signify that God had led them through the arid land of the desert to a delightful land. It was also called the "feast of gathering" or "assembly," because at that time the necessities for the expenses of divine worship were collected from the people. And it signified the unification of the people and the peace granted in the promised land.

But among those anniversary feasts, three were major, namely ***Passover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles***, as is clear from Exodus 23:14 etc. and Deuteronomy 16:16; and others were minor, namely the feast of trumpets and atonement.

These were instituted by Judas Maccabeus (1 Maccabees 4) in memory of the dedication of the temple. From which comes ἐγκαίνια <note>original: *enkainia*</note>, that is, renewals or dedications. And John 10:22 mentions the "Feast of Dedication" <note>original: *Encania*</note>. Regarding this passage, Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a prominent French Protestant theologian and successor to John Calvin.</note> observed that the temple was consecrated by solemn dedication three times: first by Solomon (1 Kings 8) in the seventh month, which is Autumn; then after its restoration by Nehemiah, on the third day of the twelfth month, which falls in February and March (Ezra 6:15, Nehemiah 12); and thirdly by Judas Maccabeus after the temple was cleansed (1 Maccabees 4). In the first two dedications, no feast was instituted, but in the last one, as is clear from 1 Maccabees 4, it is expressly recorded that a feast was established in memory of that event, to be celebrated by Judas Maccabeus in the month of Kislev <note>A month in the Hebrew calendar falling in November–December.</note>, which for the most part corresponds to our December.

Furthermore, the feast of *Purim* was celebrated, which the Jews kept in memory of the miraculous liberation they obtained when the wicked Haman plotted the slaughter and fatal extermination of the entire people. Hence the "days of Purim" (Esther 3:7 and 9:26, 28, etc.) from the Persian word *pur*, meaning *lot*, which Haman ordered to be cast for the slaughter of the Jews. This feast is still celebrated today by the Jews in the month of February, and on the 11th, 12th, 13th, 14th, and 15th days; with unique ceremonies, they read the book of Esther, which is called by the Jews מגילה <note>original: *megilla*</note>, "The Scroll," from which reading this feast takes its name. Afterward, they eat, drink, lead dances, and act excessively wild, even more so than the Pagans in the festivals of Bacchus <note>original: *Bacchanalibus* — ancient Roman festivals characterized by drunken revelry.</note>. The Talmudists <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note> relate more about this feast in the *Seder Moed, Book of Megillah*, as Johannes Buxtorf <note>A celebrated Hebraist (1564–1629) known for his authoritative studies of Jewish customs and the Hebrew language.</note> also observed in his review of the Talmudic work. But leaving those things aside, come now, let us discuss the more solemn annual feasts, and first, the Passover.

Passover was celebrated among the Jews on the 14th day of the first month, Abib or Nisan, which corresponds to our March (Leviticus 23:4-5, etc.). First, it was a memorial <note>original: *μνημόσυνον* (mnemosynon)</note> of the liberation from Egypt; second, it was a significant type <note>original: *typus σημαντικὸς* (typus semantikos)</note> of the redemption from spiritual Egyptian servitude through Christ. ### 768

[The festivals are so] designated, which is not derived from πάσχω <note>original: *paschō*, "I suffer"</note>, *I suffer*, according to the opinion of certain ancients who were deceived by their ignorance of the Hebrew language. Rather, it comes from the Hebrew פסח <note>original: *Pesach*</note> and the Chaldaic termination פסחא <note>original: *Pascha*</note>, which signifies a *passing over*. But we shall omit those points of our own accord, as well as other matters regarding commonplaces that are usually discussed in a *System of Theology*.

The Christian Passover succeeded that Jewish Passover; for according to the testimony of Paul in 1 Corinthians 5: *Christ our Passover is sacrificed*. First, the ancients disputed more sharply than was proper concerning the celebration of the Passover. Some, like the Easterners, celebrated it no differently than the Jews on the 14th day of the Moon; others, however, like the Westerners, celebrated it on the Lord's Day <note>Sunday</note> which followed after the 14th day of the Moon. Indeed, Pope Victor excommunicated all the Easterners, whom they used to call by the taunt *Tessarecadecatites*, or *Quartodecimans* <note>From the Greek and Latin words for "fourteenth," referring to those who insisted on the 14th of Nisan.</note>, from the fourteenth day of the Moon.

But indeed, to begin the matter from the very beginning <note>original: *ab ovo*, literally "from the egg"</note>, the ancients doubted whether the Jews and Christ celebrated the Passover on the same day, on account of the passages of Scripture in John 13 and 19. For in John 13:1, it is said that *Christ held the supper before the feast of the Passover*. And in chapter 19:31, it is held thus: *The Jews therefore, that the bodies might not remain on the cross on the Sabbath, because it was the Day of Preparation <note>original: *Paraſceue*</note>, (for that was a great Sabbath day), asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and they be taken away*. Nevertheless, it seems to be proven from this that Christ did not eat the Passover on the same day as the Jews; because Christ, who had come to fulfill the Law, not to abolish it, wished to sacrifice the Passover according to its prescription on Friday "between the two evenings" <note>A technical Hebrew term for the afternoon period of sacrifice.</note> and on the fourteenth day. Thus, on the same day, both the typical Passover <note>The sacrificial lamb</note> and the true, figured Passover <note>Christ himself</note> were sacrificed. But the Jews, following a very ancient observation, because the Passover fell on a Sabbath that year, sacrificed the Passover on that day [the Sabbath] so that two feast days would not follow one after the other. It is for this reason that the Evangelist calls it the *Great Sabbath*, that is, one especially celebrated and solemn because of the coincidence of a double celebration. But concerning these things, see Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a successor to Calvin.</note> on Matthew 26:17, who discusses this more extensively. See also Andreas Masius <note>A 16th-century Catholic scholar known for his expertise in Semitic languages.</note> on Joshua chapter 5, verse 9, who brings forward various opinions of the Hebrews concerning the time at which the Passover ought to be slaughtered and concerning the "two evenings."

...just as with the Rabbinic commentaries regarding the institution of the Passover on account of the reproach of the Egyptians—since the Egyptians worshiped sheep as gods. For in a very ancient commentary, *Exodus Rabba* <note>original: *Exodo Rabba*; a traditional Jewish midrash or homiletic interpretation of the Book of Exodus</note>, it is written: *The Egyptians worshiped the ram above all, and they believed him to be a God armed with fire, by which he might avenge himself from contempt. Therefore God, in order to make it clear how vain those mockeries of religion were, commanded his own people to slaughter the most choice rams everywhere; and to cook them with their own weapons, that is, with fire, and then to devour them whole.* Those are certainly the most vain commentaries of those men; nevertheless, Moses spoke truly in Exodus 8:26 when addressing Pharaoh: *We cannot sacrifice in Egypt. For we must sacrifice the abomination* <note>meaning the idols or gods</note> *of the Egyptians to the Lord our God,* etc. Hence Juvenal wrote regarding the superstition of the Egyptians: *Every table abstains from woolly animals; it is a crime there to slit the throat of a young goat.* <note>Juvenal, Satire 15. The poet is mocking Egyptian animal worship.</note> There is a similar commentary by Moses Gerundensis <note>Moses ben Nahman, also known as Nahmanides (1194–1270)</note> that the Israelites were commanded to slaughter and devour a ram for this reason in the middle of this first month, in which they were leaving Egypt: so that they might understand that they were liberated by the providence of God, and not by the influence of the stars. This was shown by treating that constellation with the greatest ignominy—the ram—which at that time held the principal position in the heavens <note>The zodiac sign of Aries, the Ram, is dominant in the month of Nisan/March.</note>. Away with those trifles! For those curious men are accustomed to making up little fables once they have bid farewell to the Scriptures.

But indeed, to return again to the time in which the Passover ought to be celebrated, four things come to be observed. 

I. **The most ancient custom of the Jews**, who by the sacred institution of the law celebrated the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month of Nisan (that is, March), as is clear from Exodus 8 in the institution of the Passover, and Joshua 5:10, when the Jews kept the Passover in the plains of Jericho, and often elsewhere. At that time, the firstborn of the Jews were saved from the sword of the Angel leaping over their houses; hence some translate *Pascha* as a "leap" <note>original: *saltum*</note>, like the German *hupf*, others (like Philo) as a "crossing over" <note>original: *διάβασιν* (diabasin) or *διαβατήρια* (diabatēria)</note>. Josephus calls it a "stepping over" <note>original: *ὑπέρβασιν* (hyperbasin)</note>; but Symmachus preferred to use the plural "passings over" <note>original: *ὑπερβάσεις* (hyperbaseis)</note>. 

II. **The celebration of Christ** at the last Passover, which was performed (as we said above) on the day before the celebration of the Jews, because in that year it coincided with the Sabbath. On account of the two festivals, it is called in John 19:31: *the Sabbath...*

The Europeans, lest they should seem to be *Judaizing* <note>adopting Jewish religious practices</note>, chose the Lord's Day after the 14th [day of the] Moon. Both sides, however, boasted of their own traditions; the former invoked John and Philip for their defense; the latter, indeed, Peter and Paul; but none relied on *written proof* <note>original Greek: ἐγγράφῳ ἀποδείξει</note>; *those who received these things passed them down to their successors as a law* <note>original Greek: οἱ ταῦτα παραλαβόντες ὡς νόμον τοῖς ἐπιγινομένοις παρέγραψαν</note>. Those who received such rites from their ancestors later transmitted them to posterity as if they were law. 

But at last, in the Council of Nicaea, by the order also of Emperor Constantine, all the Churches followed the custom of the Europeans. But since (as I said) Easter had to be celebrated on the Lord’s Day after the 14th [day of the] Moon, and at that time *ephemerides*—by which the movements of the planets are calculated—were not in use; the task was given to the Patriarch of Alexandria to signify the time of Easter to the other Bishops; which he then carried out by letter, which they therefore called a "Paschal Letter," such as the letter of Theophilus <note>Theophilus of Alexandria, who served as Patriarch from 385 to 412 AD.</note> which still exists. 

Moreover, that office was entrusted to the Alexandrian Bishop because the studies of mathematics always flourished in Egypt on account of the clarity of the climate; for since it rarely rained there, the sky was not clouded over by clouds which might impede the sight of the stars, just as the flooding of the Nile brought about the use of geometry. Then the Golden Number was invented, which would show the new moons and full moons, so that always and everywhere after the true full moon...

Easter was to be celebrated. This surely did not happen without God's providence, so that it might be known to us that the Church is free to designate the dates of its festivals. No one is bound by a harsh necessity, since it is a characteristic of the Antichrist to "change the times and the seasons," as was foreshadowed in the figure of Antiochus in the Book of Daniel. This custom was later observed in the Christian Church under the rule of the Christian Emperors, as is clear from the laws of **Valentinian**, **Theodosius**, and **Arcadius** (found in Book 1 of the Code, Title 4).

He lived during the time of the Pagan Emperors, yet the book says that prisoners obtained their freedom on the day of Easter—a practice that is certain beyond a doubt to have been done only under the rule of Christians. After the celebration of Easter, there was the feast of the **first-fruits**, in which certain sheaves of grain were offered to be waved before the altar toward the four regions of the world. ...the giver, and therefore the firstfruits <term>original: *primitias*; the first part of a harvest offered to God as an act of sanctification</term> of the crops must be offered in gratitude for His favors; just as He also willed that the firstborn of animals should be consecrated to Him, according to that law: *the male that opens the womb shall be holy.* <note>Referencing Exodus 13:2 and Luke 2:23.</note> By the firstfruits, therefore, the entire batch was sanctified: hence it was not permitted to eat bread or ears of grain except after the firstfruits had been offered, since both the harvest of the crops and their use depend on God’s blessing, and specifically because God had led Israel into possession of the land of Canaan. Pentecost was also twofold, just like Passover—namely, the Jewish and the Christian. ### 773

The solemn proclamation <term>original: *promulgatio*; the formal announcement or enactment of a law</term> was made on the day of Pentecost. That the Old Law remained in force until the death of Christ, and the New Law began from that time, is established by the fact that neither Christ nor the Apostles spoke publicly to the people [of its enactment] beforehand; furthermore, the New Law ought not to have been solemnly proclaimed until all the mysteries of our redemption were completed. Thus, at His death, Christ cried out, *It is finished.* <note>original: *Consummatum est*; from John 19:30.</note>

Moreover, just as the Old Law was solemnly proclaimed on Mount Sinai on the fiftieth day after the first Passover of the Jews; so the New Law ought to have been solemnly proclaimed on Mount Sion on the fiftieth day after the first Passover of the Christians. For that the proclamation of the Old Law was a type <term>original: *typus*; a prophetic symbol or foreshadowing</term> of the proclamation of the New Law is testified by Augustine in his 119th Epistle and Leo in his first sermon on Pentecost. Finally, all the conditions for a solemn proclamation apply to that new enactment. For it was held in the royal city of Jerusalem, with people present from all nations, as Luke testifies in **Acts 2**. A sermon was delivered by Peter, who, according to Tertullian, "was the first to use the key," <note>original: *primus clauem imbuit*; a reference to Peter using the "keys of the kingdom" (Matthew 16:19) to open the Gospel to the world.</note> and in that sermon the principal chapters of the entire Gospel doctrine were included; and then, in truth, the use of the Sacraments, which are necessary to the New Law, began.

And this is perhaps the reason for the immense joy of the Ancients exulting during the days of Pentecost. For the earliest Fathers say that not only on the fiftieth day, but all those fifty days after Passover were so dedicated to joy that it was not permitted to fast during them, nor to pray kneeling, but rather standing; the very ancient author Tertullian records this in his book *On the Soldier's Crown* <note>original: *De corona militis*; a 3rd-century Christian treatise.</note>. And all those fifty days were festivals. Hence the same Tertullian says that if the individual solemnities of the Gentiles were counted, they could not fill our Pentecost—that is, those fifty days.

Although Pentecost was a Jewish feast, the naming is not Hebrew, like *Pascha* <note>Passover</note>, but Greek, from the word *pentēkostē* <note>original: *πεντηκοστή*</note>, with "day" <note>original: *ἡμέρα* (*hēmera*)</note> understood, as if you were to say, *the fiftieth day*. Since the Christian Church was coalescing from both Jews and Gentiles...

# ANTOINE CREGUT
### 774

And since the Jews used the *Septuagint* <note>original: *L XX.*; the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> edition, while the Gentiles and likewise the Jews used the Greek original <term>original: *autographo*; referring here to the primary Greek text of the New Testament</term> of the New Testament, and furthermore since the Greek language flourished in the early days of the Church, it is no wonder that the word *Pentecost* <note>original: *πεντεκοστὴ*; meaning "fiftieth" [day]</note> was devised. It was also called the *feast of weeks*, or the *feast of seven weeks*, because that was the length of time between Passover and Pentecost. It was also called the *feast of harvest*, because it fell at the time when the harvest of crops began in Palestine. Furthermore, it was called the *day or feast of firstfruits*, because the firstfruits of the gathered crops were then offered.

But indeed, just as the Greek Church from the beginning observed the feast of Pentecost no differently than the Latin Church, so it continues to celebrate it annually today; for although they do not believe as we do that the *Holy Spirit* proceeds *from the Father and the Son* <note>This refers to the "Filioque" clause, a major point of contention where the Western Church added "and the Son" to the Creed, while the Eastern Church maintained the original phrasing</note>, but rather *from the Father through the Son*, they do not for that reason deny the procession of the *Holy Spirit* or His divinity, nor do they celebrate Pentecost any less in honor of the Holy Spirit. Thus, *Bellarmine* <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a prominent Jesuit Cardinal and theologian</note> is greatly deluded in Book 2, Chapter 30 of his work *On Christ*, when he derives the schism between the Eastern and Western Churches from this. That disagreement is not of such great importance that one should "stir up a storm in a teacup" <note>original: *fluctus in simpulo excitentur*; a Latin proverb for making a large fuss over a small matter</note> over it. Therefore, that Cardinal was considering these matters carelessly when, in the aforementioned passage, he wrote that the cause of the Greeks' destruction was their stubbornness in error regarding the procession of the Holy Spirit. For, he says, on the very feast days of the Holy Spirit, Constantinople was captured by the Turks, the Emperor was slain, and the Empire was extinguished.

...perpetually on account of the spiritual captivity under the Babylonian kingdom.

The fourth festival was that of *trumpets* or *horns* <note>original: *tubarum* or *buccinarum*</note>; which fell on what is for us the first of September, as noted in Leviticus 23:23, 24, etc. And therefore in Numbers 10:1, 2, etc., God commands Moses *that he should make two silver trumpets for summoning the assembly and for commanding the departure of the camps. And He also commands that the Priests should blow them, and summon the assembly to the door of the tent.* The use of those trumpets was twofold: one *military*, the other indeed *ecclesiastical*. The *military* use was for summoning the people, the Leaders, and the Commanders of thousands <term>original: *Chiliarchas*; from the Greek *chiliarchos*, a commander of 1,000 soldiers</term>, so that the signal for the departure of the camps and the expedition against enemies might be given. The *ecclesiastical* use was so that the people would be summoned to the celebration of festivals and in the making of sacrifices, as in Numbers 10:10.

But indeed, just as the use of the trumpets was either military or ecclesiastical, so also the *manner of blowing* was varied; for sometimes the sounding was made with a *broken sound*; sometimes it was not made with a *broken sound*. Numbers 10:6: *they shall blow with a broken sound in their departures.* For when the camps were moved, it was necessary according to the prescription of the law to blow with a broken sound. At the first time of sounding, the camps placed toward the East were moved; but at the second time, the camps that were pitched toward the South were moved, as is clear in the same chapter, verses 5 and 6. And if the leaders were to be summoned, they blew with only one trumpet; but if the whole people, they blew with two trumpets. And that sound was always uniform and continuous. But in the movement of the camps, and when the army was about to descend into battle, they blew with a broken sound, which they call *tarantara* <note>An onomatopoeic word for a trumpet blast, often associated with military signals</note>. But the Hebrews add a *mixed sound*, which is composed of both. They designated all those sounds by these various Hebrew names:

I. The fixed and equal sound they call תקיעה <note>original: *tekia* (Teki’ah); a long, straight blast</note>.
II. The broken sound they called שברים <note>original: *scheuarim* (Shevarim); literally "breakings," a series of three shorter notes</note>.
III. The mixed sound they called תרועה <note>original: *Teruah* (Teru’ah); a rapid series of short, staccato notes</note>.

Hence it is that the masters of the Hebrews expressed those blasts which they produce on the feast of trumpets by various symbols: תשר"ת [TaSHRaT], תש"ת [TaSHaT], תר"ת [TaRaT]. That is: *Teki’ah Shevarim Teru’ah Teki’ah*. It should be observed, however, that in the word תשרת [TaSHRaT], the letter taken from *Teru’ah* is not the first letter <note>original: ת (Tav)</note>, but the second <note>original: ש (Shin)</note>, so that this word might be distinguished from *Teki’ah*, which itself begins with the letter ת [Tav].

### ANTHONY CREGUTIUS

Otherwise, it is unusual to use letters other than the first in abbreviations, as Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629) was a celebrated Hebraist whose work on Jewish customs was standard for scholars of this era.</note> correctly observed in his *Hebrew Abbreviations*. According to that custom of sounding on the first day of the **New Year** <note>original Hebrew: *Rosh Hashanah*</note>, the horn-blower blows the horn three times with distinct sounds, namely (as has been said) the **steady**, the **broken**, and the **mixed**. Isaiah 27:13 deals with the first: **"the trumpet shall be blown"** <note>original Hebrew: *yitaka bashofar*</note>. For the word *taka* <note>the root of *tekiah*</note> properly signifies **"to fix"**, but when the noun **"trumpet"** <note>original Hebrew: *shofar*</note> is added, it signifies **"to sound with a steady and even blast"**, according to the phrasing of Scripture, as also in Numbers 10:5. The term **"shout"** <note>original Hebrew: *teruah*</note> is taken for a **"broken sound"**, from the root *rua*, meaning **"to sound with a wavering or broken blast."** And because it also broadly signifies **"to cry out"** (as in Judges 15:14), it came about that the Hebrews also used the term for a "mixed" sound.

Furthermore, it is most worthy of observation that it was the duty of the Priests, by God’s command, to sound the trumpets. For what today might seem unusual was then practiced most excellently and not without mystery. Since the Priests, in this duty, truly represented God's role, the people were perpetually reminded that they could not gather together, or go down to battle to engage with enemies, nor even celebrate feast days, except when their supreme Leader and King, Jehovah, summoned them through His Priests. This was so they would know they were God’s **chosen people** <note>original Greek: *laon periousion*; a people for His own special possession</note>, whom God ruled like a commander. They were to understand that victory was to be won from Jehovah Sabaoth <note>The Lord of Hosts</note> alone. For this reason, they paid a tax back to God as an acknowledgment of His sovereignty, namely the **sanctuary shekel** <term>original: *siclus Sanctuarij*; a holy coin required for the upkeep of the Tabernacle and Temple</term>. God willed this to be paid until the Jewish nation was cut off from being God’s people in the time of the Romans, when the shekel tax was diverted to the Roman Capitol <note>After the destruction of the Temple in 70 AD, the Roman Emperor Vespasian diverted the Temple tax to the Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus in Rome, known as the *Fiscus Judaicus*.</note> instead of the Temple. This is why Christ condemns the Pharisees who used trumpets before themselves during fasts and sacrifices for the sake of ambition and hypocrisy.

The fifth festival was that of **Atonements** <note>original: *expiationum*; referring to Yom Kippur</note>, on which the High Priest entered into the Sanctuary. This occurred on the tenth day after the Feast of Trumpets, which is the tenth of September <note>The author aligns the seventh Hebrew month, Tishrei, with September.</note>. That day was the most solemn festival for the Jews, because then a universal—though only symbolic—atonement for all sins was made. For this reason, it was celebrated every year as an anniversary festival, and the Jews also fasted—

For this reason, that day was called not only the **Day of Atonement** <note>original Hebrew: *Yom Ha-Kippur*; original Latin: *dies expiationis*</note>, but also, preeminently <note>original Greek: *kat' exochen*</note>, **The Day** <note>original Hebrew: *Yoma*</note>. All these things are accurately taught in the second part of the body of the Talmud, which concerns the festivals, in a specific book that is therefore titled **The Day** <note>original Hebrew: *Yoma*</note>. Even today, it is celebrated with such solemnity that it verges on superstition, with a fast proclaimed for a full twenty-four hours. Furthermore, they walk with bare feet, dressed outwardly in white, praying, reading day and night, and never sleeping, so that they might all the more quickly obtain the atonement of their sins from God.

It should be observed, however, that God required such great holiness on that day that the Sanctuary itself, though once dedicated and consecrated to God, nevertheless had to be purified again, as is clear from Leviticus, chapter 16, verses 16 and 32. This was not because the Sanctuary was not holy—namely that which was called preeminently <note>original Greek: *kat' exochen*</note> the **Holy of Holies**—and thus did not need atonement in itself, but rather in respect to the whole people whose sins were typically <note>A "typical" or "typological" relationship refers to the theological belief that Old Testament events and objects serve as "types" or prophetic shadows of New Testament realities.</note> atoned for within it. All these things concerned the people themselves, since the holiness of the Temple and its vessels was merely relative, not real; just as the impurity was also relative. For the mercy seat had not sinned, but the people in whose midst it stood had made it as if polluted and contaminated by the sins committed throughout the whole year. This was atoned for by the blood of a goat in place of the blood of the people, and by typically signifying the blood of Christ.

Therefore, all those rites recorded in Leviticus chapter 16 excellently foreshadowed <note>original Latin: *adumbrabant*, literally "to cast a shadow of"</note> the atonement of our sins performed through the blood of Christ. 1. The High Priest who on that day...

As he entered the Sanctuary, he wonderfully reflected Christ the Mediator, as the Apostle teaches in Hebrews, chapter 7, verse 11. That Priestly clothing, which he was required to be adorned with upon entry, foreshadowed the majesty and dignity of the Mediator. IV. The **washing** for himself and his family, and the sacrifice, was a symbol and a confession of his own impurity; the High Priest testified that he himself sought the expiation of this impurity in the true Mediator, and therefore that he was nothing more than a symbolic <term>typological mediator<gloss>A "type" or "typical" figure is a person or event in the Old Testament believed to foreshadow a "reality" in the New Testament, specifically Christ.</gloss></term>.

These things are graphically depicted by Paul in Hebrews chapters 6, 7, and 8, and are found to be fulfilled in every detail in Christ.

VI. Furthermore, it was to signify that the Messiah was to be offered once at the end of the ages for the sins of the world.

Therefore, from this, the **Catholics** <note>original Latin: *Pontificij*; literally "the Papists," referring here to Roman Catholic doctrine.</note> wrongly repeat their "unbloody sacrifice" and the Mass, since Christ, in the same sacrifice of the cross, was both truly slaughtered and carried our sins, and was thus truly foreshadowed by the two goats. This indeed fits better and is simpler than the saying of some—namely, that the slaughtered goat signifies Christ's death, while the other "emissary" goat designates his resurrection. It was, moreover, a thanksgiving for all the gathered crops, hence the naming as the "Feast of the Ingathering" in Exodus 23. # ANTHONY CREGUTUS #

The **Feast of Tabernacles** <note>original: "festum tabernaculorum," also known as Sukkot</note> is considered very solemn among the Rabbis; for this reason, they call it **Great Hosanna** <note>original Hebrew: הושענא רבא "Hoshana Rabbah"</note>, as if you were to call it the "Great Festival of Help" or "Great Salvation." For the word *hosanna* is the same as saying "save now" or "save, I pray." They use this term because they pray for the salvation and forgiveness of the sins of the whole people, as well as for the prosperity of the newly begun year, the festival of which preceded this one, celebrated on the **first of September** <note>The author is likely referring to Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year, which usually falls in September. The "Calends" refers to the first day of the month.</note>. This is why all the prayers composed for that festival frequently repeat the word *hosanna* and almost always begin with it. From this, it is easy to guess why the prayers of this feast are called **Hosannoth** <note>original Hebrew: הושענות</note> in the plural. Thus, the Rabbis emphasize these things: *they say the Hosannoth*, or *the Order of the Hosannoth*—that is, the sequence of prayers for the Hosanna festival. Furthermore, because they carry a bundle of willow branches during that festival and cry out "hosanna" while waving them, it has become common practice to call the entire bundle a **hosanna**. Thus it is said in the **Talmud**:

> A man should not take up the Hosanna bundle with a cloth; that is to say, he should not wrap his hand in a linen cloth or a napkin. <note>This ensures direct contact with the ritual object, as required by Jewish law.</note>

It should also be noted that the Jews do not dare to **let blood** or open a vein on Great Hosanna; and this is what the seventh day of the festival is called. These matters are cited at greater length by **Johannes Buxtorf** <note>A famous 16th-century Christian Hebraist</note> from the Talmudists, and by **Johannes Drusius** in his commentary on Hebrew words in the New Testament.

Up to this point, there have been six annual festivals established in the **Mosaic Law**, besides those established at other times by holy and pious men, such as **Purim** and the **Feast of Dedication** <note>original: "Encænia," referring to Hanukkah</note>, which were mentioned above. But you might ask: why then, in Exodus 23, are only three festivals commanded to be celebrated?

> Three times you shall celebrate a feast. <note>Exodus 23:14</note>

In that passage, God commands them to gather and appear in the presence of God only three times each year. However, that is said because of the **greater solemnity** observed on those three festival days, which carried a deeper religious obligation because they commemorated the most illustrious of God's benefits. But now, among the **Papists** <note>A derogatory term used by the author for Roman Catholics</note>, the number of festivals has grown so large that whatever the Pagans or Jews observed is nothing compared to that pomp and multitude of Romish feasts. Indeed, many are ridiculous and born from a mere play on words, such as the **Feast of the Spear**—referring to the lance that pierced Christ's side—and the **Feast of the Nails**,

By the **festival of atonement** <note>The Day of Atonement, or Yom Kippur</note> is signified the cleansing from sins of the **Christian people**. By the **festival of tabernacles** <note>The Jewish festival of Sukkot, commemorating the Israelites' dwelling in booths in the wilderness</note> is signified their pilgrimage in this world, in which they walk by advancing in virtues. By the **festival of the assembly and gathering** <note>Referring to the "eighth day" of the festival, Shemini Atzeret</note> is signified the congregation of the faithful in the kingdom of heaven: and for this reason that festival was said to be most holy. And these three festivals were continuous with one another: because it is necessary for those cleansed from vices to advance in virtue until they arrive at the vision of God, as is said in Psalm 83 <note>Psalm 84 in modern English Bibles</note>." Thus far Thomas.

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS.

Just as from the Greek original of the New Testament in the centuries following the Apostles, it happened that *Pentecost*, *Scenopegia* <note>The Feast of Tabernacles or Booths</note>, *anathema* <note>A formal curse or something set apart for destruction</note>, and many other Greek terms remained in use; so too the name of the **Nazarene** remained in the Church. It is therefore the Hebrew word <term>נזיר</term> *nazir*, meaning **Nazirite** or **one who is separated**. For among the Hebrews, whoever was devoted to God by some particular worship and religion were called *separated*, because they were set apart from others by this institution. From this was born the naming of the **Pharisees** from "separation," because that word signifies the same thing <note>The name 'Pharisee' comes from the Hebrew 'parush', meaning 'separated'</note>; and the Holy Spirit seems to have alluded to this in Acts 13: *separate for me Paul and Barnabas* etc. And Paul, in Romans 1, says he is <term>ἀφωρισμένον</term> <note>original: aphōrismenon; set apart or appointed</note> to the Apostolic office.

However, it must be observed that there are two ways this word is accepted in Scripture. For sometimes it is taken *broadly* for any kind of separation, even in common and civil matters. Thus in Genesis 49:26, among the blessings of Joseph, *Jacob the parent* says: <term>נזיר</term> *let these things be on the head of Joseph and on the crown of the one separated from his brothers*. And in Leviticus 25:5: <term>נזירך</term> *Nezirecha*, *your separated [grapes]*, that is, those of the vine from which you separated yourself by pausing its cultivation <note>Referring to the Sabbatical year when vines were left unpruned</note>. The word <term>נזיר</term> is taken *strictly* for a holy and vowed separation, when the holy ones religiously and by a pious vow abstained from many things, such as from wine and from the shaving of the head. Hence <term>נזר</term> *nezer* signifies not only the Nazirite state, but also the **Hair**, which the Nazirites abstain from shaving. Therefore, **Nazirite** or **Nazarene** draws its origin from the Hebrew word which signifies two things: namely, *separation* and *abstinence* from something out of a vow and holiness. These two meanings fit perfectly with the vow of the Nazarenes, as will be seen shortly. The Arabs use the word <term>מתחרג</term> <note>mutaharraj</note> which is from the root <term>חרג</term> <note>haraja</note> which signifies *to curse, to execrate, or to be angry*. But by another naming they call it <term>נאסיך</term> *nasik*, which properly agrees with <term>נזיר</term> <note>nazir</note>; for it comes from the root <term>נסך</term> *nasak*, which signifies *to devote oneself to religion and piety: to sacrifice*. And this same word which signifies the **Nazirite state** is the same as "divine worship," and in another sense, **Continence, chastity, and temperance**. The Chaldeans <note>Aramaic speakers</note> use the word <term>נזירא</term> *nezira* from <term>נזר</term> *nesar*, "he separated," for the same reason as the Hebrews. It also signifies to abstain and restrain oneself from something. As for the Syrians, there is another reason for the name—

...of the naming, for Christ is called **Notsraya** <note>original: נצריא; the Syriac or Aramaic form of "Nazarene"</note>, from **Nazareth**, or from the Hebrew word <term>נצר</term> *netser*, meaning a **shoot** or **branch** <note>This refers to the prophecy in Isaiah 11:1 of a "shoot from the stem of Jesse"</note>. See Matthew 2:23. However, he is not named from the word <term>נזיר</term> *nazir* <note>meaning a consecrated Nazirite</note> according to the Syriac translator. The translators of the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek version of the Old Testament</note> sometimes translate the Hebrew *nazir* as *nazaraion* with an "a" [alpha], and at other times as *naziraion* with an "i" [eta]. But Matthew, in the passage cited above, substitutes an "o" [omega], saying *Nazoraios*. Perhaps this is because at that time, following the Syrian custom, they pronounced it *Nazoreth*, rather than *Nazareth* as the Hebrews did. For those words which the Hebrews pronounce with the "Camets" vowel are rendered with an "a" [alpha], but by the Syrians with an "o" [omega]. 

Thus, the word *Nazoraios* was formed according to the Syrian pronunciation. Nor do those **Nasarai** have a place here—those who were called *Nasaraioi* with a "sigma" [Σ] from the Syriac and Chaldean word <term>נסר</term> *nasser*, which means **to cut off** or **to abolish**. This was because they judged the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible</note> and the other books of the Old Testament to be fabricated and needing to be abolished. Furthermore, Greek authors sometimes translate the word <term>נזיר</term> *nazir* as "the one set apart," and at other times as "separated," "holy," "one who sanctifies," or "one who has been sanctified." Elsewhere, the Greek interpreters call those who were in positions of leadership and authority from the beginning "sanctified Nazirites."

These names from all these languages reveal to us, in some way, the nature of the Nazirite state. 

I. Since the Hebrew word signifies **separation**, it sufficiently declares the necessary condition of a Nazirite: that he be separated—that is, sanctified above others by reason of a vow and a peculiar religious institution. 

II. Since that Hebrew word, no less than the Chaldean, signifies **abstinence**, the nature of the vow is also indicated from that source. For the Nazirite (as is clear from Numbers 6) vowed **abstinence from wine and strong drink** <note>original: 'sicera'</note>, that is, any intoxicating drink. They held this in common with the Priests, who had to abstain from wine and strong drink during the time of their service (Leviticus 10). Thus, in this way, the Nazirites also approached priestly dignity. 

Among the Hebrews, this "strong drink" was <term>שכר</term> *shekar*, and in Greek *sikera*. As Jerome relates in his letter to Nepotian: *Every drink that can intoxicate—whether it is made from grain, or from the juice of fruits, or when honeycombs are boiled down into a sweet and exotic drink, or palm fruits are pressed into a liquid, or when water is colored by thick, cooked grains.* The Chaldean paraphrast <note>Likely referring to the Targum, an Aramaic commentary</note> understands "strong drink" to mean **aged wine**. For where the Hebrew text reads "he shall abstain from wine and strong drink" <note>original: מיין ושכר יזיר</note>, the Chaldean

Just as the word **nezer** signifies **hair** among the Hebrews, they allowed their hair to grow (as is clear from Numbers 6:5), which served as a symbol of their vow, so that they might be separated from others and distinguished by their own rule. Therefore, also following the sense of the Hebrew word **nazaru** <note>original: נזרו; meaning "to separate oneself"</note>, they abstained **from contact with the dead**, by which spiritual purity was signified. If a Nazirite happened to be defiled by contact with a corpse, an atonement had to be made, and this by offering a sacrifice of two turtledoves and performing the ritual of the hair twice; and furthermore, the days of his consecration had to begin again. For according to the vow, he was forced to abstain from the aforementioned things for exactly as many days as he had originally vowed to perform. But finally, once the vow was fulfilled, it was permitted to return to his former life.

It is **votive** when it was done voluntarily and by a free vow, whether by one's own will or that of one's parents. Judges 13:7: **from wine and intoxicating drink from his mother’s womb.** Likewise, the **Rechabites** in Jeremiah 35 [abstained] **from wine, agriculture, and houses**. The first of these prohibitions was derived from the Nazirite vow. However, the latter two seem to have flowed from a certain political or even ethical reasoning. For the father of the Rechabites <note>Jonadab, son of Rechab</note> wanted this kind of abstinence to be an exercise in sobriety and modesty for his sons, lest they be corrupted by the wicked examples of the city, or give themselves over to luxury, or gape after wealth and vain honors; instead, they were to remember perpetually that they were sojourners. For they were from the descendants of Jethro the Kenite, as can be gathered from 1 Chronicles 2 and Judges 4, who had joined themselves to the tribe of Judah, and yet had lived separately outside of the cities until then. **Pareus** <note>David Pareus, a prominent Reformed Protestant theologian (1548–1622)</note> also relates (in his commentary on Romans 14) that their father wanted to prepare them through a harder life to bear the public calamities in the destruction of the kingdom, which he had foreseen.

iii. There was also a certain **excellence** <term>ὑπεροχὴ; *hyperochē*, meaning preeminence or superiority</term> of the Nazirite vow arising from leadership. For this reason, a Nazirite is also named from **nezer** <term>נזר; *nezer*, meaning crown or diadem</term>. In this way, Joseph was a Nazirite (Genesis 49:26): **a Nazirite among his brothers** <note>original: נזיר אחיו; *nazir achiv*</note>, which is to say, **separated from his brothers as if to obtain the leadership**. And in Deuteronomy 33:16–17, it is said: **let these blessings come in abundance upon the head of Joseph, and upon the crown of the one separated from his brothers.** This **excellence** <term>ὑπεροχὴ</term> and leadership of Joseph over his brothers was truly and realistically fulfilled in **Christ the Nazarene**. Hence it is that, according to some, the title of Nazirite is attributed to men of primary dignity and **excellence** <term>ὑπεροχῆς</term> in Lamentations 4:7: **Her Nazirites were purer than snow; they were whiter than milk; they were more ruddy in body than corals; their polishing was like sapphire.**

Furthermore, some Nazirites were **temporary**, while others were **perpetual**. The **temporary** ones were those who kept the vow for a certain time; for just as it was a matter of free choice to make the vow, so it was permitted to vow until a certain time and afterward be released from the vow. The **perpetual** Nazirites were those who were made so by the command of God, such as **Samson** (Judges 13:5, 7 and 16:17) and **John the Baptist** (Luke 1:15). These were not "common" Nazirites like others who vowed the Nazirite state, but were **singular**, because they were called to that profession by the will of God for a singular purpose...

# REVEALER OF SECRETS. 789

...and to signify a mystical meaning. The **Rechabites** (Jeremiah 35) can also be referred to those perpetual Nazirites. And this was not so much by their own vow or God's command as by that of their parents. Regarding temporary Nazirites, **Münster** <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), a German cartographer and Hebrew scholar</note> thinks the ordinary time of the vow was a month, that is, thirty days.

And this is the necessary division of the <term>genuine Nazirites</term> <note>original Greek: γνησίων ναζαραίων; *gnēsiōn nazariōn*</note>. But if we include more broadly anyone designated by that notion, we find four kinds both in Scripture and in the Ecclesiastical authors, as observed elsewhere by **Francis Junius of Bourges** <note>Francis Junius (1545–1602), a Huguenot theologian and scholar</note>.

I. **Nazirites** <note>original Latin: *Naziræi*</note> as described in Numbers 6, whether **by birth** or **by vow**, and whether by the designation of another or by one's own.

II. **Nazaræans** or **Nazarenes**, so called from the town of Nazareth in Galilee.

# ANTHONY CREGUT

*Jesus* is a name of office. But the surname *Nazarene* signifies three things: the *person, the office, and the homeland*. From this, the wonderful providence of God is made clear; for although Christ was not able to wear the legal insignia of the *Nazariteship*—such as a royal crown, or the high-priestly turban or tiara, because external dignity was held by his enemies—he was nevertheless surnamed *Jesus the Nazarene* by that triple right of person, office, and homeland. Even if this was done by his enemies <term>by way of a title</term> <note>original Greek: ἀξιουματικῶς (axiomatikos), implying a formal designation or rank</note>, it served to signify that he was truly the <term>antitype</term> <note>The reality or person that fulfills a symbolic "type" or foreshadowing from the past</note> of the ancient Nazarites. 

Furthermore, Pilate wished the title on the cross to be irrevocable; when the Jews refused it, he threw back this final word: *What I have written, I have written* (John 19:22). > There I will make the horn of David sprout, where I have prepared a lamp for my anointed; I will clothe his enemies with shame, but upon him his (Nezer) crown or sanctification shall flourish. <note>The author highlights the Hebrew word "Nezer," which refers to both a crown and the state of being a Nazarite/consecrated.</note>

II. *They were related as to the thing itself*; because all were separated, sanctified, and consecrated to God by a singular devotion. This is most manifest regarding Samson, and clear to anyone who runs through all the analogies...

IV. The fourth part is the *Abrogation of the Nazariteship*. I understand this with respect to the *Ceremonial* aspect. For in the Nazariteship, as in other rites, one part was *ceremonial*, another *moral*, another *civil*, another *mystical*; indeed, there was even a *physical* aspect. 

The *Ceremonial* aspect concerned external rites, which were necessary for an unrefined people during that period of the Law's <term>tutelage</term> <note>The author uses the word *paedagogia*, referring to the Law as a "schoolmaster" leading to Christ</note>; but truly, when the substance arrived in Christ, all those shadows vanished. The *Civil* aspect also remained, because a people who were especially stiff-necked—as the Jews were—must be accustomed to obedience and <term>be subject to the governing authorities</term> <note>original Greek: ταῖς ἐξουσίαις ὑπερέχουσαις ὑποτάσσεσθαι (*tais exousiais hyperechousais hypotassesthai*), citing Romans 13:1</note>. 

The *Mystical* aspect remains because one must always look toward Christ, who is the true Nazarite. 

Finally, the *Physical* aspect should be noted, since those who abstain from wine due to natural infirmities act rightly: or from other foods of this kind, just as the Jews abstained from the flesh of swine and other eatables because of leprosy, to which that nation was greatly susceptible. This is according to that proverb of the physicians: *leprosy in Egypt or Judea; scrofula in Spain; goiter in Savoy; carbuncles in Narbonnese Gaul.* <note>Narbonnese Gaul refers to Southern France. The author is noting that ancient dietary laws often had regional health justifications.</note>

# THE WORKS OF ANTHONY CREGUTUS
