I. **Regarding the matter**: for the Rechabites abstained only from wine, agriculture, and living in cities; whereas the **False-Rechabites** of the Papacy abstain from eggs, meat, dairy products, and so on. 

II. **Regarding the form**: For the original Rechabites did not abstain only on fixed days, but continually; nor did they do so with a binding obligation of conscience, for it was a free vow that could be set aside in a case of necessity. This is proved by the very example of the Rechabites in Jeremiah 35, who changed their father’s vow **partially** <note>original Greek: κατὰ μέρος (*kata meros*)</note> by dwelling in the city during a time of war when they fled from the face of the army of Nebuchadnezzar. But the **New-Rechabites** <note>A polemical term for Catholic monks and friars</note> act otherwise. 

III. **Regarding the efficient cause**: because those who were not <term>legally independent</term> <note>original Latin: *sui iuris*; referring to those under the authority of a head of household</note>, such as children and wives, did not make such vows; but in the Papacy, the opposite occurs. 

IV. **Regarding the effects**: because in the past those vows pleased God and were useful; now, on the contrary, they are the opposite.

*Three things here reach their highest point: guilt, punishment, and virtue.*

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological examination of "schism" (religious division), building on the previous discussion of Korah’s rebellion. The author moves from the historical biblical event to a linguistic analysis of the word itself across various biblical and Eastern languages to show its destructive nature.</meta>

# REVEALER OF SECRETS.

Things grow through concord, and even the greatest collapse through discord. <note>The author is likely quoting the Roman historian Sallust: "Nam concordia parvae res crescunt, discordia maximae dilabuntur."</note> And there is that saying of the Gospel: *a house and kingdom divided against itself cannot stand.* What should we think of schism, which tears the strongest bond of union? It does not call forth Concord, the tutelary Goddess, with sacrifices—as the Heathens once did when their city was besieged by enemies—but rather puts her to flight upon the arrival of its "friend" <note>An ironic reference to how schismatics often claim to be friends of the truth while bringing destruction.</note>, and introduces discord in her place. The very meaning of the name strongly confirms this. For "Schism" <note>original: *schisma*</note> comes from the Greek *schisma* <note>original: σχίσμα</note>, from the verb *schizesthai* <note>original: σχίζεσθαι</note>, meaning "to be split"; because through schism the whole assembly and Church creates a rupture, so that parts previously joined together go separate ways and are torn apart. This is no less monstrous in a Political or Ecclesiastical body than it is in a Physical body; if the members were to disagree with the head, and one did not provide its service to the other, the system of the body would gradually waste away and fall into a lethal <term>wasting disease</term> <note>original: *marasma*; a medical term for a gradual withering of the body</note>. Hence, 1 Corinthians 12:25: *That there should be no division in the body.* And John 7:43: *There was a division among the crowd because of Christ.* And 9:16: among the Pharisees. And 10:19: among the Jews. And among the Arabs, the word *shachtha* <note>original: שחתא</note> signifies not only "schism" and "dissension," but also "sedition" and "stumbling block" <note>original: *scandalum*</note>. For in truth, Schism places many obstacles and stumbling blocks <note>original: σκάνδαλα</note> upon which men strike themselves and fall lethally. Furthermore, to strengthen this meaning, the Arabs use another term, *mushtaf* <note>original: משתף</note>, a word taken from the "sixth form" of verbs <note>A grammatical category in Semitic languages often denoting reciprocal action</note>, which—just like the Latin compound made from the inseparable preposition *con* and the Greek *syn*—signifies cooperation and mutual action; so that when a schism is first exerted by a few, it afterwards creeps through the whole assembly in such a way that everyone is divided crosswise into various sects. Whence the Arabic word signifies both "schism" and "perversion" or "turning across."

Among the Syrians, the word *shalahvanta* <note>original: שלהונתא</note>, which signifies "Schism," has something peculiar about it; for it is derived from a root which in <term>Chaldean</term> <note>An older term for the Aramaic language</note> and Syriac means "to flatter" or "to entice"; which can rightly be associated with schism. For although schisms sometimes arise from a certain sudden impulse, they usually arise through deceitful enticements and flatteries. For ears are not immediately lent to schismatics, but as the poison creeps in bit by bit, the impulse eventually rushes forward quickly, and the body of the Church is split down the middle.

# ANTHONY CREGUT
<meta>catchword: ...has broken apart,</meta>

Furthermore, not only is the foulness and destruction of schism revealed through those various linguistic meanings; its very nature and historical experience also prove the same. For it can truly be called a deadly plague to both civil and ecclesiastical government. Since a state unites the magistrate with the citizens and the citizens with one another through the bonds of law—and in the Church, the flock and the pastors grow together into one through the bond of faith—schism immediately disturbs this harmony. It dissects the one body into various parts, breaks the seamless robe of Christ <note>A common metaphor for the unity of the Church, referring to the garment of Jesus that the Roman soldiers refused to tear (John 19:23).</note>, and wretchedly separates what God has joined.

This was done long ago by those four leaders of schism: *Korah*, *Dathan*, *Abiram*, and *On, son of Peleth*, as is clear from *Numbers 16:1*. They divided the people from *Moses* and *Aaron* and impiously accused the priesthood established by God. The same happened in the early days of the Christian Church among the five Patriarchs: the *Jerusalemite*, the *Antiochian*, the *Alexandrian*, the *Constantinopolitan*, and the *Roman*. They said, indeed, that the Church should not be torn apart, because it is like Christ’s seamless robe, woven from the top throughout; but they also added this: *“Come, let us cast lots for whose it shall be.”* <note>original: "Euge fortiamur cuius sit." Cregut is comparing the five Patriarchs to the soldiers at the Crucifixion who gambled for Christ's clothes.</note> This is evident from the fact that every one of them wished to be regarded as the Catholic <note>Meaning "Universal."</note>, or even the <term>Ecumenical Bishop</term> <note>original: *Oecumenicus Episcopus*; a title claiming authority over the entire inhabited world.</note>. Therefore, they preferred to divide the unity of the Church rather than possess no part of it; and thus they shattered the bond of charity, the token of Christians. So also in *1 Corinthians 11* <note>The author likely means 1 Corinthians 1:12.</note>, there was schism among the *Corinthians*, when some said, *“I am of Paul,”* others *“I of Cephas,”* and others *“I of Christ.”*

Furthermore, if you except heresy itself, I see nothing more deadly than schism. And although it must be confessed that schism is not exactly the same thing as heresy—insofar as heresy contains these three characteristics:
1.  **Error in faith**, like a blindness of the mind.
2.  **Conviction**, <note>original: *Evictionem*; here meaning the state of being proved wrong by the light of truth.</note> like a demonstration of light.
3.  **Pertinacity**, or a hardening of the will.

Nevertheless, schism immediately precedes heresy, just as a proximate cause precedes its effect. Thus, schism may truly and deservedly be called the "parent of heresy." It is like a wound that first becomes inflamed, and soon afterward blood or pus is discharged. For when schism first <insert>has broken apart</insert> the bond of charity among Christians...

Nevertheless, these things are only to be understood regarding those who can rightfully and deservedly be called schismatics. For those who make a withdrawal from a church are not immediately to be considered schismatics when pure worship of God has been abolished in that church, and when detestable **idolatry** runs rampant. Thus the **Papists** <note>A historical term used by Protestants for Roman Catholics, implying they follow the Pope rather than the Bible.</note> unjustly call us schismatics, because we have departed from **Babylon** <note>A common Protestant identification of the Roman Church with the corrupt city of Babylon described in the Book of Revelation.</note> according to the Prophet’s command. For the supporters of the Pope started the schism first, when they drove us from the **Roman Church** with sword and flame, breaking the bond of charity; and since they corrupted the Church with so many heresies, it became a sin to remain in communion with the Papacy.

The Papists therefore quibble when they say we falsely pretend the Church is corrupt, and that our schism is the greatest corruption of all; they say we have been ungrateful brothers, deserting others without applying any medicine to heal them; and that we are degenerate sons, scorning our mother’s old age on the pretext that her beauty was fading, and that some **wart** or **stain** appeared on her face. But (they say) the “luxuriant branches of the tree should have been pruned, not the axe applied to the root”; nor should the “luxury of the Roman Court be condemned through pride and treachery,” claiming that such poison is more lethal because it infects the soul rather than the body. # THE REVEALER OF SECRETS

Indeed, these were schisms that struck at the vital parts of your religion. Truly, **Onuphrius** <note>Onuphrio Panvinio (1529–1568), an Augustinian friar and historian known for his chronicles of the Popes.</note> counts as many as twenty-six schisms that have emerged in the Roman Church at various times. Anyone can find schisms everywhere in the lives of the Popes, among whom there were sometimes two, and sometimes three **Antipopes** <note>A person who, in opposition to the one generally seen as legitimately elected, makes a significantly accepted claim to be the Pope.</note>, who then dragged the whole Roman Church into schism with them. One kingdom followed the faction of this Pope, and another kingdom followed that one; Spain stood for one, France for another, and England for a third.

And in the **Council of Constance** <note>A 15th-century ecumenical council that ended the Western Schism by deposing or accepting the resignation of the remaining papal claimants.</note>, three Antipopes were deposed. Indeed, in the year 1376, after the Popes moved their seat from **Avignon**—where they had remained fixed for seventy years—a massive schism arose, greater than any that had existed in the Roman Church before. See the historians who described the lives of the Popes on this matter; they record various and long-lasting schisms.

Observe, however, that a schism ought not to be made for a trivial reason. For if the rightly Reformed withdrew from the Roman Church, it was because the causes and foundations of this breach were not light but momentous. In the same way, Protestants are rashly divided among themselves; those called **Lutherans** have wrongly separated themselves from the **Calvinists**, since it would have been easy to communicate with one another even if they disagreed on certain points—just as there were dissensions in the Church of Corinth in the time of Paul. And today in France, our Lutheran brothers take communion with us in our Churches according to the decree of the **Synod of Charenton** <note>A 1631 gathering of the French Reformed Church which allowed Lutherans to participate in its sacraments, viewing their differences as non-essential.</note>, and no danger or scandal arises from it. This we have demonstrated at length in our **Apology** <note>A formal defense or justification of a position.</note> for that Synod. 

Similarly, in ancient times, the **Donatists** <note>A 4th-century Christian sect in North Africa that broke away from the main church over the perceived corruption of clergy who had lapsed during Roman persecutions.</note> were condemned by **Augustine** and others because, having started a schism, they separated themselves from the Church not because of errors in faith, but because of certain trivial disagreements. # BY ANTOINE CRÉGUT

...that we departed from the Roman Church of our own accord, when they themselves drove us out through bloody persecutions. Furthermore, they are deeply deluded when they minimize their errors and call them merely "spots and wrinkles" on a beautiful face, when on the contrary they are a pestilential plague of heresies and a deadly gangrene. And since the Roman Church first defected from Christ the head, and handed her spouse a <term>bill of divorce <note>original: *βίβλον ἀποστασίου* (biblon apostasiou), a biblical term for a certificate of divorce.</note></term>, why then does she complain that we have continually clung to the spouse? Indeed, the schism or "tearing" was made in that particular corrupt Church, rather than in the invisible Church and the mystical body of Christ; or even in the universal Church, from which no one defects who creates a division with the Roman Church—unless, of course, one wishes to include the whole world within a single city [Rome] and <term>the whole inhabited world in a single house <note>original: *πᾶσαν οἰκουμένην ἐν οἴκῳ* (pasan oikoumenēn en oikō).</note></term>. The <term>Papists <note>original: *Pontificij*. A term used by reformers to refer to those loyal to the Pope (the Pontiff).</note></term> complain that we have created a division from the Roman Church, as if we were ungrateful sons deserting a most excellent mother. But the Reformed protest against the Papists with better right: that it is they who defected from the supreme Parent, that they have not persevered in His truth, and that they have defected not from a particular church (as we have), but from the universal Church.

Indeed, that the complaints of the Papists are most unjust is sufficiently recognized from the fact that they themselves foster and establish the schism, once made, by every means and artifice. You Papists complain that the Reformed have deserted your communion, and for that reason you call us schismatics? Yet your own Policy confirms that schism more and more. For you refuse our communion even in things conceded and in matters "related by blood" in respect to doctrine (as the ancient doctors like to speak). You establish it as a mortal sin to read our books, or to hear our prayers, whether in churches or at the dinner table; even if someone were to recite those words which were perpetually on the lips of Augustine, *Thanks be to God* <note>original: *Deo gratias*.</note>. To this end, that butchery of bodies and souls was devised, which can truly be called a part of <term>Gehenna <note>A historical term for Hell.</note></term>, but which they commonly call the **Holy Inquisition**. Do not all these things strike at the principles of true religion, whose root is truth, whose branches are charity, and whose fruits are good works?

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS

### HHHHh ij

...the schisms among you, born within the very bowels of the Roman Church? Indeed, these are schisms that strike at the most vital parts of your religion. Truly, <term>Onuphrius <note>original: *Onuphrius*. Refers to Onofrio Panvinio (1529–1568), an Augustinian historian famous for his chronicles of the Popes.</note></term> counts as many as twenty-six schisms that have arisen at various times within the Roman Church. Everywhere in the lives of the Popes, one encounters schisms between rival claimants to the Papacy; sometimes there were two, and at other times three <term>Antipopes <note>A person who claims the papacy in opposition to the one canonically chosen.</note></term>, who then dragged the entire Roman Church into schism with them. One kingdom followed the faction of this Pope, while another kingdom followed that one; Spain stood for one, France for another, and England for a third. 

Even at the <term>Council of Constance <note>An ecumenical council (1414–1418) that settled the Western Schism.</note></term>, three Antipopes were stripped of their authority. Certainly, in the year 1376, after the Popes changed their seat from <term>Avignon <note>A period known as the "Babylonian Captivity," when the Papacy was based in France rather than Rome.</note></term> (where they had remained for seventy years), a massive schism broke out, greater than any that had ever existed before in the Roman Church. Look to those historians who have described the lives of the Popes; they record various and long-lasting schisms.

Observe, however, that a schism should not occur for a trivial reason. For while the rightly Reformed departed from the Roman Church because the causes and foundations for this "tearing" were not light but weighty, the Protestants themselves have been divided too rashly. Those they call <term>Lutherans <note>Followers of Martin Luther’s theology.</note></term> have wrongly separated themselves from the <term>Calvinists <note>Followers of the Reformed tradition associated with John Calvin.</note></term>, when it should have been easy to remain in communion with one another even if they disagreed on certain points—just as there were disagreements in the Church of Corinth during the time of the Apostle Paul. 

Today in France, our Lutheran brothers take communion with us in our churches according to the decree of the <term>Synod of Charenton <note>A 1631 meeting of the French Reformed Church that officially allowed Lutherans to participate in their services, recognizing them as brothers in the faith despite differences in the theology of the Lord’s Supper.</note></term>, and no danger or scandal arises from it. We have demonstrated this at length in our *Apology* for that Synod. Long ago, the <term>Donatists <note>A 4th-century schismatic group in North Africa who believed only the "pure" could belong to the Church.</note></term> were condemned by Augustine and others because, having started a schism, they separated themselves from the Church—not because of errors in faith, but because of certain trivial disagreements. For <term>Cardinal Perron <note>Jacques Davy Duperron (1556–1618), a French cardinal who attempted to convert prominent Protestants.</note></term> admits this when writing to <term>Isaac Casaubon <note>A famous classical scholar and Protestant intellectual.</note></term> in Letter 48: he says the Donatists agreed with the Catholics on the doctrine of the Creed and the Scriptures, and on the Sacraments; but they disagreed regarding the "spirit of unity," the "bond of peace," and finally, regarding the Catholic Church itself. They differed (says the Cardinal) on a single article of unwritten tradition...

<meta>This page continues Crégut’s discussion on the nature of church division. Having previously argued that the Roman Church itself has suffered many internal schisms (citing the historian Onuphrius), he now examines the theological distinction between "schism" (a break in unity) and "heresy" (a break in doctrine), using historical examples from the Bible and the early Church.</meta>

# ANTHONY CRÉGUT

...namely, whether baptism administered by heretics was valid or not: since they themselves baptized those heretics who came over to them. But the Catholics did not rebaptize, but only <term>laid hands upon them <note>The "laying on of hands" was a gesture of reconciliation or confirmation, used instead of a second baptism for those returning from a sect to the mainstream Church.</note></term>. Similarly, the ten tribes of Israel, in the time of <term>Jeroboam <note>Jeroboam was the first king of the northern Kingdom of Israel who led a revolt against the house of David, resulting in a political and religious split.</note></term>, are rightly condemned because, for the sake of a political schism, they also created a rupture in the Church, deserting the temple at Jerusalem and erecting <term>high places <note>original: *excelsa*. These were elevated sites used for worship and sacrifice, often associated with illicit or pagan rituals in the Old Testament.</note></term>. Yet this was not held against the "elect" among them; for as the Apostle testifies in Romans 11: *seven thousand have not bowed the knee before Baal*.

It is, therefore, greatly dangerous to rashly make a secession from the Church. For what is in the beginning a slight thing and merely a schism, if hatred persists and Christian charity is extinguished, is transformed into heresy. For just as marine crabs, when they see oysters open, immediately cast little stones into the shells so that they cannot be closed again, thus enabling the crabs to devour them more easily—so too, when schismatics see the <term>bowels <note>A common early modern metaphor for the internal or most vital parts of an institution.</note></term> of the mother Church standing open, they immediately throw in heretical <term>tares <note>original: *zizaniam*. Refers to the "weeds" sown among wheat in the biblical parable; here meaning false doctrines.</note></term> so that any reunion of the members is hindered, and thus the schism is transformed into a lethal heresy. 

In this way, although the <term>Donatists <note>A 4th-century North African sect that broke away from the Church over the issue of "traditors"—clergy who had surrendered scriptures to Roman persecutors.</note></term> had first created a schism from the Catholics by rejecting Bishop Caecilian (who had been inaugurated by other bishops) on the grounds that he had handed over the Scriptures to persecutors, they later slipped into the further error of rebaptizing the faithful. Thus, once the door is opened to sedition and conspiracy, other errors immediately leap forth. Therefore, once union and the bond of charity are removed, schism arises, and then heresy follows when the parts that were once united and associated are torn apart. This is why the Hebrews called heretics *minim* <note>original: מינים (*minim*). In Rabbinic literature, this term refers to sectarians or heretics.</note>, a word that signifies both "species" and "heretics," and thus both union and separation are signified.

It is clear, then, that heresy is something worse than schism. For where there is heresy, there is schism, but the reverse is not true—where there is schism, there is not necessarily heresy. These things grow by degrees. A simple error is less than heresy, because heresy is a stubborn error maintained even after conviction. Hence <term>Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), the influential theologian who wrote extensively against the Donatists.</note></term> said: *I can err, but I do not wish to be a heretic.* After an error, schism follows, which also extinguishes charity, and finally, heresy occupies the final degree.

<meta>This page continues Crégut’s exploration of the distinction between schism (division) and heresy (false doctrine). # REVEALER OF SECRETS.

Paul seems to describe a progression in 1 Corinthians 11: *I hear that there are schisms among you, and I partly believe it; for there must also be heresies among you.* <note>original Latin: *Audio schismata esse inter vos & partem aliquam credo, oportet enim esse inter vos hæreses.*</note> However, you should understand these terms according to their church usage, not their secular one. Among the ancient philosophers, "heresy" <term>heresy <note>From the Greek *hairesis*, meaning a "choice" or a "school of thought." In a secular context, it simply meant a particular philosophical sect, like the Stoics or Epicureans.</note></term> referred to a sect or the specific opinion of a philosopher; hence the phrase, "I am in this heresy," simply meant, "This is my opinion." Indeed, in the early Church, the word "heresy" did not have such a negative reputation, as is clear from Acts 24:14 and 22: *According to that Way, which they call a sect* <note>original Greek: *τὴν διὰ ὁδὸν, ἣν λέγουσιν αἵρεσιν*. Here, the early Christians are being called a "sect" or "heresy" of Judaism.</note>. In later centuries, however, these notions of "heresy" and "heretic" came to be viewed very poorly. Because of this, the Jews, who burn with hatred for Christians, call them *Minim* <term>heretics <note>original Hebrew: מינים (*Minim*). In rabbinic literature, this term was used for sectarians or heretics, and was frequently applied to early Jewish Christians who were seen as deviating from traditional Judaism.</note></term>; and the Kabbalists say of them, *Let the name of the wicked rot.* <note>original Hebrew: *שם רשעים ירקב* (*shem resha'im yirqav*). A curse based on Proverbs 10:7.</note> This is the standard imprecation used by the Rabbis against heretics and Christians. Finally, the horror of heresy became so great that, much like a crime against nature, it was considered a sin even to name it or to revive an old, outdated one, following the well-worn proverbs: *Do not move Camarina, for it is better left alone* <note>original Greek: *μὴ κινεῖν καμαρίναν*. This refers to a marsh in Sicily that protected a city; when the inhabitants drained it against divine advice to stop a plague, their enemies were able to cross the dry land and capture the city. It means "don't stir up a settled trouble."</note>, and *Do not move an evil that is well-placed.* Some even believe that heretics, after their "hereticating" (for so the ancients used to speak), should be shunned.

But truly, before we leave this subject of our secession from the Roman Church on account of heresy, let us dismantle that "horned dilemma" <term>horned dilemma <note>A logical trap that offers two choices (the "horns"), both of which lead to a conclusion the opponent wants to avoid.</note></term> which the Roman Catholics constantly repeat with a <term>cuckoo-call <note>original Greek: *κοκκύσμῳ* (kokkysmo). Crégut is mocking the repetitive, bird-like chanting of the same argument by his Catholic opponents.</note></term>, by which they call us schismatics and cry out that our rupture and secession were done wrongly. They argue: "Either those who were under the Papacy before the secession were godly, or they were ungodly. If they were ungodly, then there was no Church within the Papacy—which is an even more impious thing to say. And if there was no Church, then those who left the Roman Church were themselves ungodly; therefore, they claim the title of 'Reformation' falsely. But if they were godly, why did they secede? Why did they tear apart the vitals of Mother Church with such a deadly schism? Could not those who lived so long and so piously in the heart of the Roman Church have continued to draw the life-giving sap of that best of mothers? Could they not have sucked that rich and sweetest milk from her breasts? If anything dreggy or unhealthy was encountered, could they not have cleaned and..."

<meta>This page continues Crégut's argument regarding the necessity of the Protestant Reformation. Having previously discussed the nature of heresy and schism, he now addresses the "dilemma" of how pious individuals could have existed within the Roman Catholic Church before the official break, using the analogy of a besieged city and the biblical "Babylonian Captivity" to justify the eventual separation.</meta>

# ANTHONY CRÉGUT

...was it very easy to purify? It is no different than how Mother Nature herself purifies the watery discharge <note>original Latin: *ichores*</note> and waste products of the blood.

I respond to the first part of the dilemma. Those who remained hidden in the Roman Church before the Reformation were pious, and as long as that **Babylonian captivity** <note>A common Protestant metaphor, popularized by Martin Luther, comparing the Roman Church to the forced exile of the Israelites in Babylon.</note> lasted, they were obliged to remain there, because there was no other Church in the West with which they could enter into communion. But after the day of liberty dawned, and the time fixed by the **Prophecy** arrived—*Come out of Babylon* <note>original Latin: *egredere Babylone*. A reference to Revelation 18:4.</note>—then a separation <term>secession <note>original Latin: *secessio*. The formal act of withdrawing from the Roman Church.</note></term> became necessary. This is just like a city besieged by hunger and unhealthy food where the inhabitants are exhausted; but after the siege, when grain flows in abundance, there is a different way of eating and satisfying oneself.

But indeed, from what has been granted, an even weightier difficulty arises. For we seem to have silently conceded that those pious people could live in communion with the Roman Church. If this is true, then that Church could not have been so corrupt that it deserved such a great division and separation. That objection is certainly not to be dismissed; however, it can easily be cleared up by a distinction. For one can conceive of two types of communion with the Roman Church: either **external** or **internal**. 

**External** communion is when someone remains in that society and visible assembly, even if they do not believe all its heresies; therefore, they take care as much as possible not to be polluted by idolatrous worship. 

**Internal** communion is when someone thinks the same as the Roman Church and is infected by the same errors and worship. The pious who were in the Roman Church were of the former kind, not the latter. This is why they eventually made a separation, because there was a danger that the Church in the West would perish from having swallowed poison for so long. Indeed, there were perhaps many who believed that many things in the Papacy were taught more soundly than they actually are, and therefore they lived piously according to their own understanding in that Church. For example, many do not believe that the Saints are to be invoked, nor images adored, nor that the body of Christ is truly sacrificed in the **Mass** <note>The central act of worship in the Roman Catholic Church; Crégut refers to the doctrine that the Mass is a literal "propitiatory sacrifice" of Christ's body.</note>. 

And this last point is explained by **Cameron** <note>John Cameron (c. 1579–1625), a highly influential Scottish theologian who taught in France and developed nuanced views on grace and church authority.</note> with this distinction: *Worship is one thing in itself; it is another thing in relation to someone.* The Roman worship is idolatrous **in itself**; but in **relation** to those pious individuals who lived under the Papacy before the Reformation, the worship was not idolatrous, for then...

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS. 807

...they did not believe that the Pope was the **Antichrist**, nor that such monstrous things were taught in the **Papacy**, until God opened their eyes so that they might perceive the Popish errors and make a <term>secession <note>original: *secessionem*. A formal withdrawal from a religious body.</note></term>. Hence, the opposite is said of them than what is attributed to the most noble historian **Jacques Auguste de Thou** <note>original: *Ioh. Now, if we descend to the **hypothesis** <note>The specific application of the theory to a particular case.</note>, we shall also assert that the schism of those four princes was the worst of all. First, *by its origin*, because it was the oldest of all; for they were truly called the first "schismatics" through so many centuries, and they showed the way of seceding to so many others. Second, *by the nature of the schism*, because that schism was **representative**, and consequently the most deadly of all. 

For just as the Roman Catholics <note>original: *Pontificij*</note> distinguish the Church by saying it is either **representative** or **collective**. The former is the assembly of prelates, both the "clothed in purple" <note>referring to Cardinals</note> and others who belong to the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy; the latter is the assembly of the faithful, whom the Papists call the Laity. So in a schism—which in the Church is a <term>deviation <note>original Greek: *παρέκβασις* (parekbasis). Literally a "stepping aside" or an aberration from the healthy state.</note></term> and a disease—we distinguish, for the sake of teaching, between the **representative** and the **collective**. 

It is **representative** when the schismatics not only withdraw from the Church and from the government of the pastors, but also form a "representative church" of their own, so that the schism stands out and, as is commonly said, **an altar is built against an altar**. They follow the example of their parent, Satan, who, wherever God willed a temple and altar to be erected, there the Demon founded a chapel. It is **collective** when the schismatics indeed withdraw from the Church and gather some assembly, but without pastors; they do not build an altar against an altar. What we call a **collective schism**, the theologian **John Cameron** <note>original: *Camero*. A famous Scottish Protestant theologian (1579–1625) who taught in France.</note> calls "negative"; and what we call **representative**, that Doctor calls "positive." We have preferred to distinguish them this way because Cameron's distinction seemed more obscure to us, as it is too general in its terms; and secondly, because I do not sufficiently see how...

...that which is truly and really a schism can be called "negative." For where there is a withdrawal of many from the pastors and the healthier part of the Church, a schism is not denied, but affirmed. Finally, because our distinction is opposed to that most common distinction of the <term>Representative and Collective Church <note>In traditional theology, the "Representative Church" usually refers to the hierarchy or councils, while the "Collective Church" refers to the entire body of believers.</note></term>. Truly, therefore, the schism of those schismatics will be called **representative**, since they represented, as it were, another Church with their followers, sharply opposing themselves to Moses and Aaron; *erecting altar against altar and despising the institution of the Aaronic Priesthood.*

III. The horror of the schism is also confirmed by the fact that it was begun against the Magistrate and the High Priest, such as Moses and Aaron were, and therefore it was simultaneously a **political** and an **ecclesiastical** schism. 

IV. V. The unique punishment abundantly signifies the horror of the fault. For those first schismatics seem to have been thrust down into the <term>Tartarean abysses <note>original: *Tartareas abyssos*. A classical reference to the deepest pits of the underworld or Hell.</note></term> in body and soul at the same time, so that they might make an eternal schism and withdraw from the <term>Church Militant <note>The Church on Earth, still struggling against sin and error.</note></term> and <term>Triumphant <note>The Church in Heaven, having achieved victory.</note></term>.

It is clear, therefore, that schism is pestilential in whatever way it is taken, both in <term>thesis <note>The general principle or theory.</note></term> and in <term>hypothesis <note>The specific application or case study.</note></term>. And just as a good citizen can never be made out of a seditious man in the state, so a true believer will never be produced from a schismatic in the Church. For as that author <note>Crégut likely refers to a Church Father such as Cyprian or Augustine.</note> skillfully says: *What kind of city is happy in sedition? What kind of family is peaceful in strife? What kind of soul is defiled in the battle of passions, and what kind of believer is tranquil in schism?*

Thus far we have dealt with schism in thesis and hypothesis; there follows now the second member of our discussion, which is **regarding the causes of schism.** The real causes are the same as those of heresy: namely, ambition and pride; envy and impatience. From those "mothers" arose the **Arian heresy** <note>The 4th-century belief that Jesus was a created being, subordinate to God the Father.</note>, when the priest **Arius** wished to appear more learned than his own Bishop, **Alexander of Alexandria**; and therefore he armed his sophistry against him. **Tertullian** <note>An early Christian author (c. 155–220 AD) who eventually joined a rigorist sect.</note> also defected to the side of the **Montanist** heretics on account of the insolence of the Roman Clergy. And truly, schisms and heresies have been stirred up by Bishops and Noblemen rather than by commoners. And only...

# REVEALER OF SECRETS. 809

...priests or Bishops were once able to foster factions of schisms or heresies; and to ensure that, according to the elegant saying of <term>Gregory Nazianzen <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and one of the "Cappadocian Fathers," known for his influential writings on the Trinity and his defense of orthodoxy.</note></term>, even when the flame is extinguished, the coals remain troublesome; namely, when they fanned them with new bellows, they erupted into far more sorrowful flames.

Nevertheless, they pretend other causes, which were fictitious, and three in number: these were the same crimes charged against Moses and Aaron. 

**I.** They objected to a **tyrannical domination** over a free people, as is clear from verse 3 of this 16th chapter: *Why do you lift yourselves up above the congregation of Jehovah?* And perhaps they further reproach them with unjust plundering, since Moses, defending himself, retorts in verse 15: *I have not taken even a donkey from them.*

**II.** They objected to the **unjust usurpation of the Priesthood**, because Aaron claimed it for his own family when it belonged to the whole <term>Levitical tribe <note>The tribe of Levi was set apart for religious service, but the specific office of the High Priest was reserved for Aaron and his descendants. Korah, a Levite but not a priest, challenged this hierarchy.</note></term>, as is clear from verse 3: *And gathering themselves against Moses and Aaron, they said to them, let it be enough for you; for all this assembly, all of them are Holy, and Jehovah is among them.*

**III.** They pretend **betrayals and deceptions**, as if they had mocked the people with vain promises. Verse 14: *And you have not brought us into a land flowing with milk and honey, etc.* <note>A common biblical idiom for a land of abundance and fertility.</note> But on the contrary, whatever the schismatics pretended, they were ambitiously attempting to claim the Priesthood for themselves; indeed, the very height of authority, rebelling against both Moses and Aaron. Moses sufficiently uncovered this wickedness in verse 11, saying: *You have gathered yourselves together against Jehovah.*

But what does Moses say to these accused crimes? Truly, Moses responds with a simple denial of the accusations, and moreover...

<meta>This page continues Crégut's analysis of the rebellion of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram from Numbers 16. # ANTHONY CRÉGUT

...**appeal to miracles**. And this is the third part of the dissertation. 

**I.** A simple denial by the supreme Magistrate could have sufficed; since he is the Legislator himself, he is not bound to give an account of his actions to every seditious and treasonous innovator. On the contrary, if he were to exercise his legal right, he could punish those factious schismatics. 

**II.** He could have dissolved those three aforementioned pretexts <note>The accusations of tyranny, holiness of the whole congregation, and Moses' supposed personal ambition mentioned on the previous page.</note> through God’s established order and from his own experience. But so that their innocence might be more evident, and their virtue and calling more illustrious, Moses appeals to the power of God and proceeds to compete with miracles, so that their calling might be confirmed by divine authority. This is also read to have been done by **Elijah** when he contended against the **priests of Baal** concerning the highest matters of religion. Such a conviction is surely the most evident and illustrious of all, since God himself sits on the throne and pronounces in favor of His own with an irrevocable decree.

But you will say: does it not seem that Moses tempted God when he appealed to miracles? For first, it is a sin to implore the infinite power of God when sufficient arguments and means are supplied to us in the order of nature—following the example of God himself, who never uses His immediate and extraordinary power except whenever nature fails; for then the **First Cause** <note>A philosophical term for God, acting directly rather than through natural laws (secondary causes).</note> is accustomed to supply that defect. Furthermore, since miracles are not in our power, how will anyone be certain of God’s will and that God will hear him? Especially since Moses himself once struck the rock in the desert with a vain and fruitless effort <note>A reference to Numbers 20, where Moses struck the rock twice in anger and was subsequently barred from entering the Promised Land.</note>. 

I respond that these things are said quite plausibly, yet they do not convict Moses of recklessness. 

**First**, because since God alone is the **searcher of hearts** <note>original: *καρδιογνώστης* (*kardiognōstēs*). A Greek term frequently used in the New Testament to describe God’s unique ability to know human thoughts and motives.</note>, it belonged to Him to reveal the sincerity of Moses and Aaron. 

**Second**, because just as God had immediately established the former as leader of the people and the latter as Holy Priest, so it was necessary to protect both by His authority against the slanders of the schismatics. 

**Third**, regarding the obtaining of miracles: Indeed, it would be rash if anyone demanded miracles from God without a promise of being heard, for this would be <term>tempting God <note>In a theological sense, "tempting God" means putting God to an unauthorized test or demanding a sign out of doubt rather than faith.</note></term>; but it must be judged otherwise for those who, through faith...

<summary>Crégut defends Moses' decision to call for a divine miracle to settle the rebellion of Korah, arguing that while normally one should not "tempt God," Moses was justified because his authority was directly instituted by God and required divine vindication.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Balaam's prophecy, shifting from the general context of the "Star of Jacob" to the specific nature of Balaam's vision and how God uses even a "false prophet" to reveal divine truth.</meta>

816
->ANTHONY CREGUT<-

Indeed, a great wonder emerges: that a mute animal, the dullest of all others, should speak wisely, and that a false prophet, the most impious of all remaining men, should have prophesied so clearly and so divinely concerning the kingdom of the Messiah. Bravo, then! Whatever Balaam's character and profession may have been, let us not despise so excellent a prophecy. For the Creator of all, who gave a mouth and a tongue to man for speaking, just as He rendered the false prophet’s donkey wise and eloquent, so He opened Balaam’s mind so that he might contemplate the future glory of the Messiah’s kingdom from afar and announce it clearly to those present.

This most noble oracle is divided by us into three members: **I.** *Concerning the vision of Balaam.* **II.** *Concerning the object of the vision.* **III.** *Concerning the effect following it.* As for the first, Moses expressly asserts in verse 16 that such a revelation was a vision when he says <note>original Hebrew: מחזה שדי יחזה (machaze schaddai iechze)</note> *he sees the vision of the Almighty*. But indeed, it has been decided not to discuss vision in general at present, since this matter was sufficiently disputed elsewhere in the exposition of the passage in Genesis 28:22; it is better now to dip our pen more strictly into the specific kind of this vision. In truth, nothing was presented to Balaam regarding his physical eyes; for he did not behold the person of the Messiah with his own <term>autopsia</term> <note>From the Greek αυτοψια, meaning "seeing for oneself" or direct eye-witnessing.</note>, nor did he see the rising star, nor the scepter of power exposed to his sight, nor the slaughter of the nations of the Moabites or Ammonites; but rather, he contemplated all these things in his mind, with the Spirit illuminating them with the flashing light of prophecy.

Therefore, the species of this vision is rightly called prophecy or a prediction, which is a vision and revelation of future things. Vision, therefore, is subdivided into three members: **I.** Into the *type of vision*, which is prophecy. **II.** Into the *subject of the vision*, which is Balaam. **III.** Into its *circumstances*, which are of place and time. As to the first: prophecy is a distinguished vision and revelation which foresees future things as if they were present. Whence the prophets are called <term>by way of excellence</term> <note>original Greek: κατ' εξοχην (kat' exochen)</note> <note>original Hebrew: רואים (Roim)</note> *Seers*. In 1 Samuel 9:9 and Isaiah 28:7, mention is made of a *prophetic vision*. And here Balaam is called <note>original Hebrew: גלוי עינים (Galui henaijm)</note> *one with eyes uncovered*.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of prophecy, moving from the specific example of Balaam to a more general theological definition of what constitutes a prophet versus the act of prophesying, using the biblical figure of Caiaphas as a primary example.</meta>

817
### THE REVEALER OF SECRETS. ###

But in truth, not all who foresaw future things were called prophets, nor were they worthy of that exceptional title; for there is a great distinction between being a prophet and prophesying. A **Prophet** is the name given to one who is distinguished by a prophetic office <note>The author distinguishes between a "job title" or permanent spiritual gift and a one-time event.</note>, and therefore prophesies and predicts future things not just once, but frequently; such prophets were Isaiah, Jeremiah, and others. But truly, many others prophesied once, or at least rarely, and therefore did not deserve to be called prophets. Such was **Caiaphas**, who was the High Priest at the time of Christ; he truly prophesied when he pronounced that someone ought to die for the people. For although he said it without understanding its meaning, it was not said by him at random, since Christ was that man who had to die for the nation—a fact which Christ himself made known in Luke 24, saying: *Did it not behoove Christ to suffer, and so enter into his glory?* <note>original Latin: "nonne oportuit Christum pati , & sic intrare in gloriam suam."</note>

Therefore, two things are to be observed in one who prophesies, even if he is not a prophet:
1. That it happens that he prophesies only once or twice, or at least very rarely.
2. That his tongue is indeed moved by the Holy Spirit, yet the mind remains blinded; his mind does not grasp the divine message because it is not illuminated by the rays of the Spirit of God. Both of these things can be clearly observed in Caiaphas.

However, two other points occur which are considered established:
1. That the prophetic vision is from God.
2. That the thing revealed has been decreed by God and will happen in time exactly as it was revealed. 
These two points are evident to all prophets and those who prophesy; nevertheless, regarding the person of the prophet and the goal of the Holy Spirit, for the most part, both true and false prophets do not fully grasp that goal, nor are they made participants in God's secret counsel.

From what has been said, it is clearly established that prophecy can be considered in two ways: either as it has the nature of an **act**; or as it denotes the nature of a **habit**. <note>These are Scholastic terms: an "act" is a single instance of doing something, while a "habit" (habitus) is a permanent quality or disposition of the soul.</note> Insofar as it denotes the nature of an act, it is not properly a "prophecy" or the deliberate act of a prophet; rather, it is the indefinite "prophesying" of a person who does so by chance—such as a Priest, which was the case with Caiaphas. Whence it is said in John 11:51: *But he said this not of himself: but being High Priest of that year, he prophesied that Jesus should die for the nation.* <note>original Latin: "Hoc autem ex semetipso non dixit: sed cùm esset Pontifex maximus anni illius prophetauit fore vt Iesus pro gente moreretur."</note>

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of prophecy, transitioning from the specific examples of individuals like Caiaphas to a systematic classification of prophecy as a "habit"—a permanent disposition of the soul—divided into natural and supernatural categories.</meta>

818
-> ANTHONY CREGUTUS <-

Insofar as prophecy describes the nature of a **habit** <term>habitus: a settled disposition or quality of the soul or mind</term>, then prophesying is an act brought forth by the prophet, to which the act of prophesying properly belongs by reason of his inauguration and prophetic office. However, just as habits are of three kinds, so they relate to prophecy in three ways.

I. **Habits** are **natural**, such as original righteousness would have been if Adam had persevered in his first state, and as original concupiscence or unrighteousness now remains. To this category of habit belongs the prophecy of **Christ**, who is that supreme Prophet of ours. Because of the fullness of the Godhead dwelling in Him **bodily** <note>original Greek: σωματικῶς (somatikōs). See Colossians 2:9.</note>, He can truly be called a Prophet by habit, and indeed by a natural habit, because of the inherent property of that divine nature which possesses all knowledge of the past, present, and future. For this reason, He alone is believed to be a Prophet **from within** <note>original Greek: ἔσωθεν (esothen); meaning His knowledge comes from His own divine nature rather than an external source.</note>.

II. Others are **infused habits**, which proceed from God **from without** <note>original Greek: ἔξωθεν (exothen)</note> and are poured into the minds and hearts of men, such as faith, charity, etc. Among these habits, we count every kind of prophecy; whether it be that by which the prediction of future things is spoken, such as was primary in the Old Testament, or that of the New Testament, which is the gift of interpreting the Scriptures clearly. This is why Peter, in his Second Epistle, chapter 1:20, wrote that **no prophecy of Scripture is of private interpretation, or revelation.** For the phrase **of private interpretation** <note>original Greek: ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως (idias epilyseos)</note> signifies both; and if, according to a most learned interpreter, we read it as **arrival** <note>original Greek: ἐπηλύσεως (epelyseos), suggesting an external "coming upon" rather than an "interpretation."</note>, with one small letter changed—or rather, according to the ancient pronunciation, not changed at all—it would correctly align with our view of prophecy: that it was an infused habit coming upon one from without. This is because **arrival** [epelysis] seems to designate the same thing as the word **influx** [epelysis], and therefore refers to an infused grace and an instinct coming down from on high, rather than from some private and intrinsic light. 

For as the most learned **Beza** <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major French Protestant theologian and successor to John Calvin.</note> correctly noted on this passage: *Peter does not oppose private interpretation to common or public interpretation; rather, he opposes the adventitious gift of the Holy Spirit to that shrewdness or vigor of intellect which is naturally implanted in men, however gifted they may be.* Hence, the term **inspiration** <note>original Greek: ἐπηλυσία (epelysia)</note> is more often attributed by **Hesychius** <note>A 5th-century Greek grammarian and lexicographer.</note> to those who are breathed upon from the outside by a spirit and are greatly moved. On this point, that most celebrated man observes aptly that the ancients...

...the Greeks distinguished introductions into "spontaneous" <note>original Greek: ἐπιλυτικὰ (epilytika)</note> and "premeditated" <note>original Greek: προέκτητα (proektēta)</note>. The former were so named because they arose and flowed into the mind according to the occasion; the latter because they were brought from home already prepared. III. Finally, **habits** are called **acquired** when they are obtained through one's own talent; specifically, those that can be gained from three things: nature, method, and practice <note>original Greek: φύσει, μεθόδῳ καὶ γυμνασίᾳ (physei, methodō kai gymnasia)</note>. But prophecy is not a habit of this kind; for its sphere is so high that these three things can never reach it.

However, although prophecy may be conceived as a habit in this sense, if we wish to speak more carefully, it is not strictly a habit, or something existing as a permanent form; rather, it is like an **impression** <term>pathos: a temporary affection or state of being acted upon</term> or a passing light. In truth, the light of prophecy or the power of prophesying was not always present in the Prophets; they had to wait for the instinct to come upon them and flow down from above. This is evident from 2 Kings 4:27, where it is said that God hid from Elisha the death of the Shunammite’s son. Therefore (as the most learned Cameron <note>John Cameron (c. 1579–1625), a Scottish theologian and professor at Saumur, known for his work on grace and prophecy</note> rightly maintains), Divine light is not in the mind of the prophets like light in the Sun, but like a ray in the air. For in this life, we taste sparingly what is drunk most brilliantly and possessed most fully in the life to come.

Rightly, therefore, Christ is raised far above all prophets. I. Because He is a Prophet habitually—indeed (as we said above) in the manner of a natural habit due to the fullness of His divinity, and because in John 1 He alone is called "full of grace" <note>original Greek: πλήρης χάριτος (plērēs charitos)</note>, on account of the fullness of His gifts or supernatural endowments <term>charismata: spiritual gifts granted by God for the benefit of the church</term>. Other prophets, however, are not properly prophets by habit, but by "impression" <note>original Latin/Greek: πάθες (pathos/passio)</note> as we have said.

II. ...continually; for in that case, any travelers would be prophets. Instead, it is **specifically** <note>original Latin: *speciatiuè*</note>, so as to signify the condition in Christ by which prophecy is suited to Him. This is much like how we commonly say someone is "curly-haired" insofar as they "have hair." We do not say it **reduplicatively** <note>original Latin: *reduplicatiuè*—a logic term meaning "insofar as it is exactly that thing." For example, "A doctor heals as a doctor," not just as a person.</note>, for then everyone with hair would be curly; rather, we say it specifically, for one would not be curly unless they also possessed hair.

III. Prophecy in Christ is a **Mediatory office** <term>munus Mediatorium: a specialized duty or role performed by a mediator standing between God and humanity</term>, which can be said of no other mortal. As for what Moses once wrote—*Jehovah will raise up for you a Prophet like me*—this must be understood regarding Moses **typically** <note>acting as a "type" or a historical foreshadowing</note>, but regarding Christ **properly and in reality**. For just as Moses was the most illustrious **type** <note>a person or event in the Old Testament believed to prefigure Christ</note> of Christ, so he was a **preeminent** <note>original Greek: ὑποχὸς (hypochos)</note> Prophet, because he was the mediator of the Law, just as Christ is the mediator of the Gospel. He was the mediator between God and the Israelite people, just as Christ was the Mediator between God and all men. Hence, **John 1:17**: *The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Christ.* Here a comparison is made between two Mediators; one is the **type**, the other is the **antitype** <note>the reality or person that fulfills the earlier "type"</note>. 

And **Galatians 3:19**: *The law was ordained through Angels, by the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator is not for one alone, but God is one.* These words, **in the hand of a mediator** <note>original Greek: ἐν χειρὶ μεσίτου (en cheiri mesitou); Hebrew: ביד (be-yad)</note>, understood as referring to Moses, indicate his ministry, not the **sovereign** <note>original Greek: αὐτοκρατοריקὴν (autokratorikēn)—referring to absolute or independent power</note> power of the "First Cause" (that is, God) at the time the law was delivered. For even then, Christ was participating, not as Mediator, but as God. Therefore, these words are to be understood regarding Moses, not Christ. 

Moses, then, was the minister of a covenant in a way granted to no other Prophet. This is why Scripture separates Moses from the other Prophets, speaking thus: *Moses and the Prophets*. **Luke 16**: *They have Moses and the Prophets*; just as one might say **Moses and the maxims** <note>original Greek: Μωσέα καὶ γνώμας (Mōsea kai gnōmas)</note>. And Homer says: **Zeus and all the gods** <note>original Greek: Ζεὺς κὴ πάντες οἱ Θεοὶ (Zeus kē pantes hoi Theoi)</note>. This phraseology seems to indicate a certain **preeminence** <note>original Greek: ὑπεροχὴν (hyperochēn)</note> among them. Hence those things said singularly in Scripture regarding Moses: *To believe in Moses* (**Exodus 14:31** and **John 5**) and *to be baptized into Moses* (**1 Corinthians 10**). This, as Cameron <note>John Cameron (c. 1579–1625), a Scottish theologian mentioned on the previous page</note> and other theologians testify, denotes the unique ministry of Moses. Yet these things are always to be understood **typically** of Moses, so that they apply truly and in reality to Christ; for the seals of the covenant belong not to the minister, but to the...

IV. Christ alone exercised all the offices, namely the Royal, the Prophetic, and the Priestly; hence, it was not without a divine mystery that when Christ was manifested in the flesh, Kings, Prophets, and Priests had vanished in Judea, and only a faint image or shadow of those three offices remained. This was so that the faithful might be taught that the true King, Prophet, and Priest had appeared on earth, in whom that entire function of the **Mediator's office** <term>munus Mediatoris: the specific duties performed by one who acts as an intermediary between God and humanity</term> was destined to unite. For He is uniquely the Messiah or Christ—that is, the "Anointed One"—consecrated to perform these kinds of duties in the Church. All of these were also uniquely fulfilled in the **type** <note>In biblical interpretation, a "type" is a historical person or event that foreshadows a future reality, specifically Christ.</note> of Moses. For Moses took the place of a king when he was the Magistrate and leader of the whole people; he was also (as demonstrated above) uniquely a Prophet. And finally, like a High Priest, he did not merely appear before God in the Sanctuary once a year, but more frequently stood before God as a Mediator and interceded for the people in the tabernacle; thus, it can be rightly asserted that he most fully performed the Priestly role. The masters of the Hebrews obscurely sensed these things when they said, according to the testimony of **Rabbi Moses** <note>Referring to Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Jewish philosopher.</note> in the *Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: *More Neuoch.* (Moreh Nevuchim), part 2, chapter 36</note>: "Prophecy does not exist in a time of persecutions, but in the time of the Messiah (may he be revealed soon!) prophecy is destined to return to us again, as God promised."

V. The prophecy of other Prophets merely struck the ears, but for the most part, the hearts of men—being as hard as stones—were not softened so as to conceive and receive the Prophetic word within. But the Prophecy of Christ sounds primarily within and penetrates the ears of the heart, so that even the very stones are softened, and the prophecy and the Prophet himself are simultaneously conceived at the root. Thus, it is not inscribed *on tablets of stone*, but *on tablets of human hearts*, as **Paul** <note>referring to the Apostle Paul in 2 Corinthians 3:3</note> testifies.

Therefore, one will observe, not without reason, that there are not only differences between Prophets, but also various degrees of Prophecy. For, to say nothing of the false prophets, such as **Balaam** <note>A biblical figure who, though a prophet, was often cited as a cautionary tale of greed and spiritual compromise.</note>, shall we not in the first place and most **preeminently** <note>original Greek: ὑπεροχῶς (*hyperochōs*), meaning in a manner of supreme excellence or superiority</note> rank Christ among the true Prophets? # ANTHONY CREGUTUS #
<meta>catchword: those</meta>

...namely, Moses? And should we not, in the third place, include the common Prophets such as Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and others? Furthermore, among all of them, those Prophets seem to shine out who, inspired by a certain unique breath, were specifically said by the Hebrews to possess <term>רוח הקודש</term> <term>Ruach Ha-Kodesh</term>, that is, the **Spirit of Holiness**. The Hebrew teachers say that by this breath or revelation, God acted uniquely with Job, David, and Solomon; hence, their books are preeminently <note>original Greek: 'ἐξοχῆς' (exochēs)</note> called <term>כתובים</term> <term>Ketubim</term>, *Writings*—the same terminology applied to the entire body of the Bible, which is called "Scripture." For this reason, the Greeks translate <term>כתובים</term> *Ketubim* as *Hagiographa*—that is, *Holy Writings*—because they were dictated more directly by the Holy Spirit.

From this, several distinctions are drawn between the other Prophets and those who wrote the *Ketubim*:

I. While other Prophets received revelations indirectly—namely through dreams or visions, whether awake or asleep (for which reason they were called "dreamers" or "seers")—these Prophets received their writings directly from the Holy Spirit without any such intermediaries. This kind of revelation was even communicated to the wicked, such as Caiaphas and perhaps Balaam, but with this distinction (according to **Thomas Aquinas** <note>Referring to his commentary on 1 Corinthians 12, lesson 1</note>): that the wicked were inspired by the Spirit *moving* them, but by no means *dwelling* within them. The holy Prophets, however, were moved in both ways: the Holy Spirit spoke within them and also dwelled within them. This immediate inspiration was infallible, no different from that of the other Prophets; thus, it was distinguished from the "common" revelation of the faithful, which is ordinary in the Church and is not infallible.

II. Other prophets were so inspired by the Spirit of God that they were further swept into an **ecstasy** <note>original: 'ecstasin', a state of being "outside oneself" or in a trance through divine power</note> by the intensity of that motion and breath. Consequently, they went "out of themselves" and performed extraordinary movements; hence, their style of speaking was adapted to these ecstatic and violent motions. But those who were the authors of the **Holy Writings** <note>original Greek: 'τῶν ἁγιογράφων' (tōn hagiographōn)</note> experienced this inspiration without ecstasy and with calm movements, so that they were not easily perceived from the outside. Their style was adapted to this kind of inspiration. Nonetheless, regarding the inspiration of the Apostles, which was even calmer,

Nor did they perform these extraordinary things without a mystery, and that by the instinct of the Holy Spirit—namely, so that by that new spectacle of most singular repentance, the lethargy of men might be stirred up. These things, however, were accepted as singular and fitting for that prophetic economy and from the instinct of the Spirit not without reason; but now, in this [current] economy, it would be judged foolish and senseless to wish to imitate these unusual things without the instinct of the Spirit, unless one were a fanatic. Furthermore, in the first Temple, there was another type of prophecy very frequently used and quite wondrous, the nature and method of which is not even sufficiently known to the Hebrews themselves, although its practice frequently appears in the Old Testament. Perhaps more will be handed down by us elsewhere in a specific study; therefore, we will refrain from adding much more for now.

We also omit other levels and types of prophecy mentioned by the Rabbis. This refers to fruit that falls from a tree before it is fully ripe.</note> of prophecy, the comparison is most fitting. Hence it follows that the prophecy of Moses was not only the most excellent of all, but also the most evident, because he communicated with God more familiarly and more immediately, without the use of dreams, visions, or Angels; which the Scripture indicates with these words: *mouth to mouth I will speak with him, etc.* (Numbers 12:8). And therefore many prerogatives of Moses over other Prophets can be collected.

# ANTHONY CRÉGUT #

The idea that God spoke to them <note>The Patriarchs, like Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.</note> and appeared to them has another meaning; for the same Rabbi <note>Likely referring to Maimonides.</note> adds that God did not command the Patriarchs to lead men, nor did He send them as He sent Moses to cry out to the sons of men; instead, they instructed men through the mode of contemplation and discipline. <note>Genesis 12:15</note>

II. Moses possessed a unique, or at least exceptional, quality shared only with David according to the Hebrew scholars: he experienced an "intellectual vision." Unlike other prophets, Moses was not affected by any of the four ways God usually communicates with His messengers. Prophets generally record that the word of God was announced to them in roughly four different ways. First, they say clearly that an Angel spoke to them either through a dream or a vision. Second, they mention an Angel, but make no mention of a dream or vision—because they take it as an established fact that an Angel would not speak except through one of those two modes. Third, they say God Himself addressed them, either through a vision or a dream, but make no mention of an Angel. Finally, they often say that God spoke these or those things to them, mentioning neither an Angel, nor a vision, nor a dream—certainly because they assumed no one can be inspired by prophecy except through an Angel and indeed through a vision or a dream. You have examples of these in <note>Genesis 13:11, Genesis 12:15, Genesis 15:1, Genesis 22:1</note>. These matters are narrated at length by Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the influential Jewish philosopher.</note>. But in his commentary on the tenth chapter of the *Tractate Sanhedrin* <note>original: מסכת סנהדרין; a book of the Talmud dealing with law and the courts.</note>, he judges that these modes do not apply to Moses; for he says:

> *God spoke with Moses alone among all the prophets without a mediating Angel, and without dream or vision.*

And Rabbi Joseph Albo <note>A 15th-century Jewish philosopher.</note>, as cited by Andreas Masius <note>A 16th-century humanist and linguist.</note> in his commentary on Joshua, says this:

> *God spoke with Moses about things so that He might imbue his soul (which we call the rational soul) with knowledge of them without any intermediate imagination <note>original: "phantasia"; referring to the faculty of the mind that processes images.</note>, in the same way He speaks with the Angels themselves.*

For this is what is meant by the phrase: *I will speak with him mouth to mouth.* <note>Numbers 12:8; original: *ore ad os loquar cum ipso.*</note> Theologians, and even the Scholastics <note>Medieval academics who used logic to explain Christian doctrine.</note>, as witnessed by Thomas Aquinas <note>Summa Theologiae, Part 2-2, Question 174.</note>, generally agree when they distinguish between a twofold vision: namely, the intellectual and the imaginary. The former (intellectual) they attribute to Moses and David. The latter, which occurs through the medium of the imagination, they say was the specific mode of the other prophets and common to all other seers.

III. The excellence <gloss>original: מעלת (*ma’alat*), meaning degree or rank</gloss> of Moses above other Prophets was such that his knowledge was more evident, and the light of his prophecy much more splendid, just as an intellectual vision surpasses an imaginary one. However, although other prophecy may be comparatively obscure, in its own kind and simply <note>original: *ἁπλῶς* (*haplōs*), meaning absolutely or in a general sense</note> it is evident and certain. For the appearances and mental images of things are represented to the prophets much more clearly than if they were seeing those things right in front of them with the keenest eyes. From this, it follows that they know for certain that prophecy does not arise from some natural instinct or a man's imagination, or even from an evil spirit; rather, they are constantly persuaded that it is a divine inspiration. Thus, the Prophets did not hesitate to announce, with the firmest confession of soul, things to the great men, peoples, and princes which were not "tasty to the palate" <note>An idiom for unpleasant or hard truths.</note>, inasmuch as they were conscious of having been, as it were, in the council of God (as Jeremiah speaks in chapter 23:18) and of having seen and heard divine words that were not deceptive.

If, however, there are obscurities in their prophecies, this happens incidentally, in the sense that Isaiah says in chapter 29: *The prophecy is like the words of a sealed book.* On this point, Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Jewish philosopher.</note> writes in *The Guide for the Perplexed*, part 2, chapter 29: *He who does not understand the language of the man speaking knows that he is speaking, but does not know what he is saying.* Therefore, since the Prophets were Hebrews, it is no wonder if, speaking in Hebrew, they obscured the text of Scripture with various Hebraisms. Hence, regarding the Prophets and prophetic writings, that Talmudic saying can be truly asserted: *it is written hard* <note>original: איכתיב קשה (*ikthiv qasheh*)</note>. For they call a "hard writing" that which is obscure and difficult and like a puzzle, which can be debated from both sides, and for the solution of which the Prophet Elijah would be needed.

From this comes that proverbial response of the Talmudists regarding obscure passages: *Tishbi will solve the objections* <note>original: תשבי יתרץ קשיות (*Tishbi yeratetz qashyot*). For as often as they are unable to explain a very difficult question <gloss>original: בעיות (*ba'ayot*)</gloss> or "hard objections" <gloss>original: קשיות (*qashyot*)</gloss>, they summon the prophet Elijah as if he were restored to life, who is called "Tishbi" in 1 Kings 17:1. Hence it is that the Hebrews, using the symbolic word *Qasheh* <note>The word for "Hard" (קשה) acts as an acronym for the three main bodies of Jewish study.</note>, which signifies "hard" or "difficult," foreshadow three difficult things and designate them Cabalistically: namely *Miqra*, *Shna*, and *Halakha*. IV. Moses stands preeminent <note>original: *ὑπεροχῶς* (*hyperochōs*)</note> before other Prophets because, as we said above, he possessed this unique quality: that he was the Mediator of the law, a symbolic redeemer, and the Lawgiver. And the Hebrews constantly emphasized the *Law of Moses*, and they accused Christ of being a transgressor of it. Hence it is that among them it was considered a sin to read those books before one's thirtieth year, since, according to the testimony of Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Jewish scripture.</note>, they were an "Ocean of Theology from which all rivers and every sea [flow]" <note>original: *Ωκεανὸς τῆς Θεολογίας ἐξ οὗ πάντες ποταμοὶ καὶ πᾶσα θάλασσα*</note>.

Thus far let the discussion of prophecy as a most noble type of vision suffice; it follows now that we pass to another part of the subdivision, namely to the *subject of prophecy*. First, regarding the subject of prophecy, its variety caused some to be true Prophets, legitimately sent and called by God and inspired by His Spirit, such as Isaiah, Jeremiah, and others. Among the Persians, these were called **Magi**. For although the Persian word signifies "a seeker of nature," because those men abused the appearance of wisdom and in this way fascinated the credulous, it happened in later centuries that the Magi gained a poor reputation, and the word was taken in a negative sense. On the occasion of this history of Balaam, one might not unseasonably ask what should be thought of those prophecies commonly circulated in France by the Physician of Salon in the province <note>Salon-de-Provence</note> named *Nostradamus*, the truth of which seems to be frequently proven by their outcome and fulfillment. Many, therefore, rightly inquire whether those prophecies were revealed by God or by a Demon. Many maintain they are from a Demon, and among them is our own Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major Protestant theologian and successor to John Calvin</note>, whose well-known and popular epigram on the matter is:

->*We give our own, while we give words, for to deceive is our way:*<-
->*And when we give words, we give nothing but Nostra-damus.*<-
<note>original Latin: *Nostra damus, dum verba damus, nam fallere nostrum est: / Et cùm verba damus, nil nisi Nostra-damus.* This is a sophisticated Latin pun. "Verba dare" is an idiom meaning "to deceive." "Nostra damus" means "we give our own things," but sounds identical to the name "Nostradamus."</note>

And in truth, those riddles and the repeated enigmas of that distinguished storyteller <note>original: *Aretalogi*, a term for a boaster or one who speaks of miracles</note> savor more of the fraudulent delusions and machinations of the Devil—who of old was called <term>Loxias</term> <note>original Greek: λοξίας, meaning "the slanted or ambiguous one," a title for Apollo</note> or <term>Amphibolos</term> <note>original Greek: ἀμφίβολος, meaning "ambiguous" or "doubled"</note>—than of the spirit of the most truthful God. Nevertheless, many difficulties arise from the fact that demons are unable to foreknow or predict future events; yet (they say) in those prophetic *Centuries* of Nostradamus, many things were predicted which were precisely realized in the event—even regarding contingent matters which could not have been foreknown in their causes by any mortal, nor by Angels, nor recognized by any external sign.

Hence it is that others believe they hold a truer view if they say that he was mostly moved by the Spirit of God, who alone is able to predict so many events before they happen. To confirm this matter, they bring forward the example of Balaam, who was a magus like Nostradamus and a false prophet, and yet, seized by the Spirit of God, he revealed the most noble prophecy of all regarding the coming of the Messiah. And to this they apply that passage from Joel 2 and Acts 2: *I will pour out my Spirit in the last days, and your sons and daughters shall prophesy, etc.* They believe, moreover, that it greatly illustrates the providence of God that in this old age of the world, notwithstanding the enormous wickedness of men, God willed to provide for His Church in such a way that He deigned to warn it long in advance of various hardships, disasters, crosses, and slaughters <note>original: *lanienis*, literally "shambles" or "butcheries"</note>.
