# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS.

However, to express my own view on this point, it would be better to say that he was driven by the spirit of a Demon. Even if a demon cannot foreknow future contingencies <note>Events that may or may not happen, depending on free will or chance.</note>, no one is ignorant of the fact that his arts are most profound and his mysteries most hidden. By wrapping and entangling anything in various covers and riddles <note>original: *gryphis*, literally "griffins," often used to mean difficult puzzles or enigmas</note>, it eventually happens that many things will occur which seem to have been predicted long ago. Yet, before those particular events came to pass, they were unknown and inaccessible to the demons. Thus, if even once something is observed to have occurred according to a prophecy, there are infinite other things judged to be of no use or fruit; they fall apart just like **loose brooms**, with no connection of words or things appearing, but rather riddles and enigmas swarming everywhere.

Among these kinds of marvelous demonic arts, one might count the stories told about **Abbot Joachim of Calabria** <note>Joachim of Fiore (c. 1135–1202), a mystic whose prophetic theories about the "three ages" of history were highly influential and controversial.</note>, which are so astounding—if they are true—that they have been a source of wonder to everyone. For that Abbot reportedly predicted all the future Roman Pontiffs <note>Popes</note>, including their names and their external forms or appearances. Some also remember the same regarding the book of **Emperor Leo** <note>Leo VI "the Wise" (866–912), to whom a series of prophetic "oracles" regarding the fate of the Byzantine Empire were traditionally attributed.</note>, in which the future Greek Emperors and Patriarchs were found predicted. 

If these things are indeed true, it must be confessed that they are surely wonderful and worthy of amazement. For how could demons foreknow these things which were so contingent—indeed, even accidental? How could they know things that did not depend on a connection of causes, but on the will of men, which in them is **wavering**? <note>original Greek: *ἀμφιρρεπὲς* (amphirrepès), meaning swinging from side to side or undetermined.</note> 

Moreover, it does not seem reasonable that these things were predicted by the inspiration of the Spirit of God; for to what good end would God have revealed them? As if God would have favored the itching and vain curiosity of shallow men! In truth, the miracles and extraordinary works of God are not done **incidentally**, <note>original Greek: *παρέργως* (parergôs), meaning as a side-task or without serious purpose.</note> but for a necessary end and for the useful benefit of the Church.

Furthermore, daily experience shows that when it comes to miracles and such portents, men frequently devise many things and sell many fictions to deceive others. They do this so that either great men or learned men might raise themselves above others because of these "gifts" and be suspected of participating in divine counsels. Thus, long ago, the first leaders and rulers of peoples...

# ANTHONY CREGUT

Hiding under that veil, they deceived the common people. Hence **Minos**, the ruler of Crete, used to pretend he held conversations with **Jupiter**; **Numa Pompilius**, the King of the Romans, with the nymph **Egeria**; **Scipio** with Jupiter in the Capitol; and **Sertorius** <note>Quintus Sertorius (c. 123–72 BCE), a Roman general who claimed a white doe told him the secrets of the goddess Diana.</note> pretended to receive his oracles from a doe. **Muhammad**, the foremost of all impostors, used to boast that the oracles of the Holy Spirit were revealed to him daily under the guise of a dove; he had trained the bird to fly over his head and peck grains of barley from his ear, and upon seeing this, he would cry out that the Holy Spirit had spoken to him and revealed most necessary things. 

To this category some political thinkers refer the story of **Joan of Arc**, the Maid of Orléans, brought forward by **Charles, King of the French**, when everything had been reduced to the last resort and was utterly despaired of <note>original: *prosus conclamata*, an idiom referring to a situation given up for dead</note>. However, all the circumstances of history and her noble deeds argue against this, as does the frequent providence of God, which has often shone forth in preserving this kingdom, especially when ordinary human means were failing. Of the same sort are the impostures of the **Anabaptists** and **Fanatics**, who constantly emphasize and claim for themselves revelations of the Holy Spirit. But it is easy to throw back at them that passage from Ezekiel 13: *Woe to the foolish prophets, who follow their own spirit and see nothing.*

***

Thus far we have discussed the subject of the prophecy—namely, **Balaam** the false prophet and his followers. Now follow the circumstances of that same prophecy, which are designated by these words: *I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near.* By these, two circumstances are clearly described: namely, time and place. 

1. **Time**, when he says *I do not see him now.* This is surely the nature of prophecy, since prophets announce future things rather than present or past ones, as is signified by the very Greek roots of the word <note>original: *φάω* (phaō) and *φήμι* (phēmi), which carry the sense of "shining forth" or "manifesting" and "speaking."</note>. And for the Hebrews, the word *navî* <note>original: נביא</note>, that is, "Prophet," properly signifies one to whom God reveals secrets, which are primarily regarding things to come. Now, Balaam speaks this way not out of ignorance, since in truth many centuries were to pass before this prophecy was fulfilled. Thus, the eyes of the Prophets are very **sharp-sighted** <note>original: *lyncei*, meaning "lynx-eyed," a common early modern metaphor for someone with supernatural or extraordinary vision.</note>, since they are able to penetrate beyond the density of future centuries. For this reason, they are preeminently called *ro’im* <note>original: ראים</note>, or **"Seers,"** and are said to *see with uncovered eyes* in Numbers 24:1, or are called *machazeh* <note>original: מחזה</note>, **"Seers of Visions."**

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of prophecy, moving from the critique of historical impostors to a technical theological analysis of genuine biblical prophecy. The author focuses on the specific visionary language used by the prophet Balaam and the distinctions between three eras of divine communication.</meta>

# REVEALER OF SECRETS. 837

Therefore, when he said *I see him, but not now* <note>original Hebrew: ולא עתה (*v'lo atah*), meaning "and not now"</note>. These final words, or rather that adverb of time, should not be joined with the verb *I see*, for indeed **Balaam** was seeing at that moment through the **Prophetic Spirit**. Instead, it should be joined with the object of his vision, because that object was not yet present. Thus, it is the same as if he were to say: "I see, but I see an object which does not exist now, but which is to come." Or it can also be said, understanding this not of the object but of the act of seeing, that the prophet wished to distinguish the type of vision. He meant to signify that this was a prophetic vision, and therefore he was not seeing the object with his bodily eyes, but with the eyes of the **Prophetic Spirit**—or as **Moses** wrote, *with eyes uncovered and opened through revelation* <note>original Latin: *oculis retectis & per reuelationem apertis*</note>, as the Hebrew word implies.

Thus, here is shown the difference between the triple ministry of the triple <term>Economy</term> <note>From the Greek *oikonomia*, referring to God's "management" or "plan" for the world during different historical eras.</note>; namely, between the **Prophetic ministry**, the **Apostolic ministry**, and the **intermediate** <note>original: *medioxumum*</note> ministry, which occupies the middle ground between the Prophetic and Apostolic. The first looks toward a future object, and announces it a long time before its manifestation, just as "figures" <note>Symbolic persons or events in the Old Testament believed to prefigure Christ.</note> shadow forth and prefigure things. But the **Apostolic ministry** testifies that the object—namely, **Christ**—has already come, and that all things predicted by the Prophets and prefigured by the symbols have been fulfilled. 

The middle ministry, however, was that of **John the Baptist**, the forerunner of Christ. He did not announce that Christ was in the future, like the Prophets; nor did he announce him as a figure of the past or as one who had already come and fulfilled all things, like the Apostles. Instead, he proclaimed Christ as he was coming and standing close at hand. This is why in **Isaiah 40:3** he is called the *Voice of one crying in the desert* <note>original: *Vox clamantis in deserto*</note>. This voice was certainly sharper than the sound of the prophets, which was not perceived from such a distance; yet it was an "Echo" or an imperfect voice in respect to the teaching of Him who is called the *Word of the Father* <note>original: *verbum patris*</note> in **John 1**. This is why John cries out, *Behold the Lamb of God* <note>original: *Ecce agnus Dei*</note>, etc. (**John 1**). And why he is compared to the dawn or the morning star <note>original: *phosphoro*, literally the "light-bringer"</note> showing the way for the rising Sun. And why in **John 1** he denies that he himself is the Christ, Elijah, or "the Prophet." For the prophets belong to the **Old Testament**, but John belongs more to the **New**. Hence that saying: *all the prophets and the law were until John.*

Observe, therefore, that according to the variety of this triple Ministry, the voice of God has been heard and has resonated among men in three ways.

I. Hence the Prophets are called **Seers** and **Prophets** <note>original Hebrew: חֹזִים (*chozim*) and נְבִיאִים (*nevi'im*)</note>, *that is, those who see and those who know secrets from a vision, as was said above.*

II. The voice of God was heard in **John the Baptist**, which resonated more than that of the Prophets, wherefore he is said to have "cried out in the desert." Isaiah 40:3. And although this voice was sharper than that of the Prophets, it was still imperfect compared to the more forceful one.

The kingdom of the Messiah would be a temporal <note>In this context, "temporal" refers to an earthly, political kingdom rather than a spiritual one.</note> one, and in the time of Christ, the Apostles themselves dreamed of this, as is clear from the account in Luke 22 concerning the sons of Zebedee.

But indeed, these things are to be understood primarily regarding the kingdom and the coming of the Messiah, to whom all the words of the text emphatically apply. First, it is said emphatically of that most illustrious object, *I see him.* *I see* (I say) *that Messiah*, the one uniquely called the "seed of the woman," and the one singularly named <term>Shiloh <note>A prophetic title for the Messiah from Genesis 49:10, often interpreted as "the one to whom it belongs" or "the peacemaker."</note></term> (Genesis 3 and Genesis 49). I see him who is <term>like a son of man <note>original Hebrew: כבר אנש (*ke-bar enash*)</note></term> (Daniel 7). I see, I say, that promised, foretold, and prefigured Christ, so long expected, and for whom we must still wait so long; he whom so many of the faithful are <term>waiting for with eager expectation <note>original Greek: ἀποκαραδοκοῦντες (*apokaradokountes*), describing someone leaning forward with an outstretched head in anticipation</note></term>. Balaam now gazes upon him, so that he might shine forth like a torch to the Gentiles.

Secondly, he emphatically describes the coming of the Messiah *through a star out of Jacob*, which matches wonderfully with the star of the Magi that appeared at the birth of Christ, and which led those wise men on a direct path from the East to Judea and to the manger of the infant. It also matches wonderfully with the qualities of Christ, which are rightly signified by a star. For what could more graphically represent the <term>Dawn from on high <note>original Latin: *Orientem ex alto*</note></term>, the <term>Sun of Righteousness <note>original Latin: *Solem iustitiæ*</note></term>, and <term>that true Light <note>original Latin: *Lucem illam veram*</note></term> mentioned in John 1, than that star of Balaam, or the star rising out of Jacob? Truly, that star is of the first magnitude, expressing the Light of the world and the Sun of Righteousness.

Thirdly, he is emphatically described *through a sceptre rising out of Israel*. Since Christ was the King of the Jews, his kingdom is rightly signified by a sceptre, as only kings hold sceptres in their hands. Hence, in Genesis 49, in another prophecy concerning the Messiah, mention is made of a sceptre that shall not depart from Judah until Shiloh comes. For his arrival was then most seasonable and opportune, when neither King, nor Prophet, nor Priest existed in Israel, so that it might become known to the whole nation that the Messiah was that true King, Prophet, and Priest who was meant to lead the people, rising as one who carries the sceptre in Israel.

Nevertheless, since this coming of Christ was foretold, this must be understood as the first coming, or the manifestation—

I. *In prelude*, He appeared very often to the fathers of the Old Testament, and that in human and bodily form, because (says *Tertullian* <note>An early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) known as the "Father of Latin Theology."</note>) *it provided a prelude to the future incarnation*. And at those times He took up bodies like garments, which He put on and took off once His duty was performed and His mission completed. For (as the ancient Teachers say) at that time He had not come to be born, and therefore not to die; nor did He animate those bodies by <term>informing them <note>In traditional philosophy, "informing" (Latin: *informando*) refers to a soul giving life and essential nature to matter; the author argues these were temporary physical manifestations, not true biological life.</note></term>, or unite with them <term>hypostatically <note>The "hypostatic union" is the theological doctrine that in Christ’s person, a human nature and a divine nature are perfectly joined.</note></term> or personally. Rather, He moved them from place to place and was present through a kind of virtual contact. 

II. He came *in the flesh* properly, when, as it is said in *John 1: The Word was made flesh. When God was manifested in the flesh (1 Timothy 3). When He was born of the Virgin (Matthew 1).* And that coming is called the *first coming*, to distinguish it from the second or final one at the judgment. And regarding that second coming <note>The author likely refers back to the prophecy of Balaam/Moses mentioned on the previous page as looking toward this ultimate fulfillment.</note>, this oracle of Moses speaks—indeed, all the Prophets and types and ceremonies look toward it—because in it was situated the salvation and redemption of the human race. Therefore, although it was humble and *in the form of a servant (Philippians 2)*, yet it is sometimes called by Paul an <term>Epiphany <note>From the Greek *epiphaneia*, meaning a "shining forth" or "manifestation."</note></term>, that is, an illustrious coming, because in that form of a servant, the form of God and His splendor shone through, according to *John 1: And we saw His glory, etc.* 

For those words of Paul are monumental <note>original Latin: *emortualia*, which can refer to funeral rites or things pertaining to death; here it likely suggests these words are the definitive statement on the death of death itself.</note> in *2 Timothy chapter 1:10: But it has now been revealed through that illustrious coming of our Savior Jesus Christ, who both abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the Gospel.* Where the Apostle uses the word <note>original Greek: ἐπιφανείας (*epiphaneias*)</note> *appearing* or *manifestation*, no differently than when he speaks of the second and glorious coming. For although nothing more lowly than that first coming could be imagined regarding its external form, yet by that naming the Apostle wished, with wonderful skill, to lift our minds from those external things and the form of a servant into the meditation of heavenly things and the form of God, or the effectiveness of Christ’s coming; hence he adds: <note>original Greek: φωτίσαντος δὲ ζωὴν καὶ ἀφθαρσίαν διὰ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου</note> *who brought life and incorruption to light through the gospel*. ...is attributed to the coming of Christ. This single passage from the Epistle to Titus 2:13 will serve as an example for all: *Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ.* For those things are said <term>ἐπιφαίνειν <note>to shine forth or appear - original: "epiphanein"</note></term> which suddenly draw the eyes of all to themselves, because they are seen to flash forth with a certain splendor. Therefore, the Common Translator <note>Refers to the Latin Vulgate, the standard Bible translation of the Catholic Church at the time.</note> does not sufficiently express the power of the word when he coldly translates it as *coming* (*adventus*), as if the Greek were <term>παρουσία <note>presence or arrival - original: "parousia"</note></term>. Erasmus often follows him in this, robbing us of the more illustrious passages where the divinity and glory of Christ are discussed, as was rightly observed by the most learned Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a French Protestant theologian and successor to John Calvin.</note>.

III. Therefore, there will be a coming of Christ in the flesh when He shall come to judge the living and the dead. This is called the "second" and "last" coming in relation to the first when He was born of the Virgin; but also (as I said) it is called the <term>ἐπιφάνεια <note>Epiphany or "appearing" - original: "epiphaneia"</note></term> <term>κατ' ἐξοχὴν <note>preeminently or by way of excellence - original: "kat' exochen"</note></term> in relation to the first coming, which was lowly—even though the first coming is sometimes rightly and in a good sense graced with that name "Epiphany," as has been proved. The faithful wait for this final coming, <term>ἀτενίζοντες <note>gazing intently - original: "atenizontes"</note></term> as those who will attain the fulfillment of their redemption: that is, the full and total redemption of both body and soul (Romans 8; Ephesians 1) and from both sin and death, because death, that last enemy, shall then be destroyed (1 Corinthians 15). Hence it is that in Revelation 22:20, John the Theologian and other faithful ones piously cry out, *Come, Lord Jesus.* And Christ says, <term>Ναὶ ἔρχομαι ταχύ <note>Yes, I am coming quickly - original: "Nai erchomai tachy"</note></term>. *Even so, I come quickly.* These words of our Savior, used in this threefold coming, offer wonderful consolation. 

In the first coming, which was in prelude: as when He appeared to Joshua before the destruction of Jericho (Joshua 5:13) and said to him, *I have now come*. These words <term>עתה באתי <note>original: "hatta bathi" - I have now come</note></term>, according to the testimony of Rabbi David Kimchi <note>A famous medieval Jewish biblical commentator and grammarian (c. 1160–1235).</note>, carry great emphasis because they signify the ready help of the Lord [Jehovah]; although that teacher offers a more subtle interpretation which we do not accept. The same phrase is found in Daniel 10:11 & 14, and Daniel 9:22. Just as in that first <term>Economy <note>In 17th-century theology, an "economy" refers to a specific era or method of God's administration of human history.</note></term>, the face of God approached Joshua to explain the method for capturing the city of Jericho, so too in other Economies—such as in the Incarnation and the glorious coming—when He cried out *Behold, I have now come*, He truly promises singular help and help full of comfort.

For indeed, that which holds greater emphasis and even greater comfort through the phrase, *now I come*, signifies the imminent and soon-to-be-saving arrival of Christ, as if He were already standing at the doors. For it must be observed that whenever Christ speaks of His coming, He is accustomed to speak of it as a matter close at hand and, as it were, happening in an instant. The Apostles received and imitated this manner of speaking from their Master so that a greater hope might shine forth.

This seems to have been started and indicated long ago by the Prophets; while they were prophesying about Christ’s arrival, they seemed to have blended those two comings <note>The "two comings" refer to the Incarnation (first) and the Return/Judgment (second).</note> into one. However, Christ and the Apostles later distinguished them, yet they did so without separating them by a vast interval of time. Instead, they asserted their proximity so that the interval of long time and the gap of centuries would not extinguish the hope of the faithful, but rather that proximity might nourish it—using those very words: *Surely, I come quickly.* 

Hence, to lift the expectations of the godly, they did not even count by years or centuries, but only by days or weeks. From this, they are called "Prophetic days," or the *seventy weeks of Daniel*. For instance, when God told Ezekiel to lie on his right side for forty days to bear the iniquity of Judah, as found in *Ezekiel 4:6*, those were prophetic days and were taken to represent years. The Apostles imitated this phrasing in the New Testament; as in *Revelation 18:23*, <note>Though the text cites chapter 18, the author is likely referring to the 1,260 days mentioned in Revelation 11 and 12, a common focus for historicist interpretations of prophecy.</note> where the 1,260 days of the Antichrist's duration ought to be calculated as that many years. This is because, in the time of Paul, the *mystery of iniquity* was already being carried out. *2 Thessalonians 2:7*: *For the mystery is already at work.* <note>original Greek: τὸ γὰρ μυστήριον ἤδη ἐνεργεῖται</note>

The most learned Amyraut <note>Moïse Amyraut (1596–1664), a French Protestant theologian famous for his "Amyraldism," a modification of Calvinist doctrine.</note> illustrates these points we have made with a very appropriate comparison, saying: almost the same thing happens to them as to those who look at two distant towers from a distance which are placed in the same line; they appear to merge into one, but after one has come toward them, the gap between them is recognized. So the Prophets, contemplating those arrivals of Christ as if from a great distance—according to that saying of Balaam, *I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near* <note>Numbers 24:17</note>—blended both comings. But the Apostles, who were looking from a closer range and were nearer than the prophets, distinguished that twofold coming; yet they did so in such a way that...

As for the ancient Hebrews, they certainly did not confuse the double coming of Christ with the Prophets, but they obscured it with their own fabrications. They had a slight scent of that truth, yet they failed to notice two comings of the same person, Christ. Instead, they dreamed—*unreasonably and unscripturally* <note>original: "ἀλόγως καὶ ἀγράφως"</note>, or rather, *contrary to scripture* <note>original: "ἀντιγράφως"</note>—of two different persons; and furthermore, the Jews *do not agree* <note>original: "ὁμοψηφεῖν"</note> among themselves. For some completely reject what Christians say about the double coming of Christ. For when we assert that there is a double coming of Christ: one in the *likeness of sinful flesh*, *concerning sin* <note>original: "περὶ ἁμαρτίας" - a reference to the Greek text of Romans 8:3</note> (Romans 8:3), by offering Himself as a sacrifice for sin; and the other *without sin* <note>original: "χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας"</note> (Hebrews 9), where He will not offer Himself as a sacrifice for sin. In that first coming, He performed the function of a Priest; in the other, He will exercise the kingly office. The Jews immediately object, claiming there is no coming of the Messiah except for a glorious one.

On the contrary, other Hebrews, catching a little scent of the truth and seeing it as if *through a lamp-wick* <note>original: "διὰ τῆς θρυαλλίδος φαίνοντες" — an idiom meaning to see something dimly or partially, like a light seen through a small opening</note>, imagine that there were two Messiahs. The first they call the son of Nehemiah, whom *Armilos* <note>Hebrew: ארמילוס — in Jewish eschatology, a figure similar to the Antichrist</note> killed long ago (which Armilos is the same to them as the Antichrist is to us); this is, as one may guess, the Roman Empire, which they also commonly call the *kingdom of wickedness* <note>Hebrew: מלכות הרשעה (malchut ha-risha)</note>. For it seems that *Armilos* is a corrupt pronunciation of *Romulus*, the founder of the Roman Empire. But they make the second Messiah the son of David, who is to destroy *Armilos*, that is, the Antichrist. Who does not see that these things, quite enigmatically and at least under a certain veil, demonstrate the double coming of Christ? That humble coming, in which He was condemned and crucified by the Romans, with Pilate as judge and sitting before the tribunal as Caesar’s procurator; and that glorious coming, by which He will therefore trample down the power of Caesar and the Antichrist.

Nevertheless, in this fabrication, the Hebrews are mistaken in two primary ways: 
1. When they assert that something was said of two persons which is actually true of only one, but fulfilled at different times. 
2. Since they dream of nothing but external and temporal things, whereas on the contrary, the kingdom of the Messiah, according to the Scriptures—

be spiritual and internal. Hence, understanding it spiritually, when Christ was born a star rose out of Jacob, and a scepter was raised in Israel, about which the Magi inquired in Matthew 2: *Where is the king of the Jews, so that we may worship him? For we have seen his star.* Therefore, they worshiped at the manger according to the Eastern custom, and offered three gifts: *Gold, Frankincense, and Myrrh.* *Gold,* because he was a king. *Frankincense,* because he was God, to whom incense, libations, and offerings of smoke pertained. *Myrrh,* because he was a man, which was used to preserve bodies from corruption.

So much for the coming of Christ *in the flesh*; now follows his coming *in the spirit*, which is twofold. I. In the Dispensation <term>Dispensation: (Latin: *Oeconomia*) The way God manages or "houses" the divine plan during a specific era of history.</term> of the Old Testament. II. In the Dispensation of the New Testament. In the Dispensation of the Old Testament, it was again twofold. I. *In prelude.* II. *Perfectly.* In the former way, he appeared to the Patriarchs. In the latter, to Moses and the other Prophets. For although at the beginning of the world and in the origins of the Church the shadows were very thick, obscuring the "body" and the truth, they thereafter became thinner, so that the body appeared more and more clearly. Hence those epochs of the Church noted in the Scriptures, *Genesis 4:26: Then they began to call upon the name of Jehovah.* And *Exodus 6:2: I appeared indeed to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob by the name of God Strong and Almighty <note>original: "Dei fortis, Omnipotentis" — translating the Hebrew El Shaddai.</note>: but by my name Jehovah I was not known to them.* Because of this, Isaiah is eventually called the *fifth Evangelist*, because he prophesied so clearly about Christ. And indeed, under different periods, the distribution of this mystery varies—at times more obscure, at times more illustrious. This is why Scripture proceeds from confused things to more distinct ones, and from more general things to more specific ones. First, in *Genesis 3*, in the oldest of all oracles, it says: *The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent.* This was said generally regarding the "seed of the woman"; but as to who that woman would be, and where she would come from—whether from the Jews or the Gentiles—there was then a deep silence. Next, it is revealed that the Messiah would be born from the seed of Abraham: *Genesis 22: In your seed shall the nations be blessed,* etc. But it was not yet clear through which of his children, until it was said: *in Isaac shall your seed be called,* and then in Jacob. But it was still not known from which tribe; however, later, as another oracle dawned, the revelation was made that the Messiah would arise from the tribe of Judah, in *Genesis 49*.

I. *With respect to individual believers*; For as often as a believer is effectively called and thereafter daily sanctified, so often does Christ come to him. Hence it is that, according to those various comings of Christ—whether in the flesh or in the Spirit—there are also various types of resurrection. For since Christ is that life and our life-giving bread, he can never come to us without immediately giving us life and calling us from the dead. 1. <note>original Greek: τῆς εὐαγγελικῆς ἐπαγγελίας</note> **of the evangelical promise** they possessed, more so than the Heathens who lived outside the covenant and the Commonwealth of Israel—indeed, living without God, as is held in Ephesians 2:12.

For he sentenced some of the Moabites to death, and others he "made to live"—that is, according to a Hebraism <note>Hebraism: A Hebrew idiom or speech pattern translated literally into Latin or English.</note>, he left them in life and, negatively, did not condemn them to death. Add that if you carefully consider the history which is found in 2 Samuel 8 <margin>2.</margin> concerning the destruction of the Moabites, you will clearly see those two kinds of effects of Christ’s coming: namely, *in itself* and *incidentally*. <note>original Latin: "per se, & per accidens"</note> For *he struck the Moabites, and when he measured them with a cord, casting them down to the ground, he measured with two cords those whom he would put to death; but with one full cord those whom he would keep alive: and the Moabites became David’s servants, bringing tribute.* <note>Quoting 2 Samuel 8:2. All and every individual human being is evil by their own nature; therefore, God could have made them "vessels of wrath," or as Paul speaks in Romans 9, they could have been "vessels prepared for destruction." <note>vessels of wrath: A biblical metaphor for those who face God's judgment due to their persistent rejection of Him.</note> Nevertheless, God chose some and rejected others, **according to the good pleasure of his will** <note>original Greek: κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ</note> (Ephesians 1:5). David had conquered all the Moabites, and therefore by the right of war he could have sentenced each and every one to death; and yet he made a tempering of his justice and his mercy. For while he measured them all with a cord, some he brought to life—specifically those he measured with a full cord—while others he put to death, namely those he measured with two cords.

In the same way, since the whole world was "Moabite"—that is, an enemy of the true David and the King of Kings—He could have cut them all off. But by the cord sent out into the Nations, He chose some for His inheritance, so that they might serve Him and bring tribute, as is found in *Psalm 72:10: the kings of the coastline and the islands shall render tribute, the kings of Sheba and Seba shall offer a gift.* Others, however, He put to death and condemned to eternal destruction. It is for this reason that Christ’s coming produced two kinds of effects.

The first is *in itself* <note>original Latin: "per se"</note> with respect to the elect, because they were brought to life—not merely *negatively*, as the Moabites were by being left alive or by not being killed; for they were not living an "ethical death" <note>Ethical death: likely referring to a state of moral or social non-existence or exile.</note> unless you understand it as "physical death," for in that sense he brought them to life negatively. Since Balaam delivered all these words with his face turned toward the Israelites, the Eastern peoples whom the Jews subdued in their own time were behind him. But if anyone prefers to interpret this as "sons of siege"—that is, troublesome enemies by whom the Israelites were pressed by constant siege—deriving the name from the verb that means "to set up camp," as in Psalm 3:7: *I will not fear the myriads of people* <gloss>who have set themselves against me all around</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: אשר סביב שתו עלי (*asher saviv shatu alai*)</note>; I have no objection. So says Junius. <note>Francis Junius (1545–1602), a major Huguenot theologian and biblical scholar.</note>

Therefore, if we look at the <term>type</term> <note>In biblical study, a "type" is a historical person or event that foreshadows a future reality.</note>—which is King David, who subdued all those nations, as is clear by comparing this passage with 2 Samuel 8:3—that interpretation could fit by taking the name <term>Seth</term> as a common noun. Nevertheless, to freely open my mind, I believe the Spirit of God (by whose inspiration Balaam pronounced this oracle) looked further and predicted something far more splendid: namely, the glory of Christ’s kingdom. Of this, David’s kingdom was an illustrious <term>type</term>; and as the <term>antitype</term> <note>The "antitype" is the fulfillment of the "type"—in this case, Christ fulfilling the pattern set by David.</note> always displays something greater than the type, so after predicting the glory of David's kingdom and the reach of his scepter in subduing the Moabites, Ammonites, and other neighboring peoples, the text immediately mentions the most ample triumphs of the Messiah’s kingdom. This is not only in the spiritual devastation of the Moabites but also in the extermination of all peoples who dared to rise against the Messiah. All these are designated by "Seth," taking that name not as a common noun, but as a proper name.

So the sense of this oracle is: <gloss>and he shall destroy all the sons of Seth.</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: וקרקר כל בני שת (*ve-qarqar kol-bene-Sheth*)</note> The word <term>karqar</term> <note>Hebrew: קרקר</note> signifies "to destroy," as when a wall is torn down; for it comes from <term>qir</term> <note>Hebrew: קיר</note>, which means "a wall." He will therefore demolish the sons of Seth as easily as if one were reducing a wall to ashes. By "the sons of Seth," he understands all of humanity. For as in Scripture, all individual men are commonly designated as "sons of Adam," since all took their origin from that one beginning (Acts 17). So, because the entire posterity of Cain perished in the Flood, and...

->BY ANTOINE CRÉGUT<-

The descendants of Seth lived on in Noah, the second parent of the human race and a sort of <term>protoplast</term> <note>From the Greek *prōtoplastos*, meaning "first-formed." Crégut uses this to describe Noah as a second Adam, the new starting point for humanity after the Flood.</note>; hence it came about that the whole human race is denoted by the "sons of Seth." Here, therefore, is fulfilled what was predicted in <margin>Psalm 2:2</margin> *The kings of the earth stand up and the leaders consult together, against Jehovah and against his Christ.* <note>original Latin: "contra Iehovam & contra Christum eius." In this context, "Christ" refers to the "Anointed One."</note> But as it is said in <margin>verse 9</margin> *he shall break them with a rod of iron.* Thus Balak, king of the Moabites, now tries in vain against Jehovah and the Messiah. For *a star shall arise out of Jacob and a scepter shall proceed out of Israel, which shall strike the corners of Moab and destroy all the sons of Seth.*

For so great will be the glory and power of that great king, that he will not only fundamentally ruin the *Moabites*—that is, certain specific nations—but even *all the sons of Seth*, which is to say, all the peoples of the earth. A specimen of this glory and power appeared in the reign of David, who rose from the dust and from the shepherd’s crook to the scepter of a great king, even though his rivals murmured and said, *What have I to do with the son of Jesse?* <note>original Latin: "quid mihi cum filio Isai." This refers to the cry of rebellion against David's lineage in 2 Samuel 20:1.</note> Just as a star when it first rises is almost imperceptible, but soon it sparkles and then shines forth more brilliantly. This was truly fulfilled in Christ, who from the beginning was a small stone cut out from a mountain, but soon grew like a mountain and broke the statue of Nebuchadnezzar, by which the empires of the world and the four Monarchies were shadowed forth, as Daniel the Prophet prophesied.

By all these things, the kingdom of the Messiah is exalted above all the Monarchies of the world: both in respect to duration, because it will last forever while the Monarchies shall pass away; in respect to glory, because it will be more radiant than the glory of any Monarch; and in respect to power, because it will lay waste to all worldly kingdoms and destroy all the "sons of Seth." Finally, he will rule far and wide, from one sea to the other and even to the ends of the earth, as the Prophet says. Hence even the <term>Chaldean</term> <note>Referring to the *Targum*, the ancient Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> in this passage has: *he shall rule over all.*

SINCE God in the beginning created the world by His word, He established it so perfectly within the interval of six days that nothing can be added or taken away; thus, what is said of the work of grace—*It is finished* <note>original Latin: "Consummatum est."</note>—can truly be said of the work of nature. Therefore, He rested in both, as if satisfied with the perfection of the work. It is for this reason that if, by some chance, that perfection of the entire world were disturbed, all things would suddenly rush together so that no vacuum would exist in nature; rather, to fill that space and aid the whole universe, a particular nature would set aside its own specific inclinations. 

This principle holds a place in the Word of God <term>analogously <note>original Greek: $\dot{\alpha}\nu\alpha\lambda\acute{o}\gamma\omega\varsigma$ (analogos); meaning that the same logic applied to the physical world applies to the spiritual Word.</note></term>; for since it is most perfect, God takes care that nothing is added or taken away. Nor does He prohibit anything more severely than <term>will-worship <note>original Greek: $\dot{\epsilon}\theta\epsilon\lambda\omicron\theta\rho\eta\sigma\kappa\epsilon\acute{\iota}\alpha\varsigma$ (ethelothreskeias); a term from Colossians 2:23 referring to man-made religious practices that have no divine authority.</note></term>. Even the Tabernacle was constructed according to the pattern shown to Moses on the mountain; to which the Apostle perhaps alluded when he demanded that the interpretation of the Word of God be according to <term>the pattern of sound words <note>original Greek: $\dot{\upsilon}\pi\omicron\tau\acute{u}\pi\omega\sigma\iota\nu \tau\hat{\omega}\nu \dot{\upsilon}\gamma\iota\alpha\iota\nu\acute{o}\nu\tau\omega\nu \lambda\acute{o}\gamma\omega\nu$ (hypotyposin ton hygiainonton logon); a reference to 2 Timothy 1:13.</note></term>. These things are taught in those prominent words of the divine precept in *Chapter 4, verse 2*: *Do not add to the word that I command you, etc.* Here, only two points come to be explained under divine auspices: I. *The prohibition made by God*. II. *The reason for this prohibition*. The *Prohibition* is that nothing should be added to the word of God. The *Reason* is so that the Church may keep the commandments of Jehovah.

I. In this prohibition, two things must be observed: 1. *that the word is commanded by God*. II. *The substance of the precept, that nothing is to be added or taken away.* There is great emphasis and urgent significance when Moses says that the word was commanded by God; for if among men the requests of superiors are treated as mandates, how must we judge things concerning God? For first, God’s permission is itself a precept, as we have taught elsewhere from the proper meaning of the word <term>Tsivah</term> <note>original: צוה (tsivah); a Hebrew verb meaning to command, charge, or give an order.</note> and from the passage in Matthew 19 when discussing the bill of divorce; and furthermore, the precepts of God are laws or irrevocable decrees. Hence, it is rightly held that three degrees of obedience are owed to God’s precepts, beyond which no others are given.

I. We must execute God's orders with the utmost accuracy. II. It is necessary to fulfill God's mandates not only outwardly in respect to the work itself, but also inwardly in respect to the will; because just as God is Spirit and the <term>Knower of Hearts</term> <note>original: καρδιογνώστης (kardiognostes); a Greek theological term emphasizing God’s unique ability to see into the human soul.</note>, so He wishes to be worshipped in Spirit and in truth. Therefore, a person ought to strip off their own will so that they may put on His will. III. There is still required the "apex of the soul," namely the mind or intelligence, which is the highest degree of obedience. This means that we should not only wish for the same things as our God, but also feel and think the same as He does—even if we are usually ignorant of the reason for the divine precepts, as Abraham was when he *believed in hope against hope*. For obedience is a kind of <term>burnt offering</term> <note>original: holocaustum; a religious animal sacrifice consumed entirely by fire.</note> by which the whole person, without any reduction at all, is sacrificed in the fire of charity. Hence Gregory I skillfully remarked:

> Obedience is the only virtue that implants the other virtues into the mind, and guards them once they are implanted.

Wherefore Christ repaired the crime of Adam's disobedience by His own obedience <term>unto death</term> <note>original: μέχρι θανάτου (mechri thanatou).</note>. Holy was the action of Martha; holy was the contemplation of Magdalene; holy was the penance and the tears with which the feet of Christ were moistened—but it was necessary for these to happen in Bethany, that is, the *house of obedience*, to signify (says Bernard) that none of those things would have been accepted outside of Bethany. This is why a theologian of no common sort, nor of the lowest rank, has very truly said that the chief effect of the fear of God is obedience. Indeed, that is the submission of a pious mind, by which the revealed divine voice is obeyed eagerly, diligently, and constantly; not as in sacrifices where one offers the flesh of another, but by <insert>sacrificing</insert> one's own will.

...by sacrificing and offering. Just as in the study of nature <note>original: Physicis</note> lower bodies are influenced by higher ones, so human minds are influenced by the Supreme. And just as those higher bodies cause changes out of impure matter, so the light of the Holy Spirit ignites the sluggish wills of men. And as God is the first mover of all things that are moved in both the physical and moral <note>original: Ethico</note> realms; so all agents, both voluntary and natural, are bound to obey Him simply: the latter by the necessity of nature, the former by the necessity of justice. II. In this first part, the **substance of the prohibition** follows, which is: *you shall add nothing to the word, nor take away from it.* This prohibition demonstrates, above all, the perfection of the divine Word. For what is a more expressive character of a work’s perfection? Is it not immutability and invariability? Namely, when the same state endures, and not even a jot or a tiny mark <note>original: iota quidem aut apex; a reference to Matthew 5:18 regarding the smallest details of the Law.</note> is changed, added, or subtracted. This perfection is certainly owed to the word of God, no less than to its author. For God is therefore called by the Hebrews, most emphatically, <term>perfect</term> <note>original: כָּלוּל (kalul)</note> from the root <term>to complete</term> <note>original: כָּלַל (kalal)</note> because He alone possesses <term>all things</term> <note>original: הַכֹּל (haccol)</note>. The Latin word *perfection* derived from *performing* <note>original: perficiendo</note> contains a hint of imperfection, for something is called *perfect* because it has been fully *made* <note>The author argues that the Latin word implies a process of "becoming" finished, whereas God is eternally complete.</note>. The Greek word <term>perfect</term> <note>original: τέλειον (teleion)</note> also means that which has reached its goal or end. But the Hebrew word includes no such imperfection. In this third sense, the word of God is primarily called <term>perfect</term> <note>original: כָּלוּל (kalul)</note>; because it contains all things necessary—I say the word of God is perfect because it contains all things necessary for salvation. For the perfection of the divine Word or Scripture is not entirely the same as the perfection of God. For God is absolutely <term>perfect</term> <note>original: כָּלוּל (kalul)</note>, having in Himself everything that can be conceived. But the word of God is perfect <term>in a certain respect</term> <note>original: πῇ τὶ (pe ti)</note> and relative to its kind—that is, regarding the fullness of the articles of faith; or regarding the fullness of its essential and integral parts, which are the heavenly truth, the Law, and the Gospel. This is why Paul, in 2 Timothy 3:16, describes the fullness or totality of Scripture when it is said <term>all Scripture</term> <note>original: πᾶσα γραφὴ (pasa graphe)</note>; for that is properly called a "whole" <note>original: totum</note> which possesses all its [parts]...

it has its parts; than by describing all the uses of Scripture.

Yet we must not linger here too long on the quibbles of the Roman Catholics <note>original: Pontificiorum; referring to those loyal to the Pope</note>, who falsely accuse <term>Theodore Beza</term> <note>A prominent Protestant reformer and successor to John Calvin, known for his Latin translation of the New Testament.</note> of corruption and try to persuade the half-learned and those ignorant of the Greek idiom. For they say—prick up your ears—that *πᾶσα* <gloss>pasa; all/every</gloss> in Greek signifies *every* <note>original: omnis</note>, not *the whole* <note>original: tota</note>. But alas, good sirs! What would *πᾶσα* <gloss>all</gloss> and *ὅλη* <gloss>hole; whole</gloss> mean to the French? And if our language is so poor that it cannot explain the distinctions between those words, it is no different than how no language, whether Oriental or Western, can explain the distinction between the Latin words *to be unwilling* <note>original: nolle</note> and *to not will* <note>original: non velle</note>—a distinction which <term>Robert Bellarmine</term> <note>A highly influential Jesuit Cardinal and Counter-Reformer.</note> devised when explaining that passage of the Psalms according to the Latin edition: *You are a God not willing iniquity.* Would it be so hard for you if Beza borrowed the property of Latin words to express the sense of the Greek word *πᾶσα* <gloss>all</gloss>? 

For *πᾶς* <gloss>pas; all</gloss> sometimes in Scripture signifies <term>universality</term>, and sometimes <term>integrity</term>; that is, either *πᾶς* <gloss>all</gloss> signifies a **universal whole** or an **integral whole** <note>In logic, a "universal whole" refers to a category where every member is included (e.g., "every human"), while an "integral whole" refers to a single thing made of parts (e.g., "the whole body").</note>. When it denotes a universal whole, it is not correctly expressed by the word "whole" <note>original: totum</note>; for example, one would not correctly say, "the whole man is a rational animal," but rather one must say "every man," etc. But if the question concerns an **integral whole**, one would not correctly say of Peter, "Every this man consists of a head, chest, etc.," but rather "The whole of this man, etc." So it is in that proverb: *πλέον ἥμισυ παντός* <gloss>The half is more than the whole</gloss>—not "more than every." So also in Ephesians 4:16, the Latin edition translates *πᾶν τὸ σῶμα* <gloss>pan to soma</gloss> as "the whole body." Did the common translator <note>referring to the author of the Vulgate</note> corrupt the text just as Beza did? Furthermore, it is more certain than certainty itself that Scripture is an integral whole, not a universal whole.

Nevertheless, even though I said at the start that we should not linger here long, because the objections of <term>Cardinal Davy du Perron</term> <note>Jacques Davy du Perron, a French cardinal known for his efforts to convert Protestants, including King Henry IV.</note> against the King of England <note>King James I, who was a scholarly theologian.</note> regarding this passage come to mind, I wish to refute them for the time being. 
I. He says Paul says *πᾶσα* <gloss>all/every</gloss>, not *ὅλη* <gloss>whole</gloss>; and therefore it is not to be understood as "all Scripture" **collectively**, but "every scripture" **distributively**. 
II. Paul does not speak with the emphatic article, *πᾶσα ἡ γραφὴ* <gloss>the all scripture</gloss>, but without the article, *πᾶσα γραφὴ* <gloss>all/every scripture</gloss>, nor is it necessary to supply the article. For even if among Greek authors *πᾶς* is sometimes taken collectively without the article, because they published writings that were somewhat poetic and licentious <note>meaning they took linguistic liberties</note>, nevertheless...

<meta>This page continues the philological debate between Anthony Cregut and Cardinal Robert Bellarmine regarding 2 Timothy 3:16. Cregut is refuting Bellarmine's claim that because the Greek word "pas" (all) lacks a definite article in that verse, it must mean "every individual part" rather than "the entire body of Scripture."</meta>

-> # REVEALER OF SECRETS # <-

-> Ppppp iij <-

among the Apostles, whose style is simpler, *pas* <gloss>all/every</gloss> without the article never signifies a collective whole, unless it is either applied to a proper name (which compensates for the article), or to a common name joined with a proper name so that it is equivalent to a proper name, such as *the house of Israel* <note>original: domus Israelis</note>, that is, *Israel*. These things the <term>Cardinal</term> <note>Robert Bellarmine</note> discusses at length, not because he himself believed them to be true, but so that he might acquire for himself the praise of sharp wit, erudition, and eloquence, and so that by obscuring the arguments with his subtleties, he might throw dust in the eyes <note>A classical metaphor for deceiving or confusing someone</note>; a fact which the prudent reader will easily observe in this place and elsewhere throughout his work.

I respond, therefore, to his first reason by denying that the word *pasa* <gloss>all</gloss> is taken distributively <note>meaning "every single part individually"</note>; rather, it is taken collectively <note>meaning "the whole thing as a unit"</note>, as was demonstrated by us above, because Scripture is not a "universal whole" <note>a category or class</note>, but an "integral whole" <note>a single body made of parts</note>. 

II. That "loophole" <note>original: κρησφύγετον; a place of refuge or an excuse</note> concerning the emphatic article is useless. For frequently among Greek authors, *pasa* is used collectively without the article, not distributively, as is clear from the proverb cited above: *the half is more than the whole* <note>original: πλέον ἥμισυ παντός; a famous line from the poet Hesiod</note>. It is futile for him to add that those authors spoke poetically and with license; for on the contrary, according to the requirements of the sense, they sometimes add the article and sometimes omit it. Indeed, if it were added against the intended sense, it would be more a matter of "license" than the omission is. As in the example praised before, it is better to say *the half is more than the whole* <note>original: πλέον ἥμισυ παντός</note> than to say "more than *the* whole" <note>original: τοῦ παντός</note>, even though it is taken collectively. 

III. In Scripture, *pas* <gloss>all</gloss> is often taken collectively, as in Matthew 8:32: *the whole herd* <note>original: πᾶσα ἡ ἀγέλη</note> of the swine. And Ephesians 4:16, which was discussed above. But, he says, it is placed there with an article. Oh, what sharp wit! What of it? Does the article really effect a change in the sense? The article certainly demonstrates and determines the thing more specifically, but it hardly changes the sense. This is clear from the fact that the article is used with the word *holos* <gloss>whole</gloss> or *pas* <gloss>all</gloss> indiscriminately, even though the Cardinal would be forced to admit that the word *holos* <gloss>whole</gloss> is taken collectively even without the article. Thus in 1 Corinthians 12:17, it is said: *the whole body* <note>original: ὅλον τὸ σῶμα</note>. 

But let us hear the Cardinal’s "erudite wit"; for he offers us the "herb" <note>original: herbam porrigit; a Latin idiom meaning to admit defeat or to offer a peace offering, here used sarcastically</note> with such a display of genius. "The article," he says, "is always joined with the word *pas*, unless it is applied to a proper name, or to a common name equivalent to a proper name, such as *all Jerusalem* <note>original: πᾶσα Iερουσαλήμ</note> or *all the house of Israel* <note>original: πᾶσα οἶκος Iσραήλ</note>." Very well, I now seize upon what has been conceded, and I ask: is not a name spoken <term>antonomastically</term>? <note>Antonomasia is a rhetorical term for using a title or epithet in place of a proper name, or vice versa—here implying "The Scripture" is a unique title like a proper name.</note>

And does not the term <term>by way of excellence</term> <note>original: κατ’ ἐξοχὴν (*kat' exochēn*); a rhetorical term for using a common title as a proper name because it is the pre-eminent example</note> equal a proper name? Does not "the Apostle" signify Paul? And "the poet" signify Homer or Virgil? And does not "Scripture" also <term>antonomastically</term> <note>Antonomasia is the use of a title or epithet in place of a proper name, like calling a king "His Majesty"</note> signify the Law and the Gospel? Who would be so senseless as to assert that *every* writing, taken <term>distributively</term> <note>meaning "every single piece of writing ever produced," rather than the specific body of Holy Scripture</note>, is divinely inspired? Away with such monstrous ideas! By this reasoning, would not that impious book which even among the Muslims is called pre-eminently *the Alcoran* <note>The Quran</note>—that is, "the reading"—be divinely inspired?

Add to this that when Paul said *all scripture* <note>original: πᾶσα γραφὴ (*pasa graphē*)</note>, he understands this—according to Davy—as referring either to the Scripture of the Old Testament, or to the Scripture of the New Testament which then existed, or to any writing whatsoever taken distributively. I do not think the <term>Cardinal</term> <note>Robert Bellarmine, a leading Catholic theologian and opponent of Crégut</note> himself would assert this last point; for (as I said a little earlier) the *Alcoran* itself would then be <term>divinely inspired</term> <note>original: Θεόπνευστος (*theopneustos*); literally "God-breathed"</note>. He does not understand this as referring to the Old Testament alone, for that would exclude the books of the New Testament which existed when Paul wrote that epistle (which was written shortly before his death). Thus the argument would be even stronger: if the Scripture of the Old Testament alone contained all the articles of faith and was perfect, it would be true regarding the "perfection of its parts," even if not in the degree of light and revelation; for those things which lie hidden in the Old Testament are made plain in the New. But if Paul is understood to be speaking of both Testaments, the Cardinal is in agreement with us.

<term>Incidentally</term> <note>original: Παρέργως (*Parergōs*)</note>, Davy also observes that in the writings of the Apostles, "Scripture" <note>original: γραφὴν (*graphēn*)</note> is always placed with the article. But what does he gain from this, except that he still extends a hand to help us? For what does this signify except what we said above: that "Scripture" is used by Paul antonomastically, as it is elsewhere, and therefore that specific usage is mostly designated by an emphatic article; so that the Old and New Testaments would be understood to the exclusion of any other writing. Yet he could not make his observation so general that he did not find an exception himself: namely 2 Peter 1:20, "that all prophecy of scripture..." <note>original: ὅτι πᾶσα προφητεία γραφῆς (*hoti pasa prophēteia graphēs*)</note>, where "scripture" is used without the article. ...sacred writing. This little "whitewashing" of the argument <note>original: *incrustatiuncula*; literally a small piece of plaster or veneer, used here to mean a flimsy or superficial excuse</note> is invalid for the following reasons:

I. Because this would not have prevented the definite article from being added in this way: *the prophecy of the scripture* <note>original: προφητεία τῆς γραφῆς (*prophēteia tēs graphēs*)</note>. 

II. Even if the article was not placed there, I say it is to be <term>subunderstood</term> <note>a linguistic term meaning a word is implied by the context even if not explicitly written</note>, both here and wherever it is not explicitly found; because always in the Old and New Testaments, "Scripture" is taken <term>antonomastically</term> <note>the use of a title or common noun as a proper name, like calling the Bible "The Book"</note>, and for that reason, the title itself designates the article. 

III. For that same reason, I say it was better translated by <term>Beza</term> <note>Theodore Beza, a major Protestant reformer and successor to John Calvin</note> as *the prophecy of Scripture*, rather than *written prophecy*, or—as <term>Erasmus</term> <note>Desiderius Erasmus, the famous Dutch humanist who produced the first printed Greek New Testament</note> had it—*prophetic Scripture*; this ensures that only the prophecy of the Bible is understood, not the prophecies of false prophets or impious seers. 

IV. Paul does not expressly add the article for a specific reason: since the word *God-breathed* <note>original: θεόπνευστος (*theopneustos*)</note> is added, it sufficiently indicates even without an article that this is about the Scripture of the Old and New Testaments, not about secular or "profane" writings. This is similar to Romans 16:26, *through the prophetic scriptures* <note>original: διά τε γραφῶν προφητικῶν (*dia te graphōn prophētikōn*)</note>, where the article is not added because the word *prophetic* preceding *scriptures* (without an article) sufficiently determines and limits the meaning, just as in Romans 1:2, *in the holy scriptures* <note>original: ἐν γραφαῖς ἁγίαις (*en graphais hagiais*)</note> is written without an article. 

V. The French versions of the Roman Church, such as those of the scholars of <term>Louvain</term> and of <term>René Benoist</term> <note>a prominent 16th-century French Catholic theologian</note>, agree with us, as they express the article in their translations.

VI. The point that someone taught <term>Cardinal Davy</term> <note>Jacques Davy du Perron, a Catholic convert and influential diplomat and cardinal</note> is of no better quality. He lists with great pride all the famous versions—Jerome’s <note>the Latin Vulgate</note>, the Syriac, the Egyptian, the Ethiopic, and the Arabic—claiming they did not include the article. The reason for not expressing the article in those versions is the same as in the original Greek manuscript, as discussed above. Furthermore, the Cardinal ought to have known that there is a specific logic to translations; for other languages do not use articles as frequently as the Greek language does. This is why in the Syriac and Arabic versions, the article is often omitted even when it is present in the Greek, as is evident from Matthew 26:54 and six hundred other places.

Moreover, he "kills himself with his own sword" <note>an idiom similar to "he is hoist by his own petard," meaning his own argument destroys his position</note> when he says that *it follows from this that every book of Scripture, taken <term>distributively</term>, is sufficient*. That is indeed a very true consequence, and therefore our position is clear: Paul’s words must be taken <term>collectively</term> <note>referring to the whole body of Scripture together</note>, not <term>distributively</term> <note>referring to each individual part separately</note>. <meta>This page continues Anthony Crégut's theological defense of the "perfection" and sufficiency of the Bible. Having previously addressed the linguistic arguments of Cardinal du Perron, Crégut now transitions into a systematic classification of how Scripture can be considered "perfect," specifically distinguishing between the lost original manuscripts and the copies used by the Church today.</meta>

-># THE REVEALER OF SECRETS #<-

than the Greeks; and concerning these we assert that Scripture is so perfect that it is not permitted for any mortal to add, subtract, or change even the slightest bit—not even a single letter or a mark <note>original: *apicem*; referring to the smallest stroke of a pen or a vowel point</note>. This is because Scripture in its original manuscript <term>autographo: the original document written by the author's own hand</term> is God-breathed <note>original Greek: Θϵόπνϵυστoς (*theopneustos*)</note> not only in its subject and substance, but also in its words and marks, so that even the smallest alteration would be sacrilegious. As for the copies <term>apographa: transcriptions or copies made from the original manuscripts</term>, those are only perfect in their meaning—and even then, not of their own accord, but by being traced back to the originals, insofar as they agree with them. Regarding the actual words, however, they are not perfect; but can be further perfected day by day <note>Crégut is acknowledging the role of textual criticism and scholarship in improving the accuracy of Bible translations</note>.

II. *The perfection of Scripture is considered according to the matter itself, or regarding the articles of faith;* and thus we also establish that it is perfect and that it is a crime for any person to add or subtract anything from it (as Moses says), or even to change it. This holds whether we look at Scripture in the original manuscripts, or in the copies and in pure versions that reflect the original Hebrew and Greek truth.

III. *The perfection of Scripture can be weighed either with respect to the perfection of its parts, or with respect to the perfection of its degrees.* In the first way, Scripture is called perfect insofar as it encompasses all articles of faith; and in this way even the Old Testament was perfect—indeed, even the individual books of the Old Testament. In the second way, Scripture is perfect insofar as it encompasses all degrees; and in this way the Scripture of the Old Testament is not as perfect as that of the New Testament. This is because the former contained shadows, while the latter contains the body <note>a common theological metaphor: the Old Testament foreshadows what the New Testament reveals in reality</note>. The former contained figures; the latter, the truth. Therefore, the degrees of light and revelation were more brilliant in the New Testament.

IV. *The perfection of parts can be viewed regarding essential and integral parts.* Scripture is perfect in both ways: For in it is always found *heavenly and saving Truth;* all articles of faith, the *Law and the Gospel.* And even if, by God's providence permitting it, some book of Scripture were to perish, the faith and the Church would not perish because of it; since the perfection of its parts would always remain, both the essential and the integral ones. Therefore, the Romanists <note>original: *Pontificij*; literally "the Pontificians," referring to the Roman Catholic party</note> waste their effort and "lose both their oil and their labor" <note>a Latin idiom, *oleum et operam perdere*, meaning to waste time and resources on a fruitless task</note> in vain...

-># THE REVEALER OF SECRETS #<-

than the Greeks; and concerning these we assert that Scripture is so perfect that it is not permitted for any mortal to add, subtract, or change even the slightest bit—not even a single letter or a mark <note>original: *apicem*; referring to the smallest stroke of a pen or a vowel point, similar to the "jot and tittle" mentioned in the Gospels</note>. This is because Scripture in the original manuscript <term>autographo: the original document written by the author's own hand</term> is God-breathed <note>original Greek: Θεόπνευστος (*theopneustos*)</note>, not only regarding its matter and substance, but also regarding its words and marks, so that even the smallest alteration would have been sacrilegious. As for the copies <term>apographa: transcriptions or copies made from the original manuscripts</term>, those are only perfect regarding their meaning—and even then, not of their own accord, but by being traced back to the originals, insofar as they agree with them. Regarding the actual words, however, they are not perfect; but can be further perfected day by day <note>The author acknowledges that scholars and translators work over time to bring copies closer to the original wording</note>.

II. *The perfection of Scripture* is considered according to the matter itself, or regarding the articles of faith; and thus we also establish that it is perfect and that it is a crime for any person to add or subtract anything from it (as Moses says), or even to change it. This holds whether we look at Scripture in the original manuscripts, or in the copies and in the pure versions that reflect the Hebrew and Greek truth.

III. *The perfection of Scripture* can be weighed either *with respect to the perfection of its parts*, or *with respect to the perfection of its degrees*. In the former way, Scripture is called perfect insofar as it encompasses all the articles of faith; and in this way even the Old Testament was perfect—indeed, even the various individual books of the Old Testament. In the latter way, Scripture is perfect insofar as it encompasses all degrees; and in this way, the Scripture of the Old Testament is not as perfect as that of the New Testament; because the former contained shadows, while the latter contains the body <note>A reference to Colossians 2:17, where "shadows" refer to Old Testament laws and the "body" refers to Christ</note>. The former contained figures; the latter, the truth. Therefore, the degrees of light and revelation were more brilliant [in the New Testament].

IV. *The perfection of parts* can be viewed regarding *essential and integral parts*. Scripture is perfect in both ways: for in it is always found *heavenly and saving truth*, *all the articles of faith*, the *Law and the Gospel*. And although, by the permission of God’s providence, some book of Scripture might perish, the faith and the Church would not perish for that reason; because the perfection of the parts would always remain, both the essential and the integral ones. Thus, the Papists <term>Pontificij: a term used by Protestant polemicists to refer to Roman Catholics, specifically those loyal to the Pope</term> waste both their "oil and their labor" <note>An ancient Latin idiom, *oleum et operam perdere*, meaning to waste time and effort on a fruitless task</note> in vain.

...when they sweat excessively in their efforts to show that certain letters of Paul have perished, along with other books of Scripture; though in this regard they are greatly mistaken <note>original: *hallucinentur*; literally "hallucinating" or wandering in mind</note>. It is no different than in the human body, where essential and complete perfection remains even if the hair is shaved or if fluids and humors <note>original: *ichores*; a medical term for the watery discharge from a wound or serum in the blood</note> are purged, provided that the limbs themselves are not cut off.

V. *The perfection of Scripture* can further be weighed in terms of the *perfection of the part and the whole*. In both ways Scripture is perfect, but it is *absolutely* perfect by the perfection of the whole, while it is *relatively* perfect by the perfection of the part. Therefore, the book of Genesis is perfect, not with the perfection of the entire Scripture (as if it contained all the articles of faith, the whole Law, and the Gospel), but just as a hand is perfect with the perfection of a part when it has five fingers, and no more.

VI. Scripture is perfect because it describes a threefold kind of perfection: I. the *perfection of nature*, in the work of creation; II. the *perfection of grace*, in the work of the Incarnation; III. the *perfection of glory*, in the work of the resurrection.

Now, with these distinctions regarding the perfection of Scripture laid out in advance, the status of the controversy will be perfectly clear, and it will become obvious how the Papists <note>A common Reformation-era term for Roman Catholics</note> generally wander away from the true point of debate. For the question between us concerns the perfection of parts and degrees, and the perfection of essential and integral parts; and furthermore, it concerns the perfection of the whole, not just a part; and it concerns the perfection of the original manuscript <term>autographi: the documents written by the biblical authors' own hands</term> rather than the copy <term>apographi: a transcription or copy made from an original</term>, except on the premise that the copy agrees with the original. The followers of the Pope deny that Scripture is perfect even in this sense; therefore, against the command of Moses in this passage (Deuteronomy 4:2 and 12:32), they add the Apocryphal books and traditions to the Canon. Indeed, Perronius <note>Cardinal Jacques Davy Duperron (1556–1618), a prominent Catholic theologian and diplomat known for his polemics against Protestants</note>, a great champion of "accessory" traditions <note>original Greek: *παρεργοδότων* (parergodotōn); referring to things given as extras or side-works</note> and a most bitter opponent of divine traditions, titled his book *On the Insufficiency of the Scriptures*. But we, on the contrary, piously proclaim the perfection and sufficiency of Scripture; and we constantly observe that command, *Do not add to Jehovah*, rejecting those traditions.

...are discussed, the various ways "tradition" is understood must be distinguished; for here too I see the Papists <note>original: *Pontificios*; a term used by Protestant authors for Roman Catholics</note> lurking and attempting to "pierce the eyes of the crows." <note>original: *cornicum oculos configere*; a Latin idiom meaning to deceive even the most eagle-eyed or shrewd experts.</note> We must therefore see what the acceptance of tradition signifies in **Scripture**; what it means among the **Fathers**, as they call them (that is, the ancient Doctors of the Church); what it means among the **Hebrew Doctors**; and finally, what it means among the **Papists** themselves.

I. In Scripture, *tradition* <note>Greek: παράδοσις, *paradosis*</note> is sometimes taken **in a good sense**; and sometimes **in a bad sense**. It is used **in a good sense** in two ways: 1. For the true doctrine concerning faith and morals, as in 2 Thessalonians 3:6, where Paul warns the faithful to withdraw themselves from every brother who does not walk "according to the tradition which he received from us." <note>original: *κατὰ τὴν παράδοσιν ἣν παρέλαβε παρ' ἡμῶν*</note> And in 2 Thessalonians 2:15: "hold the traditions" <note>original: *κρατεῖτε τὰς παραδόσεις*</note> in which you were taught, whether by word or by our epistle; that is, by word and by epistle alike, because he taught them the same doctrine whether by living voice or by writing. He certainly does not mean the impure traditions of the superstitious.

II. Traditions are taken in a good sense for those institutes which look toward **good order** <note>Greek: εὐταξίαν, *eutaxian*</note>, for the sake of preserving decorum in the Church. 1 Corinthians 11:2: "As I delivered them to you, you keep the traditions." For in the following verses, he deals with the decorum to be observed by men and women in Church assemblies, where in verse 13 he says "what is proper" <note>original: *τὸ πρέπον*, *to prepon*; meaning that which is becoming or decorous</note> is for a woman to be covered while praying.

Furthermore, traditions are taken **in a bad sense** when men, by their own authority and not by divine authority, busy themselves with intruding doctrines of faith into the Church. This is why **will-worship** <note>original: *ἐθελοθρησκεία*, *ethelothreskeia*; self-imposed or man-made religion</note> and the traditions of men are condemned throughout Scripture, as in Colossians 2:8. Christ also frequently in the Gospel, such as in Matthew 15:2 and Mark 7 verses 3 and 5, rebukes the traditions of the Jews and Pharisees, which he contemptuously calls "traditions of men" and opposes to the Divine law, even though they themselves boasted of their traditions, which they called "traditions of the elders" and "traditions handed down by the fathers." <note>original: *πατροπαραδότων*, *patroparadotōn*</note> No less do the Papists boast today of their own traditions, which they have dared to call the **unwritten word of God**. And the Council of Trent, in its 4th session, does not blush to extol such things, saying: *Traditions are to be received with the same faith and piety as the Scriptures.* And the Catechism of the Council of Trent, book 4...

### ANTHONY CRÉGUT
<sig>Ppp3</sig>
<meta>catchword: refragatur,</meta>

...concerning the unwritten Word of God, chapter 7: *There are certain traditions which are greater in terms of their obligation than certain parts of Scripture.* <note>original: "Sunt quædam traditiones quæ sunt maiores quoad obligationem quàm quædam Scripturæ." Crégut is quoting a Roman Catholic position, likely from Bellarmine, which argues that some church traditions are more binding on a believer than some specific biblical commands.</note> What monstrous words! What monstrosities of things and persons! But it is enough for us that traditions of this kind are condemned throughout Scripture; for example, in this place, Deuteronomy 4:2 and 12:8. Also in Ezekiel 20:18 and 43:8, the Jews are rebuked for *placing their own threshold next to God’s threshold, and their doorpost next to God’s doorpost*, which is to say, they were treating their own traditions as equal to the commands of God.

Secondly, among the ancient Doctors of the Church, <term>paradosis</term> <note>Greek: παράδοσις; a "handing down" or "tradition."</note>, or tradition, is understood in many different ways:

I. They understand it as *written doctrine*, and in this way the name "tradition" coincides with Scripture itself. As Paul says in 1 Corinthians 11: *For I received from the Lord that which I also delivered to you.* <note>The Latin *tradidi* (delivered/handed down) shares the same root as "tradition."</note>

II. They understand a *tradition of the name, not of the thing.* For a name might be coined by men, while the reality itself could be a matter of divine tradition. Thus, the name <term>homoousios</term> <note>Greek: ὁμοούσιον; "consubstantial" or "of the same substance." A technical term used to define the relationship between God the Father and Jesus Christ against the Arian heresy.</note> was used against the Arians. So too the term <term>perichoresis</term> <note>Greek: περιχώρησις; the "mutual indwelling" or "interpenetration" of the three persons of the Trinity.</note>, which was familiar to John of Damascus; the Scholastic theologians rendered this word as *Circumincession*. In this same way, the words *Trinity, person, substance, hypostasis, etc.*, were "traditions of names."

III. They call *Ecclesiastical rites or ceremonies* traditions.

IV. They sometimes call *their own writings*, or *consanguinity of doctrine* <note>meaning teaching that shares the same "bloodline" or essence as the Apostles' teaching</note>, traditions; but this is the same as Scripture, insofar as they agree with Scripture in their teaching.

V. They occasionally accept traditions according to the sense of the heretics, but we must qualify this as belonging to "this or that" specific Church—just as when we say *the traditions of the Roman Church*. We do not say this to approve of them, but to disapprove of them, because they exist "by fact" but not "by right." <note>original: "de facto, non de iure." A legal distinction meaning something exists in reality but lacks a legitimate or legal basis.</note>

From these points, one can gather that the name "Tradition" was originally a general term among the Church Fathers, and it signified both written and unwritten doctrine which is passed from one person to another. This is taught by Peresius <note>Martín Pérez de Ayala (1512–1566), a Spanish theologian who wrote extensively on traditions.</note> in *On Traditions, part 1, postulate 2*, and by Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Cardinal and one of the most influential figures of the Counter-Reformation.</note> in *On the Word of God, book 4, chapter 2*. But afterwards, "tradition" was specifically taken to mean only unwritten doctrine that was passed down orally; and in this way, it was set in opposition to the written Word. Bellarmine adds, however, that tradition is called the "unwritten word," not because it was never written down at all, but because it was not committed to writing by its original author. But experience...
