...is opposed, since many Popish traditions were immediately set down in writing by their authors; such as the traditions of the Popes recorded by them in the decretals <note>Legal decrees or letters issued by a Pope to decide points of ecclesiastical law.</note>; and conversely, the book of Genesis would be considered an "unwritten" tradition, because it was written by Moses long after its events were first revealed.

But furthermore, I have seen no one who has expanded the acceptance of the word "tradition" more generally or broadly than Jacques Davy, Cardinal Perron <note>Jacques Davy du Perron (1556–1618) was a prominent French Cardinal and diplomat known for his skill in converting Protestants to Catholicism.</note>, who, writing against the King of England <note>This refers to Perron's *Replique* to King James I, who considered himself a theologian and often debated Catholic scholars.</note> on page 675 of his book, understands under the name of "tradition" whatever the Church has seen fit to hand down. For by this logic, the number of traditions would be vague and infinite, growing forever. And since Pope Boniface VIII wrote that *the Pope holds all law in the shrine of his breast*, <note>original: "Papam continere totum ius in scrinio sui pectoris." This legal maxim suggests that the Pope is the living source of all law and can interpret or create it at will.</note> so Perron says the Church has all traditions hidden within itself, keeping them like a deposit, and that they are therefore of divine institution. For he begins thus: "traditions are not of simple human institution; nor are they outside the word of God, which contains everything that God revealed to his Apostles, whether they committed it to writing, or consigned it to the deposit of the Church. Nor can they be said to be outside Scripture, since they are established by the same means by which Scripture itself is proven; just as what is entrusted to the faith of a messenger is deemed to be in the letters of the prince, because those letters give the messenger his credibility and authority." These words of Perron certainly increase the number of traditions to infinity and stretch the meaning of the word. Note, however, that by "the Church" he always means the Roman Church; which therefore dispenses all things in religion as it pleases. For that Church, the old saying of the Persian kings is common: *What pleases, is permitted.* <note>original: "Quod libet licet." A phrase used to describe absolute, often arbitrary, power where the ruler’s will is the only law.</note>

Furthermore, Davy increases the number of traditions to infinity when he includes "historical" traditions under that name, which are more about facts than about law. But since law concerns universal things and rules, while facts concern individual instances and examples, historical traditions would be endless. To this end, he lists several examples in his reply to the King of England on page 776: the mention of Jannes and Jambres <note>Names of Pharaoh's magicians which do not appear in the Old Testament but are mentioned in the New Testament (2 Timothy 3:8).</note> in *2 Timothy 3*; the trembling of Moses at the foot of the mountain in *Hebrews 12*; the idea that the law was handed down by Angels in *Galatians 3*; and that the book of the Law was sprinkled with the blood of the covenant in *Hebrews*. <note>Hebrews 9:19.</note>

**IX.** [Perron includes among traditions] that the tables of the covenant were enclosed in the ark, along with one jar of Manna, and another urn containing the flowering rod of Moses; a golden censer in the Sanctuary, and thus that the office of the High Priest was to offer incense in the inner sanctuary <note>original: "adytum," the most holy place of the Temple</note> (Hebrews 9); the tradition in the Epistle of Jude concerning the battle of Michael with the Devil for the body of Moses, and concerning the prophecy of Enoch and the Final Judgment. It remains now for us to see what the Hebrews understood by traditions: For the Jews were also superstitious sellers of traditions. From this they were called *Mecubbalim*, or *Kabbalists* <note>Derived from the Hebrew root meaning "to receive."</note>. For just as traditions are named from *handing down*, because they were delivered by word of mouth; so *Kabbalah* is named from *receiving*; it is a mystical Theology, and a doctrine delivered by word of mouth and received from "divine hearing," as they call it, regarding the mysteries of the divine law. For in Chaldean and Syriac, *cabbel* <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: קבל</note> signifies *to receive*. Hence, among them, there is a double law: the *Oral Law* and the *Written Law* <note>original Hebrew: תורה שבעל פה (*Torah she-be'al peh*) and תורה שבכתב (*Torah she-bi-ktav*)</note>. These traditions were not written down from the beginning. For although the divine law had been written by Moses from the start, God also delivered an oral law to Moses on Sinai, which he then delivered to Joshua and the Sanhedrin; then to the prophets, and after the Prophets to the men of the Great Synagogue; and thereafter to the sages of the Hebrews; until at last, lest they should be lost <note>Or "grow overgrown/distorted" (inolescerent)</note>, they were compiled in the Talmud in the year of Christ 150. From this, the text is called the *Mishna*, as if it were a *repeated law*, or a *reiteration* <note>original Greek: $\delta \epsilon \upsilon \tau \epsilon ́ \varrho \omega \sigma \iota \varsigma$ (*deuterōsis*)</note>. For when they were unable to stand against the Christians in dispute by the Scriptures alone, they called upon the Talmudic traditions for aid. Following this example, the Papists <note>A 17th-century Protestant term for Roman Catholics, referring to their allegiance to the Pope.</note>, when they felt themselves overwhelmed by the lightning-bolt of the Scriptures, [fled] to traditions...

<meta>This page continues Crégut's polemic against Roman Catholic interpretations of tradition. # ANTHONY CRÉGUT
<page-num>874</page-num>

...let us transfer [the meaning], for in the word *beyond* <note>original Latin: *præter*</note> is included the word *against* <note>original Latin: *contra*</note>. For whatever is taught regarding the articles of faith that is *beyond* Scripture is entirely *against* Scripture. For (as I said above) the status of the controversy concerns the perfection of Scripture regarding the articles of faith. But no article of faith can be brought forward *beyond* the Gospel which is not also *against* it. This is sufficiently proven from the traditions of the Papists, which were instituted not only *beyond* but even *against* the Gospel.

IV. Davy <note>Jacques Davy du Perron (1556–1618), a French cardinal and diplomat</note> and Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a central Jesuit figure in the Counter-Reformation</note> depart from the Vulgate translator, whom the Council of Trent <note>The 16th-century ecumenical council that defined Catholic dogma against the Reformation</note> alone judges as the "authentic" Scripture. The Vulgate translates it just as we do: *beyond what you have received* <note>original Latin: *præter id quod accepistis*, quoting Galatians 1:8</note>. Therefore, Perron and Bellarmine, both Cardinals, now desert their own "authentic" edition—which they claim is infallible—out of an immense, itching desire to contradict us and the truth.

V. Davy again deserts the "authentic" Vulgate edition in Romans 16:17, which does not translate the word as *against*, but as *beyond*, because it follows the proper and genuine meaning of the particle. Thus, in a spirit of contradicting the truth, he now twice contradicts his own authentic edition.

VI. Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a primary successor to John Calvin</note> correctly translates that aforementioned passage in Romans 16:17 as *against*, following the sense of the passage. For Paul signifies who should be held as the authors of dissensions: namely, those who teach anything different from the Apostolic doctrine, whom he calls elsewhere "those who teach other doctrines" <note>original Greek: ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῦντας (*heterodidaskalountas*)</note>.

VII. Just as these Doctors oppose the Vulgate edition in their choice of words, so they wrongly contradict the entire Pauline context regarding its sense. For the Apostle testifies in verse 7 that the doctrine of those men was not "another Gospel," and therefore not *against* the Gospel, but *beyond* it: *Which is not another (meaning Gospel) but there are some who trouble you.* <note>Quoting Galatians 1:7</note>

Furthermore, the Cardinal adds that the word *received* <note>original Latin: *accepistis*</note> is ambiguous, and should not be taken literally, but infinitely regarding whatever the Galatians had received either by writing or by the living voice <note>meaning oral tradition</note>. But I would like to ask of him, or another in his place, whether they believe the whole Gospel of Christ has been written or not? If the whole Gospel is written, then the Galatians received nothing that was not written. For there Paul speaks concerning the Gospel: *If anyone shall preach the Gospel to you, etc.* But if the whole Gospel is not written, then the <term>Apostles' Creed</term> <note>original Latin: *symbolum Apostolorum*; the early statement of Christian belief</note> does not contain all the articles—

### MARC-ANTOINE CRÉGUT

On this point, Perron is either deceiving others or is himself deceived, since Tertullian speaks of Scripture *collectively* <note>meaning as a complete, unified whole rather than as individual, isolated parts</note>. For on page 373 of Beatus Rhenanus’s edition, he begins thus: *Whether all things were made from some underlying matter, I have nowhere yet read. Let the workshop of Hermogenes show that it is written. If it is not written, let him fear that "woe" destined for those who add or subtract.* <note>original Latin: "An autem de aliqua subiacenti materia facta sint omnia... Sinon est scriptum timeat væ illud adijcientibus aut detrahentibus destinatum." This is a famous appeal to the "sufficiency" of Scripture against the idea of eternal matter.</note> He mentions a "workshop" because Hermogenes was a painter. Indeed, in the same place, after he had said, *I adore the fullness of Scripture, which manifests to me both the creator and the things created,* <note>original Latin: "Adoro Scripturæ plenitudinem..."</note> he immediately adds what follows: *In the Gospel, truly, I find even more: both the minister and the arbiter of the ruler, the Word.* And then he immediately places what we said above: *Whether from any underlying matter, etc.* By these words—*in the Gospel truly more, etc.*—it is clearly demonstrated that Tertullian spoke of Scripture *collectively*, not *distributively* <note>meaning he refers to the total body of the Gospel's teaching, not just a single verse or book</note>. Indeed, both are true: for the fullness of the whole implies the fullness of the part according to that part. Thus, we previously distinguished between the fullness of the whole and the fullness of a part, or between the perfection of the whole and the part.

And let these things be said briefly regarding this controversy, in which it should seem a marvel to no one if we have carried back a victory against two Goliaths of the Roman Church <note>Likely referring to Cardinal Robert Bellarmine and Cardinal Davy du Perron, the two most formidable Catholic apologists of the era</note>, since we have descended into the arena for God, for His word, and for truth against the traditions of men. And it is indeed a clear prejudice against the Roman Catholics that they are doubtful and anxious about their own cause, since they so greatly reject and decline the judgment of the Scriptures and call instead upon the traditions of men—that is, to the tribunal of the Roman Church, which is the Pope or a Council. For among them, this is still undecided, and they are ignorant of what the supreme tribunal actually is; thus they themselves are both judges and interested parties. From this come so many sarcasms against the Scriptures, and on the other hand, praises of traditions. Pierre Charron <note>A French Catholic philosopher and theologian (1541–1603)</note> says in *Truths*, book 3, chapter 4: *Scripture is the smallest particle of revealed truth.* Stanislaus Hosius <note>A Polish Cardinal and leading figure of the Counter-Reformation (1504–1579)</note> says in *Confessions*, chapter 92: *By far the greatest part of the Gospel has reached us through tradition; a very tiny amount was committed to writing.* These things were certainly said so boldly that they could have persuaded any gullible person, had not a certain auxiliary soldier arrived—whether from the volunteers or the conscripts, it is uncertain...

This is Andradius <note>Diogo de Paiva de Andrade (1528–1575), a Portuguese theologian who defended the Council of Trent</note>, Jesuit though he may be, who says in *Orthodox Explanations, Book 2*: *Of those things which a Christian man must believe, the greatest part is contained in the sacred scriptures.* <note>original Latin: "Eorum quæ Christianum hominem credere oportet, maxima pars sacris literis continetur."</note>

Thus far we have covered the first part of the dissertation, namely the prohibition made by God: *you shall not add or subtract, etc.* Next follows the second part, which is the reason for the prohibition: so that the Church might keep the commandments of Jehovah. For since God is the supreme Lawgiver <term>Legislator</term>, He alone ought to deliver commands to His people, and that Church ought to keep them with ready obedience. Hence, as we said above, God demands from us three types of obedience. For the external act of movement is not enough, nor even the internal act which affects the will and its specific choices; but He asks furthermore for the very peak of the mind, so that the intellect itself, submitting, obeys those commands of God which cannot even be grasped by the sharpness of one's natural wit—following the example of Abraham, who believed in hope against hope.

Yet you should not say that this obedience is "blind," of the sort the Jesuits and the Pope command of their servants. For that is entirely blind and irrational, as the Jesuits themselves and Cusanus <note>Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464), a prominent Cardinal and philosopher</note> call it; it does not make men compliant, but dullards, stupid, and brute slaves, for whom blind obedience takes the place of reason—just as someone once said, "for pigs, a soul serves as salt." <note>This was a common early modern proverb (originally from Cicero) suggesting that a pig has just enough life/soul only to keep its meat from rotting; Crégut uses it here to suggest the Jesuits lack true intellectual life.</note> Thus, just as Caesar defined the best soldier as the one who behaved most obediently, so these men think the best "companions" <note>A pun on the "Society of Jesus," whose members are called "socii" or companions.</note> are those who obey the commands of the veterans with blind obedience. Then they all behave toward their General and the Pope in such a way that they defend him through right and wrong <note>original Latin: "per fas et nefas"</note>. Because of this, they have dared to depict the Papal throne falling, or certainly threatening ruin, while they themselves, packed together in a dense formation <term>testudo</term> <note>meaning "tortoise," a Roman military formation where soldiers locked shields over their heads to form a protective shell</note>, support it on their shoulders. But by contrast, the obedience which God demands is rational, not blinded. For even if God's command often exceeds our understanding, it is nevertheless not against reason, nor does it strike against justice; rather, it is subordinate to a higher intellect and archetypal justice, which holds over us a right that is absolute <note>original Greek: αὐτοκρατοריקὸν (*autokratikon*)</note> and independent <term>allodial</term> <note>In law, "allodial" refers to land owned independently, without any superior landlord; here it refers to God's absolute sovereignty.</note>.

The masters of the Hebrews <note>Rabbinical scholars</note> wished to illustrate that obedience due to God subtly and meticulously from the commandments of the law, when they wrote that the precepts of the Law were some of them called negative commandments... <note>original Hebrew: מצות ל"ת (*Mitzvot Lo Ta'aseh*)</note>

This is why the sum of the law—*to love God and one’s neighbor*—even though they are affirmative precepts, binds always and everywhere: for there is no place or time in which one can be dispensed from them. There is a specific reason for this, because <term>charity</term> <note>Christian love or "agape"</note> eminently and virtually embraces all precepts, both affirmative and negative; that is, they cannot be fulfilled without charity. # REVELATOR ARCANORVM.
->REVEALER OF SECRETS<-

**Charity** is truly called by Theologians the *binding force of the law and an indivisible whole—the entire law, not just a part of the law*. Therefore, if charity is violated, the whole law is violated. As it says in James 2: *whoever fails in one point, has become guilty of all.* For because of the charity and majesty of the Lawgiver, the body of the Law is indivisible.

Observe, however, that the Teachers of the Hebrews greatly exalt obedience to the law. For they emphasize two things in particular. 1. That although the law of God is most profound and beyond human understanding, nevertheless our understanding must be taken captive in submission to the law. For thus it is said in the Midrash <note>A genre of ancient Jewish biblical exegesis and commentary</note>: *Before Solomon arose, the words of the law were like a well whose waters are deep and cold, so that a man cannot drink from them. What did a wise and clever man do? He tied rope to rope and string to string, and in that way he drew water and drank. Thus Solomon proceeded from parable to parable, and from one word to another, until he penetrated into the very pit and cistern of the law. Just as if someone has lost a shekel or a precious pearl in the innermost part of his house, he lights a candle worth a single cent and finds it again; so parables are in themselves nothing and of no value, yet through them we see and recognize the words of the Law.* The Jewish masters teach these things to signify that the meaning of the law is most profound; but we must labor with the greatest diligence to penetrate into it, so that we may then strive to keep its precepts. For the law is not theoretical, but practical; its goal is not bare contemplation, but <term>praxis: the practical application of a theory or custom</term>.

Secondly, the Rabbis emphasize that although the law of God often has no purpose or cause other than the will of God, nevertheless God's commandments must be religiously observed. For Maimonides <note>A preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar</note> says thus in the *Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original Latin title: *More Neuoch.*</note>, part 3, chapter 26: Some precepts have an evident purpose, and some do not. An evident purpose is seen in the laws against murder and theft. A non-evident one is seen in the prohibition of the foreskin <note>referring to the command of circumcision</note> and of "heterogeneous things" <note>laws regarding the mixing of different species of plants, animals, or fabrics</note>. Those whose use and utility are known are commonly called *mishpatim* <term>mishpatim: laws or "judgments" that appeal to human reason and morality</term>, that is, judgments; but those whose use is not commonly manifest are called <gloss>statutes</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: חקים (*chukim*)</note>, that is, *statutes*. Hence they often say that the giving of these precepts is not a vain thing, having no use; and if any precept seems to be such, then that comes from the imperfection of your own understanding—

**...perfection.** You also know that common saying, which they generally repeat, that Solomon knew the reasons for all the commandments, except for that one concerning the red heifer <note>The "Red Heifer" refers to a ritual in Numbers 19 that was famously considered a "statute" whose logic escaped even the wisest man, as it purified the unclean but made the pure person who performed it ritualistically unclean.</note>. The reasons for these two are set forth in Deuteronomy 17:17. However, it must also be observed that even if the Rabbis spoke magnificently about the law and its observance, nevertheless in the time of the Pharisees, whenever it came to practice, its observance was external rather than internal. It tasted more of hypocrisy and pride than of true piety; for this reason they are frequently rebuked by Christ, as in Matthew 23 <note>Original text cites Matthew 24, but the "Woe to you" rebukes occur in chapter 23.</note>: *Woe to you Pharisees, etc.* From this it follows that among them there were **least** <note>original: ἐλάχιστα</note> commandments; as if indeed **lawlessness** <note>original: ἀνομία</note> or the transgression of God's law could be a "minimal" thing, when the alteration of a single stroke violates the Majesty of the lawgiver and earns the Gehenna of fire. Indeed, what is worse, the Pharisees judged their own **traditions handed down from their fathers** <note>original: πατροπαραδότους</note> to be the greatest commandments, such as *Corban* <note>A gift dedicated to God, often used as a loophole to avoid supporting parents.</note>, *tithes, washings, fasts*, etc. Yet they wanted the Moral commandments, whether of the first or second table <note>The "Tables" of the Law: the first table contains duties toward God; the second contains duties toward fellow men.</note>, to be the **least** <note>original: ἐλάχιστα</note>. A living image of these Pharisees is conspicuous today in the Papacy; for the dispensation of divine law is made easy, both for the first and second tables. Yet the Pope's mandates are either indispensable, or if they are dispensed, the dispensation is valued at a much higher price than a dispensation from divine law. This is easy to calculate in the books of the data-collectors, where any sins are taxed and redeemed for a certain price <note>A reference to the *Taxa Camarae*, a list of fees for the granting of indulgences or absolutions for various crimes and sins.</note>.

Therefore, a "dispensation" <note>An exemption from a law or a relaxation of its rigor.</note> from divine law—since this command of Moses, *do not add, nor take away, that you may keep the commandments of Jehovah*, beats strongly against it—is such a horrendous and wicked plot against God, and a most lethal crime of **treason** <term>Lèse-majesté: a crime committed against the dignity of a sovereign or the state.</term>. For what mortal can exalt himself above that supreme Lawgiver...

## REVEALER OF SECRETS

...is it valid, that he dared to dispense with His law? Therefore, I constantly assert that any kind of divine law, and whatever their precepts may be, are indispensable <note>In a legal or theological sense, "indispensable" means a law that cannot be set aside or granted an exemption—a "dispensation"—by any authority.</note> by all; indeed, that the moral law itself cannot be dispensed with even by God. 

To understand this, it must be noted that divine law is of two kinds: one is **natural law**, and the other is **positive law**. The moral law is of natural law, while the ceremonial law is of positive law. Both are indispensable by men themselves, whoever they may be—even the ceremonial law as long as it remained in force. This is why it was called a <term>righteous decree</term> <note>original: δικαίωμα (*dikaioma*)</note>, so that men would know they could not turn away from that law without immediately turning away from justice, since the will of God which established it is the rule of justice. Conversely, now that it has been abolished, nothing is more unjust than wanting to bind men's consciences and obligate them to its performance; because once the will of God has ceased [to require it], it is no longer a <term>righteous decree</term>, but a <term>failure of justice</term> <note>original: ἀδικαίωμα (*adikaioma*)</note>. To do so would be to make the will of man the rule of justice—as if it were the will of God—or as the Pope says, making sin out of non-sin, and non-sin out of sin <note>This refers to a common Protestant critique of the Papacy's claim to "plenitude of power," which critics argued allowed the Pope to redefine what constitutes a sin.</note>.

But indeed, as for the moral law, this (I say) is indispensable with respect to both God and men. The reason is that it is of natural, eternal, and immutable law. The moral law is a <term>shadowy reflection</term> <note>original: ἀποσκιάσμα (*aposkiasma*)</note> of the eternal law, from which God can no more grant a dispensation than He can deny Himself and His own justice. Indeed, I add this: that the moral law is entirely and totally indispensable by God. 

For that reason, I cannot agree with those theologians who say the moral law is indispensable with respect to the **first table** <note>The first part of the Ten Commandments, focusing on man's direct relationship with God.</note>, but not with respect to the **second table** <note>The second part of the Ten Commandments, focusing on man's relationship with his neighbor.</note>; they argue that a violation of the commandments of the first table deforms the image of God, while the second does not, and because the former—not the latter—regards God immediately and directly. However, since the entire moral law is of natural, eternal, and immutable right (as stated above), it is in no way dispensable. And in truth, the commandments of the second table cannot be transgressed without the justice of God being struck and His image being defiled. For the love of God and charity toward one's neighbor are the image of God and His justice. And charity is a certain spark...

...which is kindled from the fire of divine love; and if that spark of **charity** <note>In this context, "charity" (Latin: *charitas*) refers to the theological virtue of selfless love for others, fueled by love for God.</note> were entirely extinguished, that flame of divine love would also perish. Therefore, if God were to grant us an exemption from the duty of charity toward our neighbor, He would certainly be granting us an exemption from the love toward Himself; for the neighbor is also His image. Thus, something would be lacking from the glory of God, which contradicts the scripture: *As I live (says Jehovah), I will not give my glory to another.*

But just as God cannot, by right, grant an exemption from the law, so in fact He has never done so. He did not grant an exemption from the law against **homicide** when He commanded Abraham to sacrifice his son Isaac. That was not properly a homicide, but a sacrifice—indeed, an illustrious **type** <note>A "type" is a person, event, or thing in the Old Testament believed to foreshadow something in the New Testament.</note> of the sacrifice of Christ. Therefore, it looked directly to God's glory and the **first table of the law** <note>The "First Table" refers to the first four of the Ten Commandments, which concern man’s direct relationship and duties to God.</note>. The mandates of the first table take precedence over those of the **second table** <note>The "Second Table" refers to the final six Commandments, regarding duties to one's neighbor, such as "Thou shalt not kill."</note>, just as everyone is bound to deny himself for the glory of God. In the same way, a particular part of nature sets aside its own inclinations for the good of universal nature, so that there is no "vacuum" in the natural world <note>The author uses a common medieval scientific principle—that nature abhors a vacuum—as an analogy for how specific moral laws may yield to the higher "universal" glory of God.</note>.

God also did not grant an exemption regarding **theft** in Exodus 12. The Jews did not "steal" the goods of the Egyptians; rather, since Pharaoh (acting as a subordinate judge) was denying them justice, God Himself—the Supreme Judge—repaid the Israelites a reward from the Egyptian goods for their many labors and hardships. 

Nor did He grant an exemption regarding **prostitution** when it is said in Hosea 1: *Take a prostitute, etc.* These events were not historically carried out but were narrated as a **parable**. Through this symbol, the Israelites were meant to see that God had long indulged this people and endured most impure wives and husbands as if they were prostitutes. 

Finally, God did not grant an exemption from the law when He permitted **polygamy** and **divorce**. He did not properly "permit" them through an ethical relaxation of the law, but rather He tolerated them through a certain **accommodation** <note>original Greek: συγκατάβασιν (*synkatabasin*). This is a theological term meaning God "condescends" or adjusts His requirements to the level of human weakness without actually approving of the behavior.</note>, without approving of them. This is no different than a Magistrate who does not simply "permit" drunkenness or usury, but tolerates them by not exacting punishments. If this is called "permission," it is a permission of fact—almost the same as a physical permission—but not a permission of right. God Himself did not take away the fault or the guilt of these actions, even though there was a suspension of civil or ecclesiastical punishments.

-> Add- <-

<summary>Cregut argues that God never truly grants exemptions from the moral law; seemingly contradictory biblical events (like Abraham's sacrifice or the plundering of Egypt) are explained as higher justice or symbolic parables rather than legal "dispensations."</summary>

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS

Furthermore, Christ demonstrated the necessity of the divine law through His own example, when He submitted Himself **according to the divine plan** <note>original: *κατ' οἰκονομίαν* (kat' oikonomian). In early Christian theology, "economy" refers to the "arrangement" or "stewardship" of God's plan for salvation, specifically how Christ lived under human conditions.</note>. For although Christ was above all things—which He clearly signaled when He entered the temple, cast out the money-changers, and punished them—He nevertheless obeyed His parents and the magistrates **according to the divine plan**, which is why He paid the tax (Matthew 17:24). In Luke 2:51, it is observed that Christ was **subordinate** <note>original: *ὑποτασσόμενον* (hypotassomenon), meaning placed in a rank under someone else or obedient.</note> to His parents. 

This was certainly not recorded by the Evangelist without reason; for why would he say only that Christ was subject to His parents, adding nothing about the other commandments of the law? Was it not to sufficiently indicate that Christ was by no means exempt from the law? Among men, children who are established in high dignity are generally not subject to their parents; for instance, a king, by right of his royal dignity, is above his mother, and she calls him "lord." Christ, however, wished this to be observed regarding Himself, since He never addressed the Virgin as "His mother," but rather as **"woman"** or **"lady."** <note>This refers to passages like John 2:4. The author argues that Christ used this address to maintain His status as Lord of all, even while He chose to submit to earthly authorities for the sake of the divine plan.</note> For even if He submitted Himself according to the divine plan, He was truly the Lord of all, whose right was **absolute and sovereign.** <note>original: *αὐτοκρατορικόν* (autokratikon), referring to supreme, autocratic power.</note>

Indeed, the necessity of the law is so absolute that if God were to grant a dispensation from even the smallest part of it, He would, in a sense, descend from His throne, and a creature would ascend to sit at His right hand—contrary to that verse in Psalm 110: *To which of the Angels did He ever say, "Sit at my right hand"?* For what is it to grant an exemption from the law other than to associate a creature with Himself and place them on the same throne? This contradicts the saying: *Majesty and love do not sit well together, nor do they remain on one throne.* For in such a case, God would be without law; and if He were without law, He would certainly not be King; for these two things walk together and at an equal pace. Hence these most true verses from a gifted poet:

->*Law without a King would be like light without the Sun.*<-
->*A King without Law would be like the Sun without light.*<-
->*The flock first chooses the law; the King and the flock*<-
->*Established the law; hence the King governs both the law and the flock.*<-

Because of this, we rightly believe those words of the **Stagirite** <note>The "Stagirite" is a common historical nickname for the philosopher **Aristotle**, who was born in the city of Stagira.</note> in the third book of his *Politics* (Chapter 11) deserve to be written in capital letters: *He who commands the law to rule, commands God to rule through His own voice; but he who commands a man to rule, commands a beast to rule.*

<header>ANTHONY CREGUT</header>

This indeed occurs if an exemption is granted from the law; for a human could easily degenerate into a beastly tyrant. This was a charge leveled against the Persians with their common saying, *Whatever pleases, is permitted.* <note>original: *Quod libet, licet.* This phrase was often used by ancient authors to describe absolute autocracy where the ruler's will is the only law.</note>

Therefore, when Thomas [Aquinas] says in the *Summa Theologica* <note>original: *1. 2. q. 92. art. 2.* referring to the First Part of the Second Part, Question 92, Article 2.</note> that there are three acts of law—namely, **to command, to prohibit, and to permit**—this third one must be understood with a grain of salt. For it is not valid regarding "ethical permission," which can never occur without a relaxation of the law, which we have already condemned above. Thomas explains himself when he adds that the "permissive act" concerns **indifferent things**, which are surely neither ethically good nor bad. <note>In moral philosophy, "indifferent things" (Greek: *adiaphora*) are actions that are neither mandated nor forbidden by moral law, such as choosing which color clothes to wear.</note> But in that same article, he is seriously deluded when he places among "indifferent things" those acts which are either "a little bit good" or "a little bit bad." For in this way, he seems to introduce **venial sins**; yet, since all sins, however small, are actually **mortal**, no "permissive act" is granted in the law. <note>Cregut is arguing from a strict Reformed Protestant perspective here, rejecting the Roman Catholic distinction between "venial" (minor) and "mortal" (grave) sins. He believes any violation of God's law is a serious matter.</note> On the contrary, that fourth act of law which he adds—namely, **to punish**—would be established instead, though that is an *effect* of the law rather than an act of the law itself.

Therefore, no one can be exempted from the observance of divine law—neither princes, nor priests, nor the people. Not the princes or magistrates: hence in Joshua 1:7, God said to Joshua: *Be strong and very courageous, that you may observe and do according to the entire law: just as my servant Moses commanded you; do not turn from it to the right hand or to the left, etc.* In the Hebrew, the words are emphatic: *le-ma'an tishmor la'asot* <note>original: למען תשמור לעשות</note>, that is, **so that you may observe to do.** For "observing to act" is the same as applying the mind to acting, and taking care that nothing prescribed by the law is omitted. <term>Nachmanides</term> <note>original: *Nehmannus Gerundensis*. Referring to Rabbi Moses ben Nachman (1194–1270), a leading medieval Jewish scholar from Girona.</note>, an acute writer, thinks that **to observe** <note>original: *lishmor* (לשמור)</note> refers to the negative commandments [prohibitions], while **to do** <note>original: *la'asot* (לעשות)</note> denotes the affirmative ones. Thus, the former declares abstinence from vices, and the latter, the practice of virtue. Furthermore, the Book of the Law was handed over and entrusted to the priests who carried the Ark; it was their duty to teach and interpret the law and to explain difficult questions within it. As messengers of the Lord of Hosts, they are to be consulted regarding the law, just as the princes and elders of Israel—that is, the magistrates—must protect the interpreters of the law. Finally, the people must follow their leaders; for the magistrates and...

Magistrates and Pastors are "laws with eyes" for the people; otherwise, as Cicero says in *On the Laws*, book 3: *they do not only conceive vices themselves, but they pour them into the state.* <note>original: "non solùm vitia concipiunt ipsi, sed ea infundunt in ciuitatem." Cicero argued that leaders influence the morality of the entire community through their example.</note> Hence the saying: *The whole world is formed according to the king's example.*

Observe, however, from this passage in Joshua 1:7, Deuteronomy 4:2, from Joshua 1:8, and other places in Scripture, that whenever the observation of the law is discussed, various emphatic words are used that properly demonstrate such a necessary thing. Sometimes with the word <term>zakar <gloss>זכר</gloss></term>, to remember. Sometimes with the word <term>shamar <gloss>שמר</gloss></term>, to observe, or <term>asah <gloss>עשה</gloss></term>, that is, to do. <term>Hagah <gloss>הגה</gloss></term>, to meditate. And others of that sort. 

i. **To remember** <note>original: *זכר recordari*</note> so that we always remember the law, and it is never surrendered to oblivion, but is stored in the chest of memory like a sacred treasure; so that she who is called the <term>Mother of the Muses <gloss>mouson mētēr / μουσῶν μήτηρ</gloss></term> <note>In Greek mythology, Mnemosyne (Memory) is the mother of the Muses. The author argues that Memory should also be the mother of Law.</note> may truly be the **Mother and Matrix of the Law.** <note>original: *τῷ νόμῳ μήτηρ & matrix*</note> 

ii. Following in order is the stage of **meditating** <note>original: *הגה à meditando*</note>, because you must not only remember the law, but also perpetually meditate upon it; hence Joshua 1:8 says: *Meditate on it (that is, the book of the law) day and night.* For to **meditate** <note>original: *הגה*</note> is to handle the mind with the thought of the things themselves in such a way that, as if bubbling up from the mind itself, words are also born in the mouth—the kind of whispering that those who meditate with themselves are accustomed to do. 

iii. After meditation on the law, one must pass over to **observing** <note>original: *שמר obſeruare*</note>, a word which denotes not only the contemplation and theory of the law, like the first two, but also its actual practice. 

iv. **Doing** <note>original: *עשה*</note> denotes the actual performance, when we proceed from the mind and heart all the way to the work itself. And toward this the sayings of the <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Jewish scholars who compiled the Talmud, a central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note> in the tractate *Sanhedrin* tend:

> *He who reads the sacred letters and does not apply them to the matter is like one who sows frequently but never reaps. Or like a woman who often gives birth but immediately buries the offspring. Or finally, like a singer singing all day long: for these have no reward for their labor.*

Nevertheless, whatever that observation of the law may be—which certainly, as I said, ought to be the greatest—I would not for that reason agree with that wise man of the Hebrews who (as found in the <term>Talmud</term>), when he was asked by his sister's son whether it was permitted for him to read the writings of the Greeks now that he had mastered the entire instruction of Moses, that Rabbi named Ishmael ordered him to look...

to study: whether there might be some hour that belongs neither to the day nor to the night. For only that hour, if any such existed, would it be lawful for men to spend on anything other than the study of the divine law. This is because it is said in Joshua 1:8, *“And you shall meditate on it day and night.”* <note>The author is referencing a famous Rabbinic debate (found in the Talmud, Menachot 99b) where a student asks when he might study "Greek wisdom" if he is commanded to study the Torah day and night. The answer given is that he must find an hour that is neither day nor night.</note> But who does not know that this is a proverbial expression? Hence Homer often says *all nights and days* <note>original Greek: "νύκτας τε καὶ ἤματα πάντα"</note>, signifying a diligence that excludes all negligence, and even more so, excludes loathing and boredom. This matches what is commanded of the king in Deuteronomy 17:19: *“through all the days of his life.”* To this point serves what the <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note> say, and what is found in that ancient commentary on Genesis, *Bereshit Rabbah*. They say that the example of the law was the banner of Joshua; and that God found him holding the law, already written out, in his hands when He appeared to him. Therefore He said to him, *“Be strong, etc. let this book of the law not depart from your mouth.” Joshua 1:7.*

Nor is it in vain what the <term>Sages <gloss>chachamim / חכמים</gloss></term> here frequently say concerning the observance of the law: namely, that one should not observe the “garments” of the law so much as the “body” itself. By *garments*, they understand the letters, words, and vowel points with which the law is engraved; and by the <term>body of the law <gloss>gufei ha-Torah / גופי התורה</gloss></term>, they understand the inner meaning, which is enclosed under the letters, small words, and points just as a body is under garments, or the marrow is under the bark. And thus they say, <term>The Law is Light <gloss>Torah Or / תורה אור</gloss></term>; that is, the Law is made into light. This is according to Proverbs 6:23. For this reason, among the Chaldeans, the law was called <term>Orayta <gloss>אורייתא</gloss></term>, as if it were light itself.

But indeed, it is no less memorable what the Hebrews teach regarding the performance of the law. After (they say) the body of the law hiding under the garments is excellently known and the law has become light, one must not stop at the knowledge of the law itself; rather, it is necessary to pass into practice. For knowledge without use is something shadowy and vanishing. And that Hebrew saying is valid: <term>Everything follows the deed <gloss>ha-kol holech achar ha-ma’aseh / הכל הולך אחר המעשה</gloss></term>. And Rabbi Chanina, in the *Ethics of the Fathers* <note>original: "Pirke abhos"</note>, chapter 3, skillfully says: *“Whosoever’s works are more abundant than his wisdom, his wisdom is lasting; but he whose wisdom is more abundant than his works, his wisdom does not remain lasting.”* In this way, the Hebrews truly and excellently proclaim the response of the fathers;

<page-num>891</page-num>
-># THE REVEALER OF SECRETS <-

**E**xperience, as our teacher, has found that God, in the work of His providence, makes use of the ministry of human beings. Yet the operation of the supreme Moderator <note>original: "summi moderatoris"; a common Latin term for God as the one who governs or regulates the universe.</note> shines forth in such a way that whatever perfection exists is drawn from Him, while whatever defect occurs arises from the "secondary cause" <note>In scholastic philosophy, God is the "Primary Cause" of all things, while humans act as "secondary causes" who can introduce error or sin into the world.</note>. Indeed, it rarely happens that a man does not mingle some vice or "serpent's venom" into the work; thus, God daily brings light out of darkness, just as He did at the very beginning of the world. 

For instance, when the patriarch **Isaac** was about to bless his son **Jacob** according to God’s decree, **Rebecca** and **Jacob** acted as the instruments in that illustrious work of God, but they did so by deceiving the good old man with tricks and fabrications. The same is certainly true regarding the institution of the **Magistrate** <note>In this context, "Magistrate" refers to any civil governor or official holding legal authority.</note>. Long ago, God had decreed that excellent institution among men; and when it was to be put into execution through the organ of secondary causes, He made use of the ambition and ferocity of **Nimrod**, who, in *Genesis 10:8*, *began to be a mighty one in the earth*, and is called *a mighty hunter before the Lord*. 

By this elegant metaphor, his fierce rule over others is signified. Hence, **Jerome**, in his commentary on *Psalm 90*, notes that a **"Holy Hunter"** is nowhere to be found in the Scriptures. For this reason, some define a hunter as: *One beast sitting upon a beast and pursuing other beasts.* As the saying goes, *those who often hunt beasts take on a beastly mind.* Thus, **Spangenberg** <note>Cyriacus Spangenberg (1528–1604), a prominent Lutheran theologian and historian.</note> writes concerning the "hunting demon." Therefore, let no one presume to disparage the sacred institution of God based on the usurpation of that tyrant, since light will always shine in the midst of darkness. 

Here, then, take notice of four points to be explained:
*I. The institution of the magistrate. II. His duty toward his subjects. III. The duty of the subjects. IV. The reward or punishment for both.*

### I. On the Institution of the Magistrate

In the *institution of the Magistrate*, one must consider its dignity and its origin. Its dignity is clearly recognized from its various names. For in Latin, a **Magistrate** (*Magistratus*) is named from "more" (*magis*) and "masters" (*magistris*). Hence, in the city of Rome, he who was inaugurated as Dictator was likewise called the **Master of the People** (*Magister populi*). This is why **Cicero** used to call **Caesar** "Master," and for the same reason, **Titus Livius** wrote that a Dictator was added to the Consuls to be their moderator and **Master**. The reasoning behind the name "Master" (*Magister*) comes from *magis* (more), because they are able to do more than others, or from the Greek *megisto* <note>original: "μέγιστο"; meaning "greatest."</note>, just as a "minister" is named from *minus* (less). Furthermore, through various naming conventions—

they are marked out, both in Scripture and elsewhere, by various emphatic titles. And that other saying: **Do not judge alone** <note>Hebrew: אל תהי דן יחידי (al tehi dan yechidi)</note>. And this court judged **monetary disputes** <note>Hebrew: דיני ממונות (dinei mamonot); civil cases involving property or finance.</note>.

Regarding its institution, see Numbers 11:16: *Gather for me seventy men from the elders, etc.* With Moses, the total was seventy-one. <header>ANTOINE CRÉGUT <note>Latin: ANTHONII CREGVTI; Crégut (1612–1666) was a French Reformed theologian and professor.</note></header>

...those political matters which God had sanctioned in his law: for because that was by divine institution, it was easily permitted by pious kings to the direction of the High Priest <note>Latin: S. Sacerdotis, likely standing for Summo Sacerdote</note> as a religious and ecclesiastical matter. But in the desert, the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme legal council of the ancient Jews.</note> of seventy men was selected indiscriminately from seventy elders. Finally, in the time of the Maccabees <note>A Jewish dynasty that ruled Judea in the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE.</note>, since the priesthood had been joined with the leadership, it is no wonder if the High Priest dealt with both political and ecclesiastical matters. It is therefore clearly established that it belongs to the Magistrate to judge, which is why Moses here uses the word <term>Shofet <note>Hebrew: שופט</note></term>, which signifies a *judge*.

Indeed, it is so true that the duty of judging belongs to the Magistrate, and not inherently to the High Priest, that no place can be found in Scripture where the High Priest is called a <term>Shofet</term> (*Judge*), even though the High Priests and Judges are very often joined together. As in Deuteronomy 19:17: *in the presence of the priests and the judges who were in those days.* Likewise in Joshua 8:33, the Magistrate is joined with the judges: *all Israel, and its elders, its officers, and its judges stood on this side and that around the ark.* Therefore, Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Cardinal and influential defender of Catholic doctrine during the Counter-Reformation.</note> wrongly wished for the "Judge" in Scripture to be understood as the High Priest, so that by this means he might attribute supreme judgment in political and ecclesiastical matters to the Roman Pontiff <note>The Pope</note>. Paulus Fagius <note>A 16th-century German Renaissance scholar of Hebrew.</note> testifies in his annotations on the *Targum* <note>An Aramaic translation or paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> of Deuteronomy 17 that this same idea pleased several others.

And certainly, that it was the Magistrate's office to judge is also inferred from the locations in which judicial acts were performed among the Jews. For they were not held in the temple, but in the gates of the cities, at the time when the Jews were under their own law; but truly, after their liberty was taken away and judicial and forensic matters passed into the power of the Romans, their acts were carried out in the praetorium <note>The headquarters or judgment hall of a Roman governor.</note>, as is sufficiently proven by the history of the death of Christ. Indeed, even when two colleges of twenty-three men were established in Jerusalem, as if in a metropolis of both politics and religion, both judged in the gates of the city; *one lower*, in the gate of the mountain; *the other upper*, which sat in the gate of Ezra, or at the gate of the courtyard. Promotions were made from the lowest to the highest. Regarding the Great Sanhedrin, if faith is to be [given] <note>The sentence continues onto the next page.</note>

### THE REVEALER OF SECRETS <note>Latin: REVELATOR ARCANORVM; the title of the work.</note> ###

...to be held, it was customary for it to be gathered in that part of the temple which was called *Gazith* <note>The "Chamber of Hewn Stone" (Lishkat ha-Gazit) in the Temple of Jerusalem, where the Great Sanhedrin met.</note>. For according to them, the process went from the judgment of each city to the judgment of the neighboring one; from there to the tribunal of twenty-three judges *at the gate of the mountain*; from there to the court sitting *at the gate of Ezra or the courtyard*; and finally to the Assembly or High Council of seventy-one gathered in Gazith.

Nor would someone rightly infer that this high council was not political, or did not belong to the Magistrate, simply because kings were excluded from it. The High Priest, however, was co-opted among the seventy men. If kings did not sit in it, one cannot therefore conclude that they were not Judges or Magistrates; rather, there was a specific reason—namely, so that their presence would not hinder the freedom of the votes. For it is not safe to disagree with those in whom the Majesty of the Empire resides. As for the High Priest, he did not sit in that high order merely because he performed the Priestly duty, but by the dignity of his office; yet [primarily] because he was believed to excel the others in the gifts of wisdom and judgment. And indeed, none were enrolled into that dignity of the seventy who did not excel others in nobility and wisdom, with the usual ceremony of the <term>laying on of hands <note>Greek: *cheirothesia* (χειροθεσίας); the traditional ritual of ordination or transmission of authority.</note></term> also being applied. Foreigners, unlearned men, and commoners were completely excluded, whom they commonly call the <term>people of the land <note>Hebrew: *am ha-aretz* (עם הארץ); a term used by the ancient Rabbis to refer to those who were uneducated in the law or negligent in religious observance.</note></term>, and hence the Rabbinic precept: *A disciple of a wise man should not marry the daughter of an uneducated person* <note>Hebrew: *Talmid chakham al yisa bat am ha-aretz*.</note>.

Furthermore, it should be observed that the privilege of rendering judgment was not taken away from kings, even if they did not enter the high council; both because they had *leaders in the house*—that is, in the kingdom of Judah, about whom we read in *2 Chronicles 19:8, 10, 11*. For (as said above) Jehoshaphat established supreme judges in Jerusalem, both Civil and Ecclesiastical; and the Magistrate, who was called the *leader in the house* <note>The author refers to the "ruler of the house of Judah" mentioned in 2 Chronicles 19:11, who oversaw civil matters.</note>, presided over the former, while the Chief Priest presided over the latter. Also, kings were accustomed to give laws to their subjects separately, as is clear from the examples of *David (2 Samuel 12:5), Solomon (1 Kings 3:16), and Ahab (1 Kings 20:30)*; and Absalom desired to be appointed judge in the land of Israel (*2 Samuel 15:4*). Likewise Moses, Joshua, and their successors judged Israel. And *Proverbs 20:8* says: *A king sitting on the throne of judgment*...

...scatters all evil <note>original Latin: *ventilat omne malum*. This refers to the duty of a ruler to dispel corruption.</note>. So it is in Judges 2:16: *Afterward, Jehovah raised up Judges* <note>Hebrew: *Shophetim* (שופטים)</note> *who saved them from the hand of those who plundered them.* And in Judges 3:9: *Wherefore Jehovah raised up a savior* <note>Hebrew: *Shophet* (שופט)</note> *for the children of Israel.* These terms emphatically signify that the Magistrate is the judge, liberator, savior, and parent of the people. And since that most well-worn proverb is true—*Let the safety of the Republic be the supreme law* <note>Latin: *salus Reipubl. suprema lex esto*</note>—how great must be the necessity of the Magistrate, in whom the safety and security of the entire people is placed! It must be confessed, however, that those judges of Israel were <term>types of Christ <note>A "type" is a historical person or event believed to foreshadow a future reality, in this case, Jesus.</note></term>, who is truly the *Judge and savior* of his people; hence he is called *Jesus* and *Judge* by way of excellence <note>Latin: *Antonomasticè*, a rhetorical term for using a title as a proper name.</note>.

Thus far concerning the first naming, "Judge" <note>Hebrew: *Shophet* (שפט)</note>, which is found in the text of Moses. For if we observe the context of Scripture, that word *Shoter* is often joined with the word *Shophet*, as is clear from this passage of Moses where these two words, according to the version by <term>Junius and Tremellius <note>Francis Junius and Immanuel Tremellius were 16th-century scholars famous for their Latin translation of the Bible.</note></term>, signify *Judges and Moderators*. Since this last word is very broad, it is more specifically explained as "prefects" or "overseers of public business."

And in Joshua 1:10: *Joshua commanded the officers of the people* <note>Hebrew: *Shotrim* (שוטרי)</note> *or moderators.* And in Joshua 8:33, *Shoter* is joined with *Shophet* and with *Zaken*, which words signify *officers, judges, and elders.* And in Proverbs 6:7, *Shoter* is joined with *Mashal*, meaning *moderator and ruler*; this correctly agrees with the meaning of the word in <term>Chaldean <note>A common historical term for the Aramaic language.</note></term>, for to the Chaldeans, *Sheter* signifies *Dominion.* And yet, the Chaldean paraphrase <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation/interpretation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> of Joshua 1:10 translates *Shotrim* as "monitors," just as in Joshua 8:33. 

But the <term>Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, often abbreviated as LXX.</note></term> translates this as "Scribes" <note>Greek: *grammateis* (γραμματεῖς)</note>. And Saint Jerome <note>The 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note> uses "princes": *Joshua commanded the princes of the people.* The Septuagint also occasionally translates it as "introducers of records" <note>Greek: *grammatosagogeis* (γραμματοεισαγωγεῖς)</note>, as if you were to say, the announcers of public letters; and once, according to the calculation of some, they have "readers" <note>Greek: *anagnostas* (ἀναγνώζοντας)</note>. From that Septuagint version, when they translate it as "Scribes," there undoubtedly arose that frequent use of "Scribes" in the New Testament. ...[he] translates as <unclear>avengers</unclear> <note>original Greek: ἐκδικητὰς, meaning those who exact justice or punish</note>, as if you were to say *avengers of crimes*. But this does not fully express the Hebrew word.

It is clear, therefore, from so many interpretations of the word *Shoter* <note>Hebrew: שטר</note> that there is little agreement among interpreters—both Jewish and Christian—as to what the term *Shoter* specifically signifies. However, if we were to offer a judgment amidst so many differing opinions of learned men, we will probably put forward two points. First, according to Hebrew style, that repetition of various terms designates the same sense regarding the overall meaning, even if they designate different things regarding the properties of the words and the immediate meaning of the terms. For example, in Joshua 8:33, the *elders, officers, and judges* <note>original Latin: Seniores, monitores, iudices</note> denote various roles according to the specific meanings of the words, as is evident; yet if you weigh the sense of the entire verse, perhaps they are all the same people—the elders, the judges, and the officers—for the duty of the elders, or the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme council and tribunal of the ancient Jewish people</note>, was to judge and to advise or moderate the people. This is such that the first term designates something more general and the following terms something more specific.

Secondly, I add this: that general word *Shoter* <note>Hebrew: שטר, meaning "moderator" or "official"</note> is limited in various ways depending on which related word it is joined with. For if it is joined with the word *Shophet* <note>Hebrew: שפט, meaning "judge"</note>, then it signifies a moderator or prefect of justice, because *Shophet* means a judge. But if it is joined with the word *Moshel* <note>Hebrew: משל, meaning "ruler" or "dominator"</note>, as in the previously cited passage of Proverbs 6:7, then it signifies a moderator and prefect of the kingdom or the political state. It is no different than the verb *Asah* <note>Hebrew: עשה</note>, meaning "to do" or "to make," which is a very broad term; according to the subject matter, it can soon signify *Bara* <note>Hebrew: ברא, "to create"</note>, when no matter is presupposed; or *Yalad* <note>Hebrew: ילד, "to beget"</note>, when matter is supplied; or *Yatzar* <note>Hebrew: יצר, "to form"</note>, when a natural whole is presupposed, from which an artificial form or figure is drawn out.

This can be confirmed by the fact that in Proverbs 6:7, *Shoter* <note>Hebrew: שטר</note> precedes *Moshel* <note>Hebrew: משל</note>, that is, the word "moderator" precedes the word "ruler." This would not happen if, as some wish, the moderators were merely the servants and attendants of the judges and princes. These views (with the kind permission of the learned) are more pleasing to me; however, if anyone prefers to follow the opinion of others, they have my leave. For the Hebrews, and some Christians who followed them, believe that *Shoter* is joined with the word *Shophet* because...

<page-num>898</page-num>
<header>ANTHONY CREGUTUS</header>
<meta>catchword: Turcæ (The Turks)</meta>

A **Shoter** <note>Hebrew: שוטר, typically translated as officer or official</note> is a **moderator** <term>moderator: in this context, an official who manages or oversees the execution of laws</term> much like a **whip** <note>Hebrew: שוט (shot). The author is noting the linguistic similarity between the word for "officer" and the word for "whip."</note> or the servant of a judge. In this view, while the Judge pronounces his sentence and gives judgment, the Moderator becomes the executor of that sentence and compels those who are stubborn. This was also the role of the **Exactors** <note>Hebrew: נוגשים (Nogshim), often referring to taskmasters or tax collectors</note>, except that their duty was more broadly extended. Thus, according to this opinion, the **Shoterim** <note>plural of Shoter</note> would be the **officers** <term>apparitores: public servants or bailiffs who attended magistrates to execute their orders</term> of the judges.

However, I believe that the more recent Hebrew scholars have used these terms based on Roman institutions. For when they saw that among the Romans, who held the majesty of the empire, the Senators and Consuls had their own **lictores** <term>lictores: attendants who carried the fasces (rods and axes) as symbols of authority and punished offenders</term> and officers, they judged in this manner that the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme council and tribunal of the ancient Jews</note> and the judges of the Hebrews had their own officers, whom they called **Shoterim**. Hence, **without the support of scripture** <note>original Greek: ἄτερ γραφῆς (ater graphes)</note>, Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval French rabbi and author of comprehensive commentaries on the Talmud and Tanakh</note> arms them with whips and leather straps, just like the Romans did their *lictores*. But the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> felt otherwise; they (as we have seen) called them **scribes** <note>original Greek: γραμματεῖς (grammateis)</note>. And yet Scribes were not merely officers; indeed, in **2 Chronicles 34:13**, **scribes and monitors** <note>original Latin: monitores</note> **are joined together**, and are said to be from the number of the Levites.

Just as some Magistrates were political and others Ecclesiastical <note>church-related or religious</note>, so those moderators sometimes managed military and political affairs, and others managed Ecclesiastical affairs. Thus, those who managed Ecclesiastical matters were chosen from the order of the Levites. This is confirmed by various passages of Scripture. So in **Deuteronomy 20:9**: *then it shall be, when the moderators have finished speaking to the people, that they shall appoint captains of the military ranks at the head of the people*. And in **2 Chronicles 34:13**, it deals with Ecclesiastical matters where the Levites were in charge: *Also over the Levites and those who were gatekeepers were the Scribes and moderators*. From these passages and other Scriptures, it seems to be concluded that those moderators were by no means the officers of the judges, but the judges themselves or the prefects and moderators of justice, as we declared above. This can also be proven from this passage of Moses, since he appointed both moderators and judges to judge. Verse 18: **You shall appoint judges and moderators for yourself in all your gates which the Lord your God gives you, throughout your tribes; and they shall judge the people with righteous judgment.** This can also be illustrated from the Arabic language; for the word **Shoter** signifies a judge, a presiding officer, and moreover an exactor, and thus corresponds to the Hebrew **Nogash** <note>Hebrew: נוגש, meaning a taskmaster or driver</note>.

He supports this by citing the role of Levites in ecclesiastical administration and linguistic parallels in Arabic.</summary>

The Turks here imitate Hebrew notions rather than Arabic ones; for as the place of judgments is called a *diuan* <note>Divan: a high council or court in the Ottoman Empire</note>, just as the Hebrew **Father of the House of Judgment** <note>original Hebrew: אב בית דין (Av Beit Din), the vice-president of the Sanhedrin</note>, so also the judges are called **Alcadin** <note>Arabic: Al-Qadi, a judge who reviews matters according to Islamic law</note>.

In addition to those names, the Apostle uses the word **powers** <note>original Greek: ἐξουσίας (exousias)</note> in Romans 13:1; this is very emphatic, for in this way it designates not so much the individual persons as the **order** <term>order: the established structure or office of government</term> itself, as well as the dignity of the Magistrate. For in individuals there are often vices and reasons for not obeying. Hence Chrysostom says, *“He does not speak of this or that prince, but of the matter itself.”* He also attributes this same concept to the Angels in Ephesians 1 and 1 Peter 3, because both Angels and magistrates are armed with power and might over others. For this reason, this title is attributed to the highest Magistrate, such as kings, who prevail over others in power; and because they also excel in dignity, he calls them **superior powers** <note>original Greek: ὑπερεχούσας ἐξουσίας (hyperechousas exousias)</note>. It is from this that they give laws to their subjects, and therefore Aristotle calls royal dignity **political architecture** <note>original Greek: πολιτικὴν ἀρχιτεκτονικήν (politiken architektoniken), meaning the "master-science" of statecraft that directs all other human activities</note>.

So much for the names of the Magistrate; as for his institution, it is without doubt divine, which can be clearly declared especially from the government of the Jewish people. For God instituted both political and **Ecclesiastical** <term>Ecclesiastical: relating to the government and organization of the Church</term> rule, and the high and subordinate leaders of both. In the Ecclesiastical, He sent Aaron and the Levites; in the political, He sent Moses and then the elders, and thereafter a succession of their followers in an uninterrupted series. At last, the form of government was changed in various ways, with God so permitting and directing. For after the judges, kings succeeded; after the kings, there were princes and the **Head of the Exile** <note>original Hebrew: ראש הגלות (Resh Galuta), also known as the Exilarch, the leader of the Jewish community in Babylon</note>. Finally, in the family of the Hasmoneans, the princedom and the Priesthood were joined together, until at last liberty was utterly lost and the people dispersed throughout the whole world under the yoke of others, without a magistrate. They bear this most impatiently, and gnashing their teeth and snarling madly, they call the Roman Empire—in an **exorcistic** <term>exorcistic: used here to mean a formulaic or ritualistic cursing</term> manner—the **Kingdom of Impiety** <note>original Hebrew: מלכות הרשעה (Malchut ha-Rish'ah), a common Talmudic epithet for the Roman Empire</note>. And they rushed into this lamentable ruin because they rejected God as King with the sacrificial crime of treason and demanded Caesar. For this reason, at the time of the Babylonian captivity, the remnants of the people still remained in Judea, and the sanctuary shekel always...

For as long as it remained in the Temple, it was hung up as a tribute to the true God, the King of the Jews. But once the nation was destroyed and the Temple overturned after the death of Christ, the **sacred shekel** <note>original: *siclus sacer*</note> was diverted and brought to the Capitol in Rome. God did not take notice of **Vespasian** <note>Roman Emperor from 69–79 AD, whose forces destroyed the Second Temple</note> bringing the shekel into the Capitol—and thus polluting it, as it was to be consecrated to a pagan idol—as He had done in the time of **Belshazzar** <note>original: *Belfchatsaris*; a reference to the Babylonian king punished for using sacred Temple vessels at a feast</note>. This was because that nation was utterly cut off and the prophecy of Genesis 49 <note>Genesis 49:10: "The scepter shall not depart from Judah..."</note> was fulfilled, regarding the removal of the scepter from Judah and a Lawgiver from his feet.

But just as God had established the Jewish state <term>polity: the form or constitution of a civil government</term> from the beginning by a special right as His own possession, so it becomes clearly known from the prophecy of Daniel what should be thought of the four Monarchies of the world. Daniel designates these through the terms **King** <note>original Hebrew: מלך (melek)</note> and **Kingdom** <note>original Hebrew: מלכות (malkut)</note>; these were required to endure, as they were instituted, until a predetermined time, so that at last the eternity of the kingdom of Christ alone and the immutability of His perennial glory might be established. Think the same of other kingdoms and princedoms of the world. Whence it is said, ***By me kings reign***, etc. <note>Proverbs 8:15</note>. Hence, even if **Julius Caesar** ascended the throne by wicked ways, yet once the empire was established and the people bound by the oath of loyalty—God so ordaining it—the murder by the conspirators is condemned as parricide. Wherefore, with God taking vengeance, the conspirators fought unsuccessfully and, in despair, brought death upon themselves **by their own hand** <note>original Greek: αὐτοχειρίᾳ (autocheiria)</note>.

Therefore, the opinion of those who madly rave that the highest magistrate arises by chance and not from the ordination of God must be detested. Already long ago, 1,400 years ago, **Irenaeus, Bishop of Lyons**, left it written that all power is from God, according to the universal words of Paul in Romans 13:1, 2, etc. This is why (as **Isidore of Pelusium** <note>original: *Isidorus Damiata*; a 5th-century monk and prolific letter-writer</note> writes) in the most ancient paintings, a hand was seen extended from heaven, placing a crown upon their heads. What of the fact that the Pagans themselves seem to hold out a light? For **Homer** himself, no less a statesman than a poet, recorded in his writings that kings are born from Jove <note>Jupiter or Zeus, the king of the gods in classical mythology</note>, and that they alone reign to whom God has granted dignity; and he very often calls them **nurslings of Jove** <note>original Latin: *Iouis alumnos*</note>. And the ancient philosophers said that God alone is king by nature, because He is **Existence** <note>original Hebrew: יש (*Yesh*), meaning "being" or "substance"</note>, independent...

...whose supreme right is **autocratic** <note>original Greek: *αὐτοκρατορικὸν* (autokratikon); refers to absolute, self-derived power</note> and **absolute** <note>original: *alodiale*; a legal term for land or rights held in one's own name, not from a superior lord</note>. Nevertheless, although every magistrate is of divine institution, a distinction must be made between **immediate** and **mediate** <note>Direct vs. indirect</note> institution. For God gave judges, liberators, saviors, kings, and other magistrates to His chosen people **immediately**, as is clear from the examples of **Moses, Joshua, Saul, David**, and others. Indeed, the Supreme Governor of the whole world himself deigned to rule His people directly; He willed to be present in their midst through the visible symbol of the **pillar of fire and cloud**, and to establish edicts and laws through the **Urim and Thummim** <note>Sacred objects used by the High Priest of Israel to determine God's will</note> or by His own living voice. Thus, the Jewish **polity** <term>polity: the form or system of a civil government</term> is a certain species of government that can be called unique, and which cannot be compared to others. For it cannot be called a **Monarchy**, an **Aristocracy**, a **Democracy**, or a mixture of these. Nor, as **Claudius Salmasius** <note>A famous 17th-century French scholar and defender of monarchy</note> said of the English government, can it be called a **stratocracy** <note>A government ruled by the military</note>; for the Roman Empire was reduced to this type of tyrannical rule when it was threatened with ruin, and when the **Praetorian guards** would tumultuously set up and depose Emperors. But the Jewish polity could truly be called a **Theocracy** <note>original Greek: *Θεοκρατία* (Theokratia)</note>, because God held the helm of the kingdom directly and acted as the supreme magistrate. Therefore, when that untamable nation demanded a king who would be like the kings of other nations, God complained that He was being rejected by His people. Yet, God did not thereby confuse political and ecclesiastical government; rather, as He is the author and institutor of both, He willed to establish the **Sanhedrin** <note>The supreme judicial and administrative council of the Jews</note> and the **synagogue** for this purpose.

But as for the rest of the nations, God instituted and governed their polities **mediately** <note>indirectly, through human means</note>. Indeed, God now acts in this way even with His own people; for a Christian magistrate is either born through succession or created through election, according to the custom of various nations. In some, only males succeed, as in the Kingdom of the Franks...

-># THE REVEALER OF SECRETS #<-

[The scripture] teaches clearly that power is an ordinance of God. *Nor are there any powers except those ordained by God.* <note>original Latin: "Nec potestates esse ullas nisi à Deo ordinatas." A quote from Romans 13:1.</note> And it teaches that princes are the ministers of God for those doing well, for their praise; but for the wicked, they are avengers for wrath, which is why they are said to carry the sword. On this point, the Emperor Trajan <note>Roman Emperor r. 98–117 AD, known for his sense of justice</note> uttered immortal words while holding a sword: *draw this sword against me, if I do not practice judgment.* <note>original Latin: "stringe hunc in me gladium, ni iudicium exerceam." This famous anecdote describes Trajan giving a sword to a subordinate, authorizing him to use it against the Emperor himself if he became a tyrant.</note> Therefore, so that <term>Magistrates</term> <note>In this context, "magistrates" refers to any high-ranking civil authorities or rulers, not just local judges.</note> might judge more justly, it is said in Psalm 82:1, *God has stood in the assembly of the gods, and acts as judge in the midst of the gods.* <note>In the Hebrew tradition, the word "Elohim" (gods) was sometimes used to refer to judges because they represented God's justice on earth.</note> If they fail in their duty, they are not only unjust to the people whom they unfairly trouble, but they are also disrespectful toward God, whose holy judgments they pollute. Because God instituted the office of the Magistrate, piety toward God and honor toward the Magistrate are often joined together. Hence Peter, in his first Epistle (2:17), commands us to *fear God and honor the King.* And in Proverbs 24:21, Solomon commands that *God and the King be feared.* By joining God with the king, he shows that the office is full of a certain holy reverence. Furthermore, in Romans 13:5, we find that excellent command of Paul: that *we should obey not only because of wrath, but also because of conscience.* And Christ said to the Jews, *Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.*

Since, therefore, God instituted Magistrates, this point must be especially observed: that Magistrates are His more distinct images. For it is a perpetual truth that whenever God has established something, He immediately expresses His own image within it; it cannot be otherwise, since He can do nothing that is unlike Himself. When He founded the world, He made it after His own image with respect to essence and existence, because the creation is concerned with the institution of nature. Likewise, when He institutes a Magistrate, He creates him after His own image; not indeed according to nature—for this status belongs to creation or birth and is shared with all other men—but according to <term>political governance</term> <note>original Latin: "regimen politicum"</note> or the exercise of justice. Thus, the Magistrate is said by this special right to be created in the image of God; for God creates Consuls, Judges, and Magistrates so that they may even be "gods."

But indeed, that image of God in the supreme Magistrate consists of two things: namely, that just like God, he claims for himself a twofold right...
