While the previous page established that the Magistrate is a "living image" of God and that their power is an ordinance of God, this page delves into the legal distinctions of that power: specifically the difference between "absolute right" and "ordained right," and how a ruler's power is ultimately tempered by divine law.</meta>

# ANTHONY CREGUT #

I. Right is called *absolute*, which is indeed independent, sovereign <note>original Greek: αὐτοκρατορικὸν, meaning "autocratic" or "self-ruling"</note>, and allodial <note>referring to land or rights held in one's own right, not subject to a superior landlord</note>; so much so that they do not depend on any man at all, but are self-governing <note>original Greek: αὐτεξούσιοι</note>, not only as other men are through the freedom of their will, but also with respect to their freedom of right and lack of dependence. This is because they are simply of their own right and emancipated from any earthly authority. Whence, relative to other men, they say (as did the Kings of the Persians) that *whatever pleases is permitted*. For although not all carry the four Persian insignia—the four β’s—in this manner: ββββ, which signified: *The King of kings, ruling over kings* <note>original Greek: Βασιλεὺς βασιλέων βασιλεύων βασιλεῦσι. While the author attributes this to Persian monarchs, this "tetragrammic" symbol is historically associated with the Byzantine Palaiologos dynasty.</note>; nevertheless, kings do not depend on others and possess absolute right.

II. They also possess ordained right, which is measured by the prescriptions of laws and by the rule of reason and justice. For they know that laws are the bond by which every <term>Commonwealth</term> <note>original Latin: Respublica. This refers to the state or the organized political community.</note> is held together, and the vital spirit which the city draws; so much so that without law, the commonwealth would be nothing in the future but a burden and a prey. Hence fundamental laws, such as the Salic Law <note>A famous code of law, most notably used in France to govern royal succession</note>, are called the *rights of the kingdom*. Hence Aristotle says in the *Politics*, Book 3, Chapter 11: *Those who bid the law to rule, bid God to rule through His own voice; but those who bid a man to rule, bid a beast to rule.* This is because a man can certainly degenerate into a beastly tyrant.

Nevertheless, this must still be observed regarding absolute right: since the Magistrate is the image of God, he ought to imitate the Archetype <note>The "Archetype" here refers to God Himself, the original model for all rulers.</note> in this way: God never uses His absolute right, but always His ordained right. For although, by the eminence of His nature, He could by right perform whatever He pleased, nor be held to give an account to any creature—who, since it is made from nothing and is itself nothing in the sight of the Supreme Being, ought not even to open its mouth—nevertheless, that supreme right is tempered by ordained right. This ordained right is governed not by the super-eminent loftiness of infinite majesty, but by the weight of the most balanced justice.

Therefore, the highest <term>Magistrate</term> among men should use his absolute right much less, but rather his ordained right. This is because his absolute right is not *simply* absolute <note>original Greek: ἁπλῶς</note>, but *in a certain respect* <note>original Greek: κατά τι</note>—not with respect to God, but only to men. For if they are not held to give an account to their subjects, nevertheless their power is subordinate to God, from whose Laws no mortal can be released.

<summary>This page distinguishes between the absolute right of a monarch (independence from other men) and ordained right (adherence to law and justice). It argues that just as God chooses to act through justice rather than raw power, human rulers must prioritize the "ordained right" of law to avoid becoming tyrannical.</summary>

### ANTHONY CREGUT

I. Law is called *absolute* when it is truly independent, <term>autocratic</term> <note>original Greek: αὐτοκρατορικὸν (autokratorikon), meaning possessing absolute power or being self-governing.</note> and allodial <note>a legal term for land or rights held independently, without a superior landlord or feudal obligation.</note>; such that these rights depend on no man at all, but are <term>self-governing</term> <note>original Greek: αὐτεξούσιοι (autexousioi). In theological and legal contexts, this refers to the power of self-determination or free will.</note>—not only as other men are through the freedom of their will, but also in respect to legal freedom and independence. This is because they are simply <term>of their own right</term> <note>original Latin: "sui iuris," a legal status where a person is not under the authority of another.</note> and emancipated from any earthly authority. Hence, in relation to other men, they say (as did the Kings of the Persians) that "whatever pleases is permitted." For although not all rulers carry the four **β**'s as the Persian monarchs did—an insignia **ββββ** which signified: <note>original Greek: Βασιλεὺς βασιλέων βασιλεύων βασιλεῦσι (Basileus basileōn basileuōn basileusi).</note> **King of kings, ruling over kings**—nevertheless, kings do not depend on others and they possess absolute right. 

II. They have *ordained* right, which is measured by the prescriptions of laws and the rule of reason and justice. For they know that laws are the bond by which every Republic is held together, and the vital spirit which the city breathes; so much so that without law, the republic would be nothing in the future but a burden and a prey. Hence, fundamental laws, such as the Salic Law <note>A famous ancient code of the Salian Franks, often cited in the early modern period to justify succession rules, particularly the exclusion of women from the throne.</note>, are called the *rights of the kingdom*. Thus Aristotle says in his *Politics*, Book 3, Chapter 11: *He who commands the law to rule, commands God to rule through His own voice; but he who commands a man to rule, commands a beast to rule.* This is because a man can degenerate into a bestial tyrant.

Nevertheless, this must still be observed regarding absolute right: since the Magistrate is the **image of God**, he ought to imitate the Archetype, who never uses His absolute right, but always His ordained right. For although, by the eminence of His nature, God could perform whatever He pleased by right and is not bound to give an account to any creature—who, being made from nothing, is nothing in the sight of the Supreme Being and ought not even to mutter—yet that supreme right is tempered by ordained right. This is moderated not by the supereminent loftiness of infinite majesty, but by the weight of most equal justice. 

Therefore, a supreme Magistrate among men ought much less to use his absolute right, but rather his ordained right; for his absolute right is not <term>simply</term> <note>original Greek: ἁπλῶς (haplōs), meaning "absolutely" or "unconditionally."</note> absolute, but only <term>in a certain respect</term> <note>original Greek: κατὰ τι (kata ti), meaning "partially" or "relatively."</note>. It is not absolute in respect to God, but only in respect to men. For if they are not bound to give an account to their subjects, their power is nevertheless subordinate to God, from whose Laws no mortal can be released.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of supreme authority, transitioning from the forms of government (Monarchy, Aristocracy, Democracy) to specific historical titles of magistracy and the distinction between shared power and absolute monarchical right.</meta>

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS

The **Prytanæum** <note>The *Prytaneion*, a public hall in ancient Greek cities where the executive council met and the city's "eternal flame" was kept</note> was said to be located on the Athenian Acropolis. It was so named as if it were a *pyros tameion*, a storehouse of wheat or a public granary. Among the Carthaginians, there were **Suffetes** <note>The chief magistrates of Carthage, similar to Roman consuls; the name is related to the Hebrew word *Shophetim* or "Judges"</note> who also exercised the supreme magistracy and were not much different from Roman Consuls. There were also **Ceryces**, which you might call **heralds** or **messengers** <note>original: *præcones* or *caduceatores*, from the Greek κῆρυξ (*kēryx*)</note>, whom Nero surpassed in a contest. Hence, Seneca says to Serenus in *On Tranquility of Mind*: *“You do not wish to administer the Republic as a Consul, or a Prytanis, or a Ceryx, or a Suffes.”*

Nevertheless, if we wish to examine these matters **more precisely** <note>original Greek: ἀκριβεστέρως (*akribesterōs*)</note>, it will be clear that although those magistrates were the highest, they did not properly possess that **absolute right** <term>ius absolutum</term> <note>Supreme power that is not legally subject to any other earthly authority</note> discussed above; rather, that is reserved for kings and monarchs alone. For although the Consuls truly used the highest power and could compel the people, decree peace or war without consulting the Senate, and were the judges of the lives and property of the citizens, they were nonetheless not kings, just like the Suffetes. This is because they were two in number and equal, which is why they could be summoned to court by one another in a charge of high treason, even though they held the power of life and death. But the character of absolute and monarchical right is to have no partner, according to that saying: *“Caesar could not bear a superior, nor Pompey an equal.”* And that line of Homer: *“The rule of many is not good; let there be one ruler.”* <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίη εἷς κοίρανος ἔστω (*ouk agathon polykoiraniē eis koiranos estō*)</note> Thus, if it is true what the Rabbis say—that the kings of the Jews were judged by the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme judicial council of ancient Israel</note> for three crimes: an excessive number of wives, horses, and the abuse of the treasury—then the power of kings was greatly limited. However, I do not know where the Rabbis fished that out; since it is found neither in the books of the Talmud, such as the *Sanhedrin* or *Maccoth*, nor in the Gemara <note>The component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis and commentary</note>. And indeed, it contradicts the history of Solomon, who took 700 queens as wives (besides others), who maintained 52,000 horses, and possessed gold without number or measure.

Furthermore, it does not prevent a Magistrate from being of divine institution even if secondary causes <note>Human actions or historical circumstances that God uses to bring about a result</note> are accustomed to create and institute them in various ways. # ANTHONY CREGUT

**Salmasius** <note>Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), a renowned French classical scholar</note> in his *Royal Apology* argues that authority is derived from the **patriarchs**, who were like kings and leaders of families. Later, as lineages grew, tribes were born, such as the twelve illustrious tribes among the Jews; from this, they were called **phylarchs** <note>original Greek: φύλαρχος (*phylarchos*), meaning "head of a tribe"</note>, essentially the leaders of tribes. For before men came together into one society, they wandered here and there across the fields like wild beasts, much like the **Nomads** <note>original: *Nomades*, referring to pastoral people who move from place to place for pasture</note> of old.

II. A magistracy is created by **election**, as when either the nobles, the people, or both choose their kings. This occurs in Poland, and the **Emperor of the West** <note>The Holy Roman Emperor</note> is today chosen by seven men called **Electors** <term>Electores</term> <note>The high-ranking princes of the Holy Roman Empire who held the right to elect the Emperor</note>. Three of these are ecclesiastical (church officials) and the others are secular; according to the following verse:

->*Mainz, Trier, and Cologne,*<-
->*Let each of these be a Chancellor of the Empire:*<-
->*The Palatine is Steward: the Duke the Sword-bearer:*<-
->*The Margrave is head of the Chamber: the Bohemian is Cupbearer.*<-
->*These appoint the supreme Lord for all ages.*<-

For although seven Electors are numbered in that five-line poem—namely the Archbishops of **Mainz** <note>original: *Moguntinensis*</note>, **Trier** <note>original: *Treuirensis*</note>, and **Cologne** <note>original: *Coloniensis*</note>, and the other secular ones, specifically the **Margrave of Brandenburg** who is the Chamberlain, the **Count Palatine** who is the Steward, the **Duke of Saxony** who is the Marshal, and the **King of Bohemia** who is the Cupbearer—nevertheless, **Albertus Krantzius** <note>A German historian (c. 1448–1517)</note> wrote that the Bohemian does not truly elect because he is not **German** <note>original: *Teutonicus*</note>.

This is confirmed by **Bellarmine** <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Cardinal and influential Jesuit theologian</note> in Book 3, Chapter 1, concerning the *Transfer of the Roman Empire*, where he begins: *“Nor should you wonder that this author excluded the King of Bohemia from the number of Electors, even though he is usually counted as the seventh Elector; for in truth the King of Bohemia does not elect with the others, except only when the six Electors are so divided among themselves that three favor one and three favor another. Then he has the right to nominate one of the two chosen.”* Hence **Hostiensis** <note>Henricus de Segusio (c. 1200–1271), a preeminent canon lawyer</note> says the seventh is the Duke of Bohemia, who is now King; but according to some, he is not necessary unless the others should disagree.

III. A magistracy is created by the **voluntary submission of the people**, when by their own will they bind themselves to a prince. This is indeed according to reason, that whoever is wiser than others should rule; whence **Plato** most skillfully said long ago that Republics would be more blessed when either **philosophers reign, or kings themselves practice philosophy.**

IV. When it is acquired by the **right of war** <note>original: *belli iure*</note>; for while among private individuals goods are acquired and preserved through civil laws and rights, among princes and those who hold supreme power, they are acquired by the right of war. From this comes that common saying, **right resides in arms** <note>original: *ius est in armis*</note>. For since princes hold absolute right and are not subject to the laws of their neighbors, when the authority of the laws is violated by anyone, those who are aggrieved then defend it with arms by the right of war. Indeed, among the ancient Latins, slaves <term>servi</term> were so named as if they were "those preserved" <term>servati</term>, because although they could have been killed by their victors by the right of war, their lives were nevertheless granted to them, provided they served them as their masters. This is why those converted in the early days of the Church were not released from their servitude to their masters; hence the Apostles commanded slaves to obey their masters. For as **Augustine** says, Christ claimed for them not a bodily freedom, but a spiritual one, and he changed their character, not their condition, making good men out of bad ones.

But truly, just as kings are established in these four ways, so after they have been established, they conduct themselves in various ways in the exercise of their duty. From this, three kinds of kings can be properly distinguished. I. There are the **good and indulgent**, such as **Titus** the son of Vespasian, **Antoninus Pius**, **Marcus the Philosopher** <note>The Roman Emperor Marcus Aurelius (reigned 161–180 AD), known for his Stoic philosophy</note>, and others. II. The **severe and gloomy**, who punish crimes harshly, such as the Emperors **Severus** and **Pertinax**, and others. III. The **ferocious and tyrannical**, such as **Nero**, **Caligula**, and others, whose decrees are: **let them hate, provided they fear** <note>original: *oderint dum metuant*, a phrase famously associated with the tyrant Caligula</note>. The first group is very much loved; the second is formidable; the third is worthy of hatred. The same can be said of parents, for there are those who are ferocious and who cast off nature itself, being more fierce than wild beasts. Yet sometimes there is an excess in indulgence just as there is in cruelty. Thus the **political theorists** <note>original: *Politici*</note> say that it is more difficult to live under an overly indulgent king, under whose rule anyone may do whatever they please, than under a cruel king. It is no different than when **doctors** are called cruel when they hide a wound by being indulgent to the sick person, and thus the **cancer** or **gangrene** <note>original: *gangræna*</note> spreads.

That third kind of kings caused such a shift in the people's hatred that they pursued the king with such loathing that it did not stop at the person of the king, but reached even the dignity of the office itself—

...had come; hence it is that among various nations the name and dignity of a King has been loathed. It is known to all how hateful the name of king was to the Romans because of the tyranny of **Tarquinius Superbus** <note>Tarquin the Proud, the legendary seventh and final king of Rome, whose abuses led to the establishment of the Republic</note>. Hence, as **Suetonius** testifies regarding **Julius Caesar** in chapter 79, Caesar brought envy upon himself by his affectation for kingship; when this became known to him, he responded to the common people who were hailing him as king, saying that *he was Caesar, not a king.* Consequently, when a diadem was placed near his head by the Consul Antony, he rejected it and immediately sent it to the Capitol for Jupiter Optimus Maximus <note>Jupiter "the Best and Greatest," the supreme deity of the Roman state</note>. Yet, beneath the statue of **Brutus** the regicide was written, *if only you were alive.* And on the statue of Caesar himself:

> *Because Brutus expelled kings, he was made the first Consul;*
> *Because this man expelled Consuls, he was finally made king.*

For although Caesar did not take the name of king because it was odious, the dignity of Emperor and king was nevertheless the same; hence, whenever **Daniel** mentions the four Empires of the world, he uses the words *malkut* and *melek* <note>original Hebrew: מלכות and מלך</note>, which signify *king and kingdom*. The same usage of the word *basileos* <note>original Greek: βασιλέως, "of a king"</note> exists among the Greeks; for this reason, the name of king is used in the Book of Revelation. Today also among the **Moscovites** <note>The people of the Grand Duchy of Moscow or Russia</note> the name of king is odious; for although their ruler may be the most powerful of kings, he is nevertheless commonly called *Knez* <term>Prince</term> or *Grand Duke*, yet he is often called Emperor by his own subjects.

But truly, if among various nations even the name of king is hateful, a contrary judgment must certainly be made regarding the subjects of the King of the **Franks**, who pursue their kings with the most ardent love and worship them with a certain veneration as sacred persons and the anointed of God. And therefore, true subjects and the **Politiques** <note>The *Politiques* were a moderate faction during the French Wars of Religion who prioritized national unity and the authority of the French Crown over religious dogma</note> have always rejected the maxims of the theologians and canonists—especially the **Jesuits**—asserting the supreme authority of our kings as independent from any man, even the **Roman Pontiff** <note>The Pope</note>. And for this reason, they detest the factions of the *Henotici* <note>Those seeking religious union or compromise, often used here in a derogatory sense regarding political agitators</note>, which are recounted by the illustrious and most truthful historian **Jacques Auguste de Thou** <note>A famous French historian and statesman (1553–1617) known for his monumental history of his own times</note> in his *History*, book 95, the last volume, and book 111, pages 414 and 520, concerning the monstrous sedition that arose in **Toulouse**. This occurred when **Jean-Étienne Durant**, the first president of the Senate <note>The Parlement of Toulouse</note>, having been pierced by various shots from a handgun <term>scloppetum</term>, was hung with a noose tied to his neck. An effigy of the King was likewise ignominiously hung opposite him, with [mockery] added for derision—

...called forward, and, wearing the kingdom—that is, the crown—upon his head, he adored him even to the kissing of his feet.

Before we leave this first part of the dissertation regarding the institution of the Magistrate, it would be worthwhile to examine that noble political question concerning the Magistrate *par excellence* <gloss>original Greek: κατ’ ἐξοχὴν, meaning "by excellence" or "preeminently"</gloss>: namely, whether an **elective** magistrate is to be preferred, or a **hereditary** one? Nevertheless, because the solution to this question is sufficiently taught in political systems, and since it must be decided differently according to the variety of nations and customs, we will for now refrain from treating it. We will observe only one disadvantage in hereditary succession, which when it occurs is very harmful: namely, when power is in the hands of a child. Hence, Ecclesiastes 10: *Woe to thee, O land, when thy King is a child.* Why so? Because a child is inexperienced, unlearned, and foolish. Thus, what the Hebrews call a youth <note>original: נער (*na'ar*)</note>, the German word *Narr* <note>meaning "fool"</note> denotes a fool, as if a fool were understood by the very word for a child. What is more unhappy than to be ruled by the foolish and the unskilled? I have seen nothing more unjust than an unskilled man, who thinks nothing is right except what he does himself. This is why in Isaiah 3, God threatens that He will give children to reign once the learned and the wise have been removed. 

And therefore, as the noble historian Jacques Auguste de Thou <note>often referred to as Thuanus (1553–1617), a French statesman and historian</note> reports in *History*, Book 57, Volume 2: the final words of **Charles IX** <note>King of France, 1560–1574, who took the throne at age ten and oversaw the St. Bartholomew’s Day massacre</note>, worthy of such a prince and a witness to his great love for his people, were that he rejoiced to be dying at that age and leaving no children as heirs to the kingdom. For he had learned abundantly by his own example how miserable the condition of child-kings was, and how deplorable the state of a kingdom where children preside over a troubled Republic; such was the state of things that the kingdom of France needed a man. However, he did not judge this to be true of his brother **Henry**; for he often repeated this saying: "The Magistrate will reveal the man." <note>original: *Magistratus virum indicabit*; a variation of a classical proverb suggesting that holding office reveals a person's true character.</note> Yet elective Magistrates do not lack their own disadvantages, which will easily occur to anyone who thinks about it.

I will add one final thing to this first part. Since God (as has been said) instituted Magistrates, do not those who rise up and conspire against them seem to be fighters against God? <term>original Greek: θεομάχοι (*theomachoi*); those who wage war against the divine</term> There are two...

...demonstrate splendor and more shining glory. **II.** **Judges**, who sit on the throne or tribunal of justice to judge. **III.** **Teachers**, who sit in the chair <note>The Latin *cathedra* refers to a formal teacher's seat, from which we get the word "cathedral."</note> to teach; as Christ said of the Pharisees that they sit in the Chair of Moses. **IV.** **Disciples**, who sit to learn; hence Paul sat at the feet of Gamaliel. Next, Christ sits as the Judge of the whole world. *John 5: God gave all things into his hands and judgment to be exercised.* Finally, he sits as the highest Teacher and Prophet of the Church. 

In this way, the Pope boasts in that triple sitting as the vicar of Christ. **I.** As king he is said to sit in the Apocalypse: *I sit as queen*, etc. **II.** As Judge in Councils, from which he is called the infallible Judge of controversies. **III.** As teacher in his Apostolic Chair, in which, while sitting, he cannot err in faith. And thus he is also said in *2 Thessalonians 2:4* *to sit in the temple of God*; where, however, in the original text it reads <term>to sit in the temple of God as God</term> <note>original Greek: "καθίσαι εἰς τὸν ναὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ ὡς Θεὸν"</note>. For as Augustine observed, he sits *against* the temple of God, even if he is in the heart of the Church itself. But he should rather sit as a disciple at the feet of some teacher, since the Popes are ignorant of the chief points of religion.

However, **Amyraldus** <note>Moïse Amyraut (1596–1664), a French Protestant theologian known for his doctrine of "hypothetical universalism."</note>, a most learned man, observed that <term>to judge</term> <note>original Greek: "τὸ iudicare"</note> signifies two things in Scripture. **1.** To solemnly and legally pronounce a sentence. **2.** To carry out a decree or judgment rendered. And **thirdly**, whenever a judgment is an acquittal and brings the remission of guilt, to judge is the same as *to liberate*. Thus when David asks of God that he establish his throne and sit there, and judge according to the cause, he intends that God judge kindly and in his favor; but indeed with great fervor...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of "sitting" in judgment, specifically focusing on the second category of those who sit: Judges and Magistrates. # THE REVEALER OF SECRETS

...and with mental intensity he cries out: *O God, judge me!* <note>original: "O Deus iudica me"</note> Without a doubt, he asks of Him to be rescued from the hands of his enemies. On the other hand, if a defendant is to be condemned, then *to judge* signifies *to punish*. In *Genesis 15:14*, God promises Abraham that He will judge that nation whom his descendants shall serve for four hundred years. And thus also the word "to judge" is used in *John 16:8 and 11*: *And when he comes, he will convict the world of sin, of righteousness, and of judgment, etc.* and in verse 11: *Of judgment, because the prince of this world has been condemned.*

A Magistrate, however, whose duty it is to judge, ought to possess these two requirements: 1. integrity, and 2. learning. Regarding the first, how shall the judge himself judge justly if he himself is unjust? For as Sallust retorted against Cicero, *He who is prepared to speak against another ought to be free from every vice*: so we shall truly assert regarding the judge, that he who is prepared to judge others ought to be free from every vice, and first the judge himself ought to be just. Nor is it more fitting for judges to judge others than themselves; and judgment is more terrible for them than for the parties involved, since they may easily deviate in judging—which Nero himself, though a monster of a man, confessed during his first five years of laudable rule, when he was asked to sign a death warrant. *I wish* (he said) *I did not know how to write.* <note>original: "Vtinam nescirem literas." Suetonius records that the young Nero said this to express his reluctance to sign a death sentence, though his later reign was famously brutal.</note> A judge, therefore, ought to imitate God, whose image he is; who, as Augustine testifies in *On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 23: *He returns evil for evil, because he is just; good for evil, because he is good; good for good, because he is both good and just; only he does not return evil for good, because he is not unjust.* For sometimes a Judge or a high Magistrate ought to use clemency and grant favor, whereby he returns good for evil. Truly, then, Papinian, the presiding officer of the sacred palace, was an ornament of Judges when he refused to defend the fratricide <note>Caracalla murdered his brother Geta in 211 AD and ordered Papinian, a famous lawyer, to write a legal defense for the murder.</note> committed by Bassianus Antoninus Caracalla with his own defense; because (he said) *it is easier to commit a parricide than to justify it; indeed, it is a crime to acquit the guilty, but a double crime to accuse the innocent of one's own accord.* <note>original: "parricidium" - literally the killing of a parent, but used here for the heinous murder of a close relative.</note> Exasperated by such <term>fearless speech</term> <note>original Greek: "parrhesia" (παρρησία) — the courage to speak the truth to those in power at great personal risk.</note>, that savage Emperor slaughtered the legal scholar by the hand of an executioner. Most wisely, therefore, the Arabs wrote in their proverbs that a Magistrate without justice is like a river without water, as if justice were not an accidental quality for them, but an essential one. Not otherwise than the poets have imagined...

# ANTHONY CREGUT

...demonstrate splendor and a more radiant glory.

II. To **Judges**, who sit upon the bench or tribunal of justice to deliver judgment. 
III. To **Teachers** <note>original: *Doctoribus*</note>, who sit in the chair <note>The *cathedra*, a seat of authority</note> to teach; as Christ said of the Pharisees, that they sit in the "Chair of Moses." 
IV. To **disciples**, who sit to learn; as when Paul sat at the feet of Gamaliel. 

In the first three ways, Christ is said to "sit." As King and Monarch of the Church, he sits at the right hand of the Father; but as the Leader <note>original: *Dux*</note> of his people in spiritual warfare, he is once said to *stand*. Thus in *Acts 7:56*, Stephen saw *the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God*, so that He might strengthen the first martyr <note>original: *protomartyrem*</note> in his confession of truth and receive him to Himself; and so that He might teach the first martyr Stephen, by His own example, that he was to be crowned with glory <note>original Greek: στεφανοῖ τῆς δόξης; a wordplay on the name "Stephen," which means "crown" in Greek</note>, if he himself should die standing, as was fitting for a leader and head <note>original: *Coryphæum*</note> of martyrs—following that saying of the great emperor, that *it is fitting for an emperor to die standing.* <note>A famous quote attributed to the Roman Emperor Vespasian.</note>

Next, Christ sits as the Judge of the whole world. *John 5: [God] has given all things into his hands and the authority to execute judgment.* Finally, he sits as the supreme Teacher and Prophet of the Church. 

In this way, the Pope boasts of that triple "sitting" as the Vicar of Christ:
I. As a king, he is said to sit in the Book of Revelation: *I sit as a queen, etc.* 
II. As a Judge in the Councils, from which he is called the "infallible judge of controversies." 
III. As a teacher in his Apostolic Chair <note>*Cathedra*</note>, in which, while sitting, he cannot err in faith. 
And thus he is also said in *2 Thessalonians 2:4* *to sit in the temple of God*; where, however, the original Greek text reads: *to sit in the temple of God as God* <note>original: καθίσαι εἰς τὸν ναὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ ὡς Θεόν</note>. Because, as Augustine observed, he sits *against* the temple of God, even if he is within the very heart of the Church. Yet he ought rather to sit as a disciple at the feet of some teacher, since the Popes are ignorant of the primary points of religion.

Furthermore, Amyraut <note>Moïse Amyraut (1596–1664), a prominent French Reformed theologian and professor at Saumur</note>, a most learned man, observed that "to judge" <note>original: *τὸ iudicare*</note> signifies two things in Scripture:
1. To pronounce a sentence solemnly and legally. 
2. To carry out a rendered decree or judgment. 
And thirdly, whenever the judgment is an acquittal and brings about the remission of guilt, "to judge" is the same as *to liberate*. Thus when David asks of God that He might raise up His throne and sit there, and judge according to his cause, he means that God should judge kindly and in his favor; but truly with great fervor, and [with intensity] of soul...

<margin>Psalm 1</margin> <note>While the margin reads Psalm 1, the quote *Erudimini qui iudicatis terram* is actually from Psalm 2:10.</note> ...he was saying, *“Be instructed, you who judge the earth.”* This instruction ought to be not only theoretical but also practical, concerning which it might truly be said what Aristotle once said of the doctor: *“practice alone makes the doctor.”* In the same way, practice alone makes the <term>jurist</term> <note>A scholar or practitioner of law</note>. But alas, what injustice! In this age, just as the practice of doctors has multiplied diseases, so the practitioners of law are nothing but vain litigants who sow disputes and controversies everywhere. Like <term>leeches</term> <note>original: *hirudines*; a common metaphor for those who drain the wealth of others</note>, they suck out the very sap and substance of families, and by constantly extorting money, they drain the purses of the wealthy.

This arose primarily from the sale of offices, and in France from the introduction of the <term>Paulette</term> <note>A tax named after Charles Paulet which allowed office-holders to make their positions hereditary by paying an annual fee to the Crown</note>. *“In this year, a most ruinous institution gained strength at the instigation of the Marquis of Rosny <note>The Duke of Sully, a chief minister to King Henry IV</note>. Because the offices in our country are innumerable—both judicial and financial—they were all placed on equal footing and ordered to be offered for sale through a most shameful and disgraceful trafficking. An annual payment, which took its name from Paulet, was imposed according to a valuation made for each office. Once this was paid, it was no longer necessary to wait the forty days prescribed by royal decrees for the office to pass to a successor through resignation; instead, the offices are preserved for the heirs, so that they may dispose of them according to their own will as if they were part of a family estate or even an inheritance.”*

It is no wonder, then, that when Ferdinand <note>King Ferdinand II of Aragon</note> sent a viceroy named Pedrarias <note>Pedro Arias Dávila, a Spanish colonial administrator</note> to the West Indies, he expressly forbade him from taking any of those jurists whom they call <term>Letrados</term> <note>Literally "lettered men"; university-trained lawyers who often held administrative power in the Spanish Empire</note> with him. For that wise king feared that those "Practitioners" would disturb the newly discovered New World with infinite lawsuits, just as they had disturbed the Old World. What would he have said about the Roman Curia and the Auditors of the <term>Rota</term> <note>The highest appellate tribunal of the Roman Catholic Church</note>, where lawsuits are made eternal? Indeed, in the <term>Comtat Venaissin</term> <note>An independent territory in Southern France surrounding Avignon that was under Papal rule until the French Revolution</note> and these neighboring regions, the habit of litigation arose from a <term>perverse imitation</term> <note>original: *cacozelia*; a Greek term for a distorted or misguided zeal in copying a style or habit</note> of the Roman court when the Popes had fixed their residence in Avignon.

...born to listen to both <note>original: *ἀμφοτέροιν ἀκροᾶσθαι*</note>. **Hear the other side** <note>original: *Audi alteram partem*</note>. **Haste is the stepmother of law** <note>original: *Festinatio est nouerca iuris*</note>. And just as it is uncivil to judge a law based on a small fragment of it, without having examined the whole law; so it will be much more uncivil and unjust to condemn a defendant unheard; for in such a way the innocent is often condemned, while the guilty goes unpunished. Hence that funereal saying: *to judge a thing unknown is rash; to condemn a truth once known is as wicked as it is rash.* This second duty of the Magistrate is praised in the <term>Areopagites</term> <note>Members of the highest judicial council in ancient Athens, famous for their impartiality</note>, who (as it is said) would listen to the accuser with one ear, while the other was saved for the defendant, so that he might not be condemned unheard.

III. It is his duty to exercise both sides of **distributive justice**, namely the avenging and the rewarding. For these are the two hands of justice; if either one is missing, justice is truly maimed and cut off by one arm. Yet, as justice is practiced among men today, who will not confess it to be crippled? For the rewarding part having been omitted, only the avenging and punishing part is in use; whence, in common speech, to be "subject to justice" or to "do justice" is the same as to punish or to fine. And in that case, the rule **"nothing in excess"** <note>original: *nequid nimis*; a famous ancient Greek maxim advising moderation</note> does not apply. Instead, there is **"extreme law, extreme injury"** <note>original: *summum ius summa iniuria*; the idea that the rigid application of law without equity can result in the greatest injustice</note>, whether too much or too little. It is justice with a grain of injustice. Justice becomes a <term>Lesbian and leaden rule</term> <note>original: *regula Lesbia & plumbea*; an ancient metaphor for a flexible or biased standard; a "lead rule" could be bent by builders to fit any shape, implying the law is being bent to fit a desired outcome</note>, and a **nose of wax** <note>A common historical metaphor for something that can be molded or manipulated to suit one's purpose</note>. Nowhere in the world is justice preserved **"without greed"** <note>original: *ἀκερδοδίκαιον*</note>, nor is any <term>Rule of Polyclitus</term> <note>original: *regula Polycleti*; the "Canon" of the sculptor Polyclitus, representing a perfect and inflexible standard of proportion</note> found that is inflexible and invariable.

IV. He must beware of **partiality** <note>original: *προσωποληψίαν* (*prosōpolēpsian*), literally "the taking of a face," or showing favoritism based on status</note>, for since the Judge is the image of God, just as that highest judge is not a **respecter of persons**, so neither should the subordinate judges be. Indeed, whether the action be judicial or extra-judicial, partiality will be a vice both in a judge and in a private man. For we ought to consider not so much the person himself, but his cause: because whether he be poor or rich, noble or ignoble, known or unknown, etc., judgment must be made according to law and equity without respect of persons. Nevertheless, these things are not to be taken so rigidly as if the "acceptance of persons" were absolutely vicious and illicit. For on the contrary, it is said in Genesis 4: *God had regard for Abel and for his offering.* For God first had regard for the person, and then for the work; but truly, when partiality is condemned, it happens...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the duties of a Magistrate. # ANTHONY CREGUT

...when the cause and the matter itself are not weighed, but rather external qualities inherent to someone, such as wealth, rank, kinship, etc. Indeed, these qualities can be viewed in two ways: either as absolute or as relative. **Absolute** qualities are those common to many and have no affinity or connection to the legal case, such as the aforementioned wealth, rank, etc. In these instances, **respect of persons** <note>original: *προσωποληψία* (prosōpolēpsia); a Greek term meaning "partiality" or "favoritism"</note> is a vice. The Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> denies that this occurs in God (Romans 2). **Relative** qualities, however, are those that have a certain connection to the matter, such as when one is a Magistrate, a Pastor, a Judge, etc. In such cases, the status of the persons is taken into account, which increases the gravity of the case; thus, one who strikes a magistrate will suffer more lashes than one who strikes a private citizen. Long ago, **respect of persons** was exiled far from the **Areopagus** <term>Areopagus</term> <note>The high court of ancient Athens, renowned for its strict impartiality</note> when the judges would deliberately judge at night, so they would neither see nor hear those to be judged; they were careful in both regards lest their eyes and ears be corrupted, for objects of the senses strongly move the feelings.

But come now, because this doctrine of **respect of persons** <note>original: *προσωποληψία*</note> is of great use in Theology, let us investigate more carefully what it is. First, regarding the **study of names** <note>original: *περὶ τῆς ὀνοματολογίας*; etymology</note>. Second, regarding the **study of the matter** <note>original: *περὶ τῆς πραγματολογίας*; the actual substance of the concept</note>. The name, as is clear, comes **from receiving the person** <note>original: *ἀπὸ τοῦ λαμβάνειν τὸ πρόσωπον*</note>. But this Greek nomenclature corresponds to the Hebrew **to lift the face** or **to accept the face** <note>original: *נשא פנים* (Nasa Panim)</note>. For as the ancient Hebrews handed down, and as observed by the most learned **John Cameron** <note>A famous 17th-century Scottish theologian and scholar of biblical languages</note>, in ancient times the gesture of those greeting someone was performed with the face bowed to the ground—a practice still found in the East today. The one being greeted would then lift the greeter up, that is, he **lifted his face** <note>original: *נשא פנים*</note>. Thus David greeted Saul with his face bowed to the earth. If the greeting was rejected or taken poorly, then there was no "lifting of the face" or "acceptance of the person." This phrase is found expressed differently in Scripture, such as in Deuteronomy 1: **"You shall not recognize the face of the person."** And in the book of Genesis, God addresses Lot in this way: **"In this I have accepted your person."** From this, it is clear that in the Old Testament, **respect of persons** <note>original: *προσωποληψίαν*</note> was perpetually legitimate. The reason is that it concerns a civil act, like a greeting and its gestures, where it is permissible to accept or not accept a person. For when there is a need—

<meta>This page continues the detailed analysis of "respect of persons" or partiality. # THE REVEALER OF SECRETS

...is purely civil, and has no moral element mixed in, it is considered a matter of discretion; but truly, when the work is ethical or supernatural <note>original: *hyperphysicum*</note>, **partiality** <note>original: *acceptio personarum*; literally "the accepting of persons"</note> is rightly condemned, because judgment ought to be weighed not from the quality of the person, but from the matter or the cause itself. And so, in the New Testament, **favoritism** <note>original: *προσωποληψία* (prosōpolēpsia)</note> is condemned, as in Romans 2, Galatians 2:6, Acts 10:34, and Mark 11:34. <note>The text cites Mark 11:34, though the author likely refers to the sentiment in Mark 12:14 regarding God's impartiality.</note>

Regarding the **study of facts** <note>original: *πραγματολογίαν* (pragmatologian)</note>, we must accurately investigate when **partiality** is condemned in Scripture and when it is not. 1. In judgment, it is condemned when the judge does not judge according to the law, but through right or wrong, being occupied by favor and prejudices. 2. **Favoritism** <note>original: *προσωποληψία*</note> is condemned when the judge gazes upon conditions and qualities which ought not to move him to the prejudice of a good cause. Thus, **favoritism** is illicit when a judge looks upon a man's face and, led by a certain beauty and grace of the sight, accepts the person to the prejudice of a good cause. To this the Pharisees seem to have looked in Mark 12:14, saying to Christ: *For you do not look at the face of men*; the Vulgate <note>The standard 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> renders this as *you do not see into the face*. So that the **Areopagites** <term>Areopagites</term> <note>Judges of the high court in Athens</note> might avoid this (as we said above), it is said that they exercised judgment in the darkness. Furthermore, **favoritism** is condemned when it is based on qualities of the mind or body, or because of external qualities such as goods, resources, and honors—whether these be true or feigned, just as actors in theaters take on the **persona** <note>In Latin, *persona* originally referred to the mask worn by an actor</note> of this or that individual. And thus Peter understands it in Acts 10:34, *when with an open mouth he said: truly I perceive that God is no respecter of persons.* This is likewise seen in the other places cited above, such as Romans 2 and Galatians 2:6.

Otherwise, God is truly a **respecter of persons** <note>original: *προσωπολήπτης* (prosōpolēptēs)</note> without any injustice. Thus, in the doctrine of **predestination** <note>The theological concept that God has foreordained the salvation of certain souls</note>, He is said to have chosen Jacob and rejected Esau, and in Genesis 4, to have respected Abel. This was not done out of a flawed **favoritism**, for there was not in those men any **predisposing cause** <note>original: *προκαταρκτικὴ* (prokatarktikē); an initial or triggering cause</note> which impelled God to choose them; rather, He was moved by His own pure **good pleasure** <note>original: *εὐδοκίᾳ* (eudokia)</note>. Finally, in human judges, **partiality** is not condemned when great account is taken of virtue, and the judges do good to the good and punish the wicked, and when (as was said above) account is taken of a person’s public status in the administration of the law rather than their private status.

# ANTHONY CREGUT

...for the circumstances of places, times, and persons add no small weight <note>to the gravity of a legal or moral situation</note>.

V. It is a duty **not to be corrupted by gifts and bribes**. For those judges are the worst of all who sell justice, which ought to be undefiled. Here, truly, those who "receive" are themselves "taken" <note>A pun on the Latin *accipiunt* (receive) and *capiuntur* (captured)</note>; indeed, like fish on a hook, here those old sayings hold sway: **I give so that you may give, I do so that you may do.** <note>original: *do ut des, facio ut facias*; these are standard legal formulas for reciprocal contracts, here used to describe bribery.</note> The gifts of enemies are no gifts at all. **I fear the Greeks even when they bring gifts.** <note>original: *Timeo Danaos & dona ferentis*; a famous line from Virgil’s *Aeneid* regarding the Trojan Horse.</note> **Do you think the gifts of the Greeks lack hidden snares?** <note>original: *Putasne dona carere dolis Danaum.*</note> Surely, when a judge or a lawyer is corrupted by gifts, the laws likewise are corrupted and are usually dragged into a worse interpretation. Hence the story of that man who collected intricate and ambiguous laws so that he might abuse them for the sake of a friend; for that reason, he placed in the margin of his book the note, **"This law is for a friend."** <note>original: *Lex ista pro amico*</note> Thus, those "fair" judges, much like the Satyr <note>Referring to Aesop's fable where a Satyr befriended a man but grew suspicious when the man blew on his hands to warm them and his soup to cool it</note>, blow hot and cold from the same mouth. It was not without merit, therefore, that in ancient times the statues of judges were crafted without hands, to signify that judges ought to be kept from bribes, lest the same thing happen to them as happened to Demosthenes. He became the talk and the laughingstock of the entire Areopagus <note>The high court of Athens</note> when he was first corrupted by the envoy of Philip; hence his opponent's sarcasm: **it is not a sore throat, but a silver throat.** <note>original: *οὐ συνάγχη ἀλλ᾽ ἀργυράγχη* (ou synanchē all' argyranchē). This is a pun: *synanche* is a throat infection (quinsy), while *argyranche* implies he is "choking" on silver (bribes).</note> Those are the "wages of sin" which bring forth death. VI. The duty of a Magistrate is **to use clemency**. For even though he must punish crimes, and justice is more frequently exercised by punishing than by rewarding, it is nevertheless better for grace or clemency to prevail over strict justice. This was once the practice among the Areopagites <note>Members of the Areopagus, the most prestigious judicial council in ancient Athens.</note>. When the votes of the judges were equal, then clemency prevailed and the defendant was acquitted. Augustine testifies to this in Book 18 of *The City of God*. Pliny records that this practice originated with Mars. He says: **"Areopagus"** <note>original: *Areopagus*; meaning Mars' Hill.</note> is to the Latins the **"Court or Village of Mars."** The reason for the name comes from the judgment in which Mars—who is called *Ares* in Greek <note>original: *αρης* (Arēs)</note>—when he was standing trial for homicide, was acquitted by six votes among the twelve gods judging in that village. For where the votes are equal, acquittal is preferred over condemnation. Hence, the supreme Magistrate for capital crimes was established there, judging with such gravity and such integrity (as was said above) that he heard cases by night, not by day; this was so that he might not look at *who* was speaking, but rather at *what* was being said, and weigh it within himself. 

Moreover, Palamedes <note>A legendary Greek figure of the Trojan War era, often credited with inventing the alphabet, numbers, and weights.</note> first discovered the ballots used there. They signified acquittal, condemnation, or even an adjournment <note>original: *comperendinationem*; a legal delay for further evidence.</note> using various marks and characters. When a defendant was acquitted, the Greek letter **Thau** <note>The letter T; often used as a symbol of life or salvation.</note> was prefixed; when he was condemned, the letter **Theta** <note>original: *$\Theta$*; the Greek letter 'Th', standing for *Thanatos* (Death).</note> was used in this manner: $\Theta$. When the days were adjourned, the letter **Lambda** <note>The Greek letter 'L'.</note> was applied, and the judges would say: **"it is not yet clear."** <note>original: *nondum liquet*; a formal legal verdict when the evidence was insufficient to convict or acquit.</note> An illustrious example of this is found in Aulus Gellius’s *Attic Nights*, where the lawsuits of Evathlus and Protagoras <note>A famous paradox where Protagoras sued his student Evathlus for his tuition fee, which was only due after Evathlus won his first court case.</note> are said to have been prolonged for an age because of the difficulty of the matter. V. The fifth duty is **not to be corrupted by gifts and bribes**. For the worst of all are those judges who sell justice, which ought to be undefiled. Truly, here "those who receive are themselves taken"; indeed, they are like fish on a hook. In this context, these sayings hold true: "I give that you may give," and "I do that you may do." <note>original: *do ut des, facio vt facias*; these are traditional formulas in Roman law describing reciprocal exchanges or contracts.</note> The gifts of enemies are no gifts at all. "I fear the Greeks, even when they bring gifts," <note>original: *Timeo Danaos & dona ferenteis*; a famous line from Virgil’s *Aeneid* referring to the Trojan Horse.</note> and "Do you think the gifts of the Greeks lack trickery?" <note>original: *Putasne dona carere dolis Danaum*; also from the *Aeneid*.</note> Surely, when a judge or a lawyer is corrupted by gifts, the laws likewise are corrupted and are usually twisted into a worse meaning. 

From this comes the story of the man who collected intricate and ambiguous laws so he could abuse them for the sake of a friend; thus, he would write in the margin of his book: "This law is for a friend." <note>original: *Lex ista pro amico.*</note> In this way, those "fair" judges—no different than the Satyr in the fable—blow hot and cold from the same mouth. <note>A reference to Aesop’s fables; it describes someone who is inconsistent or hypocritical, saying one thing but doing another.</note> It was not without reason, therefore, that in ancient times the statues of judges were made without hands, to signify that judges ought to abstain from bribes. This was to prevent the same thing happening to them as happened to Demosthenes, <note>A famous Athenian orator (384–322 BC).</note> who became the talk and the laughingstock of the whole Areopagus <note>The supreme court of ancient Athens.</note> when he was first corrupted by the envoy of Philip. <note>Philip II of Macedon, who was attempting to expand his influence over the Greek city-states.</note> Hence came his rival’s sarcasm: his ailment was not "a sore throat" but "a silver-sore throat." <note>original: *συνάγχη ἀλλ’ ἀργυράγχη*; a pun on *synanche* (a throat infection) and *argyranche* (a "choking" by silver/money). Demosthenes had claimed he could not speak in the assembly because he had lost his voice, but it was rumored he had been bribed to stay silent.</note> These are the wages of sin, which bring forth death. Romans 6:23: "For the wages of sin is death." <note>original: *τὰ γὰρ ὀψώνια τῆς ἁμαρτίας Θάνατος.*</note> The poets have elegantly expressed this corruption of judges in their mythologies, playing with these verses:

### VI. The duty of the Magistrate is *to use clemency*. 
For although he ought to punish crimes, and justice is more frequently exercised through punishment than through reward, nevertheless it is better that grace, or clemency, should prevail over justice. This was once the practice among the Areopagites <note>The Areopagus was the high court of Athens, famous for its ancient and strict legal traditions.</note>. ### VII. The magistrate's duty is first of all *to cultivate piety*.
For if they ought to observe human laws and judge according to them, they must much more observe the divine law, which is the standard <note>original: "amussis," a mason's leveling tool or rule.</note> for all laws, and to which all others are subordinate. This is why, in confirmation of this practice, the patrons or advocates in the Parliament of Paris were once not accustomed to speak without the introduction of the speech being drawn from some oracle of Scripture. This was done formerly in the time of Philip of Valois <note>Philip VI (reigned 1328–1350), the first Valois king of France.</note>, King of the Franks, by Pierre Cugnières <note>original: "Petro Cunerio." A 14th-century lawyer and advisor known for defending royal jurisdiction against the church.</note> while pleading for the King's jurisdiction as his Attorney General, as is related by Paolo Emilio and Jacques Auguste de Thou. For he began his speech thus: *Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.* Therefore, pious kings ought to imitate David and Solomon, who built a temple to God, and Josiah, who discovered the Law and restored the pure worship of God.

Let them beware, therefore, lest it be truly said of their empire what the Rabbis often say of the Roman Empire, when they call it <term>מלכות הרשעה</term> <note>Hebrew: *Malkhut ha-Rish'ah*</note>, that is, the *kingdom of wickedness* or the *impious kingdom*. And so the royal power was entrusted to him without the royal name or insignia, as Paolo Emilio relates regarding Philip I. # REVEALER OF SECRETS

...they follow, as is clear from the kings of Judah and Israel in the books of Samuel and Kings. From this comes that saying: *The whole world is formed according to the example of the King.* <note>original: "Regis ad exemplar totus componitur orbis." A famous line from the poet Claudian, suggesting that the public mirrors the behavior of their leader.</note>

VIII. **Vigilance** is required. For just as the Lion, the king of the four-footed beasts, almost never sleeps but is always watching—or if he does sleep, according to those skilled in natural history, he sleeps with his eyes open—this same vigilance is certainly appropriate for a Magistrate, lest an adversary rush in like a thief. God signifies this by His own example; in the Scriptures, He is called the guardian of Israel who always watches, and He is said to be "all eye." Even shepherds and Overseers <note>original: "Episcopi." The Greek term *episkopos* literally means "overseer" or "one who watches over."</note> are so named because of their vigilance. This is why Xenophon <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and soldier known for his writings on leadership and the ideal ruler.</note> wisely wrote concerning the political Magistrate: *His vigilance is the sleep of everyone else; his industry preserves the pleasures of all.*

But indeed, Magistrates—and especially kings—do not only watch themselves, but they also use scouts or spies. These were used long ago among the Persians, who observed what was being said and done everywhere and reported it back to the king. This was done for the safety of the king and for the preservation of both the subjects and the commonwealth. The Persians called these men the **eyes and ears of the king**. However, what was a very good institution at the beginning was later abused by tyrants. Nero used them perversely and gave them a fourth part of the goods of those they informed upon, which is why they were called "fourth-part men" <term>quadruplatores: Roman legal informants who received 25% of a convicted person's assets</term>. Tiberius valued them so highly that when the Senate decided to act on abolishing their rewards, the Emperor very strenuously prohibited it, saying that the laws are subverted if the "guardians of the laws" are removed—as if to say that spies are the guardians of the laws. Regarding these spies, some explain that passage in **Ecclesiastes 10**: *Do not curse the King, even in your own mind; for a bird of the heavens will carry that voice, and the birds will report the word.* In this passage, several learned interpreters understand "birds" to mean spies. Similarly, in **2 Samuel 18**: *Nothing can be hidden from the king*, namely, through the work of spies. It seems, however, that these spies were of two kinds. Some were permanent, even in times of peace and in respect to the king's own subjects; such were perhaps those "fourth-part men" mentioned above, for whom rewards were assigned. Others were temporary and primarily used in time of war, and not so much among subjects as among enemies.

...just as those Jewish <term>spies<note>Hebrew: *meraglim* (מרגלים)</note></term> were, who were sent by Joshua to scout the land of Canaan. Finally, before we complete this section on the duty of the Magistrate toward his subjects, we must inquire whether it is lawful today for a magistrate to judge according to the **Law of Retaliation** <note>original: *lex Talionis*; the principle of "an eye for an eye."</note>, which is found in Exodus 21:24, Leviticus 24:20, and Deuteronomy 19:21 <note>The original text mistakenly cites Deuteronomy 39:21; I have corrected this to 19:21.</note>, since Christ seems to condemn it in Matthew 5:38: *“You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’ But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil. He did not, I say, rebuke the Law of Retaliation—which was holy and just—but showed its abuse and how it was being twisted into a wicked sense. 

For, **firstly**, that law was given to **judges**, who were required to distribute punishment in proportion to the fault; just as the Moral Philosophers reason concerning **Arithmetic and Geometric proportion** <note>Arithmetic proportion involves a simple 1:1 exchange (eye for eye), while Geometric proportion considers the status of the parties or the context of the crime.</note>, and concerning proportion relative to weight and justice. It was not, however, given to private individuals, who have no right to exact punishment themselves or to seek personal revenge. For vengeance belongs to God or to the Judges who are His representatives. 

**Secondly**, Christ did not abolish the Law of Retaliation, but He pulls up the roots of brawls and quarrels so that there is no need for a Judge to vent his rage through such a penalty. For every great contention is very slight at its beginning; just as great fires start from a modest spark, and the largest rivers begin from a tiny spring. Therefore, Saint Hilary rightly writes in his commentary on this passage: *“The old law cuts off the branches of vices...”*

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological examination of the Law of Retaliation (lex talionis), specifically how Jesus Christ refined these Old Testament laws in the Gospel and how the principle of "measure for measure" appears across different cultures and legal systems.</meta>

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS

The Gospel places the ax at the roots <note>A reference to Matthew 3:10, suggesting the Gospel addresses the inner cause of sin, not just the outward act.</note>. This is illustrated by examples brought from the same chapter. The Law (says Christ) prohibited homicide, but he also prohibits anger, which is the seed of homicide; the Law prohibited perjury, but Christ prohibits the simple oath taken without necessity. The Law forbade adultery, but Christ forbade the lustful look.

iii. The Law was given among equals, for if it were maintained among unequals, it would be unjust. For the sin of a son against parents is more serious than vice versa. Whence Exodus 21:17 says: *“He who curses his father... let him die the death.”* Here the rule of Retaliation <note>original: *Talionis*</note> is not kept, since a death penalty is paid for a curse, rather than a curse for a curse.

iv. Nor is the Law of Retaliation always just among equals if the retribution is commanded by private individuals rather than by a Judge; because (as the philosopher <note>Aristotle, in his *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book 5.</note> teaches) the injured party always estimates his own injury as being more than it truly is, and he who received a wound would return death for that wound if he were able. God, however, tempered this affection naturally implanted in man, and willed that the injured be content with a similar penalty.

v. The penalty of Retaliation was not so rigid that it was not sometimes dispensable, or at least commutable. For Josephus <note>A first-century Jewish historian.</note> testifies that it was permitted for a defendant to redeem that penalty with money, if the injured party had consented.

And let these things be said concerning Retaliation, which law was also in use among the Gentiles <note>original: *Ethnicis*; referring here to non-Jewish/non-Christian nations, specifically Greeks and Romans.</note>, as is clear from Pliny (Book 7) saying that the dictator Sulla feared Retaliation. And Aulus Gellius formed the verb "to retaliate" <note>original: *retaliare*</note> from "Retaliation," corresponding to the Greek word *reciprocal* <note>original: *ἀμοιβεὸς* (amoibeos)</note>, which is the same as striking back with Retaliation. Among the Hebrews, the word responding to Retaliation is **retribution** <note>original: *שׁלם* (shillum)</note>. And the verb in the <term>Pihel form<note>The intensive form of a Hebrew verb.</note></term> means to repay or to retribute. Hence Psalm 91:8: *“...and the retribution of the wicked.”* To these things respond those words of the Rabbis in the proverbs: **measure for measure** <note>original: *מדה כנגד מדה* (middah keneged middah)</note>. For this, the Latins say, "to return like for like" <note>original: *par pari referre*</note>. To this, the Savior undoubtedly alludes in Matthew 7:2: *“with what measure you mete, it shall be measured to you again”* <note>The author provides the Greek here: *ἐν ᾧ μέτρῳ μετρεῖτε ἀντιμετρηθήσεται ὑμῖν*.</note>. For this particle "the same" <note>original: *αὐτὴ* (aute)</note> is relative here; for it does not only signify to measure again, but declares something further: namely, that the measure responds to the measure from the opposite side, as in the Law of Retaliation. See also the learned and witty things which are brought forward by Aulus Gellius in *Attic Nights* (Book 20, Chapter 1) in the dispute of Sextus Caecilius the Jurist and Favorinus concerning the laws of the Twelve Tables <note>The Twelve Tables were the earliest code of Roman law.</note>. For he says those words of the Law...

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological examination of the Law of Retaliation (Lex Talionis), moving from the general theory of justice to specific arguments against its literal application and then transitioning to the duties subjects owe to their rulers.</meta>

# ANTHONY CREGUT
<meta>catchword: bert</meta>

Concerning the Law of Retaliation <note>original: *Talionis*</note>, the rule stating, *“If he has broken my limb, let there be retaliation according to the agreement,”* <note>original: *Si membrum rupit meum, è pacto Talio esto.* This is a fragment from the Roman Law of the Twelve Tables (Table VIII), which established the principle of "an eye for an eye."</note> cannot be sustained. For (he says) beyond the cruelty of seeking revenge, a just execution of Retaliation cannot even proceed. For when a limb has been broken by another, if one wishes to break a limb in return through Retaliation, I ask: can he achieve an exact balance in the breaking of that limb? In this matter, there is first an inexplicable difficulty. Furthermore, he asks, what if someone breaks a limb by accident? <note>original: *imprudens*</note>. For that which was done through imprudence ought to be retaliated through imprudence. Indeed, a blow that is accidental and one that is intentional do not fall under the same likeness of retaliation. He asks, therefore, whether they could match the retaliation perfectly to the scale and weigh it in a balance? They then respond that reciprocal retaliations were more clever in theory than they were true in practice. See more on this, if you wish, in the writings of Gellius. <note>Aulus Gellius, a 2nd-century Roman author who discussed the impracticality of the Twelve Tables in his work *Attic Nights*.</note>

Now follows the third branch: **concerning the duty of subjects toward the Magistrate.** The first duty is to honor them; this is contained in the first commandment of the second table <note>Referring to the Fifth Commandment: "Honor thy father and mother," which was traditionally interpreted by theologians to include all those in authority, such as kings and magistrates.</note> and in 1 Peter 2:17, where the Apostle commands the king to be honored. Just as the Jewish state <note>original: *politia*</note> was the most orderly of all, and established directly by divine institution (as we have shown above), so they honored their kings above all other nations. For so great was the veneration toward them that anyone who dared to sit upon the royal throne, or carry their scepter in their hand, or ride upon the king’s horse, would be punished as if they had committed sacrilege. Both the High Priest and the prophets were required to stand in the presence of the kings; nor were the kings themselves permitted to renounce this right, otherwise they would have been guilty of treason <note>original: *læfæ maiestatis*</note>. For that right is public law, or the law of the kingdom, which not even the king can alienate or deny, for it is a sacred and divine right.

Furthermore, as Salmasius <note>Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), a French classical scholar famous for his defense of King Charles I of England.</note> observed in his *Apology for the King of England*, they were moved by such great veneration toward kings that if the king had put one of the Rabbis to death, the people did not dare to lament or wail, nor to repeat these words during the funeral rites as was customary: "Where is that pious man now? Where is the wise man? Where is the disciple of Ezra? The disciple of Hillel?" <note>Hillel the Elder was one of the most important figures in Jewish history and the founder of a major school of legal interpretation.</note> This is evident from the funeral of Judah Ben Baba, as recorded in the Talmud in the Gemara. <note>The Gemara is the component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis and commentary on the Mishnah. Judah Ben Baba was a 2nd-century rabbi and martyr.</note>

Nevertheless, even if that honor which is due to the supreme Magistrate—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the duties subjects owe to their rulers, specifically concluding the first duty (Honor) and introducing the second (Subjection) and third (Fidelity). It bridges the gap between political respect and religious devotion.</meta>

->REVEALER OF SECRETS<-

AAAaaa

[The honor] owed should be the highest form, such as kneeling and the bowing of the whole body, which among the Hebrews is represented by the word *hishtachawah* <note>original Hebrew: השתחוה; this term refers to the act of prostrating oneself in reverence or worship</note>, just as it was in the case of Abraham when he bowed before the Hittites <note>A reference to Genesis 23:7, where Abraham bows to the local people to show respect during a business transaction</note>; nevertheless, that honor is strictly political in nature, not religious. For such worship is owed to God alone, according to the scripture: 
> *“You shall worship your God and Him only shall you serve.”* <note>original: *Deum tuum adorabis & illi soli feruies.* A citation of Matthew 4:10 or Deuteronomy 6:13.</note> 
And for this reason, the Roman Emperors, in whom the Majesty of the Empire resided, were not religiously worshipped by their subjects; nor did their **Apotheosis** <note>The process of being officially recognized as a god</note> occur until after their deaths. If any, however, presumed to have the honor and veneration of gods exhibited to themselves while alive, they were few, and they were believed to be monsters among men—such as Caligula, Domitian, and Julian the Apostate, who, in order to pollute Christians with idolatry, would light incense in his own presence. From this comes the **mystery of iniquity**, when the **man of sin** offers himself to be worshipped and exalts himself above all that is called God.

II. The second duty is **subjection**. For this duty is evident from the royal dignity and from the power of the Magistrate. Since their right is absolute and independent, without a doubt all others shall be subjected and subordinated to them. However, that subjection is not coerced, such as that of slaves, but voluntary; and this is so not only by civil law, but also by divine law; therefore, it is in every way voluntary. This is why Paul says in Romans 13 that one must obey the superior powers 
> *“for the sake of conscience.”* 
For this reason, the Magistrate is granted not only <term>dynamis</term> <note>original Greek: δύναμις; meaning raw power or physical force</note> **power**, but also <term>exousia</term> <note>original Greek: ἐξουσία; meaning legal authority or the rightful power to act</note> **authority** or right. Through the former, a ruler can procure even a coerced subjection, such as that of tyrants, who subdue and subject those weaker than themselves by might and force; but through the latter, a voluntary subjection is owed to them, because it is based not so much on mere fact as it is on legal right.

III. The third duty is **fidelity**. This also stems from both divine and human law. From human law, whether the Magistrate’s position is hereditary or elective. From divine law, because the sacred name of God was invoked in the oath of fidelity. Hence, the title of "Lord" is owed to any Magistrate, by which subjection is acknowledged; and to lords, as is commonly said, "recognitions" are made, insofar as subjection is pledged, or what they call **homage**. And from there...

...the fief [feudum] took its origin. For beneficiaries hold a fief from the prince, whom political writers commonly call *Vassals*. A **fief** is a benefit conferred by a prince upon a subject, by which the subject possesses certain lands free from taxes, yet in such a way that he is bound to fidelity and to the performance of duties in a time of war for the prince. For this reason, they derive the word *Feudum* from *fides* <note>original: "fide"; the Latin word for faith or loyalty</note>. However, others prefer a Lombardic origin for the name, which is confirmed by the fact that those benefits were greatly expanded during their time.

Moreover, this duty toward the Magistrate is further illustrated according to the opinion of Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and influential political philosopher known for his theory of sovereignty</note>, who asserts in Book 1 of *The Commonwealth* that the word **FEDVM** was named from five initial letters; so that whoever gave his word of honor would use these words: *I will be faithful to my true lord.* <note>original: "Fidelis ero domino vero meo." Bodin suggests the word "Feudum" is an acronym for this oath of loyalty.</note> Vassals or holders of fiefs promise this concerning a twofold fief, whether it be **simple** or **liege** <note>A "simple" fief was a standard land grant, while a "liege" fief was the primary one that took precedence over all other loyalties if a vassal served multiple lords</note>; but let these points suffice, for other matters pertain to the political writers.

IV. **The duty is to pray for Magistrates.** Paul teaches this explicitly in 1 Timothy 2, when he commands us to pray for kings, even those who are unfaithful <note>In this context, "infidelibus" refers to non-Christian or pagan rulers</note>, because God wants all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. There is a famous passage from Tertullian <note>A prolific early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD)</note> in his *Apology against the Gentiles*, chapter 30, saying that Emperors are from God, and that Christians should humbly seek their safety from the true God, who alone can grant it. For he says explicitly:

> *Looking up there, we Christians, with hands spread out because they are innocent, with bare heads because we are not ashamed, and finally without a prompter because we pray from the heart, are all always praying for all Emperors: for a long life for them, a secure Empire, a safe home, strong armies, a faithful Senate, an honest people, a quiet world, and whatever are the prayers of a man and a Caesar. These things I cannot ask from any other than from Him from whom I know I shall obtain them, etc.*

These are the monumental <note>original: "uncialia"; while literally referring to a style of large lettering, here it means grand, authoritative, or significant words</note> words of that ancient doctor, which sufficiently demonstrate the love and fidelity of the early Christians toward Emperors, even those who were non-believers.

V. **The duty of the people toward the supreme Magistrate is to recognize not only that his right is supreme and absolute, but also perpetual and indispensable.** Therefore, under no pretext can a people subject to a king be released from his power. For who then—

Who would not shudder at the things decreed in the Council of Vienne <note>The Council of Vienne (1311–1312) was a church council that, among other things, dealt with the suppression of the Knights Templar and the relationship between church and state</note>, and those found in the *Clementine* decree *Pastoralis* concerning legal judgments? These are cited by the great jurist Charles Dumoulin <note>Charles Dumoulin (1500–1566) was a famous French legal expert known for his work on customary law and his defense of royal power against the papacy</note> in his consultation on the Council of Trent: namely, that the vassals of the Emperor could not commit the crime of <term>perduellio</term> <note>A high crime of treason or acting as an enemy of the state</note> against the Emperor if they were defending the interests of the Pope. All the doctors of Canon Law hold this view, as does Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), one of the most influential legal scholars of the Middle Ages</note> himself, a professor of law, in his commentary on the decree *Those Who Are Rebels* <note>original: "Extrauagante qui ſunt rebelles"</note>. But as Charles Dumoulin observed in the aforementioned consultation, he excuses himself in his preface. And he does so quite humorously and jokingly when he confesses that he writes this only because he is a subject of the Pope, living within his jurisdictions and dominion.

The same is taught in the Council of Trent; for which reason, says Dumoulin, it ought not to be accepted in France. For the round shape of the King’s crown symbolizes its indivisibility; any break or division of it, however small, would destroy the whole. Truly, then, and not ignorantly, did someone write concerning the Pope’s attitude toward kings what was said of the gods of the Pagans toward men: *Those gods hold kings like play-balls.* <note>This metaphor suggests that popes treat kings as mere toys or objects to be tossed around for sport.</note> From this, Atahualpa <note>original: "Atabalippa"; the last sovereign emperor of the Inca Empire (c. 1502–1533)</note>, the King of Peru, stood astonished at the Pope’s "generosity" in magnificently bestowing upon others kingdoms that did not belong to him. Thus, he frequently asked what kind of man that was, who was so liberal with another's domain.

But hey, you shuffler, hear a most powerful argument, and do not be stubborn any longer. Behold the latest interpretation of Johannes de Terrano <note>Likely referring to Jean de Terrevermeille (c. 1370–1430), a French jurist who wrote on the rights of the French crown</note>, who, regarding those words of Christ, *render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's,* <note>Matthew 22:21</note> confidently asserted that those words were valid only until the ascension of Christ. For in John 12, Christ himself said: *And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself.* <note>John 12:32; the author is critiquing a radical interpretation that uses this verse to claim all earthly power transferred to the Church after the Ascension.</note>

...used it profitably.
