VII. The duty of subjects is to obey the Magistrate in political matters. For regarding divine matters, God alone is to be heard. In those cases, that saying of the Apostle must be carried perpetually in the mouth and the heart: *We must obey God rather than men.* <note>Acts 5:29</note> Because the right of God is absolutely supreme (as we said above), while the right of kings is relative to men. Hence, render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s. This is in accordance with that most true four-line poem:

> *Every power has a beginning and an end:*
> *God alone lacks both beginning and end.*
> *The power of Caesar is indefinite, not infinite;* <note>original: "Indefinita est non infinita potestas Cæsaris"</note>
> *No one on earth can do everything.*

Indeed, this sacred tribute lasted even after the Babylonian captivity because God had not deserted His people. But truly, after the entire Jewish nation was cut off and dispersed, with the city and temple leveled to the ground, just as God no longer wished to reign over them, so the sacred shekel was diverted and transferred to the Roman Capitol. But while God demanded a shekel from His people, He did not demand it from kings—as is done today by the Roman Pontiff, who had imposed <term>Peter’s Pence</term> <note>original: "S. Petri denarium." A tax of a penny per household paid to the See of Rome</note> upon the English, and from them demanded <term>palfreys</term> <note>original: "parafredos." Even the King of Portugal was confirmed by Pope Alexander III <note>Alexander III (reigned 1159–1181) was a Pope who famously asserted the authority of the Church over secular monarchs.</note> on the condition—as is commonly claimed in Rome—that two pounds of gold should be paid annually to the Roman Church by the kings of Portugal as a tribute. Just as when the Eagle, the king of birds, builds its nest, the other birds are bound to bring some feathers for the nesting; so too, when the building of a royal house is at hand, who would be of so ungrateful a spirit as to refuse to carry a stone? Nevertheless, the exaction of tributes and taxes ought to be moderate, and a good prince must perpetually keep in mind that saying of the Roman Emperor Tiberius: *A good shepherd ought to shear his flock, not skin them.* <note>original: "Boni pastoris esse tondere pecus non deglubere"</note> Let them not do what is forbidden in Psalm 52: *They devour my people as they eat bread.* <note>Psalm 53:4 in modern numbering; the text cites the Vulgate Psalm 52.</note> When cows are milked gently, milk and butter are brought forth, but when they are squeezed too hard, blood flows out. Nor is that saying of Antigonus valid: *Alexander harvested Asia, but I am merely gleaning.* <note>original Greek: "Αλεξανδρος την Ασιαν εθεριξε, εγω δ' καλαμωμαι"</note> Nor that saying of Louis XI, King of the French, that France was a meadow that could be mown with a scythe as often as he pleased. For in the end, even the dull—much like Balaam’s donkey <note>A biblical reference to Numbers 22, where an oppressed animal miraculously speaks to protest its master's cruelty.</note>—when spurred by the goad, emit voices and complaints. They reply with that same harsh spirit of liberty found in the response given to Mark Antony the Triumvir by the orator Hybreas, when Antony commanded that the taxes across Asia be doubled. Hybreas replied that Antony should then surely command two summers and two autumns—that is, two harvests and two vintages—within the same year. Well known, too, is the story of Vespasian, who imposed a tax on urine, from which came the proverb: *the smell of profit is good, no matter the source.* <note>original: "bonus est odor lucri ex re qualibet." This is the origin of the phrase "money has no smell."</note> And there was Livius the Censor, nicknamed *The Salt-man* <note>original: "Salinator"</note>, because he took a tribute from salt. It is for this reason that the treasury <term>fiscus: the state or imperial treasury</term> is skillfully compared to the spleen. For just as the human body becomes emaciated when the spleen grows and swells, but conversely, the body grows fat when the spleen shrinks and subsides; so it goes with the state treasury and the wealth of the people. Wherefore the defenders of the treasury are accustomed to say that no fat is worse than the fatness of the people. But why say more?

It is clearly established that those frequent "blood-lettings" <note>original: "phlebotomias"; here used metaphorically for the draining of wealth through taxes.</note> kill the political body no less than the physical body.

But indeed, no matter how much a Magistrate increases taxes and violently commands their collection, there is no reason from that for rising up against him. For powers are never to be softened with arms, but with prayers and supplications, so that they might have mercy on their people. Truly, to this point belongs the illustrious testimony of the most noble historian Jacques Auguste de Thou <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617) was a French historian and statesman known for his monumental history of his own times.</note> in his *History*, book 27, Volume 2, page 11, regarding the notable loyalty of the People of the Valleys <note>original: "Conuallensium"; this refers to the Waldenses or Vaudois, a proto-Protestant group in the Alpine valleys often cited by later Protestant writers for their piety and resilience.</note> in the payment of taxes. "The People of the Valleys," he says, "pay their tribute religiously, and this is a principal point in the confession of their faith, second only to the worship of God. Even if they are prevented by civil wars, they nevertheless set aside the collected amount, and when peace permits, they take care to pay it most diligently to the royal collectors." This is truly an example of singular loyalty.

I omit here the custom of the Turks in exacting taxes. For a Christian Magistrate does not care for the barbarity of that infidel or his yoke upon subjects, which is hard and difficult to bear <note>original: δυσβάςακτον (dysbastakton)</note>. For in truth, all possessions belong to the Sultan, and the subjects are the slaves of those Emperors. Hence the subjects are called *Timariots* <note>term: Timariots (Timariotæ); holders of a "Timar," a land grant in the Ottoman Empire held in exchange for military service.</note>, because since they do not even possess a clod of earth, the Sultan hands over the fields to them to cultivate, provided they pay the tithes, which are claimed as *Timar*, that is, *dominion* or *lordship*. I say nothing of the subsidies and taxes imposed upon Jews and Christians, which are poll taxes on males from the age of fourteen; for these are examples of a monstrous tyrant.

We come finally to the last part of the discussion <note>original: συζητήσεως (syzeteseos)</note>, which concerns the reward of the magistrate and the subjects. Moses points this out in verse 20 of this chapter, when he adds: *Follow justice, most just: that you may live and possess by hereditary right the land which Jehovah your God gives you.* <note>Deuteronomy 16:20</note> That reward refers to the promise of the law. For in the first commandment of the second table <note>The "second table" refers to the portion of the Ten Commandments dealing with human relationships; the "first commandment" here is "Honor thy father and mother."</note>, God promises longevity to those honoring parents, under whom Magistrates are included as "fathers." And if, according to the testimony of Philo the Jew <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who interpreted the Torah through Greek philosophy.</note>, that first commandment was written partly on the first and partly on the second table, how much more holy and worthy of observation would that command be...

...greater <note>The Latin text begins with a fragment, likely "magnius," meaning "the more greatly."</note>, thus for those who observe [the law] the reward will be greater, and conversely, a more severe punishment must be inflicted on transgressors. Moreover, Moses speaks of the land of promise because for the Jews it was a symbol and <term>type</term> <note>In theology, a "type" is a person, event, or thing in the Old Testament believed to foreshadow something in the New Testament.</note> of all divine promises and of goods both temporal and eternal. Therefore, the possession of that land is taken as a <term>synecdoche</term> <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole.</note>, the species for the genus; for it is placed in Scripture as a sign of benefit and blessing, since nothing was more pleasing to the Israelites than the possession of the land—and especially that land which is called such <term>by way of excellence</term> <note>original Latin: "antonomastice"</note> in Scripture, and which the Lord gave to the Israelites to inhabit.

For elsewhere, in a general sense, the Rabbis divide the earth into three parts: the **sea** <note>original Hebrew: "ים"</note>, because it forms one globe with the land; the **inhabited land** <note>original Hebrew: "ישוב"</note>, that is, the land which humans inhabit; and the **desert** <note>original Hebrew: "מדבר"</note>, which is uninhabited land, or less inhabited, called *erēmos* <note>original Greek: "ερημῳ"</note> by the Greeks, from the word for "naked" <note>original Hebrew: "ערום"</note>. 

Specifically, therefore, and <term>preeminently</term> <note>original Greek: "κατ' ἐξοχήν"</note>, "the land" is understood to be Canaan, which was a type of the "land of the living." For as Origen wrote in his 26th homily on the Book of Numbers: *"There is a certain land in the kingdom of God which is promised to the gentle, which is called the land of the living and the land in the heights."* Augustine and Jerome feel the same. Thus in Psalm 37:9: *"Those who wait for the Lord shall possess the land"* <note>original Hebrew: "יירשו ארץ"</note>. Just as in this place it is promised to those who pursue justice. And in verse 11 of the aforementioned Psalm, it is promised to the *"humble"*; and in verses 22 and 29, to the *"blessed of the Lord and the righteous."* And in Matthew 5:5: *"The gentle: the mild shall possess the land by right of inheritance."*

Therefore, all the words of Moses in this passage are emphatic. 

I. In a general sense, it must be observed that the temporal promises made to the Israelites were types of the promises of eternal good or happiness. 

II. This is confirmed by the specific parts of this judicial reward: first, from the phrase ***that you may live***. For life contains all good things in an eminent way, and without life there can be no happiness. Indeed, if God himself did not live, he would be stripped of all goods, for he would not be intelligent, willing, just, good, holy, etc. Indeed, he would not even be God; because his essence is to live <note>original Hebrew: "חיה חיה"</note>. Nor is there even a point of difference <note>Meaning there is no distinction between God's existence and His living.</note>. But the life and **longevity** <note>original Greek: "μακροβιότης"</note> which God promises here and in the fifth commandment of the law is a type of heavenly and eternal life. 

Secondly, Moses adds ***you shall possess the land***, because the land of Canaan was a type of the heavenly Canaan, the possession of which foreshadowed...

...the enjoyment of blessedness. For just as the people of God used various means toward this end—the possession of that land—so do the faithful use various means as long as they are **travelers** <note>original Latin: "viatores," referring to the theological concept of humans as pilgrims on a journey toward heaven.</note> toward the possession of the **celestial Canaan**, and at last they enjoy those goods in the heavenly Canaan. For **use** pertains to the means, but **enjoyment** <note>original Latin: "fruitio"</note> pertains to the end; it is named from "fruits," because that is when the fruits of all labors are gathered.

Thirdly, Moses adds **by hereditary right**, both because the land of Canaan was not won by labor, but Jehovah gave it to Israel (as is added at the end of the verse) like a father who gives an inheritance to his children; and also because no one is able to dispute the possession of that land, since it was acquired by the highest right, namely, by **inheritance**. Hence, for the Hebrews, <term>possession</term> <note>original Hebrew: נחלה (*nachalah*)</note> is a term which is also explained in Scripture as <term>inheritance</term> <note>original Greek: κληρονομία (*kleronomia*)</note>, as we have taught extensively elsewhere. All these things align perfectly with the **celestial inheritance**, for we are *children of God*, and therefore *heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ* <note>See Romans 8:17.</note>. And in Matthew 25: *Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the inheritance, etc.* And in Peter, it is called an *inheritance reserved in heaven which does not fade away.* So it is found elsewhere throughout. Since all these things are promised specifically to the **Magistrate** <note>The civil governor or judge.</note> if he exercises justice, truly this reward elevates the dignity of Magistrates and ought to powerfully drive them to judge justly.

Since these things are so, shall we not perceive more correctly regarding supernatural things than the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras.</note> did regarding natural things? For, considering things physically, the Pythagoreans were the first to celebrate the <term>union</term> <note>original Greek: συζυγία (*syzygia*), meaning a pairing or "syzygy."</note> and marriage of heaven and earth, attributing the power of acting to the heaven and the power of suffering <note>In the sense of being acted upon or receiving influence.</note> to the earth. Therefore, the heaven was the husband, and the earth was the wife. This is indeed true regarding the generation of physical bodies, according to that saying of **Aristotle**: *The Sun and man generate man.* But considering things **supernaturally** <note>original Latin: "hyperphysicè"</note>, there is a noble <term>union</term> or bond between the **type** and the **antitype** <note>The "type" is the symbol (earthly Canaan), and the "antitype" is the fulfillment (heavenly Canaan).</note>. For the land of Canaan was an illustrious symbol of the celestial Canaan, and the <term>union</term> or marriage that was begun in the earthly Canaan was to be consummated in the celestial Canaan.

What we have said concerning the reward that is repaid to judges who practice the most just justice, the Sacred Page conversely establishes regarding those who are **unjust judges**, and against all...

### ANTHONY CREGUTUS

...author; for so that there might always be a place for wonder, he willed that most things should be hidden, and he revealed **wisdom in a mystery** <note>original Greek: σοφίαν ἐν μυστηρίῳ (*sophian en mysterio*)</note> so that man’s ignorance might be driven out through revelation, and yet, insofar as it remained a **wisdom in a mystery** and a sort of hidden wisdom, it might inspire wonder for the revealed mystery and set limits and barriers to our curiosity. This was especially pleasing to do regarding those mysteries where ignorance posed not even the slightest danger to human salvation—indeed, mysteries where knowledge might perhaps have stirred up an itch for vain superstition and given it free rein.

We assert this regarding the **Urim and Thummim**, the most ancient of all oracles. God not only willed that this oracle should cease, but it has vanished so completely that not even its method, form, or **sketch** <note>original Greek: ὑποτύπωσις (*hypotyposis*) — a structural outline or model</note> remains. Therefore, under divine guidance, this **inquiry** <note>original Greek: συζήτησις (*syzetesis*) — a joint search or philosophical discussion</note> must investigate what can be known and what must remain unknown about this excellent oracle. Come then, let us briefly investigate three things: *I. What the Urim and Thummim are, regarding their **etymology** <note>original Greek: ὀνοματολογίαν (*onomatologian*) — the study of names</note>. II. What they are regarding their **actual nature** <note>original Greek: πραγματολογίαν (*pragmatologian*) — the study of the things themselves</note>. III. Concerning their significance or mystical sense.*

I. Regarding the **etymology**; this naming is Hebrew. For *Urim* is a plural word meaning **fires**; this is because the gems of the Holy Priest's breastplate sparkled like fires and flashed like lightning. This is why the home city of Abraham was called **Ur**, the city of the Chaldeans, which means **fire**; and from this comes *Urim*, because the inhabitants were fire-worshippers, just as the **Guebres** <note>original: *Gaber* — a term for Zoroastrians or Persian fire-worshippers</note> are today in Persia, or the **Chaver** according to the Talmud. Hence, we read among the Talmudists that <note>Hebrew: אורים (*Urim*)</note> **Urim** are so called <note>Hebrew: שמאירין את דבריהן (*she-me’irin et divrehen*)</note> **because they illuminate their words.**

This was because the names of the twelve Patriarchs were engraved on stones in four rows: carbuncle, topaz, emerald, etc., as found in Exodus 28:17 and verse 21: *And these stones shall be with the names of the twelve sons of Israel, according to their names; like the engravings of a signet, every one with his name shall they be according to the twelve tribes.* In the Chaldean language <note>Aramaic</note>, *Ur* and *Urim* also signify **light** or **luminary**.

Furthermore, that oracle was called <note>Hebrew: תומים (*Thummim*)</note> **Thummim**, which means **perfections**. And this is according to the decrees of the Talmudists <note>Hebrew: שמתמימים את דבריהן (*she-matmimin et divrehen*)</note> [**because they perfect their words**]...

...because they complete their words. <note>The author is quoting the Babylonian Talmud, Tractate Yoma, chapter 7, which discusses the High Priest's garments.</note> These things aptly agree with the interpretation of Philo the Jew, which is **clarity and truth** <note>original Greek: σαφώνεια & ἀλήθεια (*saphōneia & alētheia*)</note>, that is, *perspicuity and truth*. For "Light" metaphorically refers to clarity, while "Truth" refers to integrity, which is denoted by **Thummim** <note>original Hebrew: תומים (*Thummim*)</note>. For that Hebrew word signifies *perfections or integrities*. They are expressed in the plural, according to the Hebrew custom, to signify an all-encompassing perfection or integrity, and also a most radiant light or clarity. Or perhaps it is because there were twelve jeweled stones, and thus so many fires and lightnings flashing together, which were kindled so that God’s will might be read clearly on the High Priest’s breastplate; in this way, it was a kind of extraordinary word of God. For just as in God’s word revealed to us those two are found, Urim and Thummim—*Urim*, because it is a "lamp to the feet" as Peter testifies; and *Thummim*, because Psalm 19:8 says: **The Law is perfect** <note>original Hebrew: תורת תמימה (*Torat Temimah*)</note>. So in this extraordinary word of God, those two were required: *Urim*, so that God’s will might become known, and *Thummim*, so that the same will might be made manifest to the Church not **in part**, but **wholly** <note>original Greek: κατὰ μέρος... καθ' ὅλον (*kata meros... kath’ holon*)</note> and perfectly.

And so much **concerning the study of names** <note>original Greek: περὶ τῆς ὀνοματολογίας (*peri tēs onomatologias*)</note>; let us pass to the **study of the things themselves** <note>original Greek: πραγματολογίαν (*pragmatologian*)</note> and fish out, as far as possible, what that famous oracle actually was. But the masters of the Hebrews deter us from the very threshold. For they themselves who, because of their manifold knowledge and wisdom, are called **Rabbis** <note>original Hebrew: *Rabbim*, meaning "many" or "great ones," as if they contained the wisdom of many within themselves</note> in the plural—as if they themselves were Urim and Thummim—these same men nevertheless freely confess that they do not know what the Urim and Thummim were. For Ibn Ezra wrote on Exodus 28:5 that he did not know what they were or of what sort. And here indeed the Hebrew doctors seem more sober than at other times, when they scrutinize hidden mysteries too curiously; hence Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a famous Renaissance scholar.</note> truly wrote of them that among all of them, Maimonides <note>The influential 12th-century Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note> was the first to begin to be sober, because before him the Rabbis spoke more immoderately. This was likewise blamed by Joseph's father, Julius Caesar Scaliger, in his adversary Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a polymath who often theorized about the occult and natural causes.</note>, who searched too curiously into the hidden causes of things. Hence Scaliger did not blush to say "I do not know" regarding most things; whether because these...

...the secrets of nature could hardly be known: whether because he presumed no one else could know what that *perpetual dictator of the Muses* <note>original Latin: *Musarum dictator ille perpetuus*. First, Scripture in Exodus 28:30 <note>The text reads "Exod. xx, 30," likely a printing error for chapter 28, where the breastplate is described.</note> teaches that the **Urim** and **Thummim** <term>Urim and Thummim: Oracular devices placed in the High Priest's breastplate used to discern the divine will.</term> were placed into the sacred breastplate of the High Priest. However, in that instance, God did not respond to Saul because He had rejected him: *And Saul consulted Jehovah, but Jehovah did not answer him, neither by dreams, nor by Urims, nor by Prophets.* In this passage, although no mention is made of the **Thummim** but only the **Urim**, it is nonetheless understood to be included. This is a **Synecdoche** <term>Synecdoche: A figure of speech where a part is used to represent the whole (e.g., using "Urim" to mean the entire oracle).</term>, where the whole is signified by the part; for He cannot respond through the **Urim** (as is said in the two places already praised above) unless He also responds through the **Thummim**. 

Sometimes the word **Thummim** precedes the **Urim**, as in Deuteronomy 33:8, a passage which is now explained: *of Levi he said, "Thy Thummim and thy Urim,"* etc. In this case, Scripture understands the **Thummim** to represent the entire Levitical and Priestly Ministry committed to Aaron and his descendants, and this is done **metonymically** <term>Metonymically: Using one word to stand in for another related concept; here, the oracle represents the entire priesthood.</term>. 

Furthermore, it can be proven from Scripture that the **Urim** and **Thummim** remained after the Jews had returned from the Babylonian captivity. For in Nehemiah 7:65 it is written: *For the king’s legate ordered them that they should not eat of the holy things until a Priest should arise with Urim and Thummim.* This is confirmed by Josephus, the Jewish Priest, in the *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 3, Chapter 9, who said that the **Urim** and **Thummim** ceased two hundred years before his own time, God thus avenging the transgression of the Law. Then the oracle was returned to the Priest in this way: by the power of the Holy Spirit, certain letters on the breastplate would stand out, either by their position or by their brightness, in which the Priest would read the oracle and the will of God. And these are the Urim and Thummim. For just as the law of God was written by the finger of God on stone tablets because it was truly divine, so these two shining stones, the **Urim** and **Thummim**, were fashioned by God and not by craftsmen, because through them *divine manifestations* <note>original Greek: Θεοφάνεια (*Theophaneia*)</note>, *divine words* <note>original Greek: λόγια (*logia*)</note>, and *divine signs* <note>original Greek: Θεοσημεῖα (*Theosemeia*)</note> became known. For although God could have issued His oracles without letters through the voice of the Holy Priest, whose mind He had inspired with prophecy, nevertheless those signs of the **Urim** and **Thummim** can truly be called *divine signs* <note>original Greek: Θεοσημεῖα (*Theosemeia*)</note>, and it should not be thought that they were handed to Moses by God in vain.

Other Rabbis add further that the **Urim** oracle was not within the power of the High Priest; for sometimes God gave no answer, and sometimes He did. Thus He refused to answer Saul through the prophets and through the **Urim**, because He had rejected him, and therefore Saul consulted a medium <note>original Latin: *Pythonissam*, referring to the Witch of Endor.</note>, as is held in 1 Samuel 28. When, however, God testified to His will through the **Urim**, then the stones of the breastplate would flash, and at the same time the inscribed letters, joined together, would convey a perfect meaning. From this, the reason for the naming of the **Thummim** can also be taken; both because the letters of the Alphabet were made complete by adding the names of the 12 patriarchs and furthermore three others—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—which thus totaled twenty-two, and also because the meaning of those things being inquired after was "perfect" or complete; so that each person might have the answer to their requests. <meta>This page continues the technical description of how the High Priest used the Urim and Thummim to receive divine answers, specifically detailing the mechanics of the "shining letters" on the breastplate.</meta>

-># REVEALER OF SECRETS<-

[The High Priest] judged only in grave and weighty matters, such as peace, war, the state of the whole kingdom, prophets, and so on. Thus, when matters were not only serious but also ambiguous and uncertain—such that the [regular] judges were unable to decide—the High Priest would then put on the breastplate and consult God through the Urim. The person inquiring of God’s will would look at the High Priest with his face directed toward him, while at that time the High Priest would gaze at the Urim and Thummim with intent eyes. The voice of the inquirer was low (as we have said), yet he pronounced his words moderately and slowly, so that the Priest could hear and combine and join together the letters of the Urim by which the oracle was elicited. It was not permitted to ask two questions at once except in cases of necessity. If two things were asked, the Priest would respond only to the first <term>inquirer <note>original Greek: ἐρομένῳ (*eromenō*)</note></term>, or to both if it were necessary.

The Masters of the Hebrews provide an example of this. When King David questioned God through the Urim whether he should go up into any of the cities of Judah, God answered through the Urim and through the mouth of the High Priest that he should go up—or, as it is held in the Hebrew truth, <term>go up <note>original Hebrew: עלה (*'alah*)</note></term>. How, then, did this become known to the Priest on the Urim or the breastplate? Surely, if the Hebrew tradition is true, it was very easy. For the letter **Ayin** <note>ע</note> in the name **Simeon** <note>שמעון</note> shone brightly. Likewise the letter **Lamed** <note>ל</note>, which is the first letter in the name **Levi** <note>לוי</note>. And finally, the letter **He** <note>ה</note>, which is the last letter in the name **Judah** <note>יהודה</note>. All these letters, when combined, form the word *Alah*—"Go up."

And if one trusts Josephus in Book 3, Chapter 13 of his *Antiquities of the Jews*, even the Greeks (though they were averse to Judaism) so magnified the oracle of the breastplate that they believed it to be among the most illustrious of oracles and distinguished it with the name <term>oracle <note>original Greek: λογίῳ (*logiō*)</note></term>, by which God deigned to clearly declare His will to men, no less than if it had been pronounced by His own mouth. These things are recounted in the Talmud in the tractate *Yoma*, and in the writings of the Rabbis, such as Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval commentator.</note> on Haggai 1, and Kimchi on Psalm 84, as well as others, both Jewish and Christian.

But there is, moreover, a wonderful thing which Suidas <note>The *Suda* is a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the Mediterranean world.</note> reports from a certain unknown author. "The Ephod," he says, "is a Hebrew name which signifies manifestation or redemption." And in the same place, he recounts many things about its form which I omit. But concerning...

### BY ANTHONY CREGUT

...to the response, he adds this: He sought an answer from God with eyes fixed on the **Ephod** <note>The ceremonial vestment worn by the High Priest.</note>. If God agreed to what was being asked, the **Diamond** stone <note>original Latin: lapis Adamas</note> would immediately flash. If He refused, nothing was added to its original brilliance. But if God willed that the people be slain, the stone turned black; if they were to be cast to the sword, it became blood-red. These things, however, which are reported by **Suidas** <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist.</note>, are not found among the Rabbis nor in the Scripture.

It should be observed, moreover, that the **Chaldean Paraphrast** <note>A translator of the Targums, the Aramaic paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible.</note> was more sober than the others; he did not dare to express **Urim and Thummim** in his own dialect, just as the **Septuagint** interpreters <note>The seventy scholars who translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek.</note> (as was said above) expressed them through **Truth** <note>original Greek: ἀλήθειαν (*alētheian*)</note>, and as **Philo the Jew** used **Clarity and Truth** <note>original Greek: σάφειαν καὶ ἀλήθειαν (*sapheian kai alētheian*)</note>, unless perhaps 그 paraphrast did so out of superstition. For the Hebrews were often accustomed to hide their mysteries under a "bark" <note>An outer shell or literal layer of meaning.</note> and to list names **technically** <note>original Greek: τεχνικῶς (*technikōs*)</note> rather than interpreting them in another language. Others have interpreted **Urim and Thummim**, but with words that have a broader meaning. For they either call it the **Oracle** <note>original Greek: λόγιον (*logion*)</note>, which signifies a divine utterance or discourse—as in *Romans 3:2*—or as the Latins do, the **Breastplate** or the **Rational**, which more closely expresses the word <term>Choshen <note>original Hebrew: חשן</note></term> in which the Urim and Thummim were enclosed. Hence, in *Exodus 28:15*, it is called the <term>Breastplate of Judgment <note>original Hebrew: חשן המשפט (*Choshen Ha-Mishpat*)</note></term>, because the High Priest, when about to answer regarding the law, was clothed in it, and through the Urim and Thummim which were enclosed within it, he learned the responses. The **Talmudists** <note>The ancient Jewish scholars of the Talmud.</note> interpret the **Urim** as the sacred names by whose power the hidden letters were illuminated, and the **Thummim** as those things by which the same letters were made conspicuous. The Hebrews add that responses legitimately obtained through the Urim were most certain, immutable, and irrevocable; hence *Ecclesiasticus 33:3* says: **The Law is faithful as an inquiry by the Urim** <note>original Greek: πιστὸς ὁ νόμος ὡς ἐρώτημα δήλων (*pistos ho nomos hōs erōtēma dēlōn*)</note>. From this, the Hebrews say that a Prophet’s promise can be revoked, but a response through the Urim never can. The reason is that they were consulted only concerning present matters already undertaken, or those about to happen. Hence they say that the Urim and Thummim are called <term>Judgment <note>original Hebrew: משפט (*Mishpat*)</note></term>. Just as a judicial sentence is not revoked, so neither is the Urim. But if it was not sought properly, the response came out imperfect and uncertain, as happened at **Gibeah of Benjamin** in *Judges 20*.

-># THE REVEALER OF SECRETS<-

18. ...where they asked God through the **Urim** which tribe should go up first against the **Benjaminites**, but they did not ask about the success of the victory. Relying on their own strength and the justice of their cause, they were therefore struck down by the Benjaminites in the first two slaughters, as is also testified by **Rabbi David Kimchi** and **Rabbi Levi Ben Gerson** <note>Also known as Gersonides, a medieval Jewish philosopher and commentator.</note>.

Furthermore, after so many interpreters of the terms **Urim** and **Thummim**, it will not be out of place to bring forward a certain "Christian Rabbi"—namely, the Jesuit **Bellarmine** <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a central figure in the Counter-Reformation.</note>. In order to more easily defend the doctrine of the Roman Church, he adapts the Hebrew grammar of these words to suit it, just as he adapts Philosophy to his Theology. For he derives **Urim** from *Light* <note>original Hebrew: אור (Or)</note> and **Thummim** from *Perfection* <note>original Hebrew: תם (Tam)</note> so that they signify, according to the **Septuagint** <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, *manifestation and truth* <note>original Greek: δήλωσιν καὶ ἀλήθειαν (*dēlōsin kai alētheian*)</note>, and according to the Latin Interpreter <note>The Vulgate translation.</note>, *doctrine and truth* <note>original Latin: doctrinam & veritatem</note>. In this, he plays a trick on his reader and shows little regard for his own reputation, since out of partisan zeal he investigates the roots of these words in a way that goes against grammatical logic. **Arias Montanus** <note>A Spanish Orientalist and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible.</note>, who was both much more learned and more honest, restored the native meaning to these words and correctly derived them from *Light* and *Completeness* <note>original Hebrew: אור (Or) and תמם (Tamam)</note>.

Therefore, Bellarmine wrongly concludes from this that the High Priest among the Jews was **infallible**, and consequently, so is the Roman Pope; he bases this on the Lord’s command in **Exodus 28** that "doctrine and truth" be placed in the High Priest's Breastplate of Judgment. Furthermore, even if we were to grant that **Urim** and **Thummim** signify "doctrine and truth," the infallibility of the Pope would still not be correctly inferred. Rather, as **Chamier** <note>Daniel Chamier (1565–1621), a French Huguenot theologian and critic of Bellarmine.</note> most skillfully observed in his *Panstratia* <note>A massive work of Protestant polemics.</note> while triumphing after a victory, the name was given based on the daily effect—specifically, as **Aben-Esra** <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a medieval Jewish scholar.</note> noted, because of the judgments and decrees of God which were to be known from there according to **Numbers 27**. Finally, even if we admit that some duty of the High Priest is designated here, it is a matter of *right* rather than *fact* <note>A legal distinction: the text describes what the Priest *ought* to be, not necessarily what he *is* in practice.</note>. That is, it signifies what kind of person the High Priest *ought* to be, rather than what he actually is in practice. We have a very authentic witness for this interpretation in **Paul Fagius** <note>A 16th-century German Renaissance scholar of Hebrew.</note>, who wrote: "Some believe that the Lord ordered **Urim** and **Thummim** to be inscribed on the breastplate so that the High Priest would be reminded that he must be endowed with the highest doctrine, which..."

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the linguistic roots and theological significance of the Urim and Thummim. It transitions from the views of scholars like Arias Montanus and Robert Bellarmine into a historical comparison between the Hebrew oracle and ancient pagan counterparts.</meta>

### ANTHONY CREGUT

...light and illumination is often mentioned in the Scriptures, along with the greatest integrity of character <note>original Latin: *lumen & illuminatio... morum summâ integritate*. This continues the definition of Urim (Lights) and Thummim (Perfections).</note>.

Up to this point, we have learned from the commentaries of the Hebrews and from Talmudic law what should be thought regarding the **Urim** and **Thummim**; furthermore, they wished to teach us about the duration and period of this oracle. Regarding its beginning, or the time in which it started, there is much material for doubt, since the Scripture speaks clearly that (as said above) God delivered the ***Urim and Thummim*** to **Moses**, and they were placed in the High Priest's breastplate, as is evident from **Exodus 28**. Regarding the time in which it ceased, however, the opinion among the Hebrews is not the same, as we shall soon see. In the beginning, just as that oracle was illustrious, so the devil—as "God’s ape" <note>original: *Dei simia*. A common theological term suggesting that Satan imitates divine miracles to lead people into idolatry.</note> and envious of His glory—produced opposing oracles at almost the same time. For while at that time God was bringing forth the Church within the family of **Abraham**, so **Satan** was establishing assemblies of idolaters among the Nations. At that time, two oracles were established in different regions: that of ***Hammon*** <note>Amun</note> in **Libya**, and that of ***Dodona*** in **Greece**, which **Herodotus** testifies in his second book were the most ancient of all. From this, *Hammon* is said to be named after *Cham* <note>Ham</note>—as if "Chammon"—the son of **Noah**; and the *Dodonaean* oracle from *Dodanim*, a name found in **Genesis 10**. These oracles of demons seem to correspond to two other types of the true God worshiped among the Hebrews. The oracle of **Hammon** corresponded to the **Urim and Thummim**; for both were mute, because the will of God (or the ambiguities of Satan) was signified by a symbol rather than a voice. The other was vocal—namely, from the living voice of God or a prophesying prophet—which was the same thing observed regarding the oracle of **Dodona**.

Now, if we investigate the duration of time: regarding the oracles of the Demons, it is a constant opinion that they failed and became altogether silent around the birth of **Christ**. For even the pagan authors confess this. There is the well-known book by **Plutarch** regarding the "cessation of oracles," and what he relates concerning the mournful cries of sailors shouting around the sea coasts: *"Great Pan is dead"* <note>original: *Pan magnus Deus mortuus est*. A famous legend from antiquity suggesting that the spiritual hierarchy of the pagan world collapsed at the start of the Christian era.</note>. He brings forward various causes for this matter, but they are futile, since a pagan man was unable to know the true cause—that is, the birth of **Christ**, by whom the prince of this world was to be cast out.

-># THE REVEALER OF SECRETS.<-

Regarding the **Urim** and **Thummim** and other prophecies, they indeed ceased—not because they were abolished, but so that a more illustrious revelation might follow. For as it is said in Hebrews 1:1, *“In many ways and in all forms, God spoke to the fathers through the Prophets from the beginning, and in these last days He has spoken to us through His Son.”* <note>original Latin: *Multifariam & omnibus formis loquutus est Deus...*</note> Now, the period during which prophecy endured is clear in the Scripture; for **Malachi** was the last of the Prophets, so that with the approaching arrival of **Christ**, there would be no King, nor Prophet, nor Priest among the Hebrews, because in Him alone all these offices were united. It was so that wisdom among the people of God might, as it were, grow old, while it was still merely stammering among the Gentiles.

But regarding the duration of the **Urim** and **Thummim**, the matter is not so well-established among Hebrews and Christians. For in the **Talmud**, tractate *Yoma*, chapter 1, and according to **Kimchi** <note>David Kimchi, a medieval Jewish biblical commentator</note> on Psalm 84 and Haggai 2:8: Because in the word *ve-ekabed* [“and I will be glorified”] <note>original Hebrew: ואכבד</note>, the letter *He* (ה) is missing—which, as the fifth letter in the alphabet, represents the number five—in place of the word *ve-ekabedah* <note>original Hebrew: ואכבדה</note>, he says this signifies that there were five things in the First Temple which were missing in the Second.

I. The **Divine Presence**, which delivered responses and oracles at the **mercy seat** <term>mercy seat: the golden lid of the Ark of the Covenant, or *propitiatorium*, where God’s presence was said to manifest</term>.

II. The **Spirit**, or **Holy Inspiration**, which once seized the Prophets; for (as has been said) from **Malachi** to **John**, no Prophets appeared. It is called the *Shekhinah* <note>original Hebrew: שכינה</note> by the Hebrews, from the word for “dwelling,” because it dwelt in the Temple. Hence the old and famous saying of the ancient Jews: “When two sit together and the words of the Law are between them, the **Shekhinah**—that is, the Holy Spirit—is between them.”

III. The **Holy Fire**, the keeping of which **Moses** had so anxiously commanded in Leviticus 6; for (the Hebrews say) it never appeared again after it was submerged in a well by the Priests to prevent it from falling into the hands of the wicked. This is also believed by the Papists <note>proponents of the Roman Catholic Church</note> because of 2 Maccabees 1, since that book—in which these things are recounted—is canonical to them.

IV. The **Urim and Thummim**, which was an oracle different from the preceding one, because the former was vocal, while this latter one was silent, consisting of movement and signs.

V. The **Ark** itself, along with its **mercy seat** covering, and the two **Cherubim** attached to the Ark. In these, God was said to sit, because of the abundance of Himself which He granted to the High Priests there. This is understood regarding both Arks...

However, these opinions of the **Rabbis** do not sit well with many **Jews** or **Christians**. First, they do not please the **Jews**, because **Josephus**—who was from the rank of the Priests—wrote (as we saw above) that the **Urim & Thummim** existed after the Babylonian captivity, and only failed a mere two hundred years before **Josephus** himself; moreover, **Josephus** lived and wrote his book after the destruction of the second temple. That second temple lasted 600 years, and consequently, if the **Urim** failed 200 years before the destruction of the temple, it must have endured for 400 years within the second temple. Therefore, the **Rabbis** speak erroneously when they say those five things were lacking in the second temple. These ideas also do not suit the **Christian** palate, because they see from **Nehemiah 7** that the **Urim** existed after the captivity; furthermore, many do not believe the book of **Maccabees** because this book is Apocryphal <note>meaning it is not considered part of the inspired biblical canon by all traditions</note>.

It is probable, therefore, that the **Urim & Thummim** ceased in the time of **Malachi**. For since there were two types of oracles: one vocal and the other silent <note>original Latin: *vnum vocale, alterum mutum*</note>, as we said above, when one failed, the other also failed. For as the equipment and furnishings of the old **Economy** <term>Economy: here referring to the "Old Covenant" or the specific way God managed His relationship with humanity before Christ</term> gradually ceased, God wished to show that the time of the new **Economy** was near, and that in **Christ** are found both the prophetic light and the **Urim and Thummim**, and all the glory of the former house, and something even more excellent besides. For as **Haggai** testifies, the glory of the second house will be greater than the glory of the former house. ...affects the prophetic spirit. And just as the prophetic light shone upon the Prophets, and the **Urim** upon the High Priest, so the <term>Bath Kol</term> <note>original Latin/Hebrew: *bath col*; literally "Daughter of a Voice," understood as a secondary form of divine revelation or a heavenly echo</note> affected the **Men of the Great Assembly** <note>original Hebrew: *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah*, the legendary council of 120 scribes and sages at the start of the Second Temple period</note> and resided within them. This was the same kind of voice heard on Mount Tabor during the transfiguration of **Christ** (Matthew 17) and at the baptism of **Christ** (Matthew 3). This "Daughter of a Voice," which filled the void left by the absence of prophecy, also ceased—according to the testimony of the **Hebrews** themselves—with **Simeon**, who is surnamed the **Just** (mentioned in Luke 1). This occurred so that it would be even more evident that **Christ** and his forerunner had arrived: that is, the "voice of one crying in the wilderness" (Isaiah 40) and the "Word and Speech of the Father himself" (John 1:1). These succeeded the *Bath Kol* as the perfect succeeds the imperfect.

Therefore, the **Masters of the Hebrews** are mistaken when they say those five aforementioned things were missing in the second temple. For prophecy lasted until the time of **Malachi**, and afterward, the presence of the **Divinity** was nonetheless there, since the High Priest entered the **Sanctuary** every year, standing before **Jehovah**. Secondly, the <term>Shekhinah</term> <note>original Latin: *Sechina*; the indwelling presence of God</note> was in the second temple until after the death of **Christ**. Shortly before the destruction of the temple, it deserted that holy place so that, on the day of **Pentecost**, it might rest upon the **Apostles** in tongues of fire (Acts 2). From this event, a voice was heard saying, "let us depart hence" <note>original Latin: *migremus hinc*; a famous omen reported by the historian Josephus during the siege of Jerusalem</note>. And as it is said in the *Pirkei Avot* <note>original Latin: *Pirke auoth*; "Ethics of the Fathers," a collection of Jewish ethical teachings</note>, the **Angel** who appeared at the door of the **Sanctuary** was transformed into a horrible specter; and the doors of the temple, which could barely be opened by the strength of forty men, opened of their own accord. Concerning the other items, there is indeed a deep silence in the **Scripture of the Prophets**; however, it is not sufficiently clear at what time these truly ceased.

Nevertheless, besides those five wonders of the first temple, the wise men of the **Hebrews** recount several others. Well known is what they relate concerning the <term>scapegoat</term> <note>original Latin: *hircus hazazel*; the goat for Azazel used on Yom Kippur</note>, the crimson thread between whose horns sometimes turned white and sometimes remained red. Also well known is that marvel concerning the flies: even though so many sacrificial victims were slaughtered in the temple, flies never infested the people or the **Levites**. This miracle, however, did not happen in the temples of the **Pagans**, for they were perpetually infested by an innumerable multitude of flies. For this reason, they worshipped **Beelzebub**, who was the God of the **Ekronites** (2 Kings 1:2). For **Beelzebub** is the same as the "Lord of the Flies."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Urim and Thummim, focusing on their symbolic meaning for the High Priest and a critique of Catholic interpretations regarding papal infallibility.</meta>

->### ANTHONY CREGUTUS<-

...the significance of the **Thummim**; which can be viewed in three ways: for it refers either to the **High Priest**, or to the whole **royal priesthood**—that is, the **Church**—or to the **High Priest** according to the order of **Melchizedek**, who is **Christ**.

1. With respect to the **High Priest**, the **Urim and Thummim** <note>original Latin: *Vrim & Thummim*; Hebrew terms usually translated as "Lights and Perfections," referring to sacred objects on the High Priest's breastplate used for seeking divine guidance</note> signified that the **High Priest** ought to be endowed with the light of doctrine and integrity of character. Just as the **Urim and Thummim** gleamed in the **breastplate** <note>original Latin: *rationali*; the "Rationale" or breastplate of judgment worn by the High Priest</note>, so he himself should shine before the whole flock with the brilliance of his teaching and the purity of his life. 

This does not mean, however, that the **High Priest** himself was infallible and could not err, as **Bellarmine** <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Cardinal and influential Jesuit theologian who defended the authority of the Pope</note> previously argued. For if infallibility were concluded from the **Urim** (Light), then by the same logic, an incorruptibility of character could be inferred from the **Thummim** (Perfection). Yet this contradicts the view of the **Roman Catholics** <note>original Latin: *Pontificiorum*; literally "of the followers of the Pontiff"</note>, who freely admit that a **Pope** can be corrupted in his morals; but the same reasoning should apply to both—both in regards to faith and in regards to character. 

Secondly, it is not correctly inferred (as said above) that the legal duty of the **High Priest's** office translates to what he actually is in fact. For the **High Priest** was not always what he was legally required to be. 

Thirdly, the reality signified by the **Urim and Thummim**—that is, the light of intellect (or doctrine) and the perfection of character (or integrity)—could indeed exist in the **High Priest**, but not in an absolute sense where he would be entirely infallible and perfect in character. Rather, it was relative to others in the flock, because these virtues ought to reside in the **High Priest** above all others. Furthermore, that perfection was one of "parts" rather than "degrees" <note>a theological distinction: "perfection of parts" means having all the necessary components of holiness, whereas "perfection of degrees" would mean having those qualities to an infinite or absolute extent</note>. This can be confirmed by the lives of the **Jewish High Priests**, no less than by the luxury of the **Roman Pontiffs**. 

Finally, these served to signify that grand priestly finery required in the **Church of the Old Testament**, in which dispensation there were many splendid ceremonies and trappings that foreshadowed the mysteries in the **New Dispensation** <note>original Latin: *Oeconomia*; the "economy" or divine arrangement of religious laws and symbols</note>. This is why **Josephus** in his *Antiquities*, Book 3, Chapter 7, describes the priestly vestments in ten parts—doing so with no small skill, as he was himself of priestly descent:

I. He lists the **linen breeches** first, used to cover the nakedness of the flesh.
II. The **tunic**, made of fine linen and doubled throughout.
III. The **multi-colored belt**, about four fingers in width.
IV. The **tiara** or **mitre**, made of fine linen. And...

In this way, their uncertainty would be covered by the eventual outcome, and men would believe the demons had known and predicted the matter certainly, but that the uncertainty of knowledge before the event arose from the ignorance of men, who had been unable to resolve the oracle's ambiguity. Now, however, all oracles—whether silent or vocal—have failed, both those of God and those of demons. The oracles of demons ceased, as we have said, because Christ came to stop their mouths; we have a proof of this in the Gospel, when Christ retorted to Satan as he was confessing Him, *"Be silent,"* and shut his mouth. The oracles of God, however, ceased because others were to succeed them which excelled the former ones: namely, the **Urim and Thummim of the Scriptures**, of which Paul speaks in Romans 3:2, when he asserts the excellence...

## CHAPTER XXVIII.

### *On the Death of Moses.*

In *Deuteronomy chapter 34, verses 5, 6, etc.*: "So Moses the servant of Jehovah died there in the land of the Moabites according to the word of Jehovah, who buried him in that same valley," etc.

### ANALYSIS.

Antiquity celebrated the Mausoleum <note>One of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World</note>. It celebrated the pyramids: yet the tomb of Moses excels them all. The epitaph of Moses. *Division into three parts, namely: the death of Moses, his burial, and his resurrection. The first part is subdivided into five sections.*

*The first part concerns the death of Moses. That death was intended from his birth by Pharaoh. By what means was it prevented? The necessity of death. Ordinary death happens but once. The opinion of the Pagans concerning death. The opinion of the Pelagians* <note>A group of early Christians who argued that death was a natural necessity of the human body rather than a specific punishment for original sin</note> *concerning the necessity of death. What should be thought of the book titled "The Assumption of Moses"* <note>original Greek: ’Ανάληψις τοῦ Μώσεως (Analepsis tou Mouseos), an ancient Jewish apocryphal work</note>? *What of the assumption of the Virgin Mary? Why are men called "Enoshim"* <note>original Hebrew: אנשים (Enoshim), a word for 'men' often associated with the root for 'frailty' or 'mortality'</note>? *In what sense is it true that Enoch and Elijah died? Old age was venerable to the ancients. It was especially venerable to the Spartans. Christians often refuse to "act like the stork" <note>original Greek: ἀντιπελαργεῖν (*antipelargein*); a classical term for the duty of children to care for their elderly parents, based on the belief that young storks fed their elders</note>. # ANTHONII CREGVTI

---

Antiquity spoke with immense praise of that proud Mausoleum, the tomb of the King of Caria called Mausolus, constructed by his wife Artemisia with such magnificence of workmanship that it was numbered among the seven wonders of the world; hence the poet says: *Let the immoderate Carians carry to the stars with praises the Mausolea hanging in the empty air.* <note>The author quotes a classical poet to illustrate the fame of the Mausoleum of Halicarnassus</note> Antiquity likewise spoke of those famous pyramids rising above all heights at Memphis, under which the tombs of the kings of Egypt were built; but here, *Let the barbarian wonders of the pyramids of Memphis be silent.* For the tomb of Moses, fashioned by the hand of the Architect of the entire world, far surpasses the monuments of all the Egyptian Kings and their squared pyramids tapering even to the sky—not because he was believed to be the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, but because he was the most faithful servant of the King of the heavens. Therefore, in this most singular tomb, abundant material can be supplied for an eternal epitaph, more lasting than bronze <note>original Latin: "aere perennioris"; a reference to the Roman poet Horace’s claim that his poetry would outlast metal monuments</note>.

But why do we seek an epitaph, when he himself before his death composed this immortal epitaph: *“So Moses the servant of Jehovah died there in the land of the Moabites according to the word of Jehovah. Who buried him,”* etc. <note>quoting Deuteronomy 34:5-6</note> Concerning which, almost four thousand years after his death, we investigate these three things: I. *Death.* II. *Burial.* III. *Resurrection.* Furthermore, in that first part, five things come to be considered: I. *The existence of death.* II. *Its cause.* III. *Its form.* IV. *Its circumstances.* V. *Its consequence.*

I. *The existence of death* is expressly asserted from the Mosaic text itself. For it is written, *“So Moses died there.”* Truly, before his birth he was destined for death, wherefore he was exposed to the waters immediately after birth, but if they were plotting his death... <note>The text cuts off here as it moves to the next page</note>

...men <note>The text continues from the previous page's unfinished word, likely "monumenta" (monuments)</note> had intended, but God had decreed otherwise; whence by a wonderful providence he was led out of the waters by Pharaoh's daughter so that he would not be drowned. Hence it is that in Scripture death is called the *way of all the earth*. And there is that well-known saying: nothing is more certain than death, yet nothing is more uncertain than its final hour. And for this reason, death is called by Aristotle <term>eschaton <note>Greek: ἔσχατον, meaning "the end" or "the extreme limit"</note></term>, that is, the end; hence we read of Methuselah in Genesis 5:27 that he lived nine hundred and sixty-nine years; but afterward it is added, *and he died*. Therefore, the Roman author Valerius Maximus most skillfully wrote in Book 5, chapter 10: *To all mortals, by the nature of things, a law is dictated for both receiving the spirit and returning it in the same moment; and just as no one is accustomed to die who has not lived, so neither can anyone live who is not destined to die.* One should also diligently weigh the words of the same author in Book 9, chapter 12, when he says: *The condition of human life is primarily contained within its first and last days: because it matters greatly by what omens it is begun and by what end it is closed. Therefore, we only judge a man to have been truly happy when it has fallen to him both to receive the light of life prosperously and to return it peacefully. The course of the time in between is spent according as Fortune has steered the helm, moved now by rough and now by tranquil motions: it is always shorter than our hope, while it is eagerly extended by our wishes and consumed almost without reason. For if you wish to use time well, you will make even a small number of years a most ample span by surpassing it with a multitude of achievements. Otherwise, what is the point of delighting in a sluggish delay, if you merely endure life rather than making it worthy of approval?*

To this end serve the countless maxims of authors, which not only confirm for us the necessity of dying, but even demonstrate it before our eyes from <term>autopsia <note>Greek: αὐτοψίᾳ, meaning "seeing for oneself" or personal observation</note></term>. As in that passage from Job 10: *Remember, I pray, that you have made me as clay and will bring me back into dust...*

...ral laws <note>Completing the sentence from the previous page: "To all mortals, by the natural laws..."</note>. And Genesis 3:19: *you are dust and to dust you shall return.* Man is dust in three ways: by reason of his origin, because he was formed from dust; by reason of his existence, because he always remains dust, for earth is the predominant element; and by reason of his end, because he returns to dust. Whence he was truly and skillfully named Adam <term>Adam <note>Hebrew: אדם</note></term> in the Hebrew nomenclature, not only because this word properly signifies *red earth* or *mud*, but also because mystically <term>Adam <note>Hebrew: אדם</note></term> signifies, through a <term>notaricon <note>A kabbalistic interpretive method where the letters of a name form an acronym for other words.</note></term>, <term>ashes, blood, and bitterness <note>Hebrew: אפר דם מרה (Efer, Dam, Marah). Hence Jeremiah calls man *earth before birth, earth in birth, and earth after birth*. and the Philosophers call him *earth in being, earth in becoming, and earth in preservation*. Well known is the epitaph of Cyrus, King of the Persians, discovered by Alexander the Great. Known too is the tomb of John the Almsgiver, Bishop of Constantinople; known are the mournful tears of Xerxes, King of the Persians, for his army consisting of twelve thousand men <note>original: "duodecim hominum millibus." While historical accounts like Herodotus suggest much larger numbers, the author here specifies 12,000.</note>, because every one of them was destined to die at some point. Notable are those words of the wise that death is inexorable; notable is the fatality of the Fates <note>The Parcae, the three goddesses of destiny in Roman mythology.</note>, whence sacrifice was made to death alone [to no avail], because it could be appeased by no victims, nor could its necessity be removed.

This is so true that even the <term>Pelagians <note>Followers of Pelagius (c. 354–418 AD) who argued that humans possess the free will to achieve social perfection without divine grace, and who viewed death as a natural process rather than a punishment for Adam's sin.</note></term>, who denied original sin and death itself as a punishment for sin, nevertheless confessed the necessity of death, but as an adjunct of even a "pure" nature, or a necessary consequence; hence infants die in the womb, who according to them are in a state of pure nature and without sin. All these things, and others cited by authors, we omit of our own accord, because they are obvious to everyone everywhere.

Since, therefore, Moses describes in this place the history of his own death as revealed to him by God, who will dare to deny it? Do you see, then, what should be thought of that very ancient book which has been lost, cited by some of the ancients under this title <term>The Assumption of Moses <note>original Greek: ἀνάληψις τοῦ Μωσέως (Analepsis tou Moseos). An apocryphal Jewish work describing the end of Moses's life.</note></term>, as if God had taken him up [into heaven alive]; just as today the <term>Papists <note>A term used by 17th-century Protestant writers to refer to Roman Catholics.</note></term> dream the same concerning the Most Blessed Virgin, whose <term>assumption <note>original Greek: ἀνάληψιν (analepsin), referring to the belief that Mary was taken bodily into heaven.</note></term> they celebrate; whence the Feast of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary, which Lady...

...they call their mistress <note>original: "minam suam." Referring to the Virgin Mary, continuing the thought that her feast day is a solemn occasion for some.</note>, is most solemn to them. This feast is especially observed by those whose duty it is to roast or grill meat, because *assum* <note>Latin: "roasted meat"</note> signifies that which has been toasted by fire; thus, they ridiculously play upon the sounds of the words *assum* and *assumptio* <note>Assumption—the Catholic doctrine that Mary was taken body and soul into heaven.</note> in such a serious matter. Thus do the superstitious tend to indulge in fables because no mention is made in Scripture of the death of the Blessed Virgin. Therefore (if it please God) they claim she was "assumed" and did not die. Similarly, because no one knew the location of Moses's tomb, and he did not die in the sight of his fellow people, curious men have since invented an **Assumption of Moses** <note>original: "ἀνάληψιν Μώσεως"</note>, and some suggest that the things Jude records in verse 6 <note>In modern Bibles, this reference to the dispute over Moses' body is found in Jude 1:9.</note> of his epistle regarding the body of Moses were taken from that book. That book is also cited by Origen in Book 3 of **On First Principles** <note>original: "περὶ ἀρχῶν"</note>, chapter 2, under the title of the "Ascension of Moses."

Since, therefore, there is no man, nor was there, nor will there be, who is found immune from sin, so no one can be exempted from the necessity of dying. Hence man is called by the Hebrews <term>Enosh <note>Hebrew: אנוש. This name for man implies frailty and mortality.</note></term>, to which the Latin name corresponds when men are called **mortals**. Indeed, those two unique men, Enoch and Elijah, who are commonly believed to be exempt from that shared necessity, yet if we weigh the matter more carefully, it will be clear that even they were not exceptions. For they truly died, albeit by a different kind of death than the other descendants of Adam. For there are two kinds of death: one occurs **by change**, the other **by transformation**. Ordinary death happens by change. For in this, "motion" is distinguished from "change" according to the Philosophers, because motion is successive and happens in quality (like heating), but change is instantaneous and happens in substance (like birth and decay). The former occurs in birth, when the soul is united with the body; the latter occurs in death, when the soul is separated from the body. Extraordinary death, however, happens by transformation—specifically not through preceding physical declines as in ordinary death, but **in the twinkling of an eye** <note>original: "ἐν ῥιπῇ τῷ ὀφθαλμῷ"</note>, the whole man is transformed, both in body and soul. Paul speaks of this death in 1 Corinthians 15:51: **Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet.** He calls it a mystery because that matter was still a secret and hidden, as also in 1 Thessalonians 4:17.

<meta>catchword: Messiah</meta>

*Then we who are alive, who remain, shall be caught up together with them in the clouds.* <note>1 Thessalonians 4:17.</note>

Observe, however, that this **transmutation** <term>transmutation: a miraculous, instantaneous transformation of the physical body into a "glorified" or spiritual state</term> is truly death, because the soul is separated from the body, though in a different and more noble manner than usual change. For just as in the process of generation, the soul is infused into the body by the act of creation, and created by being infused in an instant; so in this transmutation, God, by transforming the person, pours the soul out from the body, and by pouring it out, transforms it in a single moment. 

For since the soul then begins to give form to <note>original: "informare." In Scholastic philosophy, this means to provide the essential life-principle or "form" to matter.</note> the glorified body—which has been transformed—it was necessary that it should be, as it were, "poured out" from the body. This is because the soul is truly said to be separated from the body when it leaves that prior union in which the soul was like a prisoner in the body, so that it may put on a new union, where the soul is free from bodily chains and entirely glorious within a glorified body. Therefore, because the first kind of life is destroyed, in this respect it is truly called the "death of the man"; but because the soul does not remain separated from the body for long after that prior animation ceases, but is united in the same instant with the transformed and glorified body, it is judged to be "living" rather than "dying." Thus, that movement is called "transmutation" rather than "change," or "living" rather than "dying." 

Yet, in truth, just as when God creates the soul by infusing it and makes the man live, and infuses it by creating; so by pouring the soul out from the body, He transforms and kills the man, and by transforming and killing, He pours it out. For just as to "infuse" is to give form and life, so to "pour out" is to cease giving form, and thus to kill or to transform.

In this way, then, and by that kind of death, we conclude that **Enoch** and **Elijah** truly died, even though it is believable that they did not feel the "pains of death." This does not contradict Hebrews 11:5, where Enoch is said to have been "translated" into heaven by a singular privilege "that he should not see death." <note>The author interprets "not seeing death" as avoiding the *experience* and decay of death, rather than avoiding the theological requirement of the soul's separation from the body.</note> And regarding Elijah, see 2 Kings 2:11. **Melchizedek** also, in another sense, did not die, as is evident. 

What was done so extraordinarily in those two <note>Enoch and Elijah</note> (as we have said elsewhere) was so that men of the three ages of the world might be given a specimen and evident symbol of the future resurrection. For **before the Law**, Enoch ascended into heaven in body and soul; **under the Law**, Elijah likewise ascended in body and soul. Finally, **Christ** under...

<meta>This page continues Anthony Cregut's theological examination of death. <page-num>966</page-num>

# ANTHONY CREGUT #

Wherefore the same Augustus, the Supreme Emperor, when he was about to die, sent forth these verses concerning the state of the soul:

->*Little soul, wandering, charming,*<-
->*Guest and companion of the body,*<-
->*Into what places will you now go,*<-
->*Pale, cold, and naked;*<-
->*Nor will you give jokes as you were wont.*<-
<note>original Latin: "Animula, vagula, blandula..." These famous lines are traditionally attributed to the Emperor Hadrian rather than Augustus. The poem expresses the uncertainty of a soul facing the afterlife without Christian hope.</note>

But indeed, a different view must be held concerning the faithful, for whom death is most beneficial; for to them it is not a punishment or a legal satisfaction for sin, but discipline, or retribution, martyrdom, or a trial. 
<note>original Greek: παιδεία (discipline), τιμωρία (retribution/justice), μαρτύριον (testimony/martyrdom), δοκιμασία (testing/trial).</note> 
Hence it is that death in Scripture is sometimes called *sleep*, and sometimes *gain*. Philippians 1:21: *to the pious, Christ is gain in life and in death.* Psalm 116:15: *Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.* And among the ancients, the day of the saints' death was called the **birthday** <term>genethlion: literally 'birthday'; the early Church celebrated a martyr's death-day as their true birthday into eternal life</term>, because they were reborn in heaven. And Bellarmine, in *On the Beatitude of the Saints*, Book 1, Chapter 6, says: *We now call the day of death the birthday, because clearly the Saints, dying on earth, are born in heaven.* Regarding the faithful, that epitaph of the "Light of Spain," Ferdinandus Nonius, also applies; he wished for no more than these four words to be inscribed on his tomb (for so he had commanded in his final will): *the greatest good of life is death.*
<note>Ferdinandus Nonius refers to Hernán Núñez de Guzmán (1475–1553), a renowned Spanish humanist and professor.</note>

Observe, however, that Scripture makes this distinction between the death of the faithful and the reprobate; concerning the faithful, Scripture says they "delivered up the spirit," as was said of Christ on the cross. Hence the Heathen philosopher said: it was never said that a virtuous man had "died" [in the sense of being extinguished]. But when Scripture describes the death of Ananias and Sapphira, it is memorable that it says they **breathed their last** <term>exepsyxe: a Greek term implying a sudden expiration or the "shucking off" of the soul, often used in a more clinical or negative sense in this context</term>. Of Christ, it says He *handed over his spirit*.
<note>original Greek: παρέδωκε τὸ πνεῦμα (paredoke to pneuma). The distinction implies that the righteous consciously return their soul to God, while the wicked simply cease to breathe.</note>

The second part of the first section follows, which concerns the cause of Moses' death. Its cause is quite unknown, since it is not determined in Scripture. First, concerning the primary cause, there is no doubt. For to it belong (as Scripture says) *the issues of life and death. And God makes one go down to the grave and rise up from it.* 
But to bring forward the primary cause of any effect is not properly to provide "the cause," because the primary cause is universal, and is indifferent toward specific effects; it does not specify the effect by itself. Whence, regarding the death of any person, it could truly be said that God [willed it].

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS #

The Messiah performed the same. Thus, the men who have lived until now, and those who are to live through the ages, see in those three heroes <note>Likely referring to Enoch, Elijah, and Christ, who represent the victory over death in different ways.</note> an illustrious example of the future resurrection.

However, although every single person dies without exception, beware of saying that death is the same for everyone. For regarding the reprobate <note>Those destined for damnation.</note>, death is a punishment and a satisfaction for sin; for then begins a satisfaction **by extension** <note>original Greek: κατ' ἔκτασιν (kat' ektasin); referring to a punishment that stretches out or unfolds eternally.</note>, and to them, death is the **most terrible of all terrors** <note>original Latin: "terribile terribilium"</note>, because it is never without its sting. If they should rise again, and the soul be reunited with the body, that resurrection is not unto life, but unto death. For although the body lives and becomes physically incorruptible, yet "hyper-physically" <note>Beyond the laws of physical nature.</note> it always dies and is corrupted along with the soul. For to live is not to depart from the source of life; hence the worst of all evils is when they cannot die, but in dying eternally they will live, and in living they will die. A specimen of this can be seen in those who are desperate, who meet their final day **by their own hand** <note>original Greek: αὐτοχειρίᾳ (autocheiria), meaning suicide.</note>, because to them dying is better than living so unhappily. But these most wretched and unfortunate of all creatures do not see that by fleeing this life, which is death to them, they are thrown into the abyss of death, from which it is impossible to be rescued for eternity. Therefore, that Roman pagan was ignorant of the torments of hell when he wished that his enemies *could not die*, at a time when death would have been better for them than life.

Yet it must be confessed that the Pagans often looked upon the face of death as if it were pleasant and joyful, and did not shudder at it. Because of this, the Emperor Augustus, as Suetonius records, obtained an easy departure and such as he had always wished for. For almost as often as he heard that someone had died quickly and without torture, he prayed for a similar **good death** <term>euthanasia: from the Greek εὐθανασία, meaning a gentle or "well-death"</term> for himself and his family (for he was accustomed to using this word). Suddenly, amidst the kisses of Livia and with these words, he passed away: *Livia, live mindful of our marriage, and farewell.* But these were the empty comforts of a weary soul, which—even if they seemed to offer a little consolation outwardly because of their opinion of moral virtues, faith in the **Elysian Fields** <term>Campi Elysii: the mythological paradise for the souls of the heroic and the virtuous</term>, and other philosophical teachings—yet within there lurked anxieties, and they were greatly perplexed about their departure and future state.

...to be the cause of that death, insofar as it has the nature of a punishment. This seems to be pronounced more fittingly regarding the death of Moses, since from the text of Moses it appears that God completed this entire work according to his own decree. For just as in the creation of Adam, God formed man from clay with his own hand—for which reason he is said to have created him—so in the death of Moses, God wished to bury him with his own hand; but whether he assigned him to death immediately by himself is difficult to know. 

Nonetheless, because the death of Moses was not a miracle, it certainly does not seem that the greatest Prophet died from the immediate action of God; since the generation and corruption of men is the work of providence, and God governs the universe mediately <note>By using intermediate means or secondary causes rather than direct intervention.</note> and through the cooperation of secondary causes, the death of Moses undoubtedly happened in that ordinary manner. Indeed, to determine it even more specifically, that death was not violent—as when someone is killed by a sword or a gun <note>original Latin: "sclopeto"; an early modern Latin term for a firearm.</note>—but it is likely that he succumbed to a natural death. 

And speaking even more precisely, since his death was not slow and chronic (as the "sons of physicians" <note>An idiomatic way of referring to medical professionals.</note> say), but sharp and sudden, we judge that he met his final day not by **wasting away** <note>original Greek: μαρανσμῷ (maransmo); referring to a slow decline or atrophy.</note>, but **acutely** <note>original Greek: ὀξέως (oxeos); meaning a swift or sudden end.</note>. But truly, we are unable by any reasoning to indicate the type of death even more determinately, since it is a unique matter and concerns historical fact; because there is deep silence on this here, there is no need to investigate, nor does knowledge of this matter contribute to faith. This one thing is sufficient: to believe that his death was most peaceful; hence here, if ever elsewhere, that praised saying of the Emperor Augustus applies: "O, would that I had a similar **easy death**!" <note>original Greek: εὐθανασίαν (euthanasian). In this period, the term referred to a happy, peaceful death in a state of grace, rather than its modern medical meaning.</note>
