# ANTHONY CREGUT #

But even before this, God had threatened Moses because of his transgressions that he would not enter the land of Canaan, as seen in Deuteronomy 32:51: *Because you trespassed against me in the midst of the children of Israel, etc.*

The circumstances of Moses' death now follow, and first regarding the time. The time of his death was after he had reached his one hundred and twentieth year, and therefore he was satisfied with years in his old age. Longevity is numbered among God’s blessings, as is evident from the fifth commandment of the Law <note>The commandment to "Honor thy father and thy mother."</note>, where the "Macrobians" <note>original: "Macrobij"; a term for those who live exceptionally long lives.</note> are said to be children who are obedient toward their parents. For this reason, old age is to be desired by a pious man, since living itself is a great benefit from God, and even the discomforts of the flesh are useful to a godly man. For this reason, the one who said "it is good to grow old" <note>original Greek: καλὸν γηρᾶν</note> also added "and not to grow old again" <note>original Greek: καὶ μὴ γηρᾶν πάλιν</note>, "for old age does not come alone" <note>original Greek: τὸ γὰρ γῆρας οὐκ ἔρχεται μόνον</note>. For living itself is usually a "heavy burden" <note>original Greek: χάλεπον βάρος</note> to the elderly, so that they must meditate more on death and burial than on life; even the very name for old age <note>original Greek: γῆρας</note> invites us, as it were, "to look upon the earth" <note>original Greek: τὴν γῆν ὁρᾶν; a play on the phonetic similarity between the Greek word for old age and the phrase for looking at the ground, referring to the stooped posture of the elderly.</note>. Nevertheless, among the ancients, old age was so venerable that the same honor was shown to the elderly as to Magistrates; hence "Seniors" and "Senators" share the same naming convention. And those older by birth were cherished by those younger—according to Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a central Jesuit theologian of the Counter-Reformation.</note>—almost in the place of God and parents. Among the Spartans <note>original: "Lacedæmonios".</note>, old age was even more honored. Hence, when someone saw how much honor the younger men showed to the elders in Sparta, he said, *it is profitable to grow old in Sparta alone.* This custom of the Spartans condemns the wicked nature of Christians, who do not revere the elderly with due honor, so that the opposite can truly be said: among Christians, it is not profitable to grow old. Because of this, few children are accustomed to "repay their parents' care" <note>original Greek: ἀντιπελαργεῖν; literally "to act like a stork," based on the ancient belief that young storks fed and cared for their elderly parents.</note>. However, I do not dwell on those verses of the clever poet, since he was joking playfully, even if they might contain a grain of truth:

->*The youth is a laughing animal: the woman and the boy*<-
->*Are prone to tears: the withered old man has unlearned both.*<-

Therefore, since attractive arguments are brought forward from both sides regarding old age, it is clear that those who die in the Lord are blessed, as is held in Revelation 14. For to them, old age is not a burden, but a blessing. For sometimes when Scripture speaks...

However, those mourning rites and commemorations for the dead in the time of the Patriarchs and Prophets were not superstitious; but truly, after the deaths of the Prophets, superstition began to creep in gradually, which is why in the books of the Maccabees prayers are made for the dead. But superstition grew much stronger after the time of Christ, as is clear from the book *Mahzor* <note>A cycle of Jewish prayers used on festivals.</note>. Finally, these superstitions of both the Jews and the Gentiles crept into the Christian Church. This is why today, under the Papacy, indulgences are given, prayers are made for the dead, and intercessions <term>suffragia|intercessory prayers or acts of devotion offered by the living to assist the souls of the deceased</term> are performed for them; from this, Purgatory is believed. And yet, regarding all these things, there is not a "peep" or a "squeak" in Scripture <note>original Greek: γρῦ (*gry*) or μῦ (*my*), a classical idiom meaning the smallest possible sound or syllable.</note>. > I would not have you be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who have fallen asleep, so that you do not grieve, even as others who have no hope.

Where "to fall asleep" <note>original Greek: τὸ κοיμᾶσθαι (*to koimasthai*)</note> is used to mean being placed in the tomb as if in a bed, from which we shall finally be awakened and raised up. By this word, the Greeks imitate the Hebrews, who use the word *shakhabh* <note>Hebrew: שכב</note>, meaning "to lie down," but almost always with an addition, such as "with his fathers"; sometimes, however, it is used on its own, as in Isaiah 14:8 and 18. The Hebrews call those who are dead "sleepers" <note>Hebrew: ישנים (*yeshenim*)</note> in Daniel 12:2.

Among the Greeks, superstition became especially prevalent; for on an appointed day, such as those called **Pandemi** <note>original: *Pandemi*, meaning "of the whole people"</note>, that is, *the people's days*, they mourned the dead and carried food and wine to the tombs of their deceased; they burned the food, but they offered the wine to the defunct, calling them by name. *"Rise,"* (they would say) *"eat, drink, and be merry."* Epiphanius testifies to these things in *The Well-Anchored* <note>original: *Ancoratus*, a work by Epiphanius of Salamis (4th century) defending orthodox Christian faith</note>. The same thing is now done in the offertory of the **Mass** for the living and the dead.

However, abuse and superstition did not immediately prevail in the Church of God. For if we consider the origin of this mourning and of the duties toward the dead, it will be most certain that from a beginning that was not bad, the custom eventually deteriorated for the worse. For at first, those duties toward the dead were introduced into the Church by those who were divorcing themselves from <term>Paganism</term> <note>original: *Ethnicismo*; referring to the customs of the "ethne" or gentiles/pagans</note> and embracing Catholic <note>Here used in the sense of "universal" or "orthodox" early Christian truth</note> truth. as happens today in funeral orations; nor did those ancient rites in any way regard the salvation of souls, but rather the bodies, which were honorably buried and commended to God in memory and hope of the resurrection. But concerning Purgatory, not even a single little word is found in the writings of the <term>Fathers</term> <note>The "Church Fathers," influential early Christian theologians from the first few centuries AD</note>. And indeed, in the Old Testament, there was the greatest care for burial, which is why the Patriarchs—who did not possess even a clod of earth—nevertheless bought tombs, which their sons obtained by right of inheritance so that whole families might be buried there. Hence Joseph commanded his brothers that his bones be transferred from Egypt into Canaan, so that he might be with his fathers, just as the same had been provided for his father Jacob.

But concerning prayers for the dead and concerning purgatory, there is a deep silence; nor was any sacrifice or <term>lustral waters</term> <note>Water used for ceremonial purification</note> established for them, even though innumerable sacrifices were made for sins—whether voluntary or involuntary, or for *sins of ignorance* <note>original Greek: *peri tōn agnoēmatōn* (περὶ τῶν ἀγνοημάτων)</note>. A single passage is brought forward by the <term>Pontiffs</term> <note>A term the author uses for Roman Catholic authorities</note> from the book of 2 Maccabees, chapter 12, verse 43. But besides the fact that this book is <term>Apocryphal</term> <note>Referring to books not included in the Hebrew Bible; the author views them as non-canonical or of lesser authority</note>, it sufficiently shows that at that time the Jews had been corrupted by excessive communication with the Gentiles. Hence it is added by that author: *But this was not the beginning but a certain increase and progress of Gentile and foreign conversation.*

That this came from the doctrine of Plato is shown by <term>Eusebius</term> <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a historian who argued that Greek philosophy often borrowed from or distorted older Hebrew truths</note> in his *Preparation for the Gospel*, book 11, final chapter: *When the deceased have arrived at that place to which they are carried, first it is judged who lived justly and who lived otherwise; and if any seem to have lived in a middle way, they climb into their vehicles, and are carried through the Acheron* <note>In Greek mythology, a river in the underworld</note> *into the marsh, where they are purged by heavy punishment, and afterward, having been liberated, they receive honors according to the dignity of their good deeds.* The same author, in book 12, chapter 3, records these things from Plato’s *Gorgias*: *moreover, whoever has sinned curably is purged by pains, etc. But those who had sinned incurably, no benefit can ever happen to them.* 

Here you see the seeds of purgatory and of venial and mortal sins; which are there named *curable* and *incurable*. Furthermore, Plato uses the words *to cleanse* <note>original Greek: *kathairein* (καθαίρειν)</note> and *to release* <note>original Greek: *apolyuein* (ἀπολύειν)</note>, to which those lines of Virgil in the *Aeneid*, book 6, respond:

->*For some, under the vast whirlpool,*<-
->*the tainted crime is washed away, or burned out by fire.*<-

<summary>This page presents a Protestant critique of Purgatory, arguing that the concept is absent from the Bible and early Church Fathers and instead originates from pagan Greek philosophy, specifically Plato.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Cregut’s argument that Roman Catholic funerary rites and the concept of Purgatory are not rooted in Scripture, but are instead continuations of ancient "Ethnic" (Pagan) superstitions. He specifically focuses on the month of February and rituals of purification.</meta>

# ANTHONY CREGUT #

Indeed, the superstition of the Pagans <note>Latin: *Ethnicorum*; refers to non-Christian, ancient Greeks and Romans</note> had reached such a point that they sacrificed humans for the salvation of the deceased. This is testified by Jerome himself in his *Letter to Heliodorus on the Epitaph of Nepotian*: *The ferocity of the Bessi <note>A Thracian tribe</note>, who once sacrificed humans at the funeral rites of the dead, has broken its harsh screeching into the sweet melody of the cross.* And Plutarch, in his *Life of Numa Pompilius*, says: *Of the months added or transposed by Numa, the second was called February, as if it were a kind of "lustral" month <note>A month of ceremonial washing and purification</note>. For "februa" generally signifies expiation, and at that time they perform rites for their deceased parents and carry out the Lupercalia, which are very similar to a sacrifice of purgation.*

Furthermore, all these things were observed with cold formality in the mourning of Pagans for the deceased.
i. Funerals were conducted by employing *flute-players and lyre-players with torches.* Persius notes here: *the trumpet and the candle; and finally the little "blessed one" <note>A sarcastic reference to the deceased</note> laid out on a high bed.* 
ii. Annual commemorations and orations were instituted in praise of the deceased. 
iii. Banquets were held. These were later forbidden by the African Council in Canon 27 as "smelling of Paganism." 
iv. The use of beans in alms-giving for the dead. The reason, according to the followers of Pythagoras, was that the souls of the dead were believed to be in them. For this reason, beans were forbidden, and the <term>Flamen Dialis</term> <note>The high priest of Jupiter in ancient Rome</note> was allowed neither to touch nor name them, because they were thought to belong to the dead. Varro also records that the Priests did not eat them because mournful letters are found in their flowers. 
v. *Washings* of the bodies of the deceased. 
vi. *Mourning garments*, which the Romans called *anthracinas* <note>Coal-colored or black</note> from *anthrax* <note>Greek for coal</note>. Perhaps the same can be said of those tragic garments named *abolla* from the word *abel* <note>Hebrew: אבל (*avel*)</note>, meaning *mourning*, about which Athenaeus writes in Book 12 of the *Deipnosophists*. 
vii. There was a festival *of the dead*, which (as I said) was celebrated in the month of February; hence those festivals were called *februata*; and the month of February was called *katharsios* <note>Greek: καθάρσιος</note>, that is, *expiatory*. At that time those banquets were held which were called *feralia* from "carrying" (*ferendo*), because they were carried over the monuments of the deceased. And *silicernia* <note>Funeral feasts</note>, on account of the silence of the dead. In this same manner, the *Feast of Saint Peter’s Food* <note>Refers to the Feast of St. Peter's Chair</note> was instituted in the Papacy in that same month of February. And just as there were *split days* <note>Latin: *intercisi dies*; days divided between religious duties and worldly business</note> among the Pagans, so in the Roman Church there are feasts that last for only a few hours in the morning. There are also *Necysia, Ennata, Enagismata, Cterismata, Tarchismata, Triacas, Parentationes, Nouendialia* <note>A list of Greek and Latin terms for various funeral offerings, ninth-day rites, and nine-day mourning periods used in antiquity</note>.

He draws parallels between the Roman Flamen's taboos and Catholic prohibitions, as well as ancient festivals like the Feralia and Catholic feast days.</summary>

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS #

...fairs, etc., were festivals of the dead among the Pagans <note>Latin: *Ethnihos*; the text likely concludes a list of festivals like the *Parentalia* or *Feralia* from the previous page</note>. The first author who made mention of these was Tertullian <note>A prolific early Christian author from Carthage, c. 155–220 AD</note>, near the end of the second century in his book *On the Soldier's Crown*, chapter 3, where he testifies that "annual offerings are made for the dead and for birthdays" <note>original: *oblationes anniuersarias pro mortuis & pro natalitiis fieri testatur*</note>.

So far we have dealt with the first part; now follows the second, which is **burial** <note>original: *sepultura*</note>. In this section, the following points come under consideration: I. *The cause of the burial.* II. *The circumstances of the location.* III. *The adjunct; the hiding of the grave, and the battle of Michael with the Devil.* <note>A reference to Jude 1:9, regarding the dispute over the body of Moses</note> I. The cause of the burial is God himself, who deigned to bury Moses with His own hand, as the divine historian and prophet <note>Refers to the author of Deuteronomy</note> clearly testifies in verse 6: *And he* (that is, Jehovah) *buried him in that same valley*, etc. If, therefore, the piety of Joseph of Arimathea is praised—who, although a wealthy man and honorable among the Jews, nevertheless did not blush to bury Christ (a man then despised, condemned with thieves, and fixed to a cross)—what shall we say of the immense benevolence of God toward His servant Moses, whom He willed to bury? Truly, that most wise Ruler of the world does not judge as vile and rejected those things which appear so to men; for as it is said in Isaiah 55:
> My ways are not your ways, etc.
Nor does that saying of Martial <note>A Roman poet famous for his witty and often biting epigrams</note> hold any weight with Him:

->*Recently Diaulus was a Doctor, now he is an undertaker;*<-
->*What the undertaker does, the Doctor had also done.*<-
<note>original: *Nuper erat Medicus, nunc est Vespillo Diaulus; / Quod Vespillo facit, fecerat & Medicus.* Martial, Epigrams 1.47. A joke implying that the doctor killed his patients, so his job hasn't actually changed now that he is a <term>Vespillo</term> (a funeral director for the poor).</note>

Whether God buried him immediately—that is, by His powerful word and an act of will, as could have happened—or whether He used the ministry of Angels, is not for us to investigate. These are the "secrets of God" <note>original: *arcana Dei*</note>, and it does not concern us how it was done; it suffices only that God, by this act, "closed the door to idolatry" <note>A common theological interpretation: God hid Moses' body so the Israelites wouldn't turn his grave into a site of worship/idolatry</note>.

From this, however, several beneficial lessons emerge. I. By burying His faithful servant Moses, God indicated that He approved the rite of burying the dead, and by His own example, He effectively consecrated it as a ceremony that is not only political but also religious. Hence, not only Magistrates <note>Civil authorities</note> but also Pastors (as God's representatives in religious and Ecclesiastical matters) hold the primary role in comforting the relatives of the deceased. II. That burial of Moses, performed by the hand of God, is a testimony of the future resurrection. For why would God raise the body of Moses to such honor...

This page explores why God did so and contrasts Christian/Biblical views on the body with those of classical philosophers like Diogenes and Socrates.</meta>

...have perished, if we had no hope of resurrection? For Diogenes the Cynic <note>A Greek philosopher (c. 412–323 BC) known for his extreme poverty and rejection of social norms</note> believed otherwise; being little certain of the immortality of souls and the resurrection of bodies, he sought "the burial of a donkey" <note>original: *asini sepulturam*; a reference to Jeremiah 22:19, meaning to be cast out without honor</note>. **III.** God willed to bury the body of Moses for this particular reason: so that the Jews would not adore the body of that man or worship his relics. Through him, God had performed so many miracles, and with him, He had conversed so familiarly, speaking to him "face to face." Later, Satan dared to tempt people [with the location of the body], but with a failed effort <note>A reference to the tradition found in the Epistle of Jude regarding the dispute over Moses' body</note>.

It is no wonder, therefore, if men have always valued burial so highly that they willed no bodies to remain unburied; and in **Joshua chapter 8, verse 29** <note>The OCR says verse 28, but the hanging of the King of Ai is in verse 29</note>, it is said with good reason that *the King of Ai was suspended from a tree until evening*. Even the poets imagine that the unburied do not cross the Styx <note>In Greek mythology, the river forming the boundary between Earth and the Underworld</note>, nor are they carried across by that aged ferryman <note>Charon</note>. Why is this, I ask, unless it shows that the buried body pertains to the immortality of its soul, and that the soul cannot exist comfortably enough in the other life unless it is eventually reunited with its own body? Indeed, Christ willed to be buried on the same day He was fixed to the cross, so that through that **Holy Economy** <note>term: *Oeconomia*; a theological term for God's structured plan for human salvation</note> He might represent this whole mystery to us. 

However, as for the fact that the seven sons of Saul were hung and David did not permit them to be taken down from the gallows and committed to the earth until they had been sprinkled with water from heaven <note>See 2 Samuel 21:1-14</note>, this was undoubtedly done by God's counsel. For this was an atonement for God's offense; therefore, their bodies were to be left on the cross until the rain dripping from the sky showed that God had been appeased. Socrates, therefore, answered wrongly when Crito asked about his burial. Since to him the soul alone was the "man," he replied that after death nothing of himself would remain that could be buried. Nevertheless, common nature itself—which God implanted in all mortals—has always silently judged that bodies would one day live again and be restored to their souls. It incites everyone to the care of burial, not by doctrine or reason, but by a certain secret sense of its own.

Who then would wonder if antiquity celebrated three tombs of Heroes in particular: namely, those of **Caesar**, **Pompey**, and **Crassus**, which...

Furthermore, the necessity of burial is greatly confirmed by *Cenotaphs*, that is, *empty tombs*. For when men have perished in a shipwreck, or by some other kind of death in which their bodies were lost and did not come into the power of parents or friends, they nevertheless constructed Cenotaphs in honor of the deceased. They considered it better to erect tombs empty of their bodies than to have none at all. Thus, they held burial to be so necessary that they magnified it even <term>outwardly</term> <note>original: *φαινoμένως* (phainomenos) — in appearance or manifestation</note> and in appearance, whenever they <term>truly</term> <note>original: *ὄντως* (ontos) — in actual reality</note> and in fact lacked the bodies. The Laws of the Twelve Tables <note>The foundation of Roman law, dating to the mid-5th century BCE.</note> contain this rule: *Do not bury a dead man in the city.* And the Jurists state: *Do not bury or burn [a corpse] in the city.* This was later also sanctioned by the decrees of certain Emperors. Because of this, even the bodies of martyrs were buried outside the city; but among Christians, this was done not out of horror—as was the case with the Pagans <note>original: *Ethnicos*</note> who were ignorant of the resurrection—but for political <note>In this context, "political" refers to civil administration and public health concerns.</note> reasons. Regarding the location, in Leviticus 21, where God said that whoever touched a corpse was unclean, and that the place where corpses were buried was also polluted, that meaning is mystical; for it signified a mystery in the New Testament, as we have stated above.

But indeed, the Papists <note>original: *Pontificij*</note> sin greatly in excess. For the Monks say that bodies and tombs are holier the closer they are to the high altar. The Franciscans and Dominicans found this art of extorting <note>original: *emungendæ*, literally "wiping the nose of," a metaphor for swindling or cleaning someone out.</note> money, so that they might persuade the ignorant that people ought to be buried in monks' cowls and near the altar; and they abused a passage from the Apocalypse <note>Revelation 6:9</note> concerning *the souls of the deceased placed under the altar.* Hence someone rightly said, *no art of acquiring money is more proven than that of the Monks, etc.* 

From this comes the corruption of the Scripture in Apocalypse 14: *Blessed are they who die in the Lord, etc.* They interpret "In the Lord" to mean "in a cowl," for they commonly call those garments a "*Domino*." <note>The author is mocking a pun: *in Domino* (in the Lord) versus wearing a *domino* (a hooded monastic cloak).</note> For this reason, men of great name and eminent dignity have elsewhere wished to be buried in a cowl. Furthermore, they dress the relics of those they call Saints in gold and silk, swear oaths over them, and so on.

Yet the opposite was done in the burial of the ancient Patriarchs. In 2 Kings 23: when Josiah destroyed the tombs that were on the high place of Jeroboam, he took the bones out of the tomb and burned them on the altar. But when he understood that the tomb of a man of God or a prophet was not far from there, Josiah commanded: *Let him rest, and let no one move his bones from the place.* And it is immediately added, *And his bones remained untouched.* Indeed, in Jeremiah 8, among the punishments inflicted by God, this most serious one is established: *They shall cast out their bones from their graves.* 

Therefore, when in 1 Kings 31 <note>In modern Bibles, this is 1 Samuel 31.</note> the bones of Saul and Jonathan are said to have been moved—for when the citizens of Jabesh-Gilead had buried them in the grove of Jabesh, David later transferred them to the land of Benjamin into the ancestral tomb of Saul—the cause was political, for then [there was] great...

...of their families had family tombs. And the old man Barzillai is said to have rejected the dignity of the royal court so that he might be buried in the tomb of his fathers. <note>See 2 Samuel 19:37. Barzillai was a wealthy Gileadite who supported King David during Absalom's rebellion.</note> As for Joseph, his bones were carried out of Egypt into Canaan just as he himself had ordered, for another reason that was indeed sacred and religious, yet not superstitious; namely, so that his faith in the promises of the inheritance of Canaan might be made known. Therefore, the old translation of Ecclesiasticus 49 <note>Also known as the Wisdom of Sirach.</note> is corrupted, where it says *the bones of Joseph were visited and prophesied after death*, a passage which some distort to suggest that the Jews established a practice of pilgrimage to gather at the bones of Joseph. However, the Greek text uses the word *epeskepsanto* <note>original: ἐπεσκέψαντο</note>, which means to guard something as diligently as if it were protected by a covering. Indeed, these latter words are not found in this place, but were transposed from chapter 48 of the same book through the carelessness and ignorance of scribes, or perhaps by the malice of someone. For while in the previously mentioned passage this is truly said of Elisha—who, by confirming his prophecy with a miracle, can be said to have prophesied after death when his bones revived a dead man—regarding Joseph, it was stated contrary to the truth of the text.

Therefore, it is a horrendous punishment—whether for political reasons, sacred and religious ones, or even according to the superstitious—when bodies remain unburied, as is clear from Joshua 10:27 concerning the five kings of the Canaanites. Since the soul of man is not like an **Angel**, who is a **self-subsisting form** <term>forma subsistens: a being that exists independently rather than being a property of something else</term> and, in an assumed body, is an "assistant form" which operates through **intelligible species** <term>species intelligibiles: the mental images or concepts through which an intellect knows things</term> created together with it, and therefore needs no creature for its own glorification. But in truth, the soul is neither a self-subsisting form properly and insofar as it is a soul; nor is it an "assistant form" hypostatically moving the body; but it is an **informing form** <term>forma informans: a form that gives essential character and life to matter</term> giving form to the body either in actuality, when it is united with the body, or in potentiality, when it is separated from the body. Knowledge gained through reasoning or mental concepts rather than direct sight.</note>; however, when the whole person is glorified, they will enjoy the clear vision of God and intuitive knowledge. 1 Corinthians 13:12: *Now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I am known.* Therefore, the soul, even when separated from the body, cannot act or understand without the <term>passive and active intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectu patiente & agente." Terms from Aristotelian philosophy; the passive intellect receives information, and the active intellect processes it.</note>, neither of which can understand without <term>connatural species</term> <note>original: "speciebus connaturalibus." Mental images or forms that are natural to human understanding, derived from sensory experience.</note> taken from the body, or formed from sensory images. Nor is this argument valid: "Souls without bodies are punished in hell. Therefore, the souls of the faithful will be glorified without bodies." For first, I respond to the premise that the souls of the damned are punished imperfectly in hell because, after the judgment, once united with their bodies, they must be punished most severely; just as the souls of the blessed are also imperfectly glorified without their bodies. Except that just as the damned despair because they are certain of their damnation, so the holy ones hope and are most perfectly persuaded of their glory, because their souls already enjoy a heavenly dwelling. Secondly, the **consequent** is denied. For the nature of the punishment of the damned and the glory of the Saints is not the same; punishment is inflicted by God and happens through suffering, which can therefore be endured by the soul without the body; but the Saints possess glory through action—that is, by understanding, loving, and delighting—which cannot happen without the (as I said) connatural <term>intelligible species</term> <note>Mental representations required for the act of thinking.</note>. And therefore, it follows from this that the Papists wander in grave error when they make "blessedness" a step toward "holiness," as is clear from the case of **Ignatius Loyola**, who, because he did not have the favor of the Pope and the Cardinals <note>original: "purpuratos," literally "those clad in purple."</note> for some time, was only declared "blessed," but not a canonized "Saint." But they err in two ways: first, when they make blessedness a step toward holiness, whereas on the contrary holiness precedes blessedness, even in God. In us, it comes first in time, as is clear from the order of the benefits of grace in <term>Paul's Golden Chain</term> <note>original: "Pauli Armilla aurea." Refers to Romans 8:30.</note> in Romans 8:30. In God, it comes first by nature, because He is not glorious except because He is Holy. Whence, according to the style of Scripture, the faithful living on earth are called "Saints," not "heaven-dwellers." Second, they err when they believe the "blessed"—that is, the souls of the deceased—are glorified without the body,

...which, however, cannot happen for the reasons cited above. Third, add that they are gravely mistaken when they attribute infinite knowledge to the blessed based on their gazing into that **mirror of divinity** <note>original: "speculi diuinitatis." A theological concept suggesting that those in heaven see all things by looking at God, who reflects all reality like a mirror.</note>, where they contemplate all things as if they were present; this will not even happen in the perfect glory of the body and soul together. Fourth, they are also mistaken when they not only <term>canonize</term> <note>The official process of declaring someone a saint.</note> the souls themselves, but the deceased people, and therefore pray to them, even though the bodies themselves (as is evident) are not yet glorified; since the souls themselves are also not glorified without the body; and since, finally, those are being prayed to whose souls might perhaps be in **hell** <note>original: "inferno."</note>.

Therefore, it is clearly established that the **horned dilemma** <note>original: "dilemma illud cornutum." A logical trap where a person is presented with two options (the "horns"), both of which lead to an unfavorable conclusion.</note> brandished by the **papal attackers** <note>original: "Pontificiis cornupetis." A play on words comparing Catholic polemicists to animals that butt with their horns.</note> could not strike the truth, neither from the right horn nor the left. However, regarding the soul of **Eutychus** <note>A young man in Acts 20 who fell asleep during a sermon by Paul, fell from a window, and was picked up dead.</note>, there seems to be a specific reason found in the text of *Acts 20:10*. For Luke records it thus: *But when Paul went down, he fell upon him; and embracing him, he said: Do not be troubled, for his soul is in him.* And yet in *verse 9* it is said: *and he was picked up dead.* Therefore, his soul was not in heaven. This is certainly true. But surely it was not in purgatory either, because it was "in him." Various authors interpret this passage in various ways. Some maintain that Eutychus was not truly dead; for although it is written in the text, *And he was picked up dead*, it is not to be understood that he was altogether lifeless, as if the soul no longer **gave form to the body** <note>original: "informasset corpus." In Aristotelian philosophy, the soul is the "form" that gives life and structure to the "matter" of the body.</note>, but because no outward sense of life appeared due to imperceptible breathing. Thus, he is called "dead" because there was no hope of life, nor any outward act of life, but rather of death. This explanation seems probable to us; and it can be confirmed by two reasons born from the text. First, when Luke says, *his soul is in him*, that is, the soul is in him regarding its <term>potential state</term> <note>original: "habitum." The inherent capacity or presence of the soul.</note>, not regarding its <term>active operations</term> <note>original: "actus." The observable functions of life like breathing or movement.</note>; or it is in him **formatively** <note>original: "informatiue." Present as the life-force.</note>, not **operatively** <note>original: "operatiue." Functioning through the senses.</note>. Second, this explanation is proved because Luke does not say that Paul raised him from the dead, but rather that the boy was brought back alive in *verse 12*: *And they brought the boy back alive, and were not a little comforted.*

Others, on the contrary, say that he was truly dead, as is explicitly stated in the text, and yet the soul was in him, and even...

...to have risen: which three things immediately seem to be paradoxes. For how is he dead if the soul is in him? How is the soul in him if he has risen? And how has he risen if he was not dead, since his soul was in him? Those paradoxes are resolved by a single distinction. For the soul can be in the body in two ways, either <term>informatively</term> <note>original: "informatiue." In Scholastic philosophy, this means the soul acts as the "form" or life-force that actually animates and gives life to the body.</note>, or <term>hypostatically</term> <note>original: "hypostatice." Meaning the soul is present as a distinct substance in a specific location, but without providing life-giving "information" to the body.</note> (that is, by *presence*). Under the **informative** definition, the paradoxes hold true. For it is utterly contradictory for the soul to be in the body informatively, and yet for the person to be dead and to have risen. But **hypostatically**, the soul could be in some part of the body, as if in a certain "where," yet not "inform" the body itself, nor give it life; since God wished to wake the young man immediately, there was no need for Him to send His Angel to carry the soul to the heavens, but it was to be left in the body, soon to be totally reunited for the purpose of animation.

Thirdly, I answer that Eutychus was truly dead, and yet the soul was in him, and nevertheless he rose again; indeed, to add what seems a further **most paradoxical thing** <note>original: "παραδοξώτατον" (Greek: paradoxotaton).</note> beyond the previous paradoxes, the soul was in the young man not hypostatically but informatively, and yet he was truly dead and rose again. This is because those various moments of time in which all these things happened must be distinguished. For at the moment Eutychus fell down from the third story, he was picked up dead, as is found in verse 9. Just as he was also dead when Paul went down and threw himself upon him (verse 10). But when the Apostle said, *Do not be alarmed, for his soul is in him,* then the miracle was performed and the boy was raised from the dead; which was done suddenly without employing any **preparations** <note>original: "παρασκευαῖς" (Greek: paraskeuais). Referring to formal rituals or medical attempts to revive someone.</note>, as is done at other times, because Paul was busy with more important matters—the preaching of the Word and the breaking of bread—which could have been disrupted by these external disturbances.

Fourthly, the Apostle could have spoken this way not because the soul was actually in Eutychus at the same instant he was speaking—for it was in heaven—but because Paul was about to perform the miracle, he spoke as if the miracle had already happened because of the certainty of the outcome. Therefore he said *his soul is in him*. As if to say: do not be alarmed, do not hinder me with groaning and complaints...

...for them this sacred exercise of the whole Church. For even now the soul is within him. In this way, Christ, the Lord of life and death, spoke in Matthew 9:24 concerning the girl who was truly dead. "She is not," He said, "dead, but she lives," <note>original: "sed viuit." Most biblical translations use "sleeps" (dormit) here; the author may be emphasizing the immediate continuity of her life through Christ’s power.</note> because, of course, she was soon to be raised from the dead. The Jews, not understanding this, mocked Him. Fifthly, it can be answered that those words of Paul could be understood concerning the soul in respect to its **vegetative** <note>The faculty of the soul responsible for basic growth and nutrition.</note> or **sensitive** <note>The faculty responsible for sensation and movement.</note> faculties, but not the **rational** faculty. And therefore Eutychus, having fallen *from the third story* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ τριστέγου" (apo tou tristegou).</note>, was not utterly dead, even if it seemed so to the senses. For it is not foreign to common speech to say someone is "dead" when their body remains like a corpse, entirely *without feeling and without movement* <note>original: "ἀναίσθητον καὶ ἀκίνητον" (anaisthēton kai akinēton).</note>. Yet it appeared differently to the Apostle when he had fallen upon him and embraced him, for he sensed the natural spirit and the vital heat of the blood and limbs, which could not exist without the <term>information</term> <note>The process by which the soul gives life and structure to the body.</note> of the soul. Therefore he said, *The soul is in him*. This is just as it is said in the books of Moses, *The soul is in the blood* <note>original: "Anima est in sanguine." A reference to Leviticus 17:11, often translated as "the life is in the blood."</note>. For although the rational soul was not performing its functions, and although even the sensitive soul was not exercising its senses and movements due to the cessation caused by that great fall (and therefore he was picked up as if dead, and believed to be so by everyone), nevertheless Paul knew from his embrace that the soul was in him. He felt the signs of life, and therefore the presence of the rational soul in terms of its "information" of the body. 

What seems to favor this explanation above all is that Luke <note>The traditional author of the Book of Acts.</note> makes no mention of a "resurrection" <note>A rising from the dead.</note>. On the contrary, he says in verse 12: *They brought the boy alive*. It is as if he were saying: he who was believed by all to be dead was brought back alive at the time when Paul was speaking and breaking bread. This sufficiently implies that the soul had been in him, just as Paul said. For a body could fall from a high place without perishing, either because houses at that time were not very high, or because a falling body can be caught by something soft, as the illustrious... <note>The sentence ends abruptly, likely continuing on the next page.</note> told concerning Louis Civil <note>original: "Ludouico Ciuili." Likely referring to Louis de Civil (1537–1611), a French soldier famously said to have been buried alive and survived three "deaths."</note>.

...illustrious Thuanus <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a famous French historian and statesman.</note> records in his history, which he recounts as something of a miracle, that **Louis Civil** <note>A French nobleman known for surviving three near-death experiences during the Siege of Rouen in 1562.</note> always signed documents in this way: *Louis Civil, three times dead, buried, and by the grace of God raised.* We have offered various interpretations of this passage, all following the **analogy of faith** <note>The theological principle that individual Bible verses should be interpreted in the context of the whole of Christian doctrine.</note>, in no way deviating from the *pattern of sound words* <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τῆς ὑποτυπώσεως ὑγιαινόντων λόγων (apo tēs hypotypōseōs hygiainontōn logōn); a reference to 2 Timothy 1:13.</note>. Each person may choose the interpretation that is more to their taste. However, whichever is chosen—whether all of them or some individually—the Roman Catholics will find throughout them a refutation of their errors and of their **horned dilemma** <note>A logical trap (dilemma cornutum) where both possible answers lead to an unfavorable conclusion for the opponent.</note>. And although we bring forward explanations that are contrary to one another, there is no inconsistency, because this opposition does not concern the law, but the fact: namely, was Eutychus truly dead or not?

And let these things be said concerning Eutychus to illustrate the history of Moses. For although at the **Transfiguration** <note>The event described in the Gospels where Jesus is seen in glory on a mountain with Moses and Elijah.</note> the soul of Moses could have been clothed in a bodily appearance, such as those in which Angels appeared (assumed for a time), it is nevertheless more probable that the very body of Moses was truly raised from the dead, just like those of other faithful people who were raised at the death of Christ or at other times. Indeed, since Moses was the companion of **Elijah**, so that one might testify to the **Law** and the other to the **Prophets** (because the Law and the Prophets gave testimony to Christ), Moses must have had his true body, just as Elijah had his own true body, not a borrowed one. For it was worth the effort that those two, who were the leaders among the Jews and who had so strictly reformed the worship of God, should give testimony to Him who had come into the world so magnificently and solemnly to purify His Church with His own blood. Thus, just as Moses was a most illustrious **type** <note>A "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament that foreshadows something in the New Testament.</note> of Christ, so he ought to have seen Him in the flesh, whom he had previously prefigured. Furthermore, just as Moses saw the land of **Canaan** (which was the land of promise) with his physical eyes before the people entered into it, so he ought to have seen Christ the **Mediator**, promised long ago, manifested in the flesh before His ascension into heaven and before the introduction of the entire people of God into the heavenly Canaan. Finally, just as of old a singular privilege had been granted to Moses to see God face to face on the mountain...

All these scriptural proofs confirm the truth concerning the immortality of souls; therefore, it is quite surprising how the **Sadducees** <note>A Jewish sect of the time of Jesus that represented the priestly aristocracy; they were known for denying the resurrection of the dead and the existence of spirits.</note> could deny the immortality of souls and the resurrection of the flesh. For even if those Jewish heretics admitted only the **Pentateuch** <note>The first five books of the Bible (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy), attributed to Moses.</note> while rejecting the other books of Scripture, a sufficient refutation was still supplied from those very books. This was evident both from the history of the death and burial of Moses, and from the oracles drawn from them, as proven by the Greatest Prophet and their interpreter, Christ, in Matthew 22, by citing a passage from the book of Exodus. Against those **dwellers in darkness** <note>original Latin: tenebriones; a pejorative term for those who avoid the light of truth.</note>, those Pagans will rise in judgment who, led by their own reasoning and the light of nature, believed in the immortality of souls. The first of all these is said to be **Pherecydes of Syros** <note>An early Greek thinker (6th century BCE) often credited with being the first to teach the immortality of the soul in a philosophical context.</note>, so named not because he was Syrian by nationality, but because he hailed from the island of Syros, which was not in Palestine, but one of the islands of the Aegean Sea. Hence, Greece wrongly boasted of its **Seven Sages** <note>A group of seven 6th-century BCE Greek philosophers, statesmen, and lawgivers renowned for their wisdom.</note>, as if any solid wisdom could be established among those who were ignorant of the immortality of souls, and consequently, of the resurrection of bodies and eternal life. For these things are so joined together that if one is granted, the other must necessarily be granted, and if one is denied, the other is denied; this is clear from the **Pharisees** <note>A Jewish social movement and a school of thought that, unlike the Sadducees, believed in the oral law, the resurrection, and the existence of angels.</note> who admitted both, and the Sadducees who denied both. Truly, therefore, Paul says in Romans 1, <note>original Greek: φάσκοντες εἶναι σοφοὶ ἐμωράνθησαν (phaskontes einai sophoi emōranthēsan)</note> "claiming to be wise, they became fools."

But what shall we say of **Aristotle** <note>The famous Greek philosopher, often referred to by the author as "the Stagirite" after his birthplace, Stagira.</note>, who was truly called an "infinite end" <note>original Greek: ἄπειρον τέλος (apeiron telos)</note> and a **Spirit** <note>original Greek: Δαίμων (Daimōn); in this classical context, it refers to a supernatural power or a genius-level intellect.</note> because of his knowledge? What did he himself believe concerning the immortality of souls? I find a threefold opinion among authors, for he delivered his oracles concerning the immortality of the soul as ambiguously as a spirit, and indeed with double meaning. Therefore, someone might aptly have said to him what was once said to the hesitating Tiberius, who "held a wolf by the ears": **either act or desist**; or as that saying goes, "either drink, or depart" <note>original Greek: ἢ πίδι [sic], ἢ ἄπιθι (ē pithi, ē apithi); a common Greek proverb regarding social or intellectual participation.</note>. One opinion is of those who say he affirmed it. Another of those who say he denied it. The third of those who say he hesitated. And indeed, by leafing through his writings, it is difficult to know what the **Stagirite** <term>Stagirite: A common title for Aristotle, referring to his hometown of Stagira.</term> felt. In fact, it is easy to find those three opinions within his own [writings...]

...to extract and demonstrate from books. Therefore, not without merit, someone once said of him: "You would never know those with whom you are associated." <note>original Greek: ἐκ ἂν γνοίης ποτέ οἷσι μετεῖν. This is a fragment likely suggesting that the depth of a thinker's soul or their afterlife connections are hidden from common view.</note>

As for the modern Jews, they condemn those errors of the **Sadducees** <note>A Jewish sect active in Judea during the Second Temple period that famously denied the resurrection of the dead and the existence of spirits.</note> concerning the immortality of souls and the resurrection. Although many among them teach certain things about the **Secret of Revolution** <note>original: *sod haggilgol*; this refers to *Gilgul*, the Kabbalistic concept of the transmigration of souls or reincarnation.</note>, they nevertheless hand down many excellent teachings concerning the reviving of the dead. Such teachings are found in the works of **Rabbi Gedalia** <note>Gedaliah ibn Yahya (c. 1515–1587), an Italian Jewish chronicler and philosopher.</note>, who was the author of the book titled *The Tree of Life* <note>original Hebrew: עץ חיים (*Etz Chaim*).</note>.

So too the book titled *The Intellectual Adam* <note>original Hebrew: אדם שכלי (*Adam Sichli*), meaning "The Intellectual Man."</note>, which is a mystical work. Among other things, it contains the thirteen articles of the Jewish faith; in the last of these, regarding the resurrection of the dead, mention is made of the bone **Luz** <note>A legendary bone, often identified as the coccyx or a bone at the base of the skull, which Jewish tradition held was indestructible and would serve as the "seed" for the resurrection of the body.</note>. They believe this bone to be incorruptible, and they imagine—or rather, they dream—that it is irrigated by celestial dew, thereby restoring the body to the soul and causing the person to live again through its benefit.

Observe, however, my dearest listeners, that the Hebrew teachers do not hold an entirely correct view of the resurrection. For although they confess the resurrection of the godly, they do not feel the same way about the wicked. Indeed, they believe the wicked will not rise again, perhaps based on **Psalm 1:5**: "The wicked shall not stand" <note>original Hebrew: לא יקמו רשעים (*lo yakumu resha’im*).</note>. And as it is added in that same place: "In the judgment" <note>original Hebrew: במשפט (*ba-mishpat*).</note>.

The Vulgate edition <note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible that became the Catholic Church's official version.</note> states explicitly: *The ungodly shall not rise again in judgment.* **Junius** <note>Francis Iunius (1545–1602), a prominent Huguenot theologian and biblical scholar.</note> translates this as "they shall not stand forth," looking to the underlying sense; for as he says in his notes, "they will not dare to present themselves even with a raised countenance." Indeed, the Hebrew words *lo yakumu* properly mean "they shall not stand" or "they shall not endure." 

Because the Jews assert that the wicked will not rise again, the **Genesis Rabbah** <note>An ancient collection of Jewish midrashic (interpretive) commentaries on the Book of Genesis.</note> (section 28) says this about the bone **Luz**: "Even the Luz of the vertebrae, from which God will cause man to sprout again in the future, was destroyed—namely, in the Flood." For since they devise this notion that the Luz bone is the germ by which bodies are brought back to life, and because those wicked people who were drowned in the Flood are not to rise again, they believe that bone was destroyed or consumed; otherwise, even in those people, there would have been a seminal germ of resurrection. 

Hence, with respect to the faithful who are to rise again, it is said in the **Zohar** <note>The foundational work in the literature of Jewish mysticism, the Kabbalah.</note> regarding Genesis: "For behold, there is a certain bone which remains incorruptible in a man" <note>original Aramaic: דהא גרמא חד דאשתאר ביה בברנש (*de-ha garma chad de-ishta’ar beh be-bar nash*).</note> "under the earth," <note>original Aramaic: תחת ארעא (*tachat ar’a*).</note>

Furthermore, the root of this bone is from heaven itself, and it is moistened by the dew with which God will one day call the dead back to life, just as leaven acts within a mass of flour. This bone is called **Luz** <note>original Hebrew: לוז</note> because it is similar to an **almond** <note>original Aramaic: לוזא (*luza*)</note>; and it is located at the end of the eighteen vertebrae of the back. Nor are there lacking fables that the Rabbis use to prove this. For the **Yalkut** <note>An ancient compilation of Jewish midrash (scriptural commentary), specifically the *Yalkut Shimoni*.</note>, in the exposition of the 12th chapter of Ecclesiastes, says: *The Emperor Hadrian asked Rabbi Joshua, the son of Haninah, saying: "From what part will God raise man in the world to come?" He responded, "From the little bone of the spine." Hadrian asked, "How would I know this?" They brought such a bone before him and placed it in water, but it was not softened; they placed it in fire, but it was not burned; they put it in a mill, but it was not ground; they put it on an anvil and struck it with a hammer, which broke the anvil, but the bone felt no defect.* All these things recited by the Teachers of the Hebrews smack entirely of old wives' tales unless they are smoothed over by some mystical sense, just like countless other things contained in the **Talmud**. For if these things were understood literally, the Hebrews would be speaking of the resurrection as some kind of physical transformation—as if God truly required some germ or seed, such as the **Luz** bone, for the reviving of the dead, just as nature cannot generate anything without a seed. Surely He who created the whole world out of nothing is able to raise bodies from the dust of the earth? Nevertheless, if the Rabbis understood these things as a certain **moral instrument** <note>In this context, a "moral instrument" refers to a symbolic or legal tool of God's will rather than a biological or mechanical necessity.</note> rather than a physical one, their opinion would not be so absurd. For they would imply this: just as God created Adam from mud—in which there was not a **physical or privative power** but a **logical or negative power**—so on the last day He will rouse Adam and other men from the **Luz** bone. That is to say, from mud or from the dust of the earth; not that this will properly be a physical seed of this resurrection, but rather a moral instrument, which is essentially like nothing. Therefore, just as the mud did not prevent Adam from...

...[just as] the production was truly a creation, because the mud contributed no power toward the production of Adam, so too the earth from which God will form the bodies of the dead will not prevent that restoration to life from being a true resurrection and a miraculous production of God. 

Indeed, the Rabbis devise these things about the bone because they perhaps look back to the vision of Ezekiel in chapter 37, regarding the bones which return to life and upon which nerves, flesh, and skin are placed. However, whatever that mystical sense might be—which surely must often be observed in the Talmud <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah (laws) and the Gemara (commentaries).</note>—nevertheless, those sharp Doctors conduct themselves wrongly whenever they wrap those divine mysteries of faith in their own "husks" and "coverings," <note>The author likely refers to the "shells" (*kelipot*) of Jewish mysticism—the idea that spiritual truths are hidden beneath layers of literal or external tradition. A Latin idiom meaning to approach a sacred or difficult subject without proper preparation, reverence, or purity.</note> but according to the simplicity of the Scriptures. 

And let these things suffice regarding their opinion, as well as concerning the death, burial, and resurrection of Moses; with which, *with God's help* <note>original Greek: σὺν Θεῷ (*syn Theo*)</note> under God's auspices, we have completed the entire Pentateuch <term>Pentateuch: The first five books of the Bible, traditionally attributed to Moses.</term> according to our plan. Amen.

*Guilt known from three sources. Four momentous reasons concerning the knowledge of sin. That those four reasons were clear in the sin of Achan.*

The mystery within the number three. The observation of Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note> regarding the Hebrew words that signify anger.*

What kind of imputation exists in the sin of Achan? Imputation is twofold, namely proper and improper. That the sins of collateral relatives <note>Relations who are not in a direct line of descent, such as siblings or cousins.</note> are not imputed. In different senses, the imputation of Achan's sin is both proper and improper. Furthermore, imputation is threefold: natural, moral, and civil. Achan’s sin could not be imputed either by God's absolute power or by His hypothetical power. The imputation of Achan’s sin is civil. Civil imputation is a middle ground between natural and moral. What kind of imputation of sin is there regarding the sons and daughters of Achan? How God’s providence and mercy are revealed in that imputation of Achan. ### *The Curse of Achan, Joshua chap. VII.*

### SUMMARY ANALYSIS.

*Puzzles and difficulties that occur regarding the Curse of Achan. The foundations of those difficulties. The division of the entire investigation <note>original Greek: συζητήσεως (syzeteseos), meaning a joint search or philosophical inquiry</note> into three parts. Two other observations are added concerning the concepts of these languages. Two reasons for the Greek name Anathema <term>Anathema: In Greek, this originally meant something set apart or dedicated to a god, but in a biblical context, it came to mean someone or something "devoted" to destruction or cut off from the community.</term>. What Cherem <term>Cherem: A Hebrew term for something strictly forbidden or devoted to total destruction as an offering to God; it cannot be redeemed or reclaimed.</term> meant among the Hebrews. Three types of Curses among the Hebrews. The custom of the Persians when they pronounce a curse. Why do they throw dust? What does the symbol of dust signify to the Persians? Two noteworthy observations about the shaking off of dust. That in the Gospel, Christ often alludes to the rituals of the Jews. God is offended by no crime more than by contempt for His word. Why Paul uses the voice Maranatha and not Schammata <term>Schammata: The most severe form of Jewish excommunication, often involving a total social and religious banishment.</term> which was customary in the Jewish Church? Five observations are offered on the use of the word Schammata. Three types of Anathemas opposed to three laws. In what sense do the impious say "anathema" to Christ? The abuse by the Jews regarding curses. Three explanations of the passage in Matthew 15:5 and Mark 7:11 regarding Corban <term>Corban: A Hebrew word for an offering or gift dedicated to God. In the New Testament, Jesus critiqued the practice where individuals claimed their money was "Corban" to avoid the moral obligation of caring for their aging parents.</term>. The abuse of the Catholics <note>original: Pontificiorum, referring to the followers of the Pope or the Roman Catholic hierarchy</note> in their pronunciations of anathema in three ways. SINCE this history of the curse of Achan has greatly tormented interpreters until now, and has seemed to them a "crux" <note>original Latin: *crux*, meaning a cross or a particularly torturous puzzle</note>, and since not everyone seems to hold the same judgment, we also (having first implored the inspiration of the Divine power, without which all human efforts and attempts are in vain) will freely offer our modest labor. That which primarily increases the difficulty of this divine pronouncement, or causes "riddles" <note>original Latin: *gryphos*, referring to the Sphinx's riddles or complex puzzles</note> to arise, seems to be this: that God’s justice is immensely assaulted. For although Achan alone sinned and was caught and convicted of such great guilt, nevertheless the innocent are punished along with that source of the crime—and not only his children and household, but even other Israelites. These were not even members of his own tribe, but valiant soldiers; about three thousand men from other tribes went up indiscriminately, of whom thirty-six fell, as is clear from verse 5 of the same chapter VII <note>Joshua 7:5</note>. Therefore, Achan’s fault seems to be imputed to them, as well as to his children, contrary to the express testimonies of Scripture: *The soul that sins shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.* <note>Ezekiel 18:20</note> These matters must be distinctly discussed by us; however, so that the whole history may be more fully explained, we shall divide it into three chapters.

I. The first will concern the fault of Achan, which is the Accursed Thing <term>Anathema: Here referring to the "devoted things" or "curse" (Cherem) that Achan stole from the ruins of Jericho.</term>.
II. The second will concern the discovery of the curse committed in secret, which is made public by three means: 1. From God's burning indignation. 2. From the casting of lots. 3. From the confession of the guilty party himself.
III. Finally, the third chapter will be about the punishment inflicted on the defendant and others, where we shall discuss the imputation of Achan’s sin.

I. The sin of Achan is rightly considered enormous, and according to the opinions of the ancient Hebrews, it was entangled in two outrages. For as it is held in the book *Tanhuma* or *Yelamdenu* <note>original Hebrew: ילמדנו (Yelamdenu). These are titles for a collection of Midrashim, or ancient Jewish homiletic commentaries on the Pentateuch.</note>, Achan was defiled by two crimes. First, that of impiety and profanation, because he violated the Sabbath day; for since (say the Rabbis) Jericho was captured on the Sabbath day, Achan was doing his own business, not God’s; or as Isaiah speaks, by "doing his own will" <note>Isaiah 58:13</note>, he profaned the holy day. For this outrage, God, when consulted, had established the punishment of stoning, as seen in Numbers 15:35. Secondly, Achan was guilty of sacrilege because of the Accursed Thing, and therefore he is burned after having first been stoned, so that the punishment of sacrilegious men—

SINCE this history concerning the accursed thing <note>original: "anathemate," referring to the devoted or cursed items Achan took from Jericho</note> of Achan has greatly tormented interpreters until now, and has seemed to them a "crux" <note>a "crux" refers to a point that is particularly difficult to interpret or resolve</note>, nor does the judgment of all seem to be the same; we also (having first implored the inspiration of the Divine power, without which all human efforts and endeavors are in vain) will freely offer our own small service. What increases the difficulty of this oracle in the first place, or causes riddles to arise, seems to be this: that God's justice is immensely shaken, since although Achan alone sinned and was found convicted of such great guilt, nevertheless the innocent are punished along with that source of the crime. And these were not only his children and household, but also other Israelites, and those not even from his own tribe, but valiant soldiers—about three thousand from other tribes—went up indiscriminately, of whom thirty-six fell, as is clear from verse 5 of the same seventh chapter. Therefore, Achan's fault seems to be imputed to them, as well as to his sons, contrary to the express testimonies of Scripture: *The soul that sins shall die; the son shall not bear the father’s iniquity.* <note>original: "Anima quae peccaverit morietur, filius non portabit iniquitatem patris," citing Ezekiel 18:20</note> These matters must be discussed by us distinctly, but in order for the whole history to be more fully explained, we shall divide it into three chapters.

I. Will be concerning the fault of Achan, which is the <term>Anathema: things devoted to God or set apart for destruction</term>. 
II. Concerning the discovery of the accursed thing committed in secret, which is made public through three means: 1. From God's burning indignation. 2. From the casting of the lot. 3. From the confession of the guilty party himself. 
And finally, the third chapter will be concerning the punishment inflicted on the defendant and others, where we shall discuss the imputation of Achan's sin.

# I.

Achan's sin is deservedly considered enormous, and according to the opinions of the ancient Hebrews, it involved two outrages. For as it is held in the book *Tanhuma* or <term>Yelammedenu <note>original: "ילמדנו," a title for a collection of homiletic midrashim, meaning "May he teach us"</note></term>, Achan was stained by two crimes; first, that of impiety and profanation, because he violated the Sabbath day; for since (as the Rabbis say) Jericho was captured on the Sabbath day, Achan was doing his own business, not God's; or as Isaiah speaks, "doing his own will," he profaned the holy day. For this outrage, God, when consulted, had established the punishment of stoning, Numbers 15:35. Secondly, Achan was guilty of sacrilege because of the Accursed Thing, and for that reason he was burned after first being stoned, so that the punishment of the sacrilegious...

# MARC ANTOINE CREGUT

<meta>catchword: word</meta>

...by law he would be condemned. However, to judge that shameful crime, the Holy Spirit in Joshua 7:1 uses the word *mahal* <note>Hebrew: מעל, often translated as a breach of faith or a sacrilegious trespass</note> which Symmachus rendered as *contemptuous neglect* <note>Greek: καταγνώσιν (katagnōsin)</note>. Indeed, this interpretation will perhaps not seem inappropriate in this passage when dealing with the imputation of Achan's sin. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> used the word for *error* or *discord* <note>Greek: πλημμελείας (plēmmeleias)</note>: *And the sons of Israel committed a trespass and they took for themselves from the accursed thing* <note>Greek: καὶ ἐπλημμέλησαν οἱ υἱοὶ Ἰσραὴλ πλημμέλειαν, καὶ ἐνοσφίσαντο ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀναθέματος</note>. In this, however, three things must be observed. 

I. These translations do not entirely express the Hebrew naming, because *mahal* says more than "contemptuous neglect" or "to trespass." Certainly, the word *to know* <note>Greek: γινώσκειν (ginōskein)</note> with its compounds is of the greatest use in Scripture; for *to know* usually sounds different than *to acknowledge*, *to read*, and *to despise* <note>Greek: ἐπιγινώσκειν (epiginōskein), ἀναγινώσκειν (anaginōskein), and καταγνώσκειν (katagnōskein)</note>. *To know* is taken broadly for a merely theoretical knowledge of God, such as that held by unbelievers; but *to acknowledge* refers to a practical recognition of God, such as that of the faithful, which is joined with the worship of God, as is clear from 2 Peter 1:3: *through the acknowledgment of him who called us* <note>Greek: διὰ τῆς ἐπιγνώσεως τοῦ καλέσαντος ἡμᾶς</note>. 

For this reason, our Theodore Beza <note>A prominent 16th-century Protestant theologian and successor to John Calvin</note> rebukes the common translator <note>The translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> when he renders it as "knowledge" rather than "acknowledgment." For the wicked often *know* God, and in some way taste what they have known, but only the faithful *acknowledge* God as their father—though I would easily concede that this distinction is not always maintained. *To read* <note>Greek: ἀναγινώσκειν (anaginōskein)</note> adds, moreover, frequent reading and mention, which is why in the ancient Church there were *Readers* <note>Greek: ἀναγνῶσται (anagnōstai)</note> in the churches; even Julian—who was later a degenerate Emperor and apostate—had been a Reader of the Church of Nicomedia. Finally, *to despise* <note>Greek: καταγνώσκειν (katagnōskein)</note> signifies to know with contempt, or to neglect. 

But *to trespass* <note>Greek: τὸ πλημμελεῖν (to plēmmelein)</note> properly signifies to do something in a disordered and uncomposed way, as if you were to say, according to the composition of the word, "out of tune" or "beyond the melody." From this comes the metaphor for sinning, because sins take away the melody of the soul, which—as Plato testifies—is a harmonic <term>number</term> <note>original: ἀριθμὸς (arithmos). Plato frequently discussed the soul in terms of mathematical ratios and musical harmony</note>. But *mahal* sounds like something worse, namely to prevaricate, or to commit a crime. 

II. Observe that here there is a "Hebraism" <note>A Hebrew-style grammatical construction</note> *trespassing a trespass* <note>original Hebrew: מעל מעל מעלו (mahal ma’al ma’alo)</note>, just as in Joshua 22:20: *he trespassed a trespass* <note>original: מעל מעל (mahal ma’al)</note>. Since this is a redundant expression...

# THE REVEALER OF SECRETS

...the fact that a verb governs a noun derived from the same root is not only stylistically elegant but also expresses a certain vehemence and certainty regarding the action. This was noted by Rabbi David Kimchi <note>A famous medieval Jewish grammarian and commentator (1160–1235)</note> in his work *Michlol*, page 48. For example, in Zechariah 1:2, "God seethed with seething" <note>original Hebrew: קצף קצף (*qatsaph qatsaph*)</note>, meaning He seethed most vehemently. And in Genesis 2:17 <note>The text mistakenly cites Genesis 11:17</note>, it was said to Adam, *in dying you shall die*, meaning you will most certainly die. This is no different than the Greek and Latin expressions *to rejoice with joy* <note>Greek: χαρᾷ χαίρειν; Latin: Gaudio gaudere</note> or *to fight a fight* <note>Greek: μάχεσθαι μάχην; Latin: pugnare pugnam</note>. 

In this way, the Holy Spirit uses this repetition <note>The technical term used is "pleonasm," using more words than necessary for emphasis</note> not only to heighten the transgression (which was doubled because it involved both the violation of the Sabbath and sacrilege) but also to demonstrate the certainty of the crime. Even though the forbidden objects were hidden and the act was not committed in the open, all things are most certainly known to God. Paul expresses this elegantly in Hebrews 4:13 when he wrote, *all things are naked and opened to his eyes*. For according to the ancient grammarians, *to be opened* <note>Greek: Τραχηλίζειν (*trachēlizein*)</note> means *to be cut in half* <note>Greek: διχοτομεῖν (*dichotomein*)</note>, or *to be split through the spine of the back* <note>Greek: τὸ διὰ τῆς ῥάχεως σχίζειν (*to dia tēs rhacheōs schizein*)</note>. This maintains the metaphor of the "two-edged sword," signifying that even the innermost parts of a person are open to God. Indeed, the Apostle continues there with the metaphor of the joints and marrow (as seen in verse 12); for just as a *two-edged sword* <note>Greek: μάχαιρα δίστομος (*machaira distomos*)</note> reaches to the division of *soul and spirit, joints and marrow*, so in verse 13 he says *all things are laid open*, as if God were dissecting the twenty-four vertebrae <note>Greek: σπονδύλους (*spondylous*)</note> and separating the pairs or connections of every single nerve. 

III. Note here also that the Hebrew word *mahal* <note>מעל, meaning to trespass or act unfaithfully</note> can be said to be an allusion to *mehil* <note>מעיל</note>, which is derived from the same root. This word signifies a "cloak" or "robe" in Exodus 28:31 and many other places. Among the forbidden spoils of the curse was a scarlet cloak: for although the Hebrew in Joshua 7:21 uses the word *addereth* <note>אדרת</note> rather than *mehil*, this is because *mehil* signifies a simple cloak, whereas the one Achan stole was not common or vulgar, but very rich and magnificent. This is why the Scripture uses the word *addereth*, which Saint Jerome translated as a *scarlet cloak*. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> rendered it as a *variegated robe* <note>Greek: ψιλὴν ποικίλην (*psilēn poikilēn*)</note>. The Chaldean Paraphrase <note>The Aramaic translation or Targum</note> translates it as a *stole*, a word which broadly signifies any kind of garment, and more strictly a *toga*. To the word—

### ANTHONY CREGUT

*Addereth shinar* <note>original Hebrew: אדרת שנער; literally "a mantle of Shinar"</note> is a Babylonian military cloak. For even among the Romans, the Emperors used to go about *cloaked* <note>Latin: *paludati*</note> when they were armed and dressed in distinguished garments and ornaments, by which they stood out significantly and were made visible to all. **iv.** To this must be added that the translators of the Septuagint <note>The influential Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, often abbreviated as LXX</note> added on their own the word *enosphisanto* <note>original Greek: ἐνοσφίσαντο</note>, which means "they pocketed for themselves" or "stealthily took away," and they applied it to themselves so that the meaning would be more explicit; the Latin translator <note>The Vulgate</note> followed them in this, as he frequently does. **v.** Add to this that, so the enormity of that sin might be more clearly revealed, the Scripture joins the word *cherem* <note>original Hebrew: חרם</note>, that is, *anathema* <note>A thing devoted to God, often for destruction</note>, with the term *ma'al* <note>original Hebrew: מעל</note>, which designates a type of *prevarication* or *trespass*. No worse form of this sin can be given, as is clear from the example of Saul in 1 Samuel 15. He was rejected by God because he refused to utterly destroy the Amalekites, even though they had been devoted to total destruction and *anathema* by God's command. This was despite Saul pretending a good intention, such as having saved the best of the flocks and herds for a sacrifice, and having shown clemency toward King Agag. But what did Samuel say to Saul? *Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, He has likewise rejected you from being king* (1 Samuel 15:23). And in verse 22: *To obey is better than sacrifice, and to heed than the fat of rams.* Indeed, the enormity of this sin will be clearly understood if we investigate what an *anathema* is.

An *anathema* signifies a thing dedicated and consecrated to God. Micah 4:13: *And I will devote their gain to the Lord, and their wealth to the Lord of the whole earth.* For an *anathema* was a thing devoted to God and set apart, which it was not lawful to touch, nor to use for other purposes, nor to redeem, but it was necessary for it to be killed or destroyed. Therefore, *anathemata* were of two kinds: **1.** *For the sake of honor*, and to this category belong offerings, firstfruits, and the firstborn, which, however, it was lawful to redeem. **2.** *For the sake of horror and detestation*, such as lepers and others separated from the Church. And all these things are clearly indicated by the Greek and Hebrew naming. For the Greek word *anathema* <note>original: ἀνάθημα, or as the Septuagint always has it, ἀνάθεμα</note>, which the Apostle Paul also follows, is derived from *anatithenai* <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀνατιθέναι</note>, meaning "from setting apart." Since things devoted and consecrated to God are separated from human commerce and use, so also those cast out from the Church are removed from the communion of the faithful. Thus...

Photius, in the works of Oecumenius, explains *anathema* as *to be separated and alienated* <note>original Greek: χωρισθῆναι καὶ ἀλλοτριωθῆναι</note>. Budæus <note>Guillaume Budé (1467–1540), a famous French humanist scholar</note> truly says that *anathemata* <note>original Greek: ἀναθέματα</note> are "sacred" men—that is, those whose lives are dedicated to the powers below. But *anathēmata* <note>original Greek: ἀναθήματα</note>, spelled with the long "e" (*eta*), are gifts consecrated to the gods. He derives both terms *from the verb "to set up," that is, "to place upon"* <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τὸ ἀνατιθέναι, τῶτ’ ἐστὶν ἀνάτιθεν</note>, because the condemnation of those men used to be publicly posted on stone tablets, and those gifts were hung upon the walls and columns of temples.

Nevertheless (let this be said with all due respect to Budæus, who is truly *bou-daios* <note>original Greek: β8-δαῖος; a pun on his name suggesting "exceedingly knowledgeable"</note>), that distinction between *anathēmata* and *anathemata* cannot easily be proven by constant usage—which is the ultimate law and norm of speaking—even though I would not deny that *anathēma* specifically declares a "consecrated gift," as is clear from Luke 21:5, when the temple is said to be *adorned with beautiful stones and gifts* <note>original Greek: καὶ ἀναθήμασι; Latin: donariis</note>. Thus, that word could rightly have a double etymology: either *from the verb "to set apart"* <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τὸ ἀνατιθέναι</note>, that is, *to put aside*, because those gifts, having been chosen from other goods, are usually consecrated as if set apart for sacred use; or from *ana* meaning *upward* <note>original Greek: ἄνω</note> and *tithenai* meaning *to place*, because they would be lifted up and hung on columns and tablets.

In this way, *anathema* would beautifully correspond to those offerings which the Hebrews call *terumah* <note>original Hebrew: תרומה</note>, about which we have spoken extensively in our work on Melchizedek. For *terumah* comes from the root *rum* <note>original Hebrew: רום</note>, which declares the same thing: *to lift up high*. For the priest, according to solemn ritual, used to lift up the offerings he carried in his hands as if in the sight of God. But truly, the *anathema* mentioned in Romans 9:3—although it is also said to be *from the verb "to set apart"*—is of a far different meaning. For while the former is for the sake of honor, this latter is for the sake of horror. Hence, it does not correspond to the word *terumah* as before, but to the word *cherem* <note>original Hebrew: חרם</note>, which is from *charam* <note>original Hebrew: חרם</note>, used in the <term>Hiphil</term> <note>The causative verb form in Hebrew, often indicating an action performed upon something else</note> to mean *to cut off* or *to devote to utter destruction*. This term is used by all the Oriental languages to signify an *anathema*; indeed, all except Arabic use it specifically in the *Hiphil* conjugation for the sake of a greater *intensification* <note>original Greek: αὔξησιν</note> of the meaning. This is because these lives are not devoted to God by some ordinary consecration, but in a certain peculiar way; so that the *cherem* <note>the devoted thing</note> is utterly cut off and destroyed, such that we have no right to redeem it, but must utterly renounce it, so that not even...

The Apostle, burning with the zeal of God and charity, exaggerates this immensely in Romans 9:3 when he desires "to be accursed from Christ" <note>original Greek: ἀνάθεμα εἶναι ἀπὸ τοῦ χριστοῦ</note>, which last words demonstrate eternal destruction. Hence it is that according to some, that word <term>Cherem <note>Hebrew: חרם; a term for something devoted to God or banned from common use, often carrying the weight of a curse</note></term> refers to the extreme and most horrendous anathema, concerning which it is said in 1 Corinthians 16:22: *If anyone does not love Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema Maranatha*. 

For learned men complain that this Syriac phrase is corrupted, and that it should not be written as two words, *maran-atha*, but would better be said as one, *maharanatha*, because among the Arameans <term>maharanatha <note>Aramaic: מהרנתא</note></term> derives from *cherem* <note>Hebrew: חרם</note>, which signifies "Anathema."
