Or from three: *mar* <note>Syriac: מר</note>, "Lord," *na* <note>Syriac: נא</note>, "our," and *atha* <note>Syriac: אתא</note>, "has come." 

And thus a kind of extreme Anathema would be designated, the formula for which would be *maranatha*, as if the person were condemned and devoted to the Lord, delivered as if into the hands of the judge without any hope of pardon. The faithful and the martyrs also call upon or appeal to him in the Apocalypse: "Even so, come Lord Jesus" <note>original Greek: ναὶ ἔρχου κύριε Ἰησοῦ</note>, as if they were saying *maran-atha* in Syriac. 

And so that word would be taken <term>technically <note>original Greek: τεχνικῶς; used as a specific liturgical or legal term rather than common speech</note></term>, like other Syriac words used in the primitive Church, such as *Abba, Hallelujah, Amen*. And indeed, the aforementioned passage in 1 Corinthians 16:22 favors this origin, where the word *Anathema* precedes, and then *Maranatha* follows; whereas, if we were to follow the former opinion, it seems *maharanatha* should have preceded, and then *Anathema* followed as an explanation of what went before, as in Romans 8 and elsewhere: "Abba, Father" <note>where "Abba" (Syriac) is followed by "Father" (Greek) as a translation</note>. 

Nevertheless, to say in a word what I think: both notions seem to me to be of equal weight, and I consider both to be consistent with reason, since on both sides the analogy of words and inflections holds firm. Nor does it oppose the first opinion that the word *anathema* is placed before it; because *maharanatha*, as a single word from *cherem*, can be taken <term>technically <note>original Greek: τεχνικῶς</note></term>, no differently than in the other compound *maran-atha*. Indeed, it is even easier than that, according to the usage of the Hebrews who place *cherem* among the types of Anathema. And therefore *Maharanatha* could have been a technical term <note>technologema</note>, and thus one need not resort to conjectures that the scribes might have changed...

Therefore "anathema" correctly corresponds to the word <term>Cherem <note>Hebrew: חרם; a term for something devoted to God or banned from common use, often carrying the weight of a curse</note></term>, or <term>Arur <note>Hebrew: ארור; "cursed"</note></term> according to others; in Greek it is <term>epikataratos <note>Greek: ἐπικאτάρατος</note></term>, *cursed*, as in Romans 9:3.

However, it does not seem that the Hebrew Masters support us in all things here. For they establish three types of anathema in their <term>Roshei Tevot <note>Hebrew: ראשי תיבות; literally "heads of words," meaning acronyms or abbreviations</note></term>, that is, in their abbreviations, in this way: <term>N.D.Sh. <note>Hebrew: נד"ש</note></term>, which they interpret as <term>Niddu, Cherem, and Shammata <note>Hebrew: נדוי, חרם, שמתא</note></term>. Under these, Rabbi Gershom <note>Rabbi Gershom ben Judah (c. 960–1040), a famous Talmudist and Halakhist</note>, who is commonly called the "Light of the Exile" <note>Latin: *lumen captiuitatis*</note>, forbade the opening of letters; hence this abbreviation is often used on the back of letters. Yet, among those types of Anathema, the Talmudists <note>scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note> classify *Shammata* as the extreme anathema. Thus, *Niddu* is the first type of anathema or excommunication, which brings about a separation, but specifically because of impurity; the naming is derived from menstruating women, who were separated from their husbands during their period. So this word signifies more than "anathema," which by the force of its etymology designates a simple separation, as was said above. But *Cherem*, beyond separation due to impurity and uncleanness, still implies dire and horrific curses by which the ill-fated heads of mortals are devoted <note>to destruction</note>. Finally, if according to the Talmudists *Shammata* adds something as the extreme kind of anathema, it will further signify slaughter and extreme destruction, even eternal. 

Nevertheless, whatever the Talmudic doctors <note>Latin: *DD.*, abbreviation for *Doctores*</note> may have felt about this word *Shammata*, I see it confused with the word *Cherem* among the Targumists <note>translators or commentators of the Hebrew Bible into Aramaic</note>. Consequently, whenever *Cherem* appears in the Hebrew, the Chaldean [Aramaic] paraphrast translates it as *Shammata*, so that these notions are equivalent. Indeed, in the Hebrew context, the extreme anathema is always signified by *Cherem*, because this word comes from a root which signifies "to erase" or "to destroy." Therefore, whenever the Scripture deals with extreme destruction, the Hebrews use the word *Cherem*, and the Targum uses the word *Shammata*; as is clear from Deuteronomy 7:2: <insert>And you shall strike them to destruction, you shall utterly destroy them.</insert> <note>original Hebrew: וְהַכֵּיתָם הַחֲרֵם תַּחֲרִיס אֹתָם — Note: the source text has a typo 'תחריס' for the biblical 'תַּחֲרִים' (destroy)</note> So too in Deuteronomy 7:26: <insert>Lest by bringing an abominable thing into your house you be an anathema, just as it is; you shall utterly detest it and utterly abhor it, for it is an anathema.</insert> And indeed, in that third kind of anathema, nothing can be exco-

Indeed, not only is it destroyed in this life, but it is also exiled from eternal life—something which Moses, in an excess of love, desired for the glory of God, and which Paul mentions in **Romans 9:3**. <note>original Latin: *Rom. ix. 3*; Paul famously wrote that he could wish himself "accursed" or "anathema" for the sake of his people.</note> Finally, the blow of that <term>anathema <note>A formal curse by a religious authority, excommunicating a person or denouncing a doctrine.</note></term> is so violent and heavy that the one cursed could be utterly destroyed and reduced to nothingness, were it not that God, for His own glory, had decreed that this devoted head must be struck eternally. Thus, those sources which could not be struck by the anathema *intensively* <note>meaning: "in a single, infinite degree of intensity"</note> due to their finite nature, might at least be struck by everlasting destruction *extensively* <note>meaning: "in an infinite duration of time"</note>.

Hence it is that the Persians wished to exaggerate this kind of anathema with a certain symbol: namely, the throwing of dust on the head. For when the Persians call down curses upon someone, they say it thus: חרך בר שוש <note>Hebrew/Aramaic transcription of a Persian phrase</note>—that is, *let dust fall upon his head*. From this comes that blasphemous saying in honor of **Ali**: <note>Ali ibn Abi Talib, the cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad, central to Shia Islam.</note>

->*He who is not like dust before his door (Ali's), even if he were an Angel, dust covers his head. For I do not recognize Ali as God, but I know he is not far from God.*<-

These words are constantly on the lips of the Persians. From this also comes the phrase, *dust upon the head of your enemy.* The words of the Evangelist in **Matthew 10:14** seem related to this symbol of execration: *shake off the dust from your feet.* <note>original Greek: ἐκτινάξατε τὸν κονιορτὸν τῶν ποδῶν ὑμῶν</note>

From a different perspective, the Persians or Turks use the symbol of dust to testify to the highest respect, in this manner: *I am the dust of your feet.* Hence the proverb: "When I see a wise man or a blind man, I want my face to be the dust of his feet." For this reason, the Persians often contrast *the throne and the dust*, as the highest and the lowest, two extremes separated by infinite <term>parasangs</term>. <note>An ancient Persian unit of distance, roughly 3.5 miles.</note> From this comes the elegant proverb: *When a pure soul wishes to depart from the body, what does it matter then whether one dies on a throne or in the dust?*

Therefore, from that shaking off of dust, two things worthy of observation can be gathered:

1. The horror of the anathema itself, which is made clearly visible through that symbol. For it signifies that the devoted man, struck by the anathema, is worthy to be reduced immediately to the dust from which he was formed. This is proven from the name of **Adam**, if we believe the **Cabalists** <note>Followers of Kabbalah, a school of thought in Jewish mysticism.</note>. They say he was called *Adam* (אדם) because, according to a **Notaricon** <note>A Kabbalistic method of deriving shorthand meanings from the letters of a word.</note>, the name stands for *Apher, Dam, Marah* (אפר דם מרה)—that is, *ashes, blood, and gall [or bitterness]*...

But the faithful truly call Christ an **anathema**, yet in a far different sense—an **anathema** (I say) not of horror, but of honor, because he himself is the **Sanctuary of Sanctuaries** <term>Sanctuary of Sanctuaries <note>original Hebrew: *mikdas mikdaschim*</note></term>; for devoted things are often called **holiness** <note>original Hebrew: *kodesch*</note> in Scripture.

For the devoted things which the Greeks name **anathemata** <note>original: $\alpha\nu\alpha\theta\eta\mu\alpha\tau\alpha$</note> and **offerings** <note>original: $\alpha\nu\alpha\kappa\epsilon\acute{\iota}\mu\epsilon\nu\alpha$</note> are as much those things dedicated in sacred places as those which are burned and destroyed: which later the Jews in the time of Christ called **Corban** <note>original Hebrew: קרבן</note> and, by dropping the letter 'r' which has a harsher sound, **Coban** <note>original Hebrew: קובן</note>; from the root meaning *to offer*, carrying the same notion as the Greek **anathemata**. In this sense, Christ is the most precious **Coban**, since he offered himself to God the Father as a **ransom** <note>original Greek: $\alpha\nu\tau\acute{\iota}\lambda\upsilon\tau\rho\omicron\nu$</note>.

And let these things said thus far suffice regarding the doctrine of the anathema, as its parts and nature are established in the foundations of Scripture, and as they are practiced in the Jewish and Christian Church. However, here we wish to be far removed from the abuse of the erring Jews, as well as that of the **Papists** <term>Papists <note>The author uses the Latin *Pontificiorum* to refer to the Roman Catholic Church, a common term in Protestant theological works of this period.</note></term>, who for the most part rattle off "anathemas" with great pomp and effort, yet they are separated by a long distance from their legitimate use. 

For first, the Jews abused it under a great pretense of religion, when yet nothing was less of a concern to them. This is clear from that proverb or solemn formula found in the *treatise on oaths and vows* among the Hebrew Teachers: **Whatever it may be by which I might benefit you, or whatever utility you might take from me, let it be an Anathema and a devoted thing.** When someone used this vow toward anyone, no matter how closely bound by kinship—even toward their own parent—the Rabbis established that it was a sin for that person to help them with any kind of benefit or duty, lest what they had devoted to God should serve human comforts. 

This tradition Christ cites and condemns in **Matthew** and **Mark** as contrary to Moses. For Christ says in **Matthew 15:5** and **Mark 7:11**: *But you say, if anyone says to father or mother, "Corban" (that is, it is a gift) by whatever you might be helped by me, he shall be guiltless. And you no longer permit him to do anything for his father or his mother, making void the word of God by your tradition, etc.* <note>original Greek: $\Delta\tilde{\omega}\rho\omicron\nu$ $\ddot{o}$ $\acute{\epsilon}\alpha\nu$ $\hat{\epsilon}\xi$ $\acute{\epsilon}\mu\omicron\tilde{\upsilon}$ $\omega\phi\epsilon\lambda\eta\theta\tilde{\eta}\varsigma$</note>.

I. According to the Syriac translator in Mark 7:11: *If anyone says to his father or his mother, "Whatever you might have received from me is my offering":* <note>original Syriac: קורבני מדם דמני אתר</note>. II. <note>original Syriac: קורבני מדם דתהנא מני</note> It can be explained this way: The gift or anathema belongs to God, to whom all vows must be paid and who is the primary creditor; since I have consecrated everything I own to Him, there are no longer funds available to relieve your poverty.

III. Explain it this way if you like: The gift by which you could have been helped is devoted to God and consecrated to Him as an anathema; therefore, I cannot take anything from it to help you, because it would be a sin to use that anathema or make it common, for we ourselves would then become anathemas of horror.

Secondly, the Papists <note>A term used by Reformation-era writers to refer to supporters of the Pope.</note> also abuse the anathema when they brandish them through right or wrong like thunderbolts—especially the Pope, acting like another **Capitoline Jupiter** <note>The chief deity of Roman state religion; here used to imply the Pope's perceived arrogance.</note>, and the "little fathers" of the Council of Trent. Thus, if the proverb was once tossed around that kings play with treaties and oaths as children play with **knucklebones** <note>original: astragalis; an ancient game similar to dice.</note>, it is now more rightly said that the Papal councils play with anathemas as children play with knucklebones. This was made clear enough in the time of Pius IV, when an unusual weapon was brandished in the French sky against the King of Navarre and the Prince of Condé, though it was a blow struck in vain; Francis Hotman alluded to this in a mocking style in the book he titled, ***The Senseless Thunderbolt*** <note>original: Brutum fulmen. This was a famous legal and political rebuttal to the Pope's excommunication of French Protestant royalty.</note>. But the Popes sin especially because they usually brandish that triple thunderbolt of the anathema against wretched men for slight and worldly reasons.

**II.** Observe this also: since God knows sins, He cannot but be vehemently moved and grow hot with anger, because sin is like a fiery dart and the poison of the ancient serpent hurled against the nature of God. Therefore, just as in natural antipathies the whole of nature shudders, and because of opposing impulses it seems to suffer and growl through and through; so God, because of His antipathy toward sin (which, being the ultimate evil, seems to attack the nature of the highest good), shudders entirely, so to speak, and His nature—though it be most mild—nevertheless burns immensely and boils over as if with fury.

**III.** Observe also that since sin is **lawlessness** <note>original Greek: *anomia*, meaning a violation of the law</note>, it directly strikes at God’s justice. Therefore, God cannot be appeased unless His justice is satisfied, and thus punishment follows the fault, either in the sinner or in a **surety** <note>original Latin: *vade*, referring to a legal guarantor or substitute who pays a debt—in theology, often Christ</note>; God also signifies this in advance through temporal punishments, which is why among the Hebrews **sin** <note>original Hebrew: *chatta'at* (חטאת)</note> designates both the fault and the punishment.

**IV.** And add this: although God knows the sinner **inside and out** <note>original Latin: *intus & in cute*, a classical idiom literally meaning "inside and in the skin"</note>, He does not declare him by name, but having indicated the commission of the sin in a general sense, He leaves the rest to the diligence and investigation of men for various and momentous reasons, which may be recounted hereafter.

->**All these things are to be distinctly observed in the sin of Achan.**<-

Therefore, the first diagnostic sign to reveal the spiritual illness of the people is the "burning" or glowing anger of God. This is not because God is "angry" in a literal sense, for such a passion <note>an emotional disturbance or change</note> can in no way belong to a nature that is **impassible** <term>Impassibility: the theological doctrine that God does not experience pain or changing emotions from internal or external causes</term>. Thus, theologians commonly say that God is angry not in **feeling** <note>original: *affectu*</note> but in **effect** <note>original: *effectu*</note>. Not in *feeling*, because such a passion is absent from God, but it is attributed to Him **metaphorically** <note>original Greek: *anthropopathōs*, meaning speaking of God in human terms</note>; rather, it is demonstrated outwardly in the *effect*. 

For this reason, the Hebrews use the word **aph** <note>Hebrew: *aph*</note>, which properly signifies the **nose** and the **face**; and **appayim** <note>Hebrew: *appayim*</note> for the **nostrils**. From this comes the expression "to smoke from the nostrils." In Exodus 34:6, God is said to be **long of nostrils** <note>original Hebrew: *erekh appayim*</note>, which means He is **slow to anger**; just as, on the contrary, a quick-tempered man is called **short of nostrils** <note>original Hebrew: *qetsar appayim*</note> in Proverbs 14. Here, the Talmudic scholars <note>Jewish rabbis and commentators on the Talmud</note> ask why the word "nostrils" is used in the dual form (*appayim*). They answer that it is because He is long-suffering toward both the righteous and the wicked, so that both, when they sin, might be invited to repentance through God’s patience. This is indeed true, although it is better established that it is called *appayim* because there are two nostrils, and the face is divided into two parts. Just as in a man moved by rage, the heat of it is read in his face and in the steaming of his nostrils; so, by a human-like description <note>anthropopathy</note>, the same is attributed to God. This is demonstrated outwardly by the effect itself, when He takes notice of sinners and punishes them with avenging justice. For even if God permits sin by **physical permission**—that is, by not hindering one who wishes the act to be done for His own glory (for what is against His command does not happen without or beyond His will)—nevertheless He does not permit...

...ethical permission, that is, by approving and relaxing the law; for that supreme Lawgiver cannot deny himself, nor dispense with the law through such "ethical permission" as if anything were permitted to man, or as if everyone might presume what the King of the Persians once did: "whatever pleases is lawful." For although God, by a certain **concession** <note>original Greek: *synchōrēsei* — a term used to describe God "stepping down" to human weakness</note> or condescension, once tolerated certain evils in Israel—such as the bill of divorce <note>Hebrew: *keritut*; Greek: *biblon apostasias*</note>—nevertheless, God did not approve of it as something good. Rather, Moses, acting as a wise magistrate, tolerated a lesser evil for a **political reason** <term>ratione politica; refers here to the management of a civil society rather than absolute moral truth</term> in order to avoid a greater evil. Christ corrects this in Matthew 19:8, saying: **Moses allowed this because of the hardness of your hearts** <note>original Greek: *Mōisēs epetrepsen pros tēn sklērokardian*</note>. Therefore, what one obtained as a concession in the **political court** <term>forum politicum; the realm of human law and civil governance</term> can never be achieved in the **court of heaven** <term>forum poli; literally "the court of the pole/heavens," meaning God’s ultimate judgment seat</term>.

Furthermore, it should be observed that although God is slow to anger, once he is finally kindled, his wrath is most vehement. He seems to compensate for his slowness with the weight of the punishment. Scripture often expresses this with emphatic language, especially in this passage using two words: **burning anger** <note>original Hebrew: *charon aph*</note>. The first word signifies a "glowing" or "burning," while the second refers to the "nostrils" or "face." Thus, it describes an anger that stirs the breath in the nostrils and sets the face aflame. 

Yet, note the opposite as well: if God avenges sin intensely and severely, his anger does not last long. If he is slow to anger, then on the other hand, his lightning bolt passes quickly. If the torches of divine fury are slow to be lit, the heralds of peace are sent immediately afterward to announce it to sinners. Hence the memorable saying found in the *Bereshith Rabba* <note>An ancient Jewish commentary on the Book of Genesis</note>, that is, the "Great Genesis": *tribulations and adversities are often defined as lasting three days in the Scriptures.* Hosea 6:3 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Hosea 6:2</note>: **He will restore us to life after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his presence.** Genesis 42:17: **Joseph said to them, "Do this on the third day and you shall live."** Esther 5:1: **It happened on the third day that Esther put on her royal robes.** And they ascribe this "privilege of the third day" partly to the mystery of that third day on which the Law was given from heaven, and partly to the day on which Abraham is remembered for being ready to sacrifice his son to God...

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of how God reveals hidden truths to humanity. The previous page discussed the nature of divine wrath and referenced Maimonides; this page shifts to the mechanism of divine providence and the specific use of "lots" as a way to discern God's will.</meta>

# ANTOINE CRÉGUT #
### PAGE 1020 ###

...are for the most part hidden from little men <note>Latin: *homuncionibus*; a humble or diminutive term for human beings in contrast to the divine</note> and lie beyond the veil? II. God does not act immediately and by extraordinary power when ordinary means and power suffice; for it pleased God to govern the world in such a way that He might act through visible governance with visible creatures, and exhibit Himself as if to be touched within this machine of the world. III. Because the manifestation of any matter through a **lot** <note>Latin: *sortem*; the practice of "casting lots" to make a decision</note> is a divine manifestation; for when in complex and ambiguous matters no certain means are available, nor signs to distinguish something obscure, we then lawfully use a lot, committing the entire matter to the supreme Moderator and placing our trust in Him. He, by His wonderful providence governing every fortuitous event, directs the lot straight—better than an archer directs an arrow—so that it can never miss the mark. And thus a **lot** is not a physical instrument, which could produce an effect by physical influence, but is like a moral instrument and as if a certain **sacrament** given to men in secret matters to manifest a hidden truth.

Hence a **lot**, no differently than an **oath**, ought not to be used rashly, nor for a trivial reason; and he who casts a lot must be certain of the providence of God, no differently than those who had the **faith of miracles** were once certain of the power of God. For as **justifying faith** apprehends and embraces the mercy of God, and the **faith of miracles** embraces the power of God; so **historical faith** <note>In 17th-century theology, "historical faith" refers to an intellectual belief in the truth of the biblical narrative and God's promises, distinct from the "saving faith" that brings about justification</note> embraces the truth of God, which shines forth both in the works of nature and in the works of grace, and which that most truthful God deigns to reveal to us in various ways—whether by His word, or by dreams, or by lot, or by other symbols. 

And just as true **justifying faith** infallibly embraces mercy, and the **faith of miracles**, firmly embracing the power of God, obtained miracles from God—or conversely, as is clear by the example of **Moses**, who, because he was doubting while striking the rock with his staff, the water did not flow out at the first blow <note>A reference to Numbers 20, where Moses strikes the rock twice; the author suggests the delay was due to a momentary lapse in faith</note>—so also **historical faith**, firmly apprehending the truth and justice of God, will obtain the manifestation and revelation of it through a lot or through some other symbol, insofar as it is expedient for the glory of God and our salvation. Therefore, just as an **oath** serves the glory of God and for testifying to a hidden truth;

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "lot" (sors) as a sacred instrument. The previous page established that casting lots is not a game of chance but a "moral instrument" or "sacrament" used to discern God's will in hidden matters, comparing its solemnity to that of a formal oath.</meta>

-># REVEALER OF SECRETS #<-

hidden things; therefore, one must not swear an oath rashly, nor should one do so in matters of indifference <note>Latin: *adiaphoris*; things that are morally neutral or trivial</note>. In the same way, the **lot** is peculiarly governed by God, so that from it His will and the truth of a matter may be uncovered while it is yet hidden. This is what Moses intended to suggest in Genesis 27:20, when Esau says to his father Isaac: *The Lord your God caused it to happen for me*; as if he wished to say that the game had been found by chance. Here, he uses the word <term>הקרה</term> <note>Hebrew: *ha-karah*; meaning "to cause to happen" or "to meet"</note>, from which root arises <term>מקרה</term> <note>Hebrew: *mikreh*; meaning "accident," "chance," or "hap"</note>, to signify that even casual and fortuitous events are subject to the providence of God. This is also clear from the illustrious example in Genesis 22:13, when a ram was caught by its horns in a thicket of briars, to be sacrificed in place of Isaac.

For this reason, a lot should no more be used for indifferent and trivial matters than an oath should; otherwise, the lot would be something vain, according to the proverb: *if you throw the dice often, you will eventually throw something else* <note>original: *si sæpè iacias aleas aliud ieceris*; a warning that treating the divine lot like a common game of chance leads to inconsistency and error</note>. IV. Finally, God did not immediately indicate that Achan had sinned, so that the Magistrates might perform their duty, and by a very diligent inquiry, testify to their piety and obedience toward God, as well as their greatest hatred against sin; and thus, by the example of a horrendous punishment, they might strike terror into the whole people. Add V. and this: that God also took account of the sinner himself. For He wished, through so many delays, to draw out a confession from the man’s own mouth, so that the most just indignation of God might be more and more recognized, and His truth might be laid open. At the same time, this displayed His immense mercy, which invited the sinner to a confession of sin, so that he might feel shame and thus be saved, according to the proverb: *He blushed, the matter is saved* <note>original: *Erubuit salua res est*; a quote from the Roman playwright Terence, suggesting that if a person is capable of shame, they are not yet beyond hope</note>. Whence it says in verse 20: *Truly I have sinned against the Lord God of Israel, and thus and so have I done.*

Since therefore (as is evident from what has been said) the lot is governed by God, it is no wonder if Joshua used it to identify the sinner; and in truth, as is clear from the outcome, it did not err from the guilty person, any more than if God had touched him with His own hand. This is why in Acts 1:26, *They cast their lots, and the lot fell upon Matthias.* For since the Apostles ought not to have been chosen by men, but immediately by God—because their office was extraordinary—they were either chosen by Christ while He was dwelling on earth (as the twelve were), or by Christ speaking from heaven (as Paul was chosen in Acts 9), or it was necessary for them to be chosen by lot, as was done in the case of Matthias, who, the lot having been cast, [was numbered with the eleven apostles].

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "lot" (sors) as a divine instrument used to uncover hidden truths and settle matters of religious importance, specifically regarding the election of the Apostle Matthias and the division of priestly duties.</meta>

### ANTHONIUS CREGUTUS ###

[Matthias] was chosen by lot <note>Latin: *calculis*, literally "by pebbles," referring to the stones used for casting lots</note> along with the eleven Apostles; and at that time, perhaps, the disciples of Christ were imitating the ritual of the Jewish Church. For out of many priests, one was chosen by lot to burn incense to the Lord at a set time. This is the source of that passage in Luke 1: *It fell to him by lot that Zechariah should go in to burn incense.* Ambrose (in his commentary on Luke, chapter 1) and Bede testify that the Apostles looked back to this custom in the election of Matthias. However, it must also be noted that this was a special privilege of that era—whether among the Jews or the Christians—and it is not to be rashly imitated today, lest we should seem to be tempting God, since we do not have specific promises regarding this matter. This is why casting lots today would either be void, as the Hebrew or Persian word <term>פור</term> (*pur*, meaning "lot") and *Purim* seem to signify—because it would be a matter of mere chance—or it would degenerate into superstition and magic, as often happens.

Therefore, Joshua ordered the matter to be settled by lot according to the custom of the Hebrews. This was not without merit, for since the lot is the voice of God, it is no wonder if its use was very frequent even in the most sacred matters. This is clear here in the case of the "anathema" <note>Referring to the discovery of Achan’s theft of "devoted things" in Joshua 7</note>, and from the rituals of the Jews, it is clear that this same practice was very common in the Priesthood. For the members of a single <term>ephemeria</term> <note>Greek: *ἐφημερία*; a daily course or rotating shift of priests</note> divided their duties among themselves: one was assigned the incense by lot, another the tending of the lamps and wicks, another the arranging of the wood upon the altar, another the sacrifice, and another the sprinkling of blood. This is clearly stated in the book of <term>תפלות</term> (*Tefillot*), or liturgies. For the lot by no means designated the family of priests who would succeed others (for that was already established by law), but rather their specific functions for as long as their daily course lasted. Hence, in Luke 1:9, Zechariah was bound by lot <term>לקטורת</term> (*le-ketoret*) to burn incense, specifically so that no confusion or brawls might arise, and so that each man might follow his calling, which was made known by the voice of God—that is, by the lot.

Here, therefore, one must observe the corruption of the degenerate Jews, who have miserably corrupted the sacred rites of the ancients. While the lot was once used in sacred matters as the voice of God, now their descendants, adulterating all things most sacred, either celebrate festivals of "the lot" <note>Referring to the holiday of Purim</note> unseasonably with superstitious rituals, or they even impiously profane themselves and all things at once. # THE REVEALER OF SECRETS #

...[cele]brated in the month of February, on the 11th, 12th, 13th, 14th, and 15th days: the feast of **Purim** <note>Hebrew: פורים</note>, that is, of *lots* <note>The Latin text here uses *fortium* ("of the brave"), though contextually and etymologically it refers to *sortium* ("of lots")</note>, concerning which we read in the history of Esther. For this reason, they read the book of Esther with unique ceremonies; they call this book the **Megillah** <gloss>the scroll</gloss>, and the feast takes its name from this reading. Afterward, they finally eat, drink, lead dances, and behave with excessive madness—more so than the Pagans did during the *Bacchanalia* <note>The Roman festival of Bacchus, known for drunken revelry</note>. Thus, modern Jews impiously profane a sacred thing.

For as Augustine testifies in his commentary on the Psalms, "a lot is a thing which, amidst human doubt, reveals the divine will." This is what the Wise Man [Solomon] once said in Proverbs 16: *The lot is cast into the lap, but every judgment—or its reasoning—is from the Lord.* And so that the casting of lots might have more certain credibility, Rabbi Levi ben Gersom <note>Also known as Gersonides (1288–1344), a medieval Jewish philosopher and commentator</note> believes that the lots were mixed and drawn by the hands of a Prophet, in front of the sacred objects, as if in the very sight of God. It is also well known in the case of Jonah that the sailors cast lots for punishment, just as happened here, and that God directed the lot.

Furthermore, it is a memorable fact regarding lots that, although God approved of lots among His people and often revealed His will through them—both in this place and elsewhere—He did not wish the specific ritual and formula for casting lots to be detailed in the Scriptures, except for what Solomon mentioned in passing regarding "the lap" in the passage praised above. Perhaps it was not without reason that Scripture hid the method from us, namely so that we would not use it superstitiously in our own affairs or in <term>adiaphora</term> <note>Matters of indifference; things neither commanded nor forbidden by God</note>. However, Scripture did not hide one point to be noticed: that the lots were drawn before the doors of the Tabernacle, as if in the sight of God, so that they might be considered more holy.

Nevertheless, the Hebrew Teachers in the tractate **Bava Batra** <note>Hebrew: בבא בתרא; a section of the Talmud dealing with civil law, including property and inheritance</note>—in which they discuss various human agreements, such as buying, selling, partnerships, and inheritances—handed down these details concerning the ritual of casting lots. They say that two urns were placed before the Ark when the land of Canaan was divided among the Jews. Into one of these urns, the names of the tribes participating in the lot were placed; into the other, the names of the described regions. Then the High Priest, while the senate and the whole Assembly watched, shook the urns and moved them up and down. He then drew out with a "blind hand" <note>An impartial or random draw</note> the name of a tribe from one and a region from the other, just as the judgment of God offered them.

# ANTHONY CREGUT #

...the ritual and method of lots <note>The Latin text uses *fortium*, a variation of *sortium* (lots)</note>; nonetheless, if you consult other books, you will find that the ritual of casting lots was quite varied among the nations. For some, as Homer testifies in *Iliad* Book 7, cast them into a helmet. Others, as Plautus testifies in *Casina*, cast them into a bucket; according to Cicero, into a water-jar; according to Virgil, into an urn. And in Scripture, Proverbs 16:33, into the lap. Finally, they were cast into whatever kind of small vessel was available. For these were the various methods of casting lots, and the Hebrews called it *hippil purot* <note>original: הפיל פורות; "to cast lots"</note>, as well as *yarah* <note>original: ירה; "to throw or shoot"</note> and *natan* <note>original: נתן; "to give"</note>, which correspond to the Greek *ballein* <note>original: βάλλειν; "to throw"</note>, which is used by all the Evangelists in the history of the Passion regarding Christ’s tunic, and *didonai* <note>original: τοῦ διδόναι; "to give"</note>, which is used in Acts 1:26 in the election of Matthias: *they gave forth their lots.*

And let these things be said concerning the second diagnostic sign of the "anathema" <note>Referring to the forbidden items taken from Jericho that brought a curse upon Israel</note>; the third now follows, namely the confession of Achan himself, which was certainly required for the exact certainty of this crime and matter. For even if the lot were the voice of God, arguments of sophistry would nonetheless have been ready for wicked men; indeed, if we may believe the Rabbis, some tribes put on their armor to avenge such a great injustice (as it seemed to them), since a chance lot could fall upon the innocent just as well as the guilty. Therefore, two primary reasons are supplied for this third sign.

I. For the sake of certainty: because since the Jews had a defendant who confessed his guilt, no one from then on could doubt Achan’s "anathema." For what innocent man would have wished to accuse himself unless he had been convicted by the testimony of his own conscience, and unless, at those words of Joshua, Achan had trembled <term>$\dot{\nu}.$ <gloss>verse</gloss></term> 19: *My son, give glory to the Lord God of Israel, and make confession, and tell me what you have done; do not hide it from me.*

II. So that an example of divine justice, truth, and providence might be given. For thus it appeared to all Israel that God was most just and most true in that outcome, and that He had wisely directed the lot by His providence, so that it did not deflect even a finger’s breadth <note>original: *latum unguem*; a Latin idiom meaning "a hair's breadth"</note> from the tribe, the kindred, the family, and the person of Achan, but aimed directly at the mark. This certainly illustrated the glory of God greatly, even by stopping the mouths of any impious men; which would have happened less effectively had Achan not confessed his crime, for the impious easily seize an opportunity for making excuses.

III. I add a reason which is of no small importance, namely—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Achan’s sin and the method of divine discovery. Having established that the "anathema" was uncovered by lots, the author now explains the theological purpose behind the slow, step-by-step procedure Joshua used to identify the culprit, emphasizing God's patience and mercy.</meta>

-> ### THE REVEALER OF SECRETS ### <-

God wished to reveal even His mercy, for God always awaits the confession of the wretched sinner, both for the lack of excuse <note>original: αναπολογίαν (*anapologian*); a legal term for being without a defense</note> of the reprobate and for the repentance <note>original: μετάνοιαν (*metanoian*); a change of mind or heart</note> of the elect. And indeed, this is clearly proven from the whole history. For why were so many drawings of lots performed? Why was the whole business not finished with a single drawing? Why does Joshua proceed step-by-step, descending from the tribes to the clans, from the clans to the families, and from the families to the individual heads? This was not done solely for the sake of avoiding confusion. Indeed, in such a great multitude of individuals, a water-jar <note>original: *hydria*; used here as the vessel for drawing lots</note> could hardly have held the names of everyone, and there would have been no end to the drawing; one could also easily have given someone else's name instead of his own, or given none at all. 

But in the formula prescribed by God, no fraud could occur, especially since the names of all the heads were known. For there were twelve tribal leaders <note>original: φυλάρχοι (*phylarchoi*); or "tribunes"</note> who, just as each was the leader of his own tribe, so too held the number of all the kindreds by name; and the individual kindreds or clans had their own local leaders <note>original: δημάρχους (*demarchous*); heads of a *demos* or district</note>. Therefore, in the first drawing, only twelve lots were cast into the urn to represent the individual tribes; and so the lot fell upon the tribe of Judah. In the second drawing, as many lots were cast as the tribal leader of this tribe had clans, and the lot fell upon the clan of the Zerahites. In the third, as many lots as the local leader of the Zerahite clan had families under him, and the lot fell upon the family of Zabdi. In the fourth, as many lots as the family of Zabdi contained individual heads, and it fell upon Achan. Otherwise, if that order had not been observed, six hundred thousand or more thousands of men would have been cast into the jar at once. 

Nevertheless (as I have said), I believe this was done not only for those practical reasons, but also to reveal the supreme mercy of God, who demanded a confession of the sacrilege and invited it by this long delay. For when Achan saw himself being continuously sought out—first in his tribe, then in his clan and kinship, and finally in his family—and saw that the lot, as the voice and witness of God, never wandered from the mark, he might have come forward voluntarily as a suppliant before he was betrayed by name by the lot, and begged for pardon. Surely this reasoning is not to be despised, since Scripture perpetually proclaims the immense mercy of God; yet we wretched sinners...

So far, we have discussed the three diagnostic signs of Achan’s guilt. We have finally reached the last part of this dissertation, which concerns the punishment of Achan and the "imputation" <note>The legal assignment of guilt or responsibility to someone</note> of that punishment to others. I will now ensure that, under good omens, we handle this as accurately as possible.

The punishment seems to be twofold: namely, stoning and burning. For in verse 25, Joshua said, alluding to the name Achan or Achar <note>original: *Achan* or *Achar*. In Hebrew, the name sounds like the word for "trouble" or "disturber"</note>, *"Alas, you have troubled us; the Lord will trouble you this day!"* And all Israel stoned him with stones and burned them with fire and pelted them with stones, and they raised over him a great heap of stones that remains to this day. 

By these words, a double type of execution seems to be indicated. First, it is likely that Achan and his children were stoned while alive. (Note that even though Scripture speaks here in the singular, it is an <term>enallage</term> <note>A grammatical figure where one form, like the singular, is substituted for another, like the plural</note> for the plural). Then, their corpses were burned according to God’s command. It was customary to atone for sacrilege by fire; and truly the crime of the <term>Anathema</term> <note>original: *Anathema*. Referring to the "devoted things" or "the ban"—items that God had commanded to be destroyed and not taken as plunder</note> was so horrible that it could only be abolished by flames, so that it might vanish into smoke or be reduced to ashes. Indeed, so that not even the ashes themselves would remain visible, they were covered with a massive pile of stones as a perpetual monument to divine justice.

Furthermore, it is noted in the book *Tanhuma*, or *Yelammedenu* <note>Two names for a famous collection of early Jewish midrashic homilies</note>, that Achan was stoned before being burned specifically for violating the Sabbath. For they say that since Jericho was captured on the Sabbath day, Achan—pursuing his own business instead of God’s, or as Isaiah 58:13 says, "doing his own pleasure"—profaned the holy day. For this outrage, God, when consulted in the Book of Numbers, had established stoning as the punishment (Numbers 15:35). But because he was furthermore defiled by the crime of sacrilege, he could likewise only be purged by flames. A horrendous crime demands a horrendous punishment, so that the penalty matches the guilt.

But regarding the "imputation" of this act—how the guilt was assigned to others—"this is the task, this is the hard labor" <note>original: *hoc opus hic labor est*, a famous quote from Virgil’s Aeneid regarding the difficulty of returning from the underworld</note>. For first, as is clear from the history in Joshua, neither the children of Achan nor, much less, the rest of the Israelites were conscious of the crime; and yet both the children and many Israelites were killed because of Achan’s accursed thing. Therefore, the same punishment was dealt to both the guilty and the innocent...

I shall now ensure, with good omens, that this is also treated by us as accurately as possible. The punishment appears to be twofold, namely stoning and burning. > *Alas, you have troubled us, the Lord will trouble you on this day; and all Israel stoned him with stones and they burned them with fire and stoned them with stones, and they raised over him a great heap of stones, which remains to this day.*

By these words, a double kind of punishment seems to be indicated. First, it is probable that Achan and his children (for although the Scripture speaks in the singular, there is an <term>Enallage</term> <note>A grammatical term for substituting one form for another; here, using a singular pronoun to refer to a plural group</note> for the plural) were stoned while alive, and then the corpses were burned, according to God's command. For it was a solemn custom to expiate sacrilege by fire; and certainly the crime of the <term>Anathema</term> <note>original: *Anathema*. Here referring to the "devoted things" or "forbidden spoils" that Achan stole from Jericho, which were strictly set apart for God</note> was so horrible that it could only be abolished by flames, so that it might vanish into smoke or be reduced to ashes. Indeed, finally, so that not even the ashes themselves would appear, they were covered with a heap of stones as a perpetual monument to divine justice. To this is added in the book *Tanhuma*, or *Ielammedenu* <note>Two names for a famous collection of Jewish homiletic teachings on the Torah</note>, that Achan was stoned before he was burned, and that this was because of a violated Sabbath. For since (they say) Jericho was captured on the Sabbath day, Achan—acting for his own benefit rather than God’s, or as Isaiah chapter 58:13 says, "doing his own will"—profaned the Holy Day. For such an atrocity, God, when consulted, had established the penalty of stoning in the Book of Numbers (Numbers 15:35). But because he was additionally defiled by the crime of sacrilege, he could likewise only be purged by flames. A horrendous crime deserves a horrendous punishment, so that the penalty corresponds to the fault.

But truly, regarding the imputation of that crime, "this is the work, this is the labor" <note>original: *hoc opus hic labor est*. A famous quote from Virgil’s Aeneid, meaning "this is the hardest part of the task"</note>. For first (as is clear from the history in Joshua), neither the children of Achan nor, much less, the rest of the Israelites were aware of the crime; and yet, both the children and many Israelites were killed because of Achan’s "devoted thing." Therefore, the same punishment fell upon both the source of the crime and the innocent...

[the punishment] was inflicted, for the guilt was not the same. Secondly, it does not seem that Achan’s sin could have even been imputed <note>The legal or theological assignment of guilt from one person to another</note> to others, both because the Scripture contradicts this in Deuteronomy 24:16: *The son shall not die for the parents, nor the parents for the sons.* And in Ezekiel 18:2: *What is it to you, you who use this proverb concerning the land of Israel, saying "the fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge"?* And afterward in verse 4: *Behold, all souls are mine; the soul of the father as well as the soul of the son are mine: the soul that sins, it shall die.* Furthermore, it would also mean that by equal right, the sins of every single person could be imputed to everyone else in turn, and thus it would be of no use to be righteous, since one could be struck with the extreme penalty by the imputation of another’s injustice. What then shall we say? Shall any mark of injustice be branded upon the most just God? God forbid! <note>original: *μὴ γένοιτο* (mē genoito). A strong Greek negation often used by St. Paul.</note> Rather, let these most iniquitous little men be silent here; let them be struck dumb and amazed at once, since they cannot penetrate the secret counsels or judgments of God because of the far too dull edge of their little minds. Even the most sharp-sighted spirits of the <term>separate intelligences</term> <note>A scholastic term for angels, who were believed to possess pure intellect without physical bodies</note> are not able to grasp or reach these things, so far are they from being subjected to the reasoning of those entangled in manifold darkness. For as it is said in Job 39:35: *He who argues with the Almighty, will he not instruct him? Neither will he who argues with God be able to answer him.* <note>In modern Bibles, this is usually Job 40:2.</note> For this would be, according to God's testimony in Job 42:7, to speak rightly of God and to think well of Him.

Nevertheless, in order to further satisfy human curiosity <note>original: *humano pruritui* — literally "human itching," referring to the restless desire to know hidden things</note> as much as we are able, come now, let us also strive to examine these secrets with due submission of mind, and let us employ reasoning supported and propped up by the pillars of the Scriptures. First, if we were to assert that Achan’s fault was imputed to his children and the slain Israelites, the matter appears at first glance to be quite difficult. If, on the contrary, it is not imputed, no less a difficulty presses; for you would retort, why then the same punishment, if not the same guilt? It seems, therefore, that Achan’s fault is imputed to others. But I retort: by what kind of imputation? For no such kind of imputation appears in the monuments of the Holy Scriptures.

Since there are only two kinds of imputation <note>The theological or legal assignment of merit or guilt to someone</note>, namely the *improperly* and the *properly* so-called: The *improperly* so-called imputation is that which is not merely *relative*, but is founded upon an absolute quality. Therefore, it is according to what is owed <note>original: *κατὰ τὸ ὀφείλημα* (kata to opheilēma). A reference to Romans 4:4 regarding wages or debt.</note>, as is said of Phinehas <note>A priest in the Book of Numbers who killed an Israelite man and Midianite woman to stop a plague</note>. When he, burning with zeal, slaughtered the fornicators, that work was imputed to him as righteousness because it was most pleasing to God. From this followed a reward: the permanence of the Priesthood in his house. That imputation (as is evident) is founded on an absolute event—that is, on an act of justice. For that reason, that imputation is not a mere relation <note>original: *σχέσις* (schesis)</note> or assignment. Conversely, when the sins of the damned are imputed and weighed in God’s judgment, then it is imputation improperly so-called; the faithful person perpetually prays against this when he asks God not to impute his sins to him.

But imputation properly so-called is purely relative; it is pure and simple imputation, not founded on any absolute inherent quality. In this way, the righteousness of Christ is imputed to us properly and relationally <note>original: *σχετικῶς* (schetikōs)</note>, because it is not founded on any quality inherent in us. For no righteousness exists within us, but the righteousness of Christ becomes ours through imputation. Thus it is said to be given by grace <note>original: *κεχαρίσθαι* (kecharisthai)</note>, not according to what is owed, just as our sins were not in Christ inherently, but only by imputation, according to *Augustine*:

> *He made our sins his own sins, so that he might make his righteousness our righteousness.*

Since, therefore, only those two forms of imputation are given, what kind would this imputation of Achan’s sin be? First, would it be imputation improperly so-called? This does not seem likely, since that is founded (as we said) on an absolute Being and some inherent quality; but this cannot be said of Achan’s children or of the slaughtered Hebrews, since they were not conscious of Achan’s fault and his theft of the devoted things, as will be clear to anyone reading the Scripture. Therefore, a dark mark of iniquity would doubtless be branded upon God if he imputed to them a fault which they did not commit; as seen in the previously praised passage of Ezekiel 18:

> *The soul that sins shall die, and the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.*

Secondly, that imputation does not seem to be "properly so-called," for in that case, God's justice would also be struck, and this would still be against the oracles alleged above. And indeed, by what right would God have punished those Hebrews and that entire family if they were all blameless? Therefore—

->### THE WORKS OF ANTHONY CREGUT ###<-

Are they all devoted <note>set aside for God</note> and under a curse <note>original: "anathematizati"</note>, if they are immune from that impious curse? For here, the imputation of Adam’s sin is nothing to the point <note>original: "nihil ad rhombum," a Latin idiom meaning irrelevant or off-target</note>; nor is the imputation of our sins made to Christ relevant. This is because Adam was the head and root of the entire human race; since everyone descends from that first principle, it was necessary that the sin of the first-formed parents <note>original: "protoplastorum," referring to Adam and Eve</note> be imputed to them. For just as Adam had received natural gifts for himself and his posterity, so by sinning he lost them for himself and his posterity. Regarding Christ, he too was the principle and root of all those living a spiritual life; indeed, he was our sponsor and vessel who was to pay our debt and suffer the punishments of hell for us. Therefore, our sins were imputed to him, and because of them, he satisfied divine justice. 

But Achan, in contrast, was a "collateral" man <note>meaning he was of equal standing or a sibling/relative rather than a direct ancestor or "root" like Adam</note> with respect to the Hebrews who were killed; they did not descend from him, nor were they members of his specific tribe or even the same lineage. As for his children, even if they did descend from Achan, the father’s sin should no more have been imputed to them than to his "collaterals" <note>other relatives of the same generation</note>, because that sin was personal. Personal faults are hardly imputed to others without injustice. This is no different than how Adam's other sins—besides that first one—were not imputed to his grandsons; they could not be imputed by God without a stain of injustice, because Adam’s subsequent sins were personal, whereas that first one was original and concerned his very nature, and therefore was imputable to all. Therefore, Achan’s fault is much more a personal one, because there was not and cannot be any "original" version of it; thus, it will be non-imputable just like the sins of collateral relatives, and the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.

But what do we say to these things? From every side, it seems, difficulties and rough patches <note>original: "salebrosa," referring to a rugged or bumpy road</note> abound; on every side there are riddles <note>original: "gryphi," literally griffins, used here to mean enigmas</note> or a dark, foggy night. Yet, if no imputation assigns the fault to them, why, I ask you, is there punishment? Why would it be imputed at all? Nevertheless, let not the great difficulty of this matter terrify us or leave us astonished; come then, let us demonstrate this one thing which, at first glance, will seem like a paradox to most. Let us boldly assert this one thing: so far is it from the truth that neither type of imputation fits here, that we instead assert that *both* apply. First, the "improperly so-called" imputation <note>defined on the previous page as imputation based on an inherent quality or action</note>: For who among mortals is there, except for Christ, who

# ANTHONY CREGUT

[The sin] was imputed to Achan’s children and to the Hebrews routed at Ai. But alas! By God's faithfulness! How and by what right was it imputed? By what reasoning ought Achan’s personal sin be imputed also to others who were his **collaterals**? <note>Those related through a common ancestor but not in a direct line, such as cousins or fellow tribesmen.</note> Yet do not wonder: it ought, it truly ought indeed for Achan's fault to be imputed to the others by that "imputation" properly so-called. But observe further that this imputation is of three types: for one is *natural* imputation, another *moral*, and another *civil*.

*Natural* imputation is that which occurs by necessity on account of natural dependence and origin; and such was the imputation of **Adam’s sin**, which is imputed to his descendants because of their original grafting into the root and their emergence and dependence from it. For this reason, on account of that natural imputation, two things necessarily emerge and are poured back into his descendants: 

First, the propagation of original corruption, which is commonly called **concupiscence** <note>original: "concupiscentia"; an inclination toward sin or desire for worldly things</note> and, in the common phrasing of theologians, is properly called **original sin**. 

Second, that this imputation is completely universal; since it is natural, it therefore extends to all of Adam’s descendants, so that there is absolutely no one to whom Adam’s fault is not imputed—unless they are not a natural son of Adam, like **Christ**. Because of the miraculous conception by the Virgin and the birth from the **Mother of God** <note>original: "Deipara"</note>, Adam’s sin was not imputed to Him.

This type of imputation cannot fit Achan’s sin, since Achan was not the parent of the Hebrews killed at Ai, and therefore there was no natural dependence on him (such as exists in the direct degrees of ancestors and descendants on a family tree); rather, Achan was a collateral to them. Regarding Achan’s children, even though they descended naturally from their parent, this kind of natural imputation cannot take place because Achan’s fault was not a **fall of nature** but of the **person**. Therefore, the imputation could not be natural. But Adam’s first sin was a fall of nature, not just of the person, which is why it is called original sin; for *the person first infected nature, and thereafter nature infects the person,* as witnessed by **Augustine** <note>referring to St. Augustine of Hippo, a foundational Christian theologian of the 4th/5th century</note>.

Furthermore, *moral* imputation is that which does not occur by necessity like the natural type, but spontaneously and freely, whether in respect to the one who im-

For if the **sin of Adam** is imputed to his descendants, this was done (as we said) by **natural imputation**, which is necessary, not voluntary. voluntarily, not only with respect to God who imputes, but also to Christ to whom [sins] are imputed, who freely and of His own **good pleasure** <note>original Greek: εὐδοκίᾳ (*eudokia*); God’s sovereign and gracious will</note> deigned to be a vessel and a sponsor <note>original: *sponsor*; a legal guarantor who takes on another's debt</note>. It remains, then, finally, that that imputation of Achan's sin was of a third kind, that is, **civil**, which occurs when the crime of one citizen is imputed to the whole city and commonwealth. This third imputation holds a certain middle ground between natural and moral imputation. For as with natural [imputation], it is not absolutely necessary by the necessity of nature; and as with moral [imputation], it is not purely voluntary and free by the pure and simple freedom of the will; but as a **civil** matter, it is partly voluntary and partly necessary, and therefore "mixed." It is free because the object is good, and the will is freely drawn toward the good; it is necessary because the imputation occurs by necessity—yet not by an absolute necessity of nature, like natural imputation, but by a necessity based on a premise <note>original: *ex hypothesi*</note>, namely of right and of law. For in a commonwealth, each and every person is bound to follow the established law and to voluntarily obey the laws of the legislator, or else immediately suffer the penalties of **high treason** <note>original: *laesae maiestatis*; an offense against the dignity of the sovereign or state</note>. But since the entire city or commonwealth is one **Political Body** <note>original: *Corpus Politicum*; the idea that a society functions as a single organism with shared responsibility</note>, it is thus judged to have a single soul and will, whether in committing an evil, or in sharing in it, or in tolerating it, or in conniving and dissembling, or in failing to prevent it. Therefore, when someone commits a crime, others are judged to have committed it with impunity and, being involved in it, are deservedly afflicted with the same punishment. 

This is evident in the history of Achan; God, the Supreme Legislator, had captured the city of Jericho from the hands of the enemy and had delivered it to His people; and this was not by the virtue of the Jews or the force of arms, but by the blast of trumpets and His own divine blessing. In remembrance of such a great miracle and favor, as well as an act of thanksgiving, He willed that the entire city be despoiled, everything burned, and all things **devoted to destruction** <note>original: *anathemate*; a "herem" or sacred ban where items are set apart for God, usually by being destroyed</note> be cut down. Wherefore, subsequently, in vengeance for the crime, the men of Israel were put to flight...

Since God, as a **Jealous God** <note>original Latin: *Zelotes Deus*; referring to the biblical description of God’s protective and exclusive holiness</note>, willed to avenge the idolatry of the Gentiles, He desired that monuments of terrible judgment should reach posterity in that first captured city <note>The city of Jericho</note>. That city was totally burned, the things contained in it were devoted as a curse <note>original: *anathema*; property or people set apart for destruction or as an offering to God</note>, and those who would rebuild it were consecrated to everlasting curses. Since, therefore, God had commanded all these things to Israel, should they not have been punished for the transgression? For the transgression of one citizen or member is to be imputed to the whole **political body**. 

Is it any wonder, then, if after such a great victory won by the arm of God alone, the Israelites are put to flight and killed by the men of Ai in the siege of the neighboring city? This happened by the just judgment of God due to such ingratitude.

Nevertheless, let us discuss these things more distinctly and in parts, so that it may become clearer and clearer that no injustice was placed in God by this civil imputation.

**First**, thirty-six chosen men are killed because of Achan’s cursed theft. But what of it? Could God not have most justly acted even if Achan had not sinned, so that those Israelites were given over to death? For He is the **Lord of Hosts** <note>original: *Tsebaoth*; a Hebrew title for God as commander of heavenly and earthly armies</note> and He turns victory wherever He wills. Therefore, He could do so much more because of the curse through civil imputation, because the crime of one citizen is rightly imputed to others. This is done not so much as a punishment, but as an **example**, so that by this slaughter everyone might be awakened and remove the evil from their midst. 

For if in a **Physical body**, when some member is seized and corrupted by gangrene, not only is that part immediately cut off, but even a living part is removed to prevent the gangrene from spreading and the poison from corroding the whole. In the same way, in a **political body**, political Magistrates do not care what becomes of the life and resources of a **Titius, Maevius, or Sempronius** <note>traditional names used in Roman law to represent hypothetical individuals, similar to "John Doe"</note>, provided the whole republic remains safe and the fame and glory of the lawgiver is not stained. ...[the law] is immediately violated by subjects, either of their own accord or at least not against their will, when they grow sluggish through negligence and fail to keep watch as diligently as they ought—which is perhaps what happened in this case.

Secondly, we must examine the justice of God regarding the children of **Achan**, both his sons and daughters. Here, the difficulty seems even greater. **Civil imputation** <note>The legal principle where a group or family is held responsible for an individual's action</note> could certainly apply to the thirty-six men and the other Israelites, because at that time the guilty party was unknown and the curse had not yet come to light. But once the culprit had confessed his sin and the curse was exposed for all to see, how could the parent's sin be rightfully imputed to the children, causing them to suffer the same punishment as their father?

However, if we look closely, we will admit that civil imputation is at work here as well, because all individuals are members of the commonwealth. Furthermore, just as God’s justice shines through here, we shall also see His mercy and His mysterious providence radiant within it. 

First, His mercy sparkles: by using this kind of temporary punishment—which acts like a fatherly correction—He rouses and sharpens the whole body of the commonwealth. This ensures that everyone does not merely look out for themselves, but cares for the entire body, since they are bound together by an inseparable bond under one head, God. 

Next, God’s providence appears illustriously. Since nothing happens without His knowledge, and the affairs of mortals are not tossed about in confusion, He shows Himself repeatedly to be the judge of all actions. Therefore, nothing more disastrous can happen to wretched mortals than the "hiding" of divine providence. This was noted among the Hebrews by **Maimonides** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Jewish philosopher</note>, who was the first among the Rabbis to be "sober" (according to the scholar **Scaliger** <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a famous French religious scholar</note>). In his book *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: *More Neuoch.* (Moreh Nevukhim)</note>, part I, chapter 23, he contrasts this with "the hiding of the face" <note>original Hebrew: *Hester Panim* (הסתר פנים)</note>, which refers to when God’s providence is either manifested or, conversely, hidden. 

**Isaiah 26:21**: *Behold, the Lord comes out* <note>original Hebrew: *yatza* (יצא)</note>, that is, He departs from His place, specifically when He makes His providence manifest. Conversely, **Hosea 5:15**: *I will go and return* <note>original Hebrew: *ve-ashuvah* (ואשובה)</note> *to my place.* This signifies the removal of the Majesty or the visible presence of God that was among us; this is followed by the loss of God’s providence over us. Hence, in a threat of punishment, God says: *and I will hide my face from them and they shall be consumed.* For when something is deprived of God’s providence, it is then exposed to every accident that might happen to it. Because this threat is so horrific and formidable, it is therefore called— <note>The text breaks off mid-word; the full word is "cognominationem" or "designation."</note>

temporal blessings and those of the present life. The same judgment must be made, conversely, regarding threats of punishment. For when parents are at their worst—and therefore outside of the covenant because they are unworthy—and their children also imitate the sins of their parents (according to the proverb, "from a bad crow, a bad egg" <note>original Greek: *κακοῦ κόρακος κακὸν ὠὸν*; a common ancient Greek expression meaning that evil parents produce evil children</note>), then God punishes the iniquity of the fathers upon the sons. This is not because the son pays the penalty for another’s sins, for that would be unjust and contrary to the principle that *the soul that has sinned shall die.* <note>Ezekiel 18:20</note> In truth, the son is punished with a penalty because of his own personal sins; if he did not imitate the sins of his father, he would not be struck down.

However, these words of the Law must be understood through the lens of <term>imputation</term> <note>In theology, "imputation" is the legal or moral assignment of a status (like guilt or righteousness) from one person to another.</note>, because the sins of the parents are imputed to the children. This is not by a "natural imputation"—the way the sin of Adam was imputed to his descendants, which was a sin of nature and an original sin that carries the spread of corruption with it. Rather, this is a **moral and forensic imputation**. <note>A "forensic" or legal imputation refers to a judgment made in a court-like setting by God, rather than a biological inheritance.</note> When God sees the depraved character and stubbornness of the children, and knows that both the father and the sons are a "brood of vipers" <note>original Greek: *γεννήματα ἐχιδνῶν*; a phrase used by John the Baptist and Jesus in the New Testament to describe the hypocritical or wicked</note>, He shows mercy to none of them. Instead, He imputes the sins of the defiant fathers to the defiant sons by abandoning them and not communicating His grace to them. Because both are outside the covenant, God does not act toward them as He does toward those within the covenant—where He remembers His pact, as is often said in Scripture regarding Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. For as a Roman Emperor once said, "from a wicked generation, it is not even expedient for a puppy to live."

This doctrine is taught throughout Scripture; indeed, it is confirmed by various examples. For besides that law in Exodus 20:5 and 34:7, we read in Lamentations 5:7: *Our fathers sinned and are no more, and we have borne their iniquities.* And in Genesis 9:25, because of the crime of Ham, his son Canaan was made subject to a curse. In 2 Samuel 21:8–14, because of Saul’s treachery toward the Gibeonites, his sons and grandsons were crucified, with God so ordaining and approving. In 2 Samuel 24:17, because of David’s sin, seventy thousand men died, leading the king to cry out, *Behold, I have sinned, and I have acted wickedly; but these sheep, what have they done?* In 2 Kings 14, the sin of Jeroboam is imputed to his descendants. Therefore, the same was done without injustice in the crime of Achan in Joshua 7:24. Among the Church Fathers, Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Archbishop of Constantinople known for his preaching.</note> in his 29th Homily on Genesis and Tertullian <note>Tertullian (c. 155–220), a prolific early Christian author from Carthage.</note> in *Against Marcion* agree with this view.

### -> REVEALER OF SECRETS <-

And indeed, if by God’s decree and because of the sin of Adam, our soul—which is created pure by God and without inherent injustice—is nevertheless created "not righteous" (that is, deprived of <term>original righteousness</term> <note>The state of perfect moral integrity and harmony that humanity possessed before the Fall.</note>) because Adam's sin is imputed to us, from which follows the corruption and the stain of desire that is spread through the generations, why then shall the sins of parents not also be imputed to their children with even greater right? For in those children, there is not only a lack of righteousness, but also corruption and injustice—indeed, a heap of all enormous sins. Furthermore, all the sins of the fathers are inherently present in the children because they are the imitators and heirs of their fathers' injustices. Therefore, in this sense, the sins of the fathers can be imputed to them by what is called "improper imputation," which occurs when an external quality becomes inherent in them. For if Adam's sin is imputed to his descendants even if no corruption were to precede it in Adam's children (since by God’s decree and just judgment that imputation precedes what we have called "natural imputation"), then how much more are the sins of parents imputed to their children if that same corruption and depravity, stemming from the imitation of their father's disobedience and rebellion, already exists within them?

Hence, in **Matthew 23:35**, Christ threatens the unbelieving and stubborn Jews with destruction because of the sins of their ancient fathers committed long ago. Specifically, it was because of <note>original Hebrew: *שנאת חנם* (Sinat chinam)</note> **baseless hatred**—that is, because of their hatred for the Messiah—that they filled up the measure of their fathers and were partners in all their sins. *Jesus said: "Upon you will come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Berechiah."* Therefore, in respect to divine judgment and before His tribunal, no one can be justified or cry out as some once did before a judge’s bench: "I, a wretch, am innocent; if I had committed this crime, I would suffer the punishment willingly." In this way, such a person would rather be likened to the thief crucified for his crimes than to Christ, who died innocent. This, I say, has no place here, because no one is punished by God while truly innocent. 

On the contrary, even Christ Himself, when He was condemned by the Father, was regarded as guilty because *He Himself bore our sins* (**1 Peter 2**) and was the **sponsor** <note>In this legal sense, a "sponsor" acts as a guarantor or surety who takes on the legal debts or obligations of another.</note> for the sins of humanity. I. He was not "innocent" in a legal sense, because He was our sponsor. 
II. Because even though He was innocent in His own person, He could nevertheless pay the penalties for others in various respects.

# ANTOINE CREGUT

...was of his own right and held <term>self-determining power</term> <note>Greek: αὐτεξούσιον (*autexousion*), meaning acting by one's own authority or free will.</note> over all creatures; he was also <term>absolutely</term> <note>Greek: ἁπλῶς (*haplōs*).</note> independent. Therefore, he was able to give and take back his life at his own will, and thus offer himself as a pledge. 

II. Because by suffering he was able to free both himself and those allied with him from guilt, and snatch them from the abyss of both deaths <note>Referring to physical death and eternal spiritual death.</note>, without which he would perhaps have offered himself in vain as an <term>atoning sacrifice</term> <note>Greek: ἱλάσιμον (*hilasimon*), a propitiatory offering.</note>. 

This, however, does not have a place in the present subject matter, because the children of Achan were <insert>guilty</insert>—if not by that curse and sacrilege of their father (of which they do not seem to have been aware, or at least Scripture does not say so), they were nonetheless not absolutely innocent, but guilty of many crimes. 

Finally, it can also be said here in another respect that Achan’s family paid the penalty by **civil imputation**; not a general one (as discussed above) but a special one—that is, a household-based one. This is because frequently the crimes of the head of the household are imputed to the whole family, not only because they are parts of this "household body" and members of its head, but also for the sake of example. The goal is that a heavy crime might be followed by a heavy punishment, and the fall and slip of the stumbling head might drag the entire family into ruin with him. 

Thus, for a head of household guilty of <term>treason</term> <note>Latin: "laesae maiestatis", literally "injured majesty," the legal term for high treason.</note>, the whole family is inevitably condemned by a decree of the Senate; and whoever by mere chance and not by design, though acting without foresight, brought destruction upon princes, they were judged guilty. 

Jacques Auguste de Thou <note>A famous 16th-century French historian also known as Thuanus.</note> noted a remarkable example of this in the 58th book of his *History* regarding Gabriel, Count of Montgomery. When Montgomery had unintentionally inflicted a lethal wound on King Henry II in a mock battle <note>The famous jousting accident of 1559.</note>, he was condemned to death as an enemy of the state, overwhelmed by the odium of the public disaster rather than by his own crime. As a <term>sacrificial person</term> <note>Latin: "homo piacularis", an individual whose death is required to atone for a public calamity or to appease divine wrath.</note>, he could not be spared from punishment; therefore, he was struck by the axe by a decree of the Senate. 

If crimes against human majesty are thus atoned for, what will happen when dealing with **Divine Treason**, especially regarding the heavy and immense crime of an **anathema** <note>A formal curse or a thing "devoted" to God, often for destruction.</note>? Indeed, since no wickedness is worse, so an anathema ought to respond to an anathema—<term>total destruction</term> for <term>total destruction</term> <note>Hebrew: "Cherem" for "Cherem". In the Bible, *cherem* refers to things or people set apart for absolute destruction.</note>—so that the sin is cut off along with the sinner, lest it crawl into the family. Rather, as it is said of the house of Ahab, let there not be left so much as a single "little dog to urinate against a wall." <note>A common Biblical idiom for the total extinction of a male line.</note> 

Blessed forever be Jehovah, our righteousness. Amen, Amen.

<summary>Cregut justifies the execution of Achan's family by comparing it to civil laws of treason, where a family shares the leader's ruin to deter others and purge a "devoted curse" (cherem) from the community.</summary>
